_childDocuments_.review: Mostly cutscenes and Walking Simulator.I expected some, after playing the demo, but not that much.I'll give it a pass this time, I'll recommend, but with at least 50% discount.There is great effort and value put into the product, for sure, but it's sold as a game, not as a TV cartoon.Studios should learn not to pad the former with the latter. Besides, whoever is unable to tell a story through their chosen medium might want to rethink their career.Though the story is contrived and rather silly, the storytelling is excellent.It mixes creative retro-futurism, stunning perspectives, themes borrowed from Truman Show to Logan's Run and older classics, substantial characterisation, top-notch voicing (spoiler alert: Number 6 isn't played by Patrick McGoohan,) and solid world-building in an alternate reality where humans have no nose and Walt Disney was a good guy.As a result, the Passivity Simulator part is very watchable. In fact, enjoyable.Which is a good thing, since not a single second of its lengthy segments can be skipped.That's right, in 2023, there are still stragglers who code their cartoon-players like a TV receptor, with 1 feature only: the dazzling on/off switch.As interesting as cutscenes might be, their appeal drops by 100% on checkpoint reload.And remember, half of the inaction requires you to keep pressing a button to walk towards the right while you watch the backgrounds.Anyway, the lack of a Skip command single-handedly annihilates all replay value, despite the availability of a chapter selector.As for the first play value, the game part, I'll give some praise.The side-scroller is classically made of platforming, stealth, puzzles and chases.All are rather easy, with impeccable gamepad control; unless hacking is required, in which mode the selection of interactables is clumsy.Despite that fact, gameplay is always more interesting when hacking is involved.It succeeds in adding a 1st person view to a 3rd person view, an interesting sensation, and it brings more original puzzles to a gamer who has seen them all.Then there is the pure 1st person adventure, controlling the support character.Progression is also a completely linear affair, but with some freedom of movement, more open to exploration.The museum is the best example of what more of the storytelling should have been like: I looked at every display, every piece, probably, but it was optional, my choice.Right after that is the opposite: a slow, long, mandatory dark ride that recaps fluff you already know. Here the devs are showing off rather than optimising their medium by involving the player.Anyway, the 3D gameplay is equally easy and more original.You rarely do the same thing twice.You can't guess what type of challenge will come next.I liked these sections more than the side-scroller. Not sure why, they both look great and are immersive. Might just be for the illusion of freedom they manage to induce.Could have been more immersive though, with more interactive spots, or a more reactive world, or with choices.Again, some of the design effort should have shifted the bystander state into player agency.But let's not forget that, in itself, transitions between 3D and side-scroller constitute a great device, very effective.Also, in every situation, the game succeeds at conveying the appropriate mental state into the gameplay. When the story wants you to panic, you do panic; when it wants you to feel in control, you smirk.Finally, you could wait for a final layer of polish: I experienced a couple of crashes (that's when you notice how fast the game launches and loads,) a pair of events not triggering (reloading the latest checkpoint is then required,) and several instances of superposed talks, thus incomprehensible, with half the subtitles ending up out of screen.Aside from these minor technical issues, the general quality and production value are high.Superior art, superior narrative, good but reduced gameplay.If the actor/spectator ratio wasn't completely out of whack, this would be a favourite of mine.Reminds me of We Happy Few, a 2018 game with similar qualities, albeit a different impairing flaw.

_childDocuments_.review: The story is intriguing at first glance. A 70s Truman Show with some retro-futurism thrown in the mix. Its unique mix of third-person platforming and first-person puzzle solving is also promising at first. But the gameplay is severely lacking. For the first 10 minutes there is no gameplay, you are just walking to the right. After that, there is exactly one solution to every scene and puzzle that you are expected to follow to the tee. It's constant trial-and-error until you find out the exact sequence of actions the game designers preordained you to follow. The background of the plot is meanwhile brought to you in clumsy exposition dumps. Disappointing overall. Did not finish it.Edit:Some things that I forgot to mention. I like the look and the style. BUT it runs very poorly for the way it looks. This should be an easy 60 FPS on any hardware from the last decade. Yet it really makes the Steam Deck’s fans spin and drains the battery in no time. _childDocuments_.review: You can read my other reviews Routine, I think we've all felt the weight of it, or if you haven't, congratulations, you have a much more interesting life than me! I just have this hobby, of looking for cool titles and sharing them with you. In this case, I didn't even have to search much. Since the release of Call of the Sea, the Out of the Blue Games studio has carved a space in my chest. American Arcadia thus marked its territory as an interesting experience.Trevor resides in the bustling Arcadia, a retro-futuristic metropolis of the 70s. Trevor, in many ways, reflects many of us. He holds a job that pays the bills but doesn’t find it fulfilling, avoids nightlife, lives with a turtle, possesses a gaming console, and a piano. Though he prefers keeping his creative side within his comfort zone, the piano remains a safe haven, offering solace from the monotony of work.American Arcadia is viewed as a utopia but doubles as a reality show watched by masses daily. It combines elements akin to George Orwell's 1984 book and series like Westworld. The inhabitants live secluded within a dome, unaware of the external world, being filmed 24/7. Visitors can experience a few days in Arcadia, indulging in the wild '70s, but strict regulations bar modern technology or clothing beyond a certain point.As a reality show reliant on viewer interest, Trevor becomes a problem—a character lacking the allure that engages the audience. Consequently, he's slated for elimination, guided discreetly out of Arcadia, seemingly on a paradise getaway. However, Trevor's regular viewer, a resistance member abroad, warns him of being a targeted individual.Angela becomes the bearer of grim truths, revealing Trevor's reality. However, she is also the guide to his salvation during his desperate and haphazard escape. It's interesting to see how American Arcadia plays with the two types of views of each playable character. With Trevor, the player has a wide view in 2.5D, where the character only moves to one side, as if the viewer were Angela watching all the action on her workstation screen. All of this while guiding him through a hotel, a shopping center and places full of props of the most different types. As Angela, a hacker, she is equipped with mechanics that allow controlling doors, or control alarm systems that help Trevor in his adventure. All the sections with Angela are spent in a first-person 3D view with stealth elements. The blend of these viewpoints stands out as a highlight in this title—a stroke of brilliance!Each new section immerses the player in an enriching experience that keeps the action fresh. Whether in terms of platforms, mixed with small puzzles with simple mechanics placing platforms in the right places, passing through sections with vibrant orange-hued rooms, ending in psychedelic moments with sublime art elements that offer new perspectives of the tormented mind of Trevor. With Angela, the puzzles can be a bit more complicated. The stealth sections are quite fun and the attention to what surrounds the player is also super important. Angela's segments also unveil story twists through subtle clues, urging players to scrutinize every detail. It's impossible not to root for this dynamic duo to emerge victorious from the clutches of this television show. It is especially interesting to understand the concept of victory from Trevor's perspective, at the end of his adventure. American Arcadia thus enters to my top Indie Games of the year.

_childDocuments_.review: "American Arcadia" takes players on an enthralling adventure, blending a gripping storyline with immersive gameplay that keeps you hooked from start to finish. The game's strength lies in its ability to weave an intricate narrative, filled with twists and turns that consistently surprise and engage.This visual storytelling enhances the overall experience, making every moment in the game feel alive and dynamic.Gameplay-wise, "American Arcadia" strikes a fine balance between challenge and accessibility, ensuring that both seasoned gamers and newcomers can enjoy the journey. The controls are intuitive, and the game mechanics are well thought out, contributing to a smooth and enjoyable gaming experience.However, the game's ending feels like a bit of a letdown. Just as the narrative reaches its peak, it concludes abruptly, leaving players hanging and craving more. This sudden stop in the storyline can be jarring, especially given the game's otherwise stellar pacing and development. It's like being engrossed in an enthralling book only to find the last chapter missing.In conclusion, "American Arcadia" is a remarkable game that offers a memorable experience, though its ending might leave players wishing for a more polished and complete conclusion. It's a journey worth taking, despite its abrupt end.

_childDocuments_.review: I will avoid going into many details in this review to avoid spoilers.I picked this up because I enjoyed Call of the Sea, another game by the same developer (Out of the Blue Games).  While I enjoyed both very much, be aware that Call of the Sea and American Arcadia are  different games.  The store page describes American Arcadia as "a cinematic puzzle game" which is a very apt description; be aware that it is quite heavy on the "cinematic" and rather light on the "puzzle", so if you're looking for puzzles, you should move on.As the game description states, Trevor -- the 70s looking dude with the moustache and the argyle vest -- is escaping from something. As a result, there are several sections of the game that are time-sensitive, where you must outrun your pursuers or time your movements to evade detection.   Apart from those, however, the game has a casual pace, so most of the time you aren't being rushed and can take your time.

_childDocuments_.review: Review of American Arcadia: A Retro Sci-Fi Thriller That’s Part Dystopia, Part Game Show, and All FunAmerican Arcadia is the love child of The Truman Show and a 1970s sci-fi thriller, but somehow, it’s also a puzzle platformer. Picture this: a city where every resident’s life is live-streamed for entertainment, and if the viewers get bored with you? Well… let's just say it doesn't end with a contract renewal.You play as Trevor Hills, a super-ordinary guy with the excitement level of a filing cabinet, who suddenly realizes that his unremarkable existence might get him terminated — and not in the "pink slip and handshake" way. This sends Trevor into a frantic escape through an incredibly stylish retro-futuristic world, where every skyscraper and arcade machine looks like it stepped out of a 1970s dreamscape.The gameplay splits between two perspectives. On one side, Trevor’s running, jumping, and puzzling his way out of the city in a heart-pounding platformer. Meanwhile, you also play as a hacker on the outside, working to guide Trevor through security and help him avoid the dangers of being the world’s least interesting escapee. It’s like Big Brother meets Indiana Jones, if Indy was more of a desk jockey than an archaeologist.One of the best parts? The retro-futuristic art direction. Everything has this groovy vibe, as if the game’s designers asked, “What if we made The Jetsons, but edgy?” The world is all geometric shapes, neon lights, and cassette-tape computers, blending sci-fi with mid-century flair. The soundtrack even matches, with jazzy tunes that make you feel like you’re breaking out of corporate hell… in style.The puzzles are clever but forgiving, so it’s more about the thrill of the escape than banging your head against a wall. Every close call feels like a scene out of a classic heist movie. Just when you think Trevor’s caught, you pull off a last-second escape that’ll have you yelling, “Run, Trevor, RUN!”American Arcadia is thrilling, unique, and endlessly fun — like binge-watching a dystopian game show while sipping a martini. If you’re looking for a quirky adventure with style, suspense, and a plot that feels way too relatable, then American Arcadia might be your next favorite escape.

_childDocuments_.review: Full gameplay: Honestly didn’t expect this game to be this good at all, it was an amazing experience filled with lots of engaging moments, great story telling, fun and humor and charming visuals and characters. I absolutely didn’t expect this level of love in creating this game, well done team. It was almost perfect in any aspect of game design. There aren’t many games out there that can keep me excited from beginning until the end. The way that this game tells a story was a masterpiece. There are lots of different elements in this game and the way they managed to put all of these ideas and execute them in this game almost perfectly is mind blowing. The visuals are so unique and charming, the characters, the level design, the vibrant colors and art style, and the Arcadia city. All of these together managed to make an immersive experience. Exploring the Arcadia city was delightful and full of charming and cool elements. There were some areas where texture were really low quality despite playing with epic quality with no super-sampling. One of the best part of this game undoubtedly is the gameplay mechanics, I feel they tried to impalement many different styles of a gameplay into this game and somehow managed to make it be an interesting gameplay. You are in control of two characters that switches during your gameplay, one you play in 2.5D and the other in first person view. I think in 2.5D view they inspired from games like Inside and Little Nightmares for puzzles solving, escape/hide from enemies and navigating through the map. One of the characters help you by hacking devices through security cams which sometimes you need to do in combination with other character, specially when you are trying to escape from enemies which sometimes can be challenging because you have little time to react, but you can easily overcome those by understanding the mechanics. There are puzzles in this game which some of them were very hard I think and took me a long time to solve, I think overall puzzles are good but sometimes they are just very simple like opening a door through security camera which I felt they could’ve made some of them more challenging and interesting. This is where I think the game shines, as I said I started playing this game without knowing anything about the story and from the very first moment of the game it made me interested in the story, I had many different speculation throughout my gameplay about what is going to happen next but the game managed to surprise me and prove me I was wrong which was really amazing.The story’s underlying message is really powerful despite the humor and charming of the game, the way that they tell this story is so unique and wonderful that I wasn’t able to not stop playing until I understand what is happening, so many ups and downs and mysteries throughout the gameplay that I never felt any moment of boredom. The amazing characters in the game were a big part of what made this story so good and made me feel really involved in its world.I can’t think of anything negative about music and sound, it was almost perfect and complemented the whole game theme and story perfectly. Maybe there were couple of overlapping dialogues here and there but nothing game breaking.Performance was really good, I played on epic settings with no super-sampling. Got 150fps on average, although there were one or two area that my frame dropped below. I encountered couple of bugs, one crash and one bug that I wasn’t able to progress the game, had to restart multiple times and play from the beginning of that chapter but managed to pass that area. I don’t think there is any replayability in this game unless you want to get all achievements or any missing dialogues or information during your gameplay.CPU: Intel Core i9-12900KMB: MSI Z690 Edge WiFi DDR4RAM: GSkill 32Gb DDR4 3600MhzGPU: Asus GeForce RTX 3090 StrixMonitor: Samsung Odyssey G7 32" 1440P 240Hz

_childDocuments_.review: I am giving American Arcadia a positive review because I can tell the devs put some much love and heart into the game but I didn't have a great time playin the game.- Great characters with amazing voice acting!- The worldbuilding told through beautiful, well-crafted designs. The colors, the UI, the music... it's just sets the vibe so perfectly!- The story is meta and interesting and has lots of twists and turns to keep you intrigued.- I really loved quite a few of the puzzles in 3D mode. They were fun and really had fun "infiltration" vibes!Cutscenes and long bouts of dialogue are unskippable. This just sucks when you die and have to sit through a whole cutscene again. Also, the game crashes a lot on Steam Deck, which makes the unskippable cutscenes worse.The level designs may be beautiful but they can also be hard to understand where the game wants you to go. There are multiple segments where they suddenly want you to run the direction you come from, but there were zero cues to do so or a line of dialogue that comes too late. There were times that you were supposed to push something to jump on but it was just unclear that the object could be pushed because there was so much clutter on the map. There was some gameplay was inspiring and integrated into the story, especially in 3D mode, but a lot of the gameplay time was filled with waiting "puzzles" where you are just wasting your time. There's no extra dialogue to keep you entertained during these segments or anything to do except to wait and twiddle your thumbs while the game shuffled you along a boring puzzle anyone can solve at a glance, but you're forced to wait for the solution to appear because the game makes you wait. Lastly, there is a trippy section of the game that requires backtracking and it sucks. It sucks to run back at Trevor's snail pace while nothing happens except you making the awkward trek backwards. It takes so long and there is nothing to keep your entertained. Despite how beautiful the world was, there are lots of segments that feel empty and long.There are long hallways that actually lead nowhere, which could be easily fixed by not creating the hallway at all or rewarding the players with a line of dialogue or a collectable. There are long stretches of time where Trevor is just running right, as he always does, but there's nothing happening for minutes at a time. There's the horrible, confusing backtracking section where absolutely nothing happens except you walk back the way you came, wondering why the game forced you to sit through a long cutscene of the camera panning the path backwards but didn't care about your time enough to just teleport you.There's also a spoiler-y scene that I think is supposed to be of emotional importance where I don't regret playing American Arcadia. The game is filled with love and great visual design but the gameplay design is questionable. There is a lot of empty time spent in the game with nothing for you to do except wait. The gameplay design, especially in 2.5D, is simply not fun. The story is interesting, but in my opinion, could have been told in half the time that the game filled with empty puzzles and dead air.I don't recommend playing the game, but I'd recommend watching someone play the game because you would get the full story.

_childDocuments_.review: The biggest surprise hit of 2023!Started this initially out of curiosity and ended up totally enamoured with it. Such has been the quality of the last part of the year, I could have easily missed playing American Arcadia. Essentially take the Truman Show, sprinkle some 1984 and Black Mirror and a glorious faux 70s aesthetic and you get American Arcadia. You take on the role of Trevor Hills as he discovers he is living in a TV show his entire life. Unlike The Truman Show though, he isn't the star, infact he is a nobody... Upon discovering this fact, things go down!A wonderful campy romp which has two styles of gameplay woven to perfection. Puzzling-platforming is the prime part, but there is also some first-person stuff happening that brilliantly changes the pace at all the right moment. Chock full of nods and easter eggs, brilliantly acted and a story that pays homage to its influences without ever ripping them off. Might not win aby game of the year awards in such a stacked 2023 for indies, but it could wll be the biggest surprise and a late sleeper hit for 2024.

_childDocuments_.review: American Arcadia is a unique narrative-driven puzzle platformer developed by Out of the Blue. Set in a utopian 1970s-inspired city, the game is reminiscent of The Truman Show, but on a much larger scale. As the story unfolds, the main character's daily routine slowly unravels as seeds of doubt are planted, leading to a gripping escape narrative.The gameplay of American Arcadia blends two perspectives: Trevor’s 2D side-scrolling platforming and Angela’s first-person puzzle-solving sequences. At times, the game also incorporates a second-person camera, where from Angela's perspective, you observe and control Trevor, adding a unique layer to the gameplay. This duality keeps the experience fresh. That said, there are a few technical hiccups. During play, I experienced two game crashes when trying to load specific scenes, and at one point, I got stuck in the environment, forcing a reload from the last checkpoint.Visually, American Arcadia shines with its retro-futuristic aesthetic. One of the standout levels involves navigating through multiple television screens. Another memorable moment occurs when the game mimics a Twitch-like chat during a live broadcast scene, offering a fun, meta twist that feels in tune with modern streaming culture.The sound design supports the immersion in both the story and gameplay. The background music matching the retro-futuristic atmosphere. One song stands out for its pleasant melody, and the game creatively incorporates snippets of it in various scenes, sometimes even in a comedic context, which adds to the charm. The voice acting is also commendable, particularly in the delivery of humorous and emotional moments. The game nails its comedic timing, with well-executed jokes adding a lighter tone to the more intense narrative moments.The story offers a compelling look at a society unknowingly trapped in a reality TV show, much like The Truman Show but on a grander scale. Trevor’s routine slowly unravels as uncertainty and doubt creep in, driving the tension forward. The plot twists are engaging and well-executed—the twist involving Javert is pretty funny and adds a touch of humor to the narrative, while the revelation about Number 6 adds depth to it. One of the things I really liked is that the game doesn’t end with a typical happy ending. This choice is refreshing and gives the story more weight, leaving players with a sense of reflection. The balance between humor, tension, and the unexpected conclusion makes the experience stand out.Despite a few technical issues, American Arcadia is an enjoyable experience from start to finish. Its unique art style and engaging narrative make for a compelling package. While the game leans more toward delivering a focused, linear story, there are moments of brilliance in its level design and plot twists that make it memorable. The game’s replayability is minimal, making it more of a pleasant one-time experience. Personally, I don’t feel the need to play it again. However, for those who may have missed an achievement, it’s possible to replay specific scenes. That said, revisiting some of the more creatively designed segments after some time might not be a bad idea.

I want more games to take the kinds of risks this one does -- but unfortunately I just can't recommend this one.The puzzles and action sequences were badly designed, frustrating, and undercooked. The gorgeous art direction tanks in later chapters where you end up in industrial and, yes, sewer locales. And I can't overstate my disappointment in the conclusion of the story.The team at Out of the Blue clearly has talent in spades -- I will look forward to their next offering, but this one I'm never going back to.

_childDocuments_.review: American Arcadia is a fun story with interactive puzzles along the way. It's a fun story about corporations, media consumerism and the desire for freedom.The game has great characters, a wonderful art style and does an good job at conveying it's social commentary it tries to get across. If you enjoy interactive story games I would recommend American Arcadia.As much as I love this game I should mention a few flaws.Firstly, the game is incredibly linear, I didn't find any decisions that actually changed the story as far as I could tell. Personally, I think that's fine, the game wanted to tell a story and it did great, we're along for the ride to enjoy it but if you like choices you won't really find them here.The game isn't too buggy, with the few bugs I ran into such as NPCs getting stuck or running faster than they should being fixed with a simple reload of a quick save. However, bugs are in the game and they can be annoying at times.Also, on a personal level, I think Raw fury deserves all the support they can get. They've published some great titles and helped new developers find themselves on the market and really support unique games and out of the blue have started off great with American Arcadia, for sure.Overall, I highly recommend this game, I see absolutely no reason for anyone not to try the demo and the game has a very fair price for what you get. It was a wonderful experience and I wish I could play it from the beginning without knowing how it ends again.

_childDocuments_.review: I recently embarked on a journey through "American Arcadia", and after spending a solid 9 hours fully immersed in its world, achieving 100% completion, I've got quite a bit to share.First and foremost, the game's story proved to be an enjoyable ride from start to finish. The characters, despite the linear nature of the narrative, managed to capture my interest and keep me invested. The simplicity of the graphics surprisingly complemented the overall experience, giving the game a unique and charming aesthetic.One standout feature was the seamless integration of both 2D and First Person aspects within the same game. "American Arcadia" flawlessly navigates between these perspectives, providing a unique blend that added depth to the gameplay. This innovative approach created an engaging experience that pulled me into the world of the game.Despite the positive aspects, the journey was not without its hiccups. Minor bugs, including clipping, overlapping dialogue, and false triggers during backtracking, slightly impacted the immersion. Additionally, I encountered freeze-frames, a potential loading-related issue, and experienced one crash. While not game-breaking, these technical glitches were noticeable.The puzzle-solving aspect, although generally short and easy, suffered from a communication breakdown. The game struggled to effectively convey all the necessary information, leading to frustration and unnecessarily prolonged attempts to solve some puzzles. The 'Room isn't ready' segment proved to be particularly troublesome due to a puzzle-breaking bug, forcing me to reset to the last checkpoint. This incident notably heightened frustration to an otherwise enjoyable puzzle-solving experience.The story, while enjoyable, had moments of predictability. Some plot twists were foreseeable, but the narrative maintained its charm with subtle humor and numerous easter eggs, providing an added layer of enjoyment.As for the ending, my feelings are mixed. While the conclusion left me with a sense of both satisfaction and dissatisfaction, it brought up contemplation on morality and certain themes. It's a unique and thought-provoking experience that, in a way, mirrors the blend of realism and an almost unrealistic touch found throughout the game.To summarize, "American Arcadia" provides a captivating adventure with an enjoyable story and innovative gameplay. Despite technical glitches and communication issues with puzzles, the game's charm, humor, and ending make it a worthwhile, albeit imperfect, journey.

_childDocuments_.review: Once in a while, a little gem of a game comes that you start playing and cannot put down until you finish. American Arcadia is such a game. Combining an interesting premise with engaging, imaginative gameplay, good writing and a beautiful visual style, this game will keep you glued to your seat from beginning to end.No spoilers here, as you learn all of this in the first few minutes of the game: Trevor is a boring, uninteresting man. His whole life is routine, he never amounts to anything... until he finds out his entire life has been a lie. He, like most other inhabitants of his city, form part of a "Truman Show"-style reality show and their entire purpose is to entertain an audience. The problem is, Trevor isn't entertaining anyone, and those who fail to entertain must be excised. Ironically, it is now Trevor's most exciting day of his life, as he must find a way to escape the city before he's made to disappear for good.This is the basic premise, but the story goes much, much deeper. American Arcadia is a story-heavy game, and while the gameplay is fun on its own it's really the story and characters that carry it. As the story progresses and you become attached to the characters you will see many twists and turns that will keep you invested until the very end. Don't take anything for granted here. Writing in general is quite good, and the worldbuilding makes the place feel real.From a gameplay perspective, there's two main kinds of gameplay: puzzle platformer and first person exploration. In the first one you control Trevor as you make your escape, while in the second one you control Angela, who's helping him escape, as she works behind the scenes to make sure he succeds. But ocassionally you get to control both characters at the same time, and it's quite an interesting experience. Both styles also ocassionally welcome several variations that keep the gameplay fresh and engaging.From a visual standpoint, the game excels. The art style is beautiful and colorful, and perfectly fits the setting. Voice acting is pretty good and helps sell the story much better. Audio does a great job in general, though it tends to be one of those "if it's doing its job, you won't notice it's there" things, except for a few times where paying attention to the sound is necessary.The game really does excel in most areas. Sadly, there is one where its job is less than adequate and that is performance. While in general the game runs well there are a few occasions where it has suffered from slowdowns, some of them very severe to the point of nearly freezing the game, and they come and go with no rhyme or reason (you can be in the same area where nothing changes visually and the framerate will suddenly go up or down). I've managed to solve this by turning v-sync off and capping the fps, but this is an inelegant solution and you still get the framerate to drop in certain scenery-heavy scenes. Besides that, I got a crash near the end for no discernible reason. I can run the Resident Evil remakes perfectly fine, so I doubt it's a problem on my end.It really is a shame about the performance issues, because it is otherwise an excellent game. These problems don't make it unplayable (at least if you do the frame cap thing) but they are noticeable. They were present for me in the demo as well, so you can probably use that to gauge if your PC will have these issues or not before going for the full game.I still recommend the game, of course. Provided you tinker with the settings, the issues with the framerate are light enough to not get in the way (and hopefully they can be patched out in the near future), and it is a game that must be experienced. Just keep it in mind.

The only "negative" thing I'd say is that it's a short game - lasting about 6-8 hours, so it's not a game you buy for it's longevity, more-so it's a game you buy for the experience and storytelling. _childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed my time with Out of the Blue's previous title, Call of the Sea, but American Arcadia left me frustrated and rather underwhelmed. I don't want to NOT recommend this title but if I could get my time and money back I would. Minor spoilers ahead.Credit where it is due: the world of Arcadia is incredibly vibrant and the concept of alternating between two protagonists (one who interacts with a 2D world and one with a 3D world) is pretty cool. The game doesn't overstay its welcome and the abundant voice acting is generally well done.Unfortunately, the ~7 hours of gameplay here is pretty uninspiring. The 2D platforming suffers from mushy controls and too many scenes where it feels like you're expected to fail the first time before understanding what the game expects of you. You don't typically lost much progress when this happens, but it often feels unfair.MAJOR spoilers ahead:I was expecting to walk away from this game with a generally positive experience and left the door open for a late twist to really propel this game to greatness (base mostly on its narrative). The twists came and they were pretty compelling, but a (perceived) flaw in the story's logic left a bad taste in my mouth as I puzzled through what just happened: Why was Angela pulled into this scheme rather than having an actor play that role? It feels completely illogical on the corporation's part and was included just to allow the player to walk in her shoes. It may seem unfair to ding a game so severely for a single plot hole, but when the story is carrying so much of a game's weight it's pretty deflating to have that story feel undercooked at its conclusion.
_childDocuments_.name: American Arcadia

_childDocuments_.review: Game was fun and I enjoyed the whole time with it. The writing was good; the characterization was excellent and storytelling superb, but the plot itself, other than a twist or two, kinda follows what you'd expect once you know the premise. There's an obvious inspiration. The twists definitely deviate from the obvious movie inspiration, but were telegraphed enough that I saw them coming.Main thing I didn't like was the very ending - but ~8 hours of gameplay and good story do mean a positive review. It's not that the ending was bad - I get what they were going for, but the ending, despite having lead-up... just sorta stopped abruptly, played credits, then had a post-credits scene that ties up some of the loose ends, but left a number of things hanging. There are enough loose ends that I hope there might be DLC or something, though I suspect the end is the end. I really think one more gameplay scene or a cutscene was missing in the ending to make it feel like the story was fully complete.I guess I didn't touch on gameplay much. Pretty standard platform fare, but the mix of platforming and puzzles was novel. Doing platforming with the left side of the controller and hacking cameras and stuff with the right side was the sort of thing I've only seen in one other game (Pivot Pilot, which is *brutally* difficult on purpose), but here, it didn't really cause any friction. It was a novel approach that I really enjoyed. But at the end of the day, while I liked the platforming and the puzzles, and the way it jumped between perspectives... if's the writing and aesthetic, the characters that will stick with me, not the gameplay. That's not to say the gameplay was bad or lacking polish or anything, just that the gameplay was a vehicle for the story more than it was the focus.

_childDocuments_.review: Finished in 8 hours over 2 days. Fun, gripping fast-paced action-puzzle-based mashup of Logan's Run, The Truman Show, The Running Man, Brazil, and the first twenty minutes of The Matrix, with some strong themes and jokes about how capitalism consumes everything, even that which struggles against it, and then turns around and sells it right back to the one who struggles. Gameplay elements are varied and solid but simple, and play with perspective in ways that remind me of the first Psychonauts. It's more a non-stop 8-hour interactive experience than a challenging game, but it's also one of the best sci-fi comedies I've "watched" in a long while.

_childDocuments_.review: So I just finished this game. Binged it all in, as you can see, basically a 5 hour stretch of time, give or take.I'm in love.Your two heroes, Trevor and Angela, are both deeply charming, and for different reasons. Not to mention their dynamic is wonderful.The gameplay is fun. If I had to explain Trevor's gameplay, it's similar to something like "Limbo", or "Inside". No complex platforming, but the challenges are fun to beat nonetheless. For Angela's, it's a great and fun puzzle adventure game, a nice mix of simple point-and-click and puzzle game. There was a moment in each section that was hard. For Trevor's, it was admittedly...not very clear how I was meant to accomplish a certain thing. I'd have liked that section to have been improved. For Angela's, I got total elation from solving it on my own. Overall, I had a blast on both sides, and didn't want to drop the momentum either provided for a moment.The story is full of intrigue and fun, and with incredible moments. There's definitely an ongoing mystery throughout that only develops the further you go. And the way they bounce between the two sides, you never feel like the protagonists are that far ahead of you, or that you're that far ahead of the protagonists in terms of information. The way each element is revealed is done with perfect timing, both narratively, and sometimes comedically. (The humor in this game is incredible, too, btw.)The ending was great as well. I won't spoil it here, but I think it was the strongest way it could have ended. Especially if you consider everything you're told...it was the perfect way to end, logically and tonally. All the worldbuilding, and character growth...it all culminates in something great. And there are some really strong character moments, too, especially from Trevor. I will admit that not everything is fully explained, but it may be leaving lingering mysteries on purpose. Or perhaps keeping itself open to conspiracy theories.My one big criticism of the game is...well, frankly, I wish it could have gone on longer. But I think that speaks to how good it is. It's probably just big enough to not overstay its welcome. Not too challenging to hold you up for long, but not so easy that it's (as some other people seem to react to it), a "pressing D simulator". It's paced really well. I just wish I could have had more, followed Trevor and Angela just a bit longer, anything.Overall, it's really amazing. And it might speak to you directly. If you're someone who feels their life is unremarkable, and that nobody would really care...give this a shot. It'll help you find a self-worth you may never have considered before.
_childDocuments_.name: American Arcadia

_childDocuments_.review: This game is basically split into two different modes.  There's a platforming mode that works like Limbo, Inside, Stela, etc etc and those sections are perfectly tolerable.However there's also sections you play like a puzzle FPS game where a female protagonist narrates literally everything that happens, even the cutscenes you're watching.  For instance, at the very beginning of the game she has to distract her boss.  On top of the usual adventure game shtick where the character quips about everything you click on, once you do figure out how to distract her boss, the character describes in detail out loud what she's seeing.  She's essentially a living audio description track and I just find this to be an insufferable trend in modern video games.  I am not blind; my eyes are fully functional.  I am capable of watching a cutscene where the events are not spoonfed to me by the protagonist.This has to be a generational thing.  Video games twenty years ago did not do this.  This game was officially my "Oh god, I'm a millennial boomer!" moment.
_childDocuments_.name: American Arcadia

_childDocuments_.review: I was close to not recommending this game because of its numerous flaws; bugs, overlapping and repeated dialogue, cheap deaths from poor level readability, and the fact that many of the 2D sections simply involve just holding the left stick in one direction for long periods of time. But the cinematic presentation is striking to see from this genre, it kept pulling neat tricks. By the end I had a big smile on my face, and there were several moments where at least momentarily I forgot about the game's lack of refinement. Those moments were so charming I couldn't help but give the developers credit, as they clearly showed this game was made with love and passion. I'm hoping the devs patch and polish this game. It will still contain the rote level design of nearly every other cinematic platformer (dragging crates and carts, taking cover to avoid insta-death from spotlights, etc.), and characters that I personally think talk too much, but once this game irons out the rough edges, I can strongly recommend it at its normal price.

_childDocuments_.review: American Arcadia is what you'd get if you mixed The Truman Show with the Prisoner, set the whole thing in the mid-1970s, and larded on a healthy dose of biting criticism of modern social media voyeur culture. That is to say, it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ amazingly well told story, which is good for while the gameplay is fun, once you wash all the frills off it's basically a 2d platformer interspersed with a FP walking sim with occasional stealth elements. This of course goes to show what good writing, more than good voice casting, and a consistent dedication to the overall aesthetic can do to boost a basic gaming concept into something pretty close to apex.

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels like it shouldn't exist and perhaps that may be the main reason to play it. It's a mostly-on-rails game with a simplified, yet highly-effective visual style that splits its time between a rather simple platformer and a first person puzzler, though it has some genius moments where it puts them together.  That is to say, there are a handful of key moments where you are controlling one character in the platformer while you're doing stuff as the other character in first person. It makes more sense when you play it.Sadly, those moments are few and far between and the narrative necessitates them dwindling as the story goes on. What's left are the pure bits played in either environment and while I lamented that more opportunities weren't taken to mash these two elements together like in the first half of the game, the stuff left over that doesn't is still capable and fun to navigate.So yeah, here's an odd duckling of a game that will take approximately 7 hours to complete and outside of some achievement hunting, that's about it for its shelf life, but the story is compelling, the environments are gorgeous and it's terrifically acted out by veterans like Yuri and Krizia among others. It's a 2.5D set-piece platformer and an FPS puzzle game with deceptively 'simple' art direction that is expertly-realized and complex when you really stop and look at it.  It feels like a high-budget production and some of the names that top off the voice cast don't come on the cheap.  Like I said, it feels like this game shouldn't exist.Perhaps the reason why it does exist is because of the yarn it weaves rather than the gameplay it offers. It doesn't seek to give the player an intense challenge in either platforming or puzzle solving; these sections on their own aren't anything to write home about, but those moments when they're put together really give the game some unique sparkle and it fits in with the narrative perfectly so it doesn't come off as a cheap gimmick. The stakes are actually pretty low - death is little more than a reset to a very nearby checkpoint so you can try again. Anybody can play this. The focus over everything else is to tell its story so it leaves the question of whether or not it's worth experiencing. I promise no spoilers.Where the gameplay is from the playbook of  and perhaps even , the setting itself is most assuredly inspired by Walt Disney's EPCOT concept and the theme park that rose out of it after his death. For the uninitiated, good old Uncle Walt wanted to build a self-contained City of Tomorrow that would constantly serve as a model for the future by incorporating the latest technologies and civic concepts in an on-going fashion. The company of his namesake decided this was not a feasible thing to do and instead turned the idea into a theme park focused on education and entertainment, yet still looking towards the possible future.I have only been to EPCOT (formerly EPCOT Center) a handful of times in my life, but the problem of focusing a theme park around future technologies is that if you don't stay up to date, it starts to fall behind. The first time I went was as a young child, some time during its first iteration in the late 80s and everything was already feeling kind of out of date with much of the park's original concepts slathered in 70s sensibilities (the park opened in '82, but I was far too young then). Lots of carpeting, stripes, Rockwell-style art, and images of the typical Nuclear Family, but still full of bright ideas on how future cities might operate if, you know, budget wasn't a thing. The second time I went was as a teenager to check out some new motion ride there about the human body. It was this bizarre mix of new stuff they were bringing in to make the park more modern pushed against a ton of things still left over from the first iteration of the park. Yet I still loved all the old stuff - it instantly transported me to my first visit. Old rides focusing on the families of the future inside Spaceship Earth (a slow-ass ride through a giant ball featuring creepy animatronics) or the behavior of animals or one I recall being about flight that  showed the original videos from the 80s that were so horribly out of date. Yet each one felt so comfortably familiar and washed in my own nostalgia that I truly fell in love with the place despite it being the more 'boring' park of the three at the time (Hollywood Studios opened up by this time). While I did return once more, it was not the same as it was in my younger years and I really mourned the passing of the park I knew.  All this to say that the world of American Arcadia brought me back one last time to the weird, fascinating park that I remember.Only it's not a park this time around. The game examines what might have happened if the real city that EPCOT proposed existed or at the very least, if a similar project had been taken seriously and attempted, but instead of looking forward to the future, it just kind of stalls and gets stuck in a utopian version of the 70s. Obviously this game does not have Disney's stamp on it, so 'Disney' becomes 'Walton' and the Mouse is now a Dog, et cetera, but this is clearly Disney-adjacent, even right down to perpetuating the Uncle Walt myth wherein he (or rather, Walton) is posthumously glorified as a flawless, legendary visionary who simply went too soon before the sharks came and smelled blood in the water. Anyone who has visited the parks in Florida, particularly EPCOT, will understand all of the alusions being made in this game and will instantly recognize the nostalgia that visting the world of Arcadia is meant to project. Even if you've never been to the park, you'll still kind of get the idea of what the park used to be. It was never this snazzy or fully realized, mind you, but so much of it feels instantly familiar, just made grander in scope.This setting is where  begins to unravel its yarn and without actually spoiling anything at all, the idea is to ask what would happen if this utopian city really existed. What would become of it? How would it survive past its initial years and how would it maintain its vision of the world as time passes? What would people living in it be like? If those concepts are intriguing to you, then I say enjoy the rollercoaster. The journey is fun, but the ending is what really ties it all together and it's worth the trip to get there. Is it worth the dollar value? I don't know, but it's definitely a game that needs to be experienced blindly. Other reviews already sadly hint at what its themes are, but despite that, you should give it a shot whenever its price becomes acceptable to you.

_childDocuments_.review: American Arcadia is a good time if you go in with the right expectations. It's not very long, difficult, or interactive. It borders on being a walking sim at times. It takes a more cinematic approach letting the story explain itself. You the player take a more passive role watching more than playing which is appropriate given the themes of the story, but isn't particularly exciting. The blend of first person adventure and cinematic platformer is not fully taken advantage of. It's a brilliant concept on its own. However, you'll rarely have to multitask outside of a few rudimentary puzzles. You're not alternating control between Trevor and Angela to solve complex puzzles while avoiding suspicion. The game literally tells you what to do in the sloppiest way imaginable. While the voice acting is very good, having your characters speak out loud exactly what they are going to do is bizarre. I don't know why so many games need their characters to always be speaking.The game's length is fairly short. You can beat this game in a day playing blind and taking your time. It's completely linear and there are no choices to be made. This is fine in service to the narrative they wanted to tell. I wish puzzles were more challenging or at least memorable. The fact that this game has a block sliding puzzle tells me everything I need to know about how much thought was put into the puzzles. The platforming is extremely basic. You spend most of the time just moving forward occasionally having to jump. Despite the many chase scenes, it's never tense or too demanding on reflexes. The gameplay is basic and easy.The story is the main selling point here. It should be familiar to anyone who's ever seen The Truman Show. While it isn't new or unique, it has some clever twists and turns throughout. It's full of references to modern pop culture and addresses topical subjects. There's a nice plot twist near the end I won't spoil that was well executed. That said, I wasn't a fan of the abrupt ending that didn't quite tie up loose ends. The presentation is also a highlight. It's bright and colorful which make up for the simple 3D models used. The 70s retro design of Arcadia with believable level design make for a more immersive experience than what's typical of a traditional 2D platformer. It feels like you're in real locations.I'd say it's good for a playthrough. I don't think $20 is too much, but I think $15 would've been better given the short length, lack of replay value, and basic gameplay. (7/10)

The puzzles are simple, the platforming is basic bordering on slightly frustrating at times with how it expects you to react although the transition between the two is a nice spin.Everything else shines. _childDocuments_.review: American Arcadia is a modern-day Orwellian nightmare which preys on all our worst technologically-driven fears both personal and societal. A sidescroller that seamlessly weaves the narrative with its gameplay so perfectly that it's unlike anything I've seen before. Each transition between gameplay and cutscene is perfectly explained to create a cohesive, uninterrupted experience. The game constantly shakes things up by introducing new mechanics for brief yet memorable sequences. These new mechanics almost feel designed with the intention of making a mini-game out of them but none of them are incorporated in a way that makes them mini-games. Instead they are fluid variations and escalations in the narrative and the required mechanics to progress it.American Arcadia tells an incredible story. Filled to the brim with movie references, American Arcadia is overtly heavily inspired by all the things that came before it - from Walt Disney to Robocop and The Truman Show to George Orwell's dystopias. Yet none of this game feels stolen. It's wholly original, building tremendously off of famous and beloved pop culture and entertainment franchises. The story is so well integrated into the gameplay as well. It constantly does very cool things to alter how you see the narrative while still being in control of the protagonist. There's very cool ways the game allows you to multitask through two separate peoples' eyes. The game is filled with plot twists that will leave you second guessing everything you believe, wondering if the people you think are the bad guys are really all that bad, and then realizing that yeah, they're at minimum not great. The ending cements this as one of the best dystopian narratives I've experienced across mediums - from TV to film to literature to games.The art is absolutely gorgeous. Boasting a 70s aesthetic with modern, even futuristic technology and nothing in the world feels out of place. The character design brilliantly avoids detailed facial animations while keeping characters looking like real, recognizable people. There's so much charm in all the design. The background set production is out of this world, always providing eye candy to look at and details to uncover whenever you're trekking from one side of a location to the other. The game has fantastic music that really immerses you in the world in ways most first person perspective still games fail to do. I always felt like I was both witnessing the story from Trevor's perspective, a second character's perspective, as well as from an outsider's perspective. Not entirely without its flaws, there's some dialogue bugs I encountered where multiple dialogue sequences would overlap with each other, and a couple of the brief gameplay mechanics/sequences were a bit more annoying than fun. That said, no game is perfect but the experience is one worth giving a 10 out of 10. Aside from the incredible story, beautiful art, mesmerizing music, phenomenal voice performances, and astounding set design, the game does some very unique storytelling and gameplay techniques not seen anywhere else which alone would make this game worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: A surprising gem I got as part of a bundle. Possibly the best game I've played in many years. That said, it's more an interactive movie than a game in the traditional sense (and correspondingly is fairly short, warning to those who. need to squeeze 60+ hours out of every game; this is over in about 7 hours, probably 6 if you're naturally good with games). But worth it in any case.The story is so engrossing, the graphics are fresh and different, I couldn't wait to pick up my Steam Deck again to continue the adventure. It's a brilliant variation on the Truman Show, with a colourful 70's vibe. The voice acting is very, very good for a game. The chapters's structure ties playing parts with cutaway scenes skilfully (flashbacks, documentary-like interviews, relevant short "movies" from earlier times...), increasing the feel of being immersed inside a movie.The game mechanics are 2-fold: when you're following Trevor it's a 2.5D engine, where you run either to the left or to the right. Though it does get repetitive in some ways, it's not as dull as it sounds, and the Arcadia world really comes to life with depth and colour during those scenes. When you're following Kovacs, you're in a 3D mode, which is more about exploration than action. Often, you're following Trevor AND Kovacs, and use the left joystick for one and the right joystick for the other, coordinating them to match the narrative. It's a very original concept, very well executed. The puzzles are not too complicated, and overall it's very entertaining and not too demanding: my kind of game!Steam Deck advice: initially it's okay but then sometimes the fan goes crazy and the remaining battery goes down the drain; I ended up limiting TDP and GPU a bit, setting graphics quality to Low except for textures at Medium because Low hinders some gameplay, and limiting fps to 25; very playable after that, with a decent battery life.
_childDocuments_.name: American Arcadia

_childDocuments_.review: It's fine. The game is almost entirely sold on its visuals, and should be more understood as guided experience.The puzzles are inoffensive, but on the very easy side, besides a few really annoying ones.The story is pretty straight forward,  and all "twists" are telegraphed so heavily that they can't really be considered twists.I can recommend it if on sale, because it looks great, and it is an interesting experience, even if the story is not that novel. However, I wish they played more with the esthetics, it feels like they could have done more with the retro-futuristic setting.
_childDocuments_.name: American Arcadia

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent premise for a game. Unique theme and setting. Excellent voice acting. Scene transitions are beautiful and surprising.  The price of the game is fair considering its length. However, this is better than most full-priced AAA games. Everything about this game shows care and attention. Don't miss out, especially if you enjoyed Limbo, Inside, Super Mario Bros 3.
_childDocuments_.name: American Arcadia

_childDocuments_.review: Blasted through this game in one go, and I want to give it my whole hearty recommendation! I got it for €15, but I'd say it well worth the price of €20. _childDocuments_.name: American Arcadia

_childDocuments_.name: American Arcadia

_childDocuments_.review: My computer sucks and so I dealt with a lot of lag and a few crashes, but this game was so, so captivating I wasn't willing to put it down! _childDocuments_.name: American Arcadia

_childDocuments_.review: This game is basically a 2.5D Running Simulator and platformer with a few puzzles to solve along the way - although you do swap into a typical first person view for about 1/3 of the gameThat might sound like im underselling it but oh boy the story is absolute captivating and had me hooked right until the end - the main character/s are just wonderful and you are constantly cheering them on the whole wayWithout spoiling anything you are basically a character inside a 24 hour watched live show - think "Truman Show" if youve ever seen that, and you start becoming self aware and try and escape9/10 overall from the platforming and puzzling, to the whole story arc - I loved this a lot more than I expected, great experience
_childDocuments_.name: American Arcadia

_childDocuments_.review: First impressionGreat game, great concept, great execution. Super great visuals and unseen level of control over how the story - extraordinary and exceptional in itself - is presented.THE GOODThere is so many amazing features. First the story itself and the way it is narated... The groundbreaking novelty approach to what basically is a platformer :) This level of perfection that I have never seen yet in any other title. 14/10Then there is the visual aspect, which is simply unmatched. I hope this game earns big and visual artists get a big buck, because the visuals are most important part of any videogame and in this case the art is so much elaborate, everything fits. 14/10 for graphics, bceause it is extraordinary, in fact it defines a new sub-genre.THE NOT SO GOODThen there is sadly only one but big exception. {edit} Actually two. {edit} Count three after finishing the game. This game could offer much more pleasant and relaxing experience, if not for the absurdly dramatical voice acting.It is way too realistic for me to enjoy the whole thing smoothly. It breaks the atmosphere of the 70s like a giant rock breaks perfect sculpture made of glass. Even Trevor acts like todays pubescent, all the screams the hype, it does not fit at all.Yes the voice actors are great actors, they just did their job a bit too well. This is not a theatre play, but it is acted as if it was one. 8/10The dialog sequences inserted between the action are Ok. Only Kovacs is behaving pretty lousy, even inconsistent with her character. Self importantly states how she coined this or that term... That brings the overall level down a lot. The type of behaviour she expresses in those scenes is very different from anything resembling a hacker. She is a bit too relaxed, perhaps even resigned. Trevor part is better, but sometimes unnecessarily reveals too much about what is gonna happen.The riddle part of the experience is very enjoyable and satysfying, with just about the right complexity level being set for me.Now I have come across the psychedelic part near the end, which again does not fit and I wish it was not there. What to say. Devs always find a way to ruin otherwise a perfect and enjoyable experience.THE UGLYTowards the end the plot starts losing its coherence and appers to be a bit fast finished. The start is definitely much more rock solid. Which is really a major shame, because the end is the place where the deeper messages are delivered. The main plot ends in a storytelling stunt which is both hard to believe and unrealistic. While I undrestand what the intended message to the audience was, it is not delivered in a comprehensible way. The story at this point suffers from too many twists and the last revelation is just too much to put it very mildly.It kind of really hurts the devs say their main goal was to keep players surprised... Not a very high goal, there were much better options. One can only take so many twists until it is too many. More and more and more change is not always for the better. Sometimes less is more. Yeah, but that does not fit with current mainstream ideology.THE POTENTIALWhat stands out huge is the bold narative warning people of today, that possibly we are also on the way to similar Arcadia, being monitored 24/7 by figures of questionable authority for even more questionable purposes. What is sad, that the same technical measures (such as smartphones) used for monitoring people in real life today are used unknowingly by Kovacs with no warning whatsoever. Such a wasted potential. This also projects false narative on security and privacy when using smartphones. In reality you lose all the privacy and can be located and spied upon very easily. Real agent Kovacs would have to know such basic facts and would need to refrain from using a smartphone in the portrayed normie kind of way, if she was to avoid detection. Most probably she would not have used such devices at all.THE SUMMARYOverall I give a score of only 11/10 for the unnecessary realistic shouts, panic and hyped emotions although I do realize that this sadly is the norm in todays world obsessed with emotions and self-importance. And for the unfitting parts like the psychadelic break inside Visiorama. There is hardly anything positive to be said about that part. Points down for the unmet potential of explaining people better, that they are part of one such show already when using social networks and smartphones.The game peaks around its half, when it is refreshing and entertaining, then it slowly starts to fall apart and unfortunately it does not manage to keep the extremely high standard of the first episodes in many ways. Upon finishing it I do not feel acoomplishment or joy, I feel like I had to finish the mundane task which got too complicated, twisted and shattered, to be enjoyable.Still a brilliant game, at least the first half or maybe 2/3ths. Worth playing most of the time. The wasted potential though...
_childDocuments_.name: American Arcadia

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic art style, genuinely interesting script with some laugh-out-loud moments and a bit of a rug-pull ending that left me really satisfied.Some basic puzzling and platforming broken up with a split narrative keeps things clipping along at a nice pace - it's not a challenging game, but the gameplay is secondary to the story with this title. It's short, so doesn't outstay it's welcome. Here's to many more from Out of the Blue Games and Raw Fury!
_childDocuments_.name: American Arcadia

_childDocuments_.review: Really great! American Arcadia, while not an entirely unique concept, is a fantastic story game about Trevor Hills escaping from 'Arcadia', a big dome/city run by an evil media corporation.Something that really set it apart for me is the interesting switching between the two protagonists throughout the story. Trevor typically plays in a 2.5D sidescrolling perspective while Angela you play in first person, the game constantly bounces you back and forth between them both as the story advances, and it keeps the game feeling fresh and fun! Both sides have their own exploration, adventure and puzzles but nothing felt particularly difficult.The art and sound is absolutely brilliant and all the parts of Arcadia you explore both as Trevor and Angela look great and are fun to discover. The voice acting of all the characters throughout the game is top notch too, it can often feel like you're watching a TV show at times it's so good and the humour is also often on point. Honestly I'd recommend American Arcadia to pretty much anyone, there's a lot of ideas here and everything comes together really well. It's not a particularly long game, taking roughly 10-12 hours but it felt the perfect length to me.(I have finished it, not sure why Steam doesn't show many hours).
_childDocuments_.name: American Arcadia

_childDocuments_.review: Rating: ★★★★★Uraveling the secrets of Arcadia, has been an in depth, fully on the edge of your seat experience, I think you should go in with no prior knowledge other than it will be a similar gameplay experience to limbo, inside, or little nightmares. Try your best to solve the puzzles first time around, and then later look up a 4 hour walkthrough video, Have fun!!
_childDocuments_.name: American Arcadia

_childDocuments_.review: I think I can honestly say that this game is one of the gems of my collection. The story is very funny, but also has some twists that I didn't expect. The art style goes really well with this, always adding variety with new set pieces. Thanks to the voice actors, I quickly took all the characters to my heart.The gameplay felt very good for the most part. Thanks to the variety of perspectives, I always had something different to do. The puzzles were average, mostly quite simple, but one or two took me quite a long time. The first-person sections in particular were sometimes very thrilling. When both sections overlapped or there were a lot of screens to see, it was quite laggy (probably due to loading).I would particularly like to praise the soundtrack, which I really liked.I'm already looking forward to the developers' next game.Muy bien hecho chicos, seguid trabajando así.
_childDocuments_.name: American Arcadia

_childDocuments_.review: A cute story and a fun cast along with highs and lows when it comes to puzzles and alright game play. Short and sweet with a few noticeable bumps. The story had me intrigued not in how he gets out, but the certain mysteries of why things are taking place. They will get delivered to you piecemeal as the story goes along, so there's always something to think about. I never felt bored and wanted to see what was going to happen next. That's enough for me. The ending was especially great, a nice bow to tie everything together. I knew with one line being said what was about to go down in the next few seconds and they delivered in such a victorious way that it gave me a good chuckle. It lives up to the 2.5D name with about 60% of the game through Trevor, 40% of the game through the black and red haired lady. The Trevor gameplay is platforming that I think is most similar to Limbo or Inside. Moving boxes around to get to higher places, constantly going one direction with a few things to spice it up. Nothing surprising, but I enjoyed it nonetheless.As for the lady... there were some great puzzles and some others that made me feel like either I somehow completely had my wires crossed or the devs were thinking I should make the same logic jump that they did. At the beginning her puzzles are fairly straightforward and I understood them. It was neat helping Trevor by hacking stuff to get him through cops or buildings. It's also a very nice way to break apart the Trevor sections as my left thumb might have gone numb pressing the left stick for so long. Not to mention building on the story along with another character to like and learn about.However, near the end of the game in a certain facility I took almost an hour in there. I probably would have taken 20 minutes to get through it all if the devs gave me just one hint on the mindset I should have to get through a puzzle. There were lessons I thought I was learning that were then expanded upon without buildup, like a puzzle was missed that would teach me what to expect next. I don't think the puzzles themselves were bad once I got the logic behind them, but I wish there was some buildup there rather than sending me in on a wild ride. And spoiler for one puzzle: While this section frustrated me, I did manage to get through it all in about 6 hours by myself. With a few puzzles that I felt needed a bit of buildup before solving, I did have a nice, fresh run through American Arcadia. If I had to guess what the inspirations were, one would definitely be Truman Show, but the other surprising and possibly spoiler one was  unless I read that movie wrong. Even with those inspirations, they do something new with it that I think deserves a playthrough. For $20, or $18 when I bought it as it just came out, I think it was well worth the price and time.Oh, and I'll also need help from my Spanish speaking friends on all the very nice things I'm sure the lady said.Don't be a fool!
_childDocuments_.name: American Arcadia

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful game! I loved the switching from first to third person for the characters, it really added to the feeling of the watched and the watcher. Fantastic voice acting and god that ending- painful how I could def see this happening in real life... I had a great time, even if my puzzle brain was inept on occasion :DD
_childDocuments_.name: American Arcadia

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely loved this game! Such a great narrative that really kept me hooked. _childDocuments_.name: American Arcadia

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a really interesting story and is compelling from front to back.
