_childDocuments_.review: This game successfully makes me want to play Prey again instead, especially for the ideas taken from Prey Mooncrash but executed less impressively. I'll preface the rest of this by saying it's not a  game, but has definitely been overrated and not worth the full price Deluxe pre-order I splurged on in anticipation of another Arkane gem.If you're interested in a mostly generic shooter with poor stealth mechanics and a mere facade of actually having to be clever to figure something out, this is for you. This game is not what I'd call an immersive sim. While it preaches the "Play Your Way" philosophy (as in Dishonored and Prey), here that just means "you can sometimes enter through a roof or vent rather than the front door". It doesn't go very deep in providing options. The biggest offender is that there's only one way to actually go about finishing the main objective in the game... not what I'd call "Play Your Way" at all.Stealth... the AI in this game has a weird combination of being dumb and too aware at once. You can often run right up to enemies and instantly kill them without detection. Other times you can be taking out one enemy and another one waayyy across the room will instantly become alert, causing the entire room to become alert, and there goes your stealth. These extremes make stealth feel very unbalanced. Another detail which kills things compared to most stealth games is that the NPCs either never stop panicking, or take so long I simply never saw it happen. So once NPCs are alert, that's it until you die. A good stealth mechanic should allow you to hide if you mess up and try again after a short while, but I guess this game is much more combat focused. The combat can be fun in itself, but is also rather shallow.Weapons, tools and abilities are somewhat unremarkable but "fine" I guess. At one point you can unlock a sniper rifle which was probably the most unique and rewarding unlock for me and my play style (and was unlocked in a pretty fun objective). Weapon perks mostly feel irrelevant, the only character perk I was attached to was the double jump and I barely felt the need to bother with the ability upgrades.  Shift was the main ability I used throughout, and Nexus purely for time-saving, though I feel I could've easily done without it. You can only equip two abilities and there's little incentive to switch them up once you've found the ones that are most useful for you, meaning the majority of the abilities just feel like wasted time for the devs. I'd guess few will use the Chaos ability that merely temporarily makes combat easier when the others offer actually interesting mechanics. I feel the Kinesis ability might've been fun but with only 2 slots I didn't feel much freedom to experiment with abilities I didn't know were going to actually help.Exploration is a big thing I was looking forward to, hoping it would feel as engaging as Prey or Dishonored, but as you can see my game hours are a mere 24, which considering how I usually take my time in games (and was doing for a while in this game), is a bit telling. Exploration is largely forced in this game, as you need to discover the clues in order to progress through the leads, find door codes and do the multiple loop persisting stuff required to actually advance to being able to complete a full loop. This results in exploration also being largely unrewarding, with residium being too easy to obtain and the perks being easily collected from enemies instead.In Prey I might get a bonus for taking my time to explore an area beyond what the game requires me to, whereas in Deathloop I have to explore everything anyway in order to find the things that actually advance me through the game, so there's little sense of doing something "extra" for a benefit. My efforts in exploring new areas always felt anti-climactic. Even progressing through leads is usually a case of picking up notes and listening to audio logs until the game says "yes you progressed, now go somewhere else".I had a few issues with following the main quests. The documents and audio logs you have to find to progress through a quest often don't stand out very well. In one case I was missing an item in an area required to complete an objective and it turned out to be a piece of paper positioned on its side, in such a way that from most perspectives it was just a line segment. If you wanted to play this game without objective markers you would suffer as it's only thanks to them that I could know that there was something else I was missing in a room. I'd also expect such a game to provide multiple ways to complete an objective rather than relying on an exact document to be collected.PvP invasions were fun... at first. Eventually it became a repeating pattern of being in the middle of my current quest, getting the invasion notification, then groaning and having to divert from my current goal to deal with it... followed by 15 minutes of waiting or looking around a map too large for 2 player first-person PvP experiences. I'm fairly sure the other player should have your current position indicated with a marker, yet still the other player tended to either hide and try to snipe from somewhere, or be completely AWOL, either waiting for me to let my guard down and give up or trolling to waste my time... which was very effective I must say. Eventually I turned player invasions off so that the Juliana encounters were just simple head to head combat, as I believe was the more intended experience. These invasions are also particularly annoying if you want to approach the game with stealth as you will have to deal with the player and compromise yourself to any NPCs that happen to be around. That said, once you get the hang of it, both the player and NPC invasions aren't hard to deal with... basically just run towards them and spam machete attack until you get an instant kill on them. However I did have one encounter where I got repeatedly spawn killed as I was leaving the tunnels, because the other player can get on top of the entry point and do a drop attack which is instant death for you too. Very well thought out.Completing the final loop was disappointing for me, despite also being the most interesting part of the game. Interestingly I actually figured out how to kill all of the visionaries without fully following the main quest through to the end, which if I did would've apparently outright told me how to do it all. Luckily I must've been missing a couple more random documents or something so I didn't get to that hand-holdy part, but found it trivial enough to deduce what to do myself. By simply advancing through the day until I saw 3 targets in one place at the end, I knew I didn't have to kill them earlier. There were 2 who you get together as part of another quest, so that is also fairly obvious. Then there's also a trap kill I learned how to set up quite early in the game (I also just guessed how to do this without any actual in-game clues, purely based on the rest of the options being clearly wrong or obvious misleads). So while it was fun for me to figure it out this way, it kind of felt like I somehow "cheated" by being clever in the "wrong way"... but hey, finally some Play Your Way right? The "assassinations" also don't feel very satisfying, with most deaths happening off-screen. This game could take some notes from Hitman there.So by the end of this game I was rushing through to get it done as fast as possible. It wasn't  fun and I didn't feel any reason to stop playing before the end, but I also sort of cut the ending short and don't really feel any impulse to do more completion or see alternate endings... I just really want to play Prey again now.

Early game absolutely requires stealthiness. However, as you progress, you can certainly charge right in, guns blazing a bit more, and not get totally smeared. _childDocuments_.review: I’ve been an Arkane fan since I got the first Dishonored on the Xbox 360 back in 2014. Since then I’ve spent ~100 hours between the Dishonored games on Xbox. I even bought Prey a few months after release to support them. I played barely two hours before it got into my backlog, but I'm looking forward to getting back into Prey this year. As you already figured out I’m mainly a console player and just recently got myself a PC and decided that my first new game on it would be Deathloop. When I first saw the trailer for Deathloop it looked like Dishonored with a different skin to me which was a little off putting but I decided to give it a chance and go in with an open mind.For starters the game has the typical arkane look (that I like) now with a 60-70s aesthetic. Although the enemy design is pretty lazy in my opinion, all of them have masks and lack facial expressions and are all covered in paint like they just finished some kind of color run. The two main characters Colt and Juliana have great chemistry and some solid voice acting. I really enjoyed their banter throughout the game. The music is also pretty good. The game’s premise is that you are stuck in a loop and have to replay it until you gather enough information to kill the eight visionaries (the bad guys) and break the loop, which sounds like an amazing premise combined with Arkanes amazing level design that welcomes replayability and different approaches. Sadly it’s not. The story starts out pretty interesting with Colt not remembering anything and having to figure it out. Without spoiling anything the story is not at all that special or interesting. I thought that the ending was kind of abrupt and didt really answer anything, really the ending felt kind of weak. A good chunk of the story is also told through the notes and collectibles you find throughout the game, so if you aren't exploring as much I’d say the story would not make that much sense. I wasn’t expecting some kind of masterpiece of a story because Arkane aren't really known for their stories, knowing that the story was still a disappointment to me. The first loop of the game starts off with a tutorial-like part with a lot more handholding than what I’m used to, this part took me about two hours to complete. It introduces you to the base mechanics such as how the day cycle works, spotting enemies, the infuse mechanic and weapon jamming. Because the same day loops and you start over from the beginning you lose all of your equipment at the start of every new loop, that’s where infusion comes in. Colt can collect something called residium in each level by absorbing it from random objects and killed visionaries. With that residium you can infuse your equipment to keep it through the loops. All residium you didn't use at the end of the loop is discarded so you can’t just accumulate a bunch of it. Even with that I had enough to enfuse everything I wanted which totally made the jamming mechanic irrelevant because the higher rarity weapons don't jam. As soon as you kill your first visionary you can just infuse their gun and keep it for the rest of the game. At the end game I forgot that weapons could even jam. There are three slots for the guns as well although the machete has its own dedicated slot. Powers are back and almost every single one of them is a rehash from Dishonored just now under a different name. Just like Death of the Outsider there is no need for potions to restore mana, which I believe is a good change that leads to more fast phased gameplay. The detrimental setback in Deathloop is that you can only pick two different powers at a time, there are technically three slots for powers like with the guns but the reprise slab (the one that lets you die twice before restarting the loop) is permanently set in one of the slots unlike the machete. I would even argue that you can only pick and choose one other slab because the shift slab (Deathloops blink) is a must. This really takes away from the experimentation of the game. I’d prefer that you yourself could choose if you want reprise there or not. Three different slabs of your own choice at the cost of restarting the loop if you’re not careful enough.In Deathloop there is no 100% non lethal way to beat the game which i fine both of Dishonored's stealth and guns blazing approach is lots of fun, for me atleast. If I remember correctly some people were complaining that they felt judged playing Dishonored leathaly and getting the bad ending. Deathloop does away with the morality system just like Dishonored: Death of the Outsider and also the possibility to take out enemies non lethally although the only ones you have to kill are the eight visionaries, you could just sneak by all the basic enemies or in this case almost full on sprint by because the AI is really dumb and inconsistent. Most times you can just walk by the enemies and they won't notice you and sometimes they can spot you through walls and crates. There is also only one type of enemy human with a gun/machete. You can “spot” the enemies and see what weapon they’re using but that doesn't matter, machete or smg, they’ll all just run up on you no matter what. In most cases you could agro all the enemies and run off to a bottleneck location and watch them all pour in and gun them all down with ease. I’m also really disappointed with the assasination animations, they look so cheap. Colts giant machete just phases throughout the enemies like they were holograms and there’s only two assassinations that desmebers the enemy, that I’ve seen atlest. An enormous step back from the brutal Dishonored assassinations.The visionaries are also a disappointment.They all have different personalities but not really that memorable. Some of them have powers like Colt some of them don’t but even the ones who do are pretty much no different than the regular enemies. The biggest let down in my opinion is that there is only one way to get rid of the eight visionaries in one day. Compared to Dishonored where there are often three or four different ways not only to get to your target but also get rid of them, only having one resolution in Deathloop was extremely disappointing.Deathloop also has an invasion mode where you can invade another player's game with Juliana and try and stop Colt from succeeding. Interesting mechanic in my opinion that can spice up the gameplay from time to time, especially because the AI in the game is that dumb. For those who don't want other players in their game there is an option to turn off the invasion mode although that doesn't stop Juliana from still invading your game but now controlled by the AI. It's a little bit annoying that you can't turn Juliana off completely but I guess the game is easy enough so it's not too bad. When you first start as Juliana you barely have anything in your inventory and have to level up to unlock the equipment. Combine that with Colts ability with dieng three times before a game over, you can see that the game is heavily favored on Colts side. That may be a good thing considering how annoying it would be otherwise playing as Colt. Overall a pretty fun and interesting addition to the game. I have heard that other players have to wait a long while before finding a game to invade as Juliana, in my case it never took longer than a minute.         In conclusion; Deathloop is not a bad game but it's not a great game either. If this was from any other developer it could easily be a 7/10 (maybe a 6.5/10 if you factor in the poor performance), but as this is an Arkane title it really feels like a devolution and at best a 5/10. I just don’t get all the praise for this game and how “original” and “innovative” it is. All of Deathloops ideas come from Arkanes previous titles and are done worse here. 2021 was such a mediocre year for games and it sucks that Arkanes Deathloop was one of the games that made the year so mediocre.

_childDocuments_.review: Deathloop is an interesting game. First time playing it was a mediocre experience but playing it second time made me appreciate it more. This game has a bit of identity crisis because often it does not represent what it wants it to be. And kind of worst part is that you can only have two superpowers (slabs) to limit your fun. To comparison I'll give examples of both Arkane games; Dishonored(s) and Prey which are 10/10.In Dishonored, Corvo has lots of magic in his disposal. The way you play is up to you as a player. You can blink across be silent as wind, pick your targets one by one, sleep-choke and so on. Or you can be absolute lunatic. Send rats, swordfight, shoot'em'all, become murdermachine who cares? Deathloop not just limits you with powers but Colt (protagonist) is literally made of glass so all-out-combat is extremely risky. Sure you can use character upgrades but stealth is much easier and more rewarding so, what's the point?Deathloop has four maps and four timezones therefore the main idea is to comeback to the areas you visited before time and time again until you learn each map and their timezone differences. I like this idea tbh because level design is Arkane's biggest strength but it does not shine better than Prey.Before "Golden Loop" update game's ending was utterly disappointing. At least they added an extended cutscene but still feels like something was missing as well.Dear Arkane, I love you. Please I'm begging you to stop using your Void Engine. Dishonored 2 was a disaster (its fine now) and oh my God, this game never runs stable. If you can handle framedrops, be my guest.If you love immersive sims, great level design and somewhat first person shooters, you should give it a chance.

_childDocuments_.review: Deathloop is so cool.  Its hip vibe is noticeable in every aspect of its presentation.  Also, it is a fantastic game!  I don't play a lot of first person shooters, but after being so impressed with Dishonored 2, and seeing Deathloop on sale, I decided to go for it.  I'm glad I did. I initially, arrogantly, dismissed Deathloop.  Seeing that the game was based on a time loop mechanic, I thought "heh, how can anyone do it better than prime late 90's/early 00's Nintendo, I'll pass".  This is a bad habit that I have, and it almost caused me to miss a great game.  The game uses a time looping mechanic, and uses it well, while cutting out all the fat and annoying parts.  You are never waiting around for a specific time, for something to happen, which can be brutal in other "loop" games.  You do however, have those sublime moments where all the previous work you have put in on prior loops pays off, and you glide through some rube goldberg-esque quest, that would normally be close to impossible.  The game does a great job keeping track of the things you learn in a journal, but doesn't always spell out everything for you, especially when it comes to side stuff. From the moment the title screen loads, a very non-traditional one, you can tell that this game is "cool".  It marches to its own beat, its got a sense of style that is unmatched.  Its very funky and very modern.  There are four locations and four time periods.  You pick which location you want to go to in each time period, either with a specific goal in mind, or to just search around and discover stuff, usually that will pay off later.  The day ends, and then it starts over, but you now have additional information in your journal, letting you accomplish more in future loops.  Eventually you discover a way to "infuse" your weapons and power ups, letting you keep them permanently.  You can only do this at your base between missions, and the feeling of relief when you escape a location and then infuse a slab or legendary weapon is palpable.  Deathloop gives you a lot of freedom to approach things from any angle.  Guns blazing, stealth, hacking, its all on the table.  You get both weapons and powers enough to suit your loadout to how you like to play, or better yet, what you think would work best for the goal you are currently trying to accomplish.  The moment to moment gameplay is excellent, everything works well, and is a blast.  One complaint, similar to Dishonored, the enemies are super sharp, sometimes making a stealth approach frustrating.  Deathloop looks great.  I don't want to spoil much, but the island you are on, has a history, both with the current residents and many people before that, who have inhabited it over the years.  The entire thing has a very Lost vibe to it, and discovering the history and the secrets of the island is very engaging, and kept me hooked.  Everything is rendered with great care and detail, and the fact that different structures come from different time periods is noticeable and interesting.  This is a very good looking game, both in terms of the engine, and the design.  I keep comparing it to Dishonored, as I think is natural, considering they are from the same developer, and one way Dishonored succeeds and Deathloop fails is in the "realness" of the setting.  The city in Dishonored, while fictional, feels real and lived in.  The island in Deathloop, while incredibly cool and interesting, does not feel real, or lived in at all, and the characters that inhabit it just feel like cyphers, or action figures.  Part of I guess is due to the nature of the island and the "looping", for instances, most of the denizens are Eternalists, part of a cult that celebrates the loop, so of course, nothing feels permanent, but there is a fakeness that permeates the game and sometimes negatively affects the immersion.  There is an online component to Deathloop that is so fun.  You can choose to play as the character Juliana, and invade other peoples game and try and kill them while they play.  There were times, when I was stuck on a particularly difficult part, that I wanted to go offline, as the last thing you need is a Juliana invasion wrecking the mission while you are doing well.  That being said, in the name of fairness (I am a Libra) I never did go offline.  The invasions have the potential to be so fun, playing cat and mouse with Juliana, or trying to deactivate her jammer and get out of dodge before she hunts you down.  Some of my most memorable sequences in the game were due to Juliana invasions.  I only actually played as Juliana five times or so, but it was very fun as well.I loved Deathloop and recommend playing it if you think it looks or sounds at all interesting.  While I didn't finish every questline, or discover every secret, I saw a lot of the game and did not just stick to the main quest.  It was enjoyable, exciting, and challenging, it is just a solid game in every single aspect.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely brilliant and fun game!It's Outer Wilds' time loop & open exploration & puzzles -- done as a Dishonored-style FPS of guns & magic & freedom to play it your way -- with the stylin' of BioShock in a 1963 alternate history art deco.It takes the gameplay mechanic of roguealikes and makes that part of the sci-fi story itself.Four sections of the town you can visit at four different times of day/night, with many plot lines running through the day & night and crisscrossing to investigate and piece together for the ultimate goal, I'm glad they provide a clear menu to track it all.You're in control of where you go and when, and the day doesn't end & reset until you say it does (no timer) or you die.The game lets you explore these sections of the city freely, so you can play and engage however you want as you explore and go after leads & goals, much like Outer Wilds.There are a few different gun types, the usual spread, and you can only carry 3 at a time and that's fine & flexible enough. Duel wielding pistols is an option, and you always have a machete for silent melee kills & stealth murders.The magic powers are diverse and fun, providing utility as well as straight brutal offensive attacks.The hackamajig tool functions like Watch-Dogs -- point and press a button to hack the device. Love all the interactions that provides.The puzzles in the game are welcome additions. Most distill down to being a number for a locking mechanism -- but the puzzles themselves aren't always "Read this memo and note the code" (codes get automatically memorized by your character, so you don't have to write them down; very nice) but the more rewarding / extra puzzles have some actual in-world puzzle solving which is fun & interesting.By engaging more in the plots & puzzles and replaying everything many times with different personal objectives, you -- the player -- level up with your own memory & knowledge of the game more than your character -- Colt -- does by having better guns & magic powers.Farming (incidentally or intentionally) the only in-game currency, Residuum, lets you decide what weapons, slabs for magic powers, and trinkets to infuse to keep them for all as available inventory for future loops (runs).  This is similar to modern Roguealike games having progression between runs and it's great here.  All items are found in-game; there are no merchants as there is no money.NOTE: Most of the negative reviews on Steam at launch here are about performance. I haven't experienced any issues with stuttering. Deathloop runs perfectly fine on my PC, and looks gorgeous even without RTX.

_childDocuments_.review: Deathloop is a really fun game. It kept me playing through all of the run-time once, and for a few matches of its multiplayer component, which is both unique and clever. he comment you'll see repeated a lot in the reviews about the game dragging toward the end (I'd say it dragged for the last third of my play-through) is true. I don't think this is just due to the fact that the game is set on four maps though, which is the reasoning I think is set out most often to back-up the claim. The maps in this game have a learning curve which promotes mastery, which does really come in the last couple of hours of play. This is rewarding and the mechanical experience of the game never got dull for me. The reason the game drags is because it needlessly pads out its last half with busywork (particularly a latter quest which tells you to get a password, then asks you to get three more passwords, each of which requires a full loop of the game's day), and because of a quirk of the design. Because most of a player's exploration of maps and messing with mechanics will likely happen in the game's third to twelfth hours, the volume of interesting things on each of these maps goes down over time. This leads the last few hours of the game with a player just sort of ticking off stray ends, doing one or two little things a loop. This sucks the momentum when the game needs it most. I think either these needed to be slightly less main plot content, or a bit more side content which isn't busywork, because I think this sets the end game as a bit of a slog.One criticism I have seen levelled at Deathloop a lot, which I don't think is fair, is that the "tells you what to do at the end", ruining the feeling that a player had been "figuring out" the game's ending sequence. I don't really know where this comes from, because Deathloop tells you what to do, with waypoints and everything, all the way through. The player doesn't "figure out" any of its plot beats outside of a bit of environmental exploration. I think this is to Deathloop's credit. It wants to invite you to explore its world but, ultimately, to finish it.Deathloop is a good game, if a bit lopsided in how enjoyable it is (the first two thirds are definitely the best time you'll have here). I recommend getting it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Even though less complex than their previous games (this isn't an "immersive sim" or a game heavily inspired by that philosophy like Dishonored, but an action-adventure which borrows a lot from that approach; something close to Bioshock when it comes to making it accessible, for instance), this game is still a blast to play.Yes, the AI is not as reactive as the one of Dishonored and allows you tons of chances to "♥♥♥♥ up", but it does so for two reasons:-the game is balanced around the lack of checkpoints and quick-saves: sure, this has forced them to tone down the difficulty of your average encounters, but this change makes the action more fluid if compared to the save scumming vice that Dishonored 2 encouraged most people to embrace (the level design is going to pose enough threats by itself though). However, if you die more than 2 times per day you'll lose most of the gear acquired through a loop, so be careful about when to go guns ablaze or switch for a silent approach. -Invading Juliannas will be a serious threat that can ♥♥♥♥ up meaningful progress, especially during the second half of the game. She's going to demand your full attention, and your playstile is probably going to switch immediately the moment she enters your game.These two changes to their core formula do make the game very dynamic though, encouraging players to seamlessly improvise and switch beetween multiple playstiles in a single session to react to whatever the game's going to put in front of them.However, it's kind of a pity to see that they chose to rely so heavily on quest markers and massive information dumps in the beginning of the game:  level design and art direction are so solid that relying on visual and written clues wouldn't have made the game that much harder, and limiting the pleasure of true discovery for the main quests this much will take away the pleasure to see how complex and well thought out the overall structure actually is for many people.Even with its shortcomings, this game is still a blast to play, and surely one of the most engaging gaming experiences of this year.Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: I was going to write a long-winded review about how bad I felt for ignoring this game, but I'll make it short.This game is not Dishonored and it's not Prey. There...I said it, and its true. It doesn't have the freedom of exploration of Talos 1,  the scope of powers is much smaller than those provided by Neuromods or even The Outsider, the game has an overall brighter happy-go-lucky tone, the writing is more Marvel-ish, oh and everything resets after 4 sorties...or death. It's quite a departure. So why is this game still worth playing? It probably isn't if you stick to the journal and follow objectives. I urge you to ignore the journal and any sort of guide.  The way the world changes throughout the day( something you do in morning on one part of the island can affect the same or another part in the afternoon) and how you piece together what interactions are/seem useful really drew me in. It will seem repetitive at first to retrace your steps after a hunch didn't pay off or you failed, but, if you look hard enough, there are some really optimised paths where you can basically waltz through undetected (but they change depending on the time of day).  If you like to experiment and explore all possible interactions, this game is for you.I was against the loop at first, but I ended up liking how I could tackle some smaller puzzles/mysteries or get through more intensive parts depending on how much time I had. If in the middle of Dishonored you suddenly put together the solution from a 3rd mission puzzle in your head, your just like "well, next play through I guess". Here you can immediately go test something out and get it off your mind. There is no FOMO. That's one thing I hated about Dishonored: I always feel I have to find everything in one go. Every book, every place I can loot, every little story I can find. Not to mention not killing or being spotted and chaos levels. It can stress me out. For Deathloop, I kept a little notebook of things I need to do or potential quests and knocked them out at my leisure. Which leaves me to the best part of this game: it is the distilled essence of Dishonored's best gameplay moments mixed with great puzzles (some of which I still have no idea how to complete). If Dishonored is a classical piece of music, Deathloop is a jazz cover. They took  the parts of a Mozart piece everyone knows and changed the notes to better fit a sandbox. Its fast and loose, doesn't take itself overly serious, but it still has depth if you look for it.The change isn't for everyone, but please don't write this game off like I did.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, the reviews are mixed as of the writing of this review.  Dishonored 2 had a rocky start as well.But I'm recommending this game because of the content, and what you can experience if your hardware overcomes the current challenges. I really hope the devs will make this more accessible for everyone else, but in the meantime, please be patient.Now, the game is yet another Arkane gem, and is incredibly unique. It has all the good sandbox fun of their other titles, with a myriad of ways to handle obstacles, distinct abilities, all of that you would expect from an Arkane game.That's pretty much where the similarities end. This is now a game with time looping at its center  You go out, you learn more each time, you die, you try again.  You figure out all the secrets and then use that knowledge to your advantage.And the process of going out to learn and explore is a joy.  you can kill everyone to your heart's content, and have lots of creative ways of doing so. The entire world is vibrant and eye-catching, with even the NPCs displaying garish pinks and greens and so on. The soundtrack is groovy and the characters are memorable. Some find the comedy forced, but I get such a kick out of Colt and Julianna's interactions.I find the singleplayer genuinely engaging. Each of the 4 maps has 4 time presets  which drastically changes the feel, some of the layout, and even the difficulty depending on the time of day. You can manipulate events that occur later in the day with your actions earlier on - Things you won't know about until you go through some loops. And when it comes to taking down your targets, you can do everything from brute-force guns-blazing, or Hitman style environmental executions. Regardless of what you do, it will feel rewarding in the end And the  - This is largely why I'm putting so much effort into this review. I want it to thrive - Taking all the creativity from the Dishonored formula and pitting two players against each other with all of those tools at their disposal is something I'm so incredibly excited about. And so far, I really think it works well!You can play as Julianna, the rival assassin who's just as dangerous (if not more so) than Colt. When she invades, she locks up Colt's escape tunnels until he can hack the satellite and open them up again. She's on the island's team, so the NPCs won't attack her and she's free to go wherever she pleases, and also has the Masquerade ability to disguise as one of them, while also giving that NPC her form. When Colt is spotted by any NPCs, you get a ping as to where he was last seen - And if you see him first, you can point him out to them and get everyone in on the action.Colt's advantage comes with his Hackamajig, and his special ability Reprise. You can commandeer some turrets and set them up in defensive positions, scramble scanners so they no longer spot you, and set up mines (Although Julianna has some of her own, too!). And finally, Reprise is your second (and third) wind - Should you take a fatal blow, you'll zip back to a previous position in time, and respawn, invisible for a second in order to get out of harm's way. But your chances are limited, so be wary.The few matches I've played so far were lots of fun each time. You can treat it like a typical FPS,  but the one with ample preparation and a good plan is going to come out on top. You may have a great gun, but that won't do much if you let Colt lead you into a room where he's set up several turrets and placed mines for you. And that's just one small example of what's possible to achieve in the PvP.Mixed reviews on a game have always been a big turn off for me, but my previous experience with Arkane led me to give this a shot anyway - And I really am so glad I did. Please give them a chance, I'm certain that they'll sort things out eventually.

_childDocuments_.review: My second review. First time, I said I really enjoyed the game but felt it crashed way too often to recommend for the time being. Now, the game has received some patches and it seems to run a lot better for me and also crash less. But I also have finished the game in that time, and unfortunately I just don't think there's enough here to warrant a full recommendation.This is an easy 7 out of 10 game, if you get it on a sale. It's a lot of good fun figuring out all of the levels, at each time of day, and exploring locations to see what's there. After not too long though, I began to realize that there wasn't much to discover at all. Unlike other loopy games like Outer Wilds (an amazing game you should play right now, my GOTY of 2019) the purpose of the loop isn't for the story, but so you can find the next Macguffin to get to the next piece of the puzzle. It's entirely self-indulgent in that sense. Unlike Dishonored and Prey, which had intriguing stories layered over their level designs, the most story you get in this game is entirely superficial. I wish I could say I cared about any of the characters in it, even Julianna and Colt, but as fun as their banter could be, basically the only character worth caring about ended up being the computer in Charlie's level.The actual gameplay itself is fairly good and if you can get this game on a sale, you will probably enjoy it for a good several hours. The level designs are interesting enough, if not a little loose and too open-ended for their own good. You have several different objectives to be pursuing at any given time and each one changes how you see each level, and where you try to go at what times of day. This is nice and helps space out the monotony but after visiting every level a few times it gets old pretty fast. The powers and weapons are all fun and interesting, and if you like sandboxy games where you can just power your way through enemies, this is one of the best there is next to Hitman and of course Dishonored/Prey. That said, the game introduces an invasion system where you can play as Julianna and unfortunately it's very half-baked.The actual invasion experience, at its best, is extremely tense and rewarding. At its worst, it's some Dark Souls level getting-invaded-by-someone-cheesing-the-game-to-screw-you-over levels of annoyance. I was on the final mission of the game, spent an hour getting to that point on one loop, only to be killed by a clever Julianna player and had to restart that entire hour of progress again. That's just not fun. You can turn invasions "off" by setting them to AI-only, but that means you have to deal with Julianna's buggy and quite-easy in-game invasion AI that is way too easy to cheese. And if you're looking to invade your friends, good luck with that because unless they've set their game to "friends only" and you happen to be online during the few-minute window that an invasion is possible per-mission, you likely won't match with them at all or another player will be matched with them first.At its best Deathloop is approximately as good as any other Arkane game. At its worst, it's unfocused, repetitive, and not nearly polished enough with invasion balance issues to spare. If you get this game, you'll likely enjoy it but if you've enjoyed any of Arkane's other masterpieces you sadly might end up disappointed like I was. Still a good game, and I had some amazingly tense and fun moments in it. But in the end the story and balance left a lot to be desired.

_childDocuments_.review: Deathloop is something of a paradox. With one hand the game presents an open-ended world, teeming with options and a "play-your-way" laissez-faire approach to moving the player through that world. After wading into the waters of Blackreef I can report that this approach has proven to be something of a blessing and a curse for Deathloop. Without spoiling anything, the game practically begs the player to break the eponymous loop by using the tools they are able to uncover though their excursions out into the game's over-worlds, but falls flat once the few truly useful paths to success are uncovered. Forced to replay the same routs without any real variance beyond the first few "days" of looping leaves the player to simply push through the oddly linear path to success that Deathloop ultimately demands. The "play-your-way" pitch quickly gives way to a "walk at your own pace down this specific path" style that highlights some of the more shallow aspects of the game's design. Enjoyable and visually striking, Deathloop is a fun game which struggles with something of an identity crisis. I can't help but feel as if too much of this game was borrowed from other Arkane IP's such as 'Dishonored' which stood on a stronger foundation owing to it's lack of a forced replaying of levels. Deathloop's loop works against any feeling consequence the game may have otherwise instilled in the player, leaving most of the game's systems to be little more than window-dressing. While fun to a point for myself, your mileage may vary.

_childDocuments_.review: I adore the developer, Dishonored and it's sequel are a couple of my favorite games. I was expecting Deathloop to be familiar but fresh and fun. It's familiar enough, reasonably fresh, and moderately fun. There's a lot that holds this game back from being a solid recommendation, but ultimately I think it comes down to the story and characters not being engaging. The moment-to-moment gameplay is serviceable, although it feels weak and neutered at the start. When you acquire 'slabs' the gameplay options open up, but honestly the blink/shift and domino/nexus powers were the only ones that were worth it and I stuck with them the whole game. The gun variety is poor and enemies feel spongy, particularly "boss" fights with Juliana. Level design is excellent though, which has always been one of Arkane's strengths. There's tons of branching paths with excellent verticality and some hidden locations that open up to puzzles, or side quests.Where things really are plain boring is in the story and character development. The main characters bicker with each other over the in-game radio at the start of each mission but besides that have no interaction. The story is largely told to you through indirect means like notes, computer/IM/group messages, and tape recordings. There's no direct interaction between your character or any of the primary or secondary antagonists besides the opening and ending cinematics. The interesting premise of the world and it's design is wasted without valuable storytelling mechanics. The world-building is also left criminally underdeveloped with the player having to actively search out key story pieces to really understand what is happening, who we are, and why we're here. And the ending is supremely unsatisfying.The timeloop mechanic is fine and serves some unique purposes, but sometimes just results in frustration. Again, coming back to the story, you also never really understand why every single person except a small handful don't actually realize they are in a loop and perform the same actions every single day (unless you intervene). This does make it easy to begin memorizing paths, enemy placement, and plan accordingly. The level you choose and the time of day you go into the level will influence the level, enemies, loot, etc. so there's some variety to each level (4 level, 4 times of day, 16 possibilities).I had a few performance issues such as bad frame pacing shortly after launch that were cleaned up with a patch. What was a bigger problem was a constant, repeatable crash when headshotting enemies during a certain mission during a certain time of day. I had to install a beta patch to get through that section. It was more reliable, but not crash-free. I had to turn off raytraced shadows to ultimately solve the problem (which by the way is totally not worth the performance hit). It might be better now that there's a DLSS implementation to help soak up the frame loss, but I haven't gone back since the update.The game really could have been so much more. Maybe it needed more time, more development, and definitely needed more time dedicated to storytelling. It would be worth a purchase and a playthrough at a 50% off sale.

_childDocuments_.review: So, I had originally given this game a thumbs down because it was horribly optimized and ran like garbage. But now, that's mostly been fixed! I didn't love the level design, and I found the repeated cycles a little repetitive - there's nothing wrong with the concept of a roguelike stealth game, but the enemy AI is just too stupid to put up any sort of challenge, and the result is that you never *have* to try out new approaches or methods. Like I said, it isn't a bad game - but I would recommend picking it up on sale, rather than going full price.

_childDocuments_.review: It's like Dishonored's game-play had a baby with the time loop mechanics of Majora's Mask where certain missions require you to alter something earlier in the loop to attain a desired effect later in the loop. In addition to this, you have a Dark Souls style invasion mechanic, except done much better then it was in Dark Souls.While when pieced apart, this game doesn't do any one thing that's new. It all combines to make for a very unique and fun experience. As far as the game itself is concerned, I highly recommend it if you are a fan of Dishonored.Now, the port however could be better. If you have a PS5 definitely go with that platform, as I have had half a dozen crashes resetting my current day, and lots of intermittent stuttering for seemingly no rhyme or reason. Some missions it's there, others it isn't. The crashes seem to have been resolved by disabling ray tracing, but having to work around anything after buying an $80 dollar game is disappointing to say the least. And this was played on a machine with a 3900x, RTX 3080, 32GB of memory and a PCIE 3.0 SSD. There is no reason for a machine of this caliber to have any performance issues. You will likely get some yourself if you decide to buy before a patch. Ultimately, nobody knows how long Bethesda/Arcane is going to wait before patching the game so the whole invasion mechanic might be dead (i.e Dark Souls) by the time this game either gets fixed, or goes on sale. We've got an instant classic (at least for me) tarnished by a port that could have used more time in the oven. Buy on Playstation, or wait for a patch/sale.

_childDocuments_.review: As far as the solo gameplay is concerned, it's a fantastic game. Plenty of stuff to uncover and work through to 'break the loop' as Cole. A superb addition to Arkane's belt of great games. Multiple paths, upgrades, and lore through the 4 (x4 time-based setups) to uncover and beat. As for the multiplayer, invasion-based Juliana segments, it's not so great (yet?). I've tried to invade plenty of times since release, maybe 5 times per day since I've unlocked the ability to invade, but all but one of those invasions resulting in a lost connection before I was even able to load it. I'm not sure if players are just afraid of an invading Juliana (if Dark Souls is worth any evidence in this; they are) but the only one I've succeeded in connecting to resulted in a crash to desktop. Now; I love Arkane's games. Dishonored was an incredible romp through a magnificent city and Dishonored 2 and Prey were both up-to-par with that expectation. Arkane's (since cancelled) idea of 'Cross-Play' in The Crossing excited me to no end. I feel like this is a delve into multiplayer-lite territory and, personally, deserving of a bit of leniency. BUT. It isn't working so well in the few days post-release. If you're looking for the multiplayer component, wait a while. If you want a nice solo game, this is great for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Arkane does it again. Deathloop takes inspiration from many genres but in doing so becomes more than the sum of its parts. I've had a great time figuring out how to break the loop.Somehow playing variations on the same four levels gives a whole new spin on the Dishonered formula. This is a build in mechanism to make you try out different combinations and new strategies when replaying the levels. While previous Arkane games had that possibility there was never a good motivation to do it before this one.Much has been said online about the invasions by other players. Personally I loved the mechanic. It is balanced in a way so that the player doing the campaign has a rather big advantage. Which makes it so that it is never really frustrating. Even a mediocre player like myself can overcome the invader from time to time. Finishing the final level while being invaded was exhilarating. It just ups the stakes.The art style and story are great, like you expect from an Arkane game. The only thing I'm not sure about is how it spoon feeds the solution to breaking the loop eventually. By that time I had a whole bunch of notes and I would have liked to break the loop using my own build up knowledge completely - like in Outer Wilds. I can see why they didn't do that to keep things accessible but it should have been an option if you ask me. A small misstep for a fantastic game.

_childDocuments_.review: Gave it an honest try, found it to be "ok at best" but, with the gimmicky rogue-like mechanics and losing items or finally getting a decent "legendary" weapon or two only to have it lost on a random event that ends your "loop" early, I have decided to stop wasting my time and play other games. Got it on sale so I don't feel like I got burned, but there are plenty of other games in my library that do everything this game tries to do, but better.I played (and enjoyed) the Dishonored series, so I may have been going in with different expectations than what I thought I was getting. It's like playing a FPS Hitman, except there are **only 4 levels** with slight differences depending on what time of the day it is. You are tasked with exploring each of the 4 areas where something slightly different happens (depending on if its morning, noon, or night), gather clues, and use them to hunt down the targets all in one "loop" (day). Time periods don't change while in the level, so you have to leave the map, load the new time period, then come back in again. Maybe this time the Library is closed now, but a new section of the map has opened up.. you get it. Catch is each time you do, you get closer to ending the "loop" for that day and then everything resets all over again. Hope you like repetition. I feel like they really missed out on having your actions in the morning having a meaningful impact on the later time periods you have to go between. As far as the rogue-like mechanics go, you absorb residual currency off random things to keep the items you found within the map-- guns, gun upgrades, and powers/power upgrades. In my time playing, It's RNG on what upgrades drop, and their quality, so be prepared to do the same shizz over and over hoping an upgrade drops. Whatever you dont "spend" you lose at the end of each loop. Rinse/repeat. The AI is not good, the difference between going loud and silent is not meaningful enough like it was in the Dishonored series, the "hacking" is just hold down mouse button til the bar fills up. The art style is confusing, and often comes off as uninspired-- a far cry from Dishonored's iconic world-building. The voice acting is fine, though the story dialog is a bit Marvel-esque. The multiplayer consists of you "invading" another player's game and trying to kill them, and they you. Can everyone please stop trying to be dark souls? 1v1 in a mediocre shooter is a shallow direction to take, and another missed opportunity for a creative multiplayer experience. Deathloop had a lot of potential, shame it didn't live up to it... perhaps it can reach it on next loop.TL;DR: Deathloop is another game that would have been cooler as a movie or mini-series.

_childDocuments_.review: I whole-heartedly recommend this game. The gameplay is wonderfully reminiscent of Dishonored and Prey 2017 with cool powers (some pretty much copied from Dishonored), a variety of weapons to build your own unique playstyle with (and are satisfying to use and listen to), a world densely packed with places to explore and lore to discover, a highly polished and stylized 60s aesthetic that ranges from bold colors and psychedelic visuals to Cold War military bunkers reminiscent of spy/war movies), kickass music, and unique characters with stellar voice performances.  What I especially liked about Deathloop was its particular blend of immersive sim and rogue-like gameplay. I like the former more than the latter because I like taking my time to explore and steathily approach targets. I really disliked Prey: Mooncrash (a game widely regarded as the predecessor/prototype of Deathloop) because of its timed mechanic putting pressure on me to only get what I need and get out of the level. Deathloop on the other hand encourages me to explore its world, and even do little puzzles or minigames that don't really advance the main story (but do give you nice weapons or trinkets). It's also very forgiving about ending your time loop (maybe even the point of making the game TOO easy), as early on you get a powerup that allows you to revive after dying two times. The time loop is also divided into 4 segments representing each time of day (morning, noon, afternoon, night), and it autosaves after you complete each segment, so there's no pressure to complete a whole time loop in one play session.I'm also very partial to the art. The art is one of the best parts of any of Arkane's games, and Deathloop is no exception. In addition to the strong and varied 60s aesthetic, the island of Blackreef (where the game takes place) changes over the course of the day in many ways. which makes the world feel in some ways even more alive than that of Dishonored and Prey. Businesses and certain people's residences open at different times of the day. In one area, a stage is built over the course of the day to host a rock concert, and decorations are set up for a big party that takes place at night. Other places get vandalized, graffiti-ed, or straight-up blown up. Snow falls during the afternoon and evening, giving the world a whole new look half the day. The characters are quite fun too. Colt, the protagonist, starts out with "I don't know what I'm doing but I'm trying my best" energy, and has many snappy and quippy interactions with his rival, Julianna. The conversation they have at the start of every segment of the day is different, and there are so many that I don't think I've heard them all after finishing the game. However Colt and Julianna show more emotional depth as you uncover their pasts, and their relationship becomes more complex than just two assassins trying to outplay each other. The other antagonists have very standout personalities--in particular, I love (to hate) Aleksis, who is basically a sweaty tryhard rich boy turned business tycoon who is extremely narcissistic, arrogant, and thirsty af. None of the other characters take him seriously, which makes all of their interactions with him extremely funny. Honorable mention to Charlie, who is a turbo-nerd game designer who built a whole set to LARP his Among Us-like game in. And who could forget 2-BIT, a very cute AI whose grammatical errors in his speech are very endearing. "Have very fulfillment day!"The music is awesome. Not much more to say about that. BUT I will also say the sound design of the game is top-notch. The sounds your guns make are punchy and satisfying, there are thematically appropriate stings for getting spotted and stealthily killing targets, and picking up trinkets has never sounded more satisfying.I like many things about this game, but I DO have things to critique about it. I think Deathloop's marriage of game genres hurts it in some ways. The immersive exploration feels shallower than in Dishonored or Prey--there are less objects you can interact with, and you won't find as many notes and audio logs, so there's less environmental storytelling and worldbuilding going on. Random conversations between lowly NPCs occur far less, so they feel a little less like people and more just bodies to shoot at. I also dislike how limited you are with powers--you can only take 2 at a time with you per mission. And since everyone and their dog isn't gonna play the game without Blink, a handy traversal skill originating from Dishonored, you really only have 1 slot to choose a power for. Same for trinkets (buffs)--you can only take 4 with you, but since no one in their right mind would unslot the one that lets you double jump, you effectively only have 3 trinket slots to make a build with. Finally, the story ends quite abruptly, and if you didn't find all of the important pieces of lore about Colt and Julianna before advancing to the ending, their interaction might not have any emotional weight for you, and the supposed implication of whatever choice you make at the end is lost on you. Overall, Deathloop is a breadth over depth type of game, and not the type of game I want to see Arkane making more of in the future, but its moment to moment gameplay is fluid, addicting, and fun. I will definitely try to 100% achievements, as well as try out meme builds and strats just to see what happens. I firmly believe Deathloop is worth every penny of its $60 price tag.

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent game, takes a lot of what I liked about Prey and meshes it with Dishonored. I loveddd Prey, and Mooncrash, but never liked first Dishonored. The gameplay does allow the player to easily choose between tackling missions stealthy or guns blazing, or just blink around with your slab and dice people up with your machete. It's quite enjoyable. The environmental design and voice acting are extremely well done like previous titles. Some of Colt's commentary is great. The soundtrack is also excellent and deserves a highlight, plus the lone guitarist on the cliff, the dance party in Updaam's afternoon sun, and the "third rate elevator music" or whatever.I have not had performance problems but you do have to fiddle with settings a bit and see what works for your system. Mostly Ultra with some Very high, even have raytracing on although I guess on Performance mode... I am at 3440x1440, so less than 4K but more than 1440p. I would recommend setting AMD FSR to Quality, no upscaling (made anything not in your face blurry for me even with DOF off). I had a total of four CTDs, all while firing a weapon (while muzzle flash is displaying/recoil being applied), and two of those were towards the very end of a zone so that did hurt my soul a touch. I also wanted to mention the 44 karat fourpounder and eat the rich tribunal are actual weapons that are character locked. Colt gets the Tribunal, Julianna gets the Fourpounder, no swaps.UPDATE: After completing the game, it is pretty good but not mind blowing imo. Personally I still rank the story, lore and exploration of Prey above Deathloop, but I found the Deathloop to be faster paced and more fun - but a bit less high-stakes. I had a hard time connecting with the characters in here versus other Arkane games, although I did love the dialogue and banter of Colt. The ending was not super satisfying to me. I feel there are a few unanswered questions that come up during the story that don't fully resolve and most of the story is background info and like a reveal or two that are kinda obvious. Hopefully they have a prequel DLC in the pipeline...

_childDocuments_.review: I will update this once I have more time in the game. I want to start this with I have had no issues with stuttering. I know a lot of people are which really sucks but I personally havent had any issues with this game and never had issues back with dishonored 2. I have literally no clue why Arkane likes me but ya. It is not perfect but if you liked dishonored 2 then I think youll enjoy this game. I love Colt as a character. There is a mix of cheesy humor, all kinds of snarky characters, and violence. It blends together in a way I love. If you like the idea of dishonored 2 set in the 60s with super weird but fun humor and a ton of guns then totally give death loop a shot.I cant really comment much on the multiplayer yet because I really havent played it. The few instances I have have felt really off balance. I am kinda okay with that in a certain way because when I am playing it I dont have the mindset of completely destroying Colt rather I think of it more as me just trying to slow the other player down. If I kill them then awesome. If I dont then I still got xp and got to screw with them. Which I like. Now I dont want to sound like some 2 bit "oooooh look at me I am so coooool" person but it really doesnt feel as hard as people make it sound. Move the turrets where they help you. Use frags. Stab everyone who cant see you. Once you get further and can gather some guns then start going in and really tearing people apart. _childDocuments_.review: Deathloop is boring. As someone who enjoyed Outer Wilds so much, this comes as a surprise, since both games have the same gimmick.In Deathloop, there are four areas to explore, and four times of day you can choose to explore each of them in a single day before the loop resets. Depending on what time you visit an area, the environment, enemy activity, and events will change. But.. it doesn't really matter. Enemy variety is nonexistant. There is basically one enemy type and that's it. Everyone is a regular dude who dies in a single headshot. And don't even mention the machines. You have a hacking tool that allows hacking from a distance from the very start of the game. Machines are not even a hinderance since it's so easy to hack anything. In most stealth games, there is satisfaction in figuring out the best way to take out enemies without being noticed. But in Deathloop, once you get a bit of gear, stealth becomes seriously breandead and going through the same four areas quickly becomes repetitive.Your objectives are mostly about finding codes to open doors and safes. There are some moments where you find out something interesting about the Visionaries, but they are few and far between.So, are the four areas interesting to explore? No. The environments are not interesting. The look and style of everything is just a bland mix of concrete buildings and rocky/snowy terrain. The game also doesn't really look good graphically.The one thing that kept the game from being an absolute complete bore is the invasion system similar to Dark Souls where another player can suddenly join your game and try to ruin your day. This was probably the only actual fun I've had in the game so far.I've been trying to force myself through the game and I'm close to finishing it, but I've really lost all interest.

_childDocuments_.review: Arkane should have been given more time.There are so many annoyances, both big and small, that it drowns any positives. The game is not optimised. There's performance losses after a couple hours of playing and I have to restart the game to fix it.I think forced dialogue to explain gameplay is bad enough but the many back-to-back hand holding pop-ups at the start of the game was atrocious. A main cast of only trigger happy mad scientists & eccentric artists with no straight-man is aggravating and tiresome, . Now it's even more aggravating and tiresome.4 maps. There's only 4 maps. Time of day differences didn't justify only having 4 maps. Because it wasn't fun having to repeat 4 maps over and over again. Dishonored 2 had 9 missions, and I still remember that  and  were really unique and fun.There is hardly any number documents or voice recordings to pick up. Very little to learn about the island or the characters, or anything. No point asking questions, when there's zero answers.After the early sections are finished, Colt's small base turns into a menu screen. Compared to both Dishonored games, which had a physically interactive base, I can't interact with the gun bench, or the investigation wall, or even the exit door.  What is the point of making cool looking guns with cool looking reload animations, when the 'fast reload perk' causes the gun to be lowered off screen and then reloaded. Why not speed up the animation. Even something small like this has left a bad impression. I tried getting a toxic gas achievement. After failing numerous times, I search the internet and find out it's bugged. Game had already been out for a year. This was the straw that broke the camel's back. I stopped playing.Play or replay a Dishonored game instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a great game but not 10/10 like the gaming review sites are claiming. A more fair score would be around a 6/10 or a 7/10 for being average, but not extraordinary and I can only really see it winning Game of the Year since nothing has released this year as of posting this review.Deathloop is a rewarding and ambitious experience that smartly combines Arkane’s immersive sim bedrock with a fluid nonlinear structure. Its smooth gameplay and naturalistic narrative stylings are interrupted by lackluster PC performance, though it fulfills a puzzle-box Groundhog Day fantasy few other games have been ambitious enough to touch. Outside of some annoying crashes and mishaps, Deathloop remains a stellar game with a brilliant premise, refreshing mechanics, and delightful characters. You'll repeat the same day and retread the same paths over and over. But, replayability is enhanced given how you'll discover new secrets and abilities to help you progress.Pros-------- Fantastic gameplay- Excellent level design- Slick, stylish presentation- Entertaining story and characters- A harmonious blend of investigation, action and storytelling- A stunning artistic direction that works wonders for the eyes and ears- Tasty dialogues interpreted by actors well in their characters- A fascinating scenario that is a pleasure in disentanglingCons-------- Graphics don't justify the required specs- Minor performance issues- A formula that is redundant and tedious over time- The system of marking enemies sometimes annoying

_childDocuments_.review: I fear Deathloop may go down as Arkane's last true swansong, considering whats happened over the last few years post release - and this has changed my view on the game entirely. I played it on launch and didn't like it too much. The dopamine hits were great, but it really wasn't the same as the studios other work. Prey's Mooncrash has a very similar gameplay 'loop' but is done better.But the writing really elevates this title. Colt is one of the most likeable and charming protagonists I have seen in a very long time. His banter elevates this game, HUGE props to the voice actor and voice direction, without such stellar performances I can see him being a bit too cheesy, but instead we get easily the best character from a studio who created Daud, one of the best villains in video game history. The game-play itself is interesting, and better than most AAA games but coming from dishonoured or prey its effectively a much more watered down and accessible version, which as much as it pains me to say, was necessary for this game to exist. its no secret arkane games do not sell well, and trying to make it more appealing is something I support if it means keeping the studio afloat. Unfortunately I do not think the transition was done particularly great, using lots of powers is a lot of fun, but it breaks the game really easily, is a bit too forgiving (and there's no hard difficulty either!), and the powers are not as fun as they were in D2 or prey. Also I have a big issue with playtime. I would say for someone who pays attention you could complete this game in 15 hours. I do not know how people claim to have only just beaten the story in 60 or even 30 seems a huge stretch. I can see 25 if you want to get everything MAYBE. As much as I love Arkane, 50 pounds for a 15 hour experience, which, compared to both D2 and prey, has MUCH less replay-ability than those titles, doesn't fit right with me. Hence why I brought it on a sale for 10 pounds and I must admit, was a complete steal. Id pay about 30/35 quid for this thing even 40 reluctantly, but 50 is a joke. Despite my roasting it for the last few paragraphs, it is worth remembering, this is still an Arkane game, this studio (until Redfall) has made no bad games, this is still a stylish, creative, written super well and a very fun video game! It just pales a little in comparison to their other titles, and it makes me feel oh so sad that I believe this is the last good game that will come out from Arkane due to studio buyouts. Im hoping im wrong. I'd love to see a Deathloop sequel / D3 spin off (implied same universe baby!) or even a Prey 2, but I fear I am just coping. I will miss games like this and deathloop will always, always have this very personal bittersweet feeling I cannot shake whilst playing. However to all you sane people out there, its a solid recommendation, especially as an entry into Arkanes other titles.

_childDocuments_.review: Everything I had hoped it would be and more. Deathloop is a wonderfully constructed mash of Arkane's best game design with a bit of this and a bit of that. The gunplay and movement feel like Prey + Dishonored = Arkane movement 2.0 with a world that's structured to reward exploration and discover in such a huge way that within the first hour I found myself off the beaten path digging deep into an environmental puzzle.Beyond that Arkane chose to design the game around auto saves, no manual saves allowed to really cement the player's actions and deliver unalterable consequences at least during that course of that loop. Without spoiling anything there are also MANY instances where you can, in error increase the difficulty of your run or even nerf the potential of an in world resource because of said errors and not being able to simply reload a save sets those actions in stone while giving you the knowledge to correct/perfect them in a future run.In the end Deathloop come across as a long form detective/mystery game with a ton of pew pew and boom boom. Every run, every loop gives you a chance to piece together a bit more of the puzzle and make new discovers that will undoubtedly alter the way you move forward. To top it all off the VA, atmosphere, music and audio/visuals are so damn good. Colt and Julianna are wonderfully written and each time I restart the loop I look forward to hearing them banter and ♥♥♥♥♥ at each other about something new that moves the narrative forward just a bit while I unravel the rest for myself in real time.I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ love this game and I haven't even talked about the hunter mode that lets you invade other players runs as Julianna. Arkane you've done it again!

_childDocuments_.review: It is a first-person shooter game with an interesting twist. Instead of just shooting your way to victory, you have to use strategy and timing to your advantage in order to succeed. The levels are challenging and require you to think carefully about your next move, but the satisfaction of completing them is immense. The game also has great visuals and soundtracks, and its dynamic environment ensures that no two playthroughs are the same. Then beat final run with default smg no powers no trinketsdishonored 2 > prey >>>>> deathloopTo be fair, if there's anything Arkane always does well, it's creating an immersive world. I read all the pages, listen to conversations, watch world events unfold, or explore for more because Arkane always does a fantastic job with their writing. It's great to hear dialogue from really almost anyone. Watching one of Aleksis' followers jump off the wolf cliff or even just slowly watching a follower who has had too much to drink fall from a roof, it's all in the details with Arkane. However, unlike the dishonored franchise or prey, they don't allow for almost any player creativity with tackling the main storyline. _childDocuments_.review: A fun roguelite-esque addition to the immersive sim genre. You'll find a bit of Dishonored and Prey: Mooncrash here. It's like an immersive sim for people who don't normally play immersive sims.If you've played Dishonored to good effect, you'll already know how you should be moving in Deathloop: quickly, quietly, sliding everywhere, and stabbing everyone in the back. Unlike Dishonored, if your stealthy approach doesn't work, you can't and won't need to save-scum, and have the luxury of going loud.You'll need to collect information and infused items across multiple loops, and remember where things are, or write them down/take screenshots. Remember that you keep information across loops, and don't get too attached to the loop. You can always reacquire a thing on the next loop, since it is the same day.

_childDocuments_.review: Deathloop is a solid 8/10. The gameplay mechanics are fun, voice acting is fantastic, the story unfolds nicely as you play and explore (though I wanted more) and the Dualsense haptic feedback is flawlessly implemented. All of that mixed in with the fun 'loop' mechanic and detailed maps with plenty to discover leaves you pleasantly satisfied.That said, there are some flaws. Invading players can be far too strong and spawn-camp you, providing a frustrating experience. There needs to be better balancing. As for the guns, each are fun to use but the options are very limited. It would have been good to see more variety in visionary responses throughout the day when tackling the maps loud vs quiet (such as other visionaries having no knowledge of your presence vs rushing around panicked or hauling up in a shelter).Overall, brilliant fun, and here's hoping they release an expansion or something similar!

Unfortunately, it does have some issues with stuttering even on high-end PCs, however there are a few settings that can be enabled that should make the game run as smooth as butter... at least, it did for me & a couple friends.First, open your NVIDIA Control Panel (assuming you have a NVIDIA GPU) & ensure that V-Sync is enabled there.Next, launch the game & ensure these settings are accurate:• NVIDIA Reflex: On• Low Latency: On• V-Sync: Off• Upscaling: AMD FidelityFX Super Resolution 1.0• AMD FSR Mode: Ultra Quality• FPS Limiter: 120Hope these settings help out those still experiencing the stuttering so they can fully enjoy this game in all its glory!
