_childDocuments_.review: This isn't just more of Rogue Legacy, it made buying the original pointless. It has everything that made RL great and much more. It looks, sounds and plays amazingly well. I have nothing but praise, but allow me to share some thoughts I had while playing this game.Since RL was praised for its impressive replayability, it made sense to focus on that for RL2. And boy does it show. I'm not one for putting almost 40 hours into a game and yet here we are. This is a good thing, of course, but in some areas it comes across as padding, and requiring excessive grinding to progress. And the new game plus system is overly complicated, in my opinion. Again, all in the name of adding more replayability, but it has some costs.I started getting tired next to the final boss. After a few dozen tries I realized I needed to grind for a few more runs to upgrade myself and have a better shot at defeating it. But, again, I was getting tired! so I cheated myself just a liiiiittle bit of money, just to save up some few round trips. Apparently I gave myself a few too many zeros though, and I had enough to buy the whole castle three times. Which made the game trivial, unfortunately lol. But I have no regrets! I still had fun. About the plot, what's with videogames and excessively complicated lore? I see this often and it always boggles my mind. There are many characters, a rich backstory for all of them, complex interactions with mystical explanations, betrayals, wars. It's hard to engage with anything that complex when you absorb it tangentially. Like, I'm not taking a deep dive into their stories, like you do in a book, I'm running around killing monsters in a castle and occasionally staring at a wall of text filled with lore. At the same time it pretends to not see what I hesitate to call plot holes, just in case it's also explained in a tome somewhere. You play as the last successor in a long family tree, which suggests at least a few decades passed between each run, and yet the rest of the game just treats the player as a singular individual in a small time frame. Other characters stay the same and no significant events happen. Again, maybe this is explained with some magical hand waving babble.

_childDocuments_.review: I threw my money at this game as soon as I saw there was an Early Access build available -- I adored the first game (I have a PC copy, plus digital copies on at least 3 consoles....I might have a problem). And the first few times I tried it, it definitely felt like it was Early Access. So I said to myself, "I've got way too many other things to play; I'll check back in on it later." And when content updates would drop, I'd come in, take a look around, and notice the steady improvements.When the Drifting Worlds Update came down, I poked around again, and I have to say that the game feels very polished now. It performs nicely on my new-ish machine on max settings, there's plenty of content, the controls are smooth, and the humor and well-designed action platforming of the first game are on full display. I am very impressed with the creativity and design of the different classes -- they all feel very different, yet very capable. I've had a blast playing this the last week or so. It has got its hooks in me much like the first one did. It is everything a sequel should be: bigger, more ambitious, clearly built on feedback from the first game, but still keeping its core intact (unlike some Risk of Rains I might know). Highly recommended for fans of the genre, whether that genre is rogue-whatevers, platforming, or games with playable chefs outside the kitchen.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is stupidly good. I liked the first one but fell off of it after a few hours, This one has held me for 10's of hours and I expect to play at least another 40ish hours or so.The good: -Excellent replayability and controls. You usually feel great when playing as most types of characters.-Interesting unlockables. Most games have your standard characters classes but this game dares to branch out into more niche categories. I wish they would have leaned further into this but maybe we'll get a good DLC or something. (one can hope)-Lore for the nerds. I kinda skimmed past it but it seems to be interesting so I figured I'd mention it-Rewards feel satisfying to get. Some games let you unlock everything very quickly but this game makes you grind for it. Usually I can afford at least one unlock per life if I didn't get flattened immediately so when you complete your castle, it feels really good.-Customization of play style, there's some flexibility to make your character feel more focused on what you want to focus on.-Great character design and art-Wonderful boss battles which feel great. My first play through and I thought these bosses were pretty much impossible. On later playthroughs you can unlock harder versions of the boss fights and the ones I've seen so far are way harder. I'm excited to see what else they change.-Responsive Devs. The devs feel very active on the game and are tuning the numbers around based off of played feedback. This game does what the first game did but better.Critiques: This game is seriously great but I'd like to highlight some things I don't like as much-Character balancing: right now, the meta strongly favors the barbarian class. Some classes feel seriously useless like the assassin, bard, or duelist. I wish these characters really stood out and made it worthwhile to level them up-More ways to upgrade: the main way to upgrade your character is using the castle at first and then upgrading their gear. The only way to upgrade gear is to get ore but the rate of getting ore is pretty slow even with the upgrades and that makes me want to experiment less. Also, each gear has their own stats which can get a little overwhelming. I wish we could just focus more on the Unity bonuses and skip all the boring numbers. -improvement on the glossary. Sometimes, the game throws out names for stuff and the only way I was able to figure it out was to google it. not a big deal but I'd like if the glossary was all encompassing-more heirlooms. Heirlooms are basically the items that change how your character plays. Some are minor, some are major, and most are mid. As someone who loves Binding of Isaac, I'd appreciate a few more major heirlooms that do more than just give you a 10% bonus to this, or a 20% buff to that. I think they could do with a bit more creativity.-MORE classes! This is really the bread and butter of the game but the issue is that there's only a few (IMO) viable classes that are worth touching. They need to buff the crappy ones and hopefully create more off the wall type classes like "Spearmen" or "Redditor".Overall, wonderful game and an excellent time sink. can't recommend this game enough to people who enjoy roguelike

_childDocuments_.review: Updated Review after full release:The short version? This game is now much better than it was at it's first public iteration, but there are some remaining very significant issues. The first boss of the game is not nearly as broken as he was originally in early access (perhaps in part due to having a full upgrade tree available in the full release, where upgrades aren't wasted on insignificant things like rune weight as they were in early access.) Most other bosses also feel better balanced now, but on average are much more difficult than Rogue Legacy 1. This is not necessarily a bad thing, other than that without detailed strategy or grinding, a couple of them the game become a slog of grinding small upgrades to health and damage in order to combat received damage, which at times still feels cheap and inevitable.As another big plus there is a TON of content in this game in terms of grindability. It would take someone an insane amount of time to fully upgrade their castle for maximum stats. The problem, much like Rogue Legacy 1, begins to arise when you realize that the gameplay is not updating significantly in response to the colossal amount of time which is asked of you, so after the 200th time clearing the same floor of the same enemies (which might have a couple new moves, but look and act nearly identical to their previous iterations), things begin to get pretty tedious after a while without regular breaks.The primary sin I still hold even after moving from early access to full release, is that the game's upgrade system still simply feels rigged and unfair. Fairy chests are STILL set up in a way that 90% are blatantly impossible if you do not have a specific class to clear them, so they are effectively a complete waste of time unless you get lucky. It is not completely egregious, but the very irksome feeling of "Why is this room even here if it is flat out impossible for me to complete on this run?" which occurs almost every single time you play, gets extremely old when looking for new ways to progress. On top of this, the ones that are not class-locked are even more frustrating at times, as the controls are simply not tight enough to accommodate what is asked of the player in many cases. For example, setting up obstacle courses which require a player to warp from gate to subsequent gate in order to not take damage and gain an upgrade are ruined when the game does not register button prompts correctly. In games where resetting and trying again might not be a big deal, this could be excused as sloppy but acceptable. However, in a setting where you get one try and then can't get a do-over until a random point in a future run this is absolutely infuriating, and frankly a failure of design. Roguelikes in essence are slaves to the mantra "you can always succeed on your first try if you are good enough, but we will let you grind to accommodate your weaknesses if you need it." When the game itself is not tight enough in controls to let a player succeed they feel cheated by a lack of success which was never possible to begin with, but at least there is the option to simply grind your way out of issues in many cases.Overall, I don't want to sound TOO harsh, as the developers have made a game which easily surpasses their previous iteration in nearly every way. Visually, mechanically, and in pure scope, Rogue Legacy 2 delivers a much deeper and polished experienced than its predecessor. Unfortunately, the sequel does also keep most of the previous generation's mechanical issues, albeit thankfully in a lesser capacity on average. If you enjoy grindable roguelikes this is a HARD recommend which you will enjoy immensely, as the game is deep with good content, and the devs are clearly working to improve based on feedback from their player base! If you don't like doing the same fights for hours on end, however, I'd recommend looking elsewhere, as you might get very bored before clearing the game for the first time, let alone on new game plus.TL;DR: Overall: 7.5/10, Very solid game, some issues that may yet be addressed, but the developers deserve a lot of kudos for polishing things up since early access.

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Legacy 2 takes every single thing that made the original a blast to play and only ends up making them better. Every class now has their own weapon and combat style, negative traits give gold bonuses (no more playing as miner every time you have the option, for the gold bonuses!) and they've added lots of fun new features. If you get the trait that lets you see trails behind every object, you get a trail when you join showing your drop into the map.Rating Pending, Would Highly Recommend

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: I recommend Rogue Legacy 2, but only with the caveat that playing with House Rules set to the recommended "easier" settings is recommended after the 4th area. I turned it on during the 6th area because I was tired of running through the castle, one shotting most things even with them off, for tiny upgrades against a bloated boss health bar. "Easier" is in quotations because these settings aren't actually making the game easier, they're just saving you time from running through the castle over, and over, and over again. Maybe this is in bad taste but if you want a roguelite more dependent on player skill, then check out Revita which has also released in 1.0 over the last 2 weeks.Rogue Legacy 2 has a philosophy of bigger means better, and that's where the major issues with the game also lie. The predecessor was a great game that never overstays its welcome, it's challenging while allowing the player to get through at a pretty fast pace with minimal grind just by being skilled enough. Rogue Legacy 2 doesn't feel that way. It insists on overstaying its welcome with overly expensive stat upgrades, a much larger castle, repetitive room layouts, and a couple bosses that throw so much at you it's better to face tank than actually learn them. It feels as though you HAVE to grind in this game, much more than the previous. Grinding for a boss in this game can almost feel like an idle game, as you'll be one shotting enemies far sooner than you will be able to reasonably chunk through a boss. Meaning you run through the castle with your brain half off many, many, MANY times all in service of 'number go up.' The recent balance patch after launch does somewhat help, but it still doesn't feel like enough. This was a 40 hour playthrough that could have easily been 20, and nothing would have changed. On top of this there's too few unique room layouts and enemies, meaning you're chopping, punching, shooting, or casting your way through the same things again and again. The majority of enemies are also recycled from Rogue Legacy 1 with a new move or two, which doesn't personally bother me, but it may bother you. If you're okay with the grind or can accept that using House Rules makes the game much less tedious, then there's no reason not to recommend this. While it doesn't really feel as if it evolved enough over the last 9 years with its genre contemporaries, it does feel like a heightened, evolved Rogue Legacy. It feels better to play (though spin kicking should reset your double jump), the art style is much nicer, the music is pretty good, and the classes are all pretty fun and much more varied than the previous game. I will say that once I was able to lock one Valkyrie into my rotation of new heirs that I rarely strayed from them. Valkyries feel like far and above the best class to me. They can hit a ton of enemies through walls and are the only class I know of that can properly pogo off enemies with their weapon and not the spin kick. There's tons of modifiers and tweaks you can make, and some small (not enough) synergies you can find through Relics. There's a lot more lore (which isn't overbearing) and things to check out in this game, including a seemingly large post game if you still haven't had enough running through the castle. Though other reviews have made it seem as if the NG+ changes aren't all that special.All in all I feel very split about Rogue Legacy 2. It's a game I was really enjoying for the first 15-20 hours, with a sharp decline during the 4 area onwards until I finally caved and turned House Rules on to save myself the tedium of stat grinding. I actually like grinding in other games, just something about this game specifically rubbed me the wrong way. If the game didn't allow you to self balance it in some sort of way there's a good chance I'd have dropped it before fighting the final boss, because Cellar Door seems content to balance it with no care for your time.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Legacy 2 is in a weird position in that its predecessor pretty much brought an entire gaming concept into the mainstream, where it's remained a dominant style of game in the indie space ever since (yes there was binding of Isaac, but between the greater persistent progress and overt connection to Roguelikes, there's no denying that the original Rogue Legacy had an enormous impact on game development culture). That space has since become a crowded field.Does RL2 have the same impact? Does it innovate on the concept? No, I don't think so. It's very similar to the original, adding new progression elements, classes, abilities, etc., more stuff to do, and a more robust story. I think it does provide a great experience on its own, however, and is worth picking up on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: This is an EARLY ACCESS REVIEW.Like the original, but better. Graphics have been upgraded from pixel art to 3d content on a 2d plane, which IMO looks amazing. I am very much anticipating the release of more content----this game is low on locations and enemies due to it being a first early access look, BUT because it's a Roguelite you can still go back and play it over and over and over and have a different experience each time. When the game comes out of EA I will be very happy with the result unless something drastically goes wrong.

Additionally, I feel like the room layouts were more creative in the original.If you really enjoyed the original, aren't looking for an entirely new experience, and are willing to wait for new content to be added to early access I would highly recommend it so far.

_childDocuments_.review: Very good, time has passed since I had a rogue like that made me want to play it continuously for weeks, you have to be very picky to not give this game at the very least a 8/10, no bugs from my part, good amount AND quality of content, the story is there but who wants to read in a roguelike? not me lmao, art style is cute and fits very well even when at first I was reluctant and missed the pixel art from the first I got used to it and now I like it even more than the one from the previous game, very good 8/10 would pick basic swordman again.My only complain and why it is not a 10/10 is because 2 classes, the bard and the astronomer, the suck, they are not fun to play, they are slow, not great damage and they just feel more like a chore to play, which is why I never picked them from the heir selection, every other class feels way better, even the ranged that I also hate but I don't think they are a chore or bad, is just that melee is superior in almost every way, specially when you play with a controller which is what they tell you to play with.

_childDocuments_.review: Very good sequel to the first Rogue Legacy.The gameplay & the art style feel just like they were on the first game, but the models are actually 3D models that are shown in a way that they look like 2D which I found super cool when I finally noticed it.Also unlike in the first game where mana was a precious resource that you didn't want to waste, is easy to get in the sequal. Every melee hit you deal restores a portion of your mana. Yep, everyones a spellsword now.Some classes can even regenerate mana from hitting enemies with spells.In addition the game has a bunch of different weapons for you to use, that you can swap out if you manage to find a weapon cart on your travels. Personally I'd recommend something with range like a bow or a revolver to make gold collecting safer.The game also has a new feature, "house rules" that allow you to tailor the games difficulty to your tastes.Enemies hitting a bit too hard or not hard enough?Some annoying parkour bit driving you crazy?New game+ proving to be too challenging or not challenging enough?You can fix ALL of this with the house rules. I personally only use the lesser burdens for new game+ & the flight on press of a button to just skip a certain mandatory jump puzzle that I have managed to climb legit only once. The one with the saw blades.You lose nothing if you do decide to use this feature. Heck, there's even an achievement for turning it on for the first time.

_childDocuments_.review: I waited for this to come out of early access for a long time. I don't think anything has ever been on my wishlist for so long. I REALLY wanted to like it.But I just couldn't. There's no carrot on the end of the stick. You slowly (and I mean sloooowwwly) build up your roguelite capabilities over time, but it's just not well designed. You end up being really overpowered for the earlier areas of the game, and yet still have to traipse through them on every run looking for the upgrades you need to actually progress. E.g. in Hades, you start over every time weak, so there's a degree of interesting combat for the early levels as you build yourself up. This just doesn't have that. Every run just becomes this, "oh god, I guess I'll go back and do the earlier areas looking for the right upgrades."The combat is fluid. The different classes/traits seem varied, but they all just end up blending together. I know it seems stupid to give a thumbs down after 100 hours, but I really just kept thinking that it would get better and was disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: A fun game that looks to be great! I'm hopeful that a few balance tweaks as Rogue Legacy 2 leaves early access at the end of April will make this a great game. As it is it's fun with some balance issues that could use fixing. It's got a lot of charm, a wonderful idea, a variety of innovative fun characters, and so much potential.I loved my first few hours exploring a castle with knights, mages, boxers, and (my favorite), cooks, making gradual progress.Then I hit a plateau, doing the same scenery (and first boss) over and over and over and over and over, with updgrades for 1% extra critical hit damage getting gradually more expensive until they're unafforable unless you can beat the first boss. Whom you need to spend 10 minutes to an hour to get to.  I've tried 100 "Fairy Room" challenges and have failed them all. Done right, hard games can be punishing but rewarding (I love Spelunky 2, Enter the Gungeon, Blasphemous and have beaten them all. Check them out!). But this is just frustrating--I feel like I lost enjoyment retrospectively and that my time has been a waste. Feels like the developers are stretching out a great game to provide more hours of playtime but those hours are less fun.The graphics, gameplay, rogue-like level design, and story have much to offer. But when I think back on my time playing I don't look back on it with fun. I just remember feeling angry and that I wasted my time trying again.Really hoping some tweaks to the currency system or gameplay balance come in the next few weeks -- I'll update if they do.

_childDocuments_.review: I was gifted this game, but was highly skeptical whether I'd like it or not. I mainly play casual/survival games and the last time I'd played a game with a real boss in it was ~2015-16'. This was also my first rogue-lite, having seen clips of the game and my friend play Dead Cells, I didn't know whether the game would truly fit my play style. And it did.The world is vibrant, filled with various mobs and characters with silly dialogue that doesn't make you feel like you're playing a game from 2012. The music is so lovely that you won't want to turn it off.As for the game itself, each time you enter the dungeon a new map awaits you until. That is, until you unlock the architect which can ensure your map stays the same until you choose for a price (maxing out at 100% of your gold). Since there is a new map each time, fighting enemies doesn't feel like a chore.The bosses are challenging, but I never felt like I wasn't capable of killing a boss. After a bit of practice (and maybe watching someone else play), the mechanics will come easily.I have no complaints and would highly recommend this game to anyone wanting to spice things up.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall - GREAT game, one of the best roguelite's I've played in a long time. Good variety between classes, spells and weapons, a LOT of variety in Relics gives you a lot of potential playstyles, and bosses were great.My only small problems with the game are that the scaling gold cost makes the grind a lot longer than it probably should be, and because of the scaling gold costs and implementation of Souls to unlock further levels in primary stats, that it basically punishes you if you try to actually level all major stats. Forcing health drops and spin kicks to scale by Intelligence seemed like a very poorly implemented acknowledgement that damage magic is much, MUCH weaker than damage you get from normal attacks, and trying to get you to actually put points in Intelligence when otherwise few would touch it.That said, it's still a great game. Sucked me in like no game has done in years, and I'd put 50 hours in before I even really realized it.

_childDocuments_.review: I was having fun until it came to beating the bosses. They are plainly just not fun or interesting. The game acts like you have more methods to avoid damage than you do, and the projectile patterns and some boss behaviors are just flat out sadistic to a degree that isn't even remotely fun. I got through three of them, but on the wizard in the library, he has a second phase that is perhaps one of the worst boss designs I've ever seen in a game. I decided I had no motivation to keep going once I got to that, it just felt like the designers didn't respect me as a player whatsoever.On top of that, the grind just doesn't feel worth it. You spend 30+ minutes just to get a 1% increase on something. Only then to be greeted with 3 terrible options of characters to pick.The "resolve" and "weight" features ruin this game for me. Why even have them? Part of the fun of rogue-likes is picking up items and having a fun build, not picking up 1-2 because you'll have no health. Overall, if you're looking for a very challenging, unforgiving rogue-like. Look no further. But if you've played Hades, Binding of Issac, Risk of Rain, or any other rogue-likes, be ready for an unfun slog.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a little at odds here.  I will almost definitely continue to play the game, but it's really a 50/50 thing going on here.  The core issue is that it's a Metroidvania, but that doesn't really merge well with the rogue-like.  You need to gather resources and explore the map to progress, but dying resets your progress.  For fairness, the game has high points.  Movement is fluid, the classes are generally enjoyable to play, and there's definitely some fun to be had here.  But man, if it doesn't come with equal parts frustration and the ever-present knowledge that it really shouldn't be rogue-like.Let's assume my next goal is to fight a boss.  As long as I don't randomize the tower, thus sabotaging that I'll even find them before dying, I need a class I feel comfortable with that isn't also wrecked by relics or traits.  It's a great example of how randomization isn't helping, I know what I need to do.  I just need the RNG to get out of the way so I can bang my head against it.  The relic system is part of that.  It's normal in these types of games to find power-ups that will help you tackle challenges, but here they generally don't help much.  The big fly in the dip is they reduce your health.  So, you might do more damage but now you have have less life.  Awesome.  This is the best case scenario, as plenty are situational or even outright detrimental to your character.  You also can't see what those relics do until you've picked them up, which means it's often beneficial to outright ignore them.  Oh, but your character might also spawn with such a relic!  And you have no idea what their resolve is until you pick them, so you might end up with a character with a bad relic AND half life.Mangled character, reporting for duty, sir!  Enter the tower and either farm gold or just retire I guess, both options are definitely anathema to progression.  It's worth bringing up the "bad" traits as well.  These are usually meme-worthy gameplay novelties of which the worst will give you a boost in gold.  Still, the worst offenders just invalidate the character.  For example, one flaw triples your gold and reduces your hp to one.  There is probably some synergy somewhere, but you aren't going to go exploring or fighting the boss with them.  Again, you could use them to farm gold, but then again you may end up earning far less because there is no room for error and since you lose all your gold between runs you do have to earn a certain amount for it to even be worthwhile.  So here's a character apparently built to farm gold that is the worst option for it.  Why even do this?The randomization is just so poorly conceived, like it's meant to support a completely different game.  It's not even a balance issue.  It's a practical issue.  Here is a character immediately invalidated by their inability to make progress.  And so, recommending Rogue Legacy 2 would require me to assume that frustration is a necessary component of the game, but it isn't.  It's a deliberate choice, one that hampers the experience, and I would gladly throw it away for better pacing and a more reliable difficulty curve.  The really crippling bit is the developers seem to know this.  You can unlock a way to stop the tower from randomizing, you can lock classes and abilities, you can keep gold from Charon, and you unlock teleporters.  All these things reduce the rogue-like features: so if it's considered a reward or benefit to turn them off, maybe they aren't working as intended?EDIT: As a small edit here, people will sometimes wonder how someone can not recommend a game they've spent a lot of time playing.  The answer is simple: I already own it.  I'm not getting a refund and there are parts I genuinely like, but it doesn't change my review.  The second bit is a lot of polish was put into 1.0 which *helps*, some of the worst characteristics were toned down and other things buffed to make the experience better.  I still stand by my original point: this shouldn't be roguelike.  I don't know why 20XX got it right and Rogue Legacy doesn't do it for me, but while it felt like a neat little randomizer add-on there, it feels like it hurts the experience here and even after 80 hours I can't shake it.  I always stop when I get tired of the RNG and don't want to make another failed run at just trying to find a boss.  The moment-to-moment is pretty good, but the overarching game just doesn't click for me.

_childDocuments_.review: With Rogue Legacy 2 still being in Early Access, it is obviously not yet the complete experience. but so far. so good. As all sequels should, if feels like the logical next step from the original Rogue Legacy which, while wonderful fun, with a promising, intriguing twist on the Rogue-Lite genre, felt less like a complete home console/PC game & more like an Arcade Game with a Roguelike/lite twist (not that there's anything wrong with that).Even in early access, Rogue Legacy 2 feels more like that full home console experience that I was after. It achieve's this without losing the fun & easy to play/difficult to master gameplay, colourful, cartoony graphics & quirky humour that I loved from the first game. In fact, due to the increased amount of dialogue, the aforementioned humour is ramped up to the nines, without being overbearing.As I mentioned, the gameplay is similar to the original, but it has been tweaked & fine tuned enough to justify Rogue Legacy 2's existence. All the original character classes return (Knight, Mage, Barbiarian et al), however they're rounded out with a number of new classes, such as my new personal fave The Cook. The Castle building system has also been fine tuned, which not only gives the pre-dungeon village far more life & character, it also provides the player with a multitude of new upgrade options, allowing for an infinitely more customizable & in depth experience than it's forebear. Coupled with what seems to be an actual & so far quite intriguing story (the narrative is incomplete at the moment so, who knows? it may fall flat on it's face in the future), these gameplay tweaks improve the overall experience, allowing the player to be drawn far more deeply into Rogue Legacy 2's world than they would have been with the original game. I would also be remiss if I didn't reassure everyone that Charon is still in the game, continuing their role as the gatekeeper of the dungeon & retaining that endearing grin & laugh that makes you love him. Despite the fact that they're clearly running a racket. As a bonus he technically isn't just the simple Gatekeeper he was in the first game as Cellar Door Games have wisely decided to make him more true to his mythological ferryman counterpart & give him a boat! Justice! 10/10 GOTY material! However, in all seriousness, Rogue Legacy 2 is looking & feeling great so far. Building on the potential that was the original Rogue Legacy, with enough spit & polish applied to create a more rewarding & engrossing product overall, ensuring that Rogue Legacy's... Ahem, legacy is in good hands, just as Sir Pepperoni continued on the great & proud Legacy of such legends as Sir Caleb, Lady Autumn II, Sir Glauber III & Lady Sara III (But not Sir James II, who has disappointed his ancestors & shamed his descendants by dying in the first room by failing to clear a pit of spikes).As a post-script, I'm still divided on my feelings in regards to early access games. On one hand you're paying for an incomplete game, with no promise as to when the full game will be released, or as to what quality & form the final product will take. However, on the other hand, it allows developers to create a far more intimate relationship with players, giving them the opportunity to craft a potentially greater experience for gamers than they might have otherwise. The perfect example of this being Supergiant Games exceptional, Roguelike Dungeon Crawler, Hades. Which was not only my GOTY for 2020, but genuinely one of the greatest & most rewarding games I have ever played. Plus, just Like Rogue Legacy, Hades gives us another iteration of Charon who is, despite my previous praise of RL's verison, the best version of Charon in any form of fiction.Anyways, Rogue Legacy 2, while unlikely to reach the lofty heights of Hades, is providing another example to justify the existence of Early Access & I heartily recommend it. For fans of:RoguelikesRoguelitesMetroidvanias PlatformersCreating a Family Tree of Fantasy Trope Weirdos

_childDocuments_.review: I whole heartedly recommend this game. This game oozes quality from its art style, animations, sound track/effects, and variety of mechanics. The characters you interact with are fun and varied, and once you get used to it the combat is tight and satisfying. However, its a bit grindy, and I think one of the reasons why it tends to be a bit grindy is because of the stacking castle upgrade cost penalty which forces you into higher level zones, perhaps before you want to be in them. Let me explain.Basically every time you upgrade your keep, the cost of the next upgrade is increased by a fixed amount. However the player is encouraged to spread their upgrade points shallowly because putting the first point in a new trait unlocks adjacent traits you can also put points into. This kind of leads to you putting early points into a lot of things that maybe you don't want or need yet, and neglecting things you do. And when you realize "I need more vitality" or "I need more strength", its now harder to quickly stack points into there because your stacking penalty is higher.I think if they apply a flat 25% reduction to the stacking castle upgrade cost, the early grind would be more manageable. They just need to tweak the power curve a little more.If you don't mind a game with some grind, then this is a fantastic choice.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. . . What a bangerRogue Legacy 1 is a great game in its own right, but this game takes it to a whole new level. If you haven't played the original Rogue Legacy that's ok, you don't need to in order to play this one, even for the story (at least for now, maybe that will change with lore updates), and even for the 1% of information you would miss from not played RL1 you can just read that online in 5 minutes.The mechanics in this game? Smooth as butter for a roguelite/metroidvania/adventure platformer. I highly highly highly suggest using a controller. I suppose you could use a keyboard and mouse but from my experience a controller of any kind (I use a PS2 to USB adapter to play) will do you wonders. Turning feels awesome, canceling out of your dash or jump is satisfying, and the spin kicks are just perfection. Once you get good at the movement in this game its addicting to run across all the biomes and just kill enemies while gathering gold without pause.The art, music, and animation of this game are a huge step up from the original (imo). I guess the only way to describe the art is a 2D platformer with "3D aspects''. Some images appear to be in 3D while they are obviously on a 2D plane. There are some screenshots online where you can see this present (the floating spike ball enemy is a good example), so if you're not into that kind of thing, take note. The lore?. . . I have mixed feelings about. Usually the lore of games is a huge priority of mine, and this game certainly has interesting lore, but there are some issues. First off the order in which lore appears, and the convoluted overall timeline is more than confusing. I don't think I can say more because it will spoil the theme of the game, but the devs look like they are going to be adding more lore to the game, so hopefully that gives us some more world development for these awesome characters. The classes system is great, don't get me wrong, but there are some balance issues. This also goes for the skills/spells in the game but mainly its classes that seem unbalanced. If you look up "Rogue Legacy 2 tier list" you will see massive differences in the subjective rankings of classes within this game. Yet, the one class that I always see in the top tier, is Chef (understandable so). Every single class I have seen placed really high, or really low, depending on who is ranking it. Furthermore there are classes that are straight up awful, but the devs have addressed this pretty quickly, even if they still suck (cough cough  cough cough). Then there are classes who do not scale well at all, which is why I believe these rankings are just pointless, since someone who has only beat the first boss can write their rankings and pretend it applies to the overarching game as a whole. Barbarian in the early game is awesome: Tanky, big aoe attack, and an aoe skill, while hitting like a truck. But as you progress you become naturally more tanky, through castle upgrades, armor, and runes. So therefore these more agile classes who also do more damage, are becoming more tanky, making the main appeal of the Barbarian diminish quickly. What i'm getting at is if I see Barbarian (who has a fat landing lag and attack lag animation) get put in S+++ tier one or time, I'm going to assume you haven't completed the base game - or you just like the spin to win feature. This is even more apparent when I see classes like Boxer get put super super low in peoples tier list. Which is hilarious, because people who are NG+10 or so, unanimously agree that the Boxer (even if you don't like that play style) absolutely melts bosses.  To address the "grind" problems, listen, it's a roguelite I don't know what you were expecting. Furthermore there is a complaint among people who get stuck that the only advice they get told by the community is to "get good". Unfortunately, that is pretty accurate. I have seen people who claim they are lvl 200 or even 300 and cant get past the final boss (not NG version) which is just insane to me. If you learn the patterns of the main bosses and use an optimal class you are confident on, then you shouldn't need all those extra hours of grinding to get that boost. Lastly, Jonah is the best character.

_childDocuments_.review: A QUITE GOOD GAME! BUT....After 12 hours of playing I think I can leave an impression.First of all, I am a big supporter of RL1. What RL2 is cursed with: it will always be related to the first part from the players who still remember RL1 with an evil grin. So as me.Now here is what I actually miss from the first part in RL2:- The graphics. The new graphics are good so far, but I liked this retro pixel look in the first part that much.- The sound. Same as above. That Nintendo-like music was awesome. In comparison with that new mandoline-whatever-music, I prefer the old style.- The fact that every character class in RL1 had the same weapon (sword) was a good idea. Now in the 2nd part with every class having their own weapon, some classes are useless individually for each player. Less often is more.- Bash direction only in view direction? Why did they do that? The first part was more comfortable, able to bash in both directions depending on which Trigger on the gamepad I am pressing.Enough complaining...The Pro arguments in RL2 are obvious:- More char classes. Even chars who at the first sight don´t seem to have the right to exist may take a twist to a powerful char which puts you more forward than the basic chars. (How can a chef with a frying pan be more perservering than a bloody barbarian?)- A huge skill tree (about double the size of the skill tree in RL1)- The ability of some of the classes to throw projectiles back to where they came from.- The NPCs which may you help through the adventure like the pizza girl. An evidence for the creators not having left their humor. Thanks!- The system how challenges can be mastered is good. That was a clear disadvantage in RL1: The amount of money you had to bring in just to make the remix bosses easier to defeat. In RL2 every chest could contain a bonus for that challenges. Great idea!Conclusion: Even if RL2 not touches me as a retro nerd like RL1 did, it ties me with every minute of playing and still the feeling of getting better with every step through the world of Rogue Legacy makes the money I spent for that game worth every cent! SO DEAR DEVELOPERS: YOU HAVE MY PERMISSION FOR ROGUE LEGACY 3! ENJOY YOUR HOLIDAYS AND AFTER THAT GO BACK TO YOUR STUDIO AND KEEP WORKING! THANK YOU!

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Legacy 2 is solid sequel to Rogue Legacy.Pros:+ Solid Platforming+ Precise Controls (I played via controller)+ Fluid Combat+ Unique Bosses+ Great Sound Design+ Fun Character Traits+ TONS of Persistent Upgrades (I Still have a ton of upgrades to get and I'm at NG+15)Cons:- Difficulty- Weapon BalancingI don't know if I'm just playing that differently than the people who struggled, but the game was ONLY difficult at the start. And this is to be expected, as you're just learning how to play the game and you're just starting the upgrade process of your castle...the problem is that each NG+ got easier. While technically the enemies and bosses evolve and get harder, it's very short lived. Each NG+ was shorter than the previous NG and by the point of around NG+4 or 5 you will be beating every NG+ on your first try (barring you don't pick a character with the 1 hp or passive trait).You might say "well you just got better" and while that is true...I think players playing my profile, even some new players, could probably beat the game on the highest NG+ that I have unlocked on their first try. Simply because I can face tank and burst down just about everything. I no longer have to dodge every little thing to survive or play anything close to how I did on my first play through. Now, sure I have a lot of upgrades, but I haven't had to "grind" for upgrades since NG+4.(Aka, die unintentionally). Every consecutive attempt since NG+4 or 5 has resulted in me beating the game and moving on to the next NG+.While my complaint may look obtuse, since the goal of the game is to have a ton upgrades and you might think "Well you're just doing victory laps since you beat the game the first time." The problem is that you don't technically beat the game until around NG+7 when you've unlocked all the harder boss variants. By that point, while the bosses may be harder and more complex, any nuance to their new mechanics is simply moot because your character will be so strong that you hardly have to try and can just face tank them down.I don't see this particular problem being resolved since the last few updates have only made the game easier. With that said, it is still a fun game. It's just a bit of a let down as your normal character progression will quickly outpace the difficulty before you've "beat the game" on NG+7.As for weapon balancing, there are a few weapons in particular that outshine every other weapon option and then there are some that so severely underperform that I would only recommend using them on a challenge run. Thankfully the majority are usable and fun to play with.TL:DR The game is fantastic and a ton of fun to play. My only gripe is the difficulty has it's spike when you first start the game, it gets easier every consecutive NG+, which is an issue imo since you beat the game story-wise / "content-wise" around NG+7. There is still a ton of content to unlock past NG+7, both in terms of difficulty (fingers crossed it gets difficult again) and character upgrades. Don't let my small complaints deter you, you'll easily get your money's worth with this game!

_childDocuments_.review: An improvement on the first game in every regard, an excellent game to fiddle with as you're listening to a podcast or half-watching a game stream.A slight downside would be that a few of the classes are clearly superior to others - why would I switch to Bard who does the same amount of damage with an attack as the Knight, but has to recharge it with a spin kick between every attack? Why would I choose the Rogue that has exceptionally weak basic attacks and isn't even more mobile than the Knight? Why would I choose the Mage that has nothing going for it, except for focusing on the magic system?And the magic system is sort of a weirdly limited not very powerful mechanic. Sure I can lob a stone that deals 100 damage and consumes a third of my mana pool, but why would I do that if I can hit stuff with my sword for 500 damage three times between casts? I suppose you have to level your Intelligence to make it powerful but why would I prioritize spending my limited resources on something that I can only use 3 times until I run out of mana and have to swing my weapon to restore mana anyway? Just spend them on making your weapons swings better.Still, even with downsides like these, the game is very fun to absentmindedly play and grind.

Since you're very limited in how you can move and avoid damage if you have too many overlapping patterns that require a different solution you can't help but simply get hit. _childDocuments_.review: RL2 is everything you'd expect from a proper sequel—it delivers in all that areas that made the original game so beloved, which includes the "shifting," procedurally-generated biomes while introducing new combat and platforming mechanics that keep the gameplay from feeling stale. There are plenty of new traits as well as returning ones like "Nostalgic" and "IBS," and for the most part, the changes are welcome. The ability to re-roll heirs/traits multiple times (with the respective talent points) allows for some degree of customization as well.While the game doesn't present the most compelling narrative—and it doesn't really need to—the bits of lore and NPC dialogue contribute to a world that's both interesting and comedic.I highly recommend this game to anyone who was even remotely a fan of the first one.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: After a decade on ice, I thought a sequel to one of the early influencers of modern roguelikes would have more to offer. Instead, I’ve been faced with the sad reality that Rogue Legacy 2 is little more than an expansion. Many of the same problems that plagued the original game remain, and the minor alterations to address them don’t work as well as they need to. Don’t get me wrong, the game’s still fun to play until you grow tired of the progression loop. I’m sure if you enjoyed the original, you’ll enjoy the sequel, but if you were hoping for a meaningful update you might be better off playing another roguelike-platformer.More at:

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best roguelike platforming games.  7/10.Graphics are pretty nice.  Nothing outstanding.  Some handicaps or traits that you may start with can destroy this.  But it's part of the games mechanics and charm.  But at a base - everything is solid and visibility of what is going on is very good.Music is very good.  Some biomes are what the youngun's call bangers.  Given the amount of time I have in the game I will use my own music.  But certain sections and parts have very memorable tunes.Sounds, at a base, are also good.  It does seem like there was a lot more they could have done here.  Maybe have monsters make sounds in the room periodically so you could try to guess what is around you.  There would have been some nice play with the handicaps and traits.  Minor critique.I can't talk game play without revealing a little bit about how the game works.  Just a heads up.  In short, it's a ton of meta progression.  I've got almost 300 hours and still quite a bit left to unlock.  You continuously pick and unlock systems to make the game more challenging while unlocking more meta progression to help you out.  I was on NG35+ to put it in a bit of perspective how deep the rabbit hole goes.  One of the games premier gimmicks as I have eluded to is handicaps/traits or whatever you want to call them.  Not all of them are very harmful.  But a majority of them are.  Some even make a run, for all intents and purposes, unwinnable.  Especially when stacked upon one another.  So for those that like challenges this game has em in spades.I feel like the price point is very fair considering how much replay ability there is in terms of pushing yourself and hitting your limits.  Can easily recommend even at it's full price.Other than the minor complaint in the sounds section I would like to have sseen some meta progression or house rules to let you have a little more control over what traits and handicaps appear.  Since the concept of "builds" don't really exist runs get very "samey".  It's fairly easy to anticipate how a run is going to go based on starting class and traits.  It's I am playing Y class so if I find X and Z items I become strong.  There is a trait that allows you to be much more proactive with spells giving you mana regen at the cost of being squishier.  This is the most fun I've had in the game as the spells can be very fun and potent due to their limited resources.  I wish I could have it appear much more often.

_childDocuments_.review: This a VERY well made follow-up to one of the landmark rogues on Steam.The art style might turn people away, but take it from a person that's played both : the art style works very much in the game's favor here.The staples of the first game return, with more features added to the mix, such as1- more natural Biomes, with more than just " a palette swap " 2- WAY more traits, and now you can earn gold bonuses for the really bad ones3- roguevania elements Ala Dead cells, such as the air dash move, you now learn them after completing a challenge4- classes and WEPS! and the classes and weps function entirely differently than in RL1, you get special attacks and skills right from the gateSo far, been enjoying my time in this - even in Early Access - I have put 3 times the amount of playtime into it, and I'll definitely be putting more in.Controls nice, looks nice, the " one more run " feeling is VERY well done here, you will be swearing this is your last try, and then you fire it up again after seeing the new heirs.Tons more lore, maybe we find out Charon's true intentions? I'm excited to see where this one goes.The first boss is simply amazing in motion, and a really tough cookie.this is a very easy recommendation.for rogue vets, and newcomers - as the game allows you to meta progress - craft new equipment to start with, a gigantic skill tree that boots things such as attack, Hp, amount you get healed by meat, new classes, and so on.edit

_childDocuments_.review: Welp, here we are in the future and another numbs down. Pretty much everything I said about the first game is present in this game as well, BUT there are a lot more tools at your disposal to be able to deal with a lot of the challenges. That being said though, no amount of tools other than the ones that allow you to get-out-of-jail-free can deal with the overwhelming amount  of crap the game throws at you. To much of the game challenge is just blatant nonsense crap.A lot of this game's challenge feels like a downgrade from the first game, and I have a theory as to why. The devs put a menu in the game called "House Rules". This menu is basically a cheat menu that allows you to mage the game literally impossible to lose while also still retaining on the rewards. This menu is here for accessibility obviously, so that anyone body, regardless of their skill level, can complete the game. This menu is a double edged sword however. The mere existence of this menu means that actually winning without using the menu can make your successes feel hollow, which is not a way you want he player to feel.Theory time here. I wholeheartedly believe the developers skimped on making the game challenging in a fun way BECAUSE they planned this menu. They make an enemy, make it unfun and unfair to deal with a base level, and just reason, "Eh, its fine, they player can just nerf the enemy in House Rules". This is lazy and disrespectful to the playerThe game has a lot of fun aspects to it, but for every fun aspect there are plenty of frustrating, unfair, and unfun challenges that will just suck the joy out of you. Their are to many situation where there are too many projectiles on screen, to many enemies missed in with them, to many enviromental hazards and nowhere safe to be at any given point while still being able to fight back with a majority of classes. Some very common enemies require so much of you attention just to deal with them at a base level that you CANNOT be paying attention to anything but them, yet the devs make sure to put many of this one enemy coming at you at the same time missed in with snipers and other enemies that just fill all space with things that cannot be avoided. A good exampled is that when an enemy shoots a homing eletric ball at you, that must be skin kicked to eliminate, but you cant do the spin kick because their is a void wall being shot at you that requires you to do a void dash, but you can do a void dash because then you will fly into an enemy. Damned if you do, damned if you don't.Their are plenty of rogue-likes out their the respect you as a player and go out of their way to earn the money and time you spent on their game. This game IS NOT one of them.Edit: I uploaded this review before I completed the game in its entirety, I do this with a lot of games that have so profoundly failed as a product. I've developed a sense over the years to know when a game isn't going to get any better, and holy crap did a call it here. There is a challenge were you ride surf board trying to stay ahead of a wave that will kill you if it catches up. You have to traverse an obstacle coarse while doing so, but instead of the devs adjusting the games mechanics to account for the unique situation, they did nothing. You cannot see whats coming because your in the right most 3rd of the screen most of the time do to how the camera pans. You have to die over and over to every obstacle until you just have them memorized, and even then, most of them are just pure ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. This challenge was so insultingly bad that any goodwill I had towards these devs is gone. I hope they go bankrupt and have to sell the selves to EA only for EA to close the studio within a year.

_childDocuments_.review: My biggest complaint about this game is that it's not really a rogue like.My interpretation of a rogue like is Binding of Isaac, Undermine, and Hades. Every time you start, you get a new build. The items you pick up along the way affect you so heavily that each run feels like a totally different game. If you're not having fun with a run, you can just die and try again. When you are having a blast, you're absolutely on edge because you don't want to die and lose the build.But this game doesn't have that at all. There are "relics" which act as the items that modify your gameplay, but they really don't change anything at all. The best relics in the game just apply status effects to enemies or allow you to heal when you open a chest. It doesn't really affect how you interact with enemies at all.The only way this feels like a rogue like is because of the classes. There are 15 classes, but honestly there's only enough differences between them to feel like 4 classes. The Bard is the most unique class they have for sure. This part is great, but it's a little strange because you get to choose what class you want to play before you start.This may not seem like a big deal, but when you stop and think about it, it's pretty problematic. Instead of feeling like League of Legends or Dota (where you start with nothing and build into a total steamroller) you end up feeling like Valorant or Counter Strike (where you choose what you start with and you don't gain anything along the way).This, in my opinion, totally violates the core principle of rogue likes. It's more of a "play the same game over and over again with a bunch of upgrades" than a rogue like. It's kind of like Hollow Knight but with grinding... A LOT of grinding. Now even though it sounds like I'm coming down on it pretty hard, it's still a pretty good game.The upgrade system is very clearly the focal point of this game. They put a lot of time into figuring out how to upgrade anything and everything. There's an upgrade system for your castle (that upgrades your lineage), an upgrade system for your weapons and armor, an upgrade system for runes, a mastery system for individual classes, an upgrade system for loose gold at the end of runs, AND an upgrade system for all other upgrade systems.On top of that, the movement in this game is surprisingly tight. I would place it above Dead Cells but underneath Hollow Knight. They hit you some platforming early on that I was expecting to hate, but I actually came around to it. Mastering dashes and spin kicks let you absolutely thrash enemies and sprint through rooms. The bones on this game hold up under pressure.If I were to change one thing about this game, I would turn it into an actual rogue like. Currently, I don't see how anybody could play this game to the 100 hour mark. The gameplay just does not change enough to keep me interested. You can change numbers all day long, but there's just not enough actually happening on screen to keep me here for the long run. But for what it is, it's not bad.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of the original Rogue Legacy, I admit that I was excited for the sequel. Despite RL1 being a perfect standalone game, I thought RL2 would have everything I loved about the original in a much bigger castle. I thought they would stick to the gameplay formula that had made the first one absolutely amazing.I hate to say this, but I am SORELY disappointed in the experience that RL2 brings to the table.RL1 had a decent learning curve that you could easily follow, with decently-sized arenas for the bosses that you had to face--and each boss was difficult in its own way without bordering on frustration. RL2... takes that concept and grinds it up, spits on it, and then throws it out the window and into the dumpster. I've only managed to get to Axis Mundi, and I'm already noticing a sharp learning curve for bosses that can be frustrating at best and insurmountable at WORST.When you have two giant skeletons in a confined area throwing rotating bones that lop off chunks of your health with each hit, and a sizable difference in levels between you (Lv. 50+) and them (Lv. 37)... it really drives the point home that this game is very unforgiving to players like myself who played RL1 for fun and HOPED to be able to do the same with RL2. It also drives home the terrible boss programming that this game showcases whenever you eventually DO manage to make it to the boss arena.I was hoping that I would have been able to enjoy RL2 and recommend it to all my friends. However, as it stands right now with the way the game handles in certain situations... I can't recommend this game to ANYONE in good conscience. A lot of things need to be polished up before I even come CLOSE to wanting to pick up this game again--because as it stands right now, this game does nothing more than leave me frustrated and wishing I'd never spent money on it.

I saw the "true ending" on YouTube and needless to say, it was VERY UNDERWHELMING and not worth the time/effort to reach that point at all).a) Original  A  that had the right balance of content (4 worlds with bearable post-game content for completionists) and FAIR gameplay system for "gold gathering" and "upgrading your character as you progress towards the end-game" and overall just welcoming to re-play even after you've finished it entirely (In fact, I recently went back to play the entire game again after receiving it on Epic Game Store as a monthly free game and have thoroughly enjoyed my playthrough of it again).b)  A  that was too ambitious (6 worlds that felt TOO BIG to traverse and the worst part, you get VERY FEW health drops and gold-gathering is such a SLUG and PAINFUL thing to do, especially when the game is  you to select those characters with "BAD TRAITS" just to get as high of a % gold bonus as possible) and overall it's a game I have  to reach "New Game +7" (didn't even mention the "scars" which are INSANELY hard to complete on their own, especially later ones) and I have no plans to ever "re-visit" this game again in the future (unlike  which I still love and wouldn't mind doing a full playthrough of it again sometime in the future).

_childDocuments_.review: (TLDR at the end) After playing through the entire base game that's currently available, I think I'm finally ready to write a review on this. I've sunk countless hours into Rogue Legacy 1, so I had high hopes for the second game, and I think they were somewhat met. At the start, I was a little hesitant to get into it, but once things started flowing it felt so much better. I'll run over what I liked most and disliked most now.Weapons/classes:Honestly incredible job done with the variety of playstyles. While I do still love me the big ol swingy sword, it felt like a breath of fresh air to have a chance to use bows, axes, a rocket lance, or maybe even a katana or a lute if you're so inclined. I do wish mana could go higher without using relics, but having regen on hits is also pretty good. Only gripes: bard and chef are literally the worst things I've ever played. They feel horrible and their weapons are garbage. At least bard's skill is pretty good. Everything else was fantastic.Bosses:While there's no final boss, I can safely say 5/6 of the bosses that are in the game were a ton of fun. The second one was kinda lame but not bad. Super innovative, so much more depth than the first game, no bad comments here.Music:Oh my god it's such a banger. Personal favourites are the 3rd boss' track and the Phishon Dry Lake track.Enemies:I do wish there was a bit more uniqueness with the enemies in the first few areas, but when you get to the Sun Tower or the Lake, there's so many new enemies. It's nice to see familiar faces but also something new. I just really hate the shield banner elites but I think that's intended, haha.Now for my biggest issue with the game: I don't get the thought process behind it, but the devs seemed to be so anti-player exploration. In the first game, you could go wherever as long as you're confident enough to not get yourself killed, but before you hit NG+, there's so much trying to stop you from reaching new areas early. The first and second are easily accessible, but the third is literally blocked behind a giant gate that opens from defeating the second boss (unless there's another way I didn't find). The fourth and fifth are like "heehoo you need this upgrade from the third area to get in here" or you need to be using a rocket lance, and even then you need an upgrade from the fourth area to get anywhere in the fifth. The sixth area is just hella dark until you beat the fifth which makes it very unfriendly to even think of going into, not to mention the only way out is to progress all the way or return to menu so you spawn back at the entrance of the first zone. I wish it wasn't trying to force me in a linear progression, but I do think the upgrades are cool, at least. Unfortunately it's probably too late in development to change any of this, but I still needed to say it.I still have more to explore in NG+, so in 35 hours I still haven't run out of things to do. Great game, definitely worth.TL;DR Super fun gameplay, amazing music, great bosses. Poor progression, being forced to go linearly instead of exploring and getting killed for it but with a chance at success. Definitely worth getting, though, whether or not you've played the first one.

_childDocuments_.review: Far Shores Update: The original Rogue Legacy was one of few games in my adult life that truly captured my attention all the way through to the end. It's very rare that a game comes along and does that.All these years later, Rogue Legacy 2 has done it again, even in a state that could practically be passed off as just an extensive demo. Don't mind my logged playtime, most of it was offline. I bought it a couple of weeks ago, and have easily put in over 20 hours playing it sporadically, and I'm maybe halfway through the current content.Playing as the Ranger feels amazing. I love that you don't just have a sword each time, and some of the spells are really fun too. The room designs and mechanics for navigating them are really creative and compelling, and the longer I've played the more interesting and complex they've gotten. I laugh at my dumb mistakes that get me killed, then charge back in again with the next heir, just like old times. All in all it's a pretty stable and competent build.With the newest update - 3 biomes, 3 bosses, Class Masteries encouraging you to use every class, 4 different currencies to gather and spend, upgrades for every piece of armor and every rune. Armor set Unity bonuses that let you mix and match and get the most out of each character, if you want to play that way. Relics with synergy that affect how each run plays. And it just keeps getting better.I will say though, overcoming some of the challenges and roadblocks can be a bit tedious or even frustrating without the Architect to lock the castle down, which is due for a later patch. I'm having a lot of fun and playing it more than any other game right now, but the experience is definitely rough around the edges in a way that I'm CERTAIN it won't be closer to the final product. So if you want something with just a little more polish, that feels closer to the complete overall experience, you might value waiting until the next major update slated for Dec/Jan. Right now it feels a little more...."halfway there". As a huge fan of the original, I'm very happy to play what they have and enjoy discussing it on Discord, but it's definitely not for everyone in its current state.Tl,dr; While not exactly cheap or nearly finished, it has been a very engaging Early Access experience that already transcends the overall quality of the first game in many ways, with the potential to be one of the great Roguelites of this era. I really look forward to seeing it continue to develop.

_childDocuments_.review: I would post mixed review if I could. It is a good game at it's core, but developers confuse difficult vs. frustrating, and many-many  features have potential to be fun, but instead you are held back by a number of arbitrary limits, that you have to slowly grind up around.-Controls are clunky and there is no way around that, there is bunch of options to assist you with that but still, for level of precision this game demands it does not have satisfying control scheme.- You will often be in situations where getting hit is unavoidable unless you got protective skill. This happens sometimes as soon as you enter a room if it's drop down, or when facing multiple enemies that target sligthly at random instead of directly at you, or just have one enemy zone you out while another lands attack that occupies entirety of your space.- There are fun relics and classes, but you are prohibited from taking many of them until you grind up or in case of classes and weapons you are rewarded for always swapping them, thus turning each run into random mish-mash unless you want to keep skipping those nifty damage bonuses. Also equipment system forces you to choose between picking up fun relics vs getting boring stat bonuses, so just ugh.- Entire descendant theme is rather poorly integrated outside of potential for enormous grind, game in general would work much better as straightforward metroidvania... because for something thaat should be roguelite, level generation, and enemy variation is lacking, not to mention challenges that you will have to repeat with each and every class if you want to get high scores, in the end game just becomes tedious and whatever story there is ,you will stop caring due to repeated playthroughs.-...that said, you can make exactly that out of this game if you were to use architect and some house rules, but it does not offset game being flawed at it's core.In the end, most important question is, will you have fun? Depends, but will be served much better by playing actually fully well done game in genre ala Hollow Knight or Cave Story instead.

_childDocuments_.review: This game isn't fully released yet, but I feel deeply compelled to write a review for this anyway.This is already probably the best Roguelite of its kind ever made. This game is shaping up to be easily one of the best Rougelites of all time, and I've played nearly all of them.This game is basically a combination of a Metroidvania and Roguelite that uses an RPG style progression system. The world is classic 2D metroidvania with secrets and bosses, and upon death you can bequeath your gold for various upgrades that will permanently level up your character. The RPG based upgrade system here is quite robust compared to pretty much every other Roguelite on the market. You have a rich diversity of upgrade options available to you in a large skill tree, as well as a plethora of equipment and spells options you can individually upgrade. Each class also has a separate leveling system to give you even more ways to power up.Yet despite this, the game is hard! The enemies and bosses are complex and fun to engage with. Winning involves either leveling your character substantially or getting gud. Usually a combination of both. No enemy is ever really gated by power itself; you can almost always win if you're good enough. But the option to win through skill or amassed power is quite nice and makes the game extremely enjoyable to play. As such, I think it would be apt to call this game a Roguelite-Metroidvania-RPG hybrid. It combines all three of those elements into a fantastic package. If you like any of those genres, I really can't recommend this game enough.And the crazy thing is that it...isn't even finished! It already has more than double the content of the original and the game isn't done. It's shaping up to be an absolute behemoth of a game that is extremely fun to play. I've sunk over 40 hours into an Early Access game, which is something I never do...and I plan to replay it from the very beginning upon full release. I can't wait!

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR Good game, with lots of potential.  But it has very little content, so it won't be ready for months.As a big fan of Rogue Legacy, with over 100 hours in game, seeing a sequel being made both worried and excited me. Rogue Legacy to me was a simple game, it has simple enemies, simple fighting style, simple graphics, but is hard to master and to finish and I love that.  Sequels in this genre can be hard to make well.  How do you improve on a simple premise without ruining what made the first game special? Fortunately I feel Cellar Door haven't ruined it at all.  They haven't tried to reinvent the wheel or add a lot of pointless and boring mechanics.  This game is an all round improvement on the first, better graphics and animations, more enemies, more mechanics, more skills, new classes, better and more varied combat.  This game truly has the potential to become great. That being said, potential is the key word there.Although this game is fun and interesting, there isn't a whole lot of it.  You can unlock every skill in under 5 hours then its a grind for fairy chests to get runes and armour.  The overabundance of new eye destroying traits can make some ruins just feel terrible, I think they need to be slightly rarer.So what new stuff is good and what is bad in my opinion?General Gameplay:I love the improved jumping mechanics and movement in this game, it's fun and incredibly satisfying.The teleporter pipe things are an interesting and welcome addition.Combat is great, challenging but doable.The heirloom challenges are fun, a bit challenging but not too hard.As previously said, some of the vision impairing traits can be a bit much and make your runs just wanted to end early.The biggest problem so far is the skill tree, which can be filled very quickly.Classes:Ranger is a slight let down for me, I was excited to try the bow, but using a controller I find it too slow to aim and can be a real hindrance to many runs.Mage has been really fun, the new spells are satisfying and just great so far.Barbarians spinning ability can end a lil badly sometimes, but I like that it has some risk.Overall I think this is a fun game, with lots of potential and it will end up getting better and better.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who never cares about graphics or art style in video games, I really really *really* hate the art for RL2.Like for some context, I've played and enjoyed such things as:Dwarf FortressShadowbane (original and emulator)DarkfallPongYet this is possibly my least favorite art style/graphics for any game I can recall playing after thinking about it for a few minutes trying to remember other awful examples. At least out of any game genre that I would actually want to try in the first place.The visuals for Rogue Legacy 2 *just don't fit*. It feels off in an almost uncanny valley like way. This art would feel at home in a Worms game, or in a prison-architect clone, or a high-res rimworld knockoff.Coming off of the previous game, which I really loved, it just feels *so wrong* though.Rogue Legacy 1 had good quality retro-style pixel art that felt pretty inline with a slightly light-hearted westernized castlevania, which fits well with how the game actually played. The graphics weren't exactly something you could describe as "serious" or "dark", but they weren't exactly goofy either, I think "stylized" would be the right moniker.Rogue Legacy 2 however has veered hard away from the vania-like roots and retro style and into . . . low detail early 2000s educational childrens game?To make matters worse, I don't feel most of their backgrounds (which are quite good) fit well with the foreground terrain, or the characters, or the enemies. The backgrounds keep that moody dungeon-crawly roguelike vibe, while foreground terrain and characters are too soft, well lit, and cartoonish to keep the same type of appeal.Now maybe they're appealing to a child audience, you might have been able to sway my nephew more easily with this style when he was 8 years old than with the old one, but that just seems really off when creating a PC game sequel to a 2013 retro game, that still contains a lot of gameplay elements that kind of appeal to an older audience that grew up on these games.On top of which, "it's meant to appeal to children" doesn't really make me like it any more, even if it could be a sound business decision.The existence of other modern games with graphical directions that are by comparison, quite frankly amazing like Dead Cells pushes my estimation of the new art direction even farther down.Writing this negative review feels weird to me, it's something I rarely care about, and I also tend to give developers an easy time since ♥♥♥♥♥♥, it's a hard and expensive endeavor to make a game, they could use the slack typically.I just don't think I can get past this art style. I'm currently expecting to refund the game purely on this issue alone. I know other reviews have covered different issues with the game; too little content for early access, small number of enemies, technical issues, etc.Honestly I'm not too worried about that stuff, I have a reasonable degree of confidence it'll get sorted out eventually given their previous title.Unfortunately, Art direction for the entire game, all classes, all animations, and all enemies probably isn't something that can be changed just from an economics perspective, so it isn't something I can expect to ever get better.As such, I don't recommend this game, as I personally have found the art to significantly reduce how satisfying fighting enemies and progressing feels, and this gets much worse if you enjoyed the previous game.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of aspects from Rogue Legacy 1 have been improved while keeping the same spirit, and really, it's a great sequel: enough similar aspects to call it a sequel, enough new features to call it Rogue Legacy 2 instead of Rogue Legacy 1.5.The different classes are a welcome addition. I use magic more often (almost never used it in RL1). Heirlooms introduce a nice variety of moves.The game can be very, very frustrating. A lot of that frustration can be avoided by learning the ennemies patterns, and by grinding gold to improve stats.But there are still aspects of the game that will keep being frustrating and that's really a negative aspect for me. For example, I hated fairy chests in Rogue Legacy 1, I hate them even more now. I fail them 19 out of 20 times. I can't figure out the puzzles ones.The rest of the issues are more a problem of balancing the game, and for an early access game, they already did a good job on that point, I'm confident for the final release.

_childDocuments_.review: While I have not played this game for very long, I simply had to write a review on how much I am enjoying this amazing game. The general flow is very reminiscent of games like For Honor where it is still fast paced but slow enough to force you to think logically and time your movements and actions, which is what the classic Roguelikes/Roguelites are all about. the learning curve is incredibly smooth, with new mechanics available to hunt down at any time in a very interesting manner that allows you to understand when and where to use them. The enemies are constructed in a way that allows you to understand the basics of each one as soon as you see them while still being unique and fun to fight every single time. 10/10 definitely worth the price tag and I hope to see even more content released soon!

I played the hell out of the first one, but this one has more cheap gotcha moments than that one. Constant things waiting off screen attacking you, enemies winding up attacks before the room fully loads in, points where you must take this new platform mechanic to proceed and at the top is an enemy waiting to chunk you for 1/3 of your life.
