_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Legacy 2 is one of the most polished roguelites on the market. Let's be real, most of us can't be bothered to finish a roguelite. For fans of the genre, that's maybe part of the charm. But Rogue Legacy 2? I could not put this down until it was done. Why? Because the game consistently offered me PROGRESSION. Actual progression that told me: you can actually finish this one.The real selling point of the game is the combat, though. They've taken inspiration from various other games that have come out since Rogue Legacy 1 and combined them all in a really nice way. The combat is just awesome and it has so much variety for you to find your own playstyle. A big challenge in games that feature both combat and platforming is the way the two systems interact with each other. In this game, it's a flawless fit.I'm not the best at writing game reviews, but I just hope anyone reading this who is interested in the game will buy it. It's a really wonderful game. The kind of game that restores my faith in the gaming industry when I start to feel jaded.

_childDocuments_.review: I had initially given this game a tentative thumbs up. Citing issues about incompleteness and being teased with features being visible, but not accessible. But since my original review, perhaps a year ago, they've put a lot of work into this game and said incompleteness seems to be largely resolved. At least as far as I've played it since the 1.x updates.I haven't had a lot of time to try it out but I've played enough to see that there are no longer any areas (that I'm aware of) where you just come to a sign saying "coming soon" or upgrades in the menu that have similar messages. It's all been replaced with the proper content, as promised. And despite only playing for a bit, I can see they've put a lot of work and effort into the new content. Just as much, or more than the original base game.Although I haven't played the game in its entirety yet, these new updates feel like they add a lot more length to the game as well. Just based on how much longer it took to get to areas in the game which previously didn't take much time at all.So all in all, it looks like they've expanded the game a huge amount since the initial release (and my initial review) and as such, I've rewritten my review to reflect those changes. Since my past review is no longer relevant.This game was still worth the price tag when the original early release version came out. But with the added content I think now more than ever it's a good buy. Especially if you liked the original. It really expands on the gameplay of that.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is entertaining, fun, unique, and provides more than enough challenge for anyone short of a "hardcore gamer." It's primarily an RPG-light Platformer / Dungeon-Crawler with elements of Base/Deck Building, and a unique take on character progression. The Heir System is brilliant! You start as a generic hero, exploring and fighting your way through a randomly generated dungeon until you inevitably die from lack of experience or by the hands of a foe you're just simply too weak to overcome. But this is by design. For, when you die, the treasure you plundered and the knowledge you gained will pass on to one of 3 randomly generated heirs for you to choose from. These heirs range from epic OP warriors with highly efficient traits to... tiny blundering abominations that can barely open a chest without killing themselves. And that--is hilarious and entertaining and makes the game so fun to play. I've had long runs with a single character, clearing out entire dungeons, collecting multiple artifacts and hoarding thousands of gold. And... I've had very short runs with a tiny blue mage that can't see enemies, or a clown who farts and can only get hit once, or a giant boxer who shoots exploding fists that damage everything... including himself. lolAnd the thing is... It's all fun! I don't mind losing in this game. In fact, as you progress you'll find there's actually some strategic reasons to plan on losing sometimes. But that's not why I like it. I like it because even the most severely handicapped heirs have their uses if you get clever about how you play with them. And the game knows this. You can get double, triple, quadruple the gold and more for choosing a more disadvantaged heir. So it's not just for laughs, these are challenges that are part of the core experience. How long can you last as a Histrionic Cook with Aphantasia? Because that was my longest run and it was fun as heck smacking stuff with a frying pan!

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished my first little bit of dabbling in New Game+, and it feels like time to give a review for this wonderful sequel to Rogue Legacy.Rogue Legacy 2 is everything that one hopes for in a sequel: it takes what was already there, and builds / improves / expands on it. The first zone (once you finish the tutorial / prologue of the game) is clearly a direct take from the first game, with backgrounds, assets and enemies either heavily similar or straight up identical to Rogue Legacy 1. The movement, combat and character traits also seem to be nearly identical at first. For me, this is a good thing: Rogue Legacy did a good job of all of that, so don't fix what isn't broken!The more you play, though, the more you realise this is not just Rogue Legacy 1, again: they have tried to *evolve* with this entry in the franchise.One such evolution is character classes: there are more of them now, and they are more varied and unique. I'm not sure what people would consider spoilers, but let's just say that in the quite late game (or if you get lucky while exploring, in some runs) you can end up wielding a magical (maybe living?) umbrella, or pizza. Yep: pizza is not just (really good) food & healing in this game, it can eventually be a weapon too! And that's just a couple of the many options. The many classes of the game each come with unique bonuses, most of which are just stat modifiers but a few of which are really influential. Lastly, the classes serve as templates for what can become a mix & match experience with weapons, talents and spells, so the variety really is incredible in terms of builds. Another evolution is the introduction of Metroidvania progression, on top of the titular Rogue-lite mechanics. In addition to, after dying, having the option to spend your gold on upgrading your 'castle' which then enhances all future runs, there are also special permanent upgrades you need to explore to find in the castle, and once you find them you then need to complete unique challenge levels that make you use the upgrade to overcome special situations in a strange, alternate liminal space: if you succeed, this run and all future runs get access to that special upgrade at no additional cost, forever from that point out. What's more is that, like Metroidvanias, some of these upgrades are *necessary* to get into the castles other zones, in addition to also just offering utility in terms of mobility and combat. Speaking of Castle Zones, that's another way that Rogue Legacy 2 has evolved beyond its point of origin. Now there are six, not four zones in each castle run. Moreover, these zones are not just slight reskins with different (usually slightly tougher / more complex) enemies like in the first game: they all have real *character*. I'll admit, the 1st and 4th zones are very samey (and the 4th zones music drives me batty, unlike all the others which are good jams that loop nicely), but each of the other zones have unique qualities that add to world-building and make each run a little less stale. Some of the zones have inherent bonuses to gold collected in them as well, making it just a little more exciting when you can finally manage to access them and / or survive in them. As you explore the zones, you not only have the chance (or requirement) to find more Metroidvania style permanent upgrades, you also can find relics that use a seperate resource called "Resolve." These relics are like ones in a lot of other rogue-likes, and range from giving you more crit chance to letting you straight up fly (at some cost, usually, more than just resolve). Problem is, if you let your resolve fall below 100% ? It eats away at your MAX HP. So you have to choose wisely. As I mentioned before as well, there are little tents that show up as well that offer randomized weapons, talents and spells to trade out for your base one. Sometimes these might be a clearly bad choice, but you might do it anyway ... why? Because each time you use one of these "Blessings" to trade out a part of your kit, your weapon damage, magic damage or resolve is increased for that run. Many times I chose to grab a less than ideal talent because I got a little greedy with a relic and my HP was in the gutter from poor resolve. With all these aspects, the game stays relatively fresh for a lot longer than Rogue Legacy 1.And its a good thing too, because as you'll see by my hours played as of writing this, it took me 65 hours to beat the game once. And honestly, I got kinda lucky. The last boss, for me at least, was TOUGH. All of the bosses felt tough at first, but also had patterns and weaknesses that you could analyse to realise what class might be best to take them on. The last boss was on a whole other level, though. So I could easily see it taking longer for people to beat than 60 hours in some cases. Or it might take less, because there is a lot of room for skill to accelerate a playthrough (and I'm honestly just not that good, despite all the practice). All of this is to say that compared to Rogue Legacy 1, this game has a lot more meat on the bones of just a base playthrough before you even get to New Game+, and then New Game+ brings all the usual suite of options to spice things up: new enemies, enemy modifiers, level modifiers, alternate (harder) bosses. Even cooler is that NG+ gives you a chance to unlock more of the story (which, while fairly straightforward and predictable, is pretty good and an improvement from Rogue Legacy 1). I should note, before I wrap up the review, that I loved Rogue Legacy 1. I played the heck out of it. We did couch hot seat with friends, where we would just hand off the controller for a run and everyone would just watch, cheer and help strategize as whoever had the controller gave it their best. When someone had a good run and brought in a big haul of gold, we would all hoot and holler of our now-shared success. Sure, it was technically a single player game, but those moments made it richer and definitely deepen my nostalgia for Rogue Legacy 1. On top of all that, I played it again on my own years later and not only beat it, but New Game+'d twice. So, I was a fan. And there's actually more I could say, but I think if I haven't convinced you by now to give it a shot, I probably won't. But I hope you do, because Rogue Legacy 2 is a delightful, underrated gem in my books. As a love letter to Rogue Legacy 1, it succeeds and then some, growing into its own by drawing on the successes of games like Dark Souls, Hades and Metroidvania titles to become something that I've really cherished. 9.25 / 10

_childDocuments_.review: Among the best brawler roguelites I've played so far.- The gameplay is just really smooth.- I found all classes fun to play. When choosing which class to use for the next run, I always picked the one with lowest mastery level, and I never thought "eww this class again". I do have my favourites among the classes, but I don't hate any - in a game with 15 classes, this is an achievement.- The classes also feel different enough from each other - even if half of the classes are melee, all of them have clear identities which lead to different playstyles, or at the very least allows different tricks here and there.- Boss design is great. When progressing through a couple of bosses the first time, I did think that there's some unfair mechanics, but over time I learned to handle them - during the last few runs, I've been able to generally avoid all mechanics at all bosses. The few "unfair mechanics" were just a skill issue after all.- I like the progression/structure. It almost feels like a hybrid between a "normal" arpg and a roguelite. When you start out, your first challenge is to find and kill the first boss. When you manage to do that, you can start progressing towards the 2nd boss - if you die, on your next character the 1st boss is already dead and you can directly start progressing through the 2nd zone. You'll also eventually unlock a way to teleport directly to any zone. So: after killing the 1st boss, there's no need to re-clear the 1st zone/boss on every new character.- This structure sort of changes after you kill the final boss and see the credits for the first time - you can then start running NG+'s, which will reset all bosses. At this point, your "one run" starts being more about "clearing all 8 bosses" instead of "killing the next boss" - but again, if you manage to kill 3 bosses and then die, you can continue from there with your next character.

_childDocuments_.review: The original Rogue Legacy is one of my all-time favorite roguelites and I gave it a glowing review back when it was released. So of course I am excited to try out any sort of sequel to that, even if it may be in Early Access.So I'll start with the most obvious change: the art style. They dropped the pixel graphics that the original had going for it in favor of 2.5D, with most assets being in 2D, but the characters and such being in 3D. I'd be lying if I said that I didn't miss the original style, but I'd also be lying if I said that this new style wasn't good. It's a solid pick for the game and the devs really did a good job with the various models, textures, and the overall detail within the game world. It kinda reminds me of the recent Shantae games, and that's definitely not a bad thing.Now in the sound department, I wouldn't say that the game does a standout job, but it's not bad. Apparently a lot of the sound effects are currently placeholders, so this is an area that will likely be improved with time. The music on the other hand, is a bit better, but still doesn't quite match the quality of the first game. Granted, I haven't been able to hear most of the soundtrack given that the other biomes are locked, so I'll be withholding a final judgement on that for now.However, the gameplay is what we're all here for and, just as with the first game, Rogue Legacy 2 really excels at it. The core loop is all here. You enter the castle with a randomized character, take down a bunch of baddies, amass a small fortune, take on the boss, and die and repeat. In the game's current state, all of this is present and it feels nice to play. The combat is solid, the movement is smooth, and it's still just as challenging as ever. In fact, it might actually be even harder this time around. That or maybe I just got worse at video games.As the game is a roguelite, you will be dying a lot, but you get a bit stronger every time by way of the skill tree and the different items and runes you can purchase. The best mechanic though (at least, in my opinion) is the randomized characters you get at the beginning of each run. One run could have me near-sighted and unable to see enemies farther away and another may have me playing the whole thing upside down. There are a lot of these different traits, most of which make the game more difficult, but all of which I had a good time messing around with.The different classes, the random traits assigned to them, and the gold modifiers brought on by these traits really make each run its own thing. Couple all of that with the randomized nature of each level and all of the upgrades and such to find and you have a really solid foundation for a good roguelite.I say foundation because, although I like the gameplay here, it is desperately lacking in content. There's only one boss, one full biome, and four classes. It's a start, but you'll pretty much see everything in just a few hours, although it will take longer to actually unlock all the skills and such. The game is in Early Access though, so this is expected. The devs obviously focused on the core to the game first before just adding in a bunch of content, which I feel is a better place to start than the alternative of offering a large amount of content, but having broken and shallow game mechanics.Rogue Legacy 2 is a good follow-up to the original, even if its Early Access is light on content. Rather, it focuses on providing a very solid base, with all the core combat mechanics, the gameplay loop, and other such essential elements all present. All of the content that is there is fun, the only thing that's really missing is, well, the rest of it. With updates, I can see this turning into a very cool sequel, maybe enough to surpass the original. The devs already have a nice roadmap laid out, so it's only a matter of time.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: I beat it after 22 hours. I turned on house rules for the last two bosses. House rules allows you to "cheat" and lower the damage and hp of monsters.The amount of grinding this game expects from the player is absurd. Everything you acquire has levels and can be grinded for hours on end. Every upgrade makes the next one more costly and by the end the prices are crazy. If you hit a wall you will need to grind. It makes the game difficulty feel more like a numbers game than skill based. Every player will beat the bosses with different time played and the difficulty will vary accordingly. I much prefer a game like Hollow Knight, where the upgrades you can acquire are fixed and you can't grind your way to an easy victory.There are several bosses with random elements such as temporarily invulnerable adds which can force you into being hit. If you don't meet the gear requirements you will fail.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played only three hours, but i think i can do a little review about this great game.I'm a fan of the first "rogue legacy" and, with this announcement, i was really excited, but the second parts are not always good. This game is an exception. The "base game" is the same. Your PJ, a castle and explore. Now, we have a little new mechanic to jump, hitting some objects (with other button), very useful, and other to open doors with normal hit.Examinate your class, with your spell, traits... BUT choose wisely, because the traits are more important than before, since you can obtain more gold with some traits and MORE gold choosing others. It's not the same choose, for example, "dwarfing" than "vegan" or "pacifist", you really need to think about this.Now, the difference between classes is really precise. The knight is the same, but the barbarian has a new attack and that is perfect! It's a great change. The ranger class is impeccable. The mage... well, maybe could be better. You need to know what you really want to play, and, sometimes, what you really MUST to play.Well, start the game. I can't talk about the improvements you can obtain building the castle because this is under construction, but you must buy "socialism" before the others. You'll need this to obtain more gold about "traits". Then, walk, there is an old friend waiting for you to travel to the castle.Now, the game really starts. The graphics are really nice. _childDocuments_.review: The first game was fun, but this one is a huge leap forward.There's 15 classes, and--unlike the first game--each class has its very own weapon: everything from sword to polearm to magic wand to boxing gloves. Where the first game used mana to power most class talents, mana is now (usually) the exclusive fuel for spells. Instead, talents now have cooldowns. Usually these are timed cooldowns, but some talents require you to strike enemies a certain number of times, one requires you to pick up a healing item, and one even requires you to get hit. Speaking of mana, everybody is a spellthief now and gains mana back by striking enemies. The selection of spells is almost entirely new, including a massive DBZ-esque "gravity beam" attack.The miner class is gone ("relegated from a class to a trait"), but not only are traits still around (of course), the more debilitating traits all give you bonus gold. The nastier the trait, the bigger the gold bonus! You can even enhance this bonus by upgrading a certain part of your manor. (Oh right: the manor has many more sections to purchase than in the first game.)There are no longer shrines you pray at for special items, but now there's thingies called "relics" all over the place. All relics have a benefit (though many also have drawbacks), and there's a pretty huge variety of them. You start to suffer a loss of maximum HP if you carry too many powerful relics at once, though.There are more bosses, and they all have much more interesting and varied movesets than the bosses in RL1. They also have a fair amount of lore behind them, which you can dig deeper into as you get into NG+. The bosses can be kind of tough, but there's a couple of new traits that make bosses easier (while making general exploration and travel harder). Besides bosses, there's also enemies sprinkled about called "Commanders"; in addition to being tougher varieties of their monster type, each Commander has a randomly selected trait--and unfortunately for you, all Commander traits are beneficial.There's loads and loads of improvements and tweaks, QoL and otherwise. While enemies still knock you back, they can't knock you out of a room, thank goodness. There's also an air recovery now, though if you miss being knocked around willy-nilly there's a new trait that disables your post-damage immunity window. You can now retire heroes early instead of being forced to kill them off. You can look around larger rooms using the right-hand joystick, and zombie-type enemies show subtle visual clues when underground. "Special" rooms gray out on the map when you're finished with them. There's a new "magnesis" rune that pulls coins towards you, and it's a cheap rune to equip (you have a "rune weight" now instead of a limit of five runes, with some runes taking up more weight than others). Finally, there's an option to make each class have its own individualized gear and rune loadout.Not everything's perfect. Sometimes you'll open a chest and it'll spray some of its goodies into a nearby pit of spikes. Sure, magnesis runes lessen the pain, but it still feels a bit dumb. Also, when playing deeper NG+ levels, it's common to have at least one death-defiance revive--but the revival animation is pretty long, and given the difficulty of very deep NG+ levels, you'll have to sit through it quite a lot. (Especially if you're weird like me and play on 76 burdens just for the challenge--you'll see what I mean eventually.)Also--and this isn't a complaint but rather a precaution--you'll to do a decent amount of reading to get full enjoyment out of this game. For example, there's a glossary submenu, and a lot of stuff isn't clear until you reference that. Consider armor: the manor's armor unlock somewhat vaguely informs you that the "Base max block cap" is 35%, while the glossary straightforwardly states that "only 35% of incoming damage can be blocked by Armor" and that "you can raise your minimum armor block % via Runes." The glossary also lists and explains all possible Commander traits (some of which are very confusing to encounter in-game). There's also bunches of lore, and there's optional-but-significant rewards for reading it all. It's not an onerous amount of reading, though (this review is probably longer-winded!), it's just kind of a lot for an action game.All in all this game is a must-play if you like platforming games or roguelite games--or RL1--at all. Plus, you can pet the dragon.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a big fan of Rogue Legacy 1 & Hades, but I can not recommend Rogue Legacy 2...What I love about rogue-lite is that you feel like you're progressing. For example, compare the first hour of the game with the 15-20 hours of the game: you should feel that you have really grown: you become a better player & your character has become stronger! And this feeling I love in rogue-lite. It was perfectly done in Rogue Legacy 1, and Hades also has a grate narrative!The problem with Rogue Legacy 1 is that despite all the cool innovations, it becomes too overloaded and overcomplicated (in terms of abilities, not mechanics). In the beginning, progress is felt, and it is felt that the new mechanics of bounces and jerks benefit the game. But after 15 hours I realized that the game has a very poor balance! There is simply no progress. You feel like you're hitting the "ceiling" in your progress. 6 bosses before the final instead of 4 in the previous part also did not play in favor of the game. Complicated just for the sake of complicating. If was made 4 locations instead of 6 it would be better. Quality, not quantity! And in my opinion, I would be happy to finish the game at 25-30 hours of gameplay. I would enjoy it. Because out of my 40 hours: the first 15 hours are "progress", and the last 25 hours are "boredom".Played on Steam Deck, 40 hours to finish.Verdict 4/10

_childDocuments_.review: Good but definitely flawed game. I like how the areas work and the basic enemies are pretty good. I'm not a huge fan of how the bosses work personally, it promotes just running to the boss and trying over and over until you win. Most bosses are also not terribly difficult but do have quite a bit of health so you just have to try until you know all the patterns and then its relatively easy.Items also have a weight-like system that reduces your health when you pick them up, so it doesn't really feel rewarding to actually explore the areas when you are going to the bosses. With a decent high-armor build you're already nearly capped out on weight, so you can only pick up maybe 2 items before you start losing max health. Combine that with items generally not being super game changing, its not really worth looking for.I did enjoy playing it for a while though, worth picking up on sale but personally wouldn't pay full price for it. For reference I beat the main game in about 13-14 hours, with the hardest boss taking something like 12 attempts to beat. After that it kind of goes into a hades style replay system where you just make enemies harder for a bigger reward, which I don't tend to stick around for much longer.

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyed the first game ? Liked Hollow knight, metroid, but also moonlighter or Isaac ? Buy. The damn. game.This game is near perfection. 12 hours in the game and the deepness of the game design still astonish me. Each character is thought with so much consideration it's creepy. I don't want to spoil you so much, but you'll die. A lot.And that's okay ! Usually, when people talk about roguelites, they tend to think about a weird difficulty curve, like the first game had : You could just farm for gold, and be so overpowered that you can OS every boss.Now ? oh boi, no sweety. The rooms are so well design, that when ennemies aren't a problem anymore... YOU ARE. Spikes, roots, flames, arrows, traps : your overconfidence can and will kill you. It was true in the first game, but here, they nailed it. The difficulty curve is so smooth, I've never felt stuck at any point, event after many, many tries in axis mundi.  Rogue Legacy 2 is not what you can call a roguelike anymore, not even roguelite fit the genre. There isn't any other game like it out there from what I know.You could call it Metrodie & retry or Skill issue : Legacy, I guess.I'm guetting out of hand here so my point is : RG2's is a perfect mix of a metroidvania, a roguelike and the synergies inside a TCG. You could play thousands of games, with thousands of different characters... And it would still feel like a new game.Well done, guys, hyped for the future !

_childDocuments_.review: Compared to it's original title, which was a masterpiece, this is just a let down. It has too many features, too many gimmicks, and not enough of the enjoyable things from the first game.-For one, one of my favorite parts of Rogue Legacy 1 was the character traits. The characters from the first had awesome traits, things that actually made sense for a *person* to have. Like being near/far sighted, having bad depth perception, not being able to see color. But now the traits are lacking compared to that, and they aren't even humanlike traits. Like, half the traits just make you start with relics. That isn't a trait, that's just giving the player an item. And giving them extra damaging abilities doesn't make sense either. How is that a trait for a person?? It's not.-There are too many gimmicks that need to be utilized and you need a bunch of upgrades to even be able to explore areas. The first game was simple - you had attack, class ability, a spell (or 2 with wizard), a pogo, a dash, a double jump, sometimes a hover, and sometimes ONE relic that would help you a little. But now you have spin kicks, advanced spin kicks, dashing, dash slashing, void dashes, long void dashes, a resolve meter that makes it so you lose comical amounts of max health just for wanting to take an item, unique weapons to memorize for every class, sometimes special button combos per class, class talents, spells, MORE unique weapons you can find around the world, recovery moves, air recoveries, a double jump, just SO MUCH.-The areas don't even make sense anymore. The first game made a lot of sense with the zones. You had the main castle, the tower for the castle, the dungeon below it, and the outside area. But now there's the castle, the mage tower, the sun tower, a dry lake that's under the castle for some reason, an area covered with water, a big snowy area, a garden area, and then a whole new castle. It's just all over the place and it doesn't make sense.-The classes are unbalanced. Judging on new enemy behavior with this game, range is incredibly important - and there are very few classes that have good range. And all others have a disadvantage because of this, as well as classes with bad air attacks like the barbarian. Classes like the dragon lancer I can't even figure out, and seem terrible and difficult to use in any way. I like the unique weapons, but they are not in any way balanced with each other.-This last bit is my personal preference, so take it with a grain of salt. Rogue Legacy 1 had incredibly good design and music design as well, and the second feels like it's just nowhere near as good in that way. I love pixel graphic games, and Rogue legacy 2 looks so much worse than the first, almost too cartoon like. And the music is significantly less good than Rogue Legacy 1. The music in the first felt really nice, it gave energy and also a good feeling of the area you're in. But half the time with the second I just tune out the music because I don't enjoy it. It doesn't feel like it fits in properly whatsoever.I don't hate this game, but I dislike it strongly compared to the masterpiece that Rogue Legacy 1 was.

After almost 100 hours, I'm still on the lookout to try new character/relic combos. There is a lot of atmosphere and world depth. _childDocuments_.review: Rouge Legacy 2 is a fun Rougelite with a variety of different classes and weapons. Each weapon has a different playstyle, and extra things like traits, relics, armor and runes can make each player's experience different.The map generates off a seed, with important rooms being generated in a select pattern (some rooms will always spawn the southmost part of an area while others always spawn on the west- it depends on the room).For a casual player, repeat playthroughs will be fun and rewarding as you deal with punishing traits in order to get a bonus multiplier to your gold.Traits comprise of negative or positive effects that are similar to real-life traits: Colorblindness, IBS, dwarfism, even Veganism, to name a few.For those debilitated by their real-life traits, the game even has a setting for 'House Rules'. These allow you to customize your playstyle to make the game easier for you to play, or add an extra challenge for the masochistic gamer. Want to breeze through the game? Don't let anyone tell you you're playing it wrong- it's all good if it's fun for you.Now, I bought this game with the intent of 100%ing the achievements. After my first completion, I breezed through the game with House Rules at their absolute lowest. After NG+1 (New Game plus), the game expects you to beat it again.And again. And... again.While the option to cut straight to NG+7 is available, and the game allows you to play with House Rules at their absolute cheesiest... If you DON'T take the option to go straight to NG+7, you'll be beating this game at least TWELVE TIMES to get all achievements.While I totally could've skipped straight to NG+7, I instead opted to beat the game for the 6 times so I could see what was different....There wasn't much. After a first playthrough, you'll probably see about 80% of all traits and the game doesn't have much variety beyond that. The remaining 60 hours I spent breezing through NG+1 to NG+8 (and the three challenge modes I needed for other achievements) don't have much difference from the original gameplay. Burdens (challenges you need in order to increase your level of New Game +'s) add some challenge by changing area bosses, making enemies harder, faster, or lifesteal can give a bit of a twist... but the game is basically the same overall.In short, I'd recommend this game to a casual player, because it's a lot of fun. But if you're trying to 100% it... enable house rules and blast through it. It got old after the 40th hour.

_childDocuments_.review: This game represent the best gamers could hope for: the developers actually listened to the feedback given during the life of their first title and produced an impeccable game, where everything has been optimized from the first installment.Graphic design hits the spot here, rooms are bigger and overall feel "cleaner" than before.#Traits have been reworked, no more you need to be stuck with the thief just to gain more gold during early runs!Also the difficulty curve has been greatly improved, not to mention the House Rules section where you can tinker the game to your heart's content in order to find your personal balance between being challenged and being totally frustrated.Writing (characters and dialog) has been explored this time, whereas in the first game the feeling of being lonely was more palpable.Great game overall, my personal score 8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: This game just plays very badly. Your character's movement is very floaty and not precise, but the game asks you to be extremely precise constantly. The movement sections are bad enough because of the physics and this makes the combat terrible. You will walk into a room and be instantly attacked by enemies that are right in front of you, with projectiles getting thrown at you through walls from off screen. The gameplay of "attack once, then run back though the door and repeat" isn't fun, and the game basically forces you to do that constantly. Some rooms are complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, especially the challenge rooms. the challenge rooms honestly just felt like "fail a bunch of times until you memorize the pattern" which is terrible game design for a game like this where I have to restart the entire run to try again, so it's impossible to practice. I'm talking corridors filled with off screen enemies, blind drops into spikes, and extremely unforgiving timers. Playing this game feels like playing a level in super mario maker by someone who had a creative idea for some platforming sections, but then got bored and made a bunch of levels that are just awful enemy spam or extremely tedious navigation levels.I consider myself good at video games and platformers in particular. I've played through most mario games, crash bandicoot, spyro, celeste, cuphead and this game feels so awful to play I don't even want to try to get better. that is my main point of this review. I've played games like this before and enjoyed them. the boss fights are fun enough, but suffer badly from the poor movement. some platforming bits can be enjoyable like doing dash jumps into floating tubes to go into another combo of dashes etc.. but for every one of those there are 5 sections where you have to do extremely precise dash combos through small spiked corridors. And if you get hit once you fail. oh and you probably won't see this exact super precise jump setup for like 2 hours because it's random so... yeah.don't waste your time playing this game, go play shovel knight.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: If you're looking for a quick roguelite fix, a single playthrough of this campaign will definitely do that for you, but don't expect it to be a roguelite to sink 100s of hours into, as it's not really that re-playable after initially completing it. The replayability of this game feels significantly lower compared to other roguelites due to a lack of interesting decisions to make during the run, as both the relics you find AND the starting traits tied to your character are typically too minuscule of bonuses to make or break your run (except for maybe the relic that gives you an extra life). As a result, most runs will play out with you min-maxing the early regions to gain health upgrades and relics, and then hoping you have enough HP to defeat the current region's boss. There really wasn't a single run where I found a cool combo with my relics and traits; all the variability came from the starting class and the starting class alone. To go further into traits and relics, the starting traits were cool to mess with in the first 10 or so hours of the game, but you eventually find out which ones are useful and which ones are too annoying to deal with (the worse traits give you more gold, which is the meta-progression currency in this game). For example, there's one starting trait that makes the game black and white. This is fun at first, but considering that some runs can be over an hour, it's not worth dealing with just for a 30% gold increase. You'll soon find that close to half the traits are this way, and I honestly kinda gave up halfway through and just kept killing my character till I got the most tolerable/favorable traits.  The relics that you find DURING the run are again very tiny upgrades. Considering that after taking a certain amount your max hp starts to go down (though you can upgrade the amount you can take later on), you will eventually do basically the same thing with the starting traits; just exclusively take the ones that are very beneficial to your character, which is like 10% of them. Sometimes I'd go through close to 20 relics in a run and not find one that's worth getting. That being said, I do think it does a couple of interesting things that separates itself from other roguelites. The ability to go back to other regions to gather more gold and upgrades is really neat, and you can even skip over your current region and try to fight through the harder ones for extra gold. I also think the metroidvania upgrades were quite fun, as they both allowed you to properly traverse through the next region AND make the previous regions much easier to complete.Adding onto that, the regions were all very diverse from each other, and required careful thought in completing them. Each one had a natural progression in difficulty; adding fun twists on existing enemies (along with completely new ones), more diversity in platforming, and even new ways to unlock the region's boss. Considering that many roguelites focus on just changing around damage numbers and scenery for their different regions, it was refreshing to see this much work be put into making these regions so distinct from each other. The bosses were also really enjoyable to fight, well at least most of them. They all put on quite the show visually, and had fun attacks that felt satisfying to learn and combat. But I'll also say that some of the later bosses relied a bit too much on projectile spam, and some bosses seem really unfair to specific classes (mainly those who have long attack animations), but even those were still enjoyable nonetheless. The game really does favor quality over quantity with these bosses (I think there's only 8 or so in total), and I think that decision paid off really well. Overall, I don't regret buying it and I really did have a fun time with it, but if I'm being honest I don't see myself coming back to this one anytime soon.

For example, there are several that change the look of the game, turning it into a retro 1990s Mac game or painting everything in sepia tones.When they describe it as a "brutal platformer," they are not kidding. Monsters harm you just by touching them, there are death traps everywhere, and most of the sub-dungeons to gain a special power are full of tricks and deadly pain. _childDocuments_.review: I wish I could give this game a thumbs to the side, or a middling score. There's a super fun game here, honestly, but I couldn't get into it. It ultimately felt to me like each run's real goal was to make the next run easier. The grind is caked right into the DNA of the game and I didn't like it. That being said, I can easily see how many other people would love it. It's got a ton of cool content and variety from run to run and it's a clean package from front to back. As a personal pet peeve, I really disliked the lack of melee interactions. Most enemies attack with various projectiles, and while every class has an answer for those projectiles, there's no block/parry/conversion system to reward interacting with the projectiles (other than not taking damage). Especially since you take damage when touching enemies, I would have liked some kind of system that allows you to strategically interact with enemies, physically, rather than relying on movement and projectile-destroying abilities to control space. I had the same issue with Hollow Knight, which, again, is a personal issue and likely won't annoy most other people.

_childDocuments_.review: So my 82 hours of playtime is to get 100% achievements, YMMV.I generally detest roguelites. They're very popular because anyone can beat them given they invest enough time. Contrast this with Hollow Knight (one of my favorite games) for example where the devs take the view of "some people won't be able to get the good ending and that's ok."Rogue Legacy pushes back against the usual roguelite trend by rewarding skill over grinding in many areas. To try not lose the usual roguelite demographic they added in "house rules" which allows you to effectively cheat by turning on fly mode, disabling contact damage, buffing your damage output etc. Despite this there's still people in the reviews complaining the game is too hard.The point I'm trying to make is, there's people that will have loved Hades or Bastion or Skul or Dead Cells, who won't like Rogue Legacy. _childDocuments_.review: Probably can't recommend it at the moment, for the same reason a lot of people seem to be finding fault in it: the grind is insane. It's nice that they added the house rules so you can still progress even if you don't have a great deal of mechanical skills, but even if you finally give up and turn the house rules on, it'll still take you huge amounts of time to unlock everything. The combat will feel repetitive and old long before you even come close to unlocking some of the upgrades that actually let you experience the game more. I beat all the bosses once, now I wanna complete NG+1 and start turning on some of the burdens to make the game more interesting instead of just the same thing over again, but I can't because even without any burdens NG+1 is kicking my butt. I'll struggle through an hour long run, just to buy one tiny PART of ONE upgrade. They really need to work on the progression and the resolve system to allow players to actually experience some of the more fun mechanics. I've put in 40 hours and still can't afford enough of the resolve upgrades to even buy more than 1-2 relics while wearing armor. I still haven't even found most of the armor upgrades. The castle is like a third of the way completed, and I'm lucky if I can afford 1/20th of a strength upgrade after a long run. Giving players like 50% more resolve to play with and 50% more gold than they currently do would go a long way towards making players actually feel like they're continuing to progress as the game goes on.

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Legacy 2 has more of everything than the original Rogue Legacy.That's usually, but not always, a good thing.The core moment to moment gameplay is better and very satisfying, with more emphasis on platforming in some areas and more combat options and more movement options. Every class restores mana on hitting an enemy so every class can use magic throughout, and class abilities (talents) have their own variable cooldowns. Each class also has its own unique weapon with some variations possible, and a unique ability to the class. The weapon, spell and talent can be changed in specific rooms in the castle, so even a class with a weapon you don't like (Ronin with the slow Katana, for instance) can be turned into one you do (finding the Greatsword). There's a lot of incentive to switch between the 15 classes (Valkyrie is my favorite!) and do well with as many classes as you can, and most are at least good - the mix is much better than the original!However, the overall gameplay loop is hindered by the fact that there's more of it. The castle has 6 areas compared to 4 in the original, and to see all the content Rogue Legacy 2 has to offer, you have to beat NG+6. The original had nothing new beyond NG+2, and both games only scale stats past this point. There's a slow drip of new boss and challenge unlocks, and new lore and dialogue on each of NG+1 through NG+7, compared to the original where I believe you can see everything in the first NG. Rogue Legacy 2 is designed for the grind.And yes, that means there's more grind. The original caps out at 523 upgrades. I beat NG+7 at 760 upgrades, and this was far from maxed out. This is actually a good thing - the game is designed to let you keep scaling, your equipment keep scaling, and the enemies keep scaling, should you want to progress to NG+20, or 50, or 100. At about 2-2.5 hours for each clear of NG+5 through NG+7, I don't have the interest in dumping several hundred hours to make numbers get bigger when relatively, I still take 2-4 hits to defeat most enemies and still die in 6-11 without healing. It would just be more playing for the sake of more playing, and after 60 hours I'd had enough. It took me another 20 to complete everything meaningful.So what meaningful content am I talking about? Well, the characters have more personality, which is great! Between runs they can give you little bits of dialogue to add depth, and there's more of them. The docks are a nice place and fairly charming... but you spend barely any time there. Instead of 25 diary entries - of which 2 are given for free - each area has 6 to 9 diary entries or memories to access, at most one per area per character. These add a lot of depth to why the events of the game are happening and this is one place where the "more" is a great benefit. If only the endgame lore came faster...Each area has its own challenging boss. These are all well designed fights except one, and I'm willing to believe I just never hit on the right method. On each new game plus, you can choose to upgrade each boss in sequence to their prime version, making them even harder. These are also great challenges except for two. Defeating the prime versions unlocks their last memories, which are genuinely some of the best backstory in the game. About half of the information was inferrable, but in context it's always much more interesting in how everything fits together. Each boss and prime boss also unlock a scar - a specific challenge similar to the boss remixes of the original. There are 16 (really more like 15) of these, compared to 5 boss remixes in the original. These are often extremely difficult to complete and unfortunately sometimes unfair. Throwing 2 bosses in the same arena only works when you always have an out. When the only dodge is to go over, and the other boss is blocking over, you're getting hit and that's no fun. 5 of these are time challenges with a specific class to destroy targets in a specific environment, and getting gold on these requires mastering the class and the route. Ultimately, this is a good place for there to be more: though getting gold on combat scars is more of a grind than it needs to be, requiring a win with at minimum 5 different classes. And probably more like 7 or 8 in practice.Overall, there's a lot more to like about Rogue Legacy 2. Just be prepared to have to play a lot more of it than you might want to, in order to get everything you want out of it. I don't regret my time spent with the game, but unlike the original I don't think I'll have a desire to return to it.

_childDocuments_.review: Short Version:Just like the first rogue legacy but better with more stuff. Can equip gear, upgrade gear, add enchantments to character, upgrade enchantments, can level up character, can "build castle" aka upgrading character and npcs further, can complete challenges to extend all upgrades for further upgrading, new game + feature, NO MULTIPLAYER, no leaderboards, can run on a low end pc, more story/npc dialogue, fair price for content, anyone of any skill level can get achievements due to the ability to modify game difficulty as much as needed via "house rules" in options setting to make game easer OR harder if they want.Long Version:A fun and challenging roguelike that is definitely harder then the first rogue legacy (the difficulty tag given by the devs 100% warranted). The amount of upgrades you can do to your character is also MUCH larger then in the first one with armor included in this version of the game. Also just like the first one, this one is not and most likely will not ever be, multiplayer. Also just like the first it has the new game + feature and this time, there's more to it then just increase the dmg/hp/size of the monsters and bosses. Much more story and character dialogue then in the first one as well. Also, your given the option to make the game either easier or harder via the house rules in the option settings (the game is perfect by default in my personal opinion at the difficulty setting it is on). Using the house rules will not disable achievements as a heads up (there is an achievement for using/enabling house rules once, so if your an old school elitist/purist that doesint want their achievements tainted by what some might consider cheating via making the game easier or dont like changing the default game in anyway,  dont touch it). Obviously this devalue's or increases the value of the achievements to some but as i just said, you can just not enable it, ever. I personally think the game is legit perfect as is, since, like the first game, just increases in difficulty with each new game + you get and you can always grind more if your having trouble, or if you just wanna boss rush and get further, just use the architect to lock the castle until you down the bosses you need to down to get further. At the end of the day though, anyone will be able to get the achievements in this game, regardless if your a god, or a disabled gamer that has to take things a bit slower due to life giving you rotten lemons. For it is clear, the devs of rogue legacy know, that this great game of theirs is mainly about one thing, having FUN (or going ssj and throwing your controller at your pc screen, shattering it into a million pieces  in a fit of unbridled blind rage over 9000/beating your mouse worse then a serial pedo in prison who choose to stay in general population rather then go into protective custody lol which ever you prefer)Now your thinking "Is it worth the price". In my opinion it is. Their is alot more substance to this game then the first and the upgrades that you can do to your character is many times more then the first. It is almost a gaurentee that you will achieve that which every game price should be based on "Will i get at least 1 hour of fun/entertainment/gameplay out of this for every 1 dollar i spent on this".That pretty much wraps up this review. Other then everything i just talked about above, it isint  that much different then the first game. Just enough was added to it to give it a new, fresh feel, and yet not too much to make it feel like something completely different. More of the "same old, same old" saying and not like the saying "If you cant do it better, do it different". Hopefully this was helpful in helping you make decision if this game is for you, if not, just buy it, play it for an hour and 30 mins, and if you dont like it, just refund it. Steam is VERY good when it comes to refunds.Happy gaming peeps!

_childDocuments_.review: modernizes the formula that made the original successful, and implements new systems that make playing longer much more appealing. Cellar Door games clearly learned from the countless roguelites that have released over the past few years.  has more variety in classes, weapons, skills, etc. than the original, and introduces new systems in new game plus that allow you to adjust the difficulty of the game, and continue to upgrade your estate as much as you'd like. Similar to , talking to the NPC characters inside, and mostly outside of your runs provides new dialogue and eventually rewards you with resources. Furthermore,  is far larger than the original. There are six different areas to explore, each have their own gimmick that needs to be discovered and learned before being approached. I enjoyed the implementation of these mechanics because you have time to master all the prior traversal skills before unlocking new ones that allow you to tackle new areas, but also make completing previous areas and solving the game's fairy chest challenges much easier. All classes within  can be leveled up, providing permanent stat bonuses to every character you play as; this was a mixed inclusion for me, because I enjoyed the stat bonuses, but typically I stuck to the few classes that I had the most fun playing as. The art style is very similar to the first, but undoubtedly cleaner, and the same goes for the platforming. Cellar Doors has been advertising the game as a Metriodvania, and for good reason. This is some of the smoothest platforming I've experienced since I played  a few years ago. You can chain together jumps, air dashes, attacks, spin kicks, and movement talents to traverse entire areas without ever touching the ground. The music is also a major treat. I really enjoyed the different area themes. I became very addicted to this game quickly, once I completed all objectives I lost motivation to play anymore, as it essentially becomes the same grind over and over for more stat bonuses, that only scale your power to increasing danger of the castle with each run. However, I can't complain about much. I spent around 80 hours with  and made it all the way to NG+9 before calling it. It's a fantastic roguelite, wonderful platformer, and the best I've personally experienced in the genre since .

_childDocuments_.review: While I liked the concept of the first Rogue Legacy and enjoyed my time playing the game when it was released, I never finished it. It was too repetitive, the bosses were uninspired, practically the very same enemy 4 times, the difficulty curve wasn't balanced enough and so on.This one is a huge improvement over the first one. The bosses are interesting, the progression is way more satisfying and there are simply a lot more things to do. I liked what they did with the graphics. They nailed it. If I didn't know the game is actually in full 3D, I wouldn't have guessed until maybe hours into the game. There are couple of giveaways, but overall, the game looks and feels like it's genuine 2D. There are quite a lot of classes this time. Some of them I don't really enjoy playing, maybe because I don't understand how do you suppose to play with them, so I mostly used the same classes over and over again. But traits give enough vareity to make most playthroughs interesting. The only thing I think the first game handled better is the feel of succession. When your character dies and the next one takes their place, it doesn't really feel like these characters are connected to each other in any way. They seem like just the next dude to play with rather than a descendant in a single lineage. I'm not sure what the reason is, but it felt more like it in the first game. This isn't really of any importance anyway and has no impact on gameplay, so whatever.While I don't think the game is particularly groundbreaking or offers anything new or exciting other games didn't offer before it, Rouge Legacy 2 is definitely a solid rougelite and is great for killing time.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to give this game some exposure and hope the devs get a chance to improve this game further, but right now, RL2 is quite brief and limited. Devs, I hope you are listening:After 2-3 hours, you've seen everything the game has to offer, unlocked everything and killed the boss. That's obviously not great for a game like this. Even while unlocking things and making progress, knowing that the game will be over within the next hour kind of killed the mood for me.Speaking of mood, the music in RL2 is good, but not quite as energetic as in the first game.The traits are once again really cool - especially the ones that change up your regular moves!! - but the ones that impact vision are mostly too drastic. You'll sometimes start out and immediately go "Ok, I better kill myself" because you can't see anything AGAIN because of a new trait with an unknown effect.Some of the stats are not clearly laid out at all. Upgrading the amount of bonus gold from ebilitating traits for example only says "+0,2". When you spend all your gold on upgrading that only to realize that it effectively only gives 2% extra gold, you'll be a bit angry. A better tooltip would work wonders here. The classes similarly could do with a bit more information. Why not show the effect of a class on HP, MP, Int, Attack, Crit chance, Armor etc.?Some of the spells are really underwhelming while costing a ton of mana to use. The magic eight ball is simply not as fun to use as something like the bouncing spike balls from the first game. Certain spells like the molten clump (that had no activation time or lag in the first game) now stop your character dead in their tracks, which feels out of place in a fast paced action game. Lowering mana costs and lowering mana gained per hit to compensate would make mana management more meaningful and fun again.The rooms offering relics in exchange for taking massive damage feel kinda meh right now. Generally only the one that simply heals you is really worth picking up, which feels like a missed opportunity.Health pickups feel kinda off right now as well. They heal quite a lot but are completely random. Knowing where food will 100% be and saving that for when you need it was a fun part of RL1 and I see no reason why it should no longer be present.The reason why RL2 feels a bit "boring" next to RL1 right now, is that you have less possibility to make a PLAN right now. Here's an example: RL1: "I'll pick a miner and try to go to the tower straight away (even though that area is way too tough) - let me pick gold gain runes too. I'll be weak, but if I can just get a few chests it will be worth it!"RL2: "2 out of 3 choices for heirs have limited vision, so I have to go with the third. I can't change my gear because the upgrade system is incredibly limited. Guess I'll just farm some gold and die so I can get those last 2 int upgrades (which I only pick because after 2 hours, there are no other options left.)"Bottom line: The devs need to get to work! I hope they can hire more staff with the money from the EA.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is brilliant and so addicting. I'm so glad I purchased it. I played the first one quite a bit and enjoyed it, but this game is just brilliant. It's a bit more "rogue-lite" than say Dead Cells, but the huge progression path adds to the enjoyment and keeps you coming back for more. The gameplay and combat feel flawless and the progression grind gives you that incentive to keep honing your skills. Tons of class variety, tons of interesting spells, definitely going on the all time favorites list.If I had one bit of constructive criticism, I'm nearing the end of my first NG (NG+ in this game isn't just bolted on; it's a core part of the game) and I feel like the resolve mechanic just means only being able to safely take 1 or 2 relics a run at most which is kind of a bummer. Honestly, I just really don't like anything about the resolve system. I enjoy full clearing but encountering all these relics that I just can't equip is kind of a bummer. I'd love it if it were changed, or at least there was a house rule that I could utilize on at least NG to just disable it so I could see what things are like with relic stacking. I get that resolve is just another stat to grind up, but punishing deep exploration just seems to go against the spirit of a procedurally generated Metroid-vania.Anyway, if you're on the fence, definitely pick up this game. Even if you're a casual player that found the first game frustratingly difficult or find rogue-lites too challenging in general, the house rules option will allow you to customize the difficulty as you see fit, which is a great addition even if I'm not utilizing it.

_childDocuments_.review: Roguelike and Roguelite games are my favourite genre, I've played different kinds including Slay the Spire, Hades, Into the Breach, Binding of Isaac, Spelunky, Risk of Rain etc. I would say that Slay the Spire and Rogue Legacy 2 are my favourites. RL2 has amazing depth and replayability, but most importantly it is extremely fun and very easy to jump into for 10 minutes or 1 hour. It is difficult at first but when you master the movement and spin kicks it become effortless to move around the map and slay enemies. It becomes super relaxing and enjoyable, being able to plan out your build with your armour at the start, and relics you pick up on the way. When you die it never really feels bad because you instantly see cool new character options and immediately begin thinking of new builds for them and want to jump into the action straight away. The bosses are very fun and unique, the biomes are interesting and cool to explore. The randomness in the game is done very well, and it's clear the devs enjoy the idea of things being random too, and have balanced it well. The new relic that gives you 3 random relics is a great way of trying out relics that you wouldn't otherwise choose for example. Gives each run a unique experience and makes you want to play more. Overall a fantastic game and most importantly super fun! 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed Rogue Legacy 1 a lot, but lost a lot of steam after beating it once. I wasn't in a rush to pick up this game, and did admittedly during a sale. But then I got utterly addicted to it. As of writing, I managed to hit thread 22.The balance of rogue-like-ness on display here achieves what a lot of others in it's class can't do - there's a legitimate feeling of progression that's somewhat drip fed, while still giving you that chase to max out a stat or see something to the end. The platforming controls are, dare I say, some of the best I've ever played for a 2D platformer. It's nearly Mega Man-esque with how tight and precise they are, but with a rising level of speed somewhat akin to a bullet hell at some points.If you like any of those things - roguelikes, 2D platforming, Metroidvania (search action) - there's just a ton here for you to really sink your teeth into. I'm really looking forward to see what Cellar Door Games does next!

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Legacy 2 is one of the more addictive, binge-able games I've played. The progression from mid-run permanent upgrades (the more "metroidvania" style progression) and the purchased upgrades (the rogue-lite progression) combine to make you feel gradually more powerful. Combine that with your own skill improvements over time and you end up a completely different player by the end of your run. Even just playing the base game to a standard ending gets you a lot of great content and is itself pretty challenging.If you choose to pursue the additional content, come prepared. There is a TON of optional content, from side quests to collectibles to skill challenges to New Game +. The NG+ provides additional challenges that aren't just more HP and Damage on enemies, but also new types of some enemies, and completely revamped boss fights which make replaying the game a very different experience, and definitely keep it from getting too easy. All of this content could easily consume 200 hours of playtime.That doesn't even touch on the latest update, which now provides more of a true Roguelike experience, and some additional challenge modes limiting your lives.The first Rogue Legacy was a fun game, but showed its age a bit. This game looks amazing, feels great, has excellent combat and platforming, and simply improves upon the original in every conceivable way. I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: A big step up from the first game. The new classes are fun, the bosses are challenging without bordering on being annoying, the new mechanic (such as void waves you can dash through) are a nice addition, and there is enough pizza to eat. I also like the silly little additions that were added later on, such as the perks that make everything look Halloweeney or Christmasey.If there is one gripe i'd have with this game, it's that the power levels of the bosses don't feel ramped up over time. The Void Beasts were FAR easier than Lamech, and Irad was FAR easier than Enoch. I didn't have that feeling with the first game. It gave you a reason to do gold runs and upgrade your castle before fighting a boss head on, but in this game i had (mini)bosses that i killed on my first or second attempt just by brute forcing them with lots of health and damage. I barely even upgraded my mana or intelligence because why use spells when you can SLASH GOOD, SMASH HARD.I don't think i will keep playing around with the burden "new game plus" system, but it was a good 50+ hours spent.

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome game, just like the original Rogue Legacy!It has many new stuff to learn, which is, at first, really hard, but it adds so much for the game and makes it really like a whole new game.If you were/are really addicted to the first game, like me, you will probably take some time to learn those new stuffs, but it really pays off. By the time I'm writting this comment, the game is not fully complete, but the content it already has, doesn't seem incomplete at all. The things it lacks are not related to mechanical or anything, just new areas, so it doesn't break the experience. I have played for some hours and I haven't reached the moment that I thought I should go for the not realeased ares.I received it as a gift and I'm loving it.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: An example of a game sequel that does so much right to improve upon the original. The first games pixel art was well done but a bit bland, where as this games 2.5d style has consistently wowed me with both hand drawn backgrounds and characters that sometimes need a magnifying glass to tell they aren't also hand animated. But even the ones where you can tell they're 3d are still great visual designs that all feel cohesive in this world together while all being unique.Controls were responsive in the first, but a little strange with having two dedicated dash buttons for left and right, where this game feels so natural and I can never blame a failed dodge on anything other than myself. Nor have encounter designs rarely felt like I couldn't evade a hit somehow. This combined with crisp animations makes basic movement and attacks satisfying.Story is different, but in the same setting, with enough assorted bits of humor, character personality, and dashes of worldbuilding to make reading logs enjoying to seek out for it's own sake, as well as drip feeding clues for things to find through gameplay.Permanent stats and metroidvania movement upgrades come at a decent pace; unique for a rogue like, allowing distinctive challenges for each zone, and relic upgrades gives some interesting decisions to make on the fly. Cool builds can be made, and as you play longer, you get more relics and resolve to make wackier builds, and more consistently with rerolls. But you can always rely on your personal skill even without them.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: I played through the first game and it was very enjoyable, good for it's time in the infancy of roguelites. Playing through this now, and seeing all the improvements they've made, and the expansions of how the game content works, the class variety, the map and movement design improvements, and so much more. This is a fantastic sequel. They've really outdone themselves.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an utterly perfect sequel to one of the founding fathers of the modern roguelite. The movement feels like an absolute dream, the progression doesn't have walls like the first game could, the class variety is ace, the reworked relic system is fantastic, just everything is at least as good if not better than the first game. And I'm not even *really* done, because the NG+ cycles have importance now! You get new story bits and boss fights in each NG+ instead of just numbers going up, and you can customize exactly how it is that enemies scale up!For those NOT in the know, Rogue Legacy is a platformer-roguelite using preconstructed rooms in procedurally generated death labyrinths. The ultimate goal is to kill each dungeon boss and take on the final sequence of the game; progress is stored in the form of movement abilities, killed bosses, and certain other sidequests as well as equipment recipes you find to purchase completed works of back in town.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: So far, I've enjoyed what I've seen and played of this game.The new additions to the game are fun, somewhat challenging and adds more flavor to the game as its successor to an already good game.Will recommend it, but you might want to wait for it's actual release if you want to finish a game in a few sittings.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: It's pretty much the same game as the first but with prettier graphics. Extremely bare-bones, even for early access.  All current content present in the game can be seen in a matter of hours. I get the feeling they rushed this out to capitalize on the hype from the original and get some extra funds for development. I'll reserve my final judgement for the full release, but this isn't especially promising to be quite honest. Also they seem to have hired a scat (feces) fetishist for the writing as almost all flavor text and dialogue mentions it, the "humor" is atrocious. 6.3/10 in it's current state. A bit above average, nothing special. Extremely bare bones. I get that it's early access, but damn. Be aware of this before you purchase.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game's so much fun, cellar door took everything good about the first game and added more cool stuff on top of it.While it doesn't have much content at the moment, the gameplay is really good. every class feels unique and fun to play and the art style is really good!definitely pick this one up if you liked the first one, but if you want a bit more content,  then I suggest you wait a couple of months.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: one of, if not the best roguelite. It's very fun and has lots of variety and repeatability. In my opinion it has a nearly perfect learning curve, it rarely felt like I was truly stuck and more like I was making progress and learning the whole time. My only possible complaint is the enemies are slightly unvaried but they do have different abilities and slight visual changes between zones. All in all it is definitely worth the money in my opinion.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't finished this game yet and I usually wait until I finish a game to review it, but due to the Steam Game Nomination 2022 I'll write a little one early.In short this is a fantastic roguelite with crisp controls and a satisfying play loop.  I like that the combat varies based on what type of weapon your heir wields and that you only get to choose between a select random number of heirs after each death.  This keeps you learning how to use the different weapons and to find which you like best.  I found though through playing even weapons I didn't particularly like at first became fun to play as I got more skilled navigating the dungeons.The meta progression system also feels very rewarding, which for me in a roguelite is very important.  You really do feel like you're able to get stronger through unlocking meta progress but also through getting more skilled at combat and navigation.Another plus is the little puzzles that are randomly generated in the dungeon sometimes which is a nice break from just combat and they are a way to further unlock meta progress.Oh and one last thought, this is a great game for the Steam Deck because you can quite out during a dungeon run and re-enter the run later when resuming the game.  I very much appreciate that I don't have to stay to finish the entire run just because I ran out of time.  Very important with mobile gaming.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: The game makes a solid first impression but absolutely falls on its face due to bad balance and inconsistencies throughout. First off: it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. You get hit and even die many times to offscreen enemies before you can see them. There are warnings for SOME projectiles.Enemies even below your level deal huge damage. Everything hits like a truck which really does not help when most enemies fire multiple projectiles per attack. How can you prevent this damage? Get better armour? Nope. You can only block 35% of all incoming damage at base. Upgrade it? Each upgrade gives you a whopping 1% increase. (Though there is a rune that does 10%)Speaking of upgrades, most of them are so incremental and expensive that they just feel crap. You can and will spend many  runs dying and buying a single upgrade. The whole point of the game is frequent upgrading but you have to grind out whole areas with crap traits just to see more than a couple per run.Major Issues:The game is so inconsistent and it sucks to find these edge cases. Some abilities can block small medium or large projectiles. What's the difference between small and large? Size? NO. Each type of projectile just has a size you have to figure out. Some massive projectiles can be blocked with small projectile blocks. Some large projectiles can be blocked with small projectile blocks. Some projectiles just can't be blocked at all. Does it tell you this? NO. I went to fight a projectile based boss with Chef (due to the reflection ability) but quickly found it was useless since these projectiles were inexplicably unblockable.While we're talking about inconsistencies, the spin kick is awful for this. Spin kick the projectiles with the auras, right? NO. Some projectiles (like the little souls) can be spin kicked without auras. Spin kick spikes? Only sometimes. Dash attacking is the king of this. Why would I bother using a dash attack that gets me hit only on some enemies?Too much new game+ in my new game! You can't even unlock half of the armours in your first playthrough. They are locked behind scars and new game+ requirements. Scars seem like a cool extra challenge but you have to do them to get higher level armours and runes. Scars suck too by the way, the rating system is awful. S+ but no reward? ♥♥♥♥ off.Bosses feel like such sponges and they give you barely anything for beating them. I spent my whole run getting here with a decent character to kill a boss and they drop less than one good run's gold. Some of them just suck to fight too. They also have huge damage and you can easily die within seconds to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.I just got grinded out in the end. I don't want to have to farm an annoying area with a terrible character just so I can get 3 upgrades. If there was a house rule to turn up the gold amount I'd probably have finished it but there isn't, so I didn't.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: I felt that it's very hard. I can play Hades, Dead Cells, Skul, Undermine. They are hard as a Roguelike, but I feel this game is much harder. Every run feels the same, the closest is Dead Cells but with random relics that doesn't match DC's random weapon combos.It also feels very grindy. Story dialogue is not interesting.Unless you're a very skilled, fast-reflex players, I don't recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: I was just browsing through my library and stumbled upon ...Definitively my next big favourit! Just writing those lines makes me want to plug in the controller and start it up again.But, as in early access ... and not really writing reviews that early in development, just my two cents on gameplay and maybe progression of development.I really like how different the classes feel in comparion to the first game. I'd love to see more of those although i see a big balance issue between a beefy class like the babarian and the mana depending mage. I like the bowslinger and his mechanics a lot though ... Want me to expanding that list?I'd love to see an summoner kind of playstyle, maybe with his own matching theme ... I'd could see some kind of Dracomancer, throughing flames and dragon eggs against thouse skeletons and (a bit of generic but familiar at least) magic flame turrets and swinging metal glove kinda thingy fellows. Or even a dark magic force wielding Necromancer remote controling dark shadow floating clouds and 1 or 2 smaller Imps on the enemy ...And what I always loved about the series are the Heirdom and the different visual or gameplay affecting Strains of the cute little Newborn Knight I'm throwing away in the flames the next room or two, after realizing:"Julia, your pacifism just doesn't work in this cruel world."Expecting a much longer experience in the future, you may implement a few more "easy mode gameplay" kinda Gameplay Strains of Heirdom Traits. Not making it too easy but maybe affecting gameplay in a way, it's more of my own unique gamestyle way. I'm a hoarder, I never use mana or potions or any ressource a game give me.
