_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: Highly recommend, if you're looking for a creative and fun rogue lite. Mixes challenging combat with challenging jumping puzzles. Through meta progression getting deeper into a run feels natural and achievable. I enjoy playing it on the steam deck a lot, but gamepad rumble has to be deactivated in the options otherwise the game freezes on taking or doing damage.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Legacy 2 has taken everything that made the first game a lovable adventure and iterated it in clever and beautiful ways. The cell-drawn character sprites are charming and lead you to a sense of false security in how nasty and truly difficult the game can be. While numerous games have aped the iterative rogue-like formula, none achieve this level of funny, cute, and downright compelling the the Devs have achieved. I look forward to spending another 60+ hours in this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10, its new traits and random perks add so much depth and new excitement. I now go into a low chance run and have hope to somehow through relics destroy my foes! AMAZING!! Please keep the great work!The combat is vastly improved, the art is wonderful, and all around i had the best time. The title is worthy of coming years awards and i hope to play this for many more hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: Movement and attacking etc  really good. Reading some of the reviews, I was concerned about weapons or movement feeling stiff/clunky, plus I saw someone complain about threats coming in from off screen. Both of these seem like non-issues.For the weapons that force you to stop moving while attacking, you can cancel the animation with a dash so you're never just stuck in a follow-through animation, with the notable exception of one secret weapon I found that has this as a deliberate downside. This does mean you have to plan around attacking and then dashing in one direction or the other afterwards but this kind of limitation makes it more interesting since you have to constantly be planning your next move in detail.Off-screen threats/dangers can mostly be seen by scrolling the camera (hold left-alt and then move around with the movement keys). Off-screen projectiles are noted with a warning symbol at the edge of the screen.To me it feels like exactly what's promised: Rogue Legacy but bigger and better and more. Also, I personally like the art style. It's an easy recommend for anyone who likes skilly platformers and roguelikes. As for the current state of the early access, it certainly feels like it's got a purchase-justifying amount of content. I've seen four regions so far and I'm just starting to get really familiar with the second one, 11 hours into the game (presumably people who were better at Rogue Legacy 1 than I can progress a lot faster than I am, though...).
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: Watch this opinion form in real time:Rogue Legacy 2 is still very early in development, even for an Early Access game. So far it isn't doing a ton that the previous title didn't, but it is still doing it very well.Included in the game so far, as of this review, is one complete biome that features a boss, two traversal upgrades to unlock, and various blue prints and runes to find in chests. There is also an unfinished biome that is fun to explore, but doesn't serve too much of a purpose at the moment, outside of getting a sneak peak at things to come.If you enjoyed the first game, you will ultimately enjoy this as well. If you aren't interested in following along with development and just want a complete roguelike metroidvania-ish adventure to go, you might be better served for waiting for the full release, or at least some major content updates.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: Lots of content to bite with a robust New Game+ system, an extensive skill tree, and over 15 score-based challenges to find and complete.Very accessible with the unmatched House Rules system. Allowing you to reduce enemy HP and damage, disable contact damage, or even enable Flight so you can skip difficult platforming sections.You can even  enemy HP and damage with House Rules, so if you find it a bit too easy you can make it harder. I genuinely hope future games follow this level of customizability.Well worth whatever you spend.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent follow up to one of my all time favorite games. Initially, I was a little concerned when I bought into this game during early access. I definitely feel that they put the game out too early, it wasn't ready. It was unpolished and lacking content. I actually dismissed the game completely until I had it recommended to me by a friend. I figured that I own it, so I should give it another chance. I'm certainly glad that I did because the game not only lives up to the original, but even surpasses it.Movement in this game just feels so incredibly smooth. Because of this, it may be one of my favorite 2D platformers of all time. Everything concerning the movement and combat of the game just feels incredibly tight. The hitboxes are dialed in to perfection. When you die, you totally understand that it was your fault and not some jank within the game.If I had to critique the game at all, I would say that I wasn't necessarily the biggest fan of the new skill tree, it feels like there's just too much there. There are too many options and many of which feel a bit arbitrary or unnecessary. But outside of that, the game is nearly flawless. If you enjoyed the first, you'll love this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: Hoo buddy. If you liked Rogue Legacy 1, pick up this game. Now. That is literally all you need to know if you've played rogue legacy before.The content is relatively lacking as of the first release, but I've still gotten a good 7 hours in because the gameplay loop is so polished. Bugfix patches are common, as well.I can't wait to see where this game goes.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: Great gameplay mechanics and progression system with a lot of things to upgrade. Enjoyable artstyle and music. Relatively tight controls and game feels fluid especially after you get some movement upgrades throughout the game.However, some aspects of level design and enemy design hold it back a bit for me. Some rooms have so much projectile spam it makes you think you were playing a clunkier Touhou game. Also using regular mobs (with more projectile spam), supersizing them and throwing 2 of them in a small room isn't exactly the most interesting and fun boss design, which happens more than once in this game.Would still recommend as a fun roguelite game.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty fun game, but at a certain point the upgrades no longer do much of anything against the ever increasing damage scaling and it crosses over to long-run grinding for extremely expensive upgrades with essentially zero gains (without any house rules, mind you). Other than that wall there stopping the progression system dead in it's tracks, the game itself has very few faults, the controls are tight, the sound isn't grating (effects, music repetition, etc) and it is genuinely fun.Game feels tighter on PC with a controller and high refresh rate display compared to the Deck, but the Deck is where I spent most of my time with it.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game :-) I am amazed by how these guys manage scaling and the interconnections of the upgrades and skills, the team working on the back side of this game is extreamly diligent and smart!! - I already want an expansion or DLC, imagine going into the green house, deeper in the town, deeper in the fungi cave... love this game, labor of love, expertice of systems.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: Recommending the game, but also suggesting you may want to wait longer to pick it up as there isn't much content here yet. This is a game I enjoy replaying and getting it in early access just lets me keep playing it more as new content releases, though there isn't much at this time. There's a "Day till next patch" countdown in the game that just gets me excited to see what the new content will contain. I'm excited to play this through it's development!
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic game.  Kept me hooked through playing all the way up to New Game 20!  The first rogue legacy was great, this one blows it out of the water.  For any wondering, no need to play Rogue Legacy 1 before playing 2.  This is basically a better version of the first game.  If you enjoy platformers and rogue lites, this is your game.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: It's very hard, but not in a way I find fun.You can only take a handful of hits before dying. There aren't many healing options. You don't have a dodge with iframes. Bosses take a lot of hits to die, but as with regular mooks you'll die in 5 or so mistakes.You have to run through the randomized dungeon each time you want to fight the boss. I think there's an option to "lock" the dungeon into a set form, but I didn't see it. But even so, it is likely a long run through deadly monsters and traps each time.You can improve your stats over time, but I don't find this satisfying. It didn't take long to upgrade my damage to mooks would die in one or two hits. That brought the difficulty down considerably, but this feels kind of backwards to me. I feel like the game should start out kind of basic and simple, and get harder as you go. Instead it starts out real hecking brutal, and eases off as you get upgrades. I don't feel like I earned a win when I know I made a bunch of mistakes, but my time investment shifted the game's numbers in my favor. You might be thinking "well that's leveling!"  Leveling is stupid in action games. Fight me.You have a weird "spin kick" move that lets you bounce on enemies and some parts of the scenery. I'm not really a fan of bouncing on enemy's heads for 10% damage until they die, but that might be a winning strategy.The game's not all bad, though. The art is fun. The class ideas are cool. I really like the chef- they can deflect enemy projectiles and cook themselves a healing meal a few times. The duelist has a dodge roll like I'd want to be standard.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: I love the new concept of the remastered masterpiece that was the original game , Rogue Legacy.The mechanic really give a flavor of new challenges that await eager players with every single re-run of the map , providing challengers a fun and new experience with each trial.I do miss few aspects of the old game , but seeing that this is just 60% done , i am expecting to see some old features brought back up from the previous game.Overall an exciting game that isn't too expensive and provides a massive amount of hours to use in your free time.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: Very out of date design, basically no map design, no synergy. Unnecessary grinding. One tip -- don't update everything, but focus on few things to update, otherwise you will run out of coins all the time. Boss fight is very counter intuitive, difficult because of the game design. to be fair, it's an average quality because the graphic and action and everything else is not bad, you can play it while listen to podcast. But I don't think it's a good roguelike game after you played games like Hades.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: A must play, high-end of rogue lites, such as hades or dead cells... This sequel has a lot of great features. Classes are all really fun to play with a nice skill cap. Bosses have this hollow knight feelin and got enhanced versions in a large ng+ system similar to hades, nice replay value. Some easter eggs too...If you like action/plaformin games you can't pass, be brave and good luck to all of your heirs !!!
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: I thoroughly enjoyed Rogue Legacy 2.  Just a really well executed 2d platformer roguelike that's well worth a play for fans of the genre.  I put in 275 hours and I only regret something like 15 or so of the hours I spent trying to beat True Rogue mode.  The first playthrough is definitely the most fun, so if you're starting to get tired of it, don't feel pressured to play additional threads to get all the prime bosses, but if you're like me and having a good time, I did find pushing through ng+7 to get all the bosses to be a nice manageable challenge to work through.The special modes are a bit hidden (you have to create a new save slot after beating the game to play Thanatophobia or True Rogue) and are fine to skip.  I do feel accomplished for having beaten True Rogue, but the lack of healing opportunities between the last 3 bosses is just brutal after having to wade through a tough run at the whims of RNG up until that point.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: very fun. challenging like the first. Longer though and overall more difficult to keep hitting the manor upgrades. Feels like it does take a lot more grinding or otherwise some really strong runs. I don't feel the relics play a huge part in it since I find them rather rare on my runs and healing is very sparse/rare so taking any damage at all feels rather punishing. gameplay loops is great and the bosses are fun
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Legacy 2

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Legacy 2 is what you'd get if you mashed Rogue Legacy and a sequel together. Every time you die, your children will succeed you, and each child is unique. Your daughter might be a Colourblind Archer, and your son could be a Pacifistic Chef. Either way, one of them is getting conscripted.

name: Atelier Ryza 2: Lost Legends & the Secret Fairy
detailed_description: Digital Deluxe Edition [Set Contents] ● The main game “Atelier Ryza 2: Lost Legends & the Secret Fairy” ● Kurken Island Gathering Tour Progress to a certain point in the game to unlock some of the gathering areas of the previous title “Atelier Ryza”. Areas featured: Traveler's Road (from Shipyard), Pixie Forest (from Flower Guard's Garden), Maple Delta (from Sweet River), Weissberg Volcano (from Smoky Mountain Path), Meteor Castle (from Heatwave Gate) ● Another Style Costume Set A set of 21 costumes, 3 each for the following characters: Ryza, Lent, Tao, Klaudia, Patricia, Serri, and Clifford. ● Summer Memories Costume Set Includes: “Summer Adventure!” costume for Ryza that was featured as an early-purchase bonus for the previous title; “Another Fashion” costume set and “Summer Style” costume set featured in the Digital Deluxe edition. 16 costumes for Ryza, Lent, Tao, and Klaudia, 4 each. ● Helpful Items Set A set of four different items to help you out in the early game. They will be added to the Container in the Atelier. Items featured: Wind Shoes (increases movement speed), Traveler's Coat (increases EXP gain), True Handmade Staff (increases AP gain), Uni Charm (boosts stats, health recovery, and skill power). ● All You Need! Gem Pack 100,000 gems that can be used for item rebuilds and other. Gems become available as you progress through the game. Note: - Please beware that this title is can also be purchased separately, and as apart of the “Atelier Ryza 2: Lost Legends & the Secret Fairy Ultimate Edition”. Ultimate Edition [Season Pass bonus] - 'Mysterious Book Alchemist' Costume for Ryza [Set Contents] ● Atelier Ryza 2: Lost Legends & the Secret Fairy Digital Deluxe Edition ● Atelier Ryza 2: Season Pass: features 12 DLC listed below that will be released in stages starting from March 2021. [Content included in the Season Pass] ① Ryza's Swimsuit 'Tropical Summer' ② Lent's Swimsuit 'Beach Flag King' ③ Tao's Swimsuit 'School Trip' ④ Klaudia's Swimsuit 'Black Monokini' ⑤ Patricia's Swimsuit 'White Beach Corset' ⑥ Clifford's Swimsuit 'Ocean Treasure' ⑦ Serri's Swimsuit 'Bitter Chocolate' ⑧ Recipe Expansion Pack 'The Art of Synthesis' ⑨ Recipe Expansion Pack 'The Art of Battle' ⑩ Additional Area 'Keldorah Castle' ⑪ High-difficulty Area 'Flame Sun Island' ⑫ Gust Extra BGM Pack Note: - ① - ⑧⑩⑫ are expected to be released before the end of April 2021; ⑨⑪ are expected to be released before the end of May 2021. Contents of the Season Pass, release dates, and the release order are subject to change without prior notification. About the Game This story takes place three years after the events of the previous game “Atelier Ryza: Ever Darkness & the Secret Hideout,” and depicts the reunion of Ryza and her friends, who go through new encounters and goodbyes to discover a true priceless treasure. 《The Story》 Three years have passed since Ryza’s secret grand adventure on Kurken Island. Ryza, the only member of her group to remain on the island, receives a letter from her friend telling her about ruins that may be related to alchemy, along with a mysterious request involving a glowing stone. This inspires her to leave the island and venture out to the royal capital, Ashra-am Baird. However, Ryza is unaware that this will lead to the beginning of an imaginative new adventure involving a pursuit of the mysteries of the ruins surrounding the royal capital and a meeting with a strange creature that will change her life. 《Main Features》 ■ Exploring with new field actions! Ryza can now perform many new actions in the field, including diving underwater, using plants to climb walls, moving through narrow gaps, and using magic ropes to travel between separated areas. These and other abilities allow Ryza to explore various areas and ruins more fully and actively. ■ More action-filled real-time battles! Take on your enemies using an improved “real-time tactics” battle system, which is now faster and more thrilling than ever. Speedily switch between characters, choose varied skills, and utilize items in just the right moments for best results. ■ Straightforward and easy-to-use synthesis! Utilize several new synthesis systems, including the new intuitive “Linkage Synthesis” system where items are placed in cells called “Material Loops”, that are designed to allow both new players to easily learn synthesis, and experienced players to create unique customized items. Created items can also be mixed and matched with “Evolution Link” to create entirely new items. Note: - Sets that include the main game, such as “Atelier Ryza 2: Lost Legends & the Secret Fairy Digital Deluxe Edition” and “Atelier Ryza 2: Lost Legends & the Secret Fairy Ultimate Edition” are also currently on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, a good chunk of you are probably on this page because of THIGHS, or other related pieces of anatomy. But for those of you who are staring at this weird anime game and don't know what the heck you're looking at, allow me, as a skeptical newcomer-become-fan, to enlighten you.	Atelier is, at its heart, a crafting-focused RPG. You can level your characters and learn new skills and all that jazz, but you will live and die by your ability to learn the mechanics behind alchemy—the game's form of crafting—which allows you to take a bunch of plants, rocks, monster bits, and more to create weapons, armor, bombs, and maybe the cure for cancer. Seriously, though, you could probably finagle yourself a healing item in this game that heals every conceivable status effect at once; alchemy is that crazy in-depth.	If you want a clear-cut comparison, I'd say Disagaea is an apt one. Like Disgaea, Atelier looks like it's your run-of-the-mill JRPG with some quirky mechanics on the side, but the more you play it, the more you realize that the real game is learning to abuse the weird mechanics until you can *break* the game.	Like the previous entry (and probably all previous entries from what I've seen), this is both Ryza 2's greatest boon and its most fatal flaw; the mechanics are interesting and powerful enough to make you want to delve into them, but they're so powerful that you can actually trivialize the game's combat on the hardest difficulties given a thorough enough knowledge and understanding of how alchemy works. There's a middle ground somewhere in there, but by the end of the game you typically end up on one extreme or the other; you either barely scrape by with basic alchemy and feel like the game's difficulty spikes are sharp enough to impale your entire party, or you spend more time in alchemy menus than you do in the game's dungeons and laugh maniacally as you instantly end every combat encounter with a single bomb strong enough to crack the planet in half.	In short, Atelier offers that strange brand of fun where the goal of the game is to trivialize the game. I didn't think I would enjoy the first game, but I did, so I'd recommend people at least give it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: The issue with the PC port is that the game maxes out your gpu each frame which is terrible for performance and battery. For example, the game was maxing out my 3060 on PC and heated my Steam deck to high heaven. Here is how to make the performance better on PC and run amazing on the Steam deck. This fix should also work for other Gust PC ports like Sophie and Blue Reflection, but some might not launch.1. Google "atelier fix" and look for doitsujin on github. Should be one of the top results.2. Open local files in the game's properties and extract the fix to where the exe is. (Rest of the guide is for steam deck only)3. Look up how to get the latest GE Proton, there are several guides and it will help get better performance out of most titles on the deck.4. Set the in-game settings to medium. The game has an issue with saving the settings, so you may have to enter the game, save, and return to title screen. I eventually got it to work, but it was strangely resistant to saving. It might be a steam cloud issue, so playing the game for a bit after changing the settings might do it.5. Hit the "..." button and bring up the performance tab. Toggle on per game settings and set the deck to 40hrz. The game runs totally fine at 40fps, it gets you a much longer battery and the vent won't kill you anymore. Stable 40 is also way better than unstable 60 in some of the larger areas.If you could do me a favor, please hit "no" when steam asks you if "verified" is a good description for the game. Gust/KT really need to improve their PC ports or hire the person who made the fix cause this game does not deserve to be labeled as "great on the deck" without the fix.

_childDocuments_.review: Starting with a disclaimer: I've played most Atelier games in the franchise and love them all (except you, Lydie & Suelle). Now, Ryza 2 isn't a bad game at all. But if someone asked me, "Which Atelier game should I play?" I would never suggest Ryza 2. Even if that person described their preference for exactly Ryza 2's sort of gameplay, I would simply refer them to Ryza 1. That's how similar they are. But Ryza 1 had a better plot.The biggest mistake in this game is the repetitiveness. From the get-go you are told that the plot will require you to investigate 5 sets of ruins. That's exactly what you do: go to ruins, get a cutscene, complete a very long-winded collectathon for glowing orbs, get a recipe out of it, go home, make it, go back to those ruins, get another cutscene, you're done. Next set of ruins. Rinse and repeat until the game ends.Now, if you actually pay attention to the immense amount of lore written into those collectathon orbs, you'll find that there's tons of interesting, potential plot points! But, tragically, it's entirely irrelevant to the game. Characters never mention it. There's an entire history of a lost civilization written into the game, but the plot moves along as though all we know is that these ruins are old. We COULD have had a plot where we learn about the past and pick up where our ancestors left us. The crafting system was also really weak compared to other games in the franchise (except Ryza 1, which has the same exact system). You can't combine traits, and the traits we do have are really boring. The best ones just sort of boost your stats. Compare that to, say, Atelier Firis, where if I tried hard enough, I could create a set of items that effectively gives me infinite turns. I miss doing weird sh** like that. It's also boringly easy to get 999 item quality. In other Atelier games, that was something to be proud of.Lastly, the fanservice was a little over-the-top. Atelier isn't known for its modesty, per se, but this time, every woman minus the 13-year-old had crazy proportions and clothes to show them off. This is a minor complaint. I know that Koei Techmo is just capitalizing on the hype over Ryza's body from the first Ryza game. but does detract from the immersion when I have to keep wondering, "Is the point of this scene what's in the dialogue here, or am I really just supposed to be showered in boobs?"

_childDocuments_.review: Atelier Ryza 1 was my introduction to the Atelier series, and overall this feels like a successful sequel, though there were some disappointments. To anyone who hasn't played an Atelier game, if you like a more slice of life story with many character interactions, as well as a very addictive alchemy (crafting) system to create game breaking items, and a real time combat system that is turn base-esque this is definitely a game to look into.I enjoyed every minute of this game, they made major improvements on the game mechanics and quality of life improvements, such as no more invisible walls when there is a 1 foot drop, you can swim/dive now, you can see what items you get pop up in a bubble if you were to gather from something, etc. Each sub story and character interaction is just as good as the first one, and the combat system had a huge improvement with the core item drives and upgrades (except that the game pauses now when you use an item). So I would like to say overall, i still really like this gameSome negatives. The overarching story was very very very bland. Fi as a plot tool was not used very well at all except for interactions with Clifford. And being "invited over to explore 5 ruins" is a bit too on the nose for me and made it all laid out right from the get-go. What's the biggest shame though is that the ruin puzzles contained some pretty cool lore if you took the time to read them all (i didn't but the ones I did read were cool) and those could've made a great story to explore (maybe it'll be dlc i hope or be used in the 3rd game) but the overall story just felt so lazy.Combat system for the most part got improved but I really liked in the first game, the game would not pause when you were selecting an item. The tension of real time combat really evolves the turn based system and that is ruined a bit with items pausing the game now.The crafting system definitely got super dumbed down. In Ryza 1 I never go above a 400 quality item but this game I accidentally made multiple 999 quality items. Made crafting feel less accomplishing.idk how but the game is even easier than Ryza 1. The only time I felt in danger was when I was at the final boss and I went in with my party at half health.Personal gripe, I just really like Kurken island. It felt organic for there to be mysteries to explore and such. In this game we get thrown into the big city, and there just happen to be 5 humongous ruins nearby to explore.Overall: gameplay, music, graphics, side quests, and crafting system are still top notch and super fun. All the negatives don't ruin the game but I hope they get fixed in the 3rd iteration

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - Ryza is really good and pushes a lot of technical development in their game engine, needs some polish but is otherwise a big step up from older Atelier games.The combat? I really like the combat. Use basic attacks to generate AP, use AP to use skills and generate CC, use CC to use items. After using up items, instead of waiting for the long cooldowns just switch party members and continue comboing harder. So addicting. Fighting the weasel roast for fun is actually enjoyable. Wish that we could crank the difficulty up on the first run of the game, I want to use my OP gear and items on the enemies instead of oneshotting. Massive step up from the active turn combat system from Ryza 1, it's arguably an entire new system and plays faster and more fluidly.The crafting? I played Sophie 2 before Ryza 2, so going to Ryza crafting is really jarring. In Sophie 2 you spend sooo much time synthesizing and minmaxing the grid, maximizing items feels great. You can't just get all the best gathering items and expect endgame items, you work for it and it's addicting. In Ryza you just want to finish crafting and autobuild everything to get to the more fun part of the game, which is exploring and fighting. Either that, or you keep delaying that one crafting item because you just want one or two more good gathering items, only to completely powercreep it with a better item (that you also don't bother crafting because difficulty is too easy). I basically only had three main crafting periods: at the beginning of the game, at the midgame after dungeon 3, and then once more for the final dungeon 5. I guess it isn't too surprising: Ryza doesn't start off as an alchemist, but as an adventurer. This carries over to the core of the game, where you do the alchemy to progress what you REALLY want, which is the exploration and combat.The story? It's not really important, I thought the main story was fairly cohesive but not too surprising. Arguably intentionally done so that players could just drop the story at any time (handheld game). However, the slice-of-life and the characters are what really stand out. A bit tropey, but the characters are quite likeable. The designs really stand out, facial expressions and eyebrows are excellent and expressive while the character movements are quite fluid. Suffers from the unfortunate JRPG symptom of characters awkwardly rotating in place, while the other animations are perfectly fine. Also the generic NPCs that kind of stand around, walking places but might as well not exist.The graphics? The art direction is designed to run on lighter handhelds like Nintendo Switch, the game is very atmospheric in place of realism. The artistic expression is extremely vibrant (I turned off bloom sometimes, because it really is that bright, you will see). The textures for the characters are nicely detailed. However, the landscapes and terrain are a bit lacking (though this is something I feel ALL JRPGs suffer from, they sacrifice landscape textures for character textures). This is arguably a good tradeoff for something supposed to run on a handheld, it doesn't hurt the experience compared to ugly character design.They could still optimize the engine more, especially for Steam Deck. On Steam Deck, you get from 15-30 fps, especially 15 fps during the lantern sections and the most open areas. Use the atelier sync fix, your fps will hardlock to 60 on Steam Deck after initial loading of areas and it's insane why they left so much performance on the table. For PC, set power plan to high performance or max performance. Don't forget to plug in the controller. Set resolution to native, graphics level to low and then work out what you can increase from there (recommend a general order of texture/geometry quality to high, then render distances long, then shadows/bloom/AA/DOF/SSAO on for greatest visual to performance gain).The music? Super nice. Instead of the orchestral, Disney-esque music from the first, it's more of an upbeat, faster soundtrack during combat. And the music, especially during crafting, gets quite emotional and is really notable. You're not going to dislike the music, very good composer they have.In comparison to Ryza 1, Ryza 2 is a clear step up in technical development, and brings back all the nice characters plus more. Combat is astronomically superior, exploration is more vertical and engaging, while the crafting is about the same. If you played Ryza 1 and liked it, get the second. For those who didn't play Ryza 1, you will feel pain from going from 2 to 1. You want to play in order. You will not understand the characters without 1. (Also of note: there's a Ryza 3 coming out. Open world and even more adventure - might want a head start)Completing the main game takes about ~40 hours, and a few more plus googling to complete all the achievements. I would recommend to get it on a sale if you are looking for laid back games, it's a nice value for your time. It delivers a character-driven story with slice-of-life events, and doesn't overstay its welcome.

_childDocuments_.review: Ryza 2 is a more traditional Atelier game with most of the story content being purely character events with no big "happenings" while Ryza 1 was the opposite and followed a more typical JRPG plot progression where the party came across various plot twists, fought a number of big threatening monsters (the dragon, the sea monster etc) and there was even a group of antagonistic characters constantly pestering you (Bos and co). I suppose that was all done on purpose with Gust trying to go for a more mainstream appeal with Ryza 1, but in Ryza 2 they went back to their usual formula, aka a slower paced, relaxing game with lots of character events and little to no drama. If you're an older Atelier fan who was disappointed with Ryza 1, then Ryza 2 is still very much worth a try.The combat has seen improvements too and you can now use your items much more frequently and the tactics level goes up on its own without you having to spend AP on it. But at its core it's still the same ATB system and most of the time you'll be just idling and waiting for your AP and CC to go up so that you can actually do stuff. The battle system is definitely still the weakest part of the Ryza/Secret subseries. It doesn't help that the base difficulty is so low, to the point that hard feels like easy, and you have to beat the game at least once to unlock actually challenging difficulty modes (but at least on PC you can just download a clear data file).Apart from that, it's a good game that fixes most of the issues with the original. Bigger and better. More party members, more areas to explore, a huge amount of character events (all of them being fully voiced outside of only a couple minor quest chains). If you loved Firis there are a few things borrowed from that game too, such as underwater exploration and a rideable mount. Overall the game feels much more complete than Ryza 1, it has a lot more content and it's a longer game with about 50+ hours needed to reach the ending. And if you still want more, there are two DLC dungeons, one mid-game and one post-game, both have actual story content but unvoiced.

_childDocuments_.review: Atelier Ryza 2: A Sequel you can Skip. I absolutely loved the original Atelier Ryza. I was actually about to beat the game for a second time when this game was announced. When I heard it was coming soon, I immediately put down my controller so I could play it with a fresh mindset. Unfortunately, the sequel is a disappointment. Many times, I stopped playing this game, but I had some good times along the way and decided to finish it.Story (2/10): This sequel requires to you have played the first game to understand it, and it is a very poor story. The party seems to be investigating underground ruins for no real reason, and they seem to stumble through an adventure with a series of coincidences. All the original characters return, but offer no interesting dialogue and no character development. The new characters introduced are one-dimensional, and each of them focus their dialogue on a boring side-quest. Gameplay (7/10): Much of the gameplay is exactly the same as the original game. The Alchemy system is almost exactly the same, with minor additions. This isn’t so bad since crafting is fun, and perfecting synthesis feels good. Exploration falls flat, the level design now includes many narrow corridors with a small field of view, even when zoomed out. You spend much of your time in underground ruins which seem similar and bland. The new system of finding ‘clues’ through memories make you backtrack through the levels, and matching the ‘clues’ with the ‘puzzle’ is simply tedious. Combat is more fluid, I like the addition of swapping out characters, and the building of ‘CC’ points to reuse your core items. The new challenges are actually fun. Overall gameplay is OK, although the difficulty is too easy even on hard. Visuals and Audio (5/10): The graphics on this game look worse than the original. You can sometimes see the textures in the level design. Characters movements look stiff and production quality is lacking. Graphical assets look like they needed more polishing, but never really got it. The music is nothing impressive, which is a shame because this series often has some amazing soundtracks.Reused Assets: Here is one of the biggest issues. This game was produced very quickly, so a lot of assets are reused in this sequel are from the original. Many alchemic recipes and items are exactly the same and it makes it feel like we are solving the same puzzles from the original. The enemies are exactly the same making combat feel repetitive. The music is somewhat similar so no songs really stand out, and they even reuse some of the original storyline which makes this story boring and predictable.Overall, I would still give this game a passing mark. The core gameplay is quite good, and it is addictive to unlock and create new items. However, I cannot recommend this game. If they made an Atelier Ryza 3, you could skip this game and not miss anything important or enjoyable. You can buy this game and have fun with the core gameplay, but the magic of the original Atelier Ryza just isn’t here. (Review: 6.5/10)

_childDocuments_.review: This one is going to be a long one....It's very unfortunate that I am unable to recommend this game, as the developers have clearly fixed and improved on around 80% of all the complaints that I had of the first game. The graphics are better, the combat is better, the systems are better, the environments are better, the controls are better. Even the music I think is better than the first game. There are just 3 major aspects that left me sorely disappointed, and perhaps interestingly, they hit at hardest at the beginning, middle, and end of the game. It's like getting slapped three times across the face. I will briefly talk about what they fixed, and then end with the three disappointments.[The improvements]- The maps are bigger and much more interesting to traverse. You will notice you can actually jump on top and over objects and ledges. Ryza can now swim, dive, ride a mount, and you also get access to traversal items in at the beginning of the game rather than at the end (damn you wind shoes)- The combat is more engaging now. You can combo basic attacks and skills. There are no longer charges for item usage that need to be replenished by returning to your Atelier. Instead you gain item core charges by performing skill combos. Time also pauses for you now while you select items. You can now also now switch/tag-in another character, effectively bringing your party size of 3 to 4.- There is now a quest board which you can turn in excess materials for money. These also reward gold coins pretty often. You may also sell materials like before, except this time it doubles as a way to improve what NPC vendors sell you.- The crafting system has gained a Skill Tree, in which you need to spend Skill points to unlock certain recipes or tool upgrades. This works to organise gear/item progression, but should be balanced way better. (I completed the entire skill tree and had so much skill points left over)- Gear and tool progression is slower, which makes it much better. Instead of making the next tier gear, you benefit tremendously by rebuilding/re-crafting a better version of your current tier gear. You also no longer need to combine tools to make those hybrid tools, thank god.[3 Major Disappointments]: HOW did they make the camerawork even worse than the first game. There's no camera tilt settings. The zoom distance constantly resets, and the BIGGEST problem is that every time an object passes between your camera position and Ryza, it automatically zooms in! So the first 3 hours of the game I'm walking around town getting a headache because the camera just goes IN - OUT - IN - OUT - IN - OUT really quickly when rounding corners, or walking up stairs, or passing street lamps. My brain got used it eventually, but please for the love of thick thighs fix that ♥♥♥♥.: The cutscenes in this game probably make up 50% of the game time. I'm not kidding. There are 6 playable main characters and maybe about 6 side characters. Each character questline has a chain of maybe ~30 cutscenes. At 3 minutes each, we are looking at 18-20 hours of cutscenes total! These cutscenes auto play when you are either in the zone or in the vicinity. This means that there are times where I literally get 5-6 cutscenes in a row. And because these cutscenes happen dependant on you triggering them, the events that occur and the mood is often out of sequence.Example: : I never expected Ryza's story to blow my mind or anything, but the ending to Ryza 2 along with some of the character stories are some of the most anti-climatic and explanation-lacking conclusions that I've probably ever seen. I think the plot in Ryza 1 was better?-Story Ending: - Ruined old main characters: - Ruined new characters: - Starchild: - Ryza's flashbacks: So yeah, if you already didn't like Ryza 1's cutscenes and storyline, don't buy Ryza 2. If you never played Ryza 1, just know that this is a visual novel - game hybrid, half the game is dialogue and cutscenes.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - This game is good if you want more of the experience of the first game, but several QOL changes accompany a significantly easier game. Play the first if you haven't played either, pick this up if you enjoyed the first. Alternatively, play this first if you want the Ryza experience without as much grinding.There are a few issues with the game that are notable considering it is the second PC game in the series:- Really crappy console style FOV. It can be nauseating at times being so zoomed in.- Bloom is broken when turned on making everything un-viewable.- Audio stuttering issues in game and in cut scenes.- Peripherals may not be correctly detected on the first game launch, requiring a close and relaunch.- The challenging bosses are only in pirate DLC.While there are many nice quality of life changes compared to Ryza 1, the difficulty of this game, not including the DLC is significantly reduced in the base game. Not as much grinding and synthesis is required for completion as was for the first game if you just want to rush the main story.The game plays very similar to its predecessor, with the loop of explore the maps, collect materials, convert them into more powerful weapons and armor almost unaltered from the recipe used in the first. The synthesis system has changed, and a few more combat mechanics are available. While you will have to get used to the new synthesis changes, the new combat stuff can pretty much be ignored unless you want achievements.Combat is turn based, real time, where you pick from your arsenal of skills, items, or just plain old wacking things. The AI is OK, but I wish there would have been a better way to fine tune them to be more then just opposite spectrums of just slash or use all the AP. Being able to assign roles would have been nice, and setting AP thresholds or item only use would have been a great addition.The world is OK, similar exploration to Ryza 1 with a new focus on exploration via swimming. There are a pretty good amount of different maps, and you can even visit parts of a few locations from the prior game. There is a good amount of backtracking, but it is limited just below the point of being excessive.The story, IMO, is very similar to the first, but just not as good. The new story does kind of continue off of the first Ryza game, but it is forced by the introduction of the character Fi, which is the main reason why everything happens the way it does and it makes the story just seem a bit forced. Following Serri's side quest line could just have easily have been turned into the main story, and I think would have been more interesting than cleaning up the mess made by Fi. If there is a Ryza 3, maybe it will expand on the afterwards of Fi, or combine with Serri's story to let you see the outcome of all your work.At the end, the underwhelming last boss, and the story's completion just made me feel kind of empty. It seems they forgot to add the "Feeling Full L" trait to this one. However, it is still worth some time if you enjoy the Ryza world.

_childDocuments_.review: Atelier Ryza 2 is a comfy JRPG about growing up and reunions, with relatable characters and relationships backed by fun, hectic ATB combat. If you're looking for a chill, cheerful experience that masterfully straddles the line between everyday adventures and world-ending threats, Ryza 2 is for you. ...and if you're a min-maxer like I am, whose idea of fun is optimizing every last 0.1% of damage from a build, and loves finding hidden interactions and loopholes in game systems, there's a completely different - and equally compelling - game present in the crafting system. Similar to games like Disgaea or Path of Exile, this game allows you to become obscenely overpowered, both through raw numbers and by stacking effect after effect on every action you take. Armor and accessories that allow you to spam skills and items on demand? Go for it. Want gear that literally increases your stats by an order of magnitude? Why not? A potion that revives your entire team, cures all status effects, gives everyone a stat boost AND speeds up your entire party's next turn? Sure, you can do that! Elemental nuke that hits everything on the field twice, lifesteals for half your health and debuffs the enemies' speed and defense down to pathetically low levels? Feel free to combine it with an accessory that makes it cost basically nothing so you can chain a million damage off of one combo.Unlike those other games, however, the path to doing so in Ryza 2 relies little on XP grinding or farming RNG loot for drops. Instead, it focuses more on how you plan out your crafting route and how you build interim crafting materials to make trait addition easier. The multiplicauldron and essence boosting systems unlocked about halfway through the game ensure that with some problem solving, you only need to find a trait once on any material in order to duplicate it infinitely and apply it to all of your equipment on demand. However, the path to doing so may not be straightforward; at one point I had to loop a material through five different interim crafting recipes, some with specific essence boost requirements, before I could get it onto the accessory I wanted to make! Due to the differences in each player's inventory, you have to figure out your own path for your specific materials and needs instead of relying on specific guides, which can pose some fun, rewarding puzzles.All this combines to make an RPG experience that makes you feel like you've EARNED your overpowered nature, not just thrown in enough hours to make the system work. Through system mastery and abusing loopholes intentionally left in by the developer, you become an alchemical god incarnate and smite everything, including the post-game boss on the hardest difficulty, with extreme prejudice.Which leads to my one real complaint about this game - there is no post-game of any real content. The game has a variety of difficulty modes, from 'I just want the story' difficulties that won't require you to craft anything, to ones that are brutally difficult until crafting really opens up in the midgame. But by the time endgame hits and you have the ability to craft anything you want, there really just isn't much need for it. There's the final boss, which is a pushover, and then there's the post-game superboss, who hits like a truck but needs about 5x the health to really push the combat system to where it shines. There's no infinite scaling or bonus dungeon to serve as a litmus test for how truly strong your OP builds and strategies are; there's just how fast you can obliterate the Lamb Roast and Weasel Roast challenges in your room.Ryza 1 had the same problem that was eventually mostly solved by a endgame DLC and I suspect that will prove true in Ryza 2 as well, but we'll have to wait and see.Now for a quick rundown of the actual game's systems in comparison to the first Atelier Ryza game:The combat's an active time battle system that feels like a mix between FFXIII and the Tales series, of all things. There's always something to do, whether it's chaining skills, using timed blocks to reduce damage, swapping between characters, or setting up your item chain and watching things go boom. Unlike some similar systems (looking at you, XC2's earlygame!) there's very little downtime and you're constantly on your toes if you want to optimize your damage output. Compared to the first game, it's significantly flashier and faster-paced, with item use being much more common and strategic since you now earn CC per character during a fight. One of my favorite ATB systems so far.In Ryza 1, hitting max quality relied heavily on crafting quality loops and was both tedious and unintuitive to reach. In Ryza 2, crafts will always go up in quality with more ingredients added, with higher quality items providing a bigger boost. This gets rid of the awkwardness in Ryza 1 where you generally wanted to use as FEW materials as possible to not waste 999 quality raw materials, so now it's feasible to hit max quality through conventional means. Some crafts will still heavily benefit off 999 quality intermediate materials, so there's still a benefit to optimizing in that regard.The need for high quality materials also made shops, money, and even dungeon equipment chests(!) completely useless in Ryza 1. You'd never use shop materials because they'd probably lower your craft quality, buying armor was a joke when you could always craft better stuff by the time you unlocked it in the store, and the same applied to whatever gear a dungeon could provide you. This is no longer true in Ryza 2. Shops can now be developed by selling materials to Romy, which can allow you to unlock certain materials like Goldoterion and Septrim a full dungeon earlier than you normally would be able to farm them! They're usable too, because the absolute need for ingredient quality is gone. Dungeon chests follow a similar philosophy, allowing you to get low-stat gear with interesting traits earlier than you can craft them - a teaser of sorts, which incentivizes players to keep progressing so they can make their own versions for the rest of the party. In general, the whole economy and material system is significantly more fleshed out and improved compared to the first game. The characterization and relationships between the characters is held pretty consistent from the first game, with all of the banter and jokes between the cast still as great as ever. The three years of separation between everyone is treated pretty realistically, and characters have developed reasonably during that time. If Ryza 1 was a coming-of-age story, this is closer to a bunch of high-school friends coming together for a reunion after university. (I can say this because of how damn relatable it was!)The story itself is more fragmented than the first game. The game tells a significant amount of its backstory through text matching puzzles this time around, which can get boring for some. There's less of a motivation for Ryza to embark on her journey this time around, although she quickly develops more reasons to care. Some character introductions are also sloppily executed. Overall, it's a slightly weaker narrative than the first game, but the increased quantity and quality of random character interactions makes up for it somewhat.In conclusion, Atelier Ryza 2 is one of my favorite JRPGs of all time. It's comfy, cute, and consistently interesting, AND it managed to scratch my number crunching itch without making me invest several hundred hours into RNG hell. Truly a worthy successor and an improvement to the first game.This game came at a perfect time during the COVID lockdown, too. Definitely needed some comfy after another few months in relative isolation.

_childDocuments_.review: As of writing this review, I have 100% completed this game and unlocked every achievement.After doing the same for the first game, I was super excited to jump into the sequel, hoping it would somehow be even better than the original. With 59.7hrs under my best I can safely say, yes. Atelier Ryza 2 is an *even better* experience than its predecessor.If you enjoyed the first game, this game is more of that, but taken to the next logical evolution. Environments are even bigger than before, with exciting and adventurous new ways to navigated them, the scenery is stunning, dare I say breathtaking. The alchemy system also returns with plenty of new recipes, expansions, new methods of crafting and more. The cutscenes and storytelling are dramatically improved, more coherent, more impactful. I genuinely found myself emotional on a number of occasions. Seeing Ryza reunite with her old friends – especially Klaudia – was just heartwarming, and their relationship dynamic is shining brighter here than ever before.Speaking of the characters, their new designs are superb, and the new additions to the cast like Serri & Patricia are just a joy see on screen. The roster of characters, both playable and non-playable, for this sequel is leagues above the previous game. I became so immersed in the world surrounding the capital city, it all felt so alive.One could hardly talk about immersion without mentioning the soundtrack. *Somehow* it’s on par with the first games incredible OST, and in honesty most of my favourite tracks from the Ryza series come from this game over the first. Hours of beautiful, orchestral, relaxing music to listen too in this game. One of the few games I’d gladly purchase the soundtrack to.The combat however, is where the game truly shines. The original system from Ryza 1 is discarded in place of a new, faster, more energetic, more thrilling fighting style. While the Tactics & WT features make a return, they function slightly differently. Veteran players of Ryza 1 may take some time adjusting, but I found this combat system to be much much more enjoyable in almost every facet after I’d gotten my head around it.I could go on and on singing this games praises, but I hardly think I need to.Atelier Ryza 2 is a masterclass in capturing a relaxing, feel-good experience.This series as a whole has had such an impact on me, I’m so thankful I played both games, and I really truly hope you’ll give the series a shot too.It is something truly beautiful, and well worth your time

_childDocuments_.review: Initially, I liked this game. After finishing this game however, I was left with an inexplicable urge to squeeze small white flying animals that squeak. The characters in this game are so uninteresting that I just began to skip cut scenes because I couldn't care less about them. How they managed to ruin the main gang I have no idea, but they are BAD. The new characters are even worse, especially the blacksmith. Gameplay wise, I respect Gust changing how items are used, and the combat is far better than Ryza. Crafting is way better and craft, gather, combat formula persists, though alchemy is still pretty easy. The ruin discovery was neat, I was interested in the beginning, but in the end, I just brute forced through the "puzzles".  The graphics look just as good as Ryza if not better, though there is an obvious shift in style in Ryza 2 that makes me prefer Ryza far more. The style change can also be found in the music, which has devolved into generic RPG GST, especially the boss themes. Not that the music is bad, but it misses a main part that personally attracted me to the series. After completing an atelier game, including the first Ryza, I would always enter the sound gallery and listen. I didn't even look at the extras button this time. I was too busy vomiting from the ending since I couldn't skip it. I couldn't put my finger on it until I reached the end, but throughout my playthrough I felt like something was missing from the game. In all of the atelier games I've played, the atelier theme haunted me for weeks on end. Ryza 2's theme is forgettable and bland. Even though I absolutely despise this game, it isn't objectively bad. Contrary, I think its an average to decent standard RPG. However, comparing it to the other atelier games I've played, its at the bottom. In my opinion, it has stripped away the music, the art style, and the characters. If you're looking to play a regular RPG, I think you will enjoy this title far more than I did. If you crave an Atelier title to fill your addiction, turn away. Even so, Ryza 2 did relax me like other atelier titles did, just that IT RELAXED ME INTO A VEGETABLE AND I WAS DECLARED BRAIN DEAD BECAUSE I DIDN'T NEED TO THINK.I enjoyed this game in the beginning. I was excited to learn how the gang changed and I enjoyed Ryza 1. Initially, the combat, characters, and art style were good. It was only after I played a little while longer that I realized that I wasn't playing an atelier game anymore. Somewhere after the first 6 hours of playtime, the writing just dropped, and the game completely inverted. I honestly feel like I've been part of an elaborate prank. I didn't think to change my positive review until the ending, which disappointed me so much I cannot explain. Atelier games are always on the more pricey side, and they are all worth it. This is the first atelier game that I have bought that has not been a worthwhile experience. Hopefully after this rant I have expelled all my hatred for the ending and characters and I can peacefully sleep and forget about this game.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing through 5 of Gust games throughout the past year (Blue Reflection 1 & 2, Atelier Sophie 1 and Atelier Ryza 1 & 2), I can safely say that Atelier Ryza 2 is the one I enjoyed the most and the one that feels the most complete to me (with Blue Reflection 2 being a close second), as it combines all the good parts of the other Gust titles I experienced.I felt that Sophie 1 was too focused on the slice of life character scenes and didn't really have any cohesive plot. On the other hand, I felt like Ryza 1 got too focused on the main adventure plot and was lacking when it came to character scenes. Ryza 2 combines the good aspects of both by having many individual character scenes while retaining a central plot, albeit a looser one than its predecessor.Newly added characters feel a lot more fun to me than the original party.The combat is also massively improved in design over the previous game, especially when it comes to AP and core item charge generating and management. Exploration and other gameplay systems got a ton of love too with all of them being improved in one way or another.The art is as good as ever, especially the environments.The overall game feel is also improved, as the UI feels a lot more slick and modern, less like older Atelier titles and more like Blue Reflection 2, which came out a few months after this game. Same goes for the PC port. PC ports of Gust games have always been bad, especially when played with mouse and keyboard. Ryza 2 is no exception but there are still significant improvements over Ryza 1. Default key mapping and controls for keyboard are much more intuitive, and the mouse actually works and does stuff like controlling the camera... incredible, I know.Overall, if you enjoyed Ryza 1, I see absolutely no reason why you wouldn't love Ryza 2 (possibly even more) other than perhaps a less focused main story, which is balanced out by a lot of interesting lore you uncover throughout the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Takes parts of mechanics from other Ateliers (mostly from Ryza 1 and the Mysterious series) and combines them in a much better manner than previously. This leads to some interesting crafting experiences, and my favourite of the Atelier games.Combat is very action based and quick, normally I would use Speedhack to increase combat speed 3x or more, but in this game I do not go past 2x, and leave it at 1x at bosses.More character interaction than in the previous game, which I love, and the maps are large, much like in Firis.An amazing Atelier game, and I have barely unlocked the beginning. Synthesis is very fun, and you will want to do a mix of auto and manual synthesis.

_childDocuments_.review: Early impressions are very positive for me, but do be aware that some players are suffering from performance issues.So far, I think I enjoy the minor changes they made to the combat system (while I personally would prefer a return to the older battle systems, I do think the changes I seem so far here are positive, like gaining Tactical Level by using skills instead of having to save all AP for it).Early on the Synthesis system seems to be mostly the same, which is fine - Atelier Ryza had my favorite alchemy system in the series, though I'd prefer it without Item Rebuild. The "recipe tree" is a good addition to re-learn the recipes, too.Now can someone please go hammer some basic fashion sense into Ryza's head? After playing for a few dozen more hours, I must say I'm extremely happy with this sequel. The combat system in particular is a fantastic evolution of the first game one, and I say this even though I generally prefer more slow-paced combat in JRPGs. It is a really well designed and fun system.If you are already used to Atelier's crafting, I strongly recommend downloading a "clear save data" to play on the hardest difficulty on your first playthrough, as the game is otherwise too easy.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, would like to give a rundown on this game to help others understand what they are buying.1. Game is subtitles only. Yes, can be annoying having to read everything the characters say, but the voice acting is nice and the dialogue is great even if you don't understand Japanese.2. This game is story intensive. Majority of gameplay will be split between reading the massive amount of cutscenes, exploring the world and crafting your equipment. Combat doesn't take up much of your game time. Difficulty can be increased, but combat is not exactly the major point of this game. Think of this like the old flash storyboard games but with full 3d environment exploration with combat sprinkled in.3. This is not a traditional RPG even though this game has the RPG tag on it. There are no choices in this game at all. None of your actions affect the outcome of this game in any way, shape, or form. Everything is set in stone. The only thing your "choices", that is, whether you have decided to view all of the cutscenes and complete side quests or not, only affects whether or not you see additional side stories, character development and in game progression such as unlocking new merchandise at the vendors or unlocking new merchants and recipes for crafting. Hence why this is a JRPG in the most simplest and truest of descriptions. Just sit back and enjoy the story. For comparison sake, this is more closely related to the Final Fantasy series except with a more detailed story.4. Single Player only. No multiplayer content at all. No Leaderboards. Nothing. Could be a deal breaker for some.5. Story does not exactly require players to have played the first game of this sub-series to make sense, however, the first game is mentioned and talked about on occasion along with the previous setting. Can leave players slightly confused if they haven't played Atelier Ryza 1. Otherwise, is mostly stand-alone and does well enough to give the players all the major plot points that are relevant to this story (which is very little).Story: Now, I understand everyone has their own likes and dislikes when it comes to games, even when talking about games of the same genre. Personally, I think the developers did a wonderful job telling the story as a whole. Now, mind you, there are areas that could have been flushed out better, better worded, or planned in general. One such area was overlooked, mainly the lack of acknowledgment by the characters during cutscenes about the memory vestiges you have collected. Story wise the characters need the vestiges in order to progress through the "dungeons", however, respond as if they didn't read the vestiges. They were only for player satisfaction and knowledge apparently, which made the cutscenes slightly agitating to watch when they responded in a dumbfounded manner. Otherwise, no other complaints about the story. Some people will dislike the very stereotypical progress of the story, to the point it becomes predictable if the player has played the first game in this sub-series.Combat: Fun and engaging. It really rewards the dedicated player and encourages them to attempt to break their characters, especially if playing on higher difficulty modes and/or in the high level DLC zone. Just enough of a change over the last game to keep it fresh and interesting while improving upon/balancing it to give the players a slightly more challenging play through compared to the previous title. Downside, only a handful of new enemy races to fight, however, each enemy has been changed to fit the new combat mechanics and have been changed to provide a new and fresh feel to this sub-series.Crafting: Balanced and is slightly harder to break early game when compared to the previous title. Many more recipes to play around with and new ways to enhance your gear.Environment: Breath taking visuals and a great setting for this game. Especially when comparing it to other anime games which tend to have less than palatable visual work such as the Fairy Tail game or early Naruto games. Which to be fair for Naruto, was more of a limitation of the consoles than the developers at that time (possibly both). Some of the level designs didn't necessarily make sense, such as how some of the ruins layouts were designed, but still looked cool and nice regardless.Sound: Can't accurately say much about the voice actors other than they sound cool and sound like they fit with what the character looks like. You can hear the passion in all of their voices and reflects each of the characters and how they feel/look like they feel at that moment. You can tell they did a wonderful job playing their role. The soundtrack was very well done. Intense boss music, peaceful exploration music, and mood music for each zone of the game that fit with the design of those maps.Achievements: Nothing too hard, easy to obtain. Most received just by playing normally. Nothing too grindy. Which can also be a downside since none were challenging enough to warrant feeling pride in obtaining any of these achievements. Plus side, leaves more room to actually enjoy playing the game the way you want to and focus on the story.Character Development: Nothing too outrageous and definitely nothing new. However, was done really well. I enjoyed seeing how each of these characters faced and overcame their own internal conflicts and becoming even better people, including the main NPCs.Replay Ability: Sadly, this game does lack in that department horrendously. Only options for replay is a New Game + that doesn't add anything new to the game. Allows you to keep all equipped gear and nothing else. Can change to higher difficulty at any point, so, not NG+ exclusive. Doesn't change the story. However, the game does have some massively high difficulty levels, especially the relatively recent addition of Legendary difficulty. Can be fun to play again for the increased challenge. For those that don't like to see the same things over and over again, this can be a massive downside and might not be worth investing in if they want a game that'll last them longer than a few days to a few weeks of play time.I have only played the previous Atelier Ryza title. So therefore, I can't speak on whether this sub-series holds up to any of the others, but I do give kudos to the developers for making a wonderful game that I enjoyed. Again, not all will feel the way that I do and that is alright. To each their own. Personally I am looking forward to the next title in this series and might actually check out the others I have not played yet. Definitely one of my top 10 JRPG games of all time.Edit: This game gets my "Game of the Year" award nomination.

_childDocuments_.review: I played the first game on the Switch and decided to pick up the second for the PC instead. It feels pretty similar and I can't say the different platforms make that much difference to how the game plays.The stuttering that other reviews mention is definitely super prominent in the PC version and I had to change people's clothes to try and escape them constantly "ticking". It's so distracting and off putting.The game itself is super similar to the first. The same enemies are present, mostly the same characters and even the same items! It's still enjoyable to faff around doing the various systems but it did very much feel like playing the game over again.You're a woman who has gone out into the world to meet up with her old friends from the first game, but now you're in the capital city. The game is focused really heavily on the crafting system - where you gather or make items to create more items. You then use these in combat against random very very boring enemies,Honestly the crafting system annoyed me a lot. It was like a shopping list where you'd realise you forgot an item, so you had to go back and do that. And to do that item, you needed another. So you had to get that too. And oh damn, for that item you need to visit a different shop - so by the time you've got that item you forgot the original item you went for.This happened to me so much. It doesn't help that the game guide only tells you what zone the item is in rather than what it looks like, so you're often wandering for a while trying to find out what you need.Ryza 2 has added a strange mount system as well. You summon a big weasel that you run around on. You can aggro enemies on it but they'll run away from you if they can. It's handy because the volume of enemies is increased greatly in this one. It can also dig up items. Loads and loads of items. In fact, it makes the rest of the gathering almost pointless - you can get more, more easily, by using the mount.It kinda exposed for me how annoying the gathering is otherwise.In the fights you have four options. You can defend - which you can do at any point but it stops your action bar filling up - you can auto attack, you can use items or you can use your specials. Doing auto attack charges your specials and your specials charge your items. It's better than the first game because you get a lot more freedom in using your items since it's constantly recharging in fights.However it also means that you don't want your allies using up the precious points for your specials, so it means your main character (whoever you choose to use as that) is the only one who really gets to do anything. You CAN let the others do stuff but it means you're kinda sat around just attacking if you do. I did sorta like it but it becomes quite thin after a few hours. You unlock the abilities you use for the WHOLE GAME by about level 15 maybe 4 hours in. It's just samey.That's how the whole game feels I guess. It's samey. It's so much like the first one and there's so little variety in enemies and items that you start to wish there was something new to see.The biggest crime of the game for me though is that the areas you go to unlock quite an interesting story that the game NEVER references. You have a little beastie with you and it's treated as a mystery but the first dungeon tells you exactly what it is in the background story bits you pick up. You even see other beasties as ghosts! And yet the game at no point acknowledges this. It's annoying because that other story sounds really interesting! Let me play that!
