_childDocuments_.review: The sequel to the experimental Atelier Ryza, Atelier Ryza 2 did a lot of polishing of mechanics and improves on what worked in the first Ryza and drops a lot of the things that didn't work.  Story is still a weak part of both games.Combat is quite improved in Ryza 2.  The ATB-style combat remains, but the crafted item system changes.  As you do basic attacks, you build up AP, which can be spent on skills when it's your turn.  The "tactics" level goes up automatically with skill usage, this time it doesn't cost AP to increase the tactics level which removes a bit of resource management.  Like in the first Ryza, higher tactics levels improves the power of your skills.  Your AI controlled allies have action triggers just like in Ryza 2, but these are easier to hit, triggering off either physical or magical damage (abilities, certain items, and support attacks).  New in this game is a 4th combat character called a support character.  This character can be hotswapped in and out of combat at almost all times (there is a cooldown), and when swapped will do a bonus attack that is usually counted as a magical skill.  Swapping characters in and out is essential for more difficult fights.The item system is quite different this time around.  Items cost CC points, which are built up by using skills in combat.  By default, you start with 0 CC points, which reduces the usefulness and power of items in the early game which is quite different from the usual Atelier game where early game items are your most important resource.  You will eventually be able to unlock CC upgrades, including starting with a certain number of points allowing you to use items immediately.  Each character can eventually equip up to 4 items, what they can equip is dependent on their Dexterity stat just like in Ryza 1, and you can use as many items in one turn as you have CC points for.  In addition, there are "ultimate" attacks that can be triggered by using certain combinations of items once per combat.Exploration and gathering are good, the areas in this game are much larger and more exploratory than anything before.  In addition to your different harvesting tools, you have a lot of new exploration items such as a grapple beam like tool, the ability to explore underwater, and more.  Unlike in Ryza 1, there are no decisions to be made about what to bring, you have slots for everything.  The effects of the monster radar and the preview of what materials can be found with each tool are always present, you no longer need to craft this ability using rare and powerful materials and no longer have to waste a tool slot for it.That said, since the areas are so much larger it takes a bit longer to traverse.  Some of the areas have pretty complex paths with a lot more verticality so it does take more time to get to places.  Due to the much larger size of the areas, you also get absolutely flooded with materials.  You'll run into basket limits very often, and Ryza 2 is the first Atelier game I've EVER managed to run out of space in the atelier's container!  You will be doing a lot of selling and material deconstruction into gems.  Unfortunately both of these systems are lacking in quality of life features.  When deconstructing items into gems, the filter resets between uses which is unlike how Ryza 1 worked.  This makes deconstructing items into gems take way longer if you filter one item at a time (so you can deconstruct the weaker and keep the stronger or ones with high level traits).  Selling is done through "shop development", and you can only select ONE item at a time, and you'll get popups regularly during the process interrupting you.  You cannot select large groups of items to sell so it's a very frustrating, click intensive, and time consuming thing.  It's also important to have shops be any sort of value.The story, however, is pretty lacking even by Atelier Ryza standards.  While it's nice to have the return of the character events, the main story revolves around a mascot character to the detriment of everything else.  You have a bit of "tomb raiding" feel during a big portion of the story, where you do minor puzzles, craft items to restore the ruins (as part of the storyline), and collect clues which can be put together into a story of the past.  Overall it's a bit more interesting than the main story but held back by a pretty bad "research" system where you put together all the clues.Crafting is one of the main draws of the Atelier series, and this game improves upon Ryza's new node system.  It's even easier now to build up massively powerful equipment than Ryza 1.  Shockingly, this game removes the crafting level.  Instead, as you craft you earn points (you also earn points from doing ruins research), and these points can be spent on a skill tree/sphere grid type of system.  The skill tree unlocks new recipes (including for more gathering tools), skills, upgrades to your crafting prowess, and new crafting options (like duplication or combat core upgrading).  It makes crafting a bit more freeform which is interesting, but it also lets you get overpowered really fast.  Just like with Ryza 1, crafting can be material overload, where a large complex craft could be built out of 50-100 base materials.  Keeping a supply of gems and materials ready to do item rebuilds is quite important for attack items and equipment.The high power level of the items you can craft and the ease at which to get it is probably why there are some pretty stiff jumps in difficulty.  The bosses and some late game forced trash fights are a huge jump in difficulty and you really need to do some heavy crafting to make through them without much difficulty.  Don't neglect your crafting as it's easy to get stonewalled by the difficulty cliffs.Artwork improves even more, areas are very detailed and very beautiful, though in some areas the bloom and post processing are a bit much and it can make it hard to see sometimes.  This port is much improved over previous Koei Tecmo ports, with a lot more graphical settings and all of the settings accessible in game rather than by a launcher.  Sound and music are standard excellent Atelier fare.  The boss theme for the bastion bosses is my favorite of the bunch, and probably my third favorite theme in all of Atelier after Ayesha's final boss theme and map screen themes.  Like with all other Atelier games, it runs well on Linux but has regular stutters every few seconds if it's not locked to 60FPS.  I do that with this launch option: DXVK_FRAME_RATE=60 %command%There's a lot of fanservice, Ryza's new outfit is a bit more revealing, and you get a lot of scenes where the camera fixes on her butt or chest.  There's also some equal opportunity fanservice with Clifford's design.  Otherwise, the character designs are great with a lot of variety.  There are no hot springs/bathing suit scenes like some of the earlier games, so while the character designs have fanservice, the story doesn't take it into any creepy aspects.Overall, this is a great Atelier game and I quite enjoyed it.  I was mixed on Ryza 1, while I liked some aspects there are others I didn't like.  Ryza 2 just improved so much aside from story that I can't not recommend it.  Definitely worth it on sale, maybe even full price.  That said, this is a sequel and you are expected to know how the crafting works in general and the characters and story events from Ryza 1.  There are not always summaries or explanations for those who might be coming into Ryza 2 without playing the first game.  If you're going to play it, definitely play Ryza 1 first (and on sale).

_childDocuments_.review: Wanted to wait until I finished the storyline before reviewing the game. Three years after the adventure from the first game we rejoin Ryza as she heads to the city after receiving word about ruins relating to alchemy along with a unusual egg shaped stone. Familiar faces rejoin the adventure along with some new characters each with their own unique combat styles. In Ryza 2 the exploring has been changed up with the addition of climbing, swimming, diving, rope swinging and monster riding which is a welcome change to the gameplay. Alechmy has changed a bit so you'll learn recipes in various ways such as the skill tree, recipe morph, main quests and side quests. Creating and improving items has largely stayed the same from the first game so it's just a matter of having the right materials. For battles the obvious change in combat is now realtime so being indisicive will allow the enemy to land more attacks or charge up special moves but this does keep the battles moving quickly. Points for special attacks and item usage still remain along with the team calling out for specific moves to be used despite odd requests like physical attacks against golems being a weird one. After getting used to the new game mechanics I enjoyed Ryza 2 just as much as Ryza 1 even if the ending does hit you right in the feels a bit too much. Fingers crossed to 100% this one as well. It's definitely worth picking up and once again a big thanks to my friend for pointing this one out ❤

_childDocuments_.review: In short, this second instalment is a slightly refined version of Ryza 1, with some QoL changes, an overall easier game, and a somewhat lacking story, but still heavily carried by its characters. People who loved the first game will love Ryza 2.The gameplay mechanics from Ryza 1 have been improved. The alchemy system is almost exactly the same, and the battle system has really been improved (but still has some flaws after many hours of gameplay). The exploration is mostly the same, the maps are interesting, with a new swimming element (which is used way too few times...). I just regret that there is way more backtracking than in Ryza 1, to the point of almost becoming annoying.A new mechanic has been introduced, which is a sort of puzzle where you have to associate sentences with clues (which are highlighted in the sentences...). It's a waste of time to have to scroll through the entire text to find the correct line, and it could have been introduced in a more interesting way. Many voice lines around this mechanic aren't subbed, so we don't really get how Ryza is reacting...The story feels a bit lacking and sometimes repetitive: go to ruins, complete the exploration log with the mechanic I just described, fight a boss, repeat. It's not to say the game is trash storywise. It just feels frustrating for it to be at the level of the first game, while there's a lot of lore ALREADY written in the ruins, describing a whole ancient civilization, but which ends up being mentioned only superficially by the characters, and not really having any importance in the actual plot of the game.The ending also leaves a bitter taste. The final boss doesn't feel that strong compared to monsters in its area (despite being "above" the boss from Ryza 1, which actually made me struggle - in Ryza 2, I beat it on the first try by accident). The ending is very rushed, comes from nowhere, and there isn't really a feeling of completion. I still personally loved the ending because of the emotional aspect of it, but I can't say it is good. It highlights the issues with the story: it's kind of empty and hidden under some repetitiveness, which artificially inflates its scope.In the end, like with Ryza 1, I still loved the time I spent with all these characters and improving my gear. The music is still awesome, the interactions between characters are interesting,... Anyone who liked the first game will love the second one as well. Just don't go in expecting a better story than the first one.I'm still looking forward to a third instalment! (and hoping the story will be better this time).

_childDocuments_.review: Second game of the Ryza series.3 years later, invited by Tao, Ryza travels to an island across the sea, to investigate something that could be related to alchemy. Atelier Ryza 2 takes it a notch further than its previous game. The combat system was massively improved, the Alchemy Level system was dropped for a Skill Tree, alchemy mechanics were refined or new ones added, new exploration tools were added on top of the previous ones and a development system was added that improved the NPC Shops. All of it without making it feel like a pain while playing the game. However, the difficulty and length are similar to the previous game and the english voices are still missing.This time around, I found the combat system to be very enjoyable. You can combo your normal attacks into skills, which can then be comboed into higher level of the same skill once learned, different skills, or you can even use the new Switch Skill, which lets you swap your current character with the one that you chose to be in the reserve, giving you small burst of AP, on top of enabling you to extend a combo with their own skills or simply prepare for the next one. This time around, the Tactic Level system very nicely designed. By consuming AP, used when using skills, you passively increase your Tactic Level gauge, which will automatically level up your Tactic Level once a certain threshold is met. Additionally, the Core Charge system was changed so that instead of gaining a one time supply of CCs across the party, which could be renewed by temporarily disabling someone's item, CCs are gained by using skills with the individual character. A character's Core can even be upgraded further, using Core Shards, gained by using items in combat, which lets you improve a character's CC limit or their performances when using a skill or item of a specific element. Not a big fan of the camera during combat though.The alchemy system got slightly better as well. Instead of taking the average quality of all the items used during a synthesis, it now takes a certain % of each item's quality and add into to the item being synthesized. However, while a nice feature, this also makes it so you can reach high values of quality very easily, making your consumables and equipments much stronger much faster, especially with Romy's development system. While the Alchemy Level system was dropped for a Skill Tree, it didn't feel that bad, since synthesizing, completing quests and exploring ruins granted plenty of SPs. A lot of the recipes are still obtained from the Merge Recipe mechanic. The Multiplicauldron can be unlocked fairly early on, making gearing up your character very easy, if you don't mind farming some gems to dupe, Rebuild system now scales depending on how many Rebuild nodes you've unlocked with a base of 25 levels, and a few more interesting features were added; which I will let you figure out yourself.This game delivers a better exploration experience than the previous game by giving you 200 items basket, monster radar and gathering preview from the beginning. A few new tools were added, which is all fun and stuff while going through the story once. The main contender is the Spirit Beast Whistle, which lets you move faster than running speed and lets you find a few items slightly earlier than you normally would with other tools, but this comes at the cost of having to go through small loading screens when getting on or off of it, which makes it a bit of a hassle when you're trying to gather a variety of items when travelling, unless your goal is speed or items specifically obtained when Mining with the Spirit Beast.I mentioned above about Romy's development system. In this game, you can only sell your items to Romy, and by doing so, it will grant you experience points into various item categories. When leveling these up, items in the shops will get improved, whether it's quality or trait level. Additionally, a lot of items have a one-time reward, which will increase the shops' stocks further or unlock new materials in the shops, which can let you earn certain materials MUCH sooner than you normally would. I found monsters in this game to give a fair amount of standard currency, Cole, and shop prices can even be reduced by leveling up your Town Reputations, which is gained by completing side quests or from the Request Board. My main grip about the game was the Ruin Exploration system. I found the idea to be interesting, but even after forcing myself to try to get interested into the Ruins' histories, I just couldn't. I simply stopped caring after a few ruins and I would just cycle through the items until they fit into the slots. The game is just as great as the previous game, if not better, depending on how you look at it. Outside of the Ruin Explorations, everything else was just so fun and enjoyable. I previously said in its own review that Atelier Ryza was my favorite Atelier by far, well this one takes the spot. I'm really happy with how the Ryza series is turning out so far and I'm looking forward the next one, if they decide to continue the series.My Play Order at the time of this review:1. Mysterious series (Sophie +, Firis -, Lydie & Suelle +)2. Arland series (Rorona +, Totori -, Meruru +)3. Ryza series (Ryza +, Ryza 2 +)

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first time I've 100%'d a game this quickly.Ryza 2 was a blast and even more fun than Ryza 2; for the most part I find Atelier story lines to be quite boring, not really a fan of slice of life games, however Ryza 1 and 2 both got me hooked through the crafting aspects of the games.When I play an MMO, the thing that consumes most of my time isn't the plot, or the leveling, or the quest grinding, it is really the crafting/blacksmithing that gets me hooked.  Atelier Ryza 1 and 2 both got that down pat.Ryza 2 (via plot) expands upon the crafting and makes certain things more sensible (with reason, via plot gate-locks) and makes the crafting/smithing/alchemy a delight to play.  The sound effects, music, and overall crafting system got me hooked from the get go.  My hours at this time says 92.6, I would argue 80 hours alone were spent crafting various items/gears/seeds etc. that were unnecessary to advance the plot.  It's that good.The plot itself is basic slice-of-life fare, the combat isn't very difficult (I actually played most of the game on easy/normal because I hate grinding levels).  However the crafting really hooked me in, I found myself working on expanding the recipe trees "just cuz" and ended up super overpowered because I had managed to accidentally min/max weapons 1/3 of the way through the story.   But you know what, that's crafting for ya.I personally enjoy Stardew, Don't Starve, Recettear, various farming/vending/smithing type games, but the one thing that always keeps me hooked is the blacksmithing and crafting aspect.  And for that, Ryza is the game of choice.

_childDocuments_.review: is a brilliant sequel that expands upon everything that made the original great, while forging a path forward that can be further expanded upon in the trilogy’s .Not only I love how  show a great growth of character development for the original cast of charactersꓹ it also has a large amount of stories waiting for you to discover – making the character content very engaging.There is also a huge improvement in its complex alchemy systemꓹ comparing to its predecessor – and its wide expansive world are just too engrossing to explore. It also has very interesting approaches to exploration and combat on par with the fantastic soundtrack. Neverthelessꓹ the game can be pretty overwhelming due to its massive numbers of mechanics. The alchemy system is complex enough on its own, with the skill tree, item fusion, item reduction, and the aforementioned Essence system to contend with. There is ingredient gathering, of course, which requires a variety of tools such as an axe, bug net and fishing pole. While gathering ingredients in the world, Ryza can also use a grappling-hook like rope to swing around and breathe underwater thanks to Air Drops.Nextꓹ there is a combat system with real-time elements, action and item points, and a tactical system based on completing characters' in-battle requests. Then there are quests, which Ryza must complete in order to improve her reputation around town. Some quests are multi-part, and progress the character arcs of various party members and NPCs. Ryza is also in charged with helping the town's merchants develop their stores by selling them various items she gathers and makes. Finally, she can earn items and themes to decorate her atelier, as well as raise a pet Puni (a jelly-like creature) who can fetch her ingredients of varying quality depending on how well it is fed. With all the sheer amount of mechanicsꓹ there were several times during the game when I felt overwhelmed as there are a lot of information to keep track of. I personally didn't feel like I had a good handle on the game and all its various parts at the beginning until I was nearly at the end. However, this abundance of mechanics definitely does not make the game unplayable, as it could be quite refreshing and appeal to players who enjoy having lots of different things to do.Overall,  is a thoroughly pleasant game and an excellent entry in a rather unique JRPG franchise. Atelier fans will definitely enjoy it, but newbies to the series are encouraged to try it out as well. While the sheer number of mechanics may feel overwhelming at first, the result is an elaborate game with so much to do - but no real pressure to do them all if you don't want to. Besideꓹ who can refuse to explore the natural world with our adorable little Fi?

_childDocuments_.review: The original Atelier Ryza was my entry to this series, so I do not know if this is common for this series but I am extremely impressed by how Gust was able to build a completely new world, create new models for the cast alongside totally new members, improve so much on the original, and do all of this in about one year and two months only.Gust fixed almost every single complaint I had about the combat system of the original Ryza and added so many quality of life improvements that I did not even know I needed. Combat is very fluid now and does not punish you for spending your AP and CC like it did before. Everything else is improved as well. Visuals, characters, cutscenes, synthesis, and more.That is not to say the game is perfect. I only have two complaints about this game:1- The improvements to combat almost makes the game too easy. After crafting strong weapons, you'll easily blow through most enemies and bosses even on the hardest difficulty. I feel like either enemies needed to be made stronger, or more difficulty settings need to be added.2- This is somewhat subjective but it feels like side quests were a little dull in this game. Half my fun with the original was going around town and helping people with alchemy. Everyone had something unique that they needed, but in this game, the side quests all center around the main characters and their needs, only a few others are noteworthy. I would love to see the sequels put more attention to side quests.I've made it very far, but I still have not finished the game, I'll edit the review if any of my views change.

_childDocuments_.review: Atelier Ryza 2 (Something Something Fairy) is the second game in a trilogy, and I want to start by saying that I highly recommend playing all three games. The Ryza trilogy is also part of a much larger franchise, yet its gameplay is a pretty drastic departure from the rest of the series. This is both a blessing and a curse, however, as it means that anyone familiar with other Atelier games will probably want to do some research into some streams or something to see if this looks like it's worth a try, but if you're like me and don't know or don't like most of the rest of the series, the accessible easy-to-learn crafting and the fast-paced real time battles might make this the best in the series (by far, IMO).Never heard of this series? Then none of that context will help. Atelier Ryza is a game that focuses on storytelling in typical JRPG fashion; fight bad guys and get stronger to progress, but unlike Dragon Quest or Final Fantasy, your equipment is never found or earned, but always crafted. Story progress unlocks new areas, new areas have better stuff to craft with, better ingredients make better pizza.The first Ryza game is strong on its own, but Ryza 2 is way better, and one of my favorite games ever made. I loved it so much, even after playing the first two on Switch I purchased all three on Steam just to get the achievements and give myself an excuse to thoroughly play them again.If you haven't played the first Ryza, go get it, then hurry up and buy this, play this, and love this.

_childDocuments_.review: So I'm writing this review under the assumption that you've played the first game, and also as someone who as of right now has only played these two Atelier games and certainly enjoyed them quite a bit. That's both a good and a bad thing, because while the game does almost everything the first game did but very slightly better mechanically, it does so TOO similarly. The enemy variety is already incredibly small and repetitive in this game, but it's also nearly completely the same as the first game's. Many of the collectible resources are also the same early on. Despite some cool new things added such as ruin exploration and the alchemy skill tree you unlock things from it's going to feel a lot too much like the first game especially if you've very recently finished the first so I'd recommend waiting a bit before jumping into it.The story is also a bit more aimless in this one for a time. I definitely feel like though the potential for it to be better was there it really never develops the way I hoped it would but it's not "bad." The music was a strong spot for me, certain areas gave me vibes from games with awesome tracks like Xenoblade. Nothing but positives to say about the ost.Overall, highly recommended but put some space between this game and ryza 1 if you're interested. Very fun game and I really would like to see a Ryza 3.

_childDocuments_.review: Good stuff. If you liked the first one, you'll like the second.It's kind of the perfect sequel in that it doesn't deviate much from the look and feel and style of the first, if at all, but does have enough changes and minor additions to feel like you're doing new stuff. That's really appreciated.PLOTOne day they'll make an Atelier game with a truly excellent story, just not today. This tale had less stakes than Ryza 1, I felt, but also was a bit less home-y and comfortable (you are literally far from home). BATTLEThe previous battle system had a reliance on one interesting decision: do you use your AP to execute awesome moves, or do you save your AP so that you can increase your Tactics to execute awesome-er moves down the line?The Ryza 2 system removes that risk/reward decision entirely. Now, executing awesome moves increases your Tactics to execute awesome-er moves. Hm. Okay, it feels alright, but it lacks a little something.Using items in battle has never been better, however. You can now equip four items and use as many of them on a single turn as you have the CC to spend. If you can afford it, you can use a buff item, a healing item, and two attack items all in one turn! That's good. That's great, even. Love this system.MUSICI prefer the Ryza 1 OST, but there's nothing wrong with this one. It feels good, some real nice tracks.REDUNDANCIESHmmm, this is a weird category for a game. What does it mean?Ryza 2 has a lot of what I feel are unnecessary parts. Redundancies. Some of these are vestigial, as in they were part of the last game and no longer serve a purpose. Others are additions that never fully integrate and wear out quickly.Of the former variety, you still have landmarks. These are special places in the world with special names that add special markers to the map. Finding all the landmarks in Ryza 1 gave you exploration points or something like that, and also allowed you to fill in diaries written by the character of your choice. It wasn't brilliant, but it worked and made the world feel good. But you don't have that same thing in Ryza 2. You just have the landmarks. They make a nice sparkle, say the name, add a marker to your map, and then mean nothing for the rest of the game.Of the latter variety, you have Popularity. As you do quests for certain groups of people (Children, Students, Scholars, etc.), they like you more, and level up. When they level up, their quests increase in challenge and you get some discounts at the shops. The discounts aren't tracked, so they are hardly noticeable. The upgrade in quest challenge doesn't feel like a reward so much as normal quest progression. And each group of people, of which there are very few, level to max (only 3 levels) pretty easily within a few hours of basic play mid-game. This won't stop the game from reminding you that a quest is giving EXP to each group, but it will stop these notifications from being useful in any way. SP is also weird.You have a Skill Tree to unlock basic recipes and skills. As you explore the plot and craft items, you earn SP for the tree. Around mid-game, you should have more than enough SP to unlock everything from the tree, and it's just a matter of moving far enough in the plot for them to allow you to do that. So SP quickly becomes redundant. However, you never stop earning it. Meanwhile, you start unlocking Gems as a currency around mid-game, and also unlock Essences, a currency of which there are five. This means after battle, on top of items you gain, you can gain a variety of currencies:- EXP- Coins- Gold Coins- Gems- Fire Essence- Water Essence- Lightning Essence- Wind Essence- Light EssenceSo you're earning those, and also you're earning SP on the side for crafting, and Popularity for doing quests, even though these last two are now redundant. It seems like it could have been streamlined a bit. Make it so Gems work on the Skill Tree, and by the time you are near unlocking everything, you have to really decide if you want to spend Gems on new skills or use them for their inherent crafting purposes. I don't mind juggling 10 weird currencies, but it's a shame when most of these currencies lose all value while others are still being introduced.ALCHEMYThe crafting is great. I like the attempt to mix up the formula by making the Quality of items accumulative instead of an average, although the freshness is the only thing I really like about it. In the end, getting Quality is easier than it has ever been, and I prefer a little more challenge. Everything else works pretty similarly to the previous installment save the Essence System, which is kinda cool but, like most of the new ideas, not as cleanly integrated as I'd have hoped.OVERALLGood game, recommended for Atelier fans. I'll be buying Ryza 3 when it comes out.

_childDocuments_.review: So, this is my first Atelier game, and I can't compare it with the other games. But as a game on it's own -- I like it a lot. But Did they?Weeeelllll no, in my opinion.I have the same complains and then some lolThey don't ruin the game, but they can get really annoying.Such as:- Constantly getting interrupted by side-story events playing automatically.- Levels are overflowed with monsters/enemies, making exploring and collecting material and clues tedious. That until you get over leveled and they starting scurrying away and it looks hilarious!- Looking for a certain item during synthesizing is still tedious, and could use better sorting, and preferably a search function or an alphabetical order.BUT, they've also added a lot of cool stuff! _childDocuments_.review: Atelier Ryza 2: Lost Legends & the Secret Fairy is an objectively better game than the first due to the many QoL improvements from its predecessor. I enjoyed my ~40 hours with the game and revisiting my favorite apathetic Alchemist. Over, I think that Combat in Ryza 2 experienced a much more significant level of improvement compared to the Alchemy. I found myself feeling the opposite way from my previous review because synthesis was not the highlight of my experience this time around (Shocking... I know!!). To put this into context, Tao's speedy style of play made him a really popular choice for my general adventuring shenanigans. It was fun building up longer combos, generating AP at a faster rate, and then getting into a flow of using skills and items. Alternatively, I think the 7 playable characters lend a good variety of play styles that can keep things fresh throughout the somewhat short adventure. My only gripe with the combat is that it doesn't not fully utilize the perfect guard mechanic due to how the camera functions during battle.In comparison, the Alchemy in Ryza 2 felt largely the same, with some added mechanics on top that I feel didn't shake things up for me. The base or the soul of the process stayed the same, but the few things added at the top layer of end-game Alchemy felt tacked on. I completed Ryza 1 not that long ago and since the synthesis felt too similar, I got disengaged with the whole process early on. It's still a deeply satisfying mechanic, but I believe the best way to appreciate Alchemy in this sequel is to space it out from the first game. I can't believe Ryza forgot all the ♥♥♥♥ she learned and created over the last 3 years!!!To accentuate the greatly improved combat was the whole exploration diary/ruins system. I think it was a fantastic move to divide lore into research items and vestiges that combine progression with comprehension of historical events that are relevant to the present. It's a good mechanic that doesn't drag on and it was a joy to explore the beautifully designed ruins and dungeons. The exploration was easily one my favorite parts of the game.Ryza 2 is a great 40h experience that builds on the first. It's an easy recommendation for a casual JRPG or anyone new to the franchise. Ryza needs to get her ♥♥♥♥ together though!!

_childDocuments_.review: Now i will start saying Ryza as a series didn't appeal to me, I'm a long time Atelier fan and Ryza throw away a lot of the old stuff to attract new fans, of which the battle system being a big one. I'm still irked about that and I will get to that but this is a big step in the correct directionThe characters in Ryza 2 are a improvement for sure, Atelier usually has great characters so Ryza one was a let down when the main supporting roles was annoying to the point of being infuriating. Thankfully they fixed this. Notably, Tao, who in the first game did nothing but moan and cry about everything to the point of being headache inducing is now pretty good (he feels like a new character). They improved his appearance (by ageing him) and now he is more adventurous and has a thirst for ancient knowledge, he is actually a good character. Lent is a huge step back but thankfully he is pretty minor for the main story so you can look beyond it. Klaudia returns and is pretty much herself again, as possibly the only good support from the first game, this is a welcome move, she didn't need changing and thus was kept. There are some new additions too, Clifford who for me was a bit pointless and nothing special but he isn't annoying or anything so no complaints, just dull. Patty (Patricia) who is Tao's student, I liked her, she comes across as passive aggressive to Ryza due to misunderstanding her and Tao's relationship but she comes around in time and even apologises for this. I liked her. Serri is a bit like Clifford, pointless. She is intended to replace Lila but... nah, she was pretty dull but nothing to dislike.in all, good step forward here.Still sporting the live turns, they changed the system a little. Items now freeze the game and you chose what to do, this is great as it made items pointless before as you lost so much time, Otherwise it's slightly less button mashing now, you have basic attacks and skills as before but the chaining is more efficient and ties in well with CC usage. There are some new systems such as core elements but these feel more gimmicky, they serve a role to deal more damage but aren't useful outside the harder modes (legendary) as the game is easy anyway. A improvement from before, I still prefer the turn based system but I was able to enjoy the game a lot more this time due to these changes.The story as a whole is so-so. The story is mostly pretty lacking with spoilers being able to sum it up in maybe a line or so but it was somewhat enjoyable. Without spoilers, you go to the capital, meet your old friends and a new companion (Fi). You explore old ruins to assist Fi (spoiler free reasons). There is no really bigger picture. The enemy from the first game (in the gate) return but only for the end dungeon. I enjoyed exploring the ruins but more over i thought the exploration diary was a fun tool, it was simple and i can't call it a puzzle  element BUT it did offer some lore into the stories being told which was fun. All in all it was mostly enjoyable, it got pretty dull and bland at some points though, hence the so-so comment as sometimes i just wanted to move on as it was boring me. I felt this nose dived a little. Ryza 1's system was simple (which isn't a compliment for old time players) but i understand this helps newer players understand it. In two, its just as simple but made easier with the essence upgrades. You can max items so easily with no real effort at all. Thus it sucked, the fun in Atelier is spending time finding items with the right traits and then trying to use high quality items to construct the perfect end result, this is just throw stuff in and add traits, it will always be good if you put even a ounce of effort. Additionally the evolution link was dumb, other than being annoying for trial and error being the only way forward, it  doesn't work proper. Say you put in a bomb and rose bomb and it makes a new item, putting in a rose bomb and a bomb wouldn't... you have to order them which means there is endless possibilities, this might sound good but it actually feels like lazy development and stupid as a system.Overall, as a long time fan of Atelier, it still falls short of the older games but it does feel a lot more like a Atelier game. I found myself enjoying the party member events (mostly) and some side quests was fun (except the "Bandits", they was super dull, not helped by not being voiced, but their quests sucked). Alchemy is too simple and has no challenge at all. Difficulty speaking, you can start on hard but "Hard" feels like normal at best, it was seriously easy. Nothing even half killed me once. you do unlock 3 new difficulties but sadly these are upon beating the game so your not as motivated to try them. The ending was both good and bad, I loved they opted for a more sad ending, it certainly wasn't what i would call a happy end but there is a post-credits scene which has  a "White space" background, this felt lazy, It isn't easy to explain without massive spoilers but the events what happened... lets just say it would be nice to see something on the otherside.All in all, a upgrade to the first Ryza and a more enjoyable experience. Still some hiccups but they seem to be finding their way if they plan to release more in the series. I certainly wouldn't complain to them splitting the series with one following turn based combat and one using this (As Sophie 2 just released, this could be possible).So yeah, its worth buying, just maybe avoid the season pass,the content is mostly "okay" but not worth the money. Oh, and the costumes are nothing special.

_childDocuments_.review: Just what I had hoped the successor to Ryza 1 would be. It's more of the charming Ryza world and feels just like the first game. It feels very comfortable jumping into it after having played the first one, but they've made plenty of new features and improvements to the systems so that it still feels fresh and updated without being unfamiliar or cumbersome.There are new layers to alchemy that you can unlock through an alchemy skill tree (although you can unlock everything), opening the tool wheel while next to a resource node now displays the items that can be harvested with that tool, plus new layers to the town, exploration, and your atelier.One of my favorite updates is what they did to combat. A lot of it is the same, but improved. For example, the tactics level in fights is now upgraded by using your tactics points actively. In the first game you had to spend points directly to level up tactics, which usually meant I'd just auto attack enemies until a high tactics level. In this game, using skills levels up tactics, so now I'm constantly using skills and other active combat interactions.If you enjoyed the first game, you'll enjoy this too. It keeps all of the elements that I really loved about the previous game and world, and added more depth and QoL changes. Really Enjoying it.

Combat especially got the biggest overhaul with new features that makes it a lot more actiony for an ATB game.Main gripe with the game is just the overall progression of the game, but that applies for the entire trilogy. It just feels bad crafting gear early on when you're limited in gems and item slots, but then in endgame/post game, the stats from a strong but far-from-perfect set is already overkill. _childDocuments_.review: After playing the first game I was overwhelmingly pressured to continue the trilogy, and this second installment is easily the best of the bunch. While it's not as simple or story-driven as Ryza 1, it's not the jumbled, substance-driven mess that Ryza 3 was, and this game has that perfect balance.It is weak in the story department, however. Credit where it's due, the environment of Ashra-am Baird defines this game and clearly sets itself apart from the others. However, it does feel that this story is too different and it feels as if we never get a proper reintroduction of its characters or setting in Ryza 3. It feels too drastic of a change in Ryza's persona, who was developed as that child-like, innocent girl looking to make a difference in her conservative town using alchemy, and in this game she's almost completely different, establishing herself far from home as an actual difference-maker in society. Even if it does deviate from the original idea, it does play with the idea pretty well.AR2 succeeds in the same ways that the first game did, in soundtrack, atmosphere, characters, and pretty much anything you can think of. But where this game completely excels in is its gameplay. I HIGHLY enjoyed the open-ended fun combat of Ryza 2 over the rigid one of Ryza 1 and the confusing style of Ryza 3. Basically, it finds that balance between skill, grinding, and game sense. The actual alchemy mechanics were the best they've ever been and I would be satisfied if it stayed that way through Ryza 3. The dungeon research was perhaps my favorite gimmick of this game, though. I really liked the way the executed it here and I had a lot of fun playing around with it. There's a lot to like about the gameplay, but I won't spoil it all.All in all, this game was well-made. It is not perfect, and it shouldn't be, but I do like the direction this game took. I do wish that there was a bit more of a connection to the other two games and a bit of story refining, but these continuity flaws don't bring down how great this game is. The gameplay is enjoyable, and that's all that matters in the end. To put it in simpler terms: it makes the best of both worlds.

_childDocuments_.review: An improvement over the original in almost every regard!Much better combat, mainly due to the defense command and core charges needing to be built up, and separately tracked per character, meaning you have a reason to use alchemy on each character instead of leaving Ryza with your strongest tools.Character graphics are very good, with working physics this time; The terrain and backgrounds are still somewhat PS3-esque, but they take advantage of it with more expansive areas.They somewhat abuse a lot of modern post-processing effects, to the point where the game looks better with some of them turned off, but thankfully the option to turn them off is there. The PC port is a significant improvement over the intital release of Ryza 1; I'm very glad they've learned from it.If you want a comfy, low-intensity RPG with a focus on crafting mechanics, I highly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Upon finishing the first game which I felt was just a great JRPG with it's Alchemy and Gathering systems I instantly jumped onto Atelier Ryza 2, which I still recommend if you enjoyed the first game.Within the first 15mins I was so happy with the amount of QoL improvements and new features I started noticing 1 after the other, like the Combat, the removable of Roles which was just horrible in the first game, then with the Gathering Tools and so much more.After a few hours of playing I then sadly started to see some of the new features or QoL improvements to feel a bit on the negative side, like the Skill Tree and the fact that you no longer get negative Quality when doing a Synthesis with materials which makes things too easy and maxes the Quality very quickly.I feel if you enjoyed using Seeds in the first game they very much made them useless in this sequel, though some may disagree, I never found them of any use in both games and felt they were implemented without much thought to what else the game offers.The Story felt very lacking compared to the first game and just seemed as though it had no purpose or reason to exist, which only until after 40-50 hours did the Story start to pick up and become interesting and more so near the end.Although I can say I still enjoyed it, it doesn't make up for the low quality in the early parts of the game.I did again play on Medium Difficulty (Just like Ryza 1) and sadly wish I played on a Harder difficulty instead as I felt this sequel just had a big amount of QoL improvements with no balancing, It was just a walk in the park.With all that said I still recommend the game as some people may find what I said to be fine or won't effect them.I look forward to playing the next Sequel Ryza 3 very soon once I have finished the Anime, and this time I plan to play on Very Hard Difficulty.EDIT: Overall with Ryza 1, 2 and 3, I would say Ryza 3 is the best and the game I enjoyed the most followed by Ryza 1, _childDocuments_.review: Well, growing popularity of the Atelier franchise got my attention, so I deсided to give it a try. After reading tons of reviews and comments, I focused on hitting the second game about Ryza, because almost everyone considers it much better in terms of technical realization and QoL. Moreover, game almost always makes references to the previous part in dialogs and during cutscenes, thus making it easier to understand the background of Ryza and her companions. However, due to poorly written story and characters, previous adventures of the party sound pretty boring. Okay, first things first - the game has plenty of pros, so let's talk about them.- Overall visual design of Ryza as a character is pretty good and somehow unique - she can be recognized almost everywhere thanks to her attire and expresiveness. Due to overwhelming modern tendency of making dull and scary femaly characters, seeing Ryza on screen is a feast for eyes. No joke, those man-like "strong and independent" women chacters are lame and totally unnatural;- Local fast-travel system. It's simple, quick and intuitive - almost all avaliable quests are shown on the map and can be easily found. By the way, this fs doesn't require money, special items or whatsoever - you can just click and teleport wherever you want (if you've already discovered the location). That's truly amazing - you dont have to wait, waste resources or perform repeatative actions (like running around the World Tree in GoW 2018);- Relatively easy story/equipment progression. The game is not trying to set up a grindwall or lvl-cap - you can progress at you own pace with no rush, timers or other pressing issues;- Great ruins exploration system based on the small detective-like research and simple logic - first of all, Ryza gathers "echoes" of the past and memories of phantoms, then she (with the player) deduces the history of the place and finds a way to progress further. Unfortunate observation: neither Ryza nor Tao ever read the gathered notes except for the "how to get deeper in the ruins" part. As for me, I liked reading this little stories much more than following the main plot;- Cute maskot Fi - every franchise has one, I assume; Yet, aside cuteness, this creature is merely useless in terms of gameplay and even triggers local calamity;- Pleasant music and surronding;Well, I still don't recommend this game due to a variety of crucial shortcomings and drawbacks:- Horrible tech side of the game. Seriously, despite the stylish design and more or less amusing visuals, the game is horrible in every technical aspect of its realisation: game kept dropping resolution to something HD-like until I locked config file; absolutly horrible controls - all those menus/submenus/confirmation windows pop up on one another making it hard to navigate; skill tree and crafting menu are even harder to navigate and select; sometimes it's unclear whether I've pressed the right or wrong button - I had to figure it out experimentally; overall, the game looks like a guest from 2010 - those sloppy animations, flickering textures, abrupt dialog sequences... - it all reminds me of Agarest: Generations of War, yet the interface of that game despite being unintuitive served its purpose pretty well. I don't expect Ryza to hit Zelda BotW's quality of animation, but why don't they try to animate properly dialogs/cutscenes at least?- Tangled and condoluded crafting system. Many reviewers adore local gather-and-craft system, but I personally hate it. It's too massive and simply misleading. Yes, you can customize every single craftable everything, but it's too tyring after first 5 hours of gameplay. Moreover, game makes you return to craft again and again, and then you must craft something once again. I prefer ye ol' quick press-one-button crafting without all those pop-ups and fireworks;- Limited inventory and even limited atelier container. Seriously?! I'll keep praying for those let's-limit-their-inventory game designers burn in hell forever;- Plain and generic main story. Here we have another story about the upcoming apo.... Well, you guessed right. Bunch of weirdly dressed adventurers will save the world. Again. The story could be engaging if the characters were good, but they are not. By the way, Ryza is the most infuriating of them - sometimes she makes me think that she is just plainly stupid and survived another ruins exploration session just on pure fool's luck and accidental lunar-solar eclipse in the galaxy far away.- Tutorials. Dozens of tutorials. Perhaps, that's one of the worst cases of tutorial integration - dozens of tutorials pop up during the game, sometimes 4-5 in a row. Game contains many mechanics, some of them require propper demonstration, but we've got only tons of text. Besides, the most part of those mechanics will soon be forgotten and never used again (unless it's required to cover the main story).- Combat system. It's sort of turn-real-time-hybrid, but it fails to deliver tactical depth (like turn-based) or bring-it-on adreniline rush (like real-time), so it's something plain and generic at its core. The drawbacks of this combat system are clearly seen during the battles with bosses - the only option to stay alive (if the boss is of higher level than your party) is to try to stunlock it, which is hilarious.- Fetch quests, hundreds of them. Aside the main story and some character-related events, every single quest in this game implies crafting N items, gathering N items or killing N monsters, which is, after playing some of the best jrpgs, is absolute nonsense.- Zero development of the characters throuhgout the game - nothing impacts their personalities.- Weird BGM playing during combat and in some locations. The mysterious atmosphere of ancient ruins with tragic history is completely ruined by overcheerful melody and Ryza's annoying victory pose after combat.  - Absolutely lame aniclimactic ending, which controverses with the lore of the game. Of course, combined power of ancient nations that wielded advanced alchemy and magic is nothing in comparison with Ryza's gang - bunch of youngsters can easily eradicate demon lord and close the portal that can not be closed according to their own words (!). F***k that history of the ruins! We can do this! Just don't forget to believe in yourself! Oh, man...- Fanservice and merchandise. Don't get me wrong, I like merchandise and fanservice. I even have a small decent collection of anime figures, but Atelier is a different thing - everything here (in the game) is about fanservice and merchandise (countless super expensive figures of Ryza, other collectibles), thus developers don't pay much attention to the contents of the game - franchise will get its profit regardless, only by selling Ryza's face on every collectible. Well, seems like I expected too much from a pretty hyped product. As the means of killing couple of hours a day without thinking too much about the plot and game mechanics - second iteration of Ryza is a decent game, but as deep involving jrpg it's just a generic product with a cute recognizable character as the main selling point.This game is pure fanservice entity that resides atop the image of Ryza - plainly stupid and barely capable alchemist, whom I (as a player) is supposed to build the connection to. She leads a group of one-sided followers, each of whom represents an rpg-stereotype. Well, the only person who tries to improve is Bos and that's it. Moreover, this gang causes the calamity it had to deal with, which can be hardly called heroic. If every Atelier game was, is and will be like this, I don't want to deal with the franchise.

_childDocuments_.review: So, from someone who liked and played most of atelier games: This game is a bit hard to recommend with certainty because it is a very craft centered game. If you are in for the combat and how it works, sorry, but most of the important game mechanics is gonna be around the crafting system, although combat does have a few nice things. However, the crafting system in itself is incredibly well done, and with way too many options for you to choose what you want and how to do it, not to mention different ways to get around to your own thing. In short, the game has a lot of depth with the crafting system. So basically, if you think you can enjoy that, go ahead and be my guest. The story is pretty nice with its up and down moments, and you usually do end up liking the characters and their development. Do keep in mind though, that this game does have some relation in both gameplan and story to the first one, so if you are gonna start now I highly recommend going for Atelier Ryza 1 first and ONLY then trying out this one. Otherwise you are gonna get spoiled and quite confused on some stuff (finished the game a few hours ago, so I can confirm, story does end up confusing if you didn't play the first game). If you don't really enjoy thinking a bit to optimize usable items like bombs/heals/debuffs, equipment and even gathering tools, or you are not a fan of crafting stuff in games, then my friendly advice is to look somewhere else.

_childDocuments_.review: Another excellent Atelier game. The story is fun/decent so far as per normal with a good focus on the adventure part of adventure. The way they acquire the egg and the compass was badly done but it's easy to get past that. Combat feels better and crafting works really well with its new twist. I dislike that gathering has no effect on the SP you gain however, as even 1 SP per gather would be rewarding.I disagree with a lot of people, I find the exploration journal to be really engaging and further my feeling of adventure. It's a lot of fun piecing it together and reading through the clues and information it gives you. I also like the animal companion Fi. I agree that it should've been an adventure companion and not a story focus. Atelier games are always strongest when they build on their well developed characters. Focusing too much on Fi takes away that aspect.The game's biggest weakness is its start, which I understand. Atelier games have always started slow because they begin by building your connection with the characters as well as building the setting. However as a sequel and coming from the position where the majority of characters are already developed and understood the slow start ends up taking away from the story rather then building on it. It's like having a foundation and a building on top, only for you to place another foundation on top of the building before continuing to develop. Having never done this before I understand why it happened, just thought I should point out that the start of the story can be a lot more engaging if done differently.Always worth recommending Atelier games.Edit: The character interactions are really flawed in this one unfortunately. Their lack of experience with sequels shows. Fi is a good addition and the animal being used as a crutch is a symptom and not the root of the problem. Excluding new characters (which still revolve around old ones), the character events mainly focus on the already established relationship between them and each others past. When you have a time-gap and a sequel, what is interesting to the player is how the characters have changed / what they have achieved, not what has already been. This is why the story is one of the weakest once you get farther into the game. All Atelier games have a simple storyline, but most make up for it with their great character arcs. This one unfortunately didn't know what to do to achieve that and fell flat. Hopefully they can learn from this.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely solid successor to Ryza 1, a step up in every way.Cute character stories, lots of fun systems that all feed back into the synthesis loop, cool ways to continue to improve your items after synthesis. And while the synthesis itself is kind of dumbed-down compared to other Atelier games still, it does a lot to remove the tedium that may keep out new fans while still keeping enough depth to pay out for those that get really invested in it.The real-time turn-based combat has been way improved as well. There's a ton you can do to eke out more damage, lots of things to chain together, and having a fourth character you can sub in really lets you be constantly doing something instead of waiting on your next turn. I was hesitant to call Ryza 1 combat better than some of the previous strictly turn-based ones, but Ryza 2's combat is the best in probably the whole Atelier series.As for some things I didn't like as much:The exploration diary + skill tree felt like a way to get back somewhat to the Mysterious idea diary thing but kind of fell flat for me. It's not difficult to max out the skill tree a little too early, and just be left with a bunch of skill points and skill point rewards wasting away. If the later DLCs add anything to the skill tree I'll probably be able to just outright buy it out right when it comes and still have leftover.The overarching story of the game is also a little whatever. I like the individual character stuff  (Minor spoilers, opinion on state, no specific story beats. Do not read if you are already getting the game)  It's a party JRPG, and the individual member stories were more than enough to keep me going personally, so this did not affect my enjoyment of the game. I can see how this would be a detriment to others though, it's worth mentioning.Basically, if you played and liked Ryza 1 this is a must-get. This game is my new favorite Atelier game, finally dethroning Sophie -- the first one I played. , it really is a direct continuation unlike with the previous games' series where the hopping of protagonists meant each was its own contained story. A vast majority of the character story and the foundations of the game story will go right over your head without it. Ryza 1 is a good game I'd recommend as well anyways.

_childDocuments_.review: While I consider Atelier Ryza 1 probably the worst Atelier game to this date, Ryza 2 improves on literally every bad thing of Ryza 1. I can't say how the entire game is, after just 8 hours, but I can say that this is very unlikely a game I won't be able to recommend. And no, you don't need to play Ryza 1 to play this. Just note that going back from this to Ryza 1 would be absolutely awful.Gust always did this. After a bad game you'd get a game fixing a whole lot of the previous game. Mana Khemia after Iris 3. Atelier Totori after Atelier Rorona (vanilla, not plus/DX what's on steam). Atelier Shallie after Escha and Logy (which wasn't quite as bad as the other examples, but still the worst of the good Atelier games) And now Ryza 2 after Ryza 1--Cutscenes so far improved. No more terribly written characters you hate and randomly become good people without any development. (I don't know what the future of the game brings, but there are no terrible characters so far, period, so it's hard to become like Ryza 1)-The music, while still Ryza style of sorts, is much closer to what you want in an Atelier game. The main town theme alone is so good, I don't mind randomly walking instead of warping. (!)-The CC system has been vastly improved. No more item sacrificing. Actually having sustain between battles. Other characters you don't control have their own CC pool (I'm pretty sure), so swapping for items is now a thing. -Item usage in battles has been improved. You have time to choose them, can use multiple at once and other fun things, with more intuitive controls. CC are built by using skills and the "consumable" items seem, on first glance, very strong. (of course they don't actually get consumed)-The ranks in battles have been improved. You don't have 1 hit normal attacks on rank 1 anymore, which makes it take forever to upgrade. You also don't need to spend AP to increase the rank anymore, just use them.-Lot's of comfort functions, like seeing what items an object yields, are already available from the beginning-The world is bigger, and you can even go to the first Ryza's areas with.. some kind of DLC I'd assume. I don't know if all are available, but quite a few at least are there.There's more, and the world is this time actually quite beautifully made. But I think this is enough to give a good idea. If you didn't like Ryza 1, this is still worth checking out. If you liked Ryza 1, this game does everything better, provided you are fine with the game's scale being bigger. And you even have auto save now. Took them a while.edit: After playing a lot more there are mostly two things I'd like to say.-The writer is probably the same. There are still a lot of the same issues like in Ryza 1, though it's not quite that extreme. Doesn't change though that the cutscenes are extremely uninteresting. They can be skipped though, and probably should be to quite an extend.-Hard mode is about as hard as easy or even very easy in Ryza 1. You can fix that with cheat engine and set it to legendary, which is maybe a little over Ryza 1's hard mode, but it's a pretty huge issue. I was even thinking changing my recommendation here, because in all honesty, the difficulties the game allows you to choose normally will drag down the game A LOT, add to that the boring and sleep inducing cutscenes, and you have yourself a good game to forget. If you play on Legendary however it can be quite fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Gust cut as many corners as they could to get Ryza 1 out which created some blaring issues such as nearly nothing being voiced outside of the main scenario and a sparse post-game. This game fully dispelled my suspicions of a new lazy direction for them.They patched up anything I could possibly complain about with the first game while introducing a plethora of engaging mechanics throughout combat, trading, and synthesis. The soundtrack is ludicrously good, particularly the ruins themes. As far as narrative goes, it starts out pretty weak with borrowing from the first game's events, but it goes on to improve on that and introduce a lot of its own charm. I haven't had this much fun with a game from the series since A18. My only misgiving in recommending it is that you need the background from the first game's plot for a lot of it. After seeing what Gust is capable these days Ryza 1 is a really mediocre affair, but it's terse enough to bear through for these absolute diamond. I just hope the next Atelier project has a protagonist with more clothes.

_childDocuments_.review: Not that far into it yet, but I already love it. If you enjoyed Ryza's first outing, this one is definitely worth a go. One of the big things I've noticed is how a lot of the aspects and mechanics of the first game were improved. Both exploration and combat feel a lot deeper and rewarding. The musical cues and dialogue invoke nostalgia of the first game, while striking the same emotions as the previous title. The new additions, such as the Skill Tree mechanics, Ruins, and Exploration Tools are all welcome additions and give new life to an already well loved title. I'll probably edit or write a full review once I've 100% the game, but at only 13 hours in, I can't wait to sink my teeth deeper into Ryza's  second adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: Reluctant recommendation, probably neutral.It's a decent follow up to the first Atelier Ryza, it brings in some quality of life improvements and additions to the crafting process. This game is playable on its own without having played the first, as any references to the first game are minor and don't affect the enjoyment. 👍The combat is simple and fun, and improved by spending time on the alchemy (crafting) process. Which in turn is improved by exploring new areas and finding new ingredients. So all in all, it's a satisfying and rewarding loop of explore, gather, craft, dominate. 👍The music is pleasant to listen to, catchy and memorable, and some are reminiscent of the first game's soundtrack. 👎Where this entry falls over though is the mundane "story" that is rendered almost to pointlessness.  Oh, it has lore, and as the exploration progresses you uncover entries that hint at some grand events behind the scenes. But the actual story is just weak; in fact it's summarized entirely in the game's title. Lost Legends & the Secret Fairy. You uncover lost legends, and there's a secret fairy.  There is no purpose to the fairy, other than a blatant attempt at  a cheap emotional tug at the heartstrings. As for the lost legends, believe it or not, no purpose either!

_childDocuments_.review: This is an early review, as I'm only a few hours into the game and a fair amount of that time has been spent in traditional Atelier fashion: Gathering and Experimenting. As such, this is more just my observations on what I do and don't like about the game so far.Like: - The gameplay loop is familiar with some fresh spins - Most systems, like synthesis and combat, will feel familiar to anyone who has played Ryza 1, but will be easy enough to pick up for anyone not familiar with it. (Before Ryza 1 my favorite synthesis was Firis, and Ryza blew that out of the water) - With a little intuition its easy enough to ramp into synthesis loops early on - So far the characters are highly likable, though that may also be nostalgia as I was a huge fan of the Ryza 1Dislike: - While the combat handles well (and personally I'm a huge fan of the active timer system), it feels like you gain too much too quickly. Playing on normal, it was absurdly easy to level Ryza and Tao to 25+ before you even get a stable third party member - Story/Gameplay segregation: So far, two major cutscenes have left me speechless, both dealing with Volker. First is Ryza's reaction to the price of rent. "I couldn't make that in a year" except as a returning protagonist she has canonically gained that much money from single fights in the past, as an alchemist she can make an absurd amount of money synthesizing items with the Expensive trait, and within an in-game week after completing Volker's task I'd already made about that much off combat and delivery quests without stopping to do synthesis even once. There's no reason for Ryza to react as negatively as she did. Second, in a random event, Volker stopped in and said "You're not holding up your end of the bargain and helping the people". Between the first meeting and that random event I've already started nearly every available citizen questline and reported well over 2-dozen item or monster-slaying deliveries. These just left a bad taste in my mouth. I realize these things are scripted, but there should at least be some connection between the scriptwriting and your actual accomplishments outside the main plot.In the end though, I will still wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone looking for a wholesome, cute, or lighthearted JRPG experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Mechanically superior to the previous game but with the setting not being as clear an improvement.I'm not far enough along to comment on the plot.  The ruins feel a bit too much like a stereotypical JRPG dungeon you can get out of a random dungeon generator.  The lore that goes with them is far superior to the layout and implementation.  The setting feels a bit more alienated, likely a natural consequence of swapping from a village where the main character grew up to a city the main character is visiting for the first time.Crafting seems as good if not better than the previous game.  Gathering is pretty good as well, with the 'see what you can gather' being a very nice feature for saving bag space.One of the biggest improvements is how CC work for using items, making them something more than 'boss only'.  CC now charges within a battle, so using items in one battle doesn't mean you will have less uses when you get to the boss.

_childDocuments_.review: Atelier Ryza 2 is the 22nd main entry in the Atelier series. This is the first game in the Atelier series that has our previous protagonist continue as such, further developing Reisalin's character and her story.Until now we would see previous protagonists in supporting roles, this changes completely in the Ryza saga. I feel this change of direction fits the specific "Summer Memories" theme of this saga pretty well, as we can now continue working on making more memories with both old and new beloved friends.The story takes place three years after the events of the previous game. After Reisalin's friends left Kurken Island to pursue their dreams, Ryza decides to stay home, following her alchemy studies and also serving as a teacher to the younger children in the village. But she's begun to feel her alchemy skills have hit a limit...What starts this new adventure is that Ryza receives a letter from Tao, who is studying in the capital city, telling her about how ancient ruins around the city might have something to do with alchemy, and inviting her to come over. At the same time, she is asked to investigate a mysterious glowing stone. She takes the stone with her and heads to the capital, where she reunites with old friends, meets new ones, and also discovers that her stone is in fact an egg which hatches a mysterious creature that she names Fi.These events eventually lead us to the main focus of the story which is investigating the ruins around the city. You'll have to uncover the truth behind the ruins and the mysteries of the Lost Legends!The ruins also introduce a new ability which allows Ryza to see the past with a magic compass to investigate what happened in the past, rewarding us with SP and sometimes progressing the story.The main story features a more clear overall objective to work on that is quite interesting and also feels like a great improvement.It might be important to note that Empel and Lila return in this game, but they're not playable, I guess we could say that they get replaced by the new characters.Some of the new features that I enjoyed a lot in this new sequel is the new ways to move around in the field, including a grappling hook, the ability to swim and explore mysterious underwater areas and being able to summon a monster that you can mount which can also dig up materials! Reisalin's passion for adventures gets a big boost thanks to these new abilities! Areas also are slightly bigger than before and there's more verticality to each different place that improves exploration quite a lot. The battle system is similar to the previous game’s and it includes some improvements. The previous system in which characters use physical attacks to build up AP so you can use skills to build up CC to use items remains similar.You can now execute a Perfect Block which will not only reduce damage taken considerably but also boosts your AP.There's also a new Skill Chain system which allows you to queue multiple skills as a combo that also increases the power of each skill depending on how long the chain lasts.The Tactical Level now also gradually increases automatically as characters perform actions, removing the need for the player to balance AP for skills and raising its level.Every character can now also equip Core Drives, which allows you to use a special move that can be activated once in battle when using a specific combination of items.The alchemy system has also changed a bit.Recipes and upgrades are now unlocked spending SP which you can earn from synthesis or clearing sidequests and requests. This is done in a new Skill Tree menu.The "Linkage Synthesis" system from the previous installment has evolved with greater depth, enabling players to simply fill the Material Loops with the required ingredients to create everything from weapons and tools to medicine.The newly introduced "Essence" feature now allows players to alter the elemental trait of an item during synthesis, and by altering the essence of a Material Loop the final item can take on brand-new qualities.Getting to see how the main characters have changed in these three years is pretty interesting too. And I was pretty happy to see Klaudia and Tao now wield different weapons in battle! Klaudia now uses a Bow while Tao used Dual Blades.The soundtrack is still amazing and somehow even better than the one in the first game! Not only has Hayato Asano returned as the composer but we also got more variety of composers for other specific scenarios!The new area tracks are incredibly beautiful and incredibly immersive. I still love how we also get day and night variations for many of these tracks, something that I also love about the Xenoblade series.The art direction and graphics also got a few improvements. The animations both in battle and as you move in the field have improved quite a bit from the first game.This might be why the battle system also feels overall faster to me. Perhaps its that I'm having too much fun with it, and that's great!I love these series and the atmosphere that these games have, you know that happy feeling you get when you eat your favorite food? These games give me that kind of feeling everytime! Reisalin's attitude to always strive to improve and look for new exciting destinations to visit is contagious and charming, and it also shows in the excellent music in-game.I found some few things that still diminish the experience of the game for me. I expected to find more enemy variety and not as many enemy recolors as in the past title but that didn't seem to change much. I also find the Normal difficulty to be too easy, and considering some previous Atelier games I'd love to see more freedom to spend my items as much as I would like.I feel like items aren't as meaningful or have as big of an impact as they used to in the past, but perhaps I'm just a bit nostalgic.The PC version graphics settings could be improved a bit, the main feature that many probably want to see improved is the anti-aliasing for an overall cleaner image quality.And lastly, both Ryza 1 and 2 not having English voice acting can be frustrating for many, not that its my case as I think the Japanese cast is perfect as is.The Atelier series are a great definition of cozy games, comparable to a slice of life anime show like "K-On!" or "Miss Kobayashi's Dragon Maid" basically featuring cute girls doing cute things. None of these games will fail to put a smile on your face, so if you're looking for something different and you also enjoy jRPG's I'll always recommend these games!

_childDocuments_.review: Not as good as Ryza 1, but still solid.Battle system is much improved. All the awkwardness of CC and skills vs items is gone. It's a bit button spammy, and I'd still prefer to go back to the old turn-based style, but this works well enough.Gathering and exploration have also been improved. Adventuring items and gathering items now have separate slots, so you don't run out of space and don't need to craft hybrid items. You can now upgrade the gathering abilities of your staff and hands, so they now match the abilities of the other gathering methods. Exploration is a bit more varied as well, though honestly nothing major was added - you get a rope, you can swim, you get a mount (that I kinda forgot to ever use), and there are more narrow passages (mostly for pervy screenshot purposes, but hey).Alchemy is the same for the most part. There were a couple changes that help keep alchemy from being quite so easily abused in the very early game (more required materials to craft, item level limits), but the full range of abuse becomes available much earlier since you gain access to gem reduction and duplication much sooner than the previous game. On top of the normal crafting, you have other systems layered on top, like core drive, and a couple other things. These are completely unnecessary, I never touched them and don't really know what they do.Story and characters... honestly this is where the game kinda fell flat for me. I think the first game actually benefitted from its smaller cast. The larger cast in Ryza 2 brings with it a proportionally larger number of cutscenes and character events. It all gets rather tedious after a while. The story was just kinda there for most of the game - explore some ruins and solve the mysteries of your strange new pokemon friend. Then at the end there's something of a surprise twist that's not really all that surprising, but comes out of nowhere with no foreshadowing. The first game had a much better pacing in its plot.Unfortunately, there's also no postgame to speak of. I tore apart the final boss in maybe a minute. Apparently there's an extra boss after that to hunt down, but that's nothing compared to the 5-6 in the previous game. Maybe they'll add some in an update, but for now there's really no reason to craft super powerful gear.
