_childDocuments_.review: I don't how it is possible but the sequel is wayyy easier than the 1st game. The standout enemy is the last boss and that's only because I didn't pay enough attention at maximizing all equipment and consumables.One thing I absolutely hated about this game is the amount of cutscenes. They went wayyy overboard with it. They're not even interesting cutscenes, just unimportant fluff over and over.I know it's ironic for me to say this but I got crafting fatigue while playing this crafting based game. Some materials becomes obsolete mid game and there's a limited space in your inventory to keep them. Even worse are the gem reduction. Just like in the first game, you have to manually select the materials you want to reduce ONE BY ONE and that gets tiring by the end game. There's also a SP system where you need SP to unlock recipes. I totally get why they went this route, Ryza isn't an amateur anymore and she already knew all of the recipes in the game but by mid game, I've already accumulated enough SP to exceed the maximum amount of SP needed to unlock everything by 10 times. 10 TIMES. This system is clearly wasn't thought out very well.  Story is also not that great. Anyone who says otherwise is lying to themselves. It's basically another retelling of "go to 5 different dungeons to unlock the final dungeon" trope. We've already seen this trope many, many times in other JRPG and this game didn't do anything different with it.Gameplay is marginally still the same but they knew they f*cked up the core item system in the 1st game because they overhauled it completely in this game. Players can now use core items as long as they can generate CC for it instead of having a limited amount of it.However, despite my complaints, it's still a competent JRPG. No technical difficulties for me as I was playing and that's rare for PC games nowadays. Since most Atelier series comes in trilogies, I'm kinda excited for the 3rd chapter of Ryza's adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic sequel. The feeling of being a young adult hanging out with a group of new and old friends in a new place is delightful. When you go around town you really feel like you're checking up on your friends and helping them out with their problems, or simply hanging out and having fun. Ryza is a lovely protagonist that really cares for her friends, and they still feel like a warm family. The new characters fit in perfectly.The new dungeon exploration mechanics are really interesting and it feels good to investigate, find new bits of lore and connect them together. It's quite simple, but it works. The only very minor problem I have with the game is just how easy the combat is, even on the hardest difficulty you can select initially. The harder modes shouldn't be locked behind beating the game. In any case, combat feels great and attack animations look amazing.I can't wait to go on a new adventure with these characters again!

_childDocuments_.review: Compared to Ryza 1, the story is more bland as it has almost no character developement, and it starts randomly with the same chance of going out for a walk and finding a treasure box...In short, Ryza goes to the capital since Tao invited her over while he was studying some ruins around the city, and then more and more ruins keep popping out and our protagonists explore them with a minigame that requires you to collect clues and understand the story behind every ruin, which is also one big story at the end of the game. Also, the game has always had magic and monsters in it, but our protagonists were just humans using such magic and fighting those monsters, while in Ryza 2 there is a magical being from another world with the super menacing name of  that becomes Ryza's pet, and out of nowhere, she finds a whistle that can call an even bigger monster to ride on... All this kind of breaks the mood of "4 young adventurers improving themselves from scratch" and made them look like the "usual heroes of the story the world couldn't live without", which is partially true for Ryza 1, but at least there they actually improved themselves at the point the could defeat the , here, Ryza just becomes a video player of past events thanks to Fi's presence and "only her can unveil the misteries of those ruins"... meh!Ryza: Serri: Klaudia:  The other characters are Patty, a new loli girl which is also a noble who follows you just because she's Tao's student, Lent and Tao, that are grown up compared to their old selves (why not the girls then?!) and Clifford, a treasure hunter you'll forget as soon as he gets out of screen.Suggested to keep up with the series, and it's fun to play as a game, but when compared to the first chapter, it has a lot less charm to it

_childDocuments_.review: I 100%'d the game and I enjoyed it throughout.Mostly the same synthesis system as Ryza 1, so if you liked it, it's back.Combat is a little different - you won't use items much unless you unlock a non-obvious part of the skill tree.  After that, item spam ahoy mateys.The big new mechanic is the ruin exploration minigame.  I'm not sure but it feels like it probably lost a bit in translation from the original Japanese.  You now get a wheel of suggested clues + some slots to fit them in with colored hints.  So its kind of a "read the lore to continue" thing which is fine, i guess.  It probably could have been better in terms of the minigame design, but at least it forces you do some lore engagement instead of just grinding away at that cauldron.

_childDocuments_.review: I was pretty neutral despite the still inferior combat, like in Ryza 1, before this one issue. In the cafe there's a quest board. On this quest board, you gradually get more and more difficult quests, eventually requiring a 500 cole fee.Many of these supposedly more difficult quests reward close to or less than 500 cole.If you're like me, you'll assume it's a 500 cole deposite that you get back. Surely a quest that only gives a reward of 120 cole wouldn't literally reward you less than you paid... right?You would be mistaken. And this quest board was originally a good source of cole, and the only low effort source of cole. Now it's full of these quests. I just fully refreshed the whole list and made sure my quest log was empty, and I'll break down what I got.1: Every single quest this time requires 500 cole to accept. Said quests also almost exclusively pay out a few of those gold coins which are far less useful than in Ryza 1 as you get pretty low quality items for them. Normally you'd get points for the skill tree instead, and those points are incredibly useful.2: 3 of these quests require 500 cole and paying out less than 500 cole.3:  4 of these quests require 500 cole and pay less than twice that, 2 closer to 500 than they really should be.4: 3 of these quests require 500 cole and pay a reasonable amount, at over twice the fee.5: 1 of these quests gives skill points, the biggest incentive to do these. Previously every single quest gave them, but apparently higher difficulty does not mean higher rewards.There are 10 quests available. It takes 5 days to refresh them all, and there is no way to sleep for a number of days at once. So I sure hope your controller has turbo, because that's the only way to quickly refresh the quests without hammering that A button a ton due to the required fanservice sleeping pic of ryza having to sit there on screen every. single. time. Hot, yes, but it gets old very fast.So yay. I now have no way to get money with a reasonable amount of effort. And I'm only recently starting to get reasonable amounts of skillpoints from alchemy.The only real silver lining is that, despite being crappy, the gold coin items can be fed back in for free shop xp, eventually increasing shop quality to a state of usability.

_childDocuments_.review: Great balance of turn-based action, story and, of course, alchemy. All these components working in tandem keep the game consistently fresh and fun. The alchemy system is deep and progressive, acting as the core of the game. This is where things might get tedious for a lot of people, but I had a blast sinking hours into synthesizing and upgrading items. After 40+ hours I still have a ways to go, not to mention the DLC, and can see myself easily putting in twice that time, if not triple. This series in general is a divergence from many other game series in the fact that has a chill and uplifting atmosphere with a story that doesn't take itself, or it's characters, too seriously, a definite plus for me. Thankfully, the Atelier Ryza games have received enough recognition, and of course sales over the past several years that we can consider future titles as imminent, whether we see Ryza again or not. I would play through the first Atelier Ryza before jumping into this game, though the experience would still be great either way, as the game does a great job of introducing you to the characters; it'll be almost like you knew them all along! Now to the in game DLC: as someone who owns all of it, I can attest that the DLC is overpriced, consisting largely of cosmetic items. Even though I haven't done so myself, I would implore new players to beat the main game first before purchasing any DLC. The game offers a more than adequate amount of content to digest on it's own, and the season pass will eventually go on sale again, even given Koei Tecmo's history of being stringent with their pricing, it has gone on sale at least once already. Overall a fun experience and I look forward towards jumping into the past games.

_childDocuments_.review: Atelier Ryza 2: Lost Legends & the Secret FairyAtelier Ryza 2 is undoubtedly a refreshing game, and the sequel has made up for a lot of the weaknesses of Part 1. For anyone interested in this game series, here are some things to keep in mind, as the game is extremely overpriced. Even at a 30€ reduction, there is a massive lack of content. 1. it is important to know that the Atelier Game is practically an oversized crafting and alchemy simulator. Therefore, you need to have a passion for collecting and crafting.  Since the game has a very mediocre story and characters, poor sidequests, and a mediocre combat experience, you are stuck with your alchemy table.  But the alchemy system is really well fleshed out here and I love it. 2. You don't need to have played Part 1 to play Part 2, as the story takes place almost completely independently of Part 1. However, you should look up something on Atelier Wiki or Youtube about what happened at the end of Part 1. You also miss virtually no character development or relationships, as these were not present in the first game. Except for Bos. But it's not worth buying a whole game just to watch a few character scenes.Atelier Ryza 2 is a very likable game, where unfortunately the disadvantages outweigh the advantages. Pros :+Very good alchemy system+It's fun to collect materials, upgrade stores and learn new recipes.+There are many mechanics to deal with.+ The game has a relatively refreshing combat system that can be quite addictive. + The game has been designed to be very clear and well-explained.Cons :- Anyone coming here for a story should forget about it right away. The story is relatively poor in both Ryza Atelier games.- The same goes for the characters. Here it was a little better, but they are very one-dimensional and extremely boring. - The producers are extremely lazy and could hardly offer any variety in the enemies. There are 4 bosses in the game, all other bosses are just copies of those in a different color. The same goes for enemies. There are about 10 enemies and all of them are the same models with only different colors. For a 60€ game, you would expect much more.- The areas are very monotonous and small. Suitable for collecting things quickly, but unsuitable for exploration.- Treasure chests are the last garbage, no matter where, you ALWAYS have better things in the inventory than you find in the treasure chests. - Quest board and side quests are pretty meaningless and have very poor rewards. - The difficulty levels are too easy, to play Legendary or Charismatic you have to complete the game once. This massively ruins the fun of the game, since you very rarely get problems on Hard. Even the final boss was immensely easy and didn't even manage to get my HP below 80% even though I didn't use any healing potions. That is a sad achievement. ConclusionDon't get me wrong, the game is fun. But for a 60€ product, you expect much more. The quality you get here is equal to a 20€ game. And that's just disappointing. The Alchemy system is good, really good, but everything around it is average or worse.Buy this game ONLY if you are an Atleier fan or it is exactly what you need. And I NEVER recommend buying it for full price.

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings about this game, and honestly I don't recommend it mostly because this title can be safely skipped between two other Ryza games. There are things to like about Ryza 2, and some systems and ideas that show promise, but are underdeveloped or made tedious. I liked the ruin exploration system. You first do preliminary check of the ruins, which activates ability to check the ruins in details. Then you collect artifacts and notes you find in the ruins to compare them to illegible notes you have. By finding artifacts related to notes you figure out history. It's sweet, but it becomes tedious later on. The requirements to activate "full ruin" become more irritating, and the design of the ruins becomes worse, so you are forced to backtrack on huge, boring maps.As Atelier series went away from time management they seemingly replaced it with tame wasting. Maps in Atelier 2 are very big, and many of them are made in a way that makes walking on them inconvenient. They tend to be a zig-zag where they might look like areas, but really there's only 1 linear path, that just takes you all over the map. And there are no shortcuts, and the game requires you to come back there multiple times. I also don't like the new alchemy system. Instead of having recipes that consist of 3-5 ingredients you have huge maps of ingredients. By the endgame you'll be putting 9+ ingredients to create a base item, then improve it further putting even more items. Sometimes you'll put in 8 items to notice you're missing 1 item to change the recipe into another item. It's very tedious then to put the items back. It seems like game developers noticed it's tedious, as there's an option to put in ingredients automatically. But by the late game you might not want to use it, as it might use up good properties on some items. Instead of carefully selecting best items you're just stacking the same property many, many times until you get +60 or whatever the limit for given property is. It's not really fun to use.You're showered with items - to the point where I had to stop most of my gathering by the late game, as I would constantly run out of room in my container inventory (not the basket). There are systems to get rid of inventory items, but they are pretty slow to use, and I didn't find it fun to stand next to an NPC for 2 hours selecting items I don't need just to clean up my inventory.The story in this game is pretty much like a filler episode. Nothing of importance happens. It's not that uncommon for Atelier games to be light on story, but usually it's saved by fun characters. But in this game every party member and NPC with event chain is very one-note. Most of the event chains could be summarised in one sentence. And every event for the given character is pretty much the same. "We're looking for flowers". "We're looking for flowers in different place". "Again we're looking for flowers". Funnily enough the character with most fun scenes was Bos from the first game. Older games had characters feel more like people, even the first Ryza.This game introduces alchemy skill tree instead of alchemy levels. This means you can unlock alchemy abilities in the order you want. But the items on the list are not described until you unlock them, so you might end up like me not unlocking very important functions until very late in the game. This skill tree is also the reason why container gets filled so quickly - you get passive buff to the number of items you find. By the end game gathering just a few times will get you full of items.The enemies on maps are often put in a way where you can't avoid them. There's no upgrade for the pre-combat smash to instantly kill them, so even if they can't do anything to you the fight will be mandatory. The combat system itself - I didn't like. It's kind of action and turn based mix. You collect action points by doing basic attacks and blocks to use your specials. But your AP is limited by your current tactics level, and the battles go SO SLOW on the lower levels. You start the battles on level 1, or, if you hit enemy avatar before fight, level 2. Out of 5. You need to get to level 3-4 before the battles become kind of fun. But by the time regular enemies die. If I got into a fight with level 1 it was so slow it took less time to escape and then attack the enemy outside battle to fight again, but at level 2. At level 5 you can drop your levels by using a finisher, so then you have to build your levels again with slow gameplay. With stronger bosses you might want to use a finisher twice or so. Your attacks also collect item points which allow you to use your items. You can use multiple items at once, and if you use certain combo of items it will launch special attack. But if you use multiple items the wait time will be pretty long. Unfortunately this is made bad by having all playable characters share "crystal improvement points". Those points allow you to improve how good your character is at using items. The battle exp and level is synced between characters, but the ones you don't invest crystal points into end up pretty bad at using items. And near the end of the game I only had 3 characters with decently improved crystal - and I was near the max level. I would need to farm for hours to allow other characters also become decent at items.I also found myself struggling at some point, when difficulty got a sudden spike. I was killing regular monsters without losing any HP. Then a boss just destroyed my team, and I had to defeat it in order to progress. I made good enough equipment to get trough it, and very soon afterwards even stronger bosses started jumping out one after another and my equipment or levels were not up to the job - I'm not sure which. I had stronger equipment locked between items I couldn't obtain yet, and the levels weren't going up too fast. But each time I visited the map Ryza would say it looks dangerous. Anyway, it was rather frustrating later on. Those were not optional fights too. Maybe I would have been fine with it if I liked the alchemy system and wanted to experiment with improving my weapons. It didn't help that bosses were very deep on the map so walk of shame to them took a very long time.The graphics are fine, but some textures are really low res. The shirt of Ryza had pixelated seams, while the leather on Clifford was very high quality. The NPCs are noticeably much, much worse quality than any of the playable characters. The game also has very unfortunate DOF, which would make character faces very blurry in cutscenes when the focus should be on their faces. I had to disable DOF completely. Overall if you're going trough Ryza series this is a good part to skip. There's some enjoyment to have out of it, but it takes a lot of time to complete, and doesn't have enough to reward the time investment.

So, sequel time.  Do I simp for the sequel just because it contains my favorite lesbian couple in gaming?  Yeah, but in this case I still think the game deserves it.  It's an improvement over the original in many ways, including the world building.  Overall it's just more interesting and the RPG more tightly built.  There are some quality of life improvements to the crafting that don't invalidate the charm and challenge, and just like the first one you can abuse the hell out of it to make incredible things.  It feels good to craft and again shows how lazy, uninspired and vestigial crafting is in most games.If you are going to build your game around anime and crafting, this is how you do it.

_childDocuments_.review: Major step up from the first game. If you played the first game (which you should, since its a story based trilogy) expect some major changes, mostly to the combat system. Instead of waiting till your AP meter fills up, by doing nothing but basic atttacks, like in first game, this time you actively use your AP to charge up the Tactics Level. This time, you can also chain them together, right after doing basic attacks. With Tao or some other low AP cost characters, this means you get to chain up a ton of skills. Sweet thing made sweeter. You can now also have up to 4 memebers in your party, with the ability to switch them right in the middle of the battle.Speaking of characters, Patty is the goat, probably my favourite new addition to the playable roster.  Back in the first game Id say Lent had the best attack animations, in this game Id give the honor to her. Character wise she also offers plenty, shes a bit like Klaudia, but better (imo). Serri is a little boring, little whatever imo. This, however, is negated by her lack of pants and dear lord, holy , did no one tell her we dont show cheeks like that in the capital??? Fi is also there, he does this little sick flip sometimes. Locations are more fun than in the first game, exploration is more fun than in the first game (you get a dog or smth to ride) and general story is more interesting than the first game. Functionality of some field items change, as to instead of boots doing the jumping part, you now get to charge downhill at high speeds. Crafting got a little simplified, you dont have alchemist levels but only item levels, which you increase with skills (yeah, there are skills now). Essences are a brand new thing which I honestly never really used much.Oh also, final boss (the ost is called "Wish" I think) and combat soundtrack in general goes INSANELY hard for some reason, idk who let them cook like that, but I say they should let them keep on cooking.All in all, I gave first one like 7.5/10, this game, Id give like 8.5/10, . If you get this game for 60€, you got scammed. Im sorry KOEI TECMO, this game is not worth full price, it still suffers from old JRPG design, less than the first game but still. However, if you spent like 24€, which is the price game goes on sale for, I think that is a good deal, based on how good the game is and what it offers.

_childDocuments_.review: Atelier Ryza 2 takes all the interesting parts about the first game and completely revamps them into a truly interesting and thoughtful system of gathering, crafting, and fighting. The alchemy finally started to mature into a system that lets you freely break anything if you so choose—for example, I was able to beat the final boss within 3 turns because of all the magic bombs I made. The story is significantly more interesting as a whole; I was paying attention the whole way through this time, unlike in Ryza 1.          The combat this time has generally the same core idea behind it as the first game, but is completely reworked to reward actual skill-based play. There's a lot more depth to it this time around than in the first game where you really only have a couple different choices during combat and no real reason to play as characters other than Ryza. Most party members feel really fun to play as during combat (I especially liked Patricia and Clifford).           Playing on the hard difficulty, the game as a whole was generally pretty easy, but some parts do require you to understand enemy attack windups; some enemy attacks are poorly telegraphed or do the Elden Ring style of a 3 hour long windup for an attack that takes probably 2 frames to connect. The fun in this game really comes from collecting and synthesising tons of materials to overprepare for whatever situation you think you'll face. Allowing a party member to hang out on the sidelines ready to swap in for anyone is a really nice change that helps combos stay running while also providing new ways to deal damage or follow action orders.          For some reason, once I got to the late-game areas, enemies always ganged up on Patricia specifically. I don't know if this is just some cosmic coincidence or if the game just hates her and whoever swaps out with her specifically, but enemies almost exclusively targeted her instead of the other characters. This isn't really an issue I have with the game (it actually got me to play as her and other characters a lot more than I would normally), but it *was* strange.          The story is obviously nothing to write home about—you can't really go in expecting Disco Elysium or Grand Theft Auto IV or something like that—but the characters are surprisingly expressive, the voice actors add a lot of energy into their performances, and the writing and structure both see significant improvements from the first game. Unlike the first game, which sees you mostly screwing around until you stumble upon an ancient secret, this game has you actively exploring ruins and trying to solve a mystery yourself. Each character has their own questline spanning the entire game, alongside an assortment of side characters (including Romy, from the first game). This helps a lot with connecting to and understanding the characters of the story. Without it, I doubt I'd have enjoyed the main quest as much. It also adds a lot of content to the game while feeling completely natural instead of bloated—there will always be something to do at any given moment, right up until the end of the game. Certain parts of the game's story (namely the Exploration Logs) could have been used far more than they actually were. Figuring out the witch's history through the memory fragments was actually really cool (I even liked the whole sorting minigame), but I really think they could have used that part more than they actually did.          Other aspects of the game, like side quests or the shop development thing, are underused at best. I found myself frequently ignoring them until I got another thing to do for Zephine or I ran out of inventory space. The game does call you out if you don't do enough side quests, though, which was hilarious when it happened to me.          The pricing is definitely . Do not buy this game at full price. Koei Tecmo is scamming you if you do. Please don't. The DLC prices are also crazy, especially because they're almost 100% worthless. If I had to say, you should probably just buy the base game when it's on sale. The fact that this game costs the same as Dark Souls III is completely ridiculous.          overall 8.5/10 clifford has a nice ass

_childDocuments_.review: Continuing the story of Atelier Ryza three years after the events of the first game, Ryza 2 hits very hard with lots of comfy and cozy vibes combined with a large and varied crafting system. It’s more of the first game but with just plain more. New systems, new story, new items, and new game.- : Not only is the pretty in-depth Synthesis system still the star of the show, you’ve also got the returning fan-favorites, item rebuilding, equipment reinforcement, and item duplication, all which are greatly enhanced by the new systems. The most major new alchemy system added is Essence, meta-items crafted using materials obtained via gem reduction and spending gems, which are used to alter and enhance the material loops in synthesis, which allows you to get even more powerful effects on the majority of items.There’s also the new Evolution Link, which allows you to not only add special effects onto items, but also reveal entirely new items in certain cases, which will unlock new loops to fill in item rebuilding. All in all, alchemy and synthesis is greatly improved upon in this installment of the Atelier Secret series.- : The combat was also greatly improved in this game. There’s still the regular RPG elements, involving stats, limited-slot parties, and skills with skill cost, but there’s also the Ryza twist with it being real-time turn-based combat. Now that we’ve established all the first game’s elements are still here, it’s time to talk about the incredible new combat features that make everything about combat shine. The most prominent feature is the Support system, which allows you to essentially just bring a fourth party member into combat, with the caveat that you can still only have 3 on-field at a time, and that you just switch members out between your 3 on-field and the one support. Additionally, the Core Crystal system has been massively overhauled. In the original game, you had a limited number of CC that only regenerated upon sacrificing items mid-battle or returning to your Atelier, but in this version, you start out each battle at 0 CC, and can gain more throughout battle by using your skills. And even then, you can also upgrade the initial and max values of each character’s core crystal as well as give elemental bonuses. Not to mention there’s also the powerful Core Crystal versions of Fatal Drives, Core Drives, which are special attacks you can activate upon using specific items at once in battle. All the new features combined with the Ryza 1 combat make this one of the best aspects of the game.- : The segmented open world returns from Ryza 1, and it still works excellently, save for a few detriments. For example, if you want to find a certain item, all the in-game guide will tell you is what area it’s in and with what tool. Nothing else. And the fact that in this game there’s a bunch of different types of harvestable things in every area, you’ll essentially either force yourself into memorizing all the important items or just using an online list. My favorite part about exploration though, is that in Ryza 2, the effect of the Mirage Loupe from Ryza 1 is permanently engraved upon your soul. And by that I mean that you always are able to see what materials harvesting something will get you, and it updates according to the quality of your gathering tool. Unlike the first game though, you don’t ever really find yourself going back to old areas (except for the grasslands areas which have several common items)- : The already pretty good-looking graphics from Ryza 1 have been updated to be more high quality, and all the areas have been upgraded as well, making for a nice new anime-styled aesthetic. - : Once again, you’ve got the 3 standard difficulty options upon starting the game, Easy, Medium, and Hard, but upon first clear of the game, you unlock 3 higher difficulty options, which considering how broken and overpowered you can make your gear, are a welcome challenge.- : The achievement grind is a lot more forgiving in Ryza 2. The achievements with the most grind should honestly not be too much of a challenge unless you manage to screw something up terribly. Examples:	Alchemy Compilation - Unlocked all alchemy skills in the Skill Tree: This sounds demanding, but the amount of SP you get throughout the game is super high, and if you somewhat regularly complete requests, quests, and synthesize, you’ll get it in no time. I think I ended the game with like 50K SP extra.	New Super Move - Activated all Core Drives: Despite the achievement description, you only need to activate the core drives ‘Four-Star Aurora’ and the ones you unlock from the skill tree, not all the ones available.Other than that, no missable or difficulty-related achievements, just more of the ‘complete essentially everything.’- : The price of $60 is just a little bit too high for me. Personally, I got it on sale for $30 (plus about ~$10 for several DLC) and it was well worth it, I would honestly probably buy it for around $45, luckily enough, as of when this review was posted, the game is on sale for half off.- : In Ryza 2, the story and lore are very separate things. The story consists of (light spoilers) . The lore however, is given to the player almost entirely through the ruin investigation system. You can collect fragments of the past and piece together information to essentially be given a block of text on the history of that ruin and how it connects to the overarching story. Personally, I think it’s nice as it doesn’t intrude on the main story and is right in front of you if you want to read it.No major downsides, minor ones were covered in their category.- : I recommend playing this game with a controller as it’s a JRPG. I can’t speak directly to the keyboard controls since I played it entirely with a controller, but just a warning.- : Once you beat the story you can either continue your existing save to better your gear and challenge some post-game content, or convert it to a NG+ game, both options of which unlock 3 new higher levels of difficulty for a higher challenge. - : In the first game, you only had 5 total slots for your gathering tools, but way more than 5 tools, so you had to deal with this annoying system of combining them to be able to fit it all. This issue is fixed in this game by not only providing all slots necessary to equip all tools, but there’s also more slots for the new tools for new ways of traversal. This is a positive, but it didn’t fit in any of the other categories and I didn’t want to make an entire one just for this.

_childDocuments_.review: Suffers from the same issues I had with the first game, that being a slow start and an ending that just sort of fizzles out. Still, there's a moment right in between when you really begin to latch onto the gathering-crafting loop where everything clicks and powering straight through the alchemy tree feels cathartic. The changes to the game play from the first are small but incredibly effective. A skill-tree looks drab and overplayed but being able to place yourself in your progression removes the frustration of struggling to find a recipe only to find that you're not far enough in the story yet. The exploration diary seems like a lazy lore-dump but it forces you to properly scope out new locations for materials. While all these new additions are admittedly rather poorly explained and make the experience feel a little bloated, they're clear innovations on the problems of their predecessors. Given that the Ryza plot lines are really nothing to phone home about, it's the kind of sequel that does everything the last game did but better, making the previous entry somewhat obsolete. Although as it struggles to properly tutorialise a lot of its systems, some may find it a little difficult to grasp its many mechanics if they decide to forgo it entirely.

Music was mentioned already, and the battle system adds depth where the first game felt afraid to limit its' audience. I didn't even start using the item combos or switching between characters until halfway through the game and it makes a huge difference. Story-wise there's a little more depth and some occasional darker tones but it's still largely the kind of thing you could have a middle schooler understand and enjoy.I can give no spoilers and would never do that, but I do have to offer warning by way of experience; I cried for about an hour after I beat this and struggled not to immediately start a new save.

_childDocuments_.review: Atelier Ryza 2 plays a bit like comfort food. You know it's not the best but it's fun, and if you played the first game then it's familiar. It streamlines some game mechanics, borrows a lot of assets and concepts from the first game, and manages to change very little of the overall milieu while still allowing our good friends from the Ever Darkness to get back together for another adventure. If you liked the first game, then I would recommend this one, but if you haven't played a Ryza game before then you'd be better served by playing Ever Darkness before jumping into this one.In the beginning of the game, Ryza is given a magical item that she heads to the big city to research. While there she meets up with her old friends; Bos, Klaudia, Tao, Lent, and a few other fun cameos along the way. The game has a bit of dungeon crawling, lots of gathering and crafting, and a good bit more of exploration. There are several facets to exploration. You craft different items to traverse different areas of the maps throughout the game. Whether it's diving underwater, climbing cliffs, or sniffing out treasure with a mystical pet, there is lots to discover on every map. You take those rare materials back home and use them to craft potions, materials, items, weapons, armor and more. The alchemy/crafting is simple, intuitive, and leaves space for putting in your own personal strategy for how to craft items. The music is delightful, which is a staple in Atelier games at this point. The graphics were beautiful anime graphics but due to a few changes (particularly the lighting engine which might be a technical improvement but exposes a lot of flaws in the rest of the graphics) I am almost tempted to say they're worse than the first game. Almost all of the monsters were reskins/copies from the first game. The story is slow paced with lots of slice of life style cut scenes and small stories weaving their way through the game. I love how it slowly builds to the bigger conflicts, it feels very organic and takes some of the edge off typical "chosen one" protagonists in fantasy media. _childDocuments_.review: A reunion of childhood friendships, The warmth of companions in the big city.As a returning player of the first Ryza, i think this is a great recommendation to anyone who like close knitted personal stories in JRPGS. _childDocuments_.review: If the first Ryza game was a good enough game, then this one is simply magnificent. The Ryza series is my first ever Atelier game series, and this series definitely made me want to try out some other Atelier game series due to Ryza 2's impeccable quality. They improvised so many things from the first game that made it impossible not to recommend anyone who played (and liked) the first game to try this one out.Here are some things that I noticed were improved from the previous gameLet me start out with this one because I think this is one of the mechanics that has gotten a lot better compared to the first game in the series.- You can now swim! This adds more depth to the exploration mechanics. Some people might not like underwater levels in video games but I don't find it to be particularly annoying.- To add to my previous point; you can also dive underwater if the water is not too shallow and if you have the right Adventuring Tool.- You can now jump down from high places/cliffs without having to go around them. There are fewer invisible walls preventing you from going down from high places. It takes away the slight frustration I've had when playing the first game for not being able to just jump down from an elevated place.- Spirit Beast allows you to travel through a map faster while keeping you safe from monsters. Spirit Beast can also dig the ground to find rare items/materials.The combat mechanics in Ryza 2 is either a hit or miss depending on the players. They changed the combat mechanics by a lot but I personally think there weren't any devastating changes.- You can't use items immediately at the start of the battle unlike in the previous game. Makes sense since this makes enemy encounters feel like a joke since you can just one-shot them to oblivion with items. Edit: You can actually use item at the start if you've actually upgraded your Core Drive.- Combat feels more like a hack-n-slash and fast-paced since your Tactics Level doesn't rely on AP anymore. I think this is an improvement since I really am not a big fan of the idea of having to consume AP to raise your Tactics Level.- You can use more than one item at a time, given that your CC amount is adequate. Especially useful during bossfights.- Your party formation does not rely on roles anymore; there are no roles to begin with. TBH I really like this one. Having to make a piece of equipment to suit a role is kind of frustrating.- The enemies' position and your party's position are random throughout the encounter, but you can still switch targets. The position of enemies might impact the effectiveness of your items. Say for example when you're using a Craft. If the target enemy's position is far apart from the others, your Craft will not deal AoE damage. I think this is a bit of a downgrade from the previous game, but maybe not all people found it to be a huge deal.It's hard to talk about Atelier games without mentioning the Synthesizing mechanics. I don't have much to talk about this. I think that they're just as good as the previous game if not better. I do notice a slight improvement like the quality of your items won't go down no matter how low the quality of the materials you use for the synthesis, but of course, higher quality materials make for some better quality items.All in all, if you like the first Ryza game, you will probably love this game. I might be trying more Atelier games after finishing the Ryza series. :)

_childDocuments_.review: Ryza 2 improves on practically everything Ryza 1 did, and then some. It seems like Gust was being highly experimental with Ryza 1 to see how they could modernize the Atelier series, but they nailed on everything that works in 2.The unique gimmick of this game is exploring ruins to piece together what happened there a long time ago. It gives Ryza as a sub-series a very unique feel compared to the others, and is a different kind of exploration for reasons other than gathering materials. This along with the addition of new traversal tools like a rope, a giant animal to ride, and the ability to swim, the environments are much more dense and expansive which makes Ryza one of the best Atelier games to flat out explore like crazy. The main hub being a massively populated town is much more interesting than Kurken Island from Ryza 1 since there are much more NPCs to talk to and more sidequests to receive from them.The biggest improvement is the combat, which I already felt was one of the best mechanics in Ryza 1. It's got the same core foundation, but you can now chain regular attacks into skills into other skills, and even swap party members in and out of combat mid-combo. The UI makes it far easier to execute commands in quick succession, and the change of core items being something you save up points to use in quick succession also adds a lot to the strategy of the game. It's excellent, fast, and frantic.Synthesis is just about the same as Ryza 1, but the method of obtaining recipes are more nuanced rather than simple story progression, as you learn a lot more recipes by doing sidequests or using the skill tree to learn more recipes, giving you more freedom on what you want to create. They also more properly explain the importance of item quality to make better items.If you liked Ryza 1, then Ryza 2 is, like I said, better in every way. There's no reason not to play this one. Might even be one of the best soundtracks in the series too.

The Ryza games stories are all just okay at best but everything else makes up for that imo. You don't particularly have to play the 1st one though I'd recommend it just to appreciate the character development from then to now makes the characters feel more fleshed out. It's the typical Atelier loop of crafting materials and collecting things with some of the best collection loops of the series with a charming cast of characters.

_childDocuments_.review: This sequel feels like a proper evolution of the first game. Traversal, exploration, alchemy, combat and characters have all been developed, without losing the charm that the first game introduced. The characters, crafting and combat are the highlights, and the story, while not bad by any means, really just serves as a vehicle for you to experience these things. There are a lot of optional cutscenes that develop character relationships and bring a lot of life to the game. And just like in the first game, you can craft obscenely powerful equipment fairly early on and become God-like as you breeze through the story. Just absolutely demolishing the bosses never gets old. I'm both sad and excited for the 3rd and final entry in the series; it's a story I wish could go on much longer.

_childDocuments_.review: I thought the combat in this game was a lot of fun, and very fluid, and the act of discovering hidden lore about the dungeons within the dungeon gave a good reason to fully explore the dungeons. I also really liked the addition of selecting which tool to harvest materials with, in order to better focus on a specific material that you are looking for. Honestly, there's been a LOT of quality of life upgrades in this one compared to the first Ryza game.That being said, I thought the way you learned recipes (or rather, re-learned), was a little lame, as they admit that Ryza already knew the recipes, so there's no feeling of exploration of alchemy and discovering new items. Additionally, since half the characters were already friends, the relationships between the characters didn't feel fully fleshed out. Also, the lore you learn from the ruins is really really interesting, but they don't really DO anything with the information, other than have it as subtext for what happened to the ruins, and I can understand why a lot of people found exploring the ruins repetitive.Overall, I think it's in my top 3 for favorite Atelier games, but not my absolute favorite.

_childDocuments_.review: As a seasoned Atelier player, I enjoyed this installment. The graphics are the most advanced out of every other Atelier game. The Alchemy "crafting" mechanics is similar to Ryza 1 yet unique in it's own version. I didn't completely enjoy the story, because there were too many cut-scenes to wade through (but that is every Atelier game imo). The story was very predictable, but I do not play the Atelier series for the story I just want to battle monsters and craft as a cute JRPG girl. I feel as if a new player into the Atelier series will not fully enjoy this game as it is supposed to be. Most of the story has inside jokes from the first Ryza game. If you are a new player into the Atelier series, I would recommend either playing Ryza 1, the Arland trilogy, or Atelier Lulua. One of the main issues I had with the gameplay was that it was incredibly easy to craft overpowered gear, but that may be due to previous experience with the previous Atelier games. I also wish could select multiple ingredients while crafting, but that is just small detail that I can overlook. A common complaint I have seen is the absence of an English dub, however I thought the Japanese voice actors did an excellent job with the characters. Overall, I loved this game. It has enticing replay-ability, and after you clear the story you unlock higher difficulties which put your alchemy skills & battle strategies to the test. I think every fan of the Atelier series would enjoy this game, unless you prefer the previous alchemy "crafting" methods.

_childDocuments_.review: Atelier Ryza 2 builds on the success of the first game in several ways. Almost everything has had a light dusting of quality of life tweaks but the headliners are the new gameplay and traversal mechanics.Being the first Atelier game to retain a protagonist makes a huge difference, as less development time was needed to create new characters, personalities and models. Instead, that time could be focused on bringing gameplay aspects that have stagnated within the series up in line with other RPGs. Simply adding climbing, swimming, a mount and rope swinging makes the game feel much more alive, even if they aren't particularly new or innovative additions (when compared to contemporary RPGs).Changes to the synthesising mechanics, specifically taking elements from the original Ryza game and mixing them with the enhancement mechanics from the Mysterious Arc, results in a system that works really well. In my opinion this is the most refined and well-balanced version of synthesis I've seen in an Atelier game to date,  and rewards bulk grinding and specifically targeting certain materials and monsters in equal measure.Despite those improvements, the combat still feels like it's at a bit of a weird crossroads.  If pressed to describe its current form, it would be a hybrid of "turn-based, on-rails auto-battling" that feels more at home in a mobile game than a console or PC RPG, but it's not bad by any stretch. I just personally prefer a straight-up turn-based system. I'd like to see this further built upon in a future Atelier game by either jumping in full to real-time action-based combat, or stepping into the ATB turn-based system. Either would work and allow for more meaningful gear/trait and character building choices. Overall, Ryza 2 improves upon the previous game in a lot of key GAMEPLAY ways, but falls a little short in the story department by rolling out the same big "looming" force as the first game's. The pacing also falls apart a little towards the end, and there's no real justification for a lot of the late-game choices the characters make outside of "to progress the plot."I really hope there's a third instalment so we can see just how much the series can improve, but for anyone looking to jump into the series I'd still recommend Ryza's original adventure over this one.

The boss battles didn't really take me too many tries because I was spending so much time in between story quests upgrading my weapons and armor.All the new characters introduced had their own side-quests which really had me invested into their story. Although at times some quests were a grind in terms of gathering resources, these quests added pretty solid rewards. For example the cafe offers a bulletin board with daily quests that give money and sometimes gold coins which could be used in Romy's shop. The only cons I really noticed from this game include a few minor technical issues with the camera, and I had 1 movement bug during a cutscene where ryza's animation kept cutting and restarting in a spaz-like way. _childDocuments_.review: I had a kind of odd experience with this game - got it last year, played for a bit, thought it was too similar to the first Ryza (which I'd just finished at the time), got bored, and ditched it before the main storyline really started. Now, I came back to it a year later, and it turns out I had quit right before all the new interesting stuff showed up! I've played it all the way through and am replaying again because it's fun. Some things that stood out to me in this title:- Ruins exploration and fragment-collecting is something new to the series. It makes it more interesting to go around the material gathering areas, and the exploration journal gives insights into the behind-the-scenes lore (and possibly foreshadowing for the 3rd game?)- The alchemy synthesis puzzle, which is the main reason I got so into Atelier games in the first place, is well-designed and I think would be pretty easy to learn for someone new to the genre. Personally, I prefer the more complicated grid-based system of the Mysterious series, but this one is more relaxing because it feels simpler. The recipe discovery mechanics are fun, and synthesis of weapons & gear feels satisfying because how well you make it will make a difference in combat.- The action battle system is improved over the first Ryza. It's easier to see all the UI elements and learn the battling mechanics. The ability to switch characters quickly is good. I would have preferred more focus on item use, the way past turn-based games emphasized it. The points  (CC) needed to use an item in battle take a while to add up, so I end up using character skills more than the items I synthesized. But then, I don't really play Atelier games for the combat, so as long as it's not too tedious or difficult, I'm good with it.- The overall plot is interesting, but the dialogues in a lot of the cutscenes felt boring and simplistic. I'm clicking Skip a lot on my replay. Nonetheless, the story has good friendships and heartfelt moments, so if you are not put off by the banter, the cutscenes will be ok to watch.- Gorgeous artwork of course. Character designs, environment designs, the alchemy and battle special effects - all just pure eye candy.- The variety of exploration tools is awesome. This is such a big difference from early Ateliers, where you'd run across the gathering zone basically in a line (invisible walls everywhere) and have 1 way to collect a material from a gathering node. In Ryza 2 (and Sophie 2), you can, for example, use a staff, an axe, or a scythe on a tree, and each tool will give you a different set of possible materials from the same tree. It's fun to discover what each tool + gathering spot will result in. Also, there are abilities to explore underwater, jump across chasms, and other things that make the areas feel more open-world (with the use of special items available through the main plot progression). Overall, I definitely recommend this game. It's a good starting point for an Atelier newbie, and works well for someone experienced with the series as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Ryza 1 was a surprisingly good game that I thought punched above it's weight - it was definitely a niche game, but one that was fun and well-written enough to compete with the big boys of the JRPG genre. This entry, though, is on a whole other level. I liked Ryza 1, but I love Ryza 2.The Ryza games do two things well that set them apart from the JRPG pack. First of all, these games focus on an interesting form of crafting, Alchemy. At first, this was a put-off for me because I've grown used to the most JRPGs' terrible crafting systems and I couldn't imagine playing a whole game of that. But Ryza's crafting is not like those systems. For one, crafted items are central to combat because items are the source of >75% of a character's stats, usable items are the source of 50% of their abilities, and the items you find pre-made in dungeons are leagues worse than those you can make yourself. The crafting system is also very deep. Materials have a quality, an elemental value, and a set of additional traits that you have to manage while being able to mix only a limited set of items on a FFX-like sphere grid. If that sounds overwhelming, don't worry. The game lets you auto-complete recipes if you want and on normal the experience is relatively easy. But the beauty of this system is how it is totally fine with you breaking the game if you're a good enough Alchemist. By the end of the game, I had crafted an Elixir healing item that was resource-cheap enough to be cast from the first turn of combat but could revive all dead party members, heal all party members to full health, add a strong regen to them, and apply a damage-reduction buff. And then I duplicated it and gave it to my entire party. How cool is that?The second thing Ryza does well that separates it from the JRPG pack is the type of story it tells. To put it simply, the Ryza games are slice of life stories. Sure, both games have a central adventure that drives the plot, but the core of the experience is the relationships between the main characters and how they grow as people over the course of the story. Now I like my share of save-the-world plots, but it is definitely refreshing to play a game with a plot about something as relatable as "how do you grow up and find what you want to do with your life?" or "can friendship hold strong despite time and distance?" So I've talked about what both of the Ryza games do well. But why do I like Ryza 2 so much more? Well, the answer comes down to polish. As much as I liked Ryza 1, there was a lot about that game that didn't quite hit. The way the map and exploration system worked felt awkward and cramped, as you didn't get the main world map and fast-travel system until a third into the game. Usable tems felt awkward because of the limited charge system and healing items were rendered moot by Klaudia's broken healing skill. And, worst of all, the slice-of-life elements felt awkwardly integrated into the game because a) they were required to advance the main plot, despite them not having much to do with it and b) they were so obtusely placed that you had to rely on a sub-menu to tell you where to go to advance the story.Ryza 2 has none of those problems. Exploration is clean and simple, and you have the main world map and fast-travel system from ~20 minutes into the game. Combat has been refined, with a new tactics and item-charge system that encourages the player to use their resources rather than horde them. And the slice of life elements have been separated from the story into their own system and placed naturally into high-traffic locations like the game's shops, quest hub, and home base. Even areas where the last game was already good, like gathering, side questing and alchemy leveling, have seen refinements, along with improved visuals and a kick-ass soundtrack.So, should you play Ryza 2 if you already played 1? Yes. Absolutely. This game is worth every cent.Should you play Ryza 2 if you haven't played 1? Well, that's trickier. I certainly think the story and character development of the sequel hits a lot harder if you've seen these  characters grow through the first game. But at the same time, it's a pretty big ask to tell someone to play a solid but flawed game for 30 hours so they can play the gem of the sequel for 40. I'd say, if possible, play Ryza 1 first. But if you're itching to get into Ryza 2 as soon as possible, playing it immediately wouldn't be the worst decision. Just keep in mind that these characters have a lot of history together that you won't know as much about. Either way, Ryza 2 is a total JRPG powerhouse, and I'd recommend it to anyone who likes the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: This is purely a gameplay review.Atelier Ryza 2: Lost Legends is a decent JRPG with turn based combat based on a individual turn timer which you can manipulate with hastening and slow effects.Main points:Unlike JRPG that focuses on skill trees per individual character, you as an alchemist, craft items by expanding a smaller skill tree to enable more advanced crafts of items, accessories and trinkets for use in combat.Atelier ryza 2 has the traditional aspect to a JRPG where you as the player can decide if you want to push story by focusing on tactics, or by simply just grind materials to make weapons that'll make you oneshot current content.The game builds to a fairly average extend upon a system where you build relationships with branches of the city to unlock quick material gathering methods or skill tree points.The world is divided into smaller instances that can be reset by re-entering the same zone by instantly teleporting or manually walking out and in again.The game itself has a Pedia that makes for easy browsing of gathering materials and where to collect them however it can at times be very vague.The game is in ♥♥♥ voice with ENG subs however it lacks subs for the quirky lines the characters says during combat or during crafting processes which just makes it bothersome noises for those who can't understand the language.The characters are locked into a specific weapon archetype like most JRPG's are.A short diversity of actions to execute during combat and you quickly find yourself using the same rotation or weaponized items.The parties consist of 3 characters during combat with a total of 7 characters to choose from however the AI insist on using buffs for their special action skills before using attacks on most ecations even on encounters that would be finished in 1 hit.The NEW GAME+ feature is pointless.The NEW GAME+ feature allows you to start the story anew seemingly only to add a higher difficulty without additional content, however you are reset to level 5 (start level) while allowed to keep the items you've crafting during your first run, which basically negates the whole higher difficulty setting for the first 60+ levels of encounters as your gear does not have a level requirement, which begs the question, why not allow the highest difficulty from the beginning?TL;DRAtelier Ryza 2 is a decent JRPG for those seeking a quick JRPG fix, but if you just finished a Persona or a Final fantasy game, don't pick this up as you will be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: June 4th, 2020: this is an update of my initial review from May, 26th, 2020.After having played the game in 3 distinct sessions for a total of 14 hours-ish, I unfortunately feel like I can't recommend this game ON STEAM.The game itself (for 95% of it) is GREAT.Unfortunately, the game is really broken on Steam and the developer doesn't seem to be able to fix it to run a stable version that everybody can run and play....Either the game doesn't start altogether or it starts painfully but then crashes hours into it and is a hassle to restart.I actually managed to beat the game today but it crashed right after defeating the final boss and I couldn't even see what was coming after. And then impossible to start the game again after about 10 attempts which completely freeze my pc (and no, it's not coming from my PC)...very frustrating !So yeah, I don't know how the game runs on Switch, PS4 and XboxOne but it doesn't work on Steam, even 2 weeks after release.Hopefully, the game will be fixed in the future because it is a real shame that everybody can not enjoy this great game to their heart's content. This would make for an amazing speedrun, not in its current state though.On the game itself: It's great, super tight gameplay, sweet graphics, awesome locations, the mechs are fun to fight, the soundtrack is solid but above all the game is really FUN.Fun until the last boss which, to me, makes no sense whatsoever in relation to everything that's been going on in the game prior (in terms of gameplay).Fighting vs the last boss, you realize how much the controller scheme doesn't work for this type of game. If I had one recommendation to the dev (other than FIXING his game !), it would be to revamp the gameplay scheme and make it into a twin-stick gameplay instead of the super cumbersome scheme that is used atm (which works great for 95% of the game and absolutely NOT for the last boss).

_childDocuments_.review: Mechstermination Force is a pretty okay and fun Action game, so it’s time for the story. The world was at peace, but that piece was broken with the arrival of giant robotic terrifying menaces called the MegaMechs. But when all hope was lost the arrival of the Mechstermination soldiers, signified the humanity was still willing to fight.Alright the likes, well to start I really like the cartoonish colorful art/ graphics style of the game it's very pretty to look at. The robot boss designs are very cool looking, probably my favorite has to be the TriMechalon 2000 boss, it's just pretty cool especially at its last phase. The levels in the game were pretty nice to look at and were actually pretty interesting and how some the bosses used the area in the fight, like the Mechstructor ZC fight.The music is very good with some good tracks to listen too; my favorite has to be the theme for GunMech Five. The action/gameplay was fun sometimes frustrating but fun. The upgrades were pretty cool and the story was simple but good, the best part was when you were at the main Hub area and you could talk to the soldiers on base they had some interesting and sweet and sometimes funny dialogue.Alright the dislikes, well there is a bug in this game that causes the game to randomly crash/boot you off, it doesn't happen all that much it just happens randomly. Like you could be playing the game for a good hour but then the game just crashes for some reason. Also I would have liked it if you could map the controller buttons like you could map the keyboard buttons, for some reason you can map the keyboard but not a controller.Also some bosses can be a real pain, like the last boss was a pain in the ass to fight because you're fighting in space and you can move in three dimension, but due to the fact that it's such a big area and your character can be very small it's sometimes can be hard to see where you are going.All right then with all that said, Mechstermination Force is a pretty okay and fun Action game, with very cool looking boss designs, very good music and a simple but good story. So if you're looking for a fun but simple action game about just fighting bosses this game is for you.

It's unfortunate that many people have had technical issues running it. name: Bloodstained: Curse of the Moon 2
detailed_description: Koji Igarashi and Inti Creates are back with more retro sword-and-whip action! Curse of the Moon 2 brings classic 2D action and a dark, 8-bit aesthetic together with modern playability. The multiple-scenario structure of the previous title returns with an epic new story supervised by IGA (Koji Igarashi) himself. Players take control of Zangetsu, a swordsman from the far east who bears a deep grudge against demonkind and the alchemists who summoned them. Zangetsu must battle his way to the demonic stronghold, but he doesn't have to do it alone! Zangetsu can ally himself with a brand new cast of characters he meets along the way and add them to the playable roster. Three brand-new playable characters appear in Curse of the Moon 2, including the exorcist Dominique. All characters from the original Curse of the Moon game are playable, too! Each new character adds a variety of gameplay options, abilities, and ways to complete the games' many stages. Players can also create demon hunting duos in 2-player local co-op, available for the first time in the series! Work together with a friend, mix and match the strengths of two different characters, and conquer stages in tons of new and exciting ways.
