_childDocuments_.review: Leaving this a positive review, but it only just barely made the cut for me.This game prides itself on being similar to old school Castlevania, which is expected given its developer. All of the retro elements are here: The 8-bit graphics, the chiptune music, the demon castle, the arcing jumps you fully commit to so you better be sure you're not going to get knocked into a bottomless pit. There's even a difficulty setting that makes enemies respawn from offscreen. At it's best, you're landing these satisfying jumps and have the boss fights down to a science.But if you're not used to this sort of old school platforming, the game also has a Casual mode, which removes the knockback/stun you take when getting hit and gives you infinite lives. In all likelihood, you'll still be challenged on this difficulty, but it's much more prone to brute forcing. While I like the inclusion of the mode, I think it speaks to the larger issue the game has of balancing the old school elements with modern tastes.While most of the characters you control are classic in their design (Miriam straight up has a whip she must have borrowed from the Belmonts), there are two characters I can't imagine existing if this were on the NES that I have a love-hate relationship with: Hachi and Gebel. These characters are distinguished by their unique mana abilities which break the platforming sections entirely. Hachi constantly consumes mana to turn invincible, and Gebel constantly consumes mana to turn into a bat and fly past everything. Hachi's ability unsurprisingly doubles as a crutch in boss fights. I want to love these two characters. Hachi is a corgi piloting a steampunk mech, and Gebel just exudes style. But when you can so easily just ignore the platforming that should be this game's identity by farming the mana drops between screens, it's hard to fully embrace them. As I personally detest life systems, I wish that they let you have infinite lives with knockback on, but I get why they'd just want the one casual setting. The game has you replay stages enough with the multiple episodes it asks you to do.Ultimately, I think this is a really niche title that would mainly appeal to Bloodstained: Ritual of the Night fans who also like more retro titles. This title shows the RotN characters in a different setting which I appreciated, and it gave me little "aha!" moments when I saw enemies from that game here in 8-bit form.

_childDocuments_.review: Curse of the Moon 2 is a fair sequel to the original, with a weak early game that eventually becomes more appealing in its final act. It uses a new set of 3 support characters, but you eventually unlock the playable ones from the first game once you've completed two play-throughs. The main issue is that the new characters are much more niche and less familiar than the ones which were based on Castlevania 3, and the overall level design is lacking until you have access to the bat-form from the Alucard-copy. For the most part, it's just like the first game in conquering a set of side-scrolling levels, beating bosses, and then eventually doing it over again with limited character options. Unfortunately, it's far less memorable and feels like a bit of a forced sequel that doesn't really shock or surpass the first game. In this one, you have a spear-woman who can jump higher, a rifleman with a long-range attack who can crouch, and a robotic ally who does a lot of damage, turns invincible, and can ignore terrain obstacles. Only the robot has significant health to tackle the challenges, so it becomes a bit slower as you work through the game and the other characters have limited use other than in their size. The game really comes into its own when you have a full cast in the third playthrough, however, as it makes the levels less linear and gives you a ton to work with and have fun without significantly harming the difficulty.My biggest complaint is that this title doesn't feel nearly as fair as the first game, and ironically has more authentic Castlevania-eseque difficulty in pits, low health, and very cheap, unpredictable bosses. A ton of boss attacks literally just can't be avoided due to the invincibility move of the robot, and though there's a better mesh in the visual design, nothing is as memorable or fun to fight. You end up dying to random attacks coming out of nowhere, rather than being able to learn and adapt, and you just have to bang your head against the wall until you get lucky. The levels themselves are only challenging for controlling jumps and falling in pits, while almost every enemy dies in one hit and you have a huge arsenal of magic weapons and the ability to switch healthbars. Probably the best part of the game is during the shoot-em-up section near the end, where it gives you a ridiculous amount of power-ups, but goes on for a long time and shows that the developers have a good imagination for those kinds of improvements, whereas they kind of let-down with the base game. Finally, the story is also lacking; as there isn't any neat twists or good explanation for the alternate options on a subsequent go-through. I thought the first game was incredible for making you want to play more than once, whereas it seems like a gimmick to be expected here. Essentially, a decent game, but nothing special enough to make me feel that it was needed or that it could stand-up well to the other two in the Bloodstained series.
_childDocuments_.name: Bloodstained: Curse of the Moon 2

_childDocuments_.review: Equally as good as the first game, significantly harder. It has way more content than the first game while still retaining the multiple endings parts and different episodes, even has a new Shoot 'Em Up section near the end of the game, while at first glance the new rooster seems weaker than the first one, they all have their own unique mechanics.. The music is fantastic like in the first game, level design is what in my opinion makes it harder than the original even tho you can bypass a lot of hazards with , while i didn't find any boss particularly hard, i found them a bit more tedious since they have less windows of opportunity to hit them, the only exception being Boss 2 and 3. I also played all episodes from Legend since the very beginning so my perception might differ from someone that played on the other 2 difficulties. The only difference between Legend and Veteran is that if your character dies, instead of switching to another remaining character you straight up just go back to the last checkpoint, you can still switch to other characters with higher health before the character you're using dies so is not that different if you already played on Veteran in the last game, you only have 1 less extra hitpoint if u wanna see it that way. Overall a more polished game with a lot of replayability, if you liked the first one then get it for sure, if not then i wouldn't recommend it since it's essentially the same game in it's core.

_childDocuments_.review: What some people are saying about Bloodstained 2 vs. Bloodstained 1 is true—the game is *a lot* harder. I openly admit to typically playing on casual, as I'm not a fan of that Classic-Castlevania ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ where you can die because you forgot how stairs worked. Additionally, the levels are *a lot* longer, by my recollection. These things are humongous; and technically, quitting will reset the current stage. So, all of this is true, and I think it's actually very much in the "Con" list.That said, the stages are also very enjoyable and an appreciated kind of challenging for a genre that has classically used pattern-enemies. The characters are original and very distinct, the protagonist finally gets a much-needed upgrade to his equipment (was that a spoiler?) and there's a very useful war-Corgi.I'm still enjoying it, and a lot of the differences with BS1 are addressing cons I had against that game; but, caveat emptor, as always. This game sure ain't for little kids.

_childDocuments_.review: Bloodstained: Curse of the Moon 2 is truth be told is a mixed bag, but it’s still a good game, so its story time.Another dark night, another full moon and all the horrors that stalk the night have come again, but like the last time the great warrior Zangetsu as returned, having been hired by the church to draw this sword again and like last time he is not alone. Now the likes, well like the first game this game captures the feeling of an old school NES Castlevania game and like the first game you can use four different characters with their own strengths and weaknesses, but in this game when you’re at the last episode you can use not just the three new characters but all so the 3 old characters that were in the first game, letting use 7 characters to play with. The three new characters are pretty interesting like Dominique and her spells, her two best being her spell that makes health hearts appear and her resurrection spell that can revive dead party members and heal them pretty good. That spell was really useful especially towards tougher bosses. She also jumps pretty high like Miriam and her spear attack iis pretty good and has a good reach. she can also user spear the same way Shovel Knight from the game Shovel Knight can use his shovel although it's not as good as that game.Then we have Robert he has pretty low health, but makes up for it in being a sharpshooter, he has the longest reach in the game because he uses pistols, he is pretty weak though but his pistol attack does come in handy with Far Away enemies and even some bosses, his sub weapons are useful like this one sub weapon where he can shoot at rapid fire speed, another sub weapon he gas is a big gun, that's great for killing ninjas.He can also jump from wall to wall kind of like Grant Danasty from Castlevania, He can also get on the ground and crawl through difficult spaces or like being able to not get hit by certain enemy attacks like the archers.Then there is Hachi and I have to say he's probably one of my favorites because he is a cute little doggo and he Pilots a steam-powered magic suit of armor, he does have one sub weapon, but his sub weapon makes him Invincible for a time. He can also hover for a bit and he can get past most obstacles like poisoned ground and he can crush spiked floors.The pixel Graphics/art style is still amazing, very detailed and there were just some set pieces and background that were just incredible to see, like the museum level or the whole final episode to cleave the Moon. The enemy and boss designs are still very good like Vepar when you destroy her first health bar or the final boss in cleave the Moon that thing was both cool and disturbing looking. I also like in this game a lot of the bosses are more original, like they're not from ritual of the night except for one boss.The game's references to other work are still pretty fun I mean in the very first level there's a call back to Strider and in the volcano level there's a boss that would fit perfectly with Metroid.The game’s music is still incredibly good still done by the incredible Michiru Yamane. I have to say my favorite would have to be the theme for the true final boss of the game.The action/gameplay is very fun although I do have to say there were some parts that were pretty frustrating but I will save that for the dislikes. Anyway the game has three different episodes what I mean by that is when you beat the game for the first time you unlock a new episode you can play, each of those episodes has for the most part the same bosses but for the final boss. I found it an interesting way to get players to play more the game and to try different routes in the game and two see new endings.The game’s story is pretty good and it’s Goofy and a bit over the top, but in a good way. I love the goofy over the top feeling of the story, but the game’s story also has a lot of heartfelt moments and character development moments. Like my favorite is after beating a level there are these campfire settings, it basically is that after you beat a level the characters will sit around a fire doing something like relaxing, goofing off or thinking about stuff, it was very good and helped with character development without the need of words.The character dialogue in the game was very good and give good development to characters like Zangetsu and the other characters in the game which was very nice, the best character development has to go to Robert. I also like the little improvements they made for the game like when you pick up a power up the power up stays with you even if you replay a previous level and the Boss Rush was pretty good I like how adds more hearts and more sub weapons and you could turn down the difficulty.Now the dislikes, well to start this, the game can be pretty frustrating especially at the last 4 levels like the fire level and it's lava pit and the museum level, it just made the game very frustrating also the enemies and bosses can be a bit cheap like those damned Dullahammer Head and that sarcophagus boss in the museum level, some level design can also be a pain in the ass like the level muted cry.I also would have liked the bosses in the game to look different in the different episodes what I mean is that in the game bosses has a final attack and they get pretty destroyed after their attack, like the first boss in the game is this dragon and his head gets completely smashed or this one boss that gets his arm sliced off and yet when you play another episode the boss is completely fine, I would have liked to have them look a bit different and maybe new and different attack due to being Resurrected like maybe the dragon boss has a Golem head to replace the one that was destroyed.All right then with all that said and finally done I have to say Bloodstained: Curse of the Moon 2 is a mixed bag, but it’s still a good game, With a pretty good story, still amazing pixel Graphics/art style and the enemy and bosses designs are still very good. So despite the game being a bit of a mixed bag I still recommend this game if you liked the first game you may like this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Another nice classicvania style game for the new Bloodstained series. This one is something of a hybrid of Castlevania 3 and the better aspects of Konami Wai Wai World.Aside from the episode setup being a bit misleading  and a few other minor nitpicks I had a great time. _childDocuments_.review: Play the first game if you haven't before this one. 2 assumes you are familiar and got gud and isn't shy about ramping the difficulty to give fans of the series more of what they thought we wanted.A competent and gorgeous retro platforming action game, Bloodstained is a spiritual successor to the Castlevania series, faithfully reproducing the core tenets of deliberate character movement, challenging stage/enemy layouts and ruthless bosses. The setting innovates with enemies inspired by Christian mythology and a steampunk setting, mixing body horror monsters, twists on classical demons, gunplay and robots into the expected fantasy medieval setting. Although the stories in the Bloodstained setting are earnest they tend to be a bit plain with one dimensional characters. A man named Zangetsu hates the moon, or the demon behind it. That's all you need to know.Advance through stages, taking your time to learn how to navigate the hazards and strike down enemies while minimizing the damage you take. You can swap characters at will and each has unique properties and sub-weapon access that can open new paths and make fighting certain enemies a breeze. It's as though each screen is a puzzle to solve, piece by piece and kill by kill. This is faithfully reproduced from 1, although the problem of the failure spiral returns. You have four health bars and can swap to really stretch how far you can go, but if somebody loses that last hit point your entire group gives up and you go back to the last checkpoint without healing. Now you're repeating screens with even worse odds. 2 also introduces a character that can heal and revive the others but ONLY this character can. The scroll of revival was a good idea for a late stage comeback but now you have somebody who absolutely cannot die early. They also have non-healing weapons but a hearty chuckle if you'll be allowing her to use them. Two steps forward, two steps back seems to be the design philosophy of 2. Stages are bigger, more dynamic, more things going on, crazier challenges, but they're so crazy at times they feel impossible to navigate safely, especially with specific characters. The perceived obligation to raise the difficulty because This Is The Sequel really took root by Stage 5, Lethal Lava Land. This is compounded further by the presence of Doge, who rides a robot that can turn *invincible.* Although the idea of a get out of jail free card option sounds merciful, many stage screens seem poorly designed and meant to be brute forced by this. Another step back from 1, where you did get the ability to fly over everything with Not Alucard or breeze by specific challenges with very powerful sub-weapons(Alfred's Freeze, Miriam's Axe) but the entire game was elegantly designed to be cleared solo as Zangetsu, the jack of all trades. There was also a separation where bat form let you do stages more easily but used hearts quickly and was of limited use vs bosses. Hachi can barrel through stages, often punch lanterns as he goes to end up neutral or ahead on hearts and is one of the best boss fighters. He even has the best platforming mobility passively and at least three other benefits. Doge and Dominique feel like small mistakes made in the name of bigger and better sequel spice.Likewise the boss design feels much more obtuse. They're flashier, they have long intros you can't skip, they're pretty impressive but CotM2 features the first bosses in the two games I'm disappointed to see. Calling you out, Titankhamun. Some are dull slogs, many are a bit too aggressive and fast for the intentionally designed glaciers you're controlling, some just have sloppy design where their attack cues are absent, rushed or misleading. Dying repeatedly and learning things the old fashioned way gets the job done but by the end of the game I was just abusing invincibility timing to get it over with.  It's funny on the Act 2 and beyond playthroughs how much of the game becomes about just holding forward as Hachi and ignoring most of it. A level redesign absent that invincibility would have delivered an actual improvement upon the first game. In fact, if you replay the game at least three times you can see that for yourself. Absent Hachi there's some thought to navigating screens and fighting bosses again until you've reunited the entire team in the final episode. Nailing the pattern timings is satisfying. Considering the sheer joy and flexibility of the expanded team and the stage select of the final episode perhaps this should have been the only episode with Hachi arriving as a nice heavy duty crutch to clear the last two stages. And Zangetsu shouldn't lose his expanded move set. Two steps forward, two steps back. Why not gain moves per stage? Why forfeit moves in Act 2 that were a reward in Act 1? This is something that was solved in the first game!Don't get me wrong. If you want more Curse of the Moon then 2 is right up your alley. It is worth full price and brings a lot of what made 1 so enjoyable. Just be ready for things to get a little too This Is The Sequel at some point, where bigger and better leads to screens full of lava streams with two second timings to try to advance.
_childDocuments_.name: Bloodstained: Curse of the Moon 2

_childDocuments_.review: The game is really good and it has a lot of playable characters compared to the first one, however it tends to be repetitive since all the episodes are about playing the same levels over and over with a different party of characters. The game mechanics are overall well balanced, altough some bosses require the player to know in advance what sub-weapons or characters are most effective against them, otherwise they can be more difficult than they should to defeat - and in some cases, almost impossible. The final boss of the final chapter is particularly bad in this regard, since it throws hell at you and you have a serious handicap that makes dodging attacks nearly impossible  and thus the only feasible strategy I've found to defeat it is to abuse Hachi's invincibility and Alfred's flame shield. Needless to say, it seemed very cheap to me and I didn't like it. But I swear it's the only way I managed to make it to the final ending.If the somewhat unbalanced difficulty isn't too much of an issue for you, then the game is great and I highly recommend it. As for myself I enjoyed it, but maybe I've lost the patience for this kind of "old school" games.
_childDocuments_.name: Bloodstained: Curse of the Moon 2

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked Curse of the Moon 1, you must play this game, there are some great improvements with quality of life stuff, like bosses with visible HP bars and visible checkpoints.There are three new characters and they are as fun to play as the old ones, and If you play enough you unlock the old character to create the ultimate curse of the moon experience.My only problem with this game is the same one I had with the first one, the difference between Veteran mode and Casual mode is too big, I wish there was an option to just get more checkpoints, or just have infinity lives, instead if you change to casual you get more mana, more mana regen, more hp drops, etc...Overall, an incredible game, with difficult setting for all kinds of players.
_childDocuments_.name: Bloodstained: Curse of the Moon 2

_childDocuments_.review: Well made action side scroller throwback to the old NES Castelvania games (with some more SNES like elements on certain modes). Seven characters (with an unlockable ultra mode for Zangetsu), each with their own strength and traversal options (breaking walls, freezing lava, high jumps, climbing, crawling, turning into a bat). Four episodes with each having eight stages (seven repeated but with possible alternate paths). Good enemy design. Difficulty options for those that want an easier or more difficult game.Needless amount of precision to do upwards and downwards attacks, you need to be holding up or down dead center. Becomes very repetitive, having you complete the same stages over and over and over. Once for episode one, twice for episode two to unlock episode three and four, once for three, and then twice for four to unlock different modes. Including one mode that allows you to play the game solo as each character to get a unique ending for each of them. Fun game but I just ended up putting it on easy somewhere after the second episode, because it just isn't interesting playing the stages and beating the same bosses over and over and over again even with the slight changes characters can offer.Screenshots:

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great sequel which has even more references to older Konami games (Gradius)! The new characters are awesome, the stages are put together very well, the bosses are huge and once again, the soundtrack kicks ass.The increased difficulty everyone is talking about is not THAT harsh, at least not so far as I haven't completed the game yet. Of course I raged multiple times already, but, come on! It's excactly what I expect from a game like this.I highly recommend it and I hope Iga is going to create more sequels in the future.And now...back to the game...
_childDocuments_.name: Bloodstained: Curse of the Moon 2

_childDocuments_.review: The best NES Castlevania ever made.Some of the deathwalks to bosses are unreasonable. Some of the platforming is incredibly unreasonable. Check points don't work if you restart the game so you have to start from the beginning of the level. This will make you incredibly angry. Really it's about the amount of time the game demands of you walking to a boss dying and walking back. It's a disrespect or a deliberate cruelty by the designers. The game reuses content on subsequent playthroughs without adding enough new to justify replaying the game 3 times to get the normal ending, let alone the 13 playthroughs required to see all the content, while making you experience some of the most rage inducing moments over and over and over.
_childDocuments_.name: Bloodstained: Curse of the Moon 2

_childDocuments_.review: A good game but somehow I found the first one more fun, I think that one had better music and more imaginative bosses.  But this will certainly satisfy your craving for classic Castlevania style action, I just wish you didnt have to reply the same levels all the time just to see something different. Oh well.
_childDocuments_.name: Bloodstained: Curse of the Moon 2

_childDocuments_.review: Bloodstained, the spiritual successor to the beloved but now butchered Castlevania, has yet another fantastic entry into the series.  You’ll find tough as nails platforming, catchy music, character variety with their own strengths and weaknesses, and excruciatingly difficult bosses.  There are also 4 Episodes to keep things interesting and keep you busy for a while.  My one major complaint is that a character death can really hamper you since level design is geared towards certain characters, and fighting bosses without a full team can be really frustrating.  Look no further if you’re looking for an old school, retro platformer with replayability.  Is the game tough?  For sure, but it’s also incredibly fun.  I’m so glad Bloodstained is carrying on the legacy and the torch of Castlevania, and I hope we see more entries into this awesome series.  Get it!
_childDocuments_.name: Bloodstained: Curse of the Moon 2

_childDocuments_.review: A little more "difficult" than the first one, and i say "difficult" because it's "fake difficult", i.e. enemies put in cheap spots) but fun nonetheless. I still got all achievements and I did enjoy it as much as the first, but this one definitely has more annoyances. The major ting that bugs me is you have to finish the game 13 times to see all endings. 13! It's outrageous. Both main endings to the game are fun and the 2 different final bosses you can get depending on your choices are a blast, but again, not as much as the original game, and definitely not as creative. Still highly recommended
_childDocuments_.name: Bloodstained: Curse of the Moon 2

_childDocuments_.review: Basically a completely better version of B:COTM. Where the original had some cool bosses but was mostly nostalgia, and couldn't hold a candle to other modern retro-style games like Shovel Knight, it felt like this one just figured it all out; the characters feel very different, and rather than simply using one character to get through a "best route", sometimes you need to get real tricky. Jump off a wall with the sniper and switch to the robo-dog on the ascent, hold jump to trigger hover... instant death if you screw it up. Good. Feels like a good, old-school challenge. Doesn't baby you quite as much as so many others today. Shovel Knight is still the king, but this one might have finally topped CV3 for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Bloodstained: Curse of the Moon 2

_childDocuments_.review: I've played the first game and loved it. This one takes what made the first one great and ramps it up with replayability. There are several episodes to unlock and different characters to play as.The balancing is superb. On casual one can brute-force through the stages and bosses but on veteran and legend, it becomes a whole other story.Overall: If you like Castlevania and liked the first Curse of the Moon, give it a shot.
_childDocuments_.name: Bloodstained: Curse of the Moon 2

_childDocuments_.review: Great sequel, even better than the first game.Also it's kinda hardcore, and I say that as Castlevania veteran and lover of challenging games.The soundtrack is a banger and the pixel art gorgeous.The stages however can get old as you revisit them in different episodes, even with alternating and hidden paths.
_childDocuments_.name: Bloodstained: Curse of the Moon 2

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, the people willing to buy this game will likely enjoy it, but for those who are unsure, well, it's a game that takes advantage of it's graphics style to make cool levels, good music and a classic style platformer.Sadly, it's there the flaws come, this game loves cheap tricks, you can bet the game gleefully knows there is knock back every time you are hit and a lot of places have moving or small platforms with enemies nearby, you will lose a lot because of this, and sometimes checkpoints are far from each other, oh, and each time one character dies, even though you have a team, you go back immediately, and you betcha every boss fight has their cutscene repeating.Also massive difficulty spikes, oh, and the game expects you to replay a few times to see everything, while there are differences, the first time you beat it, you unlock episode 2 which starts with the same levels, just with more characters and thus new routes, which is fine, but at the end you get the same bosses with a few new tricks, also the routes are harder because difficulty spike.It just feels like it overstays it's welcome fast, there are people who enjoy this over the first, and while there is some cool stuff like Hachi, this game is frustrating and made in such a way that the only reason why i think people would like this one over the first is...because it's harder and feels more like a NES Castlevania, and again, the game really really loves abusing the knock back.Still, it's a good looking game that is well made and a good amount of content, worth getting during a sale, just be aware this game loves putting enemies next to holes that mean instant death.
_childDocuments_.name: Bloodstained: Curse of the Moon 2

_childDocuments_.review: Curse of the Moon 2 is to the first game what Dracula's Curse is to Castlevania 1 - a bigger and better sequel. There's no point in spoiling any details, Castlevania fans already own it, people who beaten the first game should buy it and anyone else should start with the first game.It's also a much more challenging experience thanks to the new "Legend Hunter" difficulty - ideal for true Castlevania veterans.
_childDocuments_.name: Bloodstained: Curse of the Moon 2

_childDocuments_.review: The game is way clunkier than I thought it would be. I knew it would be 8-bit pixel aesthetic, but they did advertise modern playability, which I really don't think this game qualified as. Definitely not worth this amount of money. I knew it wouldn't be as good as Bloodstained: Ritual of the Night, but I didn't think it would be as bad as pre-SOTN Castlevanias. I want to support IGA's efforts, but this one was crap and isn't worth anymore than 5 dollars by 2020 standards. The Gameboy Advance Castlevanias are funner than this. Requested refund.
_childDocuments_.name: Bloodstained: Curse of the Moon 2

_childDocuments_.review: I see some reviews complaining about how the game gets more punishing as you do the extra playthroughs but I think this is by design. It's actually impressive how INTI CREATES managed to make levels that can be played through multiple times with different characters and have completely different experiences throughout.As you play through more and more of the episodes, the game converges on Castlevania III style difficulty with bosses that were seemingly trivial before becoming much more difficult when certain characters are removed your roster. Everything about this game (except maybe the music but it's still excellent) is a step above the first CotM and any old school video game fan should be happy that the reins of "Castlevania" are in the hands of people who love games more than pachinko profits.
_childDocuments_.name: Bloodstained: Curse of the Moon 2

_childDocuments_.review: I played through the first Bloodstained COTM and got all the achievements so my expectations for this sequel were above and beyond. And while it did satisfy me with new characters, co-op and the same gameplay as the first game, this game did show some problems that you can't really notice until you start playing.First of all, the level design is much different from the first game, with longer levels, a whole lot more insta-death pits and ackward enemy placement that makes the game overall more difficult. With the introduction of co-op, this also meant the devs had to create new routes that can only easily accesed when playing with a second player.Another problem is the soundtrack, and while there are some good songs in it, it's nothing compared to the soundtrack from the first game in terms of quality and consistency.Lastly, the introduction of new characters also meant they mostly had to leave out the cast of the first game in order to put the spotlight on the new cast. You can play as the old crew again in the EX episode, but i would've prefered if they gave you option to play as either group of characters.While this game has some problems the first game didn't have, that doesn't mean it can't be enjoyable or fun, the Bloodvania gameplay is still there and the game's aesthetics have remained untouched and you can have some fun with a buddy of yours by playing co-op.I strongly recommend this game for fans of the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Bloodstained: Curse of the Moon 2

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game; it is very exciting and engaging.  I've always been a huge fan of 2D games, so maybe part of it, for me, is nostalgia.  Still, I think they got everything right.  The difficulty is perfect--it keeps me on the edge of my seat all the time without being frustrating.  The pix-art graphics are totally amazing.  The characters are all interesting, and it is very easy to switch between them.  The little hidden secrets make it fun to replay.  Wonderful!
_childDocuments_.name: Bloodstained: Curse of the Moon 2

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoy the game up to the last stage or two, the stained glass pursuit is obnoxious and the amount of cheap death pits starts to become awful which I wouldnt mind if they didnt make you go back to the start of the room you were in while having much more long scrolling rooms filled with death pits. 2nd chapter I found fun while I had zangetsus upgraded sword then stopped having fun once I had to give it up and I think the amount of dickish level design increased? Like I distinctly remember more death pits or at least more enemies right next to them in awkward locations causing more one shots.Currently on 3rd chapter and I started with the first stage but the enemy seemingly does not leave its self open to normal attacks with zan or miriam and 20 weapon points just don't cut it so I guess I have to find a better chapter do deal with first? I dunno I just cant destroy the fire he leaves on the ground which makes it kinda hard to avoid damage.Wish me luckI managed to get through him after figuring out the lightning wasn't to terribly fast and found out I could also get in an extra slap on him when he pulls out his lightning alien tail as all you needed to do was crouch slide from mid stage over to his head to get one free hit then you could repeat it as long as he kept it up.After that I kinda started to snow ball chapter 3, the extra health and utility of the old crew is so nice I can't believe I played through this whole game without gebel twice now.Love chapter 3 much more than 2 thus far
_childDocuments_.name: Bloodstained: Curse of the Moon 2

_childDocuments_.review: I've been a fan of both Metroidvania style and oldish Castlevania games, and enjoyed both RoTN and CoTM games IGA made. I must say that I enjoyed this game even more than the more famous Ritual of the Night. I finished all of the four episodes in Veteran Mode. Although some people are saying this game being unfair. I find it challenging and fun. Definitely, it's harder than the first CoTM game. There are unfair death traps which got me on some of my attempts. However few of them irritated me to an extend that I want to say the F word loudly, not to mention you have so many options to tackle those challenges with even more unfair abilities. Come on! Invincibility ability? Hachi alone have made it a lot easier. There are different routes you can take as well as multiple endings, but you don't have to look on the internet to find locations of power-ups or to beat the perfect ending. The game itself is quite straightforward. The Items are always located on the main branch of the routes and you can always get to the last episode whether you forge Zanmatou or not. Your old companions are going to help you out anyway.  I like straightforward games since I have trouble navigating myself and remember locations. Hollow Knight is one of the examples. Even in RoTN I had trouble recognizing that I need to kill the stupid squids. That's one reason I didn't really enjoy open world games. It also frustrates me in some of  RPGs where you need to head for the "wrong" path to find treasures. Mostly I find it boring picking one road only to realize this is the right one but I have to go back to get my treasures.The story is great for an action game. The story of RoTN is totally forgettable. Dry characters, lame plots, and unimportant cut scenes. At the end I don't even understand why Miriam is determined to save Gebel. In this game they present the stories mostly by little camp scenes between stages. You see Robert's remorse on badly treating Dominique; Dominique's effort to cheer the team up; Hachi's attachment to Robert; Zangetsu's reflection on not being able to sway the blade; and everyone's determination when they all raise their weapons. Last words, if you like challenging Side-Scrolling Platformer, definitely try it out! If you're a fan of old-school Castlevania games, get the game now!

_childDocuments_.review: - I bought Curse of the Moon 2 (CotM2) for PC.- I received a free copy of Curse of the Moon 1 (CotM1) for PC as a backer of Ritual of the Night.- I have not played the co-op mode.- As of this writing, Ver 1.3 has been announced for CotM2.I recommend CotM2 if you enjoy challenging 2D action-platformers or the old school Classicvanias (Castlevania I/III/IV/Rondo of Blood).  If you enjoyed CotM1, I absolutely recommend CotM2.  It is a better sequel compared to its predecessor, being longer, more challenging, and with more features such as having eight playable characters instead of the original’s four.If you are choosing between CotM1 and CotM2, I would recommend CotM1 first because of its lower price and lower difficulty.  Both games are excellent, and while CotM2 is bigger and arguably the better game, CotM1 delivers a shorter, but solid experience at a lower price point ($10 USD) compared to CotM2 ($15 USD). CotM2 is both a worthy sequel to CotM1 and an excellent game on its own.  Like its predecessor, CotM2 proudly wears its Classicvania inspiration on its sleeve, from the visual aesthetic and chiptune soundtrack to the old school mechanics, design, and feel.  Those who enjoyed the old school Castlevania platformers, its gothic feel, stiff jump mechanics, and merciless knockback will once again feel right at home with this game.  For those who have enjoyed CotM1, you will find CotM2 is a bigger and better sequel.The only complaints I have toward CotM2 are minor nitpicks.  CotM2 is a challenging game, even more so than CotM1, but there are times when it becomes an exercise in frustration, especially when playing on Veteran Mode.  In addition, players are expected to play through the game at least four times to completely finish the game, and while each playthrough will have its own variation, the differences don’t feel enough to justify fight your way through the entire game multiple times, especially given CotM2’s difficulty.  However, once again, these are nitpicks.I absolutely recommend this game if you enjoy 2D retro action-platformers, the Classicvania games of old, or especially, CotM1.  CotM2 stands out not just as a sequel to CotM1, but a bigger, better followup.+ Core mechanics and game design make it feel like a refined, modern Classicvania.+ Character design.  There are seven distinct characters, and they are all fun to play as.+ Level design.  The levels are distinct, challenging, and fun. + Excellent NES-inspired aesthetic.+ Excellent chiptune soundtrack.- None.As this is a sequel game, comparisons to CotM1 will be made.Both games are excellent, but CotM1 might be the safer choice, especially if you are uncertain you will enjoy this series or genre.  CotM2 might be the bigger, better sequel, but CotM1 offers a shorter and sleeker experience at a cheaper price point of $10 USD compared to the sequel’s $15 USD at this time of writing.  In addition, CotM1 is an easier difficulty compared to CotM2, and depending on the person, CotM2 can feel ‘too long’.CotM2’s premise is simple and straightforward: Demons have returned, and so Zangetsu and some new partners fight their way to their stronghold, the Demon Castle.  The story is simple enough to justify fighting through eight stages full of demons and treacherous pitfalls, but there are some twists and turns that add some extra meat to the plot.  Compared to CotM1, CotM2’s story is more complex and lighter in tone.  Optional character dialogues and between-stage interludes flesh out the protagonists as they make their way to the demons’ castle, but they also inject levity and some silliness in contrast to the darker, more serious tone in CotM1.  It feels as if Inticreates was more willing to have fun with the setting.  Among other things, one of the playable characters, Hachi, is a Welsh corgi that pilots a steampunk mecha, and plays like a Mega Man X Ride Armor.CotM2 is a challenging game and much harder compared to CotM1.  At times, it feels like it borders on Castlevania III: Dracula’s Curse level of difficulty due to a combination of its more unforgiving level design, enemy placement, boss patterns, and higher-than-expected damage.  You will be expected to learn the characters, the stage layout, the enemies, and the bosses to truly succeed, especially on Veteran Mode.CotM2 once again encourages players to make multiple playthroughs, rewarding them primarily with new story modes.  Each new story mode is distinct in that it offers a new set of characters, and while it is still enjoyable to play through, the experience could wear you down due to the main game’s length and difficulty.  CotM2’s variations, while more numerous than CotM1’s, do not feel as impactful, so it could feel as if the game “wears you down” after several playthroughs without significant enough differences.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a dumpster fire, which is sad because curse of the moon 1 was so amazingly good. And while I haven't tried out multiplayer yet, I feel I've played enough of the game to understand the game well enough to give a thorough review.First lets get the things this game actually does well out of the way. First thing I noticed was the added tips in the menu screen. This is a great addition, as players who need help can just pause and read the text to understand the game better, and if you just came back from a long hiatus a reminder will help make the process of relearning what you forgot go by quicker. However the tips are somewhat randomized, so in order to get the information you want you are going to need to pause and unpause until you get the desired tip (assuming the thing you need help with has a tip that can appear here). A better design would be to give a dedicated menu option to look at all the relevant tips. Another addition that I liked was giving the bosses health bars, this made it really easy to figure out how far into the fight I was. With the addition of the health bar they made most damage to the boss carry over to the next attempt (assuming you didn't just lose you last character). Finally they gave us more clearer checkpoints, no more wondering how far back your gonna  go after dying.With all the niceties out of the way, it's time to truly tear into this game. First problem I noticed was that the game assumes you have already played curse of the moon 1, as the helpful skeletons showing you the shortest path return, but the only tutorialization the game does is give you the controls and a couple of tips on ways you can use your abilities. The level design isn't nearly as good as the last game as it seems to be obsessed with hinting at different paths you could go if only you had a new character that can utilize it is what made the first game so good. This I find very weird because they change the locations of all the stat upgrades based on which mode you are playing (also occasionally the levels' layouts, which seem to be for story reasons rather than to better suit your new party like they do with the upgrades, again weird design decisions). Most boss fights are boring as the strategy becomes rather obvious after the first run through, and execution on said strategy usually isn't all that hard. Also, the decisions that gave the first game so much depth was taken out for some reason. In curse of the moon 1, every time you came across a new party member you had three options 1) recruit them into your party 2) ignore them 3) kill them. Each of these options drastically changed how the game would play, however in curse of the moon 2 when you come across a new party member you always get some dialogue and then they join your party.In conclusion new players will probably be a little more lost then they should be, while returning players will be left pining for everything that made curse of the moon 1 so great. If this game seems even somewhat interesting, please do yourself a favor a pick up bloodstained: curse of the moon instead.

I almost wish they would patch those levels into this game, even if the new characters break them, it would be fun to have a "complete" version of the 2 games.My only complaint is the extra lives system. You feel bad ever having to spend them, so if I started to lose characters during a stage (some members of your party can die, but you don't lose a "Life' until they all fall) I would just exit out of the stage to stave off losing a life. _childDocuments_.review: Very fun game to play (at first), but it is a step back from the first two. This is the first Bloodstained game that I feel is just too exhausting to actually beat. I'm at the Final Episode there now, and I feel like I'm forcing myself to continue playing, and that's literally a sign that it's time to stop playing for now. I do like what they've done to the final episode, but to be blunt, I feel there's like a Hachi barrier where he's locked behind the game's worst boss (Mummy Boss), and I need him to get the defense upgrade, and I simply just cannot continue because I can't beat the Mummy right now because his attacks take too much damage without the added defense. This is all based on my own personal experience though, since I feel this part of the game is randomized, but I'm now stuck and unable to finish because I've learned there's only so much frustration we can tolerate until the experience just starts to feel boring.The game is truly another great game, and getting through Episode 1 should be more than enough to get the most out of this game, however, when the difficulty feels more exhausting than it is actually difficult, that's probably a telling sign this series probably should have avoided NES difficulty and continue what they were doing. I feel this company should better communicate that extra content is certainly side content, having this game presented as episodes makes the game feel like it's all part of the main story, which it is, but I don't feel the developers ever intended most people to play past Episode 1, it certainly shows. I think one reason why this game fails in the difficulty department where Castlevania III and others pass simply boils down to the size of the game. NES games were just small games, you can get away repeated deaths over and over again. However, this game is a much larger game, and it feels like another one of those games that simply doesn't want to let you go, like it's begging to keep you playing one way or another, and I kinda hate it when games does this. Simply put, the difficulty here feels like padding, as a means to artificially make the game longer than it is, without understanding what makes difficult games actually great. So ya, not a bad game, but certainly a step backwards.Moral of the story: Less is more, please developers, stop trying to force your games to be longer than what it is. Only children complain about a short game. A game's quality is not dictated by it's artificial length.

_childDocuments_.review: 9/10 They did it again. That's all I gotta say.I wasn't expecting a sequel towards the 8 bit spinoff we got for Bloodstained: ROTN. But it's here. And I'm happy it exist. If you played the first game, you'll definitely enjoy the sequel of the spinoff. I recommend playing the first game before playing this one. If you plan on either the story, or as a warm up before playing the sequel. Cause this game is harder than the first. As in this review, I'll explain there are similarities and differences than in the first one. There will be some spoilers in this as well. Mainly, the unlockables in this game. If you don't want to be spoiled, then skip past the part that says "spoilers" in this review.You start off playing as returning character, Zangetsu. The protagonist from the first game. I won't be bothered to fully say in depth of what his playstyle is like. If you want a full in depth explanation, check out my review of the last game COTM. Although, there are minor differences on this game for him. Later on in the game, Zangetsu will get an upgrade that will allow him to use a 3 slash combo with his sword, the crescent slash while jump attacking, and all his sub weapons get a power boost. Giving them slight differences on power and effect for each sub weapon. Zangetsu can also gain his ultimate form with all abilities from the last game to this one after beating the game's entirety.Along the way in the game, you will join up with 3 new characters. Dominique (Who happens to be from ROTN), Robert, and Hachi. All have their own sub weapons and abilities that are different from each other.Dominique: She is the member of the church. She is your healer class. She uses a spear that she can thrust not only the direction she's facing, but up in the air for anti air attack. Her spear can be used to aim downward when she is jumping in midair, and can be used to bounce off of enemies and lanterns like a pogostick. (Kinda like in another 8-bit game that seems familiar.) She also jumps higher than any of the characters in the game. But her high jump could mess you up from her arch of a jump could lead you into falling to your death than the other characters. (But she's not the only female character who can jump high.) She's the healer of the team. Starting sub weapon is summoning a plant that drops health pickups to restore your health. She also has a whirlwind attack that can change to anti air when enemies are in the air, and an electric attack that is anit air. But will roll along the ceiling to take out clinging enemies on the ceiling. She also has a one time sub weapon to resurrect fallen team members to half health and heal allies' health by restoring half. However, leaves her open to enemy attacks for the long cast time. If she gets hit, it cancels her ability out. And you'll have to start it all over, or mess up if she dies. So use it when you have the opening.Robert: He's the hunter. His main weapon is a rifle that fires to cover out the distance of the entire screen. Downside to him is, each shot he has to reload the chamber of his rifle. Leaving a brief opening to an enemy attack. He also is the character who has the lowest of health in the game. So he can die easily in just a few hits. He plays like a character from the side scrolling Contra games. Why I say this, is he doesn't crouch like all the characters. He will go prone and lay on the ground. Making him able to dodge nearly all incoming projectile attacks. He can fire and crawl while prone. He can crawl under areas his friends can't reach for the most part. He can wall cling and fire while on the wall. He can kick off the wall to reach to certain areas if he can jump off from wall to wall. His sub weapons are anti air throwing spears he starts off with, frag grenades that can be thrown in an arch and roll until they hit a target, a cannon that can fire a big damaging projectile that stretches out to half the screen, but can also push him in the opposite direction from the force of fire, and a scarf that buffs him to use his rifle to now shoot in rapid fire succession.Hachi: A corgi who controls a mechanical suit of armor powered by alchemy...Yes. It's not a joke. He is the literal tank of the game! He has the highest in health, and deals more damage than any of the characters. However, just like a tank, he's slow like one. He has a slight slow hit reaction when trying to hit enemies. His crouch attack is not able to hit enemies who are touching the ground. But can be taken out with his slam attack from jumping in the air. His slam attack can also destroy certain platforms that can lead to hidden shortcuts. He can also jump and hover in the air for a short time to reach some distances that normal jumps can't reach. Also useful to time platform jumps if you're uncertain of landing the jump or not. He can also destroy certain terrain like spike pits on the ground to become walkable for his friends. Traversing on ice does not effect him. Hachi has no sub weapons. But instead, uses a overdrive ability to use and slowly drain magic points to make him invincible to enemy attacks! However, it doesn't make him resistant to certain environments. Downside to him is, he sticks out a big target for enemies. Since he doesn't use sub weapons, purple lanterns in return drop magic potions instead. Just like Gabel from the first game.Later on in the game, you will reunite on playing the returning 3 characters from the last game! Miriam, Alfred, and Gabel! Like I said before, I won't be explaining in depth about their strengths and weaknesses. Read my review on the first game if you want their specs. That's a total of 7 playable characters in this game! And they can all lead you to different paths of each stage of the game. Changing the direction for where you can go in multiple playthroughs.The new feature of the game is 2 player couch co-op! You can now play the game with a friend at home. But, with Steam's remote play, you can play the game somewhat online with a friend. Try not to die too much. For this game is harder than the first. Much harder with a friend. The game still has veteran and casual modes like the last game.The spoiler bit is right here. And this is just for unlockables. But first, there's quite a bit lacking there are slightly less multiple endings to the game. Well, noticeable ones. The only unlockable you can get in this game after certain requirements is Single Mode. The option to play the game alone playing as only 1 of the 7 characters of your choosing. Can you handle beating the game with that one selected character? They have now added the return of boss rush mode in just a couple of days since the game's release. You'll be fighting all the bosses from the game from all spanning episodes. With the exception of a certain one. Which I won't spoil for the twist in the game. Another thing I have to mention here is you can't name your save files. So there's no hidden bonuses from them. Another thing that bothers me, is there is no music playlist in the options menu like in the last game. You got an awesome 8-bit soundtrack in the last game and same for this game. Why not include a soundtrack player or sound test?All and all, if you enjoyed the old school Castlevainia style of games, or the first game to COTM, you'll love this game. Is it worth $15 though? I think it's a fair price. They added a bit more than the first game. You'll see when you play it. The co-op option can lead to multiple plays of the game with friends. Not to mention, a lot of characters who can all lead you to multiple paths in the stages you play with surviving characters who can reach them for you. Boss fights are much harder than the last game as well. Especially when you play the game a 2nd time. Music is great. But not all are catchy like the last one.At the end of this review, the game is fun, it can be challenging, and now, it features a doggo in a tank. Best boi in the game. GOTY right here.X3

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent sequel all around, but is it an overall improvement?There are things this game does better than the first, but there are ways the first game offers a tighter experience.The difficulty has been ramped up substantially. Even on casual mode some of these stages and bosses will kick your ass. The stages are longer and offer more alternative pathways than in previous games. That's good and bad - there's a ton of upgrades to be gotten, but when the game really opens up, it can be tedious to go hunting for upgrades you missed. It's kind of a crossover between Mega Man and Metroid, but games like Shantae pull it off better.The game is split into multiple episodes which also serve as difficulty levels, similar to the first game. I'll warn  you now - to get the good ending for episode two and unlock the final chapter, you need to accept a nerf to Zangetsu.I would say this game was a 100% improvement if it wasn't for the tedium and padding. That's the only drawback. It's worth it for the final mode you unlock, but this is one of those cases where the destination is better than the journey, and if you've had your fill with the first part of it, you might never reach that destination.If you adore anything oldschool and don't mind some padding, this is worth it. For $15, you can't go wrong. You'll be replaying this well after you've done everything.If you're on the more casual side of things, wait for a sale. I'd say it's worth it at $10 or below if you figure you won't complete it. The art design, the soundtrack, the character variety - they're all superb. Inti Creates has done a fantastic job all around. I think they just got a tad ambitious for their own good.Edit: Having gotten the last achievement, I wanted to add a few things.The tedium of the final episode is helped a lot by the fact that where you recruit characters is randomized, and you don't need to complete stages more than once to get all the power-ups. It's still tedious to replay 3/4 of a level to reach the item you couldn't get the first time, but when reviewers like SomeCallMeJohnny talk about the last episode taking significantly longer than the others, I'm not sure how. One, you'll be better at the game by the time you're going through the final episode, and two, navigating the stages only gets easier as you recruit more characters.It feels like all the padding was there to make coop feel like a worthwhile addition, but I haven't been able to try it so I can't comment either way.The only other quibble I can think of is how one character, Hachi, controls. He has the ability to hover. It's activated by pressing and holding jump. Problem is, it's far too easy to activate the hover by accident. I've died because I unintentionally activated it and it halted my momentum.I have no idea why they wouldn't have made it a double press. It doesn't ruin the game, but it does detract from the experience a little bit. Overall this is a must buy for anyone who loves classic games with a meaty challenge.

_childDocuments_.review:
Koji Igarashi and Inti Creates are back with more retro sword-and-whip action!

Curse of the Moon 2 brings classic 2D action and a dark, 8-Bit aesthetic together with modern playability. The multi-scenario structure of the previous title returns with an epic new story supervised by IGA (Koji Igarashi) himself. 

Players take control of Zangetsu, a swordsman from the far east who bears a deep grudge against demonkind and the alchemists who summoned them. Zangetsu must battle his way to the demonic stronghold, but he doesn't have to do it alone! Zangetsu can ally himself with a brand new cast of characters he meets along the way and add them to the playable roster. Each new character adds a variety of gameplay options, abilities, and ways to complete the game's many stages. 

Game Flow
Battle through stages filled with fearsome enemies and dangerous traps, each with a massive boss waiting at the end. A chance encounter with a potential ally awaits you after defeating a boss. Will they serve as a trustworthy partner on your perilous journey?

Increase Combat Abilities
You can instantaneously switch between allies you have recruited at any time! Allies have their own life bars, so with each ally you recruit, you're survivability is greatly increased! 

Shortcuts that Only Allies Can Access
Allies have special, unique abilities which allow them to use shortcuts to skip parts of stages or access new areas! There are no special items obtainable by taking the long way around, so take every shortcut you can find! If your allies are out of commission, you'll have to take longer routes, where stronger enemies await! When your life gets low, be sure to switch then out so they'll be available when you need them.

Multiple Episodes
The story is told over the course of multiple episodes. Only the first episode is accessible at the beginning, but more episodes will unlock as you progress through the game. The events that unfold in each episode continue into the next one, so be sure to unlock all the episodes to see the true ending. 

Curse of the Moon 2 had two play styles, "Veteran" and "Casual". 

Veteran Style
Choose "Veteran" style to experiment a difficulty reminiscent of older games. An enemy's sttack knocks the player to their death...something very familiar to retro game fans. 

Casual Style
Even if you're a fan of challenging games, sometimes you just want to take it easy! Casual mode is perfect for times like that. On Casual Style, things are more forgiving. Attacks don't knock the player back and lives are unlimited, alongside other changes. 

Changing Style
Style can be changed when starting a game, loading a save file, or on the Game Over screen.

name: SOLAS 128
detailed_description: At its heart, SOLAS is a beam deflection game. Rotate and reposition mirrors to connect light sources and unlock adjacent puzzles. Every pulse is moving to the beat at all times, and each puzzle is connected to the next. Explore this strange interconnected space, learn its rules, and discover the surprises that dwell within. Rather than ordinary light beams, however, these pulses can and will collide with each other. Create new colours, deflect them in new directions, and pay attention to their timing to unlock the path to new puzzles. Along the way you'll encounter a wide array of components which interact in unique and surprising ways. You might even discover you can pass pulses and components between puzzles. Prisms, glitches, new types of mirrors, and more lurk in the depths. For example, the filters which remove colours from pulses that pass over them. To match the otherworldly, retro, neon aesthetic, SOLAS is scored with a one of a kind synthwave soundtrack to which the entire game is synchronized. Over 150 interlocking puzzle screens A beautiful synth-inspired visual style with a story where music powers everything Designed from the ground up to be colourblind-friendly A seamless world to navigate - changes in one room will affect those that follow An original synth/chillwave soundtrack Hidden areas to discover, and secrets to decypher No text or dialogue: the visuals and music speak for themselves SOLAS is a game based around the combination and separation of these pulses, but has been designed from the ground up to not be reliant only on colour. SOLAS’ glyphs each have a unique shape and profile, and there are customisable contrast settings, making it accessible to colour-blind players. Amicable Animal : A one-person studio — part-time lecturer, part-time games developer, full-time tea drinker. He loves combining old-school mechanics with minimalist, modern game design. SOLAS is his first commercial game. Jamesy Downie : The musician behind the synthwave sound of SOLAS. Obsessed with everything 80s and VHS related, he created a soundtrack that relaxes, and hints at an underlying darkness. Steven McSeveney : Sound Designer and all-round audio nerd; he creates immersive sonic experiences to bring worlds to life. He created the sound effects for SOLAS, marrying the neon-rich visuals with the game's synth-fuelled soundtrack.

_childDocuments_.review: A splendidly fun and intricate game that will challenge you just the right amount to keep you wanting to unlock the mysteries held within. Also, what an amazing soundtrack!There is a video snuck at the back of the Steam screenshots where the developer walks you through small parts of the game. Highly recommend you watch/listen to get a good sense for the game. Hope you enjoyed it as much as I did.
_childDocuments_.name: SOLAS 128

_childDocuments_.review: 100% check out the Demo / Prologue! It's ~20 minutes and entirely its own set of puzzles, so no spoilers and no re-doing puzzles.I've only played for an hour (+20m in the demo. Just got [1]) and I'm already satisfied. It's possible the game goes to heck after the first two... chapters? events? But what I've played so far has been strong!Lots of little eureka moments, with cleverly designed puzzles that come together beautifully once you've found the right solution, and the whole thing synched to some really fitting music to zone in to.The interconnected rooms are used cleverly, and add a nice sense of curious exploration as you wonder how all these things will come together in the end.Edit: Oh! And I think it's colorblind-safe! Despite being a game about colored light, it gives lots of options to adjust the hue, along with making sure each color has a unique icon! I'm not colorblind, but I appreciate accessibility!Some feedback: I would love to be able to dial down the chromatic aberration effect. As is, I can play comfortably in a window but fullscreen makes me start to feel crosseyed.
_childDocuments_.name: SOLAS 128

_childDocuments_.review: This is a brilliantly conceived and executed puzzle game that I can't help but liken to the Zachtronics style of puzzle design to an extent; a simple, reasonably minimalist concept that gradually peels back more and more layers of complexity until you're dealing with some real brain-melting challenges. Unfortunately, the one place Solas 128 really fails is in its communication. It's minimalist to an absolute fault, to where it can be a minor challenge to even work out how to navigate the frontend to resume your saved game instead of deleting it or starting a new game by accident. Very much a sign of things to come.Naturally, this extends to the puzzle design. Something a game like this desperately needs is clear introduction to new puzzle elements as they're incorporated -- you make it clear that something new is happening, then you demonstrate basic applications of it, and  you can start taking the training wheels off and integrating it into the ongoing puzzle design. Solas does  introduce you to new concepts in relatively simple environments before working them into more complicated puzzle design, but the bigger issue is that you're given no indication of the fact that you're being introduced to a new mechanic in the first place. You can never be sure if you're missing an element of the current puzzle because you need to complete more of the nearby rooms first, because there's some new mechanic you don't know about yet, if you're maybe just being a bit dense at the moment, or possibly a combination of all three. Moreover, the hint system works swimmingly for some rooms and seems to outright break or mislead you in others because it, too, is extremely limited in what it has been designed to communicate. I have  had to reference video playthroughs to be able to continue, and I've rarely been disappointed at spoiling the solution for myself because nine times out of ten it leaves me shouting at my monitor, "How the ♥♥♥♥ was anyone supposed to intuit THAT for themselves?!"Currently I'm stuck on a room that is so horrendously designed and dependent on a complex series of maneuvers involving timing-based manual dexterity that,  I've not yet been able to complete it. It looks like some sort of harebrained unintended solution one would use to solve the puzzle because they can't figure out how it's actually intended to be played... except that is, in fact, how it is required to be played, and it is  bad. Which is a shame, because aside from these particular hideous and pronounced warts, it's a really well-designed experience with some masterfully crafted puzzles. And sure, I'd still recommend picking it up on a decent discount, but if the game weren't so adamant about keeping its lips pursed and expecting you to  it could've been a far, far less frustrating and no less enjoyable experience.
_childDocuments_.name: SOLAS 128

_childDocuments_.review: At one point I shouted 'You sexy pulsating clockwork miracle', which sounds like something Alan Partridge would say.I've not finished SOLAS 128 yet but it's shaping up to be one of my favourite puzzlers. Certain mechanics and the visual vocabulary of the game can take a little while to get used to, but once you're over that bump it's an incredibly slick, smart and satisfying puzzler with lots of 'AHA!' moments. There's Alan Partridge again.I absolutely love the larger scale interconnected puzzles here. It's stumped me a few times but thanks to the excellent music, popping synchronised visuals, a subtle hint system and non-linear structure, it's not felt quite as brutally abrupt when you come to a standstill.Highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: SOLAS 128

It's hard to count up the total # of levels while avoiding spoilers (around 100?) but as I write this I've logged 7 hours & seen ~40% of the game?Let's clarify basic mechanics. This is  in a traditional sense (like  or ). You are not timing your inputs to match a rhythm. Likewise, it's . The simplest levels do work like that, but usually you also need to . To do that it's not enough to make 2  of light intersect, you make the rhythmic  of light on the beams intersect. Often, this means moving reflectors to shift the intersection-point of the beams so the pulses arrive at the same place at the same time. You also need to direct the resulting beam to unlock the exit. Your goal is to do this, many times, to re-construct some machine that has been corrupted. Since the light is "always running" there's . Gadgets (Reflectors/splitters, etc) and required light-combinations start simple but become quite complex. Puzzles are "interconnected" - on early levels this isn't key, but . Some in-game hints are available. There's some cryptic nonsense in the background (see achievements).. But I only reached that conclusion decisively after about ~5 hours of play. A few things held me on the fence. (1) . If like me your guess is that Blue + Yellow = Green, think again, because light ain't fingerpaints.  and skip a lot of confusion. It'd be  if this info were displayed prominently in the game - minimally on a pause menu, or (why on earth not?) in those huge no-man's lands of borders/pillarboxes to the left and right of the board.(2) , and at times the game doesn't help you much. Those big borders shrink the play area, which means . Occasionally it even feels like the UI is so minimal that vital info is omitted. Look at , and work out how to visually discern the gadgets that are clearly affecting light differently. I'll wait. Ready? . It'd be nice if we could spare a few more pixels or colors in cases like this to make distinct objects more discernible. (3)  too: this is key for seeing chances to pass gadgets between puzzles/screens. I didn't learn this lesson properly, and that was frustrating: you can poke at a level for a  long time and get nowhere unless you realize what you've missed. While I think it's a solid mechanic, it's one that's obfuscated by the black and white UI at times. It'd be nice if there were a toggle in settings to make this pop-out a bit more. Having sorted through all that, as I say, I think the core design of the game is solid, and though I think it could be more accessible . To wrap up I'll survey some technical points while highlighting some burdensome stylistic choices that lead to some  you may want to consider. All in all these issues aren't game-breaking, but they might well turn some players of the game.
