_childDocuments_.review: I really really want to recommend this game, but the state it is in at this very moment I cannot. The concept is amazing, and I adore all the cute animals along with the cosmetics that are out, and the collabs they've done. Visually it is a really good, a cute cartoon-y game where you get to be a stuffed animal.Unfortunately, the community is already incredibly toxic and the game hasn't even been out more than two weeks. I am a girl and I feel like I am in a COD lobby by the amount of hate I get when speaking. It is very common to get cussed out in games and called slurs because you knocked somebody out or are just playing that game the way it is meant to be played, OR because you sound like a girl.  You would think with the game being about really cute stuffed animals the community would be nice and welcoming, but it's not. You can argue that I should just mute the voice chat or just ignore it, but the game was made with voice chat and I enjoy interacting with the wholesome section of this community, the ones that are just trying to have fun and don't threaten to un-alive you for knocking them out.And the game play, I could write an entire review just about this. You can pick up a weapon, and it is pretty much game over for everyone else without a weapon unless the weapon holder is miraculously knocked out, or they run out of stamina. If you get nun-chucks or a shovel then it is almost impossible to get close enough to that person to knock them out, especially on maps like the alligator river or airplane, because those are not at all forgiving and one misjudged jump is the end. I think weapons should have some type of cool down or some type of durability at least. There should be no reason a single cat with a pair of nun-chucks can knock out eight people in a row and win the game simply because they were the first person to pick up a weapon. It is ridiculous.Speaking of being knocked out, what is the point in playing when people can just stand over you and continuously knock you out? There have been many times where somebody is upset and targets me or another person and tries to keep them knocked out for the entirety of that game, and it is incredibly frustrating to stand up only to be drop kicked into the shadow realm once again. This is just a quality of life request really, but they should add something in the game where you can see your own stuffed animal better. This would help visually impaired individuals, because sometimes you can lose your own character in the chaos of everyone. Maybe a little glowing outline or something else to better indicate where you are in the group.Overall, I like the concept of this game. It is cute and fun with friends, but it certainly can be improved. If you are looking to buy it I would wait a little while to see if there are any updates.  They reverted back to the 2v2 modes thankfully Just updating this for the Steam Awards, (for the better with friends catergory) but I think that the changes the devs are implementing soon will definitely help the game.

_childDocuments_.review: As an experienced gamer and a fan of "Gang Beasts" and other similar titles, "Party Animals" instantly hooked me. A lot of newcomers seem to miss the essence of this game.Some complain about the physics, others about the OP weapons, and still others about the friendly fire. But that’s the beauty of the game. It's designed to be a hilarious chaos, especially when played with friends.For a version 1.0, the game is more than decent. The graphics are charming, the sound design is well-done, and the game physics bring a comedic and unpredictable element.Its so great to see a game that release polished and finished.The game is a success in my eyes, but it seems that many in the gaming community are not ready to embrace something new and step out of their comfort zone. The difficulty and new mechanics seem to scare them off.However, playing "Party Animals" with friends is pure joy. The AIs are well designed, and although there is a shop system, it's not intrusive. It's focused on skins, which, I believe, are all obtainable by playing.Strengths:- Attractive graphics- Immersive sound design- Well-guided tutorial- Comedic physics- Multiple game modes- Multiplayer and local split screen options- Keyboard and controller support- Very few bugs- A variety of mapsThe only downside is that some mechanics might need adjustments, and maybe an offline mode and no quit penality could be great, but nothing that ruins the gameplay experience. "Party Animals" is definitely a game to try if you're looking for fun with friends in a delirious and adorable environment.

_childDocuments_.review: Having played the game practically since its release, I think I have a good overview of its evolution so far and, unfortunately, since its launch. Too little has gone in the right direction...Improving on the gang beast concept, it had everything to please graphically. There are even a plethora of good arguments to recommend this game to you, but...At launch, the game was sold as an 8-player brawler featuring some twenty different maps:- 9 Last Stand maps (fighting in teams of 2 or 4)- 9 Team Score maps (4vs4 with objectives to reach)- 2 Arcade maps (can only be played by creating a private lobby or joining one).In the first few months, the Chinese studio got the job done. Just over a month after the game's release, on Halloween, the developers were already adding relative content. But at the same time, problems were already beginning to emerge as the Chinese studio partnered with Chinese streaming platforms (Bilibili and Douyin to start with) and granted them exclusive skins (for Halloween, for example) that could only be obtained by Chinese users, thus penalizing other players. This led to a number of problems, as these skins, obtained by code, could (to cut a long story short) be used twice. As a result, Chinese players, having used the code once for themselves, would try to exchange it with players from Europe, North America, South America... for a code that the studio had set up with Discord (also usable twice) and which penalized Chinese players. In this code exchange, there were numerous scams on both sides, and in the end, it created a very bad climate between the gaming communities.Shortly afterwards, the studio announced its roadmap, explaining that there would be a major update every 3 months, including a new map and new skins, which augured well for the future.The problem was that their first major update was delayed by a month. To fill the gap, they added a new map and introduced the “Friend Pass”, allowing players to invite their friends to play the game with them for free. A fine initiative, to be sure.Unfortunately, the worrying comments made by the studio were already summed up in this sentence: “We've noticed that many players are looking for a place to chat with others, rather than just fight” (patch note dated 16/12/2023). I don't know which players they're talking about, but nobody expected the studio to focus their money and energy on creating a place within the game where players could chat instead of fighting... Not only because this place already exists (the arcade maps), but also because if players have paid for a fighting game, it's because they want content related to what they've paid for!At the end of January, these concerns prove to be well-founded. Their first update for the brawler they'd sold to players introduced a UNO game renamed PAWS in one of the arcade maps, as well as a jukebox... THAT'S IT! To counterbalance the anger of the players, less than 10 days later they released a new map, which didn't convince anyone because it was too similar in principle to another existing map.The 2nd update doesn't do much better, as it also arrives a month late, and once again takes players by surprise. It introduces a new game mode with 2 missions playable solo or in pairs against bots. After 10 minutes of discovery to complete them (and I'm still being kind), you start to wonder if you haven't been ripped off, as the devs are moving further and further away from the fighting game they originally sold us.Well, I'm tempering that a little, because there's one good thing in this update, and that's the appearance of another game mode, “SMASH”, which fits into the “combat” category. It's well thought-out, it's fun and it deserves to be said.The 3rd update arrived on schedule! Are we going back to basics? No, of course not. This time, Recreate set out to offer players a Mario Kart version of Party Animals. It's certainly well done, and there's much more fun to be had in the one and only race than in the 2 challenge missions of the previous update, but when are you going to keep your promises? Where's the roadmap?But all this is nothing compared to what's to come. The ultimate betrayal that buries the game for good. In the game, there are several ways to knock out your opponents:- Light punching is the use of small punches (LP).- Heavy punch: run and punch (HP)- Dropkick: jump and kick (DK)- Headbutt is a headbutt (HB)There are two other techniques which are not explained in the game's tutorial and which have been found by players through experimentation:- The superman punch is a combination of three keys and allows the player to levitate briefly after his punch.- The fling is an improvement on the superman punch, combining 4 keys and allowing the player to project himself in the direction of his choice, knocking out anyone in his path. On the other hand, the fling is not without risk, as it can backfire if misdirected or controlled.These techniques, and the fling in particular, have rapidly become extremely popular among players, because although they are extremely satisfying to perform, mastering them requires training and demonstrates a skill that any player wishing to improve must master.Can you see it coming? At Recreate, they're doing everything they can to kill the fun. Since the release of their game, they've only done what they wanted to do, and whether we like it or not, that's the way it is. Our only treasure was the fling, but they took it away from us.Faced with the tidal wave of anger, they backed down, but in the worst possible way. The fling now consumes a phenomenal amount of stamina and can no longer be played...Worse still, the fling's nerf has created a domino effect on all gameplay, and the game's dynamics have been completely ruined:- HP has become punishing for the user, as it consumes far more stamina and hits the opponent even less than before.- The LP, which already consumed no stamina, has become much better, as it hits far more than the HP.- DK has become exceptionalBefore the nerf, the game required skill. It wasn't simply a matter of doing DK over and over again. In your desire to make the game more user-friendly for new players, you've not hesitated to scuttle the rules of the game. What you're doing is not the right solution. All you're doing is making the game less attractive. You change the rules without prior communication, without even telling the players what has changed. You're gradually destroying the trust and esteem the players had in you.At the time of writing, there are barely 3,000 daily players on the game. This pales in comparison with the 60,000 of the early days. This lack of players has prompted Recreate to find “solutions”. Already present from the start of the game, bots have become the most important player community. If you thought you were playing with a player called SnoopDogg or PapaSmurf, you're just playing with a bot. Their intelligence is disastrous, and you'll soon realize it. Bots are of no use to the game. Worse still, there's a good chance they'll get in your way or accidentally kill you.It seems vital to go back to an earlier version of the gameplay mechanics and the very foundations of the game. Until this is done, this game deserves this comment.

"Gang Beasts," on the other hand, has a more intentionally quirky and ragdoll style.2. **Gameplay Variety:** "Party Animals" may offer a broader range of gameplay modes and scenarios, catering to players who enjoy diverse challenges beyond just brawling. This can include mini-games, obstacle courses, and more.3. **Controls:** Some players may find the controls in "Party Animals" to be more intuitive or responsive than those in "Gang Beasts," depending on personal preferences.4. **Online Multiplayer:** "Party Animals" might have improved online multiplayer features or netcode, making it a better choice for those who want to play with friends or others online.5. **Development and Updates:** The ongoing development and support for "Party Animals" may provide players with more frequent updates, new content, and bug fixes, which can enhance the overall gaming experience.6. **Community and Player Base:** Depending on the platform and region, one game may have a more active and engaged player community, leading to a better multiplayer experience.However, it's important to note that "Gang Beasts" also has its own merits and a dedicated player base. Some players might prefer its more unique and quirky style, or they may have a nostalgic attachment to it since it was one of the earlier games in this genre.Ultimately, which game is "better" depends on your personal preferences, the features you value most in a multiplayer brawler, and the kind of experience you are seeking. _childDocuments_.review: I'm going to go against the grain on this one and say I'm not really having fun at all. I wish I had refunded. I get that it's a chaotic game and you're going to accidentally punch someone here or there, but I can tell when a teammate continues to hunt you down and throw you off the edge it's intentional. If you dare leave you're the one getting punished with a que ban, really? Being held hostage in bad matches isn't fun.  The controls aren't for me, they feel frustrating half the time. l2p issue, get good etc I know. Nothing feels worse than getting kicked at the start of the match when you've barely loaded in and you can't even recover before being eliminated before you got to play. Minor gripe: I don't know why a minute of character select is necessary for such a short game. People scrolling through their skins without picking until the timer runs out. It's disappointing because I was hoping for something cute and lighthearted in the same realm of what Fall Guys felt like. The animals, game modes, and humor is there, but core game play isn't enjoyable for me. Again, this is likely better with a friend group.

_childDocuments_.review: Party Animals is a quirky game filled with amusing animal characters, each offering a variety of skins that you can acquire through an egg machine or by spending cookies and in-game currency earned by leveling up or by "investing" real money. With a vast selection to choose from, there's something for everyone. (except for animal abusers ig...)The game truly shines when played with friends, creating memorable and hilarious moments. However, be prepared for a bit of chaos if someone in your group decides to become the disruptor instead of focusing on team tasks, leading to entertaining but often annoying battles and knockouts. (I'm that person, friends hate me... pls hug me and say it's gonna be alright...)I'd recommend using a controller for a smoother and more enjoyable experience, as the mouse and keyboard combo may feel less intuitive. (and you'll most likely destroy your mouse by smashing it all over your desk)The game's price point is a consideration. If you have friends to join in the fun, it's worth it. However, if you're planning to play solo, you might want to wait for a sale or explore other titles. Paying €18 for an online-only 'phone-style' game with additional microtransactions for characters and skins can seem a bit steep.In terms of maps and game modes, Party Animals delivers enjoyable and well-crafted experiences. My only wish is that there were more maps to keep the gameplay even more diverse and exciting.For my own experience, I've consistently had a blast playing Party Animals. However, I can't say the same for my friends, given that I tend to be making the game difficult for them. While I find the idea of spending extra money on skins a bit unnecessary, I'm content with the selection of free options available.Speaking of pizza, I like mine with a bit of pineapple on top. I'm crazy like that.Crazy? I Was Crazy Once. They Locked Me In A Room. A Rubber Room. A Rubber Room With Rats. And Rats Make Me Crazy!!!

_childDocuments_.review: I previously had a negative review due to what seems to a bit of confusion. Some people are reporting the game cannot be played offline at all, others say you can, still others say only on certain platforms. So if you had any doubt about that and need to play this game offline, do some research before you buy because depending on your circumstances it may not work. I keep finding conflicting information, so I'm leaving it out of this review for now.Assuming you do have online capacity however, this game is incredible. It's very clearly just gang beasts but with cute animals, but it really works. The cute animals give it a unique feel and make it stand out, and there was always a thrill in the early part of the game when you would see a new animal for the first time. You have obvious ones like dogs, cats, and rabbits, but some real odd balls that were a treat to see. They did a really good job of making the other game modes fun, I actually prefer some like the train mini game to some of the pvp maps like the ice one. The game does have a few weak points. Matchmaking is buggy right now and if you don't leave a match after the end and instead instant queue for another one, it often either crashes the game or gets you stuck in an endless loading screen. The game is heavily lootbox / microtransaction filled and many cosmetics (and even some characters) seem to only be available through these. You can get a few loot boxes from levels but after you reach max you would have to spend real money to roll the dice. I've seen about 30 different animals (albeit about 1/3 are variations of dogs and cats) and while that is definitely a lot I'm already itching for more. The game just came out so no telling how often updates will arrive but if they are frequent I think this game will last a long time. Lastly, this game really needs to have local multiplayer. It might already have this, but once again I have seen very conflicting information, and it seems like it is also platform related. In some capacity it seems at least one version of the game does have this, but it's very odd that it is not universal.

_childDocuments_.review: Lets start of by talking about the meat and bones of the game - The game play itself. And let me just say this right off the bat, it is chaotic and addicting and is FANTASTIC with friends. This is the most I have laughed while playing a game in a very long time. Its chaotic yet strategic in terms of on the fly decision making. Its goofy but can still take it competitively if you'd like. The aim of most matches to be the last person standing. Knock out every other person out of the map and you win. Simple. You can jump, punch, headbutt, kick, flying kick, roll and use whatever weapons you can latch on to at your disposal, that are raining down from above mid match, to attain victory. Its a game which everyone can get a good few laughs in. The game also includes other variations of maps which include a specific objective in mind like - scoring goals against another team in soccer and ice hockey, attempting to fuel up a moving train and reach the end while also attempting to stop your enemies team from doing the same and so much more.  There is a plethora of adorable animal characters to choose from to express yourself with, with each having costumes to obtain and different colour variants of some skins also. And the models for each one are beautifully the done. In fact, the 3D models and other assets are in the rest of the game are expertly done. Nothing feels out of place. Everything is so charming to look at and even though it is a simple design, so incredibly pleasing to the eye. Noticing tiny details on certain maps was honestly my favourite thing to do from time to time. Everything from sound design, to visuals and game play is excellent and, as I have said, I had a lot of fun playing this game. The MAJOR issue I have with it however, is the predatory monetisation and gatcha "lootbox" system implemented into an otherwise perfect game. I have seen people write reviews and dismiss it entirely saying things like "It won't effect me, I don't intend to buy anything." etc etc. And to that I say - All because YOU might not be affected does NOT mean it wont affect others. This is the exact thing that EA has gotten push back from and was forced to rethink their strategies in games like Battlefront 2. Activision Blizzard got hit so hard that they needed to release Overwatch 2 because of the major awareness of lootboxes being predatory and essentially gambling. (Because it is btw). This is a game where alot of children are going to be playing. Many parents will see the bright, colourful, fluffy animals and not realise the amount of money their children could be spending on this, hoping to get a shiny drop. Something that Fortnite got bashed for and got sued over.The game has 3 currency systems. One that you can earn, one that you can use real life money to get and another to roll for these eggs which is lootbox/gatcha system that I mentioned above. The skins themselves can go up to 25 pound which is about 30 USD. Ain't no skin on some goofy animal is worth that amount money. While I do realise that seeing it is a live service game and needs incoming funds for server upkeep, this is not the way to go about it. Here is how they SHOULD improve things: Number 1. Remove the gatcha system or make it so it is something that you can't spend real money on. Don't give the option to spend money on it. It is predatory.Number 2. Reduce the price of these 30 dollar skins. Make them cheap/affordable and I guarantee you, they will see an increase in sales. Having something that you can buy and actually see it before purchasing, all while it is within an adorable price range is something I'am completely ok with. Number 3. Increase the xp gain. I haven't mentioned this yet but with every completed match you get 500 xp. You level up this almost battle pass esc system and you earn rewards. Rewards that are included are: in game money, profile pictures, egg tokens for the gatcha system, characters, character skins other items. The gripe I have is that you get very little XP per completed match. Its becomes very grindy very quickly. While the game offers daily missions to reward you with a boost in XP as well achievements to earn that also give out XP, I still feel it isn't enough. It is unfortunately very slow to level and in turn not very rewarding.   While the game itself is top notch from game play, to sound and environmental design, it suffers from the same thing I heavily critiqued Overwatch 2 over, with extortionate prices of skins as well as Overwatch 1 and other games back in the day for the lootbox system that the gaming industry was plagued with for years. So for personal reasons I can not and will not recommend this game. I recommend finding other means of acquiring this product if you feel like you MUST have it. Don't support things like this. It hurts the gaming industry through and through and it saddens me to see games like this take such a big step backwards after so much push back of these monetisation practices within the last couple of years. If things change for the better, I will also change my recommendation. But for now, avoid it.

_childDocuments_.review: In general, do not buy this game if you are are going to be playing to win - which includes if you'll be wanting to obtain new skins, because you need to level up or obtain achievements to get them or the currency needed to get them.If you are confident you can play  casually (which may be easier in custom games that have less players, where you have more control), this game can be very chaotic and goofy fun.However,  like its other live-service cousins. It  on you having a more laid-back mindset, but the various progression, unlock, and achievement aspects often unwittingly revert you to a competitive mindset as you strive to achieve goals paved out for you.  And when  happens, the gameplay instantly devolves into watching a wheel spin for 15 minutes at a time, waiting for it to stop in the hopes that you might be rewarded a singular cookie crumb.Then again, don't just read this and think  That's not want I want you to take away from this. I just think you should examine this game very closely to see if it's right for you.TL;DR: This is a casual game, and at its core, it's fun. But it seems to think it's a competitive game, so it encourages you to play to win with cookie crumbs and breadcrumbs; and once you start playing to win, the fun instantly drains away.  or have a completionist mindset, think twice about buying this game. This game relies on your willingness to laugh at failure to be fun - but it has an achievement for EVERY map requiring you to win 5 times on each of them, as well as other achievements for every map with absurd conditions. This creates competitiveness, which drains all of the fun out of the game; failure here is very rarely your fault, and instead usually just bad luck, which is  infuriating when you're driven to win. Even besides the infuriation, if you play to win, the game just feels incredibly  because you're not laughing.You also can't leave a match you aren't enjoying, because there's a 2 minute quickmatch penalty every time you force-leave.If you're playing with friends rather than in Quick Match, this game  fun (no achievements in custom mode means no completionist drive to win), but do note that this game (allegedly)  as was originally advertised - although you can have two controllers on one computer, you need a connection no matter what. The devs claimed that this was a misunderstanding; however, I don't quite believe them, to be honest.Also: this is a . Microtransactions, lootboxes, seasons (but no passes, thankfully), the works. _childDocuments_.review: Pretty fun little online brawler. Especially fun when queuing up with a friend or playing locally. Main problems as of writing the review: AFK players and skill disparity in the community. AFAIK the developers are trying to update the game to make matchmaking more fair, but chances are if you are a casual player and aren't really into the competitive aspect of the game (especially if solo queuing) you won't have a good time. Toxicity levels are manageable, some players will focus you (again, a much bigger problem when playing solo) but voice chat is mostly harmless in my experience. Regarding micro-transactions and skins: if you are putting hours into the game - you won't have to pay a dime for pretty much anything you want. I currently only know about 1 skin pack outright locked behind a paywall. Level rewards are generous and skins that cost normal currency are basically free, especially once you hit level 100. Paid currency drops in decent amounts from level ups, I never had to buy a skin for money and even managed to gift a fairly expensive skin. The issue may become worse (or better, actually) as more content is introduced and additional levels are added (though i'm not aware of developer plans to add more levels atm) All in all, if you like competitive online games that are a bit more random Party Animals comes recommended. Queue times are not long right now and the game is not annoyingly random (though this also kinda depends on the map). Skillful players will outmatch luck 90% of the time, i'd say. Bugs are basically non existent, which is also a big plus. What little bugs i've encountered have been more fun than annoying.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a delightful, chaotic, and lighthearted escape—perfect for when you're tired of overly competitive environments. It features adorable characters and party-style gameplay that anyone can jump into!It’s not meant to be taken too seriously, but sometimes it feels like the player base hasn’t quite gotten that memo.Seriously, people need to relax—this isn’t .That aside.. I absolutely recommend this game for anyone looking to have some lighthearted fun with friends. There are a few areas where improvements could be made, but the core experience is still a blast.One of the key issues right now is the potential for harassment via voice chat. By default, all players can communicate with each other, and while that can sometimes lead to funny moments, it too often results in toxicity. I recommend turning off open voice chat by default, or at the very least limiting it to party members. It's a party game, but no one signed up for verbal abuse.There’s a common issue where players block others in tight spaces or corners for entire rounds. It’s frustrating and feels like an exploit rather than a valid strategy. Introducing a timeout penalty for players who intentionally block others would make gameplay feel more balanced and fair for everyone. Some levels involve survival elements like fog or lava, where players must manage how long they can hold out. It would be great to have a visual timer or some indicator that shows exactly how long you can stay in these danger zones before your character is eliminated. This would make it easier for players to strategize and manage their moves more effectively. The UI while navigating menus with a controller is difficult to see, especially when it comes to highlighting menu options. While the game’s matchmaking system works well most of the time, it often feels like the balance shifts unfairly when playing in a party. As a casual player, I find myself frequently matched against players with 300+ hours of experience, which can be frustrating when all I want is to have fun with my friends. Some kind of skill-based matchmaking or balance adjustments for parties would help even out the playing field.

name: Patrick's Parabox
detailed_description: Patrick's Parabox is an award-winning puzzle game that explores a unique recursive system of boxes within boxes within boxes within boxes. Learn to manipulate the world's structure by pushing boxes into and out of each other. Wrap your head around what happens when a box contains itself, and learn to use infinity to your advantage. Explore many more mechanics and recursive twists as you delve deeper and deeper into the system. It's boxes all the way down. The game has over 350 hand-crafted puzzles, which are designed to make you think, but also to guide you and showcase the beauty of the system. Each puzzle contains a new idea; there is no filler. A soothing, inquisitive soundtrack and sound design by Priscilla Snow reflects new mechanics as they are introduced. Patrick's Parabox won the Excellence in Design award in the Independent Games Festival 2020. The game was also an IndieCade 2019 festival selection and received the IndieCade Developers Choice award.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's be honest: nobody likes looking up solutions to puzzles, and nobody likes leaving puzzles unfinished, and nobody likes staring at a puzzle for hours, having your brain operate on 42069 teraflops. But if a puzzle game is too easy, then it becomes boring and there's no satisfaction.Patrick's Parabox solves this conundrum by having excellent puzzle design, a very fine learning curve with lots of teachable moments, and deciding to err on the side of being too easy rather than too hard. Don't worry; it'll still make your brain hurt in that good way... okay, I think I'd better explain myself.I don't consider myself particularly good at puzzle games; I managed to "beat" Baba is You (got to the credits) with only looking up solutions maybe 2-3 times, but every late game puzzle took me ... a pretty long time. Sometimes hours. At some point it stops being fun. Parabox, on the other hand... I managed to 100% of the main game (all puzzles, minus the post-game challenges) in 12 hours. The longest I was stuck on a puzzle was 15-20 minutes, tops, and most I've solved in around 2. I mean, I have around 260 puzzles solved, so that'd make it around 3 mins per puzzle on average?Point is, it's much easier. Once you hit the "aha" moment, setting everything up to work the way you want to is quick and pleasant. Still, no puzzle was so easy that I'd instantly know the answer just by looking at it. If I had to describe my "brain flow" here, it'd be something like this:Look -> Hmm -> Messing around -> Ok -> Sherlock Mode -> Elementary, my dear Patrick -> SolveI hope that makes sense. Let's talk about the learning curve, since that's what makes the difficulty so pleasant.The game's split into thematic worlds, which all use a central mechanic as a foundation. Of course, latter worlds include mechanics from previous worlds to keep things interesting - but they don't overuse them, and many optional side puzzles have mechanics that are unique to this particular set.Every world has the "main" path - easy puzzles which mostly just show you how a new mechanic works. Sometimes two puzzles have essentially the same solution, just are flipped around a bit; but that ensures that you really get it. Once you're done with those, you can try the "red" or even "blue" puzzles which are, in my opinion, where the real meat of the game is - they test your understanding of the mechanics, and are rather  non-trivial. But the good news is that you don't need to do them if you don't want to.So: do you want a brain workout, or would you like to just be taken on a magic  box ride through a theme park of guided "aha" moments? The game's got you covered either way. No shame.You might think that the trailer showcases this part quite well. You'd be wrong; because it gets so, so much  than that. What happens if you put a box inside itself, and then leave it? That's simple, you reappear inside, at the edge of where the "inner" box is. But what if you tweaked that situation and put the inner box's edge so that it lines up with the outer edge... and then try to leave? You'd be stuck in an infinite loop of leaving into something that doesn't exist. The game just shrugs at that paradox and calls it "infinity". It usually breaks the puzzle, but not always. The game's called "Parabox" because it's all about using and abusing such paradoxes... with boxes. And that infinity thing is arguably the simplest weird thing you'll encounter here, by the way.And the best part? The puzzle design not only explains those weird concepts very well, it also twists them around and puts them in such insane configurations that you can't help but be amazed at the sheer  required to craft this insane concoction. A prime example of the divine creativity only a solodev can wield.Flaws... there really isn't much to complain here. The biggest "problem" I can think of is that there doesn't seem to be a way to zoom on a controller, you have to use the mouse. Also, if you're smarter than me (or just good at puzzle games), you'll probably find the game too easy - but I still think you'd have fun.In a nutshell, I'd say that this game has the mechanical depth of Baba is You but the difficulty and pacing of Portal. In other words - if you even remotely enjoy puzzle games, this is an absolute must play.
_childDocuments_.name: Patrick's Parabox

_childDocuments_.review: First two worlds in the full version are 90% the same as the demo.But then there are more worlds.How many? I dunno man, I'm like 8 or 9 deep currently with no obvious way to see how much farther it goes.If you can imagine busting out a hypothetical level editor just to see "But what would happen if..." then the full game apparently has levels which rely on the answer to exactly that question to solve the puzzle.What if you could step outside a level in a different direction than you're currently pushing it?What if you could step into the smaller copy of the level you're already in directly?What happens if you try to step directly from one small level to another?What about the above but *the levels have different resolutions*?What happens when you try to step into a level that has more than one exit?Or huge exits?Or.. Christ, the level doesn't even have walls?What crazy crap goes on if you have multiple levels each nested within the other?Sokoban++ your way through this and many other questions, until you finally have mastery of every ridiculous mechanic possible!That's okay, Patrick will just tell you "congratulations! Now enjoy this NEW mechanic you've never seen before, and it renders the entire zeitgeist you've learned into a mere tip of an iceberg of new madness". And rinse and repeatAND rinse and repeat.In the late 70s Warren Robinett invented and perfected the Hyperlinked Map Mechanic to make devious, physically impossible mazes for Atari Adventure, Rocky's Boots, and eventually Robot Odyssey.I think that Warren would be floored to see how Patrick has tortured and twisted and eldritchified the mechanic here.🟨➡ 🐉...... 🦆

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first time in a while that I've felt compelled and capable to 100% a puzzle game on my own. It's a complex and difficult game, but also very fair and forgiving in ways that make it a joy to play. Puzzles are difficult because of how they re-use and re-contextualize their mechanics, rather than adding additional layers of complexity for the sake of difficulty. Solutions tend not to be particularly long. I think of the 364 puzzles, there was a total of  that I did not understand and had to brute force. That's pretty remarkable!In addition to all that, I think there's a lot of value in playing this game for the first time blind. Every time a new mechanic is introduced, it was a surprise to me - and yet, the mechanic was simple enough that I almost instantly understood it.I do not know if you'll enjoy this game to the end if you're not a puzzle game enjoyer. However, if you are, I cannot recommend it enough.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't usually recommend games due to the amount of time required to write such a review. Games like these are the exception because of either how well made or horrible the game is. In this case, its the former.I'm going to compare this game to Baba is You because I feel like where Baba failed to uphold, Patrick comes in with a solid gold plate that reads 'No Excuses'.In Baba, each level teaches you a new physic mechanic, allowing you to alter the physics of the puzzle. Each level afterward becomes increasingly difficult, which is exactly how it's suppose to be done. HOWEVER, what it failed to do is when it introduces these new mechanics, it doesn't bring those mechanics back to newer levels. Spoiler Ex: There was a level in Baba where Flag is Stop and you had a treadmill is move. How you would go about solving it is that you use the treadmill to Push you on to the Flag. I thought that was a neat mechanic but when playing the game, I have yet to see that mechanic ever being reintroduced. This is where Patrick comes in. This game will teach you core mechanics of the game, while making each one harder than the last level. Not only that, but when you are no longer in the world with that mechanic, it still reuses the past core mechanics in the future levels.Spoiler: Let's say you learn about Center. Where you can only enter the area if the Center is not blocked. You can also push blocks that are in the Center by entering said area with the block. In the next worlds, they have constantly use that mechanic, not by a lot but enough of them use it to reward you on learning about the center.I guess that's the other thing about this game, every time you clear a level it feels like a sense of accomplishment and rewards you by giving you levels that uses the mechanics you learn beforehand. And this barely covers the amount of content it provides. There are challenge levels that are optional in each world, not to mention several extra worlds that are full of challenges and surprises. This game is the best example of a perfect puzzle game. From the level design, to the simple mechanics, to all the extra stuff, all puzzle games should use this game as a blueprint for any puzzle game that they want to create.Amazing game, I can't wait to see what other games this company will put out.

_childDocuments_.review: I played most of this game when I was judging for an event, so my playtime is not accurate - I am very excited to play it all over again though.this game rips. it's SO brilliant. probably my favorite puzzle game I've played. as someone who doesn't especially enjoy sokoban games, this one is an extremely fun and satisfying one that surprises and delights at every turn with great puzzles. each one is so gracefully designed, you can scratch your head at it for a long time but the solution is always just a few short steps to implement. give this a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: Patrick's Parabox is exquisite. It's immediately one of the greatest puzzle games of all time - I'd argue top 3. For those who didn't read the blurb, it's a sokoban puzzle game whose gimmick is based around the programming concept of recursion; each block you push around can be a map unto itself that you are able to go into, and the game builds on these ideas of recursion in extremely clever ways.I was wary going into this game because it's not the first puzzle game playing with the concept of recursion. Recursed has attempted this before, and I found it to be a case test in how not to design a puzzle game; The recursive puzzles very quickly became too tangled and hard to follow, and it failed to offer any satisfying a-ha moments that you expect from a puzzle game.Thankfully, Patrick's Parabox is the complete opposite experience. It's rich with brilliant puzzles that are minimal and elegant and expose interesting idea upon interesting idea. And they don't feel needlessly hard, which I appreciate. It's not like a Baba level where you might get stuck on it for hours. In the over 350 levels I never got stuck for more than like 25 minutes. It's like the quality of a qrostar game, but more accessible (while still being plenty mind bending). If you enjoy puzzle games, you must play this. It's a treat.

_childDocuments_.review: Every third spring, a solo indie developer reinvents Sokoban.Okay, well, this certainly isn't as hard as Baba or Stephen's Sausage Roll but it's just as inventive and creative, and it's also, importantly, incredibly funny. I don't think puzzle design has ever made me laugh as hard as this game. The concepts are introduced and toyed with then integrated into future concepts smoothly, rarely do ideas feel repeated, there's a -ton- of puzzles and the challenge puzzles can get quite tricky, the aesthetic is polished and pleasant to look at, it's just an overall really clever and enjoyable puzzle game with.... no real downside to speak of, other than that it's not going to wreck your brain or stump you in the same ways as similar games, and that  but that second one is... well, really a nitpick, the game is compelling enough as-is that it didn't necessarily -need- that extra push to be awesome.
_childDocuments_.name: Patrick's Parabox

_childDocuments_.review: To infinity, and double infinity, and triple infinity, and beyond! A recursive sokoban with mind-bending mechanics. Unlike a normal game restricted to what is physically possible, this game breaks reality by allowing you to do things only abstract theoretical math allows.The game starts simple, with basic boxes you can push, and then gets more and more complicated with new abilities you have to master. First, the boxes you can push are not just simple boxes, but they can be mazes you can enter and exit, with their own puzzles inside, and there are boxes within boxes within boxes. Then you get boxes containing themselves, where going out of the box still puts you inside the box, or can form cycles with box A inside box B inside box C inside box A again. Then you get clone boxes, and flipped clones, and you become the whole level itself, and find out what happens when you push a box out of itself or into itself. What lies beyond infinity? Can you push yourself into yourself? Who shaves the barber who shaves those and only those who don't shave themselves?The mechanics of the game are incredible and wonderful, yet the game does an excellent job at making you discover them. There are 18 main chapters, each focusing on one aspect of the game, and each containing some easy levels that are there to guide you towards discovering what can be done, a few hard levels that require you to show you really understand what's going on, and a few very hard levels that require a lot of thinking. You don't have to finish all of them to progress, most chapters will let you go to the next chapter if you just finish the basic levels. At the end there is a challenge chapter with really hard levels, this time combining different aspects, plus a few extra puzzles with different mechanics. A great variety from easy to very hard. 364 levels, for more than 10-20 hours of playing. Superb. Very well done "discovery" levels, very hard levels that can be beaten with logic, with non-obvious solutions, and although there are hundreds of levels, most of them are unique. Some levels are quite similar on purpose, to show what a difference a little change makes. Very good. Unlimited undo, reconfigurable controls, clean and pleasant graphics, lots of settings, decent progress achievements, cloud saving, fast and responsive. Yes! It's expensive, but it's a very well made game, and a unique experience that must be tried. Mindbending mechanics. Nothing, this game is perfect.. another excellent game with recursion at its core, but in a platformer framing instead of sokoban., exploration/puzzle game in hyperbolic (non-euclidean) space., mindbending puzzle game where you make up the rules; also has a little bit of puzzle within puzzle gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Patrick's Parabox

_childDocuments_.review: I think a good puzzle game gives you the following four experience:-Some puzzles are easy, little confidence boosters but not especially challenging-Some puzzles are tough, making you stop and think carefully about what exactly has to happen to find the solution-Some puzzles are difficult enough that you have to leave them behind and come back when you're wiser and more experienced-And some complicated puzzles...you find yourself just moving around, not even really consciously aware of what you're doing, until suddenly a hundred moves later you find you, or perhaps your well-trained subconscious, found the solution.Patrick's Parabox has all four in just the right proportions (at least for me), and I'd recommend it to anyone.
_childDocuments_.name: Patrick's Parabox

_childDocuments_.review: I really despise Sokoban, so much so that I hated Baba Is You even when everyone else loved it, because the sokoban part of the game was constructed in a boring way that I'd seen a hundred times before, even if there were labels on some tiles. I've been doing sokoban since I was playing nethack every day and I never need to do it again unless there's a good reason.Parabox has the best Sokoban puzzles that I've ever seen. Truly, even beyond the amazing set of mechanics that are introduced per world, the puzzles themselves are lean and don't have any trick alleys designed to confuse you from the correct solution--if there is a level with a single fixed block in it, you can be certain that that fixed block is used in the ultimate solution. I appreciate this immensely--it often means that once the *concept* of a level is understood, the solution is trivial. (Also there are literal nethack tribute bonus levels, which made me so happy.)And the paraboxical mechanics are great! Recursion, references, mirroring, with very natural interactions between every one. The game really reminded me of a Zachtronics game in the sense that you are putting together a set of transformations with your movements to achieve a final product.The one complaint I would have is that the linear nature of the world unlocks means that you have to substantially complete each world before doing the next. Sometimes this causes me to bounce off games because I hit a wall, but the puzzles here are so fun and relatively easy that that hasn't happened, but I do worry about it in general for this style.
_childDocuments_.name: Patrick's Parabox

_childDocuments_.review: Peak puzzle design. One of the best puzzle games out there. Underrated, and honestly could beat one of its greatest rivals: Baba is you. If there's anything Patrick's Parabox splendidly outdoes Baba is You at, it's elegant simplicity. The difficulty isn't too hard for most puzzles. This might turn off people who want a serious brain scratcher, but other than that, if you enjoy puzzles, get it. If you really want to be cautious, the demo will give you only a tiny yet fun peak at the easier puzzles. The difficulty is well balanced imo. Neither too easy, nor too hard. You will still have to pause for a moment and have to rethink, retry and reconsider your approach for almost every solution. The pace is good too, a little on the slow side, but you will never get overwhelmed.The level design is genius, and the game manages to be so incredibly simple, contained within tiny spaces, yet have dozens and dozens of different mechanics derived from a couple core mechanics, with many fascinating applications. There are many levels (read: areas/chapters), each with a theme and a few puzzles, and they all introduce a new mechanic everytime, while never changing any rule, and almost never adding a new one. The consistency of the rules deserves credit. The depth is shockingly endless. More than a hundred puzzles is also a very fair ammount of puzzles for a puzzle game, especially since the price is reasonable.It nails the satisfaction good puzzles should provide, the Ah Hah! moment. On top of that, it also nails the "wow" factor, surprising you in new ways every puzzle and new introduced mechanic.My only gripe is that this game's potential is infinite, and it isn't fully exploited as there isn't a lot of levels that try to combine a lot of mechanics at once, which means it would benefit so, so much from an editor. There IS one, but it's just not something the average player will be able to use, unlike an editor like mario maker. It's not THAT complicated either, but still demanding more than most will have.EDIT: Small correction about the editor. The way the level creation is implemented also has some significant advantages, the biggest being the following: The ability to create new mechanics.As for other aspects including technical, i have no complaint.
_childDocuments_.name: Patrick's Parabox

_childDocuments_.review: This puzzle game has been a very pleasant surprise to me. It really delivers exploiting the possibilities of implementing fractals in sokoban-like puzzle games.At first I thought there was not much more to the mechanics that are introduced while you advance through the first 3-4 worlds but the game keeps introducing new tweaks and combining them with the known ones, resulting in complex and interesting puzzles.Strongly recommended specially if you are into puzzle games, it's a breath of fresh air.

_childDocuments_.review: Patrick's Parabox is quite a beautiful puzzle game to train your brain with. With a simple, elegant design, this Sokoban-style game takes the task of organizing boxes to new heights, or rather, dimensions.As a kid, I used to love playing Sokoban-style games, there was something so interesting about figuring out how to place each box in its place. When I learned about Patrick's Parabox, I couldn't help but be intrigued by its concept: a Sokoban game where not only can you move boxes around, but sometimes you can fit those boxes inside smaller boxes, or even fit those boxes inside themselves? Sign me right up! After all, there's something that fills me with wonder when dealing with impossible geometry, recursion, and the like, and this game has it in spades.Now, I've given a general idea of the main gameplay loop: each level is a box, filled with boxes that you have to fit in specific places. The game starts out simple: the first levels are basically your standard Sokoban puzzle. As you progress through each chapter, however, new concepts get introduced, in a very intuitive way, I'd say. The game seems to follow the principle of teaching the player a new mechanic, getting them used to it by putting some spin on it, before moving on to the next mechanic, while still incorporating those previously used.The lenght of the game is pretty decent, if I recall correctly, there's something like 200+ different levels, including challenges that really make your brain work. Still, it's pretty manageable, I only had to look up a single puzzle, I'll admit, and when I saw the solution, I was facepalming at how simple it was and I couldn't figure it out. So, my advice to you, future player of this game, is to really try to think outside the box, or inside it, or besides it. You'll figure it out eventually.Artistically speaking, as I mentioned above, the game has a rather simple, yet elegant design, with colours that really pop, so to speak. The soundtrack is also very soothing, perfect for some mental exercise. All in all, I truly enjoyed this game, and I'm a bit ashamed it took me so long to finally sit down and write a proper review for it, as I think everyone should give it a chance. So, go ahead, get this game, and let your brain start working!

I can see the design space for the mechanics to be limited after a certain point, but I certainly look forward to finishing out all the 350 puzzles and seeing what updates will come up in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: It starts simple enough. For a while, I thought it was a small cute game, which was probably hard for people who weren't as used to thinking about recursion as me...I'm now about a fifth of the way in, and I'm humbled. The puzzle are starting to seriously hurt my brain, while still being solvable.Highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Patrick's Parabox

_childDocuments_.review: Positives:- The whole experience can be described as "I can't tell you how exactly this works or why I'm doing this ... but when I do these steps, I will solve the puzzle because that's exactly how the puzzle works (even tho I'm just using muscle memory and educated guesses)".- Lots of puzzles, lots of different mechanics, lots of interactions, lots of aha-moments.- There are some really nice twists to the regular puzzles, like when you have to solve one using the string representation. There are lots of these small sets with 3-4 levels that completely change the puzzle formula, and it really shows how creative the devs got with such seemingly simple mechanics.- Paradoxes are used in a clever way. First they are just an edge case you have to avoid, but later they actually become part of the puzzles.- The level hubs give a preview of the mechanic/theme of the puzzles, which is very clever.Neural:- I can recommend playing the game in multiple long sessions so you don't lose the muscle memory of how the mechanics work. It worked well for me: by the 8th or 10th level hub (out of  total), I was still breezing through the puzzles, but the game didn't give me any sort of indicator of how much more there is, so it became a little monotonous and exhausting.- There's puzzles and that's it. (For me it's a positive, but some may prefer puzzles wrapped in a story or some form of progression.)Negatives:- It can be pretty difficult to distinguish the block "states", especially if the only difference is a change in brightness of the block's color. This makes it difficult to immediately start thinking about the puzzle solution when you first need to figure out what everything is. Same with when you don't start at the "outermost layer" of the puzzle or when some blocks are burrowed 2 "layers" deep inside other blocks.
_childDocuments_.name: Patrick's Parabox

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, it's on the easier side for puzzle games but still delivers a nice challenge with the bonus levels. My game time is how long it took me to 100% the game. I was really wondering how the game was going to be able to deliver 350 unique levels using such a simple idea, and wow did it exceed my expectations on that end, it manages to do so much with so little! The game had me giggling several times throughout my playthrough with all the hilariously absurd things it managed to pull off. What a wonderful experience this was.
_childDocuments_.name: Patrick's Parabox

_childDocuments_.review: Never have I felt so smart, clever, and ingenious, while at the same time feeling dumb as a brick. The game does a great job of introducing all its moving pieces at a comfortable pace, building steadily up in complexity. Every world has to far introduced a new concept, with levels ramping up to the challenge levels where Patrick tosses you on a flying, infinitely cloning carpet to show you the recursive world. And it is beautiful.Before you know it, you'll be muttering to yourself like a lunatic, but it'll make perfect sense to anyone who has had to bend their brain the way this game needs you to.
_childDocuments_.name: Patrick's Parabox

_childDocuments_.review: Challenging but never frustrating, which is probably the highest praise you can give to a puzzle game. The game constantly introduced new mechanics that kept it fresh and interesting over the 14 hours it took me to finish all puzzles except the post-game challenges, which I might still do. I regularly thought "This game is so smart!" after finishing puzzles, so hats off to Patrick for creating an amazing game!
_childDocuments_.name: Patrick's Parabox

_childDocuments_.review: Takes a commonly seem puzzle-game concept, and then proceeds to bend it around a 4-dimensional plane wrapped around your brain. Patrick's Parabox is a stellar puzzle game with a very impressive flow that keeps introducing new elements and expanding on pre-existing ideas, without ever feeling like it's overloading the player or bombarding them with too many unknowns. There are always options and different puzzles to challenge yourself with if you find yourself getting stumped, and the level of satisfying and "whoa..." moments are a delight. Very strong recommend to just about any puzzle-game enjoyer.
_childDocuments_.name: Patrick's Parabox

_childDocuments_.review: Not as challenging as Baba Is You's Expansion, which is good. Each of the worlds introduces a mechanic and sticks to that theme, serving as a tutorial and test for all the intricate ways that the mechanic has. By the time you reach the next world, you'll have already mastered what came before, so when they appear in the next world's puzzles, they don't distract much from that world's main mechanic.Maybe like two out of 240 puzzles are implementation heavy. Y'know, in other puzzle games where you see the solution, you know the solution, but it still takes like fifty steps to actually do? This game doesn't do that, which is great.Your mind will be blown like, once or twice per world, in such a way that the game presents as perfectly normal. Reminds me of SCP-2719.

_childDocuments_.review: An utter delight, this is a masterclass in elegant design.Maybe you already thought you were thinking with portals, but what happens when you put portals through portals eh? This game starts there... and goes everrrr deeper.The real magic of this game is that, despite invoking layer upon layer of otherworldly geometry... you STILL end up with the incredible satisfaction of learning to SEE in an entirely new way. _childDocuments_.review: Worthwhile puzzle game with a novel mechanic. _childDocuments_.name: Patrick's Parabox

_childDocuments_.review: Patrick's Parabox is easy to describe, hard to master.Its in it's essence... a Puzzler. No other way to describe it.But trust me when I say, it will literally MELT your brain.I've now 100%-ed this game in approximately 19 hours of playtime and it was a blast.This game starts out very innocent, push a few blocks, win the level. As you progress, you willpush deeper and deeper into this unforgiving challenging puzzle game, you will discover Infinities, Epsilon-Areas and Infinity-Epsilons. Thinking with portals does not prepare you for this.However, what this game is doing incredibly well is: Introducing its mechanics.You start out with a new mechanic, it teaches you the basics in an incremental way for approximately 3 to 4 levels. Each introductory level adds a twist or another challenge to the previous one in a way that its easy to follow and understand. And when you thought you got this, then the mechanic combines with the previous onesin ways that you cant even imagine. Seeing how these things interact with each other and tingle your braincells is just amazing to experience and I suggest if you like puzzlers, you should buy this one right now!
_childDocuments_.name: Patrick's Parabox

_childDocuments_.review: Play as a squishy, lil' box named Patrick as he pushes a box into another box to move a box somewhere else while meeting yourself that's in a box along the way in this recursive, Sokoban-style game. This logic, puzzle game is absolutely brilliant!The game respects players' time by offering bite-sized puzzles with clearly defined concepts. It allows for players to gradually ease themselves into the game by introducing new rules and integrating those mechanics into new puzzles in extraordinarily interesting ways. It even allows for players to jump into the deep end by giving them the option to unlock all the puzzles immediately from the get-go if they're so inclined to do so. Puzzles are cleverly made, and reaching the solutions to the puzzles will always make sense.The minimalistic art-style and the accompanying cutesy, mellow tunes work well together. They lend themselves to the mood and flavor of the puzzles quite well to deliver a nice, relaxing ambiance. Players shouldn't feel rushed or stressed while they contemplate over their next move(s), and the game does a marvelous job to encourage a stress-free environment until players reach their eureka moment over a particularly elusive solution to a puzzle they may encounter.This game is excellent for puzzle lovers! Thought and care were put in for the construction of the recursive puzzles, and they are superbly built. Hands down easily recommended for people who enjoy puzzles.  is unassumingly brilliant in its minimalistic approach yet underscoring the complexity of later puzzles. Very enjoyable and highly recommended!Edit: Corrected a single letter typo. ^^'

_childDocuments_.review: Honored to share a first name with this guy. Patrick's Parabox feels like a proper spiritual successor to Baba is You. It's far more consistent and much more intuitive in its design, and while it does have a few flaws, I found this to be far more enjoyable near the end.Patrick's Parabox takes a relatively simple idea and does a lot with it. The game features a very utilitarian design which is serves its job well. The music is nice to listen to while you play. Nothing about the actual visual or aesthetic design sticks out but it doesn't need to considering the nature of this game.The gameplay is great. Like I said, it's very intuitive. You can get a great "feel" for the game, and while some puzzles do require logic, most of them are pretty straightforward. My issue with the game is that the complexity and difficulty is VERY inconsistent. Sometimes you'll come across a puzzle that's very hard, then you'll come across an easy puzzle right after. This is mostly because the game wants to use it to teach you certain concepts before making them harder, which is a good thing, but it could have been done much better. Either way the game is great. All the mechanics are self-explanatory and used consistently and creatively throughout the game, unlike Baba is You which is very creative but not consistent at all with its use of mechanics or difficulty. This game scales very well as it goes on. It got MUCH better as it went on. The last two levels are a little too simple for me personally but it's fine; the game gives you challenges after you beat it anyway.Not much more to say about this game. It gets really good near the end because of how well the mechanics are used. It's actually impressive how many puzzles there are and how different each one is. Some of them are way too simple and easy for my tastes, but it helps keep things moving along since you'll occasionally get stuck on something really hard. Very consistent mechanics and easy to get a feel of. FAR better than Baba is You which I find very overrated and inconsistent. This game is balanced weirdly because sometimes it feels too easy but it's no big deal.Only real flaw that this game has is it starts off way too easy. For the first 2-3 areas I was considering giving this game a negative review. I'm glad I didn't. The rest of the game is very impressive. Definitely worth the $20 I spent.

_childDocuments_.review: A recursive sokoban with tons of interesting mechanics. When combined, these mechanics provide an endless possibility of ingenious puzzles, 364 of which can be found in this game.The puzzles are divided into 20 worlds (plus appendix and challenges) to smooth the difficulty curve. In addition, there is a main path to follow: the core puzzles on the main path gently introduce new mechanics and need to be finished in order to unlock the next world; other puzzles offer additional challenge and explore deeper unusual consequences of the mechanics. Thus, casual players can finish the game by completing only the 100 or so core puzzles, while more hardcore players may strive to solve the more difficult ones to their heart's content.Accessible yet with incredible depth, Patrick's Parabox is a must-play for all puzzle lovers.

_childDocuments_.review: Great concept and great level progression. New ideas and blocks are introduced at a reasonable pace. Gameplay is very smooth and responsive, and the soundtrack is bubbly and relaxing.Overall difficulty is surprisingly accessible, considering the potential for extremely complex puzzles. I've completed all ~360 puzzles in about 13 hours of playtime.

_childDocuments_.review: Concept 10/10 - an absolute bangerGameplay 10/10Difficulty 9.5/10Level design 10/10Music 9.9/10Visuals 9.8/10This game is a sokoban-style puzzle with an elegant twist - you can enter some of the boxes, you can push boxes inside of boxes, and boxes can even contain themselves. Wondering what happens when you push a box out of itself? Buy this game and find out!If you are a fan of recursion and meta-games (Recursed, Baba is you) - then this game is for you.It is less complex than Baba is you - it has way fewer components a.k.a mechanics; yet it maintains a lot of puzzle diversity and lets you explore concepts of recursion, infinity and "tail property" quite well.As a consequence, puzzles are simpler than those in Baba is you. I remember spending couple of hours on some puzzles in Baba is you - but not in this game. And that's totally ok - game isn't overloaded or bloated.Visual design is great - whole level fits in your screen at all times, which makes levels very comprehensible (looking at you Recursed).On my 18-hour journey to beat this game I haven't encountered even a single bug; so if you're thinking whether you should buy Cyberpunk or this game three times over - you should probs choose the latter. Game is well worth its 10 bucks.This game easily lived up to my expectations about it, and left me satisfied yet hungry for more. If this game will have a sequel or a DLC with more mechanics - that would be an instabuy for me.PS: the idea to have "undo" button undo a level reset is AMAZING, I hope every puzzle developer steals this feature

_childDocuments_.review: Abstract sokoban-style game with recursive mechanics, not as challenging as you’d expect. [17/20⭐, 17h🏅, 3/5💡] Patrick’s Parabox is an abstract sokoban-style game with recursive mechanics where obstacles are themselves navigable areas. The closest in mechanics would be , even though that was a platformer. There is no plot, the setting is completely abstract. The visuals are simple and abstract, and the soundtrack calm and non-intrusive. In general everything is decent but not particularly memorable. Patrick’s Parabox is a grid obstacle game where the obstacles are themselves navigable areas that can be entered. While this already introduces some interesting challenges, it gets mind bending (and paradoxical, hence the name) once levels start to be contained within themselves and have multiple occurrences. This leads to some impressive effects but without ever getting too challenging. In fact, even in more complex levels there are little paths to explore and solutions end up being rather simple (except for a few bonus levels). Granted, I felt not all introduced mechanics work, such as levels with areas with varying grid sizes that never felt natural.As any game of the kind, you can hit deadends when solving a level, but can always undo indefinitely (including after restarts). Game progress is auto-saved but not the level progress. It took me about 10h to beat the ~300 main levels and additional 7h to beat the ~60 bonus levels. You can always revisit levels, and there are multiple progress slots. There are custom downloadable levels so you can further extend gameplay (although I haven’t tried them). Achievements are mostly related with progressing the game, except requiring certain actions that naturally happen throughout normal gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Patrick's Parabox

_childDocuments_.review: Patrick's Parabox is a fantastic and delightful puzzle game, and ranks highly among my favorite puzzle games of all times.Like many of the best puzzle games (-> footnote), the game sets up a small universe of game mechanics and interactions, and then explores them to the fullest extent. However, Patrick's Parabox has a couple of characteristics that elevate it even among this illustrious company: the basic game mechanic of recursive boxes is incredibly unique and delightfully interesting; the game's great UX makes this unique mechanic surprisingly approachable and intuitive; and the game's difficulty curve is comfortably flat, so the game actually feels finishable. (Compare that latter point with Baba is You, another puzzle game I love, but which I also found frankly exhausting by the end.)The game has a fantastic progression system. You're never stuck at a single level but always have a bunch of options to proceed, e.g. you only need to solve 1/3 to 1/2 of the levels in each of the 18 main chapters to proceed to the next one. Plus individual levels are delightfully small and only consist of a small number of components, so while you might have to skip a few particularly challenging puzzles, it's unlikely that you'd get completely stuck. (In an interview, the dev mentioned that he made levels as simple as possible while still expressing the core idea, without any red herrings or superfluous elements.)The flat difficulty curve feels perfect, too. I like completing challenging puzzle games, but I don't particularly like replaying them, because it's one thing to solve a difficult puzzle once and a different thing entirely to bash one's head against a difficult puzzle again after one had already solved it previously. And yet Patrick's Parabox is one of the few puzzle games I've replayed. Another point in favor of the flat difficulty curve is that it helps completionists like me complete the game without looking up too many levels. In my initial playthrough, I only looked up 5 of the 364 levels.After playing many sokoban-style games with a par move mechanic, I also appreciated that Parabox doesn't have one. As a result, it feels like the game rewards playful experimentation: when you're stuck you can just goof around by moving around randomly, and sometimes something interesting happens that gives you an idea for how to solve the level.Ultimately, I adore this game. About the only bad things I can say about it are a) that I didn't like some of the music tracks, and b) that there are a few levels (Challenge 19-21) with multiple player character boxes, and since I couldn't make intuitive sense of their priority order, I had to write it down instead.Highly recommended.Footnote: As inspirations, the dev mentioned Stephen's Sausage Roll, The Witness, Recursed, and sokosoko as explicit influences, plus Snakebird and Baba is You. Talk about good taste!

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love this game. Enough that I'm even writing a review for it! As far as puzzles go, it's phenomenal - it keeps adding new mechanics at a nice and steady clip, and a lot of the puzzles have that really head-scratchy difficulty that makes you feel like an utter genius once you finally have that "Aha!" moment. What really sets Patrick's Parabox apart, though, is how much this game respects the player. There's the little, simple stuff - the UI is nice and clean, the animations are pleasing without being disorienting (important, given this game in particular), you can undo _and_ redo, and one touch I really like is that you can undo past a level-restart, useful when you want to remember how the puzzle was originally laid out but not lose all the progress you made.But the much bigger part of that comes from the puzzle design itself. The easy puzzles that introduce mechanics do so cleanly, giving you all the info you need about how this new weird thing works, so that once you get to the hard puzzles, you aren't left wondering what in the world is going on. And the hard puzzles _are_ hard, but each is based around a clever but logical twist that, once you get it, you don't have to spend a long time shoving blocks all over the place before you solve it. It's a really wonderful and refreshing feeling, and the only thing I wish is that there were more of it!
_childDocuments_.name: Patrick's Parabox

_childDocuments_.review: Hate to be the voice of dissent on a game with so much love put into it by the developers and community. It's a fantastic technological accomplishment, the mechanics are imaginative, and I don't wish to detract from that.I speak only for the main campaign of this game - it's... well... it's very easy. Less puzzle game and more guided tour. The thing it's a tour of is all well and good, but the game seems so terrified of asking the player to make any significant leap of logic that new ideas are demonstrated literally bit by bit before asking the player to build it themselves, yes, even in the optional levels. If you understand the mechanic after the first screen, get ready to spend five more demonstrating to the game that yes, I get it, can I have an interesting question now?The post game content is a bit better about this (obviously), but I think so much emphasis was put on making the game "accessible" that it diluted the experience. For myself I would have enjoyed to do a little more thinking during the introduction of the game's mechanics.7/10
_childDocuments_.name: Patrick's Parabox

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this one and played it to 100% completion. Not only are the puzzles fun to solve in a puzzley way, but simply moving around in these recursive spaces is very fun in and of itself. It explores the concept thoroughly and comes up with more gimmicks than you're probably expecting, each new one is really cool to discover. There is a nice length to the game as well, not too short not too long. To my tastes the length is just right, nothing ever felt like a slog.I'd also like to point out that the game structure is likely to appeal to a wide spectrum of gamers:Want to experience all the different gimmicks but afraid you'll get stuck? Don't worry, every world has a path of relatively easy puzzles to unlock the next world, so you have the option of moving forward if you're stuck or simply aren't vibing with a particular gimmick.Want a good challenge? Actually solving everything is HARD and will really force you to master the power of recursion. The hardest puzzles are roughly of a similar difficulty (maybe slightly easier) to the hardest in other popular puzzle games.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of my favourite puzzle games of all times. Now my #1, but in my top 5 for sure. What it excels at is visual communication. _childDocuments_.review: is a sokoban-type puzzle game where blocks can be entered and house puzzles within puzzles. The game is heavily inspired by  by juner.This game is an idea taken to its logical conclusion, with the idea being "blocks are also rooms that can be entered".If you've played Sokoban, you know what to expect. You need to push blocks onto specified marked squares, then go and stand your character on the goal square to win a level. The twist put on it, as previously mentioned, is that the blocks you push can sometimes be entered and house a puzzle within them.Perhaps a level requires two blocks to win, but theres only one block in the level. You can enter the block that exists however, and inside it you find the second block you need. You can extract it from this block and suddenly you have all the blocks you need to finish the level.This quickly get more complicated as you come across blocks that  the level you're currently playing, and exiting the level border makes you exit the level block inside the level you're in.Or maybe you try to enter a block as you enter the same block as you enter the same block as you enter the same block as you-Well, you get the picture. The game has paradoxes  however, and it will not let you forget that.This game is very elegant. It has a few clearly defined rules, and does a lot with them.It pushes its idea beyond what you expect as a player, which reminds me of .It's mildly challenging, nowhere near the hair-tearing difficulty that for example Baba is You can throw your way. Patrick's Parabox also knows when to stop, which is something I can respect in the current gaming landscape where things seem to be designed to grab ahold of you and do nothing but waste your time.There are of course some puzzles I did not like. Most of them were puzzles that didn't make use of the main gimmick at all, or in a way that was plain uninteresting. A few ideas were recycled several times, the small tweaks were not enough to make them interesting.The puzzles I didn't like were a clear minority though!My playtime as of this review is the time it took to do everything. I completed this game in two sittings.Might seem short, but if you like block-pushing games, you're doing yourself a disservice if you skip Patrick's Parabox.It's one of the best in the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Mind-bending puzzles, each stage has around 10 levels (including optional ones), and introduces a new mechanic each time. There is no time or move limit, the only goal is finishing the level (mostly placing the boxes in the squares).Just as you (kind of) figured out a certain mechanic near the end of a stage, your brain is then flipped upside down in the next one. This keeps it fresh and fun, IMO.Some level of willpower is advised, as it can be frustratingly difficult at times.
