_childDocuments_.review: This game is living in my mind rent free after I finished it. That’s the mark of a good game where you ponder questions after you’ve finished everything. Some questions like “Do androids dream of…” I’m very sure you’ve heard that before.But whatever dares to dream in the dark reaches of space, is scarcely imagined. For mortals to be drawn into a liminal trance outside the comfort of their blue sphere invite creatures from the infinite. One thing is true, there is a cosmic song of which all sing. Some dreamers know the secrets of that song. When the song is conducted, what lurks in the infinite bleeds into the gaps of dreamers and the Old Things assume dominance. Their thoughts are labyrinthine and surreal; their music cacophonic and impossible to escape. These dreamers turned wanderers become lost in a loop, a composition, a song, lost in a promise to be fulfilled. Wake up_Random ponderings aside (and this is a review), Signalis is a game that is lovingly steeped in inspiration from games of old. If you’re a fan of the older entries in the Resident Evil and Silent Hill franchises, you’ll be all too familiar with Signalis. It even has toggleable tank controls for you Resi purists out there. But I’m getting ahead of myself. How is the game? It’s beautiful and it’s horrifying in all the right ways, and it hits nostalgia while carving its own footprint in the space.In Signalis you play as an android mechanic, Elster, onboard a scout ship, the Penrose, searching for your human pilot, who is seemingly gone. The deeper you go into finding your partner, the more things go awry. I’ll leave the vagueness of the synopsis at that because solving the mysteries of this game are part of the charm. From opening moments, you know exactly what you’re in for. Cryptic messaging strewn throughout the opening to Raindrop Prelude by Chopin… you’ll be in for a wild ride throughout. Signalis is intentionally designed to emulate the claustrophobic hallways of Resident Evil, and the almost alien yet familiar surroundings of Silent Hill as you navigate from location to location, solving puzzles and fighting monsters all while telling a somber story to the tune of Chopin, Beethoven and Schubert.It nails atmosphere to a T. From authoritarian classrooms in a bleak dystopian off world, to a lonely spaceship that your character finds some solace in, to dark hallowed mines in holes where earth’s pores ought to suffice, the atmosphere and setting do not fail to tell its own story.The Protagonist, like young Leon Kennedy or Harry Mason, is put into a scenario where she has to adapt. You as the player learn more about who Elster is/was and what her quirks are, and why you continue to unlock the seals and enact the play… Sorry, again getting ahead of myself. The overall mystery behind everything is also something that I’ve spoken to people at length about. Remember, this game is living in my head rent free, so be warned it might do the same for you.Like your typical survival horror games of yore, you control your character with a bird’s eye view of each room you’re in. Your inventory space is limited, (there’s even an in-game explanation as to why your inventory slots are limited, much to manufactured frustrations later in the game) and your enemies are numerous. You don’t have enough resources for each of them. So each foe you’re met with requires you to use your wit and cunning to avoid or engage.This becomes a delicate dance. Resources are sparse and inventory space is purposefully small which requires careful planning to navigate through. Here is where my 1 gripe with the game lies. Having limited inventory punishes you for not knowing what’s ahead. The game rewards repeat playthroughs as you’ll slowly become familiar with repeat playthroughs but makes it very frustrating for newcomers looking to their first. As you continue to play, you’re hit with puzzles that initially feel like roadblocks, but they never overstay their welcome. Puzzles are short, sweet, and make you feel like a genius when you solve them. It’s the little things like these that makes playing Signalis enjoyable. Also I just want to highlight the fact that this game is a 2-person team. A 2-person labor of love. While yes there may be composers coming in to score, the direction this game takes is so lovingly done you’ll beg Rose-Engine to make another… On that noteArt direction in this game is superb. Its inspirations are varied. On the one hand, you have “anime wifu” androids. On the other hand the rest of the world is intentionally hard and oppressive, very much steeped in the designs that you’d find in authoritarian dentist office. The posters go the extra mile and breathe life into the world. You could probably print out every poster you find in this game because they’re that well done. The game has consistent art direction and that shines through every aspect of it.I have a friend who speaks German fluently and he would give me some insight when I finished my first playthrough on details I’ve missed. Language isn’t just thrown in for the sake of sounding cool, if you know the words you gain immense insight to a few things, so German speaking players will definitely enjoy.If the writing and the world building were a steak, I’d say they are well done. It took me a while grasp the a few of the homages, but the biggest inspiration is from The King in Yellow (if you read it, you’d be in for a treat). From writing to world building to sound design. Everything is done so purposefully. Even the music plays a purpose. Now I must admit something to you, my ear for the classical may not be as good as the average person’s, but I did enjoy the mood setting of each of the pieces picked for Signalis.1000 Eyes and Cicada Sirens do an amazing job of building a beautiful soundscape. Along with classical pieces from Beethoven, Schubert, and Chopin, (I’m sorry I’ve failed you, music teachers of my youth…) you’re in for a beautifully bittersweet mood where music absolutely sets a depressing and oppressive tone of the game.Aside from the music, the in-game sounds do a great job of setting atmosphere and of characterizing the world you live in. The screeches from the monsters to the gun sounds. To the static hum of the inventory, beeps of you mousing over different inventory slots, everything is just so sharp and austere. Even moments of respite in quiet save rooms are interrupted by a unique scream that is equally haunting and calming. Yes, the save rooms do scream and yes, it is the blood curdling scream of safety.I had rewritten this segment over and over again, but I opted to omit it since it contained spoilers. I have to agree with the overall sentiment of others: Don’t look up spoilers. This game is best enjoyed when you go in as blind as possible. So in the end what would I say about this? If you’ve a fan of old school horror games, Signalis is a no-brainer. If not for the anime android wifus, it’s the old school survival horror, it’s the setting, it’s the promise. So Wake up_

_childDocuments_.review: A really beautiful game, lovingly made. awesome one who loved the PS1 survival horror games of the late 90's this slots perfectly in with Resident Evil and Silent Hill, even with a dash of Metal gear solid. brought to tears and incredibly touched at the softer moments. the world-building is fantastic. _childDocuments_.review: It's impossible to sum this experience up in a review for me. I've only played through it once, received one ending before finding the rest, I don't normally mind doing that, because often enough the game has been out for ages, and I have it spoiled before i even touch it. That wasn't the case here, and I'm so glad that was the case. I want to touch on a few things before I go over the game as a whole. If you want to leave yourself completely raw on this, do so, buy it and play it, it will do its justice like it did to me.Horror: The game handles itself much like a proper horror game, few cheap scary things, Great enemy design with context which only makes them more terrifying when you realize what they actually are, amazing sound design and music kept me shivering and on edge pretty much the entire game, Scenery is fantastic and the graphical design works great with it. Story: A fantastic story with a great way of telling itself, many games like this have a boat load of videos telling you how the story is, and what certain things mean, and so does this game. But if you play it right, avoid spoilers, solve the puzzles yourself, you'll understand the story, and so much more.Puzzles: The puzzles are designed great, you find all the context you need and you do need to work for it. Found myself looking at things multiple times and being so pumped when I solved certain puzzles, it's a bit tedious to go back and forth all the time yes, but it's more realistic and it added to it for me.  There is one puzzle that stumped me, and it's honestly one of the only things i didn't like, the solution was right in front of me, I just assumed something was it and it wasn't, the only puzzle I needed any help on was that one.Combat: Maybe another thing that lends itself to the genre is the focus on combat, because there is little of it. The combat style is great, its difficult in a sense where you need to debate whether running is a better option, or if you can afford to spend the resources to make it safer. The boss battles are great and feature good mechanics and fantastic design.Artwork: The cut scenes and pictures, first person segments and character design, I love all of it. Perfectly erie and sci fi cool.I'm sure I'm missing some things I want to talk about, but if your reading this far, you should have or hopefully already have played it. This game created something that was so investing, so tense, so eerie, that I wrote this review about it, and I will be playing it again. Multiple times I found myself saying, "No I'm not going in there." Or something similar, many times I had to make sure I was alone in the rooms, and many times I felt for the characters, and sympathized with the story. It's very akin to dead space, which is a comparison I've been avoiding, because that's what I thought of when I saw this originally, and it is very similar. But I think this is completely different.This game is great, truly something worth playing, they killed it.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't normally review games. Much less, games that feature funny anime style protagonist. That being said, something about this game struct me in a way that few games have truly done so before. It's a strange phenomenon, especially considering that I don't usually play survival horror. I think this speaks volumes about what rose engine, a team of two people mind you, had managed to put together over their time working on this game.What got me to buy the game was a few friends who had become absolutely obsessed with the game talking about it in a voice chat one night. Curious, I looked up the game on Youtube and watched a brief analysis of the game. While I don't remember who created this analysis, I remember them saying something along the lines of, "I know this game looks like some weird anime game, trust me, I thought it too, but I am glad I gave the game a chance.". While I was still a bit hesitant, the game was relatively cheap  at the time, so I decided to take the plunge.While I'm not one to talk about game play or anything, as I'm quite bad at writing, I will say this: it's good. The combat felt decent and not too over the top, and I only had a few minor gripes with the whole "aiming" system. The six item limit also felt very limiting, and not exactly in a good way. Still, the game was more than playable. The puzzles, while definitely made me think, weren't over the top or crazy for a game of this type. Then there is the real kicker for this game, the story. This game will have you thinking about it for weeks/months after you've played it, almost constantly. Overall, I would highly, highly recommend you pick this game up. You'd be supporting the passion project of a lovely two person studio that clearly put their heart and soul into making this game. With an average first play through time of around 9-10 hours, you won't be stuck on this game for a very long time either, making it an enjoyable little experience. If you are a fan of silent hill, resident evil, or survival horror in general, this game pays a lot of homage to those titles so I've been told, and I believe you would enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: I think Signalis is a very good game, and most people will probably enjoy it more than I did.What Signalis has unambiguously going for it is its visual design and art direction, which is excellent across the board, its audio design, which is pretty solid, its soundtrack, which is a genuine delight, and its story, which is extremely compellingly presented all the way through and goes in some jolly interesting directions in the back half, and without which I would have dropped the game entirely. I found its gameplay to be distractingly derivative, though. The traversal/resource management elements will be achingly familiar to anyone who has had to make their way through the Spencer Mansion; the find the key for the door to get the key for the door to get the etc. loop is extremely reminiscent of the Project Zero games (especially the second one); and the monster designs and occasionally entire setpieces and dark world aesthetics and general tone and large chunks of the story are clearly inspired by Silent Hill 2 (among other SH entries, of course). If you have never played Silent Hill 2 or a Project Zero game but feel like you'd probably enjoy them (or you played Maiden of Black Water and thought "I bet I'd dig this if it wasn't so trash"), then you'll probably got a lot more out of this than I did. I know that sounds like a backhanded compliment, but I really don't mean it that way. Silent Hill 2 and Project Zero 2 are abandonware, and I would sincerely recommend this as just about the next best thing. I certainly found it a more engaging deliberately nostalgic horror experience than this year's 'Crow County', for instance. If you want something that scratches that itch and don't want to jump through the requisite hoops to play those games, you'll probably love this. I didn't love it, but I certainly liked it enough to finish it, and I think it's an extremely strong overall package. It just that the gameplay did almost nothing for me throughout the majority of the experience -- there's about 25% of this game that I would say I *loved* (there's a chunk in the middle I really liked and the final chapter is outstanding with an ending I thought was essentially perfect), and about 75% of the game that I'd say was just fine. It was never a bad game, though, and I have no doubt that I'll be jamming the soundtrack for the next few days.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't even know.I think everything before the  is great, fantastic even. there's some small issues I have, but I can live with them.However, after "that part" my enjoyment of the game has been thrown out the window. Since it's the last part of the game, the devs go all out, and man for a survival horror game that ♥♥♥♥ just isn't fun. Every room has like 10 enemies and you have to make 2x the trips in order to juggle all the ammo you're gonna waste with all the items you're gonna pick up. And since the rooms are all so close-quarters, and there's so many enemies, trying to actually engage in combat goes from clunky but fun to just pure frustration. Sucks.I don't even think I'm gonna finish the game, I'm having no fun anymore. I have better games to play at this point (like Tormented Souls).Edit: Thinking about it more, I just don't think the developers understood how a lot of the systems worked. Like, the reason I'm okay with RE1 having 6 inventory slots is because (as Chris) you only have 3 weapons. Along with that, stuff like knives and flashbangs don't take up an inventory slot. In Signalis you have like 6 weapons, all with their own ammo pool, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥' everything takes up an inventory slot. _childDocuments_.review: A game which has been making rounds as a very, very worthwhile title to play, so I heard. Initially, I was sceptical, owing to the fact I am personally unfamiliar and a bit uncomfortable with horror elements. However, once you give this game a real go, chances are you won’t put it down (like me). While it may appear simple at first,  has a surprising amount of depth and polish to it.And my highly personal recommendation, play it on “Survival”  “Classic” (these are the two difficulty parameters accessible in the Settings) on your first try. Yes, it  be tough, especially to those new to the genre, but is it so much more worth it in the end. I did a half-playthrough with beginner-friendly difficulty settings, and realised, heck, it’s not nearly as satisfying. I might as well go all in with this amazing gem. So, I restarted my playthrough and set in on the highest difficulty. As of writing this, I have yet to fully complete the game.  Maybe because I am a real rookie to this sort of game, but maximum difficulty is  hard. I loaded up an older save with slightly lower toughness and won my first playthrough with that.+ Very interesting plot line. The story is practically littered with all kinds of intriguing details (and clues, always keep a wary mind). I won’t say anything here as I do believe this is much better experienced first-hand. And the twist in the middle, oh, it fooled me for a few days. But here I am, back again in Hell, and loving every single moment of it.  The story is really stellar. I dare say even heart-wrenching, what with the one I got. It really does draw in the player with its intrigue and lore. The various endings at the end do take some effort to achieve, when aiming for the desired one. Do note, there does exist a secret ending, apparently. But I have no clue on how to activate it.+ Combat is straightforward and simple. It rewards patience and the occasional stint of recklessness. Resource management is key to surviving. Waste too many resources needlessly early on, and you’ll be struggling in the later chapters. With the combat accessibility, i.e. difficulty, set to “Survival”, dying is very easy so knowing when to temper bravado with caution (and vice versa) is necessary.   Hoard 12 mm ammo, i.e. the one used for the revolver.+ The artwork is gorgeous. Pixel graphics for that nice retro feel, coupled with macabre horror and sci-fi anime. Unless you’re vehemently against any one of these three (technically four) styles, it’s hard not to be immersed in the art.+ The music and audio ties in very well with the above, establishing the mood throughout. The creepy background music, echoing footsteps on metal girders, slight static-y emergency announcements left on repeat, etc. But there are also calm and tranquil sounds as well, most commonly found in safe rooms. It really does set in the feeling of respite when you hear the dulcet, gentle notes of a piano just as you stumble into a particular haven after running for your life.+/- The limited inventory management might peeve some. You may only carry a maximum of  items at any one time. Additionally, ammunition has a stack limit and you cannot carry more than one stack of a type of ammo. With the latest update, version 1.2 “Krähe”, the developers added the option, which is turned on by default, to use the new “Revised” inventory capacity, i.e. certain items do not consume Elster’s already highly limited inventory. +/- As an objective disclaimer. There is “yuri” content. But if something like that bothers you, especially in today’s day and age, I am sorely disappointed at your lack of tolerance.-  It ended... That's it, my only real gripe with SIGNALIS. Oh, how I wish there was more... If there was an expansion, or a second game in the same universe, adding more story and content, I'd very likely acquire it in a heartbeat.This is definitely a title worth experiencing. Both for its well-conceived story and immersive ambience. It has a very good blend of horror, survival, and exploration.

_childDocuments_.review: The game equivalent of a brainworm. Immediately upon finishing it I could tell this one was special, but it´s been a while since a game has stayed in my mind to quite this extent days after being done with it.Signalis is, at its core, a very straightforward (albeit excellent) survival horror game: limited inventory slots, oppressing atmosphere, awesome object-based puzzles and bullets that could be considered scarcer than PS5 stock upon launch. The cassette era sci-fi/ authoritarian government aesthetic is its distinguishing element; red and black hues melt and combine to depict this nightmarish futuristic world (galaxy?) where nothing is as it seems. The setup is also quite simple: you play as an Elster unit, a Replika, looking for your Gestalt (human) companion in a mining facility. The use of these terms make it clear right out of the bat that one of its main sources of inspiration is the NieR series, where both terms are used to describe very similar concepts. However, aside from the fact that you play as a hot robot lady, the ties might not be immediatly apparent upon boot. NieR was never a horror oriented game, though it certainly never shies away from disturbing topics, but once you get to the cutscenes and the subject matters discussed, the parallels are immediately obvious. I´m not going to go in depth as to what exactly I´m talking about on the off chance that someone is reading this, but what I´m saying is that this game is basically NieR meets Silent Hill 2, and it´s ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awesome. Sporting some of the best gameplay and design elements in the whole genre and a story that will leave you pondering the implications of the things presented here for days on end, Signalis is an easy instant recommendation if you love sci-fi, philosophy, and ambitious storytelling that leaves a lot up to your own interpretation. Or if you love videogames in general. Do not skip this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible survival horror that somehow feels retro and incredibly modern at the same time.The mechanics are very old school Resident Evil. You have a tiny inventory that you juggle with the magic safe room box, limited ammo, enemies revive if you don't burn them, lots of "solve this logic puzzle to rewire the fuse box" type stuff. Classic 90s/early 2000s survival horror.The plot and aesthetic is a masterfully done homage to Silent Hill 2 with a little Nier: Automata thrown in. It's incredibly well done, taking it's source material and presenting them in a way that is instantly recognizable while also being distinctly it's own thing. If you love horror but have never played a survival horror game from the PSX/PS2 era, you should definitely give it a try but get ready to get used to some pretty obtuse game mechanics.If you grew up with or love old school survival horror, this is a must have.

_childDocuments_.review: Who would have thought at the end of the year amongst a litany of live service and micro-transaction filled games that I'd completely by chance run into one of the best games I've ever played!  Signalis is now one of my top 5 games and it's just these two developers first game!  There's so much I like in this game that it's almost like the developers decided to make a game just for me.  I love Resident Evil and Ghost in the Shell, so combining those two with Silent Hill and another influence I won't spoil results in a game that is completely tailored to what I like whilst having a unique atmosphere and setting that I haven't really experienced before in survival horror.  On top of that, the gameplay is one of the best modern takes on classic Resident Evil that I've played.  Combining that with psychological horror and a very good and emotionally impactful story makes this even more unique in a genre full of B-movie style games (which I also love by the way)!  The music is also perfect and really captures the struggles Elster goes through, shout-out to the new rendition of Chopin's Raindrop Prelude titled The Promise!I think that Signalis is a masterpiece of survival horror and of a game as well.  I haven't played a game with gameplay and a story this good in a long time.  I have no criticisms and definitely recommend that anyone interested give it a shot.  It's nice knowing that there are developers out there still making games that they are passionate about and I'll be eagerly awaiting whatever they decide to do next!  There have been a few really great games released this year, but none of them were as impactful or are going to stick with me like this game will.  GOTY (2022)!!!

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best game of it's genre ever created. The puzzles are the perfect difficulty and I occasionally felt "stuck" but never felt the need to look anything up (except for only one part.) Each puzzle is unique and never repetitive feeling, and are very satisfying to figure out. They feel realistic rather than "video game puzzle-esque." The combat is fun and satisfying and there is the perfect amount of items and ammo/weapons to keep you feeling like you can't waste anything, but its also okay if you do. The various weapon types are a lot of fun to use and all have their specific strengths. Even with the gameplay being a blast and essentially perfect to me, it's not even the best part of the game. The story is, if you can even call it that. I have never felt so immersed in trying to piece together all the possible lore a single player game as to offer in my whole life. Also, I don't even want to know who hurt the creators of this game for them to feel such an inspiration to create such a hauntingly beautiful setting, world, characters, and story. It's the most thought provoking game ever. It also never feels boring or like certain parts are dragging on, and it rewards progression in very satisfying ways. Everything is the perfect difficulty where you can chill out while you play it and be immersed in the story, while having plenty of challenging areas too. Not to mention the music choice is just chef's kiss and originally how I actually found this game (from a youtube comment on Franz Schubert's Serenade.) Overall this is a 10/10 game, and one of the few games I can't really thing of a single thing I could do better in it's creation.Side note: Use the expanded inventory option, because there is not much inventory space as is and it doesn't change much besides making you backtrack more if you decide not to use it.

_childDocuments_.review: (See the main game website for content warnings)Whether you are someone like me who has never played a survival horror game, or are a veteran player, the descent into the horrors, tragedy, beauty of Signalis (Despite it's short play time of 6-14 hours on your first one) will leave still pondering it's mystery, story, and messages.   The general story that I can give without going into spoiler territory is that you are a Repika robot who finds herself in a strange facility looking for someone while finding clues that not all is as it seems or is obvious - as you progress further, fighting and dodging horrific shrieking enemies, you start to realize how much you don't know regarding the madness of the facility. Signalis is a game where the answer to this madness (Figuratively and literally) is your interpretation, and I think that's going to keep interest in this indie horror game for many months, if not years, to come. It's one of those games that was cleverly designed to keep you analyzing, thinking, and pondering it long after you've put down the control - much like Dark Souls and Knights of the Old Republic 2 were for me.  Even though I am taking a break from playing right now, already I'm considering doing another run on survival to see what secrets I might have missed.Signalis has a nice pixel-anime inspired style, which I think helps better convey emotion through the still images of some "near-still-image" cutscenes and the movement of the in-game play cutscenes.   and remixes a lot of elements from other horror titles such as RE and silent hill, encouraging the player to think carefully how to approach reviving enemies and though bending puzzles.If I had to critique this game for a few things, One is that it feels pretty short if you only plan on doing one play through AND you get the hang of how to out maneuver enemies you may start to realize sometimes an enemy will do a melee attack but not strike you though you still get damage.  However, as for the former, I would rather have a short game made well rather than a long game or a series made poorly.  And that craving to know more about the game has encouraged me to find some cool lore videos and even check out some mods in development for the game.  As for the latter, I am sure it will be patched in and I wouldn't consider it to be too detrimental (I would say it's only happened 3 times on my run, and it might be possible that some enemies may have had a charge attack).The achievements aren't marked as completed until you've exited the game.  If you are struggling or having any sort of trouble, the steam guides has some good tips and tricks on how to play.  Signalis is what I consider to be my first Survival horror and it has gotten me interested in other games within this genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing this was a miserable experience and I do not recommend it, however, there are sequences within this that are so striking that I do recommend experiencing some of it, as long as players understand what they're getting into. Initially, like many players, if the achievement proportions are to be believed, I decided to abandon the game in the first chapter, but then restarted and persevered to the end. In retrospect I should have stopped after the credits rolled the first time (yes, as parodied in Frog Detective: Corruption in Cowboy Country, the game has a false ending). After this point there is nothing new, only iterations on what has come before. The limited inventory is fine, but it stretches each level into a slog going to and from the storage crate as the player is slowly shown the sequence of what is needed where, which is repeated several times. The game is very poor at giving feedback to the player - bosses are either alive or dead, puzzles are either solved or unsolved - there is rarely a hint that what the player is doing is working, which inevitably means looking at the forums to understand what is expected. While rushing between the box and some goal, the player is harassed by enemies, which increase in frequency as the game continues. It's typical survival horror fare - what is at first unsettling simply becomes annoying. In some areas there is no map, which means remembering, which the game seeks to undermine by mixing up directions between areas. The final boss includes mild bullet hell elements, and dying to this is extremely tedious as the death/load sequence takes a very long time. The character faces, when these are shown in cut scenes, are all drawn in an anime style, which makes the already questionable writing impossible to take seriously. The ending, at least the one I saw, heavily implied the presence of that most beloved device of young writers, which An Occurance at Owl Creek Bridge put to rest 130 years ago.   In spite of all this, the sound and text design are masterful, with the use of Beethoven, numbers stations and deeply unsettling but sparing music. The mixture of languages and typography is very effective, conjuring up Barbara Kruger, Jenny Holzer and Peter Saville's early album covers. Parts of the game are like being inside a Laibach video. Böcklin's Isle of the Dead features heavily, in several forms. The radio feedback sequence, the first time it is encountered, is incredible, but ends up overused, and by the end becomes tiresome as other enemies that the player cannot see are mixed in. I'm glad I played (parts of) it, but I'm especially glad it's over.

_childDocuments_.review: A very aesthetic sci-fi survival horror.The first thing that grabs your attention in this game is the aesthetics and atmosphere. Despite the retro horror styling, it doesn't feel outdated, and thanks to the stylization, it looks stunning.The music deserves a special mention, clearly inspired by the Silent Hill series. There are many melancholic tracks, as well as ones that make you feel uncomfortable. The soundtrack includes both industrial sounds and tense ambient pieces.The game has a very interesting and well-developed world. Throughout the game, you constantly find notes, posters, and other items that reveal the lore, and exploring them is captivating.While the plot contains intriguing ideas, it's incredibly convoluted and presented in a very complex way. It's almost impossible to fully understand what happened during the first playthrough, and you'll likely end up watching thematic YouTube videos to figure it all out. My only issue with the story is that some key points lack clear interpretation or in-game explanation, leaving certain ideas not fully explored.In terms of gameplay, it's a classic Resident Evil style with location exploration, key collection, and puzzle-solving. The main difference in the combat system is that to deal more damage to enemies, you need to hold the aim on them for a longer time, which creates quite tense situations.The first half of the game is interesting and has a moderate pace. However, starting in the second half, you enter a location where your map is taken away, and you have to collect six keys to open a door, which feels drawn-out and dull. First, you find many items, but the inventory slots are limited, meaning you'll have to frequently return to the save room after exploring each room. Second, the lack of a map in this part doesn't add challenge, it just confuses you, making you run through already cleared areas and wasting time.One of my favorite things in this game is the puzzles. There are plenty of them, they're diverse and fun to solve. Often, to solve a puzzle, I had to write something down or take a screenshot, and solving them gave me great satisfaction.In fact, all the game's shortcomings fade in the light of its polished gameplay and aesthetics. Despite some less successful segments and the difficult plot, I still recommend Signalis. Of all the indie games using the classic survival horror formula, this might be the best one, so I highly recommend not missing it.

_childDocuments_.review: Signalis is a beautiful mess.On one hand, you have a heavily anime inspired presentation with intriguing imagery and set against a dark and mysterious sci-fi/horror setting. On the other hand, you have the abysmal and frustrating gameplay that quickly becomes a chore and makes the game unplayable.The poor experience is evident by the Das Ende achievement which is the halfway point of the game, and only about 1/3 of players have it. I can't fathom how at the time of this review the game has a 95% recommended rating, and far less than half of the players can even stomach the game long enough to get halfway through the game. It sadly doesn't deserve a recommendation.I understand why people may feel that way initially.The game's presentation in the early parts of the game make it feel like an art house film. I immediately felt I needed to buy and experience this game myself before watching any more gameplay. I understand why people would WANT to recommend this game.However the gameplay is horrendous. There are far too many frustrating and poor game design choices that conflict and make the game a true nightmare to play. I am referring to:1) Extremely limited inventory space and numerous key items appearing in each chapter of the game.2) Excessive backtracking caused by the poor layout of the game and due to the limited inventory space.3) Respawning enemies, compounded by point 1 and 2.4) Very tight hallways and rooms that prevent routing around enemies and exhausting limited ammo.5) Entering a room and being hit by an enemy before you have a chance to move.6) Boss fights that act as bullet sponges, but with puzzle elements that force several attempts and diminish the atmosphere of the game.One or two of any of these choices alone would be fine, however when combined, you get a defeating and miserable experience. I simply don't wish to play this game any further, much like nearly 2/3 of the other players.Having said all of that, I would love to see more from the game developers.I'm hoping that if others voice their opinions on the dismal game design rather than play 10 minutes, call it amazing, and uninstall, that the developers can hear this criticism and make their next project truly shine. Otherwise, I feel that the duo who created Signalis are far better off producing short films, movies, and non-interactive media.Beautiful vision, and a tragically poor execution.

_childDocuments_.review: Signalis proves again that having strong vision from your soul can lead you into greatness. This game is marvel achievement from every aspect imaginable. _childDocuments_.review: A beautiful game. A must play for any lover of artistically inspiring games. It reminds me a lot of Evangelion, both in visuals and the cryptic storytelling. There's also the clear influence of Silent Hill 2 and early Resident Evil games in the gameplay, but the user experience is vastly smoother than these reference points -the mechanics are inspired by retro horror, but redesigned beautifully to reduce the clunkiness and frustrating elements of those older games. I say it's less frustrating - but that doesn't mean it's less challenging! The puzzles in particular can be fiendish at times, but with enough careful investigation you can work them out. If you're totally stumped you can always google a walkthrough too, depending on your level of purism. Without giving any spoilers, there are some extremely hard to find secrets in this game too. I don't have the patience to go back and hunt them all for myself, but it's cool to know there are extra layers woven into a game that will reward extremely dedicated players. As for me, I'm mostly here for the atmosphere, story and aesthetics - and Signalis delivers on all of these!

_childDocuments_.review: Signalis is an excellent survival horror game. But that statement alone only begins to scratch the surface of what Signalis is. It's a story about technology, memory, identity, oppression, isolation, and love. It's also a dream more vivid than reality, a mystery inside its own solution, an impossible object brought into the real world. But above all else, Signalis is an experience. One that will get inside your head and stay with you for a long time.
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: Signalis is one of the best pieces of survival-horror i have ever experienced and is honestly a contender to be my favourite. of course, with its inspiration from RE and Silent Hill, it borrows a lot of their mechanics and fit it in with their own with gimmicks. the puzzles were challenging, but nothing unsolvable. with the foundation of its gameplay heavily built upon the genre's predecessors, Signalis doesn't need to do much but focus on its presentation, which it excels in beautifully. story, cutscenes, level, enemy and sound design, all these amalgamate to form a dark cryptic sci-fi cyberpunk aesthetic. though, as much as i praise and love the idea of media leaving questions for the player to answer for themselves, in my opinion Signalis leaves some of the details too vague, leaving me slightly confused at one point. thankfully, i was able to grasp the overarching narrative despite all the brain crunch. to conclude, i recommend Signalis to any survival-horror game fan. hell, even if you've never played a horror game id recommend this. it managed to keep me engaged for its 10 hours of playtime and i haven't been able to get it off my mind for the past week. definitely my favourite indie this year

_childDocuments_.review: This game is the perfect matchup between old survival horror and new innovative survival horror, it brings back a lot of nostalgic feelings for old school silent hill and resident evil fans while also introducing new and challenging ways to put the horror in survival horror, all that while having one of the most intriguing asthetics i've seen in any game, a mixture of sprite-based voxel, both in first-person and top down third-person, with influences and references to many beloved cyberpunk media such as (but not limited to): blade runner, Akira and (most obvious  ) Ghost in the shell. The OST is such an well crafted and implemented fusion between soothing but sometimes eerie synth and classical music with great hits made by Chopin and Tchaikovsky, all sounds effects (with the exception of the one that plays when you use items and sounds just like the among us task completion sound) are all also another big contributor to this amazing atmosphere and experience. This Entire ride is done with a intriguing and confusing (in a good way) story where pretty much everything is symbolic of something and you are never sure what's real or what's meant to mean something else, either way the game has 3 endings and 1 secret ending, but regardless which one you do it's the same experience filled with notes and posters that do the world building, puzzles that try to connect some semblance of canon lore, and are fun and a little challenging, atleast the first time you do them, if you are here just for the story you will have a day field with very ambiguous texts and "what does that mean" moments, but if you are here for the gameplay and like the aspects I have already mentioned then this is going to feel like a straight line story, you are looking for person X, you keep going until you find person X, the end, tho I find it difficult for someone to play and not get atleast curious about what does it all mean as the art style and dialogue really involves the player in the universe. The raw Survival in survival horror of this game is generally an easy game, combat is not great ,but not at all bad and tries to be different than classics like resident evil's combat (and it succeeds in my opinion), with the only bad thing in the mechanical part of the gameplay being the inventory, you have A LOT of key items, 6 weapons, each with its own ammunition and one having 2 types of ammunition, 3 different types of medications and 5 types of equipables for the taser slot, and all that doesn't stack very high in you inventory, all the while you have 6 FRICKING SLOTS TO HOLD ALL THAT, I know that the slot size has lore significance and the developer has added a casual difficulty as well as a survival one that address 2 issues, the game being too easy overall (for me atleast) and the game being too difficult (because of the aforementioned 6 slot inventory) so the survival gameplay can be tailored to fix whichever bothers you more, in general you could probably finish the game with the starting gun and without killing most enemies (that would be easy for veteran Resident Evil players) as the enemies are easy to pass by and dodge.But if combat is not your cup of tea the game has lots of hidden secrets, right at the beginning you get the ability to use a radio and it feels like almost every room in the game might have a hidden message in one of the frequencies that you can explore with your radio, you also have optional but cool interactions with the few NPCs in the game that haven't turned into gorefest monsters . LONG LONG story short this game was THE BEST survival horror experience i've had since forever, the ambiguous and mysterious endings, cutscenes and notes really kept me involved in this story to the point of getting all endings and achievements (tho I wish it had more of them) and would very much recommend this game to anyone that remotely likes any of the qualities i've mentioned as each and everyone of them this game has in troves and is enough to hook you into atleast trying it. Will be on the look out for this studio's next project and wouldn't mind more content in the same vein, or even universe, as signalis.

_childDocuments_.review: SIGNALIS is a genuine masterpiece. It is a game that made me re-evaluate what a 10/10 means. Its storytelling, music, gameplay, and design all lend themselves to the constant and persistent feeling that what you are playing is something TRULY special. How many times would you crawl through hell to keep a promise? How far would you push yourself for love?It's hard to describe more of the game without spoiling too much. If you find yourself struggling to put all the pieces together, please know that SIGNALIS is a game that will only give as much as you take from it. Don't stress too much trying to piece together all of the intentionally obscure parts of the game. Rather, let yourself be absorbed into the story and the world; how and what the game makes you feel is far more important for how the game achieves in telling its narrative.I hope that anyone trying SIGNALIS will walk away from it as profoundly impacted as I was.What a wonderful experience.

_childDocuments_.review: First time a video game has made me cry. Multiple times. This is the kind of story that's going to leave you thinking, questioning, mourning for a long time after. _childDocuments_.review: i wish tall woman holding shotgun would visit me in my bathtubThis game deserves all the love it gets and even more. It's been stuck in my heart since I played it a couple weeks ago.I only have two negative things to say about the game out of the way before I get to gushing about it instead. One is that your inventory size is 6. Sometimes that gives the game the backtracking and inventory choice tension that is a staple of the genre, but sometimes it's excessive and it ends up meaning you only take one weapon with you at any time and you're leaving a lot of items unused in the storage box. The other is this game has multiple endings and which ending you get is mostly down to how fast you're going and how aggressive you are. It's not clear and can leave you with an ending that doesn't seem like it finishes off the story at all. The endings go with each other but considering you basically need a guide to figure out how to get them all on 3 entirely different playthroughs I feel like something should have changed here. Okay we're done with the griping now on to the LOVE.This game executes top down survival horror perfectly! It plays like an old school Resident Evil game but without the horrible camera and controls. Things still feel slow and tense; for most of your weapons you can not line up shots instantly, it takes a short amount of time and forces you to make decisions on what you're doing. But you also feel completely capable of taking down enemies or sneaking past them. Your resources are limited and you'll feel the scarcity but you will make it with that tense feeling of trying to both conserve and prepare for the unknown that you're walking into. The puzzles are good and always feel immersive to the world. And the world itself is haunting. This game doesn't do jumpscares and honestly isn't very scary in that sense (I may be biased on this though, I'm not afraid of much). What it is is disturbing. The scenario you'll find yourself is already a bit disturbing but it's the actual world left from before you start that will have the most effect. I'd call this game "atmospheric" but even that isn't sufficient to describe it, which I'll explain below. Signalis is a mood on several levels. It's also going to be a game that you are not going to fully understand in a concrete way, it's very open to interpretation.This game will resonate with you more if you're LGBT. You will still enjoy the game if you aren't, you will still understand on a concrete and metaphorical level most of this game, but you might not fully "get it". A lot of the themes and moods in this game heavily evoke experiences from being LGBT, and it's not all just around the tagline of a gay android searching for her partner. It's done in a way that's not in your face, so I think anybody can enjoy it, but the entire plot is predicated on gay love, not the fluffy "yuri anime" type of gay love but the type of existential, merging of souls, alone in the universe queerness that comes from a set of experiences and state of being.It's as beautiful as it is disturbing, and if the wavelength of melancholia and love this game has resonates with you as much as it does me I think you'll feel the same way.

_childDocuments_.review: Signalis is beautiful and an enjoyable experience, but so much of the game hinges on it's plot and unfortunately it's plot turns out to be extremely disappointing. I understand why so many people want to analyze it and believe that it is brilliant and connected, but if you take a step back, this game is clearly a Five Night's at Freddy's scenario in plot. It is incredibly contradictory, so much so you can't even begin to analyze the game because the chain of events is wholly incomprehensible and defies basic reasoning. It seems that the developers wrote out separate parts of the story/game without having a way to connect them, and, rather than go through the immense amount of work it would take to rebuild most of the game to have a coherent plot, they simply released it as is. I think a lot of why that happened has to do with working within the confines of the demo while wanting to have a plot that would contradict it. Also, to you dream theory people. I understand that this does make the plot almost coherent, but do you realise that in order to do that, you had to make the plot of 95% of the game completely fictitious? It's no coincidence that the by far most plausible theory is one where the vast majority of story we are fed in the game is to be ignored and taken to be fake.

_childDocuments_.review: I looked at this game several times before playing it; it always piqued my interest. I eventually folded and bought it for full price:Entirely worth it!This game is incredibly well written with phenomenal music and enticing graphics. I don't usually enjoy survival horror games like this, but boy did this game surpass all of my expectations. The whole world built is fascinating in its own right as well. It's one of those games where you genuinely want to collect and read all of the lore and collectibles! Every detail clears the view of what is going on, gives some background, opens more questions, alludes to challenges you may face, and is just all around interesting.The game's story and ending, with going into as little detail as I can, has left me at a loss of words. It hits this unique place where it is up to the viewer to interpret it and have them fill in the vague areas with their own imagination and intuition, but it is not so loose as to lose all meaning and become trite by itself. I feel satisfied with it, but the taste of its narrative still stirs in my mouth, so to speak. The gameplay is a similar story. It isn't anything overly complex, or unique at face value, but it constantly changes and keeps the player engaged while not overwhelming them; It is clever and fun. I felt in danger but with an idea of how to survive and progress. This constant grit, combined with plenty of puzzle logic, makes the game very hard to put down. Solving puzzles was difficult, but not so hard as to detract from the satisfaction of solving them. Combat was intuitive, and as I played, I naturally figured out the general strategy and skill of it. However, it always kept me on the back foot, ensuring that I never felt too comfortable roaming through the rooms of the game. I cannot recommend this game enough. It is clever and emotional. One of the best games I have played in years. A single play-through doesn't take so long that you lose interest, but I firmly believe it is a game worth playing through multiple times; I certainly will play this time and again.A strong thank you to all the developers and the bioresonant minds of Barbara Wittmann and Yuri Stern

_childDocuments_.review: For me, Signalis squeaks by to a thumbs-up mainly on the strength of its obtuse, thought-provoking, and surprisingly personal story. That story only starts to arrange itself in the game's final hours, though, and I found it a bit tough going until then. Still, I've spent the days since finishing it consuming meta-media around it--it's the type of game that inspires hours-long takes on youtube, many of them probably pretty bad--and when something sticks with you like that, it's a good feeling.But yeah--I think this game has problems. Frustratingly, some seem to be by design. It eagerly lifts a lot of mechanics straight from retro Resident Evil games. This sounds cool in concept, but, a lot of times, it is not. Most egregious is the punishingly limited inventory system. I would estimate that I spent a full 20% of my playtime just running back and forth between safe rooms, juggling tools, key cards, knickknacks, any of four types of healing items that function the same but don't stack with each other, or ammo for one of the six weapons I'm not carrying (and never the one I am). The game does do a good job of recreating that oppressive, old-school RE feeling of always being desperate for resources, but here, I feel like more of that is just the protagonist failing to carry a backpack.It took a long time for me to warm to the aesthetics, too. This is a game about sad, blood-soaked anime robot girls in space. I think the story does end strong, but it remains very abstract and confusing for a very long time, and for most of the game I just felt like I was getting assaulted with images from a middle-school goth weeb's deviantart page, overlaid with flashes of random but cool-sounding flavor text like "ACHTUNG, ACHTUNG" or "PERHAPS THIS IS HELL" or the Chinese characters for DEATH and MEMORY. Lots of peoples' faces sloughing off and "YOU SHOULDN'T HAVE COME HERE"s, all in black and red. The options menu has a quote from HP Lovecraft. It all felt simultaneously pretentious and juvenile. It doesn't help that the superficial plot, as it first presents itself, manifests as a boilerplate zombie outbreak story. Again, I do feel that the game earns it in the end, but I also think it takes a bit too long to get there.So yeah--if those vibes don't immediately turn you off, and if you are really hungry for a throwback to old-school RE and Silent Hill, this could be worth a play. I don't think it lives up to all the sleeper horror GOTY hype, though. More than anything, it just makes me want to go back and play some of the classic RE entries I missed.

UI and save room references to silent hill (and an entire area, lol), the game itself feeling incredibly resident evil moreso than any other survival horror game, and a narrative that is deeply inspired and almost contextualized by the king in yellow, the festival, and an inhabitant of carcosa. the game wears this on it's sleeve though, and never to me felt like it was just ripping ♥♥♥♥ off, it's very clearly a deep passion project by the developers and it delivers a very unique experience that feels distinct from the works that inspired it. the narrative is vague but generates a sort of intrigue i've hardly experienced in anything else, and piecing together your interpretation of the events that transpire is just as much part of the experience as making your way through the game _childDocuments_.review: SIGNALIS is undeniably a labor of love, it's felt in every aspect and layer of the game.Gameplay wise it's an old school Resident Evil 1-3 survival horror with limited resources and inventory space where combat has to be supplemented with stealth, avoidance and route planning. If you're familiar with survival horror gameplay quirks and tropes I very much recommend playing on the hardest difficulty (yes, even for the first playthrough) to keep the tension up. The game never asks you to choose the difficulty, you have to set it yourself in the gameplay options, otherwise it defaults to normal. As one might expect there's a lot of key items to look for, items to combine and a decent amount of puzzles. Some puzzles are easier than others but many of them have a bit of an edge and might require you to activate all three of your brain cells at the same time but they never seem unfair or illogical and it feels good to solve them. While gameplay is smooth and satisfying the aesthetics of SIGNALIS is where the game truly shines. Story wise the game is very surreal and you need to be able to accept that many things will be unclear or unanswered but if you read the text documents you find, pay attention and overall absorb the visual and textual world building you'll be able to piece togeher a lot of it. Visuals are a mix of pixel art and low-poly 3D. Good art direction trumps graphical fidelity imo and SIGNALIS pulls off a superb, "thick", oppressive atmosphere with its retro art style dotted with occasional bits of reprieve via relaxing music and calm moments. Outside of combat SIGNALIS is best described as serene horror because it presses on your mind via emotion, tension and a strong sense of being inside the game world much more so than physical scares. Character design leans softly into anime but don't be put off if you don't like anime. It's very low key and free of the stereotypical garishness. Reminds me of a more subdued Ghost in the Shell visual style. Elster is pretty Motoko-like. Very serious, doesn't speak much, introverted like a black hole but with a hidden passion deep within. Similarly to GiTS this game also asks questions about the fundamentals of humanity (among other things).One thing that stands out is how tactile the game feels. Various soft clicks, hums, buzzes, crackling and other sounds accompany your interactions with buttons, handles, electronic devices, your inventory, etc. giving you a sense of "touching" things. The act of opening a safe where you push the individual buttons, turn the handle, see the door open and then lean forward to look inside feels very satisfying for something so mundane. There's more to talk about like the game's multi-lingual nature which gives it a unique flavor, use of radio and sounds/music, indirect world building and story telling but it's a lot and best discovered on your own. Whatever modest budget this game had has been used for maximum effect and in all the right places.The game has surprisingly few bugs, it's a complete experience that you can buy at release and it just works start to finish which is super rare. Personally I had no bug related problems but there have been a few complaints from others so I can't guarantee perfection. Some criticism:- You can choose alternative control schemes for both controllers and keyboard but there's no key rebinding. - When two or more enemies are close to each other your weapon might not lock on to your prefered target and things can get finnicky. - Text prompts can make object interaction during combat more punishing than it needs to be. It's best to set text speed to high or instant to mitigate the problem.

_childDocuments_.review: SIGNALIS is a masterful blend of psychological, cosmic, and survival horror. When I finished it; I was choked up, close to shedding a tear, and my brain was absolutely scrambled from all of the intricate story details now laid out in my mind. After I finished it, my head hurt from putting together the aforementioned insane amount of details the game's story presents over the course of a playthrough. Details I'm probably gonna be coming to realizations about for quite a while still. And the story is just one aspect of it all. _childDocuments_.review: Beware the Rule of 6. Signalis is an homage to old-school horror games, but it's wonderful atmosphere and generally strong puzzles have a fatal flaw--the Rule of 6. Like the games it gets its inspiration from, Signalis has a restrictive inventory system. But it takes that idea way too far.The intention is to force players to make difficult decisions about what to carry, so that you'll never feel truly safe. It's a fine idea, but it's taken to an extreme here. You have so many fiddly little items to pick up, and the tiniest key takes up the same space as a weapon. And to solve the game's many puzzles, you need to ferry tons of these little items around. It gets old. The clinching factor is that the game simply isn't very tense--combat is simple and easy. Eventually, I realized that I was just juking and dodging around enemies. It was silly and tedious, and that where I decided to call it quits. Signalis is really a puzzle game with a horror game's shell wrapped around it. Unfortunately, the two elements never gelled for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Short version, this is one of the best survival horrors that I have played. It's scary not because of jumpscare, but because the atmosphere and the sense of dread from start to finish were amazing. In the end, it gave me almost an existential crisis that you would usually get from reading Lovecraft stuff. Still, it has negative in term of how 90% of the story is referential from other medium (SH2 is a must play to understand the context) and how you probably need to do forum reading to understand the story.I think it's a love letter to survival horror and I suggest people try Silent Hill 2 (presumably before trying out this game) to get the full experience. They managed to draw a lot of inspiration there, like the red letter saving and narrative structure. It would probably be easier to digest the plot once you know how Silent Hill 2 delivers its story.Anyway, back to the game. You play as a robot trying to find your love in this weird adventure that spans across different places, with living on a communist regime in the background. The world-building was amazing and the text never felt too boring to read because they made it short.  puzzles were very clever and I got to learn some new things IRL (looking at your butterfly puzzle). The story is gonna throw you off on your first playthroughs but multiple playthroughs, watching the endings, and maybe some forum reading might be able to solidify what is going on.Now onto the negative and honestly some of them are nitpicks:-I hate how the 6 inventory system makes the second half of the game a chore, especially when you introduce tools that are mandatory to progress certain rooms but took an inventory space. The number of weapons and ammo types also made it feel like the 6 inventory system is there to make the playtime longer, instead of providing a smart challenge.- The way you get the normal endings are so arbitrary.Attaching how you get an ending based on playtime is one. If you play badly (get hit often, die often, kill all enemies, and finish longer), the game rewards you with an ending that has a better conclusion to the story. Meanwhile, if you play better (die less, dodge enemies, finish faster, interact with NPC), you are probably going to get a "bad ending" of the game.I get it, Silent Hill 2 had a similar ending mechanic where it judges you based on your actions. However, those that determine the ending are something that YOU HAVE CONTROL and most of the time require you to do something outside the beaten path. Like how you get the suicide ending if you stay near low health most of the time, or how you get the hooker ending if you spend a lot more time with her. The game does have one secret ending that you can do by doing something very different which ended with a satisfying conclusion. But unless you are invested in the story, you might just drop the game after you got that bad ending because you play well.Finally, one aspect I wanted to talk about is how a lot of the things that are referenced in the game require a lot of outside of the game real life knowledge. So let me give you an example, one of the paintings that are featured in the game is Isle of the Dead, which is a painting about something unnerving or isolation (I'm not an art historian, sorry if this analysis is shallow). This painting would be flashed all over the game and as someone who doesn't grow up with these kinds of knowledge, the meaning of these flashes was none. I don't know if this is a bad thing or not, but I believe relying too much on knowledge outside the game is just something that you shouldn't do. Especially if it's going to impact how one would understand the whole theme. Inspired by one work is great, but when your player needs to know what the heck the game is referencing to understand the whole theme, it feels like the game regards itself as better than what they are. Because only high "intellectuals" can understand this. The closest analogy I could give is like playing a movie tie-in game, where the plot continues after the movie.The biggest offender is the book that frequently appears in the game, the book is called "The King in Yellow" which is an actual old horror book. Spoiler territory, so skip this paragraph if you don't want to get spoiled much.The books appears many times and for someone who played the game twice without knowing anything about the book, I don't really get the allegory the game wants me to get. You start the game by opening the book and closing it. So maybe the game story is like a book? Yes and no? Well, what if I tell you a little bit of context about the book, it's a book about a play that makes people crazy. Add the fact that a plot relevant character read that book when they were a child, suddenly the game's story opens up allowing for multiple interpretation. Even a single line about that book you are referencing, just a sentence tldr, would save some player time instead of just forum browsing to actually understand the plot. Heck I haven't read the book and there are probably reasons why everything is so fleshy there.Now, you might ask whether I hate the game or not. No, I still loved it even with its serious flaw. It has one of the best atmospheres in horror games while improving some aspects of the old survival horror game. But it is a very very flawed game, because if you don't know or understand about the reference they are referencing, you are basically ♥♥♥♥♥♥ when it comes to understanding what is happening. I personally don't like forum reading for story, because it made you feel stupid.Edit: I'm giving this a negative because I believe this could be a better game! I think Signalis inspired a lot of artsy horror game again (like mouthwashing) and when I looked at it, it has all the aesthetic I like from Signalis, but it's plot sound even more abstract than Signalis because of random artsy delivery. I think we should stray away from artsy looking game and more toward games that uses artsy feeling. Again, signalis plot isn't hard to understand, it's just that the delivery of it is so obtuse that looking back some of the emotional moments doesn't really hit.
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: An actual masterpiece of a videogame. If you like some old school survival horror games like Resident Evil, let me tell you, this is that, and better. Mechanically very sound, learns a lot from the more classic titles. Sound, Music, Art direction, all of it is utterly gorgeous and nails it's cassette futurism aesthetic to a double T. I cannot recommend this game enough. At most, takes about 8, 8 and a half hours to complete if you're taking your time, and bad at puzzles like I am. Very good mixture of puzzles, combat, and boy is this game UPSETTING and UNNERVING. It does a very good job of making you feel uncomfortable. And the STORY? You'll just have to play it for yourself, because it's absolutely wild.Pick it up. You won't regret it.It is easily my 2022 Game of the Year.10/10
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: Signalis has excellently crafted dour atmosphere, supported by an engrossing story, unique visuals a carefully crafted soundscape, and, most of all, an engrossing story and worldbuildingAlso, the lighting, oh my stars, the lighting is EXQUISITEBe forewarned, the game is paced very slowly, letting you stew in it, but from what I've seen in the negative reviews some people were expecting a fast-paced action game with satisfying combat.It's not that. Combat is sometimes a necessity and always a risk, as in classics of the genre - ammo is scarce, fighting spaces are narrow, enemies are right bastards to fight, and given enough time, they will just get back up after getting killed, so getting into any fight is a choice you need to weigh very carefullyI honestly wouldn't have it any other way
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: Finally someone has put forth something as fun and horrific as the original run of Silent Hill games.  This game, both a love letter to the past, and something all it's own, is alluring.  Secrets and mind-bending concepts match awesome visuals and a unique story of pain and madness.If any of that sounded good to you....You should probably buy this game....
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: Signalis presents you with a gift that's beautifully wrapped and set to an excellent soundtrack, but ultimately hollow, frustrating and downright broken at points.It starts off strong, though. It sets up a bunch of cool-seeming mysteries, it presents itself strongly, it makes you want to find out what's going on and has atmosphere by the truckload. I was quite engaged with the game for I want to say... the first two hours, roughly.Mechanically, though, things are a bit worse. I realize that it's meant to be an homage to retro horror/survival games, but the amount of inventory slots is laughable. Six slots were, in one area, fought over by ten key items, five weapons, six types of ammunition, three types of healing items, a mandatory usable item(the flashlight) and two very handy consumables. Unless I wanted to literally ignore the game's mechanics by refusing to engage with the combat(though that's wise to do when it's an option, which it often isn't, for instance when entering a room has you literally clipped into a monster as soon as you spawn in), I'm stuck doing tons of shuttling back and forth between my (thankfully bottomless) storage box and where I need/want to use the consumables.I'll also note that said area is mapless and a huge pain to navigate because of how same-y every single room is, and the fact that navigation doesn't always, for instance, have you enter a room from the same direction you left from(i.e. leaving through right-side door translates to entering through left-side door). That area almost made me drop the game.But I had some friends of good taste who assured me that it would be deeply worth it to keep on pushing through! To see the final twists and turns! The excellent presentation! The cool stuff I was missing out on! So I went ahead and did so.I should get friends with better taste, as it turns out.As a caveat, I am extra frustrated with the final (third? quarter? hard to tell) of the game because it has a seemingly rare but entirely extant gamebreaking bug, and if you don't discover it until you've overwritten your save, your only way past it is to use the debug console, but getting around the bug that way also breaks some of the game's scripting, which forces you to use the debug console even more! It sucks.But, really, in a game like this, we expect some rough gameplay edges. We are here for the plot! The lore! The characters! Shame there's really none of those. The game kind of hedges its bets by not really committing to any kind of explanation for anything and instead just treating it like a Tumblr creepypasta where it tosses out ten different possible explanations and then smugly leans back while the cheapest kind of pretentious arthouse cinematics roll past. I never got the sense that the writers knew what was going on, but wanted to keep things ambiguous. Instead I felt like they just copied some visuals from Silent Hill, a bit of Lovecraft, tossed in a sprinkling of space zombies and called it a day.Just know that the explanation for it all may in fact be that a space wizard did it.I would deeply recommend against playing Signalis, you are missing out on every little.
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: Easily the best game I've played in years, and I don't even like horror games usually.Good:-very engaging story and worldbuilding, at every moment during playing I wanted to know more about the characters and lore of the world-charming PS1-style graphics-overall very fitting creepy/mysterious atmosphere, nice soundtrack, it's enough to make you feel uneasy and anxious without using cheap elements like jumpscares-yuriBad:-combat feels a little wonky, especially when fighting multiple enemies at once-inventory is very limited and can be a painThis doesn't take away much from the game though and can be forgiven, especially considering that this game was made by only two people.9.5/10 Amazing game, just play it. Now.
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyable psychological horror, influenced by ps1 games like RE1, Parasite Eve, Silent Hill etc.Some nice puzzles that are very cryptic, but if you're in the right mood I think you'll enjoy them and feel clever afterwards. The radio feature is really nice, tuning into frequencies for clues and occasionally creating a signal feedback loop to defeat certain enemies, it adds an extra layer to the environments that feels unique.Inventory system is a little clunky but you get used to it.I really hope Rose Engine make a sequel to this.

And then that again and again and again. I dropped it like a rock probably an hour away from the end. DO NOT BUY. My disappointment is immeasurable and my day is ruined.
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: Insanely good. The art direction/stylistic choices are great, in addition to the character designs. _childDocuments_.review: This ♥♥♥♥ gave me emotional damage so bad I would spend more money for a second game set in the same universe no matter the genera and then some just to experience some semblance of Signalis again I desperately wish I could play it again blind just to hurt myself over pixels all over again and despite not really understanding everything fully my first time round it still hit me in the feels that not even horrible jokes could counter and now that I have watched videos on it by people with bigger brains then mine I can conclude without a shadow of a doubt....that big pain..so congrats on the game because this piece of art is going to live in my head rent free for at least a couple months if not the rest of my life I'll be following what you two plan to do next with this or any other project you may have because this truly was an experience to remember.In other news I plan to traumatise my friends with it so they too can experience sesbian lex

_childDocuments_.review: Very well made pixel horror game with an Alien / Blade Runner / Resident Evil vibe.
