_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: Signalis has a great sense of style. The way that it plays with low-poly 3d, pixel-art, and the way that the game presents itself is genuinely impressive. There's clearly so much love put into this game, and I can see why so many people are obsessed with its world and characters. That's why it's such a shame that playing the game is miserable.Signalis is a throwback to the classic survival horror games of old- Resident Evil and the like. It's a shame that it also copied all the tooth-cracking frustration those games were full of. Six inventory slots shared between keys, guns, ammo, and health items!? Unskippable cutscenes before boss fights (Which are terrible.) Scarce save rooms. Progression locking puzzles that flip between block puzzles for toddlers and actual algebra. And, the piece de resistance; CONTACT DAMAGE!? (I hate contact damage. I've hated contact damage since the first time I ever encountered it as a child playing Kirby Superstar. I've hated it as an adult, I think I may just continue hating it after I die and finally go to Hell.)Signalis is badly designed. Which is an insane thing to say. just look at it! The art! The character designs! The everything! Signalis oozes good design! That's why it's so shocking that Signalis's core game design is bad. Rooms are too tight and filled with too many enemies, which are too fast to really avoid, particularly because they have CONTACT DAMAGE. Killing them isn't a good option, because it's a survival horror game- not only will you run out of ammo quickly, they'll also get right back up after a few minutes unless you expend another scarce and valuable resource to keep them down. Even if you've been thrifty, all these resources you're holding are filling your pockets to burst. Enemies don't always reset between being activated either (dependent on a stealth/noise mechanic that I never fully understood,) so you could walk through a door and directly into an enemy's back and take contact damage. I did that a lot. The game is filled with dozens of such dead ends where it's unsafe to stay in either room. There's an option that you can toggle to add tank controls. I think I would actually rather shut a door on my fingers. Signalis is grating, clunky, and beautiful. Watch someone else play it on YouTube.(Note: Signalis actually has several difficulty options, even ones that let you increase your inventory size! That's pretty cool, but I literally cannot stand playing games on easy difficulties.)
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: Signalis is what you get if you take the politics and tone of the unfilmed Alien 3 written by William Gibson the original Evangelion cinematic energy from Hideki Anno and bio-apocalypsepunk production design from Tutomou Neihei ... but lesbians.A bit more more Silent Hill than RE2 which I did not expect, but was gorgeous and it's not too puzzley, punishing or scary... an absolute steal at the price!
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: I freaking loved this game. May not be for everyone, but if you enjoy classic survival horror and like stories that leave you thinking after you played it, you may want to check this out.Gameplay wise I would say is very well designed and very accesible if you haven't played any other survival horror games. The puzzles make you think but are not frustrating, making finding the solution quite satisfying. Art direction is amazing and the ambiance and sound design are also great. As said earlier, the writing on this thing is quite something. I won't spoil anything, but don't fear if you feel lost or confused. It's part of the fun and it serves the storytelling quite well ;)This game feels like a passion project with a lot of love put into it. It transpires the love and passion that the team at rose-engine gave to the game. If anything I mentioned seems compelling to you, try it out, you may as well love this game.
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: SIGNALIS makes me upset. I saw the cute fan animations on youtube, the very unique and stylish aesthetic on the actual game page, and that was enough for me to try it. I wanted to like it so much, but the gameplay itself is extremely irritating and the story is cryptic to the point that I could not bring myself to care about it. The awesome art direction and overall vibe of the game fall to the wayside, completely overwhelmed by things much more negative that arrest my attention from any of the positives. SIGNALIS claims a lot of critically acclaimed survival horror games as its inspiration, but I feel like it didn't understand what made them great.THE PROBLEMS:Aiming while multiple enemies are on screen is miserable. The longer you aim at something, the more lethal your shot, and the aiming works as 'shoot nearest target to the mouse'.. your primary target is a suggestion moreso than a lock-on, so you can lose your target for one instant and then you lose all the accuracy buildup on your shot, which places you in terrible situations due to aiming issues that the player cannot account for.Backtracking. I -despise- it, and this game has an outright disgusting amount of it. You will have to visit and revisit and revisit rooms at opposite ends all the way across one given area, and sometimes you won't even have a map available to help you get to the place you know you need to go despite the multiple levels and labyrinthine mess that area layouts often turn out to be. This is also made SO much worse by..-Inventory management-. There are times where you will have five to six keys in play that all need to be carried places. There are some 6 or 7 guns, and one gun type has two ammo types. All of these things take inventory slots. As direct comparison with one of the stated inspiration games, in resident evil 2 you start with a handful of inventory slots, but you also gain inventory slots via pickups to account for all the space the player is having filled up by their new weaponry. SIGNALIS does not do this. You have six inventory slots and that is it. You cannot go from room to room collecting everything in them in one go unless your inventory is COMPLETELY empty (and sometimes not even then!), depriving you of any way to fight back against the myriad enemies, depriving you of interacting with the combat in any way, depriving you of a game to play and replacing it with a walking and key juggling simulator with occasional puzzles. If you want to actually be able to shoot things while you key-collect, you must go into the settings and choose the expanded inventory option, which allows you 8 slots instead of 6, which -still isn't enough-. I carried a single gun and a single box of ammo for it, and -still- I would see the 'inventory full' screen every 10 minutes and have to stop what I was doing to backtrack to an item box. They throw so much varied crap at you in addition to all the myriad keys that clog your slots and I can't fathom for the life of me what this decision is supposed to achieve. Am I actually being punished for wanting to be able to shoot things in the horror shooter game? Am I supposed to make the haram decision to leave all these supplies behind in the horror shooter game? Being resourceful and using everything you're given is a staple of survival horror games, but here you have to pick your punishment: Will you go on with the ability to defend yourself and thus have to backtrack to an item box seven and eight times a level, or will you go on with nothing at all in your inventory and have to backtrack for storage boxes two or three times instead while kiting enemies? There is no winning, both options suck and that's that. My time was not respected and I spent over half of the game not playing it because I was too busy revisiting the same hallways and rooms ad nauseum to funnel items and figure out where key number eleven was supposed to go in the level.God.I reiterate: I -really- wanted to like this game. I have played many of the games SIGNALIS takes inspiration from, and I thought the aesthetic alone made it worth exploring with a blind playthrough. I don't know what the hell the 96% positive reception is about, but I promise you it's not from the actual gameplay. Skip this and just look the important parts of the game up on youtube or something. The whole appeal seems to be about the meta-parts of the game and the fact that the cast and story is all about anime robot waifu lesbians, and you don't need to actually play it to experience those if that's your thing.
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: Signalis is an excellent game marred by an incomprehensible story... and I do mean TRULY INCOMPREHENSIBLE, not "poor Takareer just didn't get it", as I explain below.Pros:Almost all aspects of the game are amazing. It has a distinct, consistent art style, well-supported by its soundtrack. It doesn't have many characters, but they are all interesting. The perspective switches support the story and mystery, rather than detract from it. The general gameplay is quite fun - I feel threatened (certainly no endless DOOM-style blasting here), but I don't feel horrifically oppressed. I do have guns, and they work quite well. The puzzles are interesting, too.Cons:But the story ruins it. Sure, the worldbuilding is amazing, but when I play a game, I like it to mean something. As you progress through Signalis, you realize that everything just... doesn't make sense. Who are you, really? Where are you? You're looking for someone, are they alive? Who did you meet on your adventure? Were some parts hallucinations or dreams? Which parts? If you have an explanation, what about all those parts that contradict your theory? I expected the game to answer at least some of these key points, at least in the ending, but I was unfortunately let down. This game explains almost nothing at all. Thus, towards the end of the game I increasingly felt apathetic to the story and characters, since it seemed to be functionally identical to random rooms with random monsters and random puzzles. It's unfortunate, how clearly capable the game designers are, but I can't get emotionally invested in something that can't be understood.
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: While it's a difficult call to make, I think that SIGNALIS is my favorite video game I have ever played. It is tremendously affecting; sometimes just seeing a picture of its art or remembering a scene will make me feel like I'm getting kicked in the gut (in the best way). Its visual style and writing are both extremely evocative, and highly memorable. While I was playing it, I literally got the feeling that I shouldn't make art again because it would never compare to this. This game changed me.
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: An incredibly immersive game with arguably derivative mechanics, but more than makes up for it with it's creative storytelling and fascinating lore.Take the basic gameplay of early Resident Evil and a hint of Silent Hill. Throw in some Metal Gear Solid and Ghost in the Shell motifs. Have it mixed by someone with wide knowledge of classical art and literature and you have Signalis. The kind of game you'll think you sort of understood what is going on but then watch 2 hour lore breakdown videos and keep looking up fan art.For a game with so much body horror and lovecraftian themes, the fanbase sure is propogated by a lot of wholesome robot yuri. Not that I'm complaining.

I also noted some very slick point-and-click style interfaces that you just don't see a lot anymore.Great music, great presentation and style, solid gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: Great, classic-style survival horror gameplay with inventory management, great puzzles and a mature storyline.I'm not keen on the top-down camera perspective - it has neither the accessibility of a modern camera 3rd person nor the cinematic / artistic style of old-school fixed cameras, also the story starts to feel like a Silent Hill 2 tribute act at times.Despite these gripes, I highly recommend this game to people who enjoy survival horror and I hope to see more from this studio in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: I have been a fan of the survival horror genre for a fair number of years. Played the Resident Evil franchise extensively, massively respect the Silent Hill games, and have had my ear to the ground about new releases for quite some time. When SIGNALIS came across my radar via a couple of YouTube videos that encouraged me to go play the game for myself, I decided to pocket the videos and the game for whenever a sale arose.Despite my love for the genre, this game is far more than just something with gameplay I enjoy. It is one of the best games to have been released in the past five years at least. Hands down the best thing that I have played this year. The world of SIGNALIS is absolutely fascinating and delivered well with the lore scattered about in the world. What makes that world so unbelievably memorable is how well reinforced the world is by the atmosphere. Art direction is shockingly crisp given the retro stylization, character designs are clear and concise, and enemies are simple yet effective. What elevates this above all else is the . God, I have played so many games that have exceptional soundtracks. FromSoftware's entire library, the Last of Us, ATLUS titles; none of them feel as distinct or as entrancing as the music and sound design within this game. All of this tied together with a cosmic horror story that still manages to be a coherent tragedy at it's heart.I could go on and on about my love for this game, but begin your descent yourself. You will not regret it. And after all...

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible, super interesting survival horror game. If only Elden Ring hadn't come out this year, I'd have to say it was my game of the year. It's closer than it has any business being.It has one of those stories that leave a lot for the player to think about and solve on their own. It is similar to From Soft games in that regard. However, I think it tells a much more human and emotional story than From Soft games. I've played it twice now and still find myself wondering about the story days afterwards. Genuinely hope the dev adds some DLC or something, would love to see it expanded on.
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: Remember our promise. an absolute achievement in the horror survival genre and a genuinely beautiful piece of art. I say this as someone who never cared much for the RE/ Silent Hill formula but the presentation and fascinating narrative made me look past that. Signalis is a game that absolutely wrapped itself around my mind for days after beating it and stayed there completely dominating my thoughts, as i tried to unravel it. It can be confusing but I believe the emotional narrative is easy to follow and even if you can only follow the surface level themes, you will feel content (and sad) at the end.
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: So let's start with the obvious. Heavily inspired by old-school Resident Evil and I like that. Subverted my expectations halfway through the game. What was once assumed as a typical futuristic android beat-em-up with the plot of the Matrix only to have my opinion changed once I beat a good chunk of the game. This game is beautifully made and I love the art direction between 2D and 3D. Gonna play it a third time to get the other endings.
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: Rose Engine have created a modern-day, indie classic with their horror game, Signalis… albeit a very safe modern-day, indie classic.They have managed to marry Resident Evil, Silent Hill, with a sprinkle of Metal Gear Solid to create a game that harkens back to the ‘good old days’ of gaming. At its core Signalis is a horror game, combining the action seen in Resident Evil and the psychological horror of Silent Hill, with the camera angles and control scheme of Metal Gear Solid. Some of you might be glad to know that tank controls are not present in Signalis. The art style and sound design establishes a heavy atmosphere that will keep you on your toes and will leave you feeling apprehensive going through each door.While Signalis is a horror game at its core, it would be a disservice to the game to simply label it as just a survival horror game. Signalis does a decent job at being a puzzle game too. Though these puzzles are reminiscent of the kind you would find in Resident Evil 1-3, Onimusha and Devil May Cry 1, there is much more of an emphasis on solving puzzles in Signalis. Whether that is good or bad is up to the individual player. Personally, I loved it. Admittedly, while there were two puzzles that left me scratching my head for a while, most puzzles in Signalis are quite simple.Signalis is a fun game and while I could not wait to play more, I did come away with a few gripes. While I did not mind the limited inventory space, there are some items that could have been managed differently.Items that acted like upgrades, such as the flashlight and camera, should not have taken up an inventory slot, but instead should have been treated like a mechanic the player can use. Tactical items like stun batons, thermite, or healing items should have had their own inventory slot while equipped i.e., if you had a repair patch, stun baton and thermite, the one you had equipped would take-up that seventh inventory slot, while the others remained in your general inventory.I had a few frustrating moments over these design choices, which forced me to run back to a save room to dump my inventory before I could progress. Although this could be chalked up to poor inventory management on my behalf (and an inevitability), I would argue that the flashlight is a mandatory item, meaning you will only ever have five inventory slots most of the time. One could argue that’s part of what makes the game challenging, while I would argue it is a part of the game that makes it frustrating and does not increase the challenge in any meaningful way.Oh, and just to be completely honest… in the age of smart phones, the camera was less than useless.Rose Engine played it safe and did nothing new with the survival horror genre. With that said, a team of two made Signalis and managed to produce a solid game despite that limitation. The results of their labour, while safe, is still impressive. I am honestly looking forward to seeing what they do in the future.Just to be completely transparent, I have yet to beat the game the four times required to experience the full story, so it would be unfair if I commented on the story just yet. I have beaten it only the once.If I had to score the game out of ten, I think a solid seven would be fair.
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: As many others have said, this game is excellent - one of the best modern survival horror experiences on the market with a brilliantly tense atmosphere that's going to stick with me for a long time and excellent puzzles that, for me at least, were challenging and interesting without ever becoming too hard.  However, I have a couple of issues that resulted in the game leaving a bad taste in my mouth, one involving the game's mechanics, the other involving the ending(s), something I think is really important to cover but that I don't see anyone talking about.The first one is simple to explain: the inventory is really, really small, and it results in a lot of tedious, artificial backtracking as you ferry stuff to and from save rooms, which in turn results in enemies you've killed getting back up, forcing you to put them down again or risk health getting past them.  The backtracking problem gets worse in the final zone as the game starts blocking doorways, forcing you to take more and more roundabout paths through the level as it progresses.  As a consequence, I was just kinda waiting for the game to end by the time it actually did, and I think it would've been a better experience with one or two more slots, reducing the amount of backtracking and key item shuffling necessary.The second one kinda hurt honestly - I'll spoiler it for people who want to go in blind, but I think it's important to mention for other queer folk who want to know how they can expect to be treated.  The good news is that it's textual, there's no ambiguity about the nature of Elster's relationship with her girlfriend, which is nice.  Minor spoilers on the nature of the endings and events late in the game ahead.Anyway, that's my two cents.  I'm still recommending the game because everything leading up to the conclusion is top notch and it doesn't feel fair to leave a negative review on something I did, for the most part, enjoy, but that said, I'm probably not going to play this again.
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: Truly a great game that tells a great story.I cried at the end of this game and felt emotional throughout the experience. Games like this inspire me to pursue some sort of art form to express my life or a story, to create something to either entertain or to be remembered by.The only criticism I can have of the game is in the game-play but its more of a nitpick than anything else.It can be very tediously punishing to not have inventory space for key items and have to leave them the first time you see them.Some areas change as you complete things in them or may not have a map and be hard to orient yourself in and it can make the pathways back to the left key items very frustrating to navigate. Specifically in the Nowhere section of the game I was stuck running in circles trying every door and every pathway to find the one room I had to abandon previously, there is no map in this section and it is a 3 floor area with doors you unlock every now and then.Regardless, this game is great and I recommend it to all but mostly queers probably lolI love these space lesbians, I love my partner :3
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: SIGNALIS is a masterpiece of horror. The horror of loss. Of the merciless ravages of time, and the agony of a promise that cannot be fulfilled. Disappointment. Tragedy. The erosion of love by the cruelties of the world at large. I went into this game expecting a creepy PS1 retro horror tribute, with body horror and lots of resource scrounging and obscure puzzles to push the spook factor. Shooting at decaying anime girl robots and listening to some insanely good spooky music. Instead tragic space robo-lesbians tore out my heart and stomped it to pieces, so that I might experience a slightest fraction of their pain. SIGNALIS is about the hell of letting down those you love. Of having them taken from you by sickness and tragedy and the cold, hollow march of time. It's a type of horror that leaves your insides torn apart, a hollow frozen cavity of pain where before you were made to feel hope and light. It encapsulates despair, of knowing exactly what it is you've lost, even if you don't know why you've lost it, but more than that, knowing you can never get it back. GOOD ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game. Hard recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good classic Resident Evil / Silent Hill game. I have now played it through twice, first time on survival (hardest) difficulty and second time, to get the secret ending, on normal difficulty. 100% achievements unlocked. Its greatest strength has to be the superb aesthetics. But it's not without its flaws which I would like to concentrate on here.Being limited to 6 items is too much considering tools and key items necessary to progress the game also take slots. There's one puzzle that requires a key to the door where the puzzle is located and then the puzzle itself requires 6 items. Even if you carry nothing else you'll still had to backtrack to your storage chest as with the key included you'd had to carry 7 items to complete the puzzle. If tools/keys didn't take a slot or if we had 8 slots I think the game would flow a lot better.Combat is very similar to classic Resident Evil. If you kill an enemy it might revive later unless you burn it, though it won't get super strong when it revives unlike REmake. But there doesn't seem to be a limit on how many times the same enemy can revive. One time I had to kill the same enemy 4 times. I'm not really a fan of this as I don't like being forced into run and dodge strategy where you try and avoid every enemy or rush through the game. I know many players avoid enemies in the classic Resident Evil games, but you don't have to, I always kill 95% of the enemies even on harder difficulties. If the enemy could only revive once I think this mechanic would be a lot better. If you are like me I'd suggest you play this game on normal difficulty as the ammo was much more plenty there compared to survival.The story. Let me first say that this is my opinion and preference, not some objective fact that the game's story is bad. But I usually like, exceptions exists, stories that are clear, though not necessarily simple, with happy endings. I love the story in SOMA for instance. But I generally don't like those 2deep4u open ended stories where a lot of interpretation is left to the player. Again, exceptions exists. If you want an example of a story I didn't enjoy because of this, then watch Evangelion, the most overra- I digress. But this game is definitely on the Evangelion side of things and while you can understand quite a bit of the story in this game there's still a lot left up to interpretation. There's 4 endings, I have seen 3 (MEMORY, PROMISE & ARTIFACT) of them including the secret (true?) ending. I don't think I like any of them.I'd still recommend this game as I do think it is good game with awesome aesthetics. But it is no 10/10.

_childDocuments_.review: …so Tunic's got competition for GOTY.I'll be frank: Signalis is on my short list for favorite survival-horror games. We're talking excellent “supped-up PS1” aesthetics, horrific atmosphere, disturbing (and catchy) soundtrack, and intense gameplay right out of the golden age of the genre, pulling from Resident Evil, Silent Hill, Parasite Eve, Dino Crisis, and a metric ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of cyberpunk anime to form its own twisted identity.But here’s the rub. All of that would be cool, and a neat nostalgia trip on its own. But Signalis REALLY came to play with its story. Intricate world-building, complex characters, arthouse presentation, and mind-bending twists are the name of the game, with an ocean of cosmic horror and existential dread to drown in.I wouldn’t dare give anything away. But I’m not kidding when I say this is the closest someone’s gotten to nailing Silent Hill 2’s narrative highs.There are issues, of course. And depending on how you feel about them, they might be deal-breakers, especially if you aren’t down with some of the game’s brutal design choices. There's a super-strict six-item limit for your inventory, designed to make you REALLY think about what you're bringing to the party. But the tricky thing is that utility items count for the limit, like the flashlight and the camera. I got used to this, but I wish they were just permanent upgrades like the radio. Granted, the game becomes even more tense when you have to dodge monsters and grab items in the dark. But it’s nice to be able to see in some of the underlit environments. There’s probably a Doom 3 argument in there somewhere, but whatever.The story is also super complex, going full End of Evangelion or Twin Peaks with its perception of time, space, and psychotic breakdowns. If you really want to get into the story, it asks a bit from you, not just in perception, but interpretation. Nothing’s going to be 100% clear, and if that’s not your thing, you should avoid this like the plague. I also wish there was a bit more incentive to replay the game, outside of the four alternate endings. This genre’s famous for giving players joke endings, broken weapons, character costumes, and unlockable modes for repeat playthroughs. Something like that could do the game wonders, and I’d like to think that if this game does well, the devs would investigate something like that post-launch (the Mining Laser would be a hilarious endgame BFG).All in all, it’s actually kind of crazy to know that something THIS good just showed up out of nowhere on Steam one day. And to think that this is their first ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game is such a mind job.Highly, highly recommended, although a familiarity with classic survival-horror is a plus. Be ready to pay attention, and approach with an open mind.

_childDocuments_.review: Signalis is a classic survival horror not just in design but also in form, but that is by far a boundary to which it restricts itself to, often recurring to sections that lightly mess with the basic rules of a game. But that's all just to tell you what you'd like to know for your money's worth...I don't think anything I could tell you could really encompass the dread, the sadness and that priceless sense of wonderment at what often feels like a mystery impossible to unravel.Signalis is about and in and of itself love, bleeding, seething and gelid. Abstract like a poem, coherent as a delirious fever dream at your deathbed and even as frail certainty and shards of a story's verisimilitude elude you it'll nevertheless resonate and stick with you, whether it's a tone that recurs in your ears or a memory of a cycle.That's something money can't buy.

_childDocuments_.review: Time is a flat circle.You can play this game multiple times and catch something new every time.  After every play session even if only a little progress was made, it left me thinking about something, wondering what would come next or what horrors awaited. Not once did it disappoint. Always brought something more. No sooner I got comfortable something new would come along, whether that be an actual a monster or a troubling revelation. The game doesn't rely on cheap jump scares or over the top shock factor, the sense of unease is consistent and always present. Even the saferoom music doesn't give you a break. The atmosphere sets a sorrowful duty upon the player, the task ahead is terrible and weakness cannot be tolerated. Your only option is to push forward, no matter what you're faced with, despite the chaos. Harrowing resource management, deadly encounters, and twisted puzzles await. Every decision counts, not just a few big story moments. Every bullet fired, healing item spent, each step in the wrong direction, will test you and bring challenges their own. I didn't expect to enjoy this game nearly as much as I did. Not normally one for survival horror but a buddy talked me into it. Not one regret. Ended up getting another buddy on board beings I told them what I had gone through thus far in my run and they were interested. Finished the game on call with each other discussing what was happening. Honestly can't explain how amazing the music and art style are for building the atmosphere. Not only that but certain sequences change how you view them. Switching seamlessly between the normal camera view and first person at times, it puts you directly in Elster's shoes.

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful game with striking visuals, mixed perspectives, great directing, excellent sound design, and a bit challenging to top it off.And while it certainly passes the Vibe Check and is the exact type of graphics that appeals to me, a gamer, I just couldn’t click with it in the end—literally. It’s a great game and one I recommend, but your mileage will vary WILDLY on the story, how it’s presented, and what it ultimately leads up to.I simply didn’t understand what the hell was going on nor why I should care, period. I barely even know the name of who I’m playing until an NPC finally said it. The mix of German and Chinese for a sort of… I suppose aesthetic choice also doesn’t help, as there are key moments in cutscenes that aren’t in English. Yes, to my ignorant semi-monolingual brain it LOOKS cool, but I’d’ve rather understood what was literally being said over pure aesthetics. My feelings eventually pivoted to it being too pretentious. And to that end, what cutscenes there were made no sense to the average player, not unless you were a YouTube video game lore analyzer like VatiVidya whose actual livelihood depends on it. They chose the FromSoft method of story telling, but forgot that it was a story-centric survival horror game and not a gameplay-centric action RPG. Even Silent Hill gives you some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up idea of what’s going on some times.Simply put, 10 hours is what it took for me to beat it, but it would take another 10+ just to figure out what’s going on—and that’s not taking into account the multiple endings, which was visually great but who the hell is that and why did any of it happen?! I swear I’m not that dumb, please make it make sense!To sum up, it’s a visually incredible, creepy, challenging indie horror game worth your time. And while I personally love vague storytelling, it was far too opaque for my taste—almost like the famous novel Roadside Picnic, with cool ideas but no central thread to latch onto. I still recommend it, I enjoyed a great deal of it, but was let down by the Who, What, and Why.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: as of October 2023, the update made it so you can change inventory size, and certain key items don't take up space! That's amazing, rose-engine!I don't think I have any major, important criticism of this game. Flawless in almost every way, I don't typically do survival horror but Signalis managed to keep me so engaged from start to finish and I think I'm going to be thinking about this for a while after. What complaints I do have essentially boil down to two aspects - inventory size and sometimes-unfortunate enemy placing, meaning getting through doors can sometimes be awkward. But this is rare, and inventory management is possible, and despite those two marks on its record Signalis is worth the minor trouble in every single way.I really can't say much without spoiling the whole thing, but how can such a surreal, symbolic, non-linear tale be so impactful and devastating? rose-engine have put tangible love and care into every aspect of the game, and it's in itself a love letter - particularly the survival horror game genre, but also to horror and sci-fi in general. It's unashamed of having those inspirations, which makes the experience quite novel when you can pick up on them. Uniquely these references do not take away from Signalis's story.The story, as I've said, I can't say much about as that would relegate this to a spoiler review. However, what I can say is this - it's been a joy to discuss it with people, because everyone interprets it differently. Signalis is a game of misdirection and metaphor. Almost nothing is given to you and Elster explicitly; it's almost like a detective's case with how things need to be pieced together. Some of the greatest joy and terror I've experienced in Signalis is when I've made connections, and literally had my jaw drop in front of my screen.Art direction, soundtrack, plot and character - 10/10. One of, if not THE best game I played in 2022.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:+ Unique art direction that shines bright and uninterruptedly through various perspectives ;+ Great sound design and one of the greatest soundtracks I've ever heard ;+ Well-written cast of characters, protagonist included ;+ Great level design ;+ Uncomplicated controls and overall smooth gameplay ;+ Tension does nothing but elevate SIGNALIS due to providing a continuous sense of dread and due to an overall avoidance of cheesy jump scares ;+ A true survival horror experience of old where its atmosphere and gameplay loop is concerned ;+ Really tasty puzzles, most of them doable with a bit of thinking. You may or may not find that a couple of them take more than a bit of thinking. I did ;+ Masterpiece in slow burn storytelling ;+ Extremely compelling universe that makes collecting lore pieces addicting ;+ Despite its linearity, the game has more than just one way around things. This may or may not give you a different perspective of the narrative and your surroundings.Cons:- Developer rose-engine was stingy with inventory space, which poses a nuisance and creates a need to backtrack a little too much ;- "Full controller support" is true, but there's a seemingly inherent awkwardness to aiming your firearms with an analog stick when there are multiple targets present.__________________________________________SIGNALIS. One of my mates gifted me this game back on Christmas. "It looks like your thing", he said. Humoured - if not challenged - I went in deep about 2 weeks later. A first look and I was sold on it. The atmosphere is thick, the animations are fluid and the color pallette is the best type of bleak. Welcoming, even. The survival horror aspect of this game closely mirrors that of the early Resident Evil and Silent Hill titles, both in overall feel and in the resource management department, and suddenly you're back to 20 years ago in front of that old CRT TV by yourself. They added the filters to match, too! From the screams of the unfortunate to the eerie soundtrack, the sound engulfs you in a certain way, almost as if you knew it intimally before you heard it. It's homely. It's bittersweet. Painful. Conversely, the whole gameplay experience is mostly painless, if not for one gripe - the lack of reasonable inventory space. If you haven't played the game, I'm positive that's a bridge you'll hate to cross. In the greater picture, though, this is but a minor complaint. Another thing I personally dealt with was the awkwardness in aiming that comes with using a controller when there's more than a couple targets on screen. As such, if you're on the fence about it I would advise you to use KB+M for your playthrough. Again, a very minor grievance and it didn't keep me from fully enjoying the game, at all. Regarding the thinking puzzles, I can proud myself to have kept to my self-compromise of not looking any of the solutions up. I can recall to a day at work, looking at the pictures I had taken with my phone of what I felt were the necessary clues to solve a certain puzzle, then coming home still clueless and suddenly getting it. As long as you allow for it, many small victories like these feel earned in this game.It's hard for me to put it into words any further than I already did in the previous section of this review without entering spoiler territory, but I digress. I will say that this is one story and one videogame universe for the ages. I'm not even particularly keen on sci-fi settings and the usual accompanying lore, and that did not matter one bit. I will add that every detail feels scored in with purpose, crafted with such thought, paced in such a way that I can't help but yearn for another story in this universe, preferably made by the same people. Furthermore, I can picture SIGNALIS as a mini-series, or perhaps as a hit movie, especially if made with the stoicness of the german (much in the vein of the Netflix series "Dark", if you happen to be familiar). I dearly hope a pitch will be made at some point.SIGNALIS is an instant classic and whatever faults you may find in it, you'll also readily overlook them. I couldn't possibly recommend this more if you're an adult gamer. If you miss the gaming scene from the late 90's - but regardless, really - SIGNALIS has the potential to become one of your favorite games of all time.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best games I have ever played. Plays most similar to old Resident Evil or Silent Hill games - a horror game where you crawl through an abandoned facility, fighting off monsters and uncovering secrets. Tank controls have been abandoned (though there is an option in the menu to turn them on if you wanted to for some reason), replaced with WASD and mouse aiming. These controls make exploring the game's world and fighting off the infected much more tactile and responsive compared to the older games in this genre.The story is something else, too. You play as ELSTER, a robot lady who is determined to rescue her lover, who has gone missing somewhere within the depths of the facility. The story is touching, surreal, heartbreaking, and terrifying all at the same time. The bits of lore you find on abandoned computers or on discarded notes help to flesh out the world, illuminating the paths of two star-crossed lovers across an advanced society built on rot. The story of SIGNALIS will stick with you long after you have finished the game.SIGNALIS is an unforgettable experience. I have never found another game like it, and it is not likely I shall ever find one again. I cannot recommend it enough.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who generally has a strong dislike for the horror genre, I absolutely loved every minute of my time with Signalis. It's one of my favorite games of 2022.Excellent controls (played w/ xbox controller), moody atmosphere with great art direction, and gripping gameplay. Nearly every aspect of Signalis feels so satisfyingly polished. There's plenty of ways to deal with enemies, but unless you finish one off with a certain method you obtain in the game, they will revive the next time you disturb their bodies after enough time has passed. So even revisiting areas you've cleared before can still be dangerous. Puzzles are done well enough, though there was one in particular that felt more difficult than it needed to be (water tanks be damned).The story is both a strong and a weak point to me. Perhaps it was my own lack of comprehension but the storytelling can feel too cryptic at times. It felt harder to follow as I drew closer to the end. Despite that though you can generally get a feel for what is going on, and there were some really nice moments along the way.Signalis left me both incredibly satisfied, and wanting more. It's one of the best games of 2022, and I cannot recommend it highly enough.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to love this game.As other have mentioned, the story music and atmosphere are all great, but unfortunately that's where my praise ends.The game-play simply isn't satisfying. There's no way for any tension to build when the game forces you into the pause menu every 3 seconds to look at the map, or a clue, change your radio frequency (quickly), equip a replacement auto-injector or cattle prod, or change weapons when you inevitably run out of the 2 shotgun shells you've been able to save up. While there ARE ways to do SOME of these actions without opening the menu, it's simply not efficient to do them outside of the pause menu. Why stay vulnerable while holding down the button for my heal when I can just use it instantly through the pause menu? The same goes for reloading and managing the radio frequencies.The weapons (with the exception of the cattle prod) in the game are useless to the point where I feel their inclusion is a detriment to the game as a whole. The enemies you "kill" may just decide to get up again unless you torch their bodies with a flare (which are extremely limited). This makes shooting at enemies feel pointless, and encourages you to just ignore anything hostile and run by it, hoping you don't get hit. Once you learn how ineffective the weapons are and that your only real option is to just keep moving it removes the last bits of tension the game had to offer. It's stressful getting backed into a corner firing the last of your bullets to stay alive - it's tedious when you're walking through the same hallway for the 15th time with *another new key* and that baddie that you don't want to waste ammo on slaps your ass. I have yet to encounter the first scenario.Not sure of the right wording for this but the map design is just not good for this kind of game? This is nit-picky, but in a "survival horror experience" why in the world do you think it's good game design to put a safe room with lots of ammo and meds directly prior to a boss fight in a HORROR game. It makes sense to give players some additional supplies before an encounter in some games, it's a staple of some genres, but when you want the player to have a sense of unease, a sense of tension and stress, don't hold up a sign saying "HEY GAMERS, BOSS FIGHT AHEAD". If you want the player to have access to those supplies, have them be located inside the boss room so that the player doesn't get the massive telegraph that there's about to be a fight, have them located inside the boss room to build tension as the player has to gobble up the supplies in the heat of the moment.The puzzles are unimaginative and way too easy. I swear half of them are from children's educational games like Putt-Putt and Freddi Fish from the 90's. Most involve grade school level arithmetic and/or critical thinking.Overall I find that SIGNALIS is less than the sum of its parts, as many (good) mechanics either don't mesh well or directly clash with themselves. It feels like a game with split personality disorder, where it's not sure if it wants to be a visual novel or a survival horror game, and it ends up in a lackluster purgatory somewhere in-between.

_childDocuments_.review: So what is Signalis?Signalis was developed by rose-engine, a team consisting of two people: Barbara Wittmann and Yuri Stern, and was published by Humble Games (Internationally) and Playism (in Asia.) It was released on October 27th, 2022. On Steam, Xbox One, Playstation 4 and Nintendo Switch. First and foremost, Signalis stands out due to it's distinctive visual style and the dedication to older horror game design and execution. It plays as well as intended, and while a friend of mine had trouble with aiming: I can't say I had the same problem (both of us using gamepads.)The game plays as well as intended. Combat is quick but a product of the time. It's crunchy and brief. Few fights linger longer than a handful of minutes. At most. Inventory management is a distinctive and likely divisive choice. You have six inventory slots. You will end up having to make potentially numerous trips to a storage bin to drop off and pick up equipment and required items to progress. Puzzles, which I have more to say about that below will take some note taking, some extra effort on the player's behalf. While there were at least three puzzles that I bumbled through, they were not so inaccessible as to be impossible to solve. Do note that some puzzles have the possibility of varying between what is requested of you and what the solution is. So looking up a guide may wield mixed results. -=-=-Initial Commentary-=-=-My initial review for this was negative. A thumbs down and I still stand by the "Buyer Beware" warning that it entailed. At the 3.7 Hour mark I was very close to just outright stopping. I was tired of the exploration being hampered by puzzle after puzzle after puzzle.It felt like the pacing was awful. No matter how unique and distinctive the setting, character, presentation, and world: I kept bouncing off the fact that every time I felt like I was getting into the experience. I'd have yet another puzzle blocking the path. Note that as much as I might harp on the puzzles a lot here: they are not the worst puzzles in a game I have ever experienced. The information to solve them is there, if you are looking for it. There was three puzzles I didn't know all the information for, because some of the hints are in things you wouldn't expect that knowledge to stem from. I was about to leave it there, but the setting is what kept me thinking that I should give it another shot. Whereupon I wrote an adjustment to my original assessment at 6.2 hour mark. Which consisted of still feeling cheated or at least not being made well aware of the amount of puzzles that would be involved in this particular venture. -=-=-Changing Perspective-=-=-While I still dislike the puzzle stopgap that nearly drove me to give this up. I am happy that I didn't.The mystery of the setting and the uniqueness of the premise kept me wanting to figure it out. Learn more about this setting and it's characters.So I stuck with it and managed to make it through the game. Which took me about 10.6 hours. Granted, the puzzles slowed me down because I'd often find one. Find the next save point. Take a break and then return back to it. I recommend this because of the strong setting, world-building, and aesthetic style. Despite how intense my dislike for puzzles, I wouldn't mind knowing more about this universe and the people who live there. The game captures a fairly small explorable area but the writing implies a much larger universe. -=-=-Conclusion-=-=-If you don't mind putting forth the extra effort, and don't mind the frequent inventory management required: Signalis is surprisingly good for a new studio consisting of two people.

_childDocuments_.review: I have never really been interested in the survivor horror genre at all: the cheap jumpscares, chase sequences and repetitive objectives never really appealed to me, and in general I believe horror is a really difficult thing to be done right. However, right from the first seconds I heard the haunting beginning of the Three Note Oddity in the store page trailer, I was hooked.The dread that comes from number stations is quite something else: an uncanny robotic voice spelling out nonsense, often in a foreign language, for minutes at a time. No callsign. No addressee. No message. Except, you know that is not true: you just cannot see it, but it is there. And that is where this strange feeling comes from.I would normally wait for a promotion to buy any game. This time, however I impulse bought Signalis, and I am glad I did because it does not disappoint.The game does an amazing job at constructing and maintaining the exact atmosphere that sold me to it. Simple things like lighting and the background noise of small elements such as the wind and an electric fan really help consolidate this so hard to explain feeling. The fact that the game uses actual morse code and real life recordings of radio transmissions is also great.The mix of German and Chinese is also a really good catch: it makes you feel just enough displaced while still being recognizable and even when it is not obvious, you know there is meaning behind it - just like our number stations. While it could seem a more obvious option to go with some more cliché languages like Russian or some sci-fi looking script, the choice seems really deliberate and careful, which, together with the amazing graphical design, helps consolidate an unique visual look.On the other hand, the puzzles were, as I was somewhat expecting, kind of straightforward. They are never really trivial per se, but no solution left me especially amazed. Consistently with my little experience of games of the genre, some puzzles were simple fetch quests altogether: get a key to unlock a safe to access another key, etc.. While somewhat plain, these did not upset me at all, considering how the overall atmosphere and setting held my interest at times the objectives did not. And a great setting it is. A sci-fi distopian world; an abandoned underground facility; an isolated radio station. These settings are all loaded with really specific ambiences. It reminded me quite a lot of Neon Genesis Evangelion at several times, be it with the title cards, be it with the out-there places and concepts, and I loved that.What a great game.Edit: oh boy...

_childDocuments_.review: I couldn't bring myself to finish this. I started out really liking the game. The visuals are pretty unique, the story is interesting, and I was enjoying the puzzles and problem solving aspects. About 5 hours in though I found myself starting to dislike a few things. The inventory system is just plain awful. You can only carry 6 things at a time which in the beginning it seems like a lot, but once you get to areas where you're having to carry stuff around to open doors or solve puzzles it gets to be very limiting, especially when you've got to worry about killing enemies, healing yourself, and having a light to see in certain areas. _childDocuments_.review: I dislike horror and never played any of the classic survival horror games, and not even a fan of pixel art or the anime art style, but I saw an hour or so of this game played by a streamer and its atmosphere and world building immediately grabbed my attention. My mind kept returning to it, and I decided to go ahead and play it, and I’m glad I did.The gameplay didn’t take long to get used to. It all comes down to managing resources and planning ahead, what to take with us, where to go, which enemies to engage, which to run past. There are only a few places where we can access storage and save, can only take six items with us, and permanently killing enemies requires a specific limited item too, which creates constant tension. It worked well together with other aspects of the game to create a sinister atmosphere. I liked how there’s also some rudimentary stealth, as you can sometimes tiptoe around enemies. Most locations are a non-linear series of rooms, which we must explore to find, inspect, and combine key items, and solve puzzles. The puzzles were very well-designed and fun, neither too easy nor too hard, I just had to pay attention to the hints the game gave me. All in all, the gameplay worked well, the only issue I had was that occasionally the targeting was wonky, and having the same button for stomping on foes and entering doors sometimes messed up my plans.The gameplay complements the setting and the story wonderfully. The world building is excellent, as you slowly gain knowledge through notes, items and the environment. The developers managed to create a world that feels oppressive even before the cosmic horror and surreal elements come into play. I also loved the multilingual aspect of the game. English is usually taken for granted in a sci-fi setting, but the mix of German and Chinese here gives a unique character to the game.The retro style probably helps in establishing the mood, as it leaves some room for our brain to fill in some of the details. There’s also some charm in having retro graphics combined with modern effects, like real time shadows and reflections. It all looked nice, thanks to the strong art direction, both in the claustrophobic and often disturbing environments and in the very artistic presentation of the cutscenes. The great audio design tops it all off, combining creepy ambience, with strangely melancholic tunes at just the right moments.The story itself was the most memorable part of the game. It is told via notes, trippy visions and minimal dialogue. Despite being quite cryptic and having many aspects open to interpretation, it is a story about people, and it managed to resonate with me very much. I got quite attached to the main characters’ and found the experience very emotional and the ending heart-wrenching. There are very few games that managed to impact me emotionally like this. It will take some time for me to process it, but I’m also very glad to have experienced it.What a game. I’m really happy I stumbled upon it. It was a fantastic and memorable experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Man, I really loved this game. I hadn't heard all too much about it beforehand but it seemed like the kind of game I would enjoy. With games like Soma and movies like Ghost in the Shell and Blade Runner being some of my favorite pieces of media for the topics and philosophies they discuss, I was bound to enjoy this.The game is played as a classic survival horror like Resident Evil or Silent Hill being the games its compared to the most, and while not having played either of those I can definitely see the inspiration. The gameplay of this game is very solidly made and although probably the tamest part it was always enjoyable and as fun to play as a survival horror can be.Where the game really gets me is the story itself and its presentation of said story. Nothing in the game is really laid out for you, if you don't do a little digging and connect some dots you can come out of it not really understanding anything that happened. Now I will say even with reading everything I came across I probably understood less than half of the overall story even after a second playthrough for 100%.This kind of storytelling isn't for everyone but its personally one of my favorites and you can tell that everything is very thought out on what information is displayed and when, its not ambiguous to cover up for bad storytelling like some games but to elevate the story even more. After watching several hours of lore and theory videos I'd say I have a solid grasp on what the game was trying to say, or at least an interpretation of it and I just love it.There are some many layers upon layers and symbolism in this game its impossible to list it all. The presentation of the game is also beautiful, it goes for an older type of aesthetic, with screen glitches and even a toggleable CRT effect that I chose to play with. All these little details in the game and the way its presented add to the horror vibe in a really cool way and they also have implications on the story itself if you're looking for it.Overall I really loved the game and I think its safe to say it will end up in my favorites as its just a combination of many things that I personally really love and while I don't think its a 100% perfect game its perfect to me.

_childDocuments_.review: Signalis is a masterclass of survival horror, inspired by the classic Resident Evils and Silent Hills, it goes beyond imitation to deliver its own tale of psychological torment in cold depths of an uncaring world. Signalis's gameplay is simple: Manage your limited resources, explore the environment, solve puzzles, and chart your way forward past broken dolls who wish to drag you down with them. It follows the old design of isometric locked cameras with old tank controls, all of which are refined to prevent frustration.While one could simply face foes head on, the infected replicas have a habit of not staying down without first incinerating them, meaning fights need to be chosen well or be down efficiently to preserve supplies.Boss battles are present with only one faltering, they have mechanics and tricks that make them fun to figure out, hints left before hand on what you need to win. Unlike some titles in the genre, the game was prepared to prevent soft-locking with supplies added to the world at death-count milestones, boss mechanics rewarding survival and the all-mighty shove helping make space when desperate.Use of light, tight quarters and the radio flow into combat, puzzle and exploration, this keeps it fresh and moving at a incredible pace, the game does not outstay its welcome and truly tests you on Survival difficulty.The story is cryptic and vague but once discerned is very engaging, you are Elster, a Replica in service to the Great Nation looking for your officer and so much more: Ariane, descending into a nightmarish hell from which no-one will emerge from the same as they once were.To that end, Elster meets survivors whom are all struggling or facing the end the only way they can, plenty of notes and journals detailing the life in the oppressive Berlin Wall-esque totalitarian nation, and the suffering in the horror unfolding as you arrive.To discuss more may spoil the tale, but ultimately the journey is about how love, change and adversity of cruel indifference, the symbolism is not surface-deep at all nor only worth the reference.There are multiple endings encouraging repeat playthroughs, just be ready for some to hurt.Signalis is excellent in presentation, harking back to the PS1 console era, it uses its limitations to full effect, light, enemy design, environment and audio combine to far more than some of their parts. As for the atmosphere itself, the Aliens inspired CRT-Future tech aesthetic combined with the utilitarian and cold conditions give a dark wold to journey through.Notes, posters and journals tie things together well, adding a greater element of joy and tragedy as the monsters you cut down reflect who they were before infection, especially the gentle giant MYNR and the thought police KLBR, caring for and inspiring those around her, while the little one ravages your mind in support of her comrades.The audio design is striking; whether it be the clicking of voices, the horrific screeches of the infected, or the mechanical or otherworldly echoes, it is immersive. Music shines wonderfully, the mix of orchestra, classic music and brutal military tracks weave from one scene or action to next, setup with triggers to feel flowing and alive.Eldritch, twisted, and filled with tragedy, Siganlis is genuinely worth a journey or three into the depths of a place put back together wrong by someone who doesn’t understand.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the primary ways to classify literature, is whether it is prose or poetry. Prose is punctual, the story is usually clear and straightforward, with occasional twists and turns. Prose might move you emotionally one way or the other, but that way is predefined and as intended, by the writer. Meanwhile, poetry also conveys emotions, but the resulting state of mind is left up to each reader, because two readers of the same mind and at the same time, simply don't exist. I believe, the same classification can be applied to other art forms as well - for example, a beginner painter (also AI) "writes" prose, while a master painter paints poems... andIt is truly wonderful, knowing we've reached a point in the gaming industry, where we can play such ingenious works of art as Signalis is. No matter how you interpret its story (or 'message'), I don't believe you can play through the game, without several emotionally intense (or 'wtf') moments and whether you end up truly understanding the story or not, is in my opinion irrelevant. The story is amazing nonetheless, needless of one's understanding.As for the game play, it reminds me of old Resident Evil and Silent HIll games. Many mechanics are inspired by RE especially - corpse burning to avoid reanimation; very limited inventory resulting in strategic inventory management being a must; avoiding enemies that are unnecessary to deal with... these mechanics make the game difficult by default, and also inject you with a healthy dose of nostalgia, assuming you're older than 25 years old. The puzzles are quite witty, but not difficult enough for you to get stuck and break your immersion by requiring Googling.Fantastic animation and visual design in general, sound design is on par as well. So, all that's left is to ask - ? I would say, yes it is... most of the time. Combat can be a bit frustrating occasionally. There's no aim lock, so your character might shoot the ceiling instead of the bad guy's face or some other bad guy, who's standing in the line behind your target, which might not sound so bad... except when the guy in the front munches on your arm already. However, regardless of those insignificant hiccups, 10/10 easily.

_childDocuments_.review: SIGNALIS is a very good hard-hitting survival horror, ticking all the boxes for it to be one of the classics. The creators understand the genre well, and even manage to innovate with the occasional changes in perspective from isometric to first person for puzzles and some backstory parts, these are always a nice treat and are seamless in game. The world is very oppressive, both in terms of backstory and the events/gameplay, all of which add up to a great experience. The gameplay loop is quite straightforward, with the game being more of a resource puzzler, figuring out whether to commit resources to deal with an enemy temporarily, slip past them, or use items like thermite to kill them permanently. Much of this is reinforced by the highly limited inventory space, 6 slots, which does occasionally feel too restrictive when trying to explore. This is especially true during puzzle sections, as you cannot even drop one-use items to pick up necessary puzzle items. This can be planned for, but a significant portion of the game will just involve running from a room, back to the safehouse, swaping out items, and then going back again. The game does offset this with quite a generous healthbar, and making it through the game with minimal deaths isn't too difficult as long as you're treating the game like a horror puzzle game, rather than a shooter.The story errs just on the side of too difficult to fully understand, which is going to be part & parcel of the non-linear narrative and the fact much of the game exists in metaphorical and/or liminal space, but all the same I still have a fairly weak grasp of the overall narrative despite finising the game and trying to find everything. SIGNALIS also requires the player to decode radio signals into SSTV images to obtain the true ending. I don't even mind this as a requirement, as the radio is a constant puzzle-solving companion throughout the game, and it's possible to figure out the relevant radio frequencies as clues in the game, but the game provides no clue that these signals need to be decoded in such a way. Even ignoring this, what I find most aggregious is that the game provides no in-game tool to decode the signals. I find this especially confusing given the game even provides an in-game camera (which takes up an inventory slot) to take photos of puzzles, but requires external tools to solve an ARG game to get the 'true' ending. This is an unreasonable step, breaking immersion & player expectations, and locking 99.9% of players out being able to fully complete the game unassisted. If the game included a way of decoding the signals (say, the massive radio set present at the start and end of the game), then this could be forgiven, but as is this is just too much of a requirement.Overall 9/10, would thoroughly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: An incredible game that is terrifying, heartbreaking and absolutely gorgeous all at once. I loved the art style, and the cutscenes were beautifully animated, the gameplay is a lot like the classic Silent Hill games, bearing similarities to the combat and the honestly mind bending puzzles, and it had a story that was filled with so much emotional weight, as well as symbolism and depth to the world, characters and plot that makes me fully confident calling this game a work of art.
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: Signalis is definitely one of the best works of art I've ever had the pleasure of playing. From sound design, to art, to the areas you explore and to the enemies that block your path, everything in this game feels like it fits together perfectly, making an incredibly memorable package. It also has some of the best soft-worldbuilding I've seen in gaming, and the story that accompanies this is also touching and something that I won't forget. Thank you, everyone who worked on this project!
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: Growing up I've always been terrified and stressed out about horror games, and I initially saw this game, and while I was very interested in it, I didn't know for sure if I could play through it with this prior fear that I've had. Playing through Signalis I had that fear, and unsettling tense feeling throughout the entire game, but never beyond what I could comfortably handle. This game Single-handedly shocked me with how compelled I felt to continue on, to check every corner, to read every note, to try and make sense of it all. Even if you don't like horror, but love deeply complex stories that have no "Right" interpretation, then this game was made for you. Overall this game really took me by surprise, and I am so engrossed and in love with the story characters and themes presented by Rose-Engine and the game as a whole that I've spent so much time already breaking down all the details that stood out to me. This game is a masterpiece of it's genre and well worth the play for the experience alone. I wish I could wipe my brain just to experience it again for the first time.
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: Wow...What do you even say that hasn't been said a million times already about this masterpiece. Such an incredible atmosphere and depth. It's just dripping with details and thought put into everything. I loved everything about this game, even though i sucked balls at the combat, it was fun and stressful, adding to the claustrophobic atmosphere in the tight corridors of the mining facility. Very mysterious storytelling and characters, there is probably a million theories as to what is going on since everything is so cryptic, so i'll just spend some time absorbing the vibes everyone else got, and see how they compared to mine. Really clever puzzles with great clues to help along, this game was one of those where i keep a google doc up on the second monitor and write down my theories along the way and take screenshots of things for puzzles or write down clues i'll need. It's so enjoyable to just have something smart to sit with where you know the game isn't babying you. Highly recommend everyone gives this a shot even if you don't like horror. It's a great game that everyone should play.

_childDocuments_.review: Signalis clinically executes on the classic survival horror gameplay formula. Everything from the limited inventory, to the fixed camera angle, to the puzzles and backtracking is done as well as it’s ever been done. I really don’t have that much to say about Signalis’ gameplay. If you’re familiar with the formula, playing Signalis is like slipping into a new but invitingly familiar survival horror sleeping bag.Where Signalis differentiates itself is in its themes, atmosphere, world-building, and story. I’ve played Signalis twice now and I feel closer to understanding the basic concepts of this fictional world but much of the specifics about our characters remain shrouded in mystery. Signalis pulls inspiration from many sources: Alien, Blade Runner, Ghost in the Shell, The Shining, Resident Evil, Silent Hill, the list goes on… The truth remains however that Signalis is more than the sum of its influences. Not once do these influences pull you out of the experience. It’s quite the opposite. I believe Signalis’ strengths are its fully realized lore and the unique worlds it has created for itself.Signalis is a must-buy for any survival horror fan. I think it’s an instant classic. Oh, and it runs and plays great on the Steam Deck.
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: So I quit this game early. People loved this game. Everything I saw indicated that I would love it too. And to start out, I did!It has a cool scifi setting that I'm pretty sure is somewhat inspired by the works of manga artist Tsutomu Nihei, with some obvious Lovecraft influences (one of the first objects you interact with is a copy of The King In Yellow). It also has a very neat retro polygon graphical style.So when it originally launched the game had a thing people complained about a lot. You only had 6 inventory slots. Survival horror games are known for inventory management being important but 6 was just not enough for even a lot of the most diehard fans from what I've seen online. So they addressed this in a recent update.But... the puzzles. The puzzles.See part of the reason this inventory limit was a problem was the puzzles. See there's some really good puzzles in this game. But then there are others that require you to trek across the area a lot to collect multiple items to use in a single puzzle. Like the best comparison I can think of is getting out of the police station in RE2. Now imagine you did that, but with only enough inventory space to carry one weapon at a time, only to get into another police station. But in THIS police station there's a puzzle that requires you to solve a puzzle using a cypher pieced together from a letter from the desk sergeant's niece.The story and the world are compelling, but about halfway through the game I found myself just mechanically following a walkthrough and realizing: I was not enjoying this.To be 100% honest I'd urge you to check out other reviews because I'm SURE this is just a game that is not for me.I remember one of the Silent Hill games including an option for puzzle difficulty, which would solve a HUGE complaint here for me. But I also don't think this is something that the devs should be forced to do here.
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: Review of July 2024 version, since the game has seen updates.Technically competent, with some minor bugs.The art design intent is to look like early 3D games, especially those on PS1 with muddy textures, wobbly polygons, pixels, and general low-fidelity.A CRT display filter and film grain is available if that interests you, though I had them off.3D/2D in-game artwork is good, including 1st person interactable sequences, and meets the intent.2D out-of-game artwork, like some cutscenes and portraits just don't look good, even though it technically fits the in-game artwork.Japanese-style character portraits and cutscene artwork suffers from pixel aesthetics and oversimplicity, and give an amateur feel to otherwise good work.UI is OK but slightly annoying, because I would often trip over the many menu interactions in the inventory, map, and equipment screens.If you are coming for a story, you may be disappointed.I was expecting to have a reasonable story to follow, so I was disappointed when it was really, really poorly told.I think too much inspiration was picked from prior art and it really didn't belong.Basically it tried too hard, and the sum is worse than the parts.Even with all the story items scattered through the game, it never forms something cohesive that you can understand as you play.After completing a single pass and spending 10 hours, I couldn't retell the story because it's that confusing.This is likely why so many "lore" articles and videos seem to exist for the game, which is absurd and mostly conjecture since some details are totally missing.On a touchier subject, if the story has gay female characters, that's fine, nobody cares.I can't assign sympathy points to the story for that.I would hope the writing was not planning to lean on that to escape critique and buff perception, and maybe it wasn't.Anyway, I probably won't be playing a second time, I'm 50/50 on this review, but have to go negative for the story and how it's told.

_childDocuments_.review: Signalis is an amalgamation of old sci-fi cosmic horror. The gameplay is inspired by classic survival horror games but it doesn't go anything beyond a homage. While it doesn't particularly do anything new, the game is rather short before the gameplay starts to become tedious. Despite its shortcomings in gameplay, Signalis more than makes up for it with its story. A kind of experience that stays with you long after you finish.Angel's Egg enjoyers will understand.Excited to see what rose-engine make next.

_childDocuments_.review: The PC version of SIgnalis is my third purchase of the game, I bought the other two for the Switch and my Playstation (I'm mainly a console gamer rip). This is by far one of the most emotionally investing and driving horror games I've ever played, and if you're a fan of other survival horror games, I can't recommend giving this game a try enough. The atmosphere and world-building are fun and informative to learn about as you progress, the puzzles are abundant, and the soundtrack is amazing. Arguably one of, if not THE, best examples of lovecraftian horror in a video game on the market. Plus, lesbians <3
_childDocuments_.name: SIGNALIS

_childDocuments_.review: Should be played for its just immaculate atmosphere, less so than its narrative direction or even its gameplay. SIGNALIS is such a gorgeous game, lighting is often stark and high contrast, making the games just brilliant fixed camera compositions stunning at times. While by design, the overly cryptic nature of the plot hadn't completely dissipated by the time the credits rolled. Like I got the broad strokes, of which I thought was quite interesting, its just little details that feel like my understanding of the what happened through kinda unstable,Especially with how this game petered out with the ending I got (the PROMISE ending), I was a little disappointed. Despite that, I liked it quite a bit and would recommend it for any fans of survival horror, sci-fi, or cosmic horror. As a fan of Resident Evil, an appreciator of Silent Hill, and an admirer of Mamoru Oshii, its feels like this game was made for me. Crazy how only two people made it. An incredible achievement, let there be no doubt.Give it a shot, its well worth your time.
