_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: All I know about football is you have a ball and two teams, and you're trying to get the ball into the other teams net. You also have goal keepers. That's literally it. SO this review will be from that perspective.Football Manager 2021 is the first FM game I've played, and honestly.... one of the first sports manager games I've played. I've always had an interest in them, even though I don't follow sports, but FM21 is my first jump in. So As a complete novice in every respect I jumped into FM21 with the head cannon of "I'm a stratagist in a massive army fighting against many other armies." This honestly did help me a lot to get to grips. I'm not learning a new sport, I'm learning something I'm familiar with.And teach is something that FM21 does... decently. This game is a text heavy. There is no voice overs, no videos, it's just text explaining all the text. It's honestly a lot to take in especially if you don't know what team formations are. What is a 2-4-4-2 tiki? I don't know. And there's hundreds of different formations. The game doesn't tell you what this is. But it does have a thumbs up to tell you "Hey, you're team is pretty well equiped for this formation. Use it."And that is one extremely nice thing about the management side of things. You can deligate off basically everything to the AI if you don't want to deal with it. Training, scouting, contract nagotiations, almost all of it can be given to the AI at any time and you can take it on any time. This creates a nice enviorment that you can focus on 2 things at once, and than introduce whatever next and it doesn't seem to really affect the team, at least not in any ways that new comers will notice.That being said there is a lack of explanation with some things. For instance, during the simulated matches, you watch from the side lines and can give out callouts. Things like praise, scold, ect. Now you would think praising the team after a goal would be a good thing. A nice "Awesome job guys! Keep it up!" but NO! Praising after a goal for some reasons lowers moral during the game. I've had them at great and drop to discouraged. I guess it's something to do with praise actually being something else and you need to wait to praise until the last quarter. There's no real in game explination, just people relaying what they've figured out.In terms of how welcoming this game is to new players I'd say it's pretty decent. The hardest things will be all the info related to the sport. Knowing what teams are good, what players are good, what formations are good, what skills to look for for whatever spot you're trying to fill. But it really does have that addicting managment simulator gameplay, so even if you don't like sports that much there's still a ton of depth to be found.However the absolute lack of sounds is a hit against the game. A lack of voice acting is sad, but no music, no sound effects when changing tabs or emails or anything is just... off putting. I cranked my volume thinking something was wrong, only for a match day to start with suddenly cheers and noises to blast through my headphones. It makes the game a really silent and boring time.Overall though I do recommend this game if you're a managment simulator fiend like me. Be it that you know every football player on the pitch today or you only know the ball goes in the net. There's a ton of depth and a very big and active community to help you along the way. It is a bit quite and doesn't fully explain everything to you, but it does a good job of getting it's teeth into you and holding you there.

_childDocuments_.review: It pains me to write this but after spending more than 400 hours I have to admit: it's a poorly designed game with artifical difficulty spikes designed to keep players engaged. You can be the by far best team in the league and you will always have a seasonal rival (undocumented in-game) which will keep the pace with you. You can be a heavy-weight in a small league and there will be a team which is not better than any other in competitions which will go with the same results as you. Worst part when the game decides that it should boost your real rival. I have just one example of it: playing in UPL with Shakhtar I managed to finish the season with 28 wins and 2 draws in the 30 games. Guess what was the gap with Dynamo Kiev? 2 points. The third place was like 20 points lower. A season before I lost the league to Vorskla - it had lost points in 4 games through the whole season and my only loss was to them. I had numerous finishings in previous seasons with different teams when on the last match day the leader was losing, my team coming second won and then the third team became the first on goal difference, winning 5-0 and scoring its last goal on the last minutes in injury time. I get that it happens in football, see Man City and Aguero, but not in the course of couple of seasons in a row.Apart of that the game is addicting as ever although SI doesn't care for bug fixing (top managers have like perpetual contracts, in my 15 season save Simeone, Conte, OGS, Pochettino and Flick ALL were managing their starting cubs) and their UI designer clearly hates people - I can't find any reason to make the UI overloaded mess in dark purple color. In 2021 SI didn't even care to add additional skins leaving it to fans. Really, you become so lazy? You had to tweak a couple of lines of code to do that.Match engine looks much better until you realize that it relies heavily on the patterns. If you get that patterns, you can exploit it, and if you want to keep it natural you will face artificial difficulty spikes. Maybe in 2000s it was the same, I don't know, it all felt like an unscripted free flow and now you can guess the outcome of episode 90% times the 3D field appears.Tactics make no sense, as you can't play defensive football relying to soak the pressure - it's instantly punished by the opposition. Players with 5 in long shots suddenly pull of Roberto Carlos if you play defensive and there is no way to explain it but the match engine flaws. If the game decides that it's time to score, it will score. To play attacking you should do counter-intuitive things (deep defensive line and low pressure against the last team in a league is a must or you will be heavily beaten with the magic 30-meter screamers).On top of that you have the SI community forums with extremely gatekeeping audience which is intolerable to any criticism of their game. Moderators delete negative comments claiming they welcome meaningful discussion and constructive criticism. Like, I'm a paying customer who gets banned for stating that I'm not that happy with what I've payed for. In all my years online I've never seen more toxic and hostile community - even Reddit is friendly and supportive in comparison. Think twice before sponsoring it. I was a big fan of FM in 2005 - 2012 editions, I haven't really played for 8 years and I had over 700 extremely frustrating and unrewarding hours in 2020/21 versions. I won't buy it before they fix the UI and fire their UI designer. I can't possibly recommend the game which is made with the goal to frustrate the players and encourage exploits.

_childDocuments_.review: Football Manager 2021 hasn’t really rocked the boat in terms of enhancing the matchday gaming experience from last year. Games are as  difficult as ever to manage, and the minutiae of detail is just as overwhelming as always. Rather than a complete overhaul, there are numerous minor tweaks in Football Manager 2021, affecting tactical exploration and simulation. This time around, energy levels in particular seem to play a greater role, presumably to combat previously effective pressing tactics. In other words,  you can’t rely on your tried-and-tested methods from last year to get by.Football Manager 2021‘s biggest change seems to come in the way that you, as a Manager, communicate. Gone are the meaningless emotions while addressing people; instead, your decisions are broken down into what really matters. While talking to players, the boardroom or press, you can respond in a much more clear way. You’ll be able to choose from responses that are positive, negative, convincing, or even backing down. Better yet, the intended meaning of everything you say is clearly laid out.The communication overhaul really adds a lot to how you are judged as a manager in Football Manager 2021. Yes, results are still important, but you can really change the parameters of what your personal success is. If you aren’t doing especially well but are achieving the promises you have set out, you will be given more time.This happened to me; in my first season of managing, I had slightly underachieved. But because I had delivered on my promise to repair the financial damage of the over bloated squad, I wasn’t kicked out at the end of the season where I might’ve been in previous instalments. The next season, having been able to gain control of the finances, I was able to cultivate success. This is a new experience for me in a Football Manager game; a series I’ve been playing for over a decade. While I may have improved the finances of a club before, I have never overtly communicated my goals to the boardroom and insisted on time to deliver.Football Manager 2021 has done something that great managers do: it has acknowledged its weaknesses and improved upon them without completely rocking the boat. It still feels truly familiar as a Football Manager game, but the overhaul to expectations and communication makes for a more coherent and impactful experience. There’s more of a focus on what you say and do in your role as a manager and, over seasons, your performance is better judged. It makes a real difference to how the game can play out. The matchday experience may not be massively improved, but the improved focus elsewhere makes a real difference. For anyone who truly likes to get into the role of manager, Football Manager 2021 is a must.

However, there are still annoying bugs that irritate me, the main ones being:-Wingers running at goal from out wide, electing to shoot from the tightest of angles rather than pass.-Attacking players ballooning headers miles over the bar from point blank range for no apparent reason.-Players inexplicably running at half pace and losing out on a ball which even your 90 year old nan could get to.The changes in how player fatigue is shown seems unnecessary, as the hearts have replaced the more detailed and faultless percentage system. Now for what has really annoyed me: player attributes/ development: - I have bought various highly rated youngsters for my Liverpool team and NONE of them have improved whilst at my club. In fact they have all declined substantially, despite me giving them adequate match experience, having near perfect training facilities/ coaches and also strong mentoring groups. However, young players at other clubs seem to improve dramatically, despite their training facilities and coaches being of a poorer standard and the players competing at a lower level. - Another issue is the fact that players ability to dribble always decreases by around 3-4 points as soon as they hit age 27 for some weird reason. Is this a bug or based on real life?- The little green arrows next to a players attributes never seem to noticeably correspond to an increase in stats, however, if a red arrow appears, the attribute will usually decrease! Is this a bug?- Individual training has no effect on a players attributes! For example a player will often train on defensive positioning yet their positioning rating will then decrease! Please get back to me on these issues, as its ruining the game for me.Finally, the same bug that has annoyed me in the last 5 iterations of football manager: Player transfers. PSG, Barca, Real Madrid, Man City and Chelsea seem to throw hundreds of millions of pound around like confetti, UNLESS its for one of your players, in which case they will low ball you with an offer which is half the players market value! _childDocuments_.review: I think most people know what they are getting into with a Football Manager game. The question really is if this is a version worth upgrading to if you are still playing an older version and are content with it. The answer is a resounding "yes".We all know how great Football Manager has always been at what it does. What we really want is to waste less time in the transitions from one day to the next, when searching players, saving the game, and everything else, so we can spend that time actually playing the game. Great news! The performance in Football Manager 2021 is so much better than previous Football Manager games that makes the entire experience significantly better. No longer will you be waiting on a frozen UI to load up the database while searching for players and staff. This should have frankly been done years ago but better late than never. The UI in general feels faster, snappier and more responsive than ever, and this is while playing with a huge database (122k players). This is not restricted to the search view, it is true for everything. Moreover, this version makes players last longer, which is more akin to real life modern football. Players no longer decline as fast as they did in the past. There are 36 year old players with great fitness that still have great acceleration and pace. A huge thumbs up, this is easily the best version of Football Manager so far.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a long time fan of SI's Football Manager games. They are by far the best in the market for football managing sims. Unfortunately, years have caught up to the software and it evolved into something else.First, huge props to programmers having to deal with 20 years of legacy code, dubious frameworks and all other challenges of preserving and upgrading this enormous project. Development cycle of these games isn't long enough for meaningful changes and bug fixing. It's very hard to come up with something new, implementing it and having it completely tested on a yearly basis which could lead into things getting very stale and unexpected exploits appearing. There are also problems bleeding from one yearly version to next and so on.These games suffer mostly from years and years of problem solving and innovating for the sake of innovation and bigger sales. Because of many overpowered exploits, or sometimes need to bring something new each year, things get overly complicated and some features get gutted. For example, in older versions corners were overpowered, so to make them more realistic we now have set piece routines that need to be set up before every single match if you want to have a chance at scoring them. Of course, you can save those routines but they are dependent on your players that you rotate almost every single match every season. Training was very simple and somewhat effective, but to add some sauce it got reworked and now it's kinda impossible to mold players to your will, improving specific attributes needed to take them to a new level. Meanwhile AI has almost free reign in developing their wonderkids. "Realism" is used at will to justify many creative decisions. Yet FM presents unrealistic scenarios all the time. Not only in match engine, but for example with man management. Would a player with loyal personality throw a fit after bid from a barely higher reputable team gets rejected? Would professional personalities try to turn whole dressing room against manager for not getting a contract they required with astronomical demands? To me at least, fun is much more important than the realism.The challenge of FM games can be as difficult as you wish. Everything is possible with enough time and dedication. There are pre-made tactics which are so overpowered you don't even need to build any, if that's how you wish to manage. As time passes the games sadly boil down to recruitment (having better players than the rest) and going through the same motions which is inherently the biggest flaw of designing games like these. Unfortunately they will eventually become a chore regardless of how fun the challenge started. My frustration mostly comes from encountering same irritating things that kill the fun for me:I've probably missed many other things but it's the gist of it. These games are great to scratch the itch but over time they got overly complicated and time consuming. In older versions you could easily do a season in one sitting while this one simply eats time like a candy. Aside from that FM21 is plagued with flaws. bugs and uncreative substitutes to move the problem from one thing to another.

_childDocuments_.review: I was skeptical as I'd never played a true "management sim" before, though I do like soccer in real life and also have played EA's FIFA most years. This game has me hooked - I never thought I would be well over 100 hours in to be honest but it is very well done and has a crazy amount of depth. I've also learned a great deal about soccer because of it. Something to note is that you can automate all the parts of running teams that you don't enjoy e.g. transfers, match day's, lower tier team management, etc. This makes it easy to pick up and work your way into controlling more of the day to day as you get comfortable. Really great game, would absolutely recommend.The most underrated and rarely mentioned part of this game is the match day engine that actually allows you to influence and watch your players in real time as they face the other teams on game day. It's full 3d and looks pretty good. I've now played some other management sims e.g. Out of the Park Baseball and they don't even come close to actually making the matches/games look good compared to FM21. The FM21 match engine is one of my favorite features and is very rewarding after you've spent hours before each match tweaking your lineups and tactics to see your players in real time do their best to bring your side the win. I find myself watching full matches now sitting on the edge of my chair and shouting at my players both in real life and in the game when they make mistakes or celebrating when they find the back of the goal. Absolutely would recommend.

More options with agents, etcI know it has been a tough year and this may well have had an impact but when you compare this to say F1 2020 which is probably the strongest entry in the franchise - yep its improved the glitzy side but the driving side is also far better and far more realistic on the AI front - unfortunately FM21 is leaning more towards the Madden NFL21 where the major criticism has been that its been made to look better but with no real improvements. I want to like the game and I may well change the review if after the Beta there are some improvements but at the moment it looks like a lazy attempt for either a cash-grab or because the public demand an FM game every year when realistically this one could have waited til next year.I hope I'm proved wrong.update after over 100hrs of gameplay...........No......I was right..........Glitches galore. No live league table showing. That whole interface is awful as sometimes is shows 1 game about 3 times in a row. Crashes frequently. Can't find online games most of the time, More moans........Takes a non-league club who are worse than your average over 50s pub side over three weeks to offer you a job.......presumably the bag loads of applications took ages to sift throughDefending and defensive positioning is literally about to cause me a cranial aneurism. some of the mistakes makes Croydon v Arsenal ladies cup final that made Gray and Keys wet themselves look like a competent match of football.......god I can't say anymore......its just depressing me.........Last 5 games I played before I quit the job and went off to play Red Dead again to get some enjoyment.......drew 2, lost 5.........Over the 5 games I had over 90 shots, of which 39 were on target......scored 2 goalsThe oppo had 13 shots on target and scored 7 goals................not playing the offside trap. tight in defence, no stupid mentality.........yeah........realistic this game.Worst version of FM for years........by a very very very very long way.update after another 20 hours..........Last 5 games: 107 chances, 43 on target, 6 goalsLast 5 games oppo: 33 chances, 12 on target, 5 goalsWell done Miles........great effort sunshine..........sigh

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoy the game and love football, however, the game is far too easy, havent played a fm game in years so decided to pick it up. I won every competition with arsenal 4 seasons on the trot, played with millwall and got them promoted top of the league then won the premier league first season then the champions league straight away, with dortmund i didnt lose a match for the two seasons i played. I do have a decent understanding of football tactics but surely this shouldnt happen. I have played an arsenal campaign 5-6 times and always win everything first season in, even with minimal squad changes. I did the 5 main leagues in one career and managed to win the champions league in my first season with each club.The game really feels far too easy making it relatively boring once you know what youre doing, many interactions feel like pointless clicking. I struggled to find competition from the ai and had to abandon a lot of saves as the AI didnt provide much competition. Gestures seem pointless as once you work it out you just click the right 2-3 eventually becoming a bit of a chore and boring. Would be nice to see more negative things happen with the team off field in order to balance the ease of everything(outside of injuries). Would be good if they could make use of several  tactics instead of setting one up and beating everyone with it(certain formations should overpower others more like in rl so that you actually have to 'manage' the team).I know licensing is an issue but i shouldnt have to delete files just so german players can play in  the german team etc. Being honest the main leagues and main nations are most important, name changes dont upset me too much but national teams with random generated players is just a joke when they come from major footballing nations.I like the menus and the tactical analysis, I just wish the game was more difficult so i would feel bothered to actually look at it. If its the tactics i created that were overpowered then they should be balanced more as i was using common tactical approaches which are seen throughout modern as occasionally classic football. I find it to be a game that can be very enjoyable when a competitive element exists but winning constantly with ease becomes boring very quickly. Gegenpress with majority of tactics is too overpowered, it needs to be in the game as it is a common tactical approach but should have some weaknesses in game surely?Overall the game can be very enjoyable but if you understand football, especially the tactical element the game becomes far too easy, big clubs or even decent sized clubs are too easy to manage also. Supposedly a realistic simulator although i am yet to see it.

_childDocuments_.review: Football Manager 2021 is a game that truly shines with its Match Engine. It's been a true joy to see my team grow and develop under my guidance.Despite the many hours I've put into this game, I find myself continuing to come back to it again and again. It's just that addictive! I love the depth and complexity of Football Manager 2021, and the fact that there's always something new to discover keeps me coming back for more.My only disappointment with Football Manager 2021 is that there isn't much competition in the football management game genre. name: Fights in Tight Spaces
detailed_description: Card-Based Tactical Fighting! Fights in Tight Spaces blends deck-building, turn-based tactics, and thrilling animated fight sequences in classic action-movie settings. Learn to balance your hand, momentum, and positioning to overcome the odds to defeat your adversaries. Pick from over 200 cards as you build a deck to suit your play style and your opponents’. Encounter random events, acquire enhancements (or injuries), and make critical choices about how best to upgrade your agent for the fights ahead. Features: Control the Space: Use the environment against your adversaries Train your Abilities: Build a deck to suit your play style, upgrade your moves, and equip your agent with a range of enhancements Protect High-Value-Targets: Use your skills and abilities as you act as bodyguard to VIPs Endless Threats: With a new mission each time your play, evolve your tactics, unlock new possibilities, and perfect your strategy to defeat the criminal underworld Prove your Worth: Embark on a daily mission and compare your scores to other players on the online leaderboard Summary In an era where espionage is handled largely by data-packets being pored over by teams of analysts, Section Eleven’s approach is more hands-on, dealing with the sorts of criminal organizations who live and operate outside the realms of electronic communication. When the rest of the intelligence services have failed, they call Section Eleven. As a Section Eleven agent, it is your job to find direct solutions to emerging threats… largely by smashing people’s faces into things.

_childDocuments_.review: As an early access game it's pretty polished. It works. It has a fair amount of content at its disposal for an EA title. Graphically it's bottom of the barrel but I guess that's a design choice. Can be hard on the eyes to anyone who has issues staring at bright white for long periods of time.The TL:DR version of why I don't recommend it is it's taking a long time for them to make progress on the game. It has some stuff but not enough to really keep me invested long term. There isn't enough diversity in the starting decks and some of the cards really need rebalanced to make them more viable. Just wasn't enough on the plate to keep me wanting more out of the game so I probably won't be playing it until many many updates later.For those die-hards still reading there is one other reason, slightly longer winded, that I will add below.I'm not recommending it because the development is pretty slow and there are some odd mechanics in the games card draw system that I find questionable. If one card draw is questionable then they all are. What I mean is you will always draw a movement card regardless of chance. Someone else already tested it but I was seeing it in game for a while and chalked it up to chance and the fact that I would take movement cards almost any time they were offered. What will happen is if you destroy all movement cards but a few and you have like a 30 card deck you logically shouldn't have a movement card for a long time. What the game does to compensate for that is it pulls a movement card out of your discard pile and gives it to you repeatedly every turn. Not sure I like that. What other hidden mechanic is it screwing us over with? Don't know. This isn't exactly a negative mechanic as it gives you a chance over the computer but it's still not right. It seems like a band-aid solution to a problem they don't know how to fix yet or offer an alternative to. If that function of the game is bandaided then they have to fix a few other things in the game before I'd trust it.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game.  You know that time you watched the corridor scene in 'old boy' and thought: 'hey! that would make a great turn based strategy game!'   Well, neither did I but after playing this, I should have.  Because reliving your favorite action scenes and turn based strategy apparently is a match made in heaven, when it is done as well as here.  This is the quintessential 'easy to learn, hard to master' game.  At first you are avoiding and blocking punches with the starter pack of cards.  Just surviving room to room.  Next thing you know, you are using the number of assailants against them, throwing them against each other or making them shoot one another, as you move, kick, punch and counter like a bruce lee baryshkikov around the small confines of the room you are currently in.  Like all great games, it borrows from the best (superhot, slay the spire, into the breach) and then mix all that with its secret sauce to make a new, beautiful thing.  Now, if you will excuse me, I need to go avenge myself on the guy who kicked me in the back while I was busy punching that annoying tank with the fire sprout.  EAT MY FIST!
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this nervous_testpilot album and there was a really, really good fighting card game attached to it!I want to write more but honestly that sums up how I feel about it; I've been a massive fan of Mode7's own games and Paul's music in particular. holding them up as some of the best the games industry has to offer. I'm really happy that they're publishing games that live up to that standard.I was intrigued by the idea of using a card deck like this by Metal Gear AC!D back in the day, and I absolutely loved those. They were weird, but I think they came around at a time the PSP needed them, and I didn't see a reason why it couldn't work! The fact it's a Roguelike escaped me until I realised I needed to heal between fights and that it was a conscious choice between that or upgrading cards and so on, but in the end it works out nicely. Oh and the soundtrack is incredible. Paul has this tendency to make music that doesn't react to the gameplay, which has its place in the games they make and publish. It's fairly out of the way of what he's done for games and general listening, but I think he adapted well! There's a good amount of the much-loved nervous_testpilot noises in there to make me loop it repeatedly, which I'm still doing with the Frozen Synapse 1 soundtrack!The only thing I could ask for is a date for when Agent 11 is confirmed for Smash Bros. Good thing I don't have Twitter so I can't be groaned at for that one ;P

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good twist on a turn based card based game. It's a little repetitive, mainly due to the levels repeating themselves, after a few runs you've seen all the permutations. There are, however, a good range of cards that all have utilisation in a deck; depending on how you build of course. Not sure on the longevity of the base game as yet but I'd recommend it if you like these types of game and are looking for something well polished.The only real criticism I have is that it seems to be really poorly optimised and trying to use my full GPU to run at 300fps.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very absorbing puzzle game with nice stylistic flourishes. I think I expected it to be more fluid/dynamic, but it's very much play a card at a time and see what the results are, and that didn't bother me at all once I got into it. It's very satisfying to play 'a perfect round' where you do maximum damage and take no hits.

_childDocuments_.review: Fights in Tight Spaces is a strategic, deckbuilding, roguelite brawler. That's a mouthful! Try saying THAT fast ten times. Each turn, you draw cards that you can use to attack your enemies, defend yourself from them, and move around the board. It's quite nice that you can push and throw your enemies around, and even your strikes will push them and move you forward or backward. There's just a lot of variety in the kinds of attacks you can do, and so there are a handful of movesets to choose from before you start a run. You could also draft your own deck if you so choose.There are five stages filled with several levels, and like every other roguelite, you can choose which paths to go on depending on how you want to build your fighter. You can increase your health and heal your injuries at medical facilities, learn new moves, upgrade existing moves, or even discard some moves at the gym, and each battle arena you choose from comes with its own variety of rewards. This ranges from currency to spend at the aforementioned medical facility or gym, free health healing if you can protect a high value target, and you can even increase your maximum capacity to play more cards and build up combos if you reach a certain criteria in the fight.I can geek out forever just describing plainly how the game is played, but I'll just say it's solid through and through. The only gripe I have is that some runs can drag on a bit because the last couple stages' amount of missions are a little too much. They could have benefited from being trimmed down by even just 1/4 the amount. Roguelites are supposed to short and fun experiences, and despite of how engaging the core gameplay is, having to play a full run from start to finish could take up to 1h30m to 2 full hours.Maybe better players can do it quicker, but I've yet to do less than maybe 1h20m, but that was on a failed run. You could even start the campaign in a later stage, but the big drawback is that you won't have as many upgrades as you would if you start from the very first stage.All in all, though, super solid game with catchy music and very punchy sound design. Every hit and slam literally packs a punch. Pardon the double punch pun, but that's just how powerful the game's animation and sound design are put together. If it weren't for the strenuous length of the campaign, this would be perfect. Along with being able to choose my own angles or even customize my own camera movements for the Post Fight Replay option. Yeah you can watch your fights happen in real(ish) time with the Replay, but sometimes the camera is placed too far or behind an obstruction and it really ruins the action.But yeah I tend to babble in these reviews, and I'm hyperaware of that, and I really do try my best to keep it concise. But if I really really love a game, honestly, I just can't help it! I've always a got ton to say! And for Fights in Tight Spaces, let this lengthy and detailed review be my ringing endorsement for it!
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Once again I gotta say that this game has got all the right flavors. That spicy combat mixed in with that flavorful combat oriented randomness makes for a meal that will tingle your taste buds. Now they have added even more fighting areas and more combat cards making this plate of food even more zesty. Overall this meal is a 10/10 and I will continue to devour it anytime I have free time. See you guys next time on Diners, Drive-ins and Dives!
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: What if Metal Gear Acid took out all the lengthy moving about, and was instead like a high action John Wick fight scene? Well... it wouldn't be very Metal Gear-y, would it? But, it WOULD be very reminiscent of Fights in Tight Spaces!Fights in Tight Spaces (That's a ♥♥♥♥♥ to keep typing, I'm gonna just call it FITS, now)FITS, is kind of addicting in it's simple gameplay, and deep deck building elements. As Agent 11, you are trained in every way of combining tasty fist, with supple jaw. With 1,001 ways to push someone's teeth down through their anus, you are tasked with a handful of Secret Missions that take you from Biker Bars to Yakuza Strongholds. Once in the field, FITS becomes a procedural Rouge-like adventure. This, plus random card unlocks will ensure you're never going to have the same run twice. That said, it can be frustrating to go hours into a run, only to find out you didn't pull enough spank attacks to counter Spanky, the Spanking Clown Demon, or something. For a rouge game, the campaign really takes a hell of a minute. There are about 6 missions, and they're pretty lengthy. If you don't get a modifier to increase the amount of cards to play in a single turn, it drops down to the speed of floating across a swimming pool propelled only by your own farts. I think the game is way too ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hard. Even on the easiest difficulty, I haven't beaten it yet. The RNG and insane enemy ramp up late game is pretty unbalanced in my personal opinion. Stage 4 onward is just a big turd in the punchbowl. The enemies that just counter every single attack from each direction are a particular pain up my ass. The shotgun lads that turn to face you from every side when you try to move around them and the ones with reaching attacks that get to follow you for free are almost impossible to out maneuver. And on top of that, the developers have the gall to tell me each of these levels can be completed in like... what 3 turns? Dude... come on! Ease this ♥♥♥♥ up so I can at least beat the game I paid for. I know people say games need to be challenging, but I also want to SEE the ENDING some day. Maybe boost my stats a little as the game goes on, so I'm not tickling the balls of my enemy for 4-6 damage before sucking off the end of their shotgun? I want to love this game so damn bad! I have sunk hours upon hours into Fights in Tight Spaces, but only 60% of it is even fun. Once I get to the point where every enemy has so many additional perks and buffs, along with tons of boosted stats, I just don't even want to keep going. There is such a gem hidden in here, but I'm sick and tired of trying to FIND it. This may be one of the biggest potential favorite games I've ever grown to hate. I'm trying my absolute best, but I cannot make a dent in even beating the game... on the easiest difficulty!

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful hand to hand violence in a turn-based card world~ FiTs is a breath of fresh air, yet with enough roguelite/genre familiarity.Graphics and UI is very clear, color coded to perfection. _childDocuments_.review: For a game that just started Early Access, it's very promising!It's a less complicated deckbuilder which satisfies the itch to think around tactical combat and interactions, but doesn't become too demanding. It strikes a fine balance which works well. Think Into The Breach but more relaxed.The Gameplay's pretty fun and surprisingly polished. I also adore the animations, the soundtrack and the visuals. The game is being well-made.However, you can feel that it's unfinished. All it needs is more time to develop.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: The bones are strong, but the muscle is still weak. This edgy-sounding line kind of sums up everything about this game. It has so much potential and the game system itself is fun and stylish. It has potential slathered all over it, and those are the bones.The muscles have some problems. The black-on-white color scheme is visually striking, but the overabundance of white can make your eyes want to melt after a while. There are multiple balance issues such as random events being more dangerous than beneficial. Enemy placement at start combined with the enemy getting to move first means you might be completely surrounded and screwed before you can even take your first turn. Add in the expected early version bugs and card balance issues, and the issues can really add up.I'd give this game a neutral rating right now, but it's very early and most of the bug and balance issues can be fixed with minimal effort, so I'd recommend it in the long run.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10! One of the best games I have ever played, and most certainly my new favorite deck builder. The game-play is snappy and crunchy all at once. Every fight feels complex and challenging but still fair. The game is easy to learn and an absolute joy to improve at. The ability to draft your own starting deck and choose your game type is available from the beginning. Every section/mission feels unique and teaches a new nuance within the game. There is a HEFTY amount of cards to choose from which allow each run to feel like you are creating a new agent with their own skills. Losing a run never feels that bad. It is always because of a mistake you've made and chaining runs is always a good time.In the future I would love to see more content (new cards, enemies, levels, events, etc). I also think the game has potential for player created mission and enemies due to its visual style (which fits the game perfectly.)This is really great game and a perfect addition to your deck building collection.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: This game is made for lovers of:XCOM / Into the Breach / Slay the Spire-likeHats off for making such a beautiful blend of two different types of strategy games.The only thing I wish the developers look into is the replay feature. I don't speak for all strategy game players, but when I want to check whatever logs / replays available, I am looking for information instead of cool animations. So...why don't let us press ALT to check the information of enemies? Or a library of all unlocked enemies / cards would be good.

_childDocuments_.review: My hours may be fewer than I thought, but this game is the only puzzle game I have ever really enjoyed that wasn't portal or Helltaker. And the only ever deck building game I even paid a second glance to. When you get a deck that works - Just - right for your playstyle and managed to beat a boss it clicks wonderfully. That said, it is a puzzle game that evolves. No two scenarios are ever going to be quite the same and it plays a lot like chess in the sense it pays to think ahead. I have lost a few good runs because I failed to predict where my enemy was going to bound off to when I retreated backwards. Only to be cornered and struggling to get control back. However, when you do manage to wriggle out of a sticky situation you feel like a movie star or a tactical genius. I managed to reach the end level on my very first playthrough with an astounding amount of luck. It's not a hard game, per se, but it makes you think. And getting to see a whole mini movie of you knocking guys out cold at the end of each puzzle is just hilariously fun.

Deck management still needs some major tweaks because it still boils down to do you want to heal or do you want to make your deck better. _childDocuments_.review: I've had this game since it was available in early access on Steam. I'm glad I've waited until the full release to give a review. This game has been on a steady incline of quality, you can tell the developers are really trying to improve the game and make it fun. _childDocuments_.review: Incredibly fun, I haven't been this hooked on a deckbuilder since Slay the Spire and Across the Obelisk. Yes, it's the same sequence of levels and bosses each run, so I thought it would feel stale quickly, but the fights are very compelling and the builds are a lot of fun to experiment with. The animations and board manipulation make you feel like a complete bad-ass when the combo is working, and the game knows what its strengths are and just keeps serving up the action without any excess fluff. Alina of the Arena was another deckbuilder with spatial manipulation, but this feels like it flows more smoothly than that.Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is awesome! As much as I love fantasy stuff, it's a nice break from all the fantasy-oriented deck-builders and rogue-likes. _childDocuments_.review: So far, I’ve had a very mixed experience. All of the fun that comes while playing always seems to be sucked out by the game’s exasperating and often unfair difficulty. It's like someone looked at slay the spire and thought "The problem here is players are winning too much!" There’s been so many instances where I’ve just went, “Well that was f-ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. How? It gave me no chance!” It’s like the game doesn’t want to let anyone win. Maybe I'll change this to a positive recommendation after this game receives some serious balancing patches. Right now, wait for a big sale or wait until 1.0. Early Access: 5.5/10. Needs improvement, far too frustrating right now.Review after full release:This game remains completely unfair and unreasonably difficult even on the "easiest" difficulty. The balance is awful, and later levels are completely impossible. You will frequently be put up against enemies that will one-shot you, and have 100+ health, despite your best cards and combos rarely doing more than 12 to 20 damage at best. Not to mention, for some reason they decided to PUNISH players for doing well by taking away enhancements you have earned in your run, as if it needed to be harder! Events are still completely pointless, because you just get f-ed over 90% of the time. The demands of mission extras are so stringent that they are impossible to achieve in harder levels, and all of your rewards are minuscule. This game is unbelievably frustrating and every time I have tried to play it, I never enjoy it due to it's difficulty and unfair game design choices. It STILL just refuses to let the player win, to let the player be good. I would not recommend this game to anyone unless you just really like brutally difficult games that laugh at your frustration I guess. 1/10.

_childDocuments_.review: A tactics deckbuilder with a brilliant sense of style, this game is a fresh and addictive love letter to cinematic martial arts action. Fights in Tight Spaces is a true knockout in every way that matters.Those of you familiar with the likes of Into the Breach will recognize the format of each level. A collection of baddies spawn in and telegraph the moves they will execute next turn, leaving you to strategize a response. Unlike Into the Breach however, the emphasis is on dispatching enemies as opposed to defending objectives (although some "Rescue" levels spawn in a helpless NPC for you to protect).The glory of this game lies in the ever-evolving moveset dealt to you each round. Acrobatic kicks, brutal hand strikes, and evasive countermaneuvers file in each turn, and different starting archetypes emphasize distinct fighting styles such as counterpunching or knife combat. Not only does each string of moves link together in a truly awesome fashion, but win or lose, you have the option to watch a replay of the fight you choreographed (a smooth, briskly-paced blow-by-blow with the UI removed).There's a nice roguelike progression scheme that ties each individual fight together, forcing choices about what kind of fights to take on and when to stop for health and upgrades. The difficulty steps up at a fair clip, and the challenge is scaled well so that each fight could conceivably be your last. Multiple settings and game modes ensure that you can customize how forgiving Fights in Tight Spaces is towards your latest faceplant. The soundtrack is another point of pride, somehow suiting both moments of careful contemplation and juicy hand-to-hand combat.Aside from some minor bugs (most of which are brief, self-correcting visual mishaps that don't impact the gameplay), I'm struggling to think of any complaints I have with this plucky little badass simulator. I've had this on my Wishlist for a while now and it never seems to be on sale for more than a few dollars off, so you should be prepared to pay around $22 on the lower end (well worth it, mind you, but the indie scene's more generous sales have spoiled me a bit). Of course, it could always be expanded (more cards, levels, and enemies), but what's here is more than satisfying.Smart, snappy, and chock-full of superspy charm, Fights in Tight Spaces will have you throat-punching and frontflipping your way through hours of gameplay, and loving every second.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: You get exactly what's advertised: Fights in Tight Spaces.The game starts off very simple, but quickly gets very complex. Different enemy types, attacks, blocks, stuns, counters. buffs, debuffs. But you also don't have to think too much about all of this if you just want to have some fun. It's just satisfying to watch how enemies hit each other because you pushed them into the right place. Makes one feel smart even though your probably didn't even think too much about what you did.If you want there is a lot of room to really optimize your deck though. And considering how quickly the game gets harder, that's probably something you should think about if you want to progress. But the good thing here is that it doesn't get frustrating despite you losing very often. Especially as you still unlock new cards all the time.One thing I'd like to see improved are the replays though. Currently they seem a bit clunky and you still notice the breaks between turns. Would be nice if that could be improved with smoother transitions to basically look like a movie.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Very buggy atm, with real problems in the RNG department for now. Community is cancer, as with most cardbattlers, defending the one or two sh*tty design issues the game has, so no surprise there.That being said, it's rather well balanced, with good difficulties and rather interesting mechanics, ending up being an interesting hybrid between into the breach and classic cardbattlers.So why the thumbs down?For the price, there are just too many bugs. E.g. "throw 2 enemies off the building", yup did that, but target failed... interesting. Adding to that, I encountered several horrible performance issues (and I can play Elden Ring perfectly fine on second highest setting), softlocks and freezes in the short hours when I wrote this review and I can't say I'd recommend the game right now as it is. So I'd suggest you play the demo, and wait for a sale if you're really into it and maybe get it on sale. Maybe the devs will fix these issues, but seeing this game doesn't have a stellar playerbase, I would not expect it.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Well, as most (if not all) of the flaws I listed below are mostly adjusted,the game is at least pretty all right now.However, I do recommend playing it on Classic mode, where you are allowed to retake a fight when defeated.But, (as far as I remember) you can only retake a fight and not a mission, and only when you are defeated...Sometimes, you may want to die a few times to fight best and gain most in a fight.Well, I still really enjoy the fights as I did and said for the Prologue.And, to be honest, I am a bit nervous that it is too early for me to say my piece as I have only used 2 Deck, and played 2 missions...But, since this is Early Access, might as well do it early and change it later if necessary.Yes, if you happen to be the developer, this is meant for you!So, I am not going to include what I already said about the fights in the comment for the Prologue,But just some additional thoughts i had during playing this Early Access Version.As there are more decks and more importantly, missions, the flaws became clearer.Simply put, as a strategic card game, the deck building in this game is not satisfying.True, there are 4 decks with some difference. However, the difference are not quite significant.And, more importantly, the opportunity to modify my deck is limited.Sure, there are options to add card after a fight. Meanwhile, as i understand, player can only rearrange, or say remove cards at Gym. With currency.There isn't quite enough Gym or Currency. At least not in one mission.Which bring me to the next point.Currently, whenever I lose a fight, I lose all progress.Although, I can choose to go directly into the mission I once had access,Yet, just as the Developer warns, each mission is harder than before.And, It will be much harder to go directly into them, without the upgrades from previous mission.From my experience, it is at least still doable in mission 2, the Insider.But, it would be tough.On the other hand, if I already feel tired if i have to replay the first one to play mission 2...How would i feel when i have to redo all missions when I were in say, mission 5?!Therefore, I think there should be a function that allows player to save their modified deck,maybe even allow them to modify their deck in between mission.What if the deck got too strong?I suppose there are other fun or challenge, like some people may try to minimal their turns.And, when it got too easy, people will be bored, and they will still have the option to try conquering each mission with basic decks!Anyway, my point is just that, deck building should be at least one of the core of this  type of game,but right now, it isn't for this particular game.In addition to that, i think the possibility of upgrading is rather limited right now,like, each card has only one upgrade...Also, I saw someone mention the design for Counter cards are a bit strange.I agree.As far as i remember, when I use counter, the player character counters every incoming (that he can counter)While, the block only provide a certain exact, limited protection.They seem contradict.Personally, if one counter only works once, and when the character counters, it means he doesn't get hit and hence no damage would make more sense.Well, these are just some of my primary thoughts...I hope they can help make the game better.And, i certainly hope they can be helped!
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic Rogue-like Tactics game. I like deck-builders and I like tactics games, but I didn't realize how much I liked them together until this game.Pros:- Lets you break the game sufficiently to feel like you are at fault for 99% of your losses.- Difficulty considerations let you choose whether you embrace deck-building or the Tactics element of the game more. (like always getting a move from you deck whether you draw it or not to make it more Tactics than deck-building emphasis)- Several core builds leave many builds to explore- Draft deck building lets you go outside the core decks to get a fresh experience.Cons:- The enemy and map randomization is lite. All the maps were designed to be fun to play in with varying obstacle hazards which can make a section feel familiar.- No checkmate protection. On rare occasions enemy randomized positions will cause forced damage situations. So even with deck building elements minimized via difficulty options, if your deck is weak suffers from poor movement, low defense, low damage, or other mechanics, the positioning and enemies do not guarantee you will be able to survive an encounter (though it is 95% of the time trivial to suffer no damage). This might be a dealbreaker for Tactics genre fans.This is GOTY territory for me. Incredibly well done.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm gamedev myself and that's what I think  * Fighting roguelike overall is an interesting idea. Additionally, there are many interesting ideas, like building up combo, using obstacles (like jump off the wall), tossing enemies into their allies bullets and so on* Fights are like puzzles. You should use your surrounding, plan your moves  There are many problems:* It feels not very dynamic despite all cool mechanics* The main problem that many cards are pretty weak, amount of good strategies is very limited (for example, you cannot build counter-attack only, because you would have big problems with some enemies), permanent bonuses doesn't change gameplay much, so you're runs difference is based only on cards and, as I said, there are some problems with them* I particularly didn't like challenges in each battle. For each room you have set of 3 challenges, for example: win in n turns or push enemies 3 times which forces you to play as a game says, not as you want and also eliminates many builds not very agile to complete different challenges (you receive rewards for completing them, so they're very crucial for success). When I play rogue like games I enjoy building different stuff in runs, you know* Another problem that easier difficulties give you guaranteed movement card and I don't know why. If you wanted player to move in each round, you could make it a separate mechanic, not overcrowded his handSo overall, many problems  You can unlock new "agents" (different starting decks) and some cards. Nothing crazy, nothing terrible either Replayability is the weakest part of the game, while it's rogue likeThe problems that there are not many builds, almost no deck building and as a result it becomes repetitive pretty soonI got bored very quickly, and I personally would estimate possible play time to 5 hours. Concept great, but too many problems  Didn't encounter any bugs. I feel like UI could be better, it can be hard to tell what a card does, despite them having similar actions Worth mentioning (positive) - It's simply amazing. Cool design, smooth animationsWorth mentioning (negative) -  ❌ Challenging  ✅ Simple (minimalistic)❌ High entry threshold Great concept and amazing design, but has too many problems with gameplay and replayabilityFollow my curator page  for more reviews

_childDocuments_.review: Fights in Tight Spaces is a turn-based deckbuilder in early access. You are agent 11 and need to take out different gangs (Biker, Ninja, etc.). The game offers five missions, each with around 10 fights, four difficulty settings, four different starting decks, and a draft mode. Every mission ends with an end boss fight. On your way to the end boss, you will need to fight gang members, visit the gym or medical center or be part of an event. Events work just like in other deckbuilders (text-based with different options to choose between). The medical center is for you to heal or expand your max health while the gym will let you buy, upgrade or remove cards from your deck. For both, you will need money in exchange. Now let's talk about the fights. They are turn-based and you need cards to move around the grid, block, or attack. This is very typical in the genre. What's special about FiTS is how you use your environment combined with cards. Some maps have windows, etc. You can push enemies out of there to kill them. To do that, it needs a bit of tactical thinking and luck. Enemies have different abilities and you need to carefully analyze what they can and can't do to win. Each turn, you will see if and where enemies will attack. Aside from the generic attack, block, and move cards, there are some special cards to spice things up. Many cards need to meet criteria before being able to play. Some cards require the enemy to stand next to a wall, being down or your combo to be at 2, 3, or higher. Usually, these cards are very powerful because they are harder to play. Your combo gets higher by playing attack cards and goes down when moving instead of attacking.Combine all of this and the game's tactical depth is on a high standard. Nothing is more rewarding than pulling off enemies attacking each other and killing themselves that way. This is where the fun lies. After every fight, you can watch a video of it. This can be very fun, especially because the game is aesthetically very appealing. Draft Mode adds a lot to the game. This is like a draft mode in Magic, Hearthstone, etc. You get four random cards and need to take one of them. This will be your starting deck in the next run. Fights in Tight Spaces is in early access and already a gem in the genre. It's fun and addictive. It's easy to learn but offers a lot of depth. This is a game that deserves to be praised and called a strategy game for sure. Go get it if you're into turn-based strategy games!

_childDocuments_.review: Review based on the first main build in early access, and checking out the first raft of big changes.Fights in Tight Spaces is the slick, stylish cousin of Slay The Spire. For the moment, I've had my fill, with one successful run in 27 hours of play, but I'll absolutely be returning as the game evolves throughout early access.At its core, the game is a deckbuilding roguelike, similar to Slay The Spire. With some exceptions, cards generally deal damage or add block - so far, so similar - or move. This is the ace up FiTS' sleeve. The game takes place in 3D environments, and you and enemies close gaps, create distance and flank around each other. It's a - literal - extra dimension, creating new ways to play and new solutions to problems. By shifting your position and manipulating enemies, you can trick them into attacking each other while you escape unscathed.This is what makes FiTS so satisfying to play. There's an occasional thrill in Slay the Spire of racking up your Block to the requisite amount, but FiTS delivers moments like this so regularly. A stylish, perfectly timed slip past an enemy, pushing another into the path of an imminent bullet, and instantly killing a third by kicking them out of the arena is always a thrilling experience. The addition of 3D space as something to maneuver and manipulate makes FiTS an inherently enjoyable game.There are some issues - events are often dull coinflips rather than interesting decisions to be made, some numbers need to be tweaked as a block-and-counter build (the arguably most boring, least dynamic kind of build which leans the least into the movement play) is the most intuitive for success, and a run is ultimately too long. A successful run of FiTS has you play through five different 'chapters', taking nearly an hour each (or longer for the later chapters); while you can start on any of them, to start on anything other than chapter 1 is to heavily nerf yourself from the get-go.However, these are all things I have confidence the developer will hammer out over the Early Access period. Even the first big patch changed player upgrades from random chance to player choice, a single change that adds so much depth. There's an incredible base to build on already present and I have no qualms recommending you buy it during early access to experience its addictive, stylish play and support its development.
