_childDocuments_.review: At the time of this review, I am recommending this game solely off the fact that it is in early access. Were it to be full released in its current state, I would likely hold a very different opinion. That said, this game has a lot of potential to be really great, but there are some major systemic issues that I hope are fixed up before it leaves early access.This game feels like a slick child of Into the Breach and Slay the Spire, which is high praise from me, as these are two of my absolute favorite games, but I have had a neutral total experience with it in my 6 hours of play so far. On one hand, it has a very high ceiling, and tight play can have a great deal of reach, which is something I value, but on the other hand, at its worst, this game is obnoxious, slow and tedious.Here are a few suggestions:1. Remove currency as a bonus objective reward.The rate at which you earn money feels disproportionately low to costs overall. Earning $30 per fight when upgrades cost $25-$240, removing a card costs $80 and healing 15hp costs $40 discourages experimentation because you MUST try and get the bonus rewards in order to earn cash, meaning you must build your deck as efficiently as possible. Tying money to bonus objectives creates a compounding experience, both when winning and losing. While winning, it's not so much an issue, but while trying to recover from a rough run, it feels really miserable. Not being strong enough to achieve the bonus objectives in order to get the money to upgrade or remove cards feels bad. HP, AP and combo increases feel appropriate as bonus rewards, but the most fundamental resource in the game should be awarded for completing the primary objective.2. Your first heal should be free.This relates to the constrained resource flow. Narrowly winning a fight, then earning less than the cost required to heal a mere 15hp is terrible. 3. Ranged enemies need to be reworked.I keep finding myself in these really awkward situations where there is one ranged enemy remaining, and I spend 3-4 turns just strafing left and right because the game won't give me more than one or two movement cards in the same hand. The little dance around obstacles that you perform with the ranged AI is frustrating and boring, especially as you watch the timer tick out on bonus objectives. An easy fix to this might be to just by default allow the player to discard 1+spend 1 AP to move 1 space, which would make gap-closing far less of a chore.4. An Undo button.This game is more complex than other similar games as it functions on two totally dissimilar axes (The game stage itself and the cards) resulting in the player tracking far more moving parts than similar titles. Spending minutes thinking about a turn only to realize that you forgot that moving X to tile Y would trigger Z, and then having your whole plan fall apart because you missed a small detail is disheartening, and happens frequently. I'm not an ironman gamer; I don't hate savescumming; I'm a casual fan of the deckbuilding roguelike and tactical strategy genres and I would much appreciate a way of rolling back a neglectful or accidental play. As it stands, the game feels as though it's encroaching on a Darkest Dungeon in terms of being unforgiving toward the player, which might be enjoyable for some, but not for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: This is the most fun I've had with a strategy game in years. FiTS is a puzzle game, a fighting game, and a card game wrapped in a colorful yet mimimalist visual style. Anyone who's played the Batman Arkham games from Rocksteady will appreciate the timing and logic required for moment-to-moment, close quarters, group encounters during each card-based tactical fight. Unfortunately, there are some annoying design decisions, like being unable to save custom decks (you'll unlock really fun cards over time, but you'll almost never get to use them due to the automated deck-building mechanics). You owe it to yourself to try this game, it's really unique.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: If you like card games, tactical battles, and roguealikes you cannot go wrong with this game. It's a very satisfying experience with a ton of replayability. If you threw Slay the Spire or Monster Train in a blender with Powerstone this is what would come out. There is a huge variety of cards that make for many distinct play styles. There are a selection of premade decks to just jump in, or you can draft your own deck. So it's easy to find a play style that suits your taste.The difficulty feels challenging without being unfair. After 133 hours I still haven’t beat the game once (that damn agent…) and I’m still unlocking new cards. In all this game is a solid value.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Fights in Tight Spaces is John Wick without his gun, in a deck-builder format. The cards are, like the trailer says, highly varied, and very unique. While some are objectively worse, they are basically meant to be replaced by other cards of higher value, and the game gives you many a chance to obtain and upgrade them.The combos hit hard, the animations are fluid, and the overall aesthetic and absolute banger of a soundtrack really help you get into the groove of punching, kicking and yeeting your enemies. If you're coming from the likes of Slay The Spire, I think Fights in Tight Spaces will help you scratch an itch that is incredibly close, but also not quite the same.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Fights in Tight spaces is a fun rouge-like card game that cleverly mixes martial arts with turn based combat. You are essentially an agent going to different regions and fighting different kinds of people.The cards have a lot of variety in terms of what they can do. Enemies are also all unique and present different challenges that need to be overcome. Some enemies will even react based on if you move in front of them.The game is not entirely easy as well and can be punishing at times. This is never an unfair "nothing I could do" situation either. Usually, in 99% of situations, there is a good way to do something, assuming you don't trap yourself in a corner.The challenges on each can also be interesting. They help give you money, energy, health, etc. The challenges vary from finishing a mission fast enough, collecting a briefcase, protecting a dude, and not killing an enemy.The game is fairly well polished, although it misses a few quality of life things such as card sorting or the fact a certain kind of card literally shares the same artwork, making it hard to eye. Most of the maps are exactly the same too, so the only variety really comes from the cards and how you handle the enemies. Enemies thankfully seem to be fairly random in non boss maps.Overall, if you are a fan of deck builder, rouge-like games, I would recommend giving this game a shot!
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Strong recommendation. It's one of my favorite games of the genre, and there's a replay mode just to see how cinematic your fights are. Early level enemies tend to be a little dumb so it's not as interesting to watch, but the later stage ones can be quite interesting.Cards/engines/decks make good sense and are balanced, and the game is good at giving more cards and items as you move forward. The difficulty level makes sense without feeling like the AI is cheating too much - things like lower levels allowing replays and giving free move cards every turn.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE - the devs long ago added an undo option and a bunch of new modes and guaranteed movement cards and enhancements.  Basically everything on my with list.  Can't wait for weapon of choice DLCPlayed this + the demo for over 120 hours.  Finally beat it at the time.  I was definitely watering down my decks by adding too many cards.  Only add what you want, and focus on upgrading your deck to stay effective in the last 2 levels where the difficulty ticks up considerably.  Unless you can generate a ton of block each turn, you should have enough move cards to be able to move around each hand.  A bad start or a bad draw can be mitigated that way.  There's no UNDO option, but you can exit the game and reload and you can sometimes get a do-over of your last card.  Helpful if you don't see a transparent obstacle or you didn't realize that throwing Pocket Sand at a spiky ninja boss was going to give you thorn damage (really devs??)  I f*n love this game.  I do wish I didn't have to play it all the way through each time, I'm looking forward to the roadmap with a card draft, starting on higher levels.  I definitely would like a choice of enhancements after beating the boss.I HATE the machine gun guy!!!!!10/10 would John Wick the Spire again.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Really cool and stylish card-based hallway fight simulator. The arenas are tight and you fight alone, so you don't waste time moving without purpose,  all movements have to be purposeful. Kinda reminds me to Into The Breach in that regard. Quite RNG-based, sometime you will spawn in the corner with enemies on all your side and no way to escape, but I actually don't mind it that much.Early-access wise, there's some bugs, though not overly so, and there are balance issue, but you get a whole full game so it's worth checking already. Or you can check the prologue which is actually quite long.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good one. I'm really looking forward to what else Early Access may bring.Ever since Slay the Spire seemingly forged the deck building dungeon crawler, I haven't really seen any noteworthy ones making use of more traditional battle or tactical maps. Fights in Tight Spaces not only explores this space, it does so with some gusto; positioning is everything. It reminds me heavily of D&D 4E (the only worthwhile edition; FIGHT ME) or Into the Breach in its being a pretty intense spatial combat puzzle.Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: "I can't avoid damage in this fight, better restart...""No way to achieve the goals in this fight, better restart..."It's a great, unique concept.But after 2 hours it becomes an irritation.Each "run" has a series of fights. Each fight requires executing 10+ moves to complete. And, you have to do that near perfectly, to (a) avoid damage and (b) complete goals to upgrade your deck.However, the RNG setup, and the extremely tight goal timers mean that these aren't guaranteed or even fair.So you're stuck "rolling" for perfect runs in a system that rarely produces them, and is extremely punishing to any mistakes.Moreover, while there is RNG setup, you repeat the same fights, with only small variation, in each run. So you're going to be repeating very similar fights 10-20-30 times. It's fun a few times with it's fresh, and a few more times to explore decks, and then you realize it's a grind with design issues.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: It took me a while to finish this game. But I think I can now review it fairly well.Pros: - Cool art & anims.- Cool music.- Very solid on the tactical aspect. You need to pay attention to details, mousover the enemies and plan ahead.- Very cool combos available. - The replay function is mega nice to chill after a long fight (some fight at the end are crazy long).- Very difficult game.Cons: - Very punishing. You can lose hours in a mistake, just because you forgot this guy turns in your direction. - Imbalanced in favor of enemies. You can just arrive on a level and die with no way out. Some enemies have stupid powers that are very tough to avoid.- Imbalanced in favor of the player. You have some infinite combos, mouvement is way tooo strong and stun effects can be chained to victory.- Unlocking levels is useless as you always want to start over (unless you want some insane challenge).- The starting decks are not really good outside of Aggression. - No deck building at the beginning of each run; you have to use one of the 4 base decks. - Injuries can ruin a run. Avoid them at all cost. They are not fun and should be removed from the game.- The white can hurt eyes a little.- No female main protagonist. - Lots of symbols, signs, effects and interactions to learn that are barely shown in the tuto.Despite all its flaws, it's a very nice game for the Deckbuilder-roguelike players who want a tactical hard challenge. Don't go in there if you just want to kick ass, sling cards and watch TV while playing... Here, you need to focus. But it's rewarding. :)EDIT: I am impressed by how much the dev team listened. The recent patches made the game pretty much awesome. Nearly all the cons are gone and I love to run with a fresh drafted deck. Thanks folks!
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: So, firstly, big shoutout to Ground Shatter for letting the alpha testers keep our copies. The gameplay itself is pretty straightforward, the music is awesome. Graphics are neat.There has been exactly one time I died to bad luck (horrendous spawn on the very second map). Every other time, I died because I did something stupid, or I lost track of something that one of the enemies could do. But each time, I get further and further in.Although there was one boss fight that was underwhelming, the boss spawned right next to a ledge and I was able to kick him off the building the first turn. Which is still pretty cool.Berlin has a ninja problem. :P
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game, I spent 5 hours just playing the prologue and knew from that I would want to get the full game. I have a bit of a love/hate with card based games some of them can be way to over complicated, but for me this hits just the right balance between having to think about what you are doing but at the same time you can jump right in and have fun from the get go. Even though it is early access is plays better than some games that are fully released, I have yet to find any bugs.  I can see me sinking a huge number of hours in to this. Well done Devs for creating something a bit special.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: I also wanted to like this game. I will keep it short though.There are no good feeling decks you can put together. Want a bleed deck? Well then, good luck getting the rewards of the fights. Want to have fun kicking people of the grid? Well then, good luck killing the last boss. Want to have variety? Ok, then go conter deck that is frustrating to play.And that's it. But then again, I cannot think of another mechanic for this game. The theme limits the possibilities. Maybe a ranged-hop-around-deck? -Not in tight spaces.And why are there movement cards that are blatantly better than other movement cards and cost the same?This game is fun but not well thought out and boring when you played a bit of it. Is 4 hours worth 20 bucks?
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: 5 Stars, with a BUT.I mean, it nails everything it sets out to do. The fights, the deck building, the randomization, the STANDARD options for play through. It's super creative, after like a week of game time, I still get surprised sometimes at how certain cards play together.They just need more quality of life stuff. Tell me how many cards are in my deck when I review it. Sort it so I can see that I have 3 hammerfists, don't sort it by when I got them... On top of that, keep stats better. The game knows what we did. Let us see our highest damage dealt in 1 hit. Most fights without taking a hit, etc... FINALLY, give us sandbox. Don't offer exp or anything for it, but let us just build what we think is a perfect deck and play that. Or save a god deck for a later attempt. The randomization kills the game after x amount of tries.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Almost a not-recommend, but it's good. If the authors read this, please tighten every animation by a quarter second and add some screen-effects. It all feels so slow, too clunky. This game is functionally the same Slay the Spire, but that "card" game makes every action hit hard, every block make you feel like a tank? I want to go play that game to feel like a good fighter, compared to this game about actually being a cool fighter?!
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like everytime i play this i have that one scene in the RDJ Sherlock Holmes movie in my head where he was all like "left hook, discombobulate, hit him in the eyes" it's great i hated that movie.Gameplay is smooth and engaging very understandable and the reward system is very gratifying you always want to try a run again with a different approach and the deck building option opens you up to any playstyle you can come up with (i would suggest the obvious "play first with the pre built decks" to get familiar with the cards and what they do) overall this game delivers what it aims to and i love it and there is an endless mode so neat.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: A tough (and sometimes unforgiving) card based fighting game (think the opening bathroom scene from Casino Royale). You start off with a deck picked from a selection and can customise as the game progresses. This will largely depend on you being able to complete bonus objectives in each "fight". During the first few zones these are usually largely doable, but in the later zones those which are time dependant become increasingly difficult to be able to do.The moves of the fighters are good, and the enemy variety means things are kept interesting, along with the ability at the end of rounds to watch a "replay" where all the turns are played out without the interface etc.. The music is OK, albeit you'll be hearing it a lot so it feels a bit samey after a while.Overall I've enjoyed what I've played so far, and the Devs seems responsive to making improvements over the course of the game's EA period so looking forwards to the release.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty decent game and it's getting updated well.Hopefully it continues to improve over time. My biggest problem with the game is its pacing and dull animations. I can pull out some cool card combos, but the animations are very repetitive and consuming, I understand it's one of the features of the game, but it actually doesn't make you look like a cool action hero, it still feels like you're playing a stiff RPG.The deckmaking is interesting, but not too deep and some cards and builds are just way overpowered compared to others. I wish other strategies were more valid to allow for some variety. The routes feel very empty and the choices barely matter.This game has a great fun core, I really wish it can get refined and fleshed out in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: The markings of Early Access definitely shows here, with a lot of missing animations and visual flair, lack of long term progression, and unique cards being drowned out by a little bit too much chaff. That being said, Fights in Tight Spaces lays an extremely solid foundation for a great turn-based deckbuilder, and while its current state in EA isn't really enough to sustain 40+ hours to any but the hardcore, it could easily get there with enough additions to improve run variety and a polishing phase to add more unique animations to many of the cards.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: I'm trying hard to like it as much as I think I should. A roguelike deck builder that has a cool art style and themed on fighting, right? Should be good? I just think the pacing is a little slow. While the difference with this deck builder is that you can move your hero in 3D space on a grid system, which most deckbuilders don't have, sometimes the fights just seem a little slow and boring. So many of my moves are side steps, which aren't that interesting. And different rounds drag on for a long time, especially if you get one enemy with much higher HP and armour than the others. So many of my moves in those rounds, once I have killed the other enemies, are just punching x1 or 2, then side stepping, end turn, and punching x1 or 2 then side stepping, then end turn, etc. That's not very exciting game play. I feel like the game play sometimes does NOT benefit from having it in 3d spaces, because many of your turns are just moving towards or away from your opponents. This needs a tweak, IMO.Plus, the rewards system is really bad, in my opinion. You don't get any monetary reward for finishing a round unless you meet the in game challenges for that round, which are usually end round in 4 or 5 turns (not a very interesting challenge IMO). If you don't meet that, then you get nothing in terms of money (you will get one new card). And then, that means the rest rounds, where you upgrade cards or heal are useless because IT COSTS MONEY TO HEAL. I have no idea why it costs money to heal, but it does. If you don't defeat a round in 4 or 5 turns, do you deserve to be punished? Does it mean you played the round worse if you played it slower? I don't think so. Playing in a conservative style is a hallmark of roguelikes. You deserve SOME reward for finishing the round, in a way that helps you make use of the rest rounds later. The extra round bonuses for finishing fast or getting x combo should come on top of the regular round bonuses (in a way that lets you make use of the rest rounds). I think that would be a good change.Because of this, I'm NOT SURE I can recommend it. I think they should keep the pace moving in the game and they should give players rewards each round that let them make use of rest rounds. Then I think it would be a much better game. I think there potential for this to be a good game, but I don't think it's quite there yet.  I would wait until they start patching the game for you to buy it and play it. For now, I don't think it's quite there yet.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Now I'm really loving this game at the moment BUT it's suffering some really annoying major balancing issues tied to the overall cutthroat RNG factor and lack of player ability to the build the deck. Devs hope you could listen to my issues.Every mission you complete earns you the right to get choose a new card at random, and 2 random other bonuses (money/upgraded card/health/health increase) which are tied to some side challenges, if you can complete the mission giving objectives which is totally BS since they're tied to game turns to do X based scenarios and that's totally unfair since the cards you'll be able to play are at random(ex: sometimes the game asks you to get a briefcase in 4 turns and you're surrounded by the enemies or you don't get any movement cards/defeat all enemies in X turns but no attack cards,etc), it would be nice to have some less harsher and more tangible objectives like(defeat one enemy with X attack) or at least earning 50% money, 50% health, lower health increase and standard card instead of a upgraded one. The final mission part which is a 99% chance of failure unless RNGJesus gave you the free movement enhacement + self heal enhanced which I exploited for most the final chapter until I still got owned just 1 mission before the final boss fight, every mission has 8/9 enemies and the enemies can be anything from strong types to multiple bosses with 100+ HP at the same time which is really bad.Besides that the game is really enjoyable, the OST is really superb and the animations are great, the color scheme is pretty slick, I had just some minor technical bugs like freezing and sometimes animations not playing but overall it's a great game, aside from balancing it would be cool to be able to be able to build a deck and also a endless random mode in the future if possible.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Want to play out scene like Capt. America fighting 8 people in an elevator and coming out on top?  Jackie Chan being ambushed by thugs in a small alley, and step out unscathed after forcing all the enemies to punch, chop, kick each other while dodging out of the way?This game uses a card system to control the actions of the 'agent' character who is sent to increasingly dangerous locations where they inevitably get into fights in... tight spaces.  The game's different in the details every time, and the game's progression mid-run lets you tune your deck more and more as you come out on top.Now that the game's out of early access, they have a meta progression that you see in other Rogue Lights.  Unlocking cards, unlocking starting decks, and the like.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: This was my first foray in the deck-building genre and I was not sure what to expect: looking at videos gave me the feeling the concept for the game was inspired by those hand-to-hand combat scenes in movies such as The Transporter and John Wick series, so I decided to give it a try. Turned out to be a fun, interesting experience: the mechanics of turn-based combat and usage of cards are pretty easy to understand and it does not take long to figure out which cards are helpful and which less so. Different deck types become available the more runs through the game are attempted and so far I had the most success with the "Aggressive" deck which let me blaze through the Jade Staff mission on my very first attempt.Gameplay is challenging, but so far not to the point of being frustrating. Luck plains a not entirely small factor, because cards seem to be drawn randomly from the deck at the start of each round and getting unhelpful cards in one turn could force to play a sub-optimal strategy with potentially fatal consequences later in the fight(s). Planning moves and paying attention to the environment and to what the enemies actions and reactions will be however plays the most important role to win and survive: for example, I once slipped out of the line of fire of a shotgun-wielding thug without realizing that this move placed my character in line for an auto attack from a nearby enemy that in turn pushed me right back where I came (to receive a fatal shotgun blast at the end of the turn).Can't say whether veteran players of deck-building games will feel at home with this game, but based on my experience I'm in favor of recommending this game as a nice pick to explore the genre for those players that, like me, have never done so before and would like to give it a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: I am loving this game. If you enjoyed Into The Breach, then get stuck into this one. There's an extra layer of complexity that forces you to come up with new strategies each turn and the game logic is solid throughout - the bosses don't suddenly become immune to gravity, for example.So, if you've suddenly realised that your life won't be complete until you throw a ninja off a fire escape, this is the game for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun and challenging game which gives a real rush when things are going your way and the cards come out just right, it's very fun trying to figure out how and when to attack, defend and move in such a way to maximise damage output and minimise damage taken. However, some spawns will leave you in situations in which you are guaranteed to take damage which can immediately ruin a run and really put you off trying, especially when you get further into the game and lose over an hour progress because the enemy spawns right next to you and you have no cards to dodge or defend yourself with and die as a result of this.Overall, despite the sometimes very unfair spawns i would nonetheless recommend the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: The Good:This is a solid deckbuilder.  Slay the Spire with a mix of  Into the breach.  I really enjoy it a lot.  So far i've reached the boss of the second area but have not been able to beat him.  The Bad:The interface is the games major weakness...more than half the time I take damage it is because I misunderstood what was happening or forgot that a specific card would make an enemy turn to face me.  I really would like a feature to undo my last action, I often feel like I've been punished because I didn't understand something, not because I made a bad play.Also there are certain enemies that have large health pools, high defense, ranged attacks.....and then don't want to close and fight with you.  I feel like these could be toned down a bit as they are not very fun to play against.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: An enjoyable roguelike deckbuilder that puts you in the shoes of a secret agent doing secret agent things. Usually punching people in the face.Fights in Tight Spaces is structured similarly to other roguelike games like Slay the Spire in that you have a "map" that is made up of scenarios that are a mix between fights, events, and shops. By navigating this map you eventually come up against a boss, then on to the next map. Unlike Slay the Spire however, the way each fight plays out is vastly different. Rather than just trading blows (or blocks, or skills, or whatever), you're on a grid-based map and movement is an integral part of the fight. Proper positioning will allow you to unleash devastating combos from relative safety, but if you do it wrong you can get boxed into a corner and overpowered. It's a basic flow; you do all your stuff, then all the enemies attack, then all the enemies move.Manipulating the enemy AI is a fine art, and even if you aren't good at it you can still set up some pretty nice friendly fire scenarios with just a few basic cards. Pushing people out of the map instakills them, and it's very satisfying, but also a hazard to keep an eye out for since some enemies can push , and the same rules apply.But by far my favorite thing about this game is how forgiving it is. Not in an "incredibly easy" kind of way either. The game gives you ample access to the ability to "rollback" your turn (three times per fight on the default difficulty) if you make a bad play, and you can even start the fight over again (with the same card RNG). These forgiveness measures make each fight feel like a fun puzzle rather than a stressful scouring of your available options and all their outcomes. I can't tell you how many times I've lost a great Slay the Spire run to a stupid mistake, but if I do that here I can start over. In addition the game guarantees that you'll draw a movement card every turn if you have one available to draw, which means you can't ever get stuck due to bad RNG. I've also lost a ton of Slay the Spire runs to just not drawing enough block on turns when the enemy attacks, and while you still can draw insufficient movement to get out of any jam, you always have some options.If you're worried that might make the game too easy, you can always just not use those options. You're under no obligation to rollback a turn or restart a failed fight, and if you're really up for it you can play on the higher difficulties where you get no do-overs and no RNG forgiveness.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game dripping in style. It is so satisfying using your cards to maneuver around the field, getting enemies into the right spot to attack each other or push them off the field. You have plenty of opportunity to customize your deck by adding, removing, or upgrading cards, and there's even different deck presets to choose from.However, the balance in this game is awful. Powerful upgrades such as a higher momentum cap (this game's version of mana) are tied behind challenges in paths that can be missed. The challenge is not always achievable with the deck you've built (such as getting to a certain tile when using a counter deck without movement), and it can be punishing missing out on these rewards.The last stage in the game feels like a lazy dump of all the game's assets. Bosses from the previous levels are dropped into regular stages, with the same health pools and overpowered abilities. This results in long, tiresome battles at every node.Overall, I still recommend the game. The game is still in early access and balance issues are easily fixed. The game itself is still a lot of fun and I look forward to the finished product.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: really cool game, i love the art style and deck building element of the game, i just kinda wish it was either longer, or had more permanent progression to work on, like in hades there's always story and things to unlock back at base when you finish a run which gives incentive to do more runs, whereas here it's just about unlocking the cards through levelling up and i guess doing it on harder difficulties, but once you've done that then there's little incentive to carry on playing. but overall a great deck building stylish roguelite game.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game. It's a roguelike deckbuilder, with an emphasis on combat. In each fight, you're deployed in a tiny room with enemies, and you have to defeat them (it's quite similar to Into The Breach). You will play your cards, to move, strike or do many actions (buff, debuff, move enemies, defend, dodge and so on). You will also have to achieve objectives during the fight to earn bonus rewards.The aesthetics of the game feel refreshing, and the animations are also quite nice.I've seen a few people complaining that there are not much viable deck strategies to win, and I have to disagree with this. You can play quite a few different decks imo : offensive, defensive, dot, control, guns (with the DLC), and probably more. There are enough cards to be creative while building your deck, and since combat has a lot of freedom, it's mainly about how you play your deck.It may not have the replayability of a Slay the Spire, but there's more than enough content for the price. I highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: As it's still early days in v0.17, going to post a short writeup about this game:Having grown up watching the likes of Ip Man, Jet Li and Jason Statham - Absolutely LOVE this game. Now theere are a few blemishes here and there which I will go through, but overall I think the entire concept is a great one and one that could make a brilliant game.GREAT:Animations are fairly slick Environments are shaped to look like real environments (e.g toilet, rooftop, carpark) Decent variety of enemies from samurais to gunmen to prison bossesSOUND and MUSIC - good enough for meGOOD: Progression. Now it can be quite difficult to change your deck and this is even more so because each subsequent card upgrade increases the cost. Same for card removal. Perhaps the cost can be lowered, or there can be more ways made to get money in the game.Number of environments - sometimes I fight the same location 3 times, that shouldn't be right, but that can be made good with timeCharacter customisation - making different skins, I'm not sure how much work this would be but something to keep on the map.Random events  - As of now still a bit too much influence on the game such that your entire playthrough could be detrerminmed by the roll of a dice in the random event, IMO this should not be the case as it's primarily a strategic game and a really good player for example could get thru a tough level without taking a single point of damage.Death points - In certain maps like Rooftop, it's clear why the character died if he was thrown over. But why in like 'Toilet', would a character die after being thrown out the door? Or why in 'Prison' would the character die being thrown out of the canteen? These are things that don't make much sense, perhaps it could be made clearer to the player why the death zone is a death zone. Maybe make it a fire or a manhole or something.Overall good job and I want to play this game when it reaches v1, thank you.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly solid deckbuilder that can be simplified to "Slay the Spire meets Into the Breach" with a John Wick aesthetic. The learning curve is steep but the initial stages are designed to teach the importance of the positioning and other movement mechanics that set this game apart from similar titles.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: This game is super fun. My only complaint is they dump too much information on you right away before you even understand the game. Like specifically telling you about characteristics of different enemies that you probably won't even encounter on the first go-around.But once you learn the game, it's super fun and I highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Love the way they use the deck-builder idea to make a turn-based fighter into a different challenge. Sometimes you get the perfect combo, and sometimes you have to play defense and punt until the next hand. Enemies with new abilities appear in each update so far, and some are tough - especially when confined within Tight Spaces and limited maneuverability!

_childDocuments_.review: Neat and cool!I'd be interested in a sequel that expands upon what's here. Feels sort of "proof of concept"-y. Core mechanics are unique and fun but, so far, every run feels samey, even with different decks, and there are a lot of QoL stuff that would be nice, like better camera controls. Why can I catch bullets with my bare hands while blocking, but knives do full damage?Why am I shown tips on how to fight enemies that aren't present, and then I can't ever look up that info again?Why can I restart any fight I want, but only after dying? The rollback mechanic is already in the game. I wish the campaign were also fleshed out more: each chapter longer, with more branching paths and opportunities for upgrades. I want to make choices and experiment more, but the path is always so linear and my resources are so finite.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Still a cool deckbuilding strategy game in the vein of griftlands/ slay the spire with a chessboard mechanic added to it. The Early Access is not yet worth the pricepoint and a lot more unstable than the Prologue. It is also bad at explaining itself but that may be part of it's challenge. The RNG is unforgiving as hell and in 1 of 3 Setups I had no chance to achieve any of the somewhat randomly set objectives to obtain a bonus. In this state the factor Luck is imo still too heavy a factor and it is not so much luck of the draw with the deck but with information what to strategize for.Edit as of 12.03.21: A lot has improved towards properly explaining ingame systems and working out broken cards. There will always be a luck of the draw element and I still think the game should be right under € 20,- to be an easy pickup.Edit as of 18.09.2021: Even more improvements are implemented. Better explanations, a ton of more options and the different difficulties make it very adaptable to your taste! From this point on absolutely worht the price!Edit 07.10.2023 - DLC killed the Game. New Opponents are all Superbosses with 2or more Special Abilities (Unmovable, Dodge, any Tactical Emergence the Game had is now pure luck of the Draw and the Actual Bosses apply 2 or more Special Counter Cards (besides having up to three Dodges in the same turn) to your Deck. There is no Deckdesign anymore. Too many of the rules you could count on are now enforced randomly, like auto-attack etc.Another Example where good Ideas where confused with good execution.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: To me this game is very misleading, it plays way too slow and clunky to be thrilling and stylish as it markets itself. I've played a lot of roguelike deckbuilders and this style of game is kind of my pet-peeve, it gets very repetitive and at the same time turns and fights take a very long time. They put so many different abilities on the enemies that checking what everyone does, in which order they take their turn and so on makes it so it feels very slow and flat out bores me. The fights are mostly easy but at the same time there are a lot of them to progress through, they give almost nothing in return and take forever. Which creates in me this feeling of just wanting the game to end, just wanting to get to boss to get it over with.When I play roguelikes I want the game to clearly communicate to me what I need to do each turn, without me needing to repetitively read abilities and skills. I especially hate when normal enemies abilities are tuned to counter specific builds so if you meet them you are just dead, that's anti fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: I'd highly recommend it even in alpha. I haven't beaten it yet as the end game fights seem a little OP at this point, but overall I've been having a blast kicking people out of windows and suplexing people. There's been some visual glitches, like animations not working but generally the glitches are pretty funny and not annoying. Nothing quite like kneeing someone in the face so hard that their whole body goes through a wall except their head and hands. Pros: First 4 missions are balanced and require different strategies. The enemies are varied and each has their own weakness which makes for interesting plays. The cards are all interesting and the fighting mechanics are fun. Pushing people into another enemy's attack, stunning and throwing people, collision damage, etc. The Events are interesting as well, and some have a bit of RNG to them but most are a "risk-reward" system which I think works great. The mission objectives sometimes force you to make a choice between being reckless so that you can complete them, or ignoring them so that you conserve your health. The visual simplicity is also pretty cool and the conversations with the Boss at the end of each mission gave me a chuckle. Cons: Some cards are inexplicably rare. I never saw Throwing Knife until 40 hours in yet in my opinion it's pretty sub-par. This is also the case with Pain-killers, though I really like that card. Now throwing knife shows up nearly every game for some reason and I haven't seen pain killers in probably 10 games. Also the game likes to screw me on hands towards the end of the game. I'm not sure if I'm just unlucky or what, but I'll get hands that are all movement cards or vice versa. You always have one movement card in your hand but it sucks when you get Step when you're surrounded.The economy needs a little work as well. If you get hit, you had better hope you got lucky and found a Heal card or you have money laying around for a Medic location nearby. The Balanced deck and the Trickster deck lack damage potential so you're not going to be completing timed objectives unless you can kick people out of windows. Certain levels, like the market are really bad for trickster. I've had to go through my whole deck multiple times just to finish off the last enemy before with Trickster. If you start losing, it compounds on itself because then you can't afford upgrades or new cards. This gets really bad during i Completi and the final mission since the enemy's health goes up a lot so you can't kill them fast enough to get the time-limit objectives. A tiny base income per level, or a large reward for the boss fight would make up for this.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Fights in Tight Spaces could easily be renamed John Wick the deck-builder.  The premise is simple - each round you fight different bad guys until you either win or die.  The fights get trickier as opponents not only increase in health but gain special powers and different forms of attack.  Some will be immune to throwing attacks, some have shotguns, some have riot shields which block attacks from the front. Each turn is a constant puzzle to work out where you will move, who you will attack, whilst hopefully ending up in a position where you won't take damage yourself.  Has kept me coming back again and again since the prologue was released.  Should appeal to anyone who likes card games and deck-builders, turn by turn strategy and board gamers.  Excellent game and hats off to the developers for  a great concept masterfully realized.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Thumbs up, but with criticism. Considering that this title has been on the market for nearly three years, I'm puzzled why the game still has some very basic coding / instruction / game rule errors. Examples:1) Card states that it can be played when a value is over five. However, card can also be played when the value is five. 2) Boss enemy description implies that attacker takes damage whenever it damages boss. Makes sense, except it is only the player that takes damage, even when the boss is damaged by fellow henchmen. 3) Card rules do not clearly state whether discarding is a cost or effect. Right now it is an effect, meaning that you can play a card that requires discarding a card, even if you have no other cards in your hand (compare to M:TG rules). I do not know if this is intentional or bad coding.4) Finally, I wish the game utilized visual cues to warn the player of enemy abilities. This becomes an issue later in the game where powerful enemies can cycle through different abilities each turn. This can lead to a situation where the player ends up losing the game when they do not realize in time that the target suddenly has a new ability.Otherwise, a good purchase with rogue-lite replay value. Random deck drafting makes every run unique.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: This is an enjoyable but tough-as-nails card-based brawler. Fights In Tight Spaces can be both incredibly challenging and satisfying, but currently the difficulty is perhaps a bit too high. The game encourages you to play through the entire campaign in a single run (as starting at later levels puts you at a disadvantage), but since each run ends with your first death, this can be incredibly daunting. Also, it is entirely possible to be dealt an unwinnable match with an unusable hand, which only makes things more frustrating as you can be forced back to the very beginning after a near flawless run. This is an early access game so these issues may be tweaked or improved over time, but even with them still present the game has a lot of potential and can be great fun when everything comes together.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: It's FUN!  Edit:  STRONG WARNING!!  After playing for 50+hours, I it is sad to say I have become become violently addicted to this game.  Those who have discovered playing on "Puritan" mode with the "deck draft" system have also fallen victim to this so called "game".  I'm sure it has consumed every aspect of their life and every thought they once had to themselves.  Now all I see are grids and faceless gangsters when I close my eyes.   Always one punch away from ending hours and hours of progress.  Removing the ability to rewind which is available on standard difficulty takes it to a whole new level.  You will witness the bone crushing defeat of creating an absolutely amazing deck with a lot of luck and thought, through constant visits to the gym to strengthen  it, only to accidentally forget that one lowly thug that had a "push" prefix on his attack, which then knocks you directly in the path of a thick mobster who gut slams you off of a subway track as you sit in front of the screen in shock for an hour trying not to freak out.  But jump right back at it  being excited to see the new ways these gangsters and thugs catch you slipping for a brief second when your mental game isn't pumping at full cylinders.   10/10 gaming doesn't get any better then that.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

It's much better now.I really really want to like this game, the mechanics are engaging and the gameplay is (could be) fun, but the lack of any kind of checkpointing makes it a total waste of time. Every move is a gamble with hours worth of game progress, consequently you have to play too conservatively to have any fun with it, and eventually you still die from some random thing like not remembering the order the enemies move in, or not realizing your attack would turn an enemy a certain direction. I bought this game to support the dev from Frozen Synapse, but I'm just a casual gamer; I understand having a hardcore mode in the game, but I don't have any use for a game that only comes in hardcore mode. It's really a disappointment.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros: Easy to learnGreat replay valueLow priceRuns well on low end systemsCons:Can be a little repetitiveToo many useless cardsCustom Deck building needs some tweekingI like this game, it is simple, fun, easy to learn. The story mode is a little short and loses some of its value on replay, but trying out different style decks does make it a little more challenging. I only really have two criticisms, first, the custom deck building could use some work. A lot of times the cards you get to choose from in the custom deck building are all complete crap. The other criticism is the game needs a couple more levels. By the time you finally purchase enough cards to make a decent deck, the game is over. Other than those two things, it's a fun game and not expensive or taxing on a system.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Story: Bland and simplistic, you're an agent who beats up bad guys. Gameplay: If you eat and breathe deck building/strategy games, this may be your thing. wide variety of fighting moves, steps, and blocks. However, gameplay can get extremely repetitive. Overall: A unique game for sure, but with such a bland story and repetitive gameplay, I would wait for a big sale. Definitely not worth the current price tag. I lost interest after 20 minutes.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: FiTS is what you get when you take Slay the Spire's card-dealing resource economy and enemy-prediction mechanics and retool them to work in a grid-based tactical environment. It works MARVELOUSLY well. You know what the enemies are going to do, so step out of the way, smack them in the sides of their heads, and throw them into each others' attack paths. Controlling the board is the name of the game.I could gush about the style, but you can probably tell it's got that just by watching the trailers. I will say, however, every track on the OST is a banger and worth tracking down just to listen to on its own. nervous_testpilot is the composer.They're working on a spinoff-sequel called Knights in Tight Spaces, so I don't know that it'll be getting any more DLC than the one it has. That DLC does offer a more difficult campaign if you find the base campaign too easy, though, as well as numerous fun gunplay mechanics.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Short version: FiTS is extremely tough on normal ("Classic") difficulty but I love it!Long version: Steam says I've played this game for 1,023 hours but a lot of that was idle time because I like to leave it running in the background so I can switch to it quickly to play for a few minutes.My actual play time has to be in the hundreds of hours though — this is the type of game that I can't stop playing!I set a goal of beating the game on Classic, but kept giving up vowing to play a different game.FiTS is extremely difficult even on "Classic" mode and there are things you can't really know about the end game until you get there and die a few times.Losing hours of "work" that close to the end is awful!But I finally beat finished on Classic mode game yesterday! Hooray!!!Now I have to play the DLC. :)I tried dozens of different builds, including all the standard decks.In the end the only build that worked was creating a deck from "Draft" mode — I learned you *must* have a pistol to win.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: When you're in the mood for some punch, kick, chop, this game will satisfy that itch. I thought there would be some level progression where if you die you retain some skill.  You do, but your character doesn't level up, your brain does.  Be sure to play on classic if you're not a wimp.   Probably the last game I pre-ordered where the devs actually delivered a finished product.  Can't wait for the sequel but I always come back for some daily plays.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Not normally a card game guy but this... doesn't feel like one, because your're using the cards to move around a 3D space and execute kick-butt martial arts animations while managing your health and stats. The fights have a cool John Wick sort of flavor. It very satisfyingly violent for being turn-based. You don't get guns, but the bad guys do. Collecting the achievement becomes the primary draw after you beat the game once. I've been trying to beat it The Purist difficulty for many moons now and I haven't yet... made it right to the end but got taken out. Worth the money even at full price in my opinion.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Do you like roguelike deckbuilders? Do you like turn-based tactics games? This is the best possible marriage of those two genres. I admit I was dubious when I heard the concept was basically fistfighting in a phone booth, but I am so happy that I was completely wrong. This is the closest to a John Wick / Jackie Chan fight simulator that I have ever played. It's easily my favorite game of the last two years, and depending on how early access shakes out, it may challenge XCOM 2 for my eternal affection. Could not recommend harder.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Check the link for my review/impressions video:    This game really caught me by surprise.  It came recommended while viewing another product on Steam.  I really liked the visuals and the concept of the game and have always wanted to find a deckbuilding roguelike that I could get good at.This game is very beginner friendly yet still very challenging in places.   As one reviewer in Steam said, it has a visual style reminiscent of SUPERHOT, and the gameplay feels like Slay the Spire meets X-COM or something.  So far, I have had a blast and only wish I had more time on my hands to give it even more playtime. At the asking price, I do recommend the game for those interested in getting into the genre or looking for a good stepping stone before moving onto the more challenging games of the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: It's got almost all of the pieces right, but something about how they are put together doesn't quite hit the mark. Art, and playability is top notch and the premise is there. There's no story however, and replaying *all* the stages on each death is just too brutal. At the end of the day runs just become too similar to one another, something that kills even the best roguelike, as after a few runs you feel quite happy and you've seen it all. The balancing also feels a bit off with certain cards or combos, like countering, feeling way too good to ever pass on.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: This game is the absolute king of YASDs.I thought roguelikes were hard and embarrassing. Nope. Not even close to this masochism. And I've beaten The Pit.So many, many stupid deaths. It's a brilliant card fighting game. Deserves to be up there with the ranks of Slay the Spire and Monster Train and other luminaries. It does exactly as advertised--fights with increasingly difficult opponents in tight quarters.Then, even as you understand the mechanics, it effing humiliates you for the hundredth time. It is incredibly fair, but makes Into the Breach look like Peggle for Beginners.Love it. If you like PC card games or roguelikes (I mean ACTUAL roguelikes, the old ASCII permadeath kind) you owe yourself a play.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: I first played this game back when the devs put out that free teaser, and loved the stuffing out of it until the update where they updated the soundtrack. The old soundtrack was love at first sound. The new soundtrack... I had some choice words.It pretty much kept me from playing the game until I muted the in-game music and replaced it with the old soundtrack playing in the background via. Youtube.A great, satisfying game that I can recommend, but I'm still bitter over the new music. How about a legacy soundtrack button in the options menu? Maybe another option to use the old damage icons, too? Please, guys? I promise I won't hurt the composer's feelings any more
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic. I play a lot of card based games here on Steam, but to this day I haven't found anything that plays quite like this one. The concept is unique, the execution is really really good, and I've spent more time here than I do on some AAA titles.If I had a complaint it would be that the enemy actions aren't always clear how they'll work, but the information is there (unlike what another review I read says), you just have to slow down and actually try to find it.Other than that, it's a solid game. Well made, there is plenty of variety in card choices for replay-ability (rather important since it's a rogue-like), and the dev team is one of the great few that has pushed their game past the finish line and out of early access. Thumbs Up from me.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful card-based tactical fighting roguelike.  I know that's a lot of words, but they work well together.  You are a secret agent sharing a very limited environment (the titular Tight Spaces) with myriad criminal elements.  They will try to murder you, which you will use to your advantage.  It's a difficult scenario to quickly describe, so I'll overly simplify it: Imagine if SUPERHOT and Into The Breach had a baby and then Jackie Chan got trapped inside it.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost, this is the first deck builder game I've really played. It's very beginner friendly in that sense. After playing this game, I've been more open to trying other deck builder games such as Slay the Spire. While I do think this game is a lot of fun and have really enjoyed every run I've done, there is a limited amount of content as of right now. I've played around with a lot of the different decks in the game and have finished at least one run with each of the starter decks. Each deck does a really good job at completely changing your play style. You learn very quickly how to adapt to playing more defensively when running the Counter Striker deck versus running the starter Balanced deck. After that, you quickly jump into playing with the Aggressive pack which is on the complete opposite side of the spectrum. The enemy variety and design is all very well done. You know who you should be dealing with later and who you should prioritize over others. Some enemies are difficult to deal with using certain decks but are completely outmatched when playing other decks. For example, Heavy enemies can't be knocked down. Going up against a Heavy when playing with the Thrower deck can be difficult and sometimes frustrating. But Heavy characters can be easily dealt with when using any other deck. Another example is any enemy that can counter you. They can counter just about every attack but are very susceptible to throws as they can't counter you if they're knocked prone. I highly recommend this game to anyone who is even a little interested. I do hope they add more content soon but this game was well worth the price for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: After the first hour or so I really started to warm up to this game. Might take some getting used to but you'll figure it out eventually. It's a fair challenge and a very unique concept. It's also not as complicated as other turn based games or board game-type stuff. It also has a bit of personality with some humor here and there. I'd recommend this game to anyone trying to get into turn based games.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Kicked a dude out a window at about 350mph leaving nothing but a helmet GG.If Superhot were a card-based, turn-based game, it'd probably look like Fights In Tight Spaces. Quite simplistic but surprisingly addictive, FITS is updated regularly with new enemies, maps and decks. Despite being in Early Access, any bugs are ironed out pretty quickly so it is completely playable.Not sure if it's for you? "Fights in Tight Spaces (Prologue)" is a Free-to-Play demo of the first mission. Would 100% recommend checking it out and, if you love it half as much as I do, you should buy it!
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: overall a fun neat game but why the ♥♥♥♥ add ninjas who cannot be hurt from the front have 3 of them spawn on a tiny ass map where you can easily get trapped in a corner and get perma softlocked, like legit who the ♥♥♥♥ thought thats a great idea for a game where the map size at best is like 6x5 rectangle 2 can be managed but 3 no damage from the front enemies is beyond busted and is pretty much an instant lose situation.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a lot like into the breach. You'll know exactly what every single enemy does, before they do it. Like into the breach, you can use enemies against each other. Where it departs from into the breach however, is it's a deckbuilder, so there's an additional element of randomness to it, However, I've never felt like the deckbuilding worked against me unless I made deckbuilding mistakes, such as trying to fit every card that's good on its own into it instead of just picking things that work together. For example, if you build a deck focused on knocking down enemies, taking more than a couple of cards that instead move enemies or just deal direct damage will hamper it instead of providing alternate solutions to enemies that resist knockdowns.The animations are also wonderful, and you can feel the impact of a good head smash, or a body drop with a well placed headbutt or one-two punch combo, or kicking them into a killzone out of the map, or the way the enemies react as you suplex them execute a perfectly timed stomp to finish them off. The art is simplistic, but you can always tell what an enemy is and how they fight. Every time you see a ninja with tonfas, you know what they'll do. Every time you see a riot armored goon with a shotgun, you know exactly how to avoid them and set them up to hurt an ally.There's a lot more to the deckbuilding that I'm still exploring, but overall it's an amazing game that is absolutely worth every penny if you like into the breach, games that reward tactical thinking, or deckbuilders in general. It's incredibly satisfying to watch a well built deck flow and control the battlefield as your agent moves like a ghost bashing, smashing, throwing, and shoving enemies into each other and objects while weaving around them and avoiding every blow or turning them against enemies.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love it. I love it like a newborn puppy. You get over the shock and responsibility of owning a pet. There's a little "honeymoon" period where you forgive it for chewing on wires and defecating in your bed for the 6th or 7th time. He's just a cold lil fella. A sweet little messy bean who steals your food. But man, does it irritate me.This is a rough EA game to play. Not necessarily buggy, but the basic gameplay loop needs some serious tweaking in upcoming patches. The 4 campaigns so far have had their merits and I've enjoyed the variety of enemies to an extent, but there's just so many times I can look at the same (admittedly, well-designed) maps each time per campaign. The prison block feels like you're fighting through an entire prison cell by identical cell, for example. Enemies start resurfacing in later campaigns and they're a welcome sight depending on how well you can collect and play the right cards to kite mobs of angry faceless people in circles, but they re-appear juiced to the gills. There's a constant powercreep to fuel the roguelike experience Ground Shatter's aiming to replicate, but you're only ever as strong as the next few cards you can pull.I want to like this game more, and I feel that some simple quality-of-life tweaks to the economy would go a long way. The animations are a joy to watch, and there's a certain sense of satisfaction when your accumulated cards all fall into place at once and you rip off a solid 5 or 6 move combo. That being said...forcing me to start over and punch the same three geeks in the same tattoo parlor after a series of bad draws when I've been drawing and upgrading new cards for three campaigns straight without so much as a nod, cash bump or freebie card? Torturous. I get that game design like this is the double-edged nature of the roguelike, but other games are able to start you from a place of power through strong item drops or built-in easy routes that can get you re-energized and ready for another big run. I haven't felt that yet in FiTS.Still, this was everything I asked for when I first played the demo. I wouldn't have 30 hours of failed runs sunk into this game if I didn't enjoy the gameplay loop. I hope you continue to develop and tweak FiTS into the polished diamond of a deckbuilding roguelike it deserves to be.

_childDocuments_.review: Fights in Tight Spaces rides the line between turn-based tactics, deckbuilder and roguelite, mixing a blend of gameplay that's both highly addictive and remarkably polished, Well-designed mechanics keep you informed of the effects of every move. Stylish aesthetics make every enemy distinct and easy to tell apart, and a lighthearted tone riffing on spy and martial arts films take the edge off runs gone wrong. The game is clearly biased toward certain builds, while unlucky card drops and random events with no ideal outcomes can screw over runs too easily, but they're not enough to bring the rest of the game down.

_childDocuments_.review: It's sort of like if you mixed Slay the Spire with Into the Breach. The animations are cool, and there's a lot of enemy variety as well. My main two gripes with the game is that going for sort of a brawler build that focuses on straight up damage seems to just be a lot better than trying to go for something else like a bleed or block build, and that a couple of the enemy types are more frustrating than fun to deal with. (I'm looking at you, rifle guy.) Overall a great game, one of my go-tos for something to play while watching Youtube videos.

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR Into the Breach meets Slay the SpireThe flow state in this game is amazing. I'm fighting the ninja boss on the rooftop, I look at my cards, I look at the layout. I know what to do. Combat roll over that ninja, grapple the boss into position, slip besides him, and shove him over the edge. First turn kill. I'm a damn genius. I can even watch it as a cinematic replay and bask in my badassitude. Then, I juke left when I should have gone right, take a crowbar to the head, get shot, then shoved out the window. Or I forget that the freaking hatchetman moves when I do and end up stepping into a corner where I get mercilessly cut down. But when I fail, I immediately click restart and tell myself just one more level, which escalates into one more mission, which escalates into one more game. It's really starting to mess up my sleep.

_childDocuments_.review: I really loved the idea of a "John Wick" / action movie simulator, and this appeared to be super cool for a bit - so if you're going to play for 5-10 hours and that's the vibe you're going for, do it! Buy this game and love it! 10/10, recommend.HOWEVER... if you're actually going to try and engage this game on its own terms, I'm sorry to say, this is yet another game that has totally lost the plot of being a game. In order to actually "play" the game, you will have to go real deep on probabilities, learning deck compositions, unlocks, etc etc etc.... the design gated the game behind playing a lot.To focus on the epitome of the problem, one of the best ways to defeat an enemy is to knock them out of bounds. There are many tools you need to achieve this - a movement card to position yourself to eject the opponent, and a card to eject the opponent, for example. Maybe you SWAP places with them, then JUMP KICK them out of a door. Don't worry, despite many opportunities appearing in the earlier maps, this will practically never happen, even if you pick a deck like GRAPPLER which should focus on these tools. Speaking of which, all of your moves involve throwing enemies? How about a class of enemy that's immune to throwing, as a category. Congrats, your run is screwed!Speaking of runscrew, money and deckburn compound any early errors to the point of meaning you may have lost a game hours ago and just didn't know it.They're working on a reskin, "Knights in Tight Spaces," and I hold no optimism they'll actually consider making a game. You know, a fun thing. To play.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a pretty good game.Every deck gives you good synergies and have aggressive or defensive playstyles.Enemies have a good variety and difficulty to them.Manipulating enemy positions and getting them to hit each other is very fun.The only boring side of it is that the power build-up is a little dull. You get money, upgrade your cards for higher damage, and don't really need anything else than what you do best and mixing things are only optional. You don't really work for the build, but play it like a puzzle game with what you have.With one player character there's also not much synergies you can do strategically. For example, grapplers work really well because you manipulate the enemy, as well as aggressive styles that dish out a lot of damage, but more defensive styles like counters and bleed is counter-intuitive because you have to eventually kill your enemy and they would work better if you had other allies to protect or hide behind.

_childDocuments_.review: Fights in Tight Spaces is a pretty good tactical deckbuilder.There are some interesting choices to be made when building a deck, especially when we get the option to draft cards (picking from random options) rather than the pre-built decks, which aren't bad, just a little stale after a couple runs with them.  The maps also offer interesting choices, though it falls victim almost immediately to min-maxing, with any path containing the gym (where we both upgrade and discard cards) being of the utmost importance.The enemies are mostly straightforward, and I haven't had any major wtf moments where something behaved in a way that wasn't clearly indicated.  My chief complaint is that the arena is very whitewashed, which can make it difficult to see if furniture/obstacles are in the way.  I lost a promising run because I wanted to knock back an assassin with counter so I would be out of range of its counter attack, but it had a difficult to see desk behind it which stopped it from being knocked back and caused my death.The martial arts are pretty fun to watch.  My biggest gripe here is that I wish the replay was a bit faster paced.  If there was less delay between character turns, the replay would be much more enjoyable to watch.  I do appreciate that the option to watch a replay of the fight exists, but I feel like it could be more action movie-y.

_childDocuments_.review: A great game with some pretty big problems.FITS is a roguelike deckbuilder. If you've played Slay The Spire, you already know how it works. You beat a mission, get a card, go through a branching mission, like StS floors, fight a boss at the end. Keep going until you die or beat the final boss. Honestly, that's the best way I can describe it, because the overall unique mechanics are a bit hard to explain. You move on a grid as well as attack, so moving yourself and enemies around with abilities can keep you safe or set up enemies to hit each other, and making sure you get cards that can let you move out of a bad situation is just as important as getting cards that cause damage, if not more so.But this game is HARD. Like, too hard. The first mission is pathetically easy, while the second (out of five, as of this review) is downright frustrating. The difficulty curve spikes extremely hard, and then immediately goes down again for the next two, before spiking again for the final mission, which is to be expected. The game seems to go out of its way to punish you for doing fun things, and it's a bit annoying in that aspect. For example, in mission three, you fight ninjas that gain bonus damage for the block that you have. If you've chosen the Counter Striker deck to start, your entire deck is build around blocking enemy attacks and countering them automatically, so building into your archetype too much is actively dangerous, and I can't say that I enjoy that. After a bit, it's pretty clear that, if it moves an enemy or yourself, it's good. If it heals you, it's good. If it only does damage, it's a complete waste of time. Trying to get weird and build outside of these rules will punish you.Another issue I have is that there just aren't enough cards that do cool things. There aren't things like weapon cards with a finite number of uses or pistols with some gun-fu animations. You have punches, kicks, bigger kicks, even bigger kicks, and pushes. I'd love some cards added in the future that expand on the archetypes a bit more, because right now it's "cards that counter/stun", "cards that are free if you play enough cards", and "cards that move people around", with some variations. There is a lot of unique design space that I don't feel like has been explored yet in this regard.That said, despite my complaints, I am pretty addicted to this game at the moment. It's a satisfying, challenging experience that rewards strategic play, and it's absolutely worth the price of admission as is, and I believe that it will only get better as time goes on. It's a real hidden gem.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is awesome. Adding just a couple more arena layouts, enemies and secondary mission goals would make this more than perfect.All in all a gem of a game.

_childDocuments_.review: For the price, one of the better action/strat games I've played. It does a lot of things right. I played that lame John Wick game, and while it had the correct spirit, it lacked the mechanics and basic creativity. This is essentially a card-shuffle rogue like married to Superhot. But that engine works and you definitely feel empowered when you roll back the replay. (Something Wick lacked, although it had the same gimmick). My one negative is no option to play again with all powers achieved ala Dead Space. Would be great fun to play thru feeling totally empowered. All in all, a great game with a steep but fair learning curve. I do agree with some fellow reviews that it should offer a more relaxed almost God-like mode and the non-save system feels unfair, but that's life sometimes. Very cool and a blast. Hope they are able to make a VR in the realm of Superhot.

_childDocuments_.review: Cool card battler in which you take on the role of a special agent who, on his missions, takes out room after room full of criminals in hand-to-hand combat. The background story is a bit simple, but the gameplay is not. Fights in Tight Spaces is just that - a turn-based brawler in tight spaces. What sounds strange is incredibly fun. You choose a deck of cards, get a mission from your boss, and the roguelite card-fighting begins. As befits a secret agent, you're always on your own and have to knock out a superior number of gang members in each room and eventually the boss. In between, there are rooms to heal your character or buy new cards. After winning battles, you can also upgrade your deck with a new card. Your cards are divided into four categories: attack, defend, move and special cards. With them you can quickly start beating criminals, but to succeed you'll have to play the cards wisely and at exactly the right time. For example, to push an opponent into the firing range of another opponent armed with a handgun (who will then take the bullet intended for you), or to push an opponent with his head against the wall - for this, of course, a wall must be present. In general, the positioning of all characters is extremely important. Attacks build up a combo value, which is needed to play some cards in the first place or at least make them more effective. You can choose between four different starter decks once you have unlocked them all (by reaching certain points in the game). Each deck focuses on a different style of play -  balanced, defensive, offensive and tricky. Since the last update in April, the game has become a bit easier, as opponents no longer move in their first turn and you can choose between three rewards at the end of each fight. Also, new random events have been added, which bring a bit of variety to the game. For example, sometimes you'll have to protect a civilian and push him around the room so that your opponents can't kill him. The minimalistic graphic style is extremely well done, a successful fight looks like you are the hero in an action movie fighting his way through a room full of extras.So, is it a masterpiece? Maybe not yet, it is still in Early Access, but it already brings some new ideas to the card battler genre and is a hell of a lot of fun, at least as long as you're not being beaten up by a bunch of criminals - because it is not easy.
