_childDocuments_.review: I have been meaning to write this review about 300 game play hours ago, but everytime I went to write it, I'd load the game for a quick play through, and then the review sat in waiting.  I bought in on Early Access (thanks for the recommendation from the world's best sloth mom, Casey Explosion), and played, and played and replayed, and failed to finish it for the longest of times, and loved it.  Loved it to bits.  Then the Daily Play arrived, and 10am, Australian Standard Time, there's a new daily challenge, and it has been a joy to play through each twist, variant, and "Wait, is that even doable?" moment in the game (even the undoable Finish in Six turns on a 7 turn survival round, because I laughed so hard).  Periodicially the ragdoll physics do things with the NPC body that would make a film censor send it back in the movies, and again, there's a gleeful moment of working a sequence of moves that result in some Big Bad Boss making an unscheduled close inspection of a Train Track that sparks joy.Yes, you can Marie Kondo the hell out of the villain underground.  So, buy it.  Fresh updates, new replayability options, daily play that's fun (and a little friendly competitive with the Top 10 usual suspects club), and fun.  Just amazing amounts of fun in working out a card sequence of moves that becomes so satisfying to see work (or fail hilariously because you forgot the green one with the sword does certain things).  Did I mention buy it? Because you should.

_childDocuments_.review: I've had this game since its early access release but didn't play it too much as I knew I wasn't going to have the best experience. It's now fully released and I've dumped about 8 hours into it in a couple of days, and it is a much more refined experience than the early access counterpart.The game plays out a lot like a mix of Slay the Spire combined with Into the Breach. You use your deck of cards to manipulate the position of your Agent, and also the enemies around you. You'll push enemies into hitting each other, and you'll use the environment to your advantage. You'll also need to build a deck and choose "enhancements" that work well together. The game comes with about 200 cards to unlock, it looks like, and around 5 different starter decks that all genuinely feel different to play with. Highly recommend. I'm sure I'll be playing a lot more of this in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: A cell shaded card fighting game. Be me:it's 11PM, I've just fought through a biker bar and now I'm thrown in jail, fighting my way through the jail as the entire jail wants me dead. I have 3/50 HP, and I am crawling to the next "scene". At the end of every match, you get a new "random" skill. The skill I got was: "one inch punch"For anyone who is a Bruce Lee fan, this is an awesome easter egg. In honor of the Green Hornet, I turn on my iTunes and fire up "Kung Fu Fighting" for my headphones.The music kicks off and I click, "next fight"You get 6 cards, I get 1 move card, "one inch punch", a jump kick, and three kicks and 2 blocks. I know what must be done. I proceed to wipe the floor with my cards as the spirit of Bruce Lee "enters the dragon" in cell shaded form. I win the fight and proceed to click next, grooving to the last 1 min. of "kung fu fighting"Now while I was doing that, iTunes also activated my Panasonic sound system, with 20 watt THX speakers, which were set at 20db volume from last weekend. My neighbour didnt like that too much, and after listening to the wall reverberate at 11pm on a Sunday night, he went to pound on my door.As Kung fu fighting finishes, I hear the door, open it, apologise to them for the racket. I then show him "Fights in Tight Spaces". He, being from Hong Kong, in his boxers and needing a good story to explain to his wife, comes in and we fire up a new game. He too is grinning and we turn back on "kung fu fighting" for a quick run through the game.He goes back to his wife, agreeing to buy a game after a 11PM brohug.I close the door, and write this review.12/10. This game got everyone "kung fu fighting". Would recommend to everyone I know who enjoys punching organised criminals or punch-em-up games.

_childDocuments_.review: I love the game, but after playing it a lot I have found that I play all of the decks almost the same way in order to beat the game.  Gain movement cards and cards that knock opponents out of the field, and win.  Only difference is that I will pick up good block cards if I am making a counter deck.  In the other decks I get rid of the defensive cards and just focus on movement to win.   Also, I am not a fan of some of the randomization in the rewards.  It feels bad when you don't get any counter cards offered when you are playing the counter deck.  The game needs a little more specialization with the decks and make specific cards that will only show up for those decks.  Give some cool gadgets for the trickster deck.  Have a deck that works with throws and knockdowns so that the cards that the cards that hit downed opponents can be used more often instead of being mostly dead cards in your hand.   Make some super aggressive and defensive cards that only show up in the aggressive deck and defensive deck.   I can't wait to see what more you do to really flesh out the game because the core concept of it is fun to play.

_childDocuments_.review: Video Review:  7/10 Fighting in Tight spaces is a turn-based deck builder where you fight in tight spaces. The title basically tells you all you need to know.  The cards you are given in the game range from attack, movement, block and counter cards. You can use a set number indicated by the number on the left hand of your screen and each card has a use amount. The cards cost ranges from zero and up, the interesting concept is that you can build up a momentum and combo points to do finishing moves like a spinning leg kick that deal an absolute metric ♥♥♥♥ ton of damage. You can also use the environment to your advantage with cards like head slam that can only be used when enemies are near objects so you can Plop their heads on it like the last beer at closing time. Then in some maps you have death spots that you can push or shove enemies to and will give you the quick deaths you sometimes need especially for harder enemies. The game plays like an arena rogue lite, where you can select a mission and you are set on a branching path of arenas with buffs to enemies and random rewards for wining. Rewards like new cards and gaining more health or heath replenishment. With small objectives that will allow you to gain more cash so you can reach the gym or clinic to either heal yourself or you can use the money to upgrade your cards to make them stronger and can lower the spending cost of the card. If you beat the mission, you will unlock the other one and will still keep your upgrades, but if you die everything is lost. You can start the new mission but with no upgrades you are at a big disadvantage going in. It's still possible to beat the mission but it would have been easier with the upgrades you obtained from going through the previous. The enemies also range from your standard goons to thugs with guns or prisoners with shivs. Each providing you with countless ways to die. Some also giving buffs like more health or defense to the surrounding enemies. But the unique thing about them is that every one of them are dumber than a box of door nails. If you have a gun man aimed at you and is wanting to shoot you after you end your turn just push a goon in the line and get out of the way, Reck it Ralph will load his friends face with buck shot and move to aim at you again like he did nothing wrong. I think I'll call this one ♥♥♥♥ Cheney. But the game will make you think about your moves and plan your cards accordingly to build up momentum and the best way to avoid damage because you are given a set number in the beginning and yes, you can heal along the way but it's not a lot and you could easily lose that health in the next arena so strategy is key. I’m having a blast and the game is in early access but it feels polished and complete so the early access just means more things are meant to be added to the game in a later date. So just more fun to be had. If you are a fan of turn based, deck builders or strategy games I think you will have fun with this one.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game over two years ago and today I have completed it for the first time. A lot of blood, sweat, tears, raw energy and anger have gone into my playthroughs but my God was it worth it. If you're struggling to beat this game my tips are these:1) Keep a small deck - Once you have what you feel is a perfect deck, stop adding cards and focus on upgrades.2) Don't neglect medical - Yes, strong cards are good but upgrading health will keep you in the fight longer and alive to tell tales.3) Get rid of Step - It's garbage4) 0 momentum cards will save your life, as will cards that once upgraded become 0 momentum cards. Don't neglect them.5) Walls do 4 damage, enemies that are targeting you will hit other enemies once you move out of the way. Don't forget to knock people over the edge for easy wins.Ground Shatter you are the bane of my life. I hate you, I love you. This game is a masterpiece and I've been playing since enemies would auto-attack once you walked into their line of fire. I'm going to take a break from playing after this but thank you for being here with me throughout this journey, up and down. You guys are sadistic and I look forward to purchasing your future titles. 10/10 Bravo.

_childDocuments_.review: F.I.T.S. in its core is a deck-building strategy game in the guise of an action/fighting game. Its primary inspirations are "Slay the Spire" and "Into the Breach". That's, actually, interpreted into "many VS one" fights where playing your cards correctly you can wipe whole gangs, either by spectacularly punch and kick their guts out or manipulate their momentum into hitting / smashing on their allies instead. The deckbuilding options may not reach the levels of options of Slay the Spire or Monster Train however, there's a decent variety of achetypes of fighting styles you can choose from. On the matter of maps /terrain, the game has not the greatest range but that's a big deal, for me at least. All and all, the game is loads of fun and compellingly challenging. Highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: 100+ Hours in one month is not a common gaming milestone for me, this game truly stole my heart.The Early Access-ness of the game shows, it can feel shallow, and seems to be nearly impossible to finish since you don't carry any benefits over from run to run. It desperately needs some sort of progression between runs, and you'll quickly run through all the flavors of gameplay.BUT THE GAMEPLAY IS SO DAMN FUN. Every time you use your card's to their maximum potnetial, knock some ninja bastard out, you can feel that little hit of Dopamine that brings you back time and again. It's EXTREMELY satisfying, and getting a reward after each fight helps make up for the lack of progression over all.Although you're playing out a fight, it really reminds me most of the Hearthstone Dr. Boom Puzzle Campaign. You get your hand, you're presented with a static puzzle, and you have to figure out what the most efficient use of those cards will be. Then repeat.At launch their are enough cards to keep the game fresh for a while, and they've already released an update that solved some of my silent gripes. Very excited to see what the final product will be, and would HIGHLY recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic! Funky beats, perfectly fitting art style, and awesome flow. I'm still making new builds, and perfecting old ones, and just generally having a blast! If you have the time, give it a shot!Edit: I decided after writing a negative review on another game (that I will not name here), that I should elaborate on what I love most about this game.It respects the player's ability to choose.That may sound stupid, given what genre it is. But fights in tight spaces excels at it.Because of one crucial aspect of this game-The difficulty in it is not found in limited mechanics.Take Into the Breach- phenomenal game, in many ways- but due to its nature, you can't make many changes to your build mid-game. Sure, a few, but nothing so drastic as Fights in Tight Spaces allows.Take Alina of the Arena- also lots of fun, probably my second favorite game after this one- but you can only move as the first part of a turn, or not at all. It limits the mechanics to create difficulty.Fights in Tight Spaces throws both those flaws straight out the window.Maybe you've been making an early counter build, but you don't have enough damage- just pick some damage cards. Boom, your build can adapt.Shoot, you're surrounded by two assassins, because you couldn't be bothered to pay 50 bucks to avoid it. But wait, that one is almost dead! Shoot, how will I move after killing them? Oh wait- I can!Bam, both of the only flaws in comparable games, solved like it's nothing by this absolute masterpiece of a game.If I would phrase what I love about this game so much another way, I would put it as such- this game prioritizes choice over ingrained difficulty. If you want a difficult experience, choose a harder difficulty. If you want a relaxing time beating the utter crud out of some thugs, ninjas, and mafia members, do an easier difficulty. The game doesn't shove difficult mechanics down your mouth- it trusts you to know what kind of experience you will find satisfying, unlike so many other games that arrogantly say, "nO, i KnOw ThAt LiMiTiNg YoUr OpTiOnS wIlL mAkE iT mOrE fUn AnD rEwArDiNg."I'm sort of rambling, but seriously, if you haven't already, buy this game (and the DLC), and decide how you want to have fun.And if by some miracle, the developers of this game happen to see this- Thank you for the best experience I've ever had in a game, and have a wonderful day.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Fun deckbuilder with a monstrously banging soundtrack and sleek visual style.So, I'm thinking that I like Slay the Spire, FTL, Into the Breach and these kinds of games. Along comes Fights in Tight Spaces and I'm immediately hooked.This is essentially a deckbuilding tactical game where your cards, attacks and moves are beautifully animated as fights in tight spaces. It's in the name, really!To keep this short: It's fun, the runs can take an hour or longer but you can interrupt it anytime as it saves after each fight/node. The cards have simplistic art for now, and their descriptions are not all using the same terminology. The available archetypes are alright with the exception of the trickster. They lend themselves to certain builds and card pickups.I'm not a fan of how the upgrade shop doubles its prices after every transaction at that very same shop, some textual descriptions would absolutely be useful, as well as card cost previews when receiving free card upgrades.Since this is early access, I expect a lot of polish to be added to the game. I would absolutely love to see a female agent (Keep the suit, it's sleek!), more archetypes and perhaps archetype specific/unique cards, the ability to choose from a selection of artifacts/upgrades that you receive when beating a boss and perhaps even a custom archetype where you can draft or buy your starting deck.Also, finally, I'd like the briefcase objectives to not spawn in such a manner that makes it physically impossible to reach them even if you have nothing but moves in your hands.To the devs: You knocked it out of the park. You made a simple looking but pleasingly complex game. Thank you!

_childDocuments_.review: Fights in Tight Spaces reminds me of the old board game Rush Hour where you move the car around and try to get outbut in this case its more of an action, roguelite puzzle with a lot of beating to do!Is the game worth the full price? _childDocuments_.review: F**K I LOVE THIS GAME.Context: I generally don't like deck builders. I love isometric strategy games. This is both. I truly think is one of the most slept-on games about. It has strategy positioning, forward planning in both your placement, your move set, and your order of play. You need to predict and plan both a few moves in advance, and the whole game in advance when choosing your deck. All the best parts of deck builders with none of the s**t parts. A simplified iso strategy in some aspects, but for all that is removed from other iso games, more is added with the deck builder angle.This may seem shallow at first glance, but delving deeper you will discover more and more. 62 hours playtime as I write this, and it is a game I think about when at work, and am eager to play. It is currently 1:40am and I had to tear myself away so i can go to bed for a 6am start.If you are unsure, get it. Give it your attention for an hour and if you don't like it, refund it. It is worth the gamble and I reckon very few people will refund.Devs need to make it a mobile game too. Not that I play much mobile gaming, but it would transfer reasonably well to that platform, with minor tweaks, and would make them a killing. _childDocuments_.review: This is a surprising and underrated gem with many positives and some not so positives.Check out my gameplay as I explore the Grappler class deck and cover some of the tactics:I have to say that I never thought I would get so hooked on this game,, owned it for a couple of weeks from the time of this review and the number of hours played is rapidly rising! I don`t usually play this kind of game, but what this game does right for me is the accessibility thanks to its simple yet intuitive interface, the art style which is bold, sharp, unique and pleasing on the eye. The theme of being an agent skilled in many hand to hand combat disciplines that you build upon as you progress. The animation of the characters moves and interactions are really good which adds to the presentation.You get general fights, survival, protect and boss missions. All are turn based, affected by the class of card deck you chose from the start which in turn affects your strategy. There is no time based pressure, but each level has sub challenges that reward you with health, stat boost, new cards (moves) and money which you use to boost existing cards, purchase new ones or boost/increase health in relevant areas determined by the branching path you take on your quest (all which lead to the same goal in the end). It is thought provoking on how to best take on the mission you are on, but can be done at your own pace making for a relaxing yet satisfying gameplay. Being able to turn the AI against each other can be very satisfying if you play your cards right.You get various class or card decks to choose from including Balanced, Counter Striker, Aggressive, Slasher, Grappler and Trickster (in that order) and each deck is unlocked as you level up. All decks have some shared basic moves, but then also have their own unique moves of which you can build upon as you play which results in their own tactics. Currently I am enjoying the Grappler deck (this is featured in my video) which is mostly focused on throw moves, but can be further adapted with punches, kicks etc (required for some bosses). I have many positives for this game, my gripes are few and mainly minor. Things like the cards presented on each level does not seem random, even down to when using special cards to trade a card for new cards, they will always be the same no matter how often you restart a level. This can be an issue if you are in an impossible situation where you have exhausted all your tactics and found no way to win a level due to the hand you are being dealt. You are then forced to abandon your run and start from scratch again.Some sub missions can be impossible, such as protecting an unarmed ambassador due to the position and hand your dealt, or completing in a specified number of turns due to the same issue. This is mostly minor as these are optional goals but offer bonus rewards which could be valuable for later game and potentially make or break your run.I would like more missions to be added, but I'm not sure of the dev has any intentions on expanding it, however there is a lot of replay-ability as you expand your cards and explore new tactics for each new run. It would be cool if we could build our own class deck from scratch based on cards we have unlocked aswell as the current expanding the base class decks.This game has introduced me to a genre of game I have never previously considered playing, at this time I do think this is a unique case for me. The theme, art style and presentation is what has got me hooked and I would love to see a sequel or just see this game expanded further upon.

_childDocuments_.review: A brilliant concept, well executed. Using deckbuilder mechanics to move and attack in a limited space works really well. Enemies display what moves they'll make on their turn, making each turn a little puzzle of how best to manoeuvre yourself and your enemies to avoid getting hurt and maximise the damage they do to each other. A bit of variety in enemies and objectives keeps this fresh, with enemies that move when you do or attack off turn or push you into other spaces or counter attack when struck and so on.The execution is good but not great. The game could have used some more time in early access, it's got consistently better throughout the EA period but some basic things feel like they're not done yet. The balance in the cards is a little wonky and you'll often encounter cards that are extremely strong or extremely weak, making the usable cardpool much smaller than it has to be. You'll also find some of the best cards in the game in the starting decks and some of the worst only offered as rewards for clearing tough late game levels. The result is that the feeling of progression as you build up your deck isn't what it could be and there's a sense of missed opportunities with every inviable card that could've been the basis of an interesting deck with a few tweaks. There are a lot of small quality of life issues or little relics from the EA process like objectives tailored to a deck that's no longer the games sole deck that were never pruned or expanded. A few months spent balancing and tidying up without adding new features could've made this my game of the year.Still, the reason that the missed opportunities hurt is because the core gameplay loop is just so dang good. There's a lot to enjoy about this game as it stands and among the viable cards you'll still find plenty of different ways to play. I'd expect anyone who likes deckbuilders or small scale turn based strategy will have a blast with this, I heartily recommend it to anyone into either genre (and suggest it's a good way to try them if you're not!). The overall impression is something like a cross between Slay the Spire and Into the Breach, carrying forward some of the best qualities of both games.

_childDocuments_.review: I played a lot of the prologue and was absolutely hype for this game to be fully released. let me tell you this game is an absolutely fantastic concept. However that is completely overshadowed by the glaring balance issues.You may be thinking "Well. rogue likes are usually hard so it makes sense" this games difficulty is ridiculously rng based. Theirs so much BS "50% chance" mechanics in events that I want to die. You barely get any enhancements, the cards you get to pick from are practically uninfluencable and gyms (the shops of this game) are so few, far, and expensive, that you can't rely on them to flesh out the archetype you are going for.The issue isn't with the balancing, it's with ignoring the core game loop of a roguelike. Your power in a roguelike is supposed to come from knowledge of power-ups and abilities and how they work together and being able to create good combos of items on the fly, this game bubbles all that depth down to a 50/50 chance to get ♥♥♥♥♥♥ over or have fun.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR, feels more like an alpha or other early build of game, needing more polish.The curb appeal of this game is there; you can be like Daredevil or John Wick and fight a crowd of dudes in a claustrophobic room without needing godlike reflexes because it's turn based? Sounds cool, sign me up.First problem, there are too many variables to keep track of, and not a quick/simple way to do so. Early fights will have few enemy variants (each with their own ability, or combination of abilities), and it's easy to keep track of what enemy can do what. Later fights however, you'll likely have to check what each enemy can do most every turn. Some enemy abilities are displayed with an icon, but not all, for some reason. They could be more easily identified via colour, given the minimalist art design- but there are several similar colours so again, you're checking what each enemy can do each turn.Second, damage. Very quickly you'll realise most damage moves are, not great. doing 5-10 damage when the enemy has 40, 80, or 200 health is, again, not great. Especially given that you're normally outnumbered. There are better moves sure, but this is a deckbuilding game, so you can pull movement cards when you need damage, damage when you need block, and block when you need movement. There are better cards sure, but you have to get and/or upgrade them, and pull them on the proper turn. Some cards also require special positioning, and you'll get to play them maybe 1/4 of the time you want to, every other time they are pulled it's a dead draw, clogging your hand from a potentially useful card. Third, (building on point 2) I don't think this game benefits much (if at all) from being a deckbuilder. I know I don't have many hours in the game, and there are almost certainly some synergies out there I don't know about, but even with different starting decks, the runs I did felt samey because the same cards showed up in rewards. perhaps there are different card pools available, idk. Movement is also so critical to not dying, and some enemies can act in-between individual actions you take, so pulling enough damage to kill every enemy is not a reliable solution to not having sufficient block/movement. Feels like this game would be better as a turn based puzzle game, with any and all of your moves available but on cooldown (X movement per turn, Y energy to spend on actions)Fourth, Replays. Man... so sad. Replays are not as fluid as you'd want them to be, heck NEED them to be to be cool. It's not SUPERHOT where your actions are played back in realtime at superhuman speed. Each character moves there exact move as they did in game, pauses, then next move. It's robotic, it's janky, but mostly, it's uncool to watch. Granted simultaneous movement of multiple characters would go against what actually happened in-game, but regardless, as they are- they kinda suck.Maybe I should've watched gameplay before buying, I had played some other deckbuilders and this one seemed cool. However I don't believe this to near the replay-ability of other, similar games

_childDocuments_.review: Fights In Tight Spaces is a roguelite tactics game which combines Slay The Spire style deckbuilding with Into The Breach style grid based combat. The player is a British spy, on a mission to take down gangs of bikers, prisoners, ninjas, and mafia.•	Each run uses a node based layout which will be familiar to players of other deckbuilders. Each node could be a fight against normal enemies, an elite fight, a random event where you’ll need to make a choice which could result in a positive or negative effect, a gym where you can buy new cards, upgrade or remove a card, and a medical facility where you can restore or increase maximum health. Each act finishes with a boss fight, and there are five acts, which means a full run could take a few hours.•	At the start of combat, the player and several enemies will appear in a small room which is divided into square grid. The maps are definitely tight spaces, such as a 3x3 elevator and a 5x2 prison van, while even larger rooms like canteens have tables and other objects in the middle which restrict movement. However, when I was able to build a powerful deck, it felt more like “they’re trapped in here with me”.•	At the start of each turn you’ll randomly draw cards which allow you to attack, defend, move around the room, and perform other special abilities. You’ll also see what action each enemy intends to take on their turn.•	Most cards cost energy to play, and energy is restored at the start of each turn. Special attacks are played by spending combo points, which are gained when attacking an enemy, but reduced when moving to another tile.•	Each turn is like a puzzle where you’ll need to figure out how to deal as much damage to enemies as possible, while ending the turn in a position to avoid taking damage, either by stacking up defence, moving to a tile which isn’t being targeted, dodging attacks, or stunning an enemy to cancel their attack.•	Some enemies are equipped with a gun which gives them a longer attack range, or a shield which protects from frontal attacks, while others have special abilities such as counter attacking when you hit them, dodging your first attack each turn, moving when the player moves, and summoning extra minions.•	Enemies can hurt each other if you push them into a tile which is being targeted, and some maps also have tiles where enemies can be pushed off the map for an instant kill, such as a roof railing or the doors of a moving subway train, however enemies can also do this to the player.•	Winning fights, and completing bonus objectives such as winning in a time limit, or protecting an ally, will reward you with cards, money, upgrades to health and energy, and relics which provide powerful passive bonuses.•	There are various difficulty settings. At lower levels you can undo moves back to the start of the current turn if you make a mistake, or restart a fight if you die, but at higher levels every action is permanent.•	After winning each fight you can view a real time replay of the fight, similar to Super Hot and John Wick Hex.•	Long term replayability is limited because the node layouts are quite similar for each run, and each act has the same boss fight every time. However, there are daily challenges and an endless mode.•	I didn’t have any problems with bugs, crashes or framerate.Fights In Tight Spaces is a fun deckbuilder which fans of similar games should enjoy. Definitely worth picking up on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game, the addition of movement and spacing to a deckbulding game, emphasis on enemy AI patterns and attack methods, and the myriad ways to move yourself and enemies around, out of, and into each others' attacks, gives the game an immensely intriguing, tactical feel that naturally flows and fits the 'secret agent CQC fistfights' theme perfectly. The music is also great, a pumping electronica soundtrack that sets a great tone and compliments the game's aesthetic pretty well.But hoo boy, the rest of the game is terribly undercooked. The card and upgrade economy is all over the place, and enhancements, despite being FiTS's equivalent to 'artefacts' in other games, are nowhere near as powerful or build-defining; many of them won't even have a noticeable effect on your gameplay. Card balance is also off: your ability to draw extra cards is limited, hindering many card synergies and softly enforcing a 'quality over quantity' approach... which runs counter to the many cards designed to support or set up other actions, and the fact that you get a card draft after every battle... a card draft you're encouraged to skip most of the time to keep your deck lean. This also makes action cost less valuable as you are limited by card draw far more than action economy. This just scratches the surface; there are a collection of small(and some large) problems with the overall design that bring the experience down a lot and takes away from the otherwise precise and satisfying combat. I played a lot of the demo before the game was released as I was completely mesmerised by the combat, and hoped the rough edges would be buffed out at some point. Unfortunately, many of those problems still remain in some form, and with future updates likely not forthcoming, Fights in Tight Spaces might be stuck in this half-baked state; conceptually excellent combat with an under-developed, flawed game built around it.

_childDocuments_.review: If you love Fighting games and Roguelike Deckbuilders, this game is for you. In this game you build a deck of fighting moves and use it to defeat your enemies in melee combat. As opposed to some Deckbuiders, the base decks are not generic, but are themed for different styles of play. My favorite deck is the Counter Attack deck, where you build up lots of block and then counter attack when your enemies attack. After each round you can watch a replay of the round, seeing your character defeat all the enemies in the room. It's really cool.The only problem with this game is how long runs take. One run could take well over an hour. It is a fun time, but a long time. You can stop and save anytime.This game is an awesome combination of Fighting and deckbuilding. I have enjoyed every minute of the 60+ hours I've put into it.

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty good roguelite deckbuilder and into-the-breach combo, with some flaws.Top frustrating thing is you may or may not get missions with "add momentum" rewards, which basically determines whether you win or lose. If you have the choice of more momentum (i.e. action points), it's worth sacrificing basically *anything* to get it. Take some damage to race to the suitcase, or whatever. There's no common way to increase your base momentum other than these rewards, is the real problem - if you could buy it for 250 money that would somewhat fix this flaw (though maybe it would also highlight it - it's easily *worth* 250, and other rewards are like 30-60.) Perhaps a better fix would be to have the increase-powers rewards be some kind of token, spend 1 to increase combo or max health by 2, or 3 to increase momentum. (At that ratio I would literally never pick combo or health though, again highlighting the disparity in value!)The difference in value of the "enhancements" is also really stark, so again you can get screwed or a free win based on the choices you're offered after beating a boss. You might get "momentum mastery" (+2 action points, which from the base of 3 is amazing), a free movement card every turn, or an extra card draw every turn, or you might be stuck with "+20 money when you don't take a new card" as your best choice, which pretty much only seems worth anything if you're trying to get the 1000 money achievement.Third flaw is the different starting decks all eventually converging on the same style. It feels like you can't possibly beat the boss if you don't have a good variety of movement cards, and some blocks or throws (for when he unavoidably follows you). Counterattacks is definitely the easiest starting deck, and basically with any other deck you end up picking up counterattacks anyway and playing mostly the same way. A push-heavy deck is all well and good until you get to the bosses that can't be pushed.I preferred Alina of the Arena, in essentially the same genre; it did a better job of encouraging completely diverse playstyles. But both are good, still well worth playing!

_childDocuments_.review: Having played for several hours, I can say with full confidence that I already love this game. A huge part of it is the situation to situation combat, as the chess-like set-up of the room you're fighting changes with every move your enemies make. Furthermore, the deckbuilding is extremely interesting but at the same time very simple, allowing to mix and match different cards without any need to sit with a pen and paper trying to find a loophole or somesuch. There is also a Rogue-like approach to the game, as your agent will slowly unlock different starting decks as well run into randomly placed situations and fights, keeping you guessing about what will happen next.There is a singular problem, but that's mostly balancing. The game grants you a single pack at the start of any run, gearing for different approaches, and while all of them tend to come with their own challenge, the Defensive pack is extremely overpowered as you can essentially turn your agent into a walking counterattack machine and shrug off or dodge most attacks.There's also the fact that in general replays aren't very fluid and usually look very awkward, as the dynamics of a movie fighting sequence don't translate from a deckbuilding game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a cool concept, and it's very much my genre, but it just has too many problems which make it equal parts fun and frustrating.It takes quite a while to get used to all the different mechanics, because they're not represented very well -- the different monochrome symbols and effects become muddled and confusing until you've gotten used to them enough to know the quirks and gotchas. The explanations of how the effects work, and often how the early game cards work, are also poorly-worded and ambiguous, so you really have to use them a few times to get used to what they actually do; the written descriptions aren't enough.I spent the whole time comparing this to Alina of the Arena, because that game has exactly the same feel, a tactical movement-based deck builder roguelite similar to Slay the Spire, but Alina does it much better; the effects and cards are explained and visually represented much more clearly, the soundtrack is better, it's just a better game.I've also noticed a couple of bugs which can really be frustrating -- some around enemy effects not always triggering when they should, which can sometimes totally bork the clever set of moves you're using to maximise damage and avoid getting hit by anything, and end up taking massive damage instead.The most egregious bug, though, is with the ninja boss with the spiky armour. The premise is if you hit him you get stabbed; makes sense. The most obvious counter to that in a game like this is to set your enemies up so that *they* hit him, and not only do they beat up the boss for you, but they also take the spiky armour damage.Nope.There's a bug which makes *you* take the spiky armour damage when *your enemy* hits the boss. Given it's one of only 4 bosses in the game and it's a bug affecting the most obvious way of dealing with the threat, that's pretty infuriating.My advice would be to pick up Alina of the Arena instead of this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Ever watched a spy movie and wondered what would happen if the protagonist decided to throw strategy into the mix instead of just brute force? That's the premise of Fights In Tight Spaces, a game that transforms those adrenaline-pumping action sequences into a turn-based tactical brawl. Sounds cool, right? Well, it is, but it's not without its hiccups.In this game, you're Agent 11, a spy working for a mysterious espionage organization. Your mission? Take down crime syndicates and their bosses in procedurally generated levels. It's reminiscent of Slay The Spire but with a gritty, hand-to-hand combat twist.The combat is where Fights In Tight Spaces really shines. Picture this: You're in a cramped 3D arena, and you've got cards instead of fists. These cards represent your attacks, and they're surprisingly satisfying. You can headbutt, throw, counter, and even pull off some flashy moves straight out of a Street Fighter game. The animations are so well done that it's a treat to watch your enemies crumple under your punches.But what sets this game apart is its focus on positioning. You're not just playing cards; you're also managing your space. You'll need movement cards to get into the right spot, and there are moments where creative maneuvering is more satisfying than landing a punch. It's like playing chess with an adrenaline rush.The visuals are eye-catching, with a style reminiscent of Casino Royale's intro or Superhot. It's minimalist yet never dull. The variety of locations is impressive, from a motorcycle club to a pub, each with its distinct identity. The lighting adds depth to the visuals, making it a treat for the eyes.However, there's a glaring issue - replayability. Unlike other deckbuilders that force you to change strategies, Fights In Tight Spaces feels stuck in one playstyle. Experimenting with different deck archetypes often feels pointless, as the game seems to fight against it.The randomization doesn't do the game any favors either. After a while, fights start blending together, and random enemy encounters lose their charm. It's a bit of a disappointment when you realize you've seen most of what the game offers.That said, there's a silver lining - the difficulty settings. Classic Plus mode, for instance, allows retries and move undos, turning the game into a satisfying puzzle rather than a relentless brawl.One letdown is the lack of storytelling. It feels like there's a missed opportunity for an engaging plot in this action-packed spy world. Agent 11's silence, while fitting for some games, feels odd in a world where you're toppling crime families.In the end, despite its quirks, Fights In Tight Spaces is worth a try. The brain-engaging combat is top-notch. It's just that it had the potential to be exceptional, but it left me with an "okay" instead of feeling "wowed"

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting mix of Slay the Spire and Into the Breach.You're playing as a 007-expy, moving from one location to another, usually with branching paths that give you a choice of options of where to go. Along the routes you take, you'll hit areas where you can either refill/increase your health (hospitals) or improve/buy/remove cards (gyms) using money earned during missions. Each campaign ends with a boss fight. You keep your deck between campaigns, and, including the tutorial, there's half a dozen before the end of your career.During combat, your character is in a one-against-many scenario. The only friendly I've seen so far was a civilian I had to protect, who just cowered in place. You're able to fight off the hordes of thugs, criminals, and ninja - many of whom are wielding weapons of some sort - because they telegraph what they're going to do, and you're way more mobile then they are. You've got two currencies - momentum (energy) and combo. You start each round with 3 momentum, with cards costing between 0-4 momentum. Each time you play an attack card that hits an enemy, you earn one combo. Playing a movement or defensive card will reduce combo. Some regular cards get stronger the more combo you have, others will deal a multiplier of your combo, but reset it to 0. Some cards have a combo cost - they can only be played if your combo is high enough.Much like Into the Breach, positioning is everything. Enemies can be pushed around, bashed into walls or obstacles, or even thrown out of the arena (resulting in an insta-kill), if you position them correctly. They can also be persuaded to punch, stab, or shoot one another, if you sidestep or push them correctly.One of my favorite moments so far was on a boss fight: Two of the bosses' minions had push attacks that went off automatically if anything stepped in front of them, and they just happened to be facing each other, one space apart. I was able to kick the boss into one of the minions, who pushed the boss into the other minion, who pushed him right back, resulting in a good chunk of the bosses life getting drained.The game seems to reward glass cannon builds - many enemies have nasty effects when they hit you, some ignore armor entirely, and the values of block cards means that often, even if you block, you're likely to take some damage anyway; better to just step out of the way and dodge entirely.Overall, I'm enjoying it, although I don't know if it has the staying power of StS.

_childDocuments_.review: To celebrate the proper launch of the game, this review deserves a revisit. Not only has the game grown quite a lot since Early Access, I also played it, uh. Kind of a lot since then.And while there were some rather glaring balance issues at the start that made the game feel more stressful than it should've, most of those complaints have been adressed, and I find myself doing daily runs rather consistently.So what exactly  Fights in Tight Spaces?It's a blend between a deckbuilder and a board game with roguelike elements under a very simple premise of a story - You control Agent 11, a special agent of Section 11 who comes in two flavors: male and female, both of which are identical in stats, moveset and impeccable fashion sense, and are tasked with tackling criminal organisations around the globe. The game is fairly light on story, with barebones justifications given as to why you do what you do - this should become plainly evident from Mission 2 onward, where you are smuggled into a prison currently overtaken by rioting prisoners under the guise as a lawyer...only for Agent 11 to immediately start fistfighting inmates.As to be expected of a game that seems to try to emulate and pay homage to James Bond-style action movies, story is merely a justifaction for  cool things are happening, and it does that job wonderfully. With the pretense out of the way, what do you actually ?As mentioned, Fights in Tights is a roguelite deckbuilder, and a fairly difficult one at that. At the beginning of the game, you are given the Balanced starter deck, which serves as a good introduction to the game's mechanics; attacks, movements and actions are all represented by cards, and your deck represents your available moves. Simple! Your character has a reserve of Momentum, which amounts to the game's mana system; a resource that replenishes each turn and is required for most cards; attacking enemies builds up a Combo, another resource some cards either use up, require to be used, or benefit from. Combo persists between turns, but is reduced when you move.Of course you're not beating up malignant mannequins, but hardened criminals, so your enemies fight back - instead of using a deck, though, enemies come in "classes", each of which have a particular gameplan. The most basic thugs will try to walk up an adjacent square, and punch you - other enemies use attacks with more range, will attack more than once per turn, counter your attacks, advance when you move and so on and so forth.And that's how Battles in Close Quarters plays out - you pick a map on a path to the boss of your current assignment, you're plonked down onto a board along with your enemies, and from there on out, hijinks ensue as you try to juggle beating your enemies without getting torn to shreds while fulfilling special side objectives that reward you with monetary bonuses or stat upgrades; such as an increased life pool, higher combo limit or a higher base momentum. Money is used to upgrade cards, remove cards from your deck, or purchase new moves - it is integral to your gameplay, so these side objectives are very important.Your first runs are likely to fail.Combats in Cramped Corridors is designed to be challenging, but in a fair and rewarding way.There is little in the way of meta-progression; there are no permanent stat boosts or character upgrades. The only rewards come in the form of unlocking different starter decks, all of which cater to different playstyles; Balanced representing the reliable Jack-Of-All-Trades, Counter-Striker being a more sturdy tank-build, Aggressive making more use of the combo system to deal potentially immense damage, Trickster to play around with positioning, Slasher for a more DoT-oriented playstyle and Grappler revolving around throwing enemies for crowd control, there's a deck for most playstyles! Or, one may opt to go for Draft Mode instead; foregoing the guarantee of a specific playstyle in favor of trying to build your own little toolbox at the mercy of RNG. Aside from unlocking more tools, however, your character does not improve.You, however, do.As you learn enemy patterns, figure out card synergies, find your playstyle and learn the ins and outs of both your and enemy positioning, the game feels a lot more managable. The game is never easy, and every round is - to some degree - vulnerable to RNG messing your run up in some capacity, but the game is  rewarding in a way, since even on a poor run, your strategizing can get you very,  far and potentially turn things around.The more you play, the more you learn which maps are best played in what way - you learn to exploit chokepoints without getting yourself trapped, you learn which angles to exploit with what movement cards, you learn how to best position yourself to coax enemies setting themselves up for an instant kill ring-out, and , nothing is more satisfying than managing to manipulate enemy positioning to watch them beat each other up in a gargantuan friendly firework; watching enemies suffer a collective 40 damage in a turn by employing two 0 damage cards is just as rewarding as setting up a combo for three turns, only to have it culminate in a finisher that sends a mini-boss flying off-stage in one massive hit.The game stays on the same level of challenging, but still feels very different once you get a hold of it. You go from feeling like a more handsome Mr. Bean, blindly stumbling into auto-attacking enemies and getting booted out of the front door, to an (arguably, considering stabbing people until they bleed out and throwing them off moving trains are both legit ways to end a fight) less lethal John Wick with a penchant for punching.:Brawls in Small Halls is the best kind of challenging game, with different difficulty settings to tweak your experience but never making it a total breeze; where experience is rewarded . Where RNG might end your run sometimes, without making the game feel entirely dependent on it; where your choices and input still . The game was carefully crafted, there's actual heart and soul in it; the devs were inspired, and it shows in every facet of the game, be it the stylish presentation, snappy art style, excellent attack animations, great music or the consistent balancing tweaks that followed the Early Access release. I've no clue what the future will hold for the game, but I sincerely hope there's more to come. As for now, the game gets the strongest possible thumbs up. It's one of the best games of its kind I've ever played, and I greatly appreciate it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game, bar one feature is actually really good. I have, at the time of writing this; nearly 500 hours on this game. I have reached the maximum level you can attain and quiet possibly at the time of reading, have every achievement. Though all this positivity is unfortunately dashed by one horrid failure in game design.The game does not draw it's cards at random, nor does it do so fairly. The game makes no advertisement or mention of this fact; but the game will intentionally draw cards that minimise your potential to avoid damage. Eventually you will be caught out by this, as the game will randomly place enemies at the start of each level. This means that the longer you play, the greater the risk you will be unlucky enough to die without any fault of your own. You are then essentially forced to replay until you get lucky enough to avoid nigh-certain death.This is needless and very strange, because there is enough randomisation to ensure sufficient difficulty, the card rewards you get at the end of each level are random, the challenges for extra rewards are random and the aforementioned enemy placement is also randomised.There was no need to have this system in place, it's cheap and undermines the entire point of the game, you are not just at the mercy of chance, but the game actively attempts to sabotage you all whilst trying to conceal this fact.Only one of the six difficulties disables this, the easiest difficulty in the game. The brief tool-tip mentions this feature only in so far as to ensure you get a movement card every turn; confirming that the game does indeed calculate what best means to limit your movement unless you pick this specific difficulty. You are forced to ignore 5/6 difficulty modes if you don't want the game to actively conspire against you and ensure your failure.

_childDocuments_.review: This game takes established mechanics and combines them in a novel and engaging way. You could say that it combines Slay the Spire with Into the Breach. Because of that, I found myself enjoying the hell out of this gameYou have attack, block, damage over time, stun, and other typical variations of cards. But you also have cards that provide mobility or combine attacks with movements. Some cards even require you to be able to charge, or run along a wall, or smash an enemies head into a table. All of these elements blend to create an excellent turn based brawler.There are a couple of issues with the game however. There are several difficulty options, but they are more akin to Easy, Normal, and Hard than to a ramping difficulty system like the Ascension levels in Slay the Spire. There are several different starting decks, but no different classes. There are also no randomized bosses. These things all combine to limit the replayability of an otherwise extremely fun game. I have a few minor gripes about the art style and quality of life issues that seem to have been overlooked as well.All that said, I would highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys the deckbuilding genre and maybe to those who have never tried it. Easily worth $25

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever wanted to step into the blood-spattered shoes of a lethal, tactical genius assassin like Deathstroke or John Wick, presented to you in the form of an aesthetically minimalist puzzle combat deck-building game? Well look no further: Agent 11 is here to take down the criminal cartels of the world, beating heavily armed and armoured baddies with nothing more or less than sheer brains and brawn. Who needs a lethal weapon when you ARE one?I've seen other reviews compare this game to Into the Breach, and honestly it is an apt comparison: you fight enemies on an isometric square tile board, enemies move into position at the beginning of your turn, you get to see the attacks they will unleash at the end of your turn and can plan accordingly, dealing damage to take them down first, dodging out of the way or redirecting enemies so they hit each other. Where it differs is in the deck-building: all of your moves are determined by a deck of ability cards which you can add to and upgrade over the course of the game. This will be familiar fare for anyone who's played Slay the Spire or the like.Despite this being an Early Access title there is already a vast slew of different cards and enemy types, so the game is a decent value proposition even at this stage. There are some balance issues, as is to be expected:1. The cards are almost certainly still being tweaked, as there are some like Flying Punch that cost way too much for nowhere near enough value.2. Protect the Ambassador objectives feel more like a throw of the RNG die than anything skill-based - if he gets hit even twice he's done for, so if goons spawn all around him and he instantly gets mobbed there's often very little you can do.3. The Trickster deck feels like it gives very little reward for how hard it is to play - in particular its Wall Kick move (its only big source of damage) is so hard to activate it might as well not exist, which is a problem when you've got only one enemy left and he keeps refreshing Block every turn. All three of the other decks are easier AND more effective.Whatever gripes I may have about the game I still had a blast playing it - I've managed to get to the final mission, but my goodness does it become difficult. Still, the challenge is what makes it fun, and in most cases it feels like a fair challenge where you're rewarded for thinking ahead with your moves and building your deck according to strategy. Very solid game, looking forward to seeing how it's updated as it progresses to release.

_childDocuments_.review: While I'm still sour over Mode7's swift abandonment of Frozen Synapse 2, this game was only published by them and not developed, so it's in more capable hands. This one is pretty good, especially if you enjoy card battlers, tactical games, and specifically Into the Breach--the similarities being a tactical game taking place in a small playing field with urgent decisions to be made. The obvious difference here is there is only 1 protagonist and the randomness of the card pulls, which honestly can be infuriating at times, particularly toward movement cards (though there are difficulty options where you will always pull at least one movement card per turn). But you just gotta do what you can with what you're given, and depending on the layout of the stages. The card variety will give you those opportunities...given that you're lucky enough. Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: (EDIT: This review was written before a lot of additions to the game, such as the Dodge and Conditioning mechanics. It might not be as completely accurate as it was when it was written, but almost all of this advice still holds. For example, blocking/dodging is now a lot more viable in the late game.)An excellent strategy game with a lot of replayability. Some people say this game is too hard, but I disagree. It's got a steep learning curve at times (looking at you, mohawk riflemen), but once you get the hang of it, you can consistently win. I've won all of my last 10 games, and some of them had absolutely terrible luck. Here are a couple of tips for players who are struggling:Remove all of your "move x spaces" cards. You WILL be trapped in a corner, repeatedly, and you'll need either a slip or a shift card to get out of it. The game guarantees you will always have at least one movement card in your hand at the start of every round, so ensure it will be your best one by removing all the others. Note: this will leave your long-distance mobility a bit hampered, but trust me, that's not an issue in the vast majority of fights. In the ones where it is, bring a Stun Dart or two.Skip cards. Skip a lot of them. Yes, dealing 16 damage in all directions and dealing 8 damage twice to an enemy exactly two squares ahead are flashy, but they're very limited. It's better to just not have it at all. The one exception to this is the Wall Punch. There will almost always be a wall accessible, especially if you have the Slip card. It's a huge amount of damage and it's easy to use.Stun and throw cards are amazing. Get a lot of them. Stun Dart is my personal favorite. Suplex and Tackle are both inferior substitutes to the almighty Throw card, but are useful enough that I would recommend them if you're short on stuns/throws. Roll Tackle offers enough utility that I like taking it even when I have other throw cards. (EDIT: Throw cards no longer stun enemies when they get up. This makes them less powerful than before, but they're still excellent cards.)This might be a playstyle thing, but here's what worked for me: do not block. Block cards are a waste of deck space. In the late game, where a single hit does 30 or more damage, trying to block damage just for counters is a worthless strategy. If I start out with block/counter cards, I remove them as soon as possible (after I remove my movement cards, of course). Get a healing card or two if you're not confident in your ability to avoid getting hit. Block gets removed at the start of your turn- health doesn't.AVOID LONG-TERM INJURIES AT ALL COSTS. They are NEVER worth the risk. I don't care if there's a 66% chance of an enhancement, long-term injuries are so overwhelmingly debilitating that you're better off ignoring it.As an add-on to the last point, avoid medical centers in general. Paying 65 pounds for 4 max hp is a complete rip off, and you shouldn't be getting hit in the first place. I would consider visiting them if they could raise your maximum combo, but they don't.Overall, Fights in Tight Spaces is a great tactical game which I enjoyed a lot. Definitely worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Fights in tight spaces is a game that puts you in tough situations constantly, which allows for a super rewarding feeling when you manage to come out of it like a badass.It feels a lot like a cross between Slay the Spire & Into the Breach.Most fights will have you vastly outnumbered, and in a small environment. You have a certain number of moves you can use, and different cards can cost different amounts. So you'll need to think your moves through before committing.Cards include things like basic damage attacks, stuns, pushes and movement.There's a good variety in enemy types, which will keep you on your toes when planning your moves. Some enemies have reactionary attacks, some ignore your block etc. It's fun to figure it out everytime.The game rewards you for good positioning. You need to think of your range from enemies for some attacks to work properly, while others might require a wall or table to be nearby. There are also "out of bounds" tiles that you can push enemies into for an instant kill.The combat feels awesome, and everything is super telegraphed so that you only have yourself to blame when things go wrong. It's a deck-builder, so after every combat encounter, you get to pick new moves, upgrade them, and so on. As you progress through a run, you will have occasional stops to heal, change your deck, or even have small events where you make a choice based off a text description of a scenario. These come with risks & rewards. You also get a bit of this within missions, where the game presents you with doing an interesting side mission within a few turns, like retrieving a briefcase or fighting an undercover agent.Overall, I think the game is a lot of fun. There's a good variety in moves, environments and enemies. It doesn't have as much content as games like Slay the Spire, so I am looking forward to more being added, however for now it's still a ton of fun!If you're into the genre, I'd recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: This is more of a 'meh' game than a bad one, but I feel like it needs some negative reviews to counterbalance the 'very positive' rating because it is rather mediocre. The tactics portion of the game is pretty tight and satisfying, but the deckbuilding is very underwhelming. A deckbuilder should have options for themes and decks that synergize as they become stronger and stronger. This game thoroughly lacks that aspect. Bleeding cards are too rare and infrequent to build a deck around. Countering decks are outright useless against enemies that can push you away. A mixed deck that gives you plenty of tactical options seems like the best deckbuild for the varied types of enemies you'll encounter. In fact, relying too much on one thing is going to get you hard countered and killed at some point. And in one sense, fair enough. Having lots of options really IS the tactically superior choice. On the other hand. why include a half-assed deckbuilder in that case? If you play games like Slay the Spire and think to yourself, "Hey, why do I need to build tight, synergized decks that just roll over the enemy?" This might be the game for you. If, on the other hand, you like that sort of thing, you will find the deckbuilding in FITS very poor.

_childDocuments_.review: There is nothing like spending 30 or so hours in and around airplanes to finally coalesce my opinion on Fights in Tight Spaces (and its DLC, Weapon of Choice) from Ground Shatter by way of Bristol, GB. As I gazed out at the plane wing I grappled with my tricky opinions on this game, I considered writing something aggressive but upon further reflection I had to counterbalance my opinion. Sorry to fans of the Slasher deck, I could not figure out how to fit it into the intro there. First, for a studio that loudly proclaims style over substance you should be able to spin kick the final boss off that plane wing. With that off my chest, Fights in Tight Spaces (FiTS) is a fairly standard entrent in the deep pool of roguelike deckbuilders. It hews close to the established “standard practices” of the genre, those being a simple energy system, enemy intent markers, tossing your whole hand and drawing a new one each turn, a simple branching map, and the usual suspects populating it: “Medical”, “Gym”, “Event”, “Fight”, and “Boss”. Events will always present you with a choice and list percentages for each outcome where applicable (but if asked, you ALWAYS deserve a raise, just like real life). Gym is the shop analogue where you can add, upgrade, or remove cards. Medical is the Rest analogue where you can heal, increase max hp, or remove injuries which are permanent debuffs added to your deck as cards if you get hit by certain attacks. Fights are where we start to see the style seep in. From the map you will get a description of the location as well as what the rewards could be and what the level of enemies will be. You can even see the actual space in which you will be fighting and the transition from the map screen to the Tight Space in which you will be Fighting is satisfying. While not being able to glance ahead and see a route visually is kind of annoying, having to read the little dossier plays into the spy theme which is nice. Speaking of the spy theme, this game does a pretty good job carrying it. You’re given a choice of two avatars to represent your agent (and a third with the DLC), the music is really good and runs the gamut from Transporter 1 to James Bond, the events are all spy cliches, the 5 or so acts could all be conceivable spy movie settings and you get little quips with your handler between missions. There is only one card pool in the game and it's full of things you’d expect a spy to be packing from wall kicks to stun darts, it's all here. There's even a nice little “you put them all in the SAME prison” setup for the endless mode which most games don’t try to justify narratively. This is unfortunately where the style over substance begins to come into play, all three avatars play the same and pull from the same card pool. You do get a choice of starter deck which gives you a few cards as well as a starting perk. This unfortunately means that there is one correct deck to select based solely on its perk, even if you wanted to use a gun you are better served picking another deck and finding a gun later since the card pool is shared and one of the starting perks is simply so much better than the others. The DLC adds another difficulty setting “Brutal” as well as a slightly harder remix of the existing acts. I’ve verified these are all quite beatable using one of the starter decks and simply removing a few cards from it and upgrading a few others. No need to add cards at any time. But that's all meta/substance stuff, where this game wants to succeed is in its STYLE.So let's talk about the mechanics of fighting! The star of the show is the arena itself. There are dozens of them with various stage hazards and cover presented on a grid that you and the enemies can move about using cards. Positioning yourself and your foes to use the area to your advantage is the most satisfying part of the game and many cards exist to help you scoot around and redirect attacks into empty air or even other enemies. Every card has its own little animation, there is dynamic camera work as well to sell you on the action, everyone being a colored silhouette takes me back to the days of stick fight animations in a good way. Once you’ve finished a map you can even watch the whole fight back. After all, everything has its own animation and sometimes the end result is an enjoyable watch.Did you catch the trick just now? I had wanted to talk about the combat but got lost in the style. There are a lot of nitpicks with this game but ultimately it feels good to spin kick a guy off a cliff then spin his buddy around with a judo throw then finish with a stomp. Yes the game is a little easy, yes the unlock/progression system is terrible (and largely meaningless) but if you choose to play sub-optimally you can make a cool thing happen on the screen, I believe that's the developers intention after reading their website and that's something that is almost never the case in games like these. This is the games biggest selling point as often in these games there is a “right move” and there is in this game for sure too but not taking it can give you something much cooler visually, you can style on people in this game. Why play what works when you can instead play what's COOL?That said, I do have gripes and I’d be remiss not to mention them. The game is not balanced for one. As I said above you can win on any setting with a starter deck and a few removals/upgrades no additions required. The unlock system is tedious, requiring huge amounts of grind to unlock all the cards which you seem to be able to get before you unlock them anyway? The final unlock, Dim Mak; can be acquired from the monk events and I promise I did not grind enough to unlock that card despite my 50 hours spent plugging away. Completionists beware! One of the enemy types is totally immovable so you can’t play the fun positioning game with them, another can’t be knocked off cliffs, a particularly low blow after the intended design of The Jade Staff boss is to toss him over a ledge. The final boss is the only one with unique mechanics, the other bosses don’t really present anything new to deal with other than one being able to be thrown off the board and a couple others not.Ultimately I can give this one a soft recommendation. Sure it's lacking in challenge, and can be a little finicky here and there but at the end of the day it oozes the style they wanted it to and this could be a great way to get someone into the genre. If you’re old, and jaded, and need to be challenged, and want all the achievements, and don’t like spy fiction, by all means skip on this one. If you’re newer to the genre, if you can’t immediately identify the broken starter perk I’ve mentioned, if you like spy fiction, or if you want to choreograph a fight in a tight space. Yeah, give it a go. The DLC is there if you want more of what is on offer and while the gun does change you into a stance character I don’t find it adds meaningful depth to the game. The extra music and animations did more for me than the actual effects on the new cards.If you really like the game the DLC is a no brainer purchase. If you’re on the fence about buying it the DLC will not change your mind.

_childDocuments_.review: My entryway to Fights in Tight Spaces was Into the Breach, another turn-based tactical game with heavy emphasis on positioning.  A shared goal is to maneuver around enemies to maximize attacks while mitigating incoming damage.  But instead of a squad of mechs defending cities, you are a lone agent brawling through small rooms.  The gameplay is still a lot of fun.The other major distinction is the deck building system.  Actions are derived from a hand of cards with momentum and combo resources to play them.  It's the first deck builder I've really gotten into and I'm still learning how to be effective at it. But it feels so satisfying to make an excellent play from a cobbled collection of disparate cards.The silhouette aesthetic is simple, but fitting; reminiscence of a James Bond opening.  The fantastic music is from nervous_testpilot.  I loved their work from Frozen Synapse and these jams have similar vibes.  I highly recommend the soundtrack.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a close-quarters, deckbuilding Into the Breach with a Superhot-style aesthetic. I'm a huge fan.Suggestions: - A single-use undo button- Confirmation for non-combative cards (i.e. having to select Block twice so you don't accidentally use it when you don't want to)- A little more incentive to start at later areas so it's not so brutal dying midway- Would it be possible to speed up replay just a little so it's a little less obviously turn-based?Otherwise, the music is spot on, the visuals are great, the tactics are interesting, and the sound design is crispy. I highly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I confess: I’ve spent an inordinate amount of time on Slay the Spire, to the point that I can barely look at it anymore. And while there’s a quite a few other games available in the deckbuilding genre, none of them really clicked with me.Enter Fights in Tight Spaces (later abbreviated as FITS). While it’s pretty clear from the get got that the game was heavily inspired by the StS formula. But it also does its own thing. Instead of sword and sorcery fantasy, FITS celebrates the John Woo style of action flick – a bloody and brutal beat-em-up in… wait for it… pretty tight spaces. But how good is it?The games builds off the familiar deckbuilding formula, with a deck of cards representing your arsenal of fighting moves – kicks, throws, punches as well as quite a lot of sidestepping, dashing, pushing and shoving. As you play them one after another, it plays out an intricate martial dance which, hopefully, leaves your Agent as the last man standing against a room full of opponents.The fighting takes place in turns for your Agent and the enemies, who go about according to their pre-programmed roles which you can inspect at any time. Where the formula diverges from StS in that the whole ordeal takes place on a grid of squares, which means you now need to take rage, positioning and obstacles into account. And the mechanics get pretty in-depth. While it’s still possible to rack up defense and block hits, a much healthier approach to simply not be there when the blow lands. Even better, redirect the blow so that it hits something else. A good number of cards allow you to dodge, slip past and blindside your enemies who in the chaos of melee sometimes even hit each other. Environment also plays a role, as enemies can be pushed against walls and even out of the fight courtesy of various doors, pits or railing. This knocks them out immediately, but take care that same rules apply to everyone, including your Agent.Enemy variety is nice, featuring a variety of mechanics, all of which demand a different approach. The basic mooks will use their fists, but you will quickly discover some brought knives, tire irons and even guns to the fistfight, adding to the glorious mayhem. And that doesn’t end there. Soon enough, you will find enemies breaking the familiar pattern, like shieldbearers who cannot be harmed from the front. That’s just scratching the surface, but if there’s one thing you can count on – your fighting moves will be put to the test.  FITS features a nice variety of fighting styles (or card decks). You start with a basic, balanced fighting deck mixing offence and defense and more will be unlocked more as you play. You will find standard kicks and punches, less orthodox tactics which require more careful positioning as well as a selection of counterattacks and throws. As dictated by the StS formula, your deck will evolve as you play and pick new cards and remove unwanted ones to either refine your strategy or take it into a totally different direction. Contrary to StS, however, the starter decks are decent and only require some fine tuning to take off. Once you get bored with them, there is also drafting.When it comes to the story, the game can feel very barebones. One can see immediately that it’s merely a pretext to stringing a series of fights together as the developers clearly took “gameplay first” as their motto.As my review meanders to a finish, let me talk briefly about the presentation. The graphics are deceptively simple, but perhaps “stylized” is a better word. One thing I wouldn’t call them is simplistic, as almost every move gets its own animation, accompanied by the satisfying sound of hits connecting and punctuated by blood splatters as heads meet the curb in a staggering variety of ways. There are plenty of unique animations for almost every individual move as well as ragdoll physics, all of which you can enjoy on replays once you’ve beaten the fight. The camera gets wonky at times, and I must say that I oftentimes skip the opportunity to watch the cinematic replay because of the thrill of the next encounter, but it’s still great that the devs thought about this nifty little feature.So, anything bad to report? The aforementioned issues with the story can be the biggest turn-off for some. But for fans of the genre, I think it’s an easy thing to look past. As far as I am concerned, the game was good for a good 40 hours, at this point the sameness of the arenas and the similarities in each run you attempt slowly begin to creep in. Even so, there are still daily plays, drafting and endless mode to keep you interested. If there’s one thing I’d say is actually bad about FITS, it’s the random encounters, the ones represented by the big [?] on the map. They’re functionally identical to Slay the Spire, while it’s great that each choice now shows you the odds of succeeding, they are really unpredictable and unbalanced. Bad outcomes can immediately screw over the entire run, and very often the prudent choice is the option that doesn’t do anything.Difficulty deserves a final mention, but not necessarily as the game’s bad side. Yes, the difficulty steadily ramps up, and there often comes a point in which an apparently golden strategy that took you flawlessly through 2/3 of the game will hit a wall and get brutally checked by a boss or a new enemy type that’s introduced. At its worst, the game can feel a bit constricting due to this, but overall I think it well tiptoes the line between challenging and unfair.FITS is a nice little game, overall. I recommend giving the demo (prologue) a go if only to check out the game’s really great implementation of melee fighting.
