_childDocuments_.review: Despite my upcoming complaints, I really do like the game, the core gameplay loop of it is  designed, HOWEVER due to some card balancing issues the difficulty spikes hard late game due to overly tanky and damaging enemies which means block cards are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ useless past a certain point because of how much damage enemies end up doing. Block cards need to scale with median enemy damage otherwise they might as well be lesser versions of player injury stat effects that block you from using a card in your deck. In no universe is a card that gives you 6 block actually viable outside of early game. There's also a card that increases your overall damage for all attacks that you block or a card that knocks down enemies that attack you, but past a certain point you don't want to get hit  and block cards end up being emergency "oh god I'm out of options" plays because like, so you blocked like 12 damage, alright, well that enemy that's attacking does like 20-60 something damage to you, and you only have an average health pool of about 44 in my experience. That just chunked half of your health at best, and a hospital isn't even on the path you're taking, so you're ♥♥♥♥♥♥ unless you went with the grapple deck that disables enemies from attacking you on your average turn, and even then you can't grapple big guys.If I could give it a sideways thumb I would. This game isn't bad in the slightest and is even one of my current favorite games right now; I love the core gameplay so it still gets a thumbs up, but there are some serious balance issues in the game, past a certain point your own attacks are enemy health debuffs at best while you just hope for a grapple card that lets enemies beat the ♥♥♥♥ out of each other instead of you fighting them since that's the only way you're gonna break the armor of some enemies that have endlessly stacking armor unless you can get them in front of an out of bounds area and hope for a tile push card. I understand the intention is to add extreme tension to later rounds as even one hit can probably end your run past a certain point, but last I checked this game was called "Fights in tight spaces" not "Watch other people fight in tight spaces".

_childDocuments_.review: I love the look of this game and figured it would be sort of a tactical John Wick brawler with the stark aesthetics of Superhot. Turns out that I was right! The game is incredibly fun, easy to pick up and play for short sessions and infinitely repeatable. The cards and strategies that you can employ are all varied, and there's a lot of room for self-expression even with the semi-random nature of how you build your deck. The feeling you have when the abilities in your hand line up perfectly with the situation your'e in is extremely satisfying. Yet as much as I love the gameplay, easily my favorite aspect of the game is the killer soundtrack! The whole OST is just fantastic! I can't recommend the game highly enough. Easily in my top ten of 2021.

_childDocuments_.review: FiTS scratches the itch and jumps the gap between tactical strategy and deckbuilder. It's addictive, punishing, and can leave you feeling crazy-smart or outright cheated at the drop of a hat, depending on the literal luck of the draw and how well you plan ahead.It does have some rough edges though. Some deck styles (bleed, especially) are directly at odds with the bonus system, which normally needs you to finish fights FAST to get extra rewards. Going block-heavy doesn't scale well into the end game, where enemies deal huge amounts of damage, or may ignore block completely. Some late-game enemies completely ignore the central gimmick that certain decks are built exclusively around, rendering them fun but pointlessly doomed to fail.That said, the Devs are extremely engaged with the community, respond and incorporate feedback. It's a TON of fun, and every time I play, I find myself losing hours cracking skulls, chucking ninjas out of speeding subway trains, and kicking mafia goons through high-rise plate glass windows.

_childDocuments_.review: Look, I'm being fully open with the fact from the get go here that card based roguelites are my crack cocaine. Like you give me one, I can play hours and hours at a time. Fight in Tight Spaces adds the presentation of an action movie with aesthetics from Superhot, and well I had a blast with what I've played so far in early access.The smart design of small cramp spaces with the tech/abilities available here lead to great strategy of not only how to set yourself up this turn to not take damage, but to avoid damage two or three turns down the line, as you attempt to not pin yourself to corners or to one strategy. The different play styles of defensive and offensive cards lead to good solid bases for experimentation, while the movement/combo system adds a layer of reward for waiting for the right moment to attack or move. What I absolutely love is the ability to use enemies against each other, especially in defensive counter play, to cause them to kill themselves, and watching those ragdolls flop around will never get old.The concern over the long haul will be the variety in which the game has, and to be fair, the different layouts, enemies, and scenarios did enough here in the early going to make things feel slightly different but still familiar. I do want to see little things adjusted over time: some more enemies and some more “flavor” in terms of story (give enemies names for example) can help really sell the game over time.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is for any Alina of the Arena players who are curious about this game.The core gameplay is very similar - a grid-based deck builder - and if you love Alina, you'll probably also love this. Below I listed some of the notable differences, and all in all I found them to be significant enough to result in a refreshing change from Alina gameplay.* The grid is square (with no diagonals). That's a pretty big difference in itself.* Each enemy is facing in a particular direction, and (mostly) only attacks in that direction. The result is there is a huge emphasis on maneuvering to be able to flank enemies.* There are multiple enemy types who can react to you during your own turn.* Blocking scales better in this game; it's easier to go with a blocking and/or countering build.* Bosses are stronger than regular opponents, but not to the ridiculous extent they are in Alina.* No itemization - there are a few slots for powerful upgrades, charm/bracers style, but no weapons or consumables.* The arenas themselves are very different - there are multiple kinds, they feature obstacles and insta-death pits, and the starting locations are randomized.There are of course many more differences... but the bottom line is that the resulting core gameplay, while very familiar, is sufficient different.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun game! Easy to learn, challenging to master. Took me a few runs to finally understand all of the mechanics and finally beat it on Classic difficulty. The combination of RNG with consistent AI feels just about right so far; every run has its up and downs, but you know what to expect and how to react to new but different scenarios. It does have the occasional hiccup though; in one of my runs, I had assembled a great deck, cleanly made it up to the very last level, where i was unceremoniously murdered in the first turn because my movement card was a shift, but I was dropped into a corner with a double line of Bosses on two sides, with a wall and a ledge on the other sides. It was very frustrating yet funny at the same time.The key seems to be focusing on control (grapple, push, redirect) and movement (slip, shift) cards, because in the higher levels, your direct damage cards simply can't keep up, but the enemies damage output scales with their HP, so it's just more effective to turn them against each other. Deck size is also important, keep it small (under 40 cards), upgrade what you have, and skip most of the useless cards offered at the end of every level.Since it's an early access game, it is missing some quality-of-life stuff you'd expect in a deckbuilding turn-based game like this, like a UI display of Turn Order, as well as some kind of card stacking or sorting option (by alphabetical order, damage, cost, type etc) in the Deck display, and maybe some post-game stat tracking in addition to the score (total kills, kill types, hp lost/gained etc).

_childDocuments_.review: What is about 80% a fun and strategic experience is inevitably ruined by design decisions that force the player to be punished for rule ambiguity, a lack of info for the player, or missing 1 of 10 different moment to moment modifiers that can spell doom.IMO the two critical missing elements that would turn this ok game to great:- an Undo feature. Every turn is immediately committed once it is made. Inevitably, you will make a mistake and in later stages that mistake will often kill the entire run. It won't be a mistake of planning, or a mistake of strategy, but a mistake of remembering of the 4 enemies on screen, the specifics of their paragraph of rules.- Better player info and explanation. Will this enemy turn around to face me after I do this move? Does counter-attack fire if I just move them around? Take for example 2 very similar cards - "Swap" and "Back push" (maybe back attack I can't recall) - My run just ended because while you can "Swap"  enemies with counterattack and not be attacked in return, backpush WILL cause a counter attack. This is not made clear by anything the game tells you - no iconography, predictive info, warnings, rules explanation, etc. -- you just need to get punished for it and learn the hard way. Given the complete absence of an "undo" or save states, or restart scenario, or any such features - such incidents will often mean the entire run fails, and you start over. A frustrating capstone, and in my experience, the typical end to a good time in Fights in Tight Spaces.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is the unoffical baby of Slay the Spire, Enter the Breach, and Superhot. Let me break it down for you, card system combat like in Slay the Spire, map layout and movement like in Enter the Breach, and art style reminiscent of Superhot. The combination of these three games may not seem like a recipe for a beautiful game cake, but I beg to differ. If anyone may not like 1 or all of the games I just listed above, I beg you, try the prologue before turning away from this game. Now onto why this game is great, and why you should definitely buy it even though it says *Early Access.This game, believe it or not is pretty much finished. I know what some people may be thinking. "Oh, well I've heard that before, I get in and there's bug after bug after bug." Well, let me tell you, in my 12 hours of playtime I haven't seen a single bug in any of the runs I have done. Normally I would agree with the statement before, but that just isn't the case for this game. The devs truly know what they intend to change during its Early Access time here on Steam and it isn't game breaking bug fixes like in other Early Access games, (take a look in the description if you haven't already to see what they want to add). Anyway, they know what they are trying to bring into the game, it isn't paid cosmetics, it isn't extra decks that cost $5.99 to add to your game. No, its extra content that to me, is already a bonus to an awesome game by itself. What's insane is that this is already a fully featured 40+ hour game with high replayability and insane skill ceiling to master. The campaign, if you can call it that, involves an agent named simply Agent 11. He is tasked with stopping the operations of high profile groups that pose a threat. Those range from simple Nordic biker gangs to the Italian Mafia, not exactly what you would consider "good guys". Before you start, you get to choose from 1 of 4 decks, Balanced, Counter Striker, Aggressive, and Trickster. Each bringing their own unique twist on how you engage in fights with the enemies early on. I say early on as you may have guessed this is a rogue-like and therefore you will constantly be adding new cards into your deck that vary with each run in the game. This makes for an incredibly satisfying time as the base deck never changes so you can adapt to certain combinations and enemies easier with certain card grabs in your time playing. Personally, I love the aggressive deck, it packs a punch early on and I tend to enjoy a more aggressive playstyle. That definitely doesn't mean I don't enjoy the other decks, I definitely do. Whats even nicer is that eventually your deck will be guaranteed to have overlap with more than 1 deck as you continue on in your playthrough as the cards you get as rewards for completing stages are from other decks. Like to be aggressively passive? Add some counters into your deck. Like to out maneuver enemies and get on their blindside? Add more movement based cards (there is a ton not going to name a select few). Like to use martial arts moves that make you look ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cool, add them! The limitless scope of combination for your deck is what makes this game fun and amazing with each run through. If at this point you aren't sold on the game based on what I, or other people have said. Then I ask again, go try the prologue for this game. Its free and allows you to see if you'll actually like the mechanics for yourself. I normally don't write reviews for Early Access titles as I feel that they aren't a finished product that can guarantee a stamp of approval as everything in them is normally experimental. But for this game, it is quite different, go take a look.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: Weird design decisions, inconsistent mechanics, RNG heavy dependence, and ongoing balance changes that only seem to serve to nerf various cards make this game more frustrating than fun.Full review: This game is close to being good, but not quite. Strange design decisions (how enhancements are handled is, frankly, terrible - needing an enhancement to open up more enhancements?), inconsistent mechanics (a bleed card that triggers at 0 block works fine, but a stun card that does the same does not - and no mention of this anywhere in the game), and half the mechanics being useless at the end of the game (you can't throw or shove any of the last couple of end game bosses) makes this game more frustrating than fun. Cap it all off with it being heavily dependent on RNG if you've wasted the last two hours of your life or not (e.g. trying to play a Slasher deck but not getting a single card that synergies with it the entire game is common, or worse, rewarded with an enhancement that invalidates one of the few strengths the deck has), the game rarely feels rewarding.The recent DLC adding the Gunslinger deck did help, but only if that's the deck you're using. Not all decks are created equally, so be prepared to fail repeatedly just because the rewards and shop RNG decided you playing an Aggressive deck means you must want cards that have nothing to do with the deck whatsoever.The game has seen so many balance tweaks over such a long time has made it feel inconsistent. I want to like this game so much, but when I get frustrated and leave it for a awhile and come back only to find several of the cards reworked in a negative way (ie, nerfed), it's hard for me to like having to retool my own strategies over and over again.Difficulty of the game (I only play on Classic so YMMV) isn't the issue, but inconsistency is.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a pretty terrific game. I've followed this game for some time - from early access to its full release, and I can say with confidence that it's a well made, healthy product that fulfills its goal exceptionally well. That goal is to recreate action-movie styled fistfights in a turn-based deckbuilder format. The deckbuilding is not quite to complex as, for example, Slay the Spire, but later missions keep the pressure on the player to have a viable build, and one can lose in a flash if their deck is balanced incorrectly. (Especially on the hardest difficulty, which is the only difficulty worth playing) What sets it apart is the maps/movement system, which invoke the same brilliant system as Into The Breech. Hitting an enemy and blocking aren't nearly as fun (or effective) as pushing your enemies around the battlefield so that they hit one another, before finally tossing them over a railing. When you control the flow of combat successfully, the game becomes a real joy. The story is light, barely existent, but hits the appropriate beats for your James-Bond styled protagonist. Some of the deckbuilding strategies in the game are also a lot better than others. Bleeding-style decks (which does Damage over Time) seem particularly bad as they make many of the game's side objectives (which you CANNOT afford to miss) nearly impossible. Eventually, you discover that some cards are practically must-picks and other cards are never-ever. Unfortunately, many of the game's premade decks feel like a "challenge run" compared to draft mode for this reason - the types of decks that WORK are significantly narrower than the types of decks that the game encourages you to try. The replay system is the game's biggest disappointment. The idea is to play back a level in real-time, not turn based, so that the player can WATCH the action as a continuous sequence. A great idea, but the replays themselves are horribly stiff and slow, the turn-based animations badly floundering in real-time playback. I'm sad that I always ignore this feature, since it could have been a big selling point for the game. Those concerns aside, it really is a lovely game, which feels simultaneously casual and difficult, and certainly rather addicting.

_childDocuments_.review: This game certainly one of a kind. We might have some some similar strategy similar to this, yet it they don't exploit more their posibilities when talking about combat, space and movement. This puzzle style fighting game certainly improve what other games from the genre do, despite it's simple mechanics. First, the way the game uses the enviroment is fantastic. Not only it tranform the walls, chair and bars into handy props to increase the damage of your combos and finish off enemies, but it also attracts you with it's simple geometry. The maps are just cubes and rectangles, very simple forms divided into squares and ornamented with, as I said earlier, chairs, walls, tables, windows and dors that can be used to your advantage. in very effective and reliable ways. You can get rid of enemies by smashing their faces against furnitures, push them into walls to get decent damage or even kick them out of the ring throw the entrances and exit points. Another thing to take into account is the movement. The animations of look a bit off and need some polishing, neverthless, they are varied and allow you to take a step on the enemy according to your necessities. You can well dodge your enemie to one side, flank them, rush to a further objective, use some tricky ninja skill and get on their back, or even jump obstacles get yourself out of the rock and the hard place. Moving to another aspect of the game is the combat itself. It mixes up mechanic that rely on randomness and strategic planning, in which every turn you will get a couple cards from your deck. This cards can be obtained by completing missions, events or in the GYM, where you can also upgrade the ones you have. This cards are divided into offensive, defensive and movement cards, being the first ones the most interesting. The wide range of strikes you put a hand on have different properties that makes the more effective or useful in certain situations. Some will push enemies back, some will offer you a decent range, other will alow you to attack and move at the same time and others will give you more strategical advanteges, like stunns, enemy damage reduction, taunts that will tease the enemy, holds and forcing enemies to have a nap. The combat in overall feels great, quite orchestral, since you can manipulate space and enemies to make them attack each other or fall into a trap. The only negative aspect I can see is that the replay mode animations link with each other in a very crankky way. They look more like individual steps or moves made in very long time rather than well concatenated, fluid and rapid moves. In resume, I recomend this game, is certainly something very casual that anyone can play and very entertaining if you like to put your brain to work.

_childDocuments_.review: Great deck-builder meets Into the Breach.  This is an immediate recommend if you enjoy both of these kinds of games, and a strong recommend if you enjoy one of the types and tolerate the other.  It's immensely challenging (expect to hear the 'git gud phrase way more than you've heard in the past), but it's varied enough and fun enough that it's rewarding when you finally do figure out each randomized fight.The basics: deck-builder in that you start with a pre-made deck with a theme  or do card drafting.  Your starting deck can be added to (earning cards by winning fights), removed from (spending cash to remove cards), or upgraded (spending cash to improve cards, or finding upgraded cards in challenging fights).  That's about it.  After that, Into the Breach kicks in.  Enemies broadcast their intent - so you're always looking for the way to play the cards you do have in order to beat the level by using the knowledge of your enemy's movement to help you along.  Enemies can attack each other if placed in such a position (repositioning the enemy is a big part of this game), pushed off the game board entirely, or beat through brute force of damage.

_childDocuments_.review: I waited until I hit about 100 hours to review this for multiple reasons. The main one being this game is in early access.I started playing 3 patches ago, since then:UI has been improvedProgression system addedCard compendiumCore concept, the game nails down. You'll get an RNG hand dealt to use with specific amount of points. As you progress you get better and stronger cards, health upgrades, modifiers, etc. Each level (currently 5 excluded tutorial) is split among multiple yet converging paths that lead to different bonuses and the event spaces do offer up some funny moments. Unfortunately, there is little variation of the mission structure or even in the events. The rag doll physics of characters upon death though has yet to get old and I don't see that changing anytime soon.You'll fight the equivalent of a battalion of soldiers that get progressively stronger and in some cases more annoying than one would want. Although, the annoyance of some enemies comes down to the RNG the game has. On the 2nd difficulty, you can die but retry either the stage or take a new path (unlike higher difficulties). Keen eye players will note that the cards are going to disperse in the exact same order no matter what changes you made to the battle itself. Personally, I want the cards to disperse in a brand new order, but the developer's choice to not do that makes strategies developed boom or bust. That is part of the fun at the end of the day.It is also a rouge-like, so if you like getting your ass kicked over and over again, you'll probably enjoy this. The ability to build your own deck or select from pre-made decks are both fantastic in helping players develop their play style. Daily challenges are also available for those trying to beat a leader board.The environments do allow for different ways to disposing of enemies, which there needs to be more of. At the time, there are about 15-20 different types of environments.Once you start understanding how the cards fully work, you can and will be able to start doing ridiculous amounts of damage or create a shield that none of the final stage enemies can penetrate.The sound / music is ok, but the found the music becoming far too repetitive. I'd like more SFX and different music, something that is befitting of a spy movie or show. Maybe even take some pages from Archer.The "story" is lacking, a few chats between your handler and your agent is the extent of it. I'd like to see one liners in the middle of battle (no voice lines, the speech bubbles are fine).As of now, I'd recommend the game if you want to play a new deck builder or even want to dabble in the genre.If the game gets a full release or massive enough update, I'll update this review.

They really put the effort into that and it shows.I love, love this game, but let me tell you, it is punishing and heartbreaking. You can sync 4 hours into a run and then reach a level where a single enemy hit can end the game. It's bad when I lose because I wasn't paying attention and missed how the chain of actions would play out. It's so much worse to get dealt a bad hand where there's simply no way to escape. As much as I like the difficulty because it makes the wins feel so valuable, I stopped playing because I had one too many bad hands that ended my run in the later stages.I'll keep checking back, though. I'll play a match every couple weeks, hoping my luck is either in the cards or with a new difficulty balance that devs can work out.

_childDocuments_.review: Subtly addictive in a way that reminds me of civ, despite being very different games. _childDocuments_.review: This game is almost perfect, but there's one issue that makes me give it a thumbs down, which I only do out of concern. I bought this game before the DLC was released in 2023, and it was terrific. I enjoyed playing it in my spare time. The variety of playstyles you can unlock as you progress kept the experience fresh and a bit unpredictable, and I loved every moment.However, during the second to last mission, I encountered the Bartender. Dealing with the Bartender heavily depends on your deck composition. You're in a good spot if you have high-damage cards, like in aggressive or grappler decks. However, balanced decks might struggle, and slasher or counter decks will face significant challenges. The Bartender doesn't attack, which is a problem for counter decks, and their debuffs, high HP, and immunity to friendly fire make them challenging to handle. They reduce your actions, lower your attack, and eliminate your combo, and their AI makes them hard to pin down, leading to really frustrating gameplay that detracts from the well-designed game. It's a shame. I'll try it again if I'm in the mood in the future, but for now, it doesn't make sense to me.

_childDocuments_.review: Basically, it's the Elevator fight from Captain America: Winter Soldier. As a card game.I generally hate card games. I also generally hate rogue-likes. So why have I played so much of this game? FiTS unexpectedly became a big favourite of mine because it actually alleviates a lot of my issues with bothCard games often feel abstract and inscrutable to me. But here the rules are clear and concise, and applied to a concept that you can visually see. You can make so many attacks or moves in a given turn (tied to your "momentum"), and heavier or more esoteric moves can take more time, allowing you to do less per turn. It also takes an element from Into the Breach that I wholly approve of, in that you can see what every opponent is going to do each turn. Foreknowledge = Predictability = Player can plan their actions. As a representation of a Combat in Confined Capacities, it visually illustrates how each move is going to affect everything else. It allows you to dodge or subvert attacks by careful use of your cards and surroundings. Controlling the combat space is a big part of the game. Sometimes the best thing you can do as a player isn't to attack, but to simply get out of the way and let the enemies smack into each other, occasionally giving them a little nudge, doing the work for you.The game is randomised, but rarely if ever feels unfair. You get a decent selection of cards in each Deck, and Deck draft allows you to select from 3 each time, so you can still somewhat tailor your deck to what effect you're going after. A block heavy deck is going to depend a lot on counters. a grappling deck is about controlling positioning. And sometimes you just want brute strength and pummelling power.On a personal note: It's a turn based game and I often don't have much time to play an action game. Here each bout is breezy and quick, and I can leave the computer for ages, exit the game and come back and just continue. A whole run can take a few hours, but it's not like you have to be sitting at your computer the whole time.All in all, a very solid and easy recommend for someone who these types of games don't generally appeal to.EDIT:Well, it's been a year since the game released and you know what? No updates. There's been one minor bug fixing patch, but that's about it. The promised additional cards, levels and other updates, never happened.I can't blame the devs, the game clearly didn't do well enough for them to continue supporting it At the same time, I can't in good conscience continue to recommend this game to other people. I might have enjoyed it a lot, but at the same time I have to recognise it had a very specific appeal to me (maybe it will to you too). It's still fairly limited in scope.I'm not going to change my thumbs-up. But I will say that for someone new, try the demo, understand there's not much beyond it, and make your decision. I think it's probably not worth it for most people (maybe at a discount).Don't mind the hours played on my account: I tend to run it in the background whilst barely interacting with it. In truth maybe divide those hours by 10.EDIT 2: Well, I told myself that I wasn't going to play this game again this year. And then the devs dropped a DLC which is almost literally a "John Wick" card pack. New Pistol stances and all the kind of moves you'd expect. So, yes, unexpectedly, it got an update over a year after release, and somehow they got me back in again.

_childDocuments_.review: This is ridiculously fun - by far the most cinematic and fun to play deck builder I've experienced. If you don't believe me, search the Steam Store for the Fights in Tight Spaces prologue and play that - it's very representative of the actual experience and more developers should follow suit.This game reminds me of a lot of stick figure flash animations of protracted fight scenes, all the ones which were on Stickpage back in the day - this is the first game I've played which emulates the feeling of outwitting opponents in a fist fight as a hero in an action movie would, accurately.So many of the tropes of action movie fist fights are portrayed - using enemies to block bullets, even forcing them to punch each other; kicking enemies over ledges or out of doors for instant kills (rewarding tactical positioning), and of course the James Bond trope of bloody battles and martial arts, and in the end still being in a perfectly clean suit and jacket.The aesthetics are gorgeous, I just love the art style - there's not much more to say. I also enjoy the little touches such as Agent 11 combing his hair back with his hand from time to time.The one thing I seriously think could be improved is the transition between animation states. Watching replays can look janky because moves are very much played one after another, rather than done in a fluid way. However - I realise that transition states between moves would potentially be extremely taxing for the animation team so this is very much a "would be nice" feature, but nowhere near vital.

_childDocuments_.review: Play the role of a secret agent fighting multiple enemies at once, using a customised deck of cards that represent your moves and attacks. You take turns drawing a hand of cards and using them to deal damage or move around the combat area, all while managing your health, momentum (used to play cards, like action points), and combo (which increases when you deal damage, and can be spent to play extra powerful cards).The enemies are predictable - you're told exactly where they'll attack and how much damage they'll deal - so it's up to you to choose the best cards from your randomly-drawn hand to either block or evade enemy attacks, and to dish out damage. Watch out though, as some enemies will counter your attacks or will deal damage if you step directly in front of them. The enemy attacks are locked in once they have you in their sights - you can trick an enemy into committing to an attack, and then move away so that they hit their ally who was behind you.Use the environment to your advantage: push enemies off buildings to instantly take them out, knock an enemy into an obstacle for extra damage, or spring off a wall and deal a devastating flying punch attack. Finding the perfect way to manipulate an enemy into a vulnerable spot and then unleashing a powerful attack to knock them out is really satisfying.Pick your path through the enemy compound: initiating fights, getting upgrades, buying new cards, and making choices along the way. You can pick the harder route for extra rewards, or take it easy until you reach a hospital to recover your health. Planning is essential when it comes to managing your health and your money.The game is randomised so that it essentially has infinite replayability - each round you'll find different cards, different upgrades, different enemies, different random encounters, different path layouts, etc. There are also several starting decks, which make every new game feel different. The enemies get harder as you advance through the game, and there are boss enemies which have unique abilities at the end of each enemy compound.This is a great game to play while you're watching a YouTube video, watching Netflix, or chatting online to your friends - it's turn-based so you can take your time selecting your moves and you can pause whenever you want. It also saves your run if you quit the game, so you can always pick off where you left it last time. If things start to go south and you die, you can jump right back into a new round.If you like Slay The Spire, Into The Breach, Monster Train, or other turn-based deckbuilding games, then I'm sure you will enjoy this game. It's basically the same concept except with sweet martial arts moves!

_childDocuments_.review: The tactical mechanics of Into The Breach, the visual style of Super Hot, and the deck-building of Into The Spire. Not a bad combination.I put 15-20 hours into the demo, so this was one of the easiest and quickest purchases I've ever made.The comparisons to Into The Breach that other reviewers observe are spot-on, with enemies' intended attacks, turn order, and damage output being telegraphed before you make you make your move. Besides the cards you draw, the biggest element of RNG comes from the "Events"; a vague and unexciting opportunity to throw away your health/money for the unlikely chance of a reward.It's all still early access, though, so hopefully we'll see some variation in content such as environment mechanics (meat-grinders, breakable furniture, conveyor belts, etc). It'd also be nice to see different player types; currently, we're playing as a James Bond-looking fellow using a variety of punches, kicks and takedowns, but there's definitely room for a gun-fu character, for example. It's already an extremely replayable game, but some more distinct play styles could really spice things up.As it is, the game is as addictive as anything else I've played in recent years, and I'm fully confident it will only be improved upon. Absolutely worth the investment.

_childDocuments_.review: Love this game, and keep coming back to it (even if I'm bad at it).It has all the trapping of a classic deckbuilder, but with a solid "starting deck" concept which really illustrates and kickstarts the highly varied playstyles you an take in different deck compositions.Rather than focusing on the classics damage multipliers or modifiers (which do exist to a limited extent), the main focus here comes from the 2d grid format of the board. The player is always severely outnumbered, so managing positioning of self and enemies is always critical.Frequently find yourself surrounded? You certainly will.Maybe try a "maximum aggression" build to cull the numbers quickly so you're not overwhelmed.Or maybe focus on blocks and counterattacks; make them regret it.Or maybe the better defense is to just not be where the violence is; skirt out of the way or push enemies into danger, leveraging friendly fire....or maybe you're tired of being the better person and a gun really is the simplest solution to the problem.This game is composed of simple elements and small maps, but is capable of so many different strategies and highly varied runs. It's a brilliant concept and design.

_childDocuments_.review: I got randomly recommended this game and I gotta say, very worthwhile game. It rewards good strategy, positioning, and forward thinking. My first few runs, I thought getting past the final boss was almost impossible without god RNG, but this is simply not the case. Once I started to learn the game a lot better, I was having a lot less trouble with the tougher enemies. This game has a lot of great cards and play styles that allow you to make some absolutely insane deck combinations. I will say, however, that this game's RNG can screw you over. If you draw an unfortunate lineup of cards or if an enemy decides to move a certain way, it is sometimes just simply impossible without particular cards, especially in the 4th and 5th sections where a lot of enemies counter, move with you when you move, auto attack, or can't be pushed. This is not to say that these mechanics make victory impossible. It is possible to play around these things, and sometimes even use them to your advantage to use their own abilities against them.Overall, very fun game with great music, delightful art style, and a wide variety of mechanics and cards to keep you entertained for a while. Mastering this game is quite fun and I find myself not getting bored of the loop.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fairly standard rogue-lite.The main selling point of this game is the artstyle and characterization of the player character. The art is gorgeous and unlike most other rogue-lites, the player character actually has some amount of characterization and dialogue, which makes them more interesting.As for the gameplay itself, the combat is pretty uninspired and it doesn't resolve any of the common issues that are present in most rogue-lites. The most common issue that most deck-building rogue-lites have is that they increase your pool of available cards without giving you any ways of combatting the decreasing consistency of your decks as a result. That issue is very much present here as well. The deck-building is a also bog standard, derivative one, so with a bit of a background in other deck-building rogue-lites, you will find all the cards and the way you use them extremely familiar.That said, I like that the game is "easy". The hardest difficulty in this game would probably be considered the normal difficulty in other deck-building roguelites before ascension. All difficulties below the very hardest will help make your hand more consistent, as well as allow you to manipulate RNG in your favor when it turns out badly for you.Overall, I say pick it up, play through it once and then don't bother with it again. It's a perfectly fine game, but doesn't really do much innovative stuff, so it doesn't provide much entertainment beyond the well crafted graphics and world.

_childDocuments_.review: , further referenced as FiTS, is a deck-builder rogue-like with turn-based combat. This sounds amazing on paper and it is in its actual game form as well. It has to be noted that the FiTS is still in early access and thus a lot of things are subject to change. Nonetheless, it has to be said that the base that the game currently has is very solid and will keep you entertained for countless hours. Same as with many other deck-builder rogue-likes, you will be choosing between several paths which have combat encounters, events and shop tiles on them. It is entirely up to you which way you will choose and what rewards will you aim for. For each won combat encounter, you will be able to choose from several cards to improve and expand your deck. Events will offer various risk and reward situations, ranging from healing and getting upgraded cards to taking heavy damage. Finally, there are two different types of shops, gym and medical. Gym allows you to buy new cards for currency you gain from encounters as well as upgrade cards you already own, whereas the medical shop obviously heals you but also lets you upgrade your max health.FiTS as it stands, has 4 different starter decks that you can unlock by playing and reaching certain points in the game. Each deck focuses on different playstyle. First deck is balanced deck that, as the name implies, balances both offense and defense making it a perfect starter deck. Second deck is a defense heavy deck that features counter attacks and a lot of block cards, making this the perfect pick for careful players who are not very confident in being too aggressive. Third deck, obviously, is offensive deck, which has a lot of high damage cards to make sure you end your enemies as quick as possible. Last deck is a special one as it is a trickster deck, which focuses on outsmarting and outplaying enemies. The game has 4 major card types; attacks, blocks, movements and special cards. Each of these card types are self-explanatory but in the context of the game, they get another dimension. Because FiTS is played out on a grid in a turn-based combat, positioning and where you play each card matters that much more. You want to use the headslam card? You have to make sure that there is a surface around the enemy you can commit the headslamming on. If you want to move, there have to be empty tiles around you etc. You get the gist of it. Simply put, positioning is a big factor of the overall gameplay. As mentioned, the game is turn-based. You play your cards, which have specific "mana" cost and then enemies get to react to what you just did. It is very simple concept but as the popularity of turn-based games proves, highly effective. Just as many other tactical turn-based games, enemies can react on your turn as well. For example certain enemy types can hit you if you do any kind of action on a tile in front of them. You can move around, punch and kick people or just wait out in a defensive stance and wait your comment with the counter card you just played. In the end, the deck is your playground.Another thing that FiTS does differently is that it introduces a combo system. If you play attack cards, your combo number goes up. You might be asking yourself, what is this combo number for? Firstly, it allows you to play cards that do not have "mana" cost but instead have a certain combo cost you have to pay. Secondly, combo strengthens certain cards, giving them higher damage output. Sadly, there is a way to lower the combo, and that is by playing the movement cards and moving around, unless the card says otherwise.FiTS has a very fun feature after each combat encounter, does not matter if you just won or lost. You can always replay the whole encouter back, without the long pauses for your extensive thinking and planning. This gives the game a new dimension, where you can just enjoy the mayhem you just created and feel like a true 90s action hero.The story is also clichéd and stereotypical, you are an unnamed agent who is tasked with dismantling several gangs by beating their leaders. Nothing more is said and nothing more is even needed to say. The story is not the main focus here but it perfectly summarizes what the game is. You are an agent whipping out some well needed justice.As far as replay value goes, the game is still in early access and even though it will take you quite some time to get all the unlockables and beat all the bosses, you will start to notice repetetiveness. You can choose which path you will take but the individual fight layouts will start to feel the same, to the point of you remembering where the enemies will be in the next encounter. This is compensated a bit by the fact that you get bonus optional objectives for each fight, which give you extra money when fulfilled. These can range from defeating in x number of turns to protecting an ambassador from enemies. Honestly speaking, this game will keep you entertained but you will memorize all the possible options rather quick and then the element of surprise vanishes, except for events which are always randomized.FiTS goes for minimalistic artstyle, which works very well. Your character is black, first gang you fight is red, next gang orange, ninja green and fancy hipsters (I think at least that they are) purple. You know precisely who you are fighting and what they can do because of this color code as well as helpful descriptions enemies have when you hover over them. This simplistic yet brutal visual style is accompanied by a soundtrack that is just as minimalistic. However, this take on electro music does not get tired and absolutely fits the situations of you managing to once more beat hords upon hords of enemies.For an early access title, there is surprisingly a lot of content. It can keep you occupied for well over 30+ hours and it will still be the same fun as before. If you are a fan of deck-builders and turn-based combat, this is absolutely a must buy even at the full price, just to support the developers and help them create even more content for this already satisfying experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Simply put, it's what John Wick Hex wanted to be. This isn't a perfect game by any means, and updates are far and few. Not to mention the difficulty spikes are a little jarring the first few times you encounter them. But the base mechanics and gameplay are great. Easy to learn, hard to master.My biggest problem with the game is the amount of RNG. I understand that this is a large part of what makes a roguelike, a roguelike. But It's bad enough to where you could have a perfect deck, but be spawned into a fight with the wrong cards and have no way to defend yourself from the enemies properly. This has been a run ender for me numerous times.Other than those 2 issues, this game is worth the time and energy. Visually appealing, fun gameplay, and I'm under the impression it's still being worked on at the time of writing this, so more content could be on the way. Check it out.

_childDocuments_.review: There are a few problems with the game. I would argue that it's too grindy. Only one save file, and in a 'game over' it's a repetitive grind from the beginning. There are so many things out of your control, some bad RNG with your card draws and you could feel cheated out of a situation quite easily.Some practical things for the devs to improve on is ordering the deck overview with alphabetical ordering. It's currently hard to find your duplicate cards and keep track of your deck when the cards are all over the place. Another thing to note is how stupid the informant is, I swear he's a double agent. Let's say this is an informant with auto-attack on, he's adjacent to the player; an actual enemy is also adjacent to the player. Even if your attack kills the enemy, and that was the LAST opponent, the informant decides to murder the player, despite no witnesses remaining! Please people, fix this game!! The fight should be instantly over the moment all enemies EXCEPT the informant remains. It makes no sense why the informant proceeds to murder the player!TBH with the state of the game, I would argue $36 AUD is a bit of a robbery. I'd pay $15, or $20 (at the most) instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun game, definitely worth checking out! Reminds me a little bit of Into the Breach with how you are controlling the map. This is a really unique twist on the "deckbuilder roguelike" games that have been becoming very popular over the last several years. What is has in common with Slay the Spire is that you pick your starting base deck (like picking your character in StS) and move along a map, but this map is more like a blueprint of several buildings and pick 1 of 3 cards at the end of each battle. Along the way you will run into random events, upgrade shops, doctors visits, etc.. same type of thing like how you visit shops and events in StS.This is kind of where the similarities end because the combat is completely different. Each battle becomes more challenging and is randomly generated so each run is still unique. It's tricky to describe the gameplay, you really need to watch a short video of it. What makes the gameplay really interesting is how you shuffle around the enemies and use the environment to kill them, often making them hit each other. Someone might be pointing a gun at you from 3 tiles away with another next to you going to melee. You can flip behind the melee attacker then kick them which knocks forward one tile so now that enemy is in the path of the bullet and you are behind the melee unit so their attack won't hit you either. Turn ends, the melee misses and the gun goes off hitting the melee unit with a bullet. I'm not that far into the game yet and it's becoming fairly challenging. You will face enemies with resistances who maybe can't be knocked down or knocked backwards, perhaps they do AOE damage to anyone within 1 tile, some gain a lot of armor or block each turn. I don't like how they don't just show you how much damage will be done which makes certain moments take much longer than they need to. My attack might do 6 damage, but then it's +1 dmg per energy you have (forget what they call it, just used energy for this example) and you have 5 energy. So you need to look at the attack and go ok it's 6 damage, then it's +5 for the energy so 11, the enemy has 5 hp, but they also have 8 armor for 13 total so the attack will do -8 to the armor then -3 to the hp leaving them with +2hp. It's not that this math is difficult, but it's a bit tedious for a fast paced game. Would love to be able to just select the card, choose an enemy and INSTANTLY know EXACTLY how much damage will be applied, if it's going to kill the unit then just show a lethal icon or something over it. It really slows down the pacing of this to stop and really double check to make sure someone is going to die or not.I give them a pass on some of the smaller issues because it's in EA, but the overall gameplay loop is a lot of fun right now. I also would like to see visual changes. White background with white text is definitely not easy on the eyes. Would love to see the environment highlighted sometimes to show what is interactive. For example if you get knocked thru a door you instantly lose no matter what, but it's a little tricky to notice doors because everything is just white, it all kind of looks the same. How about a red or black outline around the door that will make you instantly lose the game so that it stands out? Would also be nice to zoom out vs just rotate the map, but it's a not a huge issue by any means.

_childDocuments_.review: Fights in Tight Spaces is a strategic Rogue-like that uses a deck-building to create new experiences each session. Despite having a turn-based nature, the game manages to feel very dynamic, due to the player having a number of unlockable options for pre-made decks focused on things like damage-over-time, grappling, blocking, countering- all of which are sufficiently different in how they function. Players eventually gain the ability to build a starting deck, though because this is accomplished by having the player choose from sets of two cards at a time (drawn randomly from a pool of all available cards), doing so can lead to being forced to include cards that are inappropriate for the deck the player intends to build, which then have to be removed from the deck throughout the run (at cost). With other random elements existing in the game, it feels more predictable to just use one of the game's pre-made decks which *are* themselves built fully around a theme, and in a way, this is a real shame. Including a true deck-building system - even if it has to be unlocked - would really elevate Fights in Tight Spaces by making the process of playing more preemptive rather than reactionary.Overall, the style and gameplay of Fights in Tight Spaces can be very, very fun, if the player is willing to tolerate the few downsides. If you're on the fence, Fights in Tight Spaces is rarely on sale, but at least there exists a demo - "Fights in Tight Spaces (Prologue) - which lets you play the entire first mission for free. Give it a shot!

_childDocuments_.review: Tips for v0.17.4432 (play-style that I personally used to finish the game)Aggressive deck,Mission 1 Death's Hand Biker Gang:Choose paths that lead to all the gyms in this mission.Focus on earning as much money as possible for each fight.Fight rewards: choose more on movements cards. If no movements card is available, choose cards that can move the enemies such as: Shove, grapple, Right / Left Spin Kick, Push.At the gym, first try to upgrade your movement cards so that they do not cost you Momentum.If you have money to spare, try to upgrade your Shove, Grapple, Swap.Mission 2 The Insiders:Choose path that leads to fights with rewards that can increase your Momentum Cap (small up arrow and plus sign)During the fight, check the top right of the screen that shows the task requirements to get this reward.Usually, in Mission 2, you need to collect a briefcase in limited turn (usually in 4 turns).Focus on grabbing the briefcase first with the upgraded movement cards and shove/grapple enemies that are in your way.I restart the game if I failed to get more than 1 Momentum increase.Mission 3 Jade StaffFocus on upgrading Attack cards and get Healing cards.Boss fight: best to lure him to the edge and push him off. Mission 4 i. CompletiFocus on increasing Health Cap and upgrade attack cards.Mission 5 Final MissionAt this point, it is nearly impossible to finish any task for extra rewards, best to take your time on each fight.Try not to stay near the walls because the number of enemies can be overwhelming if cornered.In Mission 5, make a habit to stand on a safe spot and lose your turn if you don't have any good cards on your hand. It's better than facing enemies that could end you in 1-2 hits.

_childDocuments_.review: FIghts in Tight Spaces is a solid card battler game. It's a roguelike in that cards and perks can be unlocked for future runs. The overall premise is you control the Bond inspired Agent 11, sent in for some dangerous missions requiring hand to hand combat in the aforementioned tight spaces. The gameplay takes place on a small map involves using cards to perform actions. Use an kick card to do a kick, a throw card to throw, a move card to move and so on. Each card has a cost to play and various other unique elements to it. Each map has obstacles such as walls and desks that restrict movement and cause damage when Agent 11 or an enemy is pushed into said object. There are also ledges that can be pushed into and fallen from, causing an instant KO. This sets it apart from most other card battlers, as in addition to playing cards the map being played on also needs to figure into the strategy. There are quite a few different decks and cards that can be tried out, and while the gameplay can be difficult it is also rewarding when planning out and overcoming a level.A few negatives to mention are that the story is very bare bones and there isn't much there. None of the enemies, save the final boss, have a personality other than their appearance and moveset. There are also some glitches and bugs in the game, some of which can end a run. Difficulty also spikes on the last few stages which can be frustrating.FIghts in Tight Spaces is in my opinion well worth checking out if you are a fan of card battler type games.

_childDocuments_.review: Chytře provedený mix žánrů. Myslím, že dobré hry, které by mixovali tahové strategie s kartami by se dali spočítat na jedné ruce a za mě Fights in Tights Spaces k nim rozhodně patří. Když k tomu přidám tématiku krvavých zápasů, kvalitního zpracování a díky bohu za celkem tuhou obtížnost (na rozdíl od hromady jiných her, kde se doslova nudím kvůli tomu, že cílovka vydavatele her je kdokoliv kdo ví jak ovládat myš a buď hru zpracuje s hromadou asistentů, nespočtem "záchran", nebo obtížeností pro šestileté). Vyjde z toho unikátní hra, která dokáže zabavit na pár desítek hodin.Jasně určitě se najde dost reptalů, kteří budou hejtit, že výběr 3 a více karet po dokončeném zápasu je značně náhodný a nabízené karty se jim nehodí do balíku. Podobně jako v náhodném výběru nabízených vylepšeních. Na druhou stranu málokdy projdete hrou, aniž by se pár opravdu kvalitních karet, nebo vylepšení nepodařilo vybrat. A ano budete mít hry kdy ten poměr nabízených silných vylepšení a karet bude odlišný od předchozích her...Jediné co mi na hře chybí, je možnost si sestavit svůj vlastní startovní balíček ze všech obemknutých karet, kde by měl hráč určitý počet bodů a podle kvality karet by si sestavil vlastní baliček například s omezením, že silnou kartu by mohl mít jen jednu až dvě v celém startovním balíku.+ krvavá bojovka+ hezké animace úderů, kopů a přehozů+ systém zranění a eventů+ odemykání nových karet+ variace startovních balíčku+ celkem obtížné, jedna až dvě chyby v pokročilých fázích hry == konec hry - nemožnost si namixovat vlastní startovací balíček karet- u DLC občas celkem nelogické střídání animací zandavání/vyndavání zbraně vícekrát za koloNo doufám, že do budoucna vyjde ještě nějaké nové DLC kde budou i nové mapy a prostředí. A vůbec bych se nezlobil i za nějaké fatality animace, například v posledním zásahu kde by síla útoku byla značně větší než zbývající životy nepřítele. English version:A Clever Mix of GenresI think good games that mix turn-based strategy with cards can be counted on one hand, and for me, Fights in Tight Spaces definitely belongs to them. When you add the theme of bloody fights, quality implemetation, and thankfully quite a tough difficulty (unlike many other games where I literally get bored because the target audience of the publisher is anyone who knows how to use a mouse, and either the game is made with a bunch of assistants, countless “saves,” or difficulty for six-year-olds), it results in a unique game that can entertain for a few dozen hours.Sure, there will definitely be plenty of complainers who will hate that the selection of 3 or more cards after a completed match is quite random and the offered cards don’t fit their deck. Similarly, with the random selection of offered upgrades. On the other hand, you rarely go through the game without managing to pick a few really good cards or upgrades. And yes, you will have games where the ratio of offered strong upgrades and cards will be different from previous games…The only thing I miss in the game is the ability to build your own starting deck from all unlocked cards, where the player would have a certain number of points and based on the quality of the cards, would build their own deck, for example, with the limitation that they could only have one or two strong cards in the entire starting deck.Pros:Bloody fighting gameNice punch, kick and throws animationsInjury and event systemUnlocking new cardsVariation of starting decksQuite difficult, one or two mistakes in advanced stages of the game == game overCons:Inability to mix your own starting deck of cardsIn the DLC, sometimes quite illogical switching of animations of putting away/taking out weapons multiple times per roundI hope that in the future, there will be some new DLC with new maps and environments. And I wouldn’t mind some fatality animations, for example, in the last hit where the attack power would be significantly greater than the remaining lives of the enemy.

_childDocuments_.review: The systems for this game feel so much different than your usual deckbuilder rogue. Like you still have your usual attack and defend cards but the addition of movement and the tactical grid style combat adds a new layer of strategy to it all, especially when you start to engage with other mechanics. One concept that stood out to me was the momentum mechanic. Each hit you dealt increases momentum, each time you move without attacking you lose momentum for each space moved. Some cards you need to be above certain momentum thresholds to play but are effectively 0 cost when you do get to play them (the exception being the cards that "end your combo" and set your momentum to 0). Other cards do more damage the more momentum you have so you're encouraged to try to keep your combo rolling. The other mechanic that I really enjoyed was being able to move enemies around. Pushing, sliding, and pulling enemies into each other's attack ranges really helps dwindle down their numbers quickly and you'll be paying attention to your turn counter most the game. Each room has multiple rewards, with the basic reward usually being adding a card to your deck but bonus rewards like extra money or upgrades to your cards or stats having requirements like defeating all enemies within a certain number of turns or protecting a vip or collecting a briefcase or pushing x number of enemies over the railing etc etc etc. It kept the game fresh throughout the entire run.My only complaint for the game is a single run does seem to take a while (my first from start to clear was about 5 hours) but with the game seeming to save every time you play a move at least you can put a run on hold and come back to it later. A solid game and I look forward to exploring the other starter deck types and difficulty modes.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is hellish. Great music, decent aesthetics. Some rough edges that you can blame on early access(most notable are missing animations for a couple placement-manipulation cards on some enemies, and even one or two attacks).The problem is it's so damn replayable. There's a fun variety between the enemies and their attack methods that will have you thinking about your next move. It's great when you find the magic combination of cards to play to avoid damage on a turn, just barley squeezing into a safe spot and taking out an enemy, or redirecting their attacks into each other. There's a large amount of card variety, and you can have vastly different strategies on how you approach fights from one run to the next. You can focus on blocking and counterattacking, moving enemies and yourself around the map, passive abilities, cards focused on combo, or buffs/debuffs. And you're free to mix and match with all the benefits and risks that brings.The last stage is quite fun since it just throws everything you've faced so far together in a huge brawl that tests the deck you've built up to that point. I can consistently get there but I've still never beaten the final boss fight, it's just brutal. It's incredibly frustrating when you get surrounded and suddenly all your cards are worthless, especially if you get trapped between auto-attackers. You know the pain is coming but you're completely powerless to stop it. I've even started some maps surrounded by enemies and drawing zero movement cards...it's frustrating, but I'm not sure what I'd suggest as a workaround to it. Maybe just making it so there will always be one empty spot next to the player on turn one? Either way, when I inevitably die I'm constantly catching myself going "Let me try again but this time..." and I hop right into another one. I lose way too much time to this game trying to beat it, and I can only imagine that'll get better as they add more game modes and options.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: This beautiful yet completely badass game absolutely deserves a seat at the big boy rogue-lite deckbuilder table.  In my book, this is on the same level as StS, Monster Train, Roguebook, Griftlands, and the other heavy hitters but it's also incredibly lean and there's just no wasted potential at all here.  They absolutely nailed it.  The euphoric chemical dump that occurs when you pull that necessary card in order to drop a 4x combo special move and launch an enemy's stupid ass right over a railing is genuinely hard to beat.  Starting the game on Classic Plus difficulty is a big help as this does wonders for teaching players how the game actually functions, since you can run different scenarios and see what works and what doesn't.  On harder difficulty levels, restarts are not an option but the fact that they are present on some difficulties is a welcome touch.  And there's been plenty of times when my cards were just not well put together and I was unable to proceed at a given point, which is exactly as it should be.  Classic (aka normal) difficulty will wreck your face if you're not careful though.  Works for me. The replays are a nice touch but not critical in appreciating what the game does right.  This game ended up being every bit as rad as I was hoping it would be when I picked it up 6 months ago in early access.  If you have even a passing interest in rogue-lite deckbuilders, this is required reading.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Super fun game, but not perfect by any means. Easy recommend with a few things to keep in mind.It's surprisingly unique and refreshing while blending all the best parts of "Slay the Spire" and "Into The Breach" with a unique art-style reminiscent of "Super Hot" but doesn't feel derivative.This is a strategic deck builder that uses space management and a chance to add new options EVERY combat. The thing that keeps bringing me back though, is the vibe and execution of a small part of the game; the game-feel and flavor. Nothing feels static and boring. The animations are decent for a grid combat game, and most cards do not share said animations which always feels good to see new combinations both mechanically, and visually. Every run I play, I feel like I'm a completely unique character (If you're drafting) going from defensive grappler, to aggressive counter-attacker, to a ranged monk, etc etc. and I cant overstate how well that aspect is executed.Despite this, it lacks a lot of polish, and in some instances doesn't work properly... There is a mechanic called "Bleed" which does damage over time, and the game refuses to do replays if an enemy died by bleed damage. How that was missed, I have no clue.Some cards can be upgraded, and some can't, but you can't find out when choosing cards to put in your deck... You just kind of attempt to upgrade a card and see what happens, and then you have to remember in future playthroughs.The cards feel balanced enough for the most part but the abilities aren't... You can get additional card draws every turn, free movement, and actions per turn on some abilities, and others give you temporary pseudo resources which pales in comparison... Some abilities also are just carbon copies of others but way worse. One give you temporary block equal to the enemies on screen (I've never seen more than 5 at the same time), OR alternatively you can get all attacks reduced by 3 damage forever which is just strictly better outside of fringe scenerios.Last issue I found is that the events are never worth doing if you have a choice for 2 reasons; 1 is that it literally means you aren't playing the game, missing out on fun aswell as valuable resources and cards from combat, and 2 is that the events almost never pay off... Some of the outcomes are also debilitating. One run was ended because I got a permanent debuff that made all my cards cost 1 more... Which meant I lost tons of health every combat, and couldn't win the objectives that got me money that i desparately needed to remove the injury.Even though I have my gripes, if you can get passed them, the game is very good, and honestly one of my favourite deckbuilders. I hope the devs fix those issues though.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Been playing this game on and off since early-access, but I do come back to it a *lot*.Basically: the game is like Slay the Spire (Deck-building with several acts and the ability to modify your deck or heal along the way) with two dimensions of movement added.  It is the movement (and the art-style) that makes this a big winner over StS for me. The "Stand and Swing" combat in StS got boring very quickly (not to mention that the fights were always the same), whereas having to manouevre around the field to avoid attacks and maximise your own makes it far more interesting.There's a little bit of "magic" in the game which I think it could have done without (ie, powers not possible outside the supernatural), but otherwise I find the card options, selection processes, difficulty levels and basic structure of the game to be a lot of fun with a lot of replayability.  There's a good number of different enemy types and powers you need to be able to deal with.A key difference with other deckbuilders I've tried is that in others you seem to hit a fairly abrupt wall sometimes (a boss or mini-boss that just obliterates you because you were unable to get the right cards or plan for it); in FiTS, you'll generally be able to muddle through if you pay attention to where the attacks, auto-attacks, counter-attacks and such are coming from.  Substance-wise, I think the glaring omission is the lack of a Survival mode (infinite bad guys, see how long you can hold out), which the game would be well-suited to.Otherwise, no complaints.  One of my favourite games of the recent past (a big part of that comes from the fact I can listen to my own music while playing).

_childDocuments_.review: It's like Jason Bourne or the newer Bond movies, but a card game. Gameplay is similar to Into the Breach, which is to say a dynamic puzzle game consisting of turn-based combat focused on controlling the battlefield. At the end of each level you can see a replay of the fight which really does look like something from a movie. You need to maintain your combo and your momentum to succeed. Some cards allow you to slip around enemies, while others let you tank damage, or even deal damage through counter attacks. There are four decks so far which dramatically alter how you play the game. Every turn you discard your cards and draw six more. This is how each turn plays out.If I had my way, I would wish for a female agent to play as. Also, it is hard to progress because you are encouraged to begin again from the first mission, because the later missions retain their difficulty. But I still recommend this game for fans of turn-based strategy, especially fans of Into the Breach.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible game - Slay the Spire meets Into The BreachIn it's current state, this game is more than playable, and is already one of my favourites of all time.It can be refined here and there - the replay feature is clunky, and certain moves will not play out fully if they kill an enemy.Overall, however, I have no complaints. I love the game, and the difficulty is exactly what I'd expect from a game like this - I haven't completed the final yet.I would advise that if you were to get this game, go in blind - don't look at the wiki, don't research moves, metas, playstyles or encounters. Just play the game, and you'll love it too.

_childDocuments_.review: Played the already addictive prologue / demo for 40 hours and that only had maybe half an hour of content. Then the early access for close to 190 hours. Every update refined and improved what was there, added some new cards or enemies, but always stayed true to the very well working core formula. The 1.0 release today added a lot of balancing, smoothed the presentation and UI, and introduced a new and more fitting final level.Replayability is off the charts with this one. It's a deck builder with random paths through a selection of boards / maps with increasingly difficult enemies. All tied together with a very light story arch. The game is intended to be played with permadeath, forcing you to restart if you end up dying. This can be tweaked at the start by selecting a lower difficulty with the option to restart boards on fail, or rollback a turn (reset all moves from the current turn). However, every playthrough, whether successful or not gives you progression points unlocking more cards and decks for the next games.One game takes maybe two to three hours (less if you die early) with each level (collection of boards with similar enemy types) taking 20 to 30 minutes, which makes the game perfect to play when you have a little break.I wholeheartedly recommend Fights in Tight Spaces. Not just because the game itself is immensely fun to play, but also because I can't remember a developer I've been as impressed with as I've been with Ground Shatter.

_childDocuments_.review: The theme and animations are exciting, but the game is just not balanced well enough to go the distance. Some decks are obviously not viable. For example, you get rewards for completing challenges in each level. These challenges are a rich get richer mechanic. Passing the early challenges will help you beat the later challenges. You can't afford to fail the challenges early. Most levels involve a time trail. A deck built around the "bleed" status simply won't work. You can't wait for the enemies to bleed out.This challenge mechanic also gives runs a terrible arc. If you fail a couple, you'll enter a slow and frustrating death spiral. You can't luck out and chance upon an item or combo to turn things around. The unstoppable force of entropy will inevitably grind your run to a halt. You fail the trial. You get no money. You can't afford upgrades. You fail the next trial. You get no money. Rinse and repeat.They also tied to mimic Slay the Spire's map mechanism, but the path choices aren't particularly interesting. The paths don't branch off very far. If the player could choose between different kinds of trials and enemies, that might make this part of the game interesting. All they show you is the number of enemies and the rewards. There's no real risk vs. reward or playing to your strengths.Oh. And if you get injured, you should probably just abandon your run. They're wildly unbalanced.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a big fan. As a rogue-like deck-builder it's not exactly breaking new ground, but it is a great concept, well-executed, and pleasing to look at and to play. I like it better than Monster Train, which I didn't care for. It's at this stage not up there with Slay the Spire with me, but I regard that as the current title-holder, so it's a high bar. Well done.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Fights in Tight Spaces is a game where you play a special agent working for "Section 11", a British agency that "solves" problems. And by "solve", I mean "break". And by "break", I mean "break".As is a current trend in indie games, it's a deckbuilding roguelite with reliance on RNG. And the formula works well: it's a game that can be challenging, and very rewarding when you plan out how you approach each situation.The community on the Discord is quite active, and very friendly and helpful.There's stuff that definitely needs ironing out (of course, as it's in Early Access!), but I find that the devs are very reactive when bugs and suggestions are given.All in all, I'd say you should give the demo a try. It may well not be to your taste. But if you enjoy it, don't hesitate one second (unless you have work to do, in which case you probably shouldn't, or you'll spend hours on the game).

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun deckbuilder in the John Wick/Superhot vein (John Wick because it's mostly punching, superhot for the art style). Multiple different "deck" styles, multiple different enemy types. I don't see how you would easily do this without the computer, so it works well and scratches an itch - how do I use these cards, and these circumstances, to prevail?I do wish the final boss fight was easier, but I've enjoyed it a lot and am looking forward at going back with several decks and trying to finish the whole thing. And then there's the DLC. And a prequel. :D
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: I love the idea, but the execution has some flaws. Firstly, the entire gimmick is that after the fight is over you can press the "replay" button and see the fight play out like it was real time. This is a fantastic idea, but the execution is super disappointing. Every move of every character plays out one at a time with an awkward pause between each movement. It just looks like someone played the game quickly, rather than a hollywood fight scene you directed.  And there is no reason for this, it would be incredibly easy for them to code the replay so the animations overlap slightly, and other such tricks that could make the replay actually look cool. Secondly, I have played this game for like 11 hours, and every single run I had ended in an instant KO because I misunderstood how a special enemy moved/acted. The campaigns are too long and fights too complicated for such instant deaths to feel right. The campaigns are way too long in general actually.  If they made the replay system look good (its insane that they haven't yet, with such minor tweaks I could see interesting fights from this game going viral online, this game would sell itself) and radically reduce the length of the campaign, and maybe give you one or two "rewinds" somehow so you don't instantly die then I would totally recommend it.
