_childDocuments_.review: 1.0 Launch Update: Just a brief update due to the fact that the game fully released in 1.0. I threw in another three hours for this little update. The game has improved one of my primary complaints, that being the lack of interesting variety in the final zone. It is now shorter and has a small plot to go along with it, along with new enemies. That said, it didn't do much in terms of the obscene amounts of health enemies have, so it still feels rather grindly and like a chore at that point. In addition there are some new mechanics with them that just feel lazy, like a ninja with a sonic attack that can give you an injury from anywhere on the map. Past that, the runs still take an excruciating amount of time. Roguelikes for me should round out to about an hour per run maximum, and the three hours I spent in 1.0 was in a single run which got to the final stage. This is totally a personal taste thing, but it just feels bad spending an entire session of playing a roguelike on a single run. I will say that the presentation has been cleaned up and many of the bugs that I mentioned in my previous review have been dealt with. The cards and decks do seem a bit more balanced and have more adaptability compared to in Early Access. Generally speaking to the quality of the game's technical, visual, and audio design it seems to have rectified any complaints I had, even if the art style gets a bit samey after a while. TL;DR- The game has improved since Early Access, but most of my main complaints still persist, which stem more from design choices than quality standards. The final chapter and a half still feel a bit lazy in that enemies simply have a copious amount of health and somewhat unimaginative mechanics and individual runs feel too long. Again, I wish there was a neutral review option. The game functions beautifully and can offer some hours of fun depending on the individual, but for me personally I wouldn't recommend it for the reasons I stated compared to other roguelikes/deckbuilders of similar price. But please, if the things I mentioned don't bother you, by all means give the game a try. I don't regret my purchase and I'm happy to have supported the dev in early access, but the game just isn't for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I have seen too many reviews for this game already where people don't have enough time played or experience, which leads to misinformation and incorrect judgement.  Therefore I feel the need to say that I have played through the entirety of this game content wise.  I have used all cards that I understand to be in the game, and have completed every mission barring the final mission where I lost in the final fight.  I have also played the original demo AND prologue versions of this game in their entirety.  The total gameplay hours throughout all versions can be estimated at roughly 25 hours.  This being said, I believe myself to be in the utmost position someone can be to make a review for this game.Also, this review is not focussed on describing the gameplay.  It is more to point out what I think this game can be, what I think is wrong with it right now, and as a message to the developers on what kind of love this game deserves.Overarching opinions (mostly good things): In simple terms, I love this game.  Fights in Tight Spaces is extremely fun and addicting.  I can't help but praise the idea and so far, execution (given circumstances) of the developers.  I will 100% be playing much more in the future.  The potential this game has is astonishing to me.  What can be done with this formula is great.  For me it's one of those games that in a finished state, could have 100+ hours played in a week.  Which means that if I had an entire week of free time, and slept 9 hours a day, I could see myself playing this for every waking hour I have.  This is obviously not sustainable or realistic, but this scenario can portray what level of potential I think this game has.  The only other games in this category that I have played are: Mount & Blade, Skyrim, XCOM 2, and MinecraftConsidering that this game literally came out in Early Access less than a week ago, keep in mind I said "finished state", which represents the ideal state that I think and wish this game can achieve eventually.  To compete with the Triple A - like juggernauts and personal favorites I listed, this game would obviously require an absurd amount of content and polishing.  However, if there was any game that I could preemptively guess to have a chance at reaching that level of game quality, its Fights in Tight Spaces.Criticisms: So now that i'm done talking like this game is the next coming of christ, I can point out some of its very apparent flaws.  Because like I said earlier, this game is nowhere near what I think it could be.  But I understand that an Early Access game doesn't need to be perfect by any means.-Players locked into Ironman mode- This one is something that most people seem to be asking for, and rightfully so.  Most people won't be ready for the debatably brutal consequences in place at the moment where you have to restart from the beginning if you fail.  With this game demanding near perfection in its gameplay to grant success.  Playing perfectly, especially when you don't have the desire to, can be extremely frustrating.  I am, like I said at the beginning of the review, as experienced as someone can be at this game.  But it still took me a multitude of attempts to make it to the end of the game.  Even worse, this game has no tutorial, which would explain the most basic of game mechanics to brand new players.  The game also constantly introduces new card abilities which all have nuances which are never explained and must be figured out through trial and error (all while in a forced ironman).  I very often draw a line between this game and XCOM 2.  Which was a game that I started out very inexperienced at.  I almost quit playing that game in the first 10-15 hours due to its brutal difficulty and permadeath mechanics.  The only reason I didn't quit and ended up loving the game, was because the game allowed me to work around the difficult mechanics to learn how to overcome them.  #1 it did not force its ironman mode, and #2 it allowed for manual saves with which many players (including myself) used to retry segments and learn the game.  XCOM 2’s ironman mode still offered what this game already has to whoever desired the challenge.  Simply, the function of a forced ironman mode with no workarounds in a challenging strategy gameplay system (that also is not DIRECTLY explained) is almost never a good thing.-Some levels become impossible to complete at times-What I mean by this is that there are cases where the player cannot prevent a death regardless of preparation or gameplay performance.  The limited deck modification mechanics in the game, and what I assume is random generation of enemy spawns contribute to this problem.  This is one that could be overlooked or forgiven in some cases in a game that does not force an ironman mode.  But, in a game that does (at the moment) such as Fights in Tight Spaces, it can in essence prevent someone from playing the game.  Allowing the game to be played should be the first priority of any game development.  So I would assume that this should be near the top of the priority list for fixes/changes.  Obviously in a card game that relies on chance of getting the cards you need for any given gameplay situation, these problems are bound to happen.  But reducing the likelihood of such instances is very important.  I think the dev team has already mentioned their understanding of wanting to work on this issue, so this problem could be short lived.-Lacks replayability once the game has been beaten-This game strives to be a good game mostly through its difficulty and journey to learn and get better at the game to take on harder and harder missions.  Which lends a game like this to simply just add more content  (with more missions AND card mechanics).  While such an approach will obviously lead to a longer, more fulfilling game.  It does not bring out the full potential of the game.  This game could have features such as community made missions/enemies/cards.  Or higher levels of more nuanced difficulty almost like a pokemon nuzlocke which changes how the game is played at a very core level and what parts of the game are valued in each playthrough/gameplay session.  I know these ideas can create a slippery slope for developers to find out where the line needs to be drawn in respect to what they need to do versus what the players can do on their own.  Mostly because both of the features I mentioned could in some capacity be done without direct developer influence.  I also don't know in what way or how hard it would be to implement features like this into the game.  I am not making the game after all.  But if Fights in Tight Spaces is to truly meet the high bar of potential it has set for itself, moves such as these would need to be considered.Conclusion: For anyone who read this whole thing, I would say that the price is justified for the game you would be receiving.  Especially due to the high likelihood of more content and polishing in the future.  My opinion of this game is already high, and most likely it will improve further the more this game is updated and worked on.  I can only hope that this review is read by the developers as well, because most of this review was unintentionally designed as a message to them.  I wish the best of luck to the development of this game and I would recommend this game to anyone I come across.

_childDocuments_.review: Fights in Tight Spaces is a game that scratches a few itches. First, it makes me feel like John Wick without a gun. Second, it's a deck builder with a wide variety of cards that allows me to play the game in a style I want to. Third, it always feels like I'm progressing. Fourth, it feels like chess, but with melee brawls. Fifth, it's more than just a card game because you have to move your player around the battlefield, which really makes you feel like you're in charge of the fight. I recommend this game to anyone who likes card battlers with a twist. FiTS does a great job making each level feel like a game of chess, where there is always a way to slip out of danger, or put the checkmate offensive on your opponent.While I love the game and would recommend it to anyone, it is lacking in the total freedom of creating a deck from scratch using any of the cards you have unlocked. But the devs are always updating their game, so I'm hopeful for the future of this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly fantastic game with a very addictive gameplay loop, would highly recommend for anyone who are fans of action, James Bond, John Wick, martial arts, and turn based strategy to give this a shot. There is currently a demo for the Prologue that is still available that contains the first level of the mission for anyone on the fence and wants to get a taste of the gameplay.While the premise and story is simple, it's a very innovative and well thought out game that like other reviewers have said, combines the positioning strategy of games like Chess or Into the Breach, satisfying turned based combat with stylish animations as you elbow ninjas in the face and throw mafia thugs of the roof, and deckbuilding strategy from Slay the Spire. Currently the setting is that you are Agent 11 for a currently unnamed organization setting out to topple the various differently flavoured gangs of the underworld, bikers, chain gangs, ninjas and the italian mafia. I imagine as development goes along the story, potential variation in events etc. will help to tie it all together but even then the game is both quirky but with a very sleek artstyle vaguely reminiscent to Super Hot. The gameplay is what really makes the game shine. There are currently 4 decks available for the player, that while doesn't make anything set in stone gameplay wise do result in different gameplay styles and deckbuilding focuses. These are Balanced, Aggressive, Counter Striker and Trickster. While the player starts with a Balanced deck and unlocks other 3 as they play through, and inevitably die throughout a playthrough, I find the balance between the decks to be fairly good albeit can use some tweaks, and some players will prefer some over others, but I wouldn't say there is a "best" deck. As part of the deckbuilding process, you will generally want to take cards (randomly given at the end of fights as loot) that suit the shortcomings of a deck. For example, as the Trickster deck starts off with very good mobility but is lacking in damage dealing cards, you will generally want to aim for DPS oriented cards and a few mobility to round out your weaknesses. You can very easily get far more cards than you will know what to do with, and a larger deck is not neccessarily a good thing as it means you will draw your good cards less often. This gives the player lots of decisions of whether to keep a card, aim to get rid of it, and what cards to upgrade. This keeps the gameplay fresh and no gameplay run will feel the same as another, and I look forward to see further cards and strategies added to promote new playstyles and deck builds.The game has only been recently released as of last week, but currently I would say the polish the game needs would be more towards bugfixes (the game is overall a smooth experience, but some cards feel unfinished and some have counter-intuitive descriptions compared to actual ingame behaviour), and some balance changes towards the endgame. Out of the 5 levels currently, the last 2 levels, mafia and the final mission will likely need some more work. I haven't managed to beat the game yet, and usually make it to the Final Level with the trickster deck before the brutal endgame fights with lots of enemies and often no viable moves in a turn that are safe and prevent damage to yourself before I lose. I imagine as the game gets developed, this will be fleshed out and maybe more variation in the level order (as it is currently going from biker -> prison gang -> ninjas -> mafia -> final level) would be welcome as well.Overall to summarize, I've been having a blast with this game and it can get pretty addictive to get into the loop of losing, trying a new strategy or run and repeating and scratches that itch I never knew I have to elbow people's faces and push people out windows across a variety of different setpieces, all the while with a fairly satisfying deep strategy layer to go alongside the turn based combat. Give at least the prologue a shot to see if it's your cup of tea, doesn't cost you anything but time and a significant portion of your free time gone as you struggle to find a game as stylish as this one.

_childDocuments_.review: My biggest issue with Fights in Tight Spaces now is that I want more of it. Sometimes when you play such a wonderful game, you crave for a bit more of contents, more of expansions...The game is a hidden gem. Everything is highly-refined. The game-play loop is superb - you move from room to room (in very tight spaces), fighting enemies each turn with cards representing your moves - either attacks, movements or specials. For each win, you're rewarded with more cards, upgrades to health and MP, upgrades to cards... Sometimes a room is a special event. The variety of attacks is huge, and each fight can happen in a drastically different way than you thought. The interaction with different types of enemies - with their own passives, skill sets, make every fight a huge tactical puzzle, yet thrilling with actions.Graphics are okay. It has its own style and theme, and animations of kicks and punches are well-done. Yet I wish there can be more, but I guess the investment in game-play might take away one in graphics.Highly recommended to those who like rouge-like, such as Slay the Spire, but wants more tactical choice and variety in some ways. Very very good game!

_childDocuments_.review: There is literally nothing more satisfying than making half the enemies kill each other with friendly fire, and yeeting the other half off the edge of the board for instant kills. Then watching the playback of your carefully choreographed ballet of destruction.An extremely fun, extremely addictive game that succeeds in capturing the feel it's going for. Fights are usually pretty quick and pretty decisive, and when you've got good deck synergy going along with some good draws, it'll make you feel like a badass to eliminate all of your opponents in a few, elegant, chess-like moves. I don't really have any major complaints. It would be nice to  have a little more control over deck composition - rather than a pre-set starter deck, I wish I could draft from the selection of basic cards. You're at the mercy of RNG, in terms of what cards you get offered as fight rewards and to purchase in gyms, as well as which Enhancements you can choose for beating bosses, which means that bad luck will cause some runs to fizzle as your power level just doesn't keep up with the difficulty. At the same time, there are some cards and enhancements that are so good they kind of wreck the difficulty curve in your favor. For example, Painkillers - if you're lucky enough to get that card, then HP stops being a concern for the rest of the run. But those issues are kind of inherent to the roguelike genre, I guess. And aside from a few hiccups, I think the difficulty curve is pretty good. It ramps up slowly, introducing enemies with more powerful and more disruptive abilities gradually,  so it never feels too overwhelming to keep track of what all your opponents can do. I would love to see this concept expanded into a bigger, deeper game. I wouldn't mind a map with more route choices, and visuals with a little more detail and maybe some customization options. It would be nice if the animations during fight playback were tweaked slightly to make moves flow a little more smoothly into one another. And a built-in way to share fight playbacks would also be awesome!

_childDocuments_.review: So I've put in quite a few hours ever since this game came out on the 24th and I gotta say, it's definitely a fun and addicting experience.This really feels like "John Wick: The turn-based, tactical, deck-building game".So, if that is pretty much what you were looking for, I'm definitely recommending the game to you.HOWEVER, this game definitely still feels "early acces" to me.So you might think "duh, it is".Sure, but plenty of games (like, for example, Satisfactory) are currently still in early acces but definitely don't feel like it.What I mean by "feeling like early acces", is that I've encountered various bugs in during my time of playing and some stuff definitely feels like it could be polished out more (for example, the interface could use some work on making everything a bit more clear and I'm not too keen on how much in-game content, such as new cards and abilities, is hidden behind such a steep difficulty/learning curve).Other than that though, this game has an incredible foundation and I'm really curious what kind of other stuff the devs will do with this!

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun and satisfying twist on the deck-builder rougelike sub genre. Make no mistake, this isnt some slay the spire or monster train clone. This is a very unique spin on this concept and one that works very well. Fights have an ebb and flow and when your deck synergizes just right and you get the right card draws, the replay becomes a dance of death reminiscent of the most iconic scenes from kung-fu cinema. I left many levels feeling like John Wick lol. Ive recently started playing the DLC and the new gunslinger class is really fun and a refreshing update on the existing game play which was mostly melee focused with few ranged abilities. Its taken a change of mindset to keep enemies at range rather than dancing between foes up close. The range of decks, play styles, upgrade synergies and varied enemy typed has kept me entertained for a long time. And I still have two more decks to unlock! Highly recommend this game to anyone that enjoys card battlers, tactics games or even puzzle games. Thats what levels often felt like. A puzzle that I had to solve with the right sequence of moves. _childDocuments_.review: I initially played this close to release, and though my memory isn't perfect, i do still have some opinions to share.Please keep in mind that i not only played this close to release, but i refunded it at the time too, which means i'm not certain how much of what i'm talking about is legacy content.Fights in Tight Spaces does a good job of combining turn based fighting and deckbuilding into an interesting duo (see slay the spire for another good example of this), and utilising different cards in different environments does a good job of keeping you thinking for the new levels, rather than just using one unbeatable idea for every environment, a feature that is certainly necessary in a game of this genre.The art style leaves another positive point, and the minimalism and 1-2 bit colour scheme for each character helps not only identify each enemy type with ease, but also creates a wonderfully vibrant experience when various enemy types appear in the same stage. However, the soundtrack for me felt distinctly lacking, and painfully average, though this obviously isn't a game played for the soundtrack, so i'll let it slide. On the other hand, the sound effects were refreshingly decent, and I hope as more is added to the game the soundtrack and sound effects receive an extended library.This does, however, bring me to my main point and why I decided to refund the game, and that's the state of the game itself. Fights in Tight Spaces is currently an excellent demonstration of what's to come, and the content in the game is good already, but at the time of release, the game was in version 0.15 (if i remember correctly), which, quite frankly, is an insultingly underdeveloped state to release any game in, let alone at the price the developers have said they will likely sell this at upon full release. Take any other game you love and enjoy at the moment, and imagine having purchased it for it's full price when only 15% of the content had been released. Would it still seem worth it? Even at the time of leaving this review, the game has been moved up to .18 3 months after release, which leads me to doubt their early access statement of full release being in less than a year.To the credit of the developers, it seems that they are still dedicated to the creation of this game, which is a big step ahead of some early access creators, but I just can't recommend buying a game for £20 in this state. Some highly substantial content needs to be added to this before release, and I hope that the high quality of the content that's already present shines through in the rest of their work.EDIT: as someone who commented on this pointed out, i made a mistake in here calling .15 as 15%. I had meant that in terms of their version history it's all going to be outdated but i realise my mistake.

_childDocuments_.review: Deckbuilders and turn-based tactics are two of my favorite genres, so FiTS was an immediate purchase. 13.5 hours later, after a handful of properly failed runs and one shamelessly-savescummed successful run, I think there's enough to recommend here.FiTS definitely delivers on the trailers' promises of stylish turn-based combat. The aesthetic is somewhere between Superhot and Canabalt; I dig it. The different enemies you encounter are distinct and have strong motifs, and the ability to view replays is a great touch. Repositioning an enemy so they attack another enemy never fails to feel satisfying.Make no mistake, you'll need to do a lot of that repositioning. Unless you're finishing up a level, you'll rarely have less than three enemies to deal with simultaneously. Their damage output quickly ramps past the point where tanking multiple foes' hits is possible, and they also become too spongy to defeat in a single (or even in a few) turn(s). The default five-card hand feels very restrictive in the late game, and many of your starting cards are so weak that your best move is to pay to remove them. The margin for error is  in most circumstances, and unless you deliberately craft a very lean, very strong deck, you'll be depending on the relocation of enemies and yourself to survive.Nowhere is this more apparent than with enemies you encounter approximately 2/3rds through the campaign that pack assault rifles, as well as the "Overwatch" ability from Spacehulk. They will shoot you anytime you move in front of them or attack in front of them (even if you're not attacking them, which is unusually strong by itself),  they will turn to face you if you get to either side of them. The level where I had to fight two of these Terminators was - no exaggeration - the hardest level in the game, easily harder than the final boss level. And it was halfway through the third campaign! They're so difficult to deal with that you start to wonder why your character isn't packing heat of his own, which pulls you out of the whole experience. And while I'm at it, the banality of the "You Failed Your Mission" pop-up leaves a really bad taste in your mouth at the end of an unsuccessful run. (The victory screen isn't much better.) I feel like other roguelikes have more encouraging end-of-run screens that make players feel better about the loss.Despite that, this is still a solid game, provided you have the disposition to focus on enjoying the journey rather than the destination. I look forward to the devs adding more content; in particular, I feel like a female character model for the main character would be a good addition. The level generation is strong enough that you could probably sink dozens of hours into this game before it starts feeling stale, and there's always the daily leaderboards if you're into that sort of thing.All-in-all, this feels worth what I paid.Recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: I had high hopes for FiTS when it was first announced, the demo was pretty promising - unfortunately, it ended up being a case of style over substance. It looks sleek, animations are cool, music is great, but the core game under it all is lacking - worse yet, there are instances where the style gets in the way of it.Let's start with overall balance. It's to be expected that some deck archetypes would be more effective than others, but here, it feels like there are 2 or 3 viable decks, and the rest is trash. The bleed and grapple/throws based decks suffer the worst due to how slow they can be, especially since the only way to earn cash in most encounters is to finish it in under a certain number of turns. Not getting cash early means missing out on upgrading your cards, leading to later encounters taking even longer as enemy health scales up, leading to you once again missing out on the rewards and the run being ruined. On the other hand, if you do get those early rewards, you can keep snowballing into a super-easy run - the balance feels very lopsided; either you're struggling at every turn or you're breezing through.The enhancement system also contributes to that feeling: some of them are incredibly strong, such as full-healing after every fight (at the cost of 3 damage per turn) or +2 momentum; others are completely useless. The decision to lock out 2 enhancement slots behind one specific enhancement that unlocks them is pretty odd too.To my earlier point of style getting in the way: some of the card art looks very samey, especially on movement cards, making it hard to tell them apart at a glance. It would be nice to have a better way to tell movement/attack/special cards apart as well, or have the hand sort itself in a particular order. There are times when cards cover the playing field, making you have to spin the view to aim. A lot of the crucial information about enemy behavior is poorly readable, making you rely on trial and error and memorize how each enemy type behaves rather than being able to judge the situation from a glance.I'd like to say that this game just needs more polish, but no, it really could use reworking a lot of core gameplay elements. I can't recommend it at the current state, especially at that price point.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing this game since the Prologue, and now that a 1.0 release is on the brink of the horizon, I feel compelled to try and convey the experiences I've had playing it.The gameplay captivated me from day one - it was a great mix of positional and situational tactical battles with the additional layer of board-game-style deck management. There's also some route-planning to consider, but it doesn't weigh too heavily on the course of your runs - EXCEPT when tackling Daily Play for score maximization. A full run takes about an hour to complete, and you can finish the game much faster with experience.Graphically, the art style is very minimalist, taking a leaf out of the intro to Casino Royale. This isn't a bad thing for me as it helps call attention to the amazing animations that the agent and his enemies have. Additionally, the card art has evolved beautifully since the demo, and you can see them all in the new Compendium. The replay system, though sometimes buggy, makes for some great watching and showcases the aforementioned animations even more.The game soundtrack and sound design in general is sublime. It really adds to the satisfaction of executing killer moves on your opponents.I think I've tried my best to put how much I love this game into words, but I'm a poor writer, so I'll just say that if you love tactical games in general, you will appreciate at least the gameplay of FiTS.... and  punch the shark.

_childDocuments_.review: Turn-based tactical combat *and* deck-building? Yeah, it turns out this is a pretty addictive combination. But it also makes a lot of sense for the scenario which this game presents: being thrown into a small room with a bunch of dudes who want to shove your face into the wall, and the chaotic give-and-take as you try and punch, elbow, and claw your way to victory.This is a game that frequently throws seemingly impossible odds at you. But once you get the hang of it and get a decent deck going, you'll be surprised what you can pull off. Thugs with shotguns? Subway car full of ninjas? No problem!The real fun of this game is queuing up a bunch of bad guys so they're prepped to attack, and then spinning them around and shoving them into each other's faces. Watching a chain of bikers clobber each other Three Stooges-style is immensely satisfying.My main gripes are 1) having to play the same missions over and over again gets a little dull, and 2) enemies near the end of the game get overly complex, to the point where I wind up spending most of my time carefully reading stat blocks. Overall this is a fun and surprisingly addictive little game. I'm happy to have supported some talented indie devs with my purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: Facilitating an infinitely replayable Roguelite campaign as well as merciless daily beatdowns, Fights in Tight Spaces is a Card Battler in the purest sense of these words. Its sharp-cut gameplay reflects how we all naively imagine conducting ourselves in a fight. To succeed here, you need to stay calm, which isn't easy, considering how exciting the battles are. Fix your tie, throw a handful of pocket sand in the nearest thug's eyes, slam his head against the bed, push a hunk off the balcony, sidestep, kick the ones in front and behind you simultaneously, stab a guy's pressure point with a finger, then immediately dive under his armpit, jump off the wall and end another life with a flying punch. Set it all up in such a way that the remaining few of your enemies would hit and shoot each other on their turn! After the fight is over, enjoy the gloating delight of watching a real-time replay. It's hard to overstate how gratifying and hypnotically gripping this perfectly animated asskicking is. In the beginning, you go with the flow of combat, and later - control it.Your special agent's immaculate mannerisms and appearance reflect the elegant ways this game's meant to be played. He always goes against overwhelming odds, sometimes it's disturbing to simply take a peek over your hand of cards and see him surrounded by a crowd of ninjas and hulks, each of them ready to end a run after just one mistake. But remember - they hit hard, you hit harder. Calculate and predict, do your best not to get hit since, while you can take a beating, you can't afford it. And keep in mind that you can't play it safe if you want to get paid, which turns local combat into a balancing act of risk and reward. To help you with it, the game provides a comprehensive UI that tells you all you need to know as well as a clean, precisely stylised image, featuring isometric 3D with tastefully accentuated colours. The fighting mood gets magnified by all the crunching and tearing, thuds of varied intensity, and upbeat dubstep mixed with some kind of 90s dance music, I think? The kind to make combat feel energetic and cool, with a drop of vague nostalgia and maybe even some Hotline Miami vibes chiming in.The encounters take place in such memorable locations as men's rooms, prison showers, public toilets, or even a plane wing. Bikers, prison gangs, ninjas, and Italian mafia whose business you'll get to interfere with all have their dangerous quirks and moves, so taking them on is a demanding task. You'll learn the hard way to pay attention to enemy abilities, which vary from instant action, AoE swipes and counters to following your every move during your turn. Sure enough, there're mid-bosses and a multi-stage fight against the main baddie at the end, but I won't spoil any of it. However, there's a lot of fun to be had when dealing with elites like, say, Drunken Master who restores his health and dodges attacks or a bartender who distracts you with a cocktail shaker. Yeah, this game isn't a stranger to a bit of dry humour, reflected both in enemy designs and playing with Bondiana tropes in the briefings. I'm not so sure, but sometimes Fights in Tight Spaces made me think it happens in the same world as XIII, also one of the best games made for this setting.When it comes to mechanics, this is a traditional card battler with an added positioning. You use replenishing energy, which is called Momentum, to play offensive, defensive, and mobility cards, then pass that prerogative to your enemy and pray for a good draw. Positioning is key, allowing you to take advantage of the surroundings by pushing enemies into walls, each other's attacks, and the void beyond. My favourite thing. The game's card collection allows this and much more, it's extremely thought-out and diverse. There're cards with compound effects and cards with choice, presenting an array of deadly synergies for every theory crafter's pleasure. Push, pull, grapple, throw, block, counter, melee, ranged, buffs... you get the gist. Many cards demand certain conditions: some especially powerful ones need a precise position and some can only be played when you have enough Combo Points. Those add when you strike or reposition enemies and deplete when you move. Thereby, in combat, the management of your Momentum, Health, Block, and Combo Points is paramount.You won't spend much time on the map out of combat, but you'll get to make crucial decisions nevertheless. First of all, your classic branching paths are in place, including their short descriptions and possible rewards, so you won't go in wherever completely blind. Aside from battles that could have different side goals like picking up a suitcase in a set number of turns or protecting an informant, you'll get involved with self-explanatory random events, the Clinic, and the Gym. The latter is your bread and butter that provides all kinds of crucial services like card purchases, deck trimming, and expensive upgrades. This is why you need to race for the optional turn limits. The Clinic is, uh, forget about it, it's overpriced anyway. What you shouldn't forget about are the Enhancements - those are like Relics in Slay the Spire, only not given as often. Sure enough, they have game-changing properties like increased Momentum, healing, damage modifiers, special cards, etc. Nothing too interesting, yet nothing to scoff at either. Finally, obviously, by playing the game, more cards and starter decks get unlocked.Uncommonly for a roguelite, the game presents a range of well-explained difficulty options. I opted for Classic Plus for the training wheels: Rollback (undo a turn 3 times per battle) and the ability to restart a fight or even go back to the map and pick another path. I sure abused these features non-stop, for sometimes I'm stupid, and sometimes the game puts you in a predicament you can't escape unscathed right at the start of a battle. I'm not happy with that, for I feel like the privilege of f*cking myself over is mine alone. Thankfully, you won't see it happening too often. The good news is there's almost zero RNG to the process of punching out teeth and caving in skulls, only the luck of the draw, bad news is that most of your goofs are your fault alone. To see a game in this genre, which is so fair and respects your time is an unusual occurrence. To see me buying it without a discount is an event of a legendary rarity since I'm a Scrooge when it comes to consuming stuff. Fights in Tight Spaces is an exception because it's a perfection. I'm also a giant Scrooge when it comes to calling games that.P.S. Seriously, try the demo: My curator

_childDocuments_.review: Really good for 2/3rds of a playthrough. New, fresh great mechanics that are very satisfying but the final boss stream really changes the game. All the push, throw dodge and avoid strategies get broken by an immovable counterattacking unknockdownable following repeat boss. I now know how to build to beat him... armour, grapple and counterattacks other strategies don't work and you fight him and his accompanying similar henchman 4ish times on the final chapter. I repeated the last levels enough times I got lucky and the AI messed up in my favour and shot itself a bunch but otherwise it's close to impossible. I didn't want to trash a 4 hour run at the final hurdle. TBH the generosity of replaying levels probably backfired as you can keep cracking at a near impossible situation (on the auto difficulty I recieved). An FTL or other rougelike full failure would have stopped me getting as frustrated. The retries do give it more of a Superhot "retry until perfect" feel though the game just dosn't really know which camp its in. The clarity on enemy actions also broke down where previously everything was clearly spelt out, I had to find out counterattack ranges, and how many times by trial and error. Shame, the game just needs some variation so the end boss situation isn't a known fact. But as it is, same run every time so  I can't recommend fully.End of the run I was awarded with a list of "unlocked" cards most of which I've already used so not really sure how that worked out either. Hope the developers have another crack at it some time. Got on humble bundle, had my £4 of fun. At full price its probably still okay if you know what you're in for.

_childDocuments_.review: Was looking for a deep tactics style game that is quick to pick up and play. This hits every mark with flying colors as far as I am concerned. Gameplay is your standard deckbuilder (Slay the Spire) fare with a really nice difficulty curve. You are drawn a hand of cards and you have to beat down, maneuver, and escape various enemies in a tight space. Progression comes from gaining better cards through the run. You unlock better cards based on how early you start in the set of levels as you progress. The end game cards are crazy and have a bunch of risk/reward going on.The criticisms I have for the game are numerous though. In most levels there are instant kill spots in which you or enemies can get thrown into- which means a single mistake can mean you better kiss you arse goodbye. Some card and enemy mechanics are a bit tricky to understand- you may lose a lot of life because of not reading closely as you play. The later levels get very hardcore in terms of difficulty- if the cards and abilities you have are bad you won't make it. The Trickster starter deck is very punishing and should be re-balanced- some cards in the deck can ruin you immediately if used incorrectly.I really hope they add a lot more to the game. I'd love to see an infinite mode or a 50-100 floor mode with random enemies. I'd love it if you could capture an enemies weapon and use it for awhile. I'd like to see NPCs that fight with you- this engine would do well if you expand the game to have large scale fights where you control a couple more characters (with their own unique deck).Overall this game is a 9.5/10 for me. It scratched a tactical RPG itch that I have not felt in a long time. It is a very fair price for such an involving game.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: 🔵 Rougelike card game (similar to Slay the Spire/Monster Train) but with a grid-based turn-based battle system🔵 Different starting deck provides very different playstyles🔵 Drop in and drop out anytime. Progress is saved after every move, so you can quit the game anytime and continue back at the same place🔵 Game has several difficulty options to choose from that is very useful which can allow rollovers/restarts🔵 Artsyle looks charming🔵 Attack animations looks quite satisfying🔵 Highly replayable and recent update added endless mode🔴 There's too much enemy types. Usually this is nothing I want to complain about, but in this game different enemy has very different significant buffs. The buff ranges from enemies moving as you move, enemies facing you automatically, auto-attacking, auto-counter-attacking, auto-dodging, gaining auto-block, can't be damaged in front, can't be downed, debuffing you from anywhere and a lot more which becomes extremely annoying and very unfair. This kind of buffs even makes some cards useless which is a terrible game design
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: This game- THIS GAME. I love this freaking game SO MUCH. It's the first deckbuilder I've really ever gotten into. Putting it in overly simple turns it's like Enter The Breach meets Slay The Spire meets the opening sequence to Casino Royale. I have played the crap out of this game ever since the preview of it during the summer of this year. I have bought this game for at least two friends because I have so much fun with it. The team behind it are extremely responsive and the community on Discord is very active and the devs are always reading and responding to feedback. The game is almost ready for full 1.0 as of this review but the amount of things that have been added to the game over time is awesome. There are so many fun decks you can build through drafting or the pre-established decks you unlock through playing. I know for a fact, even with my hour count, there are still cards I haven't discovered and the team is also still adding more cards as time goes along. The long and short of this is that it's a fantastic game that I find addictive as hell and incredibly stylish and you have nothing to lose giving it some of your time given steam's refund policy. Even an hour with the game should be enough to tell you if this game is something you'll enjoy. Give it a shot, it's a real blast.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: I've been excited for this game since the first preview demo, and it was worth the wait. It's extremely addictive, and my fears that it would be too easy were unfounded. It's not perfect, there's clearly plenty of work to be done before Early Access is over (I also wouldn't mind an alternate color scheme to break up the constant blast of white, but that's not super important), but there's tons of content here and the fights are engaging every single time. Even as you're burning through the early fights for the hundredth time, they're still fun and can kick your ass if you aren't paying attention. If you like roguelite CCGs, this is a top tier one.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: It is a card-based fighting game. But, the satisfaction comes not only from winning the fight, but doing it with style. Can you have your enemies wipe each other out while you dash, step, and slip your way around the room? You're not a tank, and healing opportunities are RARE, so the idea is to not get hit if you can avoid it.And THAT is where the pain of this game comes in. The set up of enemies, a level's design, and your own cards can all work against you quickly turning a great run into disaster in just a few moves.I'm 8 hours in and have just beaten the first gang. During this time I've unlocked two new decks (fighting styles), but I don't see the "deckbuilding," yet. I mean there are RARE opportunities to get a new card or two (or upgrade one or two) but that is often done instead of finding the healing you will likely need. Meanwhile, those new cards and healing are EXPENSIVE for the amount of funds you are able to collect for your efforts.And, unless I've missed something, I haven't been able to "build" my own deck or fighting style yet, just select from the three I have so far. I'd love to try and set up my own fighter.All in all, if the CQB Melee interests you, and you like card games (and the randomness therein), and you want to have some fun with those two things I'd say pick this one up.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: While I am giving this game a thumbs up I honestly can't recommend it in its current state. The base mechanics are really neat and the game makes you think on your feet every run which is nice and refreshing. The issue is there is ultimately only one way to play the game. There are bleed decks that sounds cool and good but are bad because you don't do your damage fast enough to complete challenges in levels to earn money to upgrade cards so you cant win with it. There is a throw mechanic and deck that is really cool and interesting but is unusable because you can not throw bosses and throws will be almost all you have in your deck. you run into bosses very often and basically not being able to fight them makes some fights just unwinnable. These issues are very simple to fix, with slight increases to how long you have to do challenges on a level for stuff like bleed decks and allowing you to throw bosses the game would have multiple viable ways to play. It makes 0 sense that you can not throw bosses. you are allowed to CC them with push backs and what not but you cant throw them? i can do 100 dmg to him in one turn with good use of cc and control but i cant do 12 dmg to him and throw him? why?

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, this is a great game! It offers a lot of fun and strategy with good music and good sound effects to boot. The "simplistic" art style makes it really easy to distinguish between different characters (most of the time, anyway) and makes the action very easy to read. It's a fun way to live out the fantasy of being a badass agent, beating up scores of bad guys in different locales. As someone who haven't played a lot of deckbuilders, I really enjoyed this game! It's simple enough to get into, but has enough complexity to keep you entertained. It also offers A LOT of replay value, which is nice. I've been playing this game for almost 90 hours now and even though I'm still struggling to beat the final boss, it's a lot of fun. Progress is slow, but steady.The biggest issue with this game is the RNG elements, such as which cards you draw and where you end up on the board. Most of the time, it works just fine, but there are times when the RNG can really screw you over and put you in situations where you're more or less guaranteed to fail a stage on round 1. Those times can be really frustrating, especially when you're far into a run, but even then it's not a huge hassle to start over. A little annoying at times, but definitively not enough to ruin the game for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Play this.Combining a 3D tactical grid with deckbuilding worked out great. Most other deckbuilders settle for classic turn-based RPG battles, so throwing in several new layers of strategic depth already puts FITS well above most of the competition.Many strategies and deck archetypes are available to you, with several starting decks offering unique bases to build from during a run. Defeating enemies in absurd combo chains always feels good, even if half the combo is simply dancing around them to get into position.The simple art is lovely, but the music is rather forgettable; after a couple of runs, I did not feel bad about muting the game to play my own tunes over it.Hopefully we eventually get a large expansion or a sequel to this with more play modes.

_childDocuments_.review: A mediocre rogue-lite card builder. The game is close to good, but suffers from some very poor design choices.* Many of the enemies and cards look similar, in addition to that the interface has information scattered all over the place and is hard to quickly analyze. As a result, it takes longer than it should to survey the battlefield and it can make you prone to missing some tiny detail that can ruin your run.* Enemies have stacks of special abilities and in the later stages you will find that many cards and strategies are almost entirely invalidated by what you're faced with (especially the final boss). These 2 foes cancel several of your cards, this other one makes another few cards useless and the last one makes your other option garbage. In these cases there are literally 1-2 strategies in the game that still work. Balance is quite poor because of it.* The decks are also terribly balanced. With some being very strong and others being laughably bad (I'm looking at you Bleed deck).* Choices on the map are much less meaningful than in games like Slay the Spire or Monster Train. You will always take the gym over medical and you will almost always be upgrading the same cards every time you play a deck.* The game seems to have logic that prevents you from starting a fight in a position where you must take damage, which is nice. However, it will often leave you with only one correct play, making your options meaningless for the opening turn. It does not extend this protection to the victims you must protect in some stages, they will sometimes take damage no matter what. Sometimes you will be unable to protect them without getting yourself badly injured over the course of a fight, which invalidates the health they would grant you for saving them.* The way enemy abilities act is wildly inconsistent. Sometimes you step in front of an auto-attacker and they hit you, other times they just sit there. It seems to work the same for those of the same type, but the exact same ability can differ from foe to foe.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Now that v1.0 has finally released it is fair to say FITS has grown into a very stylish and polished deckbuilding roguelite. With some exceptions, roguelites have never appealed to me since their inherent RNG nature, complex mechanics, and permadeath can feel as if they are tests of luck more than skill at times. This is not so much in the case of this game since their is a strong emphasis on good tactical positioning. As the name implies, majority of the maps are very small rooms and corridors. It is very easy to get surrounded and overwhelmed so whether you decided to fight your way out of a corner or strategically slip past enemies is all up to you. FITS is very much easy to learn, hard to master. The beginning enemies are very simple and can be easily dealt with any deck but once you start getting to the ninjas and beyond, they begin to have additional attributes to make sure your deck has some flexibility to it. For example, the grappler deck is great until heavy enemies arrive because you cannot throw them so it is necessary to supplement it with some striking cards for such a scenario. Because it is turn-based, you can take as much time you need to plan out your actions. All in all, this is very much a labor of love as I bought it during early access back in June and have enjoyed seeing update after update. I look forward to seeing what more could come out of this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is cheap as hell. The mechanics are so fundamentally flawed, they need hand manipulation to help avoid checkmate situations.I tried completing the game in Purist mode (no hand manipulation) and died at the end from not getting movement cards. Then I tried classic and breezed through the game with the greatest of ease only to die to some mfer who can auto attack multiple times (while all previous enemy can only do it once).The counter and auto attack mechanics literally encourages you to play passive and manipulate the board instead of directly attacking, slowing down the pace of the game.The problem with having characters that punish you for attacking them/playing cards while being in their line of sight is that you are forced to either use block before attacking or moving away and waiting a turn to find a set of cards that can help you attack without being punished. Oftentimes, you can't hit enemies with counter and auto attack unless you either have block or 2-3 movement cards, so you have to wait a turn of be punished for trying to damage the enemy.There is also no rewards from completing the encounters themselves; you have to complete side objectives that heavily rely on having the right cards at the right time, such as push cards while you're in position to push someone off a ledge to complete "pushing people to their death" side objectives or movement cards/block cards when you need to kill all enemies in 7 turn while having to deal with auto-attack/counters.Playing this game is like reading a contract; the UI is far behind other roguelikes in terms of readability, the cards all blend together like an anime fighting game's character select and the enemy abilities are written in fine print, with tiny little details such as the enemy being capable of auto attacking multiple times easy to miss. Miss me with that ♥♥♥♥.RNG is even more critical in this game, and the pathing/encounters often feels unrewarding, as you don't get gold if you don't complete bonus objectives or participate in rng events. Also, healing costs money so if you get the wrong cards and you take damage, you are guaranteed to be bogged down in terms of economy, unless you have the absolutely broken heal card.Overall the combat favors having a bit of everything to deal with every mechanic/side objectives in the game and praying to rng for the right cards.This game suffers a lot from some sort of downward spiral dilemna: you need to complete objectives to get $, so you have to complete the levels as quickly as possible to get cash rewards, because the encounters themselves only reward you with a card. If you don't get the right combination of cards on most, if not every board state, you could spend empty turns and fail your side missions, or you could deal damage but get hit, which is not good because healing isn't free. Since you spend your money on healing or don't complete side quests to conserve hp, you need to rely on good draws to get out of tough encounters and get enough rewards to invest into card upgrades. Thus, good card rng is essential, and that is why hand manipulation exists, yet it isn't good enough for most late game encounters. Which is why the game gets incredibly unrewarding and slow near the endgame: you spend most of your time moving away from auto attacks, blocking against counters and even grappling or pushing away annoying enemies who can chase you, not dealing damage or creating a better board for yourself.Oh yeah, and the powerups/relics are boring af. In StS, they change the way you play the game. This game has nothing that makes it interesting in the long run.Imo, binding movement to cards was a mistake. Games like Into the Breach and Dofus did turn by turn strategy right by allowing the player to move without using abilities or cards.If you didn't enjoy Slay the Spire, I believe you will hate this game even more, and I liked StS. That game did it right, this game did it wrong. If you want to play a tile by tile card game, wait for Waven.tl;dr : UI sucks, the game suffers from downward spirals gameplay loop and heavy, heavy rng, so deckbuilding feels pointless

_childDocuments_.review: The basic idea is sound for the first four levels and then on the final board the fun murder just begins and doesn't let up until the end. Every enemy is a hit point sink, every enemy does an absurd amount of damage, and your character becomes the weakest piece on the board. It feels like a card game that's afraid to let you build up any real strength. Card draw is nearly non-existent, enemies rapidly out level your attacks (by the end, it is common to have multiple enemies with 140+ health on the board), and eventually deal more damage than you can afford to block. It is Early Access, so there is a possibility all of these things will get patched over time, but the current build suggests that likely won't be the case, as the developers seem to be prioritizing artificial/unfun difficulty over the player experience.One thing that I think would improve things: allow the player (once per turn) to spend one point of momentum to draw a card.

And the devs have been very active since the early access release, so the EA label hasn't been a concern at all with this game.Also you can Spartan kick dudes off of buildings.

_childDocuments_.review: Great concept and graphic style.....no saves / game-over style He has the feeling of John Wick with challenges of the fight.You have to move thru each room and level ensuring you minimise damage and taking out the bad guys to get thru the level and back to HQ. Each level (I have played training, and the first 3) is very distinct and does take a while to work out your best placement and fighting style to use make it to the end.Really really let down by the implementation and repetitiveness of the game.  You need to conserve your health to win the game. -- not just for your current room fight (that is ok),-- not just for the current 10-13 rooms in the level (tough but fun)-- NO...your health carries thru for the entire game. (WTF!!!!)Sort of like John Wicks running injuries as the fights his way thru the movie....the difference being John did get a change to recover and heal. Earning money (to pay for healing) or earning more health is difficult and sometime impossible due to your choices several rooms back.♥♥♥♥ up once...you might lose half or more of your health. (no save games here to restore) but do it a second time and you have to restart right back at level 1 square 1 (or suffer penalties) Seems this developer loves punishing the player rather than build a challenging system that you can recover from errors without resorting to the 40year old concept of 'Game Over - Restart'Fix this issue of no healing between levels and the game is a solid 8/10As it stands....3/10

_childDocuments_.review: I gave it three runs and honestly... it just doesn't live up to what you'd expect. It's a near idea, don't get me wrong, but it's very much a game that chooses looking cool over playing well. Combat becomes stale rather quickly with how every area is the exact same just with a different layout; enemies have a wide variety, but most boil down to "they move close to punch" or "they back away to shoot." While that can sound like something you'd expect, it isn't nearly as complex as it could be. The game is somehow too complex and not complex enough at the same time. Strategy takes a lot of time to figure out, with both a board to consider, an energy meter, attack ranges, some enemies being resistant to attacks from a direction, some enemies hitting you when you hit them, some enemies having a wide attack, block to consider on both sides, some enemies always just moving out of your range, the combo meter... it just all adds up so quickly into something overwhelming, but not in a particularly fun way. So... yeah, I don't think I can recommend the game. Especially not at the $25 price.

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels so close to good, but there are quite a few nagging issues that compound to make the whole experience a bit of a slog to me.- Fights feel like they drag on and on for way too long, as the fight animations border on plodding and most early fights will last several rounds past the point you've already pretty much secured your victory. Lots of watching as you punch a dude and then take one step to the left, rinsing and repeating until all the stragglers are disposed of- Tangential to the above point, the Superhot inspired visuals and replay system are a bit of a bust. No matter how cool I tried to fight or what setting I set my replays to, the jilted animations and delay between each turn means replays don't resemble badass fights so much as sitting in on a squaredance rehearsal - Balance felt off, but I've seen others praising the game's balance so maybe I'd need more time with it. Compared to something like Slay The Spire, shops feel both like they have nothing all that cool to offer and yet are obnoxiously expensive, damage/health numbers in general feel like they could both be bigger, and the core rules of enemy behavior make them feel very "dumb" for lack of a better wordYou might dig it, but its gimmick wore thin on me much quicker than I expected and sadly the game never really felt like it came together into a cohesive and fun experience. If you haven't played this game's main inspirations, namely Slay The Spire, Superhot, and Into The Breach, I'd recommend all of those games before this one

_childDocuments_.review: Update: The game is now 1.0 and there have been several new features and improvements. I'm not going to go through my old review but I still recommend this game.Do you like deckbuilders? Do you like puzzles? It's basically a deckbuilder puzzle game. RNG is inherent to deckbuilders but it's a lot of fun.=============================old review:Plenty of style here. It's a deckbuilder tactics game built on a solid theme of cinematic martial arts.As a deckbuilder roguelike, it's a bit different from other well known titles. Unlike other deckbuilders, the goal here isn't to make some sort of infinite-draw card-advantage death-engine. You aren't looking to draw multiple hands and blow your entire deck on nuking an enemy in one turn. Instead of just maximizing something like damage output, you're looking maximize your flexibility.Fights in Tight Spaces is sort of like a puzzle game. You get dropped into a small room on a grid-space gameboard. A bunch of different enemies appear and each one acts (or reacts) in their own unique ways. Some enemies hit the target in front of them, some swing in an arc, some shoot a gun in a straight line, etc. In order to survive and win, you must be able to adapt to any layout the game throws at you. If you get surrounded, you need to have an answer. Perhaps you stack counter-attacks to repel the attackers, or maybe you have a card that lets you move past an enemy so you can push him into his friends. Maybe your strategy involves staying in the middle of the room where you can move in any direction, or perhaps you want to keep your back to the wall, to minimize the number of enemies you are exposed to at one time.The actions available to you depends on how you've shaped your deck. As I said earlier, the levels are like puzzles, and your deck is the toolkit to solve this puzzle. The more flexible your toolkit, the more situations you can handle, no matter what the game throws at you. Make the right moves and you can minimize the damage sustained and maximize the efficiency of dispatching your foes. If your deck lacks movement cards, you may find yourself unable to escape. If you lack offensive cards, you may find it difficult to dispatch foes in a timely manner. At this time, the game is currently five mini-campaigns, and four starter decks. There's a really good base here, and I think some features need tweaking or adding... But it's quite solid for what it is. Overall this game is quite promising and I do hope it only gets better from here.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: The core gameplay is nice, satisfying and well-animated. The mechanics are easy to use, easy to understand and work well together, creating an overall very nice play experience. Everything else lacks a bit of polish, though.The events in particular are too random, both in terms of results and of breaking the suspension of disbelief. (i.e going to a warehouse on the other side of the world during an undercover mission inside a prison)I didn't get any major, game breaking bugs, but sometimes the interface is wrong (i.e Hidden Blade does not boost Caltrops but you see the boost on the card anyway), and some mechanics are inconsistent. (i.e Shimmy's dodge does not stop at end of turn but Bob and Weave does)One gripe I have is with the game's progression system. The xp bar is too slow (I have every achievement except the compendium ones and I'm only level 25), and what unlocking cards really does is unclear. The game shows me I have not unlocked One Inch Punch, and yet I've obtained and used that card several times. (among several other cards in the same situation)To sum up, the game is great to play but would be a lot less confusing if the devs would update it and correct or clarify everything incoherent within it.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: A card game with solid mechanics, decent polish and a nice theme. The logic employed to win fights is very satisfying and deck building is extremely important, if a bit limited.If you can get it for around £15 then I'd say that's fair enough. Otherwise, I wouldn't mind a few more decks and something more to incentivize repeat playthroughs such as harder challenge unlocks and completion rewards.They should also speed up the replay system so it actually flows properly as I feel that's kind of the game's thesis statement but it doesn't really hold up.

If you're looking for something straightforward with a lot of depth and cool moves, I highly recommend FITS!
