_childDocuments_.review: This review may involve tips and spoilers.This game is wild. It is a puzzle based, tile based, card deck building fight scene. Play against many different gangs with different styles, looks and moves. Build a deck to continue through the ranks. The main character is a sleek secret agent taking on covert missions. Let me tell you. Wow. This game is addicting. Different decks from a standard attack or defense deck to the awesome Trickster deck which allows you to use cool moves to move about the board and Heavy Attack has some cool Matrix style moves. Using your turns to move enemies into paths of incoming bullets and samaurai sword swipes never gets old especially as you get better and use less turns to complete a mission. But be warned the enemies have an array of dangerous moves and unfortunately can use guns unlike the player. Health management is very important as you may not get card rewards or money rewards to help with health regeneration or health points throughout your game. I will say choosing the pathway to get the Clinic or any level with health bonuses is a must. One card that makes it easier is Heal Self(+). Events are random levels on pathways and be anything from a percentage based chance of gaining or losing something and can sometimes be nothing. The game itself is styled in almost a Cel Shade in a way that akins to SUPER HOT.I give this game an 8/10.Some things I'd like to see.-Melee Weapon/Gun Cards-Character/Color Customization-Multiplayer/1v1/Iron Man Modes-Deck Builder/NamerMany a time during a game there were thrills, chills, laughs and yells and I think this game could be a favorite for years to pass. Hell as long as they stay away from Micro transactions I'd play this on mobile!
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: I refunded this product because I'm satisfied with how the Prologue plays, and that's around the perfect amount of time I game in a single session. However, Fights In Tight Spaces? Fights In Tight Spaces isn't a game - it is an undercover IQ test. You'd be a fool to not play it if you're a fan of Into The Breach, or any turn-based deck-building roguelike. FITS is all about the exaggerated swagger of a black tweenager, 3/3.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: This game is X-Com meets Superhot meets Slay The Spire. It's you as a James Bond clone up against thugs from Central Casting where your attacks, movements and blocks are all determined by which cards you pull.  It's a game system that should not work at all and yet it does...beautifully. Few things are more satisfying than beating the crap out of a biker dude only to push him into the path of a gunman whose itchy trigger finger adds insult to the literal injury. Add in cards you pick up on the way, events that can help or hurt  you(depending on RNG and your own choices) and unlockable decks from making progress on your run and this is the most fun card building game since, well, Slay The Spire.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: This game ROCKS - I have played the demo like crazy, and am stoked to be able to play the early access.You really feel like a badass, kicking and punching and shoving goons around, while forcing them to attack each other - heh heh heh.One thing I'd like, though -- hit point loss over their heads during hits! I can't tell how much damage I'm doing per hit... I know I can look at the *card* but between clicking the card and the attack, sometimes my feeble lizard brain can't remember how much damage I just did. Gimme some pop-up numbers!!
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: If you like a combination of turn-based strategy, card games and deckbuilding and punching stuff, this game is perfect for you. It's a combination of these three elements with it's own creative and sometimes ingenious twists. This games is hard, and you'll have some really difficult learning curves to adjust to but the reward is well worth it. You carry one deck through a range of difficult situations and through those situations painstakingly craft your deck to suit your playstyle. By the end of your run, your deck will be unrecognisable to how it started but the general concept and idea of the deck will be much, much stronger.At the end of each run, I'm gutted that I have to start again, but am always excited to try out another style and maybe, just maybe, I'll grab that card that I was too nervous to grab before.There are issues that I have with the game, but those are mostly cosmetic, or surface level criticisms. The core mechanics of the game are super solid.A few changes I'd like to see after many hours with this game in it's full version:     - Difficulty setting adjuster for each seperate run through the stages.     - A freeform camera with toggleable settings.     - A chance to experiment and to make your own deck with various limitations (even if this was for a seperate mode and not the main game mode.     - Boss Rush mode.Those are some things that I'd love to see implemented into the game and I think they would only add to the flavour and flair of the game in it's current state.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Part deckbuilder, part rogue-lite, part Into The Breach, this game is a lot of fun. It evokes Jason Statham films, and also sort of reminds me of the game Duelyst, from a few years back. The enemy telegraphs their moves, and it's fun to make them attack each other. It's also fun to throw people out of doorways or windows.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Stellar deck building game about being a John Wickesque super hero. Utilizing card synergy with enemy placement comes naturally, with different decks favoring unique playstyles. Counter attack and throw centric decks are my favorite but occasionally I pick the offensive heavy deck for a change of pace. Despite the normal deck building limitations (e.g. amount of cards diluting tactical choice) the game feels fair yet challenging.The developer added some variation game modes like the ability to rewind turns a limited amount (or even restart the current fight). I highly recommend trying these out because the game can be punishing. But once you get into the flow you will be playing one of the best computer enabled card deck building games there is.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a blast. Very few bugs for an Early Access title, and nothing that has disrupted my gameplay. I love the concept: small-scale tactical RPG grid fights with deck-based combat. Highly recommend, especially if you've ever wished that deck-building games had just a little extra depth/flavor.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: I give this a recommend in it's current early access state. The game has a lot of potential and is fun for being in Early Access. The current decks feel bother underpowered and unbalanced. Once you get the hang of the game you can blow through the first 2-3 areas, but after that it gets into painful territory. I find with the aggressive deck it's easier, as you just continually pummel your opponents into the ground until they have more health then you can reasonably deal with. The counter deck and the trickster both suffer from not being "fast" so it's difficult to get some of the bonus objectives and you lose out on cash. Maybe I'm just not great at the game but I can't help but compare it to other deck based rogue likes, where sometimes I get bad draws and just barely drag myself through a run, but sometimes you get just the right items and cards that you blow through every round, but I feel like Fights in Tight Spaces only feels like the former and never the latter. No matter what cards or abilities I get, by the third mission I'm the underdog.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Love it. Love it. Love it! Took half an hour for me to get used to the card based fighting system ... and disliked it at first. But after that ... best game so far this year :-) I was lured in by a review/preview that compared it to "Into the Breach" (a game which think is perfect!) ... and the two games have a lot in common. The small playing area, being able to (in theory) predict all that will happen ... etc. I highly recommend Fights in tight spaces :-D
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Started off good fun with a clever concept and a puzzle to slowly and carefully unpick each turn. And then it just got worse and worse over time. Enemies started getting more and more absurdly powerful abilities that just take all the tactics out of the game and make you more and more reliant on RNG.Early in the game if you didn't have decent attack cards you could move into a safe position to the side of an enemy and outside of their attack arc and wait for a better draw. The random chance of your card draw that turn forced you to think outside of the box, but it also made it feel all the more satisfying when you had just the right tool for the right job and pulled off the perfect turn. Now all enemies automatically turn to face you when you move, or they will move every time you move (And they still get to move on their turn too). They will automatically counter attack you whenever you attack them (Even if you attack from behind). Or automatically attack you whenever you move into their attack arc (Which often takes up a significant majority of the board that isn't already covered in enemies). Enemies have huge stacks of "armour" that regenerates at the start of every turn while for you to do the same you not only need to have the card drawn but also it takes an action to do so (And don't tell me the quick block free action card exists, I know it exists but the armour it gives you is barely half what a generic enemy will deal in a single attack so it may as well not exist). Enemies are immune to damage from the front. Enemies will automatically deal damage to you whenever you deal damage to them (Not even a counter attack, just hitting them will straight up hurt you). You used to be able to get around some of this by having enemies attack each other, which was cool and fun and rewarded good gameplay and positioning. And then enemies became immune to each others attacks so that option goes out the window too. And don't get me started on the deck building in this game. A few hours in and you realise that the deck theme you had been angling for is now useless because every enemy has an ability that hard counters your decks greatest strength. It gets to a point where you aren't punished for making a mistake, or taking a risk that doesn't pay off. You are punished for literally every move you make. Every time you do anything at all the entire board changes as enemies move and attack and counter attack. Hell it isn't uncommon to find yourself in an impossible situation on the very first turn of a level. Hard pass, I wish I could refund this trash.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Great card game, captures the fantasy of close space fist fight perfectly, good depth and mechanics. Some cards have 'hidden' mechanics that intuitively make sense but not written out so it needs some experimentation. For example the card 'head smash' can ignore defense against shield-wielding enemy type who immune attack at the front because, you know, you grab that guy's head and smash it in the wall, no shield can block that.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: I find this game fun as hell. I know it's early access and there is work to do. Be nice is some of the card  and enemy description were clearer. Does Counter Stun work against enemy with Shiv and so on. I know someone will throw together wiki eventually. This game has great promise and is fun to pass the time and make ya think on many levels.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: It's basically John Wick and slay the spire combined into one. As a martial arts enthusiast, this game is perfect for me. It takes a cool spin on turn-based combat, making you really think about your next sequence of moves to deal as much damage as possible while trying to not get hit by the enemy. Enemy variation is really good, keeps the game fresh and full of new challenges. Daily plays and randomized decks bring about a ton of replayability too.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Ruthless roguelike deck-building/turn-based fighting game with an underlying action movie theme. Devs are active in updating the game, and despite frustrating you with the promise of constant deaths, seem dedicated to delivering a quality, polished game. The art style is minimalist and aesthetically pleasing, and the devs recently added a Dark Mode, which makes a surprisingly big (positive) difference aesthetically. As previously mentioned, you are practically guaranteed to die constantly, and as it is a deck-builder you may die at the hands of the merciless RNJesus at any time. Despite this, gameplay is fun enough to shrug off deaths and jump back in. The game is easily put down and return to at any time as well. A beautiful embellishing feature of the game is its playback mode, allowing for cinematic replays of your fights. Combine this with the turn-based and deck-building elements, the game fulfills its underlying action movie theme beautifully - and playing back those fights is dummy satisfying.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: I do love the game for what it is. Great deckbuilder with some great combat, theme, art style, its a great game to waste a half an hour before work or stealth play during work on my deck. Its a demanding game though. Some events are straight death if you choose combat, one wrong move can spiral into getting thrown out of a room with a kick or shove. Luckily there are alot of difficulty options to make it as casual or extreme as you want.$25? A bit steep to be honest. $15? Great buy.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Fights In Thight Spaces is an original strategic/roguelite/deckbuild game.The moves, the atmosphere and everything make you remember close combat fights like in John Wick and the elegancy of the fighting like with James Bond.The art style it's simple but great, the graphics and the details could be better but still pretty solid.The gameplay the roguelike part it's like any you already played, but the fighting part and the strategy part looks pretty stunning like... if the character is near a wall you crush it with the wall for example.I seen a lot of original deckbuildings but the idea of this one I love it ^^ Here you can see my Gameplay :
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: What an awesome game! I already spent 40+ hours with the demo version before hitting the buy button on the early access version. Think of it as chess with blood. The variety of cards and playstyles is so much fun and the relief / joy you feel when you master a complete campaign is amazing. Very often you will encounter enemies or are thrown into a room and think how am I supposed to master this only to find out that you actually can and see that a much more difficult setting awaits you in the next room. Immense replayability.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Don't let the title and the visuals confuse you: this is not a fighting game, it's a card battler / puzzle game, and to me its gameplay resembles a mix of Slay the Spire and Into the Breach.On one hand, you have to manage your deck, on the other, positions matter, and you can push and pull enemies around so they damage themselves or prevent reinforcements from spawning.Overall, it's a very solid title if you like this kind of games, and you should definitely try it, be it on sale or not.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Really makes you think. This turn based strategy is in my top 10 of all time games.Deserves way more press. Multiple martial arts styles to choose from in the form of decks. Such a stylish and interesting concept. So fun to watch your moves in action and to watch the whole match in replay is very cool. Wish there was a way to save them. Each move is calculated and important. The music is reminiscent of 90s electronic. Really gets you pumped! Would buy the soundtrack. Few if any bugs. Had it freeze up a couple times, but progress was saved and it picked right back up. Watching you crunch enemies and getting them to kill each other never gets old. 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: So obviously I've put some time into this game. I've long been a fan of deckbuilders and the like, Slay the Spire being one that constantly brings me back. From the first fight in this game I was hooked because it has a lot of what I love about Slay the Spire but also a hint of puzzle-esque combat.Current Pros:-Decent replayability. You'll likely find one of the 4 starter decks that you like and stick with that for most runs.-Good scaling as you progress. the first 2-4 "gangs" you fight are fairly easy to kill without being hit, but towards the end you might be staring at the screen for a few seconds debating which of the MANY enemies you want to risk being hit by.-Multiple ways to win. You can focus offence, defense, a mixture, or just dance around the area and shove people off buildings.Current Cons: -Some of the cards don't *quite* do what you think they will, but obviously GS is working on that.-Slightly stale events. Once you do the events you're kinda just clicking through them out of memory more than weighing your options.-Expensive upgrade/removals. The cost doubles each time you use a service, resetting once you get to a new gym. It's a little steep since unless you meet every condition of the fights before that you may be only able to afford one or the other if at all.-Sometimes unfair spawns at start of combat but as GS has shown they are putting that pretty high up on their update roadmap which is awesome.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: "OH! Why didn't they tell me that's how it works?" - The GameLots of issues with how abilities are described, which is a HUGE pet peeve of mine. For example, they need to template all enemy attack and ability descriptions to specify range (i.e. doctor's combo reduction ability) and whether abilities interact with armor (i.e. attacks that deal bleed damage). It should not be unclear whether an attack I receive will cause a status effect. That being said, it is fun, deep, and very replay-able. Just expect to curse a few times on as you learn what their descriptions don't tell you the hard way.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: fun game! it rewards different types of playstyles/decks and it's fun to see how far you can get before you meet your end. i'm a fan of repetition/grinding though, so i never found it too frustrating nor boring to figure out how to get through each level. besides, it was a great time sink. solid rec, 8.5/10!
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game. It's fun, it's quick, it has a great difficulty ramp-up and bumping music but...And I mean but...Aesthetically? It's awful. The nonstop grey and white gets tiresome and the animations are boring. It's a shame because honestly, I would say this is one of the best card games I have played in sometime. I mean, it doesn't beat Monster Train - But sheeeeeaaat, it's a great game. You should pick it up and try it.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Really good game, even here in early access. They are adding in good updates, but there are some issues with balancing and the like. The core game is great and, while the fights are short, the full run can be time consuming and I constantly find myself losing a ton of time here. There are some problems, the "overworld" map is pretty boring and there isn't really much fun in picking a path nor is there much in the way of choice there. A lot of cards don't feel all that useful. But the individual fights really shine. They feel fluid and interesting even when you duplicate a map. The enemies all have different mechanics, and, at first, their skills are unintuitive and the tool tips are there but easy to forget, so you can get screwed on a new type. All in all it is a fun time. I think it is worth it right now, although there are still kinks to be worked out. You can still have a lot of fun and the updates seem to be going in a very positive direction adding in new mechanics and smoothing out some rough patches. The game is currently above average and trending towards really great.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: I love the game, and I was playing this for a long time when it first came out. I decided to give it some time after release to fix some issues and add more content... but then it took two years to have that done. To be honest, the radio silence was deafening to figure out what was going on, so as much as I'd love to give this game another chance I don't really want to risk when they didn't even really release bug fixes on a regular basis after release.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: It's a solid game that offers a variety of styles of play and it includes lots of replay with the different cards. It's a fair bit of tight spaces to figure out how to fight in. The learning curve is not tough and is easy to pick up in a short time of play. The only real thing I would a bit difficult to play over and over are the lack of variety in the maps to fight in. There is consistency which can be respected but it does dull the desire to play over and over.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: A blend of the deck building of Slay the Spire and the grid-like tactical 'puzzle solving' combat of Into the Breach all done to the style of the intro video to Casino Royale. I really don't review games ever but this one drove me to due to the massive amount of potential there is here. Despite all the following critiques i have I still enjoyed the time i spent playing it.My first criticism is the UI. As mentioned by other reviewers its just hard to tell what you're doing or how things are going to react. One misunderstanding can really cost you a run. My second criticism is that the deck building just... doesnt feel that good. It doesn't encourage experimentation like slay the spire. You dont necessarily start with a super sub par deck that you feel like you NEED new cards (like slay the spire with strikes and defends). In fact in most of my runs i dont need new cards and a rarely find myself taking them. It seems better (for the most part) to just upgrade the ones you have rather than clutter the deck with unupgraded cards.The deck composition is another thing that bothers me. In a 3D environment it feels REALLY bad (and makes little sense contextually) to have the chance to draw 0 cards that make you move or ONLY cards that make you move. I would love to see a gloomhaven approach here where every card has a top "attack" option and a bottom "move/buff" option. Universally good attacks might have a really specific move ability and vice versa. This does clutter the cards up a bit more but i think the UI could be cleaned up to convey card effects quicker and easier. This blasts the doors wide open for that sort of 'solve the puzzle' approach i think you want with a game like this by figuring out what move and attack abilities to combo. The passive rewards are also lackluster but those should be pretty easy to solve through some balancing. Some are just WAY better than others like the "all cards you find are upgraded" and the one that lets you draw an extra card every turn. The card upgrades are also WAY too good as mentioned in another review, they usually double the damage dealt which is a bit absurd.Looking forward to what the future might hold for this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing game for a single run, but the replayability-adding variety seen in typical roguelikes isn't there just yet to be worth its price.In the deckbuilding side, there's little endgame deck variety because there's a couple of godlike cards that you always take regardless of deck builds, and acquiring a deck mostly composed of such cards leads to a very stupidly easy playthrough. Gimmick-oriented deck builds are outright discouraged by some common enemy types having total immunities against some mechanics. You'll always want to go for a deck that can ultimately deal with every side missions and enemy types the game throws at you, which restricts you to flexible cards that work in 1~2 range, moves you or the enemy to put yourself to safety, while dealing straightforward damage. There are also no exciting game changer perks or items that would alter your entire deck goal, with perhaps the sole exception of the unlimited combo enhancement.The lack of level variety is also a big one: an 'optimal' run always looks pretty much the same in terms of path selection. You look at the path that goes through the card upgrades (Gyms) and you take those, always. If you had to diverge and take any other path, it's because you screwed up in some way: you took dangerous damage that can't wait for a heal-giving mission so you go to a hospital; you failed some money objectives and you can't afford a card upgrade, so you just go for more fights. Random Events add some variety if they're in the path-- and maybe it's just my bad luck-- but their chance of leading to good outcomes have been so slim, such that I always prefer a normal fight, instead.This is Slay the Spire where you only get to play the Ironclad, and there's just one or two paths you can take in the map. This is Into the Breach where your weapons are randomized every turn, and there's only one player mech and a single protection target (at most). The potential for this game to be your 1000-hour-playtime roguelike game is there, but it isn't just yet. More updates could make this game an absolute GOTY.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: The difficulty spike of the i Completi levels eventually drove me away from the game, but I really enjoyed my time up to then. FITS has an addictive "one more turn, one more fight" quality since the round-to-round cardplay is fun, as is the gradual creation of a powerhouse deck. Besides the difficulty spike (which favours certain builds over others), my only complaint is that many runs can feel samey, since you tend to get offered the same cards for purchase/rewards no matter how many new ones you unlock.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Fun, and for sure worth the money. Though I wish the cinematic replays were less wonky and glitchy. I like how the gameplay is not based on reflexes, and instead requires you to think. I really enjoyed the events where you can choose from different options, and the way you can plan your adventure and choose a path. I would rate the game a 9.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Even though this game is in Early Access right now, it feels SOLID. I really like how much emphasis is placed on dodging enemy attacks and making them accidentally attack each other with clever movement, seems to be what makes the game stand out among other turn-based strategy games. This game is the closest I've felt to being John Wick in a video game. If you like deck building or turn-based strategy, you definitely should check this game out.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Great at what it does, but starts getting repetitive mid-run. You stall out because you can't get enough buffs because you have to save money to heal and can't heal enough because it wants you to block and can't block enough because you need to do damage and can't deal enough damage because you're supposed to upgrade your cards, but there's not enough money to upgrade the cards without getting the right enhancements, which you get one of each time you finish an entire missions series (including the tutorial, I guess), and not getting the right enhancements because it gives you 3 random choices each time you finish the mission.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Into the Breach + Slay the SpireIf you've played either of those, you pretty much know how you'll feel about this game. It's got deck building, it's got roguelite elements, and it's got a grid you can push enemies around on to make them attack each other. It's still early for this game, but it is absolutely in a fun, playable state and content updates have been steadily rolling out. The main game is challenging but not arbitrarily difficult, and daily play is quite competitive.Update: After being out for a while, the game is very good. There's a lot of content and the gameplay is still great. I'm still enjoying the gameplay, but after all the hours I've put in, I'm itching for an update.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Everything about this game is great except for one thing, the card design. A great step in deck builder evolution. The framework(taking 2D to 3D, manipulating your enemies and the environment), an awesome premise(being a secret agent and combating with only your fists) is awesome. The only issue is the card design and deck archetypes work against the core gameplay.Defeating enemies as quickly as possible is the main and often only currency generator. Without it you cannot purchase, upgrade, or remove cards (the entire underlying strat of deckbuilders) and all but two do this organically. The others require you to simply draft cards to be like the others. Good game if on discount, but low replayability
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Having been obsessed with the Prologue (demo) version of this game for quite a while, I was really looking forward to it coming out, and I'd definitely say it delivers. The full version basically includes a lot of what was understandably missing from the demo; most importantly, the later levels get really challenging, with a lot of enemies having abilities like counter-attacking or auto-attacking which means you really have to think about what you're doing.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Fights in Tight Spaces offers a fantastic blend of deck-building, rogue-like features, and strategic gameplay. Players can dive into numerous well-crafted pre-made decks or embark on the exciting journey of customizing their own deck by selecting randomly chosen cards in draft mode. What truly captivates me about the game is the plethora of options and ingenious tactics available for eliminating enemies or achieving victory conditions. The freedom to adopt various playstyles, whether it's wielding guns, throwing punches, executing kicks, brandishing knives, or engaging in grappling moves, adds a refreshing dynamism to the experience. With the introduction of the 'Weapon of Choice' DLC, the game takes on a cinematic quality, making me feel like I'm immersed in a John Wick-inspired card game adventure
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Finished the game for the first time yesterday. Really enjoyed it. There are a lot of balancing needed across different starting decks IMO. I like the Aggressive deck the most and was able to get through the last level which has absurd enemy hps. If you chose your deck correctly and know when to skip or remove card, there's a good chance you can beat the last level. I made several mistakes in the last fight, for example, but I was able to mitigate the impact with cards that changes your or other enemy's position or status.The problem with this game right now is not that there are OP cards, but that 30% of the cards are useless. Positioning and control (stun and takedown) are too crucial in this game, making the counter-attack style fairly weak.Also in the early game, being able to take down the enemies fast is too important, making the Aggressive style having much better yield comparing to the other styles.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: For those wanting a John Wick game with the satisfaction of an engine builder, FITS is a pretty great example of the 'knife-fight-in-a-phone-booth' aesthetic.I really like that while you're certainly the hero of the story and can soak bullets and punches like any good action hero, there's a definite sensation of good damage scaling. Yes, minions probably won't be taking you down in one hit, but they will swarm you, they will exhaust you, and if you're sloppy enough about it; you will eventually be overwhelmed. The deck building feels weighty, and follows the time honored system of 'get a new card after every room, and hope they're somewhat in line with the deck you're trying to make'. The game rewards variety, but only to a certain extent. Too many options and you'll never draw what you need when you need it, whereas going down only one particular route almost always means being hard boned when you meet an adversary that you don't have a good solution to. In one particular fight I found myself fighting in a 3x3 grid against two enemies with point-blank counters. While I think it could be easy to get frustrated by that; really the take away for me was that if I'd built my deck differently, I might've done alright there. I do think something this game has over others like slay the spire, or griftlands is the variety of missions. I appreciate that you've got game modes for surviving for X rounds, vs kill all dudes, vs protect a person where your displacement moves will shift them across the board (which felt very evocative of old school Jackie Chan movies where he's trying to push some hapless NPC out of the way of a fight). It's all excellent and added some great variety. Inversely, I do think there are some things FITS could take from other games. General UI improvements like letting you back up from a choice (for instance, choosing a card that lets you go through your discard, and then realising there isn't anything in the discard you needed just yet. In other games with similar mechanics, a back button is an option rather than making the player peruse their discard first, then play the card to peruse it a second time). I've also stumbled on a few minor bugs such as where enhancements just didn't work (re: "Bounty hunter"). All in all; I didn't pick up FITS thinking I was going to really sink into it; but I could definitely seeing this as a must buy for the deck-building enthusiast in your life whose marvelled at the choreography of a martial arts action movie. It's certainly consumed enough hours of my life to be a danger to my 'just one more room' syndrome.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoy this game. I would love a sort of custom deck mode or the ability to use earned coins or something to unlock cards that I can choose to guarantee as a starter card. _childDocuments_.review: The game's demo has shown great promise, and in its current state it's delivering an even better experience. I'd describe the game as a fairly standard deck builder mixed with something not unlike Into the Breach: cards are fine and all, but there's also the playing field you need to be paying attention to, with positioning being of huge importance. Opportunities to set up instakills and make opponents harm their allies are provided as well. Absolutely loving the aesthetics, the music is pretty solid too. Haven't beaten it yet. Came close once, reaching the middle of the penultimate "act", but a certain new enemy has undone too much of my health, and a couple of rounds later his colleagues sealed the deal. Looking forward to seeing what's next for Fights in Tight Spaces.

_childDocuments_.review: Mechanically, it's a really awesome deckbuilding roguelite. Content-wise, there are only a few decks/playstyles and the game only tests for a few, so you can fairly easily figure out what cards are great value versus what are "traps". So, your builds don't tend to be too diverse or exciting. Overall, it's addictive and packs a lot for a game of its type, and perhaps my main issue with it is that it has a ton more potential but likely not enough resources to reach it. So, pick it up if you want to play a charming and clean mix between Into The Breach and Slay The Spire, I got far more than my money's worth with it.

_childDocuments_.review: So far, the only game in my life I bought during Early Access. Many games in that state are little more than broken demos, but not this one. By the time I bought it, they had every single level functional (apart from the updated 5th mission, which only came out with version 1.0) and kept updating maps and enemies. They also kept creating cards (some of which were even suggested by the players). So kudos to the developers for delivering a very engaging game.The only thing I miss would be a 'minimalist' challenge of sorts - you start the game with 16 cards on your deck and it only gets bigger from there. I'd like to try and play a version where you start with the bare minimum cards (5 or 6, depending on your perks) and try to beat a small gauntlet of levels (but not too many, this challenge would get stale fast).TL,DR: good guys released a good game. Give it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: First things first! Do I recommend this game right now as it is on March 8th, 2021? No. Do I think this game has all the ground work for it to become a deck builder that compares to Slay the Spire? ABSOLUTELY. Don't take the criticisms I'm going layout here as a reason to write off the game forever. I really think this game has the potential to be one of the better deck builders out there. I was one of the many people that downloaded the demo and fell in love. Roguelike/lite games are some of my favorite types of games to play and Slay the Spire has basically taken over my life since I first gave it a shot on Xbox Games Pass over a year ago (I love that game so much that I bought the game on Steam and my Switch so I could support the devs and play it anywhere I wanted). Also, get used to my comparing Fights in Tight Spaces  (FiTS) to Slay the Spire  (StS) because IMO StS is the best deck building roguelike out there. Getting back to FiTS. I played the demo and was blown away. The game felt like StS but with your character being like John Wick. As soon as I finished playing it the first night I added the full version of FiTS to my wishlist and had every intention of buying the game on release day. I "beat" a run in the demo and then stopped playing to avoid having it get stale (only played for about 2 hours total). The day the game came out I downloaded it as soon as I got home and honestly...the spark was gone already. When I played the demo I was thinking, "Wow, this game has a few different tactics to choose from and it's only the demo! There must me a bunch more strategies in the full game!" After playing the full game for almost 5 hours now, I think I can safely say that I was wrong about that. I want to mention that I've only unlocked 3 of the 4 starting decks that are available right now (Trickster is still locked but also sounds the most interesting to me). But the three I do have unlocked aren't that different from each other. in StS, each of the classes start of pretty similar (you have attacks, defends, and one or two class specific cards) but once you start collecting cards you can see how different the classes are. The classes in FiTS feel more like one class that the devs have taken and then focused on one specialization for the starting decks. The counter deck feels like the original deck with less attacks and more counters. The attacking deck feels like the original deck with less counters and mobility cards and more strong attacks. For those of you that played StS, the starting decks in FiTS feel less like choosing between the Slient, the Watcher, etc and more like only having one class like the  Slient being available and when starting your run you are given the option to start with a deck focused more on poison or a deck focused more on Shivs. It just doesn't feel different enough. When looking at the cards themselves, they also are a bit repetitive. There are definitely some cards that have a unique feel to them but in my experience it usually just boils down to "Attack", "Defend (& sometimes counter)", and "Move". Maybe it's because of the fact that the game is based around the "real world" (as opposed to fantasy like StS is with magic and fire and shields, etc) but I constantly find myself having to read the card description of a card that I've seen dozens of times because I forget what the difference is between a jab and a quick punch, or what a "slip" is compared to a "shift". Granted, I have probably over 100 hours in StS across all devices but in that game I quickly learned what each card did. The unique card art on StS cards probably helped with that as well whereas the card card in FiTS isn't too informative or unique (attack cards show your guy attacking, mobility cards show your guy moving, etc). The other thing that I haven't seen in this game is an overall progression in the overarching game in between runs. You do unlock different clans to fight and you get to unlock different starter decks as I mentioned about but as far as I've seen you don't unlock new cards or anything for making progress in a run. This is a small gripe and perhaps I'm comparing the game too much to StS.One very minor opinion: I don't think the devs are implementing "counters" in a fun way. Right now, when you use a counter card it adds armor to your character and enables an automatic attack once you get hit. So counter cards are simply block cards that allow you to attack back with a minor amount of damage. The thing is, most counter cards I've seen don't give you that much armor so you need to use another counter or block card to make sure you cover the damage you are about to suffer from just one enemy (god help you if two or even three guys are about to attack you). You only have 3 action points so to counter an enemy attack without suffering damage usually take 2 of those 3 actions points. That leaves you with very little to do after setting up a counter. And since the counter does very minimal damage to the attacker, it's entirely possible to set up for a counter to do 4 damage, only to see that the attacker has 6 armor that replenishes every turn so your counter will do absolutely nothing. It would pay off to just move your guy using one action point to avoid the attack all together. To fix that I think the devs should change up how countering works. Off the top of my head, I think a better system would be to make countering negate a certain amount of attacks. For example, say a basic counter negate one attack and then attacks the enemy back. You would only have to use one action point, you'd still do damage and two action points would be open to doing a bit of damage to the enemy on your turn so when you counter it will actually do more than just putting a dent in the enemy's replenishing armor. Now, the part where I tell you not to just move on from this game after reading this review. The game has great potential. I really believe my problem was that I came in to the game thinking this would be fleshed out like StS was even though when I played StS it was a full game release. I started thinking how I would have thought about StS if I started playing the game and only Ironclad was available and to be honest, I think I would have thought about StS the same way I'm currently thinking about FiTS. The devs released a roadmap recently and it made me feel even more optimistic about the game. right now I wouldn't suggest getting the game but I highly recommend adding it your wishlist or at least following it so you can keep track of it down the road. If they add more cards, maybe items (like relics in StS) and more classes or at least more starting decks that feel different then I think this can be every bit as good as StS. This is a raw, uncut diamond but the potential to be a glistening diamond is absolutely there; the devs just need to put in a bit more work to get it to shine.TLDR; I don't recommend the game as it is right now but the potential for Fights in Tight Spaces to be in the tier of Slay the Spire is definitely there. If you want to support the devs, buy it now. But if you don't want to buy it and games like StS are your thing, definitely keep an eye on this one. It could be the next amazing deck building roguelike.

_childDocuments_.review: While I technically got the game for free through a beta test, I bought an actual copy.Edit: 12/2/2021: The game is finished. Everything has been improved and tightened up. As most other reviews will show, FiTS is a very unique experience that you will come back to time and time again.I like just about everything about this game. It's a homage to the various action movies throughout the years, borrows a little bit from fighting games, and features some surprisingly deep tactical combat. It also combines some unlikely ingredients into a cohesive whole: it has a deck-building aspect as well incredibly important tactical positioning, and it's surprisingly competent at both. When I say tactical deck-building brawler, no other game comes to mind. It's also a rogue-like, sort of; no two runs are the same. Soundtrack is pretty cool too.You can currently play through the game from start to finish, three hours or so if you're good, and you can think of this EA as a beta. Graphics are missing from many cards, some animations are incomplete or missing, sound effects don't play some times, and there are bugs present. But like I mentioned, the game is fully playable and balanced well enough to where there is a consistent learning curve. There are elements remaining to be balanced, specifically the content toward the end, but I've put quite a few hours in to the game and it's been entertaining for mostly all of them.What I don't like about the game, if you can really call it a critique, is that the story isn't much of anything but a set piece. It exists only to move the action along. It's very action-movie-like in a way, but I like stories. I like good stories and characters. Maybe we'll get something more involved later, but right now it's very bare bones.I'm looking forward to see where the development goes after Ground Shatter is done fixing the obvious stuff. The last major revision introduced the combo system to the game, a way to build up consecutive moves to play certain cards, so it's anyone's guess as to what will come next. I'm keeping my eye on this, and you should too.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the type of game to play if you really enjoyed playing Enter The Breach. If steam had a "Maybe" rating then I'd give it that. I've put hundreds of hours into most Slay The Spire influenced games that pop into the market. FITS doesn't really hold up as well due to a couple of things. Firstly, some mechanics are not handled consistently. There's nothing worse than lining up a turn then having the game apply rules inconsistently. I've had enemies act out of turn, push not damaging enemies, and other small issues that are frustrating. Secondly, the style of too many bosses is to just throw numbers at you. I'm sure some people enjoy this but it's a lazy formula that doesn't make encounters stand out. Finally, and this is subjective, it fails the most important test of a game. It's just not very fun. It feels like a chore to play instead of a delight. I'm sure that there's something great buried here, but it's missing its soul.

_childDocuments_.review: Fights in Tight Spaces is a rogue-like deck-builder that plays out like the fighting scenes in movies.First of all, don't make the same mistake i did by playing on the classic difficulty. The lower difficulties are much more fair and enjoyable.I liked 95% of what the game offered, the rest though is infuriatingly annoying and made me not want to replay the game after completing a single run.Starting with the things i like, the gameplay is fun especially for people who like regular turn based strategy games.Having a good deck is not enough. The game is insanely punishing and thus requires immense thinking. Lastly, it has fluid animations, great artstyle, and fantastic soundtracks. Very stylish and charming.I also have some mixed opinions on three things. First one is deck variety. You have 6 archetypes to build upon. Most of them play very differently from each other but unfortunately they are not balanced so as the cards you choose. Most cards are useless which results in you picking up the same strong cards over and over again. Second one is the upgrade system specifically the prices. For some reason cards with same specs before and after upgrading have different costs. It doesn't make any sense. Lastly, the events. either i am extremely unlucky or the %90 of the events result in something bad.Now for things i didn't like. I played 28 hours on the classic difficulty since that's what the game regards as the normal difficulty. I can easily say that it was a huge mistake. As i stated before, the game is incredibly punishing. One mistake and you start over. After having so many frustrating loses, today i decided to try the classic plus difficulty and won at my first attempt. Unless you are a masochist, i really suggest playing on the lower difficulties especially for the reason i'm about to say right now. The last boss is straight up unfair. He has every buff imaginable, hits like a truck, calls for backup and you have to face him 4 times back to back without healing a single time along the way. This boss is the only reason i wont ever replay the game on higher difficulties.I enjoyed the game and will still recommend it but the last part left a bad impression on me.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: Man this game is an absolute blast. I can't seem to get enough of it. I've played one other game in this genre called Nitro Kid and honestly it doesn't compare. Every time i pick this game up i end up hooked and look up at the clock and it's been like 5 hours just flown right by. I know this won't be everyone's cup of tea but if you like tactics games or roguelike deckbuilders i would absolutely recommend checking this game out.Pros: very satisfying attack animations, easy enough for most people on the easiest difficulty and challenging for veterans on the highest, lots of enemy types with meaningfully different attributes, lots of varied movement, ability and attack cards, several different starter decks to choose from, lots of unlockables to keep your playing, fast forward button for those who don't want to wait for animations, very fun gameplay loop, a decent path mechanic, cool mechanics like pushing opponents out of the stage and getting them to attack eachotherCons: the UI can take some getting used to sometimes i wasn't aware whether an opponent was going to attack or not until i learned to mouse over them to see if they have a target i feel like that should be more visually clear, while the starting decks are all pretty varied some are very clearly better than others and they don't have unique card pools, there's only one character you you can just choose between male or female avatar. out of all of these the lack of deck specific card pools is what i feel is the only truly meaningful con to this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Fights in Tight Spaces has a lot of potential. It is a deck-building game with strategy elements focusing a lot on positioning and chain reaction. The concept is really good and they definitely started with the right foot. The first thing I'd like to mention is that the runs do take quite some time, hours, especially if you are new to the game. Fortunately, there is a save function and you can bail out in the middle of the run and come back later on.The game introduces a lot of interesting mechanics and there are several different ways to get the job done. Either by punching an enemy in the face or inducing another enemy to do it for you. These mechanics are really what makes this game shine. Right now it has a few starting decks that reflect this variety and focus on a specific kind of skill. There's still has a long way to go before its release, but for the price I got, it was sure worth it. I feel like they could add some classes or something similar that could make use of different mechanics, the starting decks are ok, but it would be nice to play as a different character like a ninja. Improvements to the replay are also welcome, it feels too dull and I see no reason to use this feature at all. Additional objectives would be cool too. Maybe some off-run progression as well, like unlocking cards and traits for future runs.Overall, the game is pretty enjoyable and fun in its current state, it is easy to put a lot of hours into it. It can become so much more though. I'd recommend this game to anyone who likes this genre and would like to support its development.

_childDocuments_.review: There are a bunch of positive things i can say about the game, but ultimately the game discourages having an actually fun deck and utilizing enemy positioning skills when you can just stun them and kill them via raw damage. Several tough enemies are immune to pushing or grabs (with the final boss being immune to both!!!), while others have multi-range counters. Stun works against everything in the game, making it pretty much necessary to play outside of some block/counter build.I don't think this is a ~bad~ game, but there's no middle option. I'd definitely be interested in seeing this concept explored more with the addition of modding support, improvised weapons as part of the stage, being able to disarm/take enemy weapons, etc. As it stands now there's just a lot of bad cards and a handful of extraordinarily good cards.

_childDocuments_.review: I had high hopes for this game when I played the demo, and was hoping my issues with the demo would be fixed by launch. They were NOT.- Cool aesthetic- Great idea behind the game- Terrible execution of said ideas- Atrociously imbalanced. Why do armour on enemies regenerate  every turn after you've smashed their protection the previous turn? Preposterous- You can't actually edit your card decks manually. That means you're stuck using cards that may or may not fit the situation at hand. You also never actually get awesome cards. I suppose you might, late in the game, but I couldn't be bothered to keep playing the boring same fights with the boring same moves over and over  - No healing between assignments. I'm not even talking about between . Once you finish fighting the biker gang boss you move straight into the prison with the same amount of leftover HP. For the love of God, why?- Healing can only be done in certain locations. Once you get your HP down to single digits and there is no heal location immediately available, your game is basically screwed unless you can somehow start and finish the next few fights  with less than 10 HP and an RNG moveset- Furthermore, healing costs a bizarre amount of currency which is shared with card upgrade costs. Not only is it not affordable to heal, it's even less affordable to upgrade cards, and certainly not feasible to do both unless you grind an absurd number of playthroughs - There is no option for card permanence. You draw a new hand each turn regardless how many cards you used this turn. Again, ? This kills any attempt at strategy since you can never plan turns ahead. You end up only  in each turn depending on what cards you draw- There are random events available, but they're almost all ridiculous. For example, you can be given a choice between losing 50 pounds... or not losing 50 pounds... Yes, reallyI suppose the game as it is will appeal to some players, but despite my wanting to like it, I very much do not. There may be meat somewhere deeper than what I've played, but I haven't found any payoff that's actually worth the effort of slogging through the early levels.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun and really easy to pick up quickly. In the first 30 minutes I was rolling and into it. It's a little rough around the edges. The animations are sometimes great and sometimes make me wish more thought went into things like how replays look. Sometimes when you rollback a turn an animation will trigger, like a status effect, and you'll think that it happens each time, but it's really just repeating the first animation of the turn you're restarting. It's also not always intuitive where things are in the UI and it definitely took me some time to figure out what a symbol meant or what was about to happen, or why something didn't trigger when I thought it would. I'm used to games like Monster Train that tell you outcomes based on positioning and order of operations. This game requires you to track a lot of that yourself. Otherwise, it's a fun and pretty straightforward turn-based deck-builder where you have to calculate what's about to happen. I dunno that it's very deep, I'm only 3 hours in. Certain moves and card-types seem way more valuable than others. Will be interesting to see how it goes, but I'm looking forward to it.Also, love that it has both a light mode and a dark mode.

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard. It's random sometimes. It's not fair. Yet I keep playing it.. so I'm changing my review. I must enjoy it, because I dream about this game.---Mmm. Noooope. No..I keep coming back to this simple fact: If I can do nothing at all wrong, make no mistakes, have a perfect deck, and still lose in a single turn hours into a playthrough, knowing not only that I couldn't have done anything differently but there's nothing I would have even ideally, and still lost, thatis not a description of a Strategy Game.That's a dice roller that hates your time.Just straight up NO WIN scenarios where you HAVE TO take damage no matter what, where it does damage to attack and you have to attack, where an enemy that wasn't even there can drop in and change the layout of the board without any indication, where four bosses and two hours in it still comes down to the luck of the draw.That's not strategy.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a strategy, roguelike, turn based deck-builder where, as the name implies, you fight in tight spaces. Like John Wick, you often find yourself against a group of thugs who are out to end your day. Luckily, their behavior is marked on the interface, so besides hitting them yourself, you can maneuver around them around to damage each other, or kick them off ledges with your pre-made deck of moves which you improve as you go along. When the dust settles, you can watch a replay of your work, and when you manage to effortlessly avoid damage while causing them to kick one another, it's a thing of beauty.
_childDocuments_.name: Fights in Tight Spaces

_childDocuments_.review: They’re really getting creative with the card games out here these days. Increasingly often I’m finding myself hooked on a new entry in the genre with new and unexpected mechanics and features thrown into the mix. Cinematic action, it seems, is one of the popular ones that I’ve been seeing implemented with varying results recently, some of them adding some thrill to the experience while others seem underdeveloped and like more of a distraction. Fortunately, after having finally gotten my hands on Fights in Tight Spaces, I can say that it falls into the former category.Fights in Tight Spaces is a rogue-like strategic deck-builder that has you taking on the role of an agent from the organization known as Section Eleven. We don’t get much in the way of details but we get the ones that are most important: we’re a bad ass who deals with the worst elements of the criminal underground with our fists. Enemy factions include bikers, inmates, mafiosos, and even ninjas each with their own grunts, sub-bosses, and faction bosses, with every foe having a unique strategy, but predictable, strategy that they use against you. It’s mastering these predictions, making use of the space around you, and building the right combination for your deck of cards that will make you feel like a real action hero as you take them down.Every action you take is based on the cards in your hand and the momentum remaining in the turn. Cards include everything from basic jabs to spinning kicks to suplexes to throwing knives and that there’s a massive variety of them to be unlocked as you level up after each run in rogue-like fashion. The fighting style (read: deck) that you build ends up being something unique each time as you gain a new card after each fight and you may also buy them at stores along the way. One run you may end up being a combo-building kickboxer of sorts while the next you’re much closer to an olympic wrestler with both having their own unique strengths and weaknesses.The minimalist environment in Fights in Tight spaces plays well with its mechanics. The black and white environments place a focus on the characters who are also quite simple in design, yet each foe you face has their own distinct look to them. Some cards even make use of these environments as you kick off of a wall or vault over a table to maneuver to a better position or simply put a serious hurting on a foe who ended up in the wrong place at the wrong time. Railings and doorways even exist on some levels which can result in the instant elimination of a foe if you knock them through them - or the immediate end of your run if it’s you who gets knocked through them instead.It seems like a lot to seamlessly combine fighting action scenes, a minimalist art style, deckbuilding, and environmental positioning, but Fights in Tight Spaces succeeds in doing just that. Every run is exciting and different while also offering a level of challenge for everyone from casual gamers to hardcore tactical gurus. I’d originally thought that the concept looked interesting from the Steam store page but it wasn’t until I’d finally given in and played it that I discovered what is one of my favorite rogue-likes to date. If you’ve looked it over and like what you see, don’t miss out on this one. It’s a unique experience unlike any other that I’ve had the good fortune to encounter. It’s exactly as much fun as you’d expect it to be when you’re the action hero taking on hardened criminals and turning their own attacks against them.

_childDocuments_.review: Quick Description:-Fight in Tight Spaces is a turn based, tactics deckbuilder w/ the visual presentation of Superhot.  I had an absolute blast playing close to 30 hrs of this incredibly challenging and fun game.  This is probably the closest game that I have played to Into the Breach when in comes to perfect information and positioning.  If you have any interest in any of the genres I mentioned, you owe it to yourself to try this game out.What's Good:-Into the Breach is one of my favorite games ever.  Like ITB, FITS also has perfect information.  You always know exactly what your opponents are going to do and how much damage they will do, before you act.  Every decision is vitally important and makes it feel like each action is a mini puzzle.  This probably all sound familiar to ITB fans.  Positioning is king in this game, and will make or break your run.-This game has a steep learning curve and an incredibly high skill ceiling.  I found this game very intimidating during my first few runs, but found it extremely rewarding as I improved.  There is randomness to which cards you are offered for pickup or which cards in your deck are shuffled into your hand.  Outside of the deckbuilding elements, this is a pure skill game that feels similar to ITB or chess.-The roguelight elements are designed really well.  There is a good amount of meta progression as it took me close to 30 hrs to unlock all starting decks.  Each run, you will have ample opportunity to purchase new cards, upgrade existing cards, and eliminate weak cards from your deck.  Pairing the deckbuilder genre w/ the tactics genre works extremely well here and created a really dynamic and engaging experience.-There are 6 different starting decks and each one will play a huge role in how you approach your runs.  The throwing deck was probably my favorite to play w/ even though there are some negatives when facing bosses.  However, no matter which starting deck you use, you can mix and match from all playstyles to create the perfect deck for you.  This allows a ton of freedom between each run in how you are going to approach each level.-FITS opts for a minimalist style w/ the aesthetic of something similar to Superhot.  It feels sleek, modern, fresh, and fits perfectly for a game of this nature.  Too much detail on the art design may have been distracting so I think the devs made a great choice w/ the minimalist approach.Could Use Some Changes:-This game is brutally difficult!  I'm a huge fan of these types of games, but I really struggled w/ this one.  I still haven't had a winning run in 30 hrs.  In fact, I've only made it to the final section once.  I usually die near the end of the third or fourth section of levels.  You only start off w/ 40-44 hp which can be decimated in 1-2 hits by late game enemies.  You are also going to be a victim of the variance of what your deck offers, which can be frustrating at times.  I absolutely love this game, but it is one of the hardest games in this genre that I've ever played.-There are some balancing issues.  The throw deck is my favorite but you can't throw bosses which is a giant issue.  The slashing deck seems fun, but waiting for opponents to bleed out feels counterproductive.  The counter deck is really fun, but it's harder to meet time requirements for powerups.  These upgrades can make or break your run, which makes this build hard to use.  It seems that agressive and balanced decks are the easiest and safest starting decks to use.-You won't have nearly the variety in your cards that you would expect from top tier deckbuilders like Slay the Spire or Monster Train.  Since FITS is a hybrid of two genres, it isn't as big of a deal here, but it's worth mentioning.Consensus:-Best of the Best Game (Tier 1 and makes up 5% of my reviews).  I had so much fun w/ FITS!  I don't think it's quite as good as Into the Breach or Slay the Spire, which are two major inspirations for this game.  However, those are two of the best turn based games ever made.  So falling just short of those standards is nothing to be ashamed of.  I would say that this game is a near perfect tactics game, but isn't quite up to those standards in the deckbuilding department.  If you are up for the challenge, I highly recommend that you give this game a try.  I had an absolute blast and I can't wait to dive back in!

_childDocuments_.review: A nice and simple game with a nice loop of tuning your deck every couple of stages until it breaks everything. There's a big focus on predicting what cards you've drawn and what's likely to come next, even on the standard difficulty which guarantees one of your movement cards will be drawn every turn. You can have a small deck of power moves or a huge deck of one-offs that thins itself out over time; can run circles around the enemy, block everything they throw at you and counter it twofold, push them off the board, grapple them into other enemies' attacks, and throw the final boss every turn so you're fighting off his mooks harder than you're fighting him. It's possible to win in a variety of ways as long as you learn how to work around each enemy type (and stock the better movement and utility cards like Slip and Grapple). I enjoy all of the standard decks except Slasher, since bleed is the one effect that takes too much time to get going. The levels being static do make runs feel samey, but I think it's nice to break them open in different ways, especially since the AI is smart about not tripping on its shoelaces - makes it all the sweeter to plan out that one gimmicky card that can exploit it.While you cannot survive with ONLY damage, and you absolutely need some form of strong mobility, defense, or stun to survive in this game, it's still very possible to have offensive decks. For an example, the  Uncontrolled Power card is very fun if you want to play aggressively. Ridiculous base damage and has 2 range, but you're forced to play it or remove it from your hand before the turn's over or you lose health.  It doesn't even fall off in the lategame since it's still useful for movement and you typically have a surplus of allowed moves by then.There are some hidden mechanics like Option Play not triggering auto-attacks, certain special movement cards not triggering Aggressive enemies' chasing, and event spaces in general being obtuse about what they do and the odds they come with, but typically everything else is intuitive and fair. Minor gripes! Otherwise, surprisingly nice little game to puzzle with and play efficiently.

_childDocuments_.review: A combination of Into the Breach's turn-based positional fighting puzzles, and deck-building elements. I paid $12.50 on sale, and I feel I got my money's worth.The combat is fun, and has that "one more turn" engagement that pulls you in. The deck building aspect is a little under-cooked: the balance is off. Certain strategies and cards are clearly optimal, while others are chaff or highly dependent on luck. I think there are too many cards, and many of the cards you unlock are dependent on having other cards in the deck for best effect, making it difficult to adjust your strategy based on pickups the way Slay the Spire lets you. As a result, the replayability isn't anywhere close to Into the Breach or Slay the Spire, and certain starter decks feel like exercises in frustration, rather than fun variations to try, The final boss can also be a bit of a slog, they should probably have cut his health pool by 20% given his summons and how many attacks he's immune to.The graphics look like if someone took a flash stickman fighting game and turned it 3D, and complement the theme. However, this game makes my GPU work a lot harder than it seems like it should. The devs appear to be working of a sequel, so don't expect updates. My hope is that the sequel has better balance, multiple save slots, and a New Game Plus mode that isn't tied to a poorly recieved DLC. I think it could be fun to have a deck you've honed over the course of several runs.Lastly, don't take Deadly Deal, no matter how much you think you're snowballing, until you've payed through the final boss at least once.

The last chapter is extremely difficult compared to the rest of the campaign and some of the extra objectives in a fight for bonus rewards are downright impossible to do if you get unlucky with your draws. The music sticks in your head, the animations are crisp, the style is minimalist yet detailed, every turn of every fight leaves you with some new challenge, and the random events, draws, upgrades, enemies, and such make replay value the biggest draw. _childDocuments_.review: Easiest sell would be to call this Into the Breach (predictive positioning turn-based tactics) meets Slay the Spire (card-based roguelike) with Superhot aesthetics. For when you want to feel like John Wick or Captain America in that elevator scene. Overall, a very competently delivered game, though obviously leaning a bit hard on its stylized visuals. Some animation smoothing and less chunky replay options would go a long way in making gameplay feel more cool in retrospect, but it doesn't matter all that much.---In terms of minor gripes, I think there's some odd design decisions like being penalized for standing over a downed opponent to prevent them from getting up or a restrictive limit on the number of enhancements you can get in a run. The events could also use a little diversity. I also don't think the cards that kind of lean into pure hand manipulation feel great to play. Especially in replay, it just ends up with your character standing around striking poses and you don't get a sense of fight choreography like other attacks do. None of these problems matter much though and you'll probably need to get used to the system before you even notice them.
