_childDocuments_.review: Would I recommend this game? On balance, I would - but it has some flaws. Noting, I am reviewing this having only played Heat 2 before; this is not a commentary on upgrades from Heat 4. All in all, this game is a good racer. The racing is fun, and when bunched up with other cars it feels you are going fast and one wrong move could spell disaster for the group. The drafting is good in it too; and I've found that cars race differently on the different track types (e.g., speedway vs super speedway). Generally speaking, the racing is fun - which is what a game should be. But I do have some gripes: the car customisation feels a bit lacking. Sure, you can create your own paint-scheme, but it just feels a bit generic. Secondly, racing on non-oval tracks just felt so darn slow, like I was racing a bathtub around, not a fast race-car. thirdly, and this is my main gripe: the career mode is pretty lacking - hire a mechanic, make generic upgrades on car (that you don't know what they are, its just a rating... engine goes from 75 to 85, for example). Ideally the career mode should be more like F1 2020 which is top notch. Finally, sometimes it feels a bit slow. To say these cars are meant to do over 180mph, it doesn't feel like that - say if you compare it to F1 2020. Saying that, it's the only current Nascar game so I would recommend it if it was on sale. Vroooooooom

_childDocuments_.review: I'd like to recommend Heat 5. It doesn't have the audio/visual glitches that 4 had. It looks fairly nice and there's plenty of detail. I'll keep playing it, probably, for a while. But I can't say its something I'd push for others to play.Somehow the formula was perfected from 03 to 06 on consoles and never made its way to the PC games. The dirt stuff is awful. The late models feel too slow and pivot from the centre unaturally. There's a road course for some reason. The schedule is too short. The cars don't even get dirty. It's a joke. If you want dirt racing, get All American Racing. It has most of the ruleset and almost all of the cars you could want. Team management is terrible. You have your choice of exactly one skin and one sponsor. You can't manage sub sponsorships and the hire team members system is just clunky. (Thankfully removed in the aforementioned All American Racing)Racing on asphalt is fine. AI is fairly decent. DNFs are not. (I can take a drivers door hit at 180mph but I can't nose the wall at 80mph). If I would give tips to the developer they'd be simple. Use the sponsorship/skin system from Thunder 2004. Use street stocks like in dirt to daytona as the entry tier. Add all of the north american national series. (Pinty's  and PEAK for Canada and Mexico) and their schedules. Overhaul the team hire system so its less of a slog and allow Crew Chief and pit crew hires. Overhaul the rivals and social media system so that it's less repetitive. Add dirt rules for the dirt racing. Spell "Brake" correctly (Two years, really?)Add skin and custom driver support so we can add our friends and family to the game. If you want a modern nascar game experience, this game is for you. If you want the best nascar game experience, play NR2003 or console games 2004-2006.

_childDocuments_.review: Do you like stock car racing? Do you enjoy the roar of powerful engines which can be heard for miles? Do you love going fast?Then do yourself a favor and skip this game.I have been playing racing games and simulations for around 30 years. There were a lot of good ones, some mediocre and a few really bad ones. Even so I hesitate to lump NASCAR Heat 5 together with the bad ones. Not because it doesn't deserve that label, rather because the bad ones shouldn't associated with the likes of this garbage.Imagine this: NASCAR Racing 2003 (or NR2K3 for short) is an 18-year old simulation and yet it still surpasses NASCAR Heat 5 in almost every aspect except graphics (though, to be fair, mods do wonders for the looks of NR2K3). The physics of this game can't even be called such; the behavior of the cars doesn't make much sense a lot of the time. FFB is there and that's about it (though the same could be said for NR2K3, to be fair). The menus offer absolutely no mouse input whatsoever, and even if no gamepad is connected you'll still get 360 buttons displayed instead of Keyboard keys or numbered buttons based on your non-Xinput device (i.e. a wheel).Maybe this could be excused because of the additional effort needed to implement improvements, and the devs decided to spent that effort elsewhere instead. Right?Riiight, haha. As if.If you want to know how little effort went into this game, consider this: Not only does it lack any field of view adjustment whatsoever - which is absolutely inexcusable for a racing game in 2021 - but if you need to adjust even the tiniest option you need to go back to the main menu. Started a race or test session but need to change your steering axis sensitivity? Bad luck, you need to go back all the way to the main menu.This isn't shoddy programming, it's a complete disregard for any kind of enjoyment a player might want to get out of this product. Basically, a big "F U" to the customer.Going back to my comparison to NASCAR Racing 2003 and why I brought it up in the first place. You may be thinking "alright, this dude is a NASCAR Racing 2003 fanboy", but as a matter of fact I have never played the game prior to the day I wrote this review for NASCAR Heat 5. The only reason I got NR2K3 - which is now abandonware, by the way - was to try and see how it would stack up against this title. And once I got it running I was surprised by how good the physics and AI were back then; in fact, I would argue the AI was lightyears ahead of most if not all racing simulations I have played since then.So, to make a long story short: If you want to do virtual stock car racing there aren't many options out there. If you are serious about online competition, don't care about offline modes and have loads of money to spare, go with iRacing. Otherwise, I recommend you get a copy of Papyrus' NASCAR Racing 2003, which can even be downloaded for free since it became abandonware. But whatever you do, please stay as far away from NASCAR Heat 5 as you can.Okay, there's one thing that's actually pretty cool in NASCAR Heat 5. The animated pitstops look really cool. But unless you are looking for a pitstop simulator it's still not worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: In general, the Heat series has been so-so. This is as to be expected from a small dev team working on its first major title series. The games have exponentially become better. The mechanics, the graphics, and the UI have all come up to snuff with any of the previous developers. The gameplay however, has not. The career mode is lackluster at best, the racing is somewhat fun, albeit repetitive. The test session mode was a great addition. The paint booth still leaves a lot to be desired. (this has been one of the better ones so far, especially in the Heat series) The main complaint I have about this game so far is the bugs. There are so many visual and audio glitches that seem to be easy fixes that could've been fixed with a couple more weeks of polishing. Originally, I read that the game was supposed to be released in September. I found it hard to believe that the dev team was able to shave 2 months off of the total build time. I was right. This game needed the extra few months to become worth the $50 price tag. I hope that with the new engine comes a better and more fleshed out career mode, and a better overall game.

If you have Heat 4, it's obviously not a necessary purchase, but whenever the game most likely goes 10 dollars off (to 40), I'd recommend it.

I can't even drive a couple tracks unless I specifically tune the car to do so running the AI on hard or legend, which, fine, the difficulty is up so I can't complain too much about that. But the biggest complaint is the realism and bugs still. I still get a second or two freeze randomly in a race and New Hampshire's restart zone paint on the wall is all bugged out. I don't have that problem with any other racing game (Project Cars, Need for Speed). A revamp in this series is needed.Adding to my review, out of frustration. The Rival system HAS TO BE THE BIGGEST JOKE!!! I like the idea! Rough someone up, they'll rough you up. Only I get hooked, ran into the wall, slammed on restarts, just flat out wrecked FOR NO REASON and it's consistent. Naw, screw your game. name: The Pale Beyond
detailed_description: Five years ago, The Viscount and its crew set sail through The Pale Passage in search of absolute magnetic South. The ship and its crew were tragically lost to the ice, never to be seen again. Her sister ship, The Temperance shall follow in her path, hoping to find answers where The Viscount failed. A polar exploration game set in an unforgiving frozen wasteland where you embark on a treacherous voyage across the ice and through the Pale Beyond. It’s a stunning yet harsh landscape that can change at any moment. Every decision matters and the ice doesn’t care. As the expedition unfolds and the Polar Winter approaches, every decision you make will have a meaningful impact on the story as you navigate your way across the ice. You didn’t ask to lead this expedition, but here you are. Stuck in the ice, Captain missing, miles from civilisation. Someone has to take charge. Manage your meagre resources, balance safety and morale, make the hard calls, and head in the only direction you can - through The Pale Beyond. Keeping the crew (and sled dogs) safe, fed, and warm during the expedition is imperative. Surviving the ice will matter little in the face of a mutiny. Every vote will count. So keep the crew on your side. Featuring original musical compositions, shanties and accordion tunes that will dynamically evolve alongside your journey.

_childDocuments_.review: 3 Hours of Gameplay: An unconventional but fun approach to the management genre. The Pale Beyond wastes no time to introduce you to a showcase of visually stunning art-work whilst still being thought-provoking during the first few weeks on board (first few hours of gameplay). Although the options are limited, the game ensures that you feel in-control and allows you to interact with the vast range of characters with multiple emotional responses simply depending on how you feel, and for a game to be able to do that can definitely be a challenge, but the pale beyond sails to succeed *chuckle*. Overall a game with a fantastic art-style and an interesting narrative that has no intention of boring me. All hands on deck? All thumbs up!

_childDocuments_.review: The story seems good enough, and is told well. Music is beautiful, artistic values are way up there. The whole ambiance of the thing is amazing. But for me, those factors don't save the game.Started out interesting enough, but just after a couple of turns, the gameplay loop started getting boring. The gameplay is slow and unwieldy, the controls are sluggish and unintuitive, and the map icons are hard to understand. The choices are impactful, but the impact of your choices is unclear, meaning you would have to start over a lot.Most importantly though... I keep saying this for all these text-intensive graphic novel type things... WHY, for the love of all that's good and holy, are there no customizations for clicking/browsing through the endless text?Things that would have made this MUCH more playable for me:1) Option to have the next line of text appear immediately (and not fade-in). Config toggle, special key, doesn't matter, as long as I have the option to click *once* and have the next line of text in there immediately. This seems like such an amazingly obvious requirement to me for anyone who has played anything with click-through dialogs ever.2) Slider for text fade-in speed.3) Configuration for font. Size, color, spacing... Color-blindness and dyslexia are a thing that text adventure games should always consider.4) A way to read back through a dialog, in case I accidentally clicked through to the next bit. Preferably configurable keys.Why is dialoging so hard to get right for almost any dialog-intensive game?!So yeah... Maybe I'll watch a walkthrough or something. First playthrough I went for a week or nine, everyone was fine and gathering food and other stuff, and then suddenly my fate was decided and it was game over. With no warning whatsoever.Waste of time, this, very sorry to say, as it is so beautiful.
_childDocuments_.name: The Pale Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, so as soon as I started this game I got hooked. Took me 3 tries to get past Act I, and my god I got so attached to these characters. I may be biased because this game combines everything I love, but it was done extremely well.Visual novel elements manage to not be boring, and characters and their personalities are super compelling.The Pale Beyond shines with its uncomplicated resource management and survivalist themes. By keeping the actual management system relatively straightforward, the player is forced to focus on managing their relationship with the rest of the stranded characters - so while the gameplay itself is not horrendously difficult, managing the decisions of your captain plays with your feelings and makes survival feel so much harder.Compelled to write this review after reaching the ending for the first time - it was super intriguing and not at all what I expected, without it feeling like the devs just pulled it out of their arses. Very very curious to see how different decisions affect my future playthroughs.Huge kudos to the devs for creating a game that combines the survivalist and resource management genre with a compelling visual novel and reasonably character-driven story (aka, if someone dies the story persists, but it still feels like your game is forever changed). The result is a well-balanced game, where there are consequences for your actions. Big recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: Game is incredibly immersive and very fun to play. The sound track is phenomenal. There are many characters each with their own personalities and backstories that are a pleasure to get to know. My only complaints are some small QoL things, like I would love it if there were an easily accessible log of the current conversation. _childDocuments_.review: Yes, but with a huge caveat - this game should contain a very clear content warning. _childDocuments_.review: I really do want to like this game but, its rough. Very rough around the edges.I lost ALL Crew on week 8 like many did, restarted from day one like an additional 3 times but I figured out:- its actually real easy to just cheese past it every, single time.STOCKPILE people. Put 3 men on the food pantry and 3 on the coal fire every single day up until new options open up. And that's it, that's the game loop side. You manage to see yourself to the end of this very short story.I start with the positives. Kudos to the Irish devs for releasing their first game. The art style is fantastic, some of the music is orgasmic to the ears and, believe it or not, I had a few chuckles as well. The characters for the most part are likeable and memorable.Now onto more middling ground territory: it does have a taboo moment I think it deserves and it handles maturely. I never had dogs but I can see why folk were in uproar and refuse to play further.I believe as of patch 1.5 - when I picked it up they just added much requested epilogues. These seems somewhat ... rushed and tacked on? mines had a play, a cafe, a meeting with father and a prisoner...Finally, the bad and I do hope some member of the team sees this and opts to improve it.Bugs, bugs and bugs. I don't think I went a single hour without facing game breaking bugs.UI was clunky, the crew or resources disappeared but counted. I was locked out for the whole week. Maybe even two, and the re-wind. Crew would teleport around, available one second and despatched the next.If I clicked too face some events wouldn't trigger. For an english speaking team mostly, I have never seen so many grammar errors and spelling typos.And that just about wraps up my thoughts on this 5/10 game. Buy it on sale. It might pique your interest.Hopefully like to see coming back to this in a year and its got expansions and fixes and implement fan requests and if possible, even fix some of the story logic, chronology, pacing and plot holes.But most of all, fix the bugs please!On a very personal niche note before I sign off - I know it cannot be changed - it is what it is - but I feel I need to warn other viewers before buying - I really did not appreciate this 4th wall breaking b-s story they try and pull on you at the end. I feel a better more realistic approach would be better. But hey, artistic freedom and what not.TL:DR. Okay game; with story, value for money and time spent. (11 hours) But needs more work. Some adjustments and bug fixing mostly. Clunky UI, unfair difficulty curve and logic defying decisions hold it back from a solid 8/10 must buy game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm rather disappointed by this title. The underlying ideas are sound, but could have been explored better.I can recommend a single playthrough, but exploring the whole decision tree of the game to get all achievements doesn't seem worth the tedium.I think it's fair to say the team was inspired by the 2004 film The Butterfly Effect. They didn't however decide to commit fully to its story structure, which would have made for a better game. As it is the load/save mechanic is pulled into the very setting of world, into the story, but isn't central to it in a way that'd have the player use it to finish the game, to achieve an ultimate goal. One that is only achievable using it.You can save everyone on your first playthrough and there's no significant motivation to meticulously go back to every story branch and explore it. More importantly I haven't noticed any fast-forward feature that'd let you skip the hundreds of lines of dialogue you've already seen to arrive at new ones. And there's a lot of characters in this game, if you save everyone by the end you'll have like 20 conversations to click through manually every time.The language also leaves something to be desired, the writers use "they/them" out of the blue to refer to singular characters whose gender we are, or can be made aware of, and it's confusing. If it's because some of the lines can be used in regards to different characters, it's just lazy coding. If it's something else, it's not making a good impression.---Forgot to tell you what I did like...The story is of an arctic expedition and it was rather faithful to my expectations of such. I'd hazard a guess it might have been somewhat inspired by the 2018 TV series The Terror, but that was just my most memorable encounter with the subject.Most of the game you'll be managing two things: resources needed to survive, and loyalty of the crew. These mechanics aren't particularly challenging nor tedious (when playing through once), they're just enough to keep you engaged and feeling like you're two weeks away from an icy grave.The characters of the crew and passengers are mostly well-written and believable, varied in their motivations and personalities. (Except the journalist, she should have won the Darwin Award years prior.)The game could have stood on its own being just this, an expedition simulator. They tried to spice it up though, and made it feel incomplete in the process.I rate it Kinder Surprise on a scale from cold omellete to Fabergé egg.

_childDocuments_.review: The Pale Beyond is a resource management survival game where you manage the food, heat, injuries, research,  and decorum of the crew of the Temperance. This is on top of balancing the crew loyalties which lead the different groups from scientist, scouts to deckhands and engineers. Some choices can be aggravating, Descriptive text tends to lend clues about certain actions. The load system is forgiving though it can be annoying as it resets on a week basis which can lead to confusion as to what is occurring. The log entry can be quite useful in this event. However due to it's forgiving nature it is possible to munchkin a path to victory albeit time consuming. As a story its actors are engaging enough to be recommended. As a strategy game it can be limited for replay. Ultimately the challenge is not in the conversation but in the resource management of where personnel is assigned. The inability to bypass speech text can also be a little grating. Lastly even if you choose to reload and repeat different segments, the game is hardly a lengthy one.

_childDocuments_.review: At its core, The Pale Beyond is most akin to a visual novel, albeit a very good one with weighty choices that matter. As such, the following will be my best attempts to convey the essence of the game without spoilers.The story is, perhaps, not for everyone. However, it succeeds in paying homage to its inspiration. It is gritty and dark, but displays hope in that most fundamental and ineffable spirit of humanity. In a word, The Pale Beyond is perseverance. The same human perseverance that embodied the age of exploration.This story was touching. I have always longed for the days when the edge of the world was still shrouded in mystery. The Pale Beyond transports players to that final hour of discovery, the last voyage to fill in that final corner of the map. At no point are you fooled into thinking your situation will be easy going. The ice is harsh and real. You and your crew must find their motivations to keep moving forward at every turn. Sometimes there are no right choices, and you are forced to answer hard questions innate to a failed expedition into the unknown.I wanted to support Bellular Studios' first foray into the gaming market regardless of what they produced. I was happily surprised to come away with a thought provoking narrative offering a unique experience and valuable lessons to be gleaned from the pale beyond.
_childDocuments_.name: The Pale Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: A surprisingly moving narrative experience. its been a while since I played a game that has held my attention like this one did. you really get into the role of a captain that has to make tough calls for the sake of the crew. the writing and character development is great most of the characters seem real and flawed. The game play is similar in someways to frostpunk if you have played that, which works well enough but if you play your cards wrong you can softlock your self and have to reload a couple saves back which kind ruins the momentum of the story. overall though the game was a fresh breathe of air for narrative style games and I highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Pale Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: After a few hours I finished my first run. I don't want to give any spoilers, but it didn't end well. But I already can't wait to have another go and try to push further. The artwork and soundtrack are a solid 10/10. The game has an incredible bleak atmosphere, but the backgrounds and soundtrack give it a real beauty. The character design is great. The dialogue feels real and lifelike, and characters really feel like major parts of the game rather than just faceless minions to be disposed of. The game also does a great job of making you feel like you're constantly on the edge of survival. You genuinely feel as though one wrong decision could result in the end of your expedition. The save system could do with a bit of improvement, and some of the mechanics aren't immediately clear. For example research isn't explained well. The game didn't explain how filling the stew pot works. But these are small issues, overall if you enjoy narrative adventures then this is definitely worth picking up.
_childDocuments_.name: The Pale Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: This is such an interesting game, I've really never played anything like it. First, yes, I do watch their YouTube channel which is how I found out about it, but I'm not going to praise a game just because of that. That said, I'm also not very far, only on Week 6 of my first run. It really is a wonderful game, full of atmosphere, charm, and touch decisions (though I don't feel that I'm at a part where I have to make a really tough decision). The music is phenomenal in that it's not distracting, but adds so much to the ambiance, and the art is awesome too.So far, things I think could be better from my perspective:- A hair more contrast in the art design. I like it, but it does come off a bit flat. That's likely a design choice, just my 2 cents.- The journal is kind of funky with multiple empty entries for the same day. It'd be nice if those could be made to be a bit more  concise.- I know there is a control to add more sensitivity for zooming, but even at the max I feel it zooms way too slowly and feels a bit clunky.- This is a maybe as I'm not yet there, but I'm wondering how a replay will work. There's a lot to go through at the beginning of the game that is setting it up and I worry that a lot of the charm and dialogue may get a bit tedious to get back to a place where things start to matter. That remains to be seen.That said, I am loving this game (I haven't played Hogwarts Legacy since I picked it up as I'm pretty engrossed in this). I really hope there is a DLC. I'm only 3 hours in and I am dreading it being over. I honestly haven't felt that way about a game for a while.

_childDocuments_.review: The first few hours, I was getting annoyed by the game design and a bit stressed out as ensuring the entire crew's survival is hard (even on Normal difficulty) and I was becoming afraid of failing after many hours played.  But you can easily restart at any previous week (I went back one week, two times: pretty user-friendly) and I made it through with flying colors in the end, but it was scary! Keep in mind it is a small independent studio, so the game systems are relatively simple, but there are tons of dialogs, endearing and varied characters, and an original story, especially near the end. If you accept the risk that you may need (or not at all) to replay an hour or so (autosaves at the start of each week), I think this adventure is rather unique in video games.  Perfectionnist beware!  I chose to play only one ending, after a very successful survival of my crew. Criticism : a) the game system makes setting up the crew's tasks slower than it could be ; b) some ending paths have extremely long dialogs, in addition to repetitions ; c) trying to view the different endings is very tedious, as the autosave is far back (a lot of dialogs).
_childDocuments_.name: The Pale Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: This game had potential to do better in my opinion, mostly on the "choice" aspect of the game.Unless you want the whole crew to hate you and (probably) make your life more difficult eventually(?), you don't truly have a choice as to what answers to choose. Apart from a couple characters and/or conversations, the "correct" answers are always quite clear and leave little to no room to any true freedom of choice.. nor fun.I was hoping a lot more from the storyline too and more varied kinds of resources (especially for heating). There wasn't really any way to "manage" anything better or worse, as there is only one way to get resources and those are always very scarce, whatever you do.. In my case, the difficulty level of the game didn't make it more rewarding when my crew made it another week, it was just frustrating and repetitive. UI was also quite annoying and some obvious commands didn't even exist (for.ex: when assigning people to an action, there is no way to "delete" it apart from leaving the menu and coming back)Overall, a pretty game that didn't really meet its potential..It could've been fun but unfortunately it was mostly boring and lacked any real substance.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: Good game, nice story, beautiful art, but lacks depth and excitementThe game takes you on a journey to south or north pole , you face troubles with your expeditions, so you will need to balance your crew needs until you can make it out alive. There are some fun small twists and events happen during your survival time. The gameplay is assigning the crew to different jobs, like fetching food, fuel, healing ...etcI finished the game, it is pretty short (10ish hours). I enjoyed the atmosphere and the style. It reminded me of "dead in Vinland" Which i really really enjoyed. All in all, the game has all the right ingredients to make it really intriguing experience but it falls short on substance, that's why i wont recommend it to others.Where they fall short is in the gameplay. The choices are too simple and very few which makes the decision making process pretty boring. You only need 2 resources, food and fuel, and both of them you get by hunting animals, so sending a party to hunt animals is pretty much the only task you have to do. There is no cost-benefit analysis that you will have to go through to decide which aspect to give priority to and balance things, nope, just go hunting every week. There are no camp improvement options where you have to balance long term benefits vs immediate needs. There are "research" points you can gather, but they dont do anything of significance. It is not required for anything (there is no improvement or upgrades to spend it on) and the only thing i found that it allows a hunting party to happen... but you already can send a hunting party easily, so you don't need research points to do that anyway. Besides sending a hunting party every week and healing/heating any injured crewmates, i didnt feel i am made any decision. During cut-scenes you will make some choices, some make impact on the story some dont. But the choices didnt feel interesting enough and there is no clear understanding of what would be the impact of each choice, so you choose one and hope for the best, it might help, it might get one of your crew mates killed. But it doesnt matter much anyway, just a story telling mechanic.The game felt like a story book with multiple choices more than actual survival resource management game.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: friend of the YouTube team here. But there's no need to show any bias, because the game's great.This game is intentional at every step, and is very thoughtful in its approach to its themes. The art and sound is phenomenal and perfectly sets the tone of the game, and the characters are very well-written, with believable motivations and conflicts. The relationships you build with these characters matter, and your understanding of those relationships as well as your understanding of the characters themselves informs your decisions - a singular decision isn't always "good" or "bad" in a vacuum, it may be contextual based on these factors, which makes the characters feel real, makes your relationship-building feel worthwhile, and rewards you for paying attention.The resource-management component of the game is, in a vacuum, less interesting, but can't really be fairly considered in a vacuum at all. What pushes this game past being "survival sim meets visual novel" is how tightly interwoven the two ideas are. Appeasing your crew could be a drain on resources, but being too pragmatic could brew dissent. The fusion of these genres makes resource management, which might otherwise feel like busywork, feel just as core to your story as the more plot-driven choices you make throughout the game.This gameplay loop, paired with great writing and wrapped in the amazing art and sound, makes up most of what there is to love about the game. The atmosphere is perfect and you really feel the weight of leadership.Unfortunately, some of the UX leaves a little to be desired and often feels a bit too inventive for its own good. The lack of mouseover tooltips is fairly glaring, and the rotating wheel-like design for the resource allocation menus is pretty frustrating to operate (why do I have to remove every crewmember from a task if I want to change the first one I allocated? Why can't I see the entire allocation at once in a nice, simple list?). There are plenty of other examples, but these are some obvious ones. Combined with some unfortunately fairly frequent UI bugs, the actual process of *doing things* in the game can be pretty cumbersome, but not enough to massively get in the way of my enjoyment.Beyond that, there is a moderate number of typos remaining in the game that I noticed, and not all aspects of the ending will necessarily land for everyone, although it is largely a great conclusion (with, I believe, some reasonable variance based on your choices/character deaths). Without spoiling, there's also a bit of missing content that is very apparent.Lastly, and this isn't necessarily a pro or a con, but: this game may be either hilariously easy or brutally hard depending on how quickly you solve it. Players who aren't super into brainstorming hard about the game mechanics are liable to get very frustrated, whereas very technical players are likely to figure out the optimal ways of doing things pretty fast and coast through. This can be rewarding for those players, but I've heard wildly varied comments in these reviews, from remarking that the game is far too easy to solve, to lamenting how unforgiving and borderline impossible it can feel. I'm perhaps closer to the former boat, but I'm not sure of the average player's experience - I'm sure there are enough players who feel somewhere in-between, too. Regardless, difficulty settings might be a good call.If the game wasn't so good at its core, I'd probably be more frustrated with the issues that do exist. But it is, so I'm not. The issues don't massively detract from the experience at all. Updates to fix bugs and UX issues are inevitable, and hopefully even to add to the content. If you're skeptical based on the issues mentioned in reviews, I'd suggest waiting for a bit. Otherwise, go ahead and play now, the game is great. I'll update this review as things change.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR, Give it a play if you are a fan of story based resource managements, But it could be better. (Light spoilers ahead)The Pale Beyond is an interesting game, I want to like it, and I do, but there's a few things that just hold it back from being one of my favorites. What really gets me is the ending, The fruit is meant to be such a big choice, such an important thing but, it just doesn't have much impact, I suppose it may have more impact if you had to make hard choices, let people die, let someone leave, but if you make it through your first time with everyone alive, loyal, and without sacrifices being made, it really just feels lackluster, From my knowledge the only impact eating the fruit will have is that you say something about already having ate the apple when offered the choice. I almost wish that eating the fruit gave you a chance to save Everyone, Including hunt and the deserters giving you a harder situation, A crew more split in their loyalties, more extreme infighting, more mouths to feed and a harder situation to deal with, Maybe even getting stuck in the ice sooner and having less supplies to deal with it, finally leading up to a situation where you save Everyone, and you get to make a decision about the tree. (oh one other thing is that crew loyalty isn't really an issue most of the time I almost wish there were more captain votes and more importance on loyalty)Some other issuesThe UI is buggy sometimes leaving characters on the screen or showing the wrong background for the situation (EX, Getting through dialogue too quickly, or The boiler room showing instead of above deck if you pass the night down there)The items and storage is a struggle to deal with, Its hard to put items into the pot of furnace most of the time due to issues with the inventory and item management.Final thoughtsOverall, The Pale Beyond is a good game with a few kinks that need to be worked out and a potential for being a very good game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Pale Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: The Pale Beyond is a concept I didn't know I wanted in a game. Story driven choices with light exploration and resource management mechanics. The gameplay loop is surprisingly compelling--it's just a shame that it all goes out the window in the last act in favour of progressing the story to a conclusion. I would have preferred the resource management mechanics matter right up to the very end. But that's really my only complaint. Everything else about the game is stellar. Good writing, nice art, decent soundtrack, and a high degree of polish. I highly recommend The Pale Beyond to anyone interested.

_childDocuments_.review: This game manages to perfectly balance the narrative structure and plot of the progression with it's survival elements, often I had to consider how my actions affected the loyalty of the crew to me as well as having to piss them off for the good of everyone. This game throws quite a few curveballs at you at times and forces you to take sides on decisions that may detriment the crew let alone the regular decisions you make every week, do you spend your resources on a warmer night? Or a full meal for everyone? The final few acts of the game are more narrative focused, but I enjoyed them thoroughly as I had to watch the consequences of my actions come back to bite my ass.This game, based on Ernest Shackleton's Imperial Trans-Atlantic Expedition is a recommend from me if you enjoy the cold setting as well as it's survival mechanics and story focused gameplay.PS. Rogue Wave soundtrack with the sailor singing release when?
_childDocuments_.name: The Pale Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: A very intelligent and interesting game that will open up your eyes to how the world works but adds some fantastical elements to it. You will feel the cold and the desperation as the events progress but also feel the warmth of the fire and the cozyness of the tent protecting you from the elements. You set out with a crew you know nothing about, as time passes they will grow up to you. You'll know the higher ranks as if they were family members and know the lower ranks as you would on a real ship, barely but knowing you'll need them to survive and feeling the weight of every choice you make. You have the choice to be the best person as you can or choose otherwise and see the consequences. One of my favourite games and I wish there were more like this from this developer. I prefer the real-life elements in games but this one teaches a valuable lesson by implementing a bit of magic. There is a lot of replayability. Very much recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: The Pale Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: I discovered this game through looking at small indie games on YouTube and came across their dev story - very cool the follow!About the game itself:Charming setting, characters and writing. Mechanics aren't too deep, but deep enough that I really made an effort on my first (and only) playthrough to get proper resources and relationships with people, and had a very successful run. As such, it isn't the most challenging game which demands a lot of micro management of you. Instead, play it for the story, it's worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Pale Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: [9/10]The Pale Beyond presents a deeply engaging story, backed with great quality sound, art and writing. The challenge of keeping your crew alive in spite of the elements offers a fun way to dig into a game that, for the most part, plays out something like a visual novel version of The Oregon Trail.For a first title from a new studio- this is super impressive!If you want to read why I gave this score: [8/10]A fun management/survival game mashed with a visual novel that forces you to make difficult decisions to survive. You can expect to have to restart chapters at times as it's very easy to make bad decisions (which is actually pretty fun) [9/10]Beautiful, hand-drawn graphics do a wonderful job of capturing the harsh environment you're set to survive, whilst expressing the individual members of the crew really well. Only thing stopping me from scoring it a 10 is that crew members could benefit from a few extra expressions to reflect their written tone. [9/10]Would never have expected this level of polish from a first-time developer. The music and sound design are incredibly immersive and do a phenomenal job of fleshing out the world and highlighting its tone. These first game in ages I don't want to turn the sound down, even when it's not needed. [7/10]Some small technical bugs, most of which have been addressed since launch, and the rest are things the team is actively looking into. Mildly annoying at times, but barely a concern. [10/10]A good story is essential to the success of a game like this, and the Pale Beyond doesn't fail to deliver. Nuanced characters, and engaging mystery and a great sense of drama had me completely engrossed in the story [9/10]This is a really special game, you can feel the love and care put into its creation. The combination of compelling art, sound and story come together to form a game that really stuck with me.
_childDocuments_.name: The Pale Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: Look, this is not a pure survival simulation. Yes, it does have elements of that, but if you're here for straight survival, do know that this game is more narrative focused.In this game your main objective is "seeing it all through". Reaching the end, and at that point reflect on all that went right, and all that you could have done differently. Then try again, and this time, try to save everyone, and see how the story changes.My best comparison would be Nine Hours, Nine Persons, Nine Doors, and although the mechanics are totally different, by the end you understand that you have been doing something very similar: getting to know a group of characters, and by changing how you do some things, see how they react differently. It even has a branching mechanic that feels very similar to what that game does (in fact, I would have loved to see it more developed in this game).It does most things right, but I feel that for being a narrative game it's a bit lacking on unique story flags during the survival part. I mean, the characters do have story flags, but what really drives the game forward are the numbers. How hungry or cold, or sick or depressed your people are, in order not to lose any crew and get a game over. But maybe if on the way there were events that determine if you found clues to get to the ending locations, or if you find the items you need for your employer, or if you find a rescue ship at all, would have been a bit more interesting. Instead, all those developments are crammed towards the end.Also there's a loyalty mechanic which is very prominent during the survival part but is meaningless until once again the end partIn general, I recommend a lot this game, but feel that they have fallen a step short of perfection
_childDocuments_.name: The Pale Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: Chilling text survival gameThis is part visual novel part sandbox survival game.Gameplay: Make the right choices and the game is easy, there are some events that intentionally screw you over, but such things are usually well foreshadowed. Usually in these types of games there is lots of RNG screwing you over, but here the RNG is only very minor. Which leads to the curious situation of having a lack of replay ability. Story: Lots of characters lots of back story a mysterious benefactor, all the usual goodness. The ending feels a little flat, and the demonisation of the benefactor felt a little forced. Art style: Very pretty. Overall a little short, but still entertaining romp, recommended when on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: The Pale Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: I'm partial to survival games, but they often come off as cheap and unpolished. But, so far, The Pale Beyond shows an impressive amount of consideration. Thoughtful, branching conversations, excellent music and art. It's very moody, and very well written. Easy to get lost in. FINAL UPDATE, having now completed the game.Gameplay balance is challenging and well thought out. You'll find yourself thinking about how to overcome the seemingly insurmountable odds even when not playing it. That said, it is remains balanced and this is a design and narrative accomplishment."What's the replacement rate on my fuel?" "How many penguins is it gonna take to not starve to f'in death over winter?" The tension is real. There are some minor glitches and nuisances still left in the game, particularly in the latter half (ie med bay being unavailable due to narrative events, etc which can necessitate resetting a day) but it's all tolerable. Some bugs are about the only thing that is not immaculately polished. Final issue, I do agree with other reviews that the ending, while amazing and satisfying, does arrive missing a bit of background. I would recommend to the Dev to do a bit more play testing to tie up loose ends here in a more narratively cohesive way, like they've done diligently throughout the rest of the game. (ie I never made those choices, so why is this under discussion? Did I miss something?)That said, the pros vastly outweigh the cons here. Overall, I'm very impressed. One of the best survival games I've played. When the Devs make another game I'll be first in line. If a well written, well designed, atmospheric, survival game sounds like your cup of tea, don't miss The Pale Beyond. Cheers!

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished my first play through and I enjoyed it very much. The art and music is great and all the characters felt unique and special. I am excited to go back and try and get all the achievements for this game. With that all being said, I have some pretty frustrating issues with the game play mechanics. There will be spoilers for my run in the review below.Throughout my run of the game, there are a few instances where I assign my crew to various tasks, thought I was perfectly okay for the day, and without any warning, an "event" happened where I needed 3-4 available crew. I understand this is likely due to the games sense of "anything can go wrong at any moment," but for someone who enjoys strategy games, it feels pretty bad to have an unexpected event in which you were required to "play bad" and have crew doing nothing during the day. Example: Near the end of the game inside the tent and patching holes. I was given instruction that there will be holes in my tent that I would need to repair. Sure I can assign the crew to it, no big deal. I look around my camp to see no active holes in my tent. Great! I assigned my crew to other tasks and fed them dinner. At this point, a hole popped up in my tent. Frustrating since I had just assigned everyone seeing no holes, but no worries I have 2 people available. Only for this not to work because I need 4 people, no more and no less, to patch a hole. These type of random events happen throughout the game, but the way the game is laid out mechanically, you would be forced to 1. Already know this is going to happen, or 2. Play "poorly" with your given information during the same night. A simple way to "fix" this would be for the holes to appear instantly after you read the dialogue so I can prepare crew for this, or alternatively, happen the next night around. It does not feel like a "new challenge," but feels more like BS. Perhaps also a way to reassign crew to various tasks? These are just a few examples that could easily solve these issues. Another mechanical frustration I had was regarding the medic. You can use scientists to create a medicine that instantly heals your crew at the doctor. This sounds wonderful, but it fails to tell you that your doctor's beds remain full, even after using the medicine. Which does not make a lot of sense gameplay or art wise. You will assign your injured crew to the doctor, and their character will appear on the bed of the doctor. You can use the medicine you have and the character is no longer there, "freeing" up the bed space on the screen. However, you cannot assign more injured crew to the now open beds. This somewhat minor thing makes you think you can heal your entire crew in one night, but instead still only allows 2-3 people to be healed. Finally, the last issue I had with the game is the loyalty mechanic. This is a big factor in the game which leads to big decisions towards the end of your story. This is the one major writing plot point that I did not enjoy. The former captain has abandoned us for 9 months on ice, stealing supplies, getting 3 of the crew killed, and left us for dead. The head of the exposition (Templeton) has been an antagonizing force throughout 95% of the game towards the entire crew. I, as the new captain, has kept 90% of my crew alive in a situation where no one could have expected to live for more than a few weeks. However, the crew voted me out as captain at the very end of the game because of -5 loyalty on a few characters. These characters do not act like people. I kept almost every single person alive for 9 months, stranded with no assistance, but because my loyalty was not above a specific threshold, the crew claims I did a poor job. And not only that, the crew who voted against me, was loyal to me for 35/38 weeks. This is not how people would react. If I survived 9 months stranded on ice because of someone's leadership, but they piss me off for 2 weeks, I would not suddenly vote against them. Furthermore, I don't care how long you might have known the former captain, I don't believe any human would vote for their former friend after they literally left you for dead. This was the only part during the story that I raised my hands up in the air and said "this is bad writing." Overall, the game is a fun strategy game with a lot of replay value. I would say this game is worth picking up for $20. I am excited to see where Bellular Studio's goes with their next gaming title (if any) and hope they learn from the very few mistakes they made in this title.

_childDocuments_.review: MAJOR STORY SPOILERS.I don't often write reviews, but this game dipped it's toes into a concept that I absolutely adore: retained knowledge through timeline jumping.That seems extremely specific so I'll explain. A lot of games use the idea of story routes and multiple endings, while precious few games use the idea of knowledge obtained in one route being useful in another. The only games I've played that have tried this are the Zero Escape series and Doki Doki Literature Club (both anime VNs which aren't normally my thing.) Zero Escape was plagued with ridiculously bad writing and idiotic characters, but it still holds a special place for me because of how well it did this concept. DDLC was great for different reasons, and the retained knowledge mechanic was extremely minor.I didn't know that The Pale Beyond would be using this mechanic, so when I reached the ending and ate that peach, the first thing I felt was obviously some extreme excitement! The game just made it clear that my character has gained awareness of previous runs through the game which has all sorts of interesting implications. Maybe me and Hunt can discuss the whole timeline and figure out together how to handle each situation. Maybe that will create some alternative choices throughout the run! Maybe I can go back to the beginning and keep Hunt from abandoning the ship, or get him to take Kurt's advice so that the ship isn't lost. The whole story could change!But eventually my excitement died down and the problems began to occur to me... that was all basically already the case. You can rewind time whenever you want throughout the game, create alternative branches, make different decisions... the only new development is that it's now being taken into account in the actual narrative that we can do that. This makes it a hell of a lot less impactful. I feel like a better way to do this would be to have the story start at the end, with Shaw eating the peach after it's clear they've failed and coming back to the office with Hunt at the beginning. That would explain why you'd been able to do this the whole time while still keeping most of the narrative from the player. We'd wonder whether it was some kind of flashback or nightmare and we wouldn't know what the hell happened. I'm not a writer, but I think this is an ok suggestion.The biggest problem, though, is what you're able to do with this new, society-changing, reality-warping ability. The new opportunities that are now available to you, now that you've gained this power. Let's go through the list:- You can tell Hunt that Minerva's coming, which changes nothing.- You can tell Minerva that Hunt went down with the ship, which changes nothing....That's it. This is truly one of the biggest missed opportunities I've seen in a game. They did nothing with the mechanic. The endings are barely different (if at all.)There's really not much more to say here, it's just a waste. If they did this mechanic well then this game could have been one of my favourites ever. I really enjoyed the rest of the experience, but unfortunately the magnitude of this missed opportunity just left me with a feeling of disappointment. I hope that this is either something that will be released as DLC at some point, or at least something that the devs will try to improve in their next game.

_childDocuments_.review: The Pale Beyond kept me captivated for hours, extremely well written and with characters that are quite interesting. The art and music are simply phenomenal and bring a feeling of immersion like no other.As for gameplay, the controls are simple and several mechanics to keep you alert, what differentiates are the handling of resources and decision-making much more relevant than I expected, making the game difficult at first, but very satisfying. Here you need to be prepared for difficult decisions, because your resources are scarce and when it comes to the crew, be careful everything can kill them within a week if you don't have the options to treat them as soon as possible.As it was recently released, it was possible to find some bugs that were fixed during the week, so they did not become a concern, in addition to always being able to alert them of problems directly on discord.

_childDocuments_.review: Well this game has taught me one thing. Surviving in the arctic with a crew of sailor after your captain abandons you is really hard. This is certainly a difficult survival experience, but it's a very interesting one. There isn't that much decision to make, but the few ones you take have vital consequences and the management aspect, while brutal, is certainly fun. The art style of the game is amazing too.
_childDocuments_.name: The Pale Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game to support Bellular, but I wasn't certain I would enjoy it.I have been very surprised. It has an interesting story and a unique game play. It's like a visual novel on steroids. Actions matter, choices matter, resource management is constant, a lot of risk/reward/opportunity costs to consider.This is the sort of game where you can expect to fail a lot. The save system only lets you have one previous save, so if you regret a decision early on in the game, you either need to tough it out or start again.There is a lot of dialogue and story. If you don't like that sort of thing this might not be a good fit.I am just over 4 hours into the game and loving it so far, but the game will require a bit of patience.I would recommend giving it a go, you will be well within the refund window by the time you figure out if this game is for you or not - for most players I'd say 1 hour into game play.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has left me pretty speechless. Wonderful art style, a realistic and diverse cast of characters, and a story that will leave you hitting yourself or cheering out loud. Honestly I believe this is the only game that has ever sent me on such a roller coaster of emotions. Never have I felt such worry and such joy over the lives of fictional characters. I sat down to play it and couldn't stop till the end. My only real complaint aside from the rare buggy interactions (someone telling someone else to return a book to someone who was dead for example) is that I can't play more. There are multiple endings and I definitely want to try to lose less people but I feel like my second playthrough won't be nearly as impact as my first. Overall if you enjoy story driven games then there is no reason not to pick up The Pale Beyond and I know I will be counting the days till this game studio drops another masterpiece.Edit: Now that I have given it more thought and my emotions have passed I do have one other minor gripe. There are a decent few things that go unexplained or under explained in the game. For example I didn't know for a long time that wounded people never die (or take ages to die) even though the one blurb talking about it also talks about Scurvy and Frostbite which will kill in one week. Some other features are the migration paths and the tent holes. Overall these aren't too bad since you can reload weeks and it makes decisions harder since you aren't fully informed but I can see it getting frustrating if you are not as comfortable with resource management games.

_childDocuments_.review: + Persona Social Links have nothing on The Pale Beyond character interactions. + The personal, human themes of the level of Citizen Sleeper but implemented in more relatable ways.+ The balancing act of resource requirements is somewhat fairer than Frostpunk and there is WAY less stat check hindrance than The Life And Suffering of Sir Brante,+ The art. It's stunning.+ The stakes are high and it gives me pause every few minutes. Actions have consequences and are true to the time and place.+ Music pieces that make me want to just sit back for a few minutes and soak it in.+ While some mistakes can feel harsh, they can be planned for in a relative sense.+ Fair release price for launch (Meets the 'Never pay more than $20 US for a game' Monkey Island 1 rule)- Maybe some automated text movement similar to VNs would reduce the clicks for longer scenes?- Research papers could have been better utilised?- The full deal with wounds could be explained better or they might be bugged?- I had to hunt Tuskarr?!Bellular and his crew were able to put their commentary on the industry and other games into practice in their own. Nothing is perfect but here I see a clear vision, what they wanted to implement and why this operates the way it does.Having gone through Persona 3 recently and being told by all my friends 'Get a guide or you don't stand a chance' and always feeling the irritation of having to do everything in a set way, seeing the way character relations worked here was a real relief. If you bother to take the time here to understand how the characters think, you can get a better result with them most of the time. Persona's social link system required so much 'See A on Monday, B on Tuesday and Friday, etc' while also having to grind Social Qualities, which is still cumbersome and goes right to the wire on allotted time even in 5. Not to mention some dialogue choices seeming so out of place with what the character has said or done. Citizen Sleeper had the heart, warmth and bitter reality of interacting with other people but had very little else to do once you understood its overall basic system. Pale Beyond found a balance between having gravity with the interactions and having other things to do than them.Frostpunk's gameplay - while brutal - was insatiable and inspired threading the needle to survival. What it did lack was the personal factor. It never really hurt to push people to the limit. Pale Beyond gives the hard choices meaning. And while I get the issue some people have with the branching system, I think it's fair for the situation. If going back to right before a critical mistake was made can be done with one quick button click, then what is the consequence of the scenario? To be true to the plight of those that had to live out these insane scenarios, it has to actually feel like there is little in the way of redos. Getting rewinds verging on Life is Strange would cheapen the experience and meaning of such a grim situation given the context. In terms of time required, I feel it is fair overall. For something WAY more punishing, I dare you to try The Life And Suffering of Sir Brante. Stat checks every minute with huge consequences. Only being able to backtrack to the start of chapters - which were many hours long - with far more choices involved. Around 20 different stats you had to 'balance' by the end. And where only one ending of many could be considered the true end but be an utter slap in the face to what you value in life. Citizen Sleeper could suddenly give you a 'If you don't have these items in X turns without foreshadowing, goodbye to your expansion playthrough, start over from the beginning of the original with no backtracks at all.' Trust me, The Pale Beyond is more forgiving than others in resource survival/life sims.In some moments, like seeing the aurora or hearing certain music pieces, I had to sit back for a bit and take it in. It's reminiscent of those Week 1 experiences in Wrath of the Lich King, knowing you're in a harsh and perilous environment, yet you want to keep going because somehow, there is beauty here and there can be a point to being here. It's the Bellular we've listened to for years. He's been able to recreate those moments himself.To Bellular and his team - thank you. This was always a Day 1 purchase for me. I'm beyond fed up with AAA gaming and what they want to force people to like or grind to fun, or with 'reviews' clearly tailored to get the next pre-release copy. You made your intentions clear and what you wanted to portray, despite their being some obvious pushback for what that scenario will inevitably involve. Looking forward to what you do next.

_childDocuments_.review: You know its a good game when 4 hours feels like 30 mins! Amazing story in which each decision feels like it has weight. I found myself going into the game at the start asking myself, who am I? Who do I want to be? By the "end" I was full immersed, feeling the weight of each decision as I had grown to like most of my crew and truly wanted to keep them alive! _childDocuments_.review: I review narrative games based on narrative, and this is a surprisingly well-designed, well-written game. There is stuff to criticize - the mechanics of adding fuel and food are a bit fiddly, the story is sometimes so streamlined that it doesn't seem to respond very well to your actions, and the "qualities" of your main character and crew barely ever seem to actually matter - but overall, I enjoyed my time with the game. I will say that the game "deleting" saves based on moving backwards in the tree is an absolutely stupid decision. My game crashed due to a bug so I had to load instead of pressing "continue", and for some reason the game had put me 14 weeks behind where I had come to. Minor mistake from me, I should have checked the date more thoroughly, but it deleted all my progress and I had to replay an hour of game to get back to where I was.

_childDocuments_.review: Not a difficult game, but it's fun. I enjoy the characters, and it felt appropriately in-depth for the kind of game it is (regarding characters and story). However, while it tries very hard to be replayable I was satisfied with my initial playthrough enough to stick with that.Still, it's fun and if you're on the fence about getting the game, I'd recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Pale Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: I finished this game this weekend and it was amazing. Excellent narrative game with a layer of survival in different conditions. Helping your crew survive while staying popular with key figures is not always easy but there is almost always a way to correct your mistakes. The story is well-written (reminiscent of The Terror) and there is more to it than it looks at first glance, with lots of branching; and characters have their own personality, story and can die permanently. The ship itself reminds me of the Obra Dinn.I managed to bring everyone back home and everyone was loyal to me save for one guy and his goons, but it still felt satisfying. The game is always good at praising you when you succeed and advising you when you fail. It's not like Frostpunk who gives you no choice but having to make cruel decisions and then makes fun of you for being the tyrant they forced you to be. In the Pale Beyond you can really follow your own moral compass and still come on top of the challenges, even if that means letting characters disloyal to you die on the ice.I've had a look at secret achievements and there is so much more that can happen that I haven't seen. Fortunately the game allows you to reload any of the spent weeks, and near the end you can create a whole new narrative branch instead of overriding.One of my top games for this year.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: Just changed to recommended cause they added endings that made the game feel more cohesive and actually replayable in the way that they intended.Original post before changing it to recommended: I am the biggest sucker for multiple endings, I will brave through repetitive gameplay and lengthy dialogues just to get every ending possible, and though this game does offer multiple endings and *some* of your choices do matter, the endings just fell really flat (i didn’t even bother getting all of them cause the payoff just isn’t worth it). I thoroughly enjoyed the conversations with the key characters, I think building up my relationship with them was my favorite part of the game (to be fair, this is my favorite part in most games), which may be why I was so disappointed with how boring the last act was. I wish they provided a better way to wrap up your impact on the characters, or show you how your choices in the latter parts affected anything after your voyage. The endings just took away all the drama, gravitas, and excitement of the whole game. Also, the strategy aspect provided some excitement at first but didn’t really matter at the latter parts. This is best played with audio on as the game's music and sounds (and sailor songs) really help you immerse yourself in the world of the game. Also really liked the overall art style, disappointed none of the characters were romanceable. I think I could recommend this for those who hadn't really played that much choose your own adventure/visual novel type of games and want to get a feel for it. For me though, I ended the game feeling disappointed and empty-handed. Especially since the beginning to middle showed great promise.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I really enjoyed the game. I liked the variety and flavor of dialog options. I hate when I can tell what my choice will result in. Big thumbs up for RPG element, kept me engaged. The music and art were wonderful, especially with how limited our visual journey is. Controls were simple and relaxing. Game play and story kept me wanting to know what'll happen next.  I'll definitely be replaying. Initially, I failed around week 20 because I was short 1 point for food so I couldn't keep the moral up (auto fail) and my most recent save point was weeks prior so I turned off the moral system. I mean, who could keep up their hope in this situation anyway? I was worried about resource management because I tend to get overwhelmed in games but this was a good balance. _childDocuments_.review: So to get it right out: I was unhappy with the end of the game, and it ruined the rest of the experience for me. HOWEVER, I would still say that the game was, overall, good. I did enjoy it, but there were issues with it. These issues may be getting fixed in patches and the developer is very responsive, so just because I disliked the ending doesn't mean that you will. You might still have fun.The good points:It's a fun survival gameThe art is beautifulThe characters all feel like different people and by the end you know how to interact with each of themThere are several touching moments that really hit me or had me on the edge of the seat.The art- character and scenery- is beautiful. I cannot stress that enough.The developers seem very responsive and are trying to do a good job. There were a number of glitches when I first played, but it seems like they have been mostly ironed out. Awesome to see!The cons:Research points. What do they do? You don't research anything, and they didn't seem to provide anything. I could be missing it, but it felt like they were literally useless.Abrupt ending. Were you hoping for an epilogue for the people who survived? Nothing.The ending. I was... really not impressed with the answers to the mysteries presented. This might be a me thing but the game was fun and then just kind of shrugged its shoulders at the end. That said they at least did tie the ending into the mechanics, so that was neat.Overall if you like games and don't worry too much about the ending this should be a good buy. I don't resent buying it, nor do I feel like I wasted my time playing it, I just felt that there was a better conclusion and answer to the mysteries coming.Edit: Thank you for the response, Bellular Studios! It really does mean a lot to hear back from you. My game updated recently and is on the 1.3.0 version. That was not the one I played, but I do not remember with whole certainty what it was. I may have to try going through again and seeing if it fixed things and about the change to research. If those are changed then I will have to revisit the review again.

_childDocuments_.review: I've only made it to week 5 on my first playthrough, but so far I'm having a blast.   For anyone who may be unsure of what type of game this is, it's like a "choose-your-own-adventure" book got mixed in with a resource management sim and a dating sim, and then got a fat does of epic art and sound / music.  Don't take the dating sim part literally, but I didn't really know how else to categorize building relationships with your team.  Big breath of fresh air this game is, and not just because you're on a boat in the ice.  I can't think of another game that I can really compare this to directly, and that seems to be a very rare thing in the gaming industry these days.  I'm only 1.5 hours in and already eagerly anticipating my next session so I can see what happens next.  I've already had some moments of absolute panic, and I love how much weight my choices are having on the course of the adventure.Definitely the best value for the price that I can think of in recent history, and I have bought quite a lot of  games in the last 12 months.  Cheers to Bellular and crew for putting out such a fantastic title for their first game, and I really can't wait to see what else is in store for me on this adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: Writing this after I stayed up til 10am playing. I love resource management games! Rather than normally thinking "Oh, I kind of like this", or "Oh no, this is a little tricky", my brain shut off as I was figuring out the game and how the narrative played out along with the gameplay. My only incredibly personal nitpick (and this is a good thing) is that I wish I'd have been warned: I honestly didn't expect anything - I probably should have, considering the very blatant description the devs so kindly gave. The pains of storytelling are maneuvering the reality of an already dire situation and sad things occur. I was crying so hard I stayed up even longer so I wouldn't got swollen eyes. _childDocuments_.review: I absolutely loved The North Water and The Terror (TV series set on board 19th century Arctic expeditions), and had thought you could make a potentially brilliant survival/management/RPG in a similar setting. So I was pretty excited when this game popped up. Unfortunately the first couple of hours left me completely cold (wahey!) and I've ended up refunding it.This is partly down to tastes and expectations and most people do seem to have enjoyed the game, but just in case you had similar hopes to mine, here's what I found disappointing:The setting is weird. Perhaps I should have watched the trailer more closely, but I was hoping for something at least nominally realistic/historical. This is more of a steampunk-light vibe, in a completely fictionalised world where the characters feel more like they've stepped out of an jaunty anime or JRPG than a gritty Victorian adventure.The bar for the 'simulation' tag seems incredibly low these days, but this is certainly not a simulation - more of a point-and-click/narrative adventure with some fairly arbitrary and opaque 'resource management' thrown in. There's no freedom to make decisions or interact with characters outside the specific order they are presented in the story, and I never felt like I had enough information - the movie star thinks the captain should change from the current (unspecified) course to a different (unspecified) course for vague reasons about cold and dark. Do you agree? The chief engineer only has six crew on the boiler even though we've hit the ice. How many extra crew should you assign? The way these choices are presented gives it the feel of a choose-your-own-adventure rather than a sim or RPG - a bit like Suzerain, from the same publisher, which I actually loved. Others have praised the writing in The Pale Beyond but actually I think that's what finally stopped me from persevering - quality dialogue and storytelling could make a game like this work, but I found a lot of it quite clunky and shallow (see above re JRPG).Other random annoyances:-The ship feels empty even when you have 20+ crew - where are they all?-You can't explore the ship, only go to the specific locations where story events are going to happen-You're told to introduce yourself to each member of the crew but you can't, you have to wait for them to appear in the story which takes weeks. You're first mate of voyage with less than 30 people on board, three weeks in you know who less than half of them are -Early dialogue contains a glaring error, not story-breaking but still irritating in a full release-Captain says you have enough provisions for six months, turns out after giving standard rations for two weeks we're out of food, dunno what that's aboutThe art and music are very nice though.
_childDocuments_.name: The Pale Beyond

_childDocuments_.review: Rarely has an interactive fiction adventure have me cheering or smiling so much at narrative cliff hangars. Lots of Mass Effect 2 style events at the end of the campaign that hit hard based on the character writing, conversations, and time spent with NPCs throughout the campaign. The checkpoint mechanic at the start of a day is well-balanced - enough that by the end of the day it is not worthwhile to go back and play through a whole day again but not punishing enough that if you make a game-ending mistake you have to start over again through the whole prologue, for example. The game is long enough that you feel invested in the adventure, but not so long that the limited mechanics become boring or chore-like. There's a surprise behind almost every character which is fun to discover, and there are elements of role-play in the captaincy that are truly tough leadership decisions! A great title and enjoyable piece of interactive fiction and adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: Terrible gameplay design. Give out zero food one week, then double food the next and you're better off decorum-wise than if you just fed people normally. Raising boiler heat is literally free (one would assume it to require additional fuel, no?). Just all around baffling, counter-intuitive design decisions that break immersion and nudge the player towards exploits. A giant waste.The story is neat overall, but the ending makes one of the main characters completely inconsequential and with nonsensical motivations to boot. Character interactions in general are incredibly shallow. Despite the game lampshading it pretty early with a character warning you that "You can't make everyone loyal to you just by telling them what they want to hear", that's precisely what you're supposed to do.
