_childDocuments_.review: In my review for DERQ 1, I said it was genuinely one of IF/CH's best. This is not the case with this game. However, even though my feelings towards this game are mixed, as the sequel took what made the first game special and added to it while also taking out things I liked, I still had a good time, and would still recommend it if you can catch the game on a sale.PROS:- It's more DERQ. If you liked the first game, you'll probably find something to like about the second.- The character designs are really strong, even the side characters are fairly memorable.- There is no censorship for returning cast members outfits thanks to the devs polling the fans.- The substories that you watch during the day are well written and add a lot to the story as a whole.- There are a lot of qualilty-of-life additions that make progression a lot easier.- The 2nd playthrough adds a lot of extra scenes to the game that I almost want to say is required, and while a lot of them require you to complete the merchant sidequests, it'll be much easier since your levels/gear carry over from the first.- Bad ends are still here, and while there are only a handful compared to the first game, they are much easier to collect and each of them are fully voiced and come with some nice and bloody artwork.- Plot points are far less predictable this time around. I ended up feeling so stressed at a certain situation that I ended up looking up spoilers for the chapter just so I could prepare myself mentally for what was to come.- Voice acting for the JP dub is decent, Mai's stands out as a great performance.- If you're into yuri, this game will definitely feed you far more than the first game. As annoying as Rottie's pining for Mai gets because it's played as a constant gag, as I went through the story I found myself cheering for her and hoping she gets the girl in the end.- Super knockbacks are fun to trigger. Enemies bounce around like a pinball machine. It's like having the Skala summon from the first game activated ALL the time.- Difficulty is comparable to the first game, the grind still isn't super necessary.- Shina is still best girl.- CONS:- You HAVE to play the first game. The story involves returning characters and plot points that would be super confusing if this is your first entry into DERQ. Thankfully the first game is fantastic and a joy to play.- No genre switching/summons/etc. No consequence for 100% corruption, so the girls can just eat up all of those buffs, meaning there's no real point avoiding them unless they're literally just mines.- Even if Shina is travelling together with the party, she will not appear in camp or interact with the characters at all during battle unless you buy her maid outfit DLC.- Returning characters from the first game are fine if you really liked the characters, but there's no reason to stray from using the 3 new protagonists because they already cover all of the weaknesses.- The pain area this time around is more challenging than the first game, but pain is VERY fitting as you'll end up fighting the same annoying wave of enemies over and over for multiple rooms in a row.- Late game/2nd playthrough strat when you  don't want to deal with large groups of enemies: spam Rottie's Speed Star, even if enemies aren't weak to it.- There are serious audio issues with this game when it comes to balancing. Some characters are infinitely louder than others, and the volume controls range from entirely muted to make-your-ears-bleed. With there being 30+ hours of screaming and crying, if you have headphones with adjustable audio, it's much easier to just use that instead. Or just skip through the voice acting when you've read the text.- If you play with a controller, there's a bug that puts the mouse cursor in the middle of the screen every time you open a menu or enter combat. While it's a quick fix by running a third-party program that automatically hides your cursor, the bug has apparently been around a while with no indication of it ever being fixed.- You want to like Mai, but for the entire first half of the game she's pretty unlikable. The second half of the game is when she really starts to open up to her companions and shine. If you don't like characters that are entirely cold jerks, you'll initially have a hard time getting attached to her.- While the 2nd playthrough adds a lot of scenes and closes up some plotholes left by the first game, it creates just as many plotholes of it's own.DERQ 1 didn't really need a sequel, as the ending was tied up fairly neatly. But now that we're already knee deep into teasing a 3rd game, I genuinely hope this series continues. I think the mixed score is a little harsh, but I still think players that loved the first game should give the sequel a try if they can get it on sale as there's still plenty to like about it.

_childDocuments_.review: Just like the previous game, this one has a ton of potential but also there is things keeping it from being a "great game", however its interesting enough that it deserves its 15 hour playthrough, assuming you played the first game... cause honestly if you havent, you will most likely be lost, and even then, some plot points may be confusing.While the first game tried to have elements of "horror" by having random "bad endings" that would lead to some gory scenes. This game does a better job capturing the atmosphere of a horror game.The game starts with the main character Mai brutally murdering her abusive father out of self-defense. She is picked up by a social worker and told she has to live in an orphanage in some town in Europe. Little does she know that this town has a gruesome conspiracy, but as the game progresses.. she starts uncovering it, and the characters from the first game get involved. Gameplay-wise, if you liked the first game, this is more of the same with some added features, such as the "Super Knockback" which launches the enemies but much harder. As I mentioned the characters from the first game do get involved in your party, however they got extremly nerfed to the point that there is no reason to have them in your active party over the main 3 characters (also the way they join your party is kinda dumb imo).The first aspect of gameplay, is that you have your Visual Novel sections where you talk to other kids in the orphanage, which are EXTREMLY boring, unlike the first game where these sections atleast let you learn more about the mystery... in this game you reading about how a little girl wants a hug or some dumb ****. Which is a huge let down since the atmosphere in the rest of the game is great, granted this time around these sections are totally skippable, making the game even shorter. The other aspect of the game, is the exploration which happens at midnigth ripping of Persona 3 (you know one of the best video games ever made), as the town becomes this weird dark and glitchy place where corrupter monsters are walking around and the towns people seem to dissapear completly.  This is where you will be doing battles, I personally enjoyed the maps in this game better than the first game, it has an almost Silent Hill-esque vibe to it.Once you beat the game, you can replay and speed run it to get some extra scenes (you can easily skip prewatched scenes) that let you know what some characters where doing behind the scenes, but also sets up a plot line that could lead to a potential third game.Overall, if you are looking for a short, unique horror themed JRPG, and can put up with the mind numbing dialogue during the day sections, in order to get to the fun exploration sections AND you played the first game, then this is worth a quick playthrough, just prepare yourself to be pretty confused by some plotpoints even if you did/did not which hopefully get answered in a third game.

_childDocuments_.review: Death end re;Quest 2 is a sequel to the first game in the series. I already loved the first game a lot with the exploration of a video game world turned into a deadly game filled with twists and turns. I was curious to see how the sequel would turn out to be.Compared to the predecessor, Death end re;Quest 2 is primarily a horror RPG. This game was written by Makoto Kedouin of Corpse Party fame, and I also liked the Corpse Party series, especially the first game. The story revolves around Mai Touyama, an orphan who after killing her own father, finds herself in the town of Le Choara where she's welcomed into Wordsworth by Headmistress Midra. She meets up with Rottie, the daughter of Midra, and then Mai comes to the realisation that something feels wrong about this town. Indeed, at midnight the town becomes infested with deadly monsters and horrifying sights. Lots of students in Wordswordth suddenly vanishing and possibly killed, maybe even became monsters... many horrors await our heroine. But what she doesn't know is there's more to this place that meets the eye.A shocking plot twist reveals that Mai was  The story definitely had me on the edge of my seat and gave me shock and terror that asked me if I wanted to push further and see if things will get worse from here on out. Even familiar characters from the first game  This is definitely a different story from what I expected for a follow up to a game that was set in an RPG before it. Of course, there are nods to the first game but you don't need to play the first game to know what happened before.However, Death end is allowed to enjoy moments of lightheartedness when you're exploring Wordsworth and Le Choara in the daylight. Each passing day you'll get to interact with the many students of Le Choara and get to know about them better. However, while there are many students in this game, there are some that the game will present you a scenario where you can possibly save them from death. Returning from the first game are a series of choices presented to the player that can lead to possible death or the continuation of the story. Unlike the first game however, some choices can alter the story further and unlock different scenarios. This is a key factor in how your story will flow out and in some cases, could possibly have consequences in the ending. While there's only three endings, unlike Death End 1 where aside from Normal End, the True End is a series of different scenarios especially Shina's End which is considered the True True End, Death End 2 will really make sure each ending is earned by different ways. New Game + will unlock even more scenarios previously unavailable in the first playthrough so seize the chance to play again from beginning to end to unlock the three possible ends.Death End re;Quest 2 is also an RPG as well don't forget. At midnight, you will be exploring Le Choara and facing various horrifying monsters. Since Le Choara is primarily a mountain based town, the locales range from town sectors to a small farm to lake sides and hills, all of which are interconnected with each other. There's less locale variety compared to the first game as a result. In addition much of the area music has a more atmospheric feel to it adding to the chill factor here. Like the first game, your three main characters, Mai, Rottie, and Liliana all have Field Bug abilities which allow them to interact with certain world elements. For example, Mai can use special surveillance computers to unravel hidden doors, chests, and even a 5 digit passcode. Occasionally however, your journey might get interrupted by a dark evil Shadow Matter force that when you come in contact with it results in an instant game over. If I may be honest though, I never found myself getting a Game Over from this as sometimes the level design doesn't really suit the Shadow Matter's AI. Not to mention after a few moments the thing goes away so if you distance yourself you'll be fine. Unless it's the Residential Area my god I nearly died because TWO Spawned at once. Ah but this Shadow Matter CAN also show up in battle and is invulnerable to attacks and can of course, kill you in one hit if you're within its Area of Effect.Speaking of battle, combat is similar to the first game where each character takes a turn moving around an open battlefield positioning themselves and selecting up to three moves that will attack the opponent. Most core mechanics make its grand return such as the Glitch Mode, the various bugs scattered in the land, and Knockback. Unlike the first game, there's no more fun genre changing abilities. However, various quality of life improvements and various tweaks dramatically change how you approach battles. In the first game, when you learnt a skill, you'd have to remember to equip it in your Skill List cause sometimes you'd forget to do so and you'd be stuck with weaker moves. Now in DERQ2, all your skills are displayed in the Skill List. Of course, you can set your favorite skills just like the previous game to make it faster to go through instead of having to scroll further down but the Display All Skills is a needed improvement. Bugs in this game are now very much beneficial for you as most of them no longer deal damage to you or even corrupt enemies. Each bug has a different perk that will help you plan out what you need to face the battles ahead. There's healing bugs, stat increasing bugs, invincibility bugs, a bug that can instantly enter Glitch mode, and landmines that explode when an enemy is knocked back to it. You will want to run into as many bugs as possible because one more change in the battle system is, even at 100% corruption, you will never die. The game encourages aggressive approaches as a result of the reworked Bug System and each battle presents you a different set of bugs that will greatly benefit you. For example, if the game throws you various landmines, knock back a bunch of foes into those landmines and set off a chain reaction for massive damage! If a boss has a set amount of Insta-Glitch bugs, use those wisely as that could help you set off massive damage numbers. I really enjoy finding ways to approach monsters with the bugs presented. Of course, you will need to perform level grinding because this game is difficult (I have played this game in Hard mode and found myself on the receiving end of getting killed). Also the battle music has some kick to it, especially the frightening rave of the Boss Fight theme, which is a stark contrast from the atmospheric tones of exploration. Oh yeah, while some tracks do return, some are new compositions, especially for the daytime conversations.Death end re;Quest 2 is definitely the follow up I've enjoyed from beginning to end. Some elements felt familiar making me feel right at home, but the game throws several new ways to approach, while of course delivering a great horror story that's on par with the original Corpse Party. While I've only earned one end, I definitely know I'm not done and I will need to replay it again and see all the different consequences. If you have played the first game, definitely play the second one.

_childDocuments_.review: DerQ2 is a second game in an IF jrpg franchise (or third if we count a minigame released only in Japan). It takes place in city La Choara, where protagonist Mai Toyama enrolls to Wordsworth, an all-girls school in search for her younger sister Sanae. There she meets cast of odd and interesting characters and a greater, darker mystery that is surrounding town.Some fans of the earlier title will already be disappointed, because most of the time players will be spending with new characters. The new gang is likeable but it would be nice to see more of the older cast (but it is more of a personal preference). DerQ2’s plot is darker compared to earlier game, with scenes depicting violent deaths of many characters (some of them can be saved thanks to player's choices). Story has many interesting ideas, especially Lydia's subplot, but some of them are available only after finishing it for the first time (similarly to the DerQ1). However, because of some lore and character changes (which I cannot reveal without spoiling the first game) DerQ2 feels more like spin off than sequel. Combat is a jrpg turn based classic with a bit of a twist; when hit, enemies are bouncing of each other like balls in a pool table. For “veterans” of the series combat system here is streamlined; old “minigames” and summons were abandoned completely, with more focus on bouncing mechanic and buffing characters with abilities and glitches, that now can be found on every battlemap.  Graphics are looking really good, however there is an irritating post processing which is making game looking blurry and out of focus. This option can be turned off in menu, but then everything is looking darker. This issue was partially fixed in patch, and now graphics have much sharper look, but still not ideal (for my taste). When it comes to bugs, I have experienced a crashing to desktop (once or twice) and freezing menu issue (this one many times). These were fixed later, but even before weren’t a big issues, because it is possible to save during conversations and dungeons have plenty save points. Other players were experiencing more serious bugs, but I heard they were mostly fixed after patches.  Overall it is a good game and good sequel to the franchise. I wonder where story will go next, because plot is not resolved completely. If you like a bit edgy school murder mystery with monsters and strange, yet interesting, people in the background, give it a try (oh, I nearly forgot, you don’t need to play DerQ1 to understand plot of this one), especially because game dirt cheap, and is now (as of autumn sale) discounted (and probably will soon be again)

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty flawed niche "gem", since there aren't that many Horror JRPG in general, and even less nowadays.To get one thing out of the way, it is pretty buggy, mostly the menu toggles. At some point in your run you will see that when you move around in the battle menu, this might disappears and reappear, at this point you should finish the battle ASAP to save. Just be careful about this, I "freezed" my game 3 times with this. I saved into a new slot just in case, but no issues with the loading of that save.So now:Did you play and liked the previous one? Then go ahead and buy this one.You like light yuri? 'Cause that feels like 60% of the interactions between some characters.You like some B grade horror and deaths? Returning from the first game we got the "death ends" (but not that many).Do you dislike grindy games? This one doesn't need grind if you exploit the knock mechanics.So more or less, you get a nice and short (20 hours) horror jrpg with some dubious characters choices (regarding common sense) and plot (in regards to consistency, and the feeling of some things being too forced) at some points, with a spoonful of yuri, a gameplay that is not cumbersome and some pretty annoying bugs (that I guess are being worked on).It will reach very positive eventually when the bugs are gone, don't let the (current) "Mixed" make you think that it's some standard JRPG crap. Also, I don't think there are many games in the market that can scratch that itch for Horror JRPG, at least I don't remember that many since parasite eve 1 (not that this is remotely similar in any way).That's it.Any recommendations for Horror JRPG are welcome, thank!

_childDocuments_.review: , while the game is easy on the eyes (unless you suffer photosensitivity), it lacks in most other categories such as depth, plot progression, and even overall scare and atmosphere. The game is an amazing visual product, but doesn’t make for a great game, horror or otherwise.In Strobophagia, you play as a nameless faceless forest-rave attendee with hundreds if not a thousand others. At this rave, you rely on a cell phone that’s provided to you to stay in contact with the organizers, the attendees, and even . With this cell phone, you’ll connect to local reception networks to interact with the residents of that space. For the most part, this cell phone acts as your compass, camera, and context, but does little more than that. Also, you can’t use the phone’s flashlight in this game.Strobophagia is a short first-person visually-motivated horror game. You’ll experience a woodland rave where you’ll encounter the  which will slowly educate you on what’s really happening here. This game works in four self-dubbed chapters, one being the tutorial, the second being where you learn of your role in this gathering, the third is a crescendo event that emphasizes  presence, and then the fourth is a reconciliation of the games’ themes.  It’s hard to say what the actual play time of this game is, but an hour and a half might be a good estimate depending on your ability to solve riddles and puzzles. For myself, I completed the game in roughly forty minutes in one playthrough, but that was after restarting and skipping the tutorial portion of the game.It goes without saying that the strongest part of this game is its visual representations. It holds a unique theme that I haven’t really seen reproduced in gaming. While some of the animations can look a little stiff or abnormal, the whole game is essentially one-long acid trip, so I think the animations can honestly play out however they want.Another thing that I did enjoy is the overall plot device of the game -- the presence of  is not one that I commonly will see in games. The unique visuals combined with the uncommon occult influences really do tee this game up to being a unique experience, if only......things were given a little more depth. Earlier, I said that this game was short, and it realistically is. It’s hard to say how much extra-curricular content there actually is to explore aside from my understanding of there being at least two endings, but the exposure you’re given during the gameplay which seems mostly linear is water-driplike. In my specific ending, you’re essentially just hamfisted most of the explanations, such as how the party started, why the organizers wear bird masks, who are  and etc., but even though you spend seven minutes or so reading that whole exchange, there’s still a lot left to wonder. You encounter some pretty significant characters that don’t really seem to get their place in the story like Phix, Ami, or Hedonis even though they impact the game in some pretty large ways. The influence of this game was lined up to provide a strong experience, but I feel like this wasn’t done justice within the small window of time the game takes.Another thing that bothered me was the overall threat of the game. During my playthrough, I encountered two enemies -- the faceless husks and the horned beast. The faceless husks appear in the forest, but they can just be slapped away, I kid you not. They walk up, you hit them, empty handed, and they run off. I defended myself from three of them as I went from point-to-point and was not the slightest bit intimidated by their presence. For the horned beast, they run faster than you when they catch you, so if you happen to get spotted by them you can just lay down and die. There’s no tense cat-and-mouse chase, nor is there much difficulty in avoiding the beast in the mazes, and to round it all off the mazes are pretty short, so your encounter with the beast isn’t given adequate time to foster feelings of fear. Even things that may have been intended to have been well-placed or deserved jumpscares didn’t get a response because I was either frustrated with other parts of the game  the atmosphere didn’t match to get the reaction it was aiming for.A point I had made earlier that I wanted to essentially reiterate because it bothered me so much is really the length of the game. My playtime is about two hours in total, with the extra being mostly non-gameplay related. Within those two hours, I spent the first forty or so minutes in the tutorial trying to get past Oedipa’s task, but after frustrating myself with it I just decided to go find the next control box on my own. On top of those forty minutes, I experienced probably thirty minutes of gameplay before being forced to reload my game due to a bug. Thankfully, the game allows you to essentially bypass the tutorial and go straight to the last checkpoint so you can begin the second chapter -- this means that of those two hours, I only really spent forty minutes playing the remainder of the game. The amount of gameplay stored in the game seems pretty negligible for its heavy price tag of $20 USD. This does leave me conflicted, because the art assets are gorgeous and should be worth the weight of its tag, but with everything else falling short in terms of gameplay, story, atmosphere, and even music -- because I spent a good amount of time mostly in silence in this game, the visuals aren’t enough to prop the game’s value up. Everything in this game is further diminished by the need to restart it due to bugs, which brings me up to my last point.During my time, I experienced at least two bugs -- one game breaking, and one deceivingly inconvenient bug. The first I had encountered was during Phix’s riddle -- I was no longer able to see messages on my phone. This posed a significant challenge because I  and had nothing to reference. I thought this was sort of a punishment for failing the riddle earlier, but I soon understood that the game was broken when I couldn’t interact with environmental elements such as putting things into containers. When I reloaded the game, I was dropped into what could have been an infinite loading screen in the intro cutscene right before I got my phone. It took me about three minutes before realizing I could press “Escape” to leave this loading screen, and on a further reload I was given another faux-loading screen when dropping into the dream-intro scene. Since the game is short, I didn’t have to redo a lot of my progress since I could bypass the tutorial, but it does take heavy points away from the atmosphere and flow of the game when you have to retrace your steps.Also, I don’t quite know why I can’t drink the wine but I  drink the beer. Just something I wonder about sometimes while thinking about this game.Anyway, that’s all the text that we have room for. Game’s , it’s just not a very satisfying experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Strobophagia is definitely a unique and overlooked gem, yet overpriced for its length.The visuals and music are outstanding, it fits and makes a great atmosphere. The gameplay aspect was somewhat lacking, there werent many puzzles and tasks to do, and they were always quite simple to figure out. Reading through message threads on the phone, and getting clues by sharing pictures in the different stations, as well as learning the lore was interesting. The setting was perfect for some weird cult.The "rave" feel is definitely there, the music goes for a darker tone here, as this is a horror game, but that doesnt make it less rave-y. If you have been at a music festival once, you would understand that distancing yourself from where the music comes from makes it less audible, thats how it works, so I cant understand why there are negative reviews having those two things as a complaint.It ran very smooth for me, I didnt encounter bugs, nor did I have frame rate drops or similar issues, so it is safe to say that the developers fixed all the past issues with their last patch.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing! I had to review it do to people giving it down rated reviews. I dont think thats entirely fair. _childDocuments_.review: The aesthetic and the soundtrack to this game is simply fantastic, definitely very unique. Have stalled progressing the story just to listen to the tracks playing before. The character movement feels decent and the puzzles involved are fun. You use a phone picked up at the beginning of the game which is vital to continuing the plot. While other games may solely use them as a light source, this game allows you to read messages from other ravers, take photos and pick up new signals around the maps. Personally found this quite entertaining and a bit different from some other games I have played in the past.There are some issues though, the plot has very little sustenance in an occult sense. The Aleister Crowley influences are apparent but shallow, and the ending was basically an information dump that didn't really feel that satisfying. It felt rushed instead. The game is also very short for the price. Overall I would recommend this game from an incredibly biased and shallow perspective; the visuals are a treat as is the soundtrack. The character movement and phone interactions were nice as well.

_childDocuments_.review: UFFDA UUUUFFFFDA I guess 7 times the charm to beat this game! I had this game bug out forcing me to restart so many times that I became a pro speed runner at it. Legit my personal best is 13 minutes and I could even probably shave a few minutes off that! The game concept itself isn't terrible but its lacking so much polish and asking almost 20$ for the game is outragesThe movement has that walking on ice feel mixed in with the walking through sand feel. When moving the mouse back and forth you'll get a bit of a drift like you built up momentum which is an odd feeling but you strafe back and forth really slow and come to a weird dead stop when running. It's really hard to explain but imagine the upper half of your body sliding down an icy hill while the lower half of your body is trying to climb out of mud.I get that the game has a RAVE theme but it should also have a SEIZURE warning theme. The bright lights and music aren't what will get you it will be the random screeching loud scream mixed in with a bunch of different color filters that will send you into cardiac arrest. There is more than one time where the game goes a little over the time with the effects. With ALOT of polish and a few tweaks I would honestly say this game might be worth 20$ but for now I'd pass it up.

_childDocuments_.review: A great addition to today's gaming libraries, Strobophagia was a really interesting experience. While not quite a walking sim, it still kept gameplay to a minimum to focus on the story at hand. With the unique gameplay of signals and connection, this rave style festival game is honestly a work of art to experience. The atmosphere was brisk and engaging, while still being mostly linear and simple to follow. An easy going exploration horror experience, with some quick paced gameplay at the end of the run to keep things interesting.For stylization alone I would recommend it. One of the most creative art styles in a sequence to actually add to the gameplay style, this game felt like an actual festival. While the story felt limited, the way in which it was told brought the narrative together that makes up for loose threads. All and all, a must play through experience.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a unique and amazing experience. The music, the neon accents and visuals making it one of the most interesting games I've played in years. I loved the story and the premise of things but some of it felt forcefully stitched together in some parts. If you're used to being told exactly what to do and where to go the game will frustrate you, while it does show you what buttons to click, what it never really explains to you is what you can do with those functions. Most of the mechanics feel under developed and underused like the wi-fi system and sending photos. I was confused and lost a few times not knowing what to do exactly in the beginning or where to go, if you can get past the first 15-20 minutes that's when the fun starts. I appreciate that it's not horror ALL the time without letting you catch a breath, it's not a traditional horror game either. The chat function was a really interesting touch on telling the story without having it forced down your throat . The conversations felt fluent and life like.Going back on my second play through I noticed a few little details that I didn't see the first time which made sense to me only after finishing the game.Overall despite the shortcomings and some frustrating design choices it's an amazing experience and one that I can't get enough of. The visual design and music alone makes it worth the time.Hoping that there will be DLC and/or a sequel in the future as the game felt too short.I enjoyed my time with this and want to make it clear that despite the constructive criticism, I adore this game and want to see more of it.

_childDocuments_.review: Destroy All Humans! 2: Re-castratedBugs, balancing, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. A certain "" mission was cut as well as certain brain-scans.The ending was apparently altered .I don't generally mention the good things in my reviews, as I find the negatives to be more relevant to me and other people who might be interested in buying a game.That being said, I don't want it to sound like I absolutely hate the game, or that the game is even bad.So on that note, I'll start with the good.- The art style is a very nice change and remains consistent with the first remake's art style.- The level layout and design, while massively different from the original Destroy All Humans 2, is very good and looks much better than the original in my opinion.- Collectibles such as records, posters, and artwork are a welcome addition to the levels.- New optional objectives on each story mission and side mission which reward you with extra furotech cells.- If you have the skin pack from the first remake, you can use the skins in this one.- There are skins to unlock in-game through side objectives (and they don't all look lame like the first one).- The audio, particularly the dialogue, sounds a lot cleaner than the first remake's.- The movement, shooting, weapons  are all massively improved over the original.- You can refund your furotech cells and upgrade cores with brain-stems, though the game fails to mention it has an exponentially increasing cost for each refund.- You start right out the gate with infinite S.K.A.T.E. and a maxed out jet pack.- Massive improvements in the  department.- Most of the dialogue made it in, even the racier bits were left unaltered with few exceptions.- I really like this game. - Cut content. Yes, in spite of the trigger warning and all the bluster, they cut a mission and some dialogue.- Bugs, and lots of em.- The virgin  isn't even primordial slag compared to the chad .Look how they massacred my boy. It just sort of bounces things off the ground to middling effect. Gone is the ridiculous sound of whizzing objects, cars, and people flying around at mach 12. Now you have to charge a shot for over 5 seconds just to bounce a car around on the ground for 2 seconds. The thing just sucks and nobody was actually asking for it to be neutered like this. I know I've dedicated an entire paragraph to the  but come on. It also looks like they got the colors for the zap-o-matic and the  switched around. The zap-o-matic's energy is purple and the 's is blue.- The graphics settings are all tied together in the options menu. So you can't change anisotropic filtering, you can only change the "visual effect" setting from "low" to "ultra".- The game's color looks washed out and overly bloomed in certain weathers.- The physics are very unreliable and tend to just freeze objects midair sometimes, or shoot a vehicle half-way into the ground.- Free love was changed to a weapon, which is actually rather nice, but there is no reason to use it at low alert levels due to the shortness of the dance. It takes a considerable amount of time to get it into effect at higher alert levels which kind of ruins it's utility as a panic button. You also can't call an all clear during free love, probably due to a bug.- PK Follow is practically useless. Armed humans no longer act as a bodygaurd (which might be a bug) and npc's tend to just run into traffic or get stuck on the open air when under the influence of Follow. Every enemy will just target your follower as soon as you make one, so it's useless for missions too.- PK Mindflash messes with clean body-snatches and calling all clear. If you mindflash and then try to snatch while everyone is down, your new body will have aggro on it until you get out of it, even if you break line of sight or get an all clear.- Transmogrification takes too long and returns too little.- A lot of the weapons are useless against vehicles compared to just using an un-upgraded pk throw. You can one shot tanks most of the time with just humans, but it takes a fully upgraded Ion charge to destroy one.- The proximity detector really sucks at finding furotech cells. Seriously, over half of them didn't ping on the damn thing while I was standing directly on them.- Furotech cells in the world are tucked away in annoying spots that are covered up. I'm probably going to end up having to use a guide to find the last one in Bay City and I'm not even going to bother trying without a guide in Albion. Seriously, in the original game, you could see the damn things from across the map, now I can barely see them when they're 10ft away, because there's usually something obscuring it.- I hate the saucer.- The saucer sucks.- Fix the damn saucer.I'm not exaggerating when I say that just about every aspect of the saucer is out of balance.- The Death Ray sucks.It takes a continuous 5 second blast from a fully upgraded Death Ray to destroy just about any building. A simple matchstick watch tower? 5 seconds. A fish stand? 5 seconds. A small house? 5 seconds. A brick lighthouse? 5 seconds. You get the point.- The Sonic Boom sucks.It takes 10 to 12 sonic blasts (fully upgraded) to destroy anything. That's even with the "added" damage from enemy projectiles being sucked into your blasts. Keep in mind, you can only hold 30 shots max.- The Quantum Deconstructor sucks.The Quantum Deconstructor has a smaller blast radius than the sonic boom. It gets like 5% charge per pickup and you need 100% to fire it. It's max capacity is only 2 shots.- Saucer transmogrification sucks double.It takes just as long as it does on foot and you get even less ammo from it. Half of the time you end up extracting brains (because you can do that in the saucer for some ungodly reason). Over half of my time in the saucer would be spent mashing E just to get ammo if it weren't for my next point.- Saucer PK Slam mogs every single other saucer weapon.It one shots almost every building, it instantly destroys any vehicle, and it costs 0 ammo to use. It's the quickest way to destroy the entire map, which is a shame because it was actually fun to tear up the map in  the original game using all of the weapons at your disposal.The saucer pretty much boils down to PK SLAM, PK SLAM, PK SLAM, PK SLAM.Unless you try to use any of your weapons, in which case the saucer boils down to: TRANSMOG, TRANSMOG, TRANSMOG, destroy 2 buildings, TRANSMOG, TRANSMOG TRANSMOG. God help you if you actually try to use the Death Ray, it takes an absolute age to destroy just a few buildings.As I said. The game isn't bad. It's just buggy and unbalanced. I don't think it's worth boycotting over THQ Nordic censoring a few lines and one mission, but it would be nice if they grew some balls, instead of kowtowing to people who aren't even going to play their games.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun game!If you've played the original PS2 version, it's a prettier and more modern update. If you haven't played the original, it's still a great game! The graphics are nice, the gameplay is solid, the plot is all tounge-in-cheek as well as full of the cheese you'd expect from this series. Instead of being confined to 1950s USA, this game goes worldwide in the 1960s. This means more areas to explore, plenty of jokes about the cultures and tensions of the period, and plenty of opportunities to rain destruction to your heart's content!The game does have a little jank: sometimes enemies will glitch into the terrain (especially when affected by certain physics-bending effects), sometimes textures will flicker during cutscenes, and sometimes items that should be spawning in will fail to do so. It happens very rarely, but is notable when it does - especially if it affects your ability to get 100% in a mission (and forces you to start over from a checkpoint). At no point did this break the game completely, however, just please be aware of it!This is a solid remake of a great classic game, and it's wonderful to have a chance to see it brought forward for a new audience!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is better than the first gameplay wise, but the rest of it is sorely lacking.First of all, the graphics DO look good, but this comes at a price. I wouldn't  say that this game is poorly optimized, but that it's NOT optimized. Without reason, my pc stuttered and lagged out, no matter what settings you have on. Somehow, putting everything on ulta seemed to have less stutters than putting everything on low.The characters and story were extremely disappointing. Now the main crux of the humor isn't that the aliens don't know enough about this world, but that Crypto has genitals and wants to use them. This, along with the crude / referencial jokes I don't really enjoy,  means that the humor was a wash. The story is in the midpoint between taking itself seriously or not, and it  just kinda is uninteresting. The main human character girl is so unimportant and one dimensional that I won't speak about  her. The open world is expanded, but the side quests are honestly bad. You go somewhere, kill someone, then that's it. Or you go in your saucer and hold your beam at people, either to kill them or to convert them. Then repeat the exact same mission in each location. As far as I saw, there is only one way to fail a quest because you botched some dialogue, at the very start of the game. There are also escort missions that are braindead easy (apart from the hive which is nigh impossible without dying midway to refill the girl's health). Also, completing the game is a lot less fun. You're now required to use a guide, not only for the collectibles that you now need to grab (and there are maybe 300 total), but also for the SKATE missions which have a path that is extremely unclear from the  achievement  alone.As for the gameplay... yes, it is fun to use the new weapons and wreck havock with them, but I'm also not too happy about the addition of the Blisk units. Without the upgrades, they're really annoying to beat. And even with the upgrades, you only have a few good options to beat them instead of your whole arsenal, so you're very restricted if you want to be efficient. The lack of regenerating health on body snatching would make it harder, but stealth is hardly ever mandatory,  you can just make people forget and bodysnatch again, and nothing drains your bodysnatch timer anymore, so it's kind of a useless change.In the end, I found this game inferior to the first. I'd only recommend this to people that are insane  about the first game and absolutely want more, or need an alien open world game to play. Otherwise, I think other open world games could be fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been a long time fan of Destroy All Humans! The second game of all 4 is and always will be my favorite of them all. That being said, I cannot recommend this game in good conscience to anyone when compared to the original. Negatives:-Despite a warning telling you they didn't alter anything and put in the same content as the original, this is not true. They took out Dialogue from characters, mind reading lines, and even sped up dialogue in some cases. They didn't even add the trans side mission in-This game is easy. the original is much harder and it doesn't even have options to increase or decease difficulty. However, I played on the hardest difficulty and it was still a breeze. It's genuinely hard to fail a mission which should not be the case-Missions are watered down. The original game made you actually look for the person you were trying to track instead of scanning ONE persons mind and instantly marking it on your map. -The controls are just weird and over complicated. The original game had intuitive controls but Christ man, there are so many different controls in just one button. Not to mention how clunky using your PK abilities are.-Adding in Peter Griffin Bot. If there's one thing I hate, it's when writers think their audience is too stupid to understand what's going on. That little bot should be removed ASAP and is just insulting to the audience.-Side objectives in missions suck. Let me play the game how I want to play it. -Not giving us options in some missions to be on foot or in the saucer UNLIKE the original. let me play the game how I want to play it-Not getting Datacores at same spots as the original. It's okay too let their be datacores in the wild and not have them locked in missions. the mothership was destroyed, it's okay to have SOME scattered in the over world. it's too planned out and feels unnatural -From Bay City to Takoshima, they simplified the map design putting things closer together and it gives an unnatural feeling yet again. LET THE WORLD BREATHE- Some guns feel butchered: the disclocator, anal probe, and meteor strike feel awful.-The saucer sucks and feels underpowered and underwhelming-The gene pool blows chunks. remember how you could  pick up cars and transmog them in bay city in the original? Well now you have to wait until Russia!!! Plus there's a delay on picking them up :)))-general bugs. I can't even load my current game since the new patch.-Kojira instantly killing you unless you play how the game wants you to play it. Oh, and the ending joke about Kojira was removed about what crypto "did" to her, he didn't even throw her change.The Positives:-The graphics and art design are incredible. absolutely beautiful. Honestly probably where all their budget went instead of trying to make a more faithful adaptation of the game.-The moon and Tunguska felt good unlike the other places. missions felt good, some were even kinda challenging. the layouts felt very similar to the originals unlike Bay city, Albion, and Takoshima.-They Handled the Blisk well. I was surprised -Despite butchering the saucer and some of Crypto's guns they did improve how the Burrow Beast functions and the Ion Detonater.There's a lot more to be said. I feel like I barely scratched the surface for issues this game faces. Play the original until they fix this and create a more faithful adaptation. The original is way funnier too.

_childDocuments_.review: Great remake of a classic I played on the original Xbox, along with the first game. However on my copy on xbox it was bugged/seemed to have memory issues. So it's ironic as people in the reviews point out it has performance and bug issues. I didn't actually encounter many bugs (I installed a bug and performance fix mod from nexusmods), and I seem to have brute-forced my way through performance issues with a 3080/ryzen 5 3600; it ran a smooth 80-100+fps the whole way through. It did not run very well on my other PC with a 1060 though, and I think I recall I had played the first remake fine on that PC.A few notes (gripes):Like the first remake (IIRC), the progression system has been changed, and unlocking stuff feels less organic than I remember in the original. In the OG first game (and I think in the OG second, but I don't remember) you collect DNA/brains to unlock stuff and the next mission, which I think was thematically appropriate and gave you more of an excuse to mess about the open world harvesting brains and be an evil maniac. Now in this game, brains seem to only be used for refunding your already spent upgrade points? And you get those after every mission. It just doesn't "feel" right, and it feels like the balance is out of wack with how it went in the original game and when and how you unlock upgrades. It also feels more "gamey" and adds an extra currency that feels divorced thematically compared to just the one OG currency of DNA.On top of that, you get extra upgrade points if you perform certain optional objectives during missions, and these feel straight out of an Ubisoft open world game mission design; they were in the first remake as well.  It's just unnecessary fluff that again, adds little and takes away from the simple thematically appropriate progression in the original... Unless I'm forgetting that the OG games had something similar.Last point about the progression system: There's an enemy type that requires upgrades to be more effective against them. It doesn't matter too much until the final boss, who will regen health faster than you can damage them, which felt really weird. I had to restart the whole mission by refunding and respeccing my upgrades, which is hardly the worst thing, but the final mission kinda sucks (it's an escort mission and a "defend this position while I hack this door" straight out of Destiny) so it was a little frustrating.Final gripe, about the story itself: It's fun especially in the beginning and peaks in the UK, but it kinda devolves into Crypto being a massive misogynist towards the sexy femme fatale character, then he goes kinda incel at one point. I guess "that was the joke" that he's a misogynist, and like, obviously, the guy's an evil alien, and this is a game written for horny teenage boys, but coming back to it and having some resemblance of media literacy that I didn't have as a kid when I first played it, oof, it hasn't aged that well. Probably because his misogyny is instead laughed off and in the end, rewarded (in a kinda... unsettling ending for the femme fatale character where her agency is seemingly removed or sidelined) rather than receiving a comeuppance of some sort. I guess that's the trouble with writing an "evil" story for teenagers of the mid-aughts, alongside other general problems of games writing from the aughts present in this game - such as the game's depiction of Japanese people - but that's a whole other can of worms that I am not equipped to deal with.Anyway, I enjoyed my time. it's an example of a sequel that tries bigger and better with interesting results, for better or worse, but it's more for better, and this remake has finally brought it to PC, although with a few questionable changes just like the first remake.

_childDocuments_.review: What can I say about this game that needs to be said? If you played this game as a kid on the original Xbox or PlayStation 2, I'm sure you will all remember having hours of fun just messing around killing humans and having fun in the sandbox world of DaH2. This remaster just like the first is essentially a face lift and polishing of the original with the same fun missions, weapons and overall fun we all had years back on the original. The textures and visuals have been greatly upgraded in every way and the game overall looks stunning all around. The addition of skins for the saucer and Crypto himself add a nice touch of modern love to the game without changing anything we loved about the original. I did experience a few bugs when I first played on release, but nothing game breaking or unforgivable. The worst things I experienced were a few glitches during missions where I had to restart to continue progressing through the mission I was playing. I believe every one of the glitches I encountered have been fixed and nothing else came to mind when thinking about things I disliked. Maybe it is nostalgia or the fact I love this series, but either way I am very happy with the job that THQ Nordic and Black Forest Games did on reviving a love of my childhood and letting me experience all that joy and fun all over again as an adult. New players will enjoy the game and it's witty humour and silly references but players of the original will be thrilled that a game from their past hasn't been driven into the ground or ruined with a half hearted remaster.As for time played, I completed the remaster of the first DaH! game in around 12 hours with all missions and achievements completed. The game cost £24.99 and was worth the money in my opinion. This remaster of the second game cost a little more than price of the first game at £39.99 but thankfully it lasted a lot longer than the original game with me completing all missions and earning all achievements in just over 26 and a half hours. Again, I think that the game is worth the price I paid for it but others may want to wait until this goes on sale for a little less, maybe more around the £29.99 mark.In conclusion, if you're a new player I think you'll enjoy the game overall and have hours of fun getting to know Crypto, Pox and the beautifully remastered maps, weapons and models in detail. If you're a returning player from the original, I think you'll be very happy with the remaster and will 100% be satisfied with the job THQ Nordic and Black Forest Games have done.

_childDocuments_.review: My experience with the PS2 version of Destroy All Humans 2 was rather limited. While I enjoyed the original back when it was released, I merely rented the sequel. Then my brother-in-law and I just messed around in co-op and I never made it anywhere. However, the fun with physics gameplay left such an impression on me that it’s been on my hit list for years. The problem is, the memory that stuck out most for me was its ugly-as-sin graphics and oppressive draw fog.Thankfully, THQ Nordic and Black Forest Games decided to go all the way with the series and gussy up Destroy All Humans 2 in the same way it did for the original title. That means, while the graphics have been upgraded to the nines, the warts of the PS2-era gameplay are still present underneath. That’s all right with me, though, I eat a couple of early ‘00s games for breakfast every morning, so I am well prepared for warts.Destroy All Humans 2 definitely looks nice. Though the upgrade to the Unreal 4 Engine hasn’t left it without blemishes, it’s obvious the art department at Black Forest Games had an absolute blast with it. The worlds you quest through are all as lush as golf greens. If you’re just looking at the game, it’s almost impossible to tell that it was built on the bones of a much older game.Playing the game is a much different matter. I have already admitted to not having a whole bunch of experience with Destroy All Humans 2, but what little I did play already made it feel as though it was more interested in being a playground than a cohesive game. And in that respect, it provided unusual weapons that screwed with the physics.However, real-time physics was still a pretty novel thing back in 2006. We ended up with actually physics sandboxes like Garry’s Mod. Years later, the novelty has worn off. Seeing a watermelon roll around is so commonplace that we often don’t think to play with them anymore. So while it was almost worth playing Destroy All Humans 2 back in 2006 just to screw around in the environments, it doesn’t really have that to fall back on now, and that kind of blunts the experience.Thankfully, it still knows how to be entertaining. Destroy All Humans 2 takes place ten years after the first game. The Furons, Cryptosporidium-138 and Orthopox-13, are enjoying their subversive takeover of the United States. Crypto has been successfully cloned with working genitalia, and while that may seem like it should be a minor aside, it’s pretty key to the plot of these games. The first Destroy All Humans was a quest to assemble enough Furon DNA to retool a tacklebox, and here we have our heroes reaping the benefits. Crypto has been enjoying humanity’s “free love” counter-cultural movement rather thoroughly, and things kick off in the midst of this. The Mothership is destroyed by the KGB, and Pox and Crypto have to find out why and how humanity is suddenly gunning for them.Damn, that’s good stuff. Once again, Crypto is voiced by J. Grant Albrecht, doing a deliciously over-the-top Jack Nicholson impression, while Orthopox is done by Richard Steven Horvitz – best known for giving vocals to Invader Zim’s titular character – doing his best Invader Zim impression.Orthopox is given a smaller role this time around in favor of a revolving cast of other characters. Although the additional characters are all ridiculously archetypal, they give a good sounding board for Crypto. The dialogue was a big reason why I kept playing; there was always something cutting hidden behind the next choice. Sometimes it was worth it to fail a mission just to see what kind of hole Crypto could dig himself with just his tongue.As they did in the first game, the developers open with a disclaimer notifying you that the humor hasn’t been touched and is still rooted in the primitive age of 2006 as to not hurt the sensitive snowflakes that accidentally pick up this game.t may be damning with praise that the feature I appreciated most in Destroy All Humans 2 is the cutscenes. I do like both carnage and destroying humans, but the weird thing here is that there isn’t as much of that as there should be. The original Destroy All Humans approached its various mission areas by starting you off with subversion before you are let off the leash to wreak havoc, and that isn’t replicated here. Don’t get me wrong, there’s plenty of destruction to be had. It’s just often not evil enough. In fact, there’s very little cohesiveness to the mission structure at all.Take the initial city based on San Francisco, for example. It’s where Crypto learns that the KGB is targeting them, but then the missions are about stopping a mind-altering substance called Revelade. The KGB is apparently using this to subvert the hippy movement into supporting communism. Or something. But the mission design is mostly: destroy Revelade, destroy more Revelade, okay, now destroy more Revelade, fight the boss.The sub-missions make even less sense. I picked up one in San Francisco where a secretary complains about being embarrassed at a company party, so the goal of the mission is to embarrass her further. Why? I don’t even know her. She’s of no importance whatsoever. How does that help anyone? It isn’t even that malicious, she’s clearly capable of embarrassing herself.The fact that Destroy All Humans 2 looks so nice and a lot of effort has clearly gone into updating its worlds makes the disjointed mission design stand out more. You’ve got all these fantastic-looking locations all over the place, but the briefings take place in shady alleys, and action scenes take place indoors or with the most basic backdrops. I’m all aboard with keeping the core gameplay unaltered, but I wouldn’t say no to maybe scooching those story moments to some of the more charming spots.It feels like the worlds are kind of wasted. Parts of them you only really see when seeking out collectibles in the environment. It’s a massive shame.But that shame just highlights Destroy All Humans 2’s biggest problem: it’s incredibly unfocused. It doesn’t do a great job of delivering on the promise of the title, not like the first game did. It feels like the development team was having a great time right up until they realized it all had to be tied together with an actual narrative. That’s another shame since a lot of concepts that could have been better explored were left on the table. What I’m saying is that there was a lot more opportunity for ♥♥♥♥ jokes. It was rated Teen in 2006, but I feel that if one of your weapons is a literal anal probe, there’s probably a bit of breathing room for a few more bangers.Just know what you’re in for. There’s plenty of potential fun to be had in Destroy All Humans 2, it’s just a bit of a mess. And being a fun mess in 2022 isn’t as forgivable as it was in 2006. Personally, I kept playing just to hear more of Cryptosporidium’s razor-sharp attacks on counter-culture, but I definitely would have preferred it if there was a better game supporting it. Meanwhile, I am fully behind giving early-3D games a fresh coat of paint while retaining what made that era special, even if the package is a bit covered in warts.Verdict: 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: A good and mostly faithful remake. Performance is good in DX12 mode, but bad in DX11. I had to download a modded executable to get the game's cutscenes to play in 21:9 aspect ratio, which is disappointing as the first game supported it natively.In retrospect Destroy All Humans 2 is a bit of a disappointing sequel. The first game had a goofy cartoonish atmosphere but could also be fairly dark at times. The genius of Destroy All Humans was the comedic tone mixed with the fact that you are an evil alien sent to conquer Earth and enslave the human race. Destroy All Humans 2, set in 1969, ditches this idea and goes for a full on Austin Powers spy spoof aesthetic. It's a lot more wacky than its predecessor and loses its identity somewhat.In Destroy All Humans 1 there can be no doubt that you are the bad guy, but in Destroy All Humans 2 you basically play the good guy. You're not destroying all humans anymore, you're saving them. There is still an alien invasion, but it's no longer the Furon invasion. Destroy All Humans 2 has Secret Agent Crypto helping his Russian girlfriend Natalya to Save All Humans from the invasion of the Martians. I didn't like this change. Overall the writing is still great, but thematically DAH2 is a lot less interesting than DAH1.

_childDocuments_.review: Like many people have reported, I keep crashing early in the game. First at the cutscene where you meet Coyote Bongwater, and later during the fight against him. I've seen various other accounts by people experiencing consistent crashing during a quest far later into the storyline, so this seems to be an issue throughout the game.As of writing this up, the game has been out for five months, so while I could complain that such bugs at the very beginning of the game should be fixed immediately, I'll see where the game is when it nears the first year marker. Such bugs definitely shouldn't exist even at launch, let alone this far after release, so hopefully they'll be addressed and won't be neglected. It seems that the very reason this game exists - to provide a modern HD remake of the original - is the very source of the game's crippling issue; the devs were too ambitious with high res flashy visuals that most computers can't handle; you'd almost think it were made on Unreal Engine 5.For now, I'd say hold off on the game unless you absolutely feel like you need it. I had just bought and played through the first game not too long ago without issue. So that, coupled with nostalgia and a 25% off sale, are the only reasons I bought it, and will be the only reasons I won't get a refund. But I doubt I can even play it anytime soon. Hopefully fixes are rolled out sooner than later, because I have missed this game.Additionally, some have discovered that this remake has removed content from the original release in an effort to sanitize it for modern audiences, despite the game featuring a literal warning label claiming that nothing was removed from the original release and thus may offend modern sensibilities. So if that's something you take umbrage with, do keep it in mind.Edit: Despite my best efforts, I simply cannot move past the boss fight against Coyote Bongwater, even when lowering my graphics to far below what my computer can actually tolerate, leading me to suspect that the game is just not optimized for itself. _childDocuments_.review: Much like the remake from 2020, its the same game as the original DAH! 2 with updated graphics and lighting, while also adding major quality of life improvements. These QOL improvments include proper ADS, checkpoints during missions and a bunch of other little things. In addition, this version also includes local coop campaign from the original version in addition to a tennis minigame and a PVP deathmatch game mode. Compared to the remake of the original, you have more weapons, areas are bigger, you have a map for each of the five areas, actual fun side missions and a bunch more stuff. Overall, If you enjoyed the humor and gameplay from the first one, you will definitely enjoy this game and it is a must-buy for those who loved the original.However, to get into some negatives about the game, the multiplayer modes can only be played locally even though this game released today. I'm aware that this was the case with the original, but I've never really understood the idea of having a game release on PC with local coop only, as this forces players to either use Steam remote play or third party software such as Parsec (which is definitely better). Another major negative is that the multiplayer tanks FPS performance pretty significantly, with dips as low as 15-20. FPS improved significantly when i messed around with the settings and put everything on high, but it was quite a bummer seeing as how I was able to run the game with all settings cranked to max in single player with no frame drops or issues. Speaking of issues, this game also has some random texture pop-ins during cutscenes which were not present in the original game or the 2020 remake of the 1st game. While the latter two problems that I mentioned are fixable, I don't personally see themselves putting an online option for the multiplayer. 4/5 (4.5-5/5 once they fix the issues I was talking about)

_childDocuments_.review: Certainly! Buckle up, fellow earthlings, because we’re about to dive into the zany world of “Destroy All Humans! 2”. Grab your ray guns, polish your flying saucers, and prepare for a review that’s more twisted than a pretzel at an alien picnic.“Destroy All Humans! 2”: An Extraterrestrial RaveIntroduction:Picture this: It’s the swinging '60s, bell-bottoms are in, and the Cold War is hotter than a jalapeño on a summer day. And right in the middle of all this chaos? Our favorite little green menace, Crypto, back for another round of cosmic mischief.Plot Summary:Crypto’s got a new gig: infiltrate Earth’s grooviest cities, impersonate humans, and generally wreak havoc. But wait, there’s a twist! This time, he’s not just vaporizing cows; he’s also moonwalking at discotheques and attending alien support groups. Yes, you heard that right—alien support groups. Because even extraterrestrials need a shoulder to cry on when their ray guns malfunction.Gameplay:Crypto’s abilities have evolved faster than a TikTok trend. He’s got telekinesis, a jetpack, and a weapon arsenal that would make Tony Stark jealous. Want to disintegrate a nosy neighbor? Zap! Need to abduct a politician? Beam 'em up! And let’s not forget the anal probe—because nothing says “intergalactic diplomacy” like a probing session.Side Quests:“Destroy All Humans! 2” doesn’t just stop at world domination. Oh no, it throws in side quests that are wilder than a psychedelic trip. From helping Elvis record his greatest hits (yes, the King is an alien groupie) to teaching Bigfoot how to twerk (don’t ask), Crypto’s to-do list is more eclectic than a thrift store vinyl collection.City Hopping:The game takes us to iconic locations like Las Vegas, where Crypto can gamble, cheat at poker, and win big (because who needs a casino when you have alien mind control?). Then there’s Tokyo, where he karaoke-battles Godzilla and accidentally becomes a J-pop sensation. Move over, Beyoncé; Crypto’s in town!Humor:The humor in “Destroy All Humans! 2” is so sharp, it could slice a watermelon. The dialogue is snappier than a rubber band, and the satire? Oh boy. Whether it’s mocking conspiracy theorists or turning Area 51 into a tourist attraction, the game’s wit is as dry as a Martian desert.Soundtrack:Imagine Jimi Hendrix jamming with E.T. Yep, that’s the vibe. The soundtrack features '60s hits, alien remixes, and the occasional cow mooing in auto-tune. It’s like Woodstock meets Roswell, and it’s groovy, man.Conclusion:“Destroy All Humans! 2” isn’t just a game; it’s a cosmic acid trip. It’s the kind of experience that makes you question reality, wonder if your neighbor is secretly a lizard person, and laugh until your ray gun overheats. So grab your tinfoil hat, hop in your saucer, and remember: When life gives you humans, make crop circles!

_childDocuments_.review: Before I start, let me state that this would be a neutral review if it was an option. If you are curious about this game, I recommend waiting for a nice sale. As someone who loved the original, I was really looking forward to this remake. At first glance it is amazing, that is until you notice all the little details that they removed and how buggy this game can be. To begin, this game is beautiful to look at. Its fun to skate around and destroy. The missions did not age well as most are boring, but then again I feel the same about the og. However, you start to notice corners cut when remaking this game and changes here and there. Like how the cutscene for traversing to a different region is removed, the menus are more simplistic and lack charm. Or little details from the og that are missing like hitting the gongs in Takoshima no longer summon ninjas. Small details, but they add soul and charm to the game. It also seems there were things censored with a mission removed, altered cutsences, and  removed/altered voice lines. Lastly, and this is a personal thing, I hate games that just spoil your later unlocks. The remake of the first game, and this one shows you all the gun icons and names. Same issue as with Miles Morales, but whatever.Next I'll go over the bugs I've encountered so far. Some game breaking, some not. I've had the dislocator put people into the ground with no way to kill them forcing mission restarts (thank god for checkpoints), cars bugging out and traveling into buildings, into the sea, and spinning. Then I have gotten into deathloops where if I failed a mission it put me back right to when I got my gameover instead of the checkpoint leading to an infinite loading screen. Ninja's teleporting onto my saucer and crashing my game. Randomly crashing in Takoshima when just traversing in my saucer causing me to lose progress. Then there is the whole getting the quantum deconstructor and sonic boom early, fun but breaks missions to have the deconstructor early. I know this isn't a bug, but i'll list it here: the AI here is horrible at times. I don't use protect anymore as sometimes the AI wont even fight for me. tl;dr If they fix the bugs and glitches then this would be a recommend, perferbaly on a sale due to the removed details and content.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR SECTION:I was sitting on the fence on whether this game get's 'barely a pass if you can get it for 15 bucks' or 'just not quite worth your money.' Despite the re-master being more than half-a-year old there are countless performance issues that the game 1 remaster at launch simply didn't have. That was as smooth as a baby's butt. This pile of trash has horrible fps drops no matter what settings you play on. Bugs that force you to re-load a check point as some objectives are uncompletable. But the final straw were the crashes that just outright forced you to re-do entire missions. Don't buy it. HAVE LITERALLY NOTHING BETTER TO DO SO I WILL WASTE EVEN MORE TIME READING YOUR REVIEW SECTION:Having gotten the TLDR section out of the way, and the primary reason as to why you shouldn't buy this game, there are more issues which I will elaborate here. I love racist and offensive stereotypes as much as your average 1930s German, but it does reach a point where it becomes stale when you bash drug addled hippies for the 514th time or every Russian you encounter uses 'ski' at the end of every noun and professes his love for vodka at the end of every conversation.In equal measure the sex jokes become boring and repetitive pretty fast. A substantial portion of the side-quests – that are all structured pretty similarly by the way – has you reviving an ancient sexual cult/god. It feels like the dialogue was written by a horny 15yo boy who thinks he's so zany because he watches ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ 6 hours per day and thinks that mentioning 'HAHA SEX' at every opportunity remains hilarious forever. It's just a phase, man. Now tuck your ♥♥♥♥ back into your pants. As such I skipped doing the side-quests at one point and just focused on the main quests instead. There is a problem with pacing here, because quite unlike the first game, what you have to do is go to a person on the map, then initiate a conversation, during which the details of the mission are explained to you in dialogue form. Rather than just starting them from a menu. Yet none of the missions handed to you are so difficult that they require much explanation, and the developers could have done a better job, like just start the mission and have the quest-giver explain to you what you need to do as you go along, instead of being locked into dialogue sessions. Without joking, some dialogues are longer than the missions you have to do. Especially when you also factor in that you have to travel to the quest giver now, often requiring you to skate across the map for the umpteenth time. They seriously could have just copypasted the way they did it in game 1 but for some reason they decided to make the simple formula of the predecessor more difficult, which doesn't translate well for a game based entirely on one-dimensional characters. There are even dialogue options now believe it or not, and outside of some quests-objective-related ones these literally have no impact beyond Crypto making another condescending joke about humanity or sexually suggestive comment to Natalya, your Russian blonde bimbo KGB sidekick. This isn't an RPG.I have already mentioned bugs in the TLDR sections but they extend beyond just performance or quest related ones as well. NPCs T-posing, vehicles not having the correct weight proportions, crypto sometimes not responding to key input. These really aren't worth mentioning if the rest of the game was stable and good, but it isn't, so I do mention them. F you. It's not all bad though, I mean if you had fun in game 1 you will probably enjoy 2 to some extent as well. But it does feel a bit like clubbing a dead seal and makes you question whether every good game really needs a follow-up. All ideas and settings have a shelf life and it seems that for Destroy all Humans that was limited to just one game.Crypto himself and his saucer do get an expanded arsenal of weapons and abilities, but unfortunately most of these add little to the gameplay and the original arsenal is objectively superior. They are more like 'five minutes of fun' features rather than something that adds a new dimension to the game, or Crypto actually needing some of the new weaponry to combat new enemies. A fully upgraded disintegrator can mop the floor with literally everything in the game, and PK can also deal with basically everything human. Yes there are new enemies in the form of space crabs (yawn) that seem to be immune to PK, but like I said the disintegrator can deal with them too.The only new weapon that really stood out to me was the meteor strike weapon. It basically opens up a giant portal in the sky and bombards the targeted location with meteors. (what big F'ing surprise considering the weapon's name) Visually quite impressive and as far as I know the only way crypto has of destroying buildings quickly while on foot. Unfortunately however, with limited ammo and quite a lengthy charge-up the usefulness of this weapon is situational at best when used in actual combat situations. As my final statement, I will say that I have played the original destroy all humans 1 back when it came out in 2005 or something, but not 2. So there may be nostalgia involved as to why I liked 1 better than 2. Regardless, I think that the pacing, bugs, performance issues, story, setting and mission structure makes this one inferior to its predecessor.

_childDocuments_.review: Ah, Destroy All Humans 2. One of the absolute best parts of my childhood. As someone who poured many hours into the original (not leaving Bay City much since I was scared of The Blisk), I can saw with utmost confidence that this is almost definitively the best way to play the game. The one thing not improved from the original is the Dislocator, which bounces instead of flying around this time. With a handy collectible tracker that doesn't trivialise finding secrets, new bonus objectives which add an extra oomph to the missions, and a 99% preserved original feel, this is the kind of remake the original deserved.In order to make certain missions more interesting, this remake also reworks key scenes. For example, the Coyote Bongwater boss fight took place in a boring, empty bunker type place that made for an uninteresting fight. The remake has the Revelade dart Crypto's been hit with cause him to hallucinate a far more interesting arena loaded with cool little details.There are a bunch of glitches that I should mention, like Blisked civilians in the mission they're introduced getting stuck under the floor if you use the wrong weapon or enemies failing to spawn, but they didn't hurt my overall opinion.The only thing missing is the quest "Ruined! - Take It Like A Man!", which depicts Crypto outing a trans woman for being transphobic while in the closet, and that's the kind of PR nightmare you just can't risk in today's climate. The quest itself was pretty weak anyway, only having you bodysnatch and walk to a phone. There's not really any challenge or choice of approach. While it was progressive to have Crypto call out transphobia in the original, the outing thing is way too far and isn't funny like Crypto's other antics.Overall, if you're a fan of DAH2 and looking to play it all over again with shinier graphics that have a distinct style instead of the original's kinda lifeless look, this is the game for you. Here's hoping for a Big Willie Unleashed or Path of the Furon remaster, remake, or even a new game entirely. At this point I wouldn't have any other studio pick up the reins. Crypto's back, baby, and he's not messing around!
