_childDocuments_.review: In some feat of preposterous litigious contractual obligation with Epic, WRC10 has shown up on Steam before WRC9. So at the time of writing this, this game has already been superseded.  But let's take a closer look anyways because I come to this series — largely — for the career mode.Career mode is by far the most interesting aspect of WRC. You'll do manufacturer/sponsor tryouts, hire and manage crew fatigue/morale by performing well and adding rest days into the calendar. Perform training, earn money to pay for repairs in-between events. You actually perform this by responding to an email after the event is over. You're able to hire PR agents so that better potential crew members start applying as you gain reputation. Other features beyond the obvious mechanics like engineers to improve repairs allow you to hire meteorologists for a more accurate forecast to help decide what type of tires you should use for an upcoming set of events.You'll have access to R+D to improve durability, crew malleability and decrease tire wear. More XP can be earned through training events. You can also partake in historical races as well as modern.Juxtaposed to the career mode in DiRT Rally 2, they're nearly incomparable. WRC9 offers a much more robust career.I would not compare this series with the main DiRT series as that series always kind of was, but is most assuredly now, as far away from sim racing as you can get without adding rockets. So, I see the WRC series mainly competing for the attention of those playing still DiRT Rally 1 or 2 or even Sébastien Loeb Rally Evo — which was made by Milstone Srl, who has not been the developer of any WRC game since WRC4. But KT Racing has done relatively fine thus far. To use my  — if 1 is Ridge Racer, 2 is the main DiRT Series, Forza Horizon/Project Gotham Racing and a 4 is BeamNG/Assetto Corsa. WRC9 is a 2.5 — right off-center. This is due to the physics being hit and miss in practice yet the intention of being realistic keeps it from being too arcade-y.In career mode, you'll have access to increased grip and reliability on certain types of surfaces should you spec into that direction with R+D. Which seems a bit at odds with what the game is trying to be, as outside of career mode those features are effectively absent. However, I can't be certain there isn't some trickery — in that, there is lowered durability and grip, among other things, in the start of the career but the aim is to then raise them back to normal through R+D.The surfaces all feel quite different in WRC. Whereas DiRT Rally they all feel vaguely the same — there's really no discernible difference in the way gravel and snow feel in DiRT Rally for example. In WRC, the differences are much more apparent. That said, if your tires stay on the ground, the physics feel pretty good. But it's unlikely you'll have all four on the ground at all times. Having what would be a relatively minor scrape can turn into a giant disaster as your car becomes a toy and bobbles around until the tires come back to Earth.To reiterate and be more concise, if not reductive, I'm typically not a person that cares a great deal about visuals, but when the purpose of the game is to be realistic in the first place, it feels appropriate to comment on. I don't think this game looks that impressive, but  This whole series seems to use some odd rendering technique that makes everything seem hollow — even at the highest settings. I'm not sure how else to really explain it as I don't know the particular way it's being rendered but everything always seems like it's paper-thin. Were I to venture a guess, it may be an extension of the way the cars feel like they don't weigh very much but also drag themselves across the entire track on a menial turn — and when conflated with the way trees sort of  as you drive, some sort of LoD load-in presumably, (I use an m.2 NVME SSD) the visual component and car movement add up to a very surreal feeling world. And I don't think that's intentional.However, visually speaking, I think the game stands out in its weather, terrain and water effects. Especially in the extreme conditions events where thunderstorms and wind are knocking you around and moving the shrubbery about. One of the more interesting aspects of WRC is that the weather can change dynamically throughout a race.WRC has a much, much better track selection than DiRT Rally.There are daily and weekly challenges, but they pale in comparison to DiRT Rally, that's where DiRT Rally really shines. Online modes for WRC include drive clubs and e-sport events. There are also challenges outside the career and dailies that reward points that unlock more challenges.There are six VOs for the co-driver. There is also a colorblind mode.The damage modeling is decent, mechanically affecting the car — difficulty options available.Codemasters has acquired the WRC license exclusively going forward (at the time of writing) — who have themselves been acquired by EA. They've obtained the rights during the years 2023-2027. I do not know how this will affect the WRC series from Nacon. As in, I don't know if will there a be a WRC 11 or 12 or if these older games will be removed from the store entirely. — As an isolated product, it's quite enjoyable and offers a lot of content. However in context of the entire WRC series — absolutely nothing stands out about it. It's more of the same from WRC8. And there's nothing  wrong with that. But it's very difficult to suggest this one over any other one, I would wait for a sale on any of them.All said, if you're like me and enjoy rally sims as a sort of 'go-to' for in-between other games, the dailies, weeklies and monthlies that DiRT Rally offer might be more up your alley. Because the ones here are not terribly compelling.My WRC8 review

_childDocuments_.review: WRC10 is probably better than this one, but this one was a little cheaper and honestly the improvements don't seem that big.Career mode: 10/10, includes both driving and management aspects, rivals the depth of the F1 games career and it's a lot more in-depth than Dirt Rally 2.0's career mode.Physics: 8.5/10, solid rally sim physics. Better on tarmac than Dirt Rally 2.0, really good on gravel too, but probably a bit too forgiving on snow/ice. I can't say for sure, since I've never driven a WRC car in real life obviously. Could be that they have unholy levels of grip on snow.Car physics/quality: 8/10 on the WRC cars, but a 6/10 on the historic ones. If you wanna drive group b, group a, stuff like that, Dirt Rally 2.0 does a much better job on those. As you would expect, the big effort went on the licensed WRC cars.Car sounds: 4/10. I've played PS1 games that sound better. Engine sounds weirdly robotic at times, and there's 0 ambience too, you'll enter tunnels and hear no reverb whatsoever. Could be that Dirt Rally 2.0 raised the bar too high on that one, but rally cars are some of the best sounding cars in the world and this game definitely don't do them justice in that regard.Stages: 10/10, the best stages I've ever seen in any rally game except maybe for the rallysimfans mod for Richard Burns Rally. They're as close as you'll get to the real ones, and they're not watered down or made wider to simplify your life. My personal favorite gotta be the japan rally, especially ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Super tight tarmac goodness. This game completely blows dirt rally out of the water when it comes to stages, except maybe for monte carlo, I find Dirt's interpretation of sweden to be scarier, but that has more to do with the ice physics being superior in that game.Gamepad support: if you're not a hardcore simracer, you're probably gonna try to play this on gamepad. It's definitely my case. This game wasn't made for gamepad, but I find it to be reasonably playable. My tip is, remove deadzone, it will make the controls much more precise and less twitchy. With the default settings, tarmac stages are undrivable on gamepad. Gamepad support in Dirt 2.0 offers a lot more options and it's a lot better, but this one is definitely viable. Just be aware the sensitivity is very high even on low settings, so learning to make small analog inputs is key. Multiplayer: 6/10, would be a 7 but the e-sports stuff is probably gonna happen on WRC 10 from now on, so all that's really left is the daily challenges which are pretty underwhelming compared to what dirt has to offer.   Difficulty and difficulty options: 10/10. This game is perfect as a "my first rally sim" experience, because you can considerably nerf the AI on carreer mode and use upgrades and perks to make the driving easier if you're struggling, and unlike dirt 2.0, it offers infinite restarts in all game modes, so if you crashed badly (it WILL happen to you) you have the option of trying again. But at the same time, the game has some of the most challenging stages to drive on, the WRC cars are probably the fastest cars since the group b era, which makes it even harder, you can crank the AI difficulty pretty high, and if you really feel hardcore, you can use the permacrash option on your carreer mode, which basically means you can't restart stages if you mess up. So this game is both the most accessible rally game, and one of the most difficult ones, depending on what you want.Do I recommend this game? Yes, if it is on sale, and if you're a huge rally fan and/or like brutally difficult driving games. But as I said earlier, WRC 10 is probably exactly the same game as this but with improvements and e-sports stuff happening.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, coming from DR 2.0, this is not the same quality level but I knew it right from the start. Having a GeForce 1060 GTX, purchasing WCR 10 would have been a waste of money since this game needs far better specs, but WCR 9 is "old" enough for my GPU.I still love Dirt 2.0 but I wanted more tracks.Good to know :a) With a Logitech G920, use Logitech Gaming software instead of GHub, this would avoid experiencing freezes in game.b) Standard wheel parameters are not fine, so you need to find parameters from other people and finetune them personnally, especially force and vibration levels according to your own preferences. c) Do NOT use ENTER/RETURN when starting the game, otherwise the game believes you want to drive with a keyboard and you need to select the wheel. I know this is stupid, but this is the way it is, use the wheel button when entering the game. d) The cockpit view is dark and unplayable but there is a solution, on racedepartment select "WCR9 care package v 1.11" available here: e) Unfortunately the wonderful WCR 9 full mod by AgentHex 0007 does not work with this version on Steam, see the"WCR 9 Mods 1.0 Update 8" available here: I like the game for the following reasons ;a) for the extra tracks Dirt Rally does not have, such as Kenya, Japan, or Italy, and others.b) Finland rally was criticized by many people but this is my preferred one since the vehicle has more space/room to move (as in Kenya).c) it works on my old PC (7 years)d) This is a nice distraction from Dirt 2.0 I still love.e) Quick play is marvellous, you select a car, a track and that's it (I do not care a lot about the "campaign").f) Toyota Corolla 1999 (being part of the full version including all DLCs) and Lancia Delta Integrale are the best cars according to me, I am not a fan of modern cars which are the most represented in this game. I deeply regret the absence of the Subaru among cars in category "Legends". Keep in mind that some cars are unplayable such as Porsche or Lancia Stratos. The nr of cars is limited in this game.g) It works well with a wheel, after all the game has the full support of Fanatec but I saw that it is also playable with a gamepad. You better feel the car with a wheel in Dirt 2.0 than in WCR 9. WCR 9 is more an arcade game whereas Dirt 2.0 is rather a simulation. If you feel a little bit tired, it is best to play with WCR 9 since Dirt 2.0 does not forgive anything... However WCR 9 is far from easy since the wheel works best with Dirt 2.0 than with WCR 9 and the game still remains demanding in terms of concentration. h) If you also have a gamepad on top of a wheel, you can play in split screen with a friend on the same PC, something Dirt Rally does not have (even if Dirt Rally has VR, unlike WCR 9). I still regret the good old time when games were playable on LAN (like Codemasters Colin McRae Rally 2.0), it was fun to see others, internet is so impersonal.In conclusion you can own Dirt Rally 2.0 along with WRC 9 in peaceful coexistence, both games are made for different public and purpose. Having more tracks in Dirt Rally (especially Kenya and Japan) would have been perfect but WRC 9 with Toyota Corolla 1999 is really enjoyable even on an old PC.My specs : Asus ROG2 G20CB, i7-6700 CPU 3.40 GHz, GeForce 1060 GTX 6GB, 16GB RAM, 1TB HDD, Triple screen configuration with Apple Cinema Led Display 27 inch, Logitech G920.I purchased the game at 6 €, I would have never spent 40 € for it. Wait for promotions.

_childDocuments_.review: WRC 9, for me, is kind-of similar to Dirt Rally 2.0 in terms of realistic-simulation-ish physics. But both games are my favorite don't get me wrong. And this is also my first time playing WRC series rally game as well.So, for the good things I've experience from WRC 9:- The handling is absolutely satisfying to steer, even on 4WD, FWD or RWD. - For the feel of driving on different surfaces, it is fine and , but the good thing is it feels right when driving on tarmac/asphalt compare to whatever the heck Dirt Rally 2.0 does with its horrendous physics. - And for the rally tracks, as I am aware since I done some research before, is hand-made and even some of them are very exciting and challenging to play with, which is a win!- And there are plenty selection for tires types too, even though I didn't really care, but its a nice touch compare to Dirt Rally 2.0.- Adding more fun to a racing game is a must, and I'm very glad that WRC includes a split-screen mode too! Plus, I never though that a co-driver mode is possible too, which is very cool (Even though I can't find any match to try out)Other than that, I do have some negative when playing WRC 9:- Remember that I said the feeling on driving different surface is just "fine"? Well yea, this game only does an amazing job on replicating tarmac/asphalt grip but not really on gravel and some other surfaces, cuz those are either slippery or very slippery.- Car variety are extremely lacking, like seriously about 23 types of vehicles to choose from? And almost majority of the vehicle behaves the same in terms of performance and behavior. Come on, Dirt Rally 2.0 does that better with 81 cars (included DLC)- When talking about hand-made tracks, I understand trying to balancing out the feel of "too much corner" vs "bruh that was easy" is difficult, but seriously, some of the tracks have waaay too much cornering and it felt like the road is build by an idiot civil engineer.- Micro-stutter are notable when observing closely, but not destructive. Just pointing that out. - Game's audio presentation is extremely lacking. Simply speaking, audio is horrendous, from vehicle sounded like boiling water to someone putting gravel in a can and shake it to simulate gravel. Its just so horrible that I rather listen to the co-driver than whatever the sound they produce. - Career is not bad, but tedious and unnecessary imo. I appreciate managing crew morale, manufacture morale, unlocking perks and stuff is pretty standard for patting out content, but again, a lot of stuff literally is just role-playing a rally organisation that I don't care. (and I just wanna drive)Overall, WRC 9 is pretty solid game, although content wise is lacking in terms of vehicle varieties and tracks, but it can mostly be excused by the extra split-screen and unique co-driver mode as an additional fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm giving this game a thumb up, because I enjoyed it, but overall, if I could, I would give it a neutral score.This is essentially WRC 8.1, as there is some additional content and some tweaks under the hood, but nothing that couldn’t be released in the form of patches and DLC packs for the base game. _childDocuments_.review: I am a 50 yo male, most likely one of the more mature people playing this game. One Sunday afternoon, as I was driving my wife and son home from church, it started to downpour heavily. I thought nothing of it as I was driving my Camry on the same highway I always take. Out of nowhere, as I was going about 80 mph, the car started going sideways. The next thing I knew I was on a hospital bed with a cast and the dullness of pain veiled by painkillers. As soon as I had regained full mental capacity, I was told that my wife had been thrown out of the vehicle as it tumbled after hydroplaning but is recuperating in the other room, but then the doctor trailed off into silence as he saw the questioning look in my eye. It's been two years since and we stopped going to church altogether. Although I could cope with the loss as time numbs the memory, my wife could not...she became more and more addicted to prescription painkillers and always washed them down with wine. Not a day goes by without these crutches, and believe me, I've tried every option to help her. A big part of me blamed myself: Was I going too fast? Should I have checked the tread depth? If we had gone to the diner instead until the rain passed would this still have happened? After numerous sessions at the shrink, I finally took his advice on potentially getting over this guilt and PTSD. So I bought WRC and a wheel. At first, I'd thought it was just a driving game. But then the dynamic weather started pouring down on me and I had a flashback to that day when I flipped the wipers on. At first I teared up, but then I got angry and started driving as fast as I could, hitting every puddle on the way until the FFB grounded to a halt. By the time I finished the career mode, I realized it wasn't my skills or anything I did wrong to cause this tragedy. Sadly, my wife refused to try this remedy, calling it "childish" and dove back into her hill of pills. I was hoping there would be a VR mode so I can somehow get her to try a new tech fad, but sadly it isn't supported. Although this game will never bring my son back, I felt a tremendous weight lifted off my shoulder and am at peace, knowing my son is in a better place. This game is a life saver, will never be uninstalled.

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah so I really like this rally game, it is similar as WRC10 but it doesn't have the time bug of WRC10 in Monaco, where when you drive on the stages that are mixed surface stages between tarmac and snow/ice, you start lagging behind the AI that it seems drives way over a reasonable threshold where it will charge 20-30 seconds or more ahead of you on the snow parts of those stages, now. I am kind of mixed on this because at first I thought that this adds to the challenge but if I in WRC10 race in Monaco and gain on every tarmac stage 20-30-40 seconds on the AI and lose a lot or all of that advantage on those mixed tarmac and snow/ice stages putting the AI to anything high like 130% makes me by default lose Monaco stage, which is just frustrating and in this sense WRC games of Nacon seem to all have some issues like for instance.WRC Generations has kind of IMHO totally different physics than any previous WRC games by Nacon before it, which coupled with the throttle bug on that game I really cannot drive and enjoy WRC Generations, even if I really want to. I have driven WRC Generations with the mouse and keyboard in the past and the throttle bug didn't matter if I had used like mouse and keyboard to race in that game. Then the throttle bug doesn't matter really (if you're racing with the controller for instance, I think) and the physics are kind of good but as soon as I start using my steering wheel in WRC Generations that game sort of falls flat for me, and that's a big pity because that's basically only game available on the market that has the new hybrid WRC cars which are really cool and fast to drive but in this sense yeah. New WRC game from that other developer that comes out might just be the perfect replacement for WRC Generations where it's lacking because WRC9 and WRC10 are really good games with again WRC10;WRC10 has this bug where driving in Monaco on mixed tarmac / snow/ice stages the AI really drives too fast. If I put the AI difficulty too low then the rest of Monaco becomes a joke and I can't dynamically drive, to push or to be cautious to simulate a battle against the AI but if I put it too hard there is no chance to catch up. It's a big problem for me in that game because WRC10 compared to WRC9 has better physic albeit slightly, because:WRC9, this game that I'm writing a sort of review or opinion piece on I really like. It's really good and catches IMHO pretty well what it would be to drive rally just that WRC10 has slightly better physics and there are more options in WRC10 compared to WRC9 that make the experience in WRC10 slightly better / more streamlined.WRC8, that one's too archaic by now. It has an understeer issue which makes the racing experience not so pleasant. It still is kind of good and the thing is that WRC8 might have different cars available you can do a championship with than there are in WRC9/10 etc.. But the gameplay doesn't feel great like it in WRC9 and 10 is. Regardless to say.Despite of their bugs the games are nice, from WRC9 to WRC Generations even though if often like each of them seems to have their own baby issues. WRC9 is for instance somewhat old by now I think but in conclusion it is a very good rally game, it feels the least buggy and I wish that WRC10 and WRC Generations were as polished or as bug free as WRC9 is.All in all I can't say that Nacon WRC adventure that lasted a few years was a failure because the games that I have played are overall good and for me with a steering wheel now are as fun as Drit Rally 2.0 is, in which case Dirt 2.0 is by now also quite old and so here is hoping that the new Codemasters WRC game will be the perfect package that's most up to date, most polished and most realistic.I love rally games, ever since Richard Burns Rally in essence and these Nacon games were a nice experience while they lasted, truth is times change and things may become better and that's a lesson perhaps for (future) developers. Listen to your playerbase and please try to implement these changes that people are in essence begging for, because if you can't or don't then for instance as developers if you allow modders to freely mod your games, they WILL fix all the teething issues your games are left with due to restrains like time or budget limitations. I can't see bugs or shortcomings being a conscious design choice and the reality is that some of Nacon games have these leftovers in them.Nacon WRC experience was good while it lasted and overall has left me with most predominantly a sort of bitter sweet feeling because after WRC Generations, it has come to the end of an era, that could have here and there been somewhat better. WRC9 is solid though, but old by now.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not sure how this game isn't more highly rated. This is better in every way then the games that followed it (especially generations)The game is far more realistic then WRC7. Tho I'm really sad they got rid of the engine sound from 7, that was so good.But yeah, this game's career mode is excellent. It's actually really challenging to drive, because the game punishes you a lot for mistakes. Repairs take very long, so the more you advance, the longer rallies get and the harder it is to actually get to the end of a rally. You have a crew that give you bonuses and you spend skill points into better resilience or speed etc for the car, as you lvl up.Driving feels great. The setup and assists actually affect the car a LOT so be sure to mess with those to find your own difficulty. Game sounds great, looks great, good amount of stages and it's a ton of fun. Not as realistic as Dirt rally, but it's up there as one of the most fun rally games I've played.Also this game has something I've dreamed of for a long time. A co-op mode where you can play as driver and co-driver. The problem is, it's pretty poorly implemented. The pace notes aren't detailed and the game connection fails and start to desync after a stage or 2. Also you can't play an entire rally, just one stage at a time and you get a stupid score....wish they fleshed out this mode some more...But yeah, Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Well KT have flipped things around, their latest titles (WRC 9 for me) keep setting the bar higher compared to CM which have dropped the ball so low at this point, WRC is the Go-To game for your rally needs on Steam. Like I've mentioned in previous WRC reviews, KT have really found the sweet spot for a simcade rally game, you'll have fun and enjoy the rallies, going flatout in the 21km Finland stage is excellent, then take the very tight Japanese rally and you have a bit of everything. Their Single Player Career mode is very well executed and the soundtrack was tasteful.I play these games with a Xbone pad so I can't comment on wheel issues that other people have reported.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is good, however I think it has the same problem a lot of racing games have in that it doesn't do a great job of conveying speed in third person camera mode. This is a problem in particular in a rally game because there are so many rocks, ditches, ect. Hitting one of them and then completely flipping out or crashing can feel unfair or not right, until you look at your speed the next time you do it and see you're doing about 140km/ph. For this reason I found the game much more enjoyable in the cars first person camera, it better conveys speed and you can find your lines a bit better as well. The one thing I don't really like is some of the arcadey simulation, like having to do a race to do maintenance on your car. Which doesn't even make sense and is also just a time sink when I would rather be doing some other event. The "simulaiton" kinda stuff feels more like a half thought out slog, when you'd rather just be rallying.

_childDocuments_.review: Finally the game has come to steam! Since WRC 10 also is available this review will most be a comparison of these two games.WRC 9 is on its own an excellent rally game which share many similarities with WRC 10, though WRC 10 include considerable more cars and content. The stages are superb in both games with some countries in WRC 9 not showing in WRC 10 and vice versus.  Graphics quality is good, with very much details. Engine sound is also good but the quality of some soundeffects like crashes are low (much better in WRC 10).WRC 9 has a slightly different car handling compared to WRC 10: less tyregrip, game is a liitle less forgiving, bumps in the road seems to have greater impact on car/driving as also waterpuddles have and rockmaterial in the roadside have a greater influence on car behaviour. Also tracks seem more bumpy. Now, all these things are good, making WRC 9 a  rough rally experience, less easy and maybe more more realistic in terms of the handling than WRC 10. However I think both games have a superb handling model.WRC 9 doesn't have mandatory tyre management in career (like WRC 10), best tyres are automatically chosen but you can also make your own choice.If you alredy own WRC 10 I recommend to buy this game on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: As seen by a casual gamer with a life long passion for rally and racing games that enjoys playing on keyboard and external camera view.WRC 9 brings everything we liked about WRC 8, with upgraded content, fixes, better graphics, and a disappointingly late release on SteamStrong :✔ It's been a while that WRC has been recycling things. Menus, team building mechanisms, skill points, cars and more. For some reason I did not feel bad about it. Maybe because I think that these things are well designed and they just work. So what's the strength of that? Well lots and lots of bug fixes. They basically preferred to take what already works pretty well, and tried to deliver a cleaner, efficient, better performant version of it.✔ Same tracks and cars with a lot more detail. A lot of graphical updates. More detail. Better reflection quality. Better weather effects. Better splash effects. Better detail of dirt (no pun intended). Internal car design is also better and more detailed. External camera view on nigh tracks don't make the driver dashboard lights glow like a neon torch out of the back window any more.✔ Visual car damage is finally awesome to look at!!! And feels even better when you activate the realistic damages difficulty, giving a spicy sense of challenge to the races✔ Sounds design is better than before. So much better! In fact the sound of tires, environment and engine is super enjoyable. The sound the beaks make when you hit them is addictive in the beginning, And also some times I noticed that the tires make different sound over different types of gravel which brought a smile in my face.✔ Very good optimization. Better FPS that WRC 8, better draw distances and my GPU did not have to be fired up to run the higher specs. Weak :❌Couple of old bugs not fixed yet (car falling off the podium, getting off road could make the car "float" over rocky points), engine sound mutes completely at some random points (its as if im driving an EV for a bit lol) and then comes back.❌WRC 9 being an EPIC exclusive for so long that it literally released 14 days AFTER WRC 10 on Steam. This is absolutely ridiculous Nacon. Absolutely ridiculous.Thing is WRC 9 has brought me joy. I don't care about simulation setups so I'm fine enough with my keyboard. I also got the game at 50% off almost as soon as it was released on Steam.But Nacon's choice to make it an EPIC exclusive for so long was such a bad move for me. Due to not wanting to use EPIC for it, I had to wait for a ridiculous amount of time. Please don't do that again Nacon, it was a bad move.So that is that. I'm looking fwd to try WRC 10 next!I wanna see what has been updated from here on

_childDocuments_.review: Engine sound can cut off or it glitches on some cars like the fiesta r2. The career mode is fairly well made. You can basically play regular career+ the management aspect or a seasonal mode which basically makes you sign a contract and off you go racing! There is a testing area where you can drive freely. There is a challenges mode which is basically time trials on different test track layouts.The handling is an improvement. Game difficulty isn't well balanced. I found historic rallies difficulty a lot more difficult. And on the other hand rally cross stages are significantly easier which is the case with older WRC games as well. These games often sell with high discounts and they're a good deal.  If you want to experience some authentic rally racing this is the game for you. If you're fairly new into this genre i recommend you try WRC 7 first. The handling is a bit more forgiving/more fun and it's basically the same game without the management/ R&D aspect.

_childDocuments_.review: It's an okay WRC game, but it has major flaws that should have been carved out.Pros: - I like the career mode, you have to start from the bottom and work your way up.- As long as you stay in cockpit/bumper cam, the physics are pretty believable (they are not when you look from the outside or in replay mode).- Nice mix between arcade and sim, and I like that damage impacts the handling of the car.- The cars look very detailed.Cons:- The career mode is veeery basic. Not many choices, and the e-mails you get are very robotic. And for some reason there isn't an ability to do shakedown(s) before going into a rally. Shakedowns are really helpful to give you a rough idea of the surface in your next rally.- The game looks like it's from 2012, graphics are bad, even for being a few years old. (Dirt Rally games look way better.)- The gravel sound is just awful. It sounds like you're driving over flattened soda cans.- The pacenotes are mostly consistent, which makes the inconsistent ones VERY annoying. (also some of the pacenote symbols doesn't appear, etc; if a 6 right goes into a 2 right, you might not get the note for the 2 right, the co-driver will say the note, but it won't appear as a symbol on the screen).- When encountering  the car seems to just fall apart. The car gets ruined by driving. Not even crashing, it just breaks suspension parts and the engine gets messed up for no reason.Overall, I kind of enjoy this game, it's not very bad, but it could easily have been much better. I hope Codemasters will take better care of the WRC games when it's their turn.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the last Nacon published WRC game that I'd argue can be played fairly casually compared to the later entries. I don't think I've seen the Barcelona stage show up but I could be wrong.Granted, 10 and Generations are more refined and have more content in general, but it's still a fun game overall and it goes for cheap during sales.

_childDocuments_.review: The previous iterations in the series weren't up to scratch but through continual iteration they've made something excellent. The graphics are great, the car handling is great, the damage model is good and the career structure is fantastic. The content in the game is also excellent and far surpasses anything that Codemasters has ever output with the Dirt series. The graphics do have some rough edges but still looks great on a good machine. The lack of online features I'm also fine with as the Dirt series never really offered anything worthwhile or substantial. I am disappointed that the WRC license has ended up in the hands of Codemasters / EA, I have no faith at all that they will have the capability to produce something excellent. WRC9 was a sign that KT Racing had really honed their skills and it really seems like further sequels would be something to look forward to. I hope KT Racing are able to further iterate on the series without the WRC license, much like how Codemasters were able to do it.

_childDocuments_.review: Almost a No! However its still a it of fun. Handling unrealistic and too difficult. Graphics/sound very good and adjustable.I cant really explain but the car never goes straight. Its always drifting, even on a straight road and playing with control settings I'm always zig zagging and eventually loose control. This can start at speeds of 40 mph which is totally unrealistic. No one has really got the handling as good as Colin McRea Dirt did.Im quite a good driver in real life and have played rally games before but this game is too difficult. With AI setting set a easy as they will go and using lower spec cars, its really hard to win a rally. If you crash a couple of times you will never make up the time and usually come near the bottom of the results or even last. I can't see me getting addicted this like I have on other games such as F1 or Dirt 2. If you want a simulator then this is almost there but be warned you won't win a lot, if you want an arcade that you will spend hours on practising, then this will be fine.All in all its still a bit of fun and I can see I will come back to this on and off for quite a while.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to be comparing this to the codemasters Dirt Rally 2.0 game. This also applies to WRC 10 because the developers just seem to be re releasing at this point.Firstly the most important thing: the driving feel. Wrc does this well for the most part. It feels on par with DR2 until you drive any car besides the official FIA cars. Whe  you jump in to a historic car you can't help but feel like you've jumped in to a different game with far inferior physics. Thia had been the same for all recent WRC games and I don't see it changing. In DR2 however it feels the same level of care and attention was put across all cars offered which is also incidentally a far superior selection then that offered to you by WRC titles. One thing that people familiar with both titles may point out is the tarmac physics. To me they feel wanting in both games. They both feel floaty and weird where as in my opinion DR2 feels far more responsive on any surface.Nextly: the stages. This is where in my opinion WRC is undeniably the better of the two. The stages in WRC are captivating and exciting. With the exception of some notable stages in DR2, such as the ones featured in new england, they all feel somewhat samey compared to the WRC titles.The last comparison I'll make is on career modes which is a difficult choice. I feel that DR2 gives more playability with the rallycross career. However the WRC career is exceedingly more immersive. It does come down to what works best for you however.I see the superior career mode in DR2 dude to the ability to save up for mew and faster cars, entering rally events with something different each time while also upgrading your team. This is an experience not avaliable in WRC. What is presented is an experience more a kin to the F1 series. Where you are signed to a team which you grow through research points, upgrading staff and performing well to increase your reputation as a driver. It is a fun system which I believe to be restricted by the limited vehicle choice and nomsensical demands from your manufacturer team to attempt to male it to the end of rally events with nonsensical setups that if you were to take them seriously could result in you not even finishing an event, but that's what the manufacturer wants apparently. When you're about to start the longest rally in the game and find that yet again your manufacturer will be upset with you for not using soft tyres is just rediculous. "Oh you won the rally and the entire championship, but you didn't use the dangerous setup we asked you to use, looks like our relationship is rocky."When you consider all of this with the fact that this game was released without wheel support it leaves the choice of what to purchase rather obvious but it does still come down to personal taste.Care more about an immersive career and having access to this era's pro WRC cars? Purchase WRC 9 or 10.Care more about having more content avaliable with a better feeling of progression? Buy DR2.

Of course, it's a bit of an exaggeration, but it's easier then, and players like me, who are new with simulators, can enjoy the game too.Overall, it's a great game, recommended.

name: Deadly Dozen: Pacific Theater
detailed_description: In 1942, specially trained soldiers were deployed to carry out commando-style missions against the forces of Japan. They were cold as steel and could strike without warning. Through sweltering rainforests, sun-baked coral beaches and stinking mangrove swamps, these skilled heroes took the war to the Japanese. This is the story of that 12-man unit, known only as...The Deadly Dozen. Penetrate the island strongholds of Japanese Imperial forces with your squad of commandos in this tactical World War II first person shooter. Stealth, a cool head and your M1 may buy you one more day. Can you survive the hard-edged intensity of the Pacific theater? 12 men, 1 chance! Personalize your strategy and squad to best achieve each mission’s objectives. Experience movie-like action as you take on the entire Pacific campaign from the Philippines to Okinawa. Creep silently through immersive environments featuring authentic WWII vehicles, weapons, and uniforms. Due to changes in networking technology since the time of this game's original release, multiplayer is not supported for this version of the game. This game is presented in its original, unedited form to preserve the developers' intended gameplay experience. This game is reflective of the historical period portrayed and contains content that may be considered offensive or discriminatory. Player discretion is advised.

_childDocuments_.review: With heavy nostalgia, It's a game that I remember deeply. Played it off and on with my friends. We did cooperative and multiplayer and built our own communities with self imposed clans and clan death match fights. We discovered exploits and ways of breaking the game, If I close my eyes I can already map entire assets down to their geometric angles. It's safe to say that I spent a lot of time in this game. There was even a guy that custom made maps and that was in my opinion a highlight to the entire DD2 experience. It was like Garry's Mod before it was cool minus any fancy physics. I met a good friend that played with me until the very end. By end I mean the end of game spy and their support for multiplayer. I wish so much for there to be a way to play online again if only for a day. It's budget for the time but it feels so immersive if you take it seriously and slow. There was a way to cheese most of the missions so there's that. Some missions feel long for no reason and others too short. I wish we had more dynamic settings like in DD1 but I can't complain as the AI is a quantum leap from it's sister. It tries to give you different ways of doing missions providing you different paths to objectives and side missions and If you don't notice it can succeed in that but it feels very linear immediately after opening the mini map. Give it a try and expect to die often but as soon as you get the hang of it, it's too easy. With the right guy a sniper and the M1 Garand it's absolutely a walk in the park.

name: Millennia
detailed_description: Updated Roadmap August 2024 Millennia: Premium Edition About the Game Create your own nation in Millennia, a historical turn-based 4X game that challenges your strategic prowess across 10,000 years of history, from the dawn of humanity to our possible futures. Set the course of history and experience different timelines in every playthrough as you write an epic story through your actions. Lead your people through times of crisis and ages of discovery, face great challenges and opportunities, and build a civilization that prospers through the ages. Dictate the course of history across ten ages, from the first cities to space travel. Accomplish certain objectives and you can move time into a Variant Age - an alternate history with new rules, new technologies, and new units. But beware Crisis Ages; following a path of chaos and disorder may plunge the world into a future filled with war, sickness or ignorance. Then again, a wise ruler can always turn a crisis into an opportunity.... Choose the path with care, as the ages you pass through will have a lasting impact on your people and the world. Customize your nation by adopting unique Nations Spirits over the course of your game. Will you be a nation of warriors or explorers? Are your people lead by a Great Khan or a builder of monuments? Are you known for defining pop culture or for dominating global finance? What parts of your culture will reverberate across history? Manage your economy with care and create a juggernaut of growth and construction. Start with basic resources to gain food, wealth, and production. As your advance, decide how to best convert these simple goods into more valuable products through research and improvements. Specialize your regions, turning iron into weapons or tools, wood into paper or lumber, gold into coin or jewelry. Ship surplus goods where they are needed, allowing the breadbasket of your empire to feed far-flung colonies or your industrial heartland to supply troops near your enemy. Pursue knowledge to research scientific and cultural advances, unlocking new units, buildings, and improvements to grow your cities or strengthen your armies. Research Defense to train the first archers, Smelting to master iron production, or Guilds for making wine. Variant and Crisis Ages feature unique alternatives, introducing everything from Cloud Estates in the Age of Aether to underwater cities in the Age of Utopia. Achieve your ultimate success through a Victory Age. Toward the end of the game (or earlier if your strategy is sound), dominance allows a nation to dictate the winning conditions. The rest of the world must decide if they will struggle to achieve victory before the leader ... or oppose the leader's attempt. Risk everything to take victory in the Renaissance or carefully plan for triumph in the modern era.

_childDocuments_.review: This is Civilization as made by Paradox Games. Which means more and less than one pithy quip alone, since "Paradox" is a pretty broad label of stereotypes and potential influences, but here's a bit of what to expect, in no particular order:- It is "more," generally speaking, than a Civ game. Civ 5, and especially Civ 6, lean heavily towards keeping gameplay simple to pick up and easy to master. Paradox doesn't do simple, and never has. There is going to be more to chew through in any given play through: more complicated infrastructure and developments, more turn-to-turn decisions in managing your "government points" tracks, more weight on where and when to research techs (being able to ignore or delay ones in certain ages is nifty), and so on. Like any modern 4X game, once you know that you're going to win the game, you're going to be able to "autopilot" your gameplay to a certain extent, but there are so many systems running at once that the game forces you to engage more even when victory's pretty much assured to keep things from falling apart all over again, which is either nice or a pain in the butt depending on your point of view. That said...- There is essentially no tutorial. What information you're given is piecemeal and lackluster. If you hate the idea of not messing around and finding out, wait a few months until someone with far more patience writes up a proper wiki and everyone sticks in all the relevant information you'll need, and at least three different steam users write up detailed strategy guides and tier lists that you can use to get some idea of what's generally good and what isn't. Otherwise, prepare for a lot of trial, error and restarting the game.- Wars are expensive, but the AI will do it indiscriminately anyway. Failing to keep up in the arms race will result in your valuable towns and fungible resources getting burned to the ground, riots breaking out in all your cities once you try to move your garrisoned troops out to fight back and crippling you further, wasting more time/money building replacement troops to cover for your deficiencies than you would have by keeping up to par, and other sorts of ways of making coming back from a losing war difficult if not impossible. That said, trying to wage war requires you to funnel lots of time and resources into building the extra troops needed to overcome enemy defenses and vassalize their territories, and trying to make those cities your own will cause so many problems with unrest and keeping a long-distance empire cohesive that it's essentially not worth doing. So if you're not a warmonger: Military parity good, military aggression suboptimal.- Sweden is one of the playable countries, naturally. Also Flax is a resource in the game, which might not be a thing in Paradox games specifically but in my experience with eurogames flax crops up all over the place and so it being in the game feels like a similarly provincial thing, idk. Not the most important observence on here, anyway.- Building and upgrading resources is finicky and time-consuming. It's also incredibly worth it, as the bonuses you get by doing even simple conversions like wheat -> flour -> bread can send your food production (and ergo city growth) through the roof. It's worth taking turns away from constructing buildings to give yourself extra shovel points (forgot the proper term) and spend those to develop your resources, though obviously don't entirely neglect constructing buildings.- The alternate timelines mechanics are probably the most fun and unique element of the game so far, blowing Civ's golden/dark ages way the heck out of the water. They're also something that it would be handy to have forward information about, so folks who don't like messing around and finding out should, again, wait a few months until other folks catalog all the relevant information in the game. Fortunately, Paradox hit a bit of a sweet spot in terms of the effect the alternate ages have on the game; while they have a significant impact on what you'll want to and CAN do, and thus shake things up between games, you won't be screwed if you aren't ready for them. The game even shows you what age you're headed for and how close you are to it, which is a neat forewarning that makes the transition between, say, a "normal" iron ages and applying the Turbo Black Death to the entire world that much more manageable. (Sure, a lot of people are still going to die, but there's dying and then there's restarting the game, you dig?)- Despite the substantial content already in the game, it's clearly begging for mods. There are so many systems that could easily have extra stuff slapped into it: more complicated production chains, more different country paths on changing eras, a more robust and complex battle system, and so on. I don't blame the game for not having mod support at launch, since that can be tricky to implement depending on the game, but like all paradox games Millennia's longevity WILL depend on how active and passionate its modding community is, since modders are crazy and tireless and deserve far more respect than they get and they WILL be able to put out more and more interesting content than Paradox itself will be able to keep up with.- And more stuff, honestly, but I've said quite a lot already.So yes, Millennia has a lot of Paradox elements to it: Wars being costly and good production chains being important are similar to Vicky 3, unpredictable and drastic era changes are a bit like playing HOI4 with the historical option turned off and seeing the AI pick truly fUnNi focuses, awful tutorial experiences and modding being critical to the game's robustness are true of every Paradox game, and so on. But when you take all that and cram it into a civilization-shaped package, is the end result any good?My answer: Yes. It's not for everyone, and especially not for everyone right after launch, but if you were looking for a turn-based 4X game that's weightier than the biggest name in the genre, Millennia gives you exactly that. If you like Paradox's design choices in general, you'll like them here; if you like Eurogames in general, this has much more of a Eurogame feel than something like Civilization does. If you're not into Paradox's normal offerings or turn-based 4X games, Millennia won't change your mind. In my (admittedly short) time playing the game, I didn't feel like the game was trying to draw new people into the genre; it felt like it was singling out people who were already familiar with the genre, seeing what they were asking for and trying to give them just that. And in an age where so many video games seem targeted towards the uninitiated and fence-sitters first and foremost, it's nice to see a title that drops those pretensions and guns for an audience that already knows what it wants, thank you very much, so long as you don't screw it up.And to me, Millennia didn't screw it up. And that's worth a thumbs-up, i think.

_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Few hours in now and really enjoying the game. It is so distinct and unique from Civ that it is a breath of fresh air. They really tried their own path with this game and so far it seems like it's going to be fantastic. I find all the different currencies and how government changes work to be fascinating, not to mention the different era paths/branches, and there seems to be so many possibilities. The game seems much more complex than Civ6 in its tech trees and eras which was frankly boring AF in Civ6 which has the same tech and civic trees that pretty much get developed in the same order every game. I love that Millennia has the opportunity for drastically different ages that the players will be forced into that will make the game highly replayable. I really love the supply chain system as well, so much more complex than Iron -> Aluminum -> Uranium in the Civ games. There are many different resources that you can harvest, and certain buildings to convert those resources into other goods (for example, wheat into flour) which can then be used as ingredients for even further items. It isn't so cut and dry and exactly the same each time, you may want to turn your wheat into flour one game and then maybe you'll do something else with the wheat next game that takes your game in a different direction. You'll notice that most of the negative reviews are complaining about the graphics, which honestly if you care about graphics you shouldn't be playing the 4X genre. The creators of this game clearly have an affinity for old school UI choices (The developers are even named "C Prompt Games" which is a clear callback to the DOS days of old) and it looks a lot like Civ5 which I feel was the best looking Civ game by far. Civ6 was so cartoony in its presentation. Millennia has an old school feel and I really like that. The units move quick and nothing feels like it is dragging which I very much appreciate as well. I also find it HIGHLY suspect that this game had dozens of negative reviews within 30 minutes of launching. Smells very much of deceptive practices by their competition.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: It's probably the most diverse turn based 4x game i've ever played. You can go into different ages and choose different national spirits, so even after quite a few games i still have a lot to explore and try.Millennia got quite a bit of undeserved hate, but it's a great game and will remain the best newcomer until new civilization comes out. It's full of innovations and new ideas, a pleasure to spend time on.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish there was a thumb sticking out sideways for "maybe, but if I have two choice, then thumbs up - barely. Let me start by saying this: Most of the bad reviews are by impatient kids. By kids I mean people born after 1990. The game has some really good ideas, I'll bullet point them quickly:-You can shape your nation as a military, economic, scientific or exploration/colonial power house. -If you understand other Paradox 4X games and Civs, you SHOULD understand this. People who don't understand it just don't read. If you click off windows that put up and refuse to read, DO NOT buy this game. The Tutorial windows are really good - but you have to READ them. If you read the first line and go yadda yadda yadds whatever you will not get what is going on. - If you can ignore the 2005 graphics combat window, then combat is good. Unlike Civ, attacking a large fortified city is actually hard. I needed 3-1 odds (3 armies of 6 units vs 1 army of 6 defending to take a capitol. I actually lost the first siege with 2 armies and was like Wow... I lost a battle? Never seen that in Humankind. - The early game is fun IF you are a warmonger like I am. Lots of barbarians, lots of independent cities to take. (you CAN peacefully get these cities and peacefully get rid of some barbs if you choose... if you are one of these types...) - There is a chaos system, if you warmonger like me, your people can get upset or rebels can pop up. It's a bit overtuned IMO but I like it overall. - I really like the national spirits and government types. The devs were not blowing smoke when they said you can have very different games. Way more varation than Civ/Humankind imo. - The resource system is pretty cool. For example, if you found a city that has no hills or forests anywhere near it, you can still have decent production. Clay pits on grassland then brick making oven = production. You can get more food by building farms, flour mill, then bakery. You can mine and make production, OR make the metal into weapons Warfare xp OR make them into trade goods, money. Great system. - You can get rich by making allies, sending envoys, and making trade deals. The diplomacy is a bit limited but trade and research deals are quite strong. - UI is fine... I don't get the complains. I have no issue. A few hotkeys like "sleep" "Skip turn" would be nice.There are many flaws however....- Elephant in the room. The graphics are weak. Period. I hate Civ 6 cartoony graphics but these are just bland, old and weak. If you really care, don't buy it. If graphics aren't a big deal, don't worry. - Biggest issue for me: You can not raze the cities of other players (human or AI) you CAN destroy minor civs 1 city but not the 8 "players" cities. This is awful, because the AI will literally found a city between two of yours just to be a pest, it's in a garbage spot and you can't destroy it. Unacceptable. That said, there is a lot of complaining over this, I have to imagine it will be fixed. - There are no setup options. Literally 5 map sizes, pangea continents or islands. Difficulty (no description of the bonuses AI gets) Done. That's it. No built in maps, no map editor, no small or large islands, no game sped settings. - Tech and eras move WAY too fast. No fast-med-slow game settings. If you like a slow game like I do... this isn't it. Pray they give us the option, or someone who knows unity makes a mod soon. - Units move far too slow. (scout and cavalry included) An average unit has 30 "move power" and almost every terrain takes more than 10 power, a lot takes 20. Do the math. Welcome back to Civ 1-2 move speed, on maps that are much bigger. Humankind 4 moves at slowest was awesome. Hope a mod can fix this. - WAY too few units, and a lot have no upgrade path. You will have electricity and still have Viking raiders and 11th century crusaders because they have no upgrade. Also, you have stupid gaps. Guess what comes after a 1500 AD Aquebus? A 1914 machine gun. Nothing in between. Come on. - I guess this is a me issue, being an evil strait white middle aged male, but I thought Humankind was woke... this is next level. About 1/2 the units through the game are female. Longswords, city guards, scouts, cavalry, etc. Even Humankind didn't do that until age 6. FFS, can we PLEASE drop the 2020s woke fad and just admit men were (and are) 99.9% of combatants? - Maybe ironic that I say that and then this: Nations have NO identity. Everyone is exactly the same. If you want diversity, then do it with the diversity of nations... not female greatsword wielders. Here is my TLDR: If you like civ-like 4X games and want a new flavor, and know the deal with Paradox and you will need a year of DLC/patches for this to be good and want to try it to get the basics down now, buy this for $39. If on the other hand, you can't deal with flaws or are one of the ADD younger players that refuse to read, super hung up on graphics and will stomp your feet if you don't 100% understand the game in a few hours, pass this up. Right now, I'd give this game a 6/10 score. So, Get it if you like civ-like 4X and you are currently bored. All others can pass it up. I think after a few weeks, it might be a 7/10. After a year it should be a 8/10 if they put the work in.

_childDocuments_.review: "Don't judge a book by its cover" - this phrase strongly applies to this game. While it has its fair share of flaws, the base structure and general "flow" of the game is actually quite decent and entertaining.There are a lot of ways to do a lot of things, and there is no clear "best way" to do them. Finally a 4X where you're not running the same chores over and over again (build X, then build Y, then build Z, because that will give you the most optimal outcome 99% of the time).One of my favorite is the economic system, which is extremely simple yet extremely fun, you actually feel like building up industries and take care of them, not just choosing something from the queue and that's it.The AI is actually quite good also (the tactical AI is a bit meh, hopefully will get improved), but they actually put up a fight without ludicrous cheating.The variety and sudden changes with Ages, unrest, etc. adds a ton of flavor and fun on the top. I hated in other games where I was just pressing the next turn button for 20 turns because nothing happened.It needs a lot of extra content and immersion related improvements, but overall it stands on solid grounds, even if it is not super-revolutionary or super-big in scope and ambition.(I played a ton with the demo and experimented a lot with it, I'll might update the review based on the mid- and lategame)UPDATE:I'm a little bit disappointed with the late game, I expected a bit more from the energy system and more from improvements, I miss some features (merging vassals to create mega-regions, etc.), many of the late game needs don't feel necessary at all (because the others completely balance out and they're easier to get), you can beeline like crazy, creating very dubious situations (have supersonic jets but only crossbows for ranged units, for example) and other things.The most annoying thing however, is that hills can be used only for mines, quarries and wind farms. If that won't be fixed in a patch soonish (or modding won't be enabled by then so I can fix myself), then I'll change this review to negative, because that alone is extremely irritating.But I'm keeping my positive review for now, because it's a fun game and as a first step I think it's quite decent.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not Civ, and that is not a bad thing. I think a lot of the negative reviews are from people coming in trying to play this game like how they played Civ, and that just isn't going to work.I've got a lot of hours in Civ, I've been playing that game since Civ first came out, all the way through the copyright spin-offs (Call to Power I & II) and to the modern Civ 6. Those are fun games, and each one brought something new and changed the game.But Millennia isn't Civ, nor is is supposed to be. Sure, it is a 4x type of game, and some of the graphics/UI mirror Civ. But the base game is different. Honestly, it took me a bit to figure that out too, I was certainly guilty of coming in and trying to build up my nation just like I have done countless times in Civ games. And that led to a lot of "oh crap, this isn't working". As of the time of this review I have yet to complete a game on Millennia because I get to a certain point and decide to start over, using what I've learned the hard way to make my next game better. And that's where I'm really enjoying it. I don't want another Civ in Millennia, I want something new that makes me think of playing differently and forces me to change me strategy. Millennia does that perfectly.There absolutely are areas this game can improve on (some of the graphics, allowing more game setup/play options, better wiki/how to manuals). But enjoy the game for what it is - a different spin on the civilization style 4x genre. Likes:+ Eras. They force you to strategize (do I want to be the first one and get to pick the next era, can I get that really cool one, or do I need to not be the first and instead prepare for our impending negative era), and so far each of my games have been widely different because of them.+ Production. You can "build" production chains. For example, I can take lumber and turn it into logs, or paper. I can then use that paper and make religious books, or instead make educational manuals. It is a cool spin on resources. You can send resources from one region to another to complete these chains. It really forces you to think about what you want your regions to focus on, or how you are going to get resources required to make sure your regions don't revolt. You can build "towns" to expand your regions/cities and have them specialize for added benefits.+ Exploration. It goes beyond just finding villages or landmarks. Later in the game you can find things that were previously hidden, or exploit landmarks for additional benefits. I'm actually enjoying exploring the map instead of feeling like I "have to" do it.+ Barbarians. I hate, hate, hate barbarians in Civ. I started off Millennia with the same feeling. But as I played more and more I began to enjoy fighting and taking out barbs. It really made me think about were I wanted to expand too, because if I took out every single one I'd be doing the AI nations a favor and clearing ground for them. I like taking out their villages and getting the benefits, and there are even some techs later that turn barbs neutral to you (but not everyone else).Dislikes- Diplomacy. It is really lacking. While the AI can become your ally, ignore you, be hostile (can attack you in neutral territory but not your land), or outright declare war on you, there really is no substance behind it. I honestly don't know why the AI is declaring war on me, or why they want to be my ally. I can't really trade things with them, or propose a common enemy. - Region expansion. I'm still figuring out where the best spot is to found a new region, or how far apart to build towns from the main city. I'm not clear on why one region expanded in a tile when another region has been next to it longer (and I wanted that one to expand there first). Some resources can't be collected by outposts and have to be in actual city founded regions (aether for one). - Wiki/manual. At the time of this review the wiki/manual is a bit lacking. A very specific example of this is the aether resource. I was extremely excited when I advanced into the Aether Age), and I quickly founded an outpost by a chain of mountains expecting to be able to harvest aether. No matter what I did I couldn't get anything to pop up allowing me to improve the tile to exploit the resource. I had to go into the discord and ask, only to be told that the resource has to be in your actual city based region (not outpost) in order to be harvested. With the map I was playing that wasn't remotely possible, so I feel like I wasted the age. All in all, I'd highly recommend this game if you like 4x games and understand that this game is not (nor was it intended to replace) Civ. It has a lot of cool new ideas and I'm excited (and hopeful) to see where this game goes in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. It's basically Civ 5 (graphics and appearance-wise, at least; regarding the movement system, though, Civ 6) with some great additional ideas, options and possibilities.However, I also have some issues with it, that are really annoying. Still, despite of these, I'm making this a positive review, because there's still more good than bad and also because I hope that these might get ironed out later. So, in case any devs might ever read this, please do something about these:- The AI. I get it that it's certainly hard to make good AI opponents. The main problem with them isn't even that they're propped up with cheats and lots of units they could never get and support if they would be playing by the rules (lots of other games do this, so I'm used to that long ago), but rather that they ALWAYS, WITHOUT EXCEPTION, ALWAYS become hostile, attack and declare war if their power is over the players. And, since, as mentioned, they get a lot ot units dumped on them to make up for their lack of actual playing capability, this will pretty much always be the case, in every game, with every AI nation.- Or, if the idea is that good relations with AI players should be maintained via regular "improve relations" and "send gift" diplomacy actions, then at the very least, there could be some reminder/notification mechanic that warns you that your relations with this and that AI has dangerously degraded and you might want to talk to them to offset this, or they will attack soon.- Units banding together even if not intended. Say, I have a group of two units somewhere, with one slot still open for a third one. I have another unit somewhere else (just one, on its own) and I'm sending it somewhere. The group of two units mentioned before just happens to be in its way. If it has enough movement points, it runs through them, no problem, but if its movement points just happen to run out exactly when it's on the square with the two units, then they band together into a group of three and stay like that. So if the one unit had any movement orders, those are now forgotten, and if the two units were just camping out somewhere, then now all three of them will camp on happily together, and the one unit will never reach it's destination. Generally, a few extra turns pass until I notice that something isn't right, because my one unit hasn't arrived - then I look and see, ah, of course, again... great. So there might be perhaps a notification if any unit(s) join any others in this fashion - or, the game could just simply manage this, remember the units' original orders, and allow them to continue (by leaving the group again on the next turn) automatically. This would be the best.- Domain XPs. These would need some reminder/notification too when they reach an amount where you can buy another policy card with them. Sure, there are the little numbers in the red circles, but they don't really catch the eye when I'm just playing and not directly looking at them. They might perhaps flash once at the beginning of a turn, when they appear or their value increases. Otherwise I tend to forget about them and turns pass, with me still not having bought something I wanted, even though I already got the XP for it for some time.- Border-related culture powers like Claim Territory, Absorb Outpost, Create Town: if used on a tile/outpost that is adjacent to the borders of two or more of my regions, it seems to be completely random, which one will get it, making such situations quite unmanagable. It would be nice to have something like a selection window pop up in this case, where I could decide, which region should get it (like when I change which region an outpost is linked to).That's... about it, I believe. Should I encounter/remember something else, I'll expand the review, but for now, these are what have been the most annoying issues for me so far. It'd be great if these could be ironed out sooner rather than later.Still, as mentioned, overall, it's still a very good game with some great ideas and if you like this genre, I can only recommend this gem (even if it could still be polished a bit more).

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:Refreshing innovations for the 4X genre. Multiple ages paths, Not having to research every technology , getting different types of points to build and upgrade (Exploration, Warfare, Government etc) your empire makes each game feel unique.Cons:Poor graphics Game is sluggish. Zero customization. Want more or less barbarians? No options for that. Want more or less tribal villages? No option for that. Want more or less resources on the map? No option for that. Want to build a custom map or have a map that is mostly desert or tundra or somewhere in between? No option for that. You get the point.No quick restart. RNG places a starting town in a horrible spot.? There is no restart function to quickly reroll another map, you have to quit the game back to the main menu and restart.In game tutorials consist of tl;dr windows with limited quick references. For example, hovering over a resource doesn't tell you what the player needs to harvest it. Barbarians spawn out of no where in your city limits with zero warning. Just NO. Horrible game mechanic.UI is ok. Can be improved. For example Improvement points (what the player uses to upgrade lands and place harvest features) is just a small button in the bottom corner which can be forgotten about. A finish turn button that says 'allocate improvement points' would be a nice fix for that.Balance issues. Warfare points seem to be more over powered than other points allowing players to create large armies faster to steam roll competition. As much as I like Ages, the first to reach the next age dictates what happens to the rest of the players as well which can be an unfair mechanic. For example it takes one nation to not pay attention to sanitation to force the Age of Plagues on the entire map AND they can reach it first by relying on RNG to get research and culture points. Once the age starts, it doesn't matter what another player's sanitation is, they will suffer the consequences of it. This type of mechanic would have better served if half the nations have a sanitation issue and the Age only ends when 75% of the map fixes the sanitation meter.Majority of this can be fixed with patches and updates. The game mechanics are fun and enjoyable and I want to enjoy them, but there are too many cons to actually recommend this game in it's current state.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Millennia is a very interesting and idiosyncratic game that has a lot more complexity under the hood than you'd initially expect. On first pass its a Civ game with a relatively unique spin on the formula of alt-history strategy games, one that Humankind rode on quite heavily and Civ 7 is now making its own version of where-in you don't pick a civilization from some place and time in history and drag it through a series of somewhat-arbitrarily chosen eras from the stone age to the information age and maybe beyond regardless of how appropriate that is, a smash brothers of history and anthropology text-books playing all the greatest hits.Rather you construct your civilization from the ground up, collecting a limited number of cultures and signifiers from across history from each era you pass into, while humankind left it at changing from one civilization to another as you cannonball through the cliffnotes of history Millennia takes it further on the alt-history spectrum and also varies up the ways that history can play out, having multiple potential eras that society can be guided or dragged into as long as requirements are met, some good, some bad, some fantastical. Indeed you can take humanity down some wonderfully whacky alternate paths.Now these two things are obvious, they're the main selling points of the game on the steam page, where things actually get really interesting is what you actually DO in the game...And much to my shock Millennia is actually something of a factory game.Now obviously this is no Satisfactory or Factorio, neither in design or complexity, rather they've taken the various resources you can collect and produce in other strategy games like wool, copper, meat, logs, etc. and made a very interesting minigame out of it.Instead of just plopping down a farm on top of a wheat resource tile and getting a flat food bonus to your city and calling it a day, to unlock the true potential of that wheat you need to run it though a production chain. First you harvest the wheat, gaining a minor but good to have bonus to food in the settlement, but you'll notice that you're not just getting a bonus to growth, that tile, when worked by a pop, is giving that city the wheat as an item, like a luxury or special resource in Civ 6, which is THEN conferring that food bonus to the city. And that's where it gets really interesting because you can then take that material and with another building (a mill in this case) and convert it into flour, gaining a marginally superior bonus, and then again, as you'd expect, with the construction of an oven that flour is transformed into its ultimate incarnation: BREAD. And just like that you've taken a simple grain that is good enough for a community getting on its feet to a monument of burgeoning human society everywhere, the mighty loaf.Waffling aside the point is that throughout the entire game you're constantly playing this minigame in all of your non-vassal cities to take resources and turn them into more useful versions, and its not always a direct upgrade, a lot of the more advanced materials (like the numerous things paper (milled from logs) can be turned into) will take an item that produces one resource and turn it into something that produces another resource. And on top of THAT you're limited in every city by not only the amount of population that can work each tile but also the number of tiles that you have available to your cities, because nearly every step of the manufacturing processes requires a building that you physically place on the game map, taking up a tile that needs to be worked to function (most of the time) rather than being tucked away in the quantum realm that is the city centre. This constant minigame of finding efficiencies and capacities is what makes Millennia truly incredible and fun to me, it also means that what resources and terrains you have available to you will directly influence how you choose which cultures (national spirits in the game) and which government types you choose, which feels SO naturalistic and true to life, cultures formed to best adapt to their environment and that's how it is in Millennia, its a brilliant keystone that makes the idea of this sort of rogue-lite civ-building-on-the-fly game work in a way that it kind of just doesn't in Humankind (at least to me) and its an extension on one of my favorite aspects of Civ 6 which is the districts system.So in summary, the game has a deceptive amount of depth to it, a ton of replayability with a bunch of national spirits and eras to mix and match and is nice to look at to boot.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok I felt as if some higher power just instilled this fervor to really give an honest review. I don’t usually review, if at all but I feel compelled for this game actually and here’s why:Like many others here, I grew up playing Civ. I put in over a thousand hours between V and VI. I desperately wanted to like VI and I’m cautiously pessimistic about VIIMillennia, in my humble opinion, has an incredible foundation set for those who like dealing with the more complex side of 4X games. I understand there’s a sizable chunk of the market like the more casual empire building experience, but I feel this is a refreshing take on the genre and although has a bit of a learning curve, can be a very fun experience.There is so much depth in this game… from the economy with supply chains and towns from combat which is surprisingly more complex than it looks (there is also a “strategic warfare system” coming in their Q4 expansion/update). I love how customizable and somewhat historically centric it is. Everything feels reactive. Your starting point is locked for now (with nomad start option coming in Q3 expansion/update) but usually the starting spot is pretty good and your surroundings are what drives the decision of your nation. The ages were a great implementation that gives the feeling that each nation is going through their own problems as well.Diplomacy is a bit underwhelming. Just feels barebones. I hope that this doesn’t come back to bite me but I’ll give them some grace because of most 4X games nowadays usually out with their own diplomatic expansion/dlc (not that it’s right).Finally to the hot topic… the graphics. I personally like the graphics. It’s not too taxing on your graphics card but it still is very pleasant to look at. You can tell it’s more focused on the strategy side and what’s “under the hood” vs selling something extraordinary to look at but I do really like the aesthetic and maybe there will be a mod in the future that helps with it.Give this game some time. It’s very fun to play now but after these next few dlcs (and no, I don’t condone paradox’s greed with 200 dlcs to put in necessary systems) I’ll like to see where this game is at. I’m extremely interested in the development
