_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to love this game, and it's not bad by any stretch, but it doesn't really succeed with what it set out to do and the lack of Steam workshop mod support is enough to get me to say not to buy alone. However, here's some of my thoughts:-NO STEAM WORKSHOP SUPPORT!-The animations that play in combat are no different than Civ's, as there's no actual control and it's all just a numbers game. I usually end up skipping them.-The balance feels quite wack and there are very clear "meta" units. -The pacing feels way too fast for my tastes and there's no way to change it.-The idea for the ages is cool, but whoever researches them first determines them for all, so unless you go real hard into science, odds are the A.I. are deciding for you, and more often than not they seem to choose the bog-standard ones. I really believe it should be on a per-nation basis. If you want to go into the Age of Heroes instead of the Age of Blood, you should have that option, in my opinion.-Most of the "faction bonuses" are pretty underwhelming and there are some clear best-picks.-There are WAY too many tile improvements and it forces you to specialize each city, but makes it infuriating when half of them are just non-viable because they rely on other improvements that you just don't have the space for. Some may like the hyper-specialized cities, but I personally am not a fan of it.-The Barbarians are *CONSTANT*. I can count on my hands the turns that I was lucky enough not to have something try to kill me. (And yes, I was constantly hunting down their camps.)-Multiplayer dead.All in all, I do enjoy the game, but for the price tag, I really can not recommend it. I will say at the very least, games published by Paradox do get long-term support. Thus, I am at least hopeful that it'll become much better in the future. However, if it doesn't get Steam Workshop some point soon, I personally don't see myself coming back to it after I finish my current game.

_childDocuments_.review: Quite a solid 4X game from an indie developer. Cities are not restricted by the "fat cross", but rather the entire cultural expansion of the city and its dependent towns, resulting in cities being much farther apart. Armies are back, so theres some unit stacking. The differing eras is quite an interesting feature as it adds not only different mechanics, but also different techs and units which changes things up. Due to how culture works, you will most likely only have 5-8 "cities" with the rest being vassals. The National Spirit mechanic also allows you to customize and adapt your civilization as the game progresses. A couple of things I didnt like was how roads are only automatically built between towns and cities within a certain range of each other, so you often needed to use pioneers to create outposts to link your cities together. Diplomacy is also a little limited and the AI can be a little fickle. There are only a small number of map types. Its a pity it couldnt be a little more random. I also wished there were some filters for terrain so you could tell what buildings were on your tiles more easily. Overall though, I enjoyed Millennia and would recommend people to give it a try

_childDocuments_.review: I agree with most of the positive posts. And with most of the negative ones too. Having played two partial games (3-4 ages) to get a handle on the rules, I started a new game with the intention of playing through to the end. Having reached the Age of Departure, I realize I've not had fun in a while, and I'm not interested in playing even one more turn.There's just too much jank. Yes, there are UI issues. Yes, there are balance issues. And yes, there are graphics issues (though I'm happy to ignore graphics when gameplay is fun). There are also some deeper issues of game systems (looking at you, diplomacy), and at least two variant ages which were no fun. Both Plague and Alchemy felt like unnecessary make-work, chasing around the map to deal with random things that popped up (squash plague / collect arcana).For all that I admire the idea of variant ages and resource production chains, the end result isn't fun. It could be, but it's not. This bun left the oven at least a year too soon.Perhaps in time, if the devs focus on core systems rather than DLC, things will be better. But for now, I'm disappointed, and not going to finish my playthrough. I'm not having fun, and life is too short to play games that aren't fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Millennia had a rocky start.  I bought it at launch and while I enjoyed it I still bounced off it for a few reasons.  However since then there has been 5 free updates which has fixed a lot of the issues I've had.Pros+Lots of fresh ideas and a very different spin on the civ formula.+The "goods" system is brilliant.  You can have complex supply chains and specialize towns based on there resources.  +The variant eras adds good replay ability.+Each civ is effectively a blank shell and as you pick different society types during the game each run is a bit different depending on these choices (some people may see this as a con)+Lots of different systems at play under the hood.+Devs have consistently put out good free updates and are receptive to community feedback.Cons-Graphically its a bit dated (think Old World but with a slightly less polished UI), however in my opinion gameplay makes up for this.-Late game performance is still a bit of an issue.OverallIts a great game with some fresh takes.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like 4x games I highly recommend you try this game as I'm having a blast playing it.  It does have some problems but nothing near game breaking. It's biggest negative right now is the information on game mechanics.  It needs to be better and this seems to be the biggest complaint and I feel like this will be addressed in an update.  Now the game does provide you with a lot of information, it's not missing entirely, there are just some essentials that are not present, you can read more about this in other reviews as ppl go more in depth about it.  I personally don't have a problem with the combat system, I actually like it though I do also wish you could turn off the combat pop up animations.  A lot of ppl approach this game with game mechanics and expectations from other 4x games (Civilazation) in mind and it is nothing like them.  Diplomacy could use a little fleshing out but the biggest problem with it at the moment is a lack of information.  Why things happen with other civs, what affects it and how to change it can be hard to find or completely lacking. I'm not saying they don't  need to be addressed I'm saying if you like 4x don't let them prevent you from discovering this great game that gives great new concepts to the genre!

_childDocuments_.review: As an avid fan of all 4x, from Stellaris and Masters of Orion I & II into all the Civ titles, including Call to Power II and Alpha Centauri (and everything between), Millenia is really good. The gameplay and ages are great, having tons of depth and variety without being something you need to plan out with spreadsheets and a calculator. It also scratches that "one more turn" itch that can lead to you finally quitting for the night at 3 am. The catchup tech mechanic makes the game fun and competitive throughout regardless of difficulty level, cutting down on stomping way behind countries or being dumped on by a less than perfect start location in the higher difficulty levels.It's not perfect, having late game slow downs depending on system/map size. Some balance issues still exist (not as bad as in pre-release Spiffing Brit-type vids). If you like stomping stone age armies with nukes, the catchup tech mechanics will kinda suck for you. Lol. The graphics, especially the combat window, are not fantastic, but easily in line with the small indie developer (Paradox is just publisher). Should be fixed/improved at some point. Regardless, you can just skip if you don't like it either and it doesn't affect gameplay much at all.At $40, it's well worth it. $60 if you want the discount on the planned expansions.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know, maybe I should play more of it, but having few games already Millenia is a mixed bag of a exprerience.It does have crazy number of mechanics and a modular gameplay design, and it feels like the core idea that differentiates it from Civ series is fairly well grounded.However, the it has the most annoying idea from Civ cranked up to 11: players competing on completing some arbitrary task. In Civ it was wonders and great people, but here we have whole ages and core game mechanics, not to mention if you are behind a few turns you get locked out from whole playstyles. You are basically doomed to watch AI do it first, because AI only pretends to play a game and will get steamrolled with some basic tactics (as it did in Civ too).It also seems that focusing on some other victory without dedicating substantial resources to scare AI away is not possible. You are basically forced to invest into an army that just stands there. However, it you do that, it does not make sense to not use it, and you pretty much end up in a war.Of course, I write these thoughts only after a few games, and I like that this game that brings some new ideas to this genre.

But just some basic game speed multipliers would make this game so much better.Third: I feel like the AI chooses the ages way too much. they should only pick the era if the Player(s) is/are staling. if other 2 points were fixed then this may be fixed too.some other things (May add to later.):-Graphics.-Leader promotions confuse me.-I don't believe city names have a set order. Rome is the capital of Rome, not Trimomerviumus.-Expanding is hard. (Again could be fixed if 1 and 2 were fixed)-Colors of Civs are kinda limited. (No red, what?)In conclusion: I do really like this game, but it needs some things added before it becomes truly great. I want this game to do good but i can't recommend playing without a few small features.

_childDocuments_.review: Started playing during the free weekend, and I'm very glad that I did. I'd watched lets-play's of this game and the game did not grab me at all. But having now played one game to completion I have completely changed my mind. It is a great game, the different ages really makes the game shine and stand out. In my play-through I was embroiled in wars and neglected the sanitation which led us down the path towards the Age of Plague, with sickness running rampant throughout my empire I finally succeeded in bringing our world screaming into the reformation, only to tech-up to fast and after having put a man on the moon and sending a signal out into space (not expecting an answer) and thus being invaded in the Age of Visitors. The game has received 6 patches now and comes with two DLC's, both which are essential I would say. Great game and totally scratches that one-more-turn itch. Recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: Lots of innovation, like vassal cities that don't make armies but govern themselves and pay taxes or Paradox-style "Mana" resources, but at it's core rather old school. Big industry and strong armies are power, and no abstract rules stopping you from declaring war when you want to kill them and take their cities.Yes, the graphics are rather dated (and the system requirements, while not that high, aren't justified imho). The main gimmick, the variant ages, feels inconsistent. Some ahistorical ages are really distinct, others are a bit of a let down, too bland.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Under the hood, this is a great foundation for a 4X game, and I know that PDX have a history of developing games through regular updates and DLC (I own and play HOI4, Stellaris, AoW, EU, Victoria and Crusader Kings) but, in my opinion Millenia is not fit for retail release, and is (effectively) a very expensive beta test.The good? This has the "just one more turn" itch so necessary in any 4X game, to the point that you can ignore many of the annoyances like the amateurish combat screen and "guards" that will watch barbarians approaching your city and not actually yell anyone about themThe Bad? Well, unfortunately, there's a lot - almost all of which (IMHO) should have been caught in playtesting and meant that the game never got Gold status in its current form. In no particular order - the own country trading mechanism seems designed to ensure that you can't specialise cities (because you can't effectively trade between your own cities many to many only one to one). This then clashes with the almost unbelievable design decision that hills (of which there can be a lot) can't be used for anything other than mines - have a great potential mining city with lots of hills well good luck with growing it as houses, sanitation and food are all unavailable! There are a lot more but these two combine to make most games an exercise in frustration. Oh, and good luck building a communication network such as roads, the only things that create these are pioneers and settlers, both of which are on an escalating cost basis and both of whom seem to decide completely at random which cities they will create roads to when they plonk themselves down.The ugly - Barbarians, oh dear deity of your choice, the barbarians! One of the great mechanics is Chaos, I really appreciate this as an idea. Unfortunately the implementation is really, really, poor. You can be going along quite nicely when, all of a sudden, another player (or yourself if you can't pay the ransom) can spawn two barbarians at EVERY city in the WORLD who then move before you can act and destroy improvements including outposts (which you can't afford to rebuild because the pioneers who create them are on an escalating cost basis) and, did I mention that your city guards won't wake up when this happens unless they're directly attacked?As I said, the basis of the game is good, but the execution is patchy and (in my opinion) shows flaws that should have been picked up in playtesting and corrected before paid release. I like the PDX model of land the main game then expand through paid DLC but it pretty much requires that the base game is playable and, unfortunately, Millenia isn't a fully formed gold product to my mind. I'll still play it occasionally because I genuinely appreciate some of the thinking, but the implementation .......
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Very Good game lots of content, there just needs to be some UI changes and some balancing with the points. There is so much content and different ways to play.The Improvement Menu is a little tedious but it is fun.The DLC listings are very scary though.If you are trying to do multiplayer no go otherwise its fun and certainly enjoyable

_childDocuments_.review: I am having a lot of fun with this game and for me personally it remedies everything that bores me in other 4X games.Online multiplayer is unpleasant with the current systems in place. I use a 3rd party desktop streaming application to play a single player game with multiple nations in order to play with friends online.Lots of features are missing I would wait if you aren't dying to get your hands on the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting take on the 4x genre that unfortunately tries to do too many things at once - loaded with systems that don't harmonize well, I would have loved to see Millennia focus on really polishing fewer systems to make them stand out rather than the current soup of systems that all just feel jumbled together. A late game with exceedingly long AI turns and lackluster win conditions just doesn't deliver the satisfaction of playing through to the end. The first half of the game is exceedingly better than the back half - if the whole game played more like that it might be enough to sway me to recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I played the demo and gave the game a decent shot without reading any reviews so as not to taint my perspective.This game isn't finished. It shouldn't have released without being labeled "early access." The art style is all over the place, the mechanics aren't well thought out and poorly explained in the in-game "infopedia." which itself is a lazy feature to rely on.Unit movement and option selection is sluggish and unresponsive. When a unit stops on a space occupied by a unit with the "guard" action selected, the movement stops with no warning the next turn, leading to units stacking up in cities without the player meaning them to. When a unit is completed, if there are units guarding the city, the new unit just stays there, once again, without any UI options to center on the newly created unit.The national spirit mechanic is horribly balanced with clear winners and losers among the options, and said options are poorly explained, once again with a barely usable infopedia band-aided in to explain maybe 1/3rd of the key words.Perhaps least important and simultaneously most egregious, I can't launch the game through steam. When I do, I get a launcher error message that very clearly refers to a programming error relating to unexpected strings. I have to go to my local files and launch via the .exe. The game launches just fine this way, but you'd think a game that has DLCs available would ensure their game launches properly on people's machines. Yes I've done fresh installs, verified game files, etc.I enjoy the production chain mechanic they have implemented, and the different tech-age options are interesting and add replayability, but the framework surrounding these things is just so... C- at bestI see a possible future where many of these issues are solved, but I don't expect it. Don't buy this game if there are no obvious updates and/or it is still 2024.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I usually begin by reading the negative reviews, to see if they're saying something that makes sense to me.  But I was enthusiastic enough about this game that I skipped that step and just bought the game and played it.  Now I've gone back to see what people are saying, and I've got to say, it doesn't.  So here are a few points I've seen, that I feel deserve refutation.Difficulty:  Some people seem to feel that the barbarians are too tough.  I don't get it.  I'll grant they're quite a bit tougher than Civ, but in Civ the barbs are so weak you can almost ignore them, even on super-barb setting.  In this game, you'll really want to keep a (small) army at home to defend.  Why is this a problem?  Likewise, yes, there are certain Civs that you can expect to show up on your doorstep with massive armies.  But, once again, this isn't really a problem, particularly once you understand how strong the defense is in the early game.  I've found I can hold these attacks off while simultaneously building a powerful economy, and eventually eat their lunch.  Don't expect this to play like CIv.  After all, isn't that why we're buying a different game in the first place.Too many improvements:  Again, I don't get it.  My chief complaint with a game is usually lack of choices--games are literally about making choices.  I do think some of the complaints about the UI are valid, but I've been playing computer games since the Commadore 64, so I've got the patience to look through a haystack without modern conveniences.  If you don't, well, based on Paradox's history, I expect quality-of-life improvements will be forthcoming pretty promptly.  In the interim, I've found looking through a long list of improvements a better problem than not having any choices.  Economy:  Which brings me to the economy.  I laughed out loud at one detailed review that, in one paragraph, complained about "armies appearing out of no where" and in another complaining that the economy is all about production.  The latter is actually true of, for example, Civ.  But one of the things I've been most pleased with about this game is that it isn't true here.  Not to say it's not important--it is.  But once you understand the economy in this game, you'l see there are ways for you to conjure up those armies out of thin air yourself.  It is precisely the fact that there are multiple simultaneous production channels that I think makes this game so interesting.  I definitely haven't played enough to claim they're play balanced, but I've got a few hundred hours of play experimenting with that question already.  I would call a win that already justifies the purchase cost.  And given Paradox's post-launch support, I still enthusiastic about this game.I could go on, but the point is that basically every complaint I've seen seems wrong to me.  I recognize each issue they're talking about, but it just seems to me that they're reacting to their own expectations, without actually playing the game.  That means taking the next step, asking "why," and trying to figure out how to adapt.  So if that's you, you'll probably be frustrated.  But if you want to play a new game, and find learning new systems fun, I can recommend.  Although my comments are based on several hundred hours of play (according to Steam), my experience is still narrow.  I haven't even tried multi-player (and I don't really care to--I play computer games when I don't have humans to play with).  I haven't tried a bunch of different difficulties--"Adept," the default, has been an adequate challenge for me so far.  Complaints about RNG do seem valid to me; some games seem much easier to me than others.  But I'm approaching that as a puzzle--a sign that there are aspects of the game I don't fully understand.  And I'm seeing some evidence that's right, because I've been finding some ways to adapt to various starting conditions to get to a solid mid-game state.  Frankly, the biggest issue I've found is that, when you play on the "continents" map, you have no way to interact with what's going on on in the other hemisphere, and sometimes one of the AIs will blob up before you get to a tech level where you can do anything about them.  Perhaps that can be improved with fine tuning, but, for me at least, it doesn't ruin my enjoyment that I can't win every game.  Likewise, more options for setting up the game--especially map types--would be welcome.  And I expect they're coming--in fact, looking at the roadmap, I know at least one is soon to be delivered.

_childDocuments_.review: There are some things to like, and things to hate, when it comes to Millennia. Artificial restrictions on expansion for the player (or else suffer sucky AI controlled vassals) are a big no-go for me. I am like the Romans, expand or die.There are a lot of cool mechanics at play making replay very attractive, such as innovations which can lead to unique bonuses or world wonders. Different ways to do some actions are welcome, such as raising an army on the quick to defend, using build, buyout, social points, and reinforce (heal) military units on the move.Then there are annoying things ... growth penalties. Everything that grows makes it harder, from age to tech or government, size of a city, number of cities ... it effectively stagnates you. Some items are city buildings that should be map buildings (e.g. wonders) and vice versa (a mill takes up 50 hectares?). Clearing forests uses precious, precious engineering points instead of improvement points you use to build farms and mines. Sort of makes no sense and clearing comes on late so clear flat land is super critical to region placement early game. The raw materials go to processing facilities which go into refining facilities which become consumables, at differing input:output ratios and unless I havent found it there isnt any sort of tool to help manage your unused, underspent or overspent resources, making a really cool concept a real pain in the ... you get it.Overall its got terrific bones and is different enough from the Civ series to not be a simple clone with a period setting or some DLC. But it has issues and annoyances. I feel like it misses the target just a bit but you may find it awesome/dreadful. Certainly worth a sale value. Hope this helps.

This seems to be done only in part.8) despite everything in this game, this seems to be a warfare only game. you dont get to focus on building a nice empire most of the times even if that is how you would like to play. the enemies and/or barbarians decide this and ages seems to be build more for forcing you to play strong military game. _childDocuments_.review: Millennia is a delightful strategy game that will feel instantly familiar to fans of Civilization. While Civ has taken some interesting directions in recent years, Millennia offers a fantastic alternative that breathes new life into the 4X genre.One of the game's strengths is its departure from the heavy emphasis on culture selection at the start of the game. Instead, Millennia lets you customize your playstyle more dynamically through a combination of National Spirits and Government forms. This approach gives you the flexibility to adapt your strategy and doesn't lock you into a specific playthrough based on your chosen civilization—no more being pigeonholed into a certain path because you picked England or Rome.While this shift in focus may make the individual nations feel a bit more faceless compared to Civilization, it more than makes up for it with near-endless replayability. The ability to tailor your civilization's strengths and weaknesses based on evolving conditions ensures no two playthroughs are quite the same.That said, Millennia isn't without its flaws. Diplomacy, in particular, could use some refinement, and the multiplayer and modding communities are still in their infancy. However, with two expansions already released and more on the horizon, the game shows a lot of promise for future growth.In summary, if you're looking for a fresh, engaging strategy experience with deep replayability, Millennia is an excellent pick—and an exciting new contender in the 4X genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Millennia is a remarkable 4x game. The remarks begin with "Wow, these systems sound great! I can't wait to explore it" and end with a combination of frustrated and annoyed cursing punctuated by brief moments of lackluster discovery.Where to begin?The UI in this game is hot garbage. Information is actively hidden from the player or rendered opaque on the science, national spirit, government, city, and map screens (which is nearly all of them). The infopedia may not be worthless, but it does a remarkable approximation of being so. Unit information is scarce. Buildings unlocked by governments and spirits often have no description. Many unit and domain abilities have no explanation until you have unlocked and used them, which means a large number of important game decisions are made blind.Speaking of blind decision making, the age system is a brilliant iteration of the largely cosmetic eras in Civ. Unfortunately, possibly to help make it feel like a journey of discovery, the game gives you almost no information on what you can research or do in an upcoming age unless you know exactly where and how to look (you have to right click on an upcoming age option in the tech screen. Ages you haven't already gotten to don't have normal infopedia entries.) When you add to this that the AI can and frequently does choose which age is next, it can feel more like being dragged through a series of puzzle rooms blind than a journey of advancement and discovery.Speaking of ages and going in blind, the age design varies from interesting to atrocious. In the third age there is a crisis variant (The Plague Age) which kills half of your population when it begins and forces you into a whack a mole disease mini game until it ends. IT is triggered (indeed forced) when you have a deficit of sanitation in any city for an extended period of time and fill a crisisometer to 20 points. At that point the only way out is to hope an AI researches another age and doesn't also get locked into the Age of Plague. I mention this for two reasons:1. The Plague Age is very easy to trigger accidentally and difficult to avoid if you've been playing well and building a large city, as the sanitation improvement is very expensive and2.  The Plague Age is, to the best of my knowledge, the only one of the Third Ages which doesn't unlock the ability to turn production into science or wealth, an ability that can never again be unlocked in the game.I actually thought that the above abilities weren't in the game at all because I got Plague Ages so consistently, either because I triggered them, or the AI sped at full speed into them without a care. This is emblematic of the whole age system, where some ages are game changing, but not always in interesting or fun ways. The crisis ages feel more like punishment overall than an interesting or challenging "what if" detour. The variant ages are kind of busted. I appreciate the variety and think it holds promise, but it desperately needs refinement.This is true of the game overall. It feels unpolished and unrefined. Powers, spirits, governments, buildings, improvements: the whole gamut of parts and features desperately needs rebalancing and a "fun" check. It feels like a bunch of cool ideas were thrown in a blender and then the resulting slop was served up without season, spice, or adjustment. The same lack of attention paid to how it actually feels to hit a crisis age and get forced into a tedious slog is evident everywhere from the map options (Pangaea is spelled incorrectly in the age of built in spell checkers) to the barbarians (there are no options for how many there are and they spawn infinitely from villages placed at ~8 tile intervals on the map until the end of the game with the same units as turn 2) to the independent cities (which carpet the map like a plague, often is awful places to settle and give you penalties if destroyed) to the AIs (which are a combination of faceless generics without even consistent map coloring across games and schizophrenic murder hobos completely incapable of diplomacy, in part because there are almost no meaningful diplomatic interactions in the game).The straw that broke the camels back for me was that you can destroy independent cities (with a penalty) but you cannot destroy any city captured from the AI. The AI builds cities like a drowning man flounders for purchase: constantly and without heed to where or what they are moving towards. The game gives you no recourse to this. 0. Nada. In a game where tiles, and especially flatland tiles, are critical to its most interesting system (the resource system) this feels awful.Overall, it's a game with great ideas, but less polish than a raw recruit's muddied boots. It needs a lot of work. It's decent for an indie game, but atrocious for a $40 game with the full force of bombastic Paradox marketing behind it. Get it on steep sale for the novelty, or skip it and just play Old World instead.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: A few good ideas that advance the genre, but ultimately not enough here to deliver a rich experience. Great resource management and build chains are overshadowed by confusing "Chaos Ages" (half your population dies, its a plague age -- ha ha, isn't that exciting) and an uneven Points system that doesn't gel well with the rest of the game (do you really want to switch your cities over to constructing special buildings that generate Diplomacy points just so that you can interact with your neighbors? Nope!). The mechanic of "Ah-ha - extremely strong enemies randomly spawn within your borders" is repeatedly used as a crutch throughout the game, including in a way that is unavoidable and probably causes you to lose half your cities. Again, who sat around and thought this was fun?A few significant different design choices prioritizing thinking and strategy over gotcha moments and a user interface visual overhaul could have saved this from being pretty quickly forgotten.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: This game seems really, really slow paced to me, and doesn't really justify it's existence the same way that other civ style games do with something new.  There's a lot to keep track of with the individual abilities you can use and the ages you are running toward, but there's not enough here to really make me engaged. Let me be clear: this is by no means a bad game, it just doesn't have enough going for it that I wouldn't rather play one of the six million other games in the genre. It just didn't grab me enough to even finish a play through to the end (though I do have around 100 hours) I'd probably wait on discount for this if you are a huge civ style fan and avoid entirely if you aren't.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I don't really understand most of the negative ratings. This game is doing a lot of things better than any other x4 game. For me, it's already more fun than civ. And i even like the battle screen somehow, even though it feels kind of cheap. Some parts of the game are not balanced yet, especially later ages. But that's ok for now, and for the price. Hope we get some cool patches / dlc's / more "what if" scenarios! I feel that i'm going to put a lot more of my time into this game. Try it, you won't regret it if you really give it a chance.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I write very few reviews for games, as I usually feel that the score and remarks everyone else is giving (in the majority) fit close to how I feel as well. This game however, seems to be getting review bombed, and very few negative reviews reflect anything I have experienced or feel is true/fair.As someone with 1000+ hours in the Civ. franchise and close to that in the various paradox and other 4X style games, I can confidentially say this game is Civilization for adults, and 4X for those that felt Civilization was great, but simplified a little to far. Civilization was always an extremely simple version of a 4X game, easily mastered and very linear compared to the more complex and interesting 4X titles. This mixes those two styles extremely well. To touch on the two points that the reviews seem to target the heaviest that do not reflect what I have seen, or are unfair:AI: This game suffers from the same AI issues that all games like it do. For anyone that has been frustrated by Civ's AI's getting advantages - especially on higher difficulties - or doing things irrationally at times, this game suffers from all the same flaws of AI. There are improvements to balancing and decision-making that the devs can (and will) work out over time for the AI, but it will always be AI. Performance: I have not had issues with performances. I have made it fairly far into it, and it seems to run just fine. I am a PC game player with a PC made for playing PC games. I am sure it could be better optimized overall, but it runs fine from everything I have seen.Overall, its a great game that requires that you hold many ideas and concepts in your mind at once, as it does not hold your hand or remind you of every little decision you should be making (except for the things you ask it to remind you of). This is by far one of my favorite parts. It requires you to manage your civilization well, pay attention at all times, and monitor resources closely throughout the entire game.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: A stripped, skinned, and empty sack of an attempt to make a 4X video game. Those defending it by uttering that it's "Not that bad" are blind, everyone should not continue to support this culture of stripped development and extensive downloadable content. Defense is only ignorance, and advocating that you are okay with the absolute development neglect of Paradox's modern products, it is no surprise that there is nothing to enjoy, the "innovative" features are manipulated forms of common turn-based mantras, the game is horribly optimized and horrible at even running though it looks like a bleached Civ4 and Anno 1404 stuffed together, the customization is so simplistic there is not even a sense at all of identity for who you "choose" to play. _childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: In Millenia there is no one resource to end the game unlike other games. I.e if you neglect knowledge in one age then its cheaper to get it in the next age. You can use this to your advantage if you want to dodge the age of the plague or other undesirable ages by letting the AI advance to the next age while you focus on infrastructure and conquest rather than being advanced researchers in all ages. Also productivity is another resource that is vastly misunderstood. Unlike Humankind or Civ 6, you can produce troops through civic points or cultural advancements. And having fewer cities leads to more cultural points being unlocked. Making it so that there is a balance between having many cities which leads to more warfare/other points and being culturally powerful which means larger army and innovation. Thus no one way is superior to the other. But you have to understand how the different resources can be utilized to complement each other so that you can be overpowered, that is the nature of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Where do i begin?I really want to like this game, i truly do, I have played every turn base strategy game under the sun from the Endless series, Civilization and total war.So, why the negative review?I know its standard practice for the AI to cheat in these TBS games but holy moly...|The moment you met another AI faction, they go for the jugular, and I am not kidding. Waves upon waves of AI units swarm towards you until your nation either capitulates or you run out of troops, its never ending. No sooner do they offer you peace then the ai declares war on you and continues to do so.And in that time you meet another faction? The AI allies up and proceed to both beat you down.Forget about exploration, Forget about expansion. Focus solely on warfare and defending your territory for the AI can produce 100 troops per every one army you create. I had a huge army but every so often Id lose a unit, no idea why, then I realised that I had no money. Yet here is the AI with 10x to maybe 20x (I'm not kidding) more units than me, some even with leaders. This, by the way is before the 3rd age has even begun. Until they fix the AI, Until they make some seriously significant improvements to the game? I recommend to stay away and preserve your mental fortitude fro this game will make you exasperated at the level of cheating and the constant warfare the AI throws at you."There is no peace, no respite, only war, and the laughter of thirsting gods!" pretty much sums up the 4 games I had.For a 4x this is pretty much a 1x in its current state.However there is somewhere in this mess a 4x game with interesting mechanics that I would love to explore....without being beaten to the curb.2/10

_childDocuments_.review: A refreshing take on 4x, but performance is a serious issue. While I would recommend you try it, I was getting 10-20fps past turn 140 with recommended specs when changing turns, and was still very choppy during my turns, so it may be a good idea to wait until they've fixed the issue.Many systems are similar to other 4x titles (like science, wealth or production resources), so I thought I'd highlight what I enjoyed/didn't enjoy about the game so far.The good:If you're an experienced 4x player that enjoys optimising the heck out of your cities then this is the game for you. - Land. Resource chains are complex and the potential for planning out your tiles far off into the future is extremely promising. Having a lot of territory is important in Millennia as you require many varieties of tile improvements to keep your cities growing.- Population. The City growth is a fun system that rewards you early on and pushes you to keep on top of several types of resources.- Ages. The ages system is a fantastic way of introducing replayability and twists to each playthough.- Territory expansion. The way Millennia handles territory is great. I really like the town mechanic as a way to spread your Region's influence. This also neatly solves the problem that Civ 6 has with going tall - you need a lot of territory for different resources/improvements so you have to build many cities. In Millennia, you can just go extremely tall, buffer your territory with some outposts to prevent the AI from encroaching, and go as high up as you want.- Culture powers. I enjoyed the culture powers immensely, they provided a strong incentive to invest heavily in culture that isn't some sort of research tree like Civ 5/6, which I'm not really a fan of.The mixed:- The style. I am actually quite a fan of both the UI style and map style (I'm less keen on the improvements), it is quite old school, but I find it charming. Having said that, there are many reviews on here of people who really don't like the graphics of this game - so make sure you watch some gameplay and decide for yourself.- The combat. I really don't enjoy the pop up menu that comes up when you're initiate or view combat, additionally, I felt that the combat system was much more one dimensional than the Endless series or Civ. There are some cool things here, but it's not the strongest part of the game.- The learning wall. I have played the start of Millennia several times at this point just to get my head around the systems. It is very daunting to start with. There are a lot of things that you can do with what seems to be an endless conveyor belt of different resource types, but it gets a little less strenuous as you come out of the early, and into the middle game. I would hesitate to recommend this as your first 4x game.The bad:- Performance. While my PC is getting on a bit, it still exceeds the minimum specs and meets the recommended specs for many of the categories listed. Despite this, Millennia runs very badly past the early game, with extremely bad framerates even on lower graphics settings. (This is possibly because Millennia doesn't seem to want to use more than 4GB of RAM, despite the fact that it almost certainly should use more - I have 16GB for context)- Limited map customisation. If you're used to setting up the map generator with options depending on what kind of game you enjoy then you're out of luck. These are a few map presets and that is it.Overall: would recommend if it is in a runnable state, I enjoyed this a lot more than I did my first few playthroughs of Endless Legend, and if you're a bit sick of each turn taking 10-30 minutes in the lategame of Civ 6, this is a game with some fantastic (and some less so) systems that are very interesting to get your teeth into.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first ever Steam Review. I'm writing it because I thought it a shame that the current rating for Millennia is 'mixed' as I am enjoying it thoroughly. Each time i have played it through I have enjoyed it more and more. There's a lot in this game and it's difficult to absorb the sheer depth of detail in one go. The region, vassal, outpost system is pure genius and a huge intellectual delight once you have got your head round it. It was probably on my fourth play through that I had my light bulb moment.The problem with Civilisation type games  (for me) is the drudgery of the end game. Not so with Millennia (for me). As you progress through the ages you find that each age has its own set of goals and challenges. The game is full of innovative ideas. I love in particular the delightful sub quests like being the first nation to build 2 castles on outposts in the age of kings.One thing that I am missing is the nation summary screen where you can see in one place all the food, hammers of each of your regions. Hopefully this will be added to the game with an update.I am sooo glad I bought this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of complaints seem to compare this to Civ, which is isn't - very different systems all around. About the only similarity is the hex tiles. How cities expand, how you improve tiles, research - that all is wildly different than the Civ series. The foundation exists that if you came from Civ, it's a good frame of reference, but beyond that the game is very different. The inclusion of different possible ages that change the landscape of the game is neat. The military composition has more depth than Civ by far, and the domains are an interesting layer of resource management. Supply chains are an important part of the game, and while you can resource horde in individual cities easily in the late game, the early game, establishing domestic trade is important for getting higher tiered goods and the bonuses that come with them.Graphics aren't great, and the game lags a bit towards the late game, but otherwise a very solid title. Steep learning curve, but more engaging than the present Civ titles.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best strategy games I have ever played. You have to make prerequisites to advance to new ages, Enlightened, Basic, or Crisis ages, balance out your national spirits, and prepare for the future. This has Civilization beat hands down, and I've been playing that since it came out, can only polish a turd so many times. This is a whole new spin on the genre and please try it and pass it along to others. More people the better cause I know this is an instant classic, just needs more players and reviews.I'm going to say if you are not ready for a real challenge, and use to things being handed to you, or you want a cake walk where you only have to play a game once to get it, don't get this game. Nobody likes a whiner.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoy the new and different approach to the tried and true Civ series that Millenia rewrites here. The Domain and different Age mechanics really shine. That being said the game does look and feel about a decade old with some rough edges. The game is getting regular updates so I expect only an upward trend for this gem.  I would only get this title when on sale, unless you have deep pockets, as it does have some rough edges due to dated graphics and UI.After 300+ hours now I would like to add that while the game can be a joy to play while building up massive city states there are a few things that come up weak-sauce. Like Diplomacy, which feels under-cooked. Just a lack of options and overly simple. For example the AI will always be aggressive to you if they are stronger then you or neighboring you. Making it very difficult to play peacefully unless you have a large standing army in which case it would be more optimal to use said military. Another negative is the poor battle AI. It does "okay" with air units but on land they only attack other units if they have a 1v1 advantage. Meaning if they have multiple units to your one and could win if they all attack well, they won't. Unless it's an objective like a city where they will gladly suicide against. I mean the combat AI is better than Civ 6, which is a complete joke, but not by much. Also, the end game can be just as boring and overly long like some others in the 4X space meaning I tend to finish games with a conquest victory which can get repetitive but it's far better than clicking next turn over and over when the outcome is already well known. Just a quick update. Still a lot to like but like many in this genre it is under-cooked in some areas and will hopefully improve over time.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I'm updating my review now that the second DLC and its accompanying patch have hit. The diplomacy system started broken and just keeps getting worse. Last night I had AIs sending me gifts during the war they declared on me, and they still forward-settle and them complain you are too close, and try to ally with everybody so it's at best random who will end up with and against you after a DOW. I don't think I'll be playing any more.Original review:Not as polished as Civ 6, but still good. The first patch fixed the thing that caused most early professional reviews to be negative, and so far I'm pleased. Some UI and UX and QoL problems, ,and a very different early game experience (you have to gear up against barbarians, you can't just pick off the camps - in fact, the camps are small cities with a wall and will take some time to be ready to take out.With the tuning for the Age of Plague done, the main innovation here is interesting. Since the civ starting bonuses are minor, each playthrough ends up interesting as you pick development options that fit the map and your starting position.Overall the most interesting and fun 4X since Civ 6 itself came out.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know if i can fully recommend this game yet, there is a lot of work left on this game but i still enjoyed my first play through and as someone with hundreds of hours in every civ game this is a breath of fresh air.The Ugly:UI is very ugly and needs workCombat is wonky and the animation needs to either be stylized or at least there needs to be an option to disable it.balance is a bit wonkyCities (especially vassals) need to be deletable, AI builds cities way too close together and i wish i could delete at least half of them AI needs work, higher difficulties is not smarter AI its just more modifiers applied to them (same issue as Civ)Maps feel cramped The Good:I Loooove the supply chains and really hope they expand on them, maybe give goods that you make by combining resources or more branching chains.The Science system is very different from Civ and i quite enjoy it.the Ages are great.I looove the HUGE citiesAll in all its already a decent game and it probably will be a great game after some DLC's and updates

_childDocuments_.review: God I would not recommend this game. you have quick start and custom to create a single player game. I went with custom to get an idea what is going on and left everything at default. the game gives you a tutorial in a Book format and expects that you understand the UI. I even got a tutorial that was like "you can promote your units since you probably have combat experience by now." Uh no. have not run into a single thing I could fight and it was not until 3 turns later that I found a barbarian, it was stronger then me. By the time I finished my second technology. I got a cut scene that we are entering the age of bronze. I was like wow that is fast paced, its only been 10 turns. By the time I got out of the stone age, some how we entered the age of heroes! I finally understood what the book said about getting improvements in my land once I got to the age of bronze, err heroes? not sure how the thing works. are we all at the age of heroes? or is it just saying that somebody is there already. Enemy nations have three times my power level and most of the map is under somebody elses control. Game needs a 1v1 tutorial that explains each thing instead of just assuming we know what they are talking about. Just actually playing was super tedious and I felt like I was just "end turn" every 5 seconds. Game is not new player friendly I am not a fan of hand holding as much as the next guy/gal. yet it feels like the game punishes you for not squeezing out everything you can do each turn. Sorry this is a refund from me.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes...but.This game has some very neat ideas. I love the idea of the branching timelines. It adds for replay-ability and an element of uncertainty forcing you to adapt to unexpected situations. The game offers some good opportunity for strategy as you continue to master the mechanics. There are many bugs, and missing QoL features however which may bring frustration to experienced 4X players. The devs appear very responsive however and I have faith that many of these will be addressed. Despite these issues, the game has still managed to keep pulling me back for more.

_childDocuments_.review: Recommend with some caveats. Basically if you know what you are buying, then its fine, even for full price.Summary: I was done after playing about 80 hours, taking the last 20 hours to 100%. In these 80 hours i had a lot of fun, some frustrating moments and overall enjoyed my time with Millennia. 80h for full price is fine, if you get it on sale it is definitely worth a pick up.Better than FoG, Civ6 and Humankind. On the other hand, Old World is way better, but also way more frustrating.Millennia is basically a turn based civ builder with Path of Exile league gimmicks. The gimmicks are hit and miss, but discovering all of them did take me around 100 hours and they were fun, different and didn't get in the way if i didn't want to deal with them.Definitely the strongest part are the gimmicks and perk trees. Again these are too hit and miss, and by the third game it was clear to me that over half of the traits i will never ever pick. ever. What is left over is still varied and fun, and you don't get punished really picking something that hasn't got a bonus. (which in my games against the AI actually never happened, not even against grandmaster)The AI is bad, not terrible, just doesn't know most of the time what to do with anything. What keeps the AI in the game is the massive flat boni for anything (a completely burned down AI city grew several % faster than my smaller 200% capital).Unfortunately the AI "difficulty" gets a bit in the way of selecting the interesting gimmicks, because the moment you are faster to the next age than the AI the player basically won.My second game ever i beat 4 master AI within 130 turns, more or less by accident, which let me farm basically 60% of the achievements in the game, which is a bit of a shame.I did have the feeling that the AI was neutered because the early reviews complained about the too aggressive AI. This is still somewhat the case. Mostly early game until the player has most of the must have boxes ticked.I did not play multiplayer, and in IMHO there are so many unbalanced things in the game, that it might be hard to get an interesting MP going if the players are even slightly different skill level.The worst part about the game is the map generator. Spawns are unbalanced and if you are surrounded by forest and hills you are going to have a bad time. Everything takes forever and its not very fun to play at all. Other times you start with nothing but flat for miles around ...

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fundamentally un-civlike - If you like engine building board games, you might want to give this a go. If you find them 'mostly busywork' then you might not like it so much.I particularly like how your culture can be built up over time; There is no 'I am India, therefore I must build tall'Cons:Poor framerate. Although turn times are short, frames drop pretty hard when improvements start to fill every tile.It poorly explains good practice, e.g. in civ there are 'build a city here' icons when you are a new player. In Millennia it's entirely possible to screw up and place cities too close without realising. I like this, for me learning a game like this over time is fun, but others can find this frustratingLack of game setup settings. It would be fun to change world gen settings, or add more than 8 players, and so on. Overall, I am having a lot of fun with this game. I'm not sure why I wrote so much here, no-one ever reads any reviews anyway

_childDocuments_.review: I made a huge update to this review, but Steam decided not to save the changes.So in short, I like where the devs are going with the updates, and feel I can now recommend it. Most of the issues below have been addressed, except Raiders which is still very much OP, but other ideas feel now viable too.Things to address in the future: *founding regions on resources (sometimes makes sense)*civic and industry improvements in forests and hills, especially housing*ridiculously expensive outpost improvements*map generation (perhaps some more asymmetrical land masses, instead of essentially just two huge slabs*separate razing (immediate) and abandoning vassal regions*switching tiles between regions*RAIDERS! (maybe just one per spawn?)Hope someone reads this, and keep up the good work!***In its current state, I cannot recommend to buy this game. While it has some very innovative ideas and mechanics, I cannot bear to launch a new game while the major flaws have been addressed.To list a few:1) AI region rush/cannot raze region capitals: As a human player, you try to build you empire as economically as possible, which means picking good spots for your region capitals and cities which allow you to specialise according to the resources in nearby. AI however does not take the map into consideration. It spams the map with totally random region and city placement, choosing the most appalling locations. If an AI has an envoy, he will surely use it to take over a barbarian capital, paying to attention to how close it is to its borders, or how terrible the surrounding area is. The game will allow you to place up to four cities in a region, but for some AI created regions you are lucky if you can place two that would make any sense.While you can raze cities, you cannot raze a region capital. Which mostly results in a game where you don't even want to look at AI regions, since they are so unbelievably uneconomical. You can't 2) Unbalanced national ideas:If you have played a few games, you know that the only Bronze Age national idea worth picking is Raiders. Its so ridiculously overpowered, you can clear a continent of opponents before age IV on a medium map. The other warfare ideas, while slightly weaker, are still quite powerful and progress quite fast, as using the armies they will allow you to amass will generate the warfare points you need to get through the tree. Most other choices however seem actually counterproductive, especially at the start of the game.3) AI diplomacy:In a very linear, banal approach to diplomacy, the AI is only receptive if you are stronger than them. You can try dedicate a game to trying to cultivate trade with your neighbours, to keep relations positive, and they still might go to war with you even after literally centuries of peace, even if your strength ratings are on par.That said, it might still be fun to play it as a multiplayer game, once the option is added. Although I predict everyone either picking or banning Raiders.

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot recommend Millenia in its current state. What is there is really, really solid. There's a great economic simulation in there and the region system is a fantastically superior implementation of the concept than any other Civ V sequel has managed. There are however a *ton* of game breaking bugs & missing features, especially in the late game.* Combat is atrociously balanced. It is never clear who is going to win and even with overwhelming force there's a 50-50 chance you'll lose because of some hidden mechanic or bug. Any war in the industrial era or beyond is an exercise in pulling teeth, especially if trying to siege cities.* Tech racing is very much a thing in this game. Tech racing has always been the worst part of Civ games, so it's not surprising to see it here but it is shocking how bad the balance is. It seems like the AI is hardcoded to tech race and then stop to let the player catch up. No matter how you play, you will never be the tech leader, which with how the age system works means you never have control over your own singleplayer experience.* Age selection is integral to the experience of the game. BUT you the player never get to pick the next age since it is tied to being the tech leader. On the rare occasion you are lucky enough to get your three techs before the AI cheats ahead, there's a good chance you don't actually get to choose between ages since the conditions are so random to achieve.* The economy is not well explained and while it is deep, it takes a lot of learning for the player to get to grips with what works and what doesn't. It's very non-intuitive and the AI cannot just be copied as a way to learn since they cheat.* Tiles cannot be swapped between regions, and expanding thus becomes a race where you the player are always screwed. Like every other aspect of this game, it's just frustrating for no reason.There's a good game here, but it's buried under several layers of unplayable crap. Still a better game than Civ 6, not that that's saying much.

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game has potential. I had fun. Then, my capital revolted - a revolution, you might say - except, that this was a game over. Despite violent revolutions being a separate thing you can do, and peaceful revolutions being a core gameplay mechanic.This enormous inconsistency made me so disappointed I had to put the game down for while. Only buy if you have a lot of money to spare; I don't see this game standing on it's own two feet before a lot of work has been done. My faith in that happening has been shaken by Imperator Rome, and if this turns out to be another burnt chance it very well may be the last Paradox product I buy.

_childDocuments_.review: So where to begin,Millennia is a (for me at least) fresh new take on the turn-based strategy formula. I've got a few k's of gametime across alot of Civ games, (3-6) so a lot of things mentioned here will mostly be in contrast to Civ-Games.For the Lazy: tl;dr, would recommend, Ages are fun, mechanics are nice and the game feels good, albeit a bit clunky here and there.If not sure, as always, wait for Sale.Now back to it.Pros:-From the get-go have Access to "Army" meaning multiple Units attack and go on the same tile.-The "Age" where you are technologically standing is way more relevant. However, you may as well get dragged into some "unfortunate" Ages by the AI, more of that in Cons.-The variant ages are really fun to discover. May it be the Age where Alchemy gets discoverd and drives your world, or a dystopian age made possible by a reckless playstyle.-City development feels better than "grassland -> Farm". The Addition of multiple sub-cities to a mayor city really makes long-term planning exciting.-No Diplomacy spam in one turn means to actually think about what to propose.-The different aspects of the Domains and their powers are really nice to have, and planning around these values is in my opinion quite nice to do.-There is a nice System to see which City has which Tiles and what is build on them. Easy reassignmend too.-The Outpost/Vassal system is kinda nice to have, especially for the Outposts to deny AI resources or to get something you really need.-Maps are nicely generated, with kind of good resource generation. Sometimes a bit too much of the same tile at once, but it still feels "Biome Appropriate".-Late in the game, there are ways to shape the Tiles or even make new Landspace. That is, however, also Limited by the amount of Domain-EXP you can spend. So terraforming a whole ocean away is not possible.Cons:-The AI is really whacky as of right now. Alliances are mostly not worth doing, however being friendly with them also does not require an Alliance.-AI will declare Hostilitys or outright war out of the left field, try to Rush one Settlement or vassal and f*ck of right after.-You will currently be locked out of quite nice technologies if you take the Variant age or get locked into an crisis age.E.g Age of Rocketry->Age of Ecology->Final Age. There are mostly none new flying units in these Ages. Not that these are really needed, but in my opinion, at least standart-age units should also appear to be researchable, mostly because AI will stay aggressive if you are near them or they are settling near you.-The AI builds their Cities really close together, and doesn't use the Subcities muchRegarding Subcities, they can only be build through a Culture Power, which also grants (at the time) better Situational benefits. Would be nice if a Town (Subcity) could be established through a special City-project, after which a pop-up appears giving the player the choice, costing either Money AND improvement points for a new town, or denying it, loosing the Productivity generated and giving Money + Culture or something like that.Building Cities is not Settler -> City. You settle in a place of your choosing, yes, but the City is a Vassal at first, needing it to be integrated. This limits the Player to a Maximum of 7 (8 if choosing the right Domains) to actually control. I can understand that, but a bit wierd.-To my liking, there are not enough national Spirits to choose, well to actually HAVE. Throughout the whole game, you can have a maximum of 4. Would be nice to have 5 or 6 of them for flexibility, maybe nerf some perks for spirits that have already been picked. (so far i had mostly taken the Exploration/Engineering spirits)-Some resources are, at the beginning of an age, really difficult to get (Religion/Ideology/Information). -Expanding your city happens everywhere around it at once, with currently no way to focus where into. Doesn't really help that the amount of influence-Buildings is kinda small, same with Powers. You can at most use the power to "Claim" a tile i think 6-8 times. So 8 Tiles at max. Understandable on small maps, but kinda a pain on big maps.-Small Maps are really dense with resources, forcing you to forgo some resources in favor of needs.-No oil in Oceans (haven't been to Age of Utopia yet, so dunno about that), meaning desert-Tiles are the only way to get oil.Also, if turned to grassland via Domain-Power, resources and build Tiles disappear. You can bully the AI with that tho, which is fun.-Variant-Ages cannot be chosen back to back. Understandable, but an option on the side of the player to enable that for maximum shenegians would be nice.Overall, even if I wrote more about the Cons, i still had the "one more Turn" feeling i had when first playing civ 5 or 6. AI seems a bit techrushy but its manageable.Millennia is nice to learn and difficult to master (City swapping to Vassal to claim another to build it up) and its quite fun to play with the Crisis/Variant ages. I wish for more of them or at least for some to last longer until they are obsolete.Would recommend Millennia to fans of round based strategy, its really fun to play even right now, however im not sure about the announced DLCs already, thats on the side of Paradox tho (see their other titles)If you are unsure, wait for a Sale and get it then, but for a title developed by essential an Indie-Studio, its a really nice game to play deep into the night (just one more turn).
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Millennia is the most underrated game of 2024.I just had a lot of fun with this game. Love the ages mechanics. Love the EP/XP mechanics which allow meaningful reactions to difficult situations.People saying the game is like Anno are exaggerating . Yes the game has production chains and increasing demands, but it's so simplified that it only makes up a small part of the game. And is not a civ6. But it doesn't have to be. You can play both games and have fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I predict this will be a big winner if the developers stay with it.    It's the first game since Old World that grabbed me with next turn energy.    I understand the complaints but frankly I wonder if there is some Paradox hate going on.    Lots of innovative ideas.   I don't really care if they call it early access, beta or late for dinner.    Its early in the games life and it has alot to offer.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Huge 4x-fan, really wanted this to be good. Even the most basic starting options are not even in the game yet. If you want the full game more "Premium edition" is needed and even more Day 1-DLC announced with the release. _childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Do yourself a favour. Do anything elseBoot up Civ 5 again. Hell, even Civ Beyond Earth. There's some cool ideas in there, right?...This game contains 1 good idea, the economy. It's essentially several pipelines that feed into each other resulting in better value from your land. Only, you can only construct this on your city's territory, not on your land, like Civ 5 tile improvements.The second you get into any war, these places and your external towns are immediately targeted. It will take *hundreds* of turns to regrow into this.Cities can be razed in 1 turn.If you do not pick the war options you suck at war so unbelievably bad that regardless of the amount of other ♥♥♥♥ you have, there is NOTHING you can do. You will die.Millennia is an exercise in carrot and stick gameplay. The carrot is small, a simple gameplay loop with some new ideas to keep it fresh. The stick is labelled "Crusader" and has a 3x bonus against all other units, and is able to beat mustketmen, grenadiers, and tier 7 leaders, in a single attack. After settling a castle on your border and shooting your units while you are at peace with them.Oh and you get a government option that gives +575% output from vassals, or the option to pick republic, giving you two things: ♥♥♥♥, and all.Do not play Millennia.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: This is one that I'm torn on. It's fine for scratching that 'one-more-turn' itch, but something about it feels clunky or shallow. It has some neat concepts like the ages and national spirits. I see where they were going for replayability with these features but the execution could be better. I recommend it with the caveat that it if you are looking for the next Civ masterpiece, this is not it. It satisfies its genre well-enough, but that is the extent.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: For those that dont want to read too much: Its better than CIV 6.For everyone else:4xGames are never about the Visuals, but about the core mechanics. So if you are looking for a feast for the eyes you are wrong here. At the same time, the graphics are readable and useful so after a while you get used to and they dont bother you. Yes it lacks in immersion and yes it could have been better, but in the end you wont miss them over time cause you try to figure out how to develop your cities.This game has many great new mechanics, which give a new experience in 4x games.As the dud that CIV 6 was and Humankind wasnt better, we finally see a game, that actually can add a innovative game mechanic. Many things like resources and city development feel different and better.As i dont want to spoil it, i wont mention more, but there is a lot to experience.Still there a 2 things i dont like.First is the progression through the game - it is far too quick. You barely managed to build an army of Archers and Spearmen just to find out they are obsolete again. This is something that needs to be addresse or a mod that does the same. You simply cant enjoy the ages as they are over before you settled in them.Second, Custom Game settings are non existent, which in my book is one of the main things any strategy game should have. This game doesnt give you much options.I recommend this game to everyone that actually likes strategygames.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Bad/AnnoyingNo options on launcherUnable to rebind keys, sorry if you have a disability you will just have to ask for a refundOnly 3/4 mapsFar too many barbarians with no options to change frequency/aggression Any unit that moves in to a tile with another unit joins the army and stops moving, if that army was 'ignored' from a previous turn, you don't get a prompt to tell you so your settler, envoy, etc could be sat idle while you think it's moving toward the hex you chose for it to go toCombat animation looks like it was made by a middle schooler for a project, not competent game designersCan change the map size, but max of 8 players even on the largest, still had an AI spawn within 10 hexesNo research tree, so unable to map out progress until you go in to the next ageVirtually no interactions with the AI playersGoodLooks nicePlenty of buildings and improvements, making you think about what you want to spend points onGood and badFar too many choices with far too few points to spendFar too many different types of points to earn/spend
