_childDocuments_.review: First of all, I do not understand the mitigated rating of this game ; sure it's not perfect, but its really enjoyable. I have seen that many thumbs down have been given by players who did not exceed 30h of play : this game has enough depth that this is too short to grasp anything about it.Don't expect to be playing Civ. If you want to play Civ, buy civ and play it. This is another 4X game with its own mecanisms, and in that regard it boast a lot of good ideas. I won't describe the details of the game  : you can find reviews or other players evaluations for that. It would be much too lengthy to provide any serious details. Lets focus on some pints:- This game is much less forgiving that civ (barbarians are a lot more aggressive at start, which is as it should be) ; IA are not kind (it's a bit of an ennoyance ; maybe I've not yet found how to talk nicemy to them). So you should expect to have to deal with wars ; most often with opponents that have more armies than you (hopefully that are startegicallly incompetent).- This game requires some level of micromanagement ; More than civ because unlike civ, there is a chain of production between basic items (say rice) and evolved products (say alcool or better food) ; your transformation chain is anything but trivial because the products will affect some aspect of the city (more food or more luxuries or more production...) ; in addition, you can exchange goods bteween cities, and import or export goods with other civilizations. You could compare that with civ luxuries, with an additional depth).- You have to manage more resources than in civ : culture, knowledge, warfare, engineering, faith, education, specialists, government, diplomacy, arts, electricity... This makes Civ a child here.- The technologies in this game are less numerous than those in Civ, but lets face it : a lot of techs in civ bring just nothing. Here, all technologies are worth it and bring new units, buildings... and usually not one, but two, three or even more.- The ages transitions are also used in this game, and they are way more important and interesting than in civ. At worst in civ (normal game), you have a bad age and that has little impact (it may have some, but the effects are light). Here, when you change age, you may have drastic different results, such as the age of pestilence where you will have to deal with pestilence outbreaks, and where the technologies will turn around that drastic event (reduce pestilence outbreaks, build medics...). If you eschew that age, you'll never see these technologies. Each age transition can lead to three or for different ages, and the first civ that breaks through defines the age ; sometimes, you don't have a choice. e.g. if your civ was unhealthy, you may be locked onto the age of pestilence.- In general, the graphic aspects of the game are not as good as those of Civ. I could not pinpoint why, but its a personal feeling. More generally, I find it difficult to get all the info I would. This is a bit ennoying.- I also believe that the game cheats (both in terms of development as in terms of warfare) ; on normal level, the IA civ consistently seem to outproduce me (I'm no newbee in this kind of game), out reserach me and I know for sure that they also know where your units are when they shouldn't (a boat of mine was attacked in deep sea by a plane and I was sure the oppoment should not have known it's position). I don't like games that cheat.- You can have wonders, but their creation is not forthcoming ; you cannot control which you will have, if any. These come as rewards for inovation breakthrough. Hence you don't have the competition to be the first to build such or such wonder, and wonders here seldom impact your whole civilization. They are worthwhile though.All of this only scratches the complexity of this game.As a conclusion, this game is full of very interesting and inovating mechanisms. It really is worth you money if you're into that kind of game. Once again, I'm pretty sure that most negative opinions come from players who did not even scratch the surface of the game, or who felt overwhelmed.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Paradox as of late has been at total let down and this is yet another. I have always been a huge fan of Civ games and the likes. There is very little meat to this game. It is somewhat confusing, to really get anywhere you have to constantly be building armies and seed generation at times sucks. You tend to get railroaded by barbarians often. You can not control your other cities in the least bit. All and all great concept, but execution sucks. Paradox really needs to take a step back and look at the games they produced a few years ago and go back to it. In-depth, immersive, and strategic. Not dumbed down hot dog water type of games. I really have to lower my expectations now from Paradox.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Early impressions: there are legitimate critiques of the UI and the choice to treat "nations" as blank canvases but I think what really matters here, is that Millennia so far feels like a game that I can't win on turn 200 and just have to click through another 200 turns to see the win screen. It has off roads to end the game if you've run away with it, and ways the game can be ended for you if you aren't taking into the account how other people are playing at the same time. I came for the alternate ages which are thrilling but I stayed for the very fun and very deep economy. I'm still experiencing the game but I want to drop a note to encourage you to try it to, you won't be disappointed if you are a little patient and dig into it.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: It's pretty good if you care about gameplay more than the looks.+ The game is well-designed: there is always a feel "I am missing this and that", a need to choose - at least until the mid-late game, when you finally start to outpace the game. It also self-balances (e.g. by having ability costs grow)+ Opponents play reasonably well, settle and grow a lot of cities, could be more aggressive. The barbarians are a good challenge early game.+ It's possible to win the game earlier and peacefully if you are already dominating.+ Okay music and sound effects.- A bit laggy for me on my older PC. It should be better optimized, given the game's simple graphics.- Could have a bit more eye candy, tile building graphical designs could be further improved.Will be playing again, and waiting for new features, buildings, resources, and fps and other improvements.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: It is deep, it is fun, and got the potential for a long-time game. It still needs lots of improvement, though - the UI is confusing in some parts and the diplomacy interface is abhorrent, but I trust this will happen over time. The game is very very deep and you will have to learn by probably running a few sessions into the ground, getting further and further through the Ages ... while having an increasing amount of fun ... the replayability seems amazing!I'd class this as a next level Civilisation, a 4X where you truly shape your civilisation through and through.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: So much better than Civ 5 or 6 already, and seemingly a much less skeezy business model. The developers are prioritising the updates that the community are asking for. Also, this game released with enough content to be a full, deep game. This is unlike many 4Xes which can be quite shallow unless you fork out for a load of DLC. Genuinely good game which seems to only be improving.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Months away from being ready for release, this featureless game could have been a pleasant experience with only a pittance of effort devoted to quality of life. As it stands, every game of Millennia is a new episode of "Dealing with Barbarians."Because the developer chose to devote zero time to allowing the user any control over the settings of a skirmish, and because the distinctions between nations are practically nil, every game plays almost exactly the same. Minor era choices and minimal starting zone differences are dwarfed by the player's decisions about how to deal with barbarians. Once they finish developing this already-released, full-price game, the bones could lead to something lovely. Until then, it's an unfair ask of consumers that they subsidize an alpha product from a massively wealthy and well-capitalized company. Pass for now.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Relaxed turn-based game, I quite like it and find it doesn't have any of the main flaws I experienced when I tried Civ which is the most similar game that I'm familiar with.That doesn't mean however that its valid to compare to Civ when looking at features, I saw a review complaining about not having customizable resources and timing, but neither of those features seem suited to this game.I've been busy with other stuff so I haven't tried the newest version so I can't comment on the polish and the price.I have no interest in MP but I can understand that port-forwarding is quite outdated to expect

_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: The game has some very interesting concepts that make for a great 4X game... the main problem with the game is that Paradox Publishing is doing their normal business model of lacking content for the sake of adding it later as paid DLC that makes the game boring.I wanted a new 4X turn-based strategy game to play since I haven't had one that I really enjoyed since Civilization 5. This one seemed poised to offer me what I wanted and I so desperately wanted to enjoy the game. They have some fantastic new ideas in this game that help give it potential! The ability to guide the world into different ages, altering the timeline into more bloody warfare or more steampunk automation is fantastic! The ability to send out vassal states to get some resources at the cost of full control is good! The innovation/chaos system is great to provide variety to game play and encourage/discourage different actions that might be helpful now but will come with a cost later.But where the game shows its weakness is that it is really boring. When you select your starting civilization, there is no benefit to picking anything but your favorite name because you can just change the starting bonus to whatever you want, and the civilizations have no real personality since they are all literally interchangeable. The micromanagement of economies gets boring very quickly (unless your into that type of gameplay). But worst of all is that the divergent timeline aspect (which arguably is the coolest aspect of this game) always forces you back to the "real-life" timeline after you select one of these alternate ages. While I understand why this is done to keep the game play mostly together and flowing in the right direction, it is just super disappointing. And then the AI of the other factions are just so... annoying, and not in a good way. The enemy doesn't do anything that is smart to stop you or interfere, they just annoy you. Like when allied nations will forward settle you right in the middle of two of your own cities. Or move their entire armed forces to block merchants and envoys. Overall, I think this game might be great a few years and a hundred dollars of DLC's from now, but its not worth buying right now.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I have been following this game for awhile and was super excited to try it, then i saw the reviews. I was hesitant but i still gave it a try. While yes it's true the multiplayer is not yet here and the graphics are not amazing. I still think this is a good game. I played a game up until the Renaissance era and I have not run into any major issues. I enjoy the game for what it is, a 4x historical era game. The era's are creative and there are some good mechanics here. I just think will a little love the issues people have can easily be fixed. Personally I have no problem with the graphics, this is not the kind of game that demands amazing looking characters. I also don't mind playing by myself. For the people complaining about too many barbarians, get good. They really aren't that bad if you proactively go after there camps every once in awhile.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I trust PDX and I believe they will update the game to be more in depth, but as it stands right now this is a sub par historical 4x.It's been my experience that they haven't done great with their TBS's in the past and maybe that's where my mind is at right now, but everything this game does, other games do better.I also went into this hoping there would be Stellaris like gameplay, given that is PDX's prize game. Maybe that made my expectations a little too high, but that's also why I trust PDX to figure it out, long term.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: When "Millennia" was announced, I was beyond excited. The game promised to be something special. I was really looking forward to diving into this new world with friends and having epic adventures together. But now, months after the release, I'm just disappointed. A proper multiplayer mode is still nowhere to be found.Instead, I see the developers announcing a DLC – and it's paid, too. Honestly, it feels like a slap in the face. How can they expect players to spend more money when the base game doesn't even deliver on what was originally promised? I just don't get why they're focusing on additional content while the game itself still feels incomplete.It's incredibly frustrating that the developers seem to be trying to make the most out of a half-finished game without fulfilling the most basic expectations of the players. I was so excited for the multiplayer mode, and now here I am, without the opportunity to experience the game the way it was meant to be.I can't help but wonder what the future of "Millennia" will look like. Will the developers finally deliver the promised multiplayer mode? Or will the game just continue to be expanded with more paid content, without fulfilling the original promises? Until that's addressed, I'm left with a bitter taste and can´t recommend it...
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: When I first got this game I hated it but it has definitely  grown on me and now it has that "just one more turn"  obsession I haven't felt since Civilization V.  I've never really liked Civilization 6 so much with it's giant deck of cards, but that's just me. The underlying mechanics of the game and its various systems make perfect sense (cultural, governmental, military, exploration etc. ) and flow together in a fairly intuitive way.  Where you place your cities on the map and it's surrounding resources really matters and the ages system works just fine.  It also really matters how you form your military troops in combat.  The UI gets the job done, but it could be better.  The graphics are generally OK, however I don't understand the developer's decisions to make everything you plop down on the land in your cities look almost exactly the same, which is basically a plop of mud.  A trash heap looks the same as a textile factory the same as a public school etc.  Just ugly.  A simple icon would have been better.  Also, until you learn the systems and how the AI behaves, things can QUICKLY spiral out of control in this game, more so than other 4X games....it's why I hated it at first because I didn't understand why it was happening.  It takes some time.  As an aside, I still hate the AGE OF PLAGUE, even though I can get through it just fine now, it is simply tedious.  If I wanted to play wack-a-mole I would have brought  that.Overall, this is a really good take on the 4X genre and doesn't get enough credit.  I't doesn't seem very popular so I don't know how much the developers will support it along the way.I

Due to improvements system and chain of goods system (Wheat->Flour->Bread), the game feels a little like a board game. The AI is agressive and isn't afraid of going to war if they think you're weaker.My only complaint is the UI - it feels a little cluttered at times. Good graphics, and excellent game plans. difficult choices. Some may say it's a revamped Civilization or Humankind. But, it isn't. far superior to either of them. _childDocuments_.review: The game has potential however some mechanics need complete re-works. The Chaos mechanic is completely broken, losing your capital province without a fight is crazy because you don't have enough money to buy off rebels???? then you have to wait 6 turns to recapture it, then wait another 50 turns to re-incorporate it back into your own nation is crazy. You should start off at war and when you capture your cities in civil war they shouldn't be force into re-incorporation for that long, if they have the homeland trait. The Chaos meter fills too fast and has too strong of repercussions.  The religion aspect needs work, you get too much unrest with not enough buildings to quell it. I'm all for random factors but when your entire civilization falls in one turn because of the chaos meter, it becomes annoying not fun......This game feels very unfinished.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I can see a lot of potential in the game, after playing a couple hours and getting a chance to experience the mechanics.  It's a different experience mechanically from Civ template to a marked degree, but not an entirely alien experience.The greatest positive I can say is that it that it captures the attempt that Humankind made to actually grow a civilization instead of an empire, and making a new history instead of simply hitting every era and tech.  Ironically, this game deserves the name 'Civilization' more than the actual series since you're playing a growing and changing Civilization more than just a human faction going through our known history.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Having fun so far. It's been a challenge figuring out the best way to start out with all of the supply chains and various benefits you get from early choices, which is nice. It's like a more complex Civilization game in terms of management, and as someone who tends to play peaceful city-sim style in 4X games having more to manage is welcome since I don't fight as much.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: A solid 4X Strategy game.  Not the vaunted 'Civ Killer' of legend, but more than just a weak clone.  The graphics and AI are nothing to write home about, but neither are they embarrassing.  The main appeal, besides the Ages variants, are the number of levers you can pull with the various in-game options utilizing the different categories of XP that you accrue.  In so many of these types of games, you wind up hitting Next Turn repeatedly while that building or unit you're waiting on gets finished, or else slogging through late game until you can finish with a Science of Cultural Victory.  There is also more of a need to strategize and improvise based on circumstances rather than just conform to a game plan which you decided on when you initially picked your civ.  Plenty of bumps and flaws and some basic features that are not yet present which I've come to expect from this kind of game, but nothing game breaking.  I'm having fun playing it now, and looking forward to seeing how they expand on the game's collection of unique gameplay dynamics in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of wasted potential here sadly. Ages and the production chain of resources are ideas which if given more than a surface level amount of effort could add the extra replay and role-play value that 4X games can never have enough of.That is where the positives end, the barbarians are far too numerous, the AI constantly spams military units, to the point where you can easily overtake them technologically. Despite the hordes they have at their command, due to the AI being brain dead, their armies are no more dangerous than a baby with a notably large stick. Worse still, unless you force peace them the AI will NEVER peace out of a war, making an already slow game a tedious slog. The game has clearly not been tested for balance either, vassals are too powerful and you win the game as soon as you can get crusaders, due to their 3x bonus against other religions and how easily they can be spammed .Do not play this mobile game, it is an unfinished product. Play Clash of Clans or something.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I'm enjoying this game a lot. That said, the game is quite unpolished for something at this price point.-The graphics are fine, but nothing earth-shattering. Then again, I loved the original Civ graphics, so ymmv.-The battles are extremely simple. For me, this is a plus, but that may not be the case for everyone.-Though I really enjoy the way improvements function, but I don't like that I can only queue 1 building at a time, and science can't be queued at all.-The game setup is not comprehensive. There's no way to save preferences to quick start in the future, and there's little customization available both aesthetically and mechanically. Nothing to customize aggression, resources, start locations, and map types are quite limited.-The multiplayer is not fully implemented, with part of its functionality tagged "coming soon". I happen to be a solo player, but that doesn't make this an acceptable practice — the game is not labelled as early access, so it's expected that the multiplayer features would be fully implemented.I have a soft spot for Paradox, and I do like this game, but I don't think it should be recommended in its current state.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Graphics are poor. 1995 like. But gameplay is worse. Combat is auto-combat, with annoyingly stupid and bad animations. Game rushes on, tutorial is poor, it's unclear what's going on, you have no time to develop anything. Bad feeling. Maps are random trash. You start building somehting, but then in 100 turns you figure out you were not paying attention to something else. AI rushes you, game over. Why did I buy this?
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Quite unfinished, but very promising (and addictive) game.Personally I found it quite nice that you can play against yourself, trying several different National Spirits/Government types at once and testing them against each other.Alternative Ages, while sometimes underdeveloped and superficial, allow for a fun diversion from the usual progression from stone tools to space crafts.Tbh the "unfinished" part is just as important as "engaging". For example, the alternative eras sadly do not have any lasting impact, their tech and resources either vanishing or becoming instantly outdated. It was especially jarring when proceeding from steampunk-inspired "Age of Aether" into and extremely mundane  "Age of Rocketry".  Allowing to proceed from a variant Age into variant Age could've mended the problem - going from Alchemy into Steampunk and then into Utopia with deepsea living domes seems more organic than sudden drop to reality.In general, lategame seems especially unfinished, as if hastily assembled at the last possible moment, and even Variant ages don't provide for same flavor and feel as do the earlier ones.But I have hopes that the dev team will do their work and not leave everything up to modding community.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a lot of interesting features that could have meant a new era for 4x.It's not though. This feels like a early access release with confusing menus, bad art direction, and soulless AI that will leave you in the dust.It's such a shame to see something that has passion behind it be crushed in what feels like another Paradox cash grab.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: The game looks promising, if you enjoy these games single player you'll probably enjoy this one.If you have friends, Hot Seat multiplayer is the only option, it's incredibly outdated and disappointing, check back when they release a proper multiplayer.  I play these games with friends, so I'll likely wait, or refund and check back then.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Having played the game a bit, I can confidently say it's worth the asking price. I have greatly enjoyed the economic system and the chains of production. The ability to customize nations as you play is unique and although all nations are generic at the start, they do specialize heavily with very different play styles. I have played three games so far and every time my nations developed in completely different ways. For example, the hunter-gatherers ethos allowed me to mostly ignore farming and get all my food from mobile forces of hunters scouring the map for hunts. It felt completely different from playing a mound-builders civ heavily focused on space optimization and large cities. The variant ages offer a lot of replayability as well, unlocking certain new strategies. For example going for an early age of heroes gives you access to the "art" resource and the religious gameplay much earlier than through the normal tech tree and can completely change your options. Many people complain that the AI forces you into ages you might not want. Personally, I did not have this issue. Even poorly optimizing my strategy, I had no issue winning the race for the next age when I wanted to. I think the fact that nations have "real world names" is a bit misleading. Those nations are truly blank slates upon which to build any strategy. For example, starting as "Russia" I was surrounded by deserts and specialized as a spice trading caravan empire. Not very russian indeed, but the ability to adapt to the start location is great and creates engaging stories. I think people might come expecting some semblance of historical flavor and end up disappointed. Maybe having fantasy nations (like there are fantasy religions in the game) would have been a better way to drive the point that the game is all about adaptation and customization. To me this is not a flaw  but I think some people will dislike how detached it is from existing countries. The game certainly has real flaws though, notably the micromanagement which can get quite tedious in the later game as well as performance problems and the weird lack of certain features (why can I destroy barbarian cities but not cities from other players?). I also think some of the game mechanics are obscured by the interface making the game confusing sometimes, for example, your influence spreads into tiles bordering your cities, but you can't know by how much. You will see the influence you currently have and the remaining one needed, but not your gain per turn, it's just a weird oversight. I understand why people would be miffed about the lack of the advertised multiplayer especially because I feel the game would shine with others. It offers so many different strategies it's a shame you can only experience them in a sort of sandbox mod and not in competition with others. However, for me this is not a deal breaker and I'm sure they will eventually implement it. What I don't understand is people complaining about the price tag, which seems totally reasonable to me or the future DLCs. The game is perfectly playable right now and if you are willing to experiment a bit I think you can easily get 100 hours of playtime with it. For 40€ this is a fine deal in my book. If there is future DLC content then I will judge it on its merits. These DLC might end up being terrible and overpriced but Millenia as is, is a very innovative and creative game and the core mechanics were solid enough to get me hooked. This is what I base my opinion on because it’s the product I paid for and own at the moment. The different strategies are compelling and I really would like to try all the possibilities, what more to ask really?
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I don't write a lot of reviews -or- play games when I buy them very much, usually... but I put in 70 hours in two weeks, without idle time. Yeah. I think it's worth the money. It's a much more accessible version of Civ, at least to me, and the addition of national spirits and ages makes things so much more varied!Definitely love this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I am having fun, it is a fresh experience for 4x games and that is nice, this game has amazing potential and while yes it has a few things that are rough I have faith that the company will fix it. If this game is the same state it is in rn in 8 months I think then it will be time to start saying bad things but as it stands right now it is a fun game with fun mechanics.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Dealing with the enemies is the least of your concern in this irrational game. Diplomacy menu is beyond weak, it feels like you are playing a game launched 30 years ago. Despite its recent failures, civilization's diplomacy menus 2 decades ago were much much better. The main problem however is not the non-existent diplomacy, it is the civilian unrest nonsense. With only a watch to build to suppress unrest for 2 ages, you lose all your cities to revolutionary(!) civilians while you are in the middle of a successful military campaign on a rival nation. The fact that when your massive cities decide to become a brand new nation by themselves, you cannot attack them for 4 turns because first you have to declare hostilities, wait for 3 turns, and then only you can declare war on them to get your city back :D By the way, the unrest is completely baseless because you have a solid economy, flourishing cultural sphere, successful conquest campaign with massive military forces but suddenly your people decide to turn against you to an extent that they become a nation on their own. If you over expand, civil unrest, conquest, civil unrest, lack of culture, civil unrest, small but central empire with a few cities, civil unrest because of population. One of the most ridiculous, braindead settings I have ever seen in micromanaging strategy games. Civilization in its contemporary awful state even is much better than this one I'm afraid.  Devs should take a look at humankind and derive some lessons from it before it's too late to save this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Millennia looks like civ at first glance, but the economics, tech, and pacing is better balanced. The "Ages" system and the "National Spirit" system make every game different and encourage you to try different things depending on the circumstances. My last play-through was super fun for this reason.The improvements system has supply-chain interactions, which sounds complicated, but the city management screens help you wrap your head around the complexity well. This system is like, if CS2's economy worked, it would probably feel a bit like this.The population management is the most intuitive and clearly presented I've ever seen in this genre. Even better than Stellaris IMO.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I really like it so far. The UI is not the best and graphics are good enough for a 4X game. What makes or breaks a game like this in the long run is not the graphics. The battle animations are very simplistic but i enjoy them anyway. It's just a simple visualization of the calculations in the background that can help you understand why you win or lose a battle, don't take them so seriously.The game has a lot of new concepts compared to Civilization. New mechanics are added every era and you customize your nation with choices you take along the way, contrary to how you in Civ choose one bonus and play focused on that most of the game. There are alternative eras that can get triggered but i havn't played any of them yet. They seem fun and will mix up the game on re-runs. If you like 4X games i recommend Millennia if you want to try something new. Don't listen to reviews with less than several hours play time, they have barely tried the game at all. They have not even bothered to try to learn the game. Watch out for barbarians in the early game, i had to restart more than once. Skill issue, i know ;)
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I don't want to give this a negative review, but I am.Big time Paradox player. Lately disappointed in all their titles.I actually like this game. I like the potential behind it.What I can't stand is the AI - The AI cheats. HeavyI've watched their settlers go through 5+ forest tiles in one turn to settle in my lands.They constantly have armies. And they constantly declare war. Making peace is lame because it lasts 1 to 3 turns. If I build an army I'm suddenly in debt.My current run I am Egypt. I am very south on the continent and pretty far from everyone. I have a lot of land to grab. I have 5 cities(one I stole from germany who came from mid north and settled right next to my capital on the other side of a mountain)There has been 1 war between the AI. There are 3 AI nations next to each other. They all start wars with me in the deep south.And because of these constant wars and these 4-5 stack armies constantly in my territory. I now can't manage unrest. So my empire is stagnant.Am I meeting needs? Yes. All green in every province. Unrest. Constantly. My population is just dying down. My income is shattered. It's my second playthrough.The first one I realized I just had a bad city start and I was never going to compete. My second playthrough made me realize that I'll never be able to compete.idk how the AI can just spend all of it's production on armies, and then have the gold to support those armies, and never let us. Also, Barbarian spam is a real problem in this game. If you don't take out a barb city, they just spawn infinitely. Like they can support that many armies. I'll pick this up after some adjustments. Still less of a let down than Humankind was.Another thing which is not a fun mechanic. Merchants and Envoys - Why on earth can a settler kill an envoy? What's the point of these units if the enemy or semi hostile enemy just destroys these units. Makes them feel like useless units
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly can't understand the negative reviews.I've been playing Civ-style games for decades, and this game is a gem.  I love the way the economy/goods system works in particular, which brings a fresh approach to the 4x genre.The only negative I agree with is the graphics for the battle cut-scenes.  They do come across a bit dated, like something from the late 90s.  Personally doesn't bother me, but I can see the turn off for some people.Hats off to C Prompt.  They seem to be a relatively new/small outfit, and they've delivered a great game with Millennia.  The only thing that concerns me about them is from their website, when I was doing some research into the company:  "We strongly encourage applications from developers of color, female developers, and LGBTQ developers."Surely you should be strongly encouraging applications from everyone, regardless of background, skin color, gender or creed?  Statements like the above just make people who don't fit into those demographic categories feel second rate, or unwanted - which is far from helpful during these divisive times.  Just a suggestion... = )
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Finally a game that really improves the old Civ formula. I first thought the tech tree was a bit thin, but it turns out the play length is quite comfortable and it is quite comfortable. The idea with the production chains is nice, although some of them are a bit pointless and others redundant. The region system is also a good idea, but it's a bit hard to get the right balance.All in all its a creative start into a new game series and while there is room for improvement (especially the UI) I think this game has a real future in the field of CIV-likes. And even if this game does not become a huge success, I hope it will inspire the other big names in 4X to get some fresh ideas.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Game does have a great concept, interesting ideas and mechanics, and a lot of damn problems. Lack of optimization is honestly worst of them, in late game with standart game rules game runs incredibly slow, and at the later stages managing cities is the worst hell you can imagine, almost all buildings look the same and in the late game there is a ton of them on the screen, playing tall is not interesting at all (My favourite playsyle tho) If you`ll play with goal to make as much influence as possible you wont see a significant difference, and furthermore it will not pay back you as you want when playing tall, it honestly feels like average size of town that is necessary to build a self-sustained city. Nothing probably would be a problem after week or two if game have modding tools at the launch, but it is what it is?Game have a giant potential and how Paradox loves do, game will become a great product after a couple of years. Price is biting and honestly, game dont cost this price in its current state, so if you out of spare money its better wait DLC`s and patches to gain the best expirience.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: After coming back to the game after a few months, I have changed to a positive rating. The game has some strong mechanics and is a unique 4x historical strategy game. More updates will only improve on the good foundation the devs built. I also appreciate that the game is easily made to play on low end rigs, unlike other recently released games in the genre...
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: So far so good, still figuring the game out. I think the map building needs to be flushed out much better... as well as the nation building. Right now there does not really seem to be a point to the custom nation thing when the various nations in general are all fairly bland and all you can do is swap around stuff.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: At this moment and time... its not worth the money. I would recommend any other civ game except humankind. I don't know why but it feels rushed. The fact that they are planning DLC already without finishing the game scares me.Main reasons I feel like playing something else and don't recommend it at this moment:- No Multiplayer (Yes everyone else says that aswell I'm sure it will come)- To take over a settlement you need to pay it with diplomacy, the max diplomacy you are allowed is 300 after 6 settlements it costs 418.... so no more settlements there goes my dream of dominating the world.- Other comments other people have made no point repeating everything elseOverall, I think this game will be really good after lots of updates. Just at this moment I cannot recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: So far this is painfully mediocre. What hurts is that there are so many good ideas but they are all half baked. And those good ideas are like... there are too many of them and it needs better execution. Everything looks deep but ends up ultimately being shallow.Typical late game slog for 4x games as well since you know if you have won or not but have to play it out for ages and the game itself has some serious performance issues in the late game. Also missing a ton of stuff that you just expect from modern games. Quality of life, simple features. It feels like a game that needed more development but was rushed out with the idea that later updates will make it better. Maybe they will but say away for now.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: This game has potential but I can't recommend it in its current state. There are a lot of issues overall and it will take time till they are fixed.The good:- The City management is fun and evolves a lot compared to games like Civ- The ages are diverse and can completely overturn a gameThe meh:- Graphics are mediocre- Performance has issues midgame, not unplayable but the game noticeably slows down- Diplomacy, the basics are there but you can't even stop the AI from settling next to you- Unlocking things early, i.E. Religion, often leaves you unable to deal with the consequences before you are locked into a certain playstyleThe bad:- The AI, it is unable to judge your strength and acts nonsensical when at war- You can not destroy/ absorb Vassals, the AI spams the map with settlers making it impossible to build large-scale cities and you can do nothing about them. Even if you declare war on them and conquer them you can't raze them.- Balance is all over the place, some Domains (specializations) are incredibly powerful while others are useless. That is present throughout the whole game, be it improvements, units, etc.- Every other tile except for flatlands is comparable useless. On a hill you can build a mine or a quarry, that's it. On a forest, you can only build foresters till the end of midgame at which you can turn them into grassland, which is very expensive. Water tiles are Harbours or Fishing ships which are both mediocre. Having a big city with loads of plains and some hills for ore is basically the most overpowered thing there is.- The Chaos System, sometimes it spawns powerful rebels at every single city you control, at other times it only destroys a single improvement. As it is, it’s simply annoying.- The UI/ UX, late game you have so many types of mana and so many abilities, it’s very hard to keep track of things, even with the ability to set alarms. The same goes for cities, you can’t even set an improvement to inactive, so you have to babysit nonstop.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: If you are a fan of the 4x genre I cannot recommend this game enough. I am shocked that it does not have very positive reviews at the time of me writing this. I was instantly hooked as soon as I started playing. The age mechanic is very interesting and cool. There seems to be unlimited replay-ability. I will say this game is definitely different than Civ. It has the Paradox stamp of being very complex but very satisfying. While there are some rough edges at launch, such as performance difficulties (not game breaking just annoying), I am confidant that with time and some updates this game will be extremely well polished and a serious rival to the Civilization series that I love.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this game but, unfortunately, I don't think I can give the thumb up. It's clear it hasn't had enough playtesting.- Different ages are refreshing, and fun in theory, but due to the age being decided by the player who gets there first I find the AI often forces everyone into a crisis age due to how poorly they handle things like sanitation and faith.- Events are semi-random and unbalanced. Depending on what you do 'chaos' builds up increasing the chance for random bad events however these events don't seem to happen to AI players and are sometimes quite unbalanced like when my capitol, revolted, became an independent state, and all I had left was a small town.- Improvements are a neat idea but look ugly on the map and are tedious to deal with. This is more of a personal opinion but I just don't really care that two logs can be turned into paper which can be turned into books which increase faith. Production chains can be fun but it doesn't fit in a grande civilisation game. There are good ideas here but in its current state it's too complex and granular for the games scale- The battle screen. It's annoying, a testament to the hubris of the game designer who has received negative feedback for months but seems intent on keeping it. In-game popups are not fun and the animations in this popup are not good enough to make them fun to watch. - Lack of unique civ-specific units and buildings. I don't mind civs not having the same personality or specific permanent traits but part of the fun in civ-style games is unlocking their special buildings and units and then spamming them for several hundred turns. I also felt that I missed culture-specific UI and graphics. China and Germany don't look or feel different, it's difficult to have an emergent story when everything looks the same.This game has potential but needed more playtesting. Hopefully devs listen to feedback and work on it some more.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: The graphics are bad and key features (proper multiplayer, end of game score) are wholly missing. Diplomacy is a bit of a joke, random countries request to ally you and drag you into wars without being able to do anything about it. I'm unhappy that I can't immediately declare wars, I have to declare hostilities first before invading.But the core gameplay is quite strong. The Ages do feel distinct and interesting - Age of Heroes is quite exciting, Age of Generals is pretty cool too. The economy is quite complex and presents all kinds of choices - wood for timber or for books? The game is long and there's a lot to do - it took me 13 hours to finish one match in Age 8/10 - that's why it's called Millennia.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a CIV game because it's a pure war game it's like 90% war either against barbarians, rebellions or other nations or all at onceHad there been less war, the game would have been fun to play, but as it is now,The game is buggy crashes sometimes in windows, can't build some things even though I have everything feels like an early beta I don't recommend the game
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Millennia suffers hard from the paradox game syndrome. At the very beginning it was probably one of the worst Civ-like games I've played. Now with two DLC behind it, I'd say it's just below civ 5 level. Give it a few more DLC, and this game will probably be the best Civ-style game in terms of enjoyment. With that being said, it has a two core problems.1. The combat is terrible. There is very little strategy whatsoever. Just put an even number of line, support, and cavalry units in your army and maybe a general. That's it. Even the bombardment system doesn't make up for it. Battles pretty much boil down to running a bunch of identical blobs at each other.2. The first player to age up forces everybody to pick the same age, with the exception of crisis ages. I think. The age system is just convoluted, and I wish I could just steer the course of my own nation without some guy across the map deciding "Nobody gets to play age of heroes, we're going straight to the classical age!"If you enjoy building a massive economy and occasionally throwing blobs of units around, this might be the game for you. If you like being a mastermind general or a narrative gamer, I would recommend you stay away until a few more DLC release.

_childDocuments_.review: So much potential with this game but soooooo many frustration game design choices. Hoping the dev team can improve the game and especially the UI in the coming months. Would not recommend until then unless you have played every other 4X avail and need something new.The AI especially just seems completely anti player. Forward settling you nonstop then getting pissed at you for being on your borders. Then declaring war on you and never accepting peace driving up your unrest.The diplomacy system is ridiculous. Cant interact with the AI unless you get an envoy to a capital city... which they take every opportunity to kill on sight. The production chains are a cool concept but very frustrating to balance. Upgrading one building can eff over another and wont say in that screen. Can't undo an upgrade after seeing how it affects your numbers.The Age of Revolution.... just sucks. Like hard. Zero warning to the player of what is going to happen and youre almost certainly screwed if you don't know in advance to prepare for it.Never feels like you have enough tiles to build what you need. Unsure if thats something players will get better at over time or something they need to balance.Has a domestic import function but only works between one city and another city. Cant have like 1 city be your lumber city and send lumber to mult places. Pretty much have to have all the items you need for the production chain you want in that city. Which comes back to the space issue...Feels like all solvable stuff. Will definitely come back to this every major update to see how its improving.

_childDocuments_.review: I have a confession to make: my first (other than some sketchy lunch breaks playing Civ 1 on a school computer) and still favorite Civilization game is Civilization II: The Test of Time. For those who aren't aware, that's not just the official subtitle of Civ 2. ToT was an updated and expanded re-release from 1999 with improved graphics (Actual animated sprites rather than “paper chits”), balance work to make it drastically less likely for a bronze age spearman to defeat a battleship in combat, and most importantly additional and expanded game modes. It had the classical civ game, beginning in 4000 BCE and ending with a colony ship to Alpha Centauri, but also featured an Extended game where you had to actually colonize Alpha Centauri (which might already have native civs), a fantasy game loosely based on Norse myth where your choice of civ gave you a unique racial tech tree (or at least army) rather than being cosmetic, and a Science Fiction game where lost colonists from both Humans and an alien race had to colonize and conquer the planets of the Lalande system.This has informed my interface with Civ as a whole. To an extent, the “historical” flavor never really mattered to me. If I wanted to learn about History, I'd be playing Where In Time Is Carmen Sandiego?. No, the theme mattered because of the implicit scope, the vastness and grandeur of it. Millennia, in my mind, is what something around Civ 4 might have looked like if ToT, rather than Vanilla, had been the launching-off point for future editions.As you play through Millennia you'll discover a few things. First of all, this isn't the Civ you know. In some ways it has an oldschool nature to its brutality. In other ways, your skills won't transfer because it's just different; Millennia focuses more on land utilization and improvement than Civ. Even if you're a genre veteran like me, your first run (or two) is likely to be scuffed.As you get the hang of it, you'll probably start to appreciate the systems, and how the game progressively introduces them. Early on in the Age of Stone and even Age of Bronze you won't have much to manage. By the late game, you're spinning dozens of plates, but assuming you know the basics of how to spin a plate in this game, the number added doesn't really matter all that much because they're added gradually.But I think the brilliance of this game, and why I see it as something of the heir to Test of Time, is when you start exploring the realms beyond the historical. I'm not just talking about classic jank like “In 1775, Montezuma lead the aztecs to develop the first nuclear weapon” that almost any historical game can put out. I'm talking about the Variant and Crisis Ages that face the world with a wonderfully insane “What If?” - new worlds of variance and replay.Speaking of variance and replay, a lot of the game seems to understand that variety is the spice of life, and defy being discovered in a single go around. Because you only have to research about half of an era's technology to progress, and as many as half your eras could be something weird and different, you're really not meant to stick to a favorite build order: circumstances may require you research different tech in different playthroughs, and then you want to leverage what you have rather than spending the time to go back to what you're familiar with. In one game, Aqueducts were my early sanitation solution. In the next, I went to the Age of Blood where aqueducts don't exist and spent the vast majority of the game having to use precious tile space rather than buildings on sanitation.That also brings me to the Chaos and Innovation events. These are semi-random events: which ones you get seem (especially for the innovations) to be largely based on your government, national spirits, and present age, but it's clearly pulling from a fairly large list that includes things like the world wonders for Innovation and all manner of middle fingers for Chaos. Each time one fires you can accept the event or negotiate a lump sum of money (getting a payoff if you don't care about the Innovation, or paying a sum to make the Chaos go away). This both makes keeping a large bankroll – usually something less valuable than rushing this and that – appealing because you can buy off your bad karma, and gives another way in which no two games are going to be the same. Some of the Innovations and Chaos events are fairly mild, others can utterly make a run if you take them or break you if you can't make the fee. The right innovation can transform your strategy on a deep level by changing even just basic math. But of course to get innovation or its evil twin, you need to fil a bar up and let the proc happen.That said, there would be some matters that I would be remiss if I didn't quibble about. The biggest one is not the graphics. Millennia is not a looker, that much is sure, but turn-based strategy games don't need to be. It needs to have a readable map and functional feedback to tell you what happens and why, and it does.No, the biggest issue with Millennia is the AI. Your half-witted rivals, possessed of the viciousness of a school of piranha and the memories of goldfish, are adequate enemies but extremely poor diplomatic partners – a fact a bit too reminiscent of my old favorite. Sure, they play the technical game well enough: against Adept AIs (the default) it's hard to be the tech leader and control what age the world goes into, at least unless and until you do something to really establish your heft (like using the Age of Blood to render yourself alone on a continent, say). But your options for talking to other nations are bare bones without sending an envoy on a frustrating mission of getting roadblocked by “friendly” units, and still anemic if you do manage to get there. I understand some things, like repeatedly begging for open borders when denied, but even among themselves the AIs will make and cancel agreements with startling rapidity, allowing the player to watch a procession of one-turn wars and peaces if they're fortunate enough to have met everybody.Other than that, while the overall art quality doesn't precisely bother me, there are a few nagging UX sorts of complaints. For instance, winning doesn't necessarily feel good or momentous: you get a honking fanfare and a popup that features, at least in the case of the wins I've yet done, the age art. Come on, even Civ 2 gave a very rudimentary animated cutscene with its own few seconds of musical score for victory!  There's no “one more turn” option either; objectively minor and probably unnecessary, but who hasn't at least once won a relatively peaceful game and then in the postscript gone psycho and burned down all those infuriating AIs?There's certainly places where more could be done as well. I mentioned chaining ahistorical ages, and that's a place where the surface is only scratched; a couple secrets to find, nothing more. Perhaps that's some of the plan for expansions/DLC, but I feel if there were non-returning branches where the fantastical elements were allowed to build on themselves, and possibly different routes thereof, you could get to some really creative places.On the whole, Millennia is a very solid strategy experience for someone who, like me, loves oldschool Civ, but who doesn't want just the same exact thing. There's a lot of dedication and polish in the game itself, but a few rough corners where either the skillset, money, or both weren't quite there. In the age of continuing support, it shows a solid enough core that it doesn't need massive changes to go from good to great, and a competent enough skill for me to believe that it can and will.Even if no real changes are pushed out, and what we see now is what we get forever, I'm satisfied. If we get more, this could absolutely be one of the greats in the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: If this was an Early Access title, it would deserve none of flak coming its way. Instead, it deserves some of it.Specifically, it deserves flak for its poor QoL features, lack of multiplayer matchmaking (although if you only play solo, that isn't an issue), and bugs/crashes (I've had two cases of computer crashing, and once where undoing an action deleted a unit). The encyclopedia hides everything from future ages, and there are some little things like changing the connected city of bow hunters. And I can't find the option to raze cities anywhere...What this game does  deserve flak for is choices it makes different from Civ. For instance, the game has tons of barbarians, especially if someone has an early war and kicks off an Age of Blood. At first it seems like a pure annoyance, but you have multiple methods of countering them, the rewards for fighting are good, and it overall provides something to do during the early game. Similarly, the goods system is interesting, you effectively need to make choices for how you're specializing production in one city, because you can't trade between cities (and it would probably be a logistics nightmare if you could). Also, you have to space cities out a lot more than in Civ, because lots of space is needed for improvements, and you've got to make sure you're making the special resources for improvements (a replacement for workers), and there are lots of "XP" resources for critical "power" abilities, and... Well, tons of stuff that will make you have a hard time if you assume it'll be just another Civ clone, instead of learning how this game works properly.There's also concerns about balance, and the AI being not the greatest... But those are true of Civ, too. I wish they were better here, though.Overall, I say this game is worth it, because the innovations have proven to be really fun, and the problems not. The most fun part for me was actually where I got overwhelmed by barbarians everywhere during the surprise Age of Blood, and needed to employ every resource I had to hold on. Then after mopping up the barbs, I used my new armies to go conquer my nearest neighbor (taking advantage of reduced war penalties).If you're still skeptical, though, maybe wait a bit for the mess to be cleaned up.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I am actually really enjoying this game. They need something that makes the civs more unique and I hope more ages/crises. I LOVE the age system but I love the crises system more. I would also love the option for a crisis after a golden age. This game is really good for a 4x from an indie dev with the backing of Paradox. As I play more i'll elaborate more. Though most won't even read this review. I recommend it but I would also wait until more ages release.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Only in my second playthrough, but it is a very promising game. It looks a lot like Civ and it introduces some very cool new game mechanics. Cons (so far):- The game introduces a lot of new mechanics/features and it does feel like a wee bit too much complexity, but if you don't mind putting some hours into researching all the new features, it's not necessarily a bad thing. It just feels overwhelming.- Some balance issues. GO RAIDERS!- It lacks ways to customize your "pre-game" settings.- Some QoL missing in the UI. - Graphics are fine/functional, but tile improvements are often impossible to identify without zooming in. - Some micro management of tiles and workers needed.- Lacks some settings (for instance disabling the combat animation)Pros:- Stable- "Just one more turn" - Only noticed one minor bug so far.- Introduces some new game mechanics, which are really cool.Definately thumbs up.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

Even when you thing you've grasped the game rules already, it will amaze you again and again with its new ways to frustrate you. :-)Yet, it is an absolute MUST-TO-HAVE if you are a fan of the 4X genre. _childDocuments_.review: Rating: ⭐⭐½TL;DR: Paradox's Millennia is a title that seems to cater to a niche within the casual 4X strategy genre. It shines in its polished presentation and offers a unique challenge that, while perhaps unintentional, keeps players on their toes. The game's age system introduces a variety of gameplay elements as players progress, yet it falters when it comes to attracting hardcore 4X enthusiasts due to significant limitations in customization and balance.Pros:    Polish: Millennia stands out for its lack of bugs and smooth performance, delivering on its design choices (although I do question some of these choices).    Challenge: Despite potential balance issues, the game consistently challenges players through threats from barbarians and rival civilizations, demanding strategic defense and progression.    Age System Variety: The progression through different ages adds layers of variety, even if this aspect becomes tedious over multiple playthroughs. For instance, spreading your religion only becomes an option after 2-3 hours of gameplay.    Naval Strategy: The game does an excellent job at balancing naval versus land strategies. Transporting units across oceans is risky due to barbarian navies, making naval escorts essential and adding depth to the naval gameplay.    Combat : This, as a whole, is the only part of the game that I can say is hands down better than Civ6 (the AI might be another but I haven't tested it enough to say for sure). The army system is great! it allows you to form small division sized armies (3-6 units, size progresses over the ages and technology) and allows you to promote certain units to leaders which boost the performance of the other units in the army. The execution of this area of the game is very good and teedering on flawless. Cons:    Lack of Customization: Every civilization is the same aside from city names. Their is no map editing capabilities or customization choices at the start of a new game such as barbarians yes/no? starting age, features (such as religion) on/off, etc. This lack of customization options severely limits replayability and strategic depth.    Balance Issues: The effort to balance the game across different ages has led to a gameplay experience where no one can gain a significant advantage, making the game overly restrictive and not rewarding strategic play. Examples of poor balancing include the inefficient cost-reward ratio for certain buildings (example: One building which grants +10wealth per turn once completed costs 4000wealth to rush build, it will take you 400 turns to recoup that wealth based on this balance. PS: No game of mine has lasted more than 300 turns).     Tedious Progression: The cool concept of the age system is undermined by its execution. The game becomes tedious as it prevents players from significantly advancing or customizing their starting age, forcing a slow and repetitive progression through the ages. The exponential requirement for advancement (following a power of 1.5 logic) further exacerbates this issue, making each subsequent age more laborious to reach than the last. For example: you need 4 knowledge to learn an age 1 technology, 6 knowledge to learn an age 2 technology, 9 to learn age 3 tech, 14 for age 4, etc.. This formula is applied to everything else also, so combat units are typically 1.5x stronger than their age predecessors, etc. As per my balancing con earlier they designed the game to prevent you being more than 1 age ahead of everyone else because 1.5x more powerful is great (a fun challenge to overcome if you are behind or a fun opportunity to take a huge advantage if you are ahead) but at x1.5x1.5 and it’s just crazy unfair. This though makes everything very tedious because it prevents you from jumping ahead in any significant way after a new playthrough. Think of it this way : Age 1 will take you roughly 20 minutes to complete (if you skip everything else and focus on nothing else but this) you can then use the power of 1.5 formula on the time it will take you for all following ages : age 2 = 30m, age 3 = 45m, age 4 = 68m, age 5 = 102m, etc. So if you are targeting something in age 6 (which you find fun and consider this the start of your enjoyment) you would have spent 265 minutes just running through the motions just to get there. Conclusion : I believe that the game has great potential and hopefully Paradox can grant us access to this potential free of charge but that is sadly unlikely. This game is a beta test for them right now. They are using us to test their game and give them metadata in order for them to decide what features to work on next and then they will sell it to us via DLC. As much as I have been a fan of Paradox for a long long time all you need to do is look at stelaris, Hoi4 and Europa and scan through their DLC options to know how money hungry they are. Sadly for them, this is one title that I doubt I will be spending any additional money on.

_childDocuments_.review: First session + 2 full playthroughs watched review here. Alt history ages and planning depth in improvements supply chains are the features I was sold out for and I have received everything that I expected and more - played to the age 6, everything I played with in terms of mechanics feel extremely satisfying and rewarding and game designers made an extremely good job in delivering it. Resource chains are very important in getting more out of less, but design doesn't make it so that you have to manage them strictly - you can benefit from sub products as well, so it is a perfect example how you make a fun and skill based mechanic that doesn't frustrate a casual player. In accord with this dev points pool works absolutely in synergy - feels like the best choice for combo of planning and rebuilding, making these mechanics as comforting as possible. Ages system make this game feeling much more dynamic than other 4X and provide more cases where you need to adapt your strategy on the go yet still keeping a 4X multiple turns planning, contentwise it feels polished and loved by devs as wellMain chokepoints in game currently imho are hardly responsive military micro management, performance and diplomacy, so if devs will be able to improve these to the economical mechanics standard this game will be a solid new word in the 4X market, keep this work!

_childDocuments_.review: Let's get one thing out of the way. The UI and graphics are not great. They are readable, but the game doesn't make things easy for you. And another thing:  This game is its own thing and should be considered from that angle.So I really enjoy this one. This is why:1) It is a much more historic-minded take on a the historical 4X game. Unlike say Civilization which assumes your civilization has immutable characteristics from the dawn of time, Millennia takes the idea that environment, neighbors, resources, etc. are what shaped a civilization into what it is. You are building your civilization as you play, and by the end of the game will end up with a civilization that differs from others to a depth you are not going to see in classic historic 4Xes, and feels organic based on both your choices and how history evolves.2) The logistics chains are fun! A lot of civilization games end up with the non-combat part and internal development being less interesting than war and conquest, and Millennia is definitely not one of those games. Deciding what to build, where to build, and how to change things as you go through history and expand your territory is very crunchy and enjoyable3) The alternate history ages are really cool and generally feel very distinct. Each one has its own improvements, buildings, and special mechanics, and can have a big impact on how the game plays out. I haven't seen all of them yet, but almost all the ones I have seen are very cool and I look forward to see the ones I am not aware of and what modders and DLC will do with them over time.There are a lot of smaller things I appreciate too, but these are what I think are the core sale points. If you like 4X but have been wanting something that shakes the genre up and does some new things then this is definitely what you are looking for. It is refreshing and really enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: This game isn't just a 4X, it's actually civilization. As in, I suspect some of the devs used to work on previous civ games and now developed their own sequel under a different banner. So don't expect some revolutionary new take on the genre, it is just civ, with some mutations that keep it interesting throughout.The most significant differences to regular civ are the different 'ages' and the internal trading system. Every age you enter in the game - there's 10 in total - introduces some new resource you'll have to manage, such as faith or information, which will determine the health of your cities. And the trading system is like a resource building puzzle. Like, you'll need to extract two logs, build something that can make that into one paper, collect two paper and then make something that'll convert it to religious texts or something, etc. There's options to send resources between your cities so you can make the puzzle work a bit easier, but it's fairly limiting and generally a pain to keep up with as the parameters change all the time. Like, literally capable of giving you a headache with all the necessary micromanagement. And ofcourse, as is tradition in every civ game so far, by the time you reach the end game things slow down to a crawl, framerate drops like a brick, decisions matter less and less, and I would commend you for actually finishing a campaign.Overall though, any game that makes me play through a headache must have a lot of good things going for it, and that's what sticks in the end. Just an expertly crafted civ clone.

_childDocuments_.review: A rare case where I actually changed my mind after playing it some more. While I still stand by my first impression (will leave my old review below for transparency) of the game being incredibly rough, the city-building and ages mechanics have kept me hooked. It may look and sometimes play like it is from 2001, but it has its charm.There is a lot of ways to have fun with the game for sure and when you see it on sale I think it is worth a shot. Diplomacy is still embarrassingly barebones and a lot of game actions feel like they require an unneccessary amount of clicks. It is not a 4X all star.Overall the game gets a careful thumbs up from me.Old Review:(As of writing the reviews for Millenia are "mixed", which is the perfect way to describe how I feel about this game.The reason why I cannot recommend this game is not because it is all-around terrible, but rather because it simply falls behind its competition. Anyone just looking for a 4X game I would much rather direct towards games like Civilization, Old World, Humankind, Age of Wonders, Endless Legend, Solium Infernum,… all of which are superior to Millenia. If however you are a seasoned 4X player and you are looking for something new (while having already tried the aforementioned games), then Millennia might scratch that itch.It does have some things going for it. Some mechanics, such as the city-building economy side and the different ages are very enjoyable. However while it innovates in some aspects, it feels incredibly dated in others (and I am not just talking about the visuals, which are hideous): Diplomacy and interacting with AI is very rudimentary and barely functional, flavor for different nations is non-existent, and overall the game has a decent amount of yank caused by bizarre mechanics and mediocre UI.There is things to like about the game, but unless you are curious about the developments in the 4X genre and have already exhausted other avenues, I cannot recommend this game. Pick it up on sale for 10-15€, but don’t pay full price. There is simply better games out there.)

_childDocuments_.review: Although the concept is great (different ages depending on choices), it doesn't quite work. First of all, this game really is very much like Civilization only withouth some of the things that made it great. When researching new discoveries you basically have to rush or other civilization will decide which age it's going to be. That leaves little room for building and discovery. Next, you can only build a few cities (there is a cap) and the improvements on tiles are of such a multitude that I just stopped caring about them. Most improvements are also quite ugly which means you'll transform your Bronze Age lands into a paved parkinglot filled with buildings. That said, I did finish one run in the longest/stretched out possible setting. When winning all I got was a screen with: 'you won', which also was a let down. I expected something more from that. If this game was a little more stretched out, included some story perhaps, and gave more reason to care it would be a banger. Right now, it basically falls short of every aspect it could have been.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like what this game is doing. It feels pretty indie, with a lot of little QoL oversights, but there's a lot of interesting ideas here that feel well executed. While they don't bother me enough to significantly impact my enjoyment of the game, the QoL oversights can't be overlooked. The most significant to me is that while the game has quite a lot of goods that can be converted into other goods for a variety of bonuses, this information is not well relayed in the game. There's an in game equivalent to the "civilopedia" but none of the goods have any details inside of it. There's also a lot of little ones like having to go to the diplomacy screen to interact with enemy rulers rather than being able to click on any of their cities.I wouldn't go as far as others seem to by stating the game "feels early access" but there are a lot of small changes that would greatly improve the game's readability. The most important factor to emphasize is that all of the issues I feel the game has are of the QoL variety. The game feels well developed and sound from a mechanical perspective.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not Civilization, it is its own thing. If you compare one to one of course this game falls short. Graphics quality is worse, diplomacy is minimal and you don't feel that same power fantasy of living through your chosen civilization.However, if like me, you always felt like Civilization was missing something key to your enjoyment; look no further. Millennia is much more strategic and, in this way, game knowledge as well as careful planning will have much more impact. You always have to adapt to your environment and your opponents decision. Although, AI quality could be better, the game is still rewarding enough and replayability is still high. If you really want to compare it to another popular game of the genre, it feels much more like Stellaris or Age of Empires. If you're in the hope for a different Civilization this is not it. If you want a unique take on the 4X genre, I recommend strongly.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoy this game, but would give it a qualified recommendation.  I enjoy the fact that the tech tree is dynamic and that the tech leader sets the world stage, giving it some variability across playthroughs.  I love the national spirit system, which lets you tailor your civilization as you go rather than having a static start.  That said, it's not for everyone, as there's a lot of "trial by fire" to learn how city building and warfare operates, and even on the lowest difficulties, the barbs can be more threatening than other civs.  As far as multiplayer, I really wish there was a distinction between "online multiplayer" and "hotseat multiplayer" - there aren't many games these days which allow for hotseat multiplayer outside of 4x, and it's head-scratching to me that this was the *only* option at launch.  I'm not sure about the performance issues in later ages, as I haven't gone past turn 150 *yet*.  Overall, I like it, and I enjoy seeing the different techs and learning this game's unique interactions; your mileage may vary.
