_childDocuments_.review: Millennia is an amazing game.  And the current rating of Mixed is just totally unfair.If you left a negative rating, please consider deleting it, or flipping it to positive.As a person who does not have a lot of time to play, I rarely play games that have a rating of at least Very Positive.It is very likely I would not have bought Millennia, if I did not play the demo.And bought it just because I liked the demo so much.The game is as great as the demo, and I am very happy that I did buy it.I've looked at a dozen negative reviews on Steam and read many negative reviews in online publications.Most of the complains I've see are as follows:1. The game is too hard for me. (Play another game)2. The game is not like Civilization. (Go play Civ)3. The game is unfinished. (Agreed, but...)I would like to address each one in detail.For the "the game is too hard" crowd, it seems strange to leave a review at all.There are plenty of games that are challenging.  It is something that people generally enjoy about them.Millennia, I think, is only partially in this category, but it is certainly a game with a lot of depths.If anything, this is good, as it makes the gameplay more rewarding as you play more.You keep discovering something new for quite some time.Even after 23 hours in the game, I am still presented with new rules and new things to try.Ages introduce new rules and mechanics.And they are non-trivial and interesting to tackle with.In any case, I find it very confusing that someone would downvote a game because it is complex.Just do not play this game if this level of complexity is not what you are looking for.As for the "it is not like Civilization" argument, again, I fail to see how is this a bad thing.There are plenty of games that are pretty close to Civilization.And if someone thinks that Civilization is the best game ever, then why try anything else?Clearly, Civilization is the best Civilization there could exist.Millennia has a lot of mechanics that remind me of board games, and the way they are combined is great and rewarding.Some hints of Stellar.  But still, I think, it is a refreshing and innovative take in the historical turn-based games niche.In some sense, the "it is not like Civilization" argument is like saying that the latest Dune RTS is bad because it is not Starcraft enough.  I find it truly pointless.The only argument I would agree with is that the game is unfinished.It certainly could be more polished and certain UI interactions are be clearly non-perfect.At the same time, in no way it actually impacted my enjoyment of the game.I truly hope that C Prompt Games continue working on Millennia.And I would be glad to support them further by buying DLCs.Hopefully, it will turn into a great franchise, similar to Stellaris, Crusader Kings, and, well, Civilization.To everyone who left a bad review, I urge you to remove it.I am certain that Millennia is not so bad that you would actually rate it as Mixed.I can understand that it might be rubbing you the wrong way, fail your expectations and such.But consider that your review tanked the game rating so low, that a lot of people would not even try it any more.Please, please, please consider deleting your negative reviews or just flipping them to positive.Millennia does not deserve a Mixed rating, I am certain of it.

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah, it’s fun. The ages mechanic is really cool  and makes repeat runs turn out completely differently on their own. _childDocuments_.review: The game is good but lacks polish. I blame Paradox for this (just look at any of their recent releases if you don’t know what I’m talking about). Trying to sell future dlc right out of the gate is a bad look with it in its current state. The current (Mixed) rating is fair. I’m writing a review because I enjoy the game and want to tip the scales in the positive direction so Paradox doesn’t decide to abandon it. The things that got me interested in the game were the age system and the resource management system. Both are done decently well. These two systems make this game more interesting than the Civ franchise imo. I was able to experience two of these alternative ages in my first play through- the age of aether, and the age of archangels. The age of aether is really cool, and it being the first alternative age I was able to bring about made this very satisfying. I look forward to experiencing the rest at some point. The age of archangels, one of the final victory ages, however was less than impressive. Not sure how this compares to the other victory ages, but it was a total slog, which I was able to cheese somewhat by sending envoys and merchants to capitals in order to snipe them with the space laser. Also when you destroy a region with the laser, it doesn’t put you at war with the receiving nation? That seemed a little strange. And I found a bug during this age which I exploited where hostile nations aren’t able to deal damage to non-military units at sea with their bomber aircraft.All-in-all I enjoyed my first play through and look forward to the game improving in time. But I found the game falling a little short of the base asking price of $40 usd. I didn’t purchase the expansion pass and wouldn’t recommend it until the game is improved. This game has potential and I want to see it become something great. There are a lot of fair critiques of this game in the reviews, as well as some unfair ones. Some things I see that need to be improved:-Information provided in both tooltips and the infopedia-More nations-More personality for different nations-Everything about diplomacy. It’s very barebones.-More map generation options-Performance-Ability to absorb smaller regions into adjacent larger regions. Toward the end of the game I had some large regions (large land area w/40+ population) with multiple small vassal regions (~10 population) as a result of warfare scattered between them. These smaller regions were mostly useless and had land which would be incredibly valuable if it could be absorbed by their neighbor regions. To avoid this becoming OP, possibly it could be limited to situations where the larger region has double or maybe 3x the smaller region's population.

_childDocuments_.review: I like 4x games in general and I prefer MoM type AoW in particular, just to set my general bias. I did not like Humankind and did like Civ6. This game is often compared to both. Its not the AAA level of Civ6 but its  base price is only $40. Bottom line for me is that is so far has that one-more-turn feel that has me playing longer and later per session. I never really got that in Humankind. I agree with those who commented that the game could have used some time in early access. Pros:No need to buy the DLC for me as a single player but I probably willEconomy is more complicated than the earlier ages make it seemInteresting use of religion and educationAges, national spirits and government mechanics are implemented in an engaging manner that encourages replaysCons:Combat. The leader promotion system is unclear that everything promotes to a melee leader. Overall the simplification of some aspects seems a bit much for a modern game. Little benefit to viewing the combats and this should be able to be skipped.Needs a  much better tutorial to get through the basic mechanics and their interaction. I did not try their video so this might be good but I use Youtube. I usually like to learn by trying.Graphics. Functional for the map but the combat units are primitive. Not terrible, but this is a taste issue. Nothing so ugly that I wouldn't play, which is something that has kept me away from some pixel graphics games.

_childDocuments_.review: Millennia is a fantastic and engaging game that shines in almost every category, with expected imperfections that could mostly all be fixed with minor patches and updates. Different ways to play are more than encouraged, leaving you without the repetitive feeling you more than likely felt going for science or faith again in Civ 6. Each new age brings new opportunities and challenges, so don't be surprised if you don't love it while you're stuck in the stone age. Trust me, things get a lot more interesting when there's a great khan on the map eating up regions while you're busy crusading and baking bread.Does the game have it's faults? Of course. Some of the major complaints you've probably seen are the lack of multiplayer on launch and the game not being graphically impressive. I personally think these aren't the issues we should be focusing on, given that the graphics are more than passable and multiplayer is currently being worked on. I'd rather that the game came out when it did without multiplayer so we can give feedback to better refine the game before it's implemented than wait longer for a potentially lesser product.In all my playtime, I've only encountered one minor bug that was fixed by simply progressing to the next turn. My biggest difficulty was learning the game's mechanics since certain things aren't explained as well as they could be, although that's only an issue if you're just starting off in your first game. Hang on, you'll get it eventually!The game's core mechanics such as it's national spirits, warfare, culture, tech and so on feel incredibly structured with little to feel disappointed about. This game definitely has something for everybody; whether you're a bloodthirsty backstabber hellbent on destruction or a collected diplomat, building their empire so tall that even the mightiest kingdoms are jealous of your wealth.I really do hope this game succeeds the way it deserves to. I'll most certainly be playing this for years to come, even in it's current state. Just please... Don't go too hard on the DLCs too early, Paradox. Free updates go a long way to building community, especially until mod support is at it's best.AND PLEASE ADD A FLAG DESIGNER, I'M BEGGING YOU. IT'S A MUST HAVE FOR THE NATION BUILDER.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm trying to love this game really, really hard. But at present, I kinda regret buying it, because it is frustrating as hell. The AI either cheats or is braindead. AI nations just rush without a second thought into ages. Because of this, you either have to rush knowledge or just leave yourself to fate because the AI REALLY wants that Age of Plague. Rushing knowledge causes you to miss out on the requirements for variant ages or crisis ages you actually want. Age of Heroes is basically unattainable because of this, after 10 resets I can't find enough landmarks before the AI rushes to the new age, no matter the difficulty.The barbarians are a greater nuisance on any difficulty than the Civilization VI raging barbarians on deity difficulty, which is saying something. Barbarians stop any kind of progress you are making, because they multiply so fast that all cities are constantly under attack. You can't really build up towards containing the barbarians all the time, unless you are going strictly towards a warfare build. I did that on my first playthrough, but other nations were so far ahead of me on everything and were just rushing to the first age they unlock. There really should be a restraint on the AI when it comes to rushing ages, even an option to not allow them to pick a new age until they research everything in their current age first. Heck, I'd gladly put that restriction globally. AI always goes unprepared into a new age, causing them to spiral into the crisis age every time. Education? Nah, no need to research my country needs, I'll just rush to the new age and force everyone into the Age of Ignorance. Sanitation? Man, gotta get hunting camps everywhere first, so I won't have the space for people to dispose of their garbage, those plague doctor uniforms look kinda lit though, got buboes all over my body, but I'll cover them with this sick drip.All of these are basically balance issues, but it extends towards the most severe problem: lack of features. I get it, this is a Paradox game. But no real options for creating a custom game other than nations and their own difficulty? No tweaking the settings like the game speed? There is no "Altert" option for your units so they can wake up when they spot an enemy? No auto explore feature? Only picking between unit flags or formations without the possibility of both? Only two build queues? These are just some of the things that are expected to be there on launch, features which a 4X game kinda requires.Minor gripe I have with the game is the forced "standard" age. Like, come on, no fun allowed? Obsolete units should have some kind of icon, so I won't forget about those Spartans I build 6k years ago while they are marching together with my assault rifle squads. Promoting units with Warfare XP is kinda... strange, and it slows down the army progression by quite a lot. There should be an option to choose between Warfare XP and money. There should also be a bit more tooltips when it comes to certain things. Hovering over Chaos meter should give you an insight on what is giving you a Chaos score, for example.I am giving this a negative review, but there are things I love about this game:The production chain is amazing, it forces you to plan ahead and specialize your regions. The outpost and vassal system is actually a great change of pace, it can award you for playing both wide and tall, although the vassals can be a bit OP sometimes. The unique ages can make each playthrough, well, unique - if the AI stops rushing the ages (you'd think that AI would stall out the crisis age they got locked into by researching other tech, but I guess Germany really wanted that plague 4 times in a row). National focuses are amazing, great addition.All in all, I can't recommend the game in this state. Especially because it does not have mod support as of the moment of writing. Not to mention an overpriced "DLC" for an alternate look of two units... come on... The modding community will probably save this game. But until then, just play Civilization VI. I'll come back to this game in a few months to see if the issues have been resolved.

_childDocuments_.review: I see the potential, let me get that out right now. This game has a lot going for it and it could honestly become something amazing. However, it is not there yet. It honestly just could be me, but the game is tremendously difficult if you aren't utilizing exploits. Barbarians spawn on top of you constantly, the AI even on a LARGE MAP with only 6 civs total still spawn directly on top of you as well. I tested almost 20 games and in each one of them, there were two enemy AI civs within 10 tiles of my spawn as well as at least 3 barbarian camps. Getting up off the ground at all feel impossible, and I was only playing on Adept, the base recommended difficulty.Even watching guides on how to play and what everything means, which there is a ton to keep track of, I was still constantly being outdone by the AI, constantly getting overrun by barbarians, and being beaten to every single age by literally every other AI despite doing the exact recommended things that every guide offered.I don't like bashing on games, I really don't and I rarely even leave GOOD reviews, let alone bad ones, but this game feels like it wasn't even played by the ones making it. The starting bonus powers don't even matter after the first three ages, the tech tree advancement is wildly unbalanced in choosing the culture things, and honestly I didn't enjoy even a few minutes of the game and I gave it an honest try. 7 hours of gameplay and I didn't feel a single moment of "aha! Okay, this is what I was doing wrong!" - I just felt annoyed. Even lowering the difficulty to learn mechanics I was slaughtered by barbarians at every turn.There is something here, but I think this game is destined to be relegated to a foundation game. One that is looked at by someone else years later and taken to build up off of. It had ideas, it did have some good innovations that I, personally, hadn't seen - but it just doesn't feel like it has hit the mark.

_childDocuments_.review: Two notes before the review proper:1. This is a 4X game. If you've never played a 4X game before, play Civilizations, and then, if you enjoy it, come back to this. This review hereafter assumes you've played a 4X game before and curious about the merits of this game within the genre, not a review on the genre itself.2. Paradox is an excellent developer and they support games long after launch. So this review may already be out-of-date.The game itself:Pro - High replayability. Moreso than a typical 4X. There are different ages and some are bad and some are good and you'll want to try achieving an Age of Harmony or seeing if you can survive an Age of Ignorance (good luck!). These various ages up the replay factor a lot because they change the challenge of the game. For example, the Age of Revolution could fracture your empire, but even if it doesn't you'll have to fight revolutionaries in addition to your enemies. Or, in the Age of Plague you have to deal with random and frequent outbreaks. These ages are a refreshing change from other 4X games (yes, I know Humanity has ages too but they're less diverse).Con - My first playthrough I wanted neither the age of plague (triggered by a different nation getting there first while I took too many technologies) nor the age of ignorance (triggered by having too high a population when the education need suddenly took effect). I also accidentally ended up in a negative age by triggering too much chaos razing too many enemy cities, go figure. Point being, sometimes it feels like the game is kicking you when you're down.Pro - Solid mechanicsParadox gets the core game right and then just adds tons of great content to it (not to fanboy too much).The game has solid play and interesting mechanics. They really made the game their own and it feels different than Civ or Humanity despite having a very familiar feel. The improvements to land feel new and necessary, the domains are a great change.Con - The game pacing is rather breakneck which isn't terrible in itself, but it does make you have to really tailor your choices per age into what you want to do. My first game I did not choose defense and by the third age the poor choice was so poor that I had to restart. Which makes you feel a bit pigeon-holed into choices, particularly when a choice is crucial to surviving a particular part of the game.Pro - It runs smoothEven at the final turns of the game with massive empires spread across the globe and hundreds of armies, the turns took about the same amount of time as they do in the beginning. In Civ, you could click end turn and walk away, get a drink, have a conversation, come back and still wait for the computer to finish processing opponent turns. Not so in Millenia, turns come fast.Why play Civ first?Not just because it is the granddaddy of the genre, but it has all the bells and whistles. This game severe lacks them (though not entirely). For example, during the space race when you achieve spaceflight for the first time, you get a cutscene. That is a great bell/whistle. But in Civ, you get a cut scene for every wonder of the world. The age transitions feel less great after 10 of them being the same, and worse when you opponent achieves it first and you have to watch them get it instead. These feel especially missing in diplomacy. You barely get a text window for diplomatic stuff and there should be at least a static portrait of what you're looking at. I know Paradox can do better here because they do better with Stellaris. Gifts from other empires don't mention what the gift actually is and the first time I got one, I thought it was a demand for a gift from another empire. The learning curve in this game is not too steep but they do present it in way too big chunks (at the start of ages rather than bite-sized bits from tooltips or whatever). So without the bells and whistles and the not quite easiest-to-learn methods, I would recommend a different 4X first, but this would be on the list to play.Con - It doesn't feel fully finished. No one mentions there is a turn limit until 25 turns before the limit. Then it's just BAM Defeat! after the 25 turn. It was almost an after thought to have a warning at all. Civ does too, but they have options to turn off turn limits and allow/disallow victory conditions and such. But like I said, Paradox supports their games so I'm hoping that along with the new multiplayer, they add other stuff that are mostly polish. Like the review says, this is a positive recommendation, what's there is great and worth the cost full price (and a good starting price it is too!)Conclusion:If you're a fan of 4X games, this one should be pretty great fun for you.

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend the game as it presents interesting paths to follow outside the normal civilization type games.  I have Civilization and Humankind.I was initially struggling at the intermediate levels and went to the lowest challenge level to get deeper into the timeline.  While the included manual and dictionary is good, I found it easier to look for specific questions searching in the web browser that lead me to the forums and Reddit.I suspect that I will have many more hours/days playing this gamePros:Balancing the tech tiers, improvements and buildings is a challenge.  You can either build buildings or units which leads to a difficult choice in some ways.Your empire is limited in the number of regions you directly control.  If you control too many, your culture will suffer and this feature is something you want to do.  You can indirectly control regions as vassals which provide money, but don't build too quickly and are an obligation to defend.Regions have many more improvements than they do have space, you must choose improvements for tech/food/military and housing.  Some improvements like the same type of terrain.Mediocre:I'm not sure why the battles are played out via individual units.  You can fast forward too the end.  The animation is a bit crude compared to a lot of other games.  It's useful to watch the animations sometimes to see which units perform better in combat.  Besides the actual attack/defense characteristics, there is a rock-paper-scissors bonus on some units that show up in other combat gameAt the lower levels, the game sometimes takes on the flavor of a grind.Cons:At the higher levels, the barbarians are really a lot to handle.  They sometimes feel like rain in that they don't bunch up in big groups, and will attack 1 on 4 or 5 units.  While this is a loss for them, these constant attacks cause instability in your regionsThe npc players are very aggressive.While this may change as I learn more, the NPCs get farther ahead than I in both tech and expansion of their empires.  In my initial games this caused me to bail out in the pre-gunpowder timeline.

_childDocuments_.review: Not sure why this has a mixed rating - its easily the most interesting 4X I've played in years (since Endless Legend & Stellaris). The age system and the re-interpretation of a tech tree stand out particularly as really neat, while its culture/warfare/exploration and public works systems all have a vibe that positively brings to mind Call to Power.Definitely a DLC-series, like Stellaris (which I am excited for - who doesn't want a game that changes and evolves over many years?) - there are some things in the end game that feel a bit shallow, and a couple of mechanics that could do with some refining. The AI in particular is a bit bland, needs a lot more work there to  make them interesting to play with (they're not necessarily 'easy', just not engaging). Also would have been nice to have a post-game summary when I win or lose, rather than just a dialogue. I've won once and lost once, the rest of the games restarted as I learned the mechanics. Bit of a steep learning curve, but that was fun in its own. Thumbs up.

_childDocuments_.review: This game gets better, the longer you play.  Wade past the silly complaints about graphics.  They aren't spectacular, but, who plays 4X games for photo-realistic graphics.  The Pros : Interesting mechanics that arent seen in other 4x games.  Addictive "one more turn" gameplay and systems that are deep enough to take a moment to figure out.Was stable over the 5 hours I played.  No performance issues.  Cons : Tooltips need some work.  Not every item or action explains what it will do, and some things are unclear.  Luckily, you have an undo option, so, test it out and if you don't like the result, just undo it.  Needs some balancing, in my opinion.  Barb spam can become irritating, but after a certain point, your army can just walk over most anything.   If you like 4x games like Civ, Humankind, Old World, etc, this might be interesting for you.  It is sufficiently different from all of them to not feel like a clone.  Price might be a tad high.

_childDocuments_.review: Millennia is an excellent civ-like. It returns to the older style of games, before the controversial modernisation of the newest entries, and adds several very interesting tweaks of its own, two most of all.The first tweak is the Ages. The game is divided into ten Ages, which are like chapters. They define the events that can occur in that chapter. After the first two Ages, there are many variants that can be unlocked to customise the gameplay. This provides for much enjoyable replayability.Another tweak is economic production chains. Rather than simply finding a resource and exploiting it, now you can create chains of buildings to process the resources in different ways, depending on your needs. So for example wood can be turned into lumber for production, or books for knowledge, or religious tracts for faith. This customisation means there is always something to do and lots of variety in how to play.Combat is also improved, with stacks returning, but with supply limits that increase with era. Units are also grouped into a three-way system that encourages the use of combined arms forces. Armies feel like real discrete forces.There are still a few bugs but not too many and the dev team are busy patching them. Diplomacy is rudimentary, again more like the older Civ games. The graphics are beautiful and traditional, not gaudy and cartoonish like the modern Civ games.Overall this is a very good civ-like and an excellent first entry into the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't played many 4X games in the past, so take my opinion with a grain of salt. But out of all the 4X games I have tried and played, this one is the one that has pulled me in the most. The way the systems works in tangent with each other really intrigue me, the national spirits and the xp systems feel like a great way to advance or change your nation. The alternative ages are also a very interesting idea that lends the game the ability to change drastically.I will say the game does feel like a very neat concept, but it might not 100% polished yet. _childDocuments_.review: I wish I could give this a mixed review because that's what is deserves right now. Its got a lot going for it but its lacking a lot of polish.  I like the way it city growth and expansion. I like the way production chains for resources function. I like the domain and spirit of the age systems. I like the age system. Combat and armies are functionally fine but they look fresh from 2003. It is a little enigmatic as to how my regions (cities) borders are going to grow there are several things that happen in game that are kind hard to notice or see. Army movement can be a little clunky, I find my self right clicking the enemy army two times when issuing an attack from further then 1 tile away. The whole game just feels kinda unpolished at the moment. This probably means there's a lot of little quality of life and minor balance changes that need to happen. I am fully anticipating flipping this interview given time. Not sure how long it will be but i fully believe this will be a great game someday

_childDocuments_.review: Info about me: I have a few hundred hours in civ 5 and 6 yet I don't see myself as a 4X player. However, I have more than a thousand hours on multiple of paradox core games like EU4, so this review is mostly for fellow paradoxers. Also I have been playing trough the first 3 ages so far.Let's split this review up for each of the 4 X's. - 7/10This seems like a fairly standart X to me. You start with 2 units, and you move them. You can get a scout unit which can see further. There are villages and natural monuments you can discover, giving you some kind of buff. This would be 5/10.BUTThere are 2 interesting things. You have several types of mana, that you passively gain or gain from events. The scouting mana lets you raise another scout, so you don't have to sacrifise your valuable production on scouts. This is a crucial concept of the game - you can lean into the area you like, making you expand in it faster. That is +1 for me. Also, there are special government upgrades (domains) that you gain in even ages, where you can further spend this mana. There is one specially for exploring, which I did not take, but there is another +1 from me. Total: 7/10 - 6/10The basis of fighting is pretty simple rock-paper-scissors. Spears are good agains cavalry, cavalry is good against ranged, archers are good against footmen. That's a strong, if somewhat worn out, base. I give +1 for the army composition - you can have multiple units in the army, and the army occupies only one tile on the map, so you don't have an uncontrollable swarm of units like in civ. Another +1 for these cute animations, even if you gonna be skipping them in no time. But big -1 for the missed opportunity of "stack building"! There is no clear information which units take the turn first, no special synergies, nothing. There are also some special domains for the military, and the warfare mana seems abundant, but that does not feel novel, so no points for this. Total: 6/10 - 9/10This is the one this games starts to shine. If you are a fellow paradoxer, you probabbly know the concept of playing wide vs playing tall. You also know that playing tall is super rewarding, but it  like you have to go out of your way to play that way. Well, they did it. Not only it feels good playing tall in this game, it feels like the intended way to play this game. AND you can also play wide at the same time, thanks to the way vasals work! 9/10 only because it may feel frustrating running out of tiles. - 10/10It got it all. You gonna stack miniscule buffs on each other and 124X your economy. You gonna juggle ducats, multiple manas, etc. You gonna have resources in intricate supply chains.  Or you gonna supress them so they spawn rebels for you to farm warfare exp. And you gonna like it. Total: 10/10- 8 / 10

_childDocuments_.review: Well, I bought the game today and played for about 9 hours with a few breaks in between leaving the game open. There will be a short summary at the end of the post to save yourself the readingThe game has it's issues and many quality of life things are missing. The graphics are subpar, cities lack fluidity and feel more like individual city states than an empire, special eras are difficult to get to, and diplomacy doesn't feel fleshed out at all. However the game is still very strong in the areas it focuses on the hardest such as the micromanagement of your empire to keep all your cities growing, the detail and thought put into the special eras and they really can change the game, and really feeling like you're building an empire from the ground up is a major plus for me. I'm accepting the issues with the game because even with them and how annoying they are (plus any others I didn't mention) I still enjoyed the game, and with a few updates and maybe some classic overpriced dlc the game can fix these issues and really drive this game home into a classic. I'd recommend the game at a 10 - 30% off for a fair price to buy the game at, but I feel like I got my moneys worth at full price.+++Micromanagement+++Cool Era Design+++ Empire Builder Simulation++Storytelling+War Simulator---Quality of Life (Gameplay-Wise)--Diplomatic Simulator-Graphics

_childDocuments_.review: So this is very similar to Civilization.  There are things I really like about it like the visuals.   I also  like the combat cut screens (even though I'd like the option not to have to see them all the time).  I also like how the game goes through the ages.  But the game lacks some of the better features of CIV that makes it an inferior experience, in my opinion.  First, it doesn't allow you to play on a realistic map.  I like that in CIV.  Second, it doesn't give you workers even though it says you should be able to put them places (maybe I haven't played far enough).  Third, it doesn't give you the rich history and factual civilization info that CIV does.  Fourth, you don't expand as easily as you can in CIV.  You have to go through a vassal period, then integrate your vassal lands before you can improve them and it takes forever!  You don't get nearly enough GOV points to do it in a way that works well in relation to the AI that seems to be able to go around increasing territory willy-nilly.  And finally, the advisors don't quite give enough information for a beginner to figure things out.  Without CIV as a background, I wouldn't have started as successfully as I did (even though I restarted 3 times because I felt I screwed up initially).Honestly, I would rather just keep playing CIV.  This adds nothing really new or great to the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like Millennia. I really do. It's venturing down a unique path, I find Civ's dominance rote, and Humankind never really caught on. The problem with liking Millennia, however, is that you have to be able to play it. The performance is not good. It's not good in a very odd way - the graphics are... dated. There doesn't seem to be something that's causing the AI to struggle through its calculations. So why does it run so poorly?I have no idea. It's bad enough that I have a book propped up on my desk that I've been reading while the AI takes its turns. I've been reading reviews and first looks to see if the performance is just me. It's not. Why would you release it like this? It's Paradox, yes, polished releases isn't their thing. They're usually better than this though. Maybe I'm just playing 'too quickly', but my turns are a lot faster than the AI's. Every turn seemed to noticeably make the performance worse.Eventually, I just surrendered to the inevitable. I closed the game and gave my book my full attention. I've dealt with slow games before - Stellaris most notably, especially before they cleaned up good chunks of the game. It was good enough to tolerate the rough performance. Millennia?Well. Points for bravery.[Also, what is with the low amount of civilisation choices? It's only city names and a flag. Jarring to see European civilisations almost outnumber the rest of them combined. Poor Africa's just got two! There's National Spirits which are clearly based off certain empires in history that are completely absent in the game. It's baffling AND sloppy.]

_childDocuments_.review: Played during free wekend. I really wish to like this game, but it feels like a bunch of great ideas that were left completely unrefined. Ages seem less relevant and interesting than you could expect. Production cycles and converting resources into goods is a fantastic idea.. that feels very lackluster in practice, because of bad UI, lack of filtering resources and the fact every single pop works a tile on map, so switching up production in bigger settlements takes far more time and effort than you should expect. The whole management aspect is pretty messy in general, yet again in big part thanks to underdeveloped UI. The combat is another mixed bag of interesting ideas, that were left in rough state - I like how your armies become bigger trough the ages and how leader mechanics work, but when you add military power to the mix it becomes huge mess. I despise re-filling movement and healing units instantly to the extreme, it makes strategic aspect of warfare almost meaningless, especially with the fact how vulnerable and crucial to economy cities are. Not settlements - cities. They are vital extensions to settlements, expanding borders and giving bonuses based on adjacency.  So you can have your enemy get his army boosted by leader to sprint for the undefended city, basically setting you up dozens turns in one turn. It can and will happen. Of course you can do that to them and cover your 6, but it's just a mess to deal with in general.  I honestly hope things get polished in the future, the game does have that "one more turn" feeling.. but it's so under-cooked I'm happy to get through without major food poisoning. 6.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Updating my review now I've put a bunch more hours in, but it's definitely still negative. There's just way too much broken gameplay; infinite wars are one of the biggest problems; essentially you reach a stalemate/near stalemate where you have some advantage, but you don't have enough forces to take their cities. If you don't do that then the war never ends, if you force a war end through one of the cultural options then they just start the war again within a turn or two with no cooldown. Diplomatic actions do nothing so you can't dissuade them that way, it's just an infinite war that'll drag on until the game times out at 500 turns. There's just no way to get out of it at that point meaning you've completely wasted hours.This on top of other bugs like all your cities randomly rebelling leaving you with a game over with zero notice and only one city being upset, or the bug where you just don't get the colony ship project (end of game project so something you don't get until many hours in) despite building everything required is just dumb.It's really just a completely broken version of Civ, and it's hard to see what it's supposed to offer that Civ doesn't - it's just Civ with more bugs, more bad game design, significantly less features, worse graphics, and worse AI.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, so just finished my first full game - I lost by the skin of my teeth.  Overall view - a  good game, however plenty of room for improvement. Things it did well: not having to have hundreds of workers to build improvements/roads etc, and being able to upgrade those improvements as you progress through the ages, (as one other review commented, things built in 6000 BC not affecting what you do in 2000 AD). the combat screen with the undo button was also interesting - as it allowed you to roll back and switch things up if you lost a fight you started. The ability to research 3-4 techs and advance an age is good, especially as you can go back later and research older techs if needed - with one exception (see below).Things it didn't do so well: The whole world advances when you progress to the next age. This is a big one for me - as the AI auto upgraded all its units as soon as it happened - instead of having to research things first like you. In my opinion  Humankind did it better - with the ages linked to your civ only - what's the point in a tech rush if the AI basically beats you every time as soon as you go up an age? At the very least they should be stuck at whatever tech they have researched, and have to complete that 'tree' before they can move to the better techs - preferably they should have to research the techs too. No ability to see where you are in comparison to other players/AI - this would be so helpful for planning. The unrest generated when taking an opponents city after the opponent declared war is a bit odd too - I'd have thought your people would be happy if you are winning a war that was forced on you - not annoyed - but hey ho. A few bugs encountered - such as age of monuments not having a 'barracks' - the mercenary building is effectively this - but it doesn't tell you that - I had to discover it by accident.TL:DR - a good game, but needs some polish/improvements to be a great one.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this but alas there are some major issues with the game.1. The complexity of the systems is welcome, but their opacity is not. The game doesn't feel intuitive at all; it takes lots of rooting around to find out exactly how systems work, and there's little clarity in how they work together. For example, you spend much of the game acquiring a variety of currencies -- 'diplomacy', 'warfare' -- but at no point is there a display on screen showing you how much you're acquiring, and from where. City demands escalate, and require space to cater to, but the area of influence grows too slowly to account for them.2. Some systems are far too unbalanced. Chaos, for example, builds up rapidly and causes major repercussions. This causes a cascade effect which takes your civilization from decent to doomed in ten turns flat. 3. Barbarians are incredibly hostile and powerful; give up all hope of having an explorer civilization unless you're willing to field expensive armies to fight their way across the world. 4. On higher levels, the ages system is reduced to a race between civilizations trying to beeline the requisite number of technologies just to move on. This is particularly important because whoever is in the lead can set the next age for EVERYONE, so it's in your interest to be the one who changes ages first. All great for folks who like minmaxing, not so much for folks like me who like to roleplay.5. For a game that is so ugly (janky unit animations, boring city designs, that 'battle screen' that looks worse than Civ Call to Power) this game lags a tremendous amount, and crashes very frequently.There are some good ideas here, but this really felt more like a half-developed demo that hadn't been through playtesting. Come back in a year or so, if it's been patched and modded. Right now, it's not worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very fascinating game with quirks, oddities and things that simply don't work. Which makes this a tough review for a few reasons. We will start with the good, examine the bad and maybe have some final thoughts about the 4x genre.Milennia does many interesting things. First and foremost in my mind is to make the geography matter for your resources. In a very standard 4x way, pops work tiles. However, most of what pops do when working tiles is not creating your standard production or food, but rather a resource that when consumed by the city produces the various resources in the game. This allows for a civ to play by focusing on wood or on stone or on clay depending on the local geography.The innovation and chaos system gives long term or even permanent buffs or drawbacks based on good things and bad things happening in your empire. Many of the buffs relate to specific types of buildings or goods which gives some neat feedback into making your empire's feel a little unique based on the surroundings.The era system is a clever way of making history feel a bit dynamic as well as balancing the game. It allows the game to incorporate things that we would call myths or large cataclysmic event into the world. Making the ages affect the whole world at once also takes away a little bit of the player's agency in small ways to avoid massively out-scaling the AI. In full disclosure I haven't played all (or even most) of the ages.Combat works by having armies made up of individual units fight- automatically until the battle ends by one side either dying or losing morale. I actually quite like the combat. It neatly splits the difference between doom stacks and doom carpets. I also like

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game that is actually truly different with each playthrough, far beyond the realm of usual 4x fare.I've played through the game four times, and I can say that none were anywhere close to each other. From an age of plague that progressed into alchemy that solved all of my material needs, then finally to an ecological paradise and victory, to another age where heroes were the dominant force that transitioned into a deep exploration phase, airships and finally an alien invasion, the playthroughs have extremely different mechanics that actually affect the game a lot, rather than just being a cosmetic difference. Sometimes you'll lack the usual buildings or units, which in itself will mean a drastically different strategy is needed to proceed than your last playthrough.The game emphasizes "in-game" customization of your nations as opposed to using pre-packaged nations like in Civ. This means they too are very different with each playhtrough, based on your choices, and you can adapt your strategy during gameplay rather than being stuck to pursuing a single victory style already predetermined at the start of the game like in Civ6.The combat system, which seems simplistic and outdated, is much deeper than you'd think once you understand how it works and functions in a much more interesting way than the surface level makes it seem. Units have morale, retreat from battle, need to be hunted down by cavalry to be finished off, and so on. However, it does have many problems at present(before any patches), chiefly performance issues at late game that are punishing even on the most advanced hardware, which is baffling considering the graphically limited nature of the game and that it's turn based.Diplomacy is another fault, especially on higher difficulties where the AI is hyper aggressive, thus defeating the point of the entire diplomatic aspect of the game.The AI is also rather weak in it's military AI, often having trouble utilizing naval units at all, or misusing their military might in foolish ways. So the usual 4x problem.If these problems can be addressed by patches, the game will be legendary. Even now it's extremely promising, but isn't for everyone. It lacks polish and isn't as casual as something like Civ6 is. You'll need to understand the underlying systems and you can't really play it without giving it some thought as to what you're doing.If you prefer creativity and interesting ideas over polish, this is your game. If you demand a polished, user-friendly experience that can be a bit dry on the side, this isn't for you.Will change my review as the situation changes.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: The graphics are disapointing and the design overal lacks love in my opinion. It looks like a cheap mobile game. And why is there no multiplayer on release ? Oh and I couldnt even launch the game through Steam. I needed to open the folder to launch it from there. I am also a bit disappointed that different countrys are basically skins since they only bring a pre set boost that can be changed at will. I feel like they had some cool ideas but didnt manage to execute them in a rewarding way. Looks like I am going back to Civ.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Lovely complexities on top of the classic 4X features, introduced in a very natural and easy-to-understand way. I really enjoy this game. The 'national spirits' achieve what Humankind tried by mid-game civ changes without you losing the sense of continuity. The devs also seem to be keen on continuing to update
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: There are severe balance issues early game that makes learning the game to an expert level a requirement, even for the "normal" difficulty setting where no inherent advantages are given to the AI. You have way too many barbarians roaming the map and you can barely defend 2 regions while keeping your economy afloat just to keep up. There are "Diplomatic" civilizations that will declare hostilities the turn they meet you, then the next turn declare full out war. Then they will come at you with on par or overwhelming forces and put you into a standstill for several turns just to get plague stricken by a civ that you never even have met, or on another continent completely and get shut out of the game. Also all the Civ's are symmetric..which is crazy to think that they thought that was okay on launch. The Nation Builder isn't complete....you can't even delete a custom civ that you made and it will go into the civ pool forever. It just leads to every playthough being the same derivative strategy just to survive.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I will plan to add more to this review as I continue to play. But the TLDR:This game is getting a lot of criticism, but at its core it's EXCELLENT. If you like Civ or Humankind, you should love this game.But, then, why the criticism? A few things:First off, I think a lot of people criticizing the game simply don't understand all the game systems. To some extent, this is due to the developers not providing as clean and direct of a UI as possible. The reality is that it will take some trial and error to figure out how this game works, and some elements that will feel familiar from civ/humankind/etc. don't work the way you expect them to. But this isn't necessarily a bad thing!Others have criticized the graphics and performance. The graphics are on the simpler side, and have a very stylized look. In many ways, it looks a lot like Civ 6, a game that is now 7 years old (and many people criticized civ 6 graphically even back then!). So yes, it's not impressive graphically. For me, this isn't a problem at all, because I don't expect amazing graphics from a 4x—indeed, I often prefer simpler graphics, to ensure that the game's presentation is "legible", as it were, to a quick scan of the eyes But reasonable people can disagree on this.As for performance...yes, it is not well optimized. Again, for a 4x, this isn't really game-breaking, but I agree with the critics and hope they will improve this over time.Beyond those issues though, I think this is an excellent 4x game in the spirit of Civ. It has a really interesting approach to managing terrain tiles and a variety of other production-adjacent systems. I think it really advances the genre, and I have more than 3k hours in all civ games combined. I even like the approach to combat, though that's something many people disagree with (it isn't as deep as, say, Humankind, and there is little tactical decision-making for the player—but there is more depth to it at the strategic level than at first meets the eye.)This game is worth your attention! And the time (and even perhaps frustration) to learn its unique systems.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: This game is OK - but after a few playthroughs I found it tedious and not very balanced.   A lot of National Spirits don't seem to provide value and the micromanagement gets overwhelming.  The end game turns into a very long snooze fest.  The early game is very challenging due to the uber powered barbarians.  I like the concept of improvements point to upgrade your regions however after a while, there's nothing to produce except more military.  This is missing that one more turn feeling you get with good 4X games.   If you want to try something new - it's worth a try.  But it's not a game you come back to year after year like that other 4X game - you know which one :-)
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: While Millennia does have it's limitations in the current form, the game as it stands is fairly solid for an "at launch" game these days. It shows the scope of ambition that the devs have in mind, is fun to play, and the mechanics take a while to get used to if you're coming from Civ V or VI, giving you a challenge. Is it a Civ Killer? Not yet. But it has promise.The UI could do with better scaling, and there could be a clearer notification system in place. I'd like to see more customisation options for games also, but this will hopefully come in time; Set Turn limit, more map options, customised victory goals etcAll in all, a solid 7/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Are they serious with these graphics? And why would anyone play this over Civilization? It literally plays and looks like a game from 1999, and not in a charming way. The AI is also really bad. At easier difficulties, enemies are dumb as dirt. At higher difficulties, they just spam ungodly amounts of units on your borders and have unlimited resources. Instead, they should actually develop intelligent AI.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Finished my first game after being absolutely addicted to it for the last 5 days.This is from the perspective of someone who has 400 hours in civ 5, and has played a large variety of other 4X, grand strategy, and base building games.tl;dr:* Lots of really good ideas and fun mechanics to explore.* Currently a bit buggy and unpolished, but nothing that causes major issues.Positive:* Very interesting tile & city management. Feels to me like they succeeded at what Civ 6 failed to do with tiles.* A variety of super fun special ages, that look like they'll give the game a lot of replay value.There are so many different numbers that are ticking up each turn (especially Domain XP)Negative:* As mentioned, there is a definite lack of polish in some areas, and a few bugs, but they're generally just visual and audio stuff, some UI stuff, but there was nothing that was a real issue.* Compared to a lot of other 4X and strategy games, Millenia is currently not giving you as much information as I'd like. For example, sometimes an ability only says "increases knowledge gain in region" but doesn't specify by how much.The game also doesn't always fully tell you what improvements do, or where you can place them, like it does in the civilopedia, for example.It took me a while to realize that a lot of "gathering" improvements can go on various tiles, they generate goods without the tile having any special goods available to it.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a real challenge.  It is complex and well balanced.  AI is very skilled.  The room for error is slim.  Rival factions are strong.  Barbarians are beefy.  Because of the twists of fate in Age progression there is no meta for winning.  The game evolves with the slings and arrows of fortune.  Every decision matters.  You can flame out at any point in the game from beginning to end and lose all your work.  The graphics are o.k.  The music is o.k.  The mechanics are what makes the game worth the buy.  As far as I can see there are at least seven different currencies you need to keep track of.  It becomes very complex very fast.  In fact, a real head ache.  But this is Paradox.  What were you expecting?
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Do you like Civilization? Do you like Paradox Games?Well then go play Civilization and Stellaris, because this game is not it.The only game I have that regularly blue screens my brand new device. I've only got 11 hours in because this game will just crash after only 3 hours.Mechanics are overbloated on release, have no depth, and almost no engagement from that. There are too many things going on with not enough ways to deal with them, there's no reason to ever start a religion once you're able to because it will instantly send your empire into a death spiral with no way to fix it without completely dismantling all your production lines just to make paper for everyone, because apparently the instant some prophet has an idea it causes your entire population to become 100% literate.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting twist on the civ style 4x formula. Lots of similarities to civ 5 and 6 on the surface but mechanically they are quite different. From how improvements work, to resource management, to the tech tree, how combat works are all very different. Most of the uniqueness and replay ability is tied to choices you make in the game. Choices such as governments, national spirit and which ages to pursue can influence how you play. The different ages are very interesting and can greatly change your games.There are some flaws though, the UI is kinda rough, diplomacy is pretty bare bones, the AI is all over the place in how it acts. Also the barbs and AI nations are aggressive and making large armies is almost mandatory which is kinda a neutral point, some players might love it, some may hate it but it definitely influences how you play. Overall though it's pretty fun and worth checking out for 4x fans.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: It's pretty good. It's definitely not a game for kids. This is like a mix of strategy war games and the production chains that Ara made a big ol stink about that are ... pretty but pretty uninteresting. I suspect that with the DLC the game develops a lot more personality than it is as a base game. Unfortunately for all the games depth the UI still communicates a lot of stuff very poorly. Diplomacy is just a lot of numbers that don't seem to change based on anything you do. You can force peace or persuade peace. The ages do a LOT to make each play through unique though. It still seems a bit thin on the longevity though... research lets your rush ahead to new ages and just reaching a new age still carries with it advantages that swing pretty heavily. I'll grant you that actually accomplished much better an aspect that Humankind tried to do and didn't quite get there. It's good but it's also sometimes a bit too familiar, if that makes sense. Just rushing science probably won't win you games though - there is a good amount of options to balance. Lots of distinct abilities and the like. Unfortunately again, the UI, isn't helping anyone play this game easier and more coherently. There is a log but it's a separate window you open and even there the details aren't often quite what you want. Also the 'mini battles' pop up thing does get occassionally tedious. I usually like it but even I'm appaled sometimes by the extra time it adds.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Finally a studio to face Firaxis head on!I've been playing 4x games since civ2 and we've been waiting for a good successor of Civ6 for almost a decade. Millenia managed to add complexity and progress through the 4x series without taking away the fun. The way the narrative unfolds and the different paths that appear throughout the gameplay are the highs for me, as well as the way the game deals with improving and expanding the terrain. Anyway, whoever is a 4x fan should definitely put some hours in Millenia!Some basic suggestions for the developers:- Add difficulty levels in the game creation menu- Start with all random Nations in the creation menu- Give greater importance to rivers for mobility between regions, bonus for trade, bonus for the capitals, etc.With 20 hours played, that's all folks. When I have 100 hours I´ll update here. Cheers

_childDocuments_.review: Graphics aren't amazing. thats a fact, especially the combat. I for the most part actually like the world map graphics quite a bit but all thats opinion, so just look at screenshots and videos to decide that for yourself.UI is a bit messy and def needs work. _childDocuments_.review: This game has a lot of really fresh, original ideas and is a breath of fresh air in the 4x space. I played way to much Civ (and Alpha Centauri) back in the day. I play a ton of Stellaris and CK3. But I really like what this game brings to the table. I was pretty sick of the traditional Civ-style 4x game before this came out. But I've played multiple campaigns and had a great time here. It's not going to displace Stellaris for me. But it'll be something I come back to and enjoy on a regular basis. If the game sees continued development, I'll probably continue buying DLC for it.It does a lot of things right and has a lot of strategic depth. In particular, I like that it encourages adaptive play. You don't start out and go for a "build". Instead you adapt what you pick to the needs of the situation and the map that you happen to have. That keeps the game interesting and leads to much less boredom. And with all the different ages and the choices you make for each one, there's a ton of depth and content that a lot of people who played the game at launch and only did the first few ages missed out on.Similarly, you need to balance getting all the different meta currencies and can't really go "all in" on one thing to the neglect of everything else. But they make it easy to do this. For example, the large numbers of barbarians and minor cities give you plenty of opportunities to get military points early and often without having to start a war with another civilization. This encourages players to try different play styles and engage with systems they might otherwise not be inclined to try.I wish the game had been given more time to "cook" and launch with a bit more polish. A lot of the negative and mixed reviews are based around surface level complains from people who didn't "get" the game. It's genuinely good and deserves more love than it is currently getting. I like the art direction and I like that the interface lets me play the game easily on a Steamdeck. I also like that they've responded to feedback from the community and improved things in this regard.My main criticism is that the game does a bad job at teaching you and it has fairly limited discoverability inside the game. It doesn't let you browse the entire tech tree, and you can't peruse what each age has in store even after you've unlocked them for the first time. More pressingly, it doesn't do a good job of helping you learn how to be a more efficient player. As a result, a lot of people try to play it like Civ and end up disappointed. This also makes it harder to get that sense of mastery that lets you relax and enjoy the game without cranking the difficulty way down. And that's ultimately where I think the game missed the mark -- Civ is a fairly relaxing game. So is CK3. Stellaris can be when you aren't doing multiplayer PvP.But this game, due to being compressed and making every option matter, feels more intense. And that intensity plus the lack of a sense of mastery is probably turning people off from the game. Given more time and resources, I think the team could fill in the gaps in multiplayer, with the AI, and the other areas that even the positive reviews raise.I hope they get a chance to do that and "relaunch" a version 2.0 with a big marketing push down the road. Because this game has a lot of potential left on the table.Regardless, I'm happy with my purchase of both the base game and the DLC. So even as-is, it's worth playing, especially if you are an experienced 4x player and want something different and innovative.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: The best 4X game available right now (as of August 2024).Very innovative with production chains, a variety of domain-specific experience points, freely combineable national spirits, freely combineable government types, and many alternative ages.  Thus there is very good value in playing this game multiple times, every game is different and unique.I can compare to Humankind (my 2nd best), Old World (3rd), Imperiums Greek Wars (4th) and Civilization 6 (5th), having played at least one game in all of these, and half a dozen in Millenia.Humankind has the best system for military battles, Old World is best for Roleplaying and has by far the best AI, Imperiums Greek Wars has the best Diplomacy system, but this one is the best overall.In addition to the key features listed above, it is the most innovative and creative, it has a good pacing and not as much annoying micromanagement as Civ6, and fewer bugs than Civ6.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I refunded despite loving Old World, having hundreds of hours in Civ V and Civ VI, and absolutely loving the genre.There's just a lot of work that needs to be done before this game can compete with the aforementioned games. Old World married Crusader Kings style lineage management and gameplay with the Civ gameplay loop, and is much more enjoyable than this game. Civ 6 and 5 have more features that are better explained (and simply are FUN). Haven't played a lot of this game, but that's because when played my first game I noticed I was having much less fun than I have with its competitors. I just won't play this game when competitors exist that have a similar, but better, gameplay loopI think this game has potential if it isn't abandoned (it DOES introduce a few cool new features), but I'm not confident it will get there
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I can not recommend this right now. If you can get past the clunky UI, downright ugly presentation and glaring balance issues (prepare to reroll starting positions often and to be beset by raging barbarian hordes at all times) then you might actually enjoy some of the innovative mechanics. For what is on offer the price point is unjustified, this looks and feels like a small and somewhat unfinished indie game, not like an AA title. If it gets some polish after release despite the already meagre reviews it might become a gem though.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Lots of negative reviews, but I like it. The resources and upgrades are nice.  The variant ages are a neat touch for replayability.  The domain powers keep things interesting by giving you more variety in things to do (compared to the city-sprawl of old civ games). The customizing of your nation as you go through the game seems better here than in Humankind.  It is easier to get into than the current Civ which has become a bit bloated with different un-intuitive systems.  I find myself wanting to keep playing this more than with Old World.  The combat animations are garbage and the UI needs work. Overall, recommend checking it out if this genre is your thing.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: ~4 hours in. Re-playable variations seem extremely high. Learning curve is definitely present early. Combat is more interesting than Civ, less so than Humankind. I expect competitive Metas to be very complicated with the sheer number of variations that seem possible. This game has the potential to compete for top 4X with a little tuning and some workshop support. Overall I'd recommend it to anyone who likes methodical 4X gaming! 8/10 with the potential to grow into a top game!
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Unbalanced.REALLY unbalanced.Only workable strategy that seems to work is being a turtle.Trying to push against the barbarians isn't really feasible as knocking down a Barbarian camp will kill an entire army at the early game and when you start advancing forward you need siege units to break through their sudden stone walls after fighting through a half dozen barbarian units that spawned all of a sudden.5/10 - barely playable.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Genuinely entertaining little "civ-like". It could use a few patches here or there, some improvement to the AI, but it's a perfectly fine game as it stands. All of the little systems work together well and it feels like it stands on its own next to Civ, and isn't just trying to be another clone. Definitely recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Game definitely needs more work: diplomacy is abysmall, final rush to victory is lenghty and boring, some things are still unbalanced and multimedia are not satisfying.On the other hand, the game is definitely interesting and more replayable than any other civ games. It certainly absorbed me more than Humankind and Civilization VI altogether - 40 hours at the moment and still growing.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: About 100 hours of play at this point.  Great treatment of history and ages in a new way.  If you like CIV, you will like this game too.  Play, options, etc. all very different than CIV, so a lot of fun to learn how things work.  Even after 100 hours, still discovering and uncovering new concepts, etc.  Hats off to the designers and developers for coming up with a fresh and independent take on civilization!
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: This game hooked me like Civ 6 never did. It keeps me up at night because I keep thinking about the synergies between Ages, Governments, and National Spirits.The game is far from perfect - graphics are basic, the UI is clunky, and many details are not properly explained. If anything, the game's biggest flaw is the lackluster tutorial - many players approach it like Civ and their strategies don't work out here, leaving them frustrated. But if you liked Civ 5, and you are willing to either experiment or watch some Youtube let's plays, you will like this game too.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a solid foundation to build itself on, it's got some balance issues but those can be fixed with time. The core economic management and supply chains make the game engaging during peace time and there's always something to do even during peace time which I find a lot of other 4x games don't do as well. There's really never a turn where I just instantly click next turn, this could be a good or bad thing though depending on how experienced you are with 4x titles. The age mechanics really shake up and shape your play through which is a nice change of pace making each game unique. Not sure if it's a balance issue or on purpose but if you hit the Age of Plagues you don't get access to converting production to science or gold which made the game really slow as I had 2 super production cities that could only pump out improvement points. Which quickly because useless because I was constantly capped on improvement points and no real way to make use of my excess production other than building more units. AI will refuse peace so often even after you slaughter the 10th full stack army that's crossed the border. This becomes even more frustrating with the war exhaustion in cities that tick up really hard causing huge unrest, despite the fact you could take a city or two off the AI and kill a bunch of AI's they are really stubborn and wont peace out causing you to have lots of instability.TLDR-Pros:-Strong foundation to build itself up on -Fun economic management with supply chains-Population needs make it so the meta of more food = more pop brings a nice change of pace-Age mechanics are interesting and play styles feel different-National spirits are great and I always find myself debating which one I want to go with as they all feel impactful in their own way-Governments are also enjoyable where they promote different play styles and it never feels like there's a correct or wrong answer when picking one over the otherMeh:-Balance seems a bit off like the Age of Plagues issue I state above-AI difficulty seems to be a bit wonky, the normal AI seems really strong, in every other 4x game I steam roll ahead of the normal AI quite quickly but here I didn't start steam rolling until about Age 7-Graphics aren't great I feel like if they did a more stylized graphics it would give the game some charm but for a strategy game I don't feel like graphics matter compared to UI/UX not a deal breaker for me-Some supply chains could do with some extra steps or different options, the metal line is fleshed out but something like woods gets stopped instantly if not turned to paper, or not having much to do with textiles unless you get specific national spirits-The different actions you could do like expand town or claim territory really need to go down in price again after not touching them for a while because they get expensive quicklyCons:-UI/UX needs work some things are a bit hard to read and the in game mechanics book needs a search function, I wish some tooltips expanded more on what something did and why, for example Daimyo says it gives a regional bonus but not how much so until you get it you have no idea what the bonus actually is and if it's worth it-Multiplayer needs to be simultaneous, I got it to work with a friend but it just feels frustrating sitting there looking at the MP screen waiting for my turn not being able to see or plan out what I might want to do next turn-Lack of options for starting the game, no resource options, no climate or terrain options, limited choice of world types, lack of control over barbarian spawns(they are way to prolific), how many city states there should be, etc-Vassals should be expanded on, once you get a large empire or conquer a continent it quickly becomes really annoying trying to manage more than 6 cities, vassals should be able to do more and need to be a bit more interesting, its a good mechanic but needs to be iterated on -Diplomacy sucks, there's little options for engaging in diplomacy and its hard to tell what the AI is willing to accept or decline and for what reasons, AI refused peals deals despite winning battle after battle and they are very stubborn and relentless in their pursuit to kill you, just enter a war on two fronts and you will quickly find yourself in a permanent war-Performance sucks mid to late game, it lags by even moving an army and just overall needs to improve to make late game playable in a reasonable amount of time
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I understand why the reviews for this game are mostly negative (so as mine). I expected a lot from Paradox, being a fan of their games such as Europa Universalis. However, this game resembles Civilization a lot, but it lacks good interface, graphics, and AI game quality. I do think that they introduced very interesting features, like in economy, the possibility of working with product chains (e.g., if you have cotton, with proper technology you can create textiles from it). To be honest, there are too many games in this area at the moment and I think the industry would benefit more if some of these producers/publishers/developers would partner up and build games together. Paradox can definitely contribute a lot with economical, political and historical depth. But Millennia looks like a beta version of a game from 10-20 years ago. For the price, I expected more.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Lot's of unique approaches to the 4X genre and easy enough to learn if you already have experience with other 4X games. I love how the game is NOT easy, many other games allow you to follow a rinse and repeat strategy or follow specific paths to guarantee a victory, but Millennia requires more specific reactions to specific scenarios depending on how your nation and world has been built around you.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: A very good foundation. Mixes standard 4x (CIV especially) with some simple but interesting supply chain management and progression through the game.The main thing to set it apart from Civ is its 'Ages' where you can move through different ages depending on your choices. For example you can swerve from the Iron Age to an age of heroes, where you gain a heroic super unit to complete quests.Graphics wise, its ugly as sin, both in fidelity and style.The lack of proper simultaneous multiplayer is a startling omission, and really does need adding. The Devs say they're adding it, but who knows if the game will last that long without?All in all, a buyer beware recommend
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I wouldn't recommend this in it's current state. Multiplayer is Asynchronous turns only, you have to mess with ports to even get lobbys hosted. the UI is very bland. While I think the resources in game for explanation are decent , the tooltips leave a lot to be desired for information on units for example unit promotion. Once the game is more fleshed out I would say give it sometime , the devs say free updates coming, I say they are finishing an incomplete product which needs some TLC.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Bought the game because I saw a number of videos recommending it, and it seemed fun. Played for a bit, and it was! Went to play the game with my buddy, and was met with a labyrinth of nonsense the likes of which I have not seen since the early 2000s.  Don't release a game without the core systems in place. Didn't think it needed to be said. Wait a while before buying, the game-play is genuinely fun but it is absolutely not ready to have been released.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a fan of 4X games, and I've played a lot of good and bad ones. This is not a bad one, but even at 20 hours it's hard to say that it's one of the greats.I would say that it's full of interesting puzzles that engage me like crazy. Like the district system of Civ 6 it makes me think carefully about how my city grows and expands, but tile adjacency isn't a thing. Instead it has an interesting system of improving products to make much more powerful products. All of these buildings take up tile space around your cities, eating up precious tiles, and making major production hubs either very focused, or areas that other cities feed into to get the very best products.Combat is simple, but has a nice Fire Emblem style of strengths and weaknesses. If you know what your foe is mostly fielding, you can make your shock troops balanced against them, and then mop up with weaker, or less advantageous types in other armies. A lot of people find the combat screen to be too simple, but it's entirely skipable, and there are even options to speed it up natively. The part that's important from it is in an optional detail screen, which will show off the attack versus the enemy defense, which shows just how each round of combat is broken down. You can use this to adjust your army composition going forward.I really like the different currencies that you make, and their varied uses depending on your gameplay style. Like you can totally make great combinations of military points into extra moves with a force, or even post combat healing. Engineering points can be used to improved towns, gaining additional resources, or to make powerful prospectors that can straight up claim a territory to send goods back to cities that need them. Each type has things that can be useful for any kingdom, but can also be hyper focused to power up whatever strategy you like to play.Exploration is even cool, with later age options for going on multi-stage discoveries to summit mountains, or map dense rainforests. Each one can be great one time sources the point types mentioned before.And probably the biggest change from the Civ eras are the games Ages. There are the usual suspects making up the base tech up ages like bronze and iron, but then there are crazy alternate ages that can send the whole world into an a-historical offshoot. Each one has an interesting mechanic, plus a few alternate mechanics and techs.I think it's a pretty great game, just weird and different.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: This game is honestly fantastic and a great alternative to the standard civ game format. The era system feels very fresh  and unique, allowing you to stray quite far from actual history with both positive and negatives alt eras.
