The Civilization starts don't have massive differences that make one Civilization have a different play style. Instead, the tech you research and era's you unlock change every game to give it repeatability. There is the standard early - mid - late game style of resource management that every paradox game has, going from desperately micromanaging for one or two extra resource points to being swamped with resources at the end.Pro - the events are not simple RNG, your management / mismanagement will cause innovation and crisis.Tons of replayability, I just started but there are dozens of combinations of tech and eras you can stack to try and min max a build.The quirks add to the game. _childDocuments_.review: Normally I love these types of games, but there is so much about Millennia that is deeply frustrating to me the longer I play. This goes beyond just one or two common features that aren't included. There are so many aspects of the game that feel hollow next to any contemporaries in the 4X space. The game does innovate in a lot of places, but it ultimately feels like the developers were more interested in the specific ideas they had for unique game features than they were in making an all-round quality game.For instance, when generating a world, you can only choose the size and number of continents. Because there is no bias to the sort of starting location you get, like there is in Civilization, you are completely at the mercy of RNG as to what sort of environment you start with. This means you can't know what sort of resources you will have access to ahead of time, and can't make meaningful choices about what playstyle you would like to pursue. If you don't start near terrain suitable for quarries, you aren't going to be building the pyramids.The tyranny of RNG is never so fierce as it is in the early ages of the game, the ages that almost all players will spend a majority of their time experiencing. Line-of-sight and movement ranges are short enough that scouts can easily be ambushed and taken out by the hordes of barbarians that occupy every part of the map, and there is no apparent consistency in how many natural landmarks will spawn close to the player. This is especially frustrating considering how crucial scouts can be when they find good resources, and an entire age is locked behind someone finding at least 2 natural landmarks, which can vary between 'trivial' or 'impossible' based entirely on your luck as a player.This game has already promised a lot of DLC that offers new alternate ages and mechanics, but what it desperately needs is better fundamentals, and to work out all the problems that are uniquely frustrating about this game in particular.

_childDocuments_.review: I like the premise, the new ideas and certainly enjoy the alternate timelines, however it has allot of polishing needed. Religion in the game does not give you enough bonuses to pursue it and it actually takes allot more effort to maintain it than it's worth. You don't have to adopt a religion in any case  and in the late game two of the three government types are secular and so any bonuses you might have had or enjoyed from pursuing religion are removed. So pointless to even go down that route.There are certain negative alternate ages that can be attained without your input, the Age of Plague for instance can happen if other factions have poor sanitation and the counter is an aggregate of all factions. So too is the Age of Singularity, I suppose you can role play it, but it's easier to rush the next age and bypass it all together. I'd like to see the alternate ages branch off like tree limbs, once you start down a branch you have to follow it and it leads to other alternate timelines rather than being able too move back to the main branch; too easy to derail them.I do feel hemmed in somehow, the clock is ticking constantly in this game and pushes you to rush the victory. I don't get to enjoy the ages. There is a 500 turn limit but I always finish it in the low 300s. Perhaps making the knowledge cost of each tech greater would slow it down.So yeah, really an interesting 4x game. Just needs polishing.

_childDocuments_.review: This is, sadly, one of the most disappointing games in my Steam library (and I've got some real stinkers on there).It's unclear how much of the fault needs to fall on the publisher and how much on the developer, as there are some good bones on Millennia. The divergent ages are an interesting concept; the supply chains feel like they provide some nice, granular, tactical choices.But there are glaring problems. The graphics are, frankly, outdated, and not in a "invoking the nostalgia of older games" way. Elements of the UI and the combat reminded me of a mobile game, which is always a red flag for me. Performance in the mid to late game struggled.And, the cherry on top: the DLC plan, which I blame entirely on Paradox. Like so many modern games, the proposed DLC is introducing content that, honestly, should have been in the game in the first place: things like starting out in a nomadic age, which almost every single game in Millennia's genre includes as a basic feature.All in all, I cannot recommend this game in any capacity. Go play Civ 6. Heck, go play Microcivilization: even a clicker game is better than this. Millennia is just not worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played a few games now, I've won 1, and lost a few, and just lost interest in the last 2. I've got a feel for whats there. I'm on the fence about this game, although i'm more disappointed in it than I thought.  TLDR: The game has alot of issues, it seems unfinished - Even after it is finished, i'm not sure it'll be a good game.  It's almost as though it needs to be rebuilt and rethought in alot of areas. Alot of quality of life changes need to happen.  I'll play it in my 4x rotation as time goes on to keep an eye on it. If you're a die hard 4x fan like myself you'll prly get some enjoyment from this game.  That being said this prly wont become your main 4x game as is. 1. No multiplayer2. No civ specialties - most civ bonuses dont matter beyond age 1 or 23. Prepare for hordes of barbarians worse than civ 6, even with camp clearing4. AI cheats, pretty hard - In later ages they only need to research half the tech you do, and so they always lead the game, and they always lead into generic eras, except for the plague era, they love that era for some reason. 5. AI wars are weird: I've had wars with the AI where I stomp them and its easy, and I've had wars where they seem to have an ungodly amount of units somehow, just waves of 400-500 strength stacks of units. In one game I had what I thought was alot of unit stacks of 400-500 strength, about 10-12 stacks, and the AI easily had 20+ stacks despite being behind in tech and regions (cities).  Sometimes they declare war on you and just do nothing. 6. National Spirits (NS) are cool but they need love, they seem to be irrelevant after you use them so often for example you can buy an artist but if you buy too many artist's the cost of the artist will exceed the cap of the resource you can use to buy it, and there is no way to reset it. In other words you wont be able to buy them anymore, and this can happen by age 3-4. 7. The Ai spams cities like you wouldn't believe, and they build them in stupid places, and you can't raze them, and you can't absorb them into another city, they are just permanently there ruining your min max, in a game that relies very heavily on min maxing. 8. There are too  many tile improvements, and you have to micromanage them as the ages advance to optimize your city. 9. Razed tile improvements are difficult to see/notice because they just have smoke coming from them... some tile improvements already come with the same exact smoke appearance like most of the industrial age tiles., and some of the early age tiles. this makes it difficult to know which tiles were razed, so you have to to click on every tile after a war or barbarian incursion just to double check. that they weren't razed10. you run out of tiles to improve very fast, and sometimes your city will have the resources to build say computers but you wont have the space so you'll have to export your resources to another city but the catch is, if you didn't take the research to be able to do that, then you are either A. screwed because you have to give up your tech lead (if you have it) to get it, or B: just have an un-optimized city/ civ. 11.  You know in the other 4x games where you get a resource like iron and you unlock the swordsman? In this game if you have no iron you can just build the swordsman, in fact you can build any unit none of them require special resources to build.  - All resources do like iron is give your city production, or food, etc. It makes building up the iron supply chain not useless but unrewarding aside from the production it gives your city. 12. There are alot of tile improvements and they are just in a big grid-like configuration for you to choose from, and as you advance up the ages they move around inside this grid because their improvement costs change... so want to build a basic farm to mid tier farm? Just imagine a 10x10 grid full of icons that are always moving around with no way for you to organize them, and then looking for that pesky improvement that used to be at the bottom but is now at the top or somewhere in the middle, or maybe its on the side of the grid? who knows? 13.  Is there a book you haven't finished yet?  In the late game you can probably finish it between turns.14.  My first victory was building a spaceship to mars, that's fine, however it took me 75+ turns to make because it costs 5000 production and if your lucky each city can add 10 production to it at a time - it was one of the most boring ways I've won a 4x game. 15. There's a chaos mechanic in the game that adds negative buffs or events to your civ, I actually like the idea, it happens too much though. Some times I wish the debuffs would last 10 turns or so instead of the rest of the game.16.  There's no auto explore. 17. Minimal map selection - each game the maps basically look the same 2 rectangular continents side by side...18. No way to customize a game - no tech slow down, cant turn off barbarians etc. 19. I like the idea of the tech leader taking everyone into the next age, but I found myself wishing I could turn it off around game 3 or 4. 20. The game gives you bonuses in hard numbers but on  your city they are listed in percentages for some reason. You'll have 133% of something your city needs but why not just have a hard number? 21. You will have lots of money and you can buy off the chaos events, if you're playing peaceful. 22. If you're at war alot you will spiral into a chaos induced nightmare of a game which I guess can be kind of fun and random but also very punishing from achieving goals.  For example I had a war with the AI and I was slowly grinding away their units and the chaos events kept spawning rebels in my territory as well as on everyone else's territory in the game, in addition to massive waves of barbarians, then you just lose  the regions you've spent the last 20 +  turns to capture to a chaos event. Pair that with the age of revolution which spawns 5-6 rebel units per region. It can really feel like the game is against you.23.  NS happens every even age, making the odd ages feel empty as you've probably filled out the last NS tech tree you had, NS abilites are underwhelming and there are clearly some NS trees that are just obvious picks - like raider or mound builder, or silicon valley.24. No end game stats, or graphs... Did you win a game where there was endless war? Want to know how many units you killed?  how many tiles you razed? How much production you had ? So you can see which ages your falling off at?  Nope there's just an option to go back to the main screen and while you're there click exit.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't feel great about writing this review.  I do like Millenia but it has some major issues holding it back currently.   I have completed a game on the 2nd difficulty, and now I'm working on Adept.  To me, there are two glaring flaws with the game that must be addressed.  1)  The AI.  I never thought I'd see AI worse than Civilization 6, but here we are.  It's all over the place, constantly threatening you, asking for deals, declaring war, suing for peace, seemingly without any rhyme or reason.  And on higher difficulty levels, it will always be ahead of you in power.  It can field more armies, have more cities, and tech faster than the player, without suffering any of the negatives.  I understand that devs need to help bad AIs be competitive and give them cheats to compensate, but it is excessive in Millenia.  I'm convinced the AI doesn't have to pay upkeep or suffer crises events.  It's a real drag.2)  Diplomacy.  It's just awful.  Most of the time, the AI will not participate.  I have never seen an envoy or merchant from the AI.  Due to the absurd power leveling of the AI, it's always ahead of you, sees you as a threat/target, and won't bother engaging.  So what's the point of envoys?  The AI refuses to return to neutral status or engage in any sort of trading.   It's almost a non-mechanic and renders a lot of the National Spirits worthless.  No point in getting an awesome diplomatic power if it won't have any impact on your opponents.  Those are my two major gripes with the game.  It seems silly to not recommend the game base off seemingly minor nuisances, but to me, they are major problems.  I really hope the developers put some more time and effort into fixing them, because if they don't, I don't see Millenia standing the test of time.EDIT after Update 3:  The updates are certainly improving the game, but the AI & diplomacy still remain pretty bad.  The AI can field armies it should not be able to field, seemingly suffering no upkeep cost or build times at all, so going to war with the schizophrenic AIs is a total slog.  And since the AI will generally be more powerful than you according to the "power score" it will ALWAYS declare hostilities or war on you.  It's a huge drain and absolutely killing my enjoyment of the game.  I fear if the next update doesn't fix it somehow, that will be the end for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Bought it on special. Regretting spending, not because of the price point, but because it just isn't a finished product, nor one where the flaws are showing work. Wish I could refund, and would be happy to never speak of this product again if I could.I just cannot get into it. Every time I start having a little fun, the game comes and beats that fun back into submission. There's obviously (theoretically?) something very cool under here, but there are just so many systems and things that have no tooltips, no help, and are totally mystifying. If you want to have a game like this, don't make me go and watch youtubes and read reddits just to teach myself stuff that you should have made available to me. That's just a lazy admission that the devs did a crap job, and don't care either. On this basis alone, I wouldn't recommend the game, because while there may be cool stuff, you will just never know if you are doing things well or not, or using all the things you could.Its such a shame, there are so many things that might be good. I just have no motivation to discover it all while flailing around in the dark.There are a number of questionable game design decisions:1. Hiding information from the user. A tutorial would be great, but even better would be good information readily available. What things can a Hunter hunt? Why is this hidden behind a button that you barely notice?2. Why can people move further than they can see? One hex vision and two hex move just makes the game full of rubbish barbarian 'surprise!' actions all the time. Its just tedious, and reliably makes for a hoser rather than a gameplay positive.3. The combats are, to say the least, moronic. No other game has done it this way, and I think there's a good reason for that.4. The double-action civics. This civic spawn two spartans. No. It doesn't. You buy this civic and it quite specifically does not do what it says. And then the game hides the ability to spawn them in another menu. Another stupidly ridiculous layering of information.The list goes onwards.Also, the gameplay is just slow. I feel like I'm playing a game stuck in treacle. It moves so incredibly slowly, and rarely in a good direction. Every other 4x is faster, and there are more options for how to add speed and interest.I am left with the enduring question : If it is so obviously flawed, what are the devs doing focussing on new content rather than addressing quite clear flaws? It surely must be reducing their access to the marketplace, but they just don't seem to care. I think their market is now additional money from those who like it, rather than adding new users. So sad.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that has a lot of obvious passion and vision within it. It's a fun concept for a 4X game that provides a glimpse into the liquid and changing nature of cultures through the ages. And when it works, I genuinely feel like this is one of the better 4X games to release in recent history.But that's the key phrase, I find: "when it works." Currently, the game is unplayably broken. I have attempted 5-6 runs since release. Half of the games crashed before the Age of Iron. The games that remained were each afflicted with what I'd like to call the "Pepto Flood", in which a tile, usually a one tile island, would suddenly visually glitch out, then cause the game to turn bright pink, and immediately afterward, causes a full screen of what looks like pink ocean texture take over what isn't UI. The gravity of this glitch is so intense, that the UI and Text all shake along with the full screen, eventually causing all the button graphics to desync with the actual buttons as they jitter all over the screen. I don't know how a visual bug is causing so much chaos, but considering the state of this game, I'm not surprised. From the Civ IV grade visuals, to the national spirits system that barely synergizes with itself, to a diplomacy page so hidden and hard to interact with that it would make Humankind blush.I really want to be able to recommend this game, but not nearly as much as I want to be able to actually play the thing. Aside from needing to be rebalanced and better optimized, the game is being held together by shoelace, and it's direly apparent, even when the game is trying its best. Save your money till they make some MAJOR changes.

_childDocuments_.review: An innovative take on the 4x genre. The game asks a very fundamental question: "What is Production". While the Civilisation games would tell you it's the yellow hammer on the hills, Millennia tells you what makes your Industry: Steel, tools, woodwok, masonry etc. It gives you the option of creating a production chain for your industry. Anyone who is a fan of managing an empire on a deeper economic level will certainly fall in love with this game.Yet I have some gripes. The UI feels outdated and does not give you the relevant information. You cannot queue buildings or even let your units auto-explore. Chaos and Innovation are poorly defined and Unless you know how they work, you do not know what and why it is happening.The games performance also takes a sharp dip in the MID game. I don't mind the dated graphics (Though trees are waaaaay too tall) but the game runs incredibly slowly at times.I personally do not mind the missing Multiplayer but it would be nice to have at launch.Despite that, I would recommend this game to any seasoned 4x player and even Anno players. I know Paradox and this is not the state the game will be left in. After a few games, they created a wonderful foundation on which they can build and expand upon.A solid 5/7!Edit: After putting some time into the game, a few more issues arose. They did not change my recommendation, but are important to keep in mind:-The AI needs serious help. It under-preforms and has to therefore cheat-Vassal city management is comically bad. Mine built a mason on every tile without mining stone! Razing was added.-Strategic resources like coal or oil are scarce and if your vassal owns the tile, you better integrate it because you will not get it otherwise. How the hell you are supposed to get that oil in the middle of the ocean is still a mystery to me.-When the age of Revolutions hits, spread your cheeks. Even if your nation was 100% stable, 0 chaos, the "rebels", or as I like to call them: terrorists, will spawn everywhere, even under your matres and will destroy everything from towns to outposts. -Late game research snowballs too much. Nothing unique to this game, but launching rockets in 1798 feels silly

_childDocuments_.review: I was enjoying the game, a bit unpolished, needs some QOL features, but overall a good time for a long time fan of 4x games like Civ, Endless etc. Then I hit the age of revolution and the game said "make sure you keep your cities happy or they will rebel". Sure no problem. All 7 of my regions are at the lowest level of unrest. I'm in the groove, I've got my strategy setup and I'm basically just hitting end turn getting ready for the next technology I unlock to really get my empire going. Then suddenly on turn 200 ALL of my regions spawn revolutionaries with modern firepower. My entire empire is under siege. There was no warning. In my experience this game is full of "jumpscare" mechanics that essentially catch you by surprise due to bad QOL and very poor explanations. Games take a long time, and honestly its just not my vibe to have to restart because something like that bricked my run because I was unprepared for it.

_childDocuments_.review: Nov 2024 Update:  I've played another 30+ hours since my previous update and overall my feeling largely hasn't changed.  Which is a shame because the market really needs a good Civ competitor.  The game is still just lacking polish.  The alternative ages is very much the strong point to this game and the two DLC's primarily add to that which in and of itself isn't a bad thing as that's that's absolutely it's high point.  It just comes with too many low points.  If Steam had a neutral option, I'd use it here.The problem is the core shortcomings really haven't been addressed.  The AI is still bad.  For example with the first DLC you now have the option to start in the ice age with a nomad who has to scavenge for resources before it can build your first settlement.  In principal, great, as that fixes my gripe in my initial review of not getting to pick the location for my starting city.  However if you're playing with the barbarian density increased, the game will frequently end in the first few turns (often after turn 1) as all the AI players get wiped out before building a city.  I honestly struggle to understand how that's even possible.  Even with regular density, several major nations generally fail to make it out of the first age which generally only lasts a few turns.  Millennia is limited to 8 players to begin with, which is pretty low for this type of game, so even if only 3 get wiped, you're now down to a 5 player game basically right off the bat which leads to a pretty empty feeling on the map.Tile improvements are still largely overwhelming.  If you click on a particular tile, that gets you a filtered list of improvements at least, but given how restrictive some improvements are on terrain type it's still less than ideal.  While it's not as bad as Ara, the supply chain aspect of it is still a bit tedious.  IE, when you're building an improvement that need a certain resource as an input, you can't see if the region in question has said resource.  There's still no auto-explore and I still feel like (at least on higher difficulties) map generation is weighted to giving you inferior access to resources and natural wonders.***  Original review  ***I hesitated to write a review with this little playtime as I don't feel that's normally enough time to reach conclusions in a 4x.  To be clear, the game definitely has potential.  However, there's a few things that are just too immediately apparent.  At least early game, tech progression is far too fast.  Domestic trade (exporting goods) happens far too late.  You've had merchants for two ages but somehow can't get good from one city to another.  The battle viewer does nothing for me personally, and the icon to view it just gets in the way.  The lack of edge scrolling is baffling.  Tile improvements become overwhelming.  Honestly it feels like there may actually be too many options, but more importantly they need some sort of grouping/sorting.  IE, here's all the wood based ones, here's the clay based ones, metal based ones, etc.  Some of the crisis ages it's unclear what exactly you've done to create the crisis risk and what you can do to stop it.  Scouts/explorers need faster movement.  Even on easier difficulties, AI pumps out an impossible amount of troops to try to compensate for being not terribly bright.None of these would terribly hard to fix, save for probably the last one.   But right now the game just feels unfinished, like it should be an early access tile.  I can certainly see it becoming a solid game, especially if it endures like most Paradox published strategy games.  But right now, I don't think it's there yet.Hour 30 edit:  Unfortunately another 15 hours hasn't really changed my feeling.  Expeditions are a great idea, however after probably a dozen restarts I feel like their locations are weighted to favor the AI.  There's at least one AI with a wonder near or in their capital cities immediate area with multiple others very close by.  This is further aggravated by the AI's ability to pump out units meaning they likely have far more explorers wandering around than you do.  It's additionally annoying because of alt-ages based on finding natural wonders.  This is further compounded by the fact you don't get to pick your pick your cities starting location and will frequently be largely hosed on it's placement.  A lot of improvements require flat ground.  I have no issue with that, other 4X's do the same thing.  However, when your starting city is spawned in a location that's almost entirely hills and forest, you might as well restart.  At least with Civ, you can chew up a few turns looking for a better spot to plop your starting city if needed.The lack of auto-explore is also really tedious.Alternate ages, also in principal great and help add variety to play through's.  However as initially stated, some of the crisis ages are really unclear as to how you triggered it or how you could have avoided it.  AI diplomacy is just bad.  Admittedly this is pretty common in this genre.  You'll be allied with somebody, they'll cancel the alliance, then go hostile, then go to war, then ask for peace all at the minimum intervals allows for diplomatic actions.  Next thing you know, you're allies again.  Oh, did I mention when you get an alliance request, there's no mention if that's going to immediately pull you into one or more wars?  Or force you to break an existing alliance?I could give a variety of other smaller things I've come across but suffice to say, I still feel this game needs a lot more time to bake.  It's got some good ideas ideas, but it's lacking a lot of polish.

_childDocuments_.review: Love this game! The evolving tech tree using different ages is a lot of fun and challenging. I also like the concept of regions within the nations. Adding and improving towns inside each region grants buffs to production, wealth, and more. The ability to specialize the towns can increase those buffs and provide more benefits. Units can be spawned using Domain and Culture powers, which is a very helpful should a more powerful enemy suddenly declare war on your unprepared nation. Also, this game allows Armies/Fleets. Units can be combined together to increase their offensive and defensive capabilities. Leaders can be incorporated into Armies/Fleets to further boost those capabilities.The XP system is also a great addition, helping drive goals for side-quests, new technologies, special ages, and more. XP is generated by buildings, tile improvements, and unit actions, very handy if one needs to generate XP quickly to achieve a goal.There is a lot to do in this game and rarely do I fall into the "dull creep" that happens so much in other 4X games. There are some aspects of the game that need fixing. Currently, special units are locked to the age in which they are discovered, meaning that they will become obsolete quickly. The AI for diplomacy ranges from a little skittish to overtly hostile without much middle ground. These issues and several more have been acknowledged by the developer and are on the update roadmap which was just released. I'm looking forward to the upcoming Updates and DLC.This game plays more like the old-school 4X games like Civ 4 but incorporates some new gameplay mechanics that really sets it apart from the other franchises. It has the same level of replay-ability also. I'm eager to see new units and ages for this game!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is terrible. Point blank. Period. There are some things in this game that are fun, but most of it is just down right annoying. Now I play Civ once and a while, always played it when I was a kid with my father, so I do like turn based strategy like this. This game, however, is so laughably bad and has things that make no sense that it rips out any fun this game has with me and makes me just go 'Why would you add that?'To start, they have this stupid mechanic where you get 'XP' for different things. Government XP, military XP, engineering XP even something called 'Improvement XP.' These things are used to give yourself some buffs, spawn a certain unit or do certain things in the world. For example, you might get Spartans at some point and when you get a culture power point, you can spawn Spartans into the world for free and instantly. Maybe you want to integrate a vassal or bribe a barbarian to leave you alone? You would think it would be something like 'Pay X amount of money' or 'to integrate, spend this certain thing,' nope. It's XP. Maybe you need to build an improvement to your city right now. Something like a farm or a mine. In Civ, you built a builder, had him go over, build the building and done the mine is yours. In this game...........It's another DAMN XP TYPE CALLED IMPROVEMENT XP. This system is so terrible, because you don't create workers or anything. Instead, your population is just a number of people in your city that mans the improvements. So if you need a mine or something, better have that XP stockpiled like a goblin.The age system I don't hate. Instead of Civ's idea of 'just research stuff' you go through ages that can give you bonuses. There is basically 'standard age,' 'better age' and 'crisis age.' Some ages give you a benefit for getting there first while a 'crisis age' is basically a bad age that has some consequences. I both hate and like this idea. It's unique, but in my game I was on the border of going through the age of plague. Basically, my people needed sanitation. I was at 19/20 and built a few things to help, barely eeking by it as I tried to go into the next age. All of a sudden, I am hit with 'the Aztecs fell into the age of plague' and I got it REGARDLESS OF WHAT I DID. So that is in the middle to me.Honestly, the XP thing is this games greatest flaw to me. Everything else is just kind of 'I can do that in Civ,' except for the idea of creating your own nation and feeling like you don't need to subscribe to that nation's ideas. You don't need to be Teddy from Civ, which I guess can make everything feel kind of 'meh.' That and the game needs some quality of life things like an auto-scout button. Why they didn't think 'We should add an auto-scout button' is beyond me. I would say this game is an avoid because of the fact that certain main things you need are locked behind the XP idea like settlers, bribing, spawning envoys, etc. The graphics are meh as well, but I do like the fact that some things feel like a supply chain is needed. Like you need a logging camp to make logs, then a papermill to make paper and on and on for improvements, but it's also just kind of 'meh' to me.

_childDocuments_.review: Crisis ages are the only thing this game has going for it over civ. And guess what? You are rarely going to get to a crisis age. Not only do you have to fulfill conditions, you have to be the first to age up. You need a combination of lucky knowledge gains and research structures, but if you neglect military then barbarians steam roll you. I'm not kidding when I say that I died in the second age to one barbarian. He had 40 attack power, and nothing I had stood up to him. Because I did the Civ thing where I used my warrior units to scout, I only had one or two at home to defend. He bulldozed through my city and killed me before I could get back to defend. I was hoping that people were wrong and I might have a different experience, but it's as the IGN review says. Doesn't do anything interesting over Civ, the things it does interesting you will rarely experience (if you wish to keep pace with other civs), the only time I saw crisis/different ages was when youtubers were exploiting the game and got ridiculously ahead. Combat animations are mobile game tier. Graphics are nothing to write home about. Game simply doesn't do enough to keep me playing. I got bored before the refund period at least.

_childDocuments_.review: The good:- I quite like the idea of customizing your civilization as you play. It makes for interesting combinations. This is definitely the best part of the game, even though the game could use more options.- Interesting mix of playing wide and tall with ability to create vassal cities and taking direct control both taking time and costing culture.- The alternative history eras are a very cool concept.The bad:- The AI seems to cheat. A lot. Playing on adept I don't think I managed to be first to progress into an era even once. Even when I started first the AI would just jump ahead of me out of the blue. By 3rd to last era I was one tech behind when AI that I never paid any attention to suddenly started moving to the next era, by the 2nd to last era I wasn't even finished with my 2nd tech when the same AI started progressing to the last era. I still won the game (production based win con) despite the AI getting what, 7-12 turn lead to start building it. Meanwhile in the 2nd to last era I finished entire space race several turns before the next AI even started it, despite being late to the era.- In the last two eras I was running out of meaningful ways to spend my points. With 30-100 point income in every category I eventually just stopped caring about points and spent maybe last hour or two of game time just passing turns to eventually finish the victory goal.- Speaking of the end goal, it was by far the most boring thing in the game. Since I couldn't see how far along anyone else was (not that more than 2 AIs ever even reached the last era) I don't even know if there was a race worth mentioning, so I just put all my cities to build the victory project and hoped for the best.- Regions only being able to export their goods to one region seems like a massive oversight. This makes it practically impossible to fulfill religious needs for any larger city without wood => paper => religious text spam.In short: The customization aspects are neat and it was mostly fun going through the eras building a weird mix of different cultures. The mechanics start to break down a bit going further into the later eras in the sense that factions felt meaningless, space race took a few clicks and I ran out of ways to meaningfully spend my points in the last two eras.I'm hoping DLC will eventually make the game worth replaying. Right now I don't feel there is much incentive for me to do so.

_childDocuments_.review: My TLDR: If you enjoy Civ 4 or older, you should give this game a try.This is a game that wants you to read everything as you're playing, so it rewards attention to detail. Production chains, picking the right techs for your goals and circumstances, knowing what ages you want to go for, that's what this is all about. My first game was a disaster but after that I had a much better idea what to expect and did better.  The alt history ages are fun and give an interesting twist to the game. That being said, this game needs a lot of work to be more user friendly. It wants you to read everything because important information is scattered throughout the infopedia and tech tree. The user interface is difficult to read, with important information in multiple places, making it difficult to keep track of everything happening in your nation. Units don't have icons on the map and are fairly small compared to the terrain, making them hard to find at times. Combat is incredibly opaque, while I can understand the basic rock-paper-scissors aspect, how the game determines turn order or what unit to target is almost impossible to figure out. My only hint so far is the Field Marshal unit, which is listed as specifically being last in target priority. I definitely understand people complaining that the nations dont feel unique. They don't. The bonuses are lame and can be changed anyways, and there are no unique units. Clearly the idea was to use National spirits to differentiate nations, similar to Humankind. This partially works, but having a unique unit or building for nations would be nice. Overall, I'd give this a thumbs up. I'm hoping the interface will improve over time as the devs take feedback, and the enjoyable parts are fun enough to keep me engaged. Civ 4 remains one of my favorite games to this day, and Millennia reminds me strongly of it (not surprising, since they share team members). If you like Civ 4 or the older Civ games, give this a shot. Wait for it to go on sale or get some more updates if you must, but keep your eye on it. I think it will be worth it

Production chains gives a whole different vibe. Yet, upgrading them can make you mad over lack of goods.+ Non linear aging is also nice to have. Adds replayability.+ I somewhat liked how nations have no specific bonus(changeable bonuses).What I do not approve is that; - Horrible multiplayer integration.- Horrible combat scenes. Seriously, this looks like a browser game from 2000's.- Exploding optimisation in late ages.- UI needs to be better- Constant e-mails offering tutorials and as such.This game has some potential over it's great ideas. It could have been better than Humankind or Civilization. Yet the cons, really destroying the game's potential a lot. It's like looking through a window of a shop, at a hideous sight. Game needs to be polished in looks in order to attract more.I still like the game nontheless. But I really want to see radical changes over the cons I stated.

_childDocuments_.review: In Civilization you play as immortal ruler with some bonuses applicable in certain eras or terrains. Playing as a ruler gives you some sense of attachment and an impression that you can play a different game next time (with different ruler). This is generally true, but with its absurdities - like "I'm starting as a ruler who will get special flavor of WW2 fighters"...There's another observation I have after playing 200+ hours - you feel like if you don't min/max your first warrior's moves, you lost some opportunities. If you don't build some building at perfect time and place, your mistake grows to huge problems later. But this is absurd - a granary built (or not built) in ancient era has too much impact in modern eras...In Humankind you play with a promise of "billions of culture combinations" - this quickly makes you forget about which culture are you actually playing - no sense of attachment at all.Here, in Millennia there seems to be no attachment to a leader/country/culture, which may be a problem for some players. However if you look at the mechanics for a while, it seems like this is very carefully designed game. - building upgrades are non-linear, so early buildings (if not upgraded) don't have much impact in later game. - army composition matters - domains, domain powers and national spirits are really great and remind me of EU4 idea groups - just more flexible - eras are amazing - you really feel like you're progrssing through time instead of waiting "till I get this special WW2 fighter " - regions, improvements and buildings are very flexible and give you a lot of freedom and require good planningThe graphics may indeed be a problem for people expecting Civ6 style. I feel like it's the best UI designed by good ... C++ developers. Hopefully if the game succeeds (I wish it does!) there will be improvements in this area.I personally don't need "a nation's immortal leader", but some sense of uniqueness would be welcome.Game works perfect on Linux and I'm enjoying discovering of various mechanisms and strategies.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: In an attempt to "be different", the developers have managed to innovate away from anything resembling fun. The game is poorly balanced, lacks game-play mechanic polish, the user interface is overly simplistic and overly 'graphical' in parts.There are some redeeming features, but they are outweighed by decisions made by the developers in pursuit of uniqueness. Selecting a "Nation" is nothing more than a language and colour choice - which they offer allows for greater replayability - however in reality, offers no insentive to go back and try again. They offer the lack of "Custom Nations" allows you to tailor your nation to your start location, environment and unique challenges - HOWEVER - in order to successfully navigate this, one is required to have a deep understanding of all options in order to make the best choice. What happens more often than not, is the player selects what they think will be fun - only to realise too late - that their map and location doesnt allow for the play style they want. A great example of this, is the inability to plant or expand forest. So much of the game, religion included, relies upon certain techs, and paper - and there is no way to generate paper unless you have a forest nearby. Get this wrong for too long, and you'll rapidly find yourself in a chaos, unrest death spiral that ALL of the AI will take benefit of and slaughter you for. Is this ignorance realistic? Somewhat. Is it fun? Far from. I find myself playing to justify the money I put into the game (AAA cost for a poorly developed game). Once I have "finished" one play-through (easier said than done, after failing 6 times in a row) I will simply go back to playing Civ 5 - a game whos mechanics are far simplier... and far more fun. Please do not buy into the marketing and save your money. This game is an underdeveloped, and under-polished financial trap.

_childDocuments_.review: Summary: Work in Progress, with many Good Ideas. The Game doesn't necessarily need more Features, just more content. I've played 3 Campaigns so far (only completely finished one, the others were ended early because I was snowballing and getting bored).Lets break the Features down:The Points, or "Experience" System is a nice take on abstracting the resources available to a Civilization, and they would be the main way of making your Civ feel Unique. Unfortunately, you only have a limited pool of things that you can do with each Type of Experience, so past the early game you will always be able to build Experience-gathering buildings of every type, turning into a generalist empire that was exactly the same as the ones that you played before. The "Unique" ages are not as unique as I was hoping: Each Age basically just seems to have a unique resource type, and a reskinned building from the "Standard" ages which helps utilize or create that resource. They still break the game up, but not as much I'd like. One exception here would be the Age of Plague, which can really devastate your empire if you don't prepare properly. This is a bit of a noob trap, since the game doesn't communicate how to deal with/prepare for an age of plague, which is probably also why many people are complaining about it, but I welcome anything that forces players to take a different routeThe Resource System is the best example for a system that desparately needs more content: There are tons of resources that are just dead ends. The best example here is Olives: In the early game, you get a building to turn olives into cooking Oil (which is super valuable for the early game), and then... nothing. Fish is even worse: There are empire types which specialize in producing massive amounts of fish by creating mobile fishing ships, but in the end fish is consumed for a tiny bit of food, and is never processed into anything else. Ther are positive examples though: Flax can not only also be turned into cooking Oil, but it can alsobe turned into Cloth, which can be further improved into Textiles and Clothing, increasing its value with every step. These Dual-use resources are the cornerstone of an interesting resource system. (if you want a perfect example, look at against the storm: Every resource there can be used for different things, and every resource can be created from one of several other resources. It creates a web that allows players to get creative with how they want to specialize their economy.I assume that a lack of interesting resources is a result of not having enough time to fully stock the game up with content, and if C Prompt Games wants to continue devlopment with future updates, I would recommend this as the cheapest and most effective place to start.This might need a slightly improved UI though, because currently you cannot decide which resources get turned into what other resources meaning if you have 1 sawmill and 1 paper maker in a city and only 1 wood to feed them with, you cannot decide whether the paper maker or the sawmill gets the wood.Finally Combat: Combat is really not that great, it mostly involves units running into each other with the player having no agency apart from initiating the fight. Endless Space 2 has a similar system, but there they at least let the player decide which of their units goes into which "lane" of combat, and they lat the player decide on strategies that determine the range at which each lane fights. Also, the Cinemtic fights in ES2 look gorgeous while the fights in Millenia look like crap. Mostly, the fights just come down to the following: Armies with generals beat armies without generals, and sometimes the AI leaves armies running around that consist only of ranged units, so you should try to snipe those. Apart from that -> more stats = more winning. The the graphics: usually I'd say that graphics aren't very important to me as long as the gameplay is interesting, but millenia really makes you appreciate Games like Civ 6 or Victoria 3 for their excellent UI. Half of the UI Elements in Millenia still look like Dev UI and the whole colour palette is a desaturated Gray-White-Green, with most of the UI being an unadorned dark blue... it's kinda cold and uncomfortable, not the sort of thing that you want to look at for 15 hours straight when youre playing a campaignThese are a lot of points, so I'd like to summarize my personal priorities (if any C Prompt Community Managers or Game Designers are reading this :P)1 - Most Important (Must Have): Get more content into your economy system - each resource should have multiple uses! (look at against the Storm for an interesting resource tree!)2- Should have: Make the combat more interesting (Endless Space 2 is a good example of a few very simple features making the combat system much more compelling, without making everything super complicated)3 - also Should have: Get a UI Artist to go over your game. You don't need to change any functionality, but adjusting some Fonts and adding the occasional color transition can go a long way.4 - Nice to have: Add more content to your Ages. You had a couple good Ideas with the Age of plague and the Age of Heroes, I'd like more things that actually make the ages feel distinct. (knock players out of their comfort zone by forcing them to change direction, and then give them the tools to change direction)

_childDocuments_.review: Let me preface this by saying that I am in no way a good 4X player, quite the opposite in fact.  I'm the kind of guy who plays Civ VI with the difficulty set to Chieftain, only to still lose the game.  I play a lot of Stellaris, but I have never completed a campaign because the AI still beats me even though I've set the difficulty as low as it will go.  So, seeing Millennia, I thought I'd give it a try, and add it to the long list of 4X games I suck at.Sadly, I will never learn if I suck at this game, because about 1-2 hours in, the game now refuses to load my last save.  This does suck for me, because below the performance issues and lacklustre graphics, there are solid mechanics.  I enjoyed using the improvements system, I like how the game allows for multiple strategies, even if the only optimal strategy is tech rushing.  There's potential here, and C Prompt Games have built something with promise, but the execution is where it all falls apart.I believe that, with time and some patches, these teething issues can be sorted, and like I said, there are solid mechanics, but for now at least I do not recommend you get this game.  I have no doubt that if C Prompt irons out these issues, this game will eventually be worth your money, but for the £50 I spent for the Premium Edition, for now, it's just not worth that much.  I will keep an eye on it, and if my opinion changes, so will this review.In conclusion, don't buy this game .

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I was going to play more before writing review, but I think the a few main criticisms are pretty unfounded, so I'll comment on those.  I'll also discuss the main systems.Barbarians: the criticisms here are that barbarians are too numerous and aggressive.  I don't think they're that bad.  As long as you have an army defending each city you'll have no problem.  The game provides tutorial screens on barbarians, combat, and armies, so I was well-prepared.  Also, as soon as you get 30 minutes into a game, your troops can 1-shot barbarians.Age of Plague: the criticism here is that this age catches players unaware, is tedious, and ruins playthroughs.  I disagree.  When you reach the point where this age becomes a possible future age, the game has a tutorial message practically saying "WARNING: this is what age of plague does, so prepare."  The preparation is just to fulfill your citizens' sanitation need, which you likely are already doing by this point.  Also, during the age, random city tiles will become infected.  You can cleanse these tiles using 1 of 2 different resources, which you likely are already producing in abundance by this point.  Nation identity: the criticism here is that nations start out identical.  This is a game where you adapt your nation to the resources and events around you.  I like that, but others may not.Graphics and UI/UX: this is subjective, but I think the game looks good.  There are better looking 4Xs.  The UI/UX is good, but could be improved.Now onto the main systems:Age system: after researching at least 3 techs, you can advance to 1 of 3 ages (some have pre-requisites).  The player who does this first decides the age for everyone.  Each age has pretty significant different mechanics and techs.  This system adds a lot of replayability.  Some people don't like that the AI or other players can decide the next age for everyone, but I think this makes playthroughs interesting.  If you could choose your own age, then you would have no reason to choose a "bad" age.Production chains: I'm a sucker for any game with these, and they're fun here.  They encourage you to specialize cities, and demolish and replace building as you expand.Mana systems: most 4Xs have a ton of stats like culture, religion, etc. that passively effect your nation.  Millennia has this as well, but each stat also has associated active abilities similar to spells in fantasy 4X games.  I think this is very engaging and expands the usual decision space.Government/National Spirits: these are like additional tech trees that allow you to choose specializations to fit your needs.  For example, my city was surrounded by hills, so I took the national spirit focused on mining and production.  City-building: you use improvement points to build improvements, like mines, on tiles in your borders.  You can actively increase your improvement points per turn via building/tech.  I like this a loooot better than "build worker -> move -> improve.Border expansion: you take a very active role on deciding where your border will expand.  First off, it's deterministic: each turn your expansion stat is divided amongst the tiles you border, and when a tile gets enough of this stat you gain that tile.  You can build towns/outposts and research tech to influence which tiles get priority.  I vastly prefer this over any random expansion system.That's all for now.  I'll provide final thoughts after more playtime.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT originally I lead with "This is a recomendation based on what this game could be." but i have to edit it down to a don't recomend simply due to the age of plagues completely destroying a playthrough. The AIs always trigger Age of Plagues if you don't reach age of kings first, and if you're like me and you like to build stuff, you want to go for Age of Monuments, but that means you wait a bit while you meet the prerequisites. In that time the AI is completely ignoring sanitation and will certainly trigger an Age of Plagues which is going to basically stop the game for 100-200 turns while you desperately trying to research 3 techs to move out of it. It doesn't matter how much wisdom you're producing before, what took you 10 turns now takes 60. You might as well just quit out of the game right then and there.  Yes you could just go age of kings, but that means every playthrough is exactly the same. Thats not what this game is about, its best feature is that you can have very different games every time you play, if you need to follow a liner path just to avoid a badly coded event, then that's just not good. I hope the Devs see this issue and either increase what it takes to cause an Age of Plagues, or make the AI civs actually take steps to prevent it, or tone down its severity. The Black Death was incredibly destructive, killing millions and upending the social fabric of Europe, but it also didn't take until the 18th century for it to pass. There is a lot here to love. The huge amount of choices on how your civ develops gives you great control on what you want to do with your game. Want to be hyper agressive militarist? Go ahead! Diplomatic power house? Sure! Lots of improvements and actual production chains so let your inner Captain of Industry run wild. It has the most important thing a civ wannabe needs, solid just one more turn itis.BUT, right now, the game is rough. There are a lot of mechanics going on and not a lot of them are explained.  For example, chaos. I have no idea what generates it, or how to get rid of it. Once it starts building up, its extremely difficult to get it down.Probably the major issue is the hyper agressive AI, both with other civs and barbarians. If you have ever played civ with raging barbarians, you'll know what i'm talking about. Barbs spawning enlessly, their camps pop up like pimples before a date and the early game feels like Zardos with eliminators running around destroying all your farms. You'll spend most of the early game building warriors and archers to deal with them, but its never enough, you can't 1 on 1 them, you need to have a decent number of units in each army to take them out, but the barbs always spawn more. You destroyed the camp their coming from? Another one has just spawned somewhere else and its pumping out units every turn. AI Civs grab land as fast as they can, because everything counts in large amounts, and you need lots of land for the aforementioned production chains and just to satisfy your late game needs for education and power. But expanding too fast hurts, so you need to balance your expansion, but while you're doing that, the AI civ comes and grabs that land right next to 3 iron deposits. And once all the land is settled, settle in because you might not have to deal with barbarians anymore, but you'll now be fighting wars with your neighbours constantly. You'll need to maintain a strong army at all times or you'll be suffering from constant wars. Even making peace or forcing truces will only last maybe a turn again certain civs (I think civs that choose raider as a national identity will just war with you as much as possible). Also don't expect to just out tech everyone, because it has the age of Civ issue of due to the way combat works, your tanks will die to low tech enemies if things line up. Also the game seemed allergic to just letting you crush units, an enemy always need to get some kind of hit in, and it always seemed disproportionate to the damage you cause. The really cool aspect of the game is the Age system. You have your standard bronze, iron, kings etc, but you also have special ages like heroes and aether, and then crisis ages like Plague. The problem I have with the crisis ages is they effect everyone, even if you have made sure you avoided them, some other civ isn't picking up their garbage, so everyone get hit with plagues, Even if you have no contact with that civ. This wouldn't really be an issue if they weren't so insanely devistating. I lost nearly 100 turns to an age of plagues that ended up basically just hitting next turn and clearing any break outs because you just don't have any resources for anything else. Also preformance drops massively in the later game, even on an ssd with 32 gigs of ram, a 3060 and a fairly new processor. I'd hate to see what it was like on an HDD.Final Edit: This is a bad game. It forces you to do nothing but play agressively and militarily. There is no room for variations in play because if you're not prepping for war and pumping out units, you're going to lose, and that means the same game every single time. If you want to just play a game of building units, managing armies and fighting battles, you're much better served by playing a total war game.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is way too aggressive to even enjoy.There are barbarians EVERYWHERE.  They constantly assail every single one of your regions every single turn by the dozens.  Even after toning them down in the game options, they are still all over the place, albeit not as dangerous.The AI does nothing but settle towards you and then declare war and never make peace, EVER.  AI armies are:-Impossible in their production speed and size.  (Usually the AI will have five units in the time you produce one)-Impossible in the amount of gold they would need to be maintained. (Based on the amount of regions the AI has, the technology available at the time to generate gold, and the lack of gold generating improvements that the AI builds)AI Regions are:-Created at an impossible rate.  (They somehow settle new regions faster than the cooldown on settlers is)-Placed usually within 4 tiles of your capital region.  (They will forward settle you without even locating you, so I assume they always know where the player is)-Created in an impossible quantity, with regard to unrest due to number of regions.  (Each of the AI will have easily twenty to thirty integrated cities (placed maybe five tiles apart from eachother) at the end of the game on a medium map with six players, which creates insane amounts of lag)I played a game where I did nothing but beeline for a settler and place a region two tiles away from my capital region (minimum distance), thus creating a vassal.  After placing the vassal, the vision from the unintegrated vassal I just settled brought in to view the already expanded border of an already integrated region of the AI, roughly 8 tiles from my capital region.  They immediately declared war.  I could not have settled any closer to my capital and yet they have an already integrated region with a town and multiple border expansions RIGHT THERE.The AI is:-Always aggressive towards the player.  All of them will try to forward settle you and declare war before you even have two regions.  The only thing that slows them down is distance.-Immune to unrest.  Period.-Given massive bonuses to aid in their never ending quest to create regions at an impossible rate and then settle on top of you constantly so they can declare wars that they suffer no unrest from while using armies they cannot pay for.It is absolutely ridiculous how hostile this game is to the player.-I want to try new playstyles.-I want to experiment with national spirits.-I want to explore the map.-I don't want to be in a crisis age every other age.But,-I cannot try new playstyles because they always run into the same issue of every single AI I meet immediately threatening, delcaring hostilities, and then declaring war.  A war which they will never make peace with.  Even if you force a truce, they declare war again three turns later even if they have no army left.-I cannot experiment with new national spirits because the AI is always at war with me, thus making a large portion of national spirits useless since the warfare ones are basically required.-I can't explore the map because it is a sea of barbarians that delete every single army of scouts I send out.  If the barbarians don't get them then the AI sure will since they always declare hostilities upon meeting you.-I don't want to be in a crisis age, but the AI will always research the next age as soon as they can, even if it is the crisis age.  Any human player that doesn't want a crisis age would wait for someone else to research a different age, so I can only assume the AI picks crisis ages because they are immune to the negative effects, or at least they are heavily mitigated by their bonuses.I am tired of having to end my game in only the fourth or fifth age so many times due to the relentless AI and barbarians sweeping me away.  Even on the novice difficulty, the AI is still hyper aggressive and will still amass armies that they cannot afford.  I was under the impression that playing with lower dofficulty AI would give me the room to experiment with other aspects of the game, but I was wrong.  I do not want to play 4X games where I am constantly at war with every single player and barbarians occupy all of my tiles every turn.  I have played over 3000 hours of Civilization V and VI.  I have played over 1500 hours of Stellaris.  None of those games are ever even close to the amount of aggression this game throws at the player.  Deity AI in Civilization is the closest comparison to the regular AI in Millennia.  The only solution to this whole mess is to just play on the Islands map (since the AI is hydrophobic), so I guess i'm just going to do that until the AI is improved.I would suggest making the AI actually pay for their army upkeep, suffer unrest from war, and also suffer unrest in general, and implementing more AI personalities, and having AI personality as an option to select when making custom nations.  I also suggest making it so the barbarians target the AI and not just the player.  I don't know why the AI is so hostile, but I assume that they decide whether or not to be hostile based solely on if they have a higher power score, which unless the human player is spamming units they cannot afford, they will likely have a lower power score.  I'm sorry, but I was busy playing the game instead of spamming armies I cannot afford.  Guess i'll die.

_childDocuments_.review: Embarrassingly threadbare in many areas.The nation builder is nothing at all... you basically can just make the same 'nations' that already exist in the game, because the options are all existing pre-sets, aside from renaming the nation itself and selecting a different starting bonus. There aren't generic symbols or city names, and everything is stuff already used by an actual nation in the game.The level of immersion is woeful. I met France and was greeted with two short sentences saying I should be respectful of them. That was it. Even Human Kind did more than that. And this is a far cry from Civ where you meet a CPU opponent and their music plays, their leader appears, and introductory diplo options pop up. This is at the level of Lord of the Realms 2 for that first meeting of another nation or leader.There is no option for edge-scrolling, a key way I move the camera around from Civ, to Total War, to Age of Empires. That is  a mind-boggling omission.Settings in general are really, really limited. I clicked what I thought was Custom Game and got player slots to put CPUs in, and only a map type option and map seed option. So I backed out and realized no, this *is* what Custom Game entails for Millennia. Quick Game, which I didn't bother trying, must literally just throw a player into a game the moment they click on it. What on earth is this battleviewer? I saw this from screenshots and the store page ahead of time, but it's literally just a viewing option. There's no interactivity with it almost at all, other than slowing down or speeding up. Why bother with this? Even if it looked great, it's just a time sink, but it looks like something from the olden days of playing Warcraft 2 on a Pentium 1. My impression is of a budget game from the late 90's or early 2000's. The only difference is the graphics, which are decent (other than the battleviewer) and look relatively modern. But there's an overwhelming lack of polish, here. The UI has fonts that are too small and that lack drop-shadows at times, so reading the words is painful. And the yellowish font color over the top of the tan backdrop is at once generic and overused; more color-coding could have gone far towards making it quick and simple to look at a glance and see what items are regions, what are armies, etc. etc. Instead, those lists just run together when all that had to be done is to give a little color coding so that regions are tan, armies are green, navies are blue.I only put in about 20 minutes, but I am wary of going much further when I am already thinking it's time for a refund. If I find nothing on Steam that's better for $40, maybe I play a bit more and get closer to that refund cut-off, but I really want to go see what $40 back could do before I bother. Which is sad, because I like 4X's. But this is unbelievably rough, and the immersion is the worst I've seen in a 4X in some time: no voiced narrator, no leader screen and unique music upon meeting someone. This is not great.

_childDocuments_.review: No! Just No........I pre purchased this game with excitement. Fully expecting there to finally be a game to rival Civ 6, I waited for March 26th for release day.Having played 14 hours already, I don't think the devs thought this thing out fully. It starts out ok, but as the game progresses past the first Age, things begin to go awry. First of all, the barbarian attacks are relentless. They come from both land and sea and never stop. Even when you're playing on the Islands map, and have taken over the entire island, the barbarians just keep spawning. This forces you to keep building more and more forces to repel them, leaving less time to build up any sort of empire. At least in Civ, one can eliminate the barbarians by simply clicking on the no barbarians at the game setup.Secondly, no matter how many different ways I tried to build my cities, the Ages progression always landed me in the Age of Plague. Once, it brought me into the Age of Kings, only to switch to Age of Plague three turns into the new Age. The Age of Plague is tedious. Constantly doing plague cleanup either by using up engineering points or producing plague doctors slows the entire game down. Oh, and then, because there's plague, your citizens become unruly, overthrowing your government and ending the game.Another thing that caused me to not like this game was the inability to load settlers into a boat. Playing on an Island map, and producing galleys, one would think you could at least get a settler off your home island to expand. Nope. In one game, I actually had a fleet of Bomb ships roaming around. They were attacked relentlessly by barbarian ships no matter where I went. Middle of the ocean? Hordes of barbarian ships attacking me. Heading to another island to explore? Hordes of barbarians on the shore, and hordes of barbarian boats.They should have named this gamer 'Kill Barbarian Hordes'. Because you're going to spend most of your time doing that instead of actually building an empire. Or you'll be watching what you built crumble away in a plague.I can't recommend this game to anyone unless you're a glutton for punishment and enjoy being frustrated at every turn. Too many glitches, the game slowed to a crawl during the Plague Age, and the gameplay itself feels clunky and outdated. I'm actually going to uninstall this game at this point, and having already paid the 60 bucks for future DLC, see if anything gets corrected. Because as it stands, this game is not fun at all.Save your money and wait for Civ 7 to come out!

_childDocuments_.review: Would hate to see a great game get review-bombed like Imperator and abandoned despite its good bones.Millennia has the most interesting systems of any 4X game, and manages to simulate how unpredictable our history really was. From a retrospective history presents a narrative that was not at all obvious or certain at the time, and Millenia is the only 4X that attempts (and succeeds!) to model all the ways things could have gone.Rather than having complex pre-fab Civs with set bonuses in set periods of the game, in Millennia your choice of Civ at start is meaningless. What would "Egypt" have turned out like if they hadn't been on the Nile, but instead had been deep in a jungle? Well, now you can decide, because you get to pick specializations and bonuses based on your location and actions. The game also backs you up by providing additional bonuses to what you already chose through Innovations - dynamic bonuses that pop up based on the specializations you already picked. Unlike in Humankind, where the age-bonuses you pick feel stilted and silly, in Millennia you can really feel like your choices are meaningful, and all options are potentially fun.The game has a tonne of replayability even at launch and it is gratifying to see the world become more complex over time as you unlock new goods, and new production chains to stack bonuses based on your natural resources and choices.Try this game, and enjoy it for what it is rather than killing it with comparison. It's not Civilization; it's something different, and ultimately better, more interesting, more engaging, and more replayable.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very lukewarm recommend. The game is fun at its core, working with the production chain system is a nice innovation to the genre, technological ages are interesting and national spirits allow for adapting the way you play in a meaningful way. But there are a lot of things this game gets wrong, which I will rattle off.Multiplayer not being ready for launch, forcing people to play a broken, port forwarded version to play with their friends is a silly mistake. The first impressions of a game for multiplayer viability are critical for convincing people to buy the game to play it with their friends. It will not matter if the multiplayer is fixed later on, the consensus will remain it that its broken and not worth playing forever. See the Humankind multiplayer for a similar example.There is a massive lack of quality of life features which add a bunch of tedium. For instance, embarking unit requires you to move to the tile next to the water, then press the embark button and select where you want to embark. Or if you have units with multiple turn movements, you have to manually confirm the movement of each one individually and if the unit spots a 'threat' it will stop and you have to reconfirm the movement.There is no automatic scout movement and no 'wait until unit is healed' button. This names the more pressing annoyances found when playing the game but you get the picture.Visually, aside from the ascetics, the biggest issue is the visual clarity in populated areas. the tile improvements, especially in the mid to late game can look indistinguishable. If a person was shown a screenshot and told to state which tile was the paper mill out of all the factories they would struggle. The same thing can be said about the difference between an envoy and a single leader unit.Chaos and the fact that it become completely irreverent at a certain point in the game once you have enough gold feels like an oversight. This is probably a good thing for the health of the game, since the events you can get range from an incontinence to a instant save reload. The mechanic just become a tax, since you never want to risk getting the event 'Your capital region becomes independent'. The simple solution would be to offer the player to pay experience points or offer a the choice of what bad event happens.More minor things include selecting one starting bonus and having no meaning to which nation you represent is a missed opportunity. Could have added some interesting flavour or choices. Winning the game was one of the most underwhelming experiences I have had winning a 4X game. The frame rate on lower end systems is poor between turns and during unit movement. If you are behind in tech you can have a game where you cannot decide any of the ages. To sum this up, if you like similar games of the genre you will get enjoyment out of this. However, view this as a single player only experience that's rough around the edges. Go watch a video to make your own judgement.

_childDocuments_.review: It's just bad. That about sums it up really, everything is just done poorly. it has some good ideas like the towns and province mechanic or the ages but its done poorly. Ai is also over aggressive as well barley leaving the age of heroes (age2) and its got 5 to 7 full stacks invading, with the units built in the same slot as buildings i think that means it didnt build much of anything and just produced units witch never really seems fun to run up against overwhelming early on and outdated hordes later in the game.the towns tho are thre real tragedy here, a truly amazing change from the city system in civ the ability to feel like a real nation with towns and provinces. the interesting way u could develop lopsided or even frontiers feeling aproprietly empty and unsafe while the interior is built up and fortified without needing many different cities to achieve it. Building actual industries base resource production then refinement by industry sectors and maby even more down the line is a good way to simulate how an economy works and reward planning your development even perhaps realistic and strange province layout to aquire more for settlements that specialize. All wasted because the first 2 eras at least u need to spam out armies, witch prevent building in cities forcing u to focus early money at any cost, food seems to do nothing after meeting needs so why build major food industries to trade food resource with ai that hate u? and ofcourse u plop gold down on hills rather than find it, one of the most contested recources on earth and u use exploration points to get a unit that plops it down on any hill u want its a joke. Even worse rushing growth is punished by bottlenecking your growth in 2 ways outrite preventing u from growing over a limit and new needs at higher levels that create unhappyness when you reach them but it only stops u from growning after this unlocking new things u need buildings to deal with before u can acuire the buildings!finally all the cultures feel the same and boring, seemingly the same city appearance and units strange choices like modern china and shang dynasty witch is also china, the UK instead of brittaine or england, nobody cultures noone cares about instead of more major powers  the list is kinda a joke, no mongols for instance.The whole game feels poorly made from crappy flags to near nonexestant diplomacy (u need units for diplo actions it seems), no leaders means no face for nations, strange decisions like crowssbows in age 2, the whole thing feels jank and cheep. more power to those who enjoy it but i refunded after buying half off, i suggest anyone else watch a lets play or something if they r seriusly considering buying.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, now this is a bit of fresh air in the 4X civ-like scene,The game has very good core mechanics and ideas that are mostly well executed. A good resources system that make you think how to build your region (not just cities) and a good mixup of national ideas + ages that can extend the replayability of the game through different build.The biggest flaw of the game is the polishing, or fine-tuning. You can see that it's likely a small team that made this, and that paradox most likely did not inject much money into it, and a lot of little flaws of the game come from probably the decision to do with what currently and do the polishing later. Things like a crude interface, badly forwarded information, a pacing a bit too fast for ages, too little option for game creation, the world generation a bit rough, etc...All in all, I recommend it, because unlike Humankind, which is very polished but has flawed core-mechanic and design choices, Millennia is the reverse, and has very good core mechanics and design choices, but a poor polishing. However, unlike core mechanics and designs choices, polishing can be easily done with patches and updates, so I don't fear that they will correct all the little flaws.Beware for civ players, the city building is NOT the same than in civ, and very simple calculation to make your city in civ will not work in your favor here, where the city management is a bit more complex. The resources system is not a simple surface level resources system like in civ, and it will ask a bit of tinkering and planning to have a snow-balling effect, but it's very satisfying once you understand it.

_childDocuments_.review: Its fun. The mechanics are refreshing. Sure its kind of a "Civ6 ripoff," but there are more than enough differences to make it compelling. It has some issues, needs some polish, a few balance passes... maybe a DLC... but on the other hand its also only $40 bucks for a new release. A warning though, the game is quite a bit more complex than other games of the genre, and like most Paradox games, has a bit of a steep learning curve.Its a stretch to envision this will grow over time into the massive DLC-fests that other Paradox games become, but it would neither surprise me. At bare minimum this game will inspire a better Civ 7.Its a solid "C+" grade, which gets graded on a curve because of the price-point.
