_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed the game, but I'm disappointed that it's being sold incomplete. Despite numerous updates, there are still many issues to fix. They promised a multiplayer mode, but months later, there's still no release date. Developers shouldn't promise what they can't deliver. They should sell the single-player game first and release the multiplayer as an update later.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: I tried the game after the previous update and it was already way better. Will fully update this review after I try this last update. If I know anything about Paradox is that they can be trusted for the long haul.----------------------------------- Old Review -----------------------------------I actually enjoyed the game and was giving it a good review because it is an enjoyable game already but then I realized there is no "one more turn", you win/lose and the game ends... in a 4x game... Overall, though I think it's not fair to call it a finished game, it feels like it was taken out of the oven 6~12 months too early. I do hope they don't give up on it and actually finish it.From the get-go, you get extremely little control on the game settings, you can't even specify winning conditions (also, the menu resets and instead of keeping your last settings). The game feels nice but there's something misbehaving in almost everything in it. The performance degrades severely mid-game and there are a lot of bugs, nothing breaking the game but very annoying especially the the one that keeps focusing the screen on weird place on the map.The gameplay is quite good, though. I like the depth, the system they implemented and the armies. I do hope they save that game cause it really is promising if they actually finish it.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Not sure how replayable the game as it currently is right now will be, but I am really enjoying my play-throughs right now. I really enjoy Millennia's take on research and economy. There are a good amount of interesting decisions to make to try and snowball to a win, and the game rewards you by min-maxing things. The combat is fine. The pop up window can be a bit annoying, and the graphics are laughable, but I have no problems with it after the initial shock. I am a bit worried about losing interest after I explore all the different Ages, but that is probably after 5 or 6 runs. Maybe more. It is also hard to learn about the game through anything other than trial and error. The tooltip system in-game is pretty decent, but the Infopedia is fairly useless. I think there is a really solid foundation here, and the game scratched a Civ itch I didn't know I had.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game but finally uninstalled it. Something is always bothering and takes away the fun: Some of the ages you can advance to.. or get forced into by others. The AI gets a humongous bonus to all their ressources it seems. Even with going all in on research and having a lucky break or two, the AI would instantly outpace me.The ingame Wiki is dependent upon what your own civilization has researched, so no looking up units from other civilizations you don't know.There is more but I just can't be bothered anymore.The game runs fine, I did not encounter any gamebreaking bugs. Interesting battle simulator. Nice technology and improvements mechanics.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I love the game. The way the economy works is peak Paradox and allows for the player to respond to economic situations that arise by specializing their economy based on where their civilization is at that point. The progression system through the ages is a really neat take on making each play through unique and I have enjoyed the "alternate" history timelines as well. One of the drawbacks of this is that it doesn't feel like the Civilization you choose actually matters, and it's nice to be able to create different civs but it doesn't feel like there is really any reason to do so other than for flavor. All in all this is a refreshing take on the 4x genre,The game does have a bit of a "beta" or "alpha" feel to it because it isn't the most polished, however I believe that is because the devs probably focused on balancing the game which must be difficult because of how much liberty the progression system provides. The biggest things I think that they should add are a "World Map" where you can see a full screen version of the map so that you can admire the sprawl of your budding empire. The meat and bones of the game are excellent however and I believe that with continued feedback and development the game has a bright and promising future!
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic. The age system is a cool gimick that keeps the game interesting, & the economy system is beautiful. As far as game economies go, Millennia far exceeds the Civ & Humankind games. Also, you have the option to create your own custom nation, which is cool. That being said, I highly recommend skipping the battle animations in the game options. They look like they were made for a bad mobile game. Additionally, there are different types of units (line, support, leader, defense, etc) but the game doesn't really explain how they interact with each other. So you kind of have to learn what makes a good army as you go. Finally, the AI vomits cities all over the map, & they can do so without settlers-- I literally had an AI city show up on the map in a tile adjacent to my pioneer, where I knew for a fact that there was no way a settler could have gotten to that tile without my seeing it. Having the AI cheat is a dumb way to make the game harder, and when the AI has 15 cities on the map by turn 60, it's pretty obvious that it's cheating. All in all, 6/10. The economy is great, & the ages are cool. But the AI cheating is blatant & the battle animations are absolute trash.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Millennia is a good Civ clone that takes it in enough new directions to make it not feel like a cheap Civ clone. Its current state and the current priorities of devs made me ultimately refund it.Pros+ Being proactive and using all your units is rewarded a bit more than in Civ. There are 'friendly village' equivalents and barbarian encampments, but rewards here for clearing those (and exploring the map) have more meaningful impact on game progress that's more in-depth than a single bolus of gold or faith for clearing a camp.+ Supply chains add a logistical component that feels nice. For example, wheat and rice provide flat food bonuses, but these can instead be fed into a mill to produce flour worth even more food. It's a good system that adds more meaning to what you build in a city, and how you base those decisions on what resources are immediately available to you.+ Your future eras are contingent on things that your empire does and what other empires do. This adds variability to how the game can progress, and has branches rather than a straight line as in Civ. It's a unique take on Eras that seems to work well.Cons- The game released in a fairly incomplete state. Multiplayer is busted and requires you to use VPNs to run a game and set up port forwarding as well.- Day 2 reveal of DLCs when things are busted and the game released in a hard beta. I know what I'm getting into with Paradox, but this is hilariously tone-deaf even for them. Planned on holding onto the title, but seeing the announcement this morning changed that decision to a refund instead.- Like the first point above, the graphics and UI also feel like they're from the early 2000s. Personally, I don't really care much, but it feels like this art direction/graphics were selected for due to cost/effort, not because they were going for nostalgia.- An absolute dearth of customization options for games. Can't control speed or fine tune world settings, nor victory types nor turn limits. All you can change is the AI empires, their difficulty, and map type/size.Neutral/Subjective• Combat isn't very in-depth but isn't as barebones as Civ V-VI. Army stacking is prevalent and you throw stack at each other that then plays a small cutscene ala Fire Emblem. You don't have any control over which unit your units attack, and there doesn't seem to be any kind of prioritization.• Tech trees are incredibly simple with 5 choices per era.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely HATED this game until I found the Build Helper button and screen, which immensely helped me understand the mechanics of the game.   I'd recommend this game if you like the interplay of various systems in your 4X games. There is the usual food, hammers, research, money, and culture that Civ fans will be familiar with. Millennia adds Domains (governments, exploration, warfare, engineering, diplomacy, & arts), and your nation evolves over the eras via choices in governments and national spirits. It still needs improvements and you can view the roadmap, but I'm enjoying the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: There is a good game somewhere in Millenia. It has quite a few good concepts. The multiple currencies (Warfare, Wealth, Engineering, etc) is compelling. However, the Barbarian spam is horrendous. You need multiple armies to keep the barbarians in check, all of which costs Wealth. Oh, you do not have resources that helps you generate Wealth, Oh Well! Too Bad! The Barbarians do not go after the AI's towns, yet I have lost games because a wave of Barbs knock out my city, even when guarded. "Well, you should have built defenses!" True, but the AI should have to build defenses as well. But they do not have to. Have not seen an AI civ get knocked out by Barbs. They will attack an AI's troops, but only if they can not reach your troops. Barbs are basically another civ that is primarily focused on the player.Some other issues..Many of the resources are weak.Gross imbalances between National Spirits. Some are simply way stronger.Difficulty in gaining some currencies, primarily Engineering and Diplomacy, see National Spirits.The game tries to force you to be militaristic, since AI civs will forward settle you hard, especially since they do not have to deal with the Barbs like the player does.As I said, the game has great potential. I simply do not recommend the game in its current state. As the game gets refined, I will be more than happy to change my review.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Millennia is a 4x and city-building game limited by a double-A budget that splashes a bucket of ugly all over itself. Once you get over that though, you'll find a diamond in the rough full of in-depth mechanics and  explorative fiction that sets Millennia apart.  The bad: awkward combat animations; simplistic graphics; buildings all look the same unless you mouse over them; missing multiplayer features; mid and late-game performance issues when panning the map. edit: a recent update has addressed the performance issues. the game now plays noticeably more smoothlyThe good: numerous ways to 'build' your empire to fit your preferred playstyle; in-depth logistics chains to efficiently exploit your environment; game-changing 'spells' that use the currency earned from simply focusing on your playstyle; exploring alternate 'what-if' timelines; peaceful diplomacy being just as rewarding as violent conquest; and a lot more tiny details that those familiar with the 4x and city-building genres will appreciate
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Millenias falls short of delivering a fresh strategy gaming experience, offering nothing innovative or standout compared to its predecessors. This lack of originality wouldn't be an issue if there weren't superior, more affordable alternatives readily available on the market. Games like Civilization, even those over five years old, boast superior gameplay and mechanics, providing far more enjoyment. Furthermore, the game's launch state is simply unacceptable; you spend  £40 for an incomplete product, with dysfunctional multiplayer functionality and tantalizing DLC advertised. I purchased Millenias with the sole intention of enjoying multiplayer with friends, only to be met with disappointment. For those in a similar position, I strongly recommend seeking a refund and pirating the game rather than supporting such subpar quality.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: This is game that I must admit I was really looking forward to, however upon starting a game it quickly became apparent that it is effectively a glorified Civilisation. After about 5 minutes of playing and you're in the middle ages without really much happening - exactly like Civilisation. For £50 I was a bit underwhelmed, plus I know that I'm going to be expected to buy hundreds of £$€ more DLC add-ons to improve the base game :( Shame that we moved away from the realtime aspect of all previous games to a turn-based version here... I'd love a bit more depth
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: The beggining of the game is really enjoyable but it soon becomes unbalanced and it looks like it's not finished. It should have been released in early access. Besides, some assets look very profesional while others, or some pictures, look like they were done without caring. The battle simulator is ridiculous for being a Paradox game, I thought at least they would care more about the games they are distributing.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Great new entry to the 4X genre with its main unique feature of alternate ages really changing the game from play to play. The micromanaging of towns to send resources to each other opens new opportunities for developing your nation.Looking forward to seeing what this looks like if it gets the same length of support that stalwarts such as Civ, Old World and Humankind have gotten.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game, I really, really, really did. But there are some game design choices that make the overall idea of the game bag. The first, and most important one, is that if you want to choose your own age, you had better tech rush everyone else. Because whoever chooses the age decides it for everyone. Want to go the Olympian route? Better make sure you beat Greece to the technology or they'll lock you in to the Iron Age!There are some bright spots, I like that you can have specialized towns, say for mining, agriculture, forestry, etc... and they can contribute to your national economy. This is a good feature, however, being able to hire a prospector and use them to declare that there is gold in the hills is a bit silly.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: It's okay so far. At least a new take on the 'civ' formula.But then there is the same problem they all have. You can't have a single playthrough without some douchebag AI warmongering. Apart from there no aggression slider there is exactly jack nothing to adjust except four puny map options and size. So either you are stuck in a forrest with no place to build or you have no forest or hills at all. I will not recommend buying this for a year or so.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Millennia is an interesting, if flawed, take on the civilization-like experience that could be so much more with polish and time taken to it. It’s worth experiencing if you like these types of games, but it’s not going to revolutionize the genre, or dethrone Civilization anytime soon. With some polish and the right updates, it can get better, but for now it's a good, but flawed experience.Pros    Unique Ages Creating distinct gameplay    Lots of Options to Build Your Nation over Time    Complexe Production Lines and ImprovementsCons    Dated Visuals, Especially in Battle Screen    Poor UI/UX    Midgame SlogRead the full review here:
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: This game takes a whole new twist on the 4X genre, and departs from the "civilization" profile. I very much enjoy the new aspects in the game, especially how the resources are set up to build off each other.While the graphics could use a little bit of a touch up, I believe this could be a very strong competitor against the Civilization series. I have had so much fun in the first day alone and i look forward to see where the developers take the game from here.My only real gripe about it initially was the 40$ price tag. At first I felt it shouldve been more like 30$, however the more i play it, the less i cared about that 10$ difference.Highly recommend this game to anyone looking for something more than your typical Civilization game.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: *Updated Review*This game is amazing in complexity for a "Civ like" and has your brain contentiously going but!!! The combat sticks out like a bad mobile game that slipped through the cracks. I dearly hope they change that in the next update, as it's the most mentioned thing! Also, the multiplayer kinda sucks to set up and should have a look at!Game with potential! ( 4 / 8 )*Update* The multiplayer isn't yet updated with the world wide multiplayer standards and still rocks the ol "save and send" the game. It's a shame may it be changed soon
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Far from perfect but intriguing enough. There's a few table stakes things I am waiting for, like being able to set or remove a turn limit instead of it being fixed at 500. Will dive back in once Update 3 is out of beta.EDIT: Changing this to do not recommend. Updates are taking way too long to add even basic QOL features. They committed to releasing 2 DLCs this year but the base game needs to be the focus right now. The ages are interesting but rarely last long enough to really change the flavor of the game. Still bound by arbitrary turn limits. No real diplomacy to speak of. And so on.Disappointing, I really wanted to enjoy this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I wouldn't think twice about recommending this game to anyone who enjoys 4X games. It checks all the boxes for me and a lot of boxes I never knew I wanted.I could write something long, but I'll focus on the two things that really stand out to me.First, the Age system makes it feel like the game is constantly evolving. Every age you get access to new features, which means it really feels like the game has changed significantly when you enter a new age. Often seemingly minor things really add up (like the double speed of integration of vassals in the Age of Bronze). And when you get to pick a National Spirit, you really get to define your culture in ways that synergize with what you are doing.The second thing that just does it for me is the Domain system. Having only one resource felt a little constricting in Civ games but I didn't realize how constricting that could be until I played this game. I love looking at a situation and seeing multiple different paths to approach it because of my Domains. Heck, I can even create armies using a wide variety of resources and that is just amazing.I'll be playing this one for decades and hope future 4X games steal ideas from it.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: So my review will probably be lost among all the others sure to follow but I wanted to put in my two cents anyway.The foundation for this game is strong. On paper and at a surface view the game sounds and looks like it should be good. But it just isn't. Even if you take away the awful online connection issues, the awful tutorial and the excessive asking price would it be a good game then?I'd have to say...it'd be better but still no and here's why.The game's gameplay doesn't do anything new or intuitive. It gives you the same thing you've seen in dozens of other 4X games similar to it. Combine Civilization with Humankind and they'll birth this game. So it's not original or doing anything new.Except for one thing. A simulated little cutscene with every battle. That part is super cool and I wish more games would do that.But literally everything else in this game is below average. The gameplay, graphics, sound design, replayability, user interface, price. It's all below average. This game is not worth 40 dollars. I'm trying desperately to find what in this game is worth 40 dollars and the only thing I can think of is how long it'd take you to get through one playthrough. maybe that makes it worth it's money. But nothing else does. The graphics are low quality, the sound design is average, the replayability is pretty badly thought out since you can't adjust or edit the world you want to play in. Hell you can't even adjust difficulty settings. And the game's confusing and badly guided. I was studying this game, taking my time, re-reading tooltips and tutorials and still found myself confused and floundering. Also some things just aren't explained to you at all leaving you helpless.The game is like a puzzle. You've got all the pieces but instead of finding the right places to put them to create a beautiful picture, they just decided to smash all the pieces into places they don't belong giving you an ugly glob of something that could have been beautiful, but you decided to just mash everything together to create a sub-par picture. That's probably the best way to describe this game.It doesn't do anything very well and what you're left with is a confusing, frustrating mess that has a similar apearance to good versions of this game.If you'd like a more in-depth look with more information please check out the video on my YouTube Channel (link below).Otherwise thanks so much for reading and I hope I managed to help some of you out there spend your money wisely.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: The ability to create your own custom nations to play as is neat, I will admit, but this has little else going for it that you can't get out of the Civilization or Humankind titles. Units and cities don't even look different from culture to culture, meaning your units will look pasty white even if you're playing the Zulu or Egyptians. I can't recommend this in its current state.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I want to enjoy this game.Many of the systems in this game seem unique and engaging.But I can't recommend this game, at all, to anyone.Why?BARBARIANS. BARBARIANS EVERYWHERE. AN UNGODLY NUMBER OF BARBARIANS. I PUT TOGETHER THE TOUGHEST ARMY I CAN LEGALLY BUILD AND IT DOESN'T MATTER HOW MANY BARBARIANS I KILL ON THE WAY TO THEIR CAMP BECAUSE MORE COME FROM EVERY DIRECTION ALL AT ONCE. MY ARMY WINS AGAIN AND AGAIN BUT THE ENDLESS STREAM OF BARBARIANS SLOWLY WEARS THEM DOWN SO THAT WHEN ITS FINALLY MY TURN AGAIN, ALL I HAVE IS A NOTIFICATION INFORMING ME OF THE DEATH OF MY ARMY.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't had a full play through yet, but I'm about 100 turns in and although there are some things that need patched, Millennia has really drawn me into it's world, similar to what Civ V still does to this day. This game goes "out of the box" with new ideas and I'm always making tough choices. I hope they make some QOL adjustments and improve the battle system, but I love this fresh take on the 4x genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I have played over 100 hours within 2 weeks! This should say it all! The game is bloody brilliant!Of course there are still some problems, some mechanics are not balanced at all - there are possibilities to create an unending source of some points for example and the diplomatic system is still utter crap, cause the AI will just demand stuff and declare war whatever you do.Also the game is too fast paced, it probably needs an option to make it 2x or even 4x longer, especially research.I was like: Hey, I just got an inventor - I wanna place a Teslacoil......a few turns later - I am ready to place the inventor's hut now---we have WHAT NOW? Fusion power?!!? Ok, I guess no inventor :/That is the basic CIV problem right there - invent gunpowder one turn, have tanks and jets 10 turns later ... this needs adressing.Other than that - the game is GREAT! Especially the first few ages and the age system in general is enormously good!
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I like it, early mid game is great fun but late game is boring but this is something that all 4x games for me suffer greatly so nothing out of the ordinary here sadly.I loved Humankind and this has become my favorite 4x game currently.DLC was pretty poor, when I consider the content Humankind added with their DLC and then this.. and being more expensive wasn't nice at all!I do enjoy it but I do wish that the enemy would stop running around my army just to destroy towns instead of taking the fight to the fields! It's a shame when you have 2-3 stacked armies on your borders and they just walk right past you with stacks and stacks of armies and completely avoiding combat!I would love to think that in a few months after a few updates that they will get things right and iron out the bugs and silly AI moves!
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Game has promise, the core systems are there, but so much of it is half-baked. Games can barely be customized: no map options beyond size and shape, no starting ages, no research/resource slider, no barbarian/village frequency. When you finish a game there are no stats pages to see the rise and fall of each nation, just a victory condition PNG.This absolutely should have been considered an Early Access release, and Paradox is likely to blame for pushing it out the door. _childDocuments_.review: Bought this game on Launch when it first came out. At the time the game had serious issues, and whilst there were some great ideas - they were poorly executed and the game was an uphill struggle to play. I played a few turns, then shelved this in my "early access" pile. However, over the last few updates they've really turned it around. More info for the players, more ideas, and a deeper exploration of the aforementioned great ideas have turned this into a genuine Civ competitor.But not only Civ:- They've also managed to take the production lines Ara tried to do, and done it better as a subsystem rather than the game.- The gradual evolution of your Civ over time is similar to Humankind (though without the defined historical civs).- And the ages mechanism is truly unique. Whilst it doesn't have AAA graphics, the strategic depth, and game-play innovations are absolutely fantastic, and this is a contender for my current 4X favourite! The major weakness right now is multiplayer. Thus far, the synchronous play is a little buggy, and we've not managed to complete a game (though we have got to the endgame where it was pretty much decided). I sincerely hope they get that figured out. I strongly recommend this game to 4X enthusiasts, and hope it continues to be supported for years to come!

_childDocuments_.review: I was introduced into this game by several youtubers that were praising the **it out of it. Albeit it has its good moments from time to time, overall Millenia just doesn't live up to this hype. I am seriously questioning the integrity of all these people that released ~hour long videos about this game and didn't take any issue with many, many problems that it has. Also, it is kinda ironic that my youtube feed was full of this game before release and now, when this game is out, I almost can hear crickets chirpingHere's a list of pros and cons:++ System of resources. I like that there is a production chain with several steps, and that it is integrated with population. I hope that later in the game there would be transportation and trade of these goods+ Public works. Call to Power was my childhood game, and I may be biased towards a resource that is used to construct tile improvements. I think it can be seen as a streamlining of worker mechanics, and it definetely pleasurable to build them in one click instead of waiting several turns for worker to finish it+ Ages are great, at least as an idea--- Multiplayer. Yes, the elephant in the room. Yes, it is as bad as they tell you. Yes, it is borderline false advertisement. It all feels like a joke and failure to deliver anything appropriate to the price tag that they are asking--- Interface. It is cheap and convoluted. In research, there is virtually no distinction between what is a city building, what is a tile improvement, what is an instant bonus, and what is a power that is activated by mana. When constucting tile improvements, you need to learn by trial and error, because tooltips usually don't show what tiles/resources an improvement can be built on and the benefits that it will provide--- Visuals. Many people complain about the graphics, but in my opinion the problem lies even deeper. It looks like the game is frankensteined from cheap or even free assets, without any shred of unified artistic vision. Ok. I get it that a game might not have top tier graphics, but could you at least make up for it with some kind of a visual style? Because as far, as I've seen, the picture is bland at best and unbelievably ugly at worst -- Mana. You may have heard jokes about how bad is mana in EU4. But even 2,6k hours in EU4 hadn't prepared me for this. Like I've seen 6 (SIX) types of mana and the number is still counting. Each type of mana has 3-5 uses inside "drop down" menu and a couple of them have their separate full-screen menus . And yes, you need to look into separate tooltip for each type of mana in order to see how much of it you are gaining each turn-- Barbarians are atrociously balanced. There is nothing in between a suicidal man that keeps attacking you over a river and a horde of warlords that steamroll your cities. Barbarians severely punish any movement outside of your borders - either by attacking you directly or backstabbing undefended regions. This leads to a situation where you just don't want to move your units at all. I could stomach this agressiveness if it was some like a "raging barbarian" option from civ, but here you don't get to choose-- "Free cities" are more like "free real estate": they do literally nothing when they are neutral/ They instantly become a player's vassal when a player conquers them or uses an envoy. Envoys (which you get with  spending mana) convert these cities by one click, so there is no political play between players around these cities: whoever got there first (either with an army or with an envoy) gets the city- Nations have zero personality and individuality. Machanically, there is one, very generic, starting bonus, and after that nations are abolutely identical. Also, color schemes of some flags are kinda weird and off-putting- Combat is chaotic and unpredictable. There is no clear indication, will you lose a unit in an army or not, or which unit you are going to lose. Also, you can't reliably identify enemy's army composition without  a tooltip- Ages are not implemented very well. If you expect a somewhat peaceful playthrough where you steer the course of history, you more likely would be disappointed, as you need to exert considerable skill even to be the first one to progress the standard variant and even more so if you want to fulfil the requirements for special onesMillenia is deeply flawed game, and even if I would like to play it more to see what else does it have in tow, I wouldn't recommend it or hope that it would become substantially better

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game! Ever spent hours building up a strong aggressive military and sent you legions of Spartans and archers to overrun a peaceful neighbour, capturing each of their cities in an unstoppable wave of conquest, only to lose each one to armed rebellion, have your economy crash and your culture drop through the floor? Ever built up a beautiful cultured sanitary society and be poised on the edge on the next epoch only to be plunged into a despairing age of plague by some filthy turd covered neighbour? It's awesome! It's the most fun I've ever had. You can make all the plans you want, but just like real life the gods will just laugh in your face! This is the best civ-like game since Civ4's Realism Invicta mod and the most fun I've had since my first game of Civ2 way back in the day.Okay, I've played it a lot more now and I'll say the more I get into it the more subtle and clever I find it to be. _childDocuments_.review: I am a big fan of Paradox games, so buying this was an easy decision for me, that said this game definitely has some major flaws, especially considering its competition with games like Civ or even their other games like Stellaris. Im going to start with some of the good though:Concept: The concept of the game is interesting, that being the way you can choose these different branching pathways for your age and society as a whole. Did you mess up and cause an age of plague making the game more difficult? Were you extremely successful and enter an age of heroes? Its cool on paper. Gameplay: It feels like your standard 4x game like Civ, wasnt hard to pick up. That being said there is no "tutorial" so be prepared to learn as you go with pop up explanations. The Bad:Difficulty: Now I might just need to "Git gud" but, the game seems incredibly difficult compared to other 4x games, even when set to the absolute easiest difficulty settings. Bandits spawn endlessly, and they build up forces within 4-5 turns every 4-5 turns and having to constantly send armies out is a real pain. You can also easily become the most hated person in the world just for investing in your military, making trade and negotiations impossible. All because you wanted to kill bandits, and the AI doesnt seem to care about bandits either. The different Ages are linked: This ties in with the difficulty, so one of the major concepts of this game are the various ages you can enter based on your success/triggers. It is cool on paper, but a major problem with it is that once anyone on the map triggers an age, EVERYONE gets it. Even if its bad, this is can completely ruin a game. For example: I was doing really well in a game against the AI and was getting close to the age I wanted (Age of heroes), but then all of a sudden we go into an Age of Plague. Not only did this cause a whole mess of new mechanics that literally ate away at my populations, but it also completely ruined my plans for the Age I wanted. At least in Civ I can still get a Golden Age when someone gets a Dark Age. I ended up losing that match because the only way to combat the plague was to spend exploration points (because that makes sense) and I hadnt been investing in exploration much. Resource Management: I am not a fan of the resources in the game. You have Govt, Exploration, Military, Engineering, Diplomacy, culture, arts, gold, and not to mention all the other various resources. Now normally that isnt an issue, I play stellaris and CIV so crazy resources are nothing new to me. The problem is it isnt entirely clear how you build those resources, and it is really easy to get yourself stuck waiting on build up (Eg exploration exp in the plague age). Also you need those points for both game changing units (like settlers, combat units, special resource finders, etc...) but you need it for your "talent" points too, you want to advance your govt or spirit. Simple things cost so much: For example, a settler. You need to spend 25-36 govt points just to buy a settler. On top of that once you have a the settler and get them where you want them, they arent added as a new city .They are a vassal. Now you need to wait 10-15 turns in order to absorb the vassal. But in order to absorb the vassal you need to spend another 25-36+ govt points. Want to know how to do it in every other 4x game, including other paradox games? Spend X amount of money resource, and build the city. It seems needlessly complicated and expensive. OVERALL/TLDR:If you are a fan of 4x games and paradox games, it has a lot of potential and it comes down to if you want to invest in that potential. I used a gift card and paid $20 and that was worth it to me. I honestly cant suggest someone pay $40 for this though.

_childDocuments_.review: Paradox has thousands of my dollars so obviously I am content buying DLC after DLC for expanding content, but each new Paradox game is shallower and shallower at launch. It informed me I lost my first game but whether everyone lost or it was scored I have no idea as it tells you nothing before booting you to the main menu. _childDocuments_.review: There's something here, but without multiplayer the game really relies on the single-player experience which is kind of lacking. The AI is hyper-aggressive and seems to do nothing but produce as many units as humanly possible in order to attack the player. It is not uncommon to run into an AI and have them declare a half-war on you immediately so they can attack your units in neutral territory. Trying to deter, out-diplomacy, or really do anything to curb their aggression is useless, so the game quickly begins to over-focus on the 'sorta okay' combat system. The alternate ages mechanic is really cool, but since the first person to reach it gets to pick the age it means you have to fine-tune your economy to a research focus, especially if you want something that isn't the plague. _childDocuments_.review: Tried for the Free Weekend. It's alright enough for a recommend.I definitely like the National Spirits system that really pushes you in to crafting your own unique civilization although some National Spirits are too strong than the others. The City builder-esque style of resource management is also fun and unique.I think this mechanic is better than what Humankind was trying. The Age system is a 50/50 for me where your progression is tied to your actions throughout a campaign which I really like, however this mechanic should be NOT be tied to all the players and instead be player-specific. 1 player activates a certain Age then the rest are forced to go through that Age as well. While I see why the devs made it so because you can prolong tech research to so you can eventually get the Age you want, I still see potential in trying to revise this system because as it stands this aspect of the system is not fun when you try to go through the age requirements only for it to not matter albeit there is some appreciation to the challenging view of this design.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: I'll provide updates as I continue playing the game. If the game has mods and they release the tools properly I could see this game going a long way in scratching that 4x and Civ itch. A lot of my gripes can be fixed through mods and the community. And then I hit the modern era and the dei just really leapt out of the game. It had been there from the start but small enough that it didn't seem like an issue. Then you get firearms and the political anti-gun pandering starts.Edited for grammar, punctuation, and clarity.There are aspects of the game I like and dislike, and now you're going to hear about them!Likes:4X grand-strategy elements.Interesting game loops (you spend warfare XP to upgrade and promote units. Promoted leader units can retire to grant you more warfare XP, further upgrading your armies and creating more leaders).Selected technological evolutions (the ability to pick 2-3 different eras to advance into, depending on how your game is progressing and your playstyle).A good tutorial and helpful pop-ups to assist players in learning the game.High-quality sound and music.Engaging and fun land/town development.Unique domain abilities.Balanced needs for your cities/regions (not just food and goods).Overall, I'm having fun and enjoying the game.Dislikes:Limited faction selection that doesn't feel unique (any faction can have any special ability, with no unique abilities just for Japan, USA, France, etc.).Graphics are mediocre.Limited research options (only 6 or fewer techs per era).Combat can become repetitive after a while. Combat also doesn't make sense at times. Unit targeting is very wonky. AI will not prioritize knocking out enemy units, which then prevents your entire army from taking more damage. Instead the AI just attacks random units, it doesn't make much sense. This has prevented me from taking cities, routing enemy armies, and taking unnecessary combat damage.Build Queue is only one deepSome of the art is ridiculous. You can tell whoever did the pictures for the modern army has never touched a firearm and doesn't know how to draw them.Has a healthy amount of DEI in the game. Women were never in the infantry in the 17th and 18th century. The "assault rifle" is pandering when you read the quote for the unit and a good example of someone who's never seen a gun in their life based on how it is drawn.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: After not particularly liking Civilization VI compared to the previous game in the series, I started branching out and turning to other games to scratch that itch. I did like quite some things Humankind did like its region system, but bounced off of it eventually too, partly due to its rather hideous characters, oddly enough.But now that Millennia released, I suppose I found a new hex-based 4X home for myself! :)I have been greatly enjoying the game over the past weeks. It's a great idea to have fiction-inspired variant ages instead of going through the same few historical eras over and over again each game, which provides some great variety, role-playing and eye-candy opportunities. It's also just plain cool to play a civ-like 4X game where you can go through a steampunk era, a cyberpunk dystopia or even a Lovecraftian cosmic horror age depending on your choices. The game averts the typical mid- and end-game slog pretty well and I always find myself having something to do instead of spamming the next-turn button. The graphics, although many people seem to dislike them, are in my opinion very pretty and I find myself often just zooming into the map and immersing myself a bit in the world. I enjoy the art style as a healthy middle ground between Civ V's realism and Civ VI's more stylized look. The UI is easily readable.I am not too happy right now about the AIs, and some UI issues need work; notably internal trade, which for some reason is based in the city you want to export _from_, not _to_. Some historical inaccuracy and misrepresentation led to eye-rolling moments too, especially the flavor text of late-game ideologies ("Communism", "Democracy" and "Fundamentalism"), conflating liberalism with democracy, fascism with fundamentalism (while muddling it with religious fundamentalism too), and Stalinist planned economies with communism. But those issues don't stop me from having a lot of fun with Millennia.The updates have improved the game significantly and ironed out most complaints I had at release. It also runs well on my GNU/Linux system using ProtonGE.I really hope that Paradox keeps supporting this excellent game despite the (in my opinion not understandable) negative reception.

_childDocuments_.review: Millennia, a strategy game with a feeling of Sid Meier's Civilization V/VI, falls drastically short of expectations. Millennia comes off as a lackluster and unpolished attempt at the genre.The game feels like an unfinished product, similar of  titles, yet it comes with a price tag that suggests otherwise. Basic features like multiplayer functionality are either missing or so poorly implemented that they might as well be absent. The user interface lacks intuitiveness, leaving players confused by the plethora of unclear concepts and functions. Even simple adjustments could vastly improve gameplay and readability, such as providing clear indications of positive or negative attributes when making building upgradesCombat mechanics are frustratingly vague, lacking the depth and clarity found in titles like Civilization V/VI. There is not one functionality in Millennia that is better or on-par with the other Civ games. Turn order and unit targeting mechanics are unclear, leading to frustration. The inability to attack enemy units with ranged units without retaliation feels arbitrary and diminishes strategic options. Diplomacy fares no better, as every encounter with a new civilization constantly results in hostility, regardless of player actions. This lack of diplomatic nuance undermines the immersion and enjoyment of the game, leading to repetitive and extremely frustrating experiences.The behavior of AI-controlled civilizations is particularly outstandingly bad, with each encounter devolving into instant hostility and eventual war. This pattern persists across different playthroughs and difficulty levels, rendering diplomatic strategies futile and reducing the game to a cycle of unprovoked attacks. Such blatant disregard for balanced and engaging AI behavior undermines the core appeal of strategy games and leaves the player feeling unfairly targeted and frustrated. Late-game performance issues are inevitable, with long turn times and freezes. The limited campaign setup options and lack of architectural and cultural diversity between nations. There are only 18 nations to choose from, not a bad amount but could be better. Each nation only has one, quite insignificant, generic bonus."Hey mom! Can I get Civilization please?""No! We have Civilization at home."Civilization at home:

_childDocuments_.review: Played during a free weekend. Game is kinda neat, and the content might be improved by those nickel-and-dime paradox expansions, but the base game has the most frustrating UI I've ever encountered in a 4x game, and that's bad considering 4x games are nothing but menuing.The crux of the problem I found is that, the game uses worker placement for city production similar to civ. However, the game also has production chains, like a city builder or factory game. Natural resources you collect will be consumed and converted into your food/production/whatever, but you can also build improvements that will convert base resources into higher grade ones for better output. You can also trade raw materials and use them in your production line, so, this adds a neat wrinkle to diplomacy. Make your economy dependent on another civ's goods and you end up giving them leverage over your empire.This all sounds good, but, you might find yourself wondering, what happens if a worker is assigned to a building you don't have the base resources to fuel? Nothing! You'll waste your labor on diddly, with no notification or warning.That's fine, I hear you say. If you don't want to assign your workers to a tile, you can just lock the tile to prevent the game from auto-assigning workers there... not quite. For whatever reason, the developers made the bright idea to have the lock button only lock existing workers in place. As in, you _can not lock empty slots._ Locking a tile prevents the game from moving workers OUT of it, but does not prevent workers from being auto-assigned back to it. The game's AI will rejiggle your pops constantly in cities, and the ai has no consideration for what base materials you need or if a production chain gets broken. You can not manually disable auto worker assignment, so have fun manually checking the worker placement in every city you own every turn in order to fix the game's AI constantly screwing with your workers. Build an improvement before you have the base chain line up, or have your base improvement stepped on by an enemy, or your trade disrupted, and you will have to constantly reorganize worker placement. Locking empty slots is a feature in most 4x games with placement, even ones that lack production chains. There is no excuse for why it's missing here.I should also mention, it's not as simple as, look at a city, pops are right there for you to click on and move around, like endless games or even civ. You have to select the city, then open up its production queue (I say queue but you can only make one thing at a time and also this menu fills your screen), then tab over to the worker placement menu. You then have to use plus and minus buttons on the various hexes, no drag and drop. And even better, tiles are grouped by output type, so you can only assign workers to a type of output, not to a specific tile. Want to move a pop somewhere else so the barbarian about to step on it won't screw up your production chain? Tough ♥♥♥♥, you can't.Production chains and worker placement are the core mechanics that drive this game, and they're so royally undercooked.Side note: While I'm here, I'll point out, the tactical ui is also terrible. Not the combat system, other folks are already ripping into that plenty, but I'm talking about the way units are displayed on the map. The game gives a generalized strength rating underneath each army, but, that number is just the stack's combined attack and defense ratings. Not average, combined. So like, scouts that have no offensive power to speak of but get a defense buff with each tech age can have higher ratings than actual military units that can hit things. The score is also unaffected by how much health a unit has remaining, so, ratings can't help you assess from afar how dangerous a partially damaged army is. There's a combat preview in the tooltip which gives you percentages for a predicted win/lose/draw, which would make sense except the outcomes are predetermined and there's an undo button you can use freely during your turn. If the player can save scum every attack just to see what the results would look like, why not put those actual results in the tooltip? You know, like Old World, another paradox title with an undo button? Obfuscating combat results with fake percentage chances is just a waste of the player's time.

_childDocuments_.review: The situation with this game is reminiscent of the dendi game cartridges scam, where 999 games in one cartridge were indicated, but all of them were the same. So here you are promised for 40 euros "killer of civilization", but in reality you get a game with graphics from 2010, animation of battles from flash games of 2000 and lack of balance. In general, the whole game looks like it was made by 2 indie developers, but not the studio that gave the world games such as: "Crusader Kings", "Stellaris", "Cities: Skylines". I am disappointed and will hardly make pre-order games from this studio in the future.

I got quite a long way into the game in just two hours so it looks like it'll be quite quick to play, with plenty of interesting systems to engage with and a combat system that's a lot more fun than I originally thought playing the demo.It doesn't play anything like Civ either, it's a historical 4X but that's where any resemblance ends. _childDocuments_.review: Refunded.I read through the reviews where many claimed that this isn't comparable to Civ. But having played it myself, I find that it copies A LOT from Civ whilst offering very little to make it stand out.The entire time playing this game, I kept asking myself "Why would I play this over Civ?". It's not offering anything new or unique and stands in a genre that already has wildly successful titles. But it has no competitive edge to go against such titles. If you're considering getting this game, my advice would be to keep an eye on your playtime to ensure you meet the refund criteria if you end up feeling the same way I do.

_childDocuments_.review: I like games like this one.I have played all civilizations since Civ3, I played Humankind, Age of Wonders etc. There are elements I liked, that game have own identity. I like:•	Supply Chains!•	Ages – and those funky one as well.•	Exploration – that you can re-visit wonders for further events.•	Civics – That You chose paths to follow etc. •	System with smaller sub-cities etc.I don’t like:•	That you cannot integrate smaller cities into bigger one, this is the biggest fault in this game. Your cities because of computer can be suffocated on small area, even after conquering you cannot do anything with it. There is no erasing as far as I know. In my last game I end up with 1 nice city, surrounded by 5 smaller ones with only 7 tiles each. I wish there would be option to downgrade them to outpost or Tier 2 inner city. When you are strangled like that, you are unable to do supply chains etc.•	Lack of opponents’ “heads” – with basic info, if you are at war or not etc. Beacause AI loves to change their stance towards you and you can attack almost everything, you never know if you at war or not. Going into that empire view for diplomacy is annoying, and screen is confusing. I would prefer heads, flags etc. at the top with information for each nation. After Civ6 did it, this is a mandatory feature, even if I would play against 16 computers.•	In some Civics trees there are requirements which are poorly explained and you can end up with civilization which is unable to fulfil them. This is rare, I had issues that building could be placed only in jungle tile. •	That sacked outpost disappears straight away, or settlements with the land which is yours. It really should give you some time to repair it, otherwise your town can be reduced to nothing really fast. It was annoying me, when during war, someone destroyed my towns, and city border of the enemy grow immediately into my old area.There would be probably more, but this is the most urgent to repair in my opinion. That game has great ideas, but execution in some places is lacking. I wish them luck.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a lazy attempt to bring in Civilization fans in the lull of a new Civilization title- The AI will literally kill itself on your units and engage them even if it results in the complete destruction of their own armyThe UI is bad and clunky, you have to click through several screens to find the information you needThe city management screen looks like a mobile gameThe combat has essentially no user input and is just an annoying video that plays every time, and when you start spamming units it becomes annoying to click through it all

_childDocuments_.review: (About launch version) Pros:Variant ages are interesting as a mechanic. I like that the devs added a touch of other genres in there like fantasy, steampunk, eco futurism, etc. Fun to explore the unique mechanics they have to offer.Crisis ages are punishing, but can be used to get an edge over other players and are unique to play through.Victory ages are staggered throughout, so there are multiple ways to win while also giving the option to win early.Supply chains and goods are interesting and interconnect each city, where the loss of one can be catastrophic for the rest.City needs are a great system, rewarding better players with faster pop growth.Army compositions are cool and reduce click fatigue from troop movements. The auto-pathing system could use a few improvements though. Combat overall is neutral. It has its pros and cons but is mostly a game of rock-paper-scissors with more choices. Not necessarily bad or good imo.Cons:Has its problems for sure. UI needs updating, graphics aren't great (not a dealbreaker for me), information is hard to seek out, and some things are just never mentioned. (Being able to use improvement points to resolve plague tiles comes to mind)Age system is very interesting, but requires a decent understanding the game to really make good use of. AI will rush ages, which means the player needs to stay on top to enter the era they want. In my earlier hours, this was quite frustrating as the AI won't try to avoid crisis ages, they'll enter them full speed ahead after researching enough prerequisite technology.AI is incredibly aggressive, and without a way to raze player cities this can get frustrating with how they settle. With a somewhat shallow diplomacy system, war is the most often outcome, even if you don't want to play that way.Starting bonuses are very unbalanced, but also not very impactful in the long term.In contrast, the national spirits range from game-defining to almost invisible. Raiders can secure victory comically easily, while Naturalists are limited in scope for their usefulness. Later national spirits have a lesser version of this problem.Playing with vassals and conquering is the best way to play, and by far. Trying other play styles while knowing they're suboptimal is fine, but might be annoying once you realize it.Number of civilizations is very low, and weirdly so, given that each civ is just a flag and set of city names. I'm sure they could be added en masse quite easily.Very easy for an average player to out-scale the AI quickly, even without war. Every game inevitably leads to the point where the player can choose every age and and speed past the AI.End game performance can be very poor, especially for older hardware.War exhaustion is very easy to cheese, for both the player and AI. Only the attacker gets war exhaustion, so mounting a successful defense practically guarantees the annihilation of the attacker with enough time. The AI is particularly bad at handling unrest from this.Overall:If I had to rate it, it would sit at a 7 or 7.5. Don't let the size of the list of cons fool you, it's certainly an enjoyable game, probably more so for casual 4X players like myself. If you're new to the strategy genre, it might be hard to wrap your head around. But if you're acquainted with other strategy genres, you'll feel at home.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Ahoi, so I've played something around 15 hours now... what can I say, I don't quite understand why various people are defending the state of the game so much...Let's start with the elephant in the room. I don't mind at all when a title resorts to simplistic graphics, but this is a joke. I mean... the elephant hunting camp looks like I'm playing with my old animal toys. The supposedly dead animal is just the model turned on its side, which would take about 5-15 minutes (depending on the program) to at least adjust the legs accordingly. What is the combat screen for anyway? It provides no value and is simply ballast. The original MoM did that better.Unfortunately, this pattern runs through the whole game. The systems seem quite exciting on the surface, but almost all of them have not been thought through to the end. The selectable domains are extremely poorly balanced and some of them are also heavy RNG-dependent. Don't missunderstand, I'm talking about the bad kind of RNG, the kind where you only see the variables you actually need after you've made a not inconsiderable investment in that direction. To be honest, these are fundamental design problems. If a idiot like me notices this within a few test games, it's really cheeky of a developer to release it like this (no early access, no, this is supposedly a full version).

_childDocuments_.review: Missing features that were promised at launch. Extremely annoying unbalanced ai.Forced linear gameplay. They bragged about how you can customize your civ but there is no such thing in this game. Play the way the devs want you to play or suffer for it. Very small differences between starting civs. Just put it on random, it doesn't really matter. They are all generic.Too bad it takes over 2 hours to even figure out how bad this game is, or I would have refunded. That was probably the strategy all along, it seems to be the thing to do these days.- Country selections for NPCs are not saved when starting a new game, so every time you start a new game you have to reselect them all.- Hard to navigate the map by click dragging., so basically forced to use direction keys.- Can't choose where to place your first city so you're basically forced to pick specific civ-types based on where you started. - All civs are the same, the only difference is the name and flag. You are playing that country in name only. No special units or abilities unique to that country.- Selected starting bonus's don't seem to work.- Ai sucks. Will always suicide into you, even if there is another enemy closer to them.- If ai can't beat you it will just send 1000 tiny units to wreck your land. VERY ANNOYING.- Too many revolutions, not enough ways to keep them from happening, so you're basically always having them unless you play the game in a linear way.- Want ability to completely disable combat animations as well as age progression animations. They said they did this but shields still show up on the map so if you click them, guess what you're watching the boring combat scene.- Can't disable barbarians.- Age of Plagues is not fun. Games are supposed to be fun. When you add an element to a game ask yourself... does this add fun to the game? If not... don't add it to your game. I didn't buy Where's Waldo, I bought a 4x game. I don't enjoy having to scroll around searching the entire map every single turn looking for infections. SO DUMB, ANNOYING and BORING.Added 5/12: Played a lot more hours. Game still has many VERY ANNOYING "features". Still would not recommend. Every playthrough is THE SAME regardless of what they would have you believe. I have never even finished a map, I always rage-quit out of annoyance before that happens.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely love this game. A fantastic competitor to Civilisation. I love the age concepts and how it makes the game re-playable and different each time. The AI is still a bit dumb at times and don't seem to be very good at fixing problems that arise from some of the age systems, e.g. Age of Dystopia is my most hated age and it seems the AI can't handle it too as half of their improvements are still closed down with in the following ages. On the whole though, has kept me well entertained and I am still enjoying as I wait for Civ 7.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Not really sure why this is getting mixed reviews (as of writing)It is far and away the best civ-like 4x that I have played in a long time. Is it a little janky? Yeah, of course. It lacks some of the spit and shine that civ gets. It's definitely a game that puts its mechanics before its aesthetics, not that it looks awful or anything. But in terms of mechanics it is way ahead of Civ, which has become so watered down in service of being approachable that it just lost its fun for me. It hasn't really evolved in a meaningful way in decades.Millennia feels like an evolution in the genre. I will happily give up the prettier UI and aesthetics of Civ 6 for gameplay that doesn't feel utterly rote at this point. It is a bigger, more complex title. If a bigger, more complex civ-like doesn't sound like an improvement, then it's not for you I guess.My only real complaint at this point is the multiplayer. Their netcode feels like they ripped it out of a game from 2002. Integrate steam's tools or something, I dunno. But doing janky IP address stuff in 2023? People don't have to do that anymore and the many problems that arise across a player population doing multiplayer that way is going to lead to lots of complaints. I realize that the devs probably felt they had to launch with multiplayer, but given the janky connection stuff and the lack of simultaneous turns, they should've held off and let it cook before patching multiplayer in. I bet at least some of the bad reviews are specifically because the multiplayer is so... unfinished.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: Is inspired by Humankind, but doesnt play as well.The idea to have era civ traits is a great improvement, which means you can guide your specialization as the game goes, without having all the civ names reshuffle each era (like humankind). And like humankind, cities have extra towns outside the center, but you can not merge cities or detach towns.Building new cities is bad, as old smaller buildings are removed from the game as time progresses, leaving only super expensive late buildings that requires already well developed cities to build, this makes it almost impossible to start new cities. Tech tree combined with the era specializations are a bit of a mess. You end up with need for, or bonuses to tech you dont have. The differing eras is great idea. Unfortunately at any higher difficulty they will be controlled by AI, and some are badly balanced with alternative game speeds, making some negative eras almost impossible to avoid.Finally diplomacy is extremely weak, and the game super easy to snowball. No vassals, no advanced diplomatic states.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I thought I would give a short review here of Millenia for anyone who is still on the fence. TLDR: Honestly, I really like the concepts that the game is playing with, but there are significant changes needed. It feels like this should have been an early access release rather than showcased as a finished product. If the problems get fixed though and the right steps are taken then I can see this becoming a solid contender for top spots for 4X strategy games. (Current Rating 7/10)The Good:The national spirits, different governments, religion, and more all provide an excellent way to create unique civilizations throughout the game. Currently there are problems with a lot of spirits and government types due to other mechanics, but these provide a solid and interesting way to individualize the group you are playing as.The different ages mechanic is super interesting and has a lot of potential. There is a problem in that if you don’t beeline what you want then you are almost guaranteed to lose the race to the AI, often ending yourself up in a crises age (looking at you age of plague). Other than that issue, which could be fixed with better AI, I really enjoy the ages here as a fresh flavor in comparison to other 4X games.Production lines are great. Honestly, I might commit blasphemy and say I prefer it to the districts from Civ VI. I think that there is also a LOT of potential for this mechanic to be worked on and made even better in subsequent updates and DLC. It also seems to encourage playing tall rather than wide (I need more experience to be sure on that though), which I actually greatly prefer to the city spam of other 4X games. I made it through my game with only 4 cities and I honestly could’ve knocked it down to 2 or 3. There is an issue with playing wide that I will once again talk about in the bad section, so perhaps wide strats are simply not currently viable (at least without giving yourself a migraine.The Bad:Barbarians suck. Like, more than in any of the Civ games suck. I don’t know who thought giving them the ability to pop out of the ground (like daisies!) was a good idea. Seriously, they don’t even require a camp to spawn, so what is the point of the camps? The lack of ability to tune them down is also a severe misstep. In fairness, I only played with 6 other civ cultures in my game rather than 8, but I don’t think I should be required to play at max civ count just to reduce barbarian threat. This also provides significant issues with certian playstyles such as any of the spirits focused on exploration, as you will just get swamped going anywhere. Diplomacy is awful and feels deliberately anti-player. First, to initiate any level of decent diplomacy one is required to send an envoy to the other civ’s capital. This wouldn’t be terrible if not once again for the barbarian horde in between wherever you try to move. Second, even if you do manage to get an envoy successfully escorted to a foreign capital, most nations seemingly hate you. Even when playing with adept AI’s, none of the nations wanted to cooperate with me in any regard, often  preferring to be hostile to me or at constant war with eachother. This also means that unfortunatly diplomacy spirits feel rather useless as gaining diplomatic xp is essentially reliant entirely on buildings at your cities rather than, you know, diplomacy.Religion is a good basework, but has a LONG way to go. Seriously, if you don’t have meta knowledge of the game it feels as though going into the age of intolerance is inevitable. You are required to have religious buildings essentially at the begining of forming a religion which, if unprepared for, means you’re screwed. The basic religious building requires paper, a reseource which I wasn’t building at the time, and thus I was screwed. This mechanic currently seems to especially encourage tall play rather than wide as providing faith to all cities sounds nightmarish. Vassals and minor cities are useless. Seriously, this is the one aspect of the game I wish was more like Civ. It would help with the barbarian problem and would put significantly less stress on the player for dealing with everyone and their dog wanting a bite of you. Minor cities just sit there, vassals practically do nothing, and worse, you can’t even raze cities. Social Fabric is a cool idea. I really think the idea of accumulating points from different spirits over time to customize your empire is a cool concept. The only issue is that right now it is a really, really, bland mechanic. As it currently sits, the mechanic only provides percentage increases to certain values such as research. It feels downright lazy in comparison to the other ways the game allows you to build a unique society. I’m not sure what could be put in its place, because I DO like the concept, but it is kind of just a click and forget mechanic presently.The Ugly:The UI simply has too much going on in an unorganized fashion. The diplomacy button, for as useless as it is, is relegated to a small circle at the top right of the screen, the improvements screen is a jumbled mess, and the XP panel is simply doing way to much. I think that some great improvements would be sectioning the improvements into the category of production (farm, mill, baker, etc.) so that players have an easier understanding of the production lines and what to build. Giving the diplomacy button an actual place would be great, along with actually fixing diplomacy, and the XP panel simply needs work. I think having a screen for the XP like CKIII has for lifestyles might be a way to do it, but the notifications and layout of the XP is simply jarring to me currently. Other UI problems exist, but those were the standouts to me. Let me know what other terrible UI stuff you have a problem with!In game information is mediocre at best. Tooltips need to provide more information, especially when scrolling over improvements in the menu. There is simply not enough information provided easily most of the time. I wouldn’t have even found the diplomacy button if not for my love of pressing buttons. I managed to figure most things out from in game, but it was a far cry from what I would label as intuitive.Once again, I really want to love this game and I sincerely hope that it grows to being a 10/10 with subsequent updates and dlc. It is beyond me, however, that they released the game in this state without it being early access. Paradox is known for their special releases though, so I’m not out of hope for significant changes and improvements. Overall, as it currently stands, 6.5/10 but actually 7/10 for that copium of justifying the price.

_childDocuments_.review: If it was $5-$10 cheaper and/or was early access at launch, it would be a 5/5.  Being that it is not, it is a 4/5 as of this first month. Could have used another few months for graphics, cap balancing, deepening diplomacy & religion, etc. I really like its take on eras and national spirits. Nice breath of fresh air into the genre.TLDR: Its really good and itll get even better

_childDocuments_.review: Millennia brings fresh wind into the 4x genre and tries a few things differently. I really enjoy the mechanics and the potential it brings. Graphics are more on the functional side, but the gameplay is pretty good, so I can overlook that.Variety Ages add a lot to replayability, but just the lack of optimization makes end game a little bit laggy.Still gets a reccommendation from me as it is only 40€ instead of full prize 60 or 70 which normal AAA-titles want.
_childDocuments_.name: Millennia

_childDocuments_.review: I don't often write reviews, but in this case I want to because I have noticed numerous negative reviews about this game and I don't think it deserves them.The game definitely has room for improvement and it lacks the refinement phase that has taken several years for other similar games, but regardless, this is the best game of its kind seen in decades. Some of the mechanics are absolutely innovative in a genre where it is now difficult to introduce anything new.I personally really like the concatenated terrain improvements and the domain system.Among the things I would improve instead I would start with adding the auto-exploration feature and the possibility to scroll the screen by moving the mouse over the edges. Simple improvements that would make the game more playable.Please go ahead. There is definitely potential for a masterpiece but it is already a 7.5/10 as of now

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoy this game.  I just finished my first playthrough to a win and had a lot of fun in the process.  I controlled the age's after the AI took us to the Plague.  I ended up getting age of Alchemy and Utopia as my variants.  It really was a great game.some points of interest:- I had played the demo, so was prepared for the Barbs.- The game performed well till about just after turn 300.  Then I started to notice some slight performance issues, nothing earth shattering though.- Tool tips and game info need a lot of work.  That being said I couldnt figure out where all my exploration points were going during the Plague.  I didnt read the Plague doctors tooltip.  :-)- speaking of Plague.  The outbreaks were really hard to see, no need to make us blind ourselves trying to find them.  same goes for Arcana, they were not easy to see either sometimes.- I love the product chains and how they can be worked.- I liked the age system.  I'm sure the future will hold more things to do with Arcana and things,,,- I enjoyed the density issues with my cities, some could spread wide, others I had to adjust tiles as we modernised because I didnt have room for everything.  It would be nice to be able to tell what the different buildings are from the map, they really do look alike.  trying to find my religous scribe buildings to delete them after i became a democracy was a process.  - I really liked the improvement point system.  I did find that once I got a lot of tech researched the improvement tab was a little messy.  I;m not sure if it can be displayed as a tree for similar items...not a huge deal but was kind of a pain.- I loved the National Spirits...I had never played Wild Hunters in the Demo, they were awesome!- I hadnt planned for the age of Utopia, because there really isnt any info anywhere.  I did have enough room in my city cap to integrate one ocean settlement and get one extra hex for it.  The Coral did seem pretty cool, I'll know what to do next time.I'm sure I'm missing some important points, but thats probably enough.Look, the game isnt finished.  If you think that will bother you, then wait.  If you dont mind figuring some stuff out...I highly recommend this 4x game.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish steam would install a 'meh'-button because this game does not deserve a thumbs down. But neither an endorsement.Don't get me wrong, I like CIV-like games and this has some interesting mechanics but it has such a 'too early a release' feel to it. It has potential but it needs a lot of work.Combat is BORING because the units are boring. You can progress them true research but they are basically the same as the unit from previous ages with better stats. If they lvl, they get better stats. That's it. And even that is screwed up. F.e. you can get a unit called early machine gun and I hope you are not expecting an actual machine gun. Navies are basically useless except for escorting disembarked units and some things you can find. You can destroy fishing fleets but no shore bombardments for you. Neither do you have amphibious landings of any kind. Or aircraft carriers.That means that if you play on islands, you just park a cheap unit like a city guard on all shores and NO ONE WILL EVER be able to invade.Aircraft are even more useless than that. A bomber cannot even kill a rabbit. Also you get only propeller aircraft even if you fly to the moon. Oh, and no modern artillery either.The UI is clunky and far from user friendly especially when it comes to tile development. And if you win the game says Victory. No cut scene, no time laps, no ranking or whatever. There are many more issues but I'll leave it at that.Maybe there are pieces of brilliance hidden in the alien invasion ages or such but I found my play through thoroughly MEH. Hope this helps. Maybe hold on to your cash for a while and see if they polish it.

_childDocuments_.review: Graphics aren't the main thing in a strategy game, but its honestly pretty sad especially from a premier publisher like paradox. They have some neat ideas with the ages and having tile improvements produce resources that can go into production chains, leader promotions, building towns as part of the region expansion, etc, but the pacing and mechanics are poor. City growth, production, sanitation, etc are all dependent on improvements. By default no matter how many regions you have, you only earn 1 per turn. Most tile improvements cost between 12-20 improvement points. You can of course increase the amount you make per turn in various ways, but it doesnt seem to keep pace with cost and number of cities.Combat has zero nuance to it, and its based on a stacked army system but the stacks cant support each other.The combat animation window is the cheesiest thing ive seen in this kind of game in a long while and serves zero purpose other than to waste time.There is no noticeable difference between any of the civs to can play. Games are limited to 8 nations (plus the city state entities). Im sure there is plenty more i am missing but this is more than enough to highlight how it simply cannot compete with the likes of Civilisation or Humankind, or the upcoming ARA, from what I've seen so far.

Create your own nation in Millennia, a historical turn-based 4X game that challenges your strategic prowess across 10,000 years of history, from the dawn of humanity to our possible futures.

Pursue knowledge to research scientific and cultural advances, unlocking new units, buildings, and improvements to grow your cities or strengthen your armies.
