_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: Do you tire of "choices-matter" style games that offer the same depth of story telling as a "Give-Yourself-Goosebumps" book? How everything basically boils down 2 paths with a few gameovers? How gameplay mechanics never used? Do you wish that someone would actually innovate this stale format from the 90s? This game does that. The story actually branches off into entirely different genres, the gameplay mechanics actually matter for the story telling. Despite it's simplicity it offers something truly fresh.
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: Oh my goodness, this was such a wonderful game! An adorable game with a darker tint, the story was gripping, the gameplay was fun, and the narration was fantastic. There are so many endings to explore and the game easily guides you through all of them as you play through it, so you don't need to miss anything, nor replay through hours and hours of content that you've already seen in order to see all possible endings.This game had me laughing at some parts, crying at others. Such a satisfying game to play through.
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: What a twisty wild ride.  A combination of Visual novel and light RPG elements, in a choose your own adventure style story, you discover a dark secret hidden in a seemingly comfy cozy little town.  Every little twist of fate reveals more of the story, and the deeper you delve into the lore the more options you have for changing the story. At any point you can go back to a previous "chapter" and change your options to learn more or pursue a different branch of the story. The art is beautiful, the music is beautiful, the characters are complex and interesting, there are all sorts of little fun side things to do, like learning about the NPCs, cooking, or fishing. Easy 100% achievement in roughly 10 hours, spent some time exploring all the options and paths to get the full story and all endings. 100% would recommend. Delightful game. Chill, but intriguing, bright and beautiful, but with underlying (and not so underlying) darkness.
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: I was able to sit down and finish the whole game in around 7hrs on twitch. I was captured by Beacon Pines! From the incredible art to the truly motivating story, I absolutely feel head over heels for this game. Being an avid reader and gamer, having found a game that truly captures the essence of both is amazing. Truly 100,000% would recommend Beacon Pines to anyone and everyone!
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: A fun visual novel style game with an amazing narrator. It's got a fun furry atmosphere to it in all the cutness of the characters. Despite the cuteness though there is a delightful darkness that mingles with some of the creative humor that is also thrown into the story. It's very much a choose your own adventure in a way with multiple endings, but it's very easy to go back and try those different arcs as you go. I got a solid six hours out of this game and don't really see to much replayability, but it's a fun story and if I'm looking for relaxing story it's a great game I can come back to for a visual novel with some nice interactiveness to it.
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: This game is actually really good even if it's pretty short. This is one of those games that is the journey, not the ending you get. The narrator never gets grating, the plot is engaging, and in the end you feel satisfied. Actually I felt very good when I got to the end because the journey was so much fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: This is a story of Struggle. The story often ends in tragedy, but it is almost always tinged with more. Every loss leads to a bittersweet discovery, both impersonal and non. Many timey-wimey story games walk the tread of 'learning more with each passing' but few try to tell a complete story as thoroughly upon each path. Some of the sweetest, heartfelt endings are tied to horrific unavoidable tragedies. Every ending leads me to hope, and hope hurts because it begets a better tommarow, which leads you to understand the ♥♥♥♥ of today. This is a story of Strange. Most every odd remark or quirk of a character is tied to the whole mess present in the town. Most everything happening is part of the wider narrative, giving the entirety of the experience a clean cohesion. The mini-games stapled to the experiance do seem a stuter step, the best of them being a cute diversion, and the worst being boring and mildly frustrating, but they do well not to overstay their welcome. This is a story of Change. My view of every character, the relationships between characters, this world as a whole, and some elements of my own life were changed through my playtime. I was reminded of my upbringing in a small county town, of struggling parents, and the inexerable nature of time. I believe the most any story can hope is that it can change its audience, and I can only hope Beacon Pines can change you as much as it did me.
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: This is my favorite narrative-focused game. Maybe my favorite video game story of all time. I love the gorgeous art, the beautiful voice acting from the narrator, the music and the story!Oh man this story, ITS SO GOOD. There's so many set-ups and payoffs. So many great twists and turns, across every branch of the story! And they use the branching narrative to such good effect! Expertly mining it for pathos, humor and dramatic irony! I was completely enthralled from beginning to end.It's "charm" system is an incredibly clever approach to video game storytelling, ensuring that even bad endings can help your progress down a different story path, or turning bad endings into new story paths entirely. This system also cuts out all of what might be described as the "narrative backtracking" that tends to plague these kinds of game, where the player has to skip through a bunch of story they've already read just to get to the pivotal choice moments. No, your always reading new story. Always forging ahead. It's all killer, no filler from start to finish. I would love for this game's structure to become a staple of the genre. Heck, I would love for Beacon-likes to become their own genre.This is the new gold standard of video game storytelling. If you have ever loved a good story in your life, I recommend this game to you. 10/10. 5/5. Two thumbs up. Dawn is my favorite character.
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: Came for the artstyle without a clue about what to expect from the game a honestly, I am glad I did, I bought the game a bunch of hours earlier and just finished it. I loved the gameplay, loved the artworks, loved the story and the characters, loved the twists, loved every single thing, as I wasn't expecting anything from it really.Don't read anything, just dive into it, and embrace what's about to be an adventure that'll make you laugh and cry.
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: Tried to keep going but there's too many annoying things - the narrator's voice is terrible, there's no way to re-read the dialogue or storybook, which makes things extra confusing when the whole point is to go through different timeline branches. The music is repetitive to the point I had to turn it down.It's a cool concept, just not cool enough for me to finish.
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoy narrative games, you will love this. Additional bonus is that in order to get to the true end, you must play through all the other various endings first. The story gets richer and richer with every ending, and it never gets boring to retrace your steps. A well-designed, well-crafted, gorgeous-looking game. Highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: Ayo - I loveeeee this game! When I first saw it played on YouTube as a demo, I had to get it. I streamed it months ago as an awesome 1 hour demo and had no regrets. Sadly I was unable to go into KickStarter and donate. (Really want a shirt or artwork)The artwork is amazing. Super detailed and very cute characters with varying personalities! The dialogue is super natural, almost an echo of what I would say. A great, memorable narrator voice (I usually find them boring/slow). The visual novel is incredibly story rich and doesn't hide it. The freedom it gives you to explore and rewards with great finds. It encourages you to learn more about the setting and others in a way that's not overwhelming and "required". A time travel kind of element that allows to explore endings BEFORE the very end and you're not super confused about where you were last. Your choices matter but you also get to remake choices which is super good. Look I didn't finish the game yet and may edit this later when I do... but I'm sure I won't be disappointed. Just... get it!
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: An amazingly creative game from start to finish! I laughed, I cried, and I explored every nook and cranny of this game that I possibly could! I loved the narrator, the characters, and I loved that the game encouraged you to explore! The routes and charm gathering really was interesting and helped give you the story in a unique way! I wish I could play it all over again for the first time! If you want an amazing game with beautiful art and a unique, twisting story, this is the game for you!
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for February 2024, this is part of my coverage of the bundle. If you are interested in the game and it's before March 5th, 2024, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.A unique take on the Mad Libs of old. Beacon Pines was a surprise for me when I first played this.  The main mechanic of the game is that players can take Charms, essentially words that they discover by exploring the world, and then use them to fill in the blanks at junctions in the story.  This sounds simple, but the main goal is to explore different branches of the story to take the narrative in different directions and then return to the branching point and try different words.  The story is well written and there’s a lot of charm in the game, as well as a great mystery at the center.  While I’ve only seen half of it previously, I need to go back and play this whole game.At the same time, this game has a very narrative focus on storytelling and world-building but still requires players to go through the world searching for the words to use.  Also, the game can feel repetitive at times, and admittedly the game does a good job avoiding that, but going back into the story means having to see some of the same content a second or third time. Pick this up if you want an interesting or unique narrative experience.  I can’t think of many games like this, because this does something fresh and new.  The story here is extremely compelling and the mysteries are ones that players will feel a need to unravel and see what’s going on. If you enjoyed this review or want to know what I think of other games in the bundle, check out the full review on or subscribe to my Youtube channel:
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: Still processing some personal thoughts on this one, but definitely a recommend as it's been a long time since I sat down and just played a story-based game for 4 hours straight.  Sometimes it's nice to play something not terribly ambitious by a small team that still has heart, instead of pandering to the lowest common denominator that has traded their soul for higher sales.  Some themes and moments aren't given equal treatment or time to be explored, but I still enjoyed my time relating strongly to certain parts of the story, and appreciating those I could not.  I don't mind letting my mind wander to the details left unspoken, it helps to make the world a bit more mine and how my imagination would fill it out; even so I would've appreciated additional art to accompany various scenes, especially at this price point.  There was a pretty glaring oversight with one of the character's portraits depending on which way they were facing, as well.Sadly nothing else is in the works for the Beacon Pines universe according to the devs, or likely even for this game at this point, but I hope they come back to it refreshed someday and build upon the heartfelt foundation they created.  Great job and I'll be waiting to see what y'all do next.
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: This is a story about CHANGE.This game tells a story in a way no other game I've ever played has tried to tell one before.  Though in some ways it will be familiar to those who have read a choose your own adventure book.  It takes that concept, expands it, embraces it, and comes out the other side as something I find I just have to share with others.This is a story about CHANGE.Arc words for the story, that every time you hear them, every time you see them, will hit a little differently.  The game is a ride, and it just won't let you go until your done.  Make some cocoa, grab your comfort food, and settle in.  Enjoy the story.  This is a story about CHANGE.Let it change you too.
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: Gripping narrative and beautiful visuals, with a plot that plays with the conventions of time and the 'choose your own adventure' style storytelling. If there is a shortfall when it comes to this game is just how short it actually is. It almost ended too soon. I will miss this little gang of misfits and the town of Beacon Pines.
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: This is a delightful story game with some surprising wtf moments. I wish choices mattered more as it ends up being fairly linear to play through, but that didn't diminish the game for me. I could see this game potentially making players backtrack a lot if you aren't thorough enough in exploring each area as you first play through it. I'm not sure because I tried my best to do everything I could in each chapter, so I only ended up backtracking for a couple of achievements at the end of the game.I love this game. I hope the studio keeps growing and make more games in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful piece of interactive fiction that has a strong, non-linear story, and charming characters.As a heavily story-driven game, the less you know going in, the better. I was consistently surprised and always eager to learn more about the mystery surrounding the town. The game is particularly good at showing the story through Luka's perspective, and you really empathize with him throughout the adventure. You feel what he's feeling.Transitioning between different choices you made is always smooth and doesn't cause the moment to lose it's potency. The music does a great job in immersing you, but it's the narrator that really brings the story to life. She compliments the writing ideally and is incredibly talented.Needless to say, if you enjoy a good story this game is one I can certainly recommend!!
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: I played this game because I finished Night in the Woods and started missing it and wanted to find something to fill the void; now I've finished Beacon Pines and I miss it and so the cycle continues.I really did buy this because people recommended it for fans of Night in the Woods.  It's not exactly the same kind of game but I 100% see why the recommendation was made.  Like Night in the Woods, this game has minimal gameplay but it's really all about the story, the characters and their relationships with each other.  The character designs are ridiculously adorable and the portraits and animations are very expressive.  It also made me laugh more than I would have expected. The visual style is stunning and the music is really nice too.  For people who get emotionally invested in games like Undertale and OneShot for the characters, I would recommend Beacon Pines in a heartbeat.
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: The art is good, the writing is very good, the gameplay is non-existent but thats fine.In terms of gameplay... there is no gameplay. You walk around and talk to people, then watch some cutscenes and conversations. that's allright because its a heavily story focused game. Just realize that there is basically zero puzzles or gameplay apart from a few very small exceptions.Same with replay-ability, although the game is a sort of choose-your-own-adventure-esque story there aren't multiple endings really. The story can be experienced non-linearly but in order to actually get to the end you basically have to see all of the content.The writing is very good, its cute and sometimes a little more serious but it never gets to the point that you can really call it 'dark'. There's a good balance between the more serious thriller stuff and the lighter slice of life friendship stuff.All in all its a good experience, its a bit on the short side at only 5 ish hours but i kind of like shorter stories. Its up to you if its worth the money though.
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: This is a cute, and at the same time mysterieus and even disturbing story. The gameplay is fairly easy, but not straightforward. That's mostly because you jump from storyline to storyline. Sometimes back in time, sometimes fast forward in time. The story is interesting, but near the end it kept a bit dragging on too long. But it was engaging enough to keep wanting to reach the end. There's no big puzzles or challenges, so some people might find this game a bit too easy. But if you look for a cozy game that is a bit darker, than this is the game for you!
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10 Would play again. Or a sequel. Or another game by this group of creators! They really out done themselves. I backed this on Kickstarter and it was a pleasure to see it come to fruition. Art is beautiful. Story is emotional. Gameplay is convenient: You can go back to branching choices and change them at any point in the game AND "skip" to where you left off so you don't have to replay dialogue. Please make more!
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: Beacon Pines has a fantastic and emotional story with lots of twists that were often quite unpredictable, and the main mechanic of the game is something I haven't really seen before. The game is not long, took me about 8 hours and I took my sweet time, but it's well worth the asking price! The artistry of the touching and funny writing, the beautiful visual and the amazing music made it a memorable experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: What an amazing visual novel! The art direction is really cute, the characters are well written, and yet the story quickly takes a dark turn. I loved how every choice you make actually leads to completely different paths, that all help you better understand the whole story. I wish more stories were like this!
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: Heartwarming, heart dropping and oh so cozy. Like Mad Libs each word in Beacon Pines has power and shapes the story. But instead of leading you to a nonsensical and hilarious story, a word can either spell doom for Luka and the other characters, or lead you deeper into a massive conspiracy. Even if you fail (and you will) every word gets you closer to unraveling it and to that ending Luka and all his friends deserve.
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: Beacon Pines is a charming story-focused game set in a farming town with a haunted past. The game plays out in multiple chapters, with each choice you make unlocking a different branch into a new act. You're given straightforward goals in each chapter, and making progress feels pretty straightforward. One of the core mechanics in the game is the ability to go back and pick new choices; so far I've only been able to into bad ends, so the game is designed with this mechanic in mind. Through it you unlock new options for previous choices, which can unlock new scenes and uncover more clues in the mystery.In the beginning, I was a little put off by how linear the game felt — I was often pigeonholed into just one option for most choices. But there was enough intrigue in the story for me to keep pushing through, and I eventually realized that this game has a very specific story it wants to tell, and I enjoyed it much more when I allowed myself to simply go along for the ride. The choices you make do matter, but it isn't the typical "choices matter" game like Baldurs Gate 3, Life is Strange, or the typical Telltale game. There is one typical playthrough, with new choices and options unlocked in relatively the same order for everyone. But it has been a nice, enjoyable, intriguing experience so far, a story I find myself eager to discover, even if I'm not creating it.
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: A unique mystery game with a charming setting and art style. Somehow manages to be cosy and spooky at the same time.Lovely characters with a brilliant story that unfolds in different paths, dependent on your choices, that feeds you dollops of dramatic irony as you replay sections to get different outcomes to flesh out the unusual goings-on in the town.
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. While this game is not very long (I took my time at around 6 hours), it is worth every penny. Genuinely one of the best adventure games I've ever played.Incredible plot, cute art, a cosy mystery, emotional soundtrack, and so many twists and turns.Absolute perfection, wouldn't change a thing.P.S. Be prepared for some tears.
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review: Recommendation #1: Plan a day to play this whole game. It's about 8 hours (some of my playtime is idling). Due to how the game is structured, it can get confusing otherwise.Recommendation #2: While the game is cheap, probably wait for a sale. The story really takes a nose dive in the 2nd half, and there is no real conclusion to be seen. The game just abruptly and awkwardly ends. Maybe a part 2 is teased at one point but it could as easily be a meta joke. I certainly would not have gotten into this if I had thought it's a chapter 1 case. Bottom line - the narrator definitely felt much differently than I did about much of the game, which made it extra frustrating. But overall cute and interesting game.
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

_childDocuments_.review:
Beacon Pines is a cute and creepy adventure set within a mysterious book. You play as both the reader of the book and its main character, Luka.

Something strange is happening at the old warehouse, and Luka and his friends seem to be the only ones taking notice. Sneak out late, make new friends, uncover hidden truths, and collect words that will change the course of fate!

As the book's reader, you'll navigate the story's turning points using The Chronicle: an interactive story tree that branches and grows along with your choices. Exploring one set of events can unlock new charms to use on another branch, leading you to jump back and forth between entirely different versions of the story in order to unravel the mysteries at the heart of Beacon Pines.
_childDocuments_.name: Beacon Pines

name: Deadly Premonition 2: A Blessing in Disguise
detailed_description: Deadly Premonition 2: A Blessing in Disguise is an open-world survival horror video game serving as both a sequel and prequel to the original Deadly Premonition: The Director’s Cut. The story takes place in present-day Boston where it turns out FBI Special Agent Francis York Morgan will have to revisit a case he thought was solved in 2005. Through unique storytelling, venture back in time to the American town Le Carré, Louisiana and uncover the mysteries buried within this once peaceful town. Follow Agents Davis and Jones as they begin a new investigation into the Le Carré serial murders. Through the memories of a former FBI agent, go back in time to Le Carré and step into the role of Special Agent York to begin unraveling the mystery. • Return as FBI Special Agent Francis York Morgan (just call him York - everyone does) and experience a brand-new murder mystery! • Both a prequel and a sequel: A historic investigation to uncover the murder mystery in Le Carré • An open-world adventure: Travel around the town of Le Carré by foot or skateboard • Mini-games: Bowling, Bayou Ride, Skateboard Challenge, and more • Customisation: Customise your character and upgrade your skateboard for improved speed and landing more difficult tricks

name: Date Night Bowling
detailed_description: You're out at your local bowling alley for a dating event, so strike up a conversation, hop over to the bowling lanes, and try your best to make a good first impression. Play things right and you might just find your soulmate! To win over your date, you’ll rely not only on your bowling skills, but also on your ability to tell well-timed jokes, throw popcorn into their mouth, give the perfect shoulder rub, and more! An Arcadey Bowling Game—With a New Spin! Grab a drink, slip on the shoes, and let the romance begin! Choose your perfect date-night bowling experience from a variety of customizable options: Pick your player and your date from a rich cast of characters with their own special chemistries (or lack thereof…) Choose to bowl solo, pair up with an AI partner, or even face off against your friends with a local 2-player match Make your own challenge by choosing your ball weight, lane oil, and overall difficulty levels Two bowling alleys, each with their own late-night vibe and groovy original music Impress Your Date with All Manner of Skills Everyone loves an ace bowler (or so we’re told), but nothing melts hearts quite like winning the cutest toy from the claw machine. You’ll need to bring your A-game not just for bowling, but for the date night, as well. Keep your partner happy and entertained, and they might just see fit to join you for a second date!

name: Adios
detailed_description: Adios is a cinematic first-person game about sticking to a complicated decision. You're a pig farmer in Kansas. It's October. Cold, crisp mornings are the norm, and you have decided that you're no longer okay with letting the mob use your pigs to dispose of bodies. When your old friend - a hitman - arrives with his assistant to deliver another body, you finally screw up the courage to tell them that you're done. Your friend doesn't want you to stop. He knows that there's no such thing as quitting, so he'll try to convince you that you're making a mistake. You spend the day together, doing chores and exploring the nooks and crannies of an authentic environment in the American Midwest alongside the man who will be forced to kill you, if he can't convince you to stay. How you respond will determine the rest of your life. Adios means goodbye.

short_description: A pig farmer decides he no longer wants to dispose of bodies for the mob. What follows is a discussion between him and his would-be killer.

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a 90 min long meditation on DeathTold from the perspective of a complicated man, who decides to do one last good thing even if it means he'll die, so your discussion with your would be killer is less a "please don't kill me" and more of a "please remember me", you offer him anecdotes, secrets and even material possessions, all the little things that make up your person, your identity, in the hope that some part of you lives on in him and othersIn that sense it reminded me a lot of a funeral, all the eulogies and stories people tell each other, hoping to capture and preserve the essence of someone, only here it is you yourself doing it, because you have no one else left to do it for youThe game has a very strong autumn feel, both due to the impending and unavoidable ending and the constant sense of decay, you're clamoring  to the last vestiges of a heritage barely anyone cares about anymore, trying to uphold and be apart of something bigger than yourself, that you hope will endure after you're gonein the end you're left with a feeling as complicated as the man you're playing as, you appreciate the noble effort, and sense the overwhelming tragedy as well as the futility of the situation
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: You're a pig farmer in Kansas. For the last fifteen years you have helped feed chopped up body parts to your pigs for the Mob. Today, you have decided to quit. You are no longer comfortable with letting the mob use your pigs as a way of disposing of victims. Together you discuss the reasons for your decision and the consequences, whilst tending to the farm on a cold crisp morning.Have you resigned to the fact that this might be your last day on Earth or can you be talked around?  There are dialogue branches, but they are extremely minimal, plus they all end up with the same conclusion. I have played through the game a few times and there is no way to change or alter the story line. It will always end the same and your journey there will be almost identical too. Therefore, Adios is a cinematic experience discussing the reasons why you have come to the conclusion to quit working for the Mob. The dialogues are voice acted quite well and some of the conversations are poignant and emotional. The pig farmer and the mobster have been working together for fifteen years so there is some familiarity in their exchanges. Most of the interactive scenes are quite basic but the control interface is quite clunky and rudimentary. I had particular issues controlling items, during the cooking scenes. You can’t put items down, only swap them, and when you swap them, they get flung across the room and bounce into awkward places. Sometimes these are irretrievable. It can be quite frustrating.Visuals are basic but attractive in places. Character’s faces aren’t drawn particularly well. They cannot display emotion, and the weight of emotion purely rests in how the voices are spoken.I am sure some of the achievements are bugged, but it is difficult to tell as there are no guides, and I can only go by the description on the achievement. The good news is that any scene can be played after you complete the game which helps. I experienced a few bugs during my gameplay including a massive glitch with the graphics where all environments were messed up. I eventually fixed this by altering the field of view and it never came back. I experienced other graphical issues like the goat jumping across the room leaving the mobster milking nothing; there were numerous dialogue errors where previous conversations would kick in; and once the mobster got left outside the building whilst I carried on in and was talking to him. The story is difficult to discuss without revealing spoilers. It is certainly thought provoking. I’ve changed my mind a few times about whether the story should have taken a different path but the outcome is a valid one. Personally, I wanted to see more emotion and more drama in their exchanges. It didn’t feel tense and there wasn’t enough pressure on changing the farmer’s decision. The conversations are initiated by walking or running to a destination indicated by a distance counter on the screen. Certain scenes can be played in any order, although after you choose a scene and play through it, another scene may automatically follow. The scenes vary in length and vary in input. Some scenes you might not even discover unless you interact with certain objects.Occasionally, you will be given up to four choices to make to continue the dialogue. The choices only alter the conversation ever so slightly though and the main points will always be the same. I noticed in some dialogues that the choices were greyed out and could not be selected. I thought that it was because I needed to say something different in previous conversations and these would then highlight. I have tried every single dialogue choice in the game and these options are still greyed out. I’m not sure whether this is a bug or I am doing something out of order perhaps? There is a journal which acts as a check list on all the chores you need to do, so this will help you ascertain what objects you might need to interactive with. There are a lot of red herrings where objects can be examined by rotating them but they are hardly ever relevant and therefore pointless. Some do relate to achievements though and some can be interacted with. For example, taps, cookers and microwave ovens can be turned on. There are a couple of free roam opportunities where you can explore the farm and the farm house. You can run quite fast so exploring is easy but the farm is often cordoned off so there’s not too much scope for meaningful exploration. Searching the house was quite fun though. There are about five interactive scenes you can enjoy whilst you talk to the mobster. Tending to the animals, throwing horseshoes, fixing your car, fishing and skeet shooting are all activities you will encounter during the day. They’re all quite basic and easy to manage apart from the cooking scene which might prove frustrating to some. The environments are quite pleasant in places and the animals look cute and move quite realistically. Immersion is let down slightly by the mobster’s facial expressions, as there aren’t any. Voice acting is quite professional and emotion is adequately portrayed in conversations. There is no menu music, or any kind of music playing whilst you play. Maybe that would have injected some more emotion into the story?
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A sad — even tear-jerking — short story about a farmer who used to help the mob destroy bodies and now wants to quit. He knows it's a death sentence — this is so clear no one wastes their breath spelling it out; and he spends his last day with a hitman who bears him no ill will and tries to talk him out of this, but respects his choice in his own way.While the main character is burdened by his misdeeds, his choice is not presented as overly moral. He seems lonely and exhausted, stranded without his wife and tongue-tied (highlighted by greyed-out dialogue options you can't pick). It's not a story of moral reckoning, but rather of old age.Modelling everyday chores feels disingenious in gaming sometimes, but not here. What *is* there to do for a man who has just... stopped? Milk the goats one last time, visit the dog's grave, call his son... make his last meal. doesn't go into too much detail, which is for the best; it stays emotional and succinct, delivering the sadness and exhaustion though the voice acting, seemingly innocuous small talk with the hitman and short task prompts. While I've found the expetience a bit too tear-jerkey, it doesn't outstay its welcome.The visuals are clunky, and there generally aren't any impressive shots, but the great voice acting and good dialogue make up for that. Worth the two hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: is a narrative-driven walking sim with two main protagonists. A farmer who says no to his "second job" and the hitman who assigns him the task of getting rid of certain people's corpses. For that his pigs are perfect. But our hero says no and the game shows us why he made this decision and, ultimately, its consequences.We have limited mobility during the game. After the first scene we have markers showing where we can go on the farm to start new scenes (we can refer to them as chapters). Consider this a hub area but eventually we are back to a linear path till the story ends. So, why this central area is important is because the mobster decides to accompany the farmer and assist with his daily chores to see if he can change his mind.When doing chores in the limited space we have we get to hear the dialogue between the two gentlemen and - where needed - pick from the responses available. They do not change the outcome so the game has low replayability unless you want to unlock every achievement.This is a great little indie game with superb voice acting. For some reason the story takes place in the early '90s. Graphics are, therefore, stylised a bit but detailed enough for us to enjoy it. Once you are done there is a scene selection options to grab the 'cheevos you have failed to acquire. I found  a very sad, emotional game. Rarely do we see such an indie game here on Steam. Highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Despite pretty good voice acting and charming cartoony graphics, I just wasn't wowed by Adios. Adios is a walking sim with the melancholic story of a man ready to die and the hitman who's trying to coax him out of it; this is the sort of story in which you know how the story is going to play out very quickly, and there are no curveballs. You'll also do a few tasks like shooting skeet or feeding a horse, but ultimately a game like this is driven by its story, and I just couldn't find myself attached to its protagonist when I knew what his ultimate fate was going to be.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a game that I didn't particularly enjoy that I think you should buy anyways.If you've watched the trailer, read any reviews, heard any buzz at all about this game, you know what's going to happen and what to expect. You don't need me to tell you if you're going to enjoy it.What I do want to tell you, and why I feel like I should leave a review even though I don't have that many positive things to say, is that the creative minds behind this project definitely have the ambition, the drive, the passion, and the ability to make something truly great. Adios, for me, is a tech demo of more important things to come. But we live in a capitalist hellhole where good things don't get made unless a rich producer-type dude gets swindled into funding a project, feeling entitled to put his greasy fingerprints all over an artist's creative vision until it's muddied and disgusting and nobody wants to look at it anymore.But maybe, just maybe, if us commoners put in our measly dollars and leave reviews, then Doc and his team get to make their magnum opus without having to bend the knee.And that, more than any reason, is why you should buy and play Adios.Also, I like goats.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a laid back linear story. Pleasant voice acting. Multiple choices for dialogue and chapter select after completed game allows for easy achievement completion and selective replay for more story. I'd say it can be mildly unsettling for sensitive folk, but it isn't gory. Nice art style. Moves a bit slow, and I wouldn't advise doing so but you can skip conversation by pressing X. Overall I'd give it a 7/10 since as a walking simulator you're relatively limited in where you can roam.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: This game is like watching a very good show on Netflix. It is mostly cinematic, although you do get to choose some of the flavor dialogue and play some short, rudimentary game sequences. Whole thing took me about 80 minutes. What really sets this experience apart from many other similar experiences on Steam, is the wonderful top-notch voice-acting and the very good dialogue / writing that keeps things interesting from start to finish. The artwork and ambient sounds just add to the whole end product. This is one of the best narrative driven games on Steam and my nominee for "Oustsanding Story-Rich Game" for the 2021 Steam Awards. I highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is about facing a tragedy you're thirty years too late to change, and confronting the other tragedies you caused along the way. As you try to make your peace, you find your past hasn't just set you on this course - it still binds you, and it won't let you undo the damage you've done.The voice acting is impeccable throughout. It's easy to praise the farmer's voice actor - the script is delivered with such sincerity it feels alive and human, but it is the hitman's easy charisma which very nearly conceals menace to the perfect degree which makes him the perfect foil for the farmer.Is it odd to say you enjoyed the worldbuilding in a game set in the real world, or a close facsimile of it? The farmer doesn't exist in a self-contained bubble in the wilderness. He's a loner, but Adios is all about the things that tie him to the world, and to the other people in it, and how his end will leave things done or undone.This game won't excite you, or thrill you. It WILL give you an experience rarely found in games, which is to inhabit someone different for a while and let yourself feel things you wouldn't otherwise feel, for reasons you might not even understand. And you might learn a thing or two about pigs, or chestnut trees.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A one of a kind, beautiful experience. The writing and voice work do a stellar job of immersing the player - I was moved to tears twice in the span of my first playthrough by the raw emotion conveyed by the pig farmer and supporting characters. I was wonderfully gripped from beginning to end, and I only regret not taking more time to meander and marinate, but I was so desperate for more of the story that I powered through a bit harder than I should've.Please buy this if you're interested in seeing the potential for mature, thoughtful storytelling using videogames as a medium. You won't regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Hello. I'm Matthew, a grown man, and this game made me cry over a chestnut tree. You may be wondering how we got here; Allow me to explain: The narrative in this game is not adequately described by any known adjectives, however I reluctantly will settle on a concept: It is like slowly becoming the character, while being fully aware of this process, with no means/desire to halt the progress of said transformation. Dialogue options are presented. I found myself at first fighting to insert myself, my will, onto said choices. I failed in the end. Even at the threshold of the final choices, I reflexively thought to the farmer and what he should say. Would say. MUST say. The absolute crushing weight of it all was immense. And I was tired. I was sorry. I was resolved. The story was telling itself in a way that I had no right to alter, and no will to try. Knowing how it would end, yet going through the simple actions that defined his day-to-day was a feeling I struggle to describe. Anxiously freeing? Somberly satisfying? Numbly engaging? It was catharsis or even poetic justice on a level I've never experienced in my own life, sadly. I threw horseshoes. Fed a horse apples. Microwaved a burrito. And yes, learned the provenance and tragic plight of a majestic organism in the form of the North American Chestnut tree. That broke me. I largely held the game at arms length until that moment, but my father cut trees all his life, all while wanting to be an arborist. That hit me so much harder than I was expecting that I physically felt it. A gut punch. This game is a veritable minefield of such connections, and one will find you. When it does, it'll hit you like a freight train, and you wouldn't leave those tracks any more then that train would. It took me 80 minutes to finish, soaking in the details, but also not lingering on any moment for longer than it needed. I would pay the price of this game thousands of times over for that experience again, if I could see it from my initial oblivious state. I'd have paid much more had I known the absolute treasure I was getting.  Final note: If you don't enjoy games as stories, then this experience probably isn't for you. It is functional and entertaining as a game in-so-much as it allows you to be the story. It is not for highscores, leaderboards, bragging rights, co-op, fighting, action and/or challenge; With the exception of challenging your reality, morality, and ability to forgive. To forgive yourself; To be the truest and most necessary version of you despite failing, giving up, and taking the easy way out until it was almost too late. Thanks Doc.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Despite the game being all about the story, the story just isn't that good. Not sure why this needed to be a full fledged game instead of a free itchio project. I came into it hoping for something very engaging, judging by the steam reviews, but the whole thing can be summed up into about 5 minutes of dialogue.I get that the dev said some nonsense about "all the little things" being the meaningful choices, but this amounts to there being absolutely no mystery or sense of discovery. This is not what replayability is.There are a lot of games far better than this, and if you really want a completely static experience without any real gameplay, listen to an audiobook.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a morbid slice of life, as ephemeral and sensitive as its subject matter would suggest. It's a rare pleasure to play a story-based game that doesn't feel the need to run for tens of hours and pad itself out with melodrama and/or Exciting Gameplay Experiences, but instead contents itself with exploring a single character's life and relationships, drifting in and out of vignettes of his life.It's a touching piece, and while the "criminal underworld as exploration of man's nature" is a trope I've long since tired of in film, it's rare to see one so fixed on the periphery, so uninterested in bombast, and specifically focussed in the life, losses and priorities of a single man. In its ~80 minute runtime, where the average game may have just gotten to the point of giving its hero whatever justification it needs for them to spend the next few tens of hours murdering fodder, Adios manages to explore the fragile nature of being at macro and micro-level; public/performative expectations of grief; hobbies as mindfulness; and the conflict between personal relationships and power dynamics. Amongst other things. That it does all of this without feeling like a parable at any point is all the more impressive.It's a game with a lot to say, but no conclusions. And it's distressing for me to realise just how rare that is. I can't wait to see what Mischief do next.(also, the dialogue and voice work throughout was fantastic, and I will never tire of games where I can pick up and rotate items at will; thanks, Shenmue, for setting off that lifelong source of pleasure in games. More in-game handling of inanimate objects, that what I say!)
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely brilliant game, written in the way that you'd hope games would and could be written in more often. There is a good chance you've heard this described as a walking simulator or a text-heavy game, and neither is exactly right or wrong -- this is a novel or short story in game form, but one that respects both mediums implicitly. Adios could only be told as a game, but the story is a wonderful addition to the legacy of loss, blurred ambition, and age that we have seen in the best recent American literature. To say it's worth your time and attention is too mild.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: What Adios lacks in polish, it more than makes up for it with it's writing, structure and voice acting. I was drawn to buy and play this by people comparing it to Firewatch and What Remains of Edith Finch, once I saw that the average playtime was only 1.5 hours, I was sold immediately. I love short focused games and this is one of those. This was a somber experience that I won't forget anytime soon and I recommend this to anyone who's hungry for more short narrative games.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely well written short, poignant and surprisingly down to earth narrative game about regret, loss and the simple things in life. The voice acting is absolutely stellar and carries a lot of its honest but emotional story that's almost exclusively conveyed through a seminal conversation between a hitman and a pig farmer who's been disposing bodies for the mob for the past decades.I've always loved movies that can carry an engrossing story exclusively through dialogue, but I've never seen a video game pull this feat off successfully until Adios.Highest recommendation if you don't mind it being on the shorter end of the spectrum. It's a game that wastes no time, it says what it wants to say, and it does it with a tasteful, tactile oomph.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Short interactive narrative game.Not an action game.You have a shotgun, you don;t get to blast away with it whenever you want.So, if you were hoping you could- this game isn't for you.It's a story- one day in a pig farmer's life, A pig farmer who feeds chopped up bodies to his pigs, as part of his work with a hitman and the people the hitman works for.Some emotionally charged narrative bits, regarding the farmer, his family, and the choices he made over the years.Some exploration, but also lots of invisible walls, where you can see a big map that you aren't allowed to explore fully (which was a bit frustrating to me- I like to explore every inch of every map in every game...).Stylized graphics- don't expect photo-realism. The game is set in the 1990s, and it has that look to it.Some good music in the son's old room, but it'll be subjective. If you're hoping for 90s pop- you're looking in the wrong place. It's not that.Scene select after you've completed the game, so you can go back and pick up missed achievements (and there are quite a few missable achievements).If you enjoy narrative driven interactive experiences, you may enjoy it.If you are looking for something where you can Blam Blam Stabby Stabby Blam Blam- you probably won't.It's different than anything i have played before, and different than I expected. That said- I enjoyed it. YMMV.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: It's a short game, yes, but it backs a good deal of emotional depth into that time. Some dynamite characterisation - I felt like I got a good read on the protagonist early, and then filled in a good amount of the "why" of him as we went. Circumstance. Principle. It paced well, and while it's a largely linear experience it still felt like there were things you had agency over. Right on up until you didn't, of course.My favourite part: Now I think I'm gonna just quietly sit a spell and think about it some more. And that's part of Adios too, friendo.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is the final walk you take around your house and reflections on the events, things, and loved ones that lead your life down its current path and helped to form who you are while you prepare to leave your life behind. The farmer slowly putting into words all the doubts about the life he's been living for himself and for his long time friend, partner in crime, and potential killer over the course of the day. Often while your friend tries to dissuade you from your course of action or to change topics on what often starts as a more mundane subject but ends as something more personal for one or both men. Simple but beautifully somber setting, with attention to small details.Occasionally, you are able to choose from different dialogue prompts when asked a question, but who your character is and the decisions they have made is already set and no inconsequential change, horse shoe victory, flavor soda you throw your friend, or how spicy you make your curry will change the ending. That you can't alter who your character is to create some ridiculous ending and that the most narratively altering thing the conversation choices do is to offer you blocked out choices for things that the farmer really wants to say, is afraid to say, or is considering saying when overtaken by emotion only gives more insight into his state of mind.A grounded and well told story with an excellent voice cast that help to further highlight and bring the needed emotion to the the well written dialogue.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Places a bright red apple in the horses mouth. "" ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°) ╭༼ ʘ̆~◞౪◟~ʘ̆ ༽╮Yea, so this is a walking simulator with not a lot of walking and exploring. It's more of a stand still and listen/imagine simulator. I really thought I would enjoy this game; the story has a great and unique premise. I'm also not one to shy away from slow paced games. Besides the opening scene, this game just left me feeling bored. The voice acting was great, seemed very fitting for the characters. Shame that most of the things they were saying wasn't doing it for me. I don't care about the neighbors house, or the chestnut tree! Tell me more about the disposing of bodies for the mob, that was the great unique thing about this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Short and bittersweet, Adios is a tightly focused story. There's obvious backstory, and some of it is addressed, but the rest belongs to the characters, which helps make them feel like real people with real lives and history. The voice acting is probably the strongest aspect of this story, some of the best I've experienced.I'm not really going to focus on the gameplay aspects here. Could they be more polished? Sure? Are they functional? 99% of the time (I hit a weird timing condition issue while shoveling manure. It recovered fine.). Is this game doing anything groundbreaking with movement, aiming, or UX? No, not really. The "gameplay" is simple, but I think the feelings this game with leave you with are anything but. I would enjoy reading this as a short story. I would enjoy watching this as a short movie. However, I think it really shines as a game because you have to walk alongside the pig farmer and AS the pig farmer, to the inevitable outcome. Simply watching or reading as an external, removed "other" would diminish the experience. This game manages to make activities like feeding a horse, preparing dinner, and fishing for "the big one" peaceful, tragic, dreadful, and somehow, triumphant. Highly recommend, even at full price, even with an approximate 2 hour experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A quirky Indie game, good story and voice overs. Basic mechanics in terms of game-play. Overall very short and not worth the full price tag in my opinion. Completed story in about 1.5 hours, to fully complete all achievements took me only 2.3 hours! I would only recommend Adios if you can get this on a massive discount or free.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Probably one of the most overrated games of all time. I can totally understand that this is about story and not game play. Hell that's the entire reason I bought it. The problem is, the story just really isn't that good. Like at all. All the reviews talking about feeling pain and what-not don't make any sense. I've played non-story focused games with a more engaging story than this.This game is a story, the story is bad. I don't recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A fellow Narrative Designer purchased this game for me to play to explore a character-driven story to inspire my journey on crafting my own. I absolutely adored playing this game and did it all in one sitting! The greyed out options of things you wish you could've made the old man say were frustrating and I'll never forget the harrowing phone call with the son.It was a sad end to what seemed to be an attempt for the man to reconcile with his crimes and mistakes. I also really enjoyed the banter between the mob member and the farmer. Both trying and failing to listen to one another's sides and how desperate both were to leave on what they conversely thought were "good terms".Would definitely recommend to anyone as a gift or a game to play for yourself!
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, don't come to this game expecting "content." It is clearly a narrative that is driven by top-notch performances and quality art, but it is not the kind of game you repeatedly play to master some sort of mechanic (except maybe horse shoes?). It's a narrative. It's a story. It's literature. All the pieces come together to serve that purpose and it's good at it.This game is an incredibly heartbreaking story that parallels the lost soul of America. I don't want to spoil anything, so it's hard to talk about, but there is a fight going on underneath the narrative of this game between the value of capitol and the value of passion and how the former seems apt at getting otherwise good people to do terrible things. It's a story about love, regret, passion, and the meaning of life as a whole. It's a game about how we've destroyed the beauty and joy of our world in favor of consumption. It's about how systemically, it feels impossible to avoid the evil. Instead of talking too much, I'll leave you with a bit of dialog from the game:Farmer: We all end up dead in the end, don't we?Hitman: I'd rather live as long as possible.Farmer: What good is that?Hitman: Living?Farmer: What good is living if you ain't happy?Hitman: Who says I'm not happy?Farmer: I'm not.Hitman: You could be.Farmer: No. I don't think I could.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: What a great little story to get sucked into. Is the game short? Sure, but it's filled to the brim with charm and attention to detail. The authenticity of it all is striking. The voice acting and writing are top notch and if you're at all a person who enjoys a well thought out story then you're in for a treat. Worth every penny.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios was... an experience. You can finish it in a couple of hours but is such a touching experiene that you'd be hard pressed to find something as emotional as this. Not in a blatant or easy way, but in a  more subtle way: there is not asingle thing that overshadwos the rest, and when you combine them all, the writing, the voice acting, and even the game mechanics themselves, you get a taste of something truly unqiue, something that you cannot probably experience in any other form of media.Do yourself a favor, set aside a couple of hours on a lazy afternoon, and play through in a sitting without distractions. You will not regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: This is a difficult title to review on a thumbs-up vs thumbs-down basis. I really enjoyed my time with Adios, it's well-written and well-acted, the directorial vision is coherent, and the narrative is tightly packaged. I want to give it a thumbs-up for those reasons, but the issue is that Adios just isn't really much of a game. Mischief had a great idea for a very simple short story and chose entirely the wrong medium to tell it.There is no real gameplay in Adios - no meaningful interactivity with the game world, and no reason for the player to be in control at any point during its ~40 minute runtime. It is essentially a minimally-animated short where you listen to two folks exchange dialogue while walking around a farm. The content is compelling, but this really, really should have been a short film, not a game.Another tiny critique: characters in Adios don't really have facial animations. Given that the game is essentially an hour of nothing but dialogue, this feels extra wooden and surprisingly jarring, given the calibre of voice acting on display (and it is really very good).Again, Steam's review system makes this difficult to express; I think the team at Mischief are talented writers and mood-setters, and I hope they make more content, but I'm not convinced that it's worth shelling out $18 for this when watching a playthrough on YouTube will deliver a fundamentally identical experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Man, I'm disappointed. I adore walking simulators and bite-sized, story-driven games, so I *really* thought I'd enjoy Adios and its unique storyline. Unfortunately, this game just didn't do it for me. Adios takes a "tell, don't show" approach and repeatedly hits you over the head with long streams of dialogue about... basically everything in the main character's life. The topics of the five minute speeches range from discussions of the morality of war to his experiences fixing cars. It's not that it's a *bad* game, but it's less of a walking simulator and more of a "listen to someone talk "simulator. There are some events that occur in the latter portion of the game that gave some context to the rambling speeches (which are fantastically voice acted!), but by then, my interest was largely gone. It's clear from the reviews that this game really resonated with some people, but it just didn't hit the mark for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a short story about the contradiction of getting up each day to perform mundane tasks in full knowledge that they can't change your prior actions, while also needing to somehow atone for those actions. The game is not a huge branching narrative adventure, but a focused window on a single day. I don't believe it's possible for your choices to change the outcome, and while some might find that frustrating I think it plays to the themes of the story. The writing and acting is on point, and I found the whole experience quite moving.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: "I've got the notion, and the notion's got me. So, least I can do is tell you Adios"One of the best indie games of the past decade. Adios is a well made, deeply solemn 2 hour meditation on one phrase. "I can't do this anymore." Voice acting and writing are the games highlights, but that doesn't mean it's a game where you just sit and watch. You participate in conversations, chores, mini games, even cooking, all while reflecting on your life, and your mistakes. Its gameplay is somewhat minimal but engaging. You're there for the story, but its not happening at you, its happening around you. The two concepts of game and narrative are put together superfluously, which makes for an easy going but hard hitting experience.Adios is something I would be remiss not to recommend or review. Anyone who plays games or loves good stories NEEDS to buy and play Adios. I consider it essential to 2010's indie game canon.  Do NOT skip this one
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A very beautiful and solemn game about mortality, life and the choices we make along the way. An incredible amount of content and story is packed into a roughly 1hr playthrough, never overwhelming but enough to keep you plugging away at the story to see where it goes.Highly recommend if you're the sort of person that likes to consume a piece of art and then sit with it for a while, find something within it within yourself.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: This wasn't for me, for macro and micro reasons. In this review, I'll basically be spoiling the whole game, so be warned. It's short, anyway.This game, as it says in the blurb, is about a pig farmer who helps dispose of bodies for the mafia. One day, he decides to quit, knowing that that means his mafia contact will have to kill him. But that's ok, because he wants to die. Section one is the farmer and the mafia hitman going around the farm doing little activities like playing horseshoes and milking goats, all the while talking about their shared past, with the hitman trying to talk the farmer out of quitting. This first section ends when the hitman realizes the farmer's decision is final, gives him the afternoon to put his affairs in order, and leaves.Section two is another few activities. The farmer catches a fish he's apparently been after for a while, says goodbye to his beloved horse and dead dog, calls his estranged son to try to patch things up one last time, and contacts his neighbor to make sure his animals are taken care of after he's gone. Then the farmer cooks himself one final meal, sits down at his table, and the hitman comes in and shoots him in the head. The end. Roll credits. On a macro level, neither the story nor the way it was presented worked for me. The themes (an old man, a Vietnam vet, feeling lonely and detached from the world after all his loved ones have died and his son refuses to talk to him, etc.) didn't resonate with me. They're far from my own experience, so it would have taken some effort to get me to feel them. This is something a video game could have done well: it could have put me in situations that allowed me to experience these things myself. Over the course of a longer game, I could have played through vignettes from this man's life. Gotten to know his wife, and his son, and the hitman, so we could get a feel for the passage of time and the pain of having these relationships wither and die. Experience the good times, then watch the wife get Alzheimer's, have to make the difficult choice to put her in the home, and see the effect it has on the farmer's relationship with his son firsthand. That way, we would also have been more invested in the hitman's efforts to talk the farmer, his friend, out of dying. Instead, we are told, not shown, these things after the fact through a series of conversations over the course of an hour or so. None of it feels earned.The game's brevity really works against it in terms of storytelling, I feel. We just sort of have to take the guy's word for all of it--we hardly know him. For example, catching the fish doesn't feel like the epic conclusion to a long struggle, because you find out about the fish's existence minutes before you catch it. There's no relationship there, either. There was so much storytelling potential, too: maybe the farmer loved fishing with his wife, and tried to catch it as a gift for her. Maybe he tried fishing with his son when the relationship was falling apart, and desperately wanted to catch it as a last-ditch effort to impress him, or something. And only at the end of his life, when all his relationships have failed and it doesn't matter anymore, does he finally manage to catch it. That would have been poignant, a metaphor for trying to force things vs. accepting them, maybe. Here, it's an item to tick off a list. Why is the fish called the Admiral? It's never explained.On a micro level, a few overtly video game-y things kept pulling me out of the story. When you talk to the hitman, he cycles through a few different idle animations that make it blatantly obvious that you're talking to a video game NPC. And the achievements detract from the experience, too. This isn't Call of Duty--I don't need a little congratulatory pop-up to appear when I hit E on the piano. Also, during the most gameplay-intensive part (cooking the meal) the controls felt clunky and unintuitive. I kept dropping food and/or the knife on the floor.And right at the end, when you sit down to your final meal and wait for the hitman to come kill you, you have to bring up your shotgun from the cellar and it's sitting next to you on the table, ready to go. Why? I was expecting something like the end of Spec Ops: The Line, where you can decide whether or not to start shooting. That would have added a little interactivity and an interesting story note to the ending. But, no. Nothing.There were a few things I liked. The writing was fine (the dialogue was natural and believable, which I know is no easy feat), and the voice acting was good. The game looks nice. And there are a few times where dialogue choices are grayed out, which is a cool visual indicator of the things the farmer would like to say, but can't (though I could have done without the voiced "hmm" when you select a grayed-out option). But overall, this was in the vein of other story-focused games like Kentucky Route Zero or Gris that just didn't do it for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios has a lot in common with stage plays. Focus on just a few characters and a fairly simple scenario that becomes complex in understanding the characters involved. It's existence as a game allows it to more naturally have a 100% first person camera focus and the multiple-choice dialogue options are used in clever ways to say things which would otherwise remain unsaid. While the character animations are often minimalist in carrying the emotions of the characters I must applaud the voice acting in this game. Both of the leads truly lift the script to new heights and each line carries meaning in its tone and delivery. Even the lack of voice lines is used to great effect in some scenes (players of the game know which one I mean).The only caveat I have is that for a lot of players paying about 15€ for a 1.5-2 hour narrative experience is going to be too much. I can't tell you what is or what is not worth your money. If the premise or the idea of a unique, introspective narrative experience with sublime voice acting interests you I think its worth giving this game a shot.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: I wish steam had a more neutral means of reviewing a game because I don't dislike it, just' I don't think it's anything spectacular as a game. This feels like a great story that should of been done in a different medium, as any element resembling a game kind of falls apart quickly, the dialogue branches aren't different enough to justify multiple playthroughs, the "Minigames" that are here at clunky at the best, nothing at worst, and you will need to just stand around looking at models that aren't the most visually appealing. This is a good story preformed by great voice actors that does well in selling the emotion its trying to, but I just wish it was a short film or a book more than a game.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: I follow one of the guys who made this on Twitter. I told him if he liked it, I'd buy it to make him feel better. seventy minutes later and one full game completed it was well worth it. You cannot discuss Adios in the way you discuss a longer game, the story is incredibly present but its short, compared to other games non existent in length. The irony is that is the A-plot, the B-plot of Adios is tightly written alongside the main ideas the primary story is telling. Neither are bad and in a lesser writers hands it would be ruined. The story presented at Face Value of two men, discussing their lives, how they have changed what happens going forward. The plot in the background, however, speaks to a deep understanding of a certain kind of loss that is hard to execute without being cheesy in the best case or insulting in the worst. Adios is neither, a well written story, great voice acting and for me personally a believable performance from every member of the cast. The concept of how this story was delivered via the gameplay gives the scenario a tangible amount of realism; if the writer or writers lived on a farm and this was how they lived, I would believe it.I was engage, I felt the emotions they were trying to get me to feel, and I enjoyed my time with Adios completely.  Even if this review sounded negative at all, it isn't. Indi games like this are the ones you hear about in the news in terms of their quality; and Adios deserve to be praised in the most genuine way I can express. Take 2 hours, maybe less, and learn what it means to be a rich pig farmer.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Subtle Story Lovers who want something down to Earth.  Adios is one of those games where you wish that there was a bit more of a budget for the game to work with, because you know that there's a solid foundation at the surface here, but it can only get so far with what it has to work with. The game's biggest selling point is its story, which isn't bombastic or over the top like you may think with the game's store page and the crime aspects related to it, but is a character study of how one man deals with life pushing at him from every angle, and how he responds to trauma. It's emotional in the right ways, and some stellar voice acting from our two main leads helps propel the game forward and make you look into every conversation and its subtext. Subtlety isn't exactly a common skill in writing like this but the game pulls it off wonderfully, and it's a game that you'll sit and think about for hours after you play about what you'd do in the situation, and the themes surronding it.This however contrasts the cement shoes that the game is working with. I don't expect the most robust presentations for a small game like this, and model and visuals wise the game is reasonable at times. It just doesn't sell the emotions of its writing well, and can take you out of the experience very quickly, especially if you get a bug or two that breaks any sort of immersion. It doesn't help that the world feels somewhat dead, and there's a lot of space to work with but not a lot to do in a free roam. It's also clunky: UI interactions and general menu navigation has problems: from confirmations on resolution screens happening when you first launch the game despite not touching it, to the game sometimes bugging out and not letting you do a task that you need to do.The biggest gotcha however is the time of content. Don't let my hours played here fool you, some idiot named Dragnix left the game on overnight. To get through the main story, you're probably looking at 2 hours tops, and replayability is only slight with achievement hunting. Exploring the world doesn't add a lot either with a lack of interactables, and for some, the price tag is going to be too much compared to what other games in the genre are offering. It's a game worth playing, but it's a game worth playing at a price you're comfortable at for that level of content, even if the writing is quality. I'd say for most its a sale title, but watch my video review to navigate if the game is right for you.

There isn't really too much to say about the game, if you looked up anything about it you know what its about and what youre expecting is what youre gonna get.I wholeheartedly recommend it.
