_childDocuments_.review: The forest for the chestnut trees.Let me preface this with my expectations first, as this is important to my evaluation. I heard about this game by seeing a lot of folks responsible for AAA level games talk about it on twitter as if this was going to be a transformative work. I have found it to be anything but, and I will admit this added to my disappointment with the end-product.Now with that out of the way, lets talk. I'll start with what the game got right: audio + visuals. The game looks really nice, and sets the tone quite well, very few complaints here. As for the audio, what can be said? The team did a great job with the sound design and stellar voice acting. Real good stuff. Anyways, I think anyone who is interested in this game should recognize that these aren't really the reasons you're here. The main attraction of this game is the narrative experience, and as such, I mostly want to focus on that, instead of the small bugs or technical flaws that are present.The narrative component of this game, is in a word, sophomoric. In a vacuum, this story might have been something memorable, but the author really overlooked his audience, and left them hanging in a space that deflated much of the intent. It is extremely clear to me that the author wanted the player to inhabit the head space of our dear main character, and while doing as much as he can to accomplish that, he never quite achieves it. The narrative is over-transparent and under designed to that end. From square one the player is completely conscious of the fact that he (the farmer) will die, that there is no altering of fate, that there is one solution to the puzzle. This critical error results in a heavy disassociation from the character. The player is already God, he knows that there is no meaning in the battle being fought, he has no investment in the farmer's internal struggle to do right, no reason to ponder what it means to die. The time, place, and reason for death are predetermined: the player no longer has the room to occupy the farmer's consciousness, they are forced to observe in a middle ground. One without agency to change the result (or even the illusion of agency that the farmer may feel), and also one without the ability to truly empathize with the character they're meant to inhabit. Adios manages to walk the line between two narrative styles while falling victim to the drawbacks of both. I really think the author failed to understand the perspective he presents to the audience here, and all the things they are observing and feeling along the way. The game seemed so focused on its idea that it , well, missed the forest for the trees. While it might seem strange to even bring this up so deep in the review, I think it is important to be critical of the chosen medium here. This story was purposely put into game form, for better or worse. I don't entirely disagree with the decision, I think that it may have been served better as a piece of literature, film, etc. that plays more to the writers strength. There was almost no leverage of what games offer as a unique medium. In particular, on an interactive level. I felt the individual acts the player was made to do: fishing, cooking, caring for animals, etc etc simply had very little gravitas. They aren't well designed or impactful, perhaps even oversimplified. The player isn't really given any time to reflect on what is happening, or to collect their own thoughts and feelings about the situation. Either the entire time they're instead splitting their attention between the conversation at hand(which is often times way, way overwritten. We'll circle back to this in a moment)  and the task. Or as with say, the fishing minigame, it is over so absurdly quickly the player could blink and it would be over. This is a moment that above all others, probably would've benefitted from simply allowing the player to reflect and absorb, as it is with *real* fishing. That's not to say ALL of the individual tasks don't land, the phone calls for example were well executed, and maybe accounted for MOST of the emotional weight of the story. As a whole however, most of the tasks fail to make the player FEEL anything, and that's a huge miss with an experience so streamlined and pared-down.  Speaking of things that are streamlined (or maybe aren't), lets make a segue to the dialogue/writing itself, rather than just the overall structure. This is the part that really took me out of the experience. How do I put this? The writer tried real hard to come off as charming or quirky with his writing. He wants you to understand hes writing directly to you, to show you how unique he is, that he knows and sees things you don't. It comes off in a pretty annoying manner to be frank. It feels like hes a media obsessed high schooler who just came off a weekend of marathoning Palahniuk novels and Tarantino films, but without understanding any of the reasons they use the tools they do, and when to use them. The little -isms that were hamfisted into the script, the tiny environmental details and decisions, even the arrangement of some of the dialogue and item prompts (labeling a door Bill). They were all just so, so heavy handed and grating. When they popped up, it felt like a fourth wall break that just kind of left me unable to focus and be immersed. Much of the moment to moment writing can be pretty good, but I think that there is a really poor understanding of the flow of human conversation, or some really wide attempt at creating character interest by making dialogue stilted, unnatural, and awkward. I'm not sure if the author thinks that is how people talk, or just really needed to force the narrative so harshly but the end product is just whiplash. From shovelling manure to Vietnam flashbacks in the blink of an eye. Or gatekeeping the very concept of hobbies. It simply doesn't fit in a situation crafted SO explicitly to be grounded, and real: an outpouring of a dead man's soul in front of his executioner. The pieces just don't *quite* fit together in the end. Its a really difficult thing to write in a way that both generates interest, but stays grounded, and I admire the effort, but it falls just shy. At the end of the day, Adios is not bad. It feels like it could've been as good as I was lead to believe, but it outsmarted itself. I don't recommend this game/experience. I do recommend their future, unfinished work. This is sort of like a college student's thesis paper: well researched and with decent technical execution, but sorely lacking the experience and perspective to make something profound. You won't get much out of Adios that cant be had elsewhere, to more effect. Much of whats here has been seen before, and that's not necessarily bad, but I want it to be clear there isn't something new to discover here. And I certainly don't think that you'll feel much of anything playing it. But. But. Watch this team though. In the future, these dudes really could make something very special with the experience they've gained making this.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A short but moving narrative that is driven by its exceptional dialogue and performance. There's an undercurrent of dread throughout the exchanges between the two main characters -- despite being flowered with pleasantries and hobbyist-level (although interesting) explanations of farming. These long-form conversations seem fit for stage plays or Quentin Tarantino movies and successfully pull you in, helping you form a mental image of who these characters are. As such, they'll stick with you well after the credits roll.

_childDocuments_.review: You can always tell when a game is made by people who are interested in things. Not in a vague sense of "we wanted to see what would happen if we jammed this story into this other genre" or overly lofty concepts, but in small things: Trees, rivalries with fish, the method and therapy of milking a goat, the strange discomfort you get around horses. Or the relatable sense of wanting to have done something, to be able to save or preserve anything you could, long after the moment has passed. This is one of those games. A walking sim where you don't just walk, and a story that leaves aside the lumpy piles of exposition in favor of character moments that get more done in ninety minutes than most seasons of TV.Plus it has a shotgun.

_childDocuments_.review: I review walking sims for the "walking sim fan club" group so after playing a good 100 of them I feel I can confortably review this one. Truth is, it's linear, it's very short, and it's well put together so a refund wouldn't be fair. But at full price, I cannot recommend this when other games run at the same price on discount and deliver 10+ hours experiences. The 1.7h you see on my timer were spent looking for alternative endings, alternatives to ... anything really. There are none. It's more of an interactive movie where you are not in control. GFX are decent but 60fps at SUW 32:9 is a bit low. The rocks looked odd. There is support for SUW but to read the journal you'll have to switch back and forth so kiss goodbye to adaptive sync unless you like to fiddle with your G9 constantly. Overall, a disapointing experience which I hope will lead to better games.

_childDocuments_.review: Sometimes some small games get a lot of buzz happening around them, praising the storytelling or the mood of the game or what not. Adios was one of these games for me as since its release a couple of months ago, I’ve heard a lot of good things about the game, with lots of “even if it’s 90 minutes long”. And I like short and succinct story driven games, as they are a rarity and are very hard to do well. Having played the game, I must say that while I can understand someone liking it, it didn’t really do it for me.The premise of the game is listed on the store page – you play as an old farmer who was helping with disposing bodies for the mob for years, wants out. And you play through what is likely to be his last day alive, hanging out the person who is still somewhat of a friend, but will probably become his killer because of his decision, doing chores, trying to say goodbyes. There are some sections that are just dialogue, with choices that don’t matter much and some sections with simple interactions which are still mostly dialogue.And it’s moody and nice and some parts of the script were really nice. Yet, even ignoring the terrible sound mix where the voices can be barely heard most of the time, I feel like there’s not really much for you to care about unless some of the elements resonate with you personally. Curiously, even the premise that I’ve mentioned, isn’t really spelled out inside the game as well, as if the store page description is meant to be taken as part of the experience. Is the game worth spending 90 minutes on, if you stumble upon it especially on sale? Sure. Is it fine if you skip it and never check it out? Yeah, you’ll probably not miss much.

_childDocuments_.review: Last day of work.'Last days' are very interesting things. Last day of school, last day living with your parents, last day in a relationship before breaking it off, last day working at the job you've worked at for ages. People get used to things. Like a ritual you go through certain motions, you feel good when things go just like usual because you feel comfort in things not changing. When it's a 'last day', change confronts you head-on. Adios puts you in someone else's life as they go through their last day of work. You learn what their rituals were, what gave them comfort, what was given up for that comfort, and why things have to change. It acts as both "examination of life" and as "slice of life" on a day where things have gone the same for far too long. This is a change that not only effects the life you examine, but the lives of all those around them to varying degrees.This game is structured in a way where you can freely transition from scene to scene in very natural ways without having to worry about plot order or relevance, allowing it to smoothly sail along. While there are things to keep you occupied, nothing will distract you from the story as it builds, and anytime you need a break you can look around at the small details that give the game a wonderful sense of lived-in depth.I very much recommend this game. Give it time to digest, play it again a month or two after your first playthrough. Consider your own life alongside it, and prepare for your next 'last day'.

_childDocuments_.review: This review has been a long time coming, but I suppose there is no better time than a Steam sale to finally write it. Adios is probably my favorite game of 2021. I don’t deal with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ like “best” and “worst,” and I’m not terribly interested in giving you an IGN wannabe look at this game. All of this is just my opinion and what I enjoyed this year. Adios is the type of game and story that transcends its story and environment. The game is literally about a man who decides to stop letting the mob dump bodies at his pig farm, but if you’ve played it you’ll know it’s also about so much more. This game is about family and relationships. It’s about what it means to do the right thing, even if you won’t receive acknowledgment for it and if doing the right thing may actually be bad for your well-being. This is a story that could only work as a game. Through a series of vignettes the game weaves the story of a man living his last day and just reconcile that fact with the man who will probably kill him - the friend who will probably kill him. If any of that sounds intriguing pick it up. I loved the time I spent with it and I can’t wait until some of the details fade a little and I can experience it again. It’s a fantastic journey, and it respects its players as well as their time.

_childDocuments_.review: First off this is indeed a small team indie game, and I'm sure what small bugs there are will be fixed rapidly, because this comes over as such a passion project, and they didn't interfere with my enjoyment of the game. On the whole the game has visual polish and art direction that certainly can carry the weighty goals of story telling its trying to achieve. I've just started the game and I can already tell the care with which the story is being setup and the quality of the dialogue that this is quite something different.  Its cinematic, not in cut-scenes or in a way we normally associate with games, but rather in the story its trying to tell and the scenes it is recreating. I'd say the experience is sort-off like stepping into a "No Country for old Men" or even some of the scenes of American live in the Preacher graphic novels, where violence and hardship might not be immediate, but something under the surface always present.A slow exploration of country living that is so uniquely american its often hard for Europeans or other suburbanites to fully comprehend.  Even after just the first dialogues, you can feel the hidden layers behind the languid and deliberate dialogue setting, are you underestimating what is unfolding?, or is it  truly about someone giving up? And you want to find out by sheer strength of storytelling. The voice acting, especially of the lead character, is exceptional, now I'm not an american so I get fooled pretty easy, but it did put me in the mood of so many a film I've enjoyed, be it westerns or modern shows like Fargo.  I think this is a game that needs to be supported it takes you too places you've never been before, which is what I play games for!.

_childDocuments_.review: It's going to be some time before I can play this through a second time.  I wont give any spoilers here.* The game is short, should take 70ish minutes to run all the way through.* I personally experienced no bugs; some people have. Some have already been fixed by the time you read this.* Could this have been a Visual Novel or even an Audio Drama? Possibly. Putting it in the first person, I believe, is necessary for the experience.* The graphics aren't exactly bleeding edge. The mouth movements are kinda funky and limited. The farm, however, is vast and beautiful. The game looks damn good.The reason you're playing this is to experience the story. You're not spending 70 minutes reading the story, either. I can't say you have a whole lot of agency here but you are here to experience a day in the farmer's life. You have a lot of conversations about yourself, about life, about the world with a good friend who's trying to convince you of something.The voice work is impeccable. Some of the best and most emotive and genuine voice acting I've heard in a game.Is the game worth 18 bucks? To me it was worth $1,241.31 and I'll leave you wondering why that number is so specific.It's worth everything if it gets this team a chance to make another one.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful thing. Worth every cent.If the Criterion Collection were to start a curated games section and publish them to disk, I'd see this being one of the first. _childDocuments_.review: Adios is a short journey worth taking.This game has a strong focus on story in which you are free to roam about a small American farm.There are horses to feed, goats to milk, and mini games to play.If you enjoyed games like Firewatch and Edith Finch - consider it highly recommended.The story of Adios captured me from the very first scene. While the setting and activities you can partake in are relaxing and peaceful, the inevitable trajectory of the story adds a sense of tension from the very beginning. It's clear that there was a lot of care put into that atmosphere which elevates it above many games of similar length.The voice acting is one of the highlights. It is top tier and feels authentic to the setting.The game's dialog serves it well. I particular appreciated how the game allows us to know what the character is thinking - even when they say nothing at all - it adds more weight to some of the themes, such as regret. Yep, this ain't no Barbie Horse Adventures.Adios controls like the FPSs we know and love (HL2?) - and the shooting that it allows feels just right. I didn't experience any of the bugs that might have been present in early releases.It's a job well done for a small team that have made something bigger than the sum of its parts.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: I'm barely recommending this......there is some good storytelling on display here in what is essentially a first-person, walking simulator style visual novel, and some cracking voice acting, but everything devolves down to the same actions and more or less the same voice responses, regardless of what dialogue options you choose, and there's truly no way to avoid the eventual outcome of the tale.The graphics are a little too stylized, but still more than sufficient to convey what is supposed to be going on, the writing and voice acting is decent, and the subject matter is handled in a weighty fashion.However........sometimes things get a little hamfisted, and the interactivity is VERY limited (and the less said about the mechanics of preparing your final meal {meals if you replay the chapter multiple times to get all the cheevos} the better.....yeesh!).So, ultimately a flawed by still enjoyable little piece of noirish storytelling, hampered by moments of clumsy writing, clumsy gameplay, and virtually non-existent story influence by the player.Recommended, but get it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a narrative adventure game (or what the kids would call a "walking simulator") developed by a game developer named Mischief. I don't really know much about this game's history in the slightest, all I personally know is that I either ran into a Youtube playthrough one day or a friend of mine wishlisted it and it said "Disposed of bodies for the mob" and I instantly got giddy and wishlisted it as I love playing games with guys like Paulie and Joey as they eat fettuccine and beat up guys while wearing see through socks and track suits. That being said, this is not that game. In fact I'm going to go out of my way to tell you the gameplay here, as I said it's a "Walking simulator", you go around your farm doing chores and conversating about life with your mafia handler and so you do a lot of walking and clicking on stuff. Personally for me, I was okay with that because primarily it's a story game and it's a game whose themes really resonated in some ways for me.The story goes like this, as stated in the steam store page, you play a Pig Farmer who doesn't want to dispose of bodies and feed the meat to his pigs anymore; all your reasons for doing this arrangement are now gone and you're left with the inevitability of what's to come: regrets and death, something we all will have to come to grasps with eventually in our lives. What follows is you and your mob buddy going around your farm and doing activities such as milking goats, shoveling s h i t, playing horseshoes and more as he tries to convince you not to sever ties. One thing I like about this game is how convincing the relationship between the handler and the farmer; they have a professional relationship and yet they respect each other and joke around, and it upsets him that he won't just continue their business together not only because it's convenient but that because you can't get out of your association with the mafia unless it's through the feds or death and for the farmer, he just wants to die anyways. His life has gone downhill,  mix that in with mortality issues such as death and thoughts on religion, and just wanting there to be some positive end even if there's no sure way that it'll really work due to his past actions.There were many scenes that were poignant to me, the two especially being the section called  a feeling that is all too relatable to me. But however, the most memorable would have to be when  The Farmer isn't a perfect man, in many ways he reminds me of a lot of my father figures; he means well and tries his best, only taking up the job because he wanted to support his family; but ended up messing up a lot of his relationships along the way (not that it excuses their actions).The story is something whose themes I'm not sure I could articulate fully without it actually being experienced as the writing REALLY does it's job well and made me empathize with all the characters in game, each having things that I can identify with in a sense (minus the whole mob shooting people thing of course). The voice acting is phenomenal too, Resident Evil fans will recognize D.C. Douglas (of Albert Wesker fame; EDIT: didn’t know he was a creeper too, the things you learn off the internet ) as your handler but Rick Zieff is the highlight with his farmer, whose voice carries a lot of weight as he shifts emotional tones trying to strike these tough conversations with people, a tone that embodies the character of someone who wishes he did better, something to me that's identifiable. I guess to finish off the review, the graphics the usual indie graphics affair, (the most I could really notice is that the Handler walks kind of funny to me personally), but the design of the farm where you live captures the Early 90s country farm feeling. Everything looks beautiful, but empty; alone, like the Farmer himself. It's a short game, you could complete it in an hour and a half to two if you're going for all the achievements and what I will say here is that the price for this game personally to me is a bit high at 18 dollars but I guess the value is up to the player themselves, as to others the game's handling of themes could more than make up the price and I wouldn't blame them as I'd also recommend plaything through the game multiple times to really digest it emotionally but to me, I'd say wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I love short, narrative driven games, especially those that cover darker or more emotional subject matter, like Adios does, which is why I was really disappointed and surprised that I didn't enjoy this game as much as I thought I would. A lot of the reason for this I think is that the game is just extremely boring. The dialogue was admittedly solid at times but there was also tons of filler that just dragged out the scenes in the game. This isn't helped by the fact that in 90% of the scenes you can't actually do anything so you're stuck standing there looking at this very ugly model of a guy talk about some nonsense. The dialogue in this game is like a 4 year old picking through a salad. 90% of it is awful bland lettuce and only 10% of it is yummy delicious chicken. I found myself looking at my phone, or eating a snack a lot of the time because I just couldn't be asked to listen to the crap being spoken. The visuals are honestly pretty terrible. The animals especially are hideous, and while graphics don't play a big part in my general ranking of a game, in a game like this where all you're doing is staring at them, they were painfully bad. If the dialogue was better, or the game a little bit more interactive I could definitely see myself really enjoying this game, but as it stands now, it's just not fun or interesting at all, which was a real shame. I had to witness the knife flying across the kitchen several times.All in all, fantastic game, highly recommend! Also, support the developer!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a very loquacious person with a lot of thoughts on my mind that I have to keep myself from spilling on a page, but I'm starting to learn that you don't need all the words, the utmost perfection, all the flashiness, all the awe in the world to express what matters to you. _childDocuments_.review: Probably one of the most solid examples of a "traditional" narrative in video game form. Adios is a very short game that follows a linear path, but puts you in the driver's seat for all of it. It's a beautiful story with a couple of twists and turns and a brutal, impactful ending. I think Adios is worth the price and playthrough of it, but do be wary of spoilers as it can suck away a lot of the game's punch. It's not for everyone, it's a quiet and low energy game with next to no gameplay, but if you like good short stories then do try this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is yet another one of those video games that feel like a real good short story. Compared to the likes of Edith Finch, Gone Home, and Firewatch its gameplay mechanics aren't as well synthesized with the story, but the writing, dialogue, and atmosphere really make it worthwhile. It’s a powerful game about death and regrets and the voice actors do a fantastic job bringing it to life.  Definitely worth checking out if you’re looking for a good narrative game.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A very interesting premise that feels kind of wasted. I liked learning about the farmer's life, but it felt like he was vomiting a lot of exposition at someone that is supposed to be an old friend. In a story like this you shouldn't get the whole picture of this person's life, but there still felt there were gaps preventing me from really understanding him.Nearly all the gameplay moments were immersion breaking, like throwing food against a wall when I want to set it down and one chore I couldn't do anything but watch my friend (please ignore me if I missed some button prompts).It's hard to recommend this even on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels like walking through a life you even forgot you have lived in the first place, being confronted by what you've done and what you can (or can't) do to make up for it. It's beautiful and very charming, the dialogue and voice acting are incredible and the grey dialogue options (pay attention to it!!) are a incredible touch.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not entirely sure what to say about this without giving up what makes it so special. To be clear, there isn't some crazy twist or anything. What Adios says on the store page is exactly what it is. If that narrative doesn't interest you, you won't enjoy this game. It's a lot of listening to two friends discuss things, and hitting the number key that corresponds with what you want to say. Sometimes, some answers show up that aren't actually possible to choose, which I thought was kind of a nice touch. They are often the "perfect" answer in the middle of heated arguments, and as in real life, it'd be too easy to have these available. They come as thoughts, not as actual words.Adios is going to stick with me while I lay in bed tonight, and that's probably the highest praise I can give to a game like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: I wish i could say i like this game. So many mechanical issues and narrative directions i find less than, solid. Buggy achievement 'pops'. One scene bugged out so i had to restart it, and another one so hard i actually had to restart the game itself. And the experience doesn't feel worthwhile for the price. But *still*. 'Adios' has ideas, thoughts and a heart i truly respect.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Short, sweet, and poignant.Adios is broken up into "scenes," each one being a conversation, either between you and the Hitman or you and yourself. You can often choose which of these scenes to interact with first. At first the animations for the Hitman were a bit offputting, but the writing, acting, and atmosphere make it fade into the background after 15 minutes or so. Each scene is surprisingly interactive, and there are certain points in the conversations where your actions can interrupt or slightly change the flow of conversation.I encountered a few small bugs here and there, but never anything too distracting. Unfortunately the game didn't run very well for me, despite my machine vastly outpacing the system requirements. But the game doesn't really require any twitch reflexes, so it was easy enough to deal with.Play it.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A well story driven game. There's nothing too much more than that to it. Nor was there meant to be (Well, besides some interact-able objects).When you play this game, just take your time with it. Soak it in. Put on some nice headphones and let the game go. It'll do it's own thing. You? You just do yours. :)I will say, it's a very short game. You can probably beat it in one to an hour and a half. Depends on your pacing. I sat there soaked it in, felt the waves and at the end I did all the achievements for the game. Its a really well written game. If you love games that mostly just do story telling for you, then this game will be for you! It has voice acting and all. :D

_childDocuments_.review: Do you know that scene in HL2 when you first meet Dr Kleiner and instead of listening to him you send items through the mini teleporter and throwing books at people? Well this game is that whole scene but without being able to throw books at people or use the teleporter.I thought I would be entering into something interesting but it was basically just a long boring dialogue between 2 people I really didn't care about. Turn on subtitles and skip dialogue with X to save yourself a lot of time.The voice acting is quite good but the story and the interactive parts are just boring, it would have better served as a short film as I spent half the time just wanting to play the game. Whats that? You like to repair old machines, cool, but don't lock me in a room with nothing to do whilst you spew irrelevant dialogue at me for 10 minutes.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a game with complex controls, rules, collectibles, and skill ceilings, look elsewhere. If you're looking for a game that puts you in the shoes of another person and uses smart narrative design to help you understand their life and experiences, this is worth your time.For a game as short and as small as it is, the stellar writing and voice acting do some phenomenal heavy lifting to the point where you feel like you've known the two main characters a lifetime, all without patronizing verbal exposition. There's a tragic warmth to their relationship that, when all is said and done, makes you wish they'd met under better, far different circumstances. The narrative beats through the entire experience made me wish things could have been different; a sentiment the farmer probably agrees with.The level and game design are simple and straightforward. You're on a farm. You do farm things. The beautifully somber farm is much smaller than your average open world experience. The few live characters are clearly working on budgetary constraints that are fairly well hidden underneath their visual style. But even with all that considered they use every part to their fullest. Arguably the most brilliant execution is how they gate the farmer's dialogue to show you the things he wishes he could say out loud.I wish more games were this small and straightforward. But until then at least I have this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: You ever lie down on the grass and watch the clouds roll by? Its beautiful, and sad. Sad because its a fleeting moment, something that will not and can not last forever. That's how I felt playing Adios. I was moved by how beautiful the characters were. Their writing and voice acting was phenomenal, and with such a short time with them, I quickly and easily empathized with them. And found myself crying at the end of the game.There were parts where I felt the need to just... stop. To stop moving and just enjoy the scenery. And I really liked that about Adios.Adios is a beautiful, fleeting moment of melancholy. A game that hopes that maybe just maybe you feel a bit more empathy for others. 10 / 10
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Short, but extremely tightly made "Last one out, hit the lights"-toned game. Impossible to talk about without spoilers, but it's very much one of the finest examples of narrative as gameplay. If Disney can charge 30 dollars to watch Mulan's trashy live-action adaptation, Adios can charge 17 for a very-well written story that's about the same length and lets you experience it in any order that feels right.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a good, emotionally engaging story, and I will probably forget about it in a year. To start with the good stuff: The acting and dialogue in this game are largely superb. You like and feel for the characters, even though one of them is an unrepentant murderer who is dead-set on killing the protagonist if he leaves his life. They have depth, although in the case of the hit man, his depth includes a curious lack of depth. While the game is linear, it play with your expectations in places, particularly with the dialogue options. While the character models resemble something from the PS2, they're charming. My criticism, however, centers around the fact that the game part of the game feels tacked on. Doc Buford, the game's writer, discussed on Twitter that he doesn't want to create a "solipsistic" game, where the main character is an extension of the player. The ability to step into another human being's shoes is important for the writer, and I can respect that. That's well and good for the game's plot and dialogue. However, the game permits comparatively little exploration of the character beyond the dialogue that's presented. While some environmental storytelling exists in the game (you have the option to explore some of the character's house, for instance), it feels more like an afterthought. If I were to compare it to another medium, it would be like having a movie with a single emotionally-engaging scene, but the rest consisting of a text crawl. At the end of the day, I am not the center of the universe. But I'm also not a pig farmer with a moral crisis. I'm a tourist in this pig farmer's mind. The game sometimes seems to try and actively stymie the exploration of the character and his life at times. There are multiple buildings in the game which serve only a decorative purpose. They don't really serve a role, beyond being something for the player to walk towards, only to sigh and turn away when they see the Unbreakable Padlock of Doom. Telling a story of the inevitable is all well and good, but I'd prefer not to have my hopes raised with the possibility of more information, only for them to be dashed by a building that only serves to ruin the view of a lovely-looking little pond. The game is also rather buggy in places. However, I'd still recommend it. Maybe wait for a sale though.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: The writing is excellent. The subtlety is sublime, and the voice acting delivers the subtlety and significance of its lines. As a video game, it can be a bit buggy or counterintuitive i.e. when replaying a section of the game for an achievement, I got a soft lock that require me to restart the game. But I do enjoy what it does with some of its dialogue choices or lack thereof ― a simple, subtle way of telling its story through its game mechanics. That being said, it mostly feels like a short play put within a video game, so for everyone else, unless you are really into story games, I cannot recommend buying the game unless it is on sale. Nonetheless, to put it in another perspective, if you are the kind of person that would pay the cost of about 1-2 movie tickets to watch something like Of Mice and Men or 12 Angry Men, then I can recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: an absolutely beautiful experience  games in general allow for such an intimate relationship with the atmosphere,places and characters in them and adios is one of the best in allowing you to just experience a vibe, a feeling and a life through a placeeverything about the game is packed with love, care and attention it also has some of the most creative narrative design decisions in recent memory, cannot remember scene cuts or dialogue option being done this way in any other game in recent memory(and i fear i will never be the same after seeing thats what can be done lol) and all this is just a side note to an extremely tight story that will make you feel many things if you are in a melancholic mood (and/or maybe want cry your eyes out and feel some things), please buy this game

_childDocuments_.review: This game has two things going for it:- excellent voice acting- excellent writingFortunately, for a narrative game, these are the two most important elements, and it mostly knocks them out of the park. Not only are both of the principal characters well sketched out and well portrayed by their respective actors, even the small, side characters are as well. For these reasons alone, I clicked the "Yes" for recommending it....which is fortunate, because everything else about this game is a bit of a hot mess. I got this and played it on release day, and I know a patch was also released today, so by the time you read this, sometime in the future, my principle complaint might be fixed: The game is buggy as ... well, I can't even think of a comparison. It's definitely the buggiest single piece of software I've ever used. Very little in it works -- certainly more things don't work than do -- and lots of the bugs are game-breaking. I had to quit right out of the game and then relaunch and sit through an entire scene over again on multiple occasions because something bugged out so hard it couldn't be recovered from. Once I got launched into the stratosphere, which was actually sort of fun and allowed me a really good view of the neighbourhood (the tree lines go surprisingly far out), but I also never game down so that was a quit-and-relaunch. Also, the settings menu doesn't work, which seems so basic that I don't even know how it could be released that way. And in its current state, make sure nothing ever interrupts your gameplay at all, because if you pause it (by bringing up the menu, for example), when you unpause it (by using the undocumented secret feature to press ESC -- the menu doesn't have an option for exiting it otherwise without quitting or restarting the scene) the dialogue will continue, but having skipped a considerable amount of time, so you'll have to go back and rewatch the whole scene to see what you missed. Most objects aren't interactive, but the ones that are will almost always do something bad, and putting things down is nearly impossible without throwing them around the room. The climactic moment of the entire game involved a character clipping right through the wall, which robbed it of a lot of its impact because it was so goofy. The whole final scene was full of goofy glitches that ruined the mood of the whole thing.That's really why the bugginess was such a big deal to me, in the end. I don't mind an indie game being relatively restrictive in what you can do, but the developers tried to make this much more "open" than it needed to be, and in the process, they completely ruined the tone of a lot of scenes, by way of having serious and emotional moments be accompanied by bugs that were anywhere from mildly irksome to outright ridiculous.Which is too bad, because otherwise it's a great, solemn story that deserved to be treated better.Ultimately, though, the game is a bit less than 90 minutes long and while it would have made a MUCH better podcast than a video game, it's still worth checking out on sale. I can't really say CA$20.99 is worth it for under an hour and a half of buggy gameplay in good conscience, but heavily discounted, it's a worthwhile experience that you'd be remiss to pass up. Even in AAA games, I've seen little writing and acting that compares.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a game about the journey not the destination.In an hour you get to learn so much about this man, his family and his relationship with the mob, every dialogue brings new information in a way that feels organic and just right, the word choice communicates so much about the characters it's amazing.The art style may clash a bit with the tone of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A short but incredibly poignant storytelling game.The graphics are pretty basic but I think that's fine, and possibly helps me focus more on the story being told, instead of how flashy it's being told. Despite the simplicity, the visuals are clean and somewhat muted in color, making for a very distinctive look.The audio is where this game really shines. From the lack of any music, to the subtle but immersive wind in the background, and most of all the outstanding voice-acting. It really makes this game shine, and the emotion in just the voices, even with only simple graphics to support, evokes feelings that will last quite a bit longer than the length of the game. Major props to all the voice-actors.So, to conclude: Adios is a fantastically written, brilliantly voiced narrative that, while short, will stick in the memories of those who play it. I would highly recommend this to anyone and everyone I know.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a delightful narrative experience, largely driven by Rick Zieff's incredible voice work. His performance as The Farmer is captivating, and drives home every emotional beat the script needed him to hit.And this game largely lives or dies on its script & voice work, there are some tasks and interactions that help you inhabit The Farmer and bring life to this final day but nothing on the level of a bigger budget game like Edith Finch. It's greatest gameplay quirk is offering you dialogue options that your character thinks, but just can't bring himself to say, a tool that is introduced slowly and then delivered on with devastating effect.This game made me tear up, and then it made me weep like a baby. 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a bit short, a bit linear, and has a couple little control issues. That concludes my negatives about Adios.This is ultimately a playable story, and so whether you like it is mostly going to be based on three things: what you think of this kind of story, how well-written (and acted) it is, and how well it uses the medium of a game to tell it. For my money, the acting is great, the writing is great, and it while this definitely isn't an especially "gamey" game, it does communicate some things in neat ways that only really work in videogame form.That just leaves how much you get on with this kind of story.This game is quiet, and subtle. Your character is in a situation he is certain he is not going to escape from, and so escape isn't his goal. You don't spend the game pleading for his life, but reminiscing about it; one simple day, telling his stories, before the big Adios. And that put me in an odd position because... This isn't the kind of story I generally like. I'm into bombastic action, emotional highs, the good guys winning and a happy ending to cap it off, and this doesn't fit the bill... But it's also not the kind of thing I hate, tales of relentless misery with no end in sight. (If there's one thing this game has, it's an end in its sights.)I think, in the end, that's why I enjoyed it. I haven't quite seen this story before. In its own quiet way, it's pretty revolutionary.I can imagine the cost is going to turn some people off, and if that's a barrier for you, I get it; money doesn't come for free. For me, I'm happy with my purchase, and happy I'm supporting the people making this. Nice work, team.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: The game is great, I loved the story. It got to be dragging on after while, then it just ended. This game took 2 hours to beat and is not worth $18, it is worth $10. Would I recommend this game to a friend? If they had extra money lying around, YES! I think games from this developer will be better in the future, but this is a great start from them!
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: I love slice of life stuff so much! Even if that slice of life is surrounding a fellow who wants out of a nefarious business and knows without a doubt his life will be sliced.It was a cool blend of walking simulator with the feeling of a visual novel. The voicing acting was a nice touch and the atmosphere was dense. Everything felt stiff and stale like an expired loaf of bread. Normally one would use this in a negative context. But not here. Given the subject material and the medium it was presented in, it's anything but moldy. Just dry. Perfect for breadcrumbs. Perfectly digestible and immersive.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: What appears at first like a fairly simple story grows with each scene, offering the story of a person who is too tired to really continue with the life he's lived. The choices made throughout the game grow and often offer surprising options. This is well worth your time if you're looking for a nice, albeit heartstring pulling story.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A deep meditative look at regret and the resolve it takes to go through with a hard decision. I rarely get emotional over games but the conversation about doing one good thing with the hitman nearly brought me to tears. I wholeheartedly recommend this product to anyone who wants a short, powerful experience. Well worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: I give this one a cautious recommendation. It's less than two hours long, and unapologetically a walking sim, but the polish of the voice acting and writing along with the premise lets it say something worth listening to. There are currently some issues on the gameplay side I ran into which made things counterintuitive and in one case halted progress, but I'm reviewing shortly after launch day and I expect they're easily patchable. I can see how I would have been gripped through a lot more of it if those issues didn't crop up.I was pleasantly surprised when the point where I expected an ending was only the halfway point. It gets stronger as it goes.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Melancholy. That's how I'd describe Adios.The feeling when you're about to leave something that's dear to you behind, and only have little time left before you have to say goodbye. Wishing time could give you forever to appreciate everything that's dear to you before it's all gone.But there's no going back. This is Adios.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: This is a short game but it's worth picking up. The writing is incredible, and unlike other "walking simulators" you have a lot more you can actually *do* during the game, like fishing, playing a game of horseshoes, cooking a meal, etc. The art is just *slightly* surreal in a great way, and if you play the game slowly (don't spend all your time running with the SHIFT key down like I did) you will really be able to feel the environment, which is lovingly constructed. The game alternates between "freeform" stages, where you can move wherever you like on your farm, and set-piece scenes that trigger when you get close or interact with something. The scenes tell a compelling story, so make sure you listen to the dialogue. But even in the set-pieces you can usually do something fun. I got only 9/25 Achievements in my first play-through so I definitely missed a lot of stuff. Highly recommended for the unique experience, gorgeous environments, and some of the best writing I've ever experienced in a video game.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: If there's one way I'd describe this game, it's that it's lean. It fits everything it needs to into 1-2 hours of playtime, with an extremely tight script, excellent voice acting, and a story that knows precisely what beats it needs to hit. The pacing here is , and while not particularly complex, the interactive parts provide a perfect backdrop as the story plays out.Even if you're not into purely-narrative driven games, please give this one a go! I'm a very mechanics-first player, and Adios  had me gripped.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: 1 hour 10/10, 10/10 8/10 5/10 5/10  5/10, 7/10You buy this game for the story. You don't buy it for the gameplay or the graphics. Let me say that this game has incredibly written dialogue, with amazing voice acting. It'll make your heart yearn with some of the dialogue that is presented in the game. The story is the simple discussion of if it is too late to do the right thing. We spend an hour doing the mundane things this pig farmer would traditionally do, being accompanied with a member of the mafia. The sense of dread and ending that is presented throughout the game is very much so fantastic. You get very engrossed into the character. I very much enjoy the fact that there are dialogue options that are grayed out that you cannot select, as they represent the thoughts of your character and how he wants to say what is on his mind but he cannot.The setting of the simple farm in Kansas is done excellently, providing a good amount of depth to your character. In addition, the art design is one that I liked to see and enjoyed, but I would see why others would not like it so much.There are some sound cues but there isn't really a soundtrack. The graphics for this game are not great, they are simply serviceable, and I do believe they do not subtract from the plot and dialogue so it does its job there. The gameplay is pretty mundane, mostly a walking simulator with some interactive parts here and there, but it is ultimately serviceable to the main plot. The sound design is also not out of this world, but it is good and helps with the main plot.If you want a short game that deals with a moral crisis that people will face at some point in their life, I highly recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: It's nice. Simple, yet very evocative and made me feel things.Characters and dialoge feel very detailed and believable.I love the art style and the location.Gives off the impression of letting you have a say in things, when the game clearly states where it's heading and how.A big AAA game would absolutely give you the option, but for all the wrong reasons, and that's why it's good that Adios sticks to its guns or rather the absence of them and delivers an experience I've never had before.Well worth your time, if you ask me!P.S.: Looking forward to whatever Doc Burford and Mischief cook up next. I'm sure it won't be white goop.

_childDocuments_.review: A pig farmer who catch fish and deals with an existential crisis. Simply an American southern gothic tale, beautifully crafted as an interactive media and piece of art. With the great care and effort put into this, you can feel the midwestern literature and the overall sense the game brings with it. ps: I love these kinda games with meta-narrative and self-reference. If you find this one interesting, definitely try Paratopic.

_childDocuments_.review: Lots of beautiful craftsmanship on display here, from the 3D, to the 2D, from the writing to the acting. An expertly crafted digital story. There are tons of great details and environmental storytelling (my favorite is the box adamantly labeled SOAP). So many heartfelt moments and even fascinating history. The characters were so nuanced I felt like I didn't truly understand them until the credits rolled. This story is going to stick with me for a long time.

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a satisfying movie-length reflection on death. Whereas some games are walking simulators, Adios is a talking simulator based around some minor mini-games. It's fun, it's meaningful, and it has really good voice acting. Adios feels like a reflection on the American Dream and finding peaceful moments in everyday activities. I'm glad I played Adios, but I think it's probably about $5-$10 too expensive for what you get.

_childDocuments_.review: Decided to purchase this to support its writer who's usually got interesting things to say about video-game as a medium on Twitter. I was invested in the story it was telling, but the nature of it, being fairly scripted and offering no real differentiated path through completion, makes it a limited experience at the 20$ mark. It's got bits of ludonarrative experience but nothing in the story or it interactivity makes me think videogame was the medium to tell that story. This could have been a medium length movie or a short story. As it is, and because I was not fully invested in the tasks, it felt like a radio-novella, a good one though. Not much would have been lost in the experience, if it were. It's exemplified by a scene where you're supposed to move the manure around in a cart. Your cart's path is scripted, all you have to do is to click forward, and I don't think it's as immersive a tool as many developers think it is. At that point, it feels quite similar to manually rotate a cinematograph's lever so that the pictures move to tell the story. So, about the story. SPOILER SECTION:It goes through some of the tropes you'd expect about pastoral representation of farmers, as the main character, a pig's farmer, is the focaliser. Through his eyes, a farmer's life as represented is idealized, and city life is seen as vapid, lacking morality, other characters are compromised in some way, became morally corrupt, while the main character seems like the only visible character to be able to afford a moral crisis. My issue also with this, is that he's never confronted about wanting to go to heaven by the other main character. If you make a choice, motivated by the wish to go to heaven, then your decision is not a moral one. We end up discovering that's not why he did it, but I think it would have been an interesting conversation to have, since the other character believes so.But  I think the thing that bugged me most about the main character was the story bit about him having gone back to Vietnam in the press corps, and it creates this weird "american hero" perspective: he was not a conscientious objector, but had, arguably, one of the very few jobs as a soldier that had a positive impact and changed things for the better, and that's clearly how it's framed. I insist on this as it's used to explain his decision, but also to frame him as a moral character. So I guess, there's something gamelike, about playing someone who, for all intent and purposes, has the moral backbone and fortitude other characters around him lack.  In that regard, it perpetrates the trope about the main character being better, stronger, smarter, more active, than others, and that might be way you might want him to be the player's surrogate. And I think that's what bugged me most. The whole framing about him representing is something so quintessentially American, so Eastwood like..It did get better with the phone call the character gave to his son (though this is also a very "Gran Torino" like trope) as the repercussions of his actions on those around him actually challenge his moral decision, but it is clear, for the purpose of the narrative, that there is no turning back. One thing I really liked, and I think it made good use of the branching dialogues: some dialogue choices were only available to you, you could not choose them, those only exist in a world where the character didn't make the decision he made. So they were grayed out. And if you wanted to access them, they disappeared, as they contradicted the choice made by the character. But it goes back to the game being extremist in its determinism: The story is about a character who made a decision you can't go back on, though the very nature of his decision is that, in spite of the exterior pressure, it was his to make and he stuck to it. So the game has to be deterministic in how you play it, in order for the character to retain his free will.  You end up looking at life through his eyes for a little bit, never really living it like him. So in the end, it's a story about a videogame character than has made a decision, while you can't. It can't be a game about having to live with the consequences of your action. You didn't choose this. Maybe the only decision the player has then, is whether or not he buy the game or not, and that constitutes the only choice. Once you bought the game and you start it, the choice is made.END OF SPOILERSI guess my whole point about this though, is that the game would have worked as a game about the decision the character makes, once the has all the elements and understands the ramifications. I think it'd be a more potent, more radical experience, to have you make the choice to allow this character to be a moral absolutist, or someone who decides, ultimately to not challenge the status quo.I know this is not what the game makers wanted, and they're crystal clear in their perspective that this game is not about making a decision, it's about living with it. But it's not because it's a conscious decision on their part, that it's a sound one. By doing so, they make way with what could have been an actual game, and we as player, become viewers, who push a button to see the machine make its thing, without us having a single impact. It's a bit ironic that the main character is into soda dispensers as those only do one thing when you push the button, and you can push different buttons if you want, but you're gonna have the same aluminum can, just with a different coating. Overall, though, for his story and overall presentation, I liked it. Can't say the 20$ mark makes it good enough. Even when the main character can be a sanctimonious jackass:  it humanizes him a little bit. But I think the developers might need to ask themselves what is the actual best medium for people to experience the story they want to tell.

Animations could be better and help conveying the emotions of the characters. _childDocuments_.review: Adios' farmstead is a temple to life's pleasures, and an imperishable monument of one's regrets in equal fashion. However, there are no illusions of grandeur; the farm has little in the way of splendor or exuberance. Just you, your goats, your pigs, your trusty horse, the hazy fog and autumn leaves... and the man who doesn't want to kill you.Games are so frequently focused on accomplishing big goals; repel the invading army, defeat the big bad guy, conquer All The Things. But Adios isn't interested in the player imposing their will on others. It's interested in closure - illustrating the ways in which life can feel like it can box us in, and how we want to push back on the walls it places us within the confines of. And, in letting us say goodbye.Adios evokes such strong pathos by leaving so little in the way of excess, and by focusing so squarely on the excellently voiced and written main characters. The farmer has the all world-weariness you'd expect of an old man with a life full of regrets, but it's met in equal measure by a sense of sorrowful earnestness that permeates every part of his vocal performance. The hitman is equally sharp in his delivery, but he's a bit of a younger man full of witty sarcasm, a surprising amount of compassion, but a layer of sadness that permeates his character. The farmer wants out of the life he has, but the hitman knows that's now how things work. After all, he's boxed in, too. Adios being so presently focused on the emotions of our characters gives it a power other games of this type don't always capture. Finding what happened prior to you picking up the controller can be powerful in and of itself, but it also isn't always good at capturing the "in-betweens". Adios dodges this by giving us a story that has yet to see it's conclusion, and is buoyed by the museum exhibit-like structure that is common in cinematic first-person titles. By the time the credits rolled, the impermanence of life's pleasures and of our innocence became so much more raw and palpable. I have failed a lot in my own life - in some ways that I still have to reckon with today. Some may never forgive us for our sins, nor are are they obligated to. But it would behoove us all to try. It's never, ever too late to try. If not for others, then for ourselves. Adios does a lot with is short runtime. Give it a go, and you might find something worthwhile.

_childDocuments_.review: It's rare for a game to truly deliver on its one-sentence pitch.  is a brief, emotionally intense game centered around a complicated decision. It's one of the few games I've ever felt had some literary weight to it - a quality that frequently gets overlooked or lost in other games. Just a sublime, emotionally resonant experience. Luxuriate in it while you can.

_childDocuments_.review: Strong delivery by a small team. Hits really hard if your life has brushed against some of the situations shown in the scenes. Set aside an afternoon or evening and really devote your attention to it, and listen closely to the conversations. Read what was left unsaid. Think about the tough choices we all have to make sometimes.
