_childDocuments_.review: Short and heavy. I was kind of waiting for the game to open up a bit more but, what you see is what you get. Some of the gameplay sections don't feel like they gel with the dialogue that is unfolding but, this is still a really ambitious game from a small team. The voice acting really shines which is very important for a game like this. All in all I'd say give it a go if you like other games in this genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: adios is about goodbyes and the many different faces that a single goodbye can hold. there's an overwhelming sense of somberness that permeates from adios that i just absolutely adore. being able to walk around in the shoes of a character who isn't just a tool to deliver the story to us but making him man who has made choices in the past that we have to accept the ramifications of as we slowly weave our way in and out of the narrative is powerful. if you're a fan of first person narrative games then i highly recommend it if you have a good two hours to dedicate to a solid powerful narrative video game.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A quiet and personal story about a man who's prepared for the end. There's a lot of very powerful writing in this game, driven home by some really fantastic voice performances. If you're a stickler for polish, some the edges of the game might bother you — like the very basic UI design and some seams in the animations — but the strength of the story far outweighs it.Would definitely recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a day in the life of a pig farmer. You do your chores, you admire the fruits of your hobby, you go skeet shooting with a pal, you catch a fish.It's a shame today is your last day alive.Though short, extraordinary writing, magnificent voice performances, and a fleshed out setting make Adios a great experience that will stick with you for years. A must-play for fans of narrative games.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: The writing and performances are the main focus here and really stand out to deliver a tender and meaningful exploration of guilt and trauma. The gameplay - short, simple activities between walks to different vignette-style settings rarely adds to the experience, mostly due to poor implementation but the achieved sense of place and atmosphere created by the beautiful environment art and lighting really sell the story in a neat package.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: this is a walking simulator(ish?) game.  it's a lot better than most walking sims at getting you to participate in the story as an actor - the dialogue is expertly written and voiced, and the interactive elements take you through the main character's thoughts in interesting ways.it's very good and made me very sad.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: So there's this bit in the game where by the end of the day you open up your fridge and there are some carrots, an onion, a pack of frozen peas and steak. You can fry the steak. You can chop carrots and add spices. Make a good stew.Or you can just microwave a taco, because it's been a long day. The most human thing I've seen in a video game.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: I started this afternoon contemplating the peaceful but solitary day to day life in one little pig farm in Kansas. By the end of it, being in the boots of this man consumed by remorse had left me in anguish. One of those stories that gets elevated by the immersive nature of videogames and knows how to take advantage of the medium. Just be careful, peas don't belong in curry. Learned it the hard way.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: There's really great voice acting and an interesting art style throughout. The story is emotional and kinda sorta tense. However, Adios is more concerned with being a character study than placing you into a role. Being locked into a series of small areas with not much to do as unskippable conversations play themselves out just didn't justify how dry and straight-forward the story is. As much as I wanted to stay interested, I ultimately found myself checking my phone during conversations. This could've been a "just fine" short film as it is.Perhaps it would've been more compelling to put the player in the role of the farmer's friend and give the player a choice as to how to interpret the Farmer's request? Would the player be warm and understanding or cold and uncompromising? How deeply would you be willing to dig to get a complete picture of the Farmer's situation before deciding how your relationship ends? I get the feeling there would be so much more to debate and internalize if the player took on that role instead.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: This game has stayed on my mind since I played it on launch and likely will for the far future. The world building is elevated by the stellar voice work in helping pull the player into the world of man facing the end of his life. Even minor things like playing old records or cooking a meal take on a special significance given how the game tells you the likely outcome upfront. I found myself wondering "is this my last X." Adios is a very special game that made me feel a connection to someone I'd only known for about two hours. Not many games have been able to do that even with much longer play times.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Everyone is right that the voice-acting is top-notch, the art style distinctive, and the story is row and powerful. What I want to highlight is that Adios let's the player express their character with more than just dialogue choices.To avoid spoilers I'll stick to the first scene. You friendo pulls up with a van full of bodies to dispose of; you tell him you're done with this life. But there is still a van full of bodies to deal with. You might lend him a hand as you tell him your plans, or you might stand defiant while he does the work himself, good-naturedly. What really stands out about this scene (and many others) is how the actions you take express ideas about the character; it's a game you could replay to discover new facets of the character, not by uncovering secret content, but by finding different ways to act.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a good game. It's short and focused, doing everything to immerse you in its story and atmosphere. I liked the way the story is told: it's nuanced and trusts you to understand the subtext of what's going on, but is never convoluted. It's not a mystery to solve, more like an experience to live through.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: It's difficult to talk too much about this game without going heavily into spoilers. I would say if you like a very engaging story about someone who wants to leave the mafia, this was a very understated take on the subject. By not having either character be over the top, it made it seem more real and grounded. The reasoning behind each man's decision was reasonable and especially pithy for the character we play.  The game does some clever things with the dialog response options, especially towards the end, I didn't even realize that I had been playing the game for over an hour and a half until I saw the Steam message afterwards.I enjoyed this quite a bit and hope other people do as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great! It sure isn't a game you want to play with other people though; I played it in a discord call with some friends, and it was hard to tell what was going on, and so at the end of the game we thought there might have been a suicide happening (there wasn't). This is a fault of our own, and the story told is great, definitely check it out.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: So. I had heard about this game; read reviews and even had a pretty certain understanding of its content before starting.Even still I was so pleasantly caught off guard and surprised with how moving it was. Yes I cried at The Dog, yes I was so happy to play horseshoes (objectively the best yard game, feel free to @ me).And I will be thinking about the horse off and on for likely the rest of my life. Excellent game, wonderful little story. Couldn't recommend it enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is an experience that is short and simple, but touching and deeply human. The game relies almost exclusively on its dialogue, the voice actors delivering an incredible performance, each conversation captivating and drawing you in. It doesn't have much in the way of gameplay and it doesn't need it. Set aside about an hour or so and just let yourself take it in (especially if it is on sale).
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Massive story spoilers but it's impossible to review this otherwise. There are two main themes here. One is of a man saying goodbye to the world. He is not dying of old age though, instead it's his moral choice to die. The other theme is his, at times pathetic, need to preserve the memories of things that were important to him by forcing them on other people. It's hard not to look at the tree, soda machine, car, as ultimately worthless hobbies in comparison to relationships that he failed at. The issue here, going back to the first theme covered, is that he is choosing to die. He has the option to live for days, weeks more and change. He refuses to do that despite the clarity of old age. To add insult to injury, he chooses to force his death on his friend, like he tried forcing the useless soda machine on him. Why not do the deed himself? Ultimately the man comes across as a pathetic person and I don't believe that was the author's intention.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a short form linear walking simulator game about a pig farmer that has decided to cut his ties with the mob.What transpires is the last conversation that said farmer has with his would be killer.Whilst this game definitely doesn't have anything groundbreaking or particularly new, it is a nice and interesting little story with some side lore and just enough questions unanswered so your imagination can roam.The gameplay is very rudimentary with some little mini games to just keep you occupied so you don't just sit there and listen to dialogue for the whole game (which i think is a nice touch).The graphics are very basic, that of an indie game, however they definitely aren't jarring and fit the setting well.The chat system, whilst technically completely pointless (since it has little to no impact on the conversation) is again a tactic of keeping the person playing involved (though there is one side use during the phone calls that I thought was very fitting).There are a few bugs that don't seem to be ironed out in the game (mostly related to the end chapter where you can't put down items as per the objective), however these were not completely game breaking so it gets a pass.The main selling point of this game is the story (as usual for walking simulator type games) and it is decently written and did capture my attention.Overall, Adios is a short laid back linear story game. Its not something you HAVE to play and it will definintely not amuse a lot of people, particularly people who like fast pace, action packed games as opposed to walking simulators. However if you do like walking simulator type games and want something easy to digest and short, Adios is a definitely a candidate.Dont expect to be blown away, but if you get it on sale its a game that definitely gets at least a passing grade.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: An incredible experience that perfectly exemplifies the power of storytelling that video games have to offer. Not only does this game has two of the single most stellar voice acting performances found on the Steam store but the cinematic-like cuts, the interactive chores and the genius handling on the dialogue system all comes together to tell a deeply sad tale of a man who's finally had enough and wants to save what's left.The chores reminded me of home and the little *ahem* chestnuts of wisdom spread throughout were great to experience, but the phone calls are the true masterpiece of this game and delivered a genuine shock to my core.Took me a while to have £14 spare, but it was well worth the wait and more than worth the price. Do not sleep on this game. I look forward to seeing what Mischief does next.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Its not really much of a game, the graphics are crude and some textures look out of place, the map is big but mostly empty and non interact-able, the game-play is basic almost non existent, but it does have excellent voice acting and a story that really sucks you in. It gets a recommendation just about. I'd definitely wait for a sale though.Note the game does not support mouse invert and the developer has said it will never be added. If your happy to play with a controller then you can enable invert via steam input which the game does support. I can confirm it plays quite well with a controller.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Decent adventure walking sim. But you should know that the game mostly consists of dialogue, voice acting and writing is pretty good though. However the game is pretty short (90 minutes for a playthrough, 120 minutes for 100%).I think the asked price is too high for that though. If you can get it cheaper, go for it.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a game well worth experiencing, but it's a game more about the melancholy getting to the end, rather than the ending itself. You know what they say, it's the journey and not the destination that's important, and that's especially true in this case. I highly recommend giving Adios a play, and hopefully you'll get to empathize with the life of a pig farmer who no longer wants to dispose of bodies for the mob.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a game about choice and about liminality.The primary gameplay of Adios is in walking, listening, and making choices in the form of sparse statements that lead to lengthy monologues written with equal parts weight and realism.  These choices are wherein the heart of Adios lies.  They don't affect the  of the story.  They can't.  It's impossible.  But they affect what you experience.  They affect the way you perceive it.  Which story are you going to hear.  What is the level of connection between these two men?  Spoilers for mechanics but not plot: Secondly, is the game's feeling and tone,  Throughout its comfortable length you are constantly teetering on the precipice of...something.  You hope, with every fiber of your being, that this ends any way other than violence.  But you know, as surely as something beyond your being, that there is only one way this can end.  That precipice is the gateway between life and death; it's the space between forgiveness and condemnation; it's the acquiescence to believing in hell because it means there must be a heaven.  The beauty of Adios is that it doesn't show you what's on the other side of that gateway.  Adios ends just at the moment of stepping through the door.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Last night I was watching 'Bones' with a friend and there was this ex-hitman who had become a pig farmer (he was obviously the murderer, OR WAS HE?) - I was like, "WOW, THIS IS JUST LIKE THIS GAME ADIOS EXCEPT DIFFERENT, LEMME TELL YA" and explained. It was not the first time that I have been able to discuss hitmen and pig farmers with visible enthusiasm since playing Adios, and none of the other times even required a forensic detective procedural to make pigs eatin' people for the mob a smooth conversational transitions. I know that now I will be fun at parties. 10/10 also it made me feel a complicated sadness which is my favorite genre of game
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Short but nice story about a pig farmer who doesn't want to dispose of bodies for the mob anymore.You already know how it ends, but the fun lies in how you spend your remaining time in this world.If you're a gameplay-oriented player like me, it can work nicely as a palate cleanser due to its focus on story & drama. It's well-made (except for minor glitches/clipping), doesn't waste your time, ends right when it's supposed to.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend it, as long as you don't read the store page first... if that's possible.Everything looks and sounds nice. The voice acting is great. Some of the mechanics are a little clunky, but it's nothing major.My biggest issue with this game is that SO many reviews talk about how awesome the story is, but one of the most major plot points is given away in the store description.I somehow managed to miss reading the whole thing, so the end honestly came as  a bit of a surprise to me, which was awesome. I wouldn't have had the same experience if I had already had it revealed to me.I don't know. I was/am conflicted.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Make no mistake—even though Adios takes place in one area over the course of a day, it fits squarely within the adventure genre the same way other recent darlings like Firewatch and Virginia do. (A 2-hour-ish experience that feels like classic Americana short fiction, but interactive.)I especially like the fact that this could probably just have been a walking sim and instead the game makes use of various kinds of interactivity and minigames to expand the world of the story outside its boundaries. This also makes it feel paradoxically more literary. Imagine that! A game that embraces the fact that it's a game and is even better because of it!Of course I wish it had been longer; but that's more or less the point. I can't wait to see what Mischief gets up to next :D
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: I think I'm the perfect person for this game: I love short stories, love stories about the mob, love this sort of gritty genre in general. But...I still just thought this was OK. Some of the animations look awkward and the story and dialogue, while great, didn't wow me necessary, just kept me entertained enough to keep pushing forward. I don't think it's a bad game so I'm not gonna *not* recommend it, but at the same time, I'd still exercise caution in light of so many positive reviews. I'm also confused how you're supposed to get the greyed out dialogue boxes (unless they're for the player's info?) and sometimes objectives could be a bit unclear (like with the fishing minigame). Decent enough game, I'd say above average due to the excellent premise and solid enough VA and writing.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: This is a straight-forward narrative about someone wanting to quit the mafia.It's basically the game equivalent of a short story, and there's not a whole lot of interaction or influencing the plot. Instead, it's about putting yourself in the protagonist's shoes and thereby starting to think about all the story's themes.For me this game is about peace. Making peace with past mistakes, doing your best to correct them and also making peace with the consequences that you cannot fix. It's kind of sad and short, but that's exactly why you should take an hour or two to play through it.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: The contemplation of a life and the choices we make to survive.Can we live with all we've done in a lifetime of morally grey decisions?Great writing and some truly sterling vocal performances. While the visual and mechanical presentation is merely serviceable, it's a genuinely moving and insightful short story to experience at least once.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Voice acting is perfect, the story is a good kind of somber and it made me think about mortality.The only issue is the graphics. It did not mesh for me. I'm not talking about the technical part of it, mind. I mean the visual direction and the style. Just doen't fit here (for me)Still a good one though, support it :)
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Despite my disagreement with the premise and some technical jank, I still quite liked the experience. Across Adios' short runtime, you really get a solid sense of who the main character is and what he's thinking, which is an impressive achievement. The writing and voice acting are extremely solid, allowing each scene to feel fully realized and be impactful on their own while ultimately coming together beautifully into one single day in a life. The farm is also equally lovingly created, with lots of little details that make it really feel lived in and containing a lot of beauty to see. Overall, if you want to have a strong experience of immersion in one man's living space and headspace, this one's for you.(PS. For a fun time, jump over the fence while guiding your visitor around.)
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoyed the game. Not much left to say that the other reviewers haven't already said way better. It lives off its natural dialogue and the voice acting which is absolutely freaking excellent, especially for a small game like this. Also liked the visual style very much. Rock-solid achievement here. Kudos to the devs!
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a surprisingly emotional portrait of a man who has decided he's had enough and the man who doesn't want to kill him. This is the kind of story that requires you actually inhabit the character and spend time in his shoes. With outstanding voice acting and writing, there's nothing else quite like it out there.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a short game but it can leave an impact on you. The story of a man who is done with his current way of life in the hopes that he can save the rest of it. A game about life and loss, friendship and family. This game walks right up to you and says, "This conversation right here was designed to make you cry." And if that one doesn't, there is another one right after. This is a beautiful game that takes its time, but only requires an hour to play. The dialogue is natural, the characters feel like real people rather than walking screenplays. It is worth your time and money. Please enjoy.Also if it gets to 100,000 sales we get Big Horse mode and I want that.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: This is fundamentally a game about endings and, in a sense, closure. Adios sets you at the last moments of the protagonist's narrative where others might have you uncover the aftermath. This makes for a refreshing interactive human drama that succeeds in a familiar walking simulator framework by sharing the protagonist's internal conflicts with their own catalysts. Adios cherishes in the contrast of both the colorful and haunting qualities of humanity with the mundanity of everyday life. What it excels at is delivering a beautiful slice of writing complimented by absolutely fantastic performances that elevate the narrative. I enjoyed my time with it.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Not only is the game worth picking up, it's quick enough that you can finish it in one sitting. But more than that, it's a heart wrenching narrative experience. What would you do if you knew today was your last day? Who would you talk to? What story would you tell? How would you prepare?While there are a few mechanical quirks that frustrated me (like trying to pick up the steak for dinner), I really enjoyed it. I paid $10 more for it than it was priced because I like and appreciate the designers that much. I can't wait to see what they do with a bigger budget and more time.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: I've been following the development of Adios very closely. Doc is one of my favourite people that I have on Twitter, and seeing more and more of the game up until launch and hearing him speak so fondly of the story and game that he and the team had been putting together really intrigued me. I couldn't quite get a grasp on what sort of game it was, or what it was trying to be, and ultimately I sort of thought that it could end up being too... 'filmic' and just a game story that could happily be better off as a book or a short film. I'm glad to say that Aidos is  not that. It can only be a interactive experience. It delivers a truly special twist on 'conversation options' as a game feature / trope that  you've come to expect from games over the years and the team have managed to take the anxiety & fear of saying how you really feel to someone, and turn it into a great narrative mechanic.Recommended for fans of narrative driven experiences, but also for people wanting something a little different. PS. There's a great little nod to Paratopic that I got a massive kick out of!Follow and support everyone involved with this production, the world NEEDS to see what they do next.

_childDocuments_.review: contrary to popular belief, sadly, i didn't like this game. I wish I did, but I don't. _childDocuments_.review: This is one of those games that isn't for everyone -- but everyone should try.A lot of people would call it a walking sim. "Oh, so it's not a GAME." Listen. No. It's absolutely a game, but it's not the kind where the goal is to win. It's the kind where the goal is to have an experience shared in a way that is more visceral than non-interactive works. It's structured play in service to a story and a hotbed of complex thoughts and experiences that are difficult to convey unless you are in the shoes of a man who is trying to accomplish a task and also make the difficult choice to push back against a demand the protagonist can no longer find reasonable. It's a story to be played, not simply witnessed.And Adios is a sublimely executed story, in large part thanks to its moving parts which you are free to mess with and examine and toss around at decent length.With a runtime of about two hours, you could conceivably knock it out in an afternoon. However, I came back to this one a few times and poked around at all the ways the narrative branches and comes back in on itself, and some moments I revisited simply because... well, they're impeccably done. The stellar voice acting that would have a lot of AAA games sweating certainly helps, but the script and structure carry equal weight.Adios is a game that pretty much knows exactly what it wants to be, and is not trying to provide you the foremost in entertainment; instead, it is an experience worth having at least once, with the understanding that, yeah, you're here, you're playing inside a story-first game that carries a lot of weight. Let it happen, meet it on its own terms, and play in the space, and you'll find something that hits surprisingly hard if you let it.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay full disclosure my friends worked on this so I'm automatically biased, but I love it so much. I don't want to say too much because I don't want to spoil the experience but man, Adios just wants to show you the most interesting possible version of every detail it conjures. _childDocuments_.review: Adios means goodbye. As a creator myself, it's so refreshing and encouraging to see a story, let alone a game have a strong idea of what it wants to do, and follow through on it on every front. There is a level of care and consideration placed on the things that really matter. If more games were like Adios, I wouldn't mind it at all.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting narrative experience with simple Gameplay interations. You can tell this game was made with a lot of heart by a small team. It explores an interesting character dynamic in a way rarely seen in video games. There's a lot of depth to the writing and the Voice Actors did a great job with their performances. The game can easily be played in one sitting. I enjoyed my time with it a lot.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a well-written, wonderfully performed narrative-driven game that adds to the expected walking sim formula by staging conversations around odd-jobs or activities that add to the organic feel of the interactions as well as presenting dialogue options that reflect thoughts the protagonist is unwilling or incapable of saying out loud. The relatively short runtime makes it a perfect experience for those dipping their feet into the walking sim style of game, while long term fans of the genre will find a worthwhile experience that respects their time.Played to completion on the Switch, but writing the review here because this game inspires conversation.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: さよなら(sayonara) means goodbye.Reference to the Steam description out of the way,  is a story-driven first-person , developed by indie development team , a studio name rather antithically whimsical for the subject matters of their first title.The game centers around a Vietnam War veteran turned farmer, and follows their entanglement with the mob. I would tag this as a spoiler, but these themes are rather swiftly established within the game, and are listed all over the game's marketing and store page. Gameplay largely consists of walking between areas, completing simple minigames, then moving to the next area. These minigames are somewhat integrated into the story, but are largely inconsequential.Even more inconsequential are the dialogue trees. Chapters are self contained, and although there are branching dialogue options, your choices regarding dialogue seem to have little effect on the narrative. For such a short experience, being able to shape the story by means of your own decisions would have been far from an insurmountable task, though .Graphically, Adios is okay. The scenery isn't on par with some other 'walking simulators' I've played, but some of the more intricate details are rather nicely put together. The character models aren't animated in a particularly expressive way, which rather softens the impact of potentially heavy narrative moments. Most of the time characters are just idling while flapping their mouth hole, leaving a window into the strange untextured interior of the character model.The voice acting and writing carries any emotional weight the game has to offer, and these two elements at least are worthy of praise. The dialogue feels cinematic, and though it doesn't nail down the 'calm before the storm' banter of a Tarantino film, it's consistent, and not too many lines feel out of place.While some of what Adios has to offer might be worth a recommendation, the game failed to emotionally resonate with me or get me invested in the characters. With a price tag of around $20, Adios doesn't give a huge amount for your money either. I wish that it could have left a more lasting impression, but instead all I have is the feeling that there was something more that it could have been. Something more that could have been said.Arrevederchi.5.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Hey, you! I see you! You, on the couch, with the buttered popcorn. Settling down for movie night? Why not play this game instead?You play, as the steam description says, as "a pig farmer [who] decides he no longer wants to dispose of bodies for the mob. What follows..." is a short but sweet game you'll be thinking about for a while.This is the best paced story I've seen in games, and one of the best voice-acted too. Scenes flow into each other unintrusively, like watching a film play out but with you as a gentle hand on the controls, and VA performances working in concert with the game's simple dialogue choice system brought me to tears.If you're expecting a mindblowing high-concept story, you'll be disappointed, but if you're willing to sit back and emotionally connect to the characters, exist in this small farm, you'll have a lot to think about. I want to see more intelligent stories told like this in games,Doc knows what he's doing, and so does everyone else on this project. Fork over the cash for this game (and don't refund it, ya stinker), because there's a lot more cool ideas coming from this team once they have the funding. You're not gonna want to miss out.

_childDocuments_.review: A farmer sways back and forth on a porch swing. It's mighty creaky. Birds are singing. The sky is a hazy purple. Then a truck with headlights on pulls up to the farm. It looks like early morning. The farmer opens his journal. It says "Tell him I'm done.". A pig's squeal is heard. Cut to black. "THE CONFESSION" shows up in big bold letters as a chapter title. An unnamed man in a blue suit and green tie with brown slicked back hair is in the farmer's face. Farmer: "I can't do this anymore."Suited man: "What?"Farmer: "This."Suited man: "What, mornings?"Farmer: "No, all of this."This is a story of regrets. He lives alone on a farm with red wattle pigs, goats, horses, and chestnut trees. However, his past life in the mob has caught up with him in the form of this suited man. He propositions to spend the day with you as the farmer. To try to convince you to change your mind to get back into that violent life. You take up his offer. Your boundaries are set, though. No "just one last job and I'm out" cliche. This is the meditative and introspective aftermath of a mobster life, which barely gets a highlight in media or it may just be a short footnote at the end. And it's not just his past life he has regrets about. It's a unique premise for a videogame. There is a serene synchronisation of gameplay mechanics and storytelling in that they're both minimalist. It's a firstperson adventure game (not walking sim because you can sprint!) where you walk around, do little activities, and make dialogue choices with this suited man. The dialogue is similarly minimalist, with a real economy of words employed by the farmer, as if he doesn't want to give up much and wants this all over with so he can go back to raising his farm. Doc Burford's writing for the game is measured and beautiful. So are Andrea Jorgensen and Zachary Northcott's art in depicting an idyllic Americana setting. There are even jump cuts to continue that economical format (there's a perfectly timed late title drop), which were also used in Doc Burford's previous game . Nonetheless, he will wax lyrical about many aspects of his farm, animals, items, and people. Violent people (or post-violent in the farmer's case here) engaging in non-sequitur dialogue is a tired trope now since Quentin Tarantino's , so thankfully this is a deeper exploration of both characters' wants, drives, emotions, and fears. Rick Zieff brings a lot of elegiac maturity to his performance as the farmer, which is unlike any of the roles he's done in the past for cartoons, TV, or films. DC Douglas brings a youthful and humorous touch to the suited man but there is empathy along with frustration just beneath the surface of this noticeable tension between both characters. This frustration drew out into me as a player too, after the many exchanges between both, I just wanted to be left alone as the farmer to tend to my private life. It's all about the little actions here. There are many verbs that get played around with. You can milk a goat, feed your horse with apples, play horseshoes, play your son's tapes and records, make telephone calls, cook meals, and even shoot a gun but against clay targets (the game recognises if you try to shoot the other man). Personally, I was hoping for more reactions from my actions, maybe the expectations were set after I threw a soda can at the man and he caught it or that I love immersive sims, but again that's a matter of resources at the hands of the developers. The shooting still feels good, despite how little it's used. Devon Palmer's animation work is minimalist too (there is no firstperson awareness here with hands being drawn in which could be down to this being a very indie game) and aside from my love of firstperson body work in videogames, it's not distracting and works for the readable simplicity. With the sombre elegiac tone, there is a yearning for closure with the farmer. Or at least an attempt for it. Familial relationships are strained, and this beat about his son and Sadie brings out the tragedy of the tale. There is a real truth and sadness to that situation that struck me with my experience as a mental health professional. Although, there's plenty of opportunities to balance out the serious tone with humorous dialogue, interactions, and opportunities. Like me playing both the vinyls and tapes at the same time, or putting all the food on the ground, cutting them up on the floor, and then putting them into the pan. It has been those little sad moments that have stuck with me long after I finished the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a very short but somewhat predicable, vaguely interactive narrative driven first person adventure.   You work for the mob, and when you decide to quit, it's time to have a few awkward conversations that give a little backstory to an otherwise remarkably uneventful game with an all too predictable ending.If this was $1 I'd say, sure, why not, it's not made so badly, even if it's short, I've seen thousands of games worse than this (quite literally). But they're charging an eye watering $18 USD for this, for which you can get pretty much any older AAA game you might want.   This costs more than you can get Hogwarts Legacy for if you shop around.   No "B minus" console port is worth that kind of money.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a cool story. But I don't know that the story being told as a game helps it any. As far as gameplay goes, this is about as boring and non-interactive as they come. So the game relies entirely on the story and artwork to keep the player engaged. Neither of which, the story or the artwork, I believe are outstanding enough to make of for the lack of engagement. Overall, I would say this game was essentially a let-down.I look at it this way. It took X hours to turn this story into a game. If you had taken those same X hours and applied it to another medium, say music, film, or a book, the result would have probably served the story much more effectively.It has a few brief moments that are deep, funny, or sad, but that's about it. And they're brief.I regret the purchase, and cannot not think of anyone I would recommend this to.

_childDocuments_.review: Brilliant game. Superb writing and voice acting, and I appreciated being able to keep my hands busy during conversation. A few bugs that others have mentioned, and I think perhaps the greyed out options could have been a bit clearer (I didn't even notice they were greyed out at first, and with only one instance in the first act I can see why others would be confused) but otherwise... bravo. Buy this game. The team deserves your money and your appreciation for this moving game.

_childDocuments_.review: I love walking/listening simulators a lot and I’ve always clapped back on people who play a game and say “why isn’t this another type of media” but if someone asked me why Adios isn’t a short film I really wouldn’t have and answer for them. It’s uglier like this and the interactivity adds nothing at all. Dialogue options being grayed out because your character can’t bring themselves to say is a hacky and clumsy tactic to communicate something that are better communicated just in moments of silence. I don’t need to be in this guys head to know what he’s thinking and I think it would be more interesting if I knew less anyways. Was really excited to play this and wanted it to be good or at least we’ll written but it really just isn’t anything special at all.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: Good story, not really a game. Has some bugs. I wanted to recommend it. Get it on sale?This is one of those reviews where I really really wish Steam had a neutral rating, but I'm going to say I don't recommend this game. I'm sorry Doc (@docsquiddy), I follow you on Twitter and I really wanted to like this game, but overall I ended up being disappointed.I have to start by saying I absolutely love the concept of the game. It's what hooked me. That being said, this could have been a short film. I didn't find this style of gameplay interesting. For the most part it was walk to location, listen to characters talk, maybe interact with the scenery. The voice acting is good, the art direction is cool, but the game is lacking something. I kept expecting some form of gameplay change or story twist to happen, but the game played out exactly the way it told me it would. Again, I just feel that this story was in the wrong medium. I would have just given it a pass with a yes recommendation and a meh essay review, but the ending pushed it hard into the negative for me. There are two objectives at the end that when I tried to execute them the game kind of broke, and I couldn't continue without breaking the experience a bit, which ruined the build up to the ending. Also, the other thing you put on the table? Why? What purpose did it serve? Did I miss a story beat?Also the game glitched out at the VERY end of the game, and the way it did without spoilers led me to think maybe the game wasn't over, but it was just a bug.That all being said, there is good stuff in here, I wanted more. I closed the game feeling like I wanted more. I genuinely can't wait to see the next thing the dev puts out.Also, this is just a serious nitpick but, aren't granny smith apples green?

_childDocuments_.review: Well I looked at recent and all reviews as Very Positive and love a good original title so purchased Adios a long time ago but really wish I hadn't bought it.  Apart from the voice acting I can't see where the money went.  The game achieves setting up a soulful mood.  But it is actually pretty frustrating to 'play' even though it is just trotting out 2.5 hours of linear sequences - move here watch this cut scene, move here watch this cut scene, all triggered by doing some trivial action.  Even though it is only a couple of hours long I abandoned it for months half way through because it was so unrewarding.  I have just this morning decided to finish it so I can free up some drive space... one of the last sequences involves chopping ingredients and preparing a meal. The frustration of that experience (ingredients falling on floor, hiding behind furniture, knife dropping on floor hiding behind furniture) had me wishing for the end in more ways than one.  I really do not understand where all the positive reviews have come from, the story could have been so much better told, the graphics and movement through the story could have been fluid and enjoyable, conveying the beauty the character was leaving behind.  I don't often take the time to write a review, but feel this is so weak that I would not wish it on someone even at its now low price point £7.69 on 45% promotion.

_childDocuments_.review: A lovely, sombre game about a fellow taking responsibility for their actions. The performances are excellent, and really sell one on the farmer and the hitman having known each other for some time now. The hitman knows his side of this tale all too well, truly hoping this farmer's just another guy having one of those days, but...He's not. He knows he's had enough. You come to realize he's had enough. That harmony of understanding only makes the melancholy of it all hit that much harder.If there's any fault to be found in the game, however, it's that the...Ah, cooking, takes one out of the experience at something of a key moment. It's all too clumsy, but by then, thankfully, one has hit most of the high notes, so it doesn't ruin anything. It would be nice to see it adjusted to be less clunky, though, to end things on...Well, not a high note, but a more...Resonant note.Nevertheless, that notwithstanding, everything else is wonderfully done, and if you're looking for an adeptly written and performed game, you'd do well to play this.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm still unsure whether I do recommend this game or not, just because it's such a different experience from other games. However, I find the 15€ tag to be a bit over the line for the duration, polish, and story/message. Maybe I'm not the target player, maybe it just didn't click for me, maybe I've been spoiled by the massive amount of incredibly cheap great games out there. Details below;The game lasted just over an hour for me; I didn't walk everywhere by the end of the game, but I didn't rush it either, just skipping a single dialog by accident. Overall, it feels unpolished; no animations on the menu, no look sensitivity, no support for 2k on borderless fullscreen, lackluster animations... These aren't deal breakers by any stretch of the imagination, specially in this kind of game, but end up making the game feel unpolished, way more than other indies.This kind of ties with the duration, and I guess it's technically a spoiler, but by the end of the game, I wasn't attached at all to the farmer, and his death didn't really mean anything to me. It kind of makes you think about that situation, and how mafias won't let you "quit", but just like hearing about that situation would. Maybe if it had been longer, if I had interacted with the farm, if you had even seen/played through the past for a bit, or something, I would have felt something for him, or left me thinking about it. But it didn't.

_childDocuments_.review: Since I can't get a refund, this will be the next best thing. This game is not worth the money. It really sucks because the story is interesting, the framework is really good, but then they take that framework and make essentially one long quicktime event with minimal interaction. There is a lot of "hinted" plot points that never pan out. There is little to no "game" here at all.Now I know some will think I simply don't like story heavy games. But this isn't the case. Adios, to me, falls in line with games like Stanley Parable, or The Beginner's Guide (both highly highly recommended). But Adios is too short and too restricted. I beat the main story (the only story mind you as there are not multiple endings despite what the game leads you to believe) in 66 minutes. I already posted but am editing to add an additional thought. The writing for the Pig Farmer is phenomenal. The son too. However! The writing for the suited men is abysmal. Literally spends half the game asking you why you have farm animals on your farm. What the ♥♥♥♥ even.TL;DR Adios is a long cutscene at best, and a poorly crafted game (if you can call it that) at worst. Don't get this for anymore than 7$.

_childDocuments_.review: So I just finished this "game," well, be careful calling it a game. I'm not big on reviewing stuff but still I feel I need to give my opinion on this product here so others know what to expect.Overall, yes I liked the experience. It's more of a good story though than an actual game. I'm all for using the gaming media to tell good stories so I'm not going to fault this dev for using that approach, but I would caution people unfamiliar with this product to think it's a game.Bottom line, many will consider refunding this because of the length and the price. I did 1.8 hours to complete this and did probably 20 mins of replaying of the last chapter because of a bug. Overall, I liked the experience though. I am older guy and can't spend 40-60 hours very often playing games, so I've learned to appreciate the more concentrated story telling games in my older age. But I don't know if I can actually call this a game, there are no real game-play machinates in this product, it's more of a real-time experience.Voice acting is very, very good. The idea and story they are trying to get to the viewer is very good. I certainly didn't cry like some other reviewers said they did multiple times, it's far from a crying experience I think. But this is very much like a sad song, almost like working overseas and not being able to see your family for more than a year because you can't get back home because your wife lost their job, you're the bread winner, your son is in school and the month you have off for vacation requires 4 weeks of quarantine given both counties requirements. You feel sad when 'playing' this experience, which is a high complicate to the story tellers who crafted this 'experience.'I personally won't refund this, but I can see how many people would want to given what they get from this. At ~$20 CND this is honestly priced way to high, this (I think) is more of a $9.99 CND experience. Good story, great voice acting, good experience, very shallow on gameplay and very weak on replay value for the story. I can only honestly recommend this at a lower price point given what else is out there.

_childDocuments_.review: My feelings are mixed. The "gameplay" of Adios is a little weak, barely rising above the level of a to-do list with not much visible creativity outside of when you conduct a few phone calls. The lip syncing on the actors and a lot of the animation is clunky, and really breaks immersion.On the other hand, the story is pretty good, and the voice work is masterful. _childDocuments_.review: This is an EXCELLENT narrative game. Think of it as the gaming equivalent of a really good short story. Something that doesn't necessarily take much time to get through, but it sticks with you for the rest of your life afterwards. It's a really concentrated experience documenting the twilight days of a man who disposes of bodies for the mob on his pig farm. It gets into things like his relationship with his son and also his friend, a charming hit man. It has some of the best executed dialog options I've ever encountered in a game. It makes you feel like you're having a real conversation. There's even some really--not just clever, but really meaningfully executed stuff, like how sometimes you can think something, but you can't say it. This is a game that really plays to the strengths of the videogame medium in terms of storytelling. It was made by a very very small team and Im really impressed by how much of a punch it packs in its small frame. If you'd like a really intimate, auteur experience, one that is very refined and mature in a thoughtful way, please check out Adios.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A touching short story about a man preparing to commit suicide. The narrative is great, and you really get in the shoes of this guy (great voice acting, too!) who is... well, just tired of everything and doesn't see a way to improve his life. There is no big epic drama, it's just that the contradictions of his life have caught up with him. The game really resonated with me, and I recommend it to everyone.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: This might be the most unique idea for a game I've ever seen.And I really really want to love it.I do love so much the game does. The dialogue great. Its subdue and meandering and it leaves a lot unsaid.Its great. But there's so much I don't love. All the ...erm...minigames? activities? you do during the conversations are janky and more frustrating than anything. I get that player needs to do something during those long dialogues, and the idea is fine in theory but its as it is its either awkward or annoying to actually do.Graphics are bad. Thats usually not a problem as long as its not distracting. But unfortunately it is. Especially in the scene where characters talk about a horse. We listen to the dialogue about how beautiful horses are, and you just stare at that barely animated, unblinking thing that looks like its from some third rate bootleg lego knock-off. Its unintentionally comical.And the cooking. Wow. It was the least fun I had probably ever. I get the aim. Its to show how much farmer is not used to cooking. I get that. It should be awkward. But after the fourth time I have failed to put a potato on a table it the last thing I cared about was artistic expression, I just wanted to PUT. THAT. POTATO. DOWN.oh and spoiler for the end:As it stands I still recommend Adios (even if its a bit pricey for what it is) because the premise is so absolutely unique and it has amazing atmosphere.

_childDocuments_.review: For a walking simulator, this game is pretty gripping (just take a look at the completion rate on the Steam achievements page).  A play through lasts about 80 minutes and it's completely sold by the voice acting, and although it does feel like this might work as a short film, I think given the dialogue options that you can choose between and the game's pacing, this story telling works pretty well as a game.  While I think you can replay the game to hear other dialogue options for a bit lengthier gameplay, this is on the short side which does make the original price a bit on the high side.  If you can find this on a deeper discount, this may be worth having a look if you're looking for an interesting, dialogue heavy game.

_childDocuments_.review: Much like the meal I cooked for myself towards the end of this experience, Adios is a bunch of nice, thoughtful ingredients that just don’t add up to the meal I thought I was making. This isn’t a bad game, it’s actually quite good for its narrative, but as it stands in the Steam store I cannot recommend it at anywhere near the full price. I’ve always been a proponent of “if the experience is worth it to you then who gives a ♥♥♥♥ about price,” but to me it’s positives and negatives cancel each other out and you’re left with an anticlimactic experience that’ll take an hour to play on average with little reason to come back aside from a trophy hunt. While labeled a walking sim, this is actually closer to a standing sim in that it’s about a dozen vignettes around singular setting and more than half of them are you bound to an invisible box while dialogue plays out. The other half you get some basic “pick up the thing and put it down over there” busywork but for two third of this hour long experience you’re just standing there letting the exposition happen.  It’s not bad exposition though. The dialogue and voice acting are really natural and well done. I could listen to the two main characters go on for much longer than they do. There’s really no depth to the story but it’s effective and the main character/actor sells it. The ending wasn’t a surprise but how quickly it came was. As a short form narrative, Adios is great and I don’t regret playing it. But as an $18 purchase, fugetaboutit.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is quite simply a very touching game. It has a ton of love put into it, you can tell. The writing took me a bit of time to really understand how fine-tuned and masterfuly crafted it was, and it all started when the game .A short, but really effective game. I think I'll replay it from time to time just to listen to it again. It's really nice.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: An hour (and a bit) of gradually mounting tension between well-rounded characters as casual, affectionate conversations slowly fail to suppress the dreadful reality approaching from beneath.A quiet, heartfelt piece of writing that had me sitting in contemplation for about as long as its runtime afterwards. Pick it up while it's on sale if you love a good narrative.

_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: This small indie game has that surprisingly rare combination of smart writing and stellar voice acting that so few games manage to capture. For some reason, most video games, even the expensive ones, have a dialogue quality that can best be described as a direct-to-DVD martial arts movie from the early 2000's. Characters rarely speak like actual human beings, which is especially jarring when the graphics are near-photo-realistic. You could argue that video games are about the gameplay so it shouldn't matter, but so many games are trying to sell you an emotional story, so this stuff really impacts the intended experience.This game, however! I was fully engaged in the story and often moved, which is a testament to how engaging the dialogue is. In my opinion, everyone should give this game a try just to experience it themselves. We don't have to put up with direct-to-DVD quality just because it's a video game.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: The best description of Adios I've managed to arrive at is "Digital Theater As Viewed From The POV Of The Lead." I think that description is useful because I think, upon reading it, a  portion of curious onlookers will know whether not they'll have any time for this one. One of Adios's core tenets, in my reading, is that a lot of seemingly contradictory things can be true at once. In that spirit; Adios is not much of a game, really. Mostly you walk around. Sometimes you choose dialogue options, though not always. You press a button to do chores or shoot skeet or shovel manure. At the same time, what it achieves, and I would argue that its achievements are significant, would not be possible in another medium. It matters that you're with the Farmer instead of just watching him. That his choices are yours, sometimes, when there's a choice to make at all. Because sometimes there just isn't. Or there used to be, but it was made a long time before you got here.Adios is a straightforward yet slyly complex story, infused with a depth of humanity and certain rural, anxious weariness.It's simply drawn and densely layered. It's also about an hour and change long. Some people will look at the price and determine it to be a poor value proposition. That's their prerogative. I can only tell you that the story stuck with me, and that I found it to be a worthwhile use of my time and money. It took an hour of my time and $18 from my pocket and in return it made me think and feel and grapple with what it meant. I'm happy with that.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Well written, harrowing, and tragic, this is the story of the pig farmer. A narrative focused piece of story telling, you're here for the story and the dialogue. There won't be any gunfights, unless you count targets. This is a story about making difficult decisions, and the subtle and not so subtle interactions that tie all of us together.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: There are many titles that reach for emotional resonance; that can make you angry, sad, or relieved, but Adios accomplishes this with an economy and efficiency - it is not a 'short' game but rather an accurate one, and it knows exactly how it wants to make you feel.  I was surprised by how I had to periodically stop and just think about what the main character was saying, or what other characters were dancing around saying.  The game's artstyle is well suited to conveying the simple charm of a rural Kansas farmstead, and the VA performances bring the narrative solidly home.  Unexpected, and affective.

It's a one track game in which you cannot change your fate and it's sad and you have mixed feelings about the main character. It's different and I like different. I do not think it is worth 18 bucks. _childDocuments_.review: I've been thinking about this game a lot since I played it. At first I wasn't sure how I felt about it as a game; it has very little real gameplay, so I was thinking maybe it would have been better as a comic or something. _childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Bacon tastes good, but do you know what pigs used to eat?Brilliant narrative, terrifyingly and painfully peaceful. As you walk through everyday chores you start to understand. Every generation has its sins and regrets, sometimes done for a better future. But we are not that different from pigs. So, what do you eat?This narrative-driven game is a great experience, and for me very unique. If you have 2 hours… this is an excellent way to spend it on a nostalgic, emotional, tragic also, but very peaceful story. Feel the moment on this Kansas farm, listen to the October wind and do this one last thing. Well... maybe a few things. This is a farm, right?

_childDocuments_.review: It's been a while since I felt so invested in a game I move the camera during cutscenes to where I think the character would look during the scene.Very engrossing story, and the voice acting is pheNOMemal, like, the story is ridiculously well-written, but some of the narrative beats really hit hard because of the voice talent. _childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is one of those games that gave me this weird vibe, which alone makes it a great experience in my opinion.The plot of the game is written in the description so there is no real mystery there but the writing, even though it seems simple, often it carries a deeper meaning. It also helps that the voice actors involved are great and made conversations feel life-like. Most part of this relatively short game (2-3 hours I think) you will be listening to those conversations combined with some mini-games that perhaps are a bit pointless but fun nonetheless.The graphics may not be anything special but did feel very smooth, especially combined with the quite odd character designs. Adios may not be a game for everyone and the regular price is a bit steep but it's a game you will not soon forget. I recommend playing on a sunday morning in autumn.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A rare storytelling gem not just in its dialogue, but how it is able to brilliantly distill so much history between the characters into just a single day. The environment is breathable, the voice acting is deep, and it leaves you with a feeling that you need to immediately pick up the phone and call someone dear to you.

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a Raymond Carver story in playable form, where a farmer and his murderer discuss the empty philosophy of an average life. It is a game about loneliness, meaninglessness, grief, and death. It is one of the most haunting and memorable games I have ever player.FINAL SCORE: ONCE-IN-A-LIFETIME/10
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is very brave for the fact that it's confident in its own way of telling the story, its length, the tone, and the subject of such story. Adios simply tells a story of a man deciding to choose his own way. The game takes place within a single day, within a single plot of land. Voice acting, color palette, and overall mood of this game come together for a nice 60-minute story that conveys so much emotion. Adios shows that, a good writing, convincing voice acting, and a steady tone are all you need for one of the most realistic and memorable storytelling I've seen in a while.8/10 short, impactful, set my standard for storytelling.

_childDocuments_.review: I did not think I would like Adios.The premise is great - your character knows that an old friend might be on the way to kill him - and I was excited about the prospect of a small, focused game about convincing the friend not to do it, or setting up a Home Alone scenario to try to turn the tables and survive. It is not really a spoiler to say that it becomes abundantly clear in the first few minutes of the game that this is not going to be the case. I therefore expected to be bored by the dreaded "walking simulator". Instead I found a simple, straightforward narrative that had me completely absorbed for its short runtime, made me cry at least once and will stay with me for some time.Adios is a game that does not give you much in the way of choices, because you are stepping into the shoes of a character who has made all of his choices already; the game begins with him making his final choice. It wouldn't be appropriate for it to be a game of choices and consequences; you are not playing as a player-insert cipher, but as a fleshed-out human being who has taken a very specific and deliberate path. The game shows this quite cleverly by presenting the player with dialogue options that can't actually be chosen; things the character is thinking and maybe wishes he could say, but can't or won't. The main mind behind the game, Doc, is known for his writing on game design, so it is perhaps surprising that Adios doesn't have a lot of "game" to it. What it does have is a surprising range of verbs through which to interact with the game world; in the course of an hour or two max,  you will milk goats, feed horses, pat long-gone dogs, make a complete arse out of trying to make a stew (if you're like me and forget to chop your onions) and yes, even fire guns, proving that it is a real video game. Doc's fondness for a well-designed shotgun is sadly let down by the shotgun here being quite unsatisfying to fire, but given the budget and the lack of extensive war sequences, this can probably be forgiven that it isn't quite Mindbender's Ambition.Despite playing as a man in his middle-to-late years, the player can sprint and jump around like Gordon Freeman, I believe largely because Doc firmly considers it more important for a game to be pleasant to play on a basic control level than to stick strictly to narrative cohesion. As someone who spent large portions of Half-Life 2's endless talking scenes bouncing nearby cacti off a scientist's head and requires constant stimulation, I can certainly appreciate this. While all of the interaction is fairly perfunctory, it does its job of keeping the player occupied in the everyday, meditative tasks that the player carries out over the game's short runtime, which I personally appreciated and found kept me engaged in a few that few other games in the genre manage, comparable to What Remains of Edith Finch. At no point did I look for a cactus to bounce off any heads. I often approach games looking for them to justify why a video game was the medium chosen to tell their particular story, and Adios is one of the minority of "walking simulators" to reach that. Even where the player is railroaded, it serves a purpose; again, this is a character who has made his choices and we are only on board for the consequences. There isn't much else to say about Adios; do not play it if you're looking for a thrilling immersive sim about trying to foil a hitman who knows your character's routine and habits, do play it if you want to experience a great narrative that (other than the aforementioned disappointing shotgun) also happens to be enjoyable to play and will stick with you for a while after its brief playtime.
