_childDocuments_.review: I have a problem with crying, a few years ago something happened and i lost the ability to cry, no idea why that's so but now the only thing that makes me produce tears is lack of sleep. But this game is one of the only things that has come close to making me ball my eyes out. Please buy Adios you won't regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty good!There were a lot of times where I noticed that the subtitles didn't match what the voice actors were saying, so it can be a bit disorienting if you play with those enabled.  The jump you have doesn't let you clear the white picket fence around the house, either.Those were the only things I could think of when thinking of things I didn't quite like about Adios (and they are pretty minor, if I do say so myself).  Everything else about it is great!  Great voice acting, great writing, moving around felt great, etc.As for how it made me feel, I have this habit of taking a deep breath and letting out a sigh after seeing the credits of something I really enjoyed. After beating Adios and letting out a sigh, I kinda sat back in my chair and  for a while, feeling sad and satisfied at the same time.  I figure that the 'satisfying' aspect of Adios makes it really stand out among it's genre, since it's nice and short too, the fact that the game is as fulfilling as it is is a major plus.So, if you're in the mood for a short yet satisfyingly somber time, be sure to check out this game! It'll set you right.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: What an amazing game, been a long time since i played any narrative games and Adios is definitely some of the best i've ever played. It's short but it just hit the right emotions. The dialogues and the dynamics between the hitman and the farmer is just awesome, and the voice acting is also just on point. Bought this game to support Doc, and ended up getting an awesome experience. Here's hoping for Adios 2 and Waifu Death Squad!
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: I played this game a grand total of one (1) time a couple months ago and I'm still thinking about it today.  Games rarely hit home quite like Adios does, there's a very frank conversation about hobbies and passions that I've had with myself in the past, and It's honestly changed the way I look at what I'm doing.  Change your brain chemistry for only $17.99 + tax
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: I'll keep this short simply because I think this game is best experienced. A simple game where you do chores as a pig farmer while having an engaging conversation with a mobster that will make you want to reflect and introspect on your own life in ways you probably hadn't considered before. If it's on sale, definitely buy it cause it's worth it even at full price
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: I had been hearing about this game for over a year. That it was an emotional experience and it was best to go in blind, and they were right. The dialogue, the characters, scenario and the emotions involved all feels real. You feel empathy and emotion for the people in the story, till you are ready to burst into tears. It is a short game, but i am not sure you actually want this to last any longer. I am almost scared of what the developer comes up with next.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: This is a remarkably delicate game. I've often been sceptical of games with a strong narrative focus but this is a wonderful counter-example which proves that the right script- and talented voice actors and artists- can produce something truly impressive.There's also cleverly designed interactivity throughout the experience that keeps it engaging- it's not 'sitting through a cutscene'. There was a particular kitchen mishap I made (entirely caused by my clumsiness) that I won't spoil here, which wasn't a scripted moment, but it really made me smile and made the story uniquely 'mine'.For what was presumably a modest budget, to hit this level of subtlety is very, very impressive, something that AAA almost never achieves.As I said in my (updated) Paratopic review, I really, really want to see what this designer is capable of on a larger budget game, so I hope you consider picking this one up.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: There are so many dimensions of excellence in this game that it is hard to tell where to start. The experience uses every element of gameplay to tell the story and include you in it, both through the actions available to you and those that aren't, and through the emotions and state of mind it provokes. Playing through it I felt trapped, I felt like there was no way out, I felt  remorse for things in my own life that could be compared to things in the main character's life, and I felt frustrated about what I could do and what I couldn't do. This game accomplishes in it's short form what few other games have ever managed. In short, this is a masterpiece. And I truly mean that. There is no element of this game that is not perfectly tuned and designed to achieve a precise effect. And that includes the short length and the relatively few choices you get along the way. This is an incredible example of how to use the video game medium for dramatic and emotional effect. I expected a lot from this game and still my expectations were exceeded. The more I reflect on it the more I enjoy it. 12/10
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: I would love to see more indie games with this style of production. The graphics, while not cutting edge, do a great job of delivering the clear visual aesthetic that the team had in mind. The voice acting has a real edge to it that a lot of AAA games seem to miss, and it lends a special chemistry between the NPCs especially.It would be a disservice to dismiss this game as a walking simulator; I felt engaged throughout the playthrough and there's plenty to do in this game even if there isn't a strictly defined lose-condition.Keep an eye open for future releases. Looking forward to seeing where this dev goes next.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a somewhat spiritual journey that reminded me mostly of Nicholas Cage's Pig, in being a fairly serious and dower look at a man's life and what he wants to do in it. The involvement of pigs in both is a coincidence though, as they mean different things. Pig's, well, pig, is somewhat of a metaphor for innocence and simplicity in a world filled with rage and go-getters. Adios's use of pigs is closer to an acceptance of the circle of life and how at the end, no matter how much work has gone into maintaining your favorite car or taking care of yourself in memory of a long lost love, you are food for the pigs. Adios made me feel solace in the meaningless meaningfullness of life, and that's pretty neat.There's an argument to be made that Adios is not a good
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: I've been putting off reviewing this game because I haven't been able to adequately find the words to describe how *good* it is, but going any longer without adding my voice to the chorus of people screaming about this masterpiece would be unfair.It's just... really effing good. It made me feel things that I didn't know video games could make me feel. If I won the lottery, my first order of business would be to give Mischief twenty million dollars and let them make whatever game they want, because it would surely be the best game ever made.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know if I' the kinda guy for some of it, but out of all the l'il narrative games I've played this is the best.While I have small gripes with the visuals (I think the game is too bright (for me) lacking gamma settings, especially in the kitchen - and the goats move a bit weird), it's written ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ well, and feels like a damn good complete package.While I'm a bit biased since the writer is the one who led me to get the game, I really love the way characters are written - instead of loredumping, it's just a glimpse into a day in a man's life.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Personally, I cannot yet enjoy a game that deals so clearly, so closely, with such an intimate scene as the last time friends can spend a morning together. I am not strong enough.That being said, I believe this is one of the few times I've experienced a video game as something other than a means to escape my own situation. It's a short experience that tells me a great deal about the developers. I look forward to their next game.10/10, would recommend this game to anyone unconditionally.So I am.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Short and sweet. The game is frequently overwritten (the breakfast scene, for one, is intensely exposition heavy in a way that took me out of it), but its moments of brilliance leave me excited for its developers’ outing. Fishing after two devastating phone calls, watching the reflections of autumn tinged trees rippling in the water. The greyed out dialogue options continuing out of the frame, telling us so much more than the dialogue itself. When the script steps back and lets itself breathe the game is great. I just wonder if its author didn’t trust it to convey all of its messages without some heavy-handedness. Will definitely check out doc’s next!
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: One of, if not the, best examples of the artistic power of video games. You're given a direct line to the main character's thoughts in the form of dialogue choices within a deeply human and limited story of The Pig farmer who wants to quit the Mob work and why he got that way. I cannot recommend this game enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Not the most exciting game, most of the play involves listening to dialogue and periodically choosing how to respond, none of which have a big impact on the story. But the story is there and it's a fierce one. Recommended, but probably not at full price--you're not getting a game so much as you're getting a brief narrative experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A short narrative game about letting go, moving on, and decisions.Adios establishes everything a game of this genre should: Little things, scenery, dialogue, and moments that are hard and relatable. The phone calls hit especially close to home.I can see why people could/do think this game is a bit overpriced, but I got a lot out of it.8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A short and bitter-sweet narrative experience that takes around an hour to finish. A narrative game with a heavy emphasis on narrative. If that's not your thing, you probably won't like it.Adios takes a certain way of interacting with it to fully enjoy in my opinion. Don't approach it as if you were to play a game. Approach it as if you were to watch a movie. As stated before, there is very little 'game' here and the elements that are there only serve to support the narrative.Fully recommend if you're in the mood for something that will make you feel things.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios feels more like a playable movie than really any other game that tries to get the feel of a movie. But in no way would this work as a traditional movie. Being the one who control what the character adds an extra layer that you wouldn't get from a movie or even, for lack of a better term, "walking sim". You are experiencing what another character experiences. You have no control of the narrative. But you see through their eyes the story that unfolds.If I had to compare the storytelling structure, I'd say it hues closest to The Lighthouse.You're just experiencing a time and a place with a few people. And the game doesn't ask you to feel anything. To agree or disagree with what characters say and do.It just asks to inhabit to the story.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A walkin' and talkin' sim, this is a story that reminds me of Hemmingway's Hills Like White Elephants, but better. It's a long goodbye with a setting that is interactive in a way that feels logical.Only got my feet wet so far, but even the short amount i've played feels like its worth the value. Gone Home was $20 and that felt worth it. This game is even better.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: It took me a short while to get the way Adios goes about telling its story but it soon captured and ignited my imagination. It steadily feeds you bits to fill in the picture of who the characters are and escalates the story as an umbrella for some exploration, "mini games" and environmental storytelling and interaction. With the general Americana a lot of us are exposed to the character motivations and setting are quite accessible.As a somewhat impatient player in general, I'm sure I skimmed past some elements that flesh out the experience even more but that doesn't stop me from thinking of Adios as a thoughtful and quite charming 'experiment' worth your time.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: adios is a thoughtful, dark game that fits a moving story in a well packaged indie title. i would highly recommend this game; exploring the harsh and emotionally rich story of it's main character through the mundanity of farm life while keeping itself concise, replayable, captivating, and visually beautiful. kudos to the team
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: It's a slow, contemplative experience about living with your decisions.The story isn't groundbreaking and won't blow your mind, but perhaps expectations to always have experiences like that are unreasonable. Instead, this is like spending time in a well made short story. Long enough to endear you to your characters and understand their respective predicaments and that both are essentially stuck, their hands forced into an inevitable ending.Although you'll know the ending, that doesn't deter from willing yourself forward, taking everything in.Graphically, the game is rudimentary without a ton of animation flash, but the graphics aren't there to wow, nor are they distracting. The sound design and writing do enough to make it all work.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is an experience where you see through the eyes of a man who has decided that today will be his last day on earth. It is an experience I believe is worth having, in totality. It is short, to the point, and manages to deliver all of its thoughts and contemplations in the time it takes for many games to get started. There are more things I wish to say on the game but much like the farmer, I am having difficulty expressing my feelings through words, so all I will say is that I believe you should purchase the game and listen to its musings on life, death, grief, loneliness, and above all, saying goodbye.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adious reminds me of the kind of ghost stories that you come across every once in a while that aren't about horror, but the longing and crushing emotion of things left unsaid and undone, whether by choice or necessity.  You feel that weight on every line the characters say, and I'm left chewing on what they (didn't) say.  The love and attention to the story is felt, and I can't even begin to describe the delivery and work that the voice actors put into this.I know that I've made two references to weight as a concept, but I really have to put emphasis that Adios is a heavy game.  I laid in bed, trying to sleep, after playing it and just running over the ins and outs in my head over and over again.There's a scene right before letting you cook that really hit me hard.  Cooking of course is a cool down activity, but considering I had a lot of trouble just getting the ingredients without throwing them or the knife across the room, I couldn't stop laughing.  In a way this could seem like the cheese factor has ruined it for me, but this just made me laugh and appreciate this all the more.Adious is a 10/10 experience and a great example of what video games CAN be.  Play it.  Now.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: This is the story of a regretful pig farmer whose life is in shambles, he decides to stop his job for the Mafia and his friend and future executioner decides to try change his mind.While it's short and most of the time is spent doing mudane activities, it's strenght lies in the narrative and the culmination of emotions at the gut wrenching points of the story, wich the outstanding voice acting manages to bring forth.Be mindfull though, it's very short, under 2 hours. And if short moments of melancholic emotional story-telling is not what you want, then there is not much else this game can offer you.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: It's not something I'd recommend to people that value pure gameplay over storytelling.  If you need that to enjoy a game this isn't the one for you.But if you, like me, are curious how we can use interactivity to tell wildly different stories...  Well, you're here.  This is one of the greats.  It's contemplative, it's slow, it's a simmer that pulls you in to its main character's situation and asks you to color in the details.  Just give it a shot, it's absolutely worth even full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A interesting and unique game! The voice acting was really effective and I found the narrative quite compelling in presenting a moral choice. I'm not a big fan of the 'tell, not show' trope being used in some of the dialogue to flesh out the background of certain characters but it's also an inevitability when trying to tell a weighty and mature story in a format like the one in the game, so I understand why it was written in the way that it was (as well, the environment often ties back to these pieces of backstory/worldbuilding). I think the design was handled well, and I really appreciate the level of interactivity found within the experience as I think it adds a layer to how the player handles the central choice. I thought the sound design was also well done and really gives your decisions weight at the end of the game  as well as bringing your attention to considering the core concept of it all. I wanted to know more about these characters once I had finished the game, and I think that really speaks to the quality of the world building presented. Bravo!
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent narrative driven game that uses the aspects unique to the medium to convey its story.  Highly recommend this to anyone who enjoys a good story, good games, or both.  All the little touches and attention to detail, the little things you can do, the minigames, just superb all around.  What a great experience!
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Pros: Great story, amazing voice actors, the writing and dialog between the characters is amazing. The style and artwork of the world is one of a kind and helps pull you in to the game. Cons: Sometimes character animations are a bit jank, but they don't take away from the story. If your a big fan of walking sims I highly recommend this game. 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: I'll probably revisit this some time in the future. Played through it once, and I'm very impressed. I'm not a terribly difficult crier, but it's still not often a game makes me cry, and even in such a short amount of time. There's some really good writing in here, and everything else supports it incredibly well. The characters struck me as just a little cartoon-y, and the horse's humongous eyes took me out of it a little (small detail, could just be based on a breed I'm not familiar wtih though), but I eased into it quickly, and then it just helped. The lighting and the environments provide the perfect, melancholic ambience too. What surprised me the most was the quality of the voiceover. Really, really good stuff that's crucial to making something like this work.Well worth your time.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A short story put into game form that still remembers it's a video game. Many moments in this game will stick with you, from the discussion about extinct chestnut trees, to the heart wrenching phone call to the farmer's son, to beating his soon to be assassin in horeshoes and futzing around with the in game musical players. I like this game a lot and you will too.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Saw Casey liked a tweet about this game, bought this game, was very pleased. Great writing, great atmosphere, and pretty good voice acting too. It's short obviously, but I got it for like $15 on sale and I'd buy another game by the same dev in a heartbeat. Honestly might replay it too to see how different dialogue options go. _childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know if he will go to Heaven.You would think that someone who sinned all his life don't deserve such thing. And yet, at the same time, the basis of the very faith, the reason the Son of God were nailed on a cross was to redempt us, to show us that we could, in fact, wash away our sins.I never asked myself if I will go to Heaven. First because I'm only 19 as the time I'm writing this but also because I think I don't want to know. I don't want my actions to about "being good enough so that Saint Peter opens up the door" like if angels were some kind of bouncers.So about this game, right ? It ain't so much a game because it's not really fun. I mean, how are you supposed to have fun ? You can't have fun when you know the end. Each passing seconds, we are trying to borrow us some time, just long enough to that the grave fits us like a glove. Maybe he will, after all. Being scarred, starving, sick and acting in response isn't bad. I mean, it ain't good but can you help it ? Is that bad to run away when you can't deal with stuff ? I'm too stupid to run but that's because I'm stupid enough to have a deathwish. You could arguee he got such a deathwish after all, it was his choice. "Accorde-lui, Seigneur, l'éternel repos et que brille à ses yeux la lumière sans déclin."
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A very contemplative game. I mean, I've been thinking about it a lot since I finished it.It's impactful while being mundane. It says a lot with just a little, the voice acting is excellent, and the scenes play out in a way that's simultaneously affecting and fluid.For me, playing Adios was like reading a soliloquy on ifs and buts. It is absolutely worth your time and money.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good story, and well told. Not much in the way of player choice and you're not going into this for a 'whiz bang shooty' kind of good time, but it sticks with you for some time afterwards. Less like a popcorn action flick and more like something you spend an evening with over a single good drink.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: It's a walking simulator. It's very very short. It's animations are very budget. Your choices don't affect the story.If you are okay with all of these things, Adios is a series of interactive cutscenes telling a tragic story with natural dialogue between multi-layered characters in a brutal scenario. It reverse-engineers very specific feelings of bleak disconnected sadness, loneliness, and grief.It should be pretty easy to figure out whether it's your type of game or not, it's not that complex of a genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Generously speaking, I've had maybe three great moves in my lifetime, the "pack all your stuff and go" type moves. The third time, I'd been hurt and I'd done some hurt, and I decided to cut my losses and leave. By the time I'd set my things in order to get out, the entire thing had the momentum of a moving train. Too many plans had been made, too many loose ends tied up, too many goodbyes. Even though there was a part of me that wanted to stay, there was another part of me that had set too much in motion to stop. You can build an inertia and a trajectory in your life that propels you, even if you're ostensibly the one in the driver's seat. To me, Adios is about that aching velocity pushing you to an end, leaving in its wake the things you wished you'd said and the people you wish you'd said them to, all the while knowing the first push was your own.There are some great and surprising moments in Adios where I found I was holding my breath, wading through the fantastic tension built up between the main characters and between where I knew the story was headed and my own desperate, lizard-brained attempts to steer it elsewhere. I also have to praise the stellar voice acting, lending such a great, weighty regret to the story.Sit down for an evening, turn down your lights a bit, and play Adios.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: There's a certain level of sentimentality that comes from growing up in rural areas that a lot of people don't understand. As the world changes around us we have to adjust to the way things are; rather than the way they used to be. Adios displays a level of quaint and sentimental writing that says a lot more in it's short run-time than what is actually spoken between the characters. There is no right or wrong way to do things. Sometimes we make mistakes, and people misunderstand our intentions. We don't always see eye to eye, but that doesn't make either party 'wrong'.  It's also never too late to fix something. We can heal from past mistakes and find beauty in the mundane. For those playing the game. Feel free to ruminate on the dialogue a bit. There's no catch-all way to experience the game. You simply get out of it what you put into it. I've thought about the topics presented in this game quite a bit before, so it hits a little close to home. Narrative and characterizations are stellar. Be aware that the experience is only an hour or two long, but it has a lot of heart. Don't be afraid to take your time and explore the game. I think you get more from it if you go around and look at everything.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: That a game could exist that tells such a succinct and beautiful story, that manages to make me actually feel something and stop and think, to take a step back from the business of life and just... contemplate the questions it asks, is absolutely wonderful. Adios is, I think, some of the best media I have consumed in a long time, and something I will be thinking about for a long time to come.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly when I first read the description I was sold on the game. And it did deliver on that sweet catharsis I was craving when I bought this. It's a lovely experience, and it got me to cry a couple times, something that I haven't had many stories do.I'll probably be badgering my friends to pick it up it's so good, and I think I'll come back to it a couple times myself. The characters and the writing were interesting and I felt for them, and their troubles. I love the dialogue system, the idea of giving false options so you can see more into your characters headspace is incredible! I also love the art style, the mossy rocks look quite fun. There's more I want to write but it'd all be spoilers so I'll cap it off here.

_childDocuments_.review: Very well-crafted walking simulator about dealing with loss, grief and past mistakes. It's fairly short, but don't let that stop you; it's got a decent replay value(different conversation paths, achievements) and it's well worth it for what you pay for it.It's a very immersive setting; the world feels just right, the wind blowing through the trees and the animals walking around in the background. Conversations with other people are very natural, unlike many other games; it actually feels like you're talking to another person. That said, the story is sad / hard to swallow, and it does a real good job at making you feel like you are the main character. I'm writing this right after playing the game, still a little dazed from the experience. Think I'll need a little time to myself to process the game's story. I'd highly recommend this game if you liked games like Firewatch. It's got compelling and believable storytelling, great attention to detail on the sound/environment design and an interesting story. In my opinion it's very much a worthy addition to your steam library.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: It's kind of hard for me to describe this game without spoiling it to some degree. Outside of the overarching plot, you're treated to a well crafted story about a man, his farm, and his family. The writing is great, elevated by an amazing cast of voice actors bringing some amazing fluidity to the already well done dialogue. Hats of to this team for putting together such concise, yet fleshed out experience. It's great at making you relate to the plot and the people while also having you feed a corpse to pigs. Like listening to my grandpa talk about stories I haven't heard yet, but with a looming sense of existential dread.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot of reviews talking about how much of an emotional wreck they are after completing Adios, I can't relate to that. Not to be disrespectful to the people who've connected to the incredible voice talent and direction of all the characters, or the messed up situation that our protagonist finds himself in, but for me, the connection I felt with the game, and the promised ending meeting it's expectations left me feeling not emotional, but almost empty. If I could put it succinctly- I felt like a fixer with nothing left to fix. Sometimes that's okay. Do yourself a favor and pick up Adios, whenever you have a couple hours to kill.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: (I should point out that while I own the game on Steam, I played on my Xbox copy instead for convenience, yes, I bought the game twice.)Yes, the game is as good and well written as you have probably heard by now because you're reading these other reviews before you come to mine anyway. It's a "short and sweet" experience and doesn't waste your time while still giving you fulfillment. So... because you'll have already read or possibly heard about all of that before, I will have to be different. Thus, I will amuse myself and you as I muse a bit on my own non-spoilery thoughts.  Deal with it.First off, I will state for the record that I agree with "the friend" against the protagonist. I can't state my reasons without spoiling, but I just do. I am also a overly logical cold B-D, so take from that what you will.Second: I don't believe for a second that Bill isn't a hipster. I heard his music, I saw his posters. I would call him a hipster to his face.  I already hated him before this and now we are enemies.Third: I appreciate how much freedom the game allowed me during my "attempts" at testing my/its limits of what I was allowed to do.  No wasting energy on exploding fruit here either.Fourth: The eggs were good, but needed pepper.Fifth:  Curry.That's all I feel I can say without spoilers. If nothing else, play multiple times for different results (and your achievements if you care about that sort of thing), and then tell your friends to play (and spend money on) it so you can discuss without spoiling each other. Wouldn't that be nice?In conclusion:Support more indie devs, support THIS specific indie dev with YOUR MONEY or so help me, I will find you and do something terrible to you that you will not like and continue doing it until your wallet and your friends' wallets has been thrown at this game.  How else can we get a sequel out of it (and also achieve a different good deed)?Thank you for coming to my TEDTalk."Be good to your neighbors and we are all neighbors."
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best written games I have played in a very long time. The animations can be a little rough at times, but at no point did it hinder my experience of this genuinely engrossing story. The voice acting is very good and really facilitates immersing yourself into the story with some really interesting characters. The phone call with Bill hit me in a really hard way, it was rough. I also absolutely loved the story telling mechanic of the grayed out options and how they're used to deepen the character you play, and also contextualize some of the conversations in a way that is significantly more effective than if it were just simply stated. I'm trying to avoid spoilers so this review might come off a little shallow, but going into this game knowing not much more than the premise is the best way to experience it. Allowing yourself to get caught up in the characters, and having a game that, when it comes to story telling, respects it's audience enough to read between the lines and make inferences. It doesn't spell everything out for you, at least not emotionally, and the story is stronger for it.I highly recommend this game. I recommend buying it, I recommend playing it, I recommend reviewing it, and I really recommend keeping an eye on this team of creators, because if they get to create more works of art in this medium like this, they will quickly become some of the best story tellers in this medium, and I, personally, can't wait to see what they do next!

_childDocuments_.review: It's short and sweet. I'm not good enough with words to really say why you should play this game, but if you need to fill out an afternoon, this game's a great way to do it.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: I've thrown away more time trying not to think about or confront difficult stuff in my life than I'd care to consider. Stepping into the shoes of Adios' main character for this short spell felt more familiar to me than any video game I can remember, in a way that was simultaneously heartbreaking and comforting. Being invited to inhabit a space where I couldn't help but take a long, hard look at myself, even if that self was – in this case – someone else's, felt pretty dang special.(Note on playtime: I'd already completed the game on Xbox before I picked it up again on Steam; I think my first playthrough was around two hours. This time I just played until I could access his son's bedroom, which, with the foreknowledge from my previous playthrough, hit me hard enough that I had to stop playing for a while)

_childDocuments_.review: Simply put if you enjoy media that makes you feel, in this case sad, be in in music, movies, or video games then this is right up your alley.  It is hard to say how much of this type of game you could just watch as a movie but there is a certain feeling of people part of the world that you can only get from interactive media. that ability to look around and notice small things that would be in frame of the camera or to take as long as you need to take in a moment or screen not just what the director allots for that makes it something special. _childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Let me tell you what's great about Adios.The dialogue. The writing is excellent and these small scenes feel real and inhabited in a way that few games can accomplish. The voice acting is also just stellar. The main character and the hitman both have warm and realistic voices, and this adds a lot of weight to the story. I'm not sure I've heard voice acting and writing on this level since Firewatch. Really excellent work.The game itself is very good, but you should know what you're getting before you purchase. This is a 90 minute to 2 hour experience that is closer to a small play than a traditional game. If you're familiar with "walking simulators" you might have some idea of how this would function, but this is less walking simulator and more "interactive stage play" in my view. In other words, there is just slightly less to do and slightly more dialogue relative to other narrative first person titles.If I have any criticism at all, it's that some of the scenes run a few beats long and the player has run out of objects to interact with and things to do before the dialogue ends. This can create a kind of "mashing B during an unskippable cutscene" type gamefeel. But after a while, I just turned up the volume and stepped back from my PC and just listened and loved it. This *might* be addressed with just a few more interactable items or relative "activities" during these scenes? Or no? Similarly, a few small details that reward exploration during the more open bits could help. (also I accidentally clicked the timer and ended up eating a single boiled potato but... that's on me).In conclusion, Adios is an excellent 90 minute experience and I highly recommend it. The writer has a particular talent for dialogue and this is just a pleasure to listen to. I sincerely think there could be an easy adaptation to a stage play or a small audio drama with the script, and I'd honestly love that also. Only thing I didn't love was feeling a bit "fidgety" during a few scenes due to lack of relative activities.TL;DR Adios is very good and the whole thing sings like a particularly memorable scene in a Coen Brothers or Tarantino movie. Great work!
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: The only thing holding this game back is its budget. Please. I need more game stories that aren't blander than butter on bread.Anyway, call your dad. He misses you.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: All and all, this is a game worth your time. However, there are some issues I had with it.The biggest issue is that it is a game. It feels like this should have been a short story, or a movie you would see at a film festival. I can't help but think that the overall experience is dragged down by this being interactive. I'm not saying it suffers from being a low budget indie game, though the game mechanics themselves aren't good, I think I would have the same issues even if this were a big budget AAA game. Part of the problem is that this isn't even really a walking simulator type game. For more than half the game you are standing around talking with someone else. You can move around and do some small tasks while these conversations are happening, and interact with items here and there, but for the most part it just feels like I'm waiting around, not doing much.The second biggest issue I had are with the game mechanics themselves. For the first half where you are just chilling with your executioner the game has you perform various tasks such as feed the horse, milk the goats, etc. These are all unobtrusive, and as I said earlier should have just been a movie or something. But once you get to the second half-ish part of the game it has cook dinner as a much more involved task. The other second half game tasks add a contemplative few moments to the game, the closing moments of someones life. The cooking dinner task was not fun at all however. It was still a fairly short task, but the mechanics got in the way and pulled me out of the narrative. It was very clunky and led me to chop potatoes on the floor, and chop carrots and onions while they were still in the fridge. It was bad enough that I didn't even bother to explore the rest of the house to see any extras, I just wanted to push the story forward.The writing is impeccable. I felt myself disliking the player character at certain moments because of what he said, but that was because he felt real and I know people like him. Stubborn, waxing poetic nonsense about hobbies, can't reconcile with his son. It felt real. I was moved. I even got tears in my eyes at a couple of moments. Even with the very low budget facial animations that were almost comical, I was able to see these people as real.As a final thought, I never felt like the player character was me. This goes with me thinking this should have been a movie. Even though I was the one controlling the character I almost felt like I was intruding on an intimate conversation. It felt like I was in the room with these men, watching real people discuss death, and hell. It felt like I was sitting with this man when he was saying goodbye to his dogs grave. But I didn't feel like him. I felt like I was with him.In the end, this game has some issues. But it feels like a promise of something more down the line. I am very much looking forward to what they make next.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: the most compelling narrative experience i've had in recent memory.its approach to world-building is an approach i'd like to see more: characters who reveal details about their little quirks and sensibilities organically by grounding them in stories from their past. too many games these days focus on 'lorebuilding' in a hamfisted way, and i just wanna get to the good stuff.in exploring reasons why a man would be willing to die, it reveals little bits of what we can practice to live our own lives in the fullest.i loved this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is about an hour long story game for 1 play through.If you're not into stories, where there isn't much gameplay to be had and some minor exploration, but mainly observing a story then this is a really great one. It moved me a bit, got me noodling about some personal stuff of my own and that is hard to do. You want to change things not just in the game, but it's a lot of it is about coming to peace with things. Past mistakes, current mistakes, and more. It's touching and moving. I also have a special place for animals in me so a scene or two got me sniffling, so there's some great effort in the writing and the voice acting. Shout out to the Audio Wizard in the credits too.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a short and fantastic experience. Its insanely well written and insanely well voiced. Its a simple story with incredibly well fleshed out and realized characters. Its a walking simulator but it still involves the player and keeps you engaged in simple yet meaningful ways. It quietly establishes its own world in the background that I'm curious to see more of in the future. The voice work is in incredible as well. Its games like this that are good to point to and show people the potential of projects with real passion and how much we don't need to crunch employees into dirt for improved grass physics. This game did a whole lot with not very much. Its hard not to talk about it and sound pretentious but this game is good. Also 420 lol.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, very much recommended. I'm not going to spoil the story, for that is it's main feature. Just buy it, play it.There were two very minor issues I had: The audio cues are a little off (they played too soon and got cutoff by about 0.1s) and the game could do with subtitles. The voice actors do an incredible work and they are understandable, but as a non-native English speaker, I like having subtitles on anyway as it does help.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is an engaging and emotional story about a pig farmer who wants to stop working for the mafia.It doesn't have the deepest gameplay, nor the flashiest visuals, but gosh darn, it definetly brought me to tears. The dialogues are fantastically written and acted, and you can really feel everything the game wants to say to you.It's short and sweet, play it if you want to immerse yourself in a refreshing and well crafted story.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is the perfect example of game developers doing more with less. Yes Adios is a short game, but that actually works to its benefit. In no way does this game leave too quickly or overstay its welcome. The characters are so fully realized and fleshed out you can hear it in everything they say. It is clear there are experiences guiding their actions that, while we never get to see, adds a layer of complexity to every interaction. This game left me with more to think about and more stimulated than many multi-million dollar games I have played for the last few years. I am very excited to see what Mischief does next.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: I never played a game that made me feel so powerless in the actions and decisions I would make, the only other game that made me feel so powerless was Mass Effect 3. Unlike Mass Effect 3, I enjoyed feeling powerless. It felt purposeful. The dialogue, voice acting, and writing is phenomenal. Everything in this game has a purpose.I loved it and I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: A very contemplative little game, that feels like it takes cues from Thirty Flights of Loving, Coen Brothers films, and quiet american plays. The voice acting is stellar, which is very much the focus of the game. Interactions are neither particularly compelling or obtrusive, but it is well worth the hour it takes to play.

_childDocuments_.review: This game will stay with you, and its themes are beautiful, and the dialogue lives up to the Coen Brothers comparison, but I want to quibble with it, because I respect artistically what it's trying to do.***Spoilers Follow***Adios doesn't deliver on the promise of its own dramatic question. "Game about sticking to a complicated decision" seems deliberately contrived to avoid claiming it's about "making" a complicated decision, because there is no player choice. But in the absence of even the suggestion of agency, the player isn't "sticking to" anything either. From the player's perspective, this game doesn't contain any complication or decision. The "Nice Try" achievement is the closest Adios comes to exploring a tension that could have been mined in a fascinating way.I share the dev's frustration with The Last of Us franchise, in part because there's no meaningful meditation on what it means to "choose violence" when the game never presents any other choice. This, similarly, walks right up to an interesting meditation on suicide, but prevents me from engaging with it because (as the description says) it's a cinematic, not an interactive, story. I'm aware that's the point, but for me that made it far less effective. Even a fakeout - presenting us with a (fake or unsuccessful) possibility of effecting the outcome - would help, and I guess that's what the phony dialogue options are trying to do, but after the horseshoe sequence I hoped for some kind of escalation on that, and not just more of the same. Again: I get the point. But the only way you get to, say, "An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge" type-payoff is if you let us dream for a second that the grim and inevitable might be averted. The big twist is that "how you respond" will not in any way "determine the rest of your life," but the Steam description does far more to suggest otherwise than anything in the work itself.That said, you get to pet the horse. ⭐⭐⭐⭐
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Really interesting and engaging story that while short definitely doesn't leave you feeling unsatisfied. I think this story works really well in the context of a game and what limited interactions you have are there to further engage you in the narrative. This small team really put together an emotional and effecting piece of story telling and I think they deserve all the praise in the world for it. Hope they get to explore more ideas and stories with a bigger budget someday. I believe they could do something really great.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: There are multiple paths to explore, and I'm left wondering what tidbits I might've missed the first time.  This game encourages you to try again to see a different facet of a life.  Perhaps best described as a 3D Visual Short Story, Adios lets you reflect on the consequence of choice as its characters are revealed in the dialogue.  What could easily be an arthouse indie film has been provided to you in an easy-paced game format.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Narrative in games is always hard to quantify. Gameplay and story segregation is something only this medium really has to think about, and even then, not a lot of video game stories are both well-written and respected by the entire project. Good writers are rare, and projects that can put good writers to good use are even rarer.Adios is both very well-written and makes excellent use of everything in it. Stellar writing, incredible voice acting, amazing art direction and a clear goal from inception. It is exactly what it says it is, and delivers exactly what it wants to deliver. We're finally at a time when it's okay to have games just doing cool stuff that doesn't need to conform to any specific mold. The fact that there isn't anything quite like Adios out there isn't a huge exaggeration to try and get you to buy it -- it's just a simple fact, because video games are cool and you can do some cool stuff with them. Adios is rad, I really enjoyed it. Can't wait to see what else the devs put out.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A touching narrative about a man who has lost his will to keep going and the friend who tries to talk him out of it. Very well written, my only real gripe is that theres a lot of moments where the conversation keeps going but you still have free range of movement without anything to do so you just kind of stand there or distract yourself from the story by messing with the surroundings.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like narrative focused games, you need to play Adios. _childDocuments_.review: Ever play a game that stops you dead in your tracks?I at least kind of knew what I was getting into (obviously with the description being what it is), but I wasn't expecting it to feel...breezy, for as long as it did. The mobster's voice acting really sells it--his wry charm and charisma makes it feel like two old friends trying to avoid an unthinkable conversation. The protagonist, old, tired and grizzled, is flawed, but not in a bad way. He's made mistakes in life, done a few truly selfish things, and feels weighed down by them. He has a lot on his mind, has a lot he wants to say, but clearly isn't always totally certain how to express them, verbally or emotionally-- so he's sometimes just left grasping for words that may not even exist.I don't want to go into the whole story, because though it's not a long game (not that I personally think that matters) it's worth buying and discovering yourself. Needless to say, I like it. A lot.

_childDocuments_.review: SOME SPOILERS below.As many of you already may be aware, this is a SHORT game. I mean, REALLY short. And while it's not expensive as far as many games go, I'm not sure $18 isn't a tad too expensive regarding how short the game is. But that's my only "negative" with "Adios."It's a beautiful, cell-shaded, narrative "dialogue simulator." A few chores here and there. The game leads you (via a journal) from point A to point B. At times, you can (before or even during a chore) wander around the "farm." Or your "house." But there are invisible walls which limit your wandering. Still, a large space to wander: a house w/ 2 floors, several rooms and a basement, a shed with a gorgeous 60s car in it, a horse to visit, a pigpen, a goat shed, even a surprise shed where the protagonist tends to his hobby (you'll see).Examining many articles (cans, teapot, etc) don't lead anywhere, but you can pick some things up and look at them if you want to. Even play records or 8-track tapes! One of the chores is even having to catch a fish at one point. Or feed your horse. Or milk a goat! The farm itself, and the house, is quite charming. Restful in fact, a nice irony considering the line of work our protagonist is in.Plus, the voice acting is superb with all characters. You really care about the protagonist's life and his regrets. There are some tender moments. His "boss" obviously doesn't want him to "quit" the bloody business he's in, and tries to talk him out of it, but the protagonist won't have any of it. Will he pay for it in the end or get a chance to live out his life in peace and quiet? Play with him as he ponders his choices. Since the voice acting is superb throughout, you are absolutely drawn into the game as he ponders his life choices and shares his regrets with his boss. And especially when he calls his son. Or has a tender conversation with his departed pet dog. Just a sweet,melancholic game.The environmental design/artwork is gorgeous and a welcome addition to the cell-shaded genre. Not a lot of music or ambient noise to speak of, but you DO feel as if you really ARE on a farm. The animations of the only characters you see are a little on the bare side, but the story is so good you rarely notice.The game picks up at the last "scene" you left off in if you haven't completed it yet when you last quit. Once the game has been completed, you can select a replay of interactive scenes.So ADIOS is definitely worthwhile. A well-optimized, gorgeous, cell-shaded indie game. Full of melancholy and all voice acting is great. Just: a SHORT game no manner how long you pad it out if you choose just to take in the sights. I think it could have been cheaper, seeing how long it is (90 min tops), but I fully support creative and talented indie teams and if this game is a sign of things to come, I'd absolutely recommend paying the $18. If only for the heartstrings that are being clutched!

_childDocuments_.review: Only you can know you, and what's right for you.In the case of Adios, the focus is on accepting and preparing for more terminal consequences, even in the face of protestations from those operating from mixed positions of personal interest and societal mores, but it kind of rings universally for a lot of big changes that way.It's about doing what you feel (or know) you need to, even if it's not enough a counter to regrets that may have led you to that decision to do something in the first place.It's about how going through the motions is fine, as we're the ones who decide which motions to go through.It's about how there is often still a present to be had even when the past has slipped away and the future is cloudy at best, sometimes more than one such present.It's the closest a game's ever felt, to me, like the messiness of simply being, regardless of whether the cessation of that being looms nigh.Thanks.

_childDocuments_.review: I think the best way I can describe Adios is to talk about something that happened to me while I was completing the last few achievements, seeing all the tiny moments that I'd missed. I had just finished a part of The Confession, and was moving on to The Shotgun. I selected that scene, and appeared in the house's kitchen holding a shotgun. I tried to move, and fell through the ground to the sub-ocean a few metres below. The ground was no longer relevant. I saw the farm in its entirety; I saw the horse, moving around its paddock; I saw the grave beneath the General's branches; I saw the shed hiding the farmer's last love - everything but the hitman. And then the farmer began talking to himself, as if there was someone else there, though the only other thing I could hear was the wind moving through the trees. At that moment, with the hitman fully excised from the story, I think I understood the farmer better than I could have otherwise. Death still hung heavy over everything, even though the reaper itself was absent.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked this game, it was a nice moment with someone who's lived a long and hard life. Despite the morbid subject matter, I found it a comforting experience for myself. My grandfather owned a ranch in rural Texas, and he passed last year. Going through his house and seeing so many memories of my childhood, and years before that of his life, was a somber but blissful time. I miss him, but that time in that house, checking every corner and hearing stories of him from my mom made it a crucial moment of my life personally. I inherited some coats and books from him, and I appreciate their presence.     This game tapped me back into it, while it's context was dramatic, it still held that somber exploration of all of the rooms of a house that tells a life well lived. The back room of the house with tools and rainboots I could almost smell the wet dog stench that remains in that room to this day from my grandfather's. I remember harvesting and eating the... well walnuts instead of chestnuts as a kid. My family even found old records of his opera singing in his prime, making Bill's room oddly familiar too. and whilst the game took place in Kansas, rural Texas in fall has a very similar air to it. This game made me reflect on my relationship with my grandfather, I loved him but we weren't close. As I got older, it became harder to talk to him. Partly because I wasn't in Texas anymore, but also because even when given the opportunity I never had the courage to ask him of his musical years, or tell him of my own progress as an aspiring music composer. I couldn't relate with him with my newfound appreciation for ranch work and farming when I was at a charter school either because I didn't know how to bring it up. I wish I could have talked to him more because I knew he probably would have loved that. This game is really good, and I appreciate it's ability to tell a story that can hold it's narrative weight whilst also tapping into something so grounded. Made me reflect and made me want to do better to remember my grandfather.

_childDocuments_.review: A dark, lovely, and brooding game with fantastic voice acting. I mentally put it in the same bucket as interactive fiction, as there's a narrative that you interact with and you make choices that impact the dialog. There's some interesting subversion as well. Can be completed in one sitting, but don't rush through it.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A game with heavy and mature themes, that tells a simple yet profound story in few choice words and scenes.Adios is that one last walk around your home you take before you say goodbye to it forever, and the development team has ensured that every scene has the right amount of emotional weight and catharsis. The ability to choose how you will spend your time with your would-be killer is certainly a unique kind of narrative tension that I've not experienced in any other medium - and can likely only be achieved in a video-game format. The developers take this a step further by giving you dialogue options your character will refuse to say due to the context of the setting, further developing the characters and story through denial of gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most strangely heartfelt games I've played. I've never been moved to tears as often in such a short amount of time, in any form of media. I feel that it's hard to talk about this one without spoiling the beauty of the game, so just play it yourself and see what it's all about.
