_childDocuments_.review: I have really enjoyed my time with Adios, I completed the story in about one hour, and I really appreciate the courage that it takes to make a short game. Adios has a simple yet good story to tell, and respects my time as a player. Playing Adios is like being the main character in a good TV series episode or a 90 minute movie. I recommend playing and I hope more short games like this get made.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A short narrative experience that takes place over a series of scenes where you talk to your friend/murderer. You have decided to stop working for the mob, and the (brilliantly acted) conversations over the course of the game go into the events and reasons that lead you to your decision. During these conversations you complete simple mini-games and make a few choices regarding what you say. While the choices ultimately don't change much, both these things provide enough interactivity to bring you into the moments (there are some points that play with the dialogue options in a really nice way as well).
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a brilliant little game that will take at most 2 hours for you to complete. Even then the main choice in Adios (to stop feeding bodies to pigs for mob) is made before the game even starts. It doesn’t ruin the game though — it makes it shine. The tension and emotions are born of characters reflecting on this choice and what led to this point in time.Adios resonates with the player HEAVILY. The game offers a situation unfamiliar to most of its players (I hope), yet it is easily understandable. Motives, goals and even the entirety of the plot are conveyed to the player in the first minute of the game. That’s how tension is created – we see subtext in every dialogue, we know the stakes, we feel for the characters. Effectively delivering this info makes room for us to follow characters more closely than twists and turns of the plot.What may be as important is that Adios effectively employs the features of the medium it chooses to tell this story in. It effectively uses dialogue tree to highlight thoughts our protagonist wouldn’t dare to voice. By giving us minute things to do during dialogues it makes us embody the Farmer and live through his memories.It’s a game driven by characters, focused on characters, effectively conveying emotions in all the right places and very much medium-appropriate. I truly believe Adios exemplifies character-based drama. Give it a try, if you haven’t already.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A quaint little story with fantastic voice acting, telling the final chapter of a troubled protagonist, that uses some quirky tricks to mess with the player and further expand the storytelling in a way unique to the medium.A bit steep if you're not the kind of person to want to replay a story based experience, but what you're getting here is worth the price even if you're only riding once.Uncertain if there are multiple endings, some things imply it but it seems the kind of thing that's bound to end a certain way.Either way, I very much enjoyed it, and think most people looking for a calm, somber story will too.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: It's a pretty good game! You can finish it in like less than an hour and a half (I was afk for a bit), so I really can't say too much about the story without spoiling it besides saying what's on the box: There's a farmer who doesn't want to dispose of bodies for the mob, and a decent chunk of the game is walking around and talking with the hitman about the farm and his life and all that. It's an easy recommend from me, as I tend to enjoy games that are closer to movies or TV shows with light interaction like TellTale and Dontnod's work (specifically The Wolf Among Us and Tell Me Why). Now, it's not up there with some of my all-time favorites. You can kinda tell where it's going pretty early on, and some of the dialogue is pretty on the nose here and there, but for the most part it's real enjoyable to listen to these two friends talk to each other over just about anything. The voice acting is impressive, but really only for the scale of the game on display, otherwise it's just okay (WHICH IS STILL A GOOD THING). The atmosphere is seriously well done, and I liked the use of  One weird thing though is that they keep saying that the hitman character is supposed to be pretty old (I'm guessing mid to late 40s by the way they're speaking), but honestly he looks like he could be in his late twenties. I bought the game day one because I was really excited for it, and only just now got around to playing it because I was in the middle of some other games when it came out. It was definitely worth it, and I hope it does well enough to let the people who made this game continue making things, because there's a real talent here that I want to see again in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great and heart felt experience. The story, voice acting, and dialogue really build a strong foundation for this game. There's little tidbits of details in the world that help make everything believable and feel lived in. This game hits some neat emotional notes that left me feeling a bit maudlin. Pros:Visuals. There's a charming cel shaded mixed with some stylized characters and design. It's really neat and enjoyable. Some hiccups here and there with animations and the animal proportions seem a touch strange sometimes, but overall still pretty great. Story. You kinda get where this is going from the summary of the game and right from the start. The more you learn about the relationship between the main character and the people around him, including his would-be-killer, your dried shriveled up heart starts to weigh a bit more or at least mine does. Voice acting. The voice acting is truly a performance rather than just dialogue being read to you. Everyone feels like a person you know and it feels natural. I could listen to the neighbor rant all day. ConsThere's certainly a discussion to be had about value here. It's $17.99 US and I finished a playthrough in just under 2 hours. It's like purchasing a movie I suppose, but with games it just feels weird. The experience is quality and more money doesn't always mean more gametime, but I did want just a bit more from it. I had one bug with the ending (no spoilers) but I literally just saw a hand get kind of glitched and the game ended. I replayed it and I realized it was a bug. Minor, but that was the end of the game, kind of a pivotal moment that was marred for me by a bug, but that's still pretty minor. If you like walking sims like Gone Home, this is an easy recommendation if you're okay with a 2 hour quality experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: I like that this game trusts you to roleplay a predefined character (e.g. fishing for me was anxious procrastination rather than relaxation, and the choice not to sprint was to enjoy one last walk while the wind blew through the woods). I'm proud of Farmer for seeing this through, and I hope Bill is OK and can find forgiveness and peace.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is exactly what it promises to be. It is a story about a man who has made a decision. It doesn't give you choices that effect outcomes - the meaningful choices have already been made. But it does exactly what it intended to do: it evokes a feeling. It produces a melancholy mood that will stick with you.The writing is excellent. The voice acting is excellent. Many reviews complain about bugs, I only saw one, and it did not ruin the experience in any way.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a short, linear, but very emotional experience.The writing and voice acting is stellar and are - perhaps obviously - the standout features of the whole game. The dynamic of the pig farmer and his contact is great, and so is their individual characterisation.It should be noted that while there are some dialogue choices, they do not affect much in my experience, and the overall story is always the same. Personally, I am more than fine with that, but don't expect this to be a "choices matter" type game. It is more about subtly expressing yourself while you go along with the story presented to you.There are some interactive scenes, such as skeet shooting or throwing horseshoes, but they are very basic and clunky to control at times. They do serve as a nice thing for the player to do while you're having a conversation, though not all dialogue scenes have such a "minigame" attached to them and so some scenes will have you standing still or jumping around inappropriately (I am more of a jumping around type).I was subtly impressed by the audio work. The environment FX feel very natural and work well in establishing the contemplative nature of the game.I recommend playing this game when you have the time to let it really sink in and not rush through the tasks given to you. Adios is one of those games where the interactive nature of it being a game is very subtle. How long will you sit by the lake before you get back inside and call your neighbour? It's imperceptible choices like these that elevate Adios in my opinion.Finally: should you buy it? I definitely recommend it if you are in the mood for an emotional, mature story. However the playtime is quite short with 1-2 hours and there isn't much in terms of replayability. So while this definitely isn't the most "bang for your buck" game on Steam, it offers something that few games do, and I love it for that.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a contemplative experience, it allows us to briefly fill in the shoes of a man that makes a difficult decision. It's difficult to talk about without spoiling it, all I will say is that it left me feeling raw in a way that few games had. Admittedly it didn't leave me overly emotional over the events, rather it gave me time to reflect on the idea of finality. This is a well written and well crafted experience, it is worth your time and I hope this sees enough success so that the talent behind it can go on to craft more like it.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: The premise of the game is rather obvious and you can see where it will end, still it is a good one, the dialogue and voice acting that leads you to it is what makes it worth it, there are some "questionable" decisions that i have seen people complain about but i think with its low price it is a good bite sized experience, if you can buy it i recommend you to do it and play it, and to experience it with someone. At first i also questioned the multiple dialogue options decisions but after the second one and reading what the option that wasnt really a option was you understand what they are going for, and it contrbutes to the overall feel and atmosphere of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A very, very good narrative game. It has a beautiful, somber feeling of finality to it. It offers a lot of thoughtful insight into, uhm, life, in it's short, almost vignette-like scenes.Remember all those conversations about how the different dialogue options in The Walking Dead where all thoughts running through the main character's head? Well, Adios takes that idea and runs with it, and it couples the interactivity of a dialogue system the fact that you're inhabiting an actual character, and this leads to something powerful that I don't want to "spoil". I want folks to experience it first-hand.Definitely worth playing!
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: I'd pay this much to own a movie I wanted to watch more than once, and I'd pay this much to own this game.The story is astoundingly well written, and the actors give incredible performances. Though some aspects of the game's design feel a bit iffy as a player  (I'm looking at you, inscrutable horseshoes game) , the game delivers an effective and emotionally impactful message using all the tools it has available.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios Is genuinely enthralling little game about trying to write the wrongs of a conscience you sold off long ago.Despite it's brevity, you get to explore most of a mans life, learn the decisions he made along the way, how they shaped him, and the regrets he has.It's narrative laser focus is akin to a James Sallis Novel, pulling no punches whilst not overstaying its welcome.I loved every bit of it, check it out!
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is one of those games where I want to try and write down some real thoughts, rather than just observations about the voice acting (good) or the graphics (serviceably minimalistic and evocative.) The aim of the 'game' as it were, or the aim of the experience, is to try to get you to inhabit the situation or the life of somebody else for a moment. And it succeeds at this very nicely. In just an hour and a half you get a feel for who this person is. What they gave gone through. How they think. How they relate to their life and to others. What the 'mood' of their world is like. Initially this is conveyed through a series of discussions with the hitman character, which take place alongside a number of mini activities. But the strongest section is the last quarter in my opinion. When you engage in a few final activities by yourself, say farewell to your horse and your dead dog, and have a particularly difficult phone conversation. Maybe I'm wrong about this, but the first 3/4 of the game feels like it's what gives all the weight to that final 1/4. And of course, all of the game as a whole is what makes that final scene have such impact. Excellently structured, and showing remarkable restraint. I could imagine other games stretching the dialogue out to two or three times the length. Maybe adding lots of letters to find and read through, or something similar. Adios doesn't do this, and it's excellent because of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is In my opinion, a tense and very introspective look in to making a difficult decision with no real correct answer-It has been one of the most deeply moving personal experiences I've had with a piece of media, let alone a game. You know those moments that make you set down the controller/back up from the keyboard for a moment to reflect? Such moments are here, and crafted quite well. All I'll say regarding specifics is, I didn't feel as though I'd relate so much to a pig farmer- but little did I know I'm well acquainted with being way too deep in a situation of my own choosing, without a clear right/wrong answer. I can't recommend this experience enough. I'd like to leave you with a bit of advice that may pertain to the game and certainly does to real life.If you ever find yourself in Hell, regardless of how you got there, just keep walking forwardThe alternative is much worse.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: It's a game that makes you think about past choices from your life. Voice acting was great. The only feedback I can give (for future games) is that it would have been interesting to have multiple endings available, depending on your answers throughout the game (e.g. choose to continue the deal, reconcile with your son, etc).
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely good little slice of storytelling finesse. Made my heart ache at certain points in the best of ways. It's not the most video-gamey video game (despite some "pointless" indulgences like having a jump button because jump good) but it's a great experience of being in the head of someone who's led a long hard life and tries to make one last good choice in it. Price might be a bit high to some but I like to think of it as a ticket to a very good movie, and it's certainly worth the immense amount of passion that clearly went into every bit of the game, from the art direction to the writing to the acting.This is definitely something special, and will hopefully lead to many more amazing things from the creatives behind it.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios manages to tell a compelling crescendo of a complicated man's life in its short run-time. It's buggy sure, but Bethesda games are buggy as ♥♥♥♥ and they aren't made by a small team. The devs are actively fixing bugs as far as I can tell too. Pick it up if you have the money to spare (especially since one of the main writers is having major trouble paying his medical bills).
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is an excellent short story in game form. The writing is sharp that these characters feel so vividly drawn within such a short time frame. You feel like you live in the main character's shoe by the end of it.However, I will warn that the game is a little glitchy that can lead to you restarting a scene when something does work correctly.Even with this caveat, I would recommend this game to anyone looking for an interesting experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A restrained, pastoral gut punch of a narrative further elevated by some extremely high quality voice acting and direction. I have seen a lot of reviews ask why this needed to be a game. Well, for one, it's a game because those who made it wanted to make a game. Second, what other medium allows for this much intimacy and embodiment of the characters? Sure, you could write a story in second person or film from first person and capture a modicum of that, but those are either more imperative or more detached. What this allows you are quiet moments of your own to walk about a farm, and reflect, or the opportunity to just go ahead with it all if you want to face the inevitable quickly.Also, crucially, you can bunny-hop.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Brilliantly written, quietly powerful. 'Adios' is a game with the patience and the focus to really hone in on it's message and deliver to players a steady stream of mounting emotional tension from the very start, while simultaneously introducing a world and characters that are lived in and full realized. And along with the wonderful writing is some truly nuanced vocal performances all around.It's an excellent meditation on life, death, the jobs we do, the reasons we do them, and the consequences of knowing when to stop.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: For a lot of games grey morality is players making a distinctly good or bad choice and then having a consequence that seems counter to the action, or good choice bad consequence. Adios takes a different approach, the player doesn't get a say in the choice, it's already been made. The player then gets to follow along as the game justifies that choice and why there is no changing the character's mind. It's a melancholic and intimate look into having to make a decision that will result poorly for you as an individual but is ultimately the right thing to do, going through the motions of a normal day, that you know ultimately will be your last. The writing and voice acting are well above what you would expect for such a small title. The graphics are appropriate for the setting, and almost weird video gamey American Gothic, which only reinforces the fairly simple gameplay mechanics of walking around and doing basic farm chores while talking to the man who you know will be coming to kill you later.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a beautiful game with a short, melancholic story. Had some moments that really took me by surprise in the best way. For a game that takes place in one house over one day and took one hour to get through, I sure think about this one a lot.  For folks who enjoy powerful short stories I can't recommend this enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Instead of slog through another somber narrative about death, the game actually takes its time to not only humanize the PC but also the hitman. It evokes the fears and insecurities that come with aging. Hours turn into minutes. Weeks into days. The years begin to weigh you down.Loneliness, purpose, love, death and its uncertainty.Many have maligned the art style but I rather liked it. With its smooth textures, washed out palette, and distorted character models it perhaps unintentionally replicates the way thoughts appear in your head or dreams as they are recollected. Almost as if all of this is flashing before the player right before the game's climax. This is complimented by the vignette presentation.Adios is a great game and it makes the argument that there is a place for minimalist interactive experiences. Games like this strip away even more "gameplay" than your average walking sim, but in doing so create an experience with just enough interactivity that its like being a part of a play.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios reminds me of a one-act play. It took me a little over an hour to get through the story, but it's a damn good story. You really feel for the characters. The voice work is really well done and really brings the characters to live. I recommend this game if you're someone who likes narrative driven games, and if you have an hour to get through the incredible story.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is really good! The voice acting is great, the writing is moving, and the art style is distinct. It has a meandering pace -- which helps bring home the idea that this is the story of someone saying goodbye -- until it reaches its fast and intense conclusion. I played through it in one sitting and can't wait to see what the team does next.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Incisive and tactful study on the harshness of departures. A goodbye always involves detaching from a part of oneself and this piece explores every remaining corner of a person's soul. There's something especially difficult, not to mention scary, about having to say goodbye when it's necessary rather than when the time comes on its own. This game does an excellent job at approaching that.Give it a go. It's a 1-2 hour-long playthrough and at first glance it might seem rather overpriced but the quality of the writing, voice acting, narrative structure, and general work put into those 2 hours easily make up for it. You'll be playing it more than once.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: It's a pretty solid, tight little narrative game! It's less about making choices, and more about congenially doing an activity together while you talk - which turns out to be a pretty neat way to deliver a game narrative. Writing's great too!Oh, tip on the cooking: there's recipes, read it. I just kinda uh, threw stuff in, and my guy ended up eating a microwave burrito instead, in shame.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to have to run through it a few more times to see everything, but but this is really a really good interactive story. The voice acting is top notch and while I think the writing is spectacular, I think that may partly be because The Farmer in outlook, accent, and timbre remind me of someone specifically from my past. I think a lot of the criticisms are primarily reactions to trying to force Adios into being something it's not. Adios isn't really something you can "win". There is no Big Bad and there aren't a bunch of different dialog trees. Just let go of your expectations and just sit back and enjoy the ride.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: This recommendation is contingent on if you can find enjoyment solely in the story. If you are expecting something more akin to an elevated game narrative, you may want to come back to Adios when it is on sale.I want to like this game more than I do. There is a lot to love; the meticulous design of the farmland, the deep characterization and sublety in the dialogue, and the astounding vocal performances. The interplay between the two characters is compelling, but only about as much as other media I've experienced. The gameplay leaves a lot to be desired. Interactivity is limited to a fault; dialogue choices are the main focus (as they should be), but everything around it seems too shallow. The player actions such as feeding the horse, shoveling, and catching fish do a lot for the setting but almost nothing for the narrative. I had no idea how the horseshoe score was calculated, or why it even mattered. The goat milking interaction was the best but it felt a bit janky. I wanted to do more with the soda machines. The dialogue is expertly written and beautifully performed. The game is about killing yourself through choice. Unfathomable choices about family and heritage, and what it means to witness tragedy. In my personal opinion, this kind of story would be much better served as an audioplay, stageplay, or short film. I felt connected to the voices rather than the characters. The level of skill demonstrated in the dialogue was incongruent with the game as a whole.  To conclude, this game is worth your time. It's a narrative that runs deep through the 90's American midwest psyche without being preachy. I did not personally empathize with the story but I'm sure many people will. Buy this game so that Mischief makes more.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: The premise is compelling, the characters rich & writing sincere; delivered believably by the voice actors. It's gentle and understated, but it's also experimental at the edges. The character & dialogue controls are separate so you can juggle the talking with mundane tasks such as milking goats, eating eggs & feeding neatly packaged murder meat to pigs
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: So I finished my first day as a pig farmer. A special farmer, but also a very ordinary one. Full of love for... his own projects, his own animals. The game will not fill you with awe for its design or music. It will take you in for its story, its plot, its settings, and will keep you immersed in it from start to end. Plenty of irony, sadness and good dialogue. A little narrative masterpiece. Respect.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: The heart and soul of Adios is the writing. Performances by the cast are also very strong. Given a larger budget, I would love to see what this team is capable of. The only objective issue I have is the price in Australia. $25 for something of this scope is a bit steep. That said, I really enjoyed my time with it and would recommend people give it a go for the reflective narrative.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Howdy kiddo's you ever tried to fix the unfixable issues that you have either created or perpetuated? Have you finally learned to tell yourself that you're ready to accept the eventual outcome; Not because you're ready for said outcome, but because you know that you have no power in getting a better conclusion? And that all you can do is give as much as you can give in the end and hoping that God will sort you out right?Well, this game's generally about that, it's good in that it is laser focused on this journey of irreparable consequences and self loathing in a nice two hour package, so I certainly think it's a nice ride. It does unfortunately fall too much into the melodramatic and over embellished for it to hit me personally, but solid atmosphere and great voice work elevate it to a nice little sad story.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot of things to be said about Adios but I feel like much of it has either already been said, or ultimately won't amount to anything in regards to convincing someone to play it.If I were to encapsulate the game as best I can, I'd describe as the season finale of a very very engaging TV show, with a direct comparison for me being Ozark. The episode(s, i'd view it as a 2 parter) focuses more on the choices, and subsequent fate, of a prominent side character; instead of having your regular plot mcguffin or direct obstacle the characters must overcome, it's pure character drama with stellar performances and ultimately will make you start crossing your fingers for a 2nd season.However it should be noted that the medium of being a video game doesn't go unused, as with certain dialogue options that you can't actually say giving you insight into your characters thought processes, and the various chores you end up doing giving you a better sense of time. There's a few issues here and there, but in regards to low budget storytelling you can't do much better than this.That's all I really have in regards to selling people on the game/singing its praises, so now I just want to bring up 2 things I think could've been improved. Firstly, the noise the PC makes when you attempt to select a grayed out dialogue option doesn't really fit the tone of situations those options usually come up in. It's an almost upbeat or curious "hmm" noise, but every instance with them is usually very somber or sad.2nd, (some spoilers) Bill's room is filled with posters that look like rock bands, possibly even punk bands, and there's a record player and a tape player with tapes and records scattered around you can play, but every single tape and record plays classical piano songs. Not that I think someone who decorates their room with rock posters would never listen to classical, and I do understand WHY those songs were chosen, it just seems very odd that someone with said posters wouldn't have any music associated with them lying around, and it sticks out like a sore thumb.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A short, interactive story. A bit thin on content with fewer interactions than expected but succeeds in an area where few video games still do in telling a complete story without wasting the audience's time. There's still room for additional polish here like a lack of sound effects where you'd anticipate having them but overall a satisfying story game.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: From the start I knew Adios wouldn't end with a gunfight. This is not a story about resisting outcomes, about changing how things are going to go. Sometimes you chose to do something a long time ago and it's influenced your life ever since. Sometimes you can't do a job anymore, even when the benefits are holding your life together. All you can do is try and get someone to understand why you made the decision you did. And sometimes even then, with nothing to lose, there are things you can't bring yourself to say.Adios is the story of a man who is trying to share his life, his little corner of the world, with someone else. It's a lovely, atmospheric, emotional narrative game.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished this game, and I was absolutely blown away. The dialogue in this game was profoundly beautiful, all the more so for being about a character who struggles to express himself. Even when the dialogue choices seem similar, the subtle changes in tone feel incredibly significant, and the use of non-selectable dialogue options adds so much weight to the story. I can't recommend this enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: This is a superb meditation on so much, with an excellent economy in terms of the verbs that are tied perfectly to the story. It never does anything it doesn't need to, nor does it remain too long. The voices are both well written and acted bringing heart to every character and showing you who everyone is. This game is up there with Firewatch, Gone Home, Tacoma and Paratopic for walking simulators - for me.Since this is a first person game my suggestion is to make use of the controls you have to further embody the main character. You're a man, a farmer, a vet who doesn't have problems talking but can struggle to express your emotions. Don't just stand there as scenes play out. Move, touch things - be who this person is. Show how uncomfortable it would be to say what you're saying. Revel in the space and actions available.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Like a short film, but interactive. The scene setting and context clues remind me a lot of Fullbright's Gone Home or Tacoma. But you're not so much "discovering" audio cues here. The scenes are more guided and contain plenty of interactive moments to help you embody the character of the farmer as the story progresses. Great writing and voice acting really brings the dialogue between the farmer and his friend to life.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: It took me a bit to start this review, because Narrative-focused games like this one typically aren't my first choice. I love narratives, character dives, but it's tough for a game to sway me if it doesn't compel me in a gameplay way.Reason I picked it up is because I initially caught wind of it through Paratopic and Hardspace, the writing history of Doc Burford. The reason I stayed to write this, however, is because of how this game draws you in. Laid bare as it is, it still compelled me.I'll speak little on the story, but I do want to touch on one early moment. The shed. I could feel the frustration in trying to explain coming to terms with things in your own way, of being expected to react a certain way, to be expected OF. The pig farmer speaks of (Minor content spoilers)  And that got me blubbering.The gameplay complements the story, but doesn't get in the way of it, either. It goes quickly, if you want it to. Hell, there's even a sprint button. It's small, and I'm sure other "walking sims" include a run option, but it was notable enough for me, in something I thought would be a slower, controlled experience. I almost didn't press it every opportunity I had, just so I could take a moment, since I knew what I was eventually rushing towards anyway. Might as well take a few looks at the scenery. Wonder about the offhand details that the conversations unearthed, and maybe see if there's any secrets tucked away.Adios comes in, gives you a man and his life, and then says goodbye. You might finish it quickly, but I feel like that's by intent. It was never meant to last, and you choose how quickly it goes.The team did a wonderful job on this... I'm desperately hungry for more and I wish Mischief all the best.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A big fan of narrative type games and this one does not disappoint. I would say this is on par or above most of the recent games in the genre, the story is phenomenal and the voice acting is just on point. The stylistic choices lend well to making a focus for the story without distracting from it. Right now my favorite game of 2021.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent short yet poignant experience.There is not too much in terms of gameplay, basically just on-rails minigames, but gameplay is not the focus here, instead it focuses on telling a story about life, death and everything in between through excellent voice acting and good pacing.There are some bugs as of the time of writing this review, but never found one that was gamebreaking and eventhough it could be finished in one hour by rushing through it, if you like stories like the ones in Firewatch, Dear Esther or even shorter games like Wide Ocean Big Jacket you definitely should play this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a short, closed experience that really  gives you a lot to think about and puts a lot of thoughts in your head about the  themes it wants to convey. It has a few quiet things to it that really enhanced the experience, especially the way some of the conversation options work (pay attention to them). This is a fantastic narrative experience and I recommend it to anyone who likes this sort of game.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: This game is more along the lines of an interactive walking simulator (think Firewatch) with a very rich narrative and quite a few interesting set pieces. I hesitate to really delve into talking about the story too much because that's why you should be here. There is no run and gun action, a very light crafting mechanic at the end, no 'We saved the world!' moment. It is a small story that grows into a vast depth that really grinds in the sting of loss, betrayal, and mourning. One specific mention that is astounding is the voice cast. They are exceptional at making the dialogue sound organic and authentic. It is well worth the entry price for the journey.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Elicited a feeling of nervous dread better than most horror titles. Well written and acted, and leaning into a sort of flat-shaded comic book style. I appreciate how the dialogue choices allowed you to help characterize the farmer, and show some of his internal monologue naturally. I also really appreciate that there's only one ending. I think a typical videogame-ey ending where you can right all the wrongs and fix everything would have only made the experience weaker.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: All I need in a game is for it to tell me its story while not being frustrating to play. Adios does that while also fully putting me into the head of the main character. Don't need a long time to make me feel a lot of feelings, and it did that perfectly. It was everything I could have asked for it to be, and huge kudos to the team for that.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an hour I won't forget easily.I bought this game because I follow the writer and lead on twitter and wanted to support him and his team, it lived up to his hype.This game also hit a little close to home and I think everyone should give it a go, not just because it's a piece of art that I feel needs to be respected but because I want to see what this studio can do in the future, so shut up and go give them your money!!!
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: This game is worth the time it takes to play it.I don't want to say much about it as i feel that could ruin the experience, But on the whole its fantastic.The Voice Acting and Writing very much take centre stage and they don't disappoint.It's not perfect now, it does get a bit dull at points but that's down to the type of game it is, so don't expect something action packed. There are some glitches but I did play Day 1 and there has already had a patch released just after I finished my playthrough so I would hope some of the bugs I ran into are fixed, but none of them where Game Breaking.Do yourself a favour and experience this Game, Your emotions will thank you.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Holy hell. This is an absolute masterpiece of emotional gaming. While a couple of bugs/issues came up, this was a wonderful story driven game that had me both knowing and not knowing what was coming next. Play this. You owe it to yourself. It is THAT good. The atmosphere, writing and voice acting is on point. 100/10 despite some minor (and I do mean MINOR) tech issues.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first time I ever cried in a game.There's a few bugs, and the Audio settings are wonky (for example, turning down the sound effects doesn't do anything in the menu, and makes it hard to hear the voices), but for such a clean game done by a small team, I couldn't have asked for more.I am asking you to buy this game and support the devs.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: It's a game about being a pig farmer who decides to stop disposing of bodies for the moborwellit's a game where the main character is a pig farmer who decides to stop disposing of bodies for the mob.it's a game about putting your affairs in order, and about things left unfinished.it's a game about the things we want to say, but can't quite bring ourselves to do so.it's a game about goodbyes.it's short (took me about 2 hours, there's probably 3 hours of game in there, I know steam says 0.5 hours but the playtime counter and the clock in front of me all disagree so I don't really know), it's brilliant, it's sad, it left me breaking down in tears in places.the art takes a minute to get used to, but it does the job really well and it really grew on me.the mechanics are limited in scope, but range from good, simple ways to convey a sense that yes, these are two friends talking, and not simply random strangers, without requiring too much player oversight, to a simple UI choice that might feel cheap elsewhere but here it works beautifully for conveying a sense of the character.In short, this game is beautiful, and if you like narrative, atmospheric, story rich games, I would fully recommend Adios, it is well worth the price tag.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Less than an hour long, set entirely in one location and read with the cadence of a stage play, Adios is a low-key meditation on living a fulfilling life. Kinda ironic that a game about someone trying to ABANDON the sort of lifestyle that would make most other games exciting is, in fact, one of the most exciting premises an indie studio can produce right now.I'll say, though: I didn't like the ending. It's abrupt and turns the camera back around to the player, seemingly asking us to project ourselves onto an otherwise very well-sketched protagonist. But I still hope the game does well so we can possibly see more like it.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR belowVery good voice acting and dialogue. It's the sort of game to play in silence and take your time. The 2 main character's discussions are interesting and thought provoking. The art direction is nice and the game looks very pretty at sunsetThe controls can be a bit awkward sometimes when it comes to interacting. Sometimes interact is E, sometimes it's left click and it's not always clear. I got stuck on doors in the house at the end which was just annoyingI also encountered 2 bugs :1. I couldn't stand up from the chair in the shed, so I pressed space and started to fly in to the sky, I had to restart the scene to fix it.2. ENDING SPOILER --> I also think it's important to know that the game is around 1h30 to complete.Great story, dialogue and voice acting. Slightly buggy, 1h30 for 15€. I really hope that this game gets a small patch to fix the little things that can break immersion.

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a moving experience that you need to play for yourself. This is an incredibly well written game, and the voice acting really sells that writing. The game is very satisfying while only being an hour or two long. It doesn't overstay it's welcome and every scene matters. Plus, since it's not too long, it's easy to jump in and play all the way through without worrying about having to commit a lot of time to a new game.The game does have a few bugs (although this review was written on launch day, so they may be patched out)  but nothing game breaking. You can restart the current scene from the menu which seems to fix most problems without sending you too far back. Nothing big enough to do serious damage to the overall experience.I highly recommend this game
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a game that takes after an interactive short film - one that is full of thoughtful care, nostalgic melancholy, and the sense of a life fully lived, mistakes and all. If you are looking for a slow burning, emotional gut punch and can spare a few bucks for this short and sweet experience (lean and efficient to the point of wanting more, which is in no way a criticism), you owe it to yourself to pick up Adios.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a game about acceptance and regret. What it sets out to do it does very well. It instils a sense of finality that's subtly interlaced with dismal rays of hope, the feeling that maybe things can be different smothered by the knowledge that it's too late, the die has been cast and no matter how much you wonder what you could have done to change the outcome the only thing you can do is say adios and move on.As for the gameplay, it's pretty solid. Nothing flashy here as this is the first game of a small studio, but it works and nothing hinders it, which is a surprisingly scarce quality in a video game these days. The only bug I discovered involved jumping over the fence and experiencing a foreboding dread as the owlman stared at me while running away. If that sounds confusing then jump the fence, you'll see what I mean. I can definitely see Mischief blooming into a great indie dev for mature and serious audiences with the seeds they've sown with this game and I look forward to seeing what they do next.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Been a while since I had a good cry at a story. Adios was such a wonderfully emotional experience. The writing shines big here. I can't remember the last time I played a game that delivered it's characters & conversations so well. The sort of narrative that you can feel in your bones, the sort that truly feels "human" in a way the medium rarely manages to capture. I would love to see more games like this in the future not just from the Adios team but from the industry as a whole. Bravo to the whole team at Mischief.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a gorgeous little game which, to me at least, wrestles with the struggle of moving on vs giving up. Composed like a classic American short story, its story beats play out over a fairly short runtime (1-2 hours) but each hint at a huge wealth of meaning and significance. Ultimately, the melancholy wins out in this one, so be sure to expect a touching but saddening story. There's a few bugs here and there but nothing honestly that breaks the game or takes you out of it, so don't worry about that.Found out about Adios through the narrative designer Doc Burford and his excellent work on Paratopic (plus his great commentaries on Twitter). Have to say though, everything about Adios, from the voice acting to the graphics is really great, so I'm definitely looking forwards to whatever else this team can put together.Seriously though, check Adios out, its a really nice and thoughtful indie game which presents its story really nicely, plus this studio really seems like one who deserves the support.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: To put it shortly: fudge yeah you  play this game. I really want to see more games that bring such unique emotions to the player. The voice cast and character writing bring wonderfully complex characters to life and the farm is a really nice hand crafted lived in space. It hit a lot of personal notes for me in ways that I haven't experienced before even in other games that aim to provoke an emotional response.That is something really special, and this is something really special.The game took me about 1 to 1 and a half hours to complete. I believe it is worth every penny of it's price tag. I hope you buy it and you take the game slowly. I just explored and enjoyed each and every moment, like I would want to do on my last day on Earth.
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: Adios is a short game ruminating largely on the subject of a life and when it's time to move on. The experience is centered around the dialogue exchanged between a Hitman and a Farmer who hides the mobs bodies. Within moments of the games starting the information is dropped that the Farmer wants to quit - a death sentence for someone that hides bodies for the mob. Over the years the two have become friends and the Hitman doesn't want to end the farmer's life so he spends the day reminiscing to try to change his long time associates mind.Most of the game you'll spend wandering around the farm into little events that build the narrative that is the Farmers life. Gradually you'll learn more about the reasoning behind his choice as the Hitman tries his best to negotiate a change of mind throwing every obligation out he can like family, responsibility, happiness all the things that keep people going .Interestingly you'd expect perhaps a degree of tension in the presentation but it really feels more sad, a melancholy acceptance of a decision already made. The Hitman (played by DC Douglas notably) is warm and kind, you get the sense this isn't about the job but his friend's life. A life you will learn about as while the story itself isn't full of enormous twists and turns there's good depth in the character of The Farmer that makes learning who he is as a person satisfying.While clearly the main focus here is on the conversations being held and despite there being a few strong visual moments in the game the small size of the team shows in several other aspects of the game with the character animation range being a little limited and some awkward interactions with environmental objects. Thankfully it's not a deal breaker and the farm itself is well detailed.Overall a solid and quite different experience but one that you definitely need to be in the mood for due the heavier topics being broached. It's called Adios and really is it possible to change someone's mind if their whole life has inevitably lead to this moment?
_childDocuments_.name: Adios

_childDocuments_.review: A pig farmer decides he no longer wants to dispose of bodies for the mob. What follows is a discussion between you, and the hitman who will have to kill you if he can't convince you to stay.

name: PAYDAY 3
detailed_description: YEAR 1 EDITION The PAYDAY 3: Year 1 Edition offers everything needed to get started in the heisting world. The Year 1 Edition includes all major content releases, along with the many free updates and improvements released over the game’s first year. It features: The base game Payday 3 Payday 3 Year 1 Pass: The Season Pass includes four major DLC bundles - Syntax Error, Boys in Blue, Houston Breakout and Fear & Greed - each introducing a new heist, a variety of weapons, and numerous cosmetics. Preacher pack (including 1 outfit, 1 weapon) Drifter pack (including 1 outfit, 1 weapon) Heavy Hitter pack (including 1 outfit, 1 weapon) Assassin pack (including 1 outfit, 1 weapon) Island skin Dark Sterling Mask Skull of Liberty Mask and Golden Slate Gloves About the Game Step out of retirement back into the life of crime in the shoes of the Payday Gang, the envy of their peers and the nightmare of law-enforcement wherever they go. Several years after the crew’s reign of terror over Washington DC has ended, they assemble once again to deal with the threat that roused them out of early retirement. The legendary Payday Crew, dreaded by the law and underworld alike, is back. Ripped from their peaceful retirement to rejoin the criminal world by a new threat, one born from the chaos the Crew left in their wake. In order to identify and crush this new threat, the Crew is leaving their Washington DC roots behind them and moving to New York City. A new location will bring with it new challenges, but also new opportunities for a heister with a plan. Give outlet to your greed and let loose in PAYDAY 3. In addition to gold, cash and jewelry and any other valuables they might come across, you’ll be able to build a sizable collection of weapons, cosmetics and accolades. It won’t be as simple as showing up and gaining goodies. You’ll have to work hard and plan smart to get away with as much loot as possible. Gain experience, unlock new skills and gain proficiency in weapons to steadily grow your power to handle the tougher challenges. A professional heister knows it takes planning, hard work and a good amount of luck in order to execute a successful heist. In PAYDAY 3 the choice is put in the hands of the players, deciding how to tackle the heist, whether you sneak or go in guns blazing, whether you let your hostages go or keep them around as pawns, whether you go at it alone or bring friends. The choices are endless and in your hands, they will vastly change how the game plays. Not just anyone is worthy of standing at your side for something as important as a heist. Likewise, PAYDAY 3 is best enjoyed with close friends in mind, whether you bring them from your childhood or make them along the road. The PAYDAY-series has always valued the bonds made through hardship and tries to reflect that in the actions and words of our heisters while in the game, and through our community while on the outside.

_childDocuments_.review: They have capitulated to the trolls who were never actually interested in buying the game three times now. It will surely become another Back 4 Blood.This game makes Payday 2 look like crap. There are a few minor issues that'll be quickly patched out like not being able to reorganize your inventory and minor stuttering during the first heist every time you launch the game (the  first launch the stuttering is less minor), but the game itself is perfectly fine. Don't listen to all the trolls who are saying Payday 2 is better, or that this game is unplayable, or any of the other flamebait they spam on the forums. They're almost never able to actually say what's wrong with the game, instead just repeating over and over again that they already did. The few times they do actually say something that's "wrong with the game" it's a blatant lie, a complete non-issue (like there not being the timewasting mechanic where you spend 5-30 seconds waiting after every single match to get something like an amount of money that's effectively $0), or just mad that this game isn't Payday 2 (despite them also saying this is a cash grab that shouldn't be purchased  it's so similar to Payday 2).The skills system is incredible, complex, and interactive, unlike Payday 2's. The cop health is great and doesn't scale with difficulty (even specials die in 1-3 headshots depending on gun & perks), unlike Payday 2. The heists are more interactive and freeform. The civilians are an interesting mechanic now. The shooting is better, the stealth is infinitely better, the AI is better, the movement is better, the health & armor is better, the deployables are way better, the multiplayer is incomparably better (no more teammates sliding around desyncing seeing things completely different than you). Every single aspect of the game is a big improvement over Payday 2. There's so much this game does right it will easily be the best game released in the last several years if they just don't listen to the trolls and keep going with what they're doing. The only advantage Payday 2 has over it is that there's more heists it received over 10 years than this game has on launch, but most of the heists in Payday 2 aren't nearly as good as the ones in Payday 3.The best example that the game is great and the only people who pretend to dislike it are trolls is the thread glued to the front page telling everyone you can refund it regardless of playtime before the game's official launch. These guys are literally refunding the game after playing it for  in  because the main menu has an Arial font.Plus, the game is $40. That's half the price of what games cost now. Great deal, definitely worth picking up.

_childDocuments_.review: Never in my life have I struggled so much between a thumbs up or a thumbs down. Never in my life have I wished more than I do now for a more gradient form of review score. Because never in my life have I ever seen a game that can exhibit so much technical and game-play improvement over its predecessor, while also relegating itself to complete inferiority compared with its predecessor due to some baffling and entirely unnecessary design choices.We'll start with the good news, because that will be a shorter list. Stealth is massively improved. With the addition of Hitman style distinction between Public, Private, and Secure areas, no longer will you fail stealth because you bumped into a security guard on the sidewalk outside a jewelry store. Some heists can even be completed while never masking during the heist, since you can do a lot more without wearing your mask in this game.  If caught in a Private area that is not deemed a Secure area, guards will opt to escort you from the premises, provided you are not wearing your scary clown mask. No longer will security guards choose lethal force as their first (and only) course of action.Of course, these improvements are compounded by the fact that Payday 3 is not using an aging, repurposed racing game engine, but rather Unreal Engine. No longer will you or a suspicious body bag be spotted by a guard on the roof, through the roof windows, two floors down, behind a bench simply because there's a single pixel gap somewhere in the polygons. Combat is also massively improved, for much the same reason as stealth. Gunplay is smooth and clean, hits have impact, and enemies are better designed. The curse of Jules has been banished. No longer are enemies specifically designed to be miserable to play against, but are rather designed like...enemies in a game. (Truly revolutionary.) Tasers, for example, now called "zappers" can only zap you if they have clear line of sight, and only if they are close. Otherwise, they opt to lay electrical mines. Cops with shields now have a weakness in the form of the narrow window on the shield, which means "guy with sniper rifle" is no longer a mandatory part of every team. The addition of the Grenadier is another intelligent choice, especially since its grenades cause poison clouds. Of course, most people have seen the "special forces" makeover the cloaker has received. Suffice it to say, I no longer resent the cloakers. They are fair and balanced, and cause a surprising number of horror-esque moments. Clearly, Payday 3 sees special enemies as strategic units whose purpose is to apply pressure to the player in unique ways, rather than simply being one-man kill squads, with their primary weapons being absurd DPS and HP numbers.By now, you are no doubt confused, as this surely seems like glowing praise. Indeed, this is the note I would end on, but Starbreeze has somehow found a way to foul up Payday 3 like a public matchmaking lobby of players on Shadow Raid. (If you know, you know...)First, I'll get it out of the way now, yes, the game is online only. Yes, there is no legitimate reason for it to be online only. And yes, the matchmaking servers are pretty slow. What you've heard is true, post launch, when the flood gates opened, Payday 3 was unplayable for DAYS. Because in addition to being online only, Payday 3 has NO SOLO PLAY. Even if you set your lobby to invite only, and invite no one, the game will still make you wait in a matchmaking queue, presumably because the servers still need to allocate resources to you. For what, I have no idea. I don't know what neurosis Starbreeze suffers from, but it really seems like they want to force us to play Payday 3 in multiplayer mode, or not at all. As of their most recent announcement, solo play is not even planned as an addition to the game. Apparently, it's just so important to the devs that we experience everything matchmaking co-op play has to offer. Like failing a stealth only heist over and over again because of that one player who keeps triggering the alarm. He claims he can't see the camera, but by the 4th restart, I begin to have my doubts.Or players on a certain loud mission where you can't allow ANY civilians to escape in order to get an achievement...what do they do? They drag a hostage to the edge of the map where cops can instantly rescue them. Or players who refuse to walk to the escape point, and simply troll until everyone dies.You get the point. Intricate stealth missions and public matchmaking simply do not mix. Public matchmaking is simply incompatible with any game type where one player can fail the objective for all players. Payday 2 suffered from these issues as well, which is why I never played public multiplayer in Payday 2. I played offline, and I used all the mods required to add all the quality of life features Starbreeze refused to. Any you know what? I had an absolute blast. Peak Payday 2 is offline solo play with 30-40 mods. Change my mind. You won't.But alas, like a heister sneaking into the private areas of a bank, I get the distinct impression that, as a player, I am not welcome in Payday 3. Starbreeze doesn't seem to want players like me.In hindsight, this train of thought has more merit than an idle lament, it's visible in every design aspect.That leads me to my last remark, Payday 3 lacks much of the personality and charm of Payday 2. Gone are the detailed, photo-realistic stop motion shots of the contractors. Gone is the unique, deep-web inspired UI flavor. Gone is the presence of , really. It's mentioned, sure, but it's not really something you interact with. Instead, Payday 3 features passable but generic music and a UI and loadout screen that looks suspiciously like it was ripped straight from CS:GO. (Or your favorite battle royale.) Voice acting is hit or miss, much like Payday 2, but it also lacks the excellent voice acting that certain characters would bring. (It helps some of them were voiced by actual celebrities, but still...) I feel like I'm queuing for some generic shooter whenever I start a match in Payday3, and many of the missions, despite their technical improvements, don't have the personality to make up for the terminal deficit.In conclusion, Payday3 is a game that, despite being out of early access, still feels very much like it should remain there. It holds a lot of promise, and features a lot of improvements over Payday2, but this promise is very much overshadowed by the nonsensical, and frankly anti-consumer design choices made by the developers. This is not a game for those without a healthy stock of friends to play with, and I fear this might not even be a game for those who liked the previous game. But whatever the intended audience is, there is nevertheless significant enjoyment to be had here if you have at least one human being who will tolerate you long enough to play with you. For now, I rate it 5 Deposit boxes out of 1 thermal drill, and hope that Starbreeze will turn this ship around, so I can change this review before too long.

_childDocuments_.review: To begin with: Do NOT purchase this game yet. It currently cannot even be played. The servers have been offline for almost 95% of the time the game has been launched, and there is no options for offline play.I have been through a handful of horrible launches for online games. I cannot even count them on both hands and feet. However, what I can only count on one hand, is the amount of releases I haven't been able to play AT ALL on launch day, or the day following.1. Why is it acceptable for companies to push out games in what would have previously been considered an Alpha build that would have never even left the studio?2. Why is it acceptable for games to release without any server stability testing? I get that companies can only expect and predict so much, but if EVERY game has this issue, you would think that some company may take control of this issue and, I don't know, maybe plan on some overhead for the first month of the game? Instead of pocketing all the savings they get on not investing into more/beefier servers? I cannot say I'm even mad about the no offline mode option. I do believe that having that as an option would have negated *some* of the issues. However, taking into account the game released on a week day, during school / work for most people, and the only stability was...quite literally just then - for the people who took time off of work and school - is absolutely horrible.tl;dr: Get your ♥♥♥♥ together. It's beyond sad when indie game devs are putting AAA devs in the dirt with on-release server stability, or release with a usable peer-to-peer system. Don't buy the game for another few days.Edit: After a week or so of struggles, I can happily say it seems like the game has been MOSTLY seamless and playable. Still a few issues here and there with matchmaking errors. Game feels fun, now that there is actually a way to play the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Payday 3 at it's core with gameplay is good fun, but fails in the progression system, Loud Gameplay variety, online-only services, etc. After grinding to Level 100 (soft cap, 150 is hard cap) and playing for 80+ hours, I can finally give my opinion on this new installment in the Payday Series.As you may already know, the launch of this game was horrible and completely unplayable. There are absolutely no excuses. While server stability has improved and the game is playable, this can happen again. Add offline support please.Core gameplay is exactly the kind of thing community members of the Payday series should be familiar with improvement. The stealth has been dramatically improved with interesting and unique objectives (One repeated but will get to it later) with casing mode being a viable playstyle due to heists alllowing no-mask runs and guards escorting you out to public areas or cuffing you instead of instantly shooting you. Oh also there are also distinct areas such as Public, Private, and Secure which give the player certain freedoms/restriction like being able to wander/sprint freely without worry of going loud or secure areas where you cannot sprint or risk a guard investigating last position. There are security modifiers at Very Hard and Overkill which supposedly will change every week with things like an endless radio guard to avoid killing, 5 second timer limit to camera loop, Titan camera's like Payday 2, and more to come. The stealth part of the game can be easily mastered after a few hours of gameplay with skills improving your experience. Standing still in circular floor objectives for 10 or so seconds to allow Shade, Payday 3's Bain, to "hack" feels like another waiting for the drill situation. It is present in 3 heist that come to mind out of the 8 at launch. It's uninspiring and a boring part of stealth. The rest feels great.Loud, however, is a different story. Yes, it does feel like the classic horde shooter or whatever you would call the Payday series, but since this is a sequel it falls very short in changing loud with new experiences like they did with stealth. I prefer stealth gameplay, but I do love loud whenever I want to go guns blazing and have that feeling like I am playing L4D but with waves of police. The problem with loud is the samey feeling that is present in every single heist. Heists like Touch the Sky, Under the Surphaze, Dirty Ice, and 99 boxes, have little difference in loud and stealth gameplay partner aside from a helicopter to pickup loot at the end. Objectives deviate little and the way to complete those objectives also don't change much. The Touch the Sky heist comes to mind. The great parts of loud involve using the new Overkill weapon, facing special enemies like bulldozers, cloakers, zappers (not tasers anymore), and a grenadier, The difficulty from Normal to Overkill does not change enemy health and instead it improves AI Police tactics and intelligence (and possible damage output but not certain). Armor is very important, at the time of writing this, and leagues above ammo bags and medic bags. Sentry turret is eh. Though once you run out of armor you better hope you are nearly done with the heist because otherwise you are screwed since zero armor drops throughout the heist aside from possible team AI dropping armor bags alongside ammo and meds or "pre-planning" favors. Team AI are non-existent on Overkill Difficulty but are very helpful below this difficulty. I would like to see possible security modifiers to loud like are present in stealth, but with obvious loud only implications. Overall, I wish they made loud more unique from Payday 2 since it's obvious a lot of work went into stealth. Less drills present is a plus from me, however. More love to loud players please.Progression in this game is heavily tied to challenge completion. These challenges range from heist completions to weapon kills/attachment unlocks and uses. I'd say you can get to around Level 50 by just playing the game without looking at the challenges tab, but beyond that feels like a necessity. You can get Level 100 anywhere between 60-90 hours depending on your playtime efficiency with challenges. A gimmick right now is to play the Touch the Sky heist, sit in one of the bathrooms with a hostage and farm kills all-day. At the time of writing, the most efficient way to get weapon levels, aside from exploits, is speed-running Rock the Cradle in max 4 minutes. All of this to me is a problem because it goes against what the developers intended with progression. They want you to play the game in all of its glory, not stick to one or two heists, but that's what weapon challenges/leveling force upon you. It's even worse when it is better to play solo to complete certain challenges when their intention for this game is to play with other players. It's just a mess. You can also get money very quickly (positive) which you can spend on masks, weapons, suits, etc. C-stacks are another currency (not a micro transaction) which you buy with in-game cash you earn by playing which serve as a another way to buy certain items like weapon presets and specific attachments and masks/suits. C-stack pricing is a bit too much for far too little reward, but they will change this as players continue to progress and/or with feedback. The changes I'd like to see with progression specifically is rewarding heist completion with Infamy Points (Also known as XP) and increase it based on difficulty (Like what was Present in Payday 2). Another change with progression can be to give more xp based on certain actions within heists such as killing no guards, completing heist without your mask, slipping in and out without sounding alarm, escape with all loot, escaping with all teammates alive, base objective completion xp/infamy points, etc. These would be a massive improvement over what we currently have.Skills, on the other, feel very good in this game. Skill lines are here which are like a skill tree but in lines. Many skills revolve around 3 unique performance modifiers or passives which are Rush, Grit, and edge which give either movement speed, percent damage output, or percent damage mitigation. Skills can help to activate these passives throughout a heist. I don't really have a problem with it, but it can feel required to activate on harder difficulties to be successful. There are base skills and mastery skills which can be equipped separately. System is good and does not feel like a requirement to Play on Normal and Hard difficulties. You can get away with having zero skills on Very hard and Overkill, but requires you to have a vast knowledge of game mechanics which is perfect.This will be bullet point list since I've written too much by now.- Loot bag transport is no different to Payday 2 and again feels like a bag moving sim. It is the most boring part of the game, especially if you are playing solo. Even with other players, it still feels like an old mechanic. There will be an upcoming skill line called Transport which will allow you to carry 2 bags, among other things, but the core problem is still present. Since we are in a technological world and setting, then there should be a reason to add maybe drones to help transport loot or a robotic RC car or something to make this more enjoyable. - Menus feel uninspiring and convoluted.- Heist selection screen is a downgrade from Crime net.- Story/lore is great with interesting cut scenes in-between heists.- Mask customization is lacking.- Outfits feel bland on launch.- Add voice chat in-game/chat in lobby.- Pre-planning screen is non-existent and is a downgrade.- Main characters are back and improved visually. Female character heisters also a very great addition.Not Perfect but fun. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Although this is a positive review, I am reviewing the game itself rather than the absolute disaster that is the current server system. Everything that you have read in every other review about the servers is completely correct.PAYDAY 3 is a solid game, but it doesn't feel as inspired as PAYDAY 2. The first time I played PD3, the word that came to mind was "charm", as in its absence was noted when compared to PD2. To wit, Shade (your handler) is a far inferior version of Bane/Locke. Maybe that shouldn't count for much in a game like PD3; I enjoyed the accompaniment of Bane and Locke in PD2, but I find everything that Shade says to be trite and obnoxious. For example, the Surphaze heist seems to be a protracted exercise in the tired critique of pretentious art snobs, and everything that Shade says would be the first thing that a person with a gun to their head would sputter if they were asked to list "pretentious art snob" tropes.The heists themselves seem to be solid as a tasting menu, but I long for heists with the nuance of Firestarter, Framing Frame, Golden Grin or Big Oil. The thing that drew me in to PD2 was that you could see and feel the inspiration of the developers with every new heist. While we were playing Rats 10 years ago, many of us were also watching Breaking Bad as it was airing, and it felt like PD2 was growing in concert with it and shows/films similar to it.Right now, PD3 feels like a game that has been refined from the experience of the last ten years rather than being one that has something new to say, new characters to introduce, or new depth to be explored. Without a doubt, the game has areas that have been carefully crafted - stealth is a new experience relative to PD2 - but the attention to detail feels mechanical, rather than the labour of love that PD2 seemed to have been.All of this might make one wonder why this is a positive review. I just enjoy the game; the challenge of figuring out how to approach a heist is still there, even though it is a massive shame that preplanning is no longer a part of the game. Combat is serviceable, but I am mostly interest in solo stealthing, as I imagine are most players. And, on Overkill difficulty, some of the stealth heists can be a bit of a handful at first. Again, I assume that the heists that we currently have will be iterated upon and will lead to greater diversity and difficulty in the future.So, I choose to be optimistic. Starbreeze has been transparent about the server/matchmaking issues (though this is no excuse for how poor the release has been), and they have earned a lot of goodwill for what they did with PD2. I only hope that they will once again dare to take risks with their designs because, at the moment, it feels like most are somewhat upgraded versions of heists that existed in PD2.

_childDocuments_.review: Payday 3 significantly improves upon Payday 2's gameplay, particularly in stealth mechanics. Stealth is less punishing, allowing for more mistakes. Detection in restricted areas leads to being escorted out. If caught in a highly secure area, you’re handcuffed, but your teammates can continue the stealth approach and even uncuff you. The game has also removed the concealment mechanic, allowing for a wider choice in weapons during stealth missions and smoother transitions from stealth to loud during heists. And in casing mode, you’re granted more freedom - you can run, open and close doors, and interact with various objects. You can now pick up bodies directly, steal keycards from NPCs without killing them, and distract NPCs with sound or visuals.The attachment system has been streamlined, eliminating the need for side jobs to acquire them. The overall gameplay is slower and more strategic, like the original Payday: The Heist. Automatic armor regeneration is removed making the game more balanced with it slower pace. Hostages can now be traded for resources like medkits or additional time if the assault hasn’t started yet.However, the lack of VR support is a disappointment. While Payday 2’s VR mode wasn’t popular due to its gimmicky implementation, it became a highly enjoyable and replayable VR shooter with the help of mods like VRPlus and Unofficial VR Patch. I hope that Payday 3 will eventually introduce a well-designed VR mode, complete with a variety of comfort options similar to the Half-Life 2 VR mod. Given the game’s replayability, a robust VR mode could potentially make Payday 3 one of the best VR games available.The matchmaking system is currently missing several key features that were present in Payday 2. These include the ability to express your preference for a stealthy or loud approach in the lobby, the option to seamlessly continue playing with the people you just completed a heist with, and the convenience of a lobby browser to check which heists are currently active. And the ability to unready when waiting in the case people leave.The UI could benefit from some enhancements, particularly in terms of efficient space utilization. Currently, there are instances where space isn't used optimally. In the heist lobby screen, the process of purchasing placed items for the map is a bit disjointed, as you're required to navigate to the loadout screen to buy favors.Furthermore, the method for purchasing and modifying a selected gun is somewhat unintuitive, especially on PC.Overall, the game has made significant improvements in terms of gameplay. However, in all other areas such as UI, matchmaking, and the heist lobby, the game has unfortunately experienced a decline in quality.

As for the DLC comments, this is how they make their money with season packs or individual DLC it's been that way since the first game.While there isn't as much functionality to the maps i.e. no forward planning there are benefits like unlimited hostage ties and so on so they have played with the format of the game a little but not that much that it breaks from the previous games. When you are playing with randoms or pick up groups however you call it now there is still no change from previous games there will always be that one clown that messes the game up because they want to go in guns blazing while everyone else is doing stealth. That's just the people of the internet. get use to it.I'd happily play with my friends if they had got this but looks like the selfish bad reviews have done their job and scare people off. Lets change that this is a good game and not to be missed especially if it is on sale.
