_childDocuments_.review: Future me: I'm just waiting for updates after reaching 120+ infamy. Luckily they're letting us get XP after heist completionAfter the first server maintenance, I can see steady progress with stabilizing the servers and ensuring that everyone can play. I have been enjoying my time inside Payday, and I can see and feel the passion Starbreeze has in making this the best game. Almir has been hosting daily LIVE Updates streams where he updates players on what's happening, what they're doing and what they plan to do in the future. They also answer the communities' questions and respond to feedback, being as transparent and honest as they can possibly be. The most requested feature, Offline mode, was answered. They DO plan to add it!Starbreeze is listening to the community. With today's gaming world, where there is always this divide between company and consumers, Starbreeze is one of those companies that has overcome this divide and reached out to players to assure them and provide an outlet for players to give feedback about what they would like to see in the future. More importantly, since it is a LIVE update stream that anyone can join in, players get LIVE replies about their enquiry. As stated above, I am enjoying my time with Payday 3. The core gameplay loop of killing cops and completing objectives is still as satisfying, if not more, than previous games. With only 8 bareboned heists, it is able to keep me entertained to continue playing it. The current heists are very short and to-the-point, which does not match up with current heists in Payday 2, where heists are so big that you cannot stay in the same place the whole heist. In Payday 3, you could very well find a spot in the map to camp and be able to come back in between objectives to brave the assault wave. I'm not saying that this is a bad aspect of the game, because this teaches new players about how to pace themselves when completing objectives between assault waves and regrouping phase.Starbreeze has mentioned that they are focusing on the foundation of Payday 3. So having concise, comprehensive heists can assist the developers in finding out what type of objectives is fun for the players, and what objectives they should avoid when making new ones.However, there are 2 main issues with the current build of Payday 3. 1st is the progression for player's level, and 2nd is the matchmaking.Progression is currently locked behind challenges, which goes a little something like this:- Complete [Insert Heist] on [Insert Difficulty] on loud "X" amount of times.- Complete [Insett Heist] on [Insert Difficulty] on stealth "X" amount of times.- Kill "X" amount of cops with [Insert Weapon]- Kill [Insert Special Enemy] "X" amount of times...You get what I mean.Since all heists, less "Road Rage", have both Stealth AND Loud options, you have to complete it the same amount for stealth AND loud.Starbreeze stated that they are doing it this way because they want players to know that if they see a high level player, they can be assured that they have the experience befitting that level. You know, since challenges forces you to use different weapons, play different heists, at different difficulties. Because otherwise, they don't give ANY Infamy Points for completing the heist. You could easily have stealthed "No Rest For The Wicked" (NRFTW) the 100th time on overkill and make it out with all bags and no civs/guards killed, but at the end game screen, you will be give ZERO points because you didn't complete any challenges (Because you've already completed them!)The other issue I have, Matchmaking. It is hard to find an active lobby of players. There is no garauntee that you'll find someone else playing on the same difficulty. As someone who loves to play co-op, I find this to be very ineffective. Payday 2 had a very well done lobby browser in the form of Crimenet. I could easily see that players are playing Fire Starter, Big Oil, or Hoxton Breakout at different difficulties. All I had to do was select the lobby I want to join and meet the randoms inside it.In Payday 3, I have to guess what heist and difficulty the other players would be playing in and what difficulty they chose. If I were to guess wrong, I'd be put into an empty lobby. A scenario where I faced this issue is that I really wanted to play Touch The Sky. But I matchmade for ALL 4 of the difficulties, just to get an empty lobby all 4 times.Monster Hunter Rise also suffered for the same issue. I loved the emergency SOS flare system in Monster Hunter World because I am garaunteed to play with people when I search for them. But in MH:R, if you wanted to hunt a specific monster, you had to pray that someone is hunting the same monster. However, MH:R had a quick match system to put you in ongoing quests, albiet a random monster that you can't choose every time.Starbreeze also addressed this, saying that they plan to add a lobby browser because newer additions of heists will reduce the chances of players finding a lobby by matchmaking for a specific heist. Overall, I am proud of Starbreeze for being transparent like they always do, and continue to put my trust in them for the betterment of the Payday series. They have acknowleged all the issues I faced, and even gave a positive answer that I can look forward to. With much more stable servers and uptime, I can finally recommend this game to my friends and really justify the $40+ they will cough up to buy this game. If you wanted to read my previous review of the game, I have left it as it is below. Take note, these were before Starbreeze came out to say anything about the server issues.I played the stress test and early access. Servers were fine, but I noticed that the matchmaking would take a very long time to find a lobby. Even when it did, I was put into an empty lobby. Had to forcefully play through on my lonesome for the whole early access.But after the release, I can see all the issues with the Always Online scheme. No way to create lobbies, no way to stay in a lobby with people who I'd love to heist with again, not even a guarantee that there might be people playing the exact heist on that exact difficulty that I've been dying to play.Coming from a player who had thoroughly enjoyed Payday: The Heist and pre-ordered  the Criminal Career edition of Payday 2, I really had high expectations from the third game in the series. Especially with the matchmaking. Coming from Payday 2 makes this game feel like a massive downgrade in terms of finding a heist to play. Payday 2 even had  AT LAUNCH!Even with all these bad experiences, I've had a blast playing Payday 3. The gameplay loop is satisfying if you loved the previous Payday games. I'll continue to play it and grind my way to completion. However, I will not recommend this game to my friends. I do not want to subject my friends to a bad experience right after sinking in $40+ on this game.I believe that StarBreeze will fix these issues with due haste, and the game will one day be the best game in the market. For now, I will leave my review as it is, as of 23rd September 2023.We all love a comeback story like No Man's Sky. But I wish to return to the good old days where I could proudly and confidently pre-order games without hanging my head in shame because of glaringly obvious game-breaking issues that has caused the whole community to turn against the developers.

_childDocuments_.review: Although I want to have faith in these devs, it seems very apparent that they've failed to understand what made PD2 so great. It feels like they wanted to change things up for the sake of changing things.The issues I have with the game as it stands:1. Leveling system is atrociousHaving challenges being directly tied to your level is one of the silliest choices they made with this game among other things. I'm unsure why they decided to make this change in the first place as I would say people praised the leveling system in 2. Having your experience tied to money is such an obvious and good incentive, and this game does not have that at all. As much as I want to sit in a bathroom on Touch The Sky for 30 minutes with some weapon I don't want to use and have no plans on using just for the sake of leveling is a terrible feeling. Have fun getting your 1000 kills with your garbage default pistol, that assuming you want to get all your skill points to properly make and try different builds, sorry pal, eat ♥♥♥♥.2. Skill TreesEver since release, I questioned why it seems the skill trees have been so incredibly neutered compared to PD2 and even Payday: The Heist. To me, it seems almost like the developers are scared to make the players powerful, which is literally why you'd want to play the game. I understand the defense of PD2 requiring so many overhauls to get some skills right, but even at launch we had skills like Inspire, or infinite ammo on ammo bag placement, to even smaller things like throwing bags further. In it's current state, everyone is using the same point allocation with a very, very minor variance as there's not really any other way to play since skills aren't that impactful in the slightest aside from ammo / armor / health usages.3. Recent changes are still not addressing issuesI held off from really talking about this game much as I wanted to see what their approach to community response was and what changes they'll do. As we've now reached the first "content drop", have had a new skill line added along with some other changes, I can say with confidence that the developers don't have an identity for this game. The implementation of XP gains after a heist completion, while appreciated, completely misses the actual argument at hand. The challenge system is not a beneficial system for anyone involved, it makes the game a checklist, and since money has no correlation to leveling (Aside from the newly implemented all bags XP) it ironically flushes its replay value down the toilet. Offline mode would be nice as well, but as that's the lowest hanging fruit for things to complain about, it is what it is.4. Stealth ChangesWith things like Stealth having a complete overhaul, I originally liked the idea of no longer having a detection rating. This meant you could use any gun you want, and it doesn't make a difference! In execution, I think this is a negative as it lessens the depth and reason to modify weapons in certain ways. Majority of people are going to use the same gun(s) with the same attachment(s) because of this is what I'm getting at. Alongside this, other changes such as the hacking circles are changes that feel more of knee-jerk "We don't want players to just sit there and wait!" reactions rather than actual thought being put into them as you almost literally end up doing the same thing. Waiting with occasionally holding W to get to the next circle.5. Half-Baked IdeasI would say a lot of their ideas for this game were originally in good faith, a large majority of them have fallen flat with some glaring negatives as to "This is why this idea sucks". One of the main ones being this Rush, Edge, Grit skill system. I strongly believe that if this system gets completely overhauled or straight up removed with everything else skill-wise changing because of it, that would be an incredibly beneficial move. As it stands, your skills are all basically locked behind having some variation of one of those 3 skills in order to actually proc any other skill. Ex. I need Rush in order to not be seen by cameras, or I need Edge to one shot headshot heavy swats with whatever gun. I just don't see the point in locking the player into these corners. There isn't any sort of benefit in doing it this way, and only negatives as far as I can see.The good:1. Core gameplay is pretty solidThe enemy variety is not super great, but it will get better as time goes on. The gunplay could definitely be better, but it's definitely fun enough to want to keep playing. Although I don't like the 3 skills system with Edge, Grit, and Rush, it's at least kind of fluid enough to maintain their up-time in combat. By that same coin though, I believe this is a core reason of why the skill system kinda sucks as everything has to be locked to those 3 modifiers / skills.2. MusicPD: The Heist & PD2 both have some of the greatest OST's of any game in this genre. I think Gustavo is honestly giving PD3 such high quality music that is so far above the rest of the game, it's a strange dynamic. Ironically, whenever they've done interviews with the staff, he seems to be one of the ones most in tune to what the game should be.3. Enemy SpecialsAs I said, the enemy variety isn't all that spectacular which is to be expected with a game like this at launch. Aside from this though, the ones that are in the game do make a fairly large impact on the game and have a lot of interesting and cool quirks. Cloakers being able to do some naruto ♥♥♥♥ and jump off walls to actively dodge you is really cool, the dialogue is quite funny as well. Bulldozers are a significantly higher threat (mostly) compared to PD2, and have very humorous voice lines. If you're unfamiliar, try flashbanging a bulldozer or interacting with them in some way. I think Tazers need an overhaul (Not sure why they changed them from Tazers to "Zappers"?) as they aren't really a threat at all with low health and aren't nearly as punishing. Naders are a good addition to the game as their area denial is something that was missing in PD2, and it is quite punishing.I'm very curious to see what comes of this game in the next year or two as these devs are no stranger to completely overhauling their game and mechanics, but it's a pretty dark tunnel from where we're at.Thanks for reading, I stream at

_childDocuments_.review: So, first things first, I've played both Payday 1 & 2. If you enjoy Payday 1, this is your game, but if you enjoy how ridiculous Payday 2 is, this is not for you.- Payday 3 is more of a story game than Payday 2 ever was. It has a story played out through stylized cutscenes between each heist, which is very difficult to fully understand due to the shortness and lack of context for a lot of the scenes. -  is not a thing in this game, and the brokers are not characterized like they were in 2. Ice-T shows up for one cutscene and gives you one heist, but that's it, it felt like they just thought it would be cool to have him in the game, so they did. - Bain just disappears, which, if you've played the other two games, is a big deal. Bain was the one who was always talking in your ear. I know that he "dies" in payday 2, but still man. I can't even remember her name, but his replacement is just down right bland. - C-stacks. I understand the issue of making your characters lose all of their aquired money between games, to explain away reseting stats, but this new way for "offshore accounts" working is just rough to be honest. C-stacks are a crypto that you use to buy specific items, such as cosmetics and preset wepons, but they are so expensive that I, personally, can't justify putting a lot of my money into it. (Not IRL money, which is a plus though)- The lack of heists are an issue. I know that the game just came out and it's somewhat unfair to compare it to Payday 2's sheer scale when it comes to heists, but still. There are a lack of variety of heists in this game. There are eight heists in this game, compares to Payday 2's launch at 12. It might not seem like much, but when you look at the fact that it had a third more than this one, it's a lot less replayable. Which, replayabilty is a big part about this series. - Preplanning is gone. I know that a lot of people wouldn't use the preplanning phase for it's intended purpose, but that's sort of what made the game more immersive. You are heisters, you need to devise a plan when going in to rob a bank or a highly protected area. - Favors, they are also almost completely removed. Favors were different things that would help you along on your heists. From body bags, to a giant pig that dropped a big drill to help get into the vault quicker. Now all we have are Ammo, Health, Armor, and the occasional favor to help you with stealth/zip lines. Might I add, you can only pick one? And you have to purchase BEFORE heists.- Online only. I know that a lot of people will only be playing this on their desktop at home, so it doesn't sound like too much of an issue, right? Wrong. You have to queue up for a solo game, you can disconnect from a solo game and you can't even play the game without Nebula (Overkill's own social hub, similar to rockstar's club)- Weapons, there are only 17 base weapons. I understand that Payday 2 had only a handfull on launch too, but this is embarrassing. The ARs don't do any damage, the semi-autos are terrible, there aren't ANY melee weapons and I believe the overkill weapons are a terrible addition to the game. I found myself getting the ability to use the overkill drop ,getting it and never actually wanting to use it because it had low damage with slow reload. There are only two overkill weapons, a Grenade launcher and sniper (unlocked at lvl 40). You have to level up each weapon to unlock more attachments for them, which is better than how the system first was in payday 2, but payday 2 fixed this with the Continental coins. Along with the previously stated, low damage output, I found myself only using the pump action that I unlocked really early into the game. - Stealth isn't really important. I understand that people mainly play loud for this series, but I still enjoy the option to complete a heists as if no one even knew until I'm miles away. - Skills feel like they don't do much at all. The skill tree is a disaster in and of itself with researching and using that one skill to unlock more in that tree, but I feel like they didn't do much to change my game. I enjoyed the idea of running into a group of cops in a two piece suit, dodging bullets like the matrix and killing everyone, or beating someone over the head with a spoon to terrify everyone around them, OR getting shot a million times just to pull out my flask, take a shot and be back to full health. None of that is possible in this game, making it feel like they don't do anything other than give me a 10% buff in either health, damage or movement speed for a few seconds. - Masks, the customization was one of the defining features of Payday 2. You're a heister, you want to be unique, the paints and patterns aren't anything special. The lack of mask selection is not something that I would ever have been a thing after all of the masks in 2. Not to mention the fact that they stripped the whole mask customization process, it's the exact same as the gun customization.All in all, my roommate sums this game up perfectly by accident. She walked in on me in the loading screen and said "I didn't know that Call of Duty got an update." Which, to be honest, is a perfect description of this game at launch. My best piece of advice, wait about a year from release to even consider purchasing this game. That pains me to say because I've played payday ever since it released on the PS3, it was one of my favorite games, my steam profile proves that with my hours in payday 2 and achievements in it. I will be looking forward to seeing Overkill continue to work on this game and listen to their community's input on what they like and dislike about the game, which I hope they do after their involvement with Payday 2 for as many years as they did. But for now, we all have to wait and see what these DLCs have in store for us.

_childDocuments_.review: At first i still wanted to recommend the game beside its flaws and terrible Launch, because i like the base game and was hopeful they would fix all my major gripes I had. The heists have depth, the gunplay is solid, graphics are decent and the skills feel interesting enough. However, in the recent Dev Streams they have announced that they wouldn’t fix, or it would be low priority, to fix the issues I had with the game and thus I can no longer recommend the game.Obviously, the servers are ♥♥♥♥♥♥. There is no way around it, by the time you’re reading it they are hopefully fixed. But they do not work most of the time right now.But when you even get into a server you will usually not have teammates, which is why is specifically I can NOT recommend this if you don’t at least have 1-2 people you can regularly play with. The stealth is very set up for at least 2 people (one person masked up and one person in casing). And the matchmaking is trash. 50% of the time you get zero teammates, and no teammates will join over any amount of time (I stealthed a heist for 2 hours and the 4th slot never got filled). The bots they give you are borderline useless. Especially if you are alone, as they do not revive each other, so you are just constantly babysitting these bots. Playing with bots feels like you are playing one difficulty up over what you are actually playing. I can do with very hard with team mates no problem, but you got 2 bots? It’s a struggle every time. If you have played a Payday game before, this will come to a surprise to you, but I would take the average pub player over a bot, yes, they are that bad. I would take David.Gonzalles2008 (Level 10) over Hoxton bot. At least they will try to attempt to use cover or move bags, Bots don’t. I usually don’t bother reviving bots a lot of the time on very hard because they have died in the middle of nowhere (Because they have no sniper resistance, do not attempt to hide from them or shoot back. It is commonplace that you will hear 2 sniper shots and the sound of a bot going down) And I will lose more resources trying to rez them then I would gain from them being alive. On overkill they might not be there, they instantly go down without any value. In the current meta-Shield bags are king, and half the time they drop useless ammo so not even their resources make them worth. (Being able to choose the resources would be nice, or at least lower the ammo chance) You also often only have the assault breaks to move bags and obviously they don’t help with that. You can put bags on them but because they don’t keep up with you it’s an annoying process. (A “Collect all bags you come across and move them to x area if you are next to it” would be incredibly useful.) Also, you can do certain objectives during negotiation as long as you don’t get to close or shoot. Bots don’t care they will immediately open fire when they see the cops and trigger the assault.They have not said that the overkill system is getting any changes or not, so assume they won’t. but it just feels bad to use. What should be a big “OH ♥♥♥♥” tide turner is reduced to the sniper being an easy dozer killer and that’s its only use. The nade launcher does more damage to yourself then the enemy. Its detrimental to use the weapon. It’s it’s a pain in the ass to get it, then you have to walk out of the heists during an assault (On some maps like the art gallery is so far out where it really does not feel like its worth it at all) Then you basically can’t do anything with it while you carry it. If there is a single guy in front of you, you can either: 1. Take the damage and run past 2. Waste your precious ammo you had to get out of your way to get it 3. Throw it down for 2 seconds, kill the guy, and pick it up again for 3 seconds. Why its “hold f to pick up” is beyond me it should be press, it makes the whole system feel so clunky, regardless of being unable to literally anything else when you carry it. My suggestion is that you can always take it out and put away by pressing the ovk weapon button (hold to call?) and then it drops a special ammo bag instead that you pick up.They said they are happy with the current progression system. I have never seen a less satisfying progression system. You only get exp through challenges and not heists themselves. I recently spend 2ish hours stealthing and beating 99 Boxes for the first time on overkill. I got ZERO exp for it. Thanks a lot, sure felt rewarding. Don’t care if its bugged or not the challenges should add onto the progression does not replace it. There should be a base exp gain based on heist, difficulty, and bags amount. Having to do stuff based on what an unorganized spread sheet tells me rather than what is most fun to me sucks. That the game gets incredibly girindly does not help at all. I’m at level 60 (and the exp gain feels terrible slow now) and have 30 hours and it takes as much exp to get to 70 then to get to level 100. And exp gain only slows down as the challenges get grindier and rarer. There is only 8 Heists in the game. You will either have to do some stupid grind Strat or burn yourself out on 70-100 hours of the same 8 heists just to get all the weapons or skills, the max level is 150 and unlocks more cosmetic stuff.The customization system is also extremely basic and sad, and what is there, is locked behind such a comical level requirement that you must had played 100 hours before you can make a mask or gun that doesn’t look like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ nerf gun. You can tell that they kept all the good things for the paid packs and the microtransactions they have already announced in a FAQ page.Other annoyances:Can’t que for “loud only/Stealth only/both” (not that you can que at all…) even tho pd2 had this feature.-The main menu buy system is just kinda annoying to use, little stuff like buying a weapon and it not putting into your inventory but keeping you in the store page. Who wants to buy more then one of the same weapons? Especially given that you only need one build of the gun with no concealment in this game. -Can’t ping codes and have to manually write them down (rip console users)-Glass cutting is def made for controller and feels annoying on pc-No chat in preplanning-No Unready button-Why do I have to buy favors? 10k is such a comically small amount, if they cant charge in the preplanning screen because their system sucks they should be free.-The special favors just randomly appear, and the game doesn’t tell you how to get more. Also doesn’t refund them when the server ♥♥♥♥♥ the bed, or you quit, so if you use your rare favor and you have to remake the lobby because the restart doesn’t work youre just out of luck.-No votekick so if a player is trolling you just must reque (and risk not getting into a new match…) In general, I am extremely dissatisfied with their response to this terrible launch. Given that the only thing saving them from bankruptcy was the community buying overpriced dlc for pd2 (and pd3 has the exact same model plus microtransactions soon) I would assume they would do right to their community, however I doubt they will. They will try sweeping this disaster under the rug.When somebody is uncertain and angry the last thing the community needs is an uncertain “idk we might look into an offline mode because our always online was clearly a mistake, not promises tho”. They want to have their cake and eat it too, and this is not what the community needs right now. It needs strong commitments to basic features (offline mode, lobbies, reworks of the exp system and bots) the game should have had at launch because overkill can’t do always online to save their ass.The game needed at least 3-6 more months in development and till they fix the above-mentioned issues I cannot recommend it. Which is a shame because a lot of the game is fun.

_childDocuments_.review: PAYDAY 3 is the sequel to one of the most popular co-op shooters ever. Since its release, PAYDAY-players have been reveling in the thrill of a perfectly planned and executed heist. That’s what makes PAYDAY a high-octane, co-op FPS experience without equal. Step out of retirement back into the life of crime in the shoes of the Payday Gang, the envy of their peers and the nightmare of law-enforcement wherever they go. Several years after the crew’s reign of terror over Washington DC has ended, they assemble once again to deal with the threat that roused them out of early retirement. The legendary Payday Crew, dreaded by the law and underworld alike, is back. Ripped from their peaceful retirement to rejoin the criminal world by a new threat, one born from the chaos the Crew left in their wake. In order to identify and crush this new threat, the Crew is leaving their Washington DC roots behind them and moving to New York City. A new location will bring with it new challenges, but also new opportunities for a heister with a plan. Give outlet to your greed and let loose in PAYDAY 3. In addition to gold, cash and jewelry and any other valuables they might come across, you’ll be able to build a sizable collection of weapons, cosmetics and accolades. It won’t be as simple as showing up and gaining goodies. You’ll have to work hard and plan smart to get away with as much loot as possible. Gain experience, unlock new skills and gain proficiency in weapons to steadily grow your power to handle the tougher challenges. A professional heister knows it takes planning, hard work and a good amount of luck in order to execute a successful heist. In PAYDAY 3 the choice is put in the hands of the players, deciding how to tackle the heist, whether you sneak or go in guns blazing, whether you let your hostages go or keep them around as pawns, whether you go at it alone or bring friends. The choices are endless and in your hands, they will vastly change how the game plays. Not just anyone is worthy of standing at your side for something as important as a heist. Likewise, PAYDAY 3 is best enjoyed with close friends in mind, whether you bring them from your childhood or make them along the road. The PAYDAY-series has always valued the bonds made through hardship and tries to reflect that in the actions and words of our heisters while in the game, and through our community while on the outside.

name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante
detailed_description: JOIN THE COMMUNITY ON DISCORD About the Game The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante is a narrative-driven RPG that comes to life on the pages of the protagonist's journal. Set in a ruthless world where any form of dissent is mercilessly crushed, the story follows a man who has dared to challenge the existing order. Set out on a lifelong journey and become an individual able to carve out their own destiny... But remember that freedom never comes cheap. Life in the Great Arknian Empire is harsh and its hardest Lot is yours by the circumstance of birth. You are a commoner, holding no rights and no title. To seize your fate and become the rightful heir to the legacy of the Brante family you will have to come to grips with ossified tradition and prejudice. Embarking on a life-long journey from one's birth until true death, you will have to endure great upheavals, face adversity, and make many difficult choices. Every decision will affect not only the protagonist, his family, and loved ones, but may even topple the foundation of the Empire itself. Key features At the turn of time Every imperial citizen's life is predetermined by their estate. The deities known as the Twin Gods have bestowed this truth to the world, dividing mortals into Lots. The nobles lead and rule over others, while the clergy guides people on the one true path, and the lowborn suffer, toiling away for the glory of the Empire. You may accept your fate without question, but it is also in your power to change the cosmic order that governs all. Your choice is not an illusion Divided into chapters, the game keeps track of the player's deeds, the skills they acquired, as well as other overlapping circumstances that shape a unique plotline for each playthrough. Every decision has its consequences and you will be held accountable throughout the entire journey. To protect your family and loved ones, to impose the rule of the Emperor and make a fortune, or to try and change the world as you see fit... Make your choice, but beware of the follies of pride and ambition. Fight for your life One man is anything but omnipotent in this realm yet under your guidance, Sir Brante may become a person who can endure every trial fate throws at him and rewrite the very laws that govern his world! Develop and train your character, leveling up such traits as determination, sensitivity, and endurance. All of the hero's skills, starting with those acquired in infancy, will affect his personality, worldview, and relationships, ultimately unlocking new talents and possible storylines. Find your own path The first complete walkthrough can take you upwards of 15 hours! Numerous branching paths that affect the unfolding story will make every playthrough a unique experience: become a noble judge, learn the ways of the inquisition, plot a revolution as a member of a secret society, or embrace an entirely different purpose. Be brave and fate itself shall bend to your will! There and hereafter Resurrection system allows the character to keep his experience upon death, letting the player reevaluate past steps and make adjustments to their strategy going forward. Take control not only of your life but also your demise, then put everything at stake in this cycle of death and rebirth!
about_the_game: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante is a narrative-driven RPG that comes to life on the pages of the protagonist's journal. Set in a ruthless world where any form of dissent is mercilessly crushed, the story follows a man who has dared to challenge the existing order. Set out on a lifelong journey and become an individual able to carve out their own destiny... But remember that freedom never comes cheap. Life in the Great Arknian Empire is harsh and its hardest Lot is yours by the circumstance of birth. You are a commoner, holding no rights and no title. To seize your fate and become the rightful heir to the legacy of the Brante family you will have to come to grips with ossified tradition and prejudice. Embarking on a life-long journey from one's birth until true death, you will have to endure great upheavals, face adversity, and make many difficult choices. Every decision will affect not only the protagonist, his family, and loved ones, but may even topple the foundation of the Empire itself. Key features At the turn of time Every imperial citizen's life is predetermined by their estate. The deities known as the Twin Gods have bestowed this truth to the world, dividing mortals into Lots. The nobles lead and rule over others, while the clergy guides people on the one true path, and the lowborn suffer, toiling away for the glory of the Empire. You may accept your fate without question, but it is also in your power to change the cosmic order that governs all. _childDocuments_.review: The game is a masterpiece of interactive storytelling, with a rich and immersive world, complex and realistic characters, and branching paths that lead to multiple endings. The game is a must-play for fans of choice-based games, as well as for anyone who enjoys a gripping and emotional tale of struggle and sacrifice.

_childDocuments_.review: This experience was the most invested I've been in a game in a long time.  It's tense and stressful, but also so rewarding when everything comes together.Choices matter.  We've been pitched that line countless times from countless game developers.  But in The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante, the makers of the game managed to do exactly that.  The game is one choice after another, and every single one of them feels significant and meaningful.  More than that - they're difficult.  There's not necessarily a "right" answer, and I found myself choosing what my interpretation of Brante would have chosen, even if I knew it might not end well.  In eight hours of gameplay with probably hundreds of decisions, I can count on one hand the number of times I chose because it seemed right for the "game," rather than right for the character.You are Sir Brante, recounting your experiences from birth until death, and every single year in between.  Every choice you make impacts the game in some way - some significant way.  It's not like your standard RPG where you get +1 morality for this choice or -1 faction favor for that choice.  Instead, they serve to drive the narrative itself, opening up one path or forever closing another.  You determine what happens with your family, your friends, your faith, and your fate itself, up to and including death.The criticism you're most likely to see for this game is that choices matter TOO much; you're forced to min/max your stats and carefully craft your decisions to reach the ending you want.  I say that's nonsense, and anyone playing with the results of their choices shown in advance (there's an option to hide them) is already missing the point of the game.  Don't let the game become numbers.  Play your own character, and make your own decisions.  Yes, sometimes things will turn out bad as a result.  But that's part of the experience, and really a part of life.  Nothing is good all the time, and, well...choices matter.Perhaps I'm too willing to praise the game because I achieved a positive ending on my very first attempt.  Not just a positive ending - exactly the one I wanted.  I imagine it's crushing to have grand plans that fall around you despite your best efforts.  But, looking back, not everything WAS perfect.  My family never realized their noble ambitions and ended up fractured and despised.  My brothers went down bad paths I wish they hadn't.  My love interest and I held irreconcilably different beliefs, ultimately leading to mutual hatred for each other.But through it all, I was true to myself and my beliefs.  I poured myself into Sir Brante and was rewarded in kind.  And THAT'S what this game can become for those willing to meet it on its own terms.  It's not a game for everyone, true.  But it has the potential to become one of the most memorable gaming experiences you've ever had.

_childDocuments_.review: A very good choose-your-own-adventure game. I was very happy with the choices I was able to make and I was rewarded with a satisfying ending. You can choose to be able to see the immediate consequences of your actions (how they affect the stats of the character and the world) and can choose to restart a chapter if one of your choices made you unhappy with how the story went, but you can also choose to disable both of these abilities if you want to only make choices by your own code and want to be forced to live with the consequences. There are also many different paths to go down, which will affect the final outcome of your character, your family, and the order of the world, which helps replayability (on my first playthrough I only unlocked about 20% of the game's achievements, each one for a different choice made). I highly recommend it to anyone who likes choose-your-own-adventure books/games.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, the good: the music and art direction are amazing, and the world-building is genuinely well-done. Now, for the bad, and this is gonna be long.The first two chapters had me hyped up for an amazing, nuanced experience. I thought that going down the noble path and supporting commoners would make me a leader of the revolt due to my influence and reputation. But nope, Sophia is hell-bent on genociding everyone and literally has no plan whatsoever for replacing the Empire with a better system, and your champion-of-the-commoners character can't convince anyone otherwise because she has **magic** eyes.Basically, this game took its title - the "suffering" part - too seriously without having any nuance, and turned into a parody of itself at some point. None of the characters have good characterisation, most are straight-up tropey (someone return Nathan to whichever Dostoyevsky novel he came from), and practically no one has an arc where the events they witness transform them in some believable way. Also, I cannot overstate how much the **magic** of Sophia irritates me. She has the unexplained ability to override all of your character's influence and power (and your whole army of rogue legionnaires) by using her mind-control magic, which is cheap and plays into stereotypes of the animalistic crowd who listen to whoever is the most violent. It is strongly in favour of the status quo and pretends that revolutions only lead to chaos and massacre, ignoring the fact that in our world, we owe a lot to the French and Russian revolutions (the former of which seems to have been a particular inspiration, with the expression "Reign of Terror" appearing directly in the game).In the end, I hoped this game would explore themes of suffering in a nuanced way, but it was just edgy.

_childDocuments_.review: "The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante" is a captivating mix of visual novel and RPG, making you feel like you're living out a compelling story with added animations and sounds. If you're into games like Pentiment (closest to this one based on setting; religion, social classes etc.), Disco Elysium or Yes, Your Grace, this one's for you.You play as Sir Brante, shaping his life from childhood through crucial choices that define his character. These decisions earn points in traits like "Determination", which grow and change as you progress. While you can see the "consequences" of your choices, I highly suggest to turn that off (you can do it before starting a "new game") for a more immersive experience.The game offers different life paths, letting you mold Sir Brante into who you want him to be. As you play, you'll gain insights into decision-making and see the story become more complex and intriguing.Pros:+Lots of content for the price.+it's highly replayable.+Animations, music, and effects enhance the storytelling.+Keeps you hooked with its twists and turns.+Every decision feels important, shaping the story.Cons:-Sometimes sound effects don't quite fit.-Lots of reading so, might not be for everyone.-New characters can make things confusing, so take breaks.Overall, "The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante" offers a deeply engaging narrative experience with meaningful choices. Despite lack of action like other similar games, it's a must-play for anyone who loves a good story.

_childDocuments_.review: It was well worth the money. I just completed my first playthrough and the story gripped me from start to finish. It will reward you and pusish you for your choices, but so is the way of life. There is a lot to explore in this world and i belive it hs significant repleyability, with each of the 3 mayor paths  diverging into more compex and compelling stories that manage to capture the divission and struggle of society. Do you even want to be remembered? Will you manage to overcome the compex situations and dificculties, or will you fail to complete your missions and dreams? It is for you to decide and find out. Write your own story, try to become what you long to be.

_childDocuments_.review: The art style, setting and overall story is great.What is not so great is that in a game about choices you lack the ability to make these choices. _childDocuments_.review: A big thing about the game from the beginning is that you can’t always make the choices you want, and you can’t control the outcome of them either. As an example, before I chose my Lot the game made sure I understood I was making a big choice, and I ultimately . Rarely, a choice can be a little polarized, like when I . I didn’t want to refuse  , but that was still my response. I was still able to  later without any  consequence, and yet I’m genuinely curious to know what that would’ve been like had I chose differently. There are even several choices that gave me only one option. It was a natural result of how I had played up to that point. That said, I didn’t feel any less free here than I did with the “demo.” They might not have all been what I wanted most, but I made a choice. Or, rather, I couldn’t make a choice as a result of my previous ones.I realized rather early on with this game that it isn’t . It’s about what you do or don’t have control over and how you adapt with your options therein. It feels very natural to me, especially as something text-based, which I know sounds strange with everything I’ve described up to this point but it was a surprise to me too. If I wanted to roam around and do anything I want on a whim then I’d play a different game, maybe something like Skyrim or .I only wish there was a native way to copy an Ironman save and rewind, there are a handful of specific choices I’d like to see a “what if” for, and I can understand why a player could want to have consequences visible. That just isn’t something  want for a first playthrough of a choice-driven game like this.Life isn’t fair, you don’t always get what you want. Some suffering is bound to come with it and it can either embolden you or destroy you.  the message of the game for me. I would highly recommend this if you’re into grimdark or Fallout: New Vegas, or even if you aren’t necessarily. Chances are, if you’re here, you’ll find what you’re looking for with The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante. Oh, and don’t mistake anything I’ve said here as any given choice not mattering, odds are it’ll be a slippery slope down…

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome stuff. Make the wrong choices and you'll die, miss out on stats, or both. Make other choices often requires stats to be at a certain level and / or to have enough "willpower", a resource that lets you go against the status quo for your own gain or curiosity.E D I T :This is mostly in response to the most "helpfully" rated review right now which just so happens to be negative. The author of this review states that the game shoehorns the player into set outcomes regardless of previous decisions and that the game requires you to select the "right" choices. Games are always about the "right" answers. The vast majority of narrative driven games have a single ending point that serves as the climax most people will reach, just with a slightly different set-up (whether it be their gear, character traits, etc.) Mass effect (not just the final game, even the first and second games in that series do this), Divinity: OS2, many widely lauded games that focus on plot shoehorn players into a specific ending or set series of events.That is how games are made, period. No game is entirely unique for every single person that plays it and to criticize the game because there is a system that prevents players from doing that is absurd. I cannot imagine the author playing a game like Crusader Kings, where the game clearly tells you (as does this one) that you simply cannot do things because the statistics don't work out in your favor. For example: "no player, you can't invite that person to your court because they won't accept your invitation because you're insane and they hate you." So, in Crusader Kings, the game simply prevents you from even attempting to invite the person. A similar system is in place in this game. Don't have the stats available? Can't do it then can ya? In no way is the game "railroading" you, frankly the reviewer is doing the game a disservice by implying nothing you do matters because "plot reigns supreme" (it does not). Though certain things happen to everyone that will play, most people, if they so choose, will have a much different life experience, for the most part than others. Every time you begin a new section / chapter of the game, you are literally presented with a list of possible outcomes that you can work towards. Anyone complaining that the game locks decisions they wanted due to stats need to actually read.The best part of this game's most helpful review (which is a thumbs down one) is the very end, where the last paragraph argues against itself:"In this game, however, you start a journey from point A to point B. But instead of having multiple solutions to reach point B like above, you must pick a "correct" path, or else you will never reach point B. Meaning; that you don't actually have a choice. That choice is taken away from you, and you are forced down to take a singular path."So the game doesn't have multiple solutions to reach point B, you just have to select a correct path (out of many, which the author conveniently leaves out) to reach point B. Sounds....... like there are multiple solutions then, huh? I don't get what this review is trying to say. To me, the review reads more like someone frustrated they didn't get the ending they wanted.The review also states that priests need to focus on theology stat, nobles on fighting stat, etc. I can tell you right now, as I'm finishing the game, Eloquence has been extremely common in my playthrough as a priest, and manipulation has come up more times than I can count on my fingers as well. The author is wrong when he said "you must focus on only 1 stat" because frankly, you may not even know what stat you will need for the hidden events the game doesn't tell you about until you need to make the decision. These decisions usually happen in between chapters and make up the majority of them, and almost all are predicated precisely on what decisions you made and what the outcomes were. Whenever you finish a plot point or event, the game literally informs you in the relation panel what "state" that relationship is in. Later down the line, if you were paying attention, you will notice that some events will have the exact same title as those relationship "states."  So why would you *have* to focus on one specific stat, and in significant what way does the game not take into account your actions? It makes no sense whatsoever.

_childDocuments_.review: The game's great, but for the love of all that is holy, PLAY. WITH. OPEN. CONSEQUENCES. It's the way the game is designed to be played, and not knowing what the consequences of your decisions will be utterly ruins the game.Also, my advice is to play the game once. Maybe twice if you want to experience a different route. Your choices matter alot, but the game doesn't have as much replay value as it might seem. It's best played with the illusion of dozens of possible routes intact. My first playthrough was mindblowingly good, my second was mediocre, and I can't bring myself to play it a third time.This game is really good, but it doesn't have much replay value and therefore is best experienced once or twice. Or you can treat it like a book and reread it very sparingly. Just don't replay it too many times in quick succession, is what I'm saying.

_childDocuments_.review: I will never forget Francis Brante, who came from a childhood of curiosity and learned to hate the nobility and what it represented, when his grandfather turned out to be a ♥♥♥♥ and the cute girl-from-next-door was almost trampled over by uncaring horse riders. He tried to keep his family and friends together and succeeded more often than he failed. In the end he followed the woman he loved on her bloody path of revenge and destruction of the old world before prostrating himself before the gods and teaching them about forgiveness. Francis left a trail of blood and despair in his attempt to change the world and while he certainly succeeded, he was unsure whether it was for the better or worse. Still, nobody could deny his place in history and his influence on the future of the world. Francis Brante, the Butcher of Anizotte.------------------What a glorious game. Inspired by Roadwarden (my game of the year) to play more text-based choose-your-own-path story games, The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante managed to engage me for almost 8 hours straight and was an absolute treat. I did notice a higher frequency of grammar mistakes in the final chapter, but other than that I was glued to my screen the whole time, both trying to forge a path for Francis that would lead to peaceful revolution and keep his family, friends and acquaintances alive -- I failed utterly, as you can imagine from the first paragraph. Francis' good intentions never quite clicked with his circumstances and the game got seriously tough at times, but engaging nonetheless, when trying to decide between outcomes. I will replay another Brante in the future for sure, making different choices and seeing how the game changes course.Strongly recommended.------------------Update: I will never forget Adam Brante, a spiritual, perceptive man who became a prophet at 16 years old and managed to shape the world and his family with his unwavering belief in good. He became known as the liberator of Anizotte and apostle of the New Faith, while reuniting his family, keeping his partner Jeanne and best friend Tommas alive and by his side until the end. The brokered peace with the Overseer, united the lots and made the world a better place, at least for a while. Adam Brante was taken to the Peak of the Shining Pillar.[Second playthrough, all in one day. What a beautiful game.]

_childDocuments_.review: I have not been this invested in a game's story for quite some time. This game is essentially a chose-your-own-adventure narrative, but in those choices lies incredible strength. I have agonized over options, regretted them instantly or years later... but also triumphed in their results and outcomes. Suffering is quite literally part of the name of the game, and with good reason. You can't do everything. Sometimes, you can't do . But with careful planning, consideration, a little luck, and a quick prayer to the Twins, you can make that suffering more than worthwhile. I've completed the Life in 11 hours and plan to return to it after a while to try something completely different.  I already cannot wait.

However by including abilities tied to stats that change throughout your playthrough, the game can lock you into or out of certain choices. Has Brante been forcing himself into too much work recently? Then he won't have enough willpower left over to make certain other choices. _childDocuments_.review: I loved this game. Had never heard of it but got it and 7 other games for $12 in the Humble Bundle. What a steal.I played through this game three times across 24 hours. I only unlocked 40/89 achievements doing so, so there's still a decent amount of content I didn't see.This game has 3 main paths you can choose, and each path has at least two different ways to ago about them.For example, in the Judge career path, you are have to balance Justice and your Career. The Nobles are used to getting their way and expect you to rule in their favor always, even when it's blatantly against the law. Doing so will be good for your career but bad for Justice, which means the common folk will feel the Law is just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and revolt. Do the opposite, and your career will be in shambles. Whichever path you choose and the stats you're trying to balance will give you different relationships  with different characters and thus different ways to handle situations.In addition to the three main paths, there are plot lines revolving your family that are always present and intersect with the three main paths you choose.Overall this game is well written with a ton of content. The writing is paced well, you're never bogged down. I laughed, I teared up, I had a blast. If you like RPGs this is a no brainer.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the most painful review I've made, perhaps on par with Cyberpunk.  This could be a rant, so I'll try and be short and sweet, and to the point.  The game feels very rail-roaded, and seems to greatly encourage both meta behaviour and min/maxing.  So much so the game, by default, enables you to see the outcome of your choices, to an extent (I played with this off since I don't like meta-info in a game like this). The start of the game you have to think, rather than by your logical thinking, but by how much Willpower you want to spend to accumulate certain skill-points. In the first half, you spend Willpower in choices, and the choice you choose attributes to a corresponding skillpoint. Not bad, except you either have to completely min/max through the well written story, or ignore the skills and choose which is logical, which will immediately drain all your willpower and doom you to stupid, default positions later. The latter half of the gain, you now very rarely spend willpower, and instead have what choices are open to you be decided by your skills, which you gained in the first half.  However, again, logical thinking plays next to no part, as you will regularly have to make retarded choices because you don't have the skills necessary to choice a logical one. This happens, constantly, and if you played the game like me, paying attention to the story and then trying to choose logical choices, your stats are completely jumbled and a wreck, meaning it's incredibly difficult to make any form of logical path forward.  Early on, I decided I wanted max Valor, which is 20, however gaining skills are extremely hard, unless you min/max your choices towards getting a skillpoint. This is where the writer's pure illogical retardation shows, as you are waiting for the option to let your character train fencing, yet it never occures.  Neither any other option to train a skill.  So you must go through the game, praying you will hopefully one day get the stat you want high by half luck, choosing the right options (Which if doing so will force you to make illogical choices, just to get the skillpoint). Overall, very good story, but they should've just made a book.  They were so obsessed with making the game so replayable, with so many endings, they forgot to make the core experience fun and rewarding. It just feels meta and unfair to a degree that goes beyond the game's intent.

_childDocuments_.review: Purely based upon the merit that this is a captivating, worthy and lengthy throwback to "choose your own adventure" RPG books of old, I will recommend this - ALTHOUGH it also certainly has some (major flaws). Starting with the positives, the art style is bold and strong right out of the gate, picturing little vignettes of the story in beautiful detail as you read along. The music is very sedate, but also very effective in it's placing and when it flares up to emphasize certain pivotal moments. The storytelling is utterly captivating, managing to immerse you in your own version of "Brante", while also providing some very worthwhile and seemingly deep gameplay mechanics; allowing you to choose not only your path of your life in the story, but also honing stats/skills and forming relationships. The seeming pure VARIETY of choices and "options" here should be commended above all else, you really feel like you could play this game over and over and REALLY have another entire different experience altogether and that in itself is an ACHIEVEMENT of writing and design in my book. HOWEVER, unfortunately and tragically the game undermines it's own admirable strengths thoroughly at times, marring an otherwise superb RPG experience and leaving a trace of frustration instead.First of all, SOME of the writing (albeit the minority) is definitely not on par with the rest of the game, sporting typing errors, weird grammar, grammatical errors, baffling expressions or straight up just... very elementary school level writing. This in of itself wouldn't be nearly enough though to ruin the experience, what really ruins it is how you start to feel more and more railroaded the further you play the game, furthermore choices and consequences there of, become so frustratingly entwined that you feel actively cheated by the game. Not only are you faced with a series of decisions that tasks you with managing your stats and ressources to reach one of the possible outcomes, that then wildly spin of out of control, denying you the outcome you actually WORKED towards because you failed to say raise one stat ONE point higher 7 decisions ago. That SUCKS. What sucks even MORE is how contrived some aspects of the game feel. I decided to become a master duelist in my first playthrough. When I was done with chapter 2 of the story, I had a MAXIMUM SCORE (20) in the stat that supposedly governs how well you are with a blade (yes I took fencing lessons, won the tournament etc), the GAME ITSELF classifies a score of 20 to be SUPERB and allowing you ONE GREAT FEAT, because of your MASTERY. So naturally my Brante went on to loose and/or die in every duel from then on. I guess the story demanded that you pay with deaths on your part, to make the decision more harsh and the resource management more difficult, but come on, at this point the game is breaking it's own rules. It's own established world building. I WORKED TOWARDS BEING A GREAT DUELIST, YET I CAN'T EVEN WIN A DUEL AGAINST SOME RANDO, OR SOME HENCHMEN IN THE STREETS. This really erodes the foundation of this game, of giving you options, of giving you stats. This is ultimately less a "choose your own adventure game" (although you can play it that way and then probably "lose") and instead more of a calculated "play the optimal path according to the math" kind of game. It rewards min-maxing and actively PUNISHES your own decisions, a realization which saddens me greatly. I wish this was better than that. It felt better than that. It felt like the game I always wanted to play and then it cruelly dashed my hopes on it's sharp rocks of nebulous skill requirements and railroading overall story decisions that are imposed upon you.

_childDocuments_.review: This game... I love CYOA books, and especially CYOA that involve a sort of gameified system where your character has defined stats, and maybe even a bit of gameplay like combat or puzzles. However, this story is an excercise in futility in both a good and a bad way. Narratively I enjoyed the idea about how the world just kind of sucks, and if trying to do something good, it may not matter much, or may even bite you in the ass somehow. My issues arise once you hit the youth stage. About halfway through it, you may begin to notice that you're not able to pick many options at all, and the writing seems to be very heavy-handed about what your character is deciding to do, without your input. It only gets worse. As the story progresses you begin to lack the 'resources' necessary to make basic decisions that should just be doable. In some cases your character outright does things that make no sense to what you've been roleplaying or doing in general. I.E. Extremely forced romance with a terrible character I 200% hated from the second I saw her. This persists through the rest of the game by the way, it's not a one off thing.I can't recommend this game. There's grammar issues all over the place, which isn't the main problem, but it's annoying for me. It's got compelling world building and some really great characters, but the only part I enjoyed was tending to the Brante family. Everything else fell apart and was so horribly put together that I was constantly going "What? Why is this happening? That doesn't make any sense."I gave it an honest effort, but you should wait for it to be much more on sale, or just read about the story online.

_childDocuments_.review: Ultimately, when I play a game I want to have fun. Yes, I want to be challenged. Yes, I want the illusion of 'grittiness.' But at the end of the day, I'm playing a game because I want to be the hero, or the villian, or the enigma. Life & Suffering is tantalizing, but quickly devolves into decision-making based on what it will do for your stats, regardless of outcomes. But the stats turn out to be meaningless: in my latest playthrough I maxed out Valor, which theoretically helps you with combat, but then proceeded to die in two duels, and a clubbing by thugs. What is the point of being maxed out in a skill if it has no bearing on your storyline?The game simply doesn't have enough storyline variety to start over, altering my emphasis on Valor, just to try to avoid the duel situations. There are three paths, I've quickly died on two of them. Also, one quick pet peeve that I lay at the feet of the writers of this game. They want so badly to create the hero standing up against nobility, sticking it to the rich, but they want to have their cake and eat it too: shoehorning your character into an affair w/ a member of the royalty. At every turn in my latest playthrough I attempted to avoid this path, as it in no way fit with the character of Sir Brante in my playthrough. Why would a man who's dedicating his life to bringing unchecked nobles to justice then choose as his only love interest a woman from that group? Can there be an option wherein Sir Brante is flattered, but has the courage to turn down an offer of romance? Not for these writers. Turning down the noblewoman is seen as a deep offense, with major negative repercussions. They're writing a Robin Hood, more obsessed with getting into bed with Maid Marian, than class equality. It's tired.

_childDocuments_.review: The life and Suffering of Sir Brante. OH BOY that was a fun ride. Clocking in at 11 hours from start to finish, it is quite the Tale. You take the role of, Sir Brante, 3rd child of the Brante family. From the day of your birth to a Revolt in your home town. You live in the Blessed Arkian Empire, a society that uses a "caste" system. From Commoners to Nobles to the Clergy to the Arkians themselves (in that order). They worship the Twins, a pair of gods that formed the world in which you live, and everyone is expected to "Live by their Lot" in life.As you play, You shape the kind of man Sir Brante is. Your actions have consequences Both good and bad, as Brante's life goes on, your actions will effect more then just Him, but his Family, the Province in which he lives and even how the Revolt plays out.Ultimately their are 4 life paths to ping from in your Youth, each of which seem to have 2 paths which branch from them as well. So their is PLENTY of replay/reread value here to make different choices. You can even replay each chapter mid run if you so choose.

_childDocuments_.review: Firstly to get it out of the way, this is a choose your own adventure novel, not a game per say.With that out of the way, I highly recommend the experience for those with a tolerance for long reading, it is presented well, clean and easy to navigate and use. With some immensely well written storylines / characters and finally a place where choices matter and not only matter, but 'really' matter.It explores a lot of themes without judging them unduly, if you want to be a noble despot who sits on the poor and uses them for wealth, you can be that, but you can equally be the polar opposite or anything in between. It really allows a freedom to explore the world as the character and in whatever way you choose to make them.Some people complain that the choices ease off towards the end in many ways, where you might be presented with six or so options and only able to pick one or two, to me, this is logical, as its a consequence of the choices you made before, better to hold to the choices of your past than just pretend they didn't happen and I feel it really makes you reflect on what you did (and didn't!) do in life.After finishing, I think I spent about an hour just reflecting upon it all and wondering, at least in my playthrough, where it all went wrong. Without spoilers, I seemed to get the worst possible ending I could envision, but equally it seemed right. Because that is the life and suffering of Sir Brante.Buy the game if it seems your kinda thing, its a hidden gem.An easy 9/10 Story that I shall replay in due course.

_childDocuments_.review: While at times interesting, I felt put off by the stat requirements for story choices in the game. You have to level certain stats for being able to even make future choices, which leads you to naturally pick options that bring you best results stat-wise for later, instead of roleplaying.There is an ingame toggle that hides the results of these choices (stat increases and others) but certainly then you won't get a story outcome/choices you were hoping, since you'll get locked out at one point or another.Sometimes being locked out makes sense because the choice wouldn't make sense compared to what happened before. However, at times the most logical choice (for your character) is not available, simply because you didn't level the stat enough.Ultimately I feel this harms the experience more than it does good. There are several different life paths I could go for in a future playthrough but I don't really feel compelled to replay after one go at it.The game does let you replay from certain points in the game to redo choices, but I still feel like the stat requirement system is flawed.As a minor complaint I also spotted a fair number of typos.

_childDocuments_.review: We now are able to follow Brante’s story up until the end of The Revolt when he is 30 years old over 5 total arcs. The Childhood and Adolescent arcs are identical to how they were in the demo so I skim read them as I rebuilt my Brante. The Youth arc is when you actually get to choose your path in life and steer your Brante down it in adulthood/ Peace Time. There are 3 major paths with a few branches: Noble, Priest and the Lotless. The overall stories told are pretty good with some good dilemmas. I was really interested in all the new events.Nonetheless, there is definitely some illusion of choice. You will be funneled into some common events that’re slightly modified to fit your path like a duel gone wrong being either about religion or Lot. Likewise, some events play the same regardless of your reputation with a person or choice. At most there is some very minor dialogue differences. This creates some tonal dissonance as roleplay is being disregarded in these segments. For example, you will ALWAYS become friends with Tommas no matter what you pick. I did 3 major playthroughs, one for each path with several other failed/ experimental games: Overall, I think the narrative is good and entertaining, a nice trip for fans of choose-your-own-adventure games. I expected a bit more polish in the finished product but being able to steer Brante in the direction you want is still really fun. There are a lot of interesting characters to meet and they all really help set the stage for your path. Choices can still be pretty brutal in terms of outcomes and moral choices and I found myself deliberating some for a few minutes.     Gameplay is exactly the same as the demo. You mostly read and make choices for Brante on how to deal with a given situation. Each decision has multiple answers, each raising or lowering a different stat. You need high stats in order to pass more difficult skill checks in lategame. After playing several runs, I feel that stats are weird in that they are both super important and not important at all.    Dedicated roleplaying is punished to some degree. Following a clear but narrow path leads to many complications such as tanking your family or career status or causing you to build a Brante ill-equipped to meet skill checks. Skill checks are entirely pass/fail with no consideration for your proficiency. For example, I maxed out Valor (combat prowess) but still ended up dying in a choice involving fighting and requiring high Valor. What is the point of maxing out a stat if you are not rewarded for it?Likewise, I wanted to roleplay a righteous judge but the best outcome for a dilemma required leveling Manipulation, a stat labeled for the Lotless job. I wasn’t able to increase it reliably since the Judge focuses on Diplomacy and Valor. The result of my low skill was that I had to let a friend die, much to my chagrin. Despite having almost maxed out my Diplomacy I could NOT use it in any capacity to aid my friend. In this regard, blind playthroughs are a bit annoying since your build may end up short of doing the actual things you want.   There is also the issue of getting railroaded into a no-win situation if you lack the correct stats. Without spoiling too much, the Judge has to get a prominent person removed from their military position. You MUST have high job stats in order to pass. I had moderate and even job stats because getting one too low gives a rather punitive event setting you back quite a bit. If you don’t have the stats you MUST pick the True Death/ game over option. The end result is you having to rewind the story to get the appropriate stats or try your luck with other routes/ jobs. I was definitely bummed out when this happened since it felt like metagaming for stats was more important than being immersed in the story and roleplaying.   The aforementioned illusion of choice didn’t help either. Some events resolve the same way in the end with minor differences. This makes decisions have considerably less weight, causing the overall experience to feel way more scripted/ linear. In a game entirely about making choices, I wish scenarios were more varied to directly reference Brante’s actions and make you feel the true weight of your actions, both good and bad. Willpower got a slight modification in the final game. Now you will sometimes gain a stat increase alongside Willpower. You still get back-to-back Willpower options but it is slightly easier to keep it high in the full release. Keeping your family happy is very difficult and unless you min-max everything someone is always going to end up sad or your family stats will tank. Becoming disgraced has some pretty nasty debuffs so be wary of how you treat your family. The game has a map tab to summarize key locations but still lacks an encyclopedia tab. The sheer amount of people and events is mind boggling and I struggled to remember everything and everyone, especially in my Inquisitor run with all the different schools of thought and lore. In summation, gameplay is overall good but there isn’t nearly as much freedom as the game says it gives you. The game retains is beautiful monochromatic ink drawings. There are now cutscenes but they have rather limited/ stilted movement with characters and objects just sliding across the screen. The journal aesthetic is still very strong and thematically appropriate. Character portraits are all great. Not much else to say as the game is very narrative focused.  The music and sound effects are still great overall. I was always in the right mood thanks to the music. The orchestral sounds really sell the “classic” aesthetic the game is going for. Sound effects add a layer of immersion I really appreciated even if they do get recycled a little bit much. I liked Brante’s VO overall.  The game ran well overall. However, it locked up once after mashing through dialogue following the Sacrament scene. Cutscenes lack any form of subtitles which is a very weird decision in a text-based game. Options are rather sparse but the game isn’t terribly taxing and should run on most computers.  I feel like I can recommend the game but it honestly fell short of what I was hoping for. The narrative and intertwined gameplay definitely felt clunky since roleplaying and metagaming were at odds with one another. Trying to be in character may require stats you didn’t earn yet, resulting in only bad choices being offered. The railroading and common events also stripped some fun away from each path. However, all the fun and enjoyable stuff I mentioned in my demo review still stands true for the most part. While Brante's destiny is to suffer, it is unclear if this is due to the Twin Gods’ will or simply because of the game design.

_childDocuments_.review: Cannot recommend enough. A stellar example of the artistic potential within CYOA games. Great art, a captivating story with lots of moments of joy and heartbreak.
