_childDocuments_.review: 9/10 Excellent.Probably one of the most well-written and conceived choose your own adventure games (or life sim, whatever) out there.You take the role of Sir Brante, a man born into a unique world, with interesting religious views where the Gods actually exist, and grant you three lives, meaning you can die three times before your fourth death is a permanent affair.It is a clever way of introducing a way to fail without failing too hard, a way to ensure that you can take some risks, and that you'll have some falls along the way in your chosen life.The world divides people into three lots, the noble's lot is to rule, the priests'  listen to the gods and tell everyone how to live, whilst the commoners are born just to toil and suffer.Brante takes an unusual position in that he's born to a noble father and a commoner mother. Thus, he has the opportunity to evolve his life into each of the three lots, and that's essentially how the story goes. You take control of Brante literally from birth, making choices and watching as he grows into a toddler, to a youth and eventually an adult. Each choice tends to raise certain attributes, and the sum of your childhood attributes combine into your adulthood skills.You can endeavour to strive to become a noble, remain a commoner or become a holy man, and each potential path offers a unique storyline within it once you unlock that path. There are multiple ways for each path to resolve, you could become a noble driven by a sense of duty, or become a tyrant, rich on corruption and focused only on advancing your career. Similar choices and paths exist throughout for the priest and the commoner routes, and it is only when you play all three routes and their variations do you get to see how neatly the pieces on the board fit and how the story manages to progress with or without each type of Brante existing.Overall, the game is simplistic, but that's fine, we're here primarily for story and characterisation, and this has both in spades. These games, CYOA games are by no means easy to produce, the effort and planning required to get lengthy and consistent storylines is quite a challenge, and I'm happy to say that I think here, they managed to get the balance just right.A solid recommendation to anyone who likes Choose your own adventure games, or offshoots of the visual novel genre.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: It has a couple troubles. Definitely not historical in any way, very low fantasy and grimdark to the point that I couldn't take some characters seriously or consider doing some paths outside of just seeing what happens / getting the achievements.Still, there's something interesting here. The writing can be fun, the characters that aren't made out of cardboard are generally cool to interact, and the mechanic of building yourself is generally fun too. I can see these devs making something much better in the future with this solid base.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: This game offers an exceptional experience. Overall, on the surface, it might seem minimalistic in appearance and gameplay, but there is so much depth to it, it's quite difficult to describe. The visuals and art entirely justify the overall setting the game is trying to achieve, which in my opinion is the time of turmoil of the Holy Roman Empire - civil war, theological schism, new military tactics, new ideas for governship and civil rights in circulation, the lead-up to the Defenestration of Prague, the War in the Spanish Netherlands and the foundation of the Dutch Republic, and so on - but all in a believable and original fantasy setting with its own world, lore, and feeling. The story and narrative is indeed rich and well thought-out, leaving one sincerely and emotionally invested in characters and events. The game will force you to make difficult decisions, and I found myself almost abandoning it two-thirds in, leaving me split between loving it and hating it. However, with a little more thought and persistence (which the game entirely justifies and earns), one can manage on forward to a satisfying conclusion. Overall, highly recommended to anyone who appreciates narrative rich games and difficult decision making.P.S. - at the time I wrote this review, I only have a single playthrough of the game - disregarding deaths and restarting, for there was one path I aimed to follow. However, it is quite evident, that the replayability value is very high, and I am looking forward to seeing how else the story could develope.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: The game is an fantastic rpg, with lots of interesting pathways and endings for the player to go through. I highly recommend deactivating the ability to see the consequences for your actions, as it makes the experience more immersive. The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante reminds me very much of the times in Europe during the Protestant Reformation, even if the game is entirely fictional, and really made me feel like a person of that time felt: Unsure about what is true in the world, when the highest authority for the last several centuries falls apart from the inside and revolt with the status quo loses all restraint. In a world where God really exists without doubt, but people don't know how exactly their deity must be worshipped. I embraced this question in my playthrough, becoming a priest to satisfy my doubt, and talking to different priests and sects to uncover the truth. When I died, as it is inevitable, I found out if I was right or wrong in my assumptions of what is the divine will, and the answer was, in my opinion, one of the greatest twists in the history of video games. I can't recommend this game enough. The only bad thing about it is that it starts a little too slowly and with too much system-exposition
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante is overall a good game but it missed the chance of being a great game by making some weird design choices. All this game needed was a disco-elysium-like skill check system. Instead, they chose to chapter-lock some skills and this concscious choice greatly impacted overall game experience. I am well aware that they took  a "you should own your choices" approach but in the end, this approach forced me to take so many out-of-character routes it was frustrating. But I can say this happily that the people at Sever are great storytellers who have a knack for a possibly-great RPG game(s). If given necessary funds, I am pretty sure they could be next RPG powerhouse. If you wanna read and be a part of a good fantasy novel give this game a chance. You won't regret it. And to Sever, I would love to see you doing a classic RPG game. You had my curiousity, now you gotta have my attention.

_childDocuments_.review: I will concur with other negative reviews that this game has an extremely major flaw - its over-reliance of stats and mechanics that in end hobbles the player's ability to truly role-play. It is really disappointing too as the game has so much potential, but after 3 hours I start to realize that I was no longer playing the way I want to, but instead was being very conscious of "gaming" the system, and that honestly is not fun when you are way too conscious of the mechanics behind the game rather than "playing" it. And all this is because the game does not allow me to make the decisions I want to, like not being able to save Sophia just because I was too "tired" (from what??) due to my previous choices. After trying to play and couple of times with different decision paths, I realize I was just not empowered by the choices given to me, and ultimately I started becoming disinterested and not invested enough to see any of them through.  Excellent games of similar nature like Roadwarden and Disco Elysium do a fantastic job in making the mechanics serve the story, rather than the other way round. I just wish that this game did the same for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, so I haven't finished the game and have just reached the next stage in my life in the game, but I know a bit about the start to say if it can get you hooked or not. I am going to go through some possible spoilers, so if you don't want them, do not read on.This game is NOT AN OPEN WORLD RPG OR OPEN CHOICE GAME. You are on a set path towards a set place in the character's life. You are not playing YOUR character, your are playing as Sir Brante. You can name him whatever you want like 'Sir Jet Brante' or something, but it's not like you are controlling everything in his life. It's a choose your own adventure with set choices. Sometimes, choices are locked behind stats you have to have. In your childhood, your stats are just three things, willpower, insight and I forget the other one (basically strength.) These stats change based on what you do in the story. If you kind of take an easy route, you will get some willpower. If you choose something a bit harder, you might get strength and same goes for insight. The story so far is pretty good. It has an interesting world, story, art, etc. but it isn't anything flashy or in your face beautiful. You don't have a lot of color, mostly black and white with grey. There really aren't any bad things to the game glitch wise, maybe a slight spelling mistake here or there, but a pretty solid running game (but if you expected more from a game about reading and some still art, you might need to reevaluate your graphic decisions xD.) It is a game about goods and bads. Should I do this which might hurt my willpower, but maybe give me something special in my timeline, or take an easier road and get the stat boost or willpower up? Now some choices are locked behind stats, so don't think it is always a good idea to be full on min/maxing in this game. Sometimes you might see a choice that might have given you a nice benefit or something, but you can't get it because you don't have that specific stat. There really isn't much else to say. Nothing really bad, but nothing really that pops out aside from the unique art, story and the world itself in the game. I would say if you like a game where reading and choice making is a high priority, but it is still on rails, this is a game for you. If you are more of the fan of choosing your own destiny from square one, do not buy this game. This is not YOUR story, this is Sir Brante's story. Keep that in mind when looking at this game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't expecting as much as I got from this game. Rich lore and characters weave a moving and convincing narrative. _childDocuments_.review: Life and suffering of Sir Brante is a bit difficult to review for me. It is entirely text based game with some rpg elements set in a wonderfully realized medieval world. It is one of the few games where choices you make actually do matter which is, interestingly, both its biggest strenght and weakness.PROS:- presentation is beautiful. You, as Brante, are flipping through the pages of the book chronicling your life. Book is wonderfully illustrated with black and white drawings that truly bring the story thats being told to life. Soundtrack fits the setting and story perfectly. Entire presentation is top notch-world/story/lore You are living life as Brante from his birth to its end. There are 3 main paths you can take that change the middle of the story drastically. These paths further diverge into more possible paths making what feels like endless options for you to take. Story focuses on themes of class, politics, family and religion and is very reminiscent of Game of Thrones. Penultimate chapter of the game is the longest, most intriguing and its probably at this point your Brante's fate will be decided. -replayabilityFirst playthrough, if you read everything, should take you 8-10 hours which is decent but there are so many different paths you can take it seems impossible to experience the exact same playthrough twice. Once you start skiping familiar text playthroughs can be done in about an hour, maybe less.BOTH PRO AND CON-gameplayIts a choice based visual novel. There isnt much you can do differently with these types of games. It does have light rpg elements, though, in form of various skills. These skills start developing during Brante's childhood and then morph into new skills as he grows up. Skills are tightly connected with your choices as you need to pass various skill checks to make a choice. I like this system but its also the game's biggest problem. Some skill checks become so rigid near the end of the game that you need to be pitch perfect and plan a lot in advance just so you can make a choice that you want to make. Even slightest mistep that doesnt seem all that important can derail you into oblivion. It all comes to end in an extremely dissapointing and rushed last chapter where you are forced into one of two main paths regardless of what you did before. Its not Mass Effect 3 level of dissapointing but still...I found this extremely annoying and it made me not want to do more playthroughs.CONS:- as I mentioned above, extremely tough late game skill checks and restrictive last chapter- some choice based incosistencies. For example..character that ends up in one situation after a choice is made is in entirely different position in his next scene. It seems like devs didnt make a story point for situation like that which is understandable due to insane amount of diverging and mutually exclusive choices. Still, its very immersion breaking.Overall, I think this is a really good game. I thought it was incredible during first 2-3 playthroughs but then flaws in the design started to become more and more apparent. Still, I would recommend anyone who likes stuff like Game of Thrones or Witcher to play through this game at least a couple of times.

_childDocuments_.review: I was really looking forward to this game.  I put it on my wishlist and considered playing it for months, but I wanted to make sure I had ample time to play regularly as I knew that it was likely not the kind of game you can put down and then come back to after weeks of inactivity.  Disappointing. This is essentially like one of those free-to-play mobile app games.  It has a nicer interface, is longer, and perhaps better developed, but it also failed to live up to any potential.  Early game I felt like I was in control of my choices, and I was really creating the type of character that I wanted to role-play.  The later chapters, however, all real choice is taken away from you. The game essentially boils down to a scenario that you read, and then a single choice you can make at the end of that scenario.  Rinse and repeat, from one chapter to another.  As you progress in chapters, you meet new people, gain access to new stats that can rise or fall, and develop various relationships.  All of this seems fine and good on the surface.  But none of it really matters at the end, where the game becomes a frustrating series of clicking the only option available to you.  And I thought that I was developing the necessary skills to succeed in the game.  Not that you get much of a chance to do so, your skills rising and falling based on the choices you make and only the choices you make.  It seemed to me that I was always 1 point too low to choose the option I wanted.  I'd raise the skills, and then I'd still be 1 point too low.  It was very limiting, where at the beginning of the game you could choose between 4 different outcomes for every scenario, and at the end of the game 3 of the 4 choices are locked and you're forced to do something that seems incredibly out of character. But it goes further.  There were times when the plot of the game wouldn't make sense.  At one point I made the choice to "lock up" my best friend so he was out of reach of his enemies, and just a few scenario choices later he's on the streets being chased by those exact same enemies that I was trying to protect him from, forcing me to make the single choice to help him which, despite having developed my combat skills, resulted in a lesser death.  All 3 of my lesser deaths occurred in such quick succession without any real ability to prevent them, at least from the point of view of the player.And it seems like such a simple thing to fix.  Instead of completely locking choices, make every choice available and subject to some RNG outcome modified by the relevant skills.  Give us that role-playing aspect to the game so our characters can at least attempt to do the things that we expect them to do.  The last 3 hours or so of my gameplay was basically suffering, and the last few scenarios I just clicked my way through skimming the text because I knew it didn't matter and that I was already locked into a certain ending.And you have to mention the blatant typos and grammar mistakes in the game.  For a game that is 100% text based, you have to make sure you proofread.  Even a single mistake is too much, and I noticed half a dozen.I am left with bitterness, and a resentfulness for having spent money on this game.  I would have been better served by downloading free CYOA games from the App Store.

_childDocuments_.review: Prepare to cry when you hide the consequences (optional but i recommend it) of your actions for I certainly did thinking what I was doing was "right" when really I felt horrible. For in one society beforehand this was a norm it really makes you question  on an individual perspective of change and tradition. I am just lucky enough to not be born in a time where this type of world was just reasonable. The only differences is that its a very fictional rendition since well you can't die a certain amount of times in real life or even see the wisdom of higher beings which really just cemented my feeling of despair in this game. Initially I got the reign of terror ending and I did meet an old man whom asked me a question if I were a higher being how would I treat the world and its people, would I care? would I free everyone? leave it as it is or the other options this brought me to tears for I thought I was doing was "right" but I ended up destroying and killing everyone on my first run.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, what a beautifully drawn, pleasantly scored, rich in detail, engaging story! I have not reached the end of my (first) journey yet, but regardless of the outcome it is already very, very memorable.I heartily recommend the game, with only one caveat, reinforced in an upfront manner by the game itself: the setting is somewhat grimdark, and it is a not a place of heroes. What this means is that if setbacks or shortcomings will upset you, this game will probably be very frustrating. You probably cannot win at life. If, on the other hand, you want to try your best at some interpretation of who Sir Brante is and see where that will take him, then the continuous twists and turns and juggling of hard choices are very rewarding. A nice touch is that the game has a few levels of disclosure that may help min-max the consequences of your choices... but personally I am playing blind and iron man, and that is working great for me. I'm acting according to a few character priorities, and while it is obviously impossible to succeed at everything (or even most things), so far I have been able to guide all story developments that I consistently cared about in a positive direction. So by no means min-maxing is necessary to avoid frustration. Just enjoy the ride. Not only I am enjoying it, but I can already tell the branching paths are diverse enough to warrant significant replayability for other Sir Brantes that I can imagine...
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: is a text heavy & choice focused visual novel/ RPG. The player takes on the role of Sir Brante making his way in life while choosing 3 main paths each having their branching choices (Path of the Lotless, Nobleman or Priest). The story is set in the middle ages and the game makes a really good job in making the player understand right off the bat that the world is cruel, unfair and more often than not you'll have to make sacrifices in order to progress. You cannot make everyone happy or save everyone. There's tension in the society within the different classes, the nobles believe that each class should not step out of the boundaries of what they are supposed to do, if you're born a noble (or get the mantle through great effort) then you're meant to rule over everyone else, if you're born lotless then you're meant to hold your head down, listen to the nobles and do physical work. On the other hand the common people are sick of the poor treatment that they're receiving from the nobles, conflicts and revolts are brewing. The inked artstyle does a good job with conveying the game's story. The whole choosing aspect of the system is quite flawed. You need willpower AND certain stats to be able to make any important choices. Because of it you lock yourself out of certain decisions even when it doesn't make sense in all of the situations. Now you can leave on the notes that will tell you what consequence the choices are going to have and what stats you need for them or you can turn them off for the real "suffering" experience especially for the very first playthrough. As a timeline Sir Brante's life story also goes from infancy to early adulthood years but after that no matter what happens at the end of the game, the rest of his life is not shown anymore. Other than that the freedom to make your character focused on certain values is still there. Is your Sir Brante going to perpetuate the noble caste corrupted habits, is he going to fight for the good of the common people or is he going to align with other values entirely ? You decide. Good at a sale or if you got it in a bundle.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: I'm really impressed by this game a lot. Excellent writing and presentation and it seems like the choices will offer replay value. The small amounts of voice over narration at some moments aren't amazing but they are rare and not a big detraction really. If you enjoy story heavy games or choose your own adventure style games this is the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Total leftist propaganda. You can tell that the story is written by fedora-tipping atheists and fat women with dyed hair who are mad their moms made them go to church or something.The first 2 hours of the game tries as hard as possible to tell you that societal hierarchy is immoral, and that if you value or follow it, then you're basically a bootlicker. The writers barely even try to show the value of the Lots (social classes) or show the Old Faith (Catholicism) in a good light at all. All the conservative characters are portrayed as needlessly cruel just for the sake of it, while the lower classes and liberal characters can only be victims. The game tries as hard as it can to make the right wing faction and system as unsympathetic as possible.And to top it all off: You can't side with the Old Faith (the right wing faction) unless you pass a skill check, whereas to side with the liberals you don't need to pass anything. This shows it's the path the game WANTS you to take. Choices should never be behind a skill check.Very disappointed by how unintelligent this actually is beneath the fancy writing and nice art.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: Masterfully crafted game. ignore my "time played", it's many hours higher. i did 3 full playthroughs, most was offline. each of the three main paths you can take are significantly different and worth an additional playthrough, which is kind of the whole point of choice-based games, that not only is THAT choice different but all that happens to you and what choices come before you afterwards as a result of it is different. i only got the ending i was aiming for in my third playthrough, but i still loved the others. you try to push for the outcome you want, and it is attainable, but it's difficult, and you don't have complete control over how your actions will affect the people around you. as an example, First play, I became a judge and pushed for peaceful reformation. It's hard to tow that middle line and my pro-reform decisions led to a bloody, horrible revolt. That feels realistic, because to a large extent, YOU contribute to the outcome, I did encourage the people to push for change. even if you don't get the outcome you were striving towards. The "ideal" outcome is attainable though, even if you aim for the middle ground (hardest target). It's got an immersive world and a good soundtrack, good for any game but imperative for one without "play" mechanics (choices only).
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: Told my partner I've been playing a "choose your own adventure book game" for the past 3 days. The world-building in this game is compelling and brutal. Making a positive impact is hard and you'll likely have to sacrifice a lot for it. I ended up going back and replaying the game from various checkpoints each time I met my final end, making different choices until I felt I'd 'beat' the game. There's still a whole story branch I didn't go down (priest), and another that I messed up and died halfway through (conspirator). So I've really only seen half of what the story has to offer.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most frustrating visual novel type games I have ever played.The writing and world are fairly interesting, although you'll often feel like the game stuffs way too many actions and implications into singular choices, and even with consequences visible it's not always clear what the actual ramifications will be, how you actually achieve the goal you selected.But the way the game handles choices and certain mechanics is often rage inducing. You'll be the one suffering here, not your character.Frequently you'll be presented with choices that often feel gated behind some really arbitrary requirements. You really don't have *any* chance of getting a decent outcome for a lot of decisions without meta-game knowledge or a guide, and the game happily taunts you by giving you a list of greyed out options and your singular choice which might as well just be a big ♥♥♥♥ you sign. Relationship with a character a point too low? Sorry, your only option is death. Often the ways to actually achieve the conditions required to choose some very sensible, logical outcomes are contradictory, and some I'm not even sure how you'd achieve without doing a 180 face-turn of your character for no reason.SpoilersMy first two playthroughs of the game were as a priest. This path is the only one where you have access to literal divine miracles through the twins. You never actually get to employ these as an option at any point in the game - for example, you are more than capable of healing severe wounds with this. At one point toward the end of the game, your mother is dying of illness. You can -literally- talk her better, but you can't call upon your divine power to just heal her.This all comes to a head in the final chapter, the big revolution. This is clearly intended to be the payoff for the character you have built and the choices you have made, but it just ends up making the meat of the game into a lame exercise in optimising your stats and choices just so you can unlock the option to not stab yourself in the face because you didn't make enough sneaky plans earlier.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible game until you want to get a great ending, then the difficulty is punishing and you won't know whether one or two of your 40 choices were correct enough or you'll find out you have to betray someone or yourself because you are one point shy.  Restarting chapters is an illusion of choice because (to this games credit) the games depth is immense that trying to fix a one point error opens up 3 other problems that you can then try again and see if you can rebalance.Suckering people in with the first 2 chapters free was brilliant.  I loved my first 3 games with the 3 paths until I figured out that your choices are an illusion if you want the story to play out in good ways.Very cautiously checking any future games from you. A shame.  Had I been able to get the best ending on my 4th try with 3 chapter restarts, this would have been a FULL recommend.  Shame there was no way to get the best ending and find that out instead of wasting time to resuscitate a corpse.Either lower the point threshold or give us a tracker that tells us how many points remain to get and a warning that this is your last chance to gain a point if you want to reach the best ending.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: After playing the demo, I was hooked but didn't want to buy the game at full price. So instead I went on a long excursion to find a visual novel that would satisfy me with it's storytelling. A few titles later being half played, none sufficed. Still being a penny pincher, I went further instead to binge reading several hugo award winning books to fill that void. A week or two passed, good times I may add. A game discount aggregator notified me that this game was on sale, to which I immediately purchased. So here is my experience with the game.It exceeded many of the popular Japanese visual novels with it's deep world building, decent writing on par with fantasy novels. The games of this genre typically have a focus on a dating aspect requiring choosing between different heroines to romance. In this game, romanticism is there but only there marginally. The world is socially divided between three groups, the nobles, priests, and peasants. The peasants suffer deeply having no rights, close to being slaves. Due to the brutal narrative of the game many may be turned off with some of the horrific events.The game design is similar to the Choice of Games series on the android and ios platforms. There are many choices to make which decides the path of plot to take. In this game, added stat values creates an increased complexity. Many choices and events require a stat threshold making actions have weight and importance. This function gives it a RPG feeling rather than a "choose your adventure" novel.My first playthrough pointed me the way of the faith, eventually becoming a priest. I wholeheartedly followed the rules my social status called the "Lot" sometimes making me cross the line I wouldn't have crossed in general. After one mistake of a seemly insignificant but major choice, was forced to become exceptionally brutal which caused me to face my true death (I died) before the final Act begun. I did get a good ending on my next playthrough. There were plenty of poor reviews suggesting that the game was flawed and every choice was bad towards the end. I didn't have the same experience but I understand how they got that ending. Once you understand what this game is about, I have no doubt you'll reach a good ending every time. I recommend this game for gamers who don't like to read, but love stories. Hopefully, you'll start picking a reading habit like me.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: Largely a well written story in an interesting world with great characters. Why largely? Because Sophia exists and she really just shouldn't. Depending on how you play, her arc sort of works, or it just doesn't at all. But she is a fixed component of every story and is one of only a few characters, for which this is true. Out of them she is by far the worst written and least fitting in many of them. She's somewhere between demagogue  and mouthpiece of the people in the literary sense and these two functions constantly clash, as she sometimes acts as an independent character and sometimes as a literary device.All this leaves me wondering why she exists. The people didn't really need a face, they are more interesting faceless, and as sort of lancer to the protagonist, she's drawing far more attention than any other character. Not a single other character comes close in terms of how important they are, in fact she is in many ways far more integral to the world than the protagonist is and while a protagonist (especially a heroic one) gets a sort of free pass at this in video games and stories at large, side characters really don't.The only guess i have as to why she does exist, is her being a remnant of a planned, but never implemented second main character acting as his mirror.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: This is absolute hidden gem of narrative story rpg. Literally EVERY decision has matter, many options to choose. The title describes the game perfectly. Sir Brante's entire life is suffering for the protagonist and the player because of the choices you make and the world "you" must live.I planned to play more times but after my choices on the first playthrough, the game made me "game depressed" and at this moment  i can't play another time.In conclusion, if you want to be happy after playing a game, don't play this game. In other cases it's must have.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a role-playing game, really. It's a choose-your-own-adventure with a lot of overt stat-tracking so you can see the numerical consequences of your choices. The world-building is great, and the story points were all believable and compelling. I really enjoyed making choices about my character, his family, his position in society, and how he used his influence to steer events. I'm going to replay it to make very different choices.The game has a serious flaw in the last act, where a number of choices are hard-gated due to stats and prior choices. It makes sense that some choices would be more difficult, or even cut off to you given the choices you made previously. But some of the gating logic doesn't make a lot of sense. There were also critical junctions where the choice I would want to make wasn't even an option under any circumstances. This is probably inevitable, since they can only cover so many options. But I would have liked to see a better job of considering all the options at the critical last act. It felt a little too constrained. Still well worth playing.

Taking a break, but I will likely play again, possibly multiple times, just to see the possible alternate choices I can make.  Very engaging story. Even the sadder or more upsetting moments contributed overall.

_childDocuments_.review: I do recommend this, but with a caveat. It feels much more like a puzzle game rather than a choose your own adventure game. My first playthrough (Noble/Judge) I did the typical choose your own adventure style. Especially when it came to the Peace Time chapters I fell into a very railroaded experience where a lot of my choices were limited due to having 2 skills nearly maxed (I have a pretty solid pattern to what I was deciding) but also having those skills maxed didn't do anything for me either. My second playthrough of the Noble/Judge line, knowing how the mechanics worked, it felt much more like a puzzle game, balancing skills and choices not by if I'd really do them, but because I wanted to store that willpower, instead of max skills build up all the skills pretty evenly, and make sure I wasn't doing anything absolutely devastating to my character. I don't think at all in my two playthroughs I ever had any options that required or were changed due to a skill being maxed, so it seemed better to keep them all around that 10-14 range and build them up evenly while using willpower when needed. This ended up in me having a lot more narrative options and a "better" ending. The problem was, I had more options open, but to keep those options going I had to usually pick something I didn't want to do because it buffed my skill I needed to build up more instead of something cooler for the story. This doesn't make it not fun though. I enjoyed the style and story, I do like how some things are punishing and you have some hard decisions to make, I just wish there was more change or reward for maxing a certain skill out, instead my first playthrough while fun and very involving with the story, by the end of it I was in multiple areas where I only had 1 option to pick and it snowballs into okay because I couldn't pick that option and get that destiny then this next one I'm stuck with just this option, and it spirals a bit. It was just as fun going back and trying to build the "perfect" character to get a better ending. So I do recommend it, it is fun, the story is good, I plan on plaything the other paths too and even if they aren't as good I got good fun out of the noble/judge line, I just thing it's really more of a puzzle game trying to make the right character balance and such rather than a choose your own adventure, because if you go for the more roleplay experience you'll find yourself really railroaded into certain options. Hopefully some of this is addressed later on, maybe with some more special options if you have certain skills maxed or like an outcome might be changed (ie. if you suffer a lesser death in a duel with a 12 valor, then maybe with a maxed 20 valor you get beaten up but don't take the lesser death) because currently maxing things out just really doesn't do anything for you.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't believe there aren't more games like these. I admit, I am a sucker for story based games so this little review might be biased. At first I thought it was gonna be a quick experience, maybe 1 replay and that's it, but I got hooked. Hard. And having finished it 4 times already I want to share my views on it, because honestly this games deserves it. The first impressions one might have regarding this game is that is more of the same but that couldn't be further away from the truth. The first thing that stands out for me is the universe itself and the way the world-building is presented and complemented by the gorgeous art style. It's not through codex entries or long diaries, but rather through the interactions with other characters and the world itself. Sure the story might not answer all the questions it presents or that the player might ask themselves  , but the answers were sufficient. In fact one could also argue that, that same lack of answers helps deepen this worlds appeal. Another aspect of the story and plot itself is that you are not "the chosen one" or anything like that, the world does not revolve around you. Political plots and cultural rejection might fester in the background of your story but you only see their effects and are not deeply involved in them. The choice making aspect is also something to praise, as it does the best it can to track all of your choices and motivations, and it does so to a surprising and effective extent. It's not perfect though, as it sometimes the game poorly justifies the presence of some characters in scenes when they shouldn't be making previous efforts feel useless. But at this point I think I'm just nitpicking. Overall I fell in love with the world the developers have crafted. They seemed to have put a lot of passion into it and it really shows. I'm just sad that I now have to look for another game to obsess over...
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: Despite the elaborate plot, I found that no matter what you do, you are always extremely limited in the options of progressing into a successful path to the end of the game, and I never ended up getting there. _childDocuments_.review: I was too hyped compared to what the game offers. There are definitely some good points to the game. The art style is unique and the story is rich, the combination makes it very nice for a visual novel game. The first few hours of the game are great, the story builds up, you gain stats which then open up more of the story, choices matter, you are buildings up your own adventure.Then hours later, the choices started to vanish, I went for max theology and eloquence with some diplomacy and manipulation, I thought I'd make a great Inquisitor, so an Inquisitor I became, my theology was so high that it was marked as "prophet" yet my brother Nathan becomes the prophet. I raise inquisition to the maximum level and somehow, the options vanish. My only options are to do nothing, and only watch, I am an prophet Inquisitor, defender of the Empire, and all I can do is watch as events unfold. I obtained great power from the Twins to heal and attack my enemies with my will, yet my only option is to accept my death.OK. I accept my death, and go on to meet the twins, The most lackluster of endings ever. The twins ask me questions which I answer truthfully, then the time for judgement is here, and I receive no judgement, I vanish, I am no-more. I am now the twins and I need to pass judgement on the Inquisitor before me, on whether he will go to the bottom or the top of the Spire.TL:DR Has some replay value, good story building, lackluster ending. Overall, it was unsatisfying.

_childDocuments_.review: Ah, The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante — a game that promises you a rich, medieval narrative experience and delivers... well, mostly suffering. If you’ve ever wanted to experience what it feels like to make morally agonizing choices, get emotionally attached to characters, only to see them crushed by the weight of fate, then this game will have you saying, "Wow, I didn't think life could be this depressing!"You start as Sir Brante, a poor soul who never had a say in his own destiny. First of all, the game makes you feel like the least important Brante in the Brante family, where even your grandma’s knitting seems more consequential than your existence. From childhood, every decision matters — but spoiler alert: most of them matter in the sense that they’ll haunt you forever, no matter what you do.Remember that time you tried to make a friend in the playground? Yeah, turns out they betray you later. Or when you thought your choices could prevent your brother from becoming a hot-headed lunatic? Surprise! You were wrong. In fact, you’ll learn very quickly that the true moral of this story is that no matter how hard you try, life will constantly find new and creative ways to kick you down.But the real charm of The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante is how it makes the Renaissance era feel like a very, very bad day on loop. You think you're making progress, climbing the societal ladder, getting close to fulfilling your grand purpose, but then the game decides, “Nope! Here’s a plague, a political coup, and a personal betrayal all at once. Good luck!”The graphics and sound design are beautiful, of course, because there’s nothing quite like somber music and detailed parchment-style art to remind you of the futility of life. But don’t let the pretty art fool you — behind those lovely visuals lies a relentless barrage of existential dread.In conclusion, The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante is an amazing game for anyone who enjoys making impossible choices, feeling miserable about them, and questioning whether or not they've just wasted hours of their life on a character whose only guarantee is more suffering. 10/10 would recommend for a rainy day when you feel like embracing your inner medieval philosopher.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: If you don't mind doing a lot of reading, this is a cool story set in an interesting backdrop that will force you to decide whose life you're living this for. My recommendation is turn off the stat-related outcomes and the ability to go back and just play this game through your first few times, and experience the regret of bad choices. It's the kind of game that makes you think about more than just the game in front of you.

_childDocuments_.review: DO NOT BUY IF YOU WANT TO MAKE YOUR OWN CHOICES IN A GAME!!!Here's why:- no matter what you pick (i went with being a lawyer and becoming a noble, went fine for the first two/thirds of the story, then the 2nd to last stage comes before the end and it just all falls apart....- if you pick to your moral compass, you will end up not finishing the game because of how much it limits you based on "trait points"- missing out on all trait points from every chapter severely limits you, except for 2 or 3 choices (that I have seen) which save your job but do nothing else. If you do not get your traits high enough in your childhood and teenage years you are pretty much done for if you want the freedom to make choices.for example: You are given a chance to do 3 things about a certain secret organization which you may or may not want to save from being discovered. You can either:A - give up their location and arrest everyone B - not give up their location but risk losing your job and getting the members killedC - not give up their location but try to convince their leader (who you may like) to leave and disband the illegal society to save themIf you do like their leader (which most people do), you would pick C which is best for you and the society, but if one of your stats isn't high enough, you can't even try!!! this and many other scenarios frustrate me to the point of no end, which is why you should not play this game and go play the many wonderful "choice of" games which are way better in freedom of actual choices.or just go outsidegame is 1/5 stars

_childDocuments_.review: I had this game on my wishlist for a really long time before pulling the trigger.  I am not sure what pushed me over the edge but I am glad I finally bought this game.  Then it sat in my library for months until I finally had a reason to try it out.While the system design of this game is pretty straight forward (it's all stat and faction based) the storytelling is what sets it apart.  If you play the game just chasing Stats and Factions at the expense of the story I think you'll have less fun.  However, even doing that can lead to an interesting and entangled narrative.  The complex story forces you to make decisions which echo throughout the rest of the game.  And sometimes the decisions are difficult.  I willingly went to my final death with the hope I did so to make the world a better place.The presentation and graphics are rough, as you can see, but once you get taken away by the story and the relationships it hardly matters.  I would have like to have had better UI and UX, there was a lot of loading a new splash page rather than just keeping to flipping through the book.  These were supposed to have been times to punctuate the story with important exposition, but I found that throwing up a new screen got pretty annoying.  I think it would have worked just fine as a double page spread in the book UI.I was totally engrossed in the narrative that the time passed very quickly.  I am not sure I'll be ready to play the game again any time soon, it definitely takes an emotional toll, but even one playthrough was worthwhile.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a roughly 10-12 hour per run game with beyond excellent writing and storytelling, for once actually meaning- AND impactful decisions, then this game is precisely what you should play!There are three main paths through the eponymous Life of Sir Brante, and within each of those three paths are people you will meet, maybe fall in love with, maybe learn to despise from the bottom of your heart, or maybe simply don't understand at all... and the game will force you to constantly make decisions without telling you what the results will be, but you can rest assured that sooner or later, you are going to find out.More often than not: the hard way.I cannot say this too often:The writing is phenomenally great, the way the story is presented, the characters are brought to life, it draws you into a deeply immersive world quite like an actual, real book would.Precisely because the visuals so closely resemble a "Choose your own adventure" book, the "reader" is left to apply their own phantasy to fill out the scene *precisely* as *they* think it would, or maybe even: should appear.This is helped in no small way by the outstanding sound design, so that this game actually manages something quite outstanding in its own right: to bring together the best of both audio- and real books.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: [TL/DR version: Mostly great picturebook-style game which i cannot fully recommend because of the way the ending is presented.]At its core, The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante plays like a visual novel: you read some really well-written text about the tribulations of the game's namesake character in a dark medieval world of absolute rule, stratified society and unrelenting gods. You gasp at the amazing black-and-white illustrations and listen to a rather fitting soundtrack, both made to help immerse you into the story, and they do it swimmingly. The only caveat - every decision you select during your playthrough will change some of your character's numerous stats or opinions of other characters, with some decisions being unavailable  if a particular stat is not high enough. And this caveat greatly emphasize the choices you make during the game and making your first playthrough more "dynamic" - you will often take not the option you thing is the absolute best, but selecting an option you CAN select, as many would be stat-locked. No matter which decisions you make, they will ultimately affect the game's world: would act honorably and miss profitable opportunities, or will you take every bribe you can get and make your family wealthy? Would you push the church towards religious reforms, or keep true to the cruel ancient traditions? Will you try to keep your family together, or use the conflicts between family members for your own objectives? The possibilities are numerous and generally feel pretty organic.But even if all of the above does sound amazing, there is still a rather big problem with this game, and it is its Ending. Basically, on the final in-game day, you will be presented 5-6 options, and the one you select determines the ending you get, each option having steep stat requirements, so you will have only 1-2 options unlocked at any given playthrough.And that would be perfectly fine, however, it felt like only 1 of those options leads to a "good" ending, the rest either making you feel like an absolute jerk even if you tried to roleplay an absolute jerk before, or just being a watered-down "good" ending. This heavily devalues the player's choice, as it basically implies there is a single "correct" way to play the game if you want to "clear" it and reach the only good ending. It also feels like the developers trying to push their own set of morals to the player, which does feel really unnecessary for a game dealing with such controversial topics like politics and religion.So, do i recommend this game? If a possibility of the game pushing the "correct" set of morals to you doesn't seem like a big deal, then i do, by all means, recommend it, as its production value is extremely high.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: One of the greatest stories i'v ever seen. I am a big fan of classic and dark fantasy books and this game(actually a visual novell) made its place among the best of them. Huge thanks to the developers who'v made this excellent experience avaliable for us. The thing i want after 2 complete Sir Brante stories - next game in this beautifull universe.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: This game did something no other game has done. . Starting the game as a child my goal was to become a noble like my father, and make the family proud to have me as a Brante. Much how real life tends to go, my plans changed. I didn't meet the requirements to ennoble myself, I was doomed to be a commoner from the start. The new development led me down a path I never imagined taking when I started the game, and it did it time and time again as things changed and priorities shifted. No other game has made me change the course I had set for myself. In, "The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante," you are simultaneously the master of your own fate and a victim of fate, an experience any fan of Text Based Games will adore.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: This is a negative review because Steam enforces an either/or-decision while I would like to give an as-well-as-rating.(+) Positives: I like this kind of interactive story-telling, even if it consists in plain text. The story is a nice plot of a historical novel with some fantasy elements, roughly modelled after Europe's Reformation epoch. The underlying »engine« of class struggle, elite factions, and religious schism seems well thought-out to me. Biography is well tailored into the development of historical events (a plausible micro-macro connection is most important for me, because this literally gives meaning to life), allowing for a broad choice of individual career, and conflicts do not feel arbitrary.(-) Negatives: I don't like it when the developers' sense of plausibility suddenly kicks me out of options because somewhere and somehow I missed a point which later proves to be a mandatory prerequisite for continuation. Of course I can't expect to freely switch between the Path of the Commoner and the Path of the Noble. But running into a choice between death, death, and death which subjectively comes out of the blue because all alternative choices are barred, is not really satisfactory. I'm expected to swallow this because in-game, I cannot argue with fate and fortune, but as a player I know that there's a developer behind fortune which I expect to be reasonable.Unfortunately, I am not the type of player happily going back to change preceding decisions, especially when I do not see my point-of-failure, which might lay way in the past. So replay value for me is limited, unless I want to try out an entirely other path. Maybe that here I've fallen into the trap of moral over-identification with a specific conduct of life.I got the game with a discount, so I will not complain about the price. And I'm still going to come back for another game, hoping that disappointment doesn't run in development studios.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: This game has *really* sucked me in. I'm not sure if the story itself is the most compelling, or the game design with meaningful choices. For most of the important moments in the character's life, the game will show you 3-5 choices you *could* take, but you may only be able to take 1-2 either because of past choices you made, the stats your past choices have put you at, or the amount of willpower you have currently.This is not a happy game, but it's a weighty game. You might be able to get good endings for your family, but not for your city - or vice versa. Or perhaps you can accomplish your goals for both, but only by dying in the effort.The story and the writing are very good (although it is translated to English, and there are a few minor errors). You're the son of a medieval noble and a low-born woman in a fictional world that effectively has a caste system, and two gods who you're told will send you to this world's version of hell if you don't follow the lot you were born into.The choices you're presented with often just have bad outcomes, like you'd expect from life in this world, so sometimes you have to think hard about which choice will be the least terrible - but there are bright moments in the game as well.Ultimately, your choices will shape your own destiny, your family's, and the empire itself. I can't imagine how this game could be more "choices matter", so if that tag sounds appealing, pick it up.

_childDocuments_.review: The ideia behind this indie game by a Russian developer is great: a mixture of CYOA visual novel and RPG. As the story develops, you gain (or lose) stats that may allow better choices for your character. I hope more games like this are released _ as long as they're greater than this one, because I have some qualms about it. The writing is not bad, but not wonderful either (I heard people saying that this was as well-written as "Disco Elysium", but unfortunately that's not true); there are some typos and mistakes, but nothing serious. The story is well structured, following the life of your character from birth to adulthood, in a setting that mixes religious fantasy (I know, all religions are fantasies, but bear with me) and a French-Revolution-like environment. There is a ficticious race called Arknians that oppresses humanity, and even humans are divided in castes (two classes of nobles and the lowborn); you will be lowborn at first, but with a chance of rising to nobility, depending on how you play. Also you'll have to choose from 3 different occupations when you grow up.From the start, the game tells you that you'll go through childhood to adulthood, with a revolt waiting to happen in the last chapter. Also, in each of the 5 chapters, the game reveals to you possible conclusions (I did my best to not look at them to not spoil myself). And, by default, the game warns you about the outcomes of your choices (I had to disable this in the settings; I also turn "Ironman Mode" on, because I didn't want to savescum). It'd have been better if the game were more mysterious about what's to come. In my case, my first ending (which happened after a little less than 24 hours of play) came abruptly at chapter 4, even though I still had 3 lives left (there are 4 in total). Although the destiny of my character wasn't nonsensical, it happened suddenly and without giving me any room for avoiding it, so it felt partially unfair. Besides, I thought that the final judgement by the Twins (this world's deities) would be more interesting _ in the end, you end up , and your answers  . Still, I was entertained by this story and all the conflicts it presented me. Beware that there's a lot of violence happening (but isn't that the case in most games?). I've got only 12% of the achievements in this playthrough, so obviously it's a game that demands to be replayed. I intend to do it, eventually, but even with more knowledge I suppose it won't be easy getting to the end.

_childDocuments_.review: This is where a simple Like/Dislike recommendation fails to fully articulate my feelings. I would say it's more apprehensive than outright negative, but what can you do.I found the writing and world building to all be of high quality, but the game's over-reliance of its mechanics and stats impacted the ability of roleplaying, a sentiment that I share with other reviews I have found. Spending years of my life working to build up my family's station, commit to the promise of equal law, while giving commoners/people of lower Lots a chance to have their rights represented in a fair manner all collapsed within just a few story beats. To have my choices suddenly not matter in the end felt as if the negative ending is indeed the only proper outcome of the game. The game poses really interesting questions of free-will, fate, and the power one person can have on their society, and all in a way that felt as if no one decision was incorrect. Then everything came crashing down around me; my maxed out Diplomacy apparently wasn't enough to save my family from falling apart to inner squabbling, or my years-planned court case to be destroyed the moment before the crucial turning point of the game. And from what I can tell, I don't know why everything went to hell in a hand basket so quickly.Perhaps those previous questions of fate did indeed have a concrete, intended answer by the devs; perhaps the negative outcome is the only real one. After this game is called the Life and SUFFERING of Sir Brante. Perhaps not being able to follow decisions I would've made in character simple because the game deemed I was not able to may well be the only true outcome. However, it feels as if I was purposely robbed of a satisfying ending, despite seemingly following a path with its own rewards and sacrifices. Perhaps I may try again and see if I can carve out a better ending than the one I was forced into, but right now I'm not so sure. I feel as if I would only struggle and, well, suffer, a new storyline I do not believe in only to receive the same outcome. Perhaps the only way for Sir Brante's suffering to truly end is to stop playing the game.TL:DR: A great premise with great writing, but railroads you into a dissatisfying ending where it feels your stats and choices throughout the game did not matter.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: Just, wow... I've never played a "game" like this in my life. To be honest, I don't care much for reading novels, but I hardly skipped over any words. The reason being: I felt like I was truly taking part in the unraveling of an awe-inspiring story.The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante first and foremost offers you meaningful characters, both of the Brante family, and many many others. You grow to like some characters, dislike some, and remain indifferent to others. This is directly corresponded in the game by different statuses, and is nearly always accurate. The fact that you can grow attached to these characters further makes you interested in the story plot... the plot where changes ACTUALLY DO MATTER (unlike many other games suggesting so). I couldn't tear myself away and finished a playthrough (though an early death) in a little over 8 hours. I'm not sure how replay-ability will be, given that the choices I made were my own and were true.... however, given the immense amount of potential plot twists, I could see giving it another go. And let me tell you, some of the choices you have to make feel very difficult, again, because the characters grow on you.In my opinion, The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante is a true masterpiece that will appeal to anyone with a heart, as it musters emotions that games rarely could. I can't speak highly enough of the development team, Sever, on creating this. I must assume it was truly a passion project. Thank you, Sever!

_childDocuments_.review: On what is currently my fifth or sixth playthrough, I can say with the utmost confidence that this game is well worth its expense and then some.You play as a young man of a minor noble house in a grim medieval fantasy setting, where the choices you make in the story, will have consequences that shape the world around you. In this game, you essentially have 3 main "career" paths -- Judge (Noble path), Priest (Priest path), and Lotless (Rebel path). From these choices, you have several options that will lead you down several interconnecting substories that add more detail to the general story, and the setting as a whole the more times you play and different paths you take.Be mindful of your choices, as what may seem good in the present, can become your downfall if not carefully thought out. Overall, I gives this game a very strong recommendation for anyone who likes story driven games with a lot of replayability.

_childDocuments_.review: Chapters 1 & 2 are possibly one of the best examples of how a solely story-oriented game can become a masterpiece.In chapter 3 players are introduced to more stats which begin to interfere with how you wish for the story to progress. While annoying it still pretty much allows you to forge your own destiny.The issues begin with chapters 4 & 5 where you're introduced to even more stats that depend on your previous choices. Some of these make no sense and some decisions are locked behind statistics solely for the sake of it. I feel like the game suffers from it tremendously because the abundance of those statistics and the dependence on them lead players to basically min-maxing the statistics instead of actually choosing the choices they wish to make.Not to mention the fact that you had no idea the game was gonna add those statistics in the first place. So if you haven't played the game before you won't even be ready for what is coming which could possibly lock you from the choices you desire to make.It leads to players feeling like their progression was meaningless as now they're basically being forced into making choices they wouldn't normally do. Everything feels like a big game of mathematical calculations rather than a story-driven novel. In the end, all choices will come down to getting enough Reputation, Unity, etc instead of actually forging your own story and seeing the consequences of those choices.Therefore I feel like a much better choice would be to get rid of the majority or even all the unnecessary statistics and base the game solely on player choice. Allowing players absolute freedom in choosing how they want to progress without seeing the consequences of their actions.The story itself is phenomenal and I strongly suggest picking it up on this merit alone.

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game I truely do, it's difficult to describe but it's rare for video games to ever really get me attached to characters enough to the point I genuinely remember them let alone feel sympathetic to what their going through. It's easy to admit the art style and music are perfect for this game and the different stats (in theory) gives you alot of different options to approach situations and the feeling you get when you've played the long game on a hunch of where the story was going was exhilarating.......but the thing is.That's all i can really say positive the story was interesting filled with intique and betrayal, family drama that hit me right in the feels with brilliant writing, but it doesn't really matter because in truth you have no REAL control over anything. Sure there are many options but besides the allure of possible things to consider its near to impossible to fulfill many of the opportunities before you because despite the game being set over many years there isn't that many moments to gain new skills that will help you. Theres not enough to help you in the milestone you're in and surely not enough to help you in the ones to come. You'll be tearing your hair out trying to figure out why these random stats are even related to one another to complete a task, why is it in your early childhood you're given so few opportunities to gain new skills if it's supposed to be several years before you reach the next milestone. I've been marathoning this game sense it came out for the past 13ish hours and I don't know what the game expects of you? Sure I get it "suffering is fun" "sacrifices" ect, ect, but when theres so many things expected of you, so many objectives that's needed to completed otherwise risking "true death" (that whole concept is really cool btw) you don't have many opportunities to complete even 1 or two of them let alone several more than likely you'll just drop the game because of how frustrating it is to accomplish anything. TLDR liked the game but there needs to be some better balance wither lessen the requirements to some task or provide more stat points to keep it modestly balanced and leave the option to complete task in different ways open than just max stating the entire way through.

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked this game overall, but I also want to echo some of the criticisms that others have mentioned in their reviews.The positives of this game are numerous. The world is interesting and well-fleshed out. The writing is good, and really is the driving force of the game. The characters are complicated and compelling, and the multiplicity of story arcs and choices makes for quite a bit of replay value. This last feature of the game is especially well-done, for the narrative of the game is itself cyclical in a manner that gives continuity to your successive lives while still leaving room for you to make different choices each time. That said, if you approach this kind of game with an intent to get "the best ending," then you will likely be disappointed. I've done several playthroughs, and while all have been meaningfully different, most have ended with my character dying horribly and with the city/empire he lives in destitute and riven by conflict. Furthermore, despite multiple attempts there are several paths that I was never able to complete successfully. For instance, I never managed to raise my family to the status of nobility, nor was I ever able to resolve the main conflict of the story peacefully. Still, I would definitely recommend this game, especially if you can get it on sale like I did! As long as you go into it taking the "suffering" part of its title seriously, you'll have a rich and varied narrative experience that is both thoughtful and enjoyable.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely one of the best narrative games I've played. The choices actually do matter and there is large number of events that you won't experience in one playthrough. The game is fairly explicit about the possible events and their conditions, which gives you a sense of control over the story, unlike others that leave you guessing for what a given dialogue line actually entails.  I've finished it without reloading in about 20 hours (some offline playtime didn't sync) and will likely replay in a year or two.The writing is pretty good, though could use a bit more character, in my opinion. And above else, I really liked the art style, the book-form presentation and the subtle visual and audio cues to punctuate the prose. I've been looking for something like this for a while and finally found it. A must for anyone who enjoys narrative games.

_childDocuments_.review: Sir Shuna Brante - Noble of the Mantle, Arbiter of Imperial Justice, Devoted Servant of the RealmAfter a mere 7 hours, I've finished my first run with Sir Shuna Brante, and first experience with the game, in Iron Man mode and being unable to see the impacts of my own actions. And I must say, it was an immersive experience. Well worth the price of admission, and I've barely begun my 2nd run. The writing is high quality, the immersion is impressive, and the music is surprisingly good for something that repeats ad infinitum. The aesthetic is gorgeous, and although the prologue had a future inconsistency, that can be handwaved away.As to who my Sir Brante was, he was a nobleman who fought constantly for peace within the Brante family, equality among the people, and the separation of State and Church. As a child and teenager, he witnessed the unfairness of the lots, the remorseless views the Arknians and Nobles had, and he sympathized. As an adolescent, he fought with the system many times, doing little to help it remain, and much to help it change. Yet, he did not like the New Faith. As a Judge, Sir Shuna Brante languished in the despair of loneliness, his only true ally Sir Augustin El Borne, Prefect of Anizotte. As a human, he suffered the fights of his family, the need to tie it together in the coming trials, yet fearing the failure he could only dream of preventing. As a noble, he endured the dual adversity of mistrust by the Commoners, and the suspicion of his fellow Nobles. And as a loyal servant of the Empire, he stomached the unjust treatment of all mankind by the Arknians, and the impossible barrier between Uther Tempest and the troubles of the common man, Noble or not.However, he was not only in suffering. Finding fidelity in his co-dependence with Augustin El Borne, and his secret, yet infinitely fulfilling relationship with Octavia Milanidas, he braved the many torments of the soul and person, overcoming trial after trial to bring to fruition many dreams since adolescence. And yet, as someone who fought and suffered for the common people, he was betrayed by fate in the Anizotte rebellion. Shocked by the abhorrent and lawless behavior of the rebellion, he fought to control it, to bring it to strength in purpose, and yet was killed by the very men and women he protected in life, a fate soon to befall his only life-long friend, the Just and Fair Augustin El Borne, Prefect of Anizotte.I will gladly say this game is perhaps not for people who cannot fluff their stories. TLaSoSB is not so long, as much as it is exploratory. The high points are betrayed by the length, and the willpower mechanic can easily annoy those unwilling to change the stories they want to tell for the Machine God they end up obeying. For me, though, and people who can fluff the stories they tell and truly inhabit the mind of the game, of telling a story of a man's historical significance, the game is a solid 9/10, and a full 10/10 so far.

_childDocuments_.review: I never buy a game on the first day of release and I never write reviews for Steam - until now. The devs made the bold choice of making the first two chapters of the game available for free, and after playing through that demo I decided it would be a day one purchase.You probably know what you need to know about this game - it's essentially an RPG visual novel, but has an interesting and well-conceived setting that lifts it beyond a lot of the generic fantasy/anime tropes of that kind of genre.It's full of interesting, difficult decisions that you have to make among a cast of nuanced and colourful characters and most of the time there's no clear right or wrong answer. Of course, if it were simply a case of choosing the answer you wanted then that would be one thing, but many answers will be locked depending on the build of your character or your previous decisions. This alone would make the game replayable, but with the choice of three different vocations, and within those the decision of whether to support the old order or try and establish something new, this is one I can see myself playing over and over just to explore its nooks and crannies.Sometimes, due to the weaving political threads and naming conventions, it can be a little hard to follow which character is on which side, and the temptation can be to skip the odd page or two of reading because you can feel yourself getting lost. I just want to get to the next decision! Furthermore, the limits to your choices caused by whether or not you have the right stats, though generally consistent and good, can sometimes lead to a bit of frustration - for example, a chain of events might lead to your family going from being on pretty good terms to totally falling apart over the span of two or three choices simply because you were one point short of some crucial stat at a critical moment. It might feel unfair, but then no-one said life would be fair, not even for Sir Brante.Oh, and the game end is much more rewarding than I was expecting, even if you finish up an abject failure.This is definitely one for fans of games with an emphasis on building a story or those who like the idea of RPG elements in a Choose Your Own Adventure setting. I'd wholeheartedly recommend it for anyone who thinks that might be something that would interest them.Then game will always tell you what the consequences of your choices will be in terms of stat and relationship changes, but you can set it so the consequences are hidden. I think it's would be a good idea to play through a run with hidden consequences early (before you know too much of what is waiting for you...). You can always go back and play again, trying hard to manipulate outcomes in your favour - but be warned, that is much harder to do than you might think.I definitely don't regret my purchase and am pleased to be able to reward the devs for creating something really interesting and being willing to make a fair chunk of the game available as a demo.

_childDocuments_.review: I’m going to recommend this game because it does some things so extremely well that it absolutely deserves credit for, but at the same time it utterly fails in its execution in other places and completely undermines itself. I’ll start with what I felt were the strongest parts of the game.First off, this game does an exceedingly good job of making you feel like your choices matter and have a huge impact on who your character is, his relationship with his family, and the world as a whole. I don’t think I’ve played a narrative game other than maybe Disco Elysium where choices have the same amount of narrative impact. The highs of being able to save someone or reconcile differences in your family feel just as good as the lows of being forced to betray a friend because of other obligations you have or the greater good. This aspect of the game really is executed almost perfectly.Another aspect I really enjoyed is the game’s approach to world building. From the very beginning you are introduced to the very basic foundations of the game’s world and as time goes on it builds on cultural norms, politics, societal expectations, etc. The pacing is perfect. I never felt like I was overwhelmed by the world and every time you felt like you knew everything a new layer of depth or intrigue is introduced to keep you invested.Overall, the game’s writing is great. It does an amazing job of making you invested in your relationships, side characters and overall plot points. There are plenty of characters to love and hate, and it’s easy to become invested in any of the overarching causes the game presents to you.Now, with all of those positives the game builds up during the first 90% of it, in my opinion the execution utterly fails in the final act. Unless you have perfectly made decisions for the first part of the game, you will be railroaded to AT MOST 2 choices in each stage of the final act. It is extremely hard to get an ending that doesn’t amount to you or your entire family dying, the empire being locked in years of bloodshed, or any other number of bad endings. The ending really makes it feel like your choices up until that point didn’t ACTUALLY matter, like the developers had a clear set of decisions in mind that you MUST choose in order to get a decent ending. You want to try and save your family? Sorry you should have chosen to side with a noble and consign a commoner to execution two chapters ago so that your diplomacy score was 14 instead of 15.You may be thinking ‘well just make better decisions’ but believe me, when you are invested in the characters and trying to role play, making ‘perfect’ decisions is impossible. You would pretty much have to look up a guide or something to get one of the good endings which I think completely defeats the purpose of the game.I can’t stress enough how disappointed I felt by the last chapter. It is difficult for me to recommend this game, but the middle portion of it is executed so brilliantly that I feel like I must.
