_childDocuments_.review: I'm still not sure whether a negative rating is fair but I just did not have enough fun to justify a thumbs-up. The game was a chore. And the reasons for it are the game mechanic and the writing.In the beginning you'll get asked a question: Is it fate, is it our surroundings or is it ourselves that determines our course of life? After playing the path of the Noble I can say Brante truly feels like a plaything of fate. Fate (whether you believe in that concept or not) is unfair, illogical, frustrating, just like the choices I was forced to make.However, I can put up with frustration, as long as the writing grips me. This was not the case. What I found myself in was a world of black and white, not what I expected after the first two chapters which showed us the intricate problems of family life in an unfree society.I did not yet play the other two paths (and it's not itching me to do so) but the image I got so far is: we roughly have a 'good' and 'bad' side of every path. The baddies are the friends of nobility, the followers of the old faith, the violent revolutioners - the good guys are the advocates of the commoners, the followers of the new faith and the moderate revolutioners. This is just...not interesting. We get the same story beats, the same worn-out imagery we have in so many medievalish fantasy settings. I found myself skimming and skipping over the text windows, characters were not properly introduced, their purpose was one-dimensional, our relationships with them and their ideals were not sufficiently explored and most of them disappeared completely in the last 30 minutes or so as if the devs have lost interest in their own creation. It's not all bad of course, the presentation is lovely, as is the soundtrack, but the essential element of a text adventure - the writing - is severly lacking. Still I don't regret buying it and thereby helping the devs in establishing themselves and hopefully developing more well-rounded games in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Ill try to keep this both detailed and to the point for anyone reading this. First off, the only other time I've ever played anything even close to a dialogue-driven game was the Obra Dinn. I usually do grand strategy war games like Civilization and Crusader Kings, so I was really stepping out of my comfort zone for this when I impulsively picked up this game. If I had to describe this game to others, I feel like the best comparison I could make in terms of objective and gameplay would be 'Papers Please', which I know is a rare gem of a game in a genre that can be kind of trash. I was already suspicious that games that held branching story patterns always tend to railroad you back to 2 or 3 conclusions by the game's end, with games like Papers Please always being the exception, but I did not feel like thats what happened in this game. 20 hours through the game I finally emerged to my first good ending, and there are definitely some different paths that can be taken from beginning to end that I am curious to unravel. Now for actual advice: For those of you who do play this game, i STRONGLY encourage you to make peace with the fact that you will not get a 'good' ending the first few playthroughs. I literally was 20 hours of play time through the game, and started putting together an Excel Spreadsheet of in game events and outcomes, before I was able to figure out how to best set myself up to succeed. That speaks to how invested you can get into this game and the level of complexity behind the story. Once I figured out what some of the more important story plot elements were, and how to beat/overcome them, then I could on a later playthrough get the skills required and events in order so that i could get on the path towards a 'good' ending... It is by no means easy to get a good ending, but once you do get one, it is incredibly satisfying, and there's enough beef in the game that there are other routes you can take to other 'good' endings as well. Perhaps the biggest frustration that can be encountered in the game is when you get towards the end of the narrative. You see, some of the choices you can select as your characters actions are pretty wide open at the beginning of the game, but as you advance more and more through the story making different selections, then by the end of the story you may have at best 2 or 3 options to pick from. If you misplay your choices early in the game it can very easily ♥♥♥♥ you over by the end of the game, and if you're not prepared to deal with that mechanic like I almost wasn't, then this game can be a tough time for you. Once you have failed a couple times and get an idea of what you have to aim for though, then the game becomes easier to overcome and then those good endings feel like a real triumph.  Minor spoiler warning:My playthroughs usually took me down the path of the noble judge, and I regularly would screw things up and get bad endings one way or another. Once I figured out though that it is PIVOTAL to do whatever necessary to convict this character Otton of his crimes, and later on that another character Sophia could NOT be left in charge of the revolt, that finally allowed me to score my first 'good' ending after several failed attempts. I felt solid joy at finally being able to get a good victory in the game after so many failed attempts, to the point that I now wanna go back and explore entirely different narrative paths to see what the hell else is in this game. /minor spoiler warning. In short, if Papers Please ever intrigued you as a game, if you are looking for a choose-your-adventure story that does require you to carefully select choices, and if you are prepared to really struggle the first couple of attempts before finally getting all the way through, then this game is a great game to give a go. It might not be quite like Papers Please, but should you play the cards right after failing enough times, it is a rewarding feeling that feels well worth the purchase price for the game. May the Twins bless the soul of Daniel Brante <3

_childDocuments_.review: Man, this game made me rage. And I mean that as a compliment. What the game did is take one of the most ingrained storytelling choice-based conventions and burned it to the ground. Then made a little dance on the ashes. The convention that every possible choice is always available to you to pick. This game drives the point home that you cannot make a hard choice after a hard choice without your will wavering. It also drives the point home that a world-hating, bitter cynic will not become a hopeful idealist just because you were nice to her once, but I'm getting ahead of myself. So, first a DISCLAIMER:This game is not for you if you want to play to "win", since it does not have a "golden ending". It only has crushingly miserable endings, up to bittersweet-if-you-squint-and-play-pretend endings. You start your life (and suffering) as Sir [YOUR NAME HERE] Brante, a child born to a civil servant and his lowborn wife. Your elder brother is born of your father's first wife, a noble, who died in childbirth. Your elder sister is your mother's child, and a bastard child in a family that strives to push its way into the noble ranks. And your grandfather is pretty much Tywin Lannister, obsessed with bloodline and legacy. See the trouble brewing already? It gets worse. Gods exist in this setting, two of them to be exact, and they enforce a very strict caste system, called the Lots. To act against your Lot is a sin that will condemn you to eternal torment in the Hereafter. There are the Chosen Peoples called Arknians who rule above all; then there are two classes of Nobles - hereditary, and the second-class ones who earned their title through civil service, their Lot is to rule and bear responsibility; then there is the Clergy, whose Lot is to guide the people and bring the word of the Twin Gods to them; and finally there are the Lowborn whose Lot is to break their back and accept abuse of their superiors with gratitude. The only thing the lower-caste folks get is that they get to be sent back up to three times after they die, while the Arknians and other prominent figures of power only get one life. See the trouble brewing already? Finally, the Lowborn have been squeezed dry by the power struggles between the factions of nobility (with the side that wants to provide for the commoners and improve their lives losing), and are getting rather desperate. There's a schism in the Church of the Twins that's about to rear its head, and an increasing number of the Lowborn have been joining underground resistance. See the trouble brewing already?The game starts at the final hour of Sir [YOUR NAME HERE] Brante, as a journal that pledges to recount his life, and back to the womb you go. No, really, the first decision you'll make is who you touch first after you're born. From then on, you will grow up and make your place in your home, the city of Anizotte, and finally the world. The world, which, as noted above, you can see trouble brewing in.There are three possible paths, each with its own love interest (no happy endings, sorry) and dynamic as your life progresses from birth to the age of 28 years. And that's when the events culminate into an inevitable resolution, and the fate of your home city of Anizotte, as well as the Empire will be decided. What skills have you acquired along the way? What connections have you made? Whom can you trust? Who can trust you? And what of your family? Most importantly, what are the events you missed because you can't be everywhere at the same time? (Hint: Replay value)You stand at the shores of destiny, Sir [YOUR NAME HERE] Brante, and you may be able to tip its scales, decide the fate of the Empire, and even the Twin Gods themselves! Or not. It all depends on the decisions you have made. Sir Brante can lead many lives, many different stories can be written. None of them is more or less "true" or "canon" than another. None of them is a "win". They're all fraught with sacrifices, tough choices, and the final realization - you cannot save everyone. The world is too big for one man to decide alone. There are no heroes, there are no villains. Only the sum of choices all the people, from the lowliest of commoners, to the highest of nobles, have made. That is history. But how will history remember you? Try and see. This game has earned my respect.

_childDocuments_.review: It is with these kinds of games that I wish Steam had a neutral review button. The game has some amazing points. The artstyle is unique and refreshing, the music is captivating, the lore is mind-bogglingly intricately crafted, and the characters are multi-layered and complex. And the story, by god the story is simply brilliant. It is clear that a lot of work and love went into creating Sir Brante's world, and making it feel as real as possible. If this were a book, I would stop the review here. And as a game, the gameplay kind of flops. The store description and tags make it seem like a free-choice RPG, but it's more like a choose-your-own adventure visual novel. You're not playing your own character, you're playing as Sir Brante. And Sir Brante has a specific path in life that he must follow closely lest you want to have future choice options locked out due to lack of stats. It's similar to the Paragon/Renegade system in ME1 and ME2, where if you didn't stick to your path, it would heavily limit the number of choices later in the game. And the same is the case for Sir Brante. Once set on your path and personality, you are railroaded to a pre-set destiny, and any deviation from the path could lead to locked-out options in the future, death, or even a game over.Stats are probably the worst aspect of this. The stats are grossly inconsistent. Some stats, despite being "important" to your chosen path, end up being barely used and essentially wasted choices that could have been used to improve other stats. Some choices are locked behind stat requirements, and you will be forced to min-max your choices in order to reach those required stats (even though those choices might be out of character for your Brante). If you fail to reach those requirements, there will be little chance to gain extra points in those stats for future choices, causing a positive feedback loop where you will always not have enough stats for story options. The most egregious examples of this are some story choices that  And to add to all this, once you max out a stat, there is no reason to ever touch that stat again; you gain nothing out of choosing options that improve a maxed out stat, again forcing you to min max and make out-of-character choices.(TL;DR) All this results in a game with a gorgeous universe, lore and characters, but that is strictly limiting as to the path you can choose for Sir Brante. If you enjoy these kinds of choose-your-own adventure visual novels, where your choices end up on a railroad, more power to you, you're probably going to love this game. However, if you were looking for a text-based RPG with free choice, you need look elsewhere.EDIT: Should also mention the game gives you the option to hide the consequences (i.e. stat gains/losses) of your choices. The devs "recommend" leaving consequences on, but in actuality you're required to do so. Playing with hidden consequences will ruin your experience as the game was not at all designed with that in mind. Why include the option in the first place, if it clearly wasn't part of the design process, is beyond me...

_childDocuments_.review: This game has two unfortunate major flaws.1. Not being able to save (the game autosaves after every decision, but you can only load from either your last choice or major timeline landmarks which are few and far between) plus not being able to skip quickly through already-read text makes replaying pretty frustrating. Especially when you screw up one choice and you have to go back through an entire segment of the timeline to fix that one mistake. I understand the concept of wanting players to live with their mistakes but at the very least being able to skip through text like in a visual novel would be greatly appreciated.2. No spoilers, but: the last segment of the game is the weakest by far, which makes for a disappointing ending. The ending is made inevitable by events that happen between story beats (this is a downside in itself; these events are the same in every playthrough and sometimes seem to contradict your choices) but it just isn't satisfying to play through and is extremely easy to fail at. Why am I recommending this game anyway? Because everything else is so worth it. The worldbuilding in this thing is incredible and thought-provoking. While the objective best strategy is to min-max your stats to make optimum choices available later on, I still wanted to try all the options and try to make my character as logically consistent as possible just because I was immersed in my character and the story. The different paths are truly different and there is so much content in each. I've only done 2 full playthroughs so far (and in one of them I didn't even make it to end game, I died first) and while I feel the need to take breaks in between so the parts that do repeat don't get too repetitive, I am absolutely planning to do many more.This game is truly worthwhile for anyone who loves an interesting world and doesn't mind a lot of reading.

_childDocuments_.review: I decided I would have to go through each of the three branching paths before writing a review, and so that is what I did. I will list the pros and cons of choosing each for a first play through, because it will change your experience with the game significantly.Noble path:The most difficult path to choose and the one that tolerates the fewest mistakes. It's easy to get locked out of many options regarding the main story, and it's difficult to pursue your career without destroying everything else in your life. Still, this path embodies the suffering aspect of the title. It would be a good first choice, but not as an ironman play through. Let yourself mess up, go back and fix things. If you want to play straight through without ever going back, do not pick this path.Clergy path:This is the most dull choice, but the easiest. There is not a lot tiptoeing around, and it's easy to simply choose the most moral thing and what's best for your family all of the time. You can pretty freely ignore most outside pressures and lead the story where you want it to go. That being said, it's difficult to appreciate the subtle power dynamics at play on this path and I wouldn't recommend you choose it first.Commoner Path:This feels like the path that you are secretly supposed to take. You feel like a fish out of water from the very beginning. Every decision you make brings you closer to danger within the narrative, but it doesn't feel excessively punishing or difficult to balance in terms of your decision making in the game. I always felt like I had at least one or two reasonable choices to make and wasn't being forced into a corner, nor was I so free that my decisions didn't matter. I would definitely recommend picking this path first, especially if you want to play on ironman.Overall the world building is satisfying, the characters all have unique qualities even if they are somewhat one-dimensional. The simplicity of the writing makes it clear - most of the time - exactly what you are doing when you decide one thing or another, and yet there is just enough mystery about the world that you are interested in learning more. 8/10 story game.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. .. ....I'm writing this review directly after I first witnessed The Life, Suffering and Final Death of Sir Richard Brante.Right now I'm kind of awestruck. I dont think a game has made me feel so immersed in the world and made me feel so much like the character then this. It has awesome writing, deep lore and realy makes you feel with the character. I'm a person who plays RPGs (P&P and cRPGs) since 25 years now. I'm one that considers it to be the epitome of excelence if you as a GM can make your characters not witness but feel the story. If it makes you laugh in moments of joy, if it makes you cry in moments of sorrow, if it makes you curse when destiny seems to only have bad things in store for you and if it makes you feel a deep feeling of satisfaction and calm when you look at all the struggling and thrive you had to endure and of the good that in the end still prevailed.This game literally made me have all these feelings, and for that it is now within my top 5 of games I ever played. Nowadays to many RPGs put to much of their time into making a proper rulesystem and challenging combats. Other times it seems like player agency and being able to experience all content in one playthrough is weighened as way more important then to have a logical and coherent gameworld. This leads to a hen and egg dilemma. On on hand if players think of the characters they represent as reflections of themselfs and therefor want to have the right to do whatever they want instead of the characters being a living breathing person in the world they live in, with their own hopes, struggles, knowledge and restrictions, it endorces GMs or Game Developers to develop games to their liking. On the other hand if games simply do the above mentioned fault of putting to much time into creating rulesystems and challenges and freely available content, players get to know RPGs as simple stories with challenges the players (not the characters) need to find a way to overcome to "succesfully" finish the story, and characters being mere tools (or builds as people seem to call them) to achieve that.Now, I'm not saying a ruleset isn't important (on a lot of Roleplaying Conventions I stayed clear of Narrative Systems with almost no rules, and the ones I visited where often criticised by me after the session was over because a lot of them aren't good and leave to much room for GM bias), but a ruleset and challenges is not the centerpiece of a good roleplaying game, the stories are.Luckily "The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante", while having a roleplaying system integrated that isn't bad at all (although at times gives you the wrong skill increases in my opinion), is focussed on telling such a compelling story. Or more precisely multiple of them. Because even if I just finished my first playthrough, I've already seen small glimpses of what could have been, if I made different decisions. And those decisions are always meaningfull. I just realised I didn't say much about the game itself, but most of it is already on the store page. It is an interactive novel with LOTS of decisions that follow the story of a man from the moment he comes to existance until the moment his existance ends. In the beginning it tries to run the narrative that the story is experienced in hindsight by the old you who writes it down. That is the only thing I think is a failure, but that I completly forgot about until writing these lines. Just ignore the "The character is writing down his history in a book, and here it is" idea of the beginning because it doesn't make sense. The story ends AFTER you die your final death, kinda hard to write down what happened then, and the death of at least my character was kind of unexpected so he couldn't have written down everything till the point of his death either.I cant say anything else about this game. About the Developers and writers, I wish you all the best and hope you will keep to your occupation and will continue making beautiful pieces of art like this one.Edit: Since I discover another great game similar to this in the quality of writing and emotions, and since I believe games like this should be created way more often, I will endorce "Golden Treasure: The Great Green" here, like I did the other way around. If you enjoyed one of them, chances are realy good you will enjoy the other.

_childDocuments_.review: A perfectly enjoyable CYOA game.Comparing it to the Choice of X games, namely Choice of Robots and Choice of Magics, I'd describe the differences in the following way. Choice of X series offers breakneck pacing, meaning you can easily go from 0 to 11 in under two hours, unless an untimely dead end happens to interrupt your playthrough. Humble beginnings are swiftly forgotten and replaced with something far grander. The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante, however, offers a calmer experience. Here you go from, let's say, 3 to 8, and the progression is considerably slower (it took me 8 hours to reach the finale). This lets the game rather thoroughly focus on each of its chapters, providing plenty of details and boosting immersion. Speaking of the latter, it certainly helps that the game is not 100% text-based, and as for its stat system, in my experience it's minimalistic and sensible enough to avoid pulling out the reader out of the right mindset.The game is true to its name, and the suffering is plentiful. It does allow you to snatch a fair number of various victories, but many are the cases where you will be forced to concede or just let things proceed as if you weren't there. So, if this doesn't sound acceptable, it's unlikely that there's a good time to be had here. The game is fully honest about all this, though, for what that's worth.The finale felt respectable to me. Most of the loose ends felt reasonable to me, a few I'd prefer to have eliminated, but overall I don't believe there were any major issues with it. I'm satisfied with what I got out of the game, and I'm rather strongly considering another playthrough or two to see certain other paths that Sir Brante is yet to walk under my guidance.[Update] Here's what I have to say after experiencing the game further.On one hand, I'm rather satisfied with the other major paths. They all share certain components, but there's also a fair amount of unique stuff, and for me experiencing it was absolutely worth it. On the other hand, replaying the game over and over again isn't what I'd call smooth. You will inevitably be spending time skipping bits that you're already familiar with, and there's no automatic way to handle that. In a way, I guess this is a necessary evil, but I wish they'd make things easier to handle somehow.So, the way I see it, pretty much the only sensible way to make subsequent playthroughs more tolerable in terms of user experience, so to speak, is by using guides aimed at reaching certain endings. I'd suggest doing a playthrough or two blind, and then, if you are still interested in seeing more, making use of walkthroughs.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a difficult one to review. It is probably one of the best written visual novels available on Steam, with short, evocative descriptions and strong to-the-point dialogue. Even though it's a low-magic fantasy setting, the story, stakes and themes are quite personal and character-driven. You'll have to enjoy relationship troubles, intrigue and political scheming because big dramatic moments and action scenes are rare.The fantasy setting allows the writers to examine the injustice of a rigid caste system propped up by a powerful religion, without bringing all kinds of real-world baggage into it. It's a very smart choice that leads to lots of Game of Thrones-style backstabbing and maneuvering.My issue with the game is that the choice systems seems extremely granular at first, with everything from your personality to your family's unity to the state of the empire plotted on a huge array of values that run from -10 to +10. However, in practice there are only a so many gates you have to clear to open the handful of alternative storypaths.  It seems silly to grade everything on a scale of 20 possible values when you really only need to account for three different states.Worse, this system makes it very unintuitive to predict how your decisions will affect things, despite the game relying on a very clunky bolted-on system of outright telling you which future events will be impacted (on the default difficulty.)I also encountered very significant bugs in this system where whole destiny events just disappeared from my character's bio by the time they became relevant, taking away the few strategic choices I made throughout a long storyline (e.g. in The Way of the Sword plot, the game suddenly stopped acknowledging both the Fencing Lesson and Octavia Remembers You even though I literally had those events on my character sheet at the chapter change.)Both my playthroughs feel like I've been led by the nose through very rigid storypaths and in the first attempt, I couldn't even explore the one I thought I was on.All in all, a cautious recommend. Play it for the interesting story and well-written moments but please be aware how flimsy and unpolished the underlying mechanics are.

_childDocuments_.review: This game offers a pretty good experience for the first 5-6 hours of playthrough, where choices do seem logical and story is told coherently. After that story slowly but surely becomes a convoluted mess, your choices mean less and less in a story, and most of the events seem to happen just because writers need them to happen, not because of your choices. Overall, it's an interesting experience, I would still recommend at least finishing it once. I'll try different path in this game in the future, maybe it will be more coherent.UPD So, after second playthrough I cannot say anything positive. For a game that claims to be choice-driven, your choices actually matter very little. The writing is lasy beyond any comprehension. Some events happen literally no matter what you choose. Most of the dialogue is just а couple of phrases that provide very thin layer of justification for actions of characters. Overall plot doesn't change much, whatever path you choose. In my first playthrough I chose Lotless, second time I played as a Priest, and level of similarities is just astounding. This game has literally no replayability value.

_childDocuments_.review: Most fans of choice rpgs will enjoy this one. The 'suffering' in the title is serious, if one is going for an incorruptible character in their decisions then they will face perma-death at least 3/4 of the way through the total game. As punishing as that sounds, the game does a good job of softening the hit with the after-life concept in the game, if you played the game's idea of a virtuous person of course.I would have liked the willpower point system to have applied to choices that if we had lacking attributes for then the willpower could make up the difference. Maybe make those types of choices cost more willpower than the standard willpower choices that come up?Overall, 8/10. I thoroughly enjoyed the story and design of the game, the art aesthetic I enjoyed as well.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm part way through and on the fence as to whether I finish or refund. My biggest problem is the writing--it's like it was done by Garth Marenghi, who famously contended that "subtext is for cowards". Does everything  be so on-the-nose? Do characters  announce exactly what they're thinking when they enter a scene? I get the player has to understand what's going on, but it's too much--for a game so heavily dependent on prose, this isn't good enough.Second thing is that the choice mechanism isn't amazing. It feels more like you're blindly implementing a build order than expressing character decisions. It's pretty meh.So there it is. I might have talked myself into refunding...

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an example of how you can make something very unique and special out of a format that has been around for decades, it's a choose your own adventure for the modern age but it also manages to balance narrative choices that really do change the game.I have completed this game and unusually went straight back into the game and made different choices, which is unique when I have 9000 steam games that most of them I will never play and yet this is only the third time I have done this, the other two times being the wolf amongst us, Disco Elysium and Telltale Game of Thrones ( games with the same dark undertones).Its taken me a while to actually play this game as it isn't a game you can play with distractions as the story requires thought and contemplation, so if you are looking for a game to play while watching Netflix, this isn't it.Games like this prove that computer game can be every bit as moving as a novel or film, as I said if your looking for fast action this isn't it as it's a game that you really do need to think through your actions before committing as every action has an equal opposite reaction.I solid 9 out of 10 in anyone book.

_childDocuments_.review: I got weirdly obsessed with this game- mostly weird because I don't usually play RPGs of any stripe and the only other text game like this left a bad taste in my mouth at the end.But the cradle-to-grave examination of a possible life set within such a compelling world presented in a striking art style was a strong hook for me. It's become a new favorite, and one I may come back to now and then in order to suss out the different life (and death) paths I didn't get to.If you're on the fence, try out the two free chapters that act as a demo- if you like it the saves carry over and you keep on keeping on, and if you don't you're not out any cash.For me, though, I am curious to see what the devs do in future because this game feels like a good first step. Once you replay a bunch of paths there are some annoyances- having to re-read the same texts when you're going back and trying for a new result, not having the ability to retry single decisions in case you click the wrong thing by mistake, and somewhat more frustrating to me was not being able to at least 'try' for one of the closed off options. I get that the narrative is written and the game paths balanced to have these harsh delineations but sometimes it felt like the game prohibited you from doing things.I also found the "willpower" trait a little confusing- I get the narrative purpose for calling it willpower, but whether you gained it or lost it from certain actions didn't make sense. Sometimes you'd lose willpower from doing something that wasn't put upon you by a person or institution, and gain it from blindly following orders.That all said, love the game, love the world. I hope the devs branch out with more games in this style- any setting would do, but I have gotten quite attached to the Not-So Blessed Arknian Empire and I hope this isn't the only chance I get to see it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the quintessence of what a story-rich text-based game should always be! The story is compelling, the choices you make really matter, and there is no trace of woke ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ like in Choice of Games' books. For some endings to happen, you really have to make strong sacrifices. For example, in my first story, I played a judge who favored justice for the folks over career and nobility. But defending my family's life during the revolt cost me the possibility of reaching the negotiated peace ending because, by defending my family against the mob, I lost some support from the common folks in the process (I killed some of them). So yes, choices really matter, as do your past relationships with other characters.You need a decent level of English if you're not a native speaker, but an upper-intermediate level should do.A great interactive story, a nice musical background (after a few readings, however, the music becomes a bit monotonous), and the possibility to do a chapter again if you didn't reach the result you expected make this game a success.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has enormous potential but dosent stick the landing. The only way to get anywhere towards the late game is to completely metagame it and build points to get specific outcomes which kind of ruins the point of it being a chose driven narrative. You can spend the whole time building towards something with logical steps and have really high points in your needed categories then for no reason at all be railroaded to inaction and true death which ends the game. Even if you build relationships, power, fighting skills, spy networks and get guns it wont matter all your building is for naught and despite having maximum willpower to act with your only options end up being surrender or cowardice without any real reason why. Its a shame as there is so many things about this game which are great but to invest all that time in your story and the world it takes place in just to have something pointless and often contradictory happen and end the game really wore me down. As is often the case with modern RPG games this game gives the illusion of choices and consequences when actually its just a stat builder game. Even if you chose X & Y the game will come to a halt and decide you don't have the points necessary in some stat to move to Z instead it will retcon your choices to W & X so that Y never happened and you have to pick L which leads to your character being a witless coward and dying immediately for no real reason.For example eve if you save your friend from a lord with impeccable choices it wont matter as it dosent really have that plan in place for you thus upon the next meeting your friend will just say he was on the run all this time even if you made him the commander of the guard. I really hope they continue to make games and work on them as this game shows enormous potential but needs more work on its decision mechanisms considering its a story book game thats kind of the only thing it offers and it dosent really nail it

_childDocuments_.review: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante is a neat little game that plays out through a journal. Read the text, make a choice, enjoy the artwork and continue to the next page. It is a "choices matter," "choose your adventure" type game set in a pretty cold and cruel pseudo medieval fantasy world.I do recommend this game, however, I do have some criticisms for it & the devs:If you're going to make a text based video game, the text has to be flawless. There is a handful of grammatical and syntax errors in this game.The game is pretty short. The first play through can be done in about 5-7 hours depending on how quickly you read and make decisions. Subsequent play throughs can be done in much less time.If you play this game ostensibly how it's supposed to be played, in ironman mode without being able to see consequences and such ahead of time, it can be brutally unforgiving. If you don't make the "right" sequence of choices early on, even if you think they're the right choices for the "path" you're trying to take, the game will arbitrarily force you down a certain path. So if you didn't take the "right" choice(s) for an event chain in part 1 or part 2, you will be blocked later on from being able to take the choices/decisions that you want to take, which is incredibly frustrating and personally made me not want to keep playing once I got to that point.Aside from the first name you pick at the beginning, there is no customizing your Sir Brante. Want your Sir Brante to have a glorious beard like his grandfather? Too bad.You get 2 "love interests" in the game, the first is a commoner/witch who becomes an annoying haggard looking rebel, and the other is a noble woman, who becomes an alien or something and there's apparently no way to prevent this. Would have been nice to marry the noble woman and start your own branch of the Brante dynasty with her once you become a "Noble of the Sword" but nope. Oh yea, and once you finally attain nobility (or whatever path you were going for) the game ends. This is pretty disappointing since this is where the game could really open up and become much more interesting.The game's lore is intriguing but it just didn't do much for me. I would prefer games like this to be based in our own medieval world/history instead of these half baked pseudo "historical" fantasy settings. Overall it is a good and interesting game, and if you like reading based games and medievalish fantasy settings then you'll probably like this a lot, though considering how short it is I would advise only getting it on sale. Tbh, with everything I mentioned already in mind, I'm kind of bitter that I bought it at full price and then it went on sale less than 3 days later.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: I completely agree with the negative reviews of this game, but would still recommend giving it a try. The game makes mistakes, but still makes me exited to see what this developer does next.The game is so close to great, but, fumbles when they remind you that it's a video game. Toward the middle/end, they force you into "choices" your character (as you have played them so far) would never make because you don't meet the skill check. For the most part, in the beginning these cutoffs make sense and are manageable, but as you get further into adulthood, it feels like they just were unable to consider what my previous choices were supposed to mean for the character that I was playing. In the last 20 minutes of my run I was only ever presented with one available "choice" the whole time. I was literally forced into a betrayal that I never would have picked if i literally had any other button to click. At the very least let the player choose death to live out their version of the story. It nearly ruined the experience for me.There are also some continuity issues. Without getting into spoiler territory, many actions and events I had caused seemed to be completely contradicted by cut scenes that occurred minutes later. I also notice a bug where it told me that this stage of my life was nearly over, but I still had at least 5 more subchapters in that stage to go.If you are willing to forgive these issues the game is still worth checking out for the novelty of what they are attempting. Just be aware that it will very likely fall short if you are looking to have true control over your character's actions. I look forward to seeing what they do next and hope they take these criticisms into account as it appears I am not the only one with this opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so great that I don’t even know where to start this review. I will try to keep it spoilers free as you should experience the game and read all the lore and see everything by yourself and trust me the more you play it the more you want to play it. I was unable to think about anything else or to play anything else for a few days because of this game. I finished it 3 times already and I’m sure I will finish it 10 times more not only for achievements but mostly to see all the decisions and consequences that exists in this game and to read every last bit of dialogue and lore that there is in this game.First let’s talk about settings. There is an option to pick English or Russian language, option to turn on or off animated illustrations and subtitles in cutscenes, sliders for music and sound and options to pick screen format and resolution and to turn on or off vsync. But the most important settings in my opinion shows up when you start a new game and it is a choice of game mode. You can pick if you want to enable or disable chapter restarts and if you want consequences to be open or hidden. While the game tells you that setting the consequences to open is a recommended game mode I would tell everyone to play this game with disabled chapter restarts and hidden consequences as this makes this game so much more deep and unforgiving and you have to think each time what would you do as the game hero, how would you act and what would you say to someone before picking anything instead of just looking at what consequences will each action bring. So while game says that enabled chapter restarts and open consequences is recommended way to play just trust me and set the game on disabled chapter restarts and hidden consequences – that way you will have a lot more fun with the game and you will play it for longer and it will find more ways to surprise you without you knowing the consequences.Now let’s get to the meat of things and that is gameplay. There is a lot of reading and reading and picking your responses and actions is the whole gameplay. That is why you must focus on what you read and what your choices are. You play as Sir Brante and your life is divided into 5 chapters: childhood, adolescence, youth, peace time, the revolt. I think each of these are equally important as they shape our hero and his stats and also open some choices while closing some others in our life. At all stages of our life we will be able to influence how each member of our family sees us and the unity of our family as a whole. As we grow up we will be also able to influence reputation and wealth of our family. It is also important to note that we have willpower and it is used on difficult choices we will make in our whole life and things like resting or having fun give us some willpower back but choices like that most of the times will not give us points in skills so we have to find a balance between gaining skills and willpower.Beginning and end of each chapter gives you a summary. The summary is what stats can you get in that chapter or what stats you got already, events that you can trigger that are also divided into family events and personal life events and events you already got and how much willpower you have left and also how many times you did die so far. Yes you read that right. You can die more than once in this world and it is an interesting game mechanic that makes you meet the gods and learn more about them before being reborn but every 4th death is the final one and after that death you will not be reborn. But there are also events that can trigger the last 4th death called a true death like being convicted for final death by one type of a court or being challenged to a duel to a true death by someone in front of a different type of court or by just making the gods angry with your actions. There are probably others way to get denied the lesser deaths and go straight to true death that I haven’t found yet.Childhood is our first 8 years of life and here our decisions will shape our first two skills like determination and perception. After that we have adolescence that also last for 8 years and here our decisions will shape our three new skills: nobility, ingenuity, spirituality. During these 2 chapters if we get to 4 points in any of these skills we get special events based on that skill. Also in each chapter there are some events changing the stats of your home province like wealth, order,  church status and who is in power. There will be also some events changing things in your family. The next chapter is our youth and it lasts for 4 years. This is the point where the game starts to open the most and gives us the most options and consequences that will shape the rest of our lives. Also all the skills we accumulated during first 2 chapters are now transformed into 6 skills that will be with us for the rest of our lives: diplomacy, manipulation, theology, valor, scheming, eloquence. Our options will be based on our choices and these skills and this will be the skills we will be able to increase for the rest of our live. While 4th chapter also last for 8 years like the first two chapters it is the longest one as you will make many decisions and friends and enemies during this chapter and it is your life during so called peaceful times. After that the last chapter is the revolt and it is only about what things will you do during one day that is divided into 4 parts.I just love how your choices will make you meet some characters while never get to know some others or only see some only once in your life while an other choice can make that character to be the most important person in your life. Your choices really do matter and they change who will be your ally who will be your enemy they even change if you will meet some people at all. While I was playing the same person that was most important for the plot and consequences of my choices was only seen by me once and didn’t change anything for me when I did play the second time and made different choices.But the most important thing for me was the world presented in this game. It is so deep and so rich with lore. Everything here is connected with each other and has some sense in this world. Yes just like the developers say it is a gritty world but it is such a complex world with many laws, many groups and religions and sects and types of magic and its own history and races that exists as well as these that went extinct. Everything in this world is really well thought out. The sound in this game like horse hooves on a cobblestones or the sound of the giant tree bark moving on the wind etc. really makes you feel like you are inside this world. I’m not ashamed to say that the world presented and the writing gave me tearful eyes a few times. The only problems I found were some small errors in English spelling from time to time. Things like: “Today you will you be taking” or “The” instead of “He” etc. But I think these errors will be fixed with time as developers only need to read all the text in the game a few more times to catch them all. Do you like to read and be immersed in a great living world with it’s own history and problems and reality? Do you like when your decisions have a strong lasting impact? Just buy it now! Just do it!Overall score 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: A very engrossing game set in an imaginary universe strongly reminiscent of the Enlightenment Era.You take charge of the second son Brande, name him as you wish and navigate him throughout his life. The possibilities are immense, but choices are more often than not difficult, both short and long lasting. Will you strive to be a noble, get inducted in the clergy of the Old Faith, join the heretics of the New Faith, or will you become a rebel? Will you keep the family together or are you going to seek only your own? Would you join the oppressors or the oppressed?  The choice is yours.You can restart each era if you want to explore different avenues. The game has replayability and is not a short one, so you get enough for your buck. The storyline is very interesting and you are part of it all the way through.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a wonderful narrative-driven game.  While it resembles more a traditional "choose your own adventure" style of play, it is deftly improved by the incredible variety of choices and subtlety of consequences.  It certainly has that "one more turn/click" incentive to see where the text will lead next.  This is a spartan game by design, but it does not take away from the atmosphere it creates-rather the opposite.  The evocative illustrations are superb, even when they recycle throughout the text - and I love the sparing use of sound effects that puncture the choices and story so effectively.  This is a true gem of a game - not for fast paced action; but mellow, thoughtful progression.  It has some replay value given the variety of paths you commit to throughout the story; with the only caveat that you really do not always get all that much UI on what your choices mean or may lead to - something I enjoyed as a puzzle to resolve but I can see where it might jar a more casual player.  This is a very easy recommendation - thoroughly engrossing, highly engaging and despite an ultimate rigidity rewards multiple play-throughs!

_childDocuments_.review: Stunningly intricate and well thought out, yet not without it's flaws.The story is astoundingly innovative, delving out layered outcomes concocted from series of specific, united choices that are free to be expanded by player's will alone.. The gameplay system is as balanced as it can be, fairly limiting possibilities that are not deserved with the former results. Even failure, given how articulately the circumstances are presented feels justified, giving plenty of introspective to think upon, whilst every small victory is genuinely deserved, as it is an amassment of everything you add to your path. The only bits that sour the experience are the occasional locked off progressions the requirements of which are unfairly set sky high and demand a specific route to be taken from the start, and minor typos scattered throughout the paths.I've eagerly awaited for a title like this to pop up, fusing together an elaborate story, and player freedom that's expanded enough to make consequences of choices matter and have real presence through and through. The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante made a solid attempt it at, partially succeeding but still meeting minor limitations that don't let the experience flow. And yet I'm convinced that this small success will inspire and pave the way for grander, bigger titles that will solidify a niche of truly interactive adventures, elaborateness of which will astound anyone and everyone who appreciates thought and care of deliberate cohesive writing.

_childDocuments_.review: Interactive stories are my guilty pleasure. As I was playing The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante I was impressed more and more. The story was great, my actions had consequences, everything seemed to make sense, and I was playing my character and story as I wanted. And then as things peaked all my work went to the trash bin for no apparent reason. It was unexpected. What's even worse the results I was getting from my actions and choices made absolutely no sense and were completely out of character for my character.A brief example avoiding spoilers, would be, I did take care of my family and had unity 7 which was no easy feat as I did a lot of compromises to keep peace and balance in the house. In no time, after short successive occurrences, it went from 7 -> 0 leaving my family in ruins. Another example even more important, again avoiding spoilers:-"I walked a fine line keeping peace, making concessions and trying to be a benign influence. I was doing more than fine, everything was looking promising and the majority of my personal stats were maxed - my lowest personal stat was Scheming. Apparently in the final chapter personal stats do not matter much. My choices were extremely limited. Everything led to my death because I was missing - 1 point to one stat or another to be given different choices.... so city power wasn't low enough or high enough etc. But what was worse was not that every choice led to my death achieving nothing of consequence... but having replayed the final chapter eight times the only more impactful ending I could get, and that is a major laugh, was to lead a bloodbath. HOW my peaceful, diplomatic, caring but pragmatic character ended up being a butcher and a killer.... is truly beyond me."I agree with other people's reviews that the conditions/requirements for choices offered restrict the story too much and derail it in the final chapters. Also those conditions can be random and unpredictable - there is no reason why you need this and that in order to be offered a different path. It isn't the story structure and plot that fails - it is the conditions and the numbers approach.Because of the effort put into making this game I can only rate it positively. It is a very very decent attempt into making an interactive book/game. If you even think you might like it, go for it, it will offer you plenty of entertainment. Your playthrough is certain to be different to mine as there is a great range of paths. Else skip.

_childDocuments_.review: I won't be talking much about this game; it tried to be Lone Wolf and failed. That's the long story short version.The long LONG story version is that: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante takes you into a written adventure, playing as Sir Brante from his first cry into the world, to his death... The decisions you make affect your life as Sir Brante, as well as the glory that comes with it. Now, don't get me wrong, the game's got a lot of lore... Its Grammar is very well on point (much better than my reviews, I concur) BUT, and there's a huge BUT here... this is NOT an RPG game.Let me compare it to one that follows more or less the same paradigm here; Joe Dever's Lone Wolf, a game that captivated me enough that I read through all of it, twice, because I loved the game even though I hate reading as a skill and as a hobby. Lone Wolf was a charismatic regent lord, with so many skills you could chose from to take care of certain situations! Lone Wolf would also do a lot of RPG things, like Level Up, wear armor, equip weapons, use magic, drink potions, pursue a love interest and other RPG things to do... Apart from having a bride, Sir Brante does NONE of them, on top of that, after reaching a point in the game where I could see how charismatic this dude can be; he can be as cold as stone! No matter what choice you pick up, the guy's still as lame as ever, and that's the ONLY RPG thing you can do in the game, pick choices that would increase or decrease certain nonsensical stats as well as boost or destroy your relationship with members of your family, who, by the way, are also lame and boring as all hell. The best outcome I had with Sir "Fauxnel Brante" is getting him into the clergy, and get him promoted to Patriarch Sir Brante. I mean the game is called "The SUFFERING of Sir Brante" and yet, depending on your choices, this dude can have a pretty fulfilling, great life... Make it into the clergy, put aside the current patriarch and take his own place while your family thrives in the highest positions of power? How is that a life of suffering? Uuugh, cringe!One point for the game, however, is that the writing is very good... but I hate reading, so why would I care? The illustrations in black and white are nice... sometimes shocking after I've been skipping most of the writing and following a guide to make sure I pick the right choices for my achievements ahahaha. To me, this is a  very uninspired visual novel... It's got NOTHING to do with the labels it's got on the Store Page... yes technically this IS a role-playing game, but is it an RPG? Oh, hell no.

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I want to -- I can't recommend this game. The world-building here is extremely strong, setting up a unique and interesting narrative in such a way that the divisions and structured required for the different plots feel natural and make sense, despite the contrivances required. There are enough strong characters to make the world feel lived in, and to create tension when you ultimately have to choose sides. The satirical religious and societal structures are well enough presented, however at times they feel overdone, with the sheer extremity of the regimes involved begging the question of how things have lasted this long before revolution. The possible narratives are predictable but perfectly serviceable especially when presented with such a compelling world. The problem is not the narrative -- its everything else.A choose-your-own-adventure style gameplay loop is fine, it works, as long as each decision feels meaningful, however put simply they don't. You will enter strings of decisions that each have exactly the same mechanical impact and no impact on the narrative other than additional context -- most of which is blindingly obvious before you make a decision.The action of skills and 'resources' going up or down depending on your decision, and later choices being gated behind these skills and resources feels frustrating. Some of this is clearly intentional, with contrasting decisions leading to increases and decreases in opposing pools, and several events making clear the danger and tensions involved based on the state of these pools, however it feels like more oft than not it simply gets in the way of telling a compelling story, and draws the player out of the narrative to focus on the wrong things.Together, these actions both make the game feel (intentionally) unfair at times -- this is the suffering of Brante after all -- leading to unsatisfying narrative conclusions that feel uncontrollable, whilst the overall design of the game is not nearly unique enough between different paths and options to allow for multiple differing playthroughs to feel anything but a slog through old content with the occasional interesting tidbit. The game also simply needs another couple of layers of polish -- some of the writing and grammar is downright sloppy, and it can really work to further draw you away from the games strengths. The art and sound designs are decent, and work with the overall tone of the game, however it would improve the experience between different paths if so much of it wasn't reused within different contexts to represent different things. I also don't understand the point of the narrated cutscences between stages of life -- all they did was draw the player away from the interesting parts of the narrative to a general and boring one that had to be so in order for it to be used across all possible routes. Overall, whilst the world and narrative designs are strong, the game experience is poor enough that I simply can't recommend it, as much as it disappoints me to say so.

_childDocuments_.review: Ahoy! This be ye local piratical game reviewer telling ye if The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante be worth ye gold or whether it be sent down to the sunken depths of Davey Jone's Locker! Yarr! For ease of ye reading, I've broken me thought down in te Ayes and Nays and me thoughts on each!The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante is a choose your own adventure game. When I first started the game I expected it to be more brutal, especially with the warning from the start. I found that while the game setting is quite brutal, the game itself is not. I've completed one play through and tried experience as many endings as I could from my game's worth of choices. I'll be exploring my thoughts in me ayes and me nays!The game is presented as a story book with detailed illustrations, each tab represents a slice of Sir Brate's standing in the world. From a game map, to the standing of the House of Sir Brante, Skills, Family relationships and the sort. The game itself runs smoother then a clipper with a full sail of wind. It fits the setting well.The world of Sir Brante is brutal and rigid. You are born into your lot and the world for the most part expects you to stay in your lot, It has strong ties to our own medieval times. For the typical peasant, you have no hope but to suffer and endure what fate has meted out for you.The only exception to this rule is families like the House of Brante which while considered a Minor house. It has the wealth and opportunity where you may change your lot in the world. If you choose too.You have a lot of freedom to choose but you can't have everything in this story. I found a lot of my picks had trade-offs, My Diplomacy and Valour were high but it came at the cost of my other skills. Certain choices will be closed to you depending the route you take and I like that. It actually allowed me to Role-Play Sir Brante and see the world through the lens of where he is in the world. In my main run, My Sir Brante didn't accept his lot as a commoner, he defied it, He kissed the sword, He paid for it but he was proud of his choice. He followed his father's footsteps and became a judge, He tried to change the system from the inside, He put others before himself before family and friends. They all had costs and opened and closed various doors.I've always liked Dystopia's and the world of Sir Brante is one. The main events of the game unfurl around you as you progress in life. You do have the option to participate in them although how you participate is defined by your choices. As you progress in the story, the strife continues to build until the crescendo at the end.It's like watching the start of a revolution. At the start, the problems feel very far away. My Sir Brante, Participated in the marches, he fought to get his education. It was the start of a long chain of events. When he became a judge your choices and events in the world eventually brings the revolution closer and closer to you until you're forced to deal with it.The only thing I didn't like was the endings and I'll touch on that in my Nays!Your skill choices when you're young feed into your adult skills and If I'm honest, I didn't really find them useful. Since I took the route of becoming a diplomat, I naturally took choices that would give me high diplomacy and Valour. I didn't really put much thought into it. The game itself doesn't really give you really high checks until very late in the story. I understand that a game like this needs skill checks but I had 20 Diplomacy but because of prior choices the option to use the 1 20 diplomacy check the game tells you about was actually closed off because of prior choices I made earlier in the game. Making getting that high moot. Outside skills and factional standing. You have one final stat and that's will power and sometimes it was the most frustrating thing in the game. You could meet all the requirements for a choice, You've got the skills, you've got the right support. You've done all the prep work. The choice you're about to take is completely in your Sir Brante's Character. However, because of a choice you got railroaded into 2 pages ago that you couldn't have possibly have known you've now character's now got -5 willpower and their face is too tired to make the right decision. You know, A decision that might be in their fibre of personality that they would take regardless. Yes, I get that you need to include mental state but by David Jones locker, drink some damn rum and just get on with it. Will power at times felt like an arbitrary barricade, You'd take hits out of the blue and the very next choice, you know the important one. It's too bad you spent that will power a page ago, you'll have to do something out of character! The story is great, The build up is great. However, I felt like there wasn't actually much choice in the endings. You can side with the empire or side with the rebels. You either hit the requirements or you hit a failure state. I explored as many endings as I could with my character, For the most part it's most serviceable but I dunno, I felt like there could have been more choices.I also found that to get my ideal ending, The path was open to me but I'd actually have to let my entire family die. Sending them away or fighting for them would result in either insufficient willpower or would leave the commoners state be 1 too low. Felt a tad bit Harsh considering I spent the entire time making sure they stuck together and sacrificed everything to stick together.I loved the vast majority of this game, I feel that you would have the best experience if you give your Sir Brante a few character traits and then play organically and blind and see where the story leads you.I would have given this game 9 gold doubloons out of 10 if not for the aggravation of the willpower stat and the more mediocre ending which bumps it down to a solid 8 out of 10 gold doubloons - As good as a bottle of rum. Drink these when you see 'em.If you are a strong fan of role-playing and love choose your own adventures. The Life & Suffering of Sir Brante is a no brainer. Hop aboard this ship, unfurl your sails and start your adventure. There is many a route to explore here, who knows you might even find your own Xanadu in these seas.A small note for Steam Deck users. I played through it all on my steam deck, The writing is a bit small but works fine, barely drains the battery much at all.

_childDocuments_.review: 50/50% on this game. Or should I say 25%75%Many of the other positive reviews stand, I find that this game has great writing; it's got me very invested in the story, the choices were great and didn't feel forced. I found it a very organic story.While the Introduction was great, the set-up (middle part) had its moments, mostly being bogged down by inconsistent events with the path I was taking, and the feeling that I had to "lock onto" a path meaning that I had to "play the game", which felt incongruent with how organic the rest of the game felt.The finale felt really strange, especially during the first playthrough. Many people I knew nothing about showed up, and I found very unclear which stage of the revolt I was in. The initial overview of "peaceful resolution" or "military resolution" was nowhere to be found, and as I was assuming all I had to do was fill in the requirements, I was left confused when achieving the requirement didn't complete the overarching event. All this being said, the final conclusion I found brilliant.Ultimately, I'm not writing this review thinking this game is bad. If it truly were that, I would just disregard it. I think this is a great game, which with a little chiselling would be 9-10/10. Right now, I would consider it a high 7/8, only because it left me longing for what more it could be.Since I have to pick, I think it's a worthy playthrough if you have the spare money. If the points above were resolved, it would be a definite buy*Lastly, I found it funny how out of place the american accent of the author felt in a 10th century based world. Not a huge deal, but did take me out of character hearing it

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, what a perfect matching title!This game really shows the life and especially the  of... me! But in a great way!First of all, if you don't like reading, move along. This game is a lot of text. With around 15 hours of playtime for a full game (you might be quicker if you decide to die early or skip some story lines) you get some good amount to read.But what is this game about, you might ask. And this is hard to define. I did not read anything about it and got surprised a lot. It starts as a simple medieval story in which you make some decisions. But pretty soon you realize this world offers far more and you end up in a world of magic and divine conflict.The story itself starts with your birth and requires right from very the start your decisions. (who do you look at when first opening your eyes?). Over the 5 chapters you play through your years making sometimes smaller other times bigger choices of your life. The good thing is, it really feels like you are making your choice. From your profession and personal life, first love and friendship, you pick your own LOT.And this is actually what the story is about. Soon you realize, it becomes a story where you fight for your own destiny. But not only as a matter of choices but also within the story. In a world that divides people into different classes with very little leeway for change, you will get a (mostly tragic) story of a young man trying to find his way in a horribly unfair world. Your family isn't helping much either and you will find your choices offering only tragic decisions of losses.The fun mechanic here is that each chapter (beginning at your childhood, then your youth...) offers slightly different "attributes" representing your character. Where as a child you might decide what personality you have (e.g. are you the bold one or the observing calm type etc.) these attributes might influence not only the whole story but also the next chapters in which you get new mechanics. So when coming in the years of your youth, you use these attributes to learn your profession. The observing type might learn more about the nobles lives. A bold person might become the rebel who fails when it comes to learning a profession. So instead of making my family proud by becoming an eloquent noble, I disappointed them all by becoming a brawling commoner. I wouldn't if I had chosen a different path in my childhood.This chain goes on and you feel your character growing with each year. You will loose friends and family - and don't even dare trying to make a perfect game. You will suffer and you will die - a lot.But I haven't played many visual novels that sucked me into their world so deep. Rarely have I had the impression of playing my own life. Most of these games feel like my choice doesn't actually matter but instead giving me only a slightly different dialog in the next page. Not so in this game.The game offers two play modes. The default one shows you in each chapter what consequences you might face. (e.g. someone might die, you might have success at something or fail. Etc.) It also shows the requirements for this condition. Same goes for all the decisions you make. So you can hover your mouse over them and see what they affect. This is clearly shown as "You gain +1 strength, the other person will die...".But from what I played, it feels so much better when you disable that mode. This is a novel that wants you make the decisions as you face them. And to me this spoils a lot the gameplay. I disabled this and played "blindly" since in my real life I also wouldn't know I need "a bit more money and willpower in order to find my true love in 2 years". This spoils the "this is me" feeling a lot so I can only give you the advise to accept the life you would pick. There is no perfect game anyway and usually you know the consequences more or less. (If someone draws the sword telling you to surrender and you ignore it, you don't need the tooltip to understand the severity of your actions).In any case, give it a try and enjoy the game if- you have advanced English skills (native level or a good dictionary will make you enjoy the medieval terms)- you can accept that your life will actually mean "suffering"- you like to make tough decisions even if they hurt- you like to read a 15+ hour text (which only lightens up by black & white pictures and some sound effects)- like to think about your decisions, life, society and what you want to achieve with the time you are given withDon't play this game if you- expect it to be a roleplaying game (even though it has attributes and medieval theme)- don't like to read- get frustrated when making "wrong" decisions, die, or want to restart when you didn't like your decision (you can restart a chapter but that potentially means replaying a few hours)- don't like fantasy (there is no fancy ork or dragon in here but you have some magic and spiritualism)

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing. So many choices, so much to read and experience. _childDocuments_.review: The game is a pick an ending style graphic novel where your choices throughout lead toward their end.  The game requires alot of reading and very little graphic appeal.  However, the story is engaging.  One thing I do not like about the game is the limited choices you are left with.  Often more than not you have very little choice in your decision.  By the last part of the game you are basically reading only results of choices in the previous chapters.  Leaving the option on to see all choices you find one choice or another blocked you from picking an ending you would have wanted to pick.  I find that the path to any outcome must be so specific that you really do not have much choice in your decisions.  I have found through a few play throughs that you must be evil to save the empire and being good only leads it to its ruin.  That for me is just bad story writing where you are pigeon holed into the narrow views of the creator of the game.With all that being said, I still recommended the game because it reminds me of those pick and ending books I loved as a kid.  Unfortunately just like those books, once you play through a couple of times you forgo the reading and just click through to find your result.  I;m sure someone has plotted the path to each ending by now on some wiki page.  If you want to see a specific ending might as well write down the entire choice path because I'm sure that is what you would need to do to follow the maze to the end you want.

_childDocuments_.review: TLSSB is a choice-heavy visual novel about the caste system in a dark fantasy world, and the way it collapses, reforms or survives based on your choices.Without spoiling much:As of now, my first (and only) run was the lotless one, which was pretty fun besides a few complaints on the ending which I don't want to spoil. Your choices have impact, and at several times I was given the call on whether important characters would live or die.The worldbuilding is predictable but does have a few neat twists to it, like how prominent castes are, the three reincarnations each character has, and the way gods and magic are handled. It does manage to feel genuinely oppressive and upsetting, and it complements the plot well.As for the plot, it's well written. Things make sense, actions have consequences, and characters behave believably. It kind of stutters at the end though, where the epilogue bits ended up contradicting themselves. The prose is serviceable, nothing special, but gets the point across cleanly.This is one of the less famous games I've played, and its very solid. I definitely recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: An extremely compelling visual novel. You are witness to the entire life of the titular Sir Brante, playing through key events from his moment of birth onwards. Most events require a decision from the player with both immediate consequences and a change to various game stats that will affect what options are available to you later in the game. The branching plot is quite complex and the available decisions have the feeling of real consequence. I played through once myself and watched a different game on stream and I look forward to several more replays.On the negative side, I have noticed that as you approach the later part of the game the difference between success and disaster can hinge on a single point in a single stat. Which feels a bit arbitrary. Having more "partial failure" options would be nice. But such is the nature of video games. Also, I would say that the setting is a fantasy world with a resemblance to Renaissance Europe but with the inequality and suffering ratcheted up to an extreme unmatched even by history. The awfulness can become comical in its extremity. Toning things down a couple clicks would only have improved the narrative.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: Lot's of choices. Moments of tragedy and triumph. Honour, disgrace, happiness. All Achievable but at a cost. The game makes you really feel the impact of each choice you make and never holds you're hand by making the morals black and white, right and wrong. Instead it makes you question what the "good" path is and if one even exists in the cruel world of Sir Brante. Honestly its a breath of fresh air compared to the cookie cutter morality system most games force one into.I highly recommend this game to anyone who likes to experience a good story with a warning to not assume you can win this game, as that is not the point. Its about the experience and immersing you're self into to the trials and tribulations of one man struggling to make his way through life. A long read but a good one, give this game a try if you like choose your own adventure style games and you got spare cash to burn.

_childDocuments_.review: Sir Surrik Brante was a cold and pragmatic man. He carefully plotted and defied his way into the nobility. The growing conflicts in the lands were nothing more than an opportunity to gain influence among the truly elite. Even his own life and romantic pursuits would be spent for political gain. Yet despite all that ambition, Brante could not escape his lingering traces of empathy and the pain it brought him. As he formed close bonds with others he was forced to watch them fade away due to his own ambitions. His efforts to keep his family together ultimately ruined their reputation and any hopes of being among the upper nobility. Brante ultimately lost his life subduing a revolt in exchange for nothing more than a name on a monument. The lands were ravaged and the people were more oppressed than ever before. No meaningful change was achieved. In the end, Sir Surrik Brante lived a truly miserable and worthless life.But...what if he had a second chance? Could he have taken a different path? Altered the very course of history? And what price would he have to pay?
