_childDocuments_.review: This is an astounding work of ludonarrative fiction whose quality is *almost* comparable to heavy weights in the genre (such as Disco Elysium, or Vampire the Masquerade:  Bloodlines).  The central gimmick of the game -- playing a single character from their birth all the way through their death -- is both a unique premise and deeply engaging in how it is set up.  The true meat of the story is contained within the adulthood section of the narrative (and the game conveys this clearly by calling your childhood a 'prologue'), but the choices you make during childhood reverberate through the entire story and can have significant impact on both your stats as an adult, and the shape of the narrative itself.  In addition, the game gently eases you both into its mechanics and the surprisingly deep lore of its world with each stage of Brante's maturity, allowing you the time to come to grips with how both the game and the setting function with stakes that are at first low, but quickly escalate as your character becomes older.  Although the world this game takes place in is fictional, it is very obviously inspired by historical events in late medieval/early renaissance Europe.  The conflict at the heart of the game's story is equal parts a class and religious conflict, pitting an old guard of feudal aristocrats and traditional spiritualists against the rising class consciousness of a coalition of commoners, lower ranking nobility, and progressive priests.  Your family itself is a microcosm of this conflict, with your grandfather, father, and older brother all belonging to a class called 'Nobles of the Mantle', a sort of 'earned' rather than inherited noble title, while you, your mother, older sister, and younger brother are all commoners.  Just as the conflict threatens to tear your nation apart, it too threatens to tear apart your family.  It is difficult (but not impossible) to maintain the peace within your family and between the two sides of the conflict, and the game's narrative pressures you on both the family and professional fronts to pick a side.  Happier endings require a very carefully considered series of decisions on the part of the player, as late game decisions can begin to have very difficult requirements both in terms of required stats and previous decisions made earlier in the run.This brings me to my only true criticism of the game -- there are a few points in the game's narrative where I feel that the requirements for certain choices are too steep, and occasionally lead to a feeling of the game playing itself due to you having essentially no options available to you.  This is especially true in the final chapter -- without spoiling the specifics, the endings associated with siding with the revolt have approximately four different outcomes, three of which are locked behind a specific decision whose requirements are egregiously difficult.  To make matters worse, you have no reasonable way to know how to prepare for it.  In order to achieve one of these three endings, I had to save scum multiple times to get various stats in exactly the right places to meet it, which is not the kind of experience I am looking for out of a narrative game -- I'd prefer to make my choices and live with their outcomes, but in this particular instance I felt that the game's overly strict stat checks on this one specific, all-important decision point flattened a moment that should have been tense and full of anticipation for divergent possibilities into a frustrated boredom with knowing only one ending was possible.  In my opinion, with how important this specific decision proves to be and how much is locked behind it, the requirements could have been made a little less strict for a better, more logical experience.That said, I must also give credit where it is due -- this is one of only a few times the game missteps with its mechanics, and the overwhelming majority of the time I felt that the various requirements of decisions made sense and helped imbue the game with a sense of consequence that few games achieve.  As a result, the replay value of this game is immense.  I have already completed two runs, and am planning to do many, many more.Overall, I would consider this game a flawed masterpiece -- marred by a few missteps, but ultimately a tour de force of narrative gameplay that demonstrates what is possible in the medium.  I would easily recommend this to anyone who enjoys narrative focused games with political or historical themes.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed the game and it's one of the better interactive fiction games I've played, but it's not without a few issues.The worldbuilding is solid enough, but a little flimsy. A solidly stratified society with clear divisions between peasantry, nobility, clergy, and ruling elite isn't groundbreaking, but it's done well enough. I wish a tiny bit more backstory had gone into the founding of the empire and how the Lots came to be. The game was originally written in Russian and translated to English, and for the most part it's a solid translation, but there's definitely some clunkyness and unnatural word choice.The main "gameplay" revolves around making choices that affect various stats and relationships, which in turn open up and close off paths down the line. These generally follow a logical progression, where choices made at one point have clear consequences in later events, but at a few points I was left frustrated when what I felt was the correct choice in a situation was locked off because I didn't meet an entirely arbitrary point value in one of my stats. I feel the game may have been better served by not having an attribute system, or by simplifying it to avoid these situations, especially towards the end of the game.There are 3 distinct paths you can take in the game, and I chose the one that seems most natural for the protagonist based on his family history, the Noble lot. You can, it seems, also choose to be a priest or a commoner. Those paths didn't really appeal to me - the religion in-game was a little lukewarm for me and the commoner path seemed like a dead-end - but there's definitely room here for subsequent playthroughs and multiple endings for each path. I feel I've gotten my money's worth so probably won't be replaying, but it's nice knowing the option is there.You have to be a certain type of person to enjoy these types of games. Many people will know at a glance that they won't enjoy it. But if you like reading, choose your own adventure games, and a good class struggle, you'll probably enjoy this one. It's got pretty high production value, relatively, and while the art and music are minimal what is here is pleasant.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm only tentatively recommending this game. I believe the strengths outdoes the weaknesses. I believe it's a generally enjoyable experience. But it has some pretty heavy flaws.Personally, I felt... Completely powerless in my ending. The family mechanics are bizarre near the end, to say the least. You can't choose to be close to some family members but not the rest, basically. If you do, your family will fall apart in a string of events in a bizarrely immersion-breaking manner with your house being abandoned for some reason, which will leave your character without willpower, which then also drains your ability to do anything in the end what-so-ever. You know. The most important part of the story. (In case you've played the game, I got like 4 negative events in a row, yikes) I was legit on okay-ish or great terms with everyone but one character. One. (Stephan). The game starts out by talking about 'sacrifice', but if you actually go through with sacrificing your family for your duties, you don't get either. Which is silly. Don't set up the start of the game by telling the player that "things will cost sacrifices" if it then turns out to not be true.Post credits was also just weird. People died 'because reasons' off screen. I did choose a violent ending, but even then it made very little sense. A rebellion, even if violent, shouldn't lead to random uninvolved people to die for no reason.All in all, it made it feel like someone else had taken the controller away from me. As if someone else had taken the character out of my hands and was playing the game for me. It was a very dissatisfying ending. I think most of the blame lies in the willpower mechanic. There wasn't a point in time that that mechanic felt satisfying. It's basically a stamina meter, and if it isn't filled enough when you need it, vital choices will just pass you by. And you don't know when those vital choices are (nor when you will be struck by 4-5 negative family events in a row which drains your stamina bar), so there's no real way to plan out your willpower expenditure without having played the game multiple times and hence knowing when important events arise.I did enjoy the game in general though. The worldbuilding is unique and creative, you do get drawn into the characters and their stories, and the early parts and the middle of the game is quite entertaining, at least it was on my route. (I went lotless). So yeah. A mixed bag, but ultimately more enjoyable than not, especially prior to the ending.

_childDocuments_.review: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante is an exceptionally high quality visual novel. It is extremely well written, and features a branching story, wherein each branch takes place in the same area and time as the rest - allowing each branch you follow to expand your knowledge and understanding of the world, making it ever-more interesting.It is set in a fantasy realm; multiple sentient species exist, and more existed before. The gods are a matter of fact; their rule is ever-present in your life. You play as the second son in a family, and ultimately you have three generals paths before you; the path of the commoner, the path of a priest, and the path of a noble. To avoid spoilers, I will limit myself to saying this; these paths may seem simple to choose from, but they are all more than they seem, and the additional choices thereon diversify the plot even more. In relation to technical aspects of the game, the graphical presentation is both flawless and immersive, and the music is also excellent; the number of tracks is large enough to provide for enough variance that the music always feels fresh. However, the sole voice actor of the game is extremely amateurish and sounds like he has an uncharacteristic speech impediment (especially so considering he's meant to be voicing the well-spoken main character, Sir Brante).Mechanically, the game assigns stats to you, and values of affection or contempt to people of meaning that you will interact with. It becomes a bit of a balancing act, but ultimately, it just means that you are forced to play as the character you've been playing as before; do not expect to be able to become a genius when your character has been out drinking at every opportunity, or have a good familial relationship when you've only ever cared about maintaining your studies and your reputation. There is also a mechanic called 'willpower' which can become irritating, especially towards the end of the game; however, I would recommend treating it as a narrative feature - because it is one.That leads on to my next point - a negative one. The final arc, the 'revolution' is a messy attempt to bring nearly all paths back together for one big finale. Rather than your choices in the past, there is only one thing that matters during this arc: how much willpower you stocked up before the arc started. If you didn't stock up 20-30, you will get one of the generic ends that don't apply to your story; it's disappointing, and should've had more thought, time, and effort put into it.I wholely recommend this game to anyone that enjoys a solid narrative, and enjoys exploring that narrative. However, I would strongly recommend playing through the 'noble' path the first time you play; it's lower quality than the other paths, but it's also clearly intended to be the 'first' path anyone plays through.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really good in a lot of ways. It manages to do what so many games strive for but fail to do; give you choices that are meaningful and also difficult. I have played many games with choices where there really was no choice because one option was obviously the best for one reason or another. This game presents you with options and quite often I had no idea which to pick because they all seemed equally intriguing and soon realized I would just have to play the game through multiple times to see everything I wanted to see.Little did I know how irritating replaying the game would be. There were so many times where I wanted to do one thing but I was locked out of that choice because of some other thing I had chosen or stat check I didn't pass which then  necessitated me picking an option my character would never choose and giving me terrible outcomes. This is especially telling in the last two chapters. I picked whatever I wanted to do, sometimes siding with one side and other times the other and was left in a situation where I had no hope of getting the stat checks I needed for a good ending to either one. You have to pick the fate/fates you want at the beginning and make choices to follow that path regardless of what the choices you make to get there are and even then you probably won't be able to get what you want. I realized that I had to completely ignore consistency for my character and only go for points to pass stat checks to get the ending that I wanted. Its so frustrating how everything you want to do seems to be locked behind a stat check you had to be working on from the very beginning of the game before you even knew how your childhood stats would affect your adult ones. I find this infuriating and it changes the game into more of a puzzle than anything else.Unless they update the game with a mode where there are no stat checks so you can choose whatever you want your character to do I'd say give this a hard pass. Stories aren't fun or intriguing anymore when you can't do what you want to do because of arbitrary stat checks.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: That product, for I won't call it a game, is a mixed bag. I'd still rate it , mainly for it's world building.But except interesting world itself there are many flaws. I really appreciate the concept of the in-game world, however, I won't say a word about it, for it is by far the most interesting thing to do in the game - to learn the world. That one idea of the game worked great - we get into the place which we (players) do not  know and we explore and learn it from the first days of our life.I'd love to see modding tools for the game. _childDocuments_.review: An intricately made choose your own adventure game that doesn't pull punches, as the title implies. You follow the life of Sir Brante, and make decisions to determine his destiny starting all the way from his birth.The worldbuilding is impressive, it's easy to get sucked in and gradually learn about the different cities, politics, religions and the ways of life. The gods are real, but their will is open to interpetation, which will play a big role in the story. The writing is also wonderful, having the story ranging from blissful innocence to melancholy determination. On my first playthrough (with consequence visibility turned off, it seems more fun to play by gut feeling without metagaming,) Sir Brante fought most of his life to liberate the tortured commoners from the predetermined Lots, the laws that say if you have to suffer and obey or are able to live in luxury and power. After having sacrificed almost everyone dear to him in the fight for this cause, he succeeds, but at a cost that makes it highly questionable if it was worth it, and giving up his own life in the process. ♥♥♥♥ gets real dark in this game, and for the second half i had already racked up my share of guilt over decisions made and people sacrificed. Death was looming around every corner, and i lost trust in everyone. In the end i simply didn't have the willpower to achieve my goal, leading to widespread destruction and death that went way past what i had intended to achieve. I'm eager to play it again in a completely different way to see different outcomes.

_childDocuments_.review: Not perfect by any means, but perhaps one of the best "choose your own adventure" style games out there.It's split in 5 different sections, each portraying a part of your life, each very different from one another. While your early years are formative, the real challenge of the game only starts in chapter 4. This is the one that almost broke me, because a single decision can have a cascading effect, and the only way to rectify that is to restart the entire chapter ... only to realize that you've now locked yourself out of other possible decisions.These decisions you can make are governed by other decisions you may have made hours ago, not just because they are interdependent (i.e. if you condemned someone to death they can't really help you in the future, can they?), but also because most decisions give you various stats (or make you lose them). Especially the first 2 chapters though are very vague about what these stats actually do. You only realize this at the start of chapter 3. And from that point on you can actually go down a specific route. Or try to. Only to realize that the stats you've invested heavily in don't do you any good, despite the game telling you they are important to your "class".See, you will have to choose one of three paths at some point and each path allegedly gets more use out of some of the stats. The game does tell you this, but in my case I wondered why I had ever bothered to put in that many points in valor or whatever the stat was called...I basically never needed it.Trying to keep your family from falling apart, while also trying to shape the fate of the world around you without dying your "true death" (you can die 3 times with no consequence, but the 4th is the end of your game) is challenging. As I said, chapter 4 is particularly long and brutal in that regard. At least as the "Judge" path. I've not checked out the others. I don't think I have it in me, because I've basically achieved the ending I wanted already and chapter 5 is, unfortunately, very linear. You don't have as many choices anymore, you're pretty much shoehorned into what you've chosen in the previous chapters. And that is also the chapter you can influence the least. So, if you want another ending, you'll have to replay previous chapters. In my case to achieve one more possible "good outcome" I would have needed 1 more "power", one of many, many, many stats in the game (not personal power, but power of the people), which was impossibly to achieve in chapter 5. If you want entirely different outcomes you need to go back even further and choose different paths. But now that you know how chapters 1 and 2 are relevant to that choice, you should just replay the game from the beginning and make your choices so you get the best possible stat outcomes. Which kinda makes the game boring to me. So I'm not doing it.All in all I liked it, but found it a bit too restrictive at times, especially the deaths seemed weird. I thought to myself, why would I die in this case? But then I did, and I had no other choice. And then my family broke apart, everyone died or hated me, my career was ruined, my name was ruined, I was poor, and justice wasn't served either, I had to grovel and all my hard work was for nothing. And it basically all boiled down to 1 or 2 choices... that seems, imho, too harsh.The presentation and art style is very neat, sound effects are okay, voice is barely present, but the music is pretty great.8/10 imho ... and replay value if you want to. For me, I'd have to stick to guides or trial and error I think, and that's not appealing, because of my limited time. Otherwise, yeah, sure.I'd like to say that there are enough choices here in the over 10 hours of my 1st playthrough that you, your friends or anyone else will have a different story to tell. And that's an achievement.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll admit I was initially skeptical about this game. Fantasy caste systems and "Catholic vs. Protestant" struggles are well-worn tropes. And the unrelenting grimdark of the first couple chapters was a turn off (at least for me).But I kept playing, and I was pleasantly surprised. The game turns into a gripping, engaging tale with a ton of viable options and playstyles. It lets you set your own goals and challenges, and decide where you want to be on a scale of idealism vs. cynicism. This game will obviously satisfy dark fantasy fans, but it's also great for powergamers who want to combine as many goals as they can into one run. The "best" endings require you to skillfully manage a few variables rather than just letting them max out.---I also appreciate that this game, purposely or not, offers a critique of our brutally meritocratic world. Odds are that if you're reading this, you've had a family pushing you to be a "Noble of the Mantle" in this game's terms, a commoner that ascended to a higher station through study and deeds. There's nothing wrong with that in itself. But our same world gives little credit to people who walk a very different road, and none at all to people who got lost in the wilderness. In Brante, you will meet many people who fell off the beaten path. What happens next to them is entirely up to you. Just know that while you might not be interested in certain characters and variables, everybody and everything is interested in you.

_childDocuments_.review: Kudos to the developers of  for their worldbuilding of a medieval fantasy continent, and melding roleplaying game design within an interactive fiction. But their design of the story progression acts against the very nature of that genre.Decisions are only open to a player if they've honed in on one particular path for their narrative, so that contrary to the open-ended complexity of human decision-making, this just becomes yet another exercise in min-maxing to achieve optimal desired results. That gamification is transparently provided to the player by default--they can hide it in the settings--betraying what kind of idea the developers had for this game experience.One may claim that to live according to one's shifting judgments may tend to condemn one to suffering--let alone that suffering is a baseline condition, particularly for a medieval life--and so this decision tree design is actually true to life; but when analyzing specific options grayed out to players simply because they chose not to devote all their prior decisions to one path, or go all in on whatever a particular character wanted them to do, it's sadly clear that these rails have only been erected at the whims of game designers (as opposed to actual literary writers).

_childDocuments_.review: When people think CYOA games they tend to think the games are easy or limited. Brante (the games) different stats and meters keep the game an actual game. Balancing the also means breaking character from time to time in order to make certain parties and faction happy but it will create a safety net to make bigger movies latter on in the chapter. I don't recommend an iron man playthough especially on the first go around. Even with knowing what the outcome of a choice will be you don't know what points or requirements you will need for choices latter down the line. Having 4 lives also means death might be worthy sacrifice to achieve you goals if there is no other way and there is a achievement for getting through the game without a single death. Now some people really don't like the sat system because they feel it takes away choice but I am of the option it just makes the game more repayable and fresh. As for the story, there are alot of different branches that and ways to effect the ending not just for you but for the entire kingdom, your family, your friends, your lover, and your enemies. Some of these branches lead to the same destination but there are alternative ways of getting there that are only available to your chosen path.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the greatest "visual novel" games of all time (I put this in quotes because this game is much less linear than your average VN, despite wearing the trappings of one. Deals with incredibly heavy themes of faith, ones lot in life, the cruel indifference of the universe and the powerlessness of the individual against the straining tide of the whole. The illustrations are beautiful, the music is iconic and moving, the writing is fantastic, and the background is a fascinating low-fantasy world that mirrors elements of the Protestant Reformation and French Revolution while introducing unique and novel ideas like the Minor Death, a non-human overclass, and actual, real, God-given (?) miracles. I felt that this game, more than maybe any I've played, really makes you question the circumstances of one's place in the world in an existential way. God is real and you are not his favorite, you were made to toil in the fields and worship him until you die. To step out of line will have you banished to hell for eternity. When God by all accounts is real and manifests His will on Earth, how could you possibly deny your place in it? How you react in the face of such existential cruelty (or perhaps indifference?) is the mantra of the game, and the games branching (and very significantly different) paths allow you explore this concept from a few different angles, before working their way back together for a climactic finale. The game is very good at encouraging repeat playthroughs, such that I would probably not recommend it if you want to play through only one ~10 hour run.Just be aware that despite the game being quite long, your entire first run through may be a wash depending on your perspective on bad endings. You're up against the weight of the entire world and more after all, what hope does one small person have in such a tumultuous ocean?

_childDocuments_.review: This is sort of like a gamebook, in which you take on a role of a noble's son (no ladies, sorry) in a world and time similar to the French Revolution of late 1700s and you forge his destiny, from the day you are born until your (hopefully timely) demise. I have finished this game three times already, and I think I've seen around 75% of the contet. There are a lot of hidden bits in the story, which make it impossible to see everything with one walkthrough (or even three). But since the writing is very decent, I felt the urge to go back, and back, and back, to see more of the story, the world, the characters. No two playthoughs were the same, since at one point you have to choose one of three given paths, but even if you choose the same path twice, the events may still be completely different. In the end I never reached an ending which would satisfy me fully, but each time I had to admit the "Suffering" part of the title was pretty spot on. Still, I wanted to play more.To summarize, I highly recommend this title. If you're a story buff, and you don't care for the audio-visual bells and whistles, this game will give you a solid run for your money. Looking forward to more games from those guys.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to recommend this to others because there's too much quality to be found here for anyone to dismiss it outright, but it's quite possibly the most frustrating experience I've ever had gaming. Even after surpassing 50 hours and trying out five different characters, my last run ended in such disaster despite going to great lengths to set it all just as I wanted, a cascade of negative events with no option to avert the resulting crises hit all at once in the adulthood chapter, quickly laying waste to hours of careful planning. There was no reason for it to have still hit that hard, in such an unsatisfying fashion, after I'd taken so much time to learn the game mechanics and treat them with the respect they deserved.Credit to the developers for creating a convincingly hopeless world here, with tons of believably sympathetic and awful characters full of well-written dialogue, and for doing an admirable job of illustrating how difficult it is to effect change at a widespread level, even when that change is noble in intent. I think they may have gone a little overboard, however, when it comes to creating that suffering sensation so boldly featured in the game's title. I'd probably agree that it is some form of suffering to spend hours setting up a character for a particular type of outcome only to find your stat-padded hero missing critical opportunities because his relationship with a particular character is one tick too low, or his family's reputation is just not quite high enough. By the time you could possibly get a sense of all the pitfalls to avoid in the countless disaster scenarios that pop up one after the other in the end game, you'll have read through the story so many times you won't even care to go back and get it right.For the record, I understand this game is not meant to be played to seek out a perfect ending, and I was completely accepting of this, hence my five total playthroughs. I did have one run that came as close to yielding an optimal outcome as I can imagine. I still think this is too much. I stand by that opinion. This is a good game. And I'm never playing it again.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, I like the visual representation and design of the game. Reminds me of Frostpunk. The atmosphere, story, illustrations, interface - all of it looks solid and pleases my eyes.There's a thing, though, I would say typical for such games. That being over-simplification of character development. For instance, if you were afraid of a bug / darkness / etc. when you were four, it makes impossible for you to confront your opponents when you are 10 years old! My point is, some lines of character evolution are simply way too short. I tried to play realistically. But once you find out the logic and mechanics behind your decisions in game, you may begin to play it 'mechanically'. Not for the sake of the story but because you know that acting 'badass' you'll get a 'badass' ending.PROS:- gloom and simple, yet stylish desigh- well written storyCONS:- short and overly simplified character development (not realistic enough)6,5-7 / 10

_childDocuments_.review: This is a spin on a choose your own adventure game that includes player stats. It's a good idea for a game, but the "willpower" stat practically ruins the meaningfulness of your decisions. You can make all the choices that seem best and most in line with the character you wish to create only to suddenly come to a set of decisions over which you have no control because you spent all your "willpower" on making prior decisions. In effect, you're forced into making ♥♥♥♥♥♥ decisions. It's right to include "and suffering" in the title, because Sir Brante is going to suffer no matter what you do. It's ultimately a choice between lesser evils, simply because the character you're forced to work with is weak-willed by design. That makes for an unsatisfying game that embodies the old saying, "You can't have it all." In fact, you can't have most things. You will end up siding with your family, your career, your religion, or maybe some flimsy notion of having made all the best choices you could, given you're handicapped from actually doing that. If you want to take the best thing about choosing your own adventure and throw it out the window, replacing it with a perpetual undeserved sense of guilt, maybe this game is for you. It's not for me. Willpower is not something you lose due to making good decisions. If anything, your will should harden, and you should gain resolve. The mechanics of this game express an absurdly incomprehensible misapprehension of what it means to be a human being making choices in life.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: Not everyone lives in the luxury of knowing one's Lot in life. The Blessed Arknian Empire is a place of immense segregation, as dictated by the Gods, also known more affectionately as "the Twins". The covenant that one is born into can hardly be changed without great effort, perhaps the Will of the Gods themselves can be altered by a man's stubbornness, as well? Alas, you, Sir Brante -- are a man with a dignified sense of this reality: that destiny is in a realm your perception can not yet reach. So, is it true, that the destiny of all living things is controlled by transcendental entity or law? Or that man has no control, even over his own will?Sir Brante is a true example of a Russian made game. It is obviously written and developed by individuals who grew up graciously well read. After all, Soviets and post-Soviets were raised on books. This strong basis and appreciation for higher standards of art and literature, often means that the former Communist world (which in turn, the grandchildren of religious empires and monarchies) is incredibly capable in crafting narratives, characters and story beats that often excel over that which appears in Western media. Western media and the Anglosphere, despite making some of the greatest authors of all time in the past, have increasingly become more sloppified. That is to say, the former Soviet world is not without its unique brand of slop, but Sir Brante is an example of how the diamond in the rough is sometimes brighter than the diamond mines of its contemporaries.However, it comes with significant problems. Sir Brante is a lot like Pathologic, in that it is an experiment in how amazing presentation, meaning, characterization, narrative and ambition can truly carry a story. And much like Pathologic, its inherent meaning is that often - good efforts and intentions sometimes do not prevent great tragedies. As a result, the game itself can be as miserable as life. To really appreciate a game of this sort, one must embrace the darker meanings of life. The mysterious Russian soul tells us that when drowning, sometimes its best to accept the water in your lungs, for when death comes - suffering is already over. But what of the works of say, the Japanese post-modern great - Osamu Dazai? Who more or less says that some people are given a Lot in life to suffer, to live unconventionally within a conventional world of conformity, at the cost of all happiness and dignity. The Eastern world is in love with the idea that our suffering is either for nothing and therefor noble and poetic, or that our suffering is tragic yet beautiful in the fact it is ultimately not at the consequence of the things larger than us. These themes, questions and philosophical, spiritual assertions will be asked of the player directly. One thing is for sure, Sir Brante will take you on an amazing journey. Your youth and adolescence will be formulative to how your life ends, you will have great freedom of choice with some true consequences and meaningful choices - filling you with joy, with despair... And in the end, much like real life, you may just end up too exhausted to resist the hand of that fate deals to you. In the end, by the time you are an adult, your freedom of choice is entirely gone and you are instead, railroaded into a linear mechanic of min-maxxing certain stats and giving up on any sensibility in favour of more singular, sometimes extreme loyalties. And thus, sometimes you just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ die out right and ♥♥♥♥ is unfair.This game is unfair. Its meaning is entirely coherent, and ironically, to quote Family Guy: its largest suffering is the fact that it "insists upon itself". The mechanics, while ambitious and interesting, that elevate this virtual novel into something more gamey - commits a sin. It accidentally confirms its own belief by the limitation of its own structure. The game wants to tell us and show us how hard it is to make tangible change while making compromises of your spirit or to your spirit... and yet, the best tool to hammer this thesis home is the anti-thesis itself. Sir Brante is about human nature, human culture and human life, but it's an ambitious package stuck in a game that simply cannot competently deliver the impossible task it sets forth. A beautiful irony and metaphor. Competent in design, far too ambitious in execution and a truly enjoyable experience at the cost of what makes the game parts a game and what makes the virtual novel parts a virtual novel. The perfect example of a Russian game with an artistic premise.It is so good at what it does, that no one else can touch it, but its so bad at what it is good at - it's uniquely broken and an experience in itself. Much like the numerous glitches and unfinished state of the STALKER games add charm to its world facing an existential threat from anomalies alien from traditional nature and has since, been salvaged by opportunists in more ways than one - Sir Brante is a lifetime-story about how life never goes the way you want and it is a game that never goes the way you want despite giving you the keys.Sir Brante is a car with a beautiful exterior, but not enough under the hood to get you where you want to. But, it goes far enough with the gas you already put into it.I would recommend you play the first time completely blind, on ironman and with consequences hidden. Just so you can get likely soft locked into the same ♥♥♥♥ ending I got (twice!) and from there, abuse some meta, min-max your stats and look up a guide to find a better path. Without meta knowledge, you won't get much of anywhere.Suzerain also suffered from this flaw of not being able to keep the plot coherent while keeping roleplay clarity with its systems and mechanics.My first playthrough, I was a middle-ground bastard and tried to appeal to everyone and be a centrist in a radical front, rather than a radical centrist. It ended with my family completely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ me over by being an endless tragedy machine. My second playthrough, I played the part of a zealot. My family's absolute demise was irrelevant to me, for I had ambitious beyond the mortal realm. The ending I got was dark, interesting, thrilling and one of the healthiest depictions of a loving romance I'd seen in a game of this sort was tarnished by my own inability to resist the path I set myself on. This run was one of the few where the mechanics ♥♥♥♥♥♥ me over in a way that made the game far more interesting and was working as intended. Alas, my family ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ still held me back from what would have been one of the best plot-call backs in the VN genre and I went to hell forever.My third playthrough, I was dedicated to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ my family and doing everything right. At first, I was on the side of justice, but got quickly seduced by a blue lady from the untouchable chaste above me, by many, many heavens of distance. I went from a patron of the people, to a patron of the powerful. And hilariously, despite appealing to both sides evenly, I still got completely ♥♥♥♥♥♥. My stats had me as a sword-saint and I still got murdered in almost every instance of 'combat'. The Gods took pity over me and my mission to at least save my family. ♥♥♥♥ the world, I can't save it, but let me at least save my family! Alas, I took a path that was a combination of my first and third playthroughs. The reputation and strength of a noble, with the scheming of a revolutionary. Unfortunately, since the Gods allowed me to pick a certain place to start up again, I erroneously started my young adulthood again with a build better suited for the nobility still. In the end, I still was robbed of complete freedom and despite devoting myself to loyalty under a seemingly noble, albeit dark purpose - I literally got the same ending I got the first playthrough. Once again, because of the misery of my family exhausting me.What a fitting end. I had walked all the paths, only to be doomed by crushing depression and burnout yet again.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a game that really makes you feel the consequences of your actions. Almost to the point where you want to stop playing, but that's really what you want from these sorts of games. For instance, I attempted to be a power hungry nobleman and ended up getting screwed over in a number of ways because I didn't care about family unity. That happened because I chose to not care about unity, thinking there wouldn't be any big issues to come of it. The world building and writing is good; enough to make the characters and setting feel real. The story beats will be familiar to anyone who's taken a college level European history course, but they're executed well. I hope to see more from this developer, or even updates to this game that flesh out certain paths/add more unexpected possibilities. As a gameified choose your own adventure novel it rivals the best offerings from the "choice of games" series, if not surpassing them in several key ways with its artwork, length, and multiple career paths. Whereas with those games it feels like you are playing the character the author intended you to play, here you have a bit more freedom to roleplay and face the consequences of your actions.

_childDocuments_.review: In my first game I became a righteous judge, defended the people's rights, got grilled by my power-hungry superiors, lost my family to feuds, lost my love to an alien cult, and fled from my country. In my second game I became a scheming double agent, got filthy rich by pleasing the right people with deep pockets, united my family by becoming a momma's boy, and supported my vengeful love by burning my country to the ground.Yeah, Sir Brante's suffering is pretty guaranteed alright.8/10 Writing. Deep, elaborate, clever with some twists.7/10 Game Mechanics. Min-maxing is very much needed, with options leading to well-defined routes. Still feeling like you have some semblance of freedom while being tossed here and there by the times you're in.7/10 Graphics. Simple, aesthetic, though the art style makes everyone look older by at least 40 years. 7/10 Replayability. Pretty much until you've tried all the routes there are. Cool stuff to unveil, though, especially if you care about achievements and details. There are three big routes with each their own sub-routes.6/10 Music. Ominous. Really. Don't play when you're depressed. Wait. Don't play this game at all if you're depressed. (The title should've warned you enough).And, oh, I will dedicate my third game to become an armed acolyte. With some luck I'd prevail without first plunging into zealotry or got kicked onto the streets.

_childDocuments_.review: Got this with Humble Bundle a few months ago (I think, hard to keep track) and now just getting to it.  This game is very good, though it is all text based do beware of that if you don't like to read.  Sometimes the choices are hard even if you are aiming towards a particular path.  In my childhood I thought I was going to try to find a way to "change my stars" as the concept goes from one of my favorite movies, A Knight's Tale, and aim for finding a way into the nobility.  However,  it appears my first playthrough I will be going down the path of the Inquisition.  Of course being the first time through, just starting adulthood, and not having any idea of what type of directions the story will fully go in I am interested in seeing where the chips do fall.With what I have seen so far I can definitely recommend this for people that like these types of games, especially if you catch it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent choose your own adventure story. If I had known what the last chapter was like I would have not have disabled chapter restarts. _childDocuments_.review: After playing the demo I was eager to try out the full release of The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante.I was not disappointed in the slightest, this game absolutely blew me away.The story is masterfully written, the writing kept me interested and invested in these character's lives and their eventual fate. I felt like all of my choices carried weight and affected Sir Brante's life in some meaningful way. In addition I found that even messing up and failing to achieve your desired outcome was still a fun and interesting experience. In fact, that is one of the games strongest features in my opinion. All of my misfortunes were deserved and could be traced back to mistakes I made. I never felt as if the game was being unfair or railroading me onto a certain path.I also loved the presentation of the game. The writing was great and was complimented by an amazing soundtrack and a beautiful artstyle that fit the game's tone perfectly.The ending was fantastic as well. In my experience the ending can usually make or break a game and I certainly was not disappointed in the slightest. Even though I didn't achieve my desired ending (I definitely made a few mistakes along the way) I still found my first ending to be satisfying and it made me want to play the game sometime in the future to see if I can change the outcome and possibly right a few of the wrongs I had made in my first playthrough.I also found the game to be surprisingly thought provoking. The conversations with the Twin Gods were very well written and I especially enjoyed the final talk with them before SIr Brante's final death.  All in all, this game was a great experience. Watching and influencing Sir Brante's journey from birth to death was a lot of fun and I look forward to completing another playthrough or two in the future. If you are a fan of RPG's, graphic novels, or just story-rich games in general, I am confident that you will enjoy The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a really good visual novel. The world is well-built with lots of deep lore. There are 3 main paths you can explore throughout the character's life, each with similar and unique events that can happen. I played through it 3 times and only got half of the achievements as there are events you can get locked out of based on your stats. Although I enjoyed it, I don't think I will be going back to get the rest of the achievements. The music and sound effects are a nice touch. I hated the voice acting but thankfully there was very little of it. There were also too many political names to remember and the game tries a little too hard to emphasize the importance of characters you never interact with. Also some characters were not fleshed out at all and seemed completely forgotten about (Aylis for example). Other than those small complaints, it was a really good game if you can handle descriptions of violence.

_childDocuments_.review: 5.5/10An addicting, enjoyable and frustrating stats collecting game.It is not a choose your own adventure game, there's not a lot of choices branching done here, the game loop is how to meta game to collect the most stats for the best ending, you will have to replay the chapters quite a bit until you learn what stats to collect along the way. Figuring out which stat you should pick('decision to make') isn't based on logic because if you do that you can probably max out some of your stats, and then you will lose points which will lead to a bad ending.this is why the developers recommended that you see the stats outcome for each choice you make, because they know that the game they created will only provide a frustrating choice an arbitrary choices and  consequences experience. So instead they focused on making the game loop on stats collecting until you get the best ending.The writing is mostly enjoyable, the atmosphere is good, the main issue when it comes to writing is that it likes to steal the player's agency. In many incidents you are thrown into  a situation after your character has already taken a few decisions on its own, this fits with the stats collection game narrative. You're more in it for the ride, you will get to reflect on this when you meet your makers.In my opinion the stats design stands in the designers way and made their product less good that what it could have been.The lack of saving mechanics in a game like this is a petty effort to extend the game's life. Buy on sale if you like games of this type.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game, well worth your time. This is easily one of the best VNs ever. It really is a cool life simulator where you have to balance the needs of your family, friends, career, and goals in life and manage not to die four times. It's an enthralling experience.Story-wise, the game clearly borrows heavily from Hinduism, including a rigid caste system, belief in a Nirvana afterlife and the concept of reincarnation.In my first game, I decided to become a priest and aid the reformation from within the inquisition. My family fell apart but I saved my best friend. From the looks of it, this game has many many more paths (not just the three obvious ones, but many variations between them) so I expect I'll be replaying this for a while, too.The UI is simple and effective, the stats are all clearly displayed and you get a good sense of where you can take the story. But much of what happens will be out of your control. The challenge is to do as well as you can and do as many deeds during your life.If you are a fan of VNs with lots of text and personality stats, this game is a 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: This is an excellent game and story. The developers do indeed keep their promise of making a game where decisions truly matter, and where even small ones can effect the trajectory of your life years later. The difficulties of balancing your character's family life, his personal ambitions, and his ideals provides a real challenge and often requires sacrifices to be made.Apart from that, this game also has a lot of well-written characters whom I found it easy to grow attached to. This makes it satisfying when you see them again years later, as well as tragic when your choices or lack-thereof results in their deaths or defeats. I also like how characters who are significant in one of the three career paths only play bit roles in the other two - it shows how often people we don't pay attention to have their own stories and ambitions we might only glimpse. I'd recommend this to anyone who appreciates good stories and good gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: I started The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante by playing its demo a while ago. If you aren't paying much attention to your choices if your consequences are hidden (the game allows you to pick whether to hide the consequences of your choices or not), then it will be overly punishing; but if you aren't, it'll be fine. I highly recommend the game!

_childDocuments_.review: A great text-based adventure with fantastic characters and meaningful decisions but the endgame choices are too restrictive.⠀I had a fantastic time playing through all three paths and you definitely need to do that to appreciate the intricate storytelling and the various perspectives. The writing is excellent, the descriptions are spot-on and both help breathe life into the different places and characters. The stats system is well-designed and truly gives weight to your choices, opening new possibilities while closing some at the same time. Be warned that there are rarely right/wrong choices and the outcomes are not always what you except.⠀There are not many things that rubbed me the wrong way but I wish there was a way to skip directly to the choices page after the first playthrough instead of having to manually "turn" the pages to reach it. Regarding the choices and outcomes, I didn't like how in chapters IV and V things can spin of control way too quickly, ruining the outcome you've been working toward and making many interesting choices unavailable.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this game because of its incredible art style and storytelling, but I cannot recommend it because the "freedom of choice"/"create your own story" is nothing but an illusion in this game.The choices you can make in this game are not the consequences of your previous decisions but are reduced to an accumulation of stat points. If you are trying to roleplay a certain character, no matter how consistent the character you're playing is, there is a high possibility that you won't have enough stat points to make the choice you want. Therefore, I found myself in multiple situations that I have to make the choices that do not fit my character at all, either because I do not have enough stat points or because I need the stat points to reach the requirement of some specific endings. Needless to say this is really frustrating and breaks immersion.In short, I do not think this is a bad game. It is just not what I expected.

_childDocuments_.review: A fascinating experience to say the least if you enjoy reading.The game's backstory takes place as you are a mere mortal growing up into a world slowly, but surely heading towards a bloody conflict akin to a revolution (or simply a failed revolt).There are 3 main branches in this CYOA (Choose You Own Adventure) game, with a forked path in each branch. Your interactions with people and decisions have an impact on whether or not you make it to and past the revolt in the game's final chapter.The 3 branches are:1. Clergy2. Noble Man3. LotlessAs of this review, I have completed 1.5 of the branch (as a Clergyman Prophet, both old faith and new faith). I'm currently exploring the noble man's branch and will save the lotless for last.The clergy branch is a very interesting path if you studied or read a bit of christian history involving the protestant reformation.And yes, there is even a secret sub story playing out very much like the sith if you're into the church of Jedi. That is by killing your master and seizing power while appearing to the world at large as the embodiment of god's Law and Order.

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game, since it has a good story and world setting. I specially like the "tropes": multiple routes, different endings, choices matter, etc.I have to say that it has its share of problems too. As a Visual Novel, it doesn’t have very memorable characters. The ones that are half decent are inside your family circle, since you spend the most time with.Also the game suffer from the absence of "game system". Often, you are split between the choice you want to make and the stats you gains from that choice. In a way, the game punishes you a bit for roleplaying. It would be better if the history choices wouldn't be as joint together with the stat gain choices or if the progression was dependent in a different game system.Despite its flaws, it is a fun game.

_childDocuments_.review: The game starts out with so much promise of nuance and choices in the an interesting fantasy setting akin to Revolutionary France. Yet strangely, it is once you reach adulthood that you find this world offers you all the freedom and nuance that a guillotine offers a neck. The start of the game is so promising, with a selection of interesting choices that help you get a feel for your Sir Brante and shape the character and some of the later choices were incredibly intriguing and engaging. The trouble often, is that whether you are allowed a choice is increasingly predetermined by either your stats or your previous choices, which means that much too often, you lack any choice at all. Your personal stats are often useless, as whether you can call upon them is entirely arbitrary and you are often not given the choice to apply whatever skill you may or may not have prioritised. In particular, do not make my mistake of trying to roleplay a man who tries to join the martial nobility, the only noble choice is to be a judge (despite what the game and the lore tells you) and your 'unbeatable' fighting skills (that's a quote from the stat screen) genuinely will not help you win a single fight. I also played a more cunning and rounded noble, which was much less restrictive to begin with, but eventually, I still found myself railroaded in a pretty irritating fashion. The kind where you are given 3 or 4 choices in a row, in which you simply have no choice and must simply take the single bad or out of character path left, which is very frustrating. The story itself is brilliant to begin with, as is the lore and worldbuilding, but it all fizzles out into a set of melodramatic endings which feel a bit rushed and don't really live up to the freedom and storytelling quality of the early game. I promise I'm not just writing this because there was no option to try and put Stephen in front of a firing squad at the end.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: The game is really ok for one play through, but the impact of your early life on the rest of your life is very limited and the story doesn't really branch off, which made me not recommend this game. - Wait to buy it on sale, it is really overpriced, 17,99 euro is too much for the content.It really isn't better than a 'choice of games' game, which are about 4 to 10 euro. - I did enjoy the first play through and it has some art to go along with it to enhance the experience a bit. But the main thing remains the story, and it is too linear to really enjoy more than two playthroughs. (even though there are three "paths", more like three sides to the same story) Played it through a lot of times to see what made it tick, clicked through is more the accurate description so the 21hrs isn't actual play time.- The UI could have been done better, they are contrast to the artwork and that while the artwork is rather roughly drawn, colored and animated. It all could have gotten a tad more love here and there. The expressions of the shown characters often do not match your choices due to re-use of artwork for every occasion.   - The story has multiple typos, but it's original isn't in English, so I ignored that. I mean I am not a native speaker myself so I can relate. P.S. Dear developers, a well meant tip: do not stream in English if you aren't good at English, especially if you want to explain lore, choices and story paths in detail. I am watching you think for the most part and than trying to decipher what you meant. Still appreciate the effort though!
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: This is a weird case, definitely.The short answer - I adore this game, and you should totally get it, but it's not without flaw.The long answer:This game is without a doubt well-crafted, but I think it could use a difficulty slider.Sir Brante is a game cruel and punishing, and I have no issue with that, I have countless hours on , and I've played  to both endings, I like my games to be a little hard on me, but there are some points where Sir Brante takes slapping the player in the face and turns it into punching the player's teeth out for being a dumbass - decisions you made in previous chapters can and will affect what you can do in later chapters, and the game doesn't place enough emphasis on this point in my opinion to demonstrate the full gravity of this concept - if you're not determined enough or haven't buried Sir Brante's nose in theological books, or any number of other factors, you are irreversibly locked out of certain paths for the rest of the game, unless you feel like completely restarting a certain chapter. On my first playthrough, for example, my aim was to gain nobility to change the system from the inside, whilst supporting my sister, but keeping my brother in the family. Because I had tried to balance out my skills in the very early game, though, I ended up being FORCED to become a fanatical terrorist, having been unable to make any use of my skills because I had been constantly out of willpower. On my second playthrough, I was able to rectify these issues, and for the most part, I was able to, keeping my sister in the family, though I was unable to keep my brother from leaving, and making steady progress towards social reform - I was well-educated, well-spoken, strong-willed, cunning, and good in a fight.And then I reach the end of the game and I'm completely unable to make peace or even get any form of good ending for no reason other than that I didn't grind power, a stat which seemed completely arbitrary and didn't in any way effect any of my playthroughs until that point.I was locked out of a good ending because the kingdom's political climate was perfectly balanced.These flaws leave a terrible taste in my mouth - a game based upon your choices shouldn't really restrict your choices in this way, and while you should be punished for being a dumbass, yes, I don't think you should have to grind a certain stat or restrain yourself from being a good person, just so you can gain some willpower to be a good person in the next scene. The game seems to know this sometimes, since it tends to throw you a bone every once in a while with some major choices disregarding your stats completely, but other times, this game is downright soul-crushing, and I admit with no pride that it was the first choice-based story-driven game that ground my gears so much I took a one-day break from it.I understand "suffering" is in the title, and I understand not everything can or should be perfect in a video game, especially a choice-based one, but I feel less compelled by the trauma and strife of Sir Brante and more "That's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, you're telling me I can't save that guy because I have 11 Valor instead of 12? Time to restart the chapter and grind Valor, I suppose!"Again, these are glaring issues that make the game pretty thoroughly unfun to play sometimes, but despite this, when it's fun, it's FUN, when it's sad, it's SAD. I brought up  earlier, and this game brought me to tears multiple times in the same way that game did, not from frustration or anger, but from genuine attachment to the characters. This game has a way of making you feel pretty viscerally for any and every character you choose to invest your time into, and I love it. You can feel the tension between Stephan and Gloria, and you can tell neither is a bad person, but you also understand their flaws, and don't really want either to get hurt, and this principle extends to just about every character in the game, with the exception of Otton.Overall, Sir Brante has some terrible, crushing flaws, though at the end of the day, it's a wonderfully crafted tale, but only once you actually know how to play it, which is oddly reflective of the game's world itself.Your first playthrough will NOT be fun. That is fact. But, on subsequent playthroughs, you'll likely find yourself engrossed in the story and characters, but frustrated with the lack of choice at times.Thanks for reading.

_childDocuments_.review: Just a brief review for a truly excellent game. TLDR: Choices and Consequences.TW: Child abuse. All the abuse. Rampant cruelty. Painful choices and even more painful consequences.I was a bit skeptical going into this experience. I tend to get rubbed the wrong way when game designers tell me who I'm going to play. However, after getting into it, it became clear to me that isn't what the game designers were aiming to do at all. Yes, while the character’s circumstances will be set in certain respects. However, the formation of Sir Brante (whose first name you choose) is where you begin to actually play. On a fundamental level, this game uses choices to create a rigorous character creator.I’ve been thinking a lot about what makes a good VN or a good game lately, and I feel like The Life and Suffering of Sir embodies the most important aspects. I want to enter a world that someone has put their heart into. I want to feel like the game is a collaborative process between myself and the game designers. Although I can’t make every choice, I want to feel that the choices that I do make resonate within the context of my playthrough. The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante covers all of these areas and then some.  The world of The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante is dark and ugly, and it’s easy to see why so many of the characters turn out to be cruel.  In certain aspects, it’s genuinely hard to swallow this rampant cruelty. In that same respect, it’s easier to play as a coward, or a bully, than it is to be a good guy, or a hero. The game doesn’t ask you to only make one type of choice over and over again (ex. You’ve chosen that you’re honest, just pick the honest choice each time to pass a skill-check). Instead, the game asks you to create a dynamic Brante, a person who may want to live one way, but is so greatly affected by their circumstances, relationships, desires, and policies they struggles to commit to the bare minimum. There is no easy way to get everything that you want, and I can appreciate that. It’s also worth noting here, that this game is hard. However, powering through and finding your way to the “right” ending is exceptionally fulfilling. It’s hard not to grow to love these characters and this world when you stop wanting something better, and you actually start making something better.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the beginning of the future of RPG's.  I just lived a life!  The life of Sir Brante.  And boy was there sufferings.  My Brante had a big heart and big dreams, and he valued freedom above all.  But the reality of the world beat him down.  At nearly every turn he failed.  He made a great friend, and even fell in love, but in the end he died at the end of a noblemans noose knowing he sacrificed literally his entire family and his very humanity doing dark deeds he never thought himself capable of all to fail and ultimately just leave things worse than they were to start with. _childDocuments_.review: This game is what every branching story should aspire to be. From the beginning, it is able to grip you with compelling characters and an unfair, yet enthralling world. There is really a lot of praise to give here.I absolutely adore that there doesn't seem to be a "flawless" way to go through the game. No matter how many times I go over it, there always seems to be a time when I am cornered into a subpar choice because of my previous choices. It's an amazing feature that really boosts replayability as I try and retry to reach different endings or achievements.The worldbuilding is worthy of praise that mere words cannot convey. The world is so terribly unfair that even the gods themselves in it enforce an even nastier form of feudalism than the one we know. It makes your choices surrounding it even more engaging, because the writers have done a wonderful job in making you care for that world's improvement, which is a gruelling task indeed.I will give the writers credit for not going with the easy way out in designing the revolt as flawless and pure. The revolution is a bloody, messy affair that takes innocent and guilty alike, and it takes a lot of effort to steer it towards any improvement in the lives of the people in the world. I particularly like that. It gives you the idea that, no, overthrowing tyranny is not enough by itself. There needs a little more to it than just revolution.I also adore how many things you end up managing at once. Family, realm and job, as well as your multiple relationships. I think the game does a superb job in showing how much weight there is on Sir Brante's shoulders, a man born under the right circumstances at the right time.The soundtrack and the sound effects that play out as you see the story unfold are more than adequate, immersive and beautiful. A must for any game where reading is so important, in my opinion.Every time I replay it, I become surprised, honestly. I am taken to a new plot point or a new interaction with a character, and it becomes worth it just to see how things shape out by the end.My only complaint about this game is about the minor typos that pop up here and there. They hardly hamper your reading, but I suppose I should still point them out.The fact that they are willing to give you the first two chapters for free should be enough to tell you they are confident in their writing and worldbuilding, and rightly so. I cannot recommend it enough that you try the first two chapters for yourself and see if you do not fall in love with the Brantes and their horrible world. I know I have.Edit: All of these reasons, to me, are more than enough to nominate this game for an award for its story, visual design or even its soundtrack, which still sticks with me even now. The only reason I am editing this comment is to justify my nomination and to express the shame that I may not nominate this game for more than a single category.

_childDocuments_.review: A visual novel set in pretendo Europe where you play a scion of the Brante family, would be nobles who are scrabbling to make their title hereditary in a time of social upheaval. The choices available to you as you progress through the game are based on different stats that go up and down such as your character's Valor or Perception, along with scores representing your relationships with other characters. As you progress through your life, you are even able to make choices that effect that stats of cities. However, I didn't make it much farther than this because the story didn't grab me. The character's relationships felt flimsy, and the setting didn't grab me. It's worth checking out as a decent choice-driven visual novel, and maybe you'll like the story more than I did.

_childDocuments_.review: I was really having the time of my life with this game until I hit the final chapter where... suddenly my choices were restricted in ways that didn't logically follow from anything I'd previously done. Overall I'd still recommend the game, but I would also recommend being very conscious of the stats because it's the only way you can really shape a story that makes sense once you reach the end.  So basically...PROs:-incredibly complex characters, relationships and worldbuilding.-A really interesting story with a lot of different outcomes and twists-The choice based mechanics are responsive and impactful - you really feel like you're building a person.-Thought provoking - stays with you for a while.-Some replay value due to the different factions, pathways, etc you can take.CONs:-Frustratingly restricted in narratively illogical ways in the final chapter-Replay value is limited by the inability to fast forward through text you've already seen-Romances seem a little underdeveloped to me-The choice mechanisms sometimes break with plot turns being dependent on stats instead of events and thus sometimes locking you into paths that, narratively, seem to be out of nowhere.-Pretty depressing sometimes, I mean it's a great game but kind of a downer.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: This is an engrossing biographical survival story set in the febrile pre-revolutionary days of a ~17th century fantasy world. The choices you make have a cumulative effect of shaping the game's world setting and the game pressures you to make active choices, though the outcomes of choices in later chapters become obtuse and can diverge from the expectations set by the text. This can sometimes mean being locked out of choices with late game pathways because of a minor choice missed during an earlier part of the story. However overall this is a very strong narrative game with a great deal of player agency over the Sir Brante's life and the conclusions he reaches.

_childDocuments_.review: Initially it seemed like a great game; but the more you play, the more you realise the lack of player agency is both  and . Sir Brante suffers - and so will you for playing a game with a sadistic game mechanic of ambiguously depleting willpower. Want to make a choice that is rationally consistent with your character's motivations or role? Too bad - you can't, you ran out of willpower to do so; while tackling some forced event earlier in the chapter. Want to recover from a mistake? Nope, some stat point types are extremely rare to come by and nearest the "checkpoint" the game allows for can be several hours of repetitive gameplay ago. I hope you remembered the dozens of exact choices you made.Think there is some optimal "best" outcome? There isn't. Min-Max across enough play-throughs and you'll realise that most goals are mutually exclusive - not because of plot or role selection, but because you are only given enough "willpower coins" to buy one of the three shiny things in the rewards cabinet. The illusion of agency shatters pretty quickly once you realise your player choice is simply picking  Sir Brante suffers; not  he suffers.I think the only way to enjoy this game is to play without expectation of agency; which is difficult to do, given how artfully they've disguised the railroading. The game falls into the Uncanny Valley equivalent of player agency. Too much for a 3rd person narrative; too little for 1st person narrative/role-play.
