_childDocuments_.review: , a small team from Tomsk, Russia released  just shy of two months ago and yet feels like it's been there forever! A VN dressed in the style and progression of a RPG- so the minimal gameplay is there but with a great emphasis on choices. Unlike anything I have ever played before, but would be familiar to fans of D&D or choose your own adventure type. This review took way too long because VNs tend to consume me whole and I procrastinate, like I do with my readings- and the storybook format didn't quite help! I eventually did muster up the attention span, literacy level expected me and got everyone . But I was thoroughly pleased with the journey I put my version of Brante through. And most of all, I learned that I would be eaten alive in this fictional but uncanny world. Let me tell you more, but first let's leave the crypt~ *Insert-name-here* Brante, born into an uncertain period where stratification was utterly visible, ingrained and faith heavily influential. That division prevalent in every crevice of your being; self, family and society! Currently chronicling your life, you cover every detail from your coming into the world and you leaving it- wait, that CAN'T BE right... I shall start over *ahem*. It was a warm sunny day~Get comfortable and sink in your chair or bed because it will be mentally exhausting. Well, not at first, since it's all candy and rainbows with the two "perception", "determination" stats and a currency type "willpower" that affords you some choices. But as you age, new stats form, intersperse in preparation for the personality, occupation and influence you want to exert when all goes to hell. Naturally, I modeled the character's traits after yours truly- and I ended up with the most unfavorable and neutral outcome. I typically aim for the "most ideal" playthrough and goal in "your choices matter" games, but here I didn't waver or regressed to the chapter before except for when I died a  (btw, you can die up to 3 lesser deaths until a permanent one) before the natural conclusion. I just wanted to be... me and stand by my principles. Even when robbed of other alternatives, I persevered because I know in my second playthrough, I was going to dominate LSB~ Ink blotches, striking illustrations give it that antiquated stationery look. Ideal to complement the occasional blood smears that appear during more doom and gloom parts. Short bursts of loud sound effects that dissipate after a while keep the scenes alive.The soundtrack is also simply astounding and serve as part of this ambiance. With at times pure divineness or rustic liveliness tugging on your eardrums wanting to be listened to. The rest of the time let out dangerous, somber or uneasy medieval rhythm- sitting idly by and don't detract from the gospel that are the words on the pages. Personally,  was my favorite because of the piano-music box ensemble!! Still, a lot of the score sounds posh and brazen~ The story is overly dramatic, like a soap but not quite as sappy or unbelievable. With elements of love, class, culture, religion, politics and just about anything you can think of... Better yet, I guess it was like watching a season of  or , the latter being if you're from around South-East Asia. I mean that in a good way as there's much to be loved, learned and fascinated by!! You'd want to take your time with this one, as I did and really let the weight of your choices sink in. And the supporting characters are equally properly developed with arcs and personality shifts just as you do, showing the humanness and instability to them. There were ones I flat out hated, desperately wanted to please and others just to curry their favors! But of course, my favorite is still Sir "Me" Brante~SCARY: 1st) It showed me that history is often underappreciated- things that didn't or never happened to us are usually not relatable. So, we go about our lives oblivious to all the suffering before. The very notion that progress and all the rights we have now could just as feasibly ceased to exist will give me nightmares.  2nd) The consequences to each decision may seem futile but they have unknown effects in the long run and how one decision from the past can leave its mark on what awaits is... I mean, I know this already! It's just I keep forgetting, I can't even remember what I ate last week. That's how I got into journaling~3rd) LSB's world and politics were inspired by the developers' own knowledge and research of the Russian Federation, if not also European conflicts. But as a student of Sociology myself, the whole make-up of the society hits close to home. People still fight for fair wages, voices and representation. Discrimination is deep seated, though some remain latent and religion (beautifully and poignantly portrayed) is a force to be reckoned with. Therefore, LSB reminds us we should carefully treasure the past, guard the present and be wary of the future!!I sympathize because the way choices were structured must’ve took countless mapping. That said, some consequences/motives don't seem to be proportionate. For instance, appeasing one character over another sometime hurts the other but other times it doesn't. Or the stats you’re will be gained end up lost instead. So, I can't imagine playing with "hidden consequences"...”Levelling up" your and monitoring your stats transform into second nature and mechanical. It's not about the decisions themselves anymore, but rather LSB is about fulfilling conditions to unlock events. I don't know why I would question the game design as it does work perfectly. Perhaps *too* much so... BUGS: None so far!NITPICKS:~ Occasional typos and letters switched up to form other words.~ Illustrations are heavily recycled.~ Odd choice of infrequent narration.LSB’s page-turner of a world leaves you absorbed and winced. Institutions, events may be fictive but neither their truths nor relevance can be dismissed. Choices don’t seem to matter till you’ve none~ Gameplay serves as both a trip down memory lane and tribute to the ruthlessness that is life. The plot so fleshed out and described with tact, it’s basically an interactive book! The jet-black ink and blood paints a grim outlook to the already depressing setting. Once you realize the real-life influences, LSB enters a whole new intellectual realm for you to obsess over and ponder with anxiety. Its storytelling would be untarnished had it not been for how choices became a numbers game and consequences often so unprecedented that brain cells off themselves. The few and far between typos impeded the flow, but make up for less than 0.5% of the text. Ultimately, LSB’s biggest and most memorable achievement lies in the road it paved for future video games. With exceptional writing- social analysis can be done and so emotionally tangible~

_childDocuments_.review: I'm gonna try not to go on for too long but no promises. At the time of this review, I have only completed one story path, but I plan to do as many as I can when I have the time. This game is laid out similar to a visual novel, and involves a LOT of reading. Usually I wouldn't spend very long on these types of games as I have attention disorders and can often find it difficult to read for extended periods. However the story crafted here kept me engaged and WANTING to continue playing. You make choices all throughout the game, and they actually do impact how everything plays out, so taking time to consider every outcome is important. Making certain choices will prevent you from doing certain things later on in the game, and it will likely take you multiple playthroughs to get the outcome you originally wanted, as some choices can have consequences that are extremely hard to foresee. This happened to me on my first playthough. I knew what my end goal was, and I made decisions based on that. However by the end of the game, I realized I had gone too far and it was too late to change the course of my actions. You are given to option to restart from a certain point and try again, but I decided to accept the outcome, even if it wasn't what I wanted. There are a few minor gripes I have, but they aren't nearly big enough problems to ruin the game for me. Some of the dialogue is clunky sometimes, and there are spelling errors at various points, but they are few and far between. The UI is solid, although the tabs on the side feel useless most of the time. I didn't find myself utilizing them very much, since there isn't much to memorize, but perhaps others will get more use out of them than I.Overall, I definitely say give this game a try. The story is both unique and engaging, and it never feels TOO complicated or overwhelming. There were points where I had to pause and seriously think about my past decisions and actions I might take in the future, but it was a process that I enjoyed. I'm excited to see more from this developer and I hope this game gets the attention it deserves, because it really is a hidden gem.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: I would like to call this an interactive story but it wouldn't properly convey the sheer amount of choices there is in the game. Instead, let's say The Life And Suffering Of Sir Brante is what interactive stories should be.The game is set in a very interesting world and every character is perfectly written. If you like fantasy and don't mind shedding a few tears for imaginary people, go for it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is truly the best choose your own adventure game in its class.The ability to truly watch, interact, and change the world around you is unmatched in every other game like it.Having played many story book games, especially from the "Choice of" series, this is 100x better.The characters all feel so alive, its easy to become attached. Which can be good or bad depending on your choices.The art is very pleasant to the eyes, and the UI is tailored to be easy to navigate.Each of the 3 main story paths are expertly crafted, well written, and will capture your attention for hours.If you have ever remotely enjoyed anything similar to an interactive story book, or are just considering a purchase of this game: DO IT.You wont regret it.I lived and suffered through the life of Sir Brante, and I didnt regret a minute of it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: If there is a game that is 'Dark Souls' but reading-- it's this one.This game is merciless and every bit true to its name. It is suffering. And, by the Twin Gods themselves, it is so good in its agony. The story and the world you live in, as Sir Brante, is fantastic. I have been impossibly tormented by my options and the results. I have had to restart entire chapters or an entire life just to follow the outcome I truly wanted. Partly because I kept dying and I wanted to rip my hair out. I have so much love, and indescribable hate, for this game and its core functions. And really, the hate comes from a place of love. You want things to go well, you want to succeed, you want to be the hero, you want to win! And winning is honestly close to a Sisyphean task. And that's really where the beauty of this game shines. You can't win at everything (as far as I know, I want to shake hands with the Brante that can) and it is *your* Lot to suffer. I think this is an incredible story with a lot of replayability. I don't often replay games and enjoy choosing a different path; however, my second playthrough doing something completely different was more rewarding than the first. It was so, so good, and while there are a lot of scenes that are the same, I was still shocked to learn new things about the story. If I really had to nitpick anything, I think it would be that I wish it was easier to skip over certain graphics per new chapter or jump through a scene I've read many times already. I don't think this game is for everyone, but I stepped away exhilarated. For better or for worse, this story left an impression on me.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: Less you care about collecting skill points, less agency you get in the story.Starts off great but the later part just gets frustrating, not because you have to make hard choices and live with the consequences, but because you're simply locked out of other options because you had not collected enough skill points.And intentionally collecting these points, so that you could make some specific choice in the future, goes against interacting with the narrative in an immersive and organic way.I enjoyed many parts of the experience but it left me feeling unsatisfied.

_childDocuments_.review: The game starts great, with family dynamics and the player being introduced to and invited to form their own opinion about sociopolitcs of this world.Then it throws said invitation out the window, forcing you to join the rebels at 16 just because you don't make skill checks at one particular point (choices behind the skill checks and the one without it could only come from place of strong conviction-which game hadn't yet offered you a chance to form one).And then when you join the rebels it turns out it was COINTELPRO and you either betray them (which again-game assumes you are strongly supporting their cause in the first place) or it's game over.World and story is interesting, but game mechanics cripple it with forcing your hand to do something you see no actual reason to do it.

_childDocuments_.review: Very different from anything else. I ended up judging my character to eternity in hell... which is definitely a first.The story takes place in a parallel universe french revolution. A world entirely inspired by pre revolutionary france, an environment that provides a really gritty, harsh environment with very hard decisions. Will you lead the reign of terror? Crush the revolution? Destroy your family? Fight your brother to the death? Disgrace your father? My playthrough ended when I chose to defend my family against a mob, and we all died. My only other choice was to flee and abandon them while they all die. So I fought to the death to save my family from a revolution I helped start. Uh...yep... that's pretty morally ambiguous!The writing ranges from 10/10 fantastic in the first two chapters to 5/10 disjointed during the 4th chapter (at least in the path I chose). It is definitely best when dealing with smaller, intimate situations involving your family, and worst when trying to explain out all the events (and political machinations) as society spins out of control.

_childDocuments_.review: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante is one of the games that impacted me the most. Your choices really take effect and completely change the story. Attempts to please everyone can lead to a tragic outcome. Taking sides on one side too. A mix of RPG and history books, in a universe more interesting than any other. Get ready to read a lot and try to understand the intricate web of relationships, intrigues, betrayals, deals, and lots. The characters are very well built, with all their motivations (or lack thereof).The choices are very difficult: how many times have I had my heart tight because of them? How much have I questioned my own beliefs?Simply one of the best games I've ever played.

_childDocuments_.review: The game itself is solid, but the quality varies widely depending on the chapter in focus. Chapters 1&2 are only fun the first time around since they never wary, and are plagued by the fact that there usually is a "right" way to play them, and a wrong way. Especially plagued are they by the fact that they are designed to make you specialize your character depending on your estate, but usually checks from all three are required. The fact that you usually need a medium level in a skill to increase it further, and that you reach the lv 20 cap in skills rather fast in chapter 4 reinforces this. Chapters 3&4 are more fun, mostly beacuse they wary completly between saves, and as such you get a lot of fun naration between them. However, only the occupational events wary, meaning that you still get a lot of the same events. Chapter 4 is plagued by hidden trigger events, meaning that you can't do what you want to do (for example triggering a specific outcome for an achievment), which is counter-intuative. Chapter 5 is completly lackluster and fails to be enjoyable the first time, or later times. It is TOO HARD, and the first time around EVERYONE will be slaughtered. Especially annoying is the requirement of you needing to be the leader of the rebellion in order to get any outcome which you might reasonably want. This can only be achieved by specifically planning for it all the way back in chapter 4, which is so riddled with hidden events that even on 3th and 4th saves you still won't manage it. There's also a problem with a lot of the "life events" that can happen being entierly irrelevant, and never coming up again. Examples of this is Brante's first love, which is something you assume will become relevant, but which never did. Another is the cult in chapter 4, but which as far as I know is only referenced in 1 check; and even there it changes nothing. The game however posseses great lore, and the story is great; especially aided by your ability to see it from many different angles from save to save. My first game was a very enjoyable excercice in fictional theology as I constantly looked into every bit of evidence of which of the numerous different doctirines were the "right one", in a world where nobody doubts the existance of the gods, only their will. Spare to say, my character became a willist heretic, and was promtly inncinirated by divine wrath after he finished burning the provincial bishop to death. It will take more than one character to do anything you might want in this game, but luckely it posseses some quality of live mechanics that allow you to skip quickly past previous chapters. Firstly, you can flow through events with a breeze if you utelize the -> key. Secondly: DO NOT TURN ON IRONMAN MODE. There is no reason for doing so, you still earn achievments for going without it an the game is frankly designed for it to be disabled, as you don't want to go back to chapters 1&2 after you have done them once. Thirdly, if you have turned off ironman mode, you can go back to the main menu and then reenter; then press one of the periods in your characters life to jump back to the start of that one. Alternativly, die your true death.There is however a significan lack in a specific and highly needed quality of life improvment. There is no ability to go back halfway a chapter, or go back 1 event. I've had to restart chapter 4 aproximatly 7 times beacuse of this, since I needed everything right in order to actually get the outcome in chapter 5 that I wanted. This needs to be modded in or otherwise implimented. Overall, the game is an excellent game for what it is, but gets progressivly worse the longer you play since you have to do more and more bussywork to dig for new content with every save. This is quite common in any game, and I therefore reccomend that you buy this with only the expectation to play through all the three lots. If you find afterwards that you want to achievement hunt for specific things, then you schould play onwards. Your first 12 hours will be an 8/10The following 7 will be 7/10afterwards, it will be 6/10This is acceptable, and makes it one of the best games in this specific geanra on the marked. A rare exception of a game that through inventive skill and event mechanics manages to make a non-linear visual novel wherin your decisions actually matter; and which gains increased replayability from doing so.

_childDocuments_.review: An almost exclusively narrative-driven literal RPG (it  is a Game where you Play a Role) that takes a new approach to branching narratives while exploring themes of family, politics, religion and class.Life and Suffering of Sir Brante classifies itself as an RPG; which is a good a example of why I usually dislike genres as the only descriptors of games.When you think of "RPG" - in a video game context - you typically associate it with progression systems, combat, open world, side-quests and, of course, narrative. Sir Brante completely forgoes some of that (combat & open world), has a different take on other parts (progression system & side quests) and focuses on one specific aspect (narrative) while pushing you to do something most RPGs forget to do: actually play a Role.In that sense, this game is closer to a "light" tabletop RPG than to other RPG video games. It's efforts are squarely in narrative, characters and branching paths.The key systems at play here are: decision making, extremely branching paths, stat-based progression and economy balancing; but what makes this game particularly interesting is how all mechanics are tied together.Sir Brante has a stat-based progression system but - unlike other RPGs - it doesn't use the standard strength, intelligence, dexterity or magic. Stats in this game are specific and branch out, changing depending on your own choices. It's interesting how the branching narrative is reflected on a mechanical level: an army private does not need knowledge of politics just like a lawyer doesn't need to know how to use a mini-gun.There are no levels, experience or skill points in the traditional sense. You improve your stats by making choices, which brings me back to my initial point on cohesion. Choices shape your stats which you improve by making choices which affect your economy which change the choices available to you which branch the narrative. It's all a wonderful case-study on expressive mechanics... but there's a downside to it.Even though tying all the mechanics back to the story is a nice concept (in my opinion) it also has a negative impact on the narrative impact. Story-driven games typically have you make choices for intrinsic reasons but in Sir Brante, the fact that every choice carries a mechanical, economic or progression effect, forgoing the role-playing aspect becomes very easy. At one point I was no longer driven by the story or the characters, even ignoring what I *wanted* to chose altogether; I was solely focused on the outcome and min-maxing my character. The devs do give the player the option to hide the outcome of decisions but the fact that it was on by default makes me think it's the intended way of playing.Leaving some minor typos aside, the script is very well executed.Characters are deep, with distinct personalities and priorities that come through clearly. They feel like actual people with a story, shaped by their environment. You can almost see the path they took in life that led them to their current world-view. The team also has put a lot of effort into character dialogue, making them all sound subtly different from one another. All of this makes NPCs feel natural and realistic.On a final note, one thing that does stand out about the script is the "style" of the writing. The tone is very serious and grandiose - which is something I find is often poorly executed in games - but here it works (for reasons I get into in the next section).First off, I want to commend Sever for the narrative. The entire experience is very special and one worth experiencing: an "epic" in the most classical sense of the word.Starting with the setting, the world of Sir Brante is complex and detailed. It's clear that a lot of work went into it and the effort payed off. The politics, religion and class-system are very well realized and feel justified and logical. Anizotte, Magra, the Arknian Empire... they all feel like "places": locations that exist, had centuries of history before you arrived and will have millennia more after you leave. The rules of this world are unique and something you learn about as you play. This is one of the things that bolstered by the devs choice to make you play as Sir Brante from the very beginning of his life. There's no clunky exposition or world-building, learning more about the setting here feels natural.As with any classic epic, this game (kind of) focuses on the relationship between the world and the hero. It's how the game communicates its themes and, again, Sever's choice to have you live his entire life adds to the "epic" feel. The meat of the game's narrative lies in how Sir Brante interacts with the world, and the nature of society in the Arknian Empire makes exploring its ideas interesting and thought-provoking. There are, however, two themes that the game explores that felt strange to me: religion and family.Religion is the easiest issue to explain so we'll start with that one. During the game we learn a lot about the history of the world and have the opportunity to directly experience multiple facets of its societal building-blocks. Every interaction with an NPC and their beliefs is steeped in "moral-greyness", adding to the depth of exploration. But when it comes to religion everything becomes "black-and-white". It feels like the devs wrote themselves into a corner and then realized they wanted out of it; it's something that could have been fixed either by skipping the exploration of religion altogether or by changing the rules of the world (though I understand how the latter could be complicated).However, the biggest theming issue for me is family. Like I've already stated, Sir Brante is an epic by definition: it uses an epic tone, it has a clearly defined mythos, it focuses on the relationship between the main character and the world and even has an epic hero. As part of this genre it should stick to one guiding principle: "the concern of the epic is the concern of the entire world within the narrative". In other words, the protagonist's concerns are of little importance to the story; so you can see how the theme of family might be a weird one.Don't get me wrong, the Brante household is a key part of the entire experience and a very interesting one in its own right. The sections in which you interact with your family members are great and feel like a slice-of-life in medieval times. It helps that the characters are all well developed and the dynamics within the family reflect the overall struggles of the world. But there is also a tonal whiplash when changing between the two sections. One minute your choices are shaping the world, the next you're having dinner with your family; no matter how the latter reflects or is impacted by the former, it still feel dissonant.Leaving those two minor gripes aside, I would still say Sir Brante has a very compelling narrative. It uses the genre to its fullest extent while exploring interesting themes in a thought-provoking way. It's refreshing to play an epic game that's not about a saving the world, fighting caricature villains or dealing with some inter-dimensional evil. And it's worth playing by that fact alone.Family, politics, social-class, religion, society.Altogether, this is a special experience that brings something new to the medium. It tries a lot of new things and - like with all innovation - it hits some bumps on the road. Thankfully, said bumps are incredibly minor (and honestly almost "nit-picky") and don't detract from the overall experience. I recommend you give it a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid short visual novel with tough choices and an interesting world which keeps you suspended in uncertainty about what comes next. Designed to be replayed at least 3-4 times to really get the most out of it, it feels fresh just as long as it needs to be. It can be a bit tough - as you can tell by the title - this is a game about life and suffering. I played it with the outcomes of choices turned off the first time around, and it felt much more immersive in that way - but much like real life, it can lead to some pretty rough outcomes.It seems like a smaller team made this one, given that there are a few typos and very barebones production (similar to Obra Dinn in vibe), but it's full of heart.

_childDocuments_.review: You see a little Arknian girl sleeping in an exquisite bed, surrounded by nothing but darkness. The rest of the world is only her dream.She dreams of a prison of gilded cages and noble parties and dances and mansions, all surrounded by a moat of blood that is her father's Blood Tide. She dreams of trying to flee, prying the bars apart, only to slam into the bars of an even larger cage. The Twins tower above her - the cage is their great design.The girl is crying now - she has realized that there is nothing outside the cage.

_childDocuments_.review: Story building centered around character and relations. Characters and the world is realistic enough, for a fantasy world, not to break suspension. Choice matters, even when it leaves room for regret or reaffirming your choices.Still in my first game I chose to play as a despicable pathetic character, as to avoid wallowing in grandure and imagined self importance. It really helps at developing a deeper discust for the world as it is, and I recommend the approach for those who which to replay the game. It seems like the game-creators have supplied a good experience for those of us who whant to do this, as the story does not wear thin although I make all the "wrong" life-choises. To me, that is a sign of a carefull and nuianced script, from creators who put love in their work. I'm looking forward to a replay where I try to set things right, and I think that the experience will be richer than if I did so from the start.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite the text format, believe me, the plot of the game is really deep and fascinating. Freedom of choice is not an empty phrase here, many decisions have far-reaching consequences. The plot branches into many fundamentally different lines depending on the player's choice. The characters are well written. The systems of relations with factions and characters work perfectly. The in-game lore is intriguing yet not too itricate. However, the game is not without its drawbacks. The game mode without hints about the consequences of each choice is a NIGHTMARE: often these consequences feel random, not logical, loosely related to the player's choice itself. Its not fun but causes frustration. In my opinion, if the game decides to punish you, it should at least make clear what are you punished for. I don't like plot moves like "and suddenly a piano falls on your head." Overall, highly recommended to those who appreciate good stories even without good looking graphics.

_childDocuments_.review: An original and interesting world, multi-layered characters, investing story and setting, choices which impact the game and most importantly exceptional writing. At times I was more invested in this game than in any other piece of media I engaged with in recent memory. It actually felt like I was forging my own path within the difficult world of the game, based off the principles and ideals I (Brante) acquired and I absoulutely loved that. What I love even more is how open-minded the game is if you decide to take a more questionable path or make an immoral choice - it doesn't judge you, but instead just alters the narrative in a way that would be respectful of your choices.Long story short - this would have been the best game I've played this year. But then I tried to replay it.It seriously baffles me how a game with so many possible outcomes can have such a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up save system. In the final chapter of the game I had 3 different paths to choose from. I initially went with one of them and finished the game. Then to play through the other two, I had to play through the ENTIRE CHAPTER twice as well. For some reason (presumably because it could make farming achievements too easy? but I honestly have no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ clue) the game overwrites your save whenever a new event starts and then if you want to make other choices you can only do that by replaying the entire chapter from the start. Manual saves would easily fix the entire issue, so I don't know why the devs went for such a stupid choice. I would honestly replay the game a couple of times if I didn't have to sit through all of this stuff. There is so much content in it, but it somehow feels like the devs don't care enough to give you access to it.Still, if you only do one playthrough (which is even somewhat thematically fitting - you know, every person has one life etc.) the game is definitely worth your attention - even with the lacking design. It's thought-provoking, it's original, it's very well-written and it's a very good game / interactive book.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: This is a pretty simple visual novel game/choose your own adventure style game, but there is a decent amount going on to engage you with it. As with any game like that I believe the way to enjoy them the most is to role play, but of course if you play, do it as you choose.The best part of this game is the Lore. There is a great level of detail that will give the player plenty to think about as they progress through. The way the character's believe the world works is slowly revealed to you as you go, and just when you think you've worked it out, the story will hit your with a brand new idea to get you thinking all over again.Then you get to explore these ideas through the choices, where there can be nuances hidden in each passage depending on your choice. A lot of the choices have prerequisites, which you should be able to build a strong sense of character as you progress. It's for this reason that I find the choices with the prerequisites are often better, or better suited, since they reflect the kind of character that I'm playing so they would only be available to them. You can choose to show or hide the consequences, but as you can freely change that option I like to make my mind up, then unhide the consequences. This isn't to achieve "perfect" play, but more-so to avoid the rare blunder where I might have misunderstood what the choice was doing. If I wanted to do something I thought was risky, and it turns out to be risky (even deadly), I'll still do it.The game is reasonably short, so gives you a great opportunity to play through the various paths. There are a lot of minor story arcs scattered about, so you can have several runs through each path to find them. Each chapter is centred around the players choices, which it calls upon you to make frequently. You'll have less influence over the narrative in the early game. Since you start as a child it's more about creating a personality, and forging relationships with your family. Once you reach adulthood you will begin to affect the world around you as well, should you wish to.I've played many choose your own adventure style games that threaten to kill you for making a bad choice. This does add tension, but it can also be an anti climax when your story abruptly ends. Not so much here, as death is not the end. If you do make a careless decision the game can go ahead and kill you without completely derailing things, which I think is brilliant. It's also interesting how the youthful bravado can slip away from a character once their lives start getting used up.As for the end, well there's a reason the game is "the life and suffering", as opposed to just "the life". I've found it quite difficult to actually get an ending that where it felt like everything didn't either fall apart, or I had to make too many compromises that I wasn't happy with. Still, if you find the right character who can strike that balance, it is very satisfying. Even so, if it all goes wrong, I'll know that it was my fault which is all I really need to be left happy.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: While the game seems charming and immersive at first, you will find after a few playthroughs that there is no good end to the game and you are wasting your time by trying. Reviewers will often say it it's a struggle full of hard choices, but it's really only an illusion of choice. Don't waste your time. There is no good ending. They only dangle the possibility and then snatch it away with random events. You may hit all the conditions to proc a certain event, but then the game will generate new randoms that will take your work away and then hand you a crap ending again. Waste of time.

_childDocuments_.review: A very in-depth graphic novel with an original fantasy world and paths that branch in unexpected ways. The challenge is that the longer you go, the more and more previous choices constrain later ones. I think it is impossible to have an unambiguously good life in any run. You have to make hard choices.

_childDocuments_.review: Yet another great addition to already wonderful movement of Russian existentialism. There are two things to talk about here: the STORY and the GAMEPLAY. They are both good, great even, but I'd like to perhaps shed some light so you can decide whether this is something that you'd like to experience.The story follows, well, the life of Sir Brante - a common-born son of a self-made noble. The writing is great and concise. Of note is the general setting, which I'll try to describe in points:- the world has a quite rigid system of castes - noblemen, clergy and commoners- the gods are real beyond any doubt, although they're rather non-interventionist, but there are plenty of things they left behind, and talking to them is not that unusual- there are lesser deaths, and true deaths. You die four times, you die for real. Unless you die by execution in the court of law (related to the gods). Otherwise, you literally respawn in the family crypt. This applies to you as well as others. - things are about to go down, the wind of change is howlingDue to the somewhat unusual circumstances of Sir Brante's birth, his path is his own to choose. This means you can remain a commoner, or try your luck at becoming a nobleman or a priest. Of course, this changes significantly how the story progresses, but in general the story is intriguing, full of interesting twists and quite intense at times. I'd recommend playing the game one or two events at a time due to intensity and better pacing. As for your agency? The world follows its own path, but you can influence certain events. Your choices most definitely matter, and more often than not you MUST choose. Take sides, close some doors to open others. Luckily, the game is pretty good at hinting you which choice will have what story consequences. As for status consequences...You read, you are given a choice, you choose. Standard. But there's an interesting twist: the game tells you outright what the result of your actions will be. Doing this will increase this stat, but lower this one. This will result in your (lesser) death, but will provide these stat boosts and save this person's life. Etc. If you think this defeats the whole point, let me describe the chapter system.In the beginning of a chapter, you are told the possible outcomes for this chapter. Conveniently, you are also given the stat and event requirements for this outcome to happen. As such, you can play the chapter knowing what you're working towards. This makes you feel like you're very much in control of your fate. And don't think for a moment that it makes things easy: you can only choose how to deal with what's happening. And for the most part there is no 'golden' way to solve things. You have to choose. I'd compare it somewhat to Sunless Sea - in that game you also are given the stat and event requirement for given outcomes, giving you an idea of what you need to work on. Except there's less 'direct' gameplay here, and more reading. And more choices, ultimately.The only thing that comes to mind is that you're essentially forced to replay entire chapters if you want a different outcome. My prime run was for the most part very satisfactory, but in the end I made one mistake and got a bad ending. I choose ironman so I couldn't rewind anyway, but what was OK with me, I started a new game. There I was too busy minmaxing and I messed up multiple times, and had to rewind to the beginning of the chapter. To make things worse, there's no fast forward or skip option. Luckily you can just click your way through rather quickly.Oh, and the voice over of Sir Brante is... not good. Luckily it only happens in very occasional cutscenes. It's not good because the character is very jovial which contrasts the general grim and serious atmosphere of the world. That said the faults are completely overshadowed by sheer finery of the general game experience. I'd compare it to a quality whiskey: rich in flavour, delectable in small amounts, puts you in a thoughtful mood. Sit down and pour yourself a glass. Prost!

_childDocuments_.review: The prologue of the game is fantastic. The setting, characters and choice & consequences really drew me in. However, even when consequences aren't set to hidden, the requirements for certain event options or endings are not straightforward. This really comes to the fore in the final two chapters. It is possible to role play as a noble only interested in garnering reputation, and still miss out on being ennobled because your family unity was not high enough. It is a narrative game but not a full RPG, though better written than most that I've played. The world is complex and intriguing but the writing is easy to understand and never superfluous. Each character has strong motivations and presents difficult conflicts connected to the world. The tone of the game reminds me a lot of the movie Barry Lyndon. It is a realistic take on a hero who is fallible and pays painfully for their shortcomings. ...Sir Brante is a difficult game to play and requires a lot of experimentation but the prologue is amazingly executed. Ambitious and refreshing, I encourage you to give this game a chance.

_childDocuments_.review: Half-way through my second playthrough, I have decided to write a review of this game. But a review cannot be written without first explaining the Lot (caste) system that the world of this game has. There are 3 castes in this game, each with its own Lot.First, there are the Nobles. Their Lot is to rule and govern. They have rights and privileges. Originally, only the blue-skinned Arknian race had the right to be Nobles. However, several centuries before the start of the story, humans were given the right to become Nobles of the Mantle, through their faithful service to the Empire. A Noble of the Mantle with a good enough reputation can apply to become Nobles of the Sword, making their nobility hereditary.Second, there are the Commoners. Their Lot is to work hard, suffer, obey and never complain. They have hardly any rights, and certainly no privileges!Finally, there are the Priests. Their lot is to instruct the people in the will of the Twin Gods, and make sure everyone follows the Lot they were given. The Twin Gods are supernatural beings who watch over the world, occasionally coming to people in visions, and even resurrecting them up to 3 times if they die.The protagonist of the game is born at a turbulent time for the Empire, when many of its citizens have started to question the old Lot system. They range from those members of the clergy who doubt whether the rigid Lot system is what the Twin Gods truly want, to revolutionaries wishing to dismantle the entire social order, and many other things in-between. There are also those who wish to keep things just as they are. The player has the chance to decide which of the many groups Sir Brante is going to represent and fight for.This game has often been criticised for not giving the player enough choice in the final chapter. But I believe this is a feature, not a bug! Because the choices available to the hero in the final chapter are determined by many of the choices made throughout the earlier chapters. Also, there is no way to save everyone and/or make everybody happy.From a technical standpoint, the game is a masterpiece. The unusual artstyle and nice music make for a very immersive experience. The writing and storytelling strikes just the right balance - enough detail to make you care about the characters and the game world, but not so much that you are reading endless walls of text.Overall, this is one of the best visual novels I've ever read. If this is going to be your first, it's a great starting point. If you are a fan of the genre, you are in for a treat!
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: This is a must-play for the "choose your own adventure" sub-genre. It's got a great story, interesting characters, and a consistent tone with reasonable pacing. There's a healthy amount of replay value if you want to be a different type of Brante, with certain events only occurring if you've done a long series of things in the past. The final two chapters have some issues with staging actions that don't make as much sense depending on the run, and sometimes decisions that seem logical based on past actions are locked out for arbitrary reasons. Definitely play this with choice rewards visible; it spoils things occasionally, but the effects can be very different from what you'd expect.Overall, this is a great game. I'd buy it if you're at all interested in text-based story games.

_childDocuments_.review: Where to begin with this game... Firstly, I'd like to admit that the game has flaws. Some of the translations are a bit off. You'll commonly find things in the wrong tense or missing a word to make sentences sound natural. Sometimes the storyline is sadly limited and there's plenty of opportunities that will be missed the first time around. That all being said, I love this game. If you're looking to engross yourself in a setting than this one offers more than a heaping helping of lore. From Arknians and their empire to the religious study of the Twins. It's also a game that opens you up to multiple playthroughs, I'm sure some would be rather annoyed at that but I've found that it adds a freshness to runs and actually playing the three styles has very interesting net outcomes. But the most fun, if I can say so, is playing this with a group of friends. It's amazing to make voices and have friends make up voices and get invested in your choices and how they effect their character that they voice. It's a group thing and that adds to the enjoyment overall. But, even on your lonesome you'll find this game makes you question what you really want as the system progresses. It's a storybook, feel free to read it and redo it and take a different path. I've always loved Choose Your Own Adventure Books and this is a perfectly gameified version of those wonderous little tomes. Needless to say, my friends and I thoroughly enjoy this game and I can't say it's perfect but for a cheap price you might find that this is your next favorite story.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing if you love dystopian fantasy stories. You have to choose your path in life, but that is harder than it sounds. Do you obey or not? _childDocuments_.review: The game is overall well-made and good enough to receive a thumb up, though not what i'd really recommend if you expect something exciting or extraordinary.My main issue is the stat system which is too unforgiving. You basically have to minmax your stats and stay locked on a single path during a playthrough, otherwise you will often be missing a single stat point for an obvious choice. Not that it's hard to guess the consequences of you actions and get the stats you need, even if you turn hints off, but the choice variety is lacking severely. You can't explore your opportunities and instead have to replay over to see different sides of the story. Gameplay actually feels like a sort of grind - pretty underwhelming for a game of this type.Nevertheless, the game has good style, well-written setting and interesting story aspects that make you want to replay with different choices.

_childDocuments_.review: Great story driven game with hard choices, wins, unexpected twists, and losses along the way.  I played my first run through on ironman with the hints/foresight function turned off and not really looking at what was needed to unlock events - just living Sir Brante's life choice to choice and trying to adhere to a certain character/personality.  A very bumpy, but enjoyable ride.  It didn't end well but gave me a good feel for the game.  Even though it didn't end well it was an enjoyable play through.  I then played several runs on ironman with the hints/foresight function on and looking at requirements to unlock events.  It was still enjoyable and satisfying for him to achieve "success" even though it still was not possible to win in all goal areas.  I'm not sure how much I will come back to the game at this point but I thought it was well worth the buy.

_childDocuments_.review: This game delivers a consummate interactive fiction experience. The writing suites the drama well, the choices are meaningful and distinct. I will likely update my review after i go back and play through the game a few more times, but i am satisfied by my first play of the game to recommend it. The style is consistent between the narrative and the visual design. The world-building is engaging, and the characters are compelling. The final chapter is quite unforgiving compared to the rest of the game (at least on the path i chose) and tragedy abounds. Despite this, there are many moments of hope, joy, and victory throughout. The emotional complexity and depth is the best feature of this game. The people who worked on this project should be proud of what they produced, and I wish them continued success.

_childDocuments_.review: The story is packed with political intrigue and tough moral dilemmas, and your choices have far-reaching consequences. It's not your typical game; it's more like a book you can influence. You'll find yourself pondering questions about right and wrong, and the game doesn't give you easy answers.Now, it's not for everyone. It's heavy on text, and it takes its time to unfold. But if you're into deep storytelling and don't mind a slower pace, "Sir Brante" is a rewarding journey.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

Watch out, your grandfather is cranky! Ughh...not fun, not compelling.Too late for a refund. Don't make the same mistake.

_childDocuments_.review: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante is one of the best games I have ever played (and I have played a lot). Take this game as a favorite book that you get a hand in writing. I truly recommend it. Thank you to anyone who reads this. Peace be with you.

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful game. To say the writing is engaging would be doing it a disservice. The world is so totally immersive, and the RPG mechanics of managing your personality and social stats so well integrated, that you truly feel that you not only are a part of this world, but you also experience the choices the game throws at you as grounded and realistic, despite the weight of your decisions in the story. In a game with weaker writing the plot might feel clichéd or too eager to praise the player character. But in the life of sir brante, the story beats feel natural, and the hardships your family go through make each of their small triumphs and moments of happiness feel earned.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: This is without a doubt the best game ever made at least in my opinion. However this game is not for everyone as it is a very Eastern European story and you WILL suffer playing it. Most victories are partial and all of them have a price often one that will make you question wither the victory was worth it at all. Failures are deep and crushing but rarely end your game. Morality is a point of view where you must choose between fairness and stability and often one cannot be had without the other while at the same time neglecting one will ultimately harm both. But as cruel as this game and it's world is it is also fair as in the end life is nought but suffering.

_childDocuments_.review: The whole premise is interesting. The world is quite well built. However, as you progress along the story, a lot of the choices in the second half of the game become impossible to access because of decisions you made prior. And that sounds good in theory, as consequences should exist for your actions. However, often times I was obligated to pick a single option out of 5-7 others because I didn't do specific things in the previous chapters. It felt too constrictive towards the end, with no actual choices to be made and with little personal emphasis on how those final events should be played out. And that's a shame, as that part should've been the more interesting one.Recommended for the whole setting and premise, but only on sale. _childDocuments_.review: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante (in Times of the Fall of the Blessed Arknian Empire, obviously) is a text-based roleplaying game with an emphasis on choices, consequences, and stat-management. The story takes place in a theocratic society originally built on a strict caste system. The main character is born in an inter-caste family: his father is a small fry nobleman and his mother is a commoner (lower caste more akin to peasants). This means you have a certain amount of freedom in terms of social growth and at the same time a certain amount of responsibilities and stigmas associated with your origin. You also have siblings with vastly different ambitions, desires, and outlooks on life and society, which promotes conflict inside your family. Also, the whole caste thing, while being oppressive, actually allows people to change their caste in certain cases - say, a commoner can get an education and become a nobleman, which makes people question “why even have a caste system at this point”, promoting conflict between conservative and progressive parts of society.  since the country in question is a theocratic empire, all the societal problems are traced back to religious teachings, which, you guessed it, promotes conflict and schism in church. And yes, gods are also real, every person can, for the lack of a better word, respawn three times and after every death you have a brief contact with higher beings, making things even more complicated.So yeah, absolutely every aspect of the main character’s life is an explosive barrel about to blow up in violent fires of revolt and you have to live your life in it, try to survive, achieve something and find happiness for yourself and the people around you, the last part being the least likely.The game revolves around reading text and making choices. These choices affect your stats (both character traits, the skill set, and the amount of fatigue you experience) and stats dictate the choices available to you. You start building your stats up since birth and carry them throughout your life. This is a contentious topic because stat requirements limit your roleplaying options, but they also serve an important narrative purpose - your Sir Brante is almost doomed to be flawed. He won’t always do the best possible thing in every situation either due to selfishness, cowardice, incompetence, lack of resources or simply because he’s depressed and tired of all the ♥♥♥♥ happening in his life. Sure, not being able to make an important choice by missing a stat requirement by a single point can be infuriating, but as a result, by the late game your protagonist becomes a complex, interesting character with his own set of regrets, failures, and triumphs. Also, because of how good the writing in the game is, most situations and consequences make sense, so as long as you make consistent, in-character choices, you will get a cohesive and rather fascinating human being as your protagonist.Writing is the main reason all of this works. I can’t comment on the English translation, but the original Russian text is of very high quality. It’s laconic, but descriptive, a bit dry, but heart-wrenchingly emotional at the same time. The biggest strong point of the text itself is that it feels like authors actually write from their own perspectives and experience, not from the media they consume. When your character is leaving his home to study in the capital, it's written in a way that feels raw, real, and authentic - speaking as someone who actually did leave his home and family to gain an education in another city. Descriptions of love and sex scenes (however few of them are here) in this game feel like the author actually has a goal of relating the feeling of physical intimacy, instead of retelling a porno they saw someday. Dangerous situations feel close and tense, tragedies hit hard, and every triumph and victory, especially the big ones, feel exhilaratingly satisfying. The tragedy of the Brante family, being the emotional core of the story, is particularly well done. Every family member is a complex, multi-faceted character with both flaws and sympathetic qualities and you see them throughout an entire life of your character, making you feel like you have known them for a long time. There is some stellar character development here and extremely effective tear-jerking moments. The game is also surprisingly thoughtful and deep about the religious aspects of society, going way beyond a “religion bad” argument. Overall it feels like a dark fantasy political thriller (say, The First Law by Joe Abercrombie) augmented by Dostoevsky-esque psychologism and introspection.Also, the presentation with its black and white illustrations, melancholic (and extremely catchy, might I add) music and some fantastic soundbites is great for a text-based game. The soundtrack in particular creates a very specific mood for the game as a whole and for the key scenes in it, elevating presentation.Of course, the emotional impact of a story is subjective and largely depends on the player, but I found my first playthrough to be a genuine journey of self-discovery and felt enriched from playing it. The game has a lot of adult themes - but not in a “blood and boobs” sort of way. It’s adult in a way that it attempts to resonate with the player's life experience. It’s adult in a way that it asks you to reflect on things you have done, people you have hurt, love you have given, victories you have achieved despite every circumstance and tragedy you have endured in your life.I whole-heartedly recommend this game to anyone looking for a deep story-based experience and capable of enduring some of the frustrations linked to stat management.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is masterfully crafted to put you in the shoes of Sir Brante from the first panel. It captures the essence of the "Choose-Your-Own-Adventure" style so painfully close to perfectly. Its simplicity allows you to really get emotionally involved with the story every time you have to make a decision. This is what storytelling and role-playing is all about.Two minor negatives. One, there are spelling and grammar errors in the text. With it being basically a text-only game, it does break the immersion a little. And two, in the same vane and completely my opinion so feel free to ignore this entirely, the "Willpower" system stifles true role-playing a tad. I understand that decisions have consequences, but not being able to make a truly honest decision as your version of Brante due to not having enough of an arguably arbitrary resource you have to manage constantly bugs me a little more than it really should.In summary, this game is one of the best I have ever played. It has become truly special to me and I hope it will become equally special to many. many more people.

_childDocuments_.review: This is so far the best Choose Your Own Adventure/Choices Matter game I've played. Choices actually matter, the game is lengthy (20+ hours for a single playthrough), there is replayability (2-6+ playthroughs) and there are minimal choices that had either improper requirements to choose or improper consequences for choosing them or absent choices.There are many options and branching paths, but of course not every wanted choice is present (such an ambitious project that would be, but one worth striving for I think), and most of them have great impact on your story.Only real gripe is that some of the RPG elements aren't entirely used. There is a comment about getting a stat to 20 enabling to make a singular powerful option, but I only saw one such 20 requirement and it had other specific requirements (I had 20 Saboteur, felt wasted to get it up there; never saw anything else above 16). Maybe in the other life routes? But that isn't very cool, each path should have the option for each stat check once, since I don't think you can get more than 2 stats maxed normally. Also, that too many stat-increasing choices tend to require that stat to already be leveled (I get the idea, but then Willpower should be used more as the Rule-Bending stat).And I guess the many spelling/grammar errors, but they don't break the game.So, if you're looking for a casual game that has a "just one more turn" appeal (there is a hidden consequences/ironman mode too, what I took) then definitely pick this one up.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Worldbuilding, story, music, and art are great. But get ready to mash through hundreds of pages of text if you want to see more than one ending.I want to like this game a lot. It has really detailed worldbuilding, a great story that feels cohesive across all 3 paths, and a cool art style and soundtrack. I'd say playing through it once nearly justified purchasing it.It has one major flaw though: there is no easy way to see all the endings. You can only rewind by chapter, so you need to mash through all the scenes to make different decisions. This requires a lot of trial and error, and a LOT of clicking. I mean literally hours worth of clicking.There's several ways they could have fixed this:- Being able to skip to the end of a scene right away- Having a "cheat" mode that lets you pick any decision regardless of whether you meet the requirements, as some other visual novels do- A better rewind system where you can rewind to a certain scene, or at least go back one scene. I get that they want your decisions to have stakes so you can't just go back in one turn, but ultimately the stakes just becomes "having to mash through minutes of text." They could have enabled this after your first playthrough, for example.(If they end up adding anything like these, I'll gladly change my review.)The game tells you not to worry about getting everything right, but to experience the "life and suffering of Sir Brante." But it actively incentivizes you to rewind and make exactly the right decisions, because all the good endings are locked behind playing exactly right. There's barely any wiggle room, and it sucks when you have to go all the way back to the beginning because you made some mistake in the adolescence chapter. If you play like they recommend and don't rewind, you'll almost certainly either get a game over before the final chapter or get a bad ending. If you're curious like me and want to see multiple endings, get ready to mash. I found you can mash "d" with your left hand and mash the left mouse button with your right hand to get through text faster. It still took me literal hours.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the poor man's version of sealed artifact 0-08.  You shape a man's life from birth to death and decide many people's fate via decisions at critical moments.  While the game gives you visibility of short term impacts on decisions,  the long term impact of the collective decisions are not clear and therefore make your decisions carefully. The game has great replay value as there are many different branches of how the story proceeds.  The chapter 4 alone has more than 15 possible outcomes.   The option to restart from selected chapter comes handy.Achievements in the game require you to go through most of the different branches and therefore not easy to complete.  First run will take about 10 - 15 hours and subsequent runs will be much faster as most of the text have been read. The game runs perfectly on steam deck.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, first review ever, hopefully that speaks for itself.Look, if your anything like me, you play video games to experience great stories. Some people love the action, the grind, the visuals, the music, the community, the *insert your preference here*, but I play for a great story. So giving a guy like me a choices matter game is the equivalent of straight heroin (this writer cannot actually comment on the effects of heroin). I've played damn near all of them, high budget, low budget, text based, high res, choices are meaningful, choice is an illusion, I've played plenty.This game pulls you in, keeps you there, and asks you to come back for more (an ask I accept willingly).I just got wrecked, spent 8 hours building my life, making key choices, developing key relationships, becoming a "Brante" the Brante family could be proud of...................... and my principles got me killed. Looking back at my life I probably could have done some things differently, but I guess I paid for the things I believed in. If you can me tell another game that makes you feel that way, then please shoot me a message, I need to play it.I now have to give this game another run, partially to my chagrin, partially to my excitement. Pay the $20 it is 100% worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent writing, intriguing world, unexpected course of events and difficult choices to make. I wish there were more games like this. The most beautiful thing about this game is that you can choose 3 completely different paths and experience what is exactly going on in the different regions of Anizotte. You have chosen to be a noble and supressed the revolt but you want to know what was happening in the Church in that timeline or you are wondering how the revolt was prepared to this very moment? _childDocuments_.review: I rarely write reviews. However, I felt compelled to write one for this game. I've played many games during my life; however, very few felt so memorable. As for this, I would say by far this is one of those games that really sticks with you. I believe this is a heavily underrated game. That is because most people nowadays enjoy action-packed games, and there are not many who enjoy visual novels like this one. But if you value a good story more than gameplay, I say try it, and who knows, you might develop a liking for games like this.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely stellar game with meaningful choices. I love the fact that you can see what the immediate stat/relationship results will be from each decision you make. It gives you just enough information to feel like you have agency in how you shape Sir Brante's life. It makes it easier to live with the consequences of your actions and the storylines are so drastically different that I'm extremely tempted to play through it again to get a new ending. The setting and story also pulls brilliantly from history while delving into fascinating fantasy plots.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante is an incredible story that puts you right into the shoes of a young man in a country wrestling with its outdated social and political systems and lets you live out his life (and suffering) while deciding what, if anything, to do about the issues that plague his world, as best as one man can help in affecting such massive systemic change. It is a beautiful narrative, has some of the best writing you will find anywhere (even after translation from the original Russian), is so often emotionally raw, and is deeply reactive to the player's decisions. It is the perfect blend of a RPG, a choose-your-own-adventure graphic novel, a personally-driven sociopolitical satire, and a masterpiece of Russian literature. Oh, and I almost forgot, the art is absolutely gorgeous and the music is unbelievable.It is a must play for anyone who likes to read, who is interested in the history of social and economic change, and who enjoys punishing games that do not hold your hand. It has immense replayability, but once you get it right, you may not want to see the story play out any other way.10/10Buy this game at any price as soon as you can.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played other Choose your own adventure games before, and I always had a soft spot for the genre. What I like about The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante is the level of presentation and feature to help the players with the experience. In other games, they rarely tell us why the consequences of our action happens, so I appreciate that this game does it so I can fix my mistakes for next time rather than it becoming a tedious puzzle games to figure out what I did wrong. The greatest strength is the very interesting world-building and you get to develop your relationship with the characters, family and friends alike. Although it is the game's best strength, I would also say that the amount of text possess a challenge to some players, but I acknowledge that this is the type of game that appeals to certain group of players. I hope to see more games like these with the same or more amount of presentations. The beautiful visuals really helps with the immersions and keeps me engage with the story. I can't really say anything more critical beyond continuity errors with a certain character being mentioned to be alive even though they should be dead, and some of my choices didn't fit the criteria at the end even though that I should have marked them.

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing game that perfectly captures the memories of the classic choose-your-own adventure stories.The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante pairs a medieval fantasy aesthetic, a gorgeous art style and an immersive soundtrack for an experience that far outshines any other "choices matter" RPG of its kind. The constant balancing act of building Sir Brante's stats and guiding his life makes for a game that sucks you into the story and the world of the Blessed Arknian Empire. Despite the intense amount of reading that is required due to the unvoiced dialogue, I found myself being immersed in the lives of the characters, enrapturing me in the story of Sir Brante.Your choices truly do matter, with three over-branching lives that you can lead as Sir Brante, with multiple outcomes leading to the end of your life within each, the replayability of this game easily justifies the price. Easily one of my favourite games in a long time.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played this game for some time now and honestly, it is so disappointing. There are far too many limits imposed upon the choices that you make and it makes the entirety of your effort and invested time feel completely pointless. As an example, if my judge character has 20 valour and 20 diplomacy then surely there should be a way for me to achieve a reasonable outcome. Any outcome, at all, is all that I ask for. No, it forces me in the strongest possible way to choose between the concepts of justice and my career. You can opt for the two extremities and that's it. There is no room at all for the middle ground. In certain circumstances, your choices are cut off because of a deal you made a few years ago that ostensibly bares no relevance to the choice that you want to make. For example, making a deal with Mayor Egmont will preclude you from being able to negotiate with El Vernel (if that is his name, I can't remember).It is frustrating because there is a lot of interesting world building and many of the choices that you make are interesting and meaningful but the circumstances mentioned above are far too common for me to enjoy the game. A real shame.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really frustrating game in more ways than one. I wish I liked it more, because I really dig the style, setting, and atmosphere, but the game just seems so hellbent on forcing the player into bad positions to really enjoy this thing.You pretty much have to play this with a guide, or just trial-and-error your way through until you can actually get to the ending. Maybe I'm just a bad player, and I'll accept 'skill issue' in that case, but in my opinion, it should be generally more forgiving. There are a ton of skill checks that require you to have planned ahead since the very beginning, and *yes* I understand that the point is that the world is frustrating and unfair. That doesn't give the game free rein to punish the player just because the story is supposed to be this herculean uphill battle. Even Soulslikes, vaunted for their difficulty tying into the story, generally give you the freedom to play how you want. Playing this game with a guide takes the fun and novelty out of crafting your own life in the game, but unfortunately playing without one ends up making you bash your head against a wall of skill checks.I wouldn't have even given this game a review if I hadn't read the dev's Q&A, where they justified the amount of planning/math required in the game by saying we use math all the time in games and just don't realize it. Well yeah, no ♥♥♥♥ we use addition all the time. It's probably a problem if a main complaint from your players is that there's too much math involved.I absolutely respect the devs for creating a vision for the game and sticking to it 100%, but I sadly cannot buy the whole "losing is actually more important than getting forward" shtick. I get it, and sure, the game is immersive and makes you care about your decisions and all that wonderful stuff, but after a certain point I just couldn't care less what happens. I guess my Sir Brante simply gave up because of his suffering, and that is a decision, too.

_childDocuments_.review: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante is one of those games which gives you, the player, a far greater insight into your protagonist’s life. But the game actually goes one up and lets you develop Sir Brante, the protagonist, in the image/personality that you desire. You get to develop Sir Brante from his birth to his inevitable destiny. Death and rebirth, Success and Failure; everything is in your hands.The decisions you make with Sir Brante’s personality and traits will go a long way and help determine the person he will become, as well as the world around him. Everything from how relations are forged and kept to Brante’s successes and failures. This is not your typical Story-rich, RPG, Choices matter game. Oh, no sir! Every choice has its outcomes and consequences, and your choices translate into Brante’s traits, his ambition, his estate, his occupations, and more. Plot: In the year 1118, life in the Great Arknian Empire is harsh and desolate at best. Robart Brante, a nobleman, and his commoner wife Lydia welcome their newborn to the world. First, there was peace and darkness; a never-ending silence. Now, all of a sudden, breath or air touches my (Brante’s) skin. Two shadowy figures stand right in front of me. As I reach my arm to the figures, I feel a warmth that I’ve never felt before; there is peace and safety in that touch. I gradually realize that these figues are my creators, my parents. For the coming years of my life, everything that I will learn will come from them. As I start to understand this world, I realize life isn’t easy. Everything comes at a cost and has its consequences. Every decision I make may affect my future, the person that I will become. Whether I succeed or fail rests solely in my hands and my hands alone, as do the events that will take place around me. Gameplay: The game progresses through year/years at a time showcasing different stages of Sir Brante’s life. And throughout the course of time, you have a lot of control in your hands.You get to decide who and how Sir Brante’s character will develop, and from that, all the necessary traits will emerge. The game progresses at a good pace, and having all the controls in my hand, I went through the game with ease according to my own comfort level when it comes to reading. Utilizing a minimalist UI and controls fits the game’s setting just fine, and adds a deep sense of immersion into the game’s overall theme and story arc. The game features a robust style of choosing options and direction which determines where Sir Brante ends up in his life, from before his birth to his inevitable demise. Going through each option and choice in life furthers the story, and Sir Brante either gains or loses traits according to your choices.The game also features an interesting Character Development Journal, which tracks everything from family, estate, status, titles, etc. Which seems like a no-brainer, but it’s actually very clever and features well in the game. You will pass through some major turning points in Sir Brante’s life – Childhood, Adolescence, Youth, Peace Time, and The Revolt. Hard choices will need to be made and the difficulty will vary, being impacted by your previous choices and the traits that have been gained.Game design:  Visuals and design are absolutely brilliant!  With a crude art style, design and colour scheme, there’s a strong sense of Medieval times which fits the game's narrative and story arc just perfectly.  Music and Sound effects: Although the background music is nothing to write home about, the sound effects were absolutely brilliant when it comes to a real sense of immersion and deep connection with the characters. Positives: + Brilliant Story arc+ Well-put-together immersive visuals + Interesting sound effect scheme+ Choices have impact and consequences + Journal that keeps track of Sir Brante’s life and status + Some well-developed characters + Theme appropriate visuals and UI Negatives: - Very much felt the need for more compelling background music“By the pricking of my thumbs, Something wicked this way comes. Open, locks, Whoever knocks!” - William Shakespeare. Your choices have greater impact and consequence than you think. 8/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!
