_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the better written games I've played. That in and of itself has high value for me.As you might be able to tell from the title, screenshots and clips on the store page, this is a heavyly text based reading game with a grim tone. The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante is a game about political intrigue, clergy/religion/spirituality, power struggle and it is about family (and that's what's so powerful about it). All in all very high concepts, not remotely trivial. There's absolutely no humor, albeit tons of misery. You grow closer to people and get sentimental, only to have your heart broken. The descriptions are tasteful. No vulgarity, but much violence and hatred. The aesthetics are well fit for this style and tone. Not an easy read, though.Set in a fictional world reminiscent of our middle ages, you as the protagonist are born into a situation where you have the opportunity to overcome the handicaps of your inheritance and take your fate into your own hand. Maybe even influence the world you live in on a greater scale. It's all there for you to become a man of the people or a tyrant, consumed by ambition. However, it is more likely that you attempt to balance all powers surrounding you and then fail to have a meaningful impact.One thing you need to understand while venturing forth is that this world does not follow the same rules as our reality or its history. There are metaphysical elements you have to make your peace with. Redarding lots and lesser deaths. You'll see. There are also constant mentions of the Twin Gods, which you might have heard in another game. Forget about that.There are only so many outcomes to this tale and you will need to subscribe to one of them. Trying to never step on someone else's toes and be wishy-washy while going your path causes you to lose agency in the long run and will terminally lead to a unsatisfying conclusion. The game warns you early on that you have to make tough decisions you won't want to make. In order to see your goals come remotely to fruition, you need to play the long game and sometimes take a step back so you can take two steps forward later. The game lets you decide whether you want to see the outcomes of your choices before you click it, which is kind of mandatory to make an informed decision and to steer things your way. But that extra information could also paralyze you. While it is true that you cannot see all of this game's content in one go and that it changes depending on your previous descions, the majority will be identical and once you played it with that sneak-peek feature on, you rob yourself of the opportunity to be surprised, maybe shocked. For the most part at least. So beware when you start the game.Not only is this a visual novel, it is also a roleplaying game with corresponding mechanics. Almost always are there variables in place that increase or decrease whenever you make a choice. Some of them flip a switch which has lasting consequences. You have status attributes, that only go up and should be as high as possible to unlock options at certain times. Also, there are other varying factors where it is preferable to get them into a sweet spot on the higher end of the spectrum, but not too high or it gets out of control. Can't say I've seen that in other games before.The thing with these RPG aspects is, it can get pretty frustrating. You may be confident with your development, only to find out that you are missing one point at a critical time, forcing you to take an option you can't identify with, which consequentially leads to events where you need to follow up on those choices, straying further from your desired outcome and compromising your entire run. Should you find yourself in such a situation, you may want to start the chapter over. Because of the perfidious autosave function, there is no way to quickly redo anything. So you either have to suck it up or fast-forward as much as the game allows through the start of the current chapter to have another chance. Either way, it is frustrating. But it doesn't matter, because at the end of the day everything is futile anyway as it seems. You may convinced yourself you found your niche in which you and yours can survive, only to learn how miserable and tragic it turned out in the gut punch which is the epilogue. Thanks for that.This game wants to be replayed. You can construct a different built, focusing on different talents, going down different paths and see their endings. Good luck trying that on your own, though. Should you strive to get most if not all of the achievements, you will need to have a guide handy. The alternative is way too tedious.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn’t want this game to end. But end it did, Sir Brante’s life, just like our lives will one day. Maybe this review will too?This game reminds me strongly of two other titles. We will come to those. But first, what is The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante (LSSB), and why should you care about this little game? Are you supposed to care because it is described as a hardcore RPG on Steam? It’s not an RPG. And that’s just fine.So why then? Because it is tagged as Choices Matters, the same tag that games with two alternative ending scenes get? What a ridiculous tag. Choices matter? No, LSSB is  about choices. In fact, it is the only way you can interact with the game. By making choices. And that’s just fine. Once upon a time in a distant century there was a home computer game called Alter Ego. In that almost completely text-based game, you first filled in a brief personality questionnaire that would set your in-game personality seed. Then there was a splash screen with an ancient quote by the Roman politician Sallust: ‘Every man is the architect of his own fortune.’ How true, your actions shape your destiny. And what a complete load of BS at the same time. Easy for him to say, a Roman noble who picked Easy Mode at game start and was born into power and wealth? Could a Roman slave shape her destiny? But LSSB doesn’t start that way. It plays with this very duality in life throughout.Anyway, after that splash screen in Alter Ego you were thrown into someone’s womb somewhere in America. That was the given. The rest was life choices. The text narrative progressively presented you with an array of choices that shaped your game life, be it short or long, miserable or wonderful. The game ended with your death. I was very young when I found Alter Ego, and although I couldn’t have fully grasped the mature content it still made a lasting impression on me. (Note: You can still play it today for free in web-based C64 emulators.)LSSB is *that* game. Only much longer, smarter, better written, more interesting. Illuminated with beautiful woodcut style artwork. Set not in America but in a fantasy world. And it is perfect just like that.As opposed to Alter Ego, LSSB openly shows you the “stats” influencing the storyline – how you affect these stats through your choices and how those stats in turn affect some of the opportunities and events life presents you with. You can partly hide these stats in the settings, and I recommend you do just that in your first playthrough. Immerse, and let your instincts, your ethics and your heart make the choices for you, not the stats.What is the game about then? Well, it puts you in the shoes of a titleless son of a petty noble family in a fantasy land, from birth to his death. And that’s about it. And that’s just fine. So it’s a fantasy game then? Yes but… we need to frame the fantasy in LSSB or you won’t understand the choice of setting.The style of the artwork, not to speak of the setting and certain events in the game, it is all suspiciously reminiscent of Europe in the 16-18th century. Of the social, political and religious turmoil during that period - of the estates and inequalities in society, of the religious conflicts of the Reformation, of oppression and uprising, and in a sense very accurately so, not at face value but as a parable. Then why didn’t they make it a historical game instead? After all, isn’t fantasy a bit silly? Doesn’t the setting detract from a game with such a serious address? No… it’s just that… I will make a claim, regardless of whether it is false and not at all what the developer intended, I don’t care: The developer, Sever, had to make it a fantasy game, or the illusion, the parable, would never have worked on us. It’s a narrative ploy, a #%&$ brilliant one at that.Sure, genres such as fantasy and sci-fi sometimes pick up on tendencies and ideas from our time and throw them into new light. But it’s not that. It’s this: If LSSB had indeed been a historical game about life in late Renaissance-Enlightenment Europe, a time period that laid the foundation of our values today, then how could you as a 21st century player possibly walk in the same shoes as someone born into a lower estate? As someone who actually believes that the nobility has a divine right to rule you, that you will invoke God’s wrath by questioning society and morality, because the priest said so? You can’t. Except if it is fantasy. LSSB tells you right from the start that the world is ruled by twin gods, that the current order in society pleases them, and that they will punish those who break the order, for all eternity. That includes your game save! Can you be absolutely sure these gods exist in the game? No, but in a fantasy setting you have *no reason to question the assumptions, the conditions.* And *now* you’ve put on the shoes of a citizen in Martin Luther’s Europe. *Now* you are a commoner in an uprising holding a pitchfork in your shaking hands, or a frightened noble whose castle those evil ignorant peasants just set ablaze. *Now* you are a well-educated revolutionary in France hiding in the shadows, knowing that you risk your neck anytime, fighting for your Easy Mode 21st century rights that you got at birth – for free. LSSB gives you a taste of what it must have been like. Few other games succeed in bringing history to life. There is e.g. We. The Revolution, a similar game. You have Kingdom Come: Deliverance, a very different game using a different method, with a protagonist so painfully naïve that his surroundings has to point out and explain the proper ways of 14th century Bohemia to him. It sort of works. But LSSB hits you in the guts.I was about to say even few novels have succeeded in truly bringing history to life, but there are notable exceptions. Have you read Hilary Mantel for example? If not, then you should. I’m not primarily thinking about the Wolf Hall trilogy (if you don’t have the patience for books, then at least watch the BBC TV series namesake with stellar performances by Damian Lewis, Claire Foy and, above all, Mark Rylance). I’m rather thinking about A Place of Greater Safety, a novel about the French Revolution. The thing about Hilary Mantel is her way of writing. The vivid yet accurate historical narrative, yes, but there is something even more unique about it: She doesn’t write series of static events like everyone else. She writes process, about *things unfolding.* You know that feeling, when things unfold? It’s now it all happens, your break, finally. Or that moment when your guts tell you things are about to turn to crap. That feeling when life is good because you keep doing the right things, forging your own destiny. Or when you’re miserable and realize you’re the only one to blame for your situation. Or that idea that things are going great because you’re really something, only it was just luck, circumstances. Or that other idea that you are kept hostage by cruel fate, only you’re actually not. Or those times when things around you just spiral out of control, and there is literally nothing you can do. And you may say to yourself, ‘How did I get here?’ All those things, I think they are called life. And that’s LSSB for you.Get it, LSSB I mean. It’s a wonderful little game that inspires to big words.

_childDocuments_.review: Essentially a virtual version of those old paperback choose your own adventure novels I adored as a child,  tells a depressing, yet tantalizing story about a strange magical world. You essentially follow a dude's life from birth, to his death, and witness and/or participate in drastic events in the world. Whether you decide to follow a path that your family wants for you, or strike out in something a little different, it's all really up to you. However, choices in this game NEVER come easily, and no matter what happens, expect to feel the "suffering" that's part of this game's title.  bills itself as a hardcore RPG, which feels kinda weird at first, considering there isn't really any combat or dice rolls per say, rather a set of stats you keep track of over time. It's more of an RPG in terms of playing a SPECIFIC role, which you have to decide for yourself in the dreary, dark narrative of a late medieval setting. By the end of my first playthrough I understand why it mentions this now, as you do make choices that influence events an actions available down the line in drastic ways. For those who want a great story wrapped up in important choices,  is a masterclass in this type of game. I can't wait to see what the developer comes up with next!

_childDocuments_.review: This is, at its core, a highly polished and stylized visual novel. And it is a very, very good one at that. Like the staple of the genre, it provides you multiple story pathways, based on your previous choices. What is unique about this game however, is the amount of branching pathways. An enormous amount of data is considered when you are presented with a choice, and the way you can take the story forward is locked by some of your stats and previous actions. Some may dislike that, but I don't. It adds weight to an already serious storyline and makes you reconsider when you are about to take action. The way it deals with stats is also pretty clever. Taking no action for a particular event is actually beneficial sometimes, since this is the only way to generate "Willpower", which then can be expended for more crucial choices. I think it also reflects real life very well - we may remember a moment of our weakness which motivates us in the future to take action.The Story is grand, and it is told quite skillfully. What elevates this visual novel over others is, unexpectedly amazing musical score. The nostalgic family tune still brings a tear to my eye, it is that powerful. The stylization of the game puts itself apart too, immersing you in the world of Sir Brante. The eponimous character itself, although shaped by your action, is a great protagonist, who can be as honorable or as vile as you deem to make him. All actions are valid, if your end goal is so.Finally, the game is like fine wine, to be savored one sip at a time. I have only finished one path of Brante's life, which would amount to 40% of the game. But I think I will save the rest of the game for a later date, when I wish to relax and enjoy the company of Sir Brante to the fullest.Great game. well worth the price. 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I was very impressed by this game. Combining the major revolutions in European history: the Reformation, the French Revolution and the Russian Revolutions (particularly the October Revolution) - this game follows the path of a young man from birth into his adulthood while the Empire he lives in slowly falls apart. You can view it as following one person's life, but I was drawn in by the developer's haunting descriptions of a society that's fraying and splintering. From the adolescent chapter until the end, you see a society's idea of justice transform from a religious tenet to equal protection of secular law.  The main character's family sits firmly in what modern day audiences would call the upper-middle class and the main character's father starts the story working within the civil service, but for the quickly modernizing feudal society, the main character's family sits precariously between the three estates of the aristocracy, the priesthood, and the peasantry. Due to the unusual situation of his family's social standing, the main character has reasonably clear roads to all three estates, but the roads he has open to him at birth may have quickly narrowed by the time he is only 12 years old due to his own decisions of what's important to the player at the time.  There are some supernatural or fantasy elements, but don't be fooled: this is history. When viewed through the lens of Russian history, the magic in the game isn't really magic. It's more to force modern players into a perspective of what it must have been like for rural commoners prior to 1917 (the Russian Revolutions) and particularly 1861 (the liberation of the serfs in Russia). In the game, the Arkinians are an alien race that rule over the Empire, but the Romanovs, the Russian ruling family, were viewed by rural Russian commoners prior to 1917 as something close to Godlike. Much like the Arkinians in the game, the Romanovs had relatives with very well known names (e.g. Sheremyetev, Yussopov, Naryshkin, Miroslavsky) descended from Vikings and Mongols scattered across Russia. Like the Nobility of the Sword in the game, the Russian state also had hereditary nobility descended from ethnic Slavs, but they had markers to show their Slavic roots. Finally, like the main character's family's standing as Nobility of the Mantle, there was a small layer in the Russian society that was well-educated, cosmopolitan, and at least somewhat self-made and largely populated the Russian civil service. There was a strict order within Russian society, particularly when it came to the serfs before 1861: Lots are just an in-game religious explanation for what the legal situation was for 90%+ of the Russian population. Yes, you can "win" but I found it difficult if not impossible to win on all fronts. You could become professionally successful, but you may not be very happy with your family life. You could be happy and united as a family, but your professional outcomes would be generally poor. The trade-offs are fascinating. The only mechanic that I take issue with is "Willpower" - it's the point system that the player expends when making a hard choice during what the game considers to be a difficult or emotionally/mentally/physically taxing decision. There were times that willpower was expended on what was not a particularly difficult or taxing decision. I say that, but I don't know if I have a better alternative. I do have to say that the branching alternatives, particularly for the pivotal Childhood and Adolescent chapters, would be too easy game effectively if it were not for the expense of Willpower.

_childDocuments_.review: Very good story, however, the choices you make in the game will give you points. These points will be distributed under several categories, you'll need a certain amount of points to make other choices.This system, although interesting, forces us to make certain choices in order to get enough points rather than choices that go in the direction we want. A bit frustrating but well compensated by the visual charm and the sound ambiance
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: The story is very interesting and the storytelling is good.Frustrating, however, is that you are sometimes forced to make decisions absolutely completely against your characters interest, motives and previous (long series of) choices because you miss a simple check (for example, missing just 1 point of some attribute). This has happened several times where I have taken care to stack attributes that are important to me, yet always missing out on 1 point at a crucial moment leaving me to make a frustrating choice antithetical to everything my character stands for.Unbelievably frustrating and no way to mitigate it during gameplay. Made me ragequit an otherwise very enjoyable game because this happened one time too many.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: Family issues, the game, but other than that it was fun trying to appease everyone while at the same time doing what was best for me. Gloria hated me by the end of my first play trough and I was murdered and Stephan threw away the family name at the end of my second, the grind for a good ending is real. The choices matter in this game but a lot of times you won't be able to make the choices that you want unless you have the stats from making previous choices and the game autosaves so they really want you to roll with the punches. Thankfully, this gives the game a lot of replayability especially with all the achievements.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: A massive thumbs up for this game. Its enthralling narrative and the weight of your choices feels relevant. That is rare. It is a text-based game so not everyones cup of tea. I have grown up with text adventure games so this is a rare treat these days. Last time I got this involved was when playing Disco Elysium. This is a game for those who find equal pleasure and enlightenment in literature.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: This is great! Lots of choices that matter, lots of paths that lead to entirely different scenarios and in each of these scenarios even more possible paths to find.If you don't mind reading and playing in a relaxing way. This might be the "adventure book" game you always wanted.My only complaint is that a few choices are designed a bit forcefully like a tournament you can only win by honoring a specific name beforehand or that you cannot stop a certain ritual no matter what you do. But these types of restrictions are at least partially unavoidable.8/10 for me
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: Wow... admittedly, I originally bought this game just to acquire a profile background. I am so glad that I decided to play it and give it a chance.This game is incredibly fun and had me honestly playing it for 10 hours straight (with breaks in between). The amount of choices that this game provides you, and its consequences or events that occur in your favour is just... mind blowing to me. The story, the lore, everything that relates to you and your entire family bloodline is just amazing to see unfold when you make decisions. Such a wonderful and fun story driven game. Definitely recommend that you buy this game, it's so good if you like narrative-driven hardcore RPGs. Jeanne is based. Has to be said.
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: It's not just a game, it's a MASTERPIECE.I felt like I was reading "Les Miserables" the whole time I was playing. The characters and events are so connected, there is nothing left to add, there is nothing left to take away. The plot makes you think hard before every decision and reflect on your own life. The game doesn't enforce any agenda, it's a rare thing nowadays. God bless Russian game developers. The creators managed to keep the balance between the variety of choice and core ideas. If you play the hard way, the game will literally make you suffer. Like real life at those times. So intense!The music and the sound gave me chills. Guys, I could praise this game on and on, but you just need to try it yourself.I wish I could work on such projects with the creative and industrious team that made this game and the highest praise for me when I create my own game would be if someone compared my game to The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante. 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante

_childDocuments_.review: A narrative-driven RPG set in a gritty world where a person's Lot is determined at birth, while the gods are real and preside over the fates of men. Set out on a lifelong journey and carve out your own destiny. Will you become a judge, an inquisitor, or conspire against the old order? You decide!

name: Diplomacy is Not an Option
detailed_description: Just Updated About the Game Diplomacy is Not an Option is a base-building survival RTS with an active pause, taking place in a medieval fantasy setting, where your choices can decide the destiny of the world. You step into the well-worn shoes of the minor Lord. Circumstances force you to fight. Like all the time. Always outnumbered. Build your walls, raise your armies, and experience warfare on an entirely new scale. Over 25 THOUSAND enemies assault your castle walls. You're going to master engineering, economy and even magic If you hope to survive. Your King is a mighty and powerful leader. Also, he is an egocentric pig. Adores to drink and in general he's enjoying his life. But after the treasury had emptied and even raising taxes had not helped, it became clear that he could not continue his leisurely lifestyle. Which is a problem. Mostly yours. Because peasants, who are not fond of raised taxes and hunger, are rioting in your feud. King demands you put down the rebellion and go to the distant land to get some gold. (Rumors are there is one where there are tons of it) Will you do as your sovereign bids and set sail to replenish the palace coffers ? Will you join the violent leader of rebels to bring the tyrant to justice ? Will you help poor natives of Uncharted Continent ? Or will you cast aside human nature and ambition and lead armies of Undead ? Questions, questions, questions. The one thing you can be sure of is that no matter what faction you support there will be blood anyway. And legions of archers, swordsmen, siege weapons, knights, and more will be staying by your side for you to achieve your goal. While admittedly tongue-in-cheek, the laws of physics are still deadly serious in Diplomacy Is Not An Option. Every arrow, catapult stone and enemy launched skywards is physically modeled, making for a tactile and coherent battlefield. Just make sure your troops have towers to shoot from and clear lines of sight, or you might find your best-laid plans embarrassingly blunted by your own fortifications. Consider your gates, your lines of advancement and retreat. Create kill-zones and fall-back positions. You will need to take an active role in combat to get the best from your men. Even under siege, never forget your castle was built on the backs of the peasantry. Defend your people, and they’ll serve you well. Engage in agriculture and farming, or food can become scarce, and your soldiers can starve on the battlefield. Build houses, bury fallen soldiers and peasants to prevent plague, and treat the infected when death comes knocking. If you do not care for your people you may soon find yourself overrun with the most unpleasant troubles. Like empty stockpiles, unrepaired walls and running dry barracks… or be overrun literally with swarms of zombies. And no lord wishes to see zombie apocalypse in the backyard of his castle, right ? A functional army requires a functional economy to support and feed it. Food, Wood, Stone, Iron, and Gold are the foundations of your city’s economy, and you will need to watch your supplies carefully if you are to meet the advancing foe in a timely manner. Gather resources, choose your storage locations, plan your expansions and upgrades with care. The enemy will not cede their lands willingly, and unprotected civilian expansions will have consequences of falling prey to the hostile incursion. Trade, via the impressive merchant dirigible, bringing emergency supplies of food to feed the men, or stone to rebuild the walls. Can you strike the balance between greedy expansion and security ? If life gives you lemons, make lemonade. If you’ve inherited a cursed kingdom, why not master the dark arts ? Sturdy castle walls will protect you from most ordinary threats, but in Diplomacy Is Not An Option you're also be battling undeads. So why give them a monopoly on magic ? There is a dark history of tainted power that stirs zombies and traps wayward souls. On the lighter side: it can also be used to call down really very big fireballs onto your enemies. So enjoy that too. Build magical monuments, harvest soul crystals and give a try to a maniacal laugh as searing magical beams tear through your foes and summoned ghosts to chase down the stragglers. The game has been designed with freedom as a core concept. Go beyond the campaign and crush your foes as you see fit in Endless Mode, Sandbox Mode or Challenge Mode. Develop your own personal strategies on procedurally generated maps. Go heavy on walls early, build large armies of cannon-fodder, or pursue the macro game of greedy growth and costly investments. Play battles in real-time or use pause constantly to keep everything in your hands. Will you be able to stand on a par with the most acclaimed generals in the world, like Joan of Arc and Genghis Khan ? Finding which style grants you the most success is up to you. As in real life, stupidity and greed lie behind most problems, but here it is far too late to talk it through. You have no recourse to resolve this peacefully. At this stage : Diplomacy Is Not an Option !

It's so relaxing hearing the stringed instruments while the birds are chirping and the wind is blowing. I really didn't think I'd be talking about the soundtrack mainly in the review but good grief it makes you yearn for the springtime.

The endless mode is really fun and the campaign has loads of potential.It's a really good base building strategy with all the satisfying upgrade mechanics you love to see in these kinda games.  There are only two campaign levels right now but I can't wait to see where the game goes.

Setting control groups requires several attempts, trying to select units constantly double clicks selecting everything instead of just 1 building/unit. _childDocuments_.review: Ever wanted a cool tower defense game but takes 0 actual skill and setup and you have to use guides and know your "build order" just to survive the "medium" difficulty? Ever wanted RNG in your game to make sure you have to constantly reroll maps just to have a single hope of survival? Yeah, that's this game in a nutshell. The balancing for endless more is completely off, going from the easiest mode you can take a nap and still survive, while the medium difficulty makes sure to end your entire career because you got a garbage map set up that keeps you below the difficulty curve. The difficulty scaling of waves needs to be completely overhauled as you don't even get a chance by the 4 wave. Resources a joke, everything requires wood, yet wood cannot be replanted, leading to you being forced to expand to keep up with demand, which then leads to more food demand, which leads to more food sources, which leads to more wood. In order to keep up with his crazy cycle of wood demand you have to expand and make you base bigger, but as you make it bigger you need to make more and more walls just to secure weakness, yet there are hardly any choke points in a tower defense game, so expect to expand in a 360 map just to get stone, iron, and wood which are FINITE early game. Honestly the worst economic tower defense game I've played which punishes you for expanding, yet you NEED to if you get bad mountains, stone, or metal.This game forces perfection on any difficulty just to keep pace with the waves of enemies. By far it is the least relaxing tower defense game on the market, go play any other, at least you'll enjoy your time instead of hitting the reset button after an hour of failure again and again.Edit 8/13/24: Played the game again after years. I don't think a single thing has changed. Trash difficulty curve, RNG, limited resources, literally nothing has changed. I don't even see new units, maps, or anything except the sandbox mode. The sandbox mode kind of sucks to, making your options so limited. I'd like to actually see the devs play their own game without cheating in crap or you know, surviving past wave 4.
_childDocuments_.name: Diplomacy is Not an Option

_childDocuments_.review: I have played this game in EA, and boy has it delivered on release. I am not even half way through the campaign, but it's just astonishing. Also, for me, unit balance was very important. During EA melee units were just a source of problems, spreading disease.Now they actually make sense, because of how fast they regen, AND the attacking waves include archers, who prefer focusing units behind the walls, which makes archer spam less viable, or even better, forces you to have melee units to draw fire on them.There are still a few units with limited to no use, like axeman, horseman and footknight (the alternatives are just better), but the game is already in a very good spot.Content wise, campaign is story rich, however the cutscenes could use a button to skip to next animation. I also hope we get some extended research, more naval team, etc.I know devs won't do it, but I will ask once again for multiplayer :)

There is plenty of content already and the game mechanics are really smart.Performance is an issue. Even outside large fights and with low quality video settings I am not getting above 40fps. Taking into consideration this is (very) early access, I can take it with the same dark humor the game offers :) One word to its competitor. There is another Indie Castle builder out right now: "bacastled". This one is so much better on all fronts... Have fun, lords!

_childDocuments_.review: I had to change my review from Yes to No recommendation. This game just feels really incomplete and doesn't really add anything new that other wave defenses don't already have. The campaign is only 2 missions. Endless mode isn't "endless" because resources are finite and you can't build forever. Unlike games such as They Are Billions, the resources run out. I'm not sure if that will be something added in the future but I can't recommend this currently, definitely not at the price point. The game is not near completion. Just wait until then.

_childDocuments_.review: Great blend of RTS and wave defense. The campaign's writing is charming, witty and funny. I love the back and forth between the king and his advisor. Gameplay is very well balanced, being just the right level of difficulty for me. It was very engaging trying to balance economic growth with military might.
_childDocuments_.name: Diplomacy is Not an Option

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoy this game for a number of reasons and love many of the mechanics. However... the absolutely merciless ramp up of the difficulty in the campaign on the 4th mission is insane. I've learned a few things and started to progress a little bit farther but still haven't completed it, even after dropping the difficulty down to the lowest setting. I always get to a certain point where it just seems impossible to fend off the constant waves of enemies from the south while also dealing with the regular hordes of enemies that come less frequently and doing the objectives at the same time. I end up using all of my resources on the first things I mentioned and have nothing left to trade in at an insanely bad exchange rate for gold so that I can build the troops needed to put on the ships. I begin to run out of resources in safe areas and have to build work sites that inevitably get destroyed when the next large wave comes. The time in between waves seems like just enough to recover from the previous one, only to get rewarded with a fresh wave of enemies. I feel like this would be a whole lot better without the constant wave from the south. Then I could actually focus on the other mechanics. Please fix this or ease us into this difficulty better by teaching us more about the mechanics.This is really my only complaint about the game, everything else has been pretty great. I would like to be good at this game but the learning curve is either very steep or it simply hasn't been play tested to make sure you can do it on all difficulties. Maybe the devs can do it easily, but new players will definitely struggle.
_childDocuments_.name: Diplomacy is Not an Option

_childDocuments_.review: I like the bit I played but feel like the game kinda doesn't know what it wants to be, city builder? colony management? tower defence? main thing is that it does non of them well but all kinda meh.I liked building the walls of the city and thinking how i'd defend it but when the enemies came your archers just shoot through stuff and your footmen are just really good compared to the npc (this was the very begining so maybe later it's harder) plus the combat is kinda weird like I'd click my guys to fight but half of them would just stand around while the other half actually fought or they'd ignore the enemies and just attack a hut instead. Building the city was nice it looks nice and its really easy but it does lack in depth and there's no real point in building with any order and you can't place stuff right next to each other or the townfolk would get stuck in the building meaning your city takes up way more room than you think you need.Why have a tech tree/research system? seems kinda pointless, instead just give me better stuff as I upgrade my keep, just seems like something they added because other games have it, doesn't add anything other than an annoying thing I have to check every 2 minutes which add kinda pointless upgrades.The management aspect is really basic, your guys eat food you just gotta have enough each day kinda thing which you get by placing a fishing hut etc.. It's simple and not worth noting for the most part its just really basic.I do think adding the power to shoot a laser from the sky or spawn some guys from hell is also a pointless thing and they're really op,.I do think this game could of focused on actually making good defences a more important thing rather than just lasing every enemy from orbit just seems like a kinda missed chance.Overall I refunded this game and will keep tabs on it for the future as I think it could be pretty good given some time to stew and respond to feedback :)
_childDocuments_.name: Diplomacy is Not an Option

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of Warcraft 3 castle defense maps, I tried this out and it scratches the old castle defense itch. It's more fleshed out of course than any WC3 castle defense map was and has an addictive endless wave mode. Updates here and there bring nice additions. If you like building castles and defending them without a crazy amount of complex mechanics, this is an easy buy.

_childDocuments_.review: Super dope game, it involves economics and resource management that constantly keeps you thinking, random  combat that always keeps you one step behind so you're never truly winning, monotonous tasks automated to keeps things fresh. I would recommend this to any fans of rimworld, city skylines, factorio, it combines elements of all 3. 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Diplomacy is Not an Option

_childDocuments_.review: Great game already, but with the potential to be even better. If you like base-building and wave defense games, you'll love this.A couple of things I'd love to see added eventually:- automatic trading in the market- bigger trading airships (maybe through research)- a button to send the next wave right away- bigger maps- maybe a gold mine (could be heavily defended by rebels and you first have to free it)- unique high end fighters (maybe like a wizard or Robin Hood or a Gregor Clegane or a bard)- storage and granary lvl 4 (maybe subterranean or only buildable into a mountainside)- (or) research options to unlock bigger storage space in the respective buildings- research addons for available units (e.g., more range for archers or healing for swordsmen or stealth for healers) - maybe some reward for killing rebels (scum!) ... like 1 gold for every 50 rebels from a wave or some of these magic stones (because you can't replenish the latter once all rebel settlements have been .... liberated)- also, the records for how many days you lasted should update not just when you die, but also upon saving the gameFinally, it would be cool if we could switch difficulty levels during the game (in case it's too hard or too easy) ... it could be a new category of endless gameThanks for making this.

_childDocuments_.review: Diplomacy is Not an Option - This is yet another great sandbox-style city builder.Excellent, simplified and elaborated graphics, nothing superfluous. Good gameplay without which there is nowhere and beautiful to the ears melody. Throughout the game I have not encountered a single bug or minus, if there were any minuses, only not significant.All of the above can be seen here, I advise you to buy and play in the evening with a mug of beer, just enjoy the atmosphere. All the best and goodbye

_childDocuments_.review: At the point, I'm just forced to give this game a negative review. I first bought this game in EA to support the game because I liked the idea, and the gameplay was kinda fun. However, the game has had 0 progression for almost 2 years. The dev should be ashamed. They put up all the update news to attract more attention and funds, yet I don't see them have any intention of completing the game. The campaign had 2 missions when first released, and now, 2024, still 2 missions.... with the same message telling you there will be more coming. Don't be fouled. This indie Dev don't deserve any support

Automatic thumbs down.Developer contacted me privately and asked for screenshots of what my screen looked like, and said that using a PC on a 4k TV was an "unusual" setup. _childDocuments_.review: Ever play Starcraft 2 Terran campaign?Remember the mission where you are in the middle of the map, and there are infected terran and zerg in all 360 directions, and the goal is to wipe out all enemies surrounding you? (attack during the night)Well this game is basically that SC2 mission/They Are Billions with it's own unique combat system and econ etc.if you enjoyed that mission, this game is that mission x10.Devs have an enjoyable British cheeky sense of humor.Solid seemingly balanced game after 6h.Just gimme Starcraft 3 dammit.

_childDocuments_.review: Until they release more Campaign levels I can't recommend this game. You can play endless, sandbox, or challenge mode instead if you want but $25 (at time of writing) for a singleplayer game with only two campaign levels out is ridiculous. When you load the game you can see in the campaign menu where they put something along the lines of "the rest of the campaign levels will be added when the game leaves early access."It's been in early access for almost three years now. You could just release a few levels at a time until they're all finished.I liked the first two campaign levels, I just want the rest. Don't buy the game until it's out of EA.

_childDocuments_.review: Well made and thought out, excited to complete the game as well. Hoping I don't have to run through every single level again to in order to see the alternate endings, hoping I can just pick up at the branching campaign points. Gameplay and economy system on point, seems scaling is working well as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Crashes too often in a few stages, but runs smooth on other stages.Cannot set units to follow other units, you range units will attack enemies on their flank and attract them but you melee units will walk too far away to protect them. Cannot queue moving paths for rally units, your units will rally through enemy units/base.Cannot rally to units, sending reinforcements is unnecessarily complicated.Only way to select individual low health unit out of multiple units is by zoom in and spam clicking until you pick the right one.There is no clear indication for dead units and small enemies. It is very difficult to identify them in the base where there are many other units and structures.A lot of the missions in different campaign paths are similar
_childDocuments_.name: Diplomacy is Not an Option

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game after a really long time of seeing it around. Honestly, I loved the idea but while playing it, well. . . it just feels really boring and lackluster. I feel like roads should be a bare minimum in building a structure and the development of your settlement should be a higher priority. I mean basically this is the entire game in a nutshell. Build some wood collectors, build some housing, build food, build a bigger army, repeat until you have enough, clear map, build walls to defend and put some archers on top and done, now do it on a different map. Don't get me wrong, its fun but after one game, you have pretty much played the entire game and it is time to rinse and repeat. The bigger you build, the more resources it costs and the more you need to rinse and repeat so it has some serious diminishing returns. I really am glad that every single time I saw this game, I resisted the urge to buy it and waited till it was a game in a bundle and got it like that. Honestly, I'm just surprised it is still marked as early access after so long.
_childDocuments_.name: Diplomacy is Not an Option

_childDocuments_.review: I tried the free demo of this game before purchasing it... and then 5 hours later I realized that 5 hours had passed.This is an interesting strategy game that is definitely worth the investment if you are looking for something to occupy your time.Similar types of games that led me up to this game (even though Steam recommended it to me) were Sim City 4, Cities Skylines and Tropico 5.My main dislike about this game is that I still haven't figured out how to build fast enough that I don't get terminated by the rebels before I can establish a real foothold.
_childDocuments_.name: Diplomacy is Not an Option

_childDocuments_.review: An RTS with (I am promised) epic sieges in great walled cities with hordes of thousands and spells raining down from the sky.After you get past the (for me, so far, insurmountably boring) opening levels, which entirely consist of micro-managing a small, slow ranged army to circle the map, painstakingly picking apart dozens of large, slow melee armies, while ctrl-v'ing houses and logging camps. The engine looks amazing. I'd happily skip to the bits in the ads.
_childDocuments_.name: Diplomacy is Not an Option

_childDocuments_.review: I usually don't like this play style for games but this won me over. It's an incredibly challenging and mostly fast paced game that requires lots of strategy. The game however is far too hard, even on easy mode. There is little to no room for error and success is pretty much just based on the rng of map generation. Some maps suck and you get screwed. _childDocuments_.review: This is a game I've wanted for quite some time, and it has not disappointed. It is a very fun, unique and dare I say 'cute' approach to the RTS/Tower Defense genre that scratches all the itches I have. Dev on it is steady and when content patches come out they are rather meaty so I don't get my panties in too big of a twist when they come a few months apart from one another.It is very smooth and elegant for what it is in its current state and I haven't experienced a bug or issue yet. I wish I could code like these folks do. Outside of some balancing issues (and what game doesn't experience that in its development) I'd say buy this up immediately, it's a very good time. The short story thus far is also very humorous and witty, I rarely skip a scene because the humor strikes even when I know it's coming.My suggestions thus far in the game would be more enemy types, a more strategic AI, and probably a nerf to trebuchets.  Could use a short ranged combat unit that you have to pay attention to and focus on. Keeping to the theme of filthy peasants perhaps people throwing rocks or using slings instead of a sophisticated bow/crossbow. They could also use a hunter style unit that went after your soldiers/people specifically. Perhaps a hunting dog that could burrow under walls and chew up your peasants/soldiers but wall units are safe. It seems at a certain point each level that defense stops becoming the main concern and shifts toward resources/supply. Enemy waves tend to come from 2/3 directions tops and once secured in those directions, you can leave entire sections of your fortress empty or even open. If there was some kind of 'defensive power' stat that the AI analyzed before picking an attack route before each wave, that would make levels not only more replayable, but much more interesting. Example: archers have stat of 1, a wooden wall has a stat of 2. North wall has a 3 wall section with 2 archers, south has 1 and 1, east has none, and west has 2 archers. Prior to the wave, the AI calculates the power based upon the compass directions and effectively divides the map into a big X in quadrants. It'll have a much, much higher % chance to attack from the east because it has the weakest defense stat.   ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ these things are so fun and awesome, but really, after building about 4-5 of them, you've won whatever level you're on. I don't think the power of them needs to be nerfed, actually with my thoughts to changes on them perhaps even buffed a little. I think they need to be permanent fixtures like a building once 'deployed' somewhere, increase their minimum range so they can't shoot targets within range 5 and a worker peasant assigned to them like a resource node. Each time they shoot, a peasant needs to run and get a stone from storage and bring it back to load. This provides players with choices to risk resource storage closer to front lines in order to shoot more often, and makes trebuchet's a more strategic choice of placement as they are effectively a building once deployed. You would also think twice about building random towers with trebuchets on them all over the map if you were risking peasants, stone, and pathing into your fortress to do so.All in all, a fantastically fun game, one that I've sat down to play with the intention of putting in an hour, and looking at the clock to find 3 has gone by. I'm very excited to see where this goes from here.

_childDocuments_.review: Revised Review: After giving this game another look, can start to see that developers are making the necessary changes to make the game more playable and enjoyable.  Attack indicators on the mini map make seeing where attacks are occurring a lot easier, in addition to material harvests being more fair. Other modes have been added so you can enjoy more than just the two levels they have available. Rogue units are still a thing as of writing this given that its easier to keep units and citizens from dying from hunger or being killed from aforementioned changes.Original Review: This would be a good game if not for the fact this game as of now only has two levels. I get it's in early access but come on. In addition, the rouge units being able to sneak in to my city and start causing damage is a nightmare to deal with especially on the easiest setting. In addition, with the maps being randomly generated, that  can make or break a run on a level. Also the way you can train units is also a bit of a hassle. In RTS's I've played before, as long as you have the resources and haven't gone over the unit cap, you are free to create units. In DiNO, you have create more population through houses which take resources, in addition most units also require resources that you need to spend AND you can only get more units when a day in game has passed. This creates a rough scenario if you need units stat.Theres also the issue that I always seemed to run into never having enough food for my city. Either resource gathering is too slow (even with research) or the payout for food and resources is too little. And if you don't have enough food, your city begins to starve which results in not being able to create new units for battle AND if it goes on for long enough citizens and troops will start dying. The dead need to be buried lest they spread disease, and undertakers can be killed just like every citizen or unit. And if bodies haven't been buried, they become zombies, which will in turn attack your city. The thing is, having all of this creates a stupidly delicate system where you're micromanaging your city more than you are commanding your army to complete levels. When you start losing citizens to enemy forces, this causes major disruptions to your city which ultimately causes a negative feedback loops where you just end up in an uphill battle just to win a map.The game shouldn't be that hard. There's honestly just too much going on and too much relying on the day night cycle that just to keep moving forward. And again the rogue units are also a pain in the rear because you can hardly ever tell where they are.

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty good They Are Billions clone with several changes that I think improve the game a lot. Has speed settings (unlike TAB) and pause and reasonable zoom (unlike Age of Darkness). Its unique point is the physics simulation, which mostly means if an enemy changes speed or direction during the travel of a projectile you'll miss, shooting over obstacles will reduce accuracy and range, and if your siege engines don't have clear shots they'll often impact terrain dealing no damage to the enemy hordes. While zombies do exist in the game the main enemies you will defend against are actually revolting peasants who have their own siege engines, which can be interesting. The game has several resources of which two are infinite on the map eventually (food and wood, limited in the demo but at tier 2 you can get infinite food and tier 3 infinite wood), two are finite on the map but can be traded for (stone and iron) and one that can only be traded for (gold). The fact that tier one defenses and units as well as some tier 2 units can be recruited for only food and/or wood keep them relevant longer.The game is somewhat buggy currently, and performance apparently is severely impacted on certain CPUs (12th gen i7s I've seen repeatedly), but in the ten hours I've played during the course of playing prior to this review I've found two; A wave spawning on an enclosed area that did not have a path to the rest of the map and the game crashing around day 42. Try the demo, if the basic gameplay appeals to you it's better in the main game due to the content tiers 2 and 3 add. If you don't like the demo at all you probably won't like the game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not terrible. It's a PvE RTS in the vein of They Are Billions, clearly trying to build on that foundation; and it feels a little like Age of Empires. These are good things in my book, so I kept on playing for a bit.Unfortunately, there are a million little things that annoy me here, that eventually made playing this frustrating.On paper, it's pretty classic. Food, wood, stone, iron, and later on you can trade for gold. Your guys collect stuff, deposit it in a local stockpile (provided there's room) and repeat. But in practice it creates a new layer of unnecessary complexity; having stockpiles in the right places, with the right settings, and having to constantly move them around because you keep clearing out forests... it's a little less annoying with stone and iron as these resources stay in one place for a pretty long time, but it's still the same problem.Then there's food. Long story short, it's pretty hard to tell how much exactly do you produce and how much do you need (to keep growing, you know how much you need to sustain yourself). There is a graph screen that helps you with this, but even then, planning becomes an approximation. And of course, farms need SPACE. Lots of space.Just like in They Are Billions, you have to keep expanding your town by clearing out enemies. In TAB it made sense, there were zombies everywhere, obviously you need to clear the place. But here there are enemy encampments just 'cause. Feels a little weird, but whatever.My main issue is that it always felt like there's not enough room. Ok, I need houses, farms, production facilities, military buildings. So no problem, just go expand, right? But aha, two issues here. One - the resources are somewhat sparse, you probably can't afford to just move your walls every few days. And two - the further you go, the more fortifications the enemy has. Not bases, just random towers full of archers. So there is a point where you can't just go around and kill stuff, unless you're ok with throwing units at the wall, not worried about casualties. But here's the problem with this approach.Whenever any of your people die - whether civilians or soldiers - they have to be buried, or else they'll generate disease. Your gravediggers will be walking around, collecting corpses and putting them in the designated graveyards. Curiously, only your people have to be buried, I guess the corpses of the attacking masses are disease-free or something. Anyway, let's say that a bunch of your soldiers died in an attack, and the location remains unconquered. There are bodies there. What do you do?Option 1: You send your gravediggers anyway. You might be successful, but a more likely outcome is that the gravediggers will just join the other corpses, since there are archers in the area.Option 2: You just let the bodies rot there. That's fine if you don't plan on expanding there, but you'll keep having an annoying notification that there are corpses to be buried - a notification that you otherwise should pay attention to.And even if you're just burying regular soldiers that died during an enemy attack, it's still a pain, even if you have a bunch of gravediggers on the ready. Oh, and make sure the graveyards themselves are safely tucked away, because they die in pretty much one hit and once destroyed, all the corpses you've buried there will instantly rise as annoying undead.So instead of having a more faction VS faction type of combat here, you have your units and the enemies are weaker but far, far more numerous. Again, like in They Are Billions. I feel like it makes no sense here, except to create this "sea of enemies at our walls" feeling which I personally don't care for. This works when your enemies are zombies or monsters or something, but here? Our guys with a sword are three times stronger than their guys with a sword! Can't we just have them equal and have smaller numbers?Also, uh, the... humour. It's a little like Monty Python but relying almost entirely on the comical pause. Oh, a weird situation. Characters just stare at each other for literally 5 seconds and say nothing. There are exceptions to this, some moments made me laugh, but otherwise the timing is bad, the jokes themselves are a mixed bag...Let me say for the record that I highly prefer British humour to American one (no, I'm not British, I don't even speak English actually) but even the Britishness is not enough to make these awful jokes work. But that might just be my personal taste speaking.All the time when playing this, I was thinking "I wish I was playing They Are Billions instead". So I eventually went and played a game and it was such a breath of fresh air. You can see the clear line of influences, but there the things just work.Diplomacy Is Not An Option is an attempt, but one that fails, if you ask me. I think it's a noble one, however; so I feel a little bad for this scathing critique. Still, know what you're getting into.

_childDocuments_.review: Lackluster Gameplay.Diplomacy is Not an Option is a game that promises a lot by referencing its inspiration from the Command and Conquer franchise but fails to deliver. Missions are repetitive, and you always start each mission at the same starting point, making it tedious to develop the entire kingdom again and sitting there in boredom. That's the main issue of the game: it is tedious and boring.The structure of the title is its biggest weakness, as missions could have used more variety when it comes to the starting phase, either by giving players more developed kingdoms or by breaking missions into smaller ones. When I play Command and Conquer I have fun due to the variety of objectives, the unique maps, and the situations the game throws at you. Diplomacy is not an option, you always make a base, deal with some stationary enemies, and survive waves. In addition, the game is not easy at all even in the easiest settings, making me wonder if the developer was targetting a hardcore RTS playerbase or if they never got to playtest this game.✔️An interesting take that combines RTS with tower defense.✔️The graphics are simple, making it easier to distinguish units in the field.❌Tedious gameplay, always start each mission at the same point.❌Despite having a variety of modes, all of them feel the same.❌Abrupt difficulty spikes even on its lowest difficulty settings. ❌A story that is not captivating and has scenes dragging for way too long.I am not a master tactician, but even I can beat the hardest Command and Conquer 3 missions on normal difficulty and hard. In this game on the other hand, due to a poorly explained tutorial and abrupt difficulty spikes, even the easiest setting is a nightmare for those not enthusiast of the genre. Adding to this is a lack of unit identity as they are not memorable as said a mammoth tank in CaC, and you have a stale game. Don't believe me? Check the Steam achievements, the drop rate for this game is so big that less than 8% of players have gotten past a few campaign missions. Unless you are a big fan of RTS and are extremely good at them, I suggest you don't buy this title. :) If you enjoy and find the review helpful, please follow my curator!

_childDocuments_.review: Fun, but has fairly noticeable technical and game balance shortcomings.Technical:- Saves of more than a few hours of gameplay in Endless mode will not load within reasonable timeframe (30 min or less). This is the dealbreaker for me.- Game running for a while at higher wave sizes still suffers from significant performance drops - can be somewhat helped by restarting game, but then runs into the problem above. This is with a fairly powerful rig.Game Balance:- Diversity of units is very limited. While it appears as though there are many units (~8 infantry, 3 siege), half of them are completely replaced by later units (ie. Archer by Crossbowman, Swordsman by Spear/Hammerguy) and lose all relevance once you unlock the later units (fairly quickly).- Ballista is overshadowed by both Catapult and Trebuchet in all noticeable applications. It lacks a useful niche (like good DPS or range to counter enemy catapults) to make up for having no AoE, something that the other 2 have in droves.- Upgrade system is too barebones - upgrades generally apply to only one unit, with no further progression or synergy.Would recommend a "wait and see" approach for now - it's still a fun game with potential, but still needs a good deal of polish and rework to really shine.

_childDocuments_.review: I have an issue with games that artifically are difficult by just sending more and more stuff. It's artificial and it doesn't require good balancing.For context I played semi comp Supreme Commander and CoH, so i'm fairly experienced when it comes to RTS micro but also grander scale and have therefore certain expectations to controls and the sort.All it is at some point is just to build faster and faster and faster (so the economy is done like an ECO Rts like AoE) in hopes to beat the aritficial difficulty. While painfully microing around mistakes that you only discover when the hordes of enemies are at your footstep (Like a low unit RTS like CoH).But since the enemy doesn't build a base the closest that I can think of is that this is a tower defense. Unfortunately there's not a lot of variety in here after the 3rd time you went through it. It's a game that doesn't know whether it's an RTS, City Builder or a Tower Defense. Not excelling at either of the three.A good example here is firing vision. You deal with 1000's (!) of enemies (like Supreme commander) at the same time, but your units sometimes shoot into a wall because a unit is obscured by it. Yet the AI is not capable of at least shooting at something else. So you will have sometimes a trebuchet shooting at one guy somewhere else, missing 100 shots (because they crash into a wall or stone) while an invasion is happening right next to it.Either fix that, or let shots pass through terrain / walls. This added "realism" is not helping anyone.The archer target distribution is also horrendous. The controlling aspect of the RTS side is just not good enough for a game that has you control THIS many units while fighting that many units.The tech tree is also not giving you a lot of choice which would have been one option to diversify, but most choices are obvious.A tower defense in which one mistake can destroy the last hour of progress unnecessarily. The reason why most Tower defenses are on pre set routes is to exactly avoid this and because it's easier to balance the difficulty ramp.Something feels off about this difficulty ramp method, especially since the game keeps you artifically busy with you having to clear the map constantly while there's offmap waves coming as well all the time. You either resort to cheese or you accept that the game is incredibly opaque with what's happening and what's coming at you.Also the controls are not good enough to excert the control the game implies in the trailers (with the phalanxes etc.). This also unfortunately includes the ECO side of the game. Instead of being able to define a specific limit that is auto exported we have to manually click and export resources. It does not add to tactical dept but keeps you from playing the game, like many other things unfortunately. Constantly recruiting but no Auto Build. Constantly balancing food and population.Some maps are for most people only beatable if they know where what is so they can direct and time their resources there. It's an ok game but I'm feeling quite stressed after playing it which is something I really don't want in a game.I tried loving it. But that's it.

_childDocuments_.review: So generally sppeaking, I like this game. For an early Access Game, this game looks good, is fun and is well made (no major bugs, crashes, lags, etc.) I like to take the time though to think and speak about what improvements can be made. The first category of these Ideas would be the: "Please change that, it annoys me": 1. Placing buildings should be easy. I don't care and don't want to care about people not beeing able to reach buildings. Either lat me place them whereever I want, or automatically put streets in between. The reason is, that building castles, cities etc. should: a. result in a castle that looks good b. be realistic c. be fast, since you need to concentrate to defend your stuff. 2. Gold is wierd. It slows everything down. The only case where slowing things down with the current gold system are trebuchets because they are overpowerd. But just in technical terms: In order to get gold the user has to: a. reach castle level 3b. build a market (which isn't that obivous todo) c. have resource availibled. click on a button in the market (why, isnt it where you build building e.g.? Why the extra click?) e. wait till the things are traded (~2min) f. Repeat the process after you only hear an indication that the market is ready again.  Now the issue is: this is very inflexible and you forget about the market and therefore get out of gold very quickly. How to do it better: a. have an internal market where you can exchange all resources over gold. (e.g. Stellaris Energy credits, Stronghold gold, etc. ) b. There are better means to nerv trebuchets (just more resources, longer training times etc.) c. To get gold you take taxes from the people. Its basically whats the story about isnt it ;)? 3.Range of some buildings, like the cemetary. Although a cool idea, but if I raid the peasants I dont want to build a cemetary near it because one soldier died. Also note, that you discourage offense in favour of defense, that way. 4. The game is sometimes rather undynamic. I mean that it is slow and expensive to build armys, and with the cemetary mechanic, fights are discouraged. Compare that to Age of Empires and similar, where its encouraged to fight, and loose armys if need be. So I recommend more waves and a faster and easier way to train troops. Now the category: "That would be cool!!"1. Train troops not soldiers. The only game that I know, does that properly would Lord of the Rings: Battle of Middle Earth 1 & 2. There you can train a troops instead of one soldier which leads to epic battles really quickly. 2. Walls: First of all: why can't I put troops on walls? Second: Why are stone walls so thin? They aren't fences. But I like them visually. The style is great. Maybe improve the visualls for diagonal walls. Here you can take inspiriation from Stronghold and Lord of the Rings: Battle of middle Earth 1 (not 2) 3. The enemy are peasants, but they bahave like zombies. I know you probably got inspired by They are Zillions, but they are still peasants. And peasants can use bows, can make leaders and most importantly: Ramms. The classical weakpoint of any castly is the gate, and therefore an an enemy would target that weakpoint and will not attack the closest point of wall. 4. Kavalary needs some love: First its very expensive and time consuming to create the predominant kind of middle aged military due to the gold mechanic. Secondly, they cannot overrun infantary. This looks somewhat wierd (like in Age of Empires where the elephant stops to hit a citizen a few times). You already let soldiers fly on catapult inpact, so I think it would be cool if the cavalary can charge the enemy. (Inspired by Lord of the Rings: Battle of Middle Earth) 5. Please let me play against an other castle. Then all the siege weaponry makes sense, and you have a more dynamic gameplay then a tower defence, against waves. 6. Castle upgrades, where you can build towers to the castle, that are pre-positoned. This would get around the current "street"-system. 7. I like the magic system, but I find it a bit overpowered. Maybe instead have a new soldier type: Magician, that has a specific range, or make them less op than the meteor. Although it looks quite cool, destroying a big wave with a meteor, I admit. 8. I find myself only building walls, when I see the direction where the wave is coming from, in order to save resources. However a castle is not a wall between 2 mountains to block braindeads that can't figure out another way around the wall. I would recommend more smaller waves, and attacks from more directions in order to force the player to build a proper castle. so that what I could think of. I only concentrated on mechanics because I think you are creative enough for story and content. I would expect more enemy types, and you could go more into fantasy if you want (trolls, dragons, demons, etc.). Generally I like the game, and I am looking forward on what you will make of it.

_childDocuments_.review: First off 30$ is an insane ask for this game, I got it in a bundle for 12$ and I would feel extremely ripped off paying full price for this (maybe I would have refunded if it wasn't part of a bundle of codes, i'm not sure).There is a huge difference between the lowest and highest difficulty in this game, my play is based on the highest difficulty.  Lowest is extremely easy and someone with little to no skill probably won't have much trouble with it.  One of the first levels had over 9k enemies killed at the end.One very glaring issue with the game is that the map is randomized, meaning sometimes it will generate and have a huge lack of resources, or straight up none of stone or iron anywhere nearby.I do not understand the reason for gold, a resource for tier 3 to be basically locked behind trading, finding it on the map is too unreliable.  Couldn't have just simply added a gold mine or something into the game, or just not even have this resource and it would make a lot of things much more tolerable.Resource gathering is very weird, for example the workers hit trees to get wood and bring to a lumber mill and you would think that's it but nope they then have to process it into wood, yes they are processing wood into wood.  Then have to carry it to a storage which takes an extremely long amount of time. Same but worse with iron.There is no markers on the campaign to which difficulty you beat the stages on, it's just a "clear" despite playing on highest versus lowest, this is so bizarre, they couldn't even do the most basic of things.  This is an absolutely huge slap in the face for how difficult the highest setting is.If you look at the achievements the game seems to have had a HUGE drop off of players at some point or just a lot of accounts with game codes sitting idle?13% of players have the "Now, that’s what I call a Town Hall!" which means at least 87% of the player base hasn't even finished the fourth campaign mission.25% of players "Repluse a wave" or "Built a Barracks" or "Filled a storage with food" these are all literally things that you WILL do yet 75% don't have this, it doesn't make any sense how this game has over 6k reviews.The latest short they uploaded (In the Development Diary Part 27 "courageous warriors") is EXTREMELY questionable, the dialogue is as if a literal 4 year old made it, which is actually an insult to 4 year olds...  Even without dialogue it makes no sense.  My guess is they used a cheap Chinese company to make it for them.Also the humor is really weird as well, it was funny the first few times when the random @#!(* showed up but it kept getting repeated over and over to the point it just became kinda cringe.I will eventually finish the game on the highest difficulty for I am a masochist unfortunately. I would NOT recommend this unless it's on sale at a HUGE discount or some extreme changes happen.

_childDocuments_.review: Ever enjoyed turtling up in age of empires or command and conquer, and watch coldly from your throne in cathartic megalomania as endless legions of the pathetic vermin that once dared oppose you now crashes in impotent violence against the cold, merciless might of your carefully crafted dominions, protected by the most talented artisans in the art of bloodshed and slaughter?No? just me?.....  Aaaaanyway, it seems to me that the devs are going for something like that, and did pretty good at it too, so far. It's quite similar to the games i mentioned earlier but without the clutter and micromanaging of having to balance several diferent factions, tech trees and the like. There's still some of that, enought to make a difference but not that time consuming or annoying. There's also several attacking factions with different aspects to them to keep in mind when defending, etc.All in all, an excellent primary gamplay loop with a lot of versatility but without much depth, and cathartic action that even at its most complacent moments manages to keep you engaged and on your toes. The only real con is that there's not that much variety in general and a few qualities of life improvement can be seen missing here and there, but hey, that's what early access is for. Bottom line: having a lot of fun with it and looking foward to see what the devs cook up for the next update. Also, it's ok if it isn't for you.

I had to watch a video of people playing an the hardest difficulties, to see their build order. After that, it became the "walk in the park" it promised, but this should be tought through gameplay and not by watching other people. A fix for that could maybe be a small prologue campaign that serves as an extended tutorial, that forces you to build larger economies. Right now, the fourth (if memory serves right) mission of the campaign, where you have to build those boats, is the first mission, where you have to expand to townhall lvl3, having to use the market and whilst beeing under pressure, Which results in quite a difficulty spike, until you have figured those mechanics out. _childDocuments_.review: This game is like a mix of city building, RTS, and tower defense games, and the exciting part is that you don’t have to like all of them to enjoy the game. For example, if you only want to build your dream city in peace, you can turn off the enemy altogether. However this game is very much a work in progress, it needs more content on all three aspects of the game. The city building part is especially lacking in depth: there needs to be more building types and complex mechanics for it to be interesting. As of right now, RTS and tower defense seem to be their main focus, city building feels more like a supplement to them. I enjoyed taking a small army to explore the surroundings and uncover the fog of war, and occasionally using my cavalry to crush the enemies, but there isn’t much else you can do with your units. Things like different formations, active skills, and flanking bonus from the Total War series will be good additions to the game. I also would like to see more defense towers added to the game. Currently, you just put your archers and siege weapons on the wall and that’s it. On a side note, this game desperately needs more Steam Cloud storage space. 100MB is simply not enough, considering that a single save file is 6 to 8MB. Overall, the game shows great potential and gets updated regularly. There are so many things they can add to this solid foundation. I can’t wait.

_childDocuments_.review: Seriously fun, well-made and well-balanced challenge. You probably think it's a simple castle-builder, build walls and fend off hordes. Blow em up. Looks good.What you may not be able to see yet is that there is an entire medieval city building simulator behind it. You must manage resource gathering & storage, food & starvation, housing, illness & grave-digging, research & upgrading, market trading, and the most fun part, building walls & military units.It's a genuine challenge at first. Mismanagement of any area can derail your economy. Forgot to produce enough food before building all those houses? Now everyone's starving. Forgot to bury those dead bodies? Now everyone's ill and rushing to the nearest hospital.Though soon enough you learn how to snowball the economic system and build a mighty empire. Then you can focus on building layered defences with archers, catapults, and a whole lot of swordsmen for cannon fodder, against a series of increasingly ridiculous waves of enemies.
