_childDocuments_.review: It's a cool one! I don't know if there's a game that's a closer inspiration, but I'm naturally comparing it to They Are Billions (TABs) a lot, being a PvE defense RTS city-builder kinda deal.It has some changes to the formula that I can appreciate, though it should be kept in mind that I have relatively little time in this game and I haven't actually completed a map yet.The economics are a little more detailed, with workers having to physically travel the map and transport their products to storage buildings. It's an extra layer of management with a game style that already constantly demands your attention in different places, but from what I can tell it's a manageable change considering the game seems to me to be less punishing than TABs. I do appreciate the added physicality in this game, with line-of-sight concerns and an emphasis melee combat and units to hold the line. The emphasis on setting your units up in formations as opposed to the old-school Blob-of-Death you'll find in TABs. I'm just a sucker for a good battle line. Also, to my limited understanding your army variety and the overall balance between your units seems to be greater in this than in TABs, so I can appreciate that!Having to bury your dead is a fascinating change, if a hair frustrating. Though I haven't encountered the mechanic enough to see how it pans out when the brown-stuff hits the whirly-thing.I will say that flavor-wise the game (currently?) lacks slightly for me. The visuals are clean, functional and cute. The premise and enemy are solid and novel to me. Music wise, though, I'll say that it's one of the few games that I'll mute it and put on my own music and vibe. It's functional, and I do like the main menu theme, but so far I haven't encountered anything that felt like it really elevated my experience. This is a point where I keep making unfair comparisons to TABs, because the music in that game is PHENOMENAL, especially the songs that come on during the different waves. It just does so much to enhance the mood of the gameplay in a way that DINAO lacks. Maybe this is an aspect that will get some love more towards release, I can't say.Overall, I dig it. I haven't played many of the other survival strategy options out there, so I can't say whether or not you should buy DINAO over the others, but I've been coming back to the game here and there since I've bought it at the beginning of Early Access.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game with a very promising future. The game has a good concept and it's done amazingly. The mechanics feel good and I truly have to say it's the most polished and finished early access game i've played (besides factorio). That being said there's some issues that need fixing pretty quick. Firstly and the largest is endless mode resource collection. The main reason I bought this game was to play endless and it seems to be the only glaring issue. Trading is an amazing idea but the current implementation is far far too little after any remotely high wave count. Stone, iron, and gold can't be gathered infinitely like food and wood. The only way to infinitely get these resources is to trade them through the market. Currently each market transaction is a minute and some change (after an upgrade). You can only trade around 100 stone and far less iron. Honestly this cap isn't that massive what is for me is that every minute I have to setup this transaction. There is no auto sell/buy. This is soo annoying it alone ruins late game. I don't personally find the resource limit as harming as the mindless repetition. To make matters worse if you play at faster than normal game speed this time also goes down meaning less than a minute to do something tedious. The early game is soooo good and controls perfectly. Late game needs some serious work. Balancing, resource management, troop control, and performance. I like hard games and I personally don't think the game is too hard (even on higher endless modes) what is too hard is the scaling. The first endless map (with actual waves) is too easy compared to the second endless map. It doesn't scale linear at all and there's like 8 different maps meaning it gets nuts too quickly. Resource management like I said late game needs more options for one and the current option (trading) needs wider ability. Multiple markets with each being unlocked by an increasingly expensive research would be an easy upgrade to the game. Also please quickly add auto sell buy ( if you don't have enough to sell then it waits till you do ). Troop control now this is part of were the game truly shines. Troops control amazingly and they need to. Early game you clear effectively barbarian camps so your settlement can grow. The issue is hold mode works 99% of the time. But sometimes troops will randomly leave position and walk forward and then run back (idk why truly). The bigger issue is troops moving to get a shot on enemies on the other side of the wall. Troops will even on hold decide to go across the entire map outside the walls to stand right next to a massive horde and shoot. You have to do so much micromanaging sometimes to prevent this. Regardless of ANYTHING even if archers are getting smacked in the face HOLD needs to make them HOLD. Now into performance I have a 5600x and a 3080 I have a high end system and the game well runs pretty crappy during waves. Gpu never maxes out on a 1440p ultrawide it's purely a cpu thing. And tbh the game is well made I mean I can see each threads usage and holy molly it's a even split. I've never seen a game have such a great even split on cpu threads, But when im on wave like 7 only day 60ish and am getting 28 fps it's too little. Make ai dumber. The only time it crashes down to this low is during waves. Ultimately you need to make the ai dumber. Or you can group them so 10 enemies act based on 1's guidance. So if the "leader" walks here all are told to do that as well. It sounds like it's a technical limit but many many many other games have larger armies with much more intricate ai and fps doesn't tank anywhere near as much. This is the sole point of the game massive waves if you can't get it running better then the game will die. Im not talking about late waves im talking still pretty early game. As a whole this game is soo good that when I can focus on specific issues and very narrow topics you know it's done most of it right. I am very happy this game is still in early access because it has a chance of being a long lived gem that I will continue to come back to.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: If you enjoy They Are Billions and are pining for something to fill the Stronghold-sized hole in your heart, this game promises to show you what they can do with both!I tend to put a lot and a lot of hours into games I enjoy, and while I haven't done so with this one yet, I think the promised future content, the comedic pitch of the campaign, and the sense of escalating difficulty are all draw-ins for something I can soak countless hours into. At a glance, this game is They Are Billions but played as a medieval lord. Saying this, there are some specific mechanics that are specifically changed from TAB that, in my opinion, are massive upgrades. There is no power radius for towers in order to show you where you can build. People have to walk to their jobs and back to wherever they need to store their goods, but there are very very few limitations on building (short of a perimeter around the edge of the map). With the full range of options of buildings, you are also capable of building a Stronghold-tier castle, complete with periphery buildings you do not defend behind walls and the more important Keep and Castle structures all locked tight behind walls. If you want to play like this is TAB and expand all over the map, the only limitation is how much food you can dish out to people because there are, as of writing, no self-automated defenses. Every person you want to keep from damaging you needs to be dealt with by a person you hire. I played the campaign (though making a specific choice seems to lock you out of the other option, and I'm unsure if you can reset your efforts to see the other side) as it stands for now, which for me was only two missions. I played a 4 hour session of the demo and another 4 hour session today. The content is all really good where it is, which impresses me for a month after going into early access. There are a few problems: your people have to pathfind to their jobs, and sometimes they will walk right out to the enemy if they get confused. Builders will wall themselves in. Endless doesn't (at least not in early days) seem to make use of the enemy variety established in the campaign. The enemy's directives for what they want to attack in their path seems a little odd and inconsistent sometimes.But overall? I am loving my experience with the game, and it is an easy recommend to me. 25 dollars might be a bit steep if you do not like endless modes or only want structured content, but for me, this is well worth it. I hope this game continues to impress!

_childDocuments_.review: *This review was very difficult to give a negative to as I truly believe this game will eventually be great, happy to come back and look at it again developers!*Greetings as always!  Today we’ll be looking at ‘Diplomacy is not an Option’ an RTS that puts your kingdom up against a Zapp Brannigan level of peasants who have the audacity to want freedom or maybe against a King who is out to conquer everyone who dares oppose?  I really like this genre but am always concerned at early access games, were my concerns justified?  Let’s discuss!Sire their Zombies…I mean peasants:  At the core this is a RTS with wave based attacks very similar to ‘They are Billions’ or ‘Age of Darkness’ which I’ve taken to calling ‘Survival RTS’.  The graphics are decent and enjoyable, almost more block based than anything else but not enough to annoy me (really dislike the MineCraft aesthetic) but the audio (both music and sound) are completely forgettable.  Currently what we honestly have is the great beginnings of a new survival RTS.   The main issue is that it just feels like the beginning…Just a Flesh Wound:  As stated above this game feels very similar to other games of the genre, the problem is that it feels more like the precursor and less like a new addition in its current state.  The story is forgettable with dry humor and there really isn’t much in the ways of content outside of the bare bones.  I really would have liked to see a shift from the genre in some kind of defining way.  And it ends up the same way as every survival RTS game out there; tons of walls and covering the entire map in an absurd amount of units for the final wave.Overall, this game is not a bad game and I have a good hunch this game will eventually be well worth the money, it’s just not at this time.  It doesn’t really provide anything new over other games of the genre and they feel more like a complete game.  At this time I can’t recommend it but hoping to come back one day and change my mind, Enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: What a wonderful game! I'm always down for a new RTS, this is very reminiscent of They Are Billions, only in a lighter more comedic tone with less OP individual units. It definitely scratches the itch for RTS mixed with Tower Defense.I highly recommend it, So you'll understand the loop: there is no ramp up through the campaign for new buildings or anything, it's always an individual race to level up to the third building level and create large defense obstacles between "mountains" to push enemies into small areas so you can use your god powers to wipe them out, your units are nominally stronger than the enemy but their numbers can quickly overwhelm you. Usually though you can usually take your time to do just upgrade at "leisure" with regular bandit raids throughout depending on your difficulty. The harder levels can be quite brutal though!The campaign doesn't have any special player buildings or considerations aside from enemy building/unit types, but there are some interesting wrinkles on a few of the missions that keep it fun and interesting. Also the comedy is well done if occasionally grammatically incorrect.The visuals are quite nice, I personally have some fairly robust computers so I've never had any issues with too many sprites or system lag, but I'm not sure about older systems. It's pretty cool to have a few thousand enemies attacking you though, I thoroughly enjoy setting up my 50 man squads behind walls loaded with archers and siege weapons.I give it a solid 8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: This game is like an awesome blast from the past - a faithful and interesting love letter to the old Stronghold games, but with more modern graphics and control system.I did feel that this game is missing a bit of the character of the old Stronghold games - the campaign text is funny but it might at times be a little *too* silly. It can be fun to have heroic, brave, or more interesting characters thrown in the mix as well. Also, without voice acting for the campaign, it essentially boils down to watching a long cutscene of just text bubbles, which definitely made me miss how that was handled in Stronghold. This game is still early access, obviously. The campaign isn't done yet, but the 3 missions I played were a blast. I hope they incorporate more story persistent elements (for instance, I let my peasant revolt hero die accidentally and didn't see any acknowledgement of that in the cutscene dialogue, although I can chalk that up to the game being in early access. All in all, if you want a fun, fresh Stronghold-inspired game, this is a great choice! Just be aware that although the gameplay feels fairly polished, the campaign and other elements seem pretty unfinished, although there is a good foundation there and I am excited to see where they take it!

_childDocuments_.review: This game reminds me of STRONGHOLD... and older game that had better graphics.   This is a simplified version  of the medieval warfare game of castles and catapults.  I like this one because of the "chill" factor.   The designers didn't take themselves too seriously.  They made a game where you could get a basic economy and have basic troops with some degree of difference in performance.By taking the path of least resistance, they gave us a game that has fun and strategy but goes easy on the learning curve and brain burn.  There may still be bits of that if you ramp up the level of difficulty but it is entirely possible to learn the game quickly and have fun at the lesser levels.  Graphics are not a strong point but they aren't poor either.  You can clearly make out the buildings as well as the flora and fauna.  It does not strive for strict realism but there are doses of that.  Dead bodies left littering your home area cause people to get unhappy and even ill.  Economics rears its ugly head to bring life in the game closer to reality but once you learn what to build and when, the game can be forgiving of little mistakes.Politics are ignored and I for one am pleased they are.  Health issues are left at a basic level but not too basic.  You must consider you populace while you are waging war.  This can be a fun "tower defense" game or ramped up to be a serfdom mini-simulator.   Some thought and good choices were put into the design which made it easier to enjoy this game.   If you are looking for an uber-serious simulation, keep on moving.  If you are looking for an inexpensive game that will make you think a bit about strategy while eating away time without too much stress?  This is well worth you time and effort.

_childDocuments_.review: A small, but great RTS/city building game. You start as a small castle with a meager amount of resources, soldiers, and residents; and you must expand your territory through scouting, city-building, resource acquisition/management, technological development, and military might. You must defend your kingdom from hordes that come every few days, and expand into a hostile territory whose occupants only grow in strength the further you venture from your castle. Due to the nature of hordes growing in strength as time goes on, you must research better tech and increase the proficiency/size of your army with every passing day. You must wall off your entire kingdom so hordes can't just waltz on through. Every mode ranges in difficulty, from easy to practically impossible. Once you get used to the game's mechanics, you can play this while listening to music/videos. I highly recommend this game to those who enjoy city building/horde defense games.

_childDocuments_.review: 🎮 Game Title: Diplomacy is Not an Option 🎮🕒 Hours Played: 87.8 Hours📝 Review:The campaign mode in Diplomacy is Not an Option is a solid entry point for players who enjoy strategic decision-making in tower defense gameplay. However, it has some notable drawbacks when it comes to replayability and story progression.One key issue is the difficulty in exploring all the possible narrative choices. Once you choose a side—whether it's the Crown, the Rebels, or the Sarranga—you are locked into that storyline for the duration of the campaign. While this adds a sense of commitment to your decisions, it also makes it more cumbersome to experience the other sides of the story.If you want to replay the campaign to see what the other factions offer, you're required to return to the load menu, which can be a bit of a hassle. The mission titles are not always easy to remember, and finding the right point in the campaign can be tedious. As of now, the only viable way to fully experience all of the branching narratives (Rebel, Crown, Sarranga) is by creating a new profile and replaying the entire campaign from scratch. This limitation detracts from the game's overall flexibility and could discourage players from exploring all the narrative paths.On the positive side, the campaign is engaging, with interesting faction choices and varied challenges that keep things fresh. But a more streamlined method for switching between storylines, or at least a clearer mission tracking system, would greatly enhance the replayability of the game.Additionally, I wish the developers would introduce more of the unique enemy troops from the campaign—like the bosses and even the crabs—into the endless and sandbox modes. These enemies bring variety and added challenge to the campaign, and having them in other modes would make the game feel richer and more diverse in terms of threats.Another area for improvement is housing space. The current system for building housing in the campaign is frustratingly inefficient, as housing structures take up a lot of the map’s space. It feels like a constant battle to find enough room for your buildings, especially when space is already limited. Hunger also adds another layer of difficulty, 8 frickingh lvl 2 with a lot of berry isn't enough to feed my peasants.lastly,  Acquire gold in the game is really hard or am i just stupid that there is menu that i can open or something ohh well... . It often feels like you're scraping by, and I found myself constantly wishing for a better way to earn it. I think an in-game taxation system would be a fantastic addition, allowing players to tax their citizens to generate additional gold. This would add a layer of depth to managing your economy and make it feel like you're governing a real kingdom with economic decisions to make.but all in all game is great hardcore difficulty is winnable while nightmare is bs

_childDocuments_.review: If you just wanna "chill" and build a city there are other games in my opinion. I've been seeing some people say its a chill game, others have been saying its impossible. You've got the usual babyragers crying over "scaling". I will say there does seem to be a discrepancy between difficulties. Where one is the "chill" version and the other is "WTF hard". The hardest difficulty I just don't wanna even know right now.The game is overall fun and aesthetically pleasing and pretty straightforward as far as this style of games go. There are variety of resources to gather which I like. I feel like some games only have one or two and the economy just gets boring. However there are some quality of life issues that I'm honestly having trouble getting past.Problem #1 - As far as I know there doesn't seem to be an economy "tab" I can open that shows my net gain/loss. Its really only an issue with food tbh. It shows what you consume the next day but not what you are harvesting. In resource management games (which this IS 110%) efficiency is honestly life or death otherwise you're just guessing at how much food, wood, stone, etc you are getting each day. Do I need 3 berry picking huts or can I squeeze by with 2? Well hell if I know. You also can't build structures unless you have the people to staff them. Doesn't matter if you have the wood. Which wouldn't be so bad if I knew whether I needed 2 or 3 berry huts, so I can free up those workers. Get it? There are ways around this but it's extra steps that can all be avoided with just one simple thing....an Economy Tab for an economy game.Problem #2 - Spawns in Endless Mode. Sometimes you get a GODLY spawn and you want for nothing. However sometimes they really screw you and the game is already challenging enough that if you get a bad spawn, you just start shaking your head and asking why me?! You're in the middle of a damn field with no food but berries and no natural barriers to aid in wall building and choke points. Good luck getting the resources to build all those walls. Sucker.Now having said all that I am enjoying this game, mostly because I'm still learning and I haven't hit a progression wall. I'm holding out for these things to be fixed. In the meantime I'm going to keep playing to see if maybe I can win despite it. However at the current state of the game and the current price tag, I just don't think I can recommend it. Drop the price or add an economy tab. Then I'll change my mind.Edit 3/29/22 - Oh please fix the catapult aggro. They DO NOT attack the nearest target. I have lost early game playthroughs WAY too many times because it attacks a huge cluster of enemies at the max range pulling a huge mob when I already have a mob attacking my troops i.e. "the nearest target".

_childDocuments_.review: : Great game that involves key strategy and decision making which can lead to different successful out comes in battle and defences. campaign is limited to only two missions, this is expected as the game is currently in early access hence the limited overall structures, building, troops etc. Within Missions and endless mode it seems that time flies considerately as there is just so much to do and accomplish in little time before being attacked therefore a lot of thinking and strategy is implemented which makes the game very enjoyable and at some times frustrating.: Starting I understand that the game is in early access and it can be expected that these suggestion will come to light in future production of the game. Starting with troops, every troop seems to have a major purpose to your armies and do a very good job for what they are. However, the horsemen are by far the most useless troop as they are only used for scouting which is preferred to be done in larger groups, i don't believe that they should cost 1 coin as coins are fairly hard to obtain and can only be gained by trade or carts. Implementing an upgrade within the upgrade/skills tree to allow them to do a charge attack which does small spread of splash damage to surrounding enemies would greatly imp-rove the overall use of this troop, allowing for a cavalry group to conduct a team charge to clear out lines of enemies, other wise i have never really used them and still hoping they get an upgrade. (hoping to see a lot more troops of all types as well, both enemies and friendlies). The ballistics although having great aim and damage is set to single targets making it rather useless and hope that perhaps enemy giants to combat walls will be introduced to bring use to these single hard hitting machines and please set them to attack stronger targets constantly rather than small infantry. Iron and stone farming, within late game of endless mode you seem to run out of iron and stone deposits therefore relying on trade, for wood, foresters cabins are a great addition to the game perhaps underground mining areas should be implemented allowing to access gems as well which should stay rare. Berry pickers are quite useless in my opinion when reaching town hall 2 as farms are way more productive and useful. Implementing captains of battalions, sometime the need of one army to support another in an event of an invasion is necessary however mixing the troops up by accident and not knowing which fallen soldiers belonged to either squad can be annoying, By implementing a captain means when moving the squad of those who belong to that original squad will move with him, squads should also be highlighted as different colours for example squad 1 is blue squad 2 is green etc would greatly help army management. _childDocuments_.review: Diplomacy is Not an Option plays out like a pretty conventional RTS. You gather resources, kick start your production, and hire builders and soldiers to do gruntwork. The gimmick is that your enemy doesn’t have a base of operation. Instead, they attack you in waves from outside the map boundaries, at set intervals. Sort of like in a tower defense game. You know where they come from too, giving you some space to focus your defenses. And as a last push in their final attack, they also gather up stray units from encampments around the map -- giving you some mitigating busywork to do between the earlier waves.It’s fine. But I think I might have raised my hopes up a little too high. The marketing material makes it seem like this epic tower defense game, where you defend your bastion from closing armies. A real focus on scale and excess. Huge crescendos. Massive armies. Yet, the game starts out with such humble beginnings. Small armies defending tiny castles, with barely enough resources and units to go around. It’s both slow and punishing, never really reaching those epic proportions. It sort of just fizzles, somewhat unceremoniously.I’m sure it will reach those heights eventually. I’m just not interested in playing for tens of hours just to  reach that point, when it feels like it should have been the core experience from the get-go. It’s a matter of expectations I guess. But it’s a pass for me either way. I feel like I’ve played Diplomacy is Not an Option a million times before.

_childDocuments_.review: Get the game on sale. While being fun the game does lack many QoL features and still has some balance issues to address.The good:At release balance was an issue for some players but the devs have been working on it and balance has improved. DNO is actually pretty fun with it's cross between RTS and tower defense. Along with the stylized graphics and humorous storyline DNO makes for a fun and unique experience.The game pushes you to expand quickly unlike many other RTSs that punish for expanding too quickly. You'll get the hang of it and I actually quite enjoy this way of playing.There are about a dozen maps to choose from for endless mode each balanced with higher or lower difficulty and different factions to fight against each with unique units. The undead are quite fun to play against.There five different difficulty levels to play in the campaign mode. The higher levels are quite challenging.DNO also has different paths to choose from with four different endings. So there is quite a bit of  replay ability in the campaign.The good good:The devs are active on Steam forums, Reddit and very active on Discord. The devs are on top of feedback and bug reports.You couldn't ask for more active developers.The bad:But DNO  does have it issues in the QoL department. The most glaring lack of a feature is that you are limited to just 5 auto saves, total, across all game modes. Not 5 saves per map, but 5 saves total! There is also no means to rename or even organize your saves. You also cannot rename or organize saves. Everything is limited to 5 saves. THough this can be circumvented with creating multiple in game accounts for campaign and endless modes it is still a hassle.What this means is that when you want to play a new map or hop between games modes the autosaves for any previous games will be overwritten and you will lose all progress from previous maps that you have played. This also means that you cannot hop between campaign and endless modes because all previous progress in your campaign progress will be overwritten...There are other issues such as when building different military units there is no information providing their stats before building them. Only after you have built them will you be able to see their different stats. Damage, attack speed, attack range, speed, melee and ranged damages, etc.These features should have been a no-brainier. Literally countless games over the decades of PC gaming have had these features. The devs haphazardly dropped the ball on not implementing these features.

Well it is quite apparent that they're not focusing on the game's development as much anymore when the updates were every couple of months last year to non-existent in 2023. December, October, August, June, May... all "major" updates last year, with some hotfixes between each of them as well. But It's April and the release of their new title is approaching fast. _childDocuments_.review: You would think after 20 hours I would know if I like a game or not, yet I still haven't decided because there are things I like, and things I hate about Diplomacy is Not an Option.DNO is a They Are Billions style game, for better and worse. It's not any lesser, nor is it a clone, but instead has its own style and quirks that set it apart. However, the entire game is about perfecting a build order, where you clear and build up a map in preparation for waves of attackers. There are two issues with this style of game that make it not for everyone.The first is that snowballing is incredibly important. Small gains and optimisations snowball into major changes an hour later. Getting an hour or two in and finding that you just can't win, means starting over from the very beginning. Just the time investment in such long playtime is not for everyone, and being forced to do it again can cause a lot of frustration.The second is that the game is an optimisation problem. Should you be selling wood or food? Building two or three foresters on the first day? None of this is apparent to the average person, and so getting better is often just not possible because the game doesn't provide you that feedback. Instead, getting better is done by looking up spreadsheets and build orders. This is the kind of thing that makes competitive RTS games toxic and unfun, and yet that is the path this singleplayer game has chosen.Awkward pacing, QOL, and balance.DNO suffers from a pacing issue, whether it be in the gameplay, or even in the cutscenes. Certain moments feel like a mad scramble of multitasking and chaos, but most of the game is spent waiting around. Sure, you can pause and fast forward, but that is a crutch rather than a solution to sloppy game design. Worse and most blatant are the story cutscenes, filled with long drawn out pauses that make them take 3x longer than they should. The dialog isn't that clever, and nothing is actually happening so they just feel painful to sit through and watch.QOL features could be vastly improved. The tech tree specifically feels awkward to use, needing to be reopened every time a research item finished. Easy to miss that and go half an hour without remembering to do research. There is no reason why there couldn't be a queue, or even simultaneous researches. Having to save scum to get to different paths in the story is also bizarre.Game balance is a mess, and I hope the devs actually take this complaint seriously. I'm not alone with finding certain levels to be poorly balanced with massive difficulty spikes, but the responses to these concerns has been, concerning. Pinned responses to this criticism has been effectively 'get gud', with solutions being to look up spreadsheet builds, or even save scum.Overall DNO is not a bad game, but it's issues make it not for everyone. It was a coin flip to recommend or not, but decided there would be more value highlighting the issues with DNO and the There Are Billions formula that both games share. I recommend buying TAB first as it's more refined, then you can make a more informed decision about DNO.

_childDocuments_.review: Maybe it's just because I stubbornly refuse to go lower than the 3rd difficulty "Ultra-Hardcore" but around mission 8 this game turns into the more stressful moments of an RTS like SC2 except they never stop and the games take 3+ hours. It's exhausting. The pacing is terrible. Just constant pings everywhere because you're being attacked from every direction and you have to check every single ping in case this time it's a big wave and you need to do some micro. Up until this mission the game would mostly let you know when an attack was coming and outside that window you could focus on macro. If you're familiar with the final mission in Wings of Liberty it's like that but you're attacked from any direction often 6+ attacks happening at any one time and the mission takes 3 or more hours.There's a cool magic system except the game doesn't give you a way to reliably get the resource for it until the last tech tree and even when you do the place you have to build it is invariably way outside your fortress and the maximum rate is pathetic so you may as well not bother.The early game is frustrating once the random spawns start because there's no way you can afford to build walls for every direction so again you're constantly managing individual units to fend off attacks and if you miss a single attack the normal buildings in this game are made of paper mache and get destroyed in half a nanosecond. Visibility is atrocious until tech tier 2 so your first minimap vision of an attack is a single red pixel about 2 seconds before it starts destroying your buildings.Small gripe but the screenshots and trailer are not particularly representative of a real game. The sheer amount of stuff would be comically expensive to build. It's not impossible but the base would cover half the map not a small box around the town hall. Related but in the trailer they're throwing out half a dozen meteors like that stuff is free on tap. You're lucky if you get 6 in a whole mission.To be clear I like a difficult RTS. I've enjoyed trying and retrying missions, different strats, better macro, etc. This whole "attacked from all directions" gameplay is fun. But do it continuously for hours and all it's doing is raising my cortisol.Overall it's an interesting game with bad pacing that gets exhausting and stressful to play and that is not something I'm interested in from a single player RTS.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:+Humorous campaign cut scenes+Diverse enemy types+Content that has been released is highly polished+Significant depth in city and defense planning+High Quality voice acting +Multiple game modes to keep you engagedCons: -Game is not finished yet-Not a significant need to use melee troops when towers and archers are easier to keep alive-Updates come out slowly-Only 2 playable missions in campaign-Lack of variety to units in each enemy type-No research queue Personal Opinion:Diplomacy is Not an Option (DNO) offers thrilling real time strategy that also happens to be a tower defense and city management game. The more I learn about the game the more I want to play. It can be easy to overlook the complexity and depth of city and defense layout, but it all starts by realizing how building storage next to production increases the rate of materials harvested, and how water fountains increase the population of nearby houses, or how builder houses need to be dispersed throughout the city in order to reduce the time it takes a builder to get to a construction site, and so on. There are quite a few different enemy types like undead, peasants, royal army, but there are not a large variety of units in each type, hopefully more will be added in the future. Campaign cut scenes are very amusing and I found myself looking forward to each one, which made learning the campaign isn't complete all that much more disappointing. As it currently is DNO is a great little game, and with more features to be added it should be worth looking forward to what comes next!

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun. Combines the best parts of roguelike city builders and medieval style RTS games with many systems that engage each other in satisfying ways without being overly complicated.The game runs as fast as you want to: you can adjust game speed on the fly and pressing the spacebar pauses/plays the game. You have full control of the game while it it paused: give as many commands as you like and you can unpause the game and see them carried out. This means that as a new or experienced player keeping your thumb on the spacebar means that you always have time to stop, evaluate the situation, then make a decision, whether you are microing away a weak troop or plotting out the layout of your city.Combat is not overly complicated but super satisfying. While the game does advertise itself as a "wave defense" type of game, where you have to fend off a large wave of enemies every four or five in-game days, in reality combat is a constant part of the game. You will need to micro your armies always in order to scout out the fog of war and clear out bandits which dwell around the map, in small camps or very, very large ones. You'll be using a small handful of troops to slaughter many times their number in the early game clearing bandits away from forests, minerals and food sources. Luckily all of your troops have out-combat health regeneration, and the enemy AI is fairly simple and easy to out-micro. Neither of these things are too dumbed down though: the health regen is modest and will not make up for bad decisions, and the enemy AI may be simple but it does have some tricks to keep you on your toes. Most notably, bandits will stray from their camps and into your base and start attacking civilians and structures. Outside of fortifications, there is no "passive defenses"; if you do not have manpower availible to respond in time, I have seen a small handful of bandits do damage ranging from a major inconvenience to entirely ruining a two-hour long run by blowing up a fully stocked Granary and throwing me deep into food debt. In short, combat is big part of the game and you'll be glad to know that is is satisfying and well paced, between rewarding you for constant skirmishing as well as providing large-scale battles to pour lots of resources into defending against.The logistical side of the game is really where everything shines and sets the pace for the entire game. You will need a lot of resources. A lot of food, a lot of wood, a lot of stone, a lot of steel. Later on you'll need Coin as well. Natural resources are scattered around your base, sometimes easy to get to, and sometimes not so much. In order to gather the resources fast enough to do something useful with them before you're overrun, you're going to need a lot of manpower. How do you get more workers? You need a lot of houses. Houses increase your maximum population cap and how many new people you have access to every morning. And they take up a lot of space. You'll learn pretty quickly that you will need to be really, really smart about how you place buidlings in this game. The longstanding consequences of a poorly placed Storage Pile can have you cursing yourself an hour along down the line when you're trying to maximize space for population buidings. Your soldiers, and (more importantly) workers cannot move through buildings. You'll always want to have clear avenues for people to move around while also cramming as much stuff as you can into as small of a space as possible, because you can only clear the map so quickly without investing too much into early army and hampering your long term economic health. Did I mention that you need manpower for troops too? And if any of your troops die, they will leave behind a corpse that needs to be manually picked up and dragged to a cemetery, which is an expensive task that can mean a few careless deaths clearing out early bandit camps can do a lot of damage in the long run. The theme you might have noticed so far is that you need to make a lot of important decisions very quickly, which may seem demanding, but because of the "real time with active pausing" system it never feels unfair or overwhelming.If you've actually read this so far I'm going to assume you're interested, and if you want my opinion, the game is worth it's price. It's an "Early Access" title but there's enough in the game currently that you can get your money's worth, then come back later when they've added new stuff. If you decide to pick up the game, just don't forget about Watchtowers. They're in the defense tab and they can save you a lot of headaches when you're spending a lot of wood in the early game and there's not enough resources/time/space to start walling up to keep out wandering enemies in between waves.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played this game for 8.6 hours in 2 days. That says about the enjoyment of the game. if I get bored of a game, i drop it almost completely.Good things about the game:1. The game overall just feels nice. It is hard to describe any other ways. You have points where you can just get into the game and forget time exists. It is satisfying seeing you build up your city/town and start to really scale up.2. The overall game feels sort of complete already but with flaws (I will get to that later) the combat feels good and the building is intuitive.Bad things about the game:1. The game is difficult. Like very difficult. Especially if you went the traitor route in the campaign (It isn't a spoiler, it happens super early in the campaign) the build cost of buildings seems pretty expensive for whatever you wanna build. When I first got the game, i was under the impression that I would be able to build a massive stronghold with a sizeable army to combat the horde of enemies that appear over the horizon. However, it didn't really seem the be the case. If I spend too many resources on scaling, then I wouldn't have the resources to build on the castle and army. If I were to spend too many resources on the castle, then i wouldn't have enough resources to scale up food, wood, stone, iron production. That would in turn affect my army development. So basically, if you try to focus on any aspect, then you would fall behind in others. Additionally, the enemy waves scale very hard. The first 1 -4 waves are pretty easily discombobulated. then all of a sudden, you'll get a huge enemy army charging at you that you had no idea to expect. This is especially evident in the campaign. The first couple of waves are pretty easy. Then the final wave, they will send multiple large armies from multiple directions and by then, your army is pretty lackluster compared to the sheer brute force the enemy is bring to bare. 2. You sometimes get that one or 2 enemies that hide among your crowd of citizens and they just have a murder spree as your citizens won't run away and just casually stand there like it's another Tuesday. So that will just cause a ton of your citizens to die and then you have to pick up their bodies and etc. It's pretty tedious. But I also understand that raiding parties are a thing and that I should be ready for it.3. Production is slow. Like very slow. You would think a Farm would be able to output massive amounts of food considering the amount of land they occupy, but it seems to be more time, resource, and space efficient to just spam fruit pickers when you are down bad on food. Furthermore, because production is slow, you don't have nearly the amount of resources to be able to build up to anything you can imagine. This is just my two cents, but if the costs of buildings was lowered and the production speed was higher, then it'll allow the player a lot more freedom to build up their castle.4. Weird bugs. There are sometimes weird bugs that are present in the game. For example, I was under attack and I was attempting to spam walls to slow down the onslaught while I moved my army into position to fight. However, I noticed  that I had no control over my army. I couldn't move them and that resulted in my defeat.Overall, I actually really enjoy the game, but there are some thing that I would like to tweak to make the game play slightly more player friendly. I am playing on easy for the most part and I still get dumpstered by the AI. If you have any comments to you want to make of this review, feel free to roast me.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, here’s how it went the first time I played Diplomacy is Not an Option. I jump in thinking, “Great, bit of strategy, build a castle, defend it, maybe even have time to enjoy a nice medieval sunset.” But nope. First wave of enemies shows up before I’ve even put the foundations down. It’s like trying to build a sandcastle while a toddler stomps all over it. You barely get a breather. The pace is insane. They should call it Diplomacy is Definitely Not an Option Because You're Too Busy Panicking.I’m sitting there thinking, "Maybe I’ve done something wrong. Am I missing something? Is there a setting for people who actually want to build a castle before the game turns into medieval Doom?" Nope, not in the campaign. Even on easy mode, it's relentless. I’m sweating. I’m shouting at my screen. It’s madness. And the thing is, I love strategy games! But this? This feels like they took the stress of real-time strategy and cranked it up to ‘Oh god, why did I do this to myself?’Then, miracle of miracles, I find out about the sandbox and endless modes. Turns out, if you want a more relaxed experience—where you can actually, you know, build your bloody castle before the world falls apart—they’ve got you covered. Much better. You can chill out a bit, take your time, not feel like you’re constantly under siege. But seriously, the campaign? Avoid if you don’t fancy having a heart attack at your desk.

_childDocuments_.review: At first, I thought it was just another wave defence simulator, but it's actually a pretty decent RTS and, surprisingly, a "mean" city-building simulator. Everyone can find some fun in this game, and I got sucked into the campaign for the first 8 hours. The storyline is decent  and is spiced up with good humour. I also noted the good balance and moderate challenge  for the player, where you’re not exactly on the edge, but you still need to click quickly. Everything was great until I reached a mission that many discuss in the forums, and suddenly, the game's flaws hit me all at once, burning me up:Progress in the campaign resets at every level, and at least 30 minutes  are spent repetitively handling the city-building part, which gets tedious by the fifth time. You have to start all the research from scratch, which drags the game into a more routine and tedious experience, in my opinion. They could've easily avoided this by unlocking later buildings as you progress through the levels so that you could dive deeper into the more interesting aspects of the game rather than repeating everything from scratch each time.After the waves of hordes, there's a huge lack of "auto-rebuild" for the destroyed buildings. Especially when the settlement grows, it becomes very difficult to track what was where. Considering that defending against hordes is one of the core mechanics, this often throws you off track.Up until a certain mission, I didn't have any trouble completing the objectives and easily cleared the map. But then, everything fell apart all at once, and honestly, I don't want to start all over again, knowing that I'd have to rebuild the settlement from scratch every time.I enjoyed the campaign, and I was pleasantly surprised to see that it includes choices that add new mechanics and challenges, which interestingly change and enrich the gameplay. There's also a large selection of units to choose from, just what you need for a good RTS.But man, from one mission to the next, it really started to bug me that you have to start over every time, just with slightly different starting conditions. When you're struggling with a game, you either want to overcome it and feel accomplished, expecting a reward and a sense of victory, or you think it’s just not worth it. After passing this level, I’m pretty sure the next one will force me to start from scratch again, which really spoils the game for me. People do share strategies on how to beat the notorious level by kiting the entire horde with a single unit , but the game doesn't prepare you for this at all, and it’s no StarCraft by any means. Given the sometimes downright annoying city-building part, you're forced to sit and wait for the new day to come as there's a limit on actions , which gets exhausting. But at least there are time acceleration buttons, thank goodness.My experience is based solely on , as it’s the fastest and easiest way to introduce players to the game.For now, I’m giving it a thumbs down, but , as I’ll try to beat the notorious level again. Still, I didn't expect this level of frustration—it feels like the game just wants to keep me stuck in it for as long as possible.UPD:Steam conveniently showed me how to actually beat the Ozzy level (via a live stream on the game's page), and I realized that my experience and speed were clearly not enough for that level. Maybe this level is specifically designed for RTS challengers? Like, "Can you beat Ozzy?"... But I still managed to squeeze out diamonds through sheer frustration, got a few new gray hairs, and after several completely fresh attempts, I finally beat the level, and the game rewarded me with... the next level, which involved escorting a very slow unit with a limited number of troops. I lasted about 15 minutes before deciding that I'd had enough of the campaign.UPD 2:Okay, maybe I gave the game an undeserved thumbs down, considering that it can still be quite engaging. Despite its flaws, there are other modes that are pretty fun (tried, which is a great quality, especially given the game's very reasonable price.

_childDocuments_.review: Diplomacy Is Not An Option is a real-time city builder focused primarily around turtling, or hunkering down and building up defenses in order to defeat waves of enemies. It’s similar to They Are Billions, a zombie-focused city-builder that came out of a few years ago. They Are Billions is notorious for it’s difficulty, and while Diplomacy Is Not An Option is no walk in the park, it is much more accessible to newcomers. It also has a colorful, lively art style and sense of humor, the later of which is nothing special.The setup is silly and mostly pointless. You are a bored king who’s decided to abandon his responsibilities to his people. This leads to unrest and riot, but actually it just provides an excuse for massive mobs of enemies to storm your castle walls. The story bits that set up the campaign and run between missions are very bare bones. At this point there’s no voice acting and little in the way of animation. As it stands they are pretty boring and don’t really hit home the humor they seem to be aiming for. Luckily you can skip them and get right to the action.That’s where Diplomacy Is Not An Option really shines. You have to quickly transform your meager settlement and handful of units into a formidable defense. To do this you must collect various resources like wood and stone, while also providing food to your ever growing populace. Like the best of these games, Diplomacy Is Not An Option is a delicate balancing act. You have limited resources, including works to perform jobs, so you have to prioritize right from the start. Luckily it’s easy to shuffle worker around and get your town on task early on.The first few waves of enemies are simple to deal with, but things quickly ramp up. You’ll soon have to begin walling in your city and making educated guesses on where to begin. Each wave comes from a different, random direction and you’re only a given a few minutes notice as to where it will be coming from. This leads to last minute building that you can hopefully afford and quickly requisition your builders to erect. Often times you’ll be fighting off pitchfork wielding peasants with a half-built wall and poorly positioned guard towers. Thankfully you can quickly make some soldiers to help literally fill in the gaps in your defense.While Diplomacy Is Not An Option is considerably easier than similar games like They Are Billions, it’s definitely no cake walk. The waves ramp up considerably and it’s very easy to get caught with your pants down. However, there are several difficulty options to make the game easier, or harder, and the penalties for letting small batches of enemies through are low. It just launched in early access, but already has a robust research tree and several tiers of upgradable buildings. Right now if features an endless survival mode and two campaign missions. However, you can see dozens of missions they plan to add once the game leaves early access. It seems like Diplomacy Is Not An Option already has a solid foundation that will only get better the more Door 407 builds upon it.

_childDocuments_.review: So... Diplomacy. It ain't an option, but what is this game, exactly? More or less, this is Age of Darkness : Final Stand with a more cartoony art style, and a development team not crewed by morons that don't know their gluteus maximum from a hole in the dirt. Obviously, this game has taken some pointers from They Are Billions, a game that showed Activision was WRONG when they declared RTS games dead as a genre, but they don't copy it word for word like AoD did. Instead, they expand upon it! There's a lot to appreciate here with quality of life changes and good design decisions. To start, one flaw TAB had was with its camera system. When designing towns, it was difficult to manage the entryway of buildings, especially houses, in such a way that you could make neat, orderly lines that were as efficient as possible. Diplo has a full 3D camera that can view the game from any angle you please, even getting those top-down views that allow for picture perfect placement. Nice. :)Another problem TAB and AoD has was maintenance. Everything costed a maintenance fee, which really made me scratch my head. Was there not a zombie apocalypse going on? Their payment should be a day's meal, and getting to live another day without getting turned into a brain eater. Diplo took this to heart and soldiers only cost the food required to keep them from starving to death (it can happen), and the raw materials required to create their gear, which is a nice change of pace. Much like humanity in its adolescent, medieval times, you're going to be spending most of your time focusing on creating enough food for everyone, and then raw materials like stone, iron, and wood to keep the malcontents from burning your throne room to the ground. The gameplay loop of resource collection, logistics, construction, expansion, clearing, and wave defense is really quite satisfying. A word on defense. At first glance, its very simple. You have walls, towers, and archers to shoot down from them. Even TAB had tesla towers, ballistas, and gatling guns... but FEAR NOT, dear basement dweller, Diplo has you covered. Towers can stock about 9 archers/crossbowmen at a time, giving them a nice little range boost, but they can also have catapults, and ballistae loaded instead. This gives some nice, tactical options for how you want your defense to be laid out. Oh, and your archers can also stand on walls, which is something I haven't seen since Battle for Middle Earth 1 back during the halcyon days when EA used the Sage engine! Even though it's still in early access, there's more than enough content here to satisfy even the nit-pickiest of internet denizens (though there are still many who engage in what I call “unemployed behavior”, and you can't appease someone with THAT much free time). The developers are just blazing through their development schedule too, and have released FIVE major updates, based on community feedback, in the single year Diplo has been in early access. These guys have their thumb on the pulse of the community and know precisely what they're doing. The price tag isn't overly extreme for what you get either, but wait for a steam sale if you must. I wholeheartedly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: A roguelite-ish rts-ish citybuilder-ish good time. You can pause at any time so it doesn't have the stress and frankly the inflexibility of an RTSbut includes all the important beats of an RTS like huge armies and walls. When I was a kid, all I wanted to do was create insane cities in Ageof Empires 2 map builder and I always found it disappointing that I couldn't make a 'real' city. This game splits the difference and lets youenjoy the building aspect and placement despite most of it really not mattering a ton, while still having objectives which can make some ofthose sandbox city building type games feel a little empty and pointless.Lots of trial and error, but it isn't a huge investment to restart so I never mind that. Sure, maybe the game has an annoying way of pathingthe enemy on certain maps. Sure maybe you'll lose because a random attack happened to fall at an inconvenient location/time. Oops! I didn'tbuild enough builders to keep up with construction so I can't build in time so my people all starve to death because I wasn't on top of foodwhile I was focused on army stuff. While these things are all frustrating in the moment, especially if you didn't really explicitly do anything"wrong", it just fuels your replay where you say "ah, yeah I should probably clear out this part of the map and put a wall here etc".I do wish there were more upgrades and unit variety but I think the game is going for mass over quality. At later points in the game yourtroops really meet their match which brings in another trial and error mechanic: Oops, I guess I should focus on taking the fight to the enemymore often.Ultimately the one reason I didn't want to play this game is that I was afraid it would be content bare, and to some extent it kindof is, but thereplayability and level variety is sufficient to just pick it up randomly and play through a map. The game doesn't bait me to continue all nightlong which I actually like, but it's definitely one of those games to play when I'm killing time more than wanting to fulfill an objective.9/10Could use more unit types, cavalry needs some kind of buff, spearmen could use a lategame upgrade like swordsman have, and I wouldn'tmind more trading options to pad resources up or down more than you already can.Casual enough to enjoy even if you can't quite get into RTS or this newer genre of infinite city defense but complicated enough to actuallyplay more than 20 hours.

_childDocuments_.review: I had been following this project for a long while. At least some of the dev team for this game are a huge help in the Unity Community, as they are active therein responding to questions therein. I bought this partially in recognition of the good work they do there and just wanted to mention it here as I felt it would be something that otherwise went unremarked on.And for the record, the OTHER reason I bought this, is that Stronghold + They Are Billions is neat.Diplomacy is Not An Option is great in concept. The gameplay is primarily about resource flow and making sure that you can have the resources to produce the things you need to survive as greater volumes of enemies are thrown at you. You also need to be careful about map control, as every enemy that is on the map, will eventually migrate at you during the attack waves. So if you clear the map early, you have less to deal with later. Clearing the map also rewards you with resources for summons or damage abilities. The rates of every resource are clearly marked in the UI and upgraded structures clearly signpost what cost they have for upgrading and what benefit they provide you. This is a great foundation for the game, and I have no complaints here.I only played a few hours when I got this and I encountered 1 session breaking bug, where when some of the builder villagers died, my towncenter was incapable of making more all the sudden. There have also been a few glitches during the end of a scene, where on defeat the enemy pathing would start directing all the enemy AI to a single point nearby where they were. I believe what is happening, is that the flowfield (At least I infer it to be a flowfield based on how the AI behave) is setting some point nearby after the enemy destroy the last structure, that then all enemies converge on to form a horrendous many limbed mockery of life as the enemy entities seem to stop attempting to prevent overlap and merge into one. This is merely hilarious and not actually all that impactful as it's during the like 5-10 second end of mission screen after your last building is destroyed, but I got enough of a laugh out of it, that I wanted to mention it here.I have found unit control to be a bit sticky for lack of a better term. Friendly entities are given more orders that then reset if they are to hold position or move to attack. So positioning a group of melee fighters between the enemy and archers in a hold ground stance, means clicking to move them, and then immediately clicking to get them to hold position when they reach their destination. Groups moved together do not form up prior to moving, so any moving in formation. Likewise since stance resets on move orders, you can click to move units in a heated moment, forget they aren't in a hold stance, and have them walk into 200 enemy entities and get pounded into dust, which is annoying. None of this is gamebreaking, but it is somewhat frustrating, and each issue kind of builds on others.Also I'll confess I do not enjoy the laser or summoned units, or other such battlefield abilities. I get their purpose and I would say the game is balanced at higher difficulties around you using them, but I wish they were a little less fantastical. This isn't to say the setting is some kind of super serious, historic epic conforming to the historical record; but, the ion canon from the C&C series (Except instead of the GDSS Philadelphia, it's a tactical laser granted to you by the divine power of fantasy God) is a bit stark of a juxtaposition when it is presented side by side with spearmen and catapults.So overall I only detract 1 for the session breaking bug and 2 for the control issues. It should be said that as this is an early access title, I find it likely that the control issues will be fixed with time; and, when they are fixed I will amend my score.So 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: *Original Review Before @ 11.1 hours* Synopsis: 8.5/10 | Easy going tower-defense with in progress campaign.Pros: - Good, open, and consistent communication & updates from the team, probably 9 or 10/10 as far as well-run early accesses go.- Fair price point for a game that when finished could be fairly priced at $45. Maybe get on sale if you're skeptical - Difficulty is good upon early adoption Cons: - Early Access, obviously diverse content is sparse- After getting a hang of mechanics, any of the modes become a cake walk, becomes a city-builder Myself personally, I really enjoy chill laid back games to play while I watch sports, hence the long playtime, so don't think there is THAT much content to justify the playtime. After kind of "mastering the mechanics" I feel as though it has mostly become a city-builder (on any version of Endless mode) which is fine, because I like those too. But that is to say, late-game needs balancing work done. However, like I mentioned in my pros, this is one of the most responsive and well-intentioned teams I've seen operate an early-access. Community complaints are, if not patched, then responded too within the monthly updates, and patches are discussed at length on the steam page (which is such a far cry from other EA's that force you to join their forum or follow their socials, I forgot that it was even a thing), that if you enjoy the genre, you can know that this is clearly a passion project and that throughout EA you can contribute to the direction of the game and expect regular updates. Anyway, solid tower-defense game, rough but fun mechanics, and did I mention it's gorgeous? 8.5/10 ** Previous review:8/10 from me, has work to do on balancing, such as timing of waves as well as adding in new content so it's more worthwhile to push for upgrades, but it's good enough in it's current state to justify its current price point.Have got to say, this game can't come recommended enough if you enjoy challenging tower defense games. I've got to say, it's been awhile since I've been able to find a game in this genre that is able to strike a happy balance between "shut-off brain and upgrade" and rage inducing unfair mob fest. It's a game that rewards you for noticing your mistakes and inefficiencies when you lose, making it all the more satisfying when you win.Also lends itself to replayability which is nice.No tower defense game has held me so firmly by my tennis balls since I was 10 and was obsessed with AddictingGames|com. I mean, the 12 hours on record at the time of this review were recorded in the 3 days since I bought this game - which is insane for me, who usually just has games like Football Manager in the background while I code or watch videos. _childDocuments_.review: Diplomacy is Not an Option (DNO) is classic style Real-Time-Strategy game which uses well designed and implemented gameplay to make a tightly packaged experience which both regular fans and more particularly those who enjoy the more old school and difficult examples RTS genre will find highly enjoyable. Taking place in Medieval fantasy world, you play as gruff and long suffering nobleman referred to, even by his closest advisors and friends, as 'The Lord'. As such it is your duty command your people and guide them to glory, growing from a scant handful of foot-soldiers and berry pickers into a vast economic machine that turns raw resources into an unstoppable army of knights, towers, and war machines.Having played the game for a significant amount of time, completing one campaign, and being mid-way through others, I feel like I have divined the single word which best describes DNO's style and strength within the RTS landscape. That word is 'Simplicity'. Rather than creating a sprawling morass of game mechanics, DNO instead strips down the administrative and inconsequential bloat of other designs and instead builds a highly focussed game style. You, for the most part, play as a single classic medieval faction made of knights, swordsman, archers, castles, catapults, and the like. These forces must be trained or built using classical resources of wood, stone, metal and gold, gathered from the surrounds or traded for.The game has to major modes, the story Campaign and an Endless mode. The main goal in both is much the same, build up a meagre starting force into one which can not only defend itself but also crush your enemies and bring their cities and fortifications tumbling to the ground. My focus was primarily on the campaign, where you are presented with individual missions, sometimes with more complex objectives. While in effect, most missions involve obliterating your enemy, sub objectives or specific targets change the players focus, and create a surprisingly deep need for tactics and strategy beyond simply amassing an army.Indeed, while material resources are needed to grow your army, there are three other major resources which DNO uses to drive gameplay and create difficulty for the player. The first two are food and people. As a Lord, you have dominion over your growing city, and growing is what it must do to survive. Every soldier, farmer, fisher, etc. needs to be fed and housed. More houses means more people. More people need more food. More food needs more land. And, a bigger army needs more people, more resources, and more defenses. DNO uses this simple chain, like many other RTS games do, but adds in an additional element which forces the player to work efficiently and try to roll this economic boulder down the hill. This final resource, is time, and it is an ever dwindling resource.That may sound trite, but DNO really does have a sharp and ever present focus on the passage of time. At the top left of your screen you'll see a slowly turning disc representing day and night, each one meticulously counted. In the bottom left, right beside your map is a counter showing when new enemies will next attempt to storm your city. Each one of these assaults is a horde of enemies marching towards your settlement, and they only grow with time. DNO does not allow complacency. Each moment should be put to work, and despite the games apparent focus on defensive battle, the most success is often found by being aggressive.Take too long, fail to clear out enemies fast enough, or build up your own military too slow, and the next horde will wipe you out completely. Even knowing where and when an enemy will hit you is only a small strategic boon. Knowing these things will help you place your defences, walls and warriors, but to win you'll need more that just raw strength. Often, your army will be vastly outnumbered by incoming enemies, while your offensive targets will often be frustratingly robust. So, your greatest strength is in fact your player intelligence.DNO has active pausing, letting you stop time at any point and give orders. Battles are not won by simply steam rolling the enemy with a superior wall of meat and metal, but by careful coordination of positions, formations, and movements. Enclosing an enemy will limit their movement and damage output, and the bunched up core of their forces struggle to reach the front, replacing the limited frontline as they mauled by yours. Siege equipment and marksman can be placed on fixed towers, raining death on enemies as they scramble to take down walls or maneuver around obstacles, bleeding them out. A well thought out number of healers and choke points can turn a handful of soldiers into an unbreakable wall of steel and death, cutting down entire armies as they flood towards you. DNO asks the player to embrace all these, and more. It is an RTS which feels highly tactical, and more than a simple measure of army sizes.This methodology of building on simple base mechanics, using what you have intelligently, is the real shining star for DNO. The tech-tree is similarly basic. Each major building expands the tree to provide more improvements for it's own units. These are understandable and useful, such as the speed at which resource gatherers move, which is needed for collecting and depositing materials at your various depots. The speed of building and builders, which become increasingly important as you expand, with builders rushing between sites and buildings needing to be completed before the next day dawns. Soldiers and siege gear increase in range, health, damage, a few special abilities, and training times. All these things are easily understandable, and give real improvements to you while still keeping things simple.Even graphically, the game is simple and polygonal, redolent of early RTS games. This not only allows computing power to be devoted to the massive number of units that are present in any major combat, but also moves to make everything easily recognizable. DNO leans into this artistic style, opting for a cartoonish design which I found very appealing, and shows that stylistic design can be every bit as visually enjoyable and hyper-realistic games if done boldly and sincerely.I will say, however, DNO can be very unforgiving. It can feel disheartening to spend hours on a mission only to realize the economic engine you've created doesn't have enough power or speed to beat you the level, and their is little recourse but to start over and plan better next time. I am playing on the normal difficulty, and have had a number of these moments as I learned to break out of my defensive and passive mindset.If you love stories of classic fantasy, with some comedy thrown in, but also love a challenging strategic war gaming experience, DNO will probably have something that you'll really enjoy. You can spend a great deal of time in just the campaign, and the endless mode expands this experience massively, and gives the opportunity for some battles of a truly epic scale. Overall, DNO is an RTS I have truly enjoyed, despite my own amateur skill in the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Brilliant little addition to the RTS genre, with a lot more meat to it than the cute graphics would suggest. It feels like a spiritual successor to the Stronghold series, as you work to build walls, traps, and a variety of tiny little warriors to defend your ever-expanding economy. Having to feed your troops as well as your citizens makes economic management a careful balancing act, as building too big of an army will create a deadly famine, while focusing too much of your economy will place it in danger of the ever-expanding waves of attackers.The real strength of the game, though, is the graphics. I've seen plenty of games attempt a low-poly style and end up feeling soulless and generic. This one does the opposite - it oozes character and charm. The characters, buildings, and warriors all have beautifully detailed animations, and you can happily spend a good while watching your little smiths tinker away in their forges, your lumberjacks haul logs back from the forest, or a squad of spearmen face off against a horde of peasants.The choice of enemies is similarly delightful. Huge, teeming waves of low-HP attackers make for delightfully satisfying fights, made even better by the physics-enabled impacts that throw them into the air. Even losing the game becomes a visually satisfying experience, as you watch the enemy pour into your base. And somehow, it still runs as smooth as butter - I didn't get any FPS drop even when the waves became colossal.Highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: In the current state of the game, I won't recommend it. This RTS game with Tower Defense elements is not going in the right direction. It does not have all aspects that is necessary for an RTS game. There are lots of things which they should have prioritized, but instead they prioritized on other things which will have negligible impact on the fun factor of the game.The unit type is very limited. They should have focused on adding more playable unit types. But they didn't.Lack of terrain variation. Even though they said the map is randomly generated, but you can't really tell, because they all look 95% similar. They should have created more variation of terrain textures. But they didn't.Resource distribution is quite terrible an uneven at some times. At some point, you'll get several iron ores very close to your main base. And at other points, they are very far away, so your main base is open for tons of unexpected attacks from fast-moving enemies. Hence you'll get crushed easily. Fyi, iron ores are the critical resources for your entire colony to advance. Without it, then it's practically game over soon.There's are 3 types of game mode: Endless mode, Scenarios, and Campaign. The campaign mode is just dull. Even with the added cartoon, it does not add value to the game. The endless mode is the most interesting part of the game. But sadly, they created unbalanced difficulty level. The lower level is very easy to beat. Once you're able to create a stone wall, then you're practically invincible, because they enemy waves do not have enough attack power to bring down even 1 tile of wall. On the other hand, the higher level is very hard to beat. The enemy waves will come with many powerful units, fast-moving units, and even artillery. They can easily beat your main army in open combat and easily destroy multiple tiles of wall or towers. So it's game over once your entire army is crushed. No chance to rebuild. It's the most stupid mechanics to happen in an RTS game, because the most fun aspect of an RTS game is if players always have the opportunity to always rebuild and always keep up with the incoming enemy force. In addition, with very limited playable units in Endless mode, makes this game very boring after 1 or 2 trial.The scenario mode is also not really fun and not worth replaying. It's very predictable and basically you just need to implement one style of strategy to win it. No point in trying to replay scenario, because it is not design for strategy. It is designed for you to memorize your steps in winning it. So this is another stupid implementation of the game with an RTS aspect to it. Oddly there are a lot of enemy unit types available in scenario mode, which should have been available in the endless mode.There's also no tool for mods or community-made maps. This reality makes the game much worse than They are Billions.Despite all of the negative aspects and feedbacks from players, they decided to be stubborn and still continue with their idea to create a cartoon instead, which will not be memorable. They are spending too much effort on creating a story with cartoons which nobody will even care about in the end. It's an RTS game, so why do they focus on a cartoon story? Are they trying to change the game's genre and become something like "The Last of Us" game? They are Billions don't even have any cartoon story, but they manage to acquire a huge number of players and high positive reviews.But I guess some developers just love to maintain their ego instead of selling the game to players.

_childDocuments_.review: This is basically "RTS mechanics 101" with appealing presentation value and a nice sense of the frantics. It's not subtle. The frantics come from assault waves you have to prepare for and the idiocy of your troops, you have to learn how much of everything is enough and what sorts of idiocy you have to prevent, and how.  See? RTS mechanics 101. There's one formation (you can scroll between a longer and shorter battle line) and no troop discipline to speak of at all; infantry are simply incapable of forming a line if they can see the enemy. As RTS puzzles go it's not a challenge. There's memorizing how much you'll need to build to meet wave number N (since there's no scouting the main enemy, they just arrive from off-map), figuring out how to build that much that fast (that's a genuine challenge in this game, even on the "easy" setting finding time to build and man enough walls for the 2nd, 3rd, 4th waves is not easy), and micromanaging the slaughter of the charging-straight-in horde.
