_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game! Well built and plays very well! If you are a fan of games like StarCraft or base defense games in general, you should really enjoy this one! Many of the mechanics we already know are well executed and the controls are very similar, so learning is very easy. There's not much to complain about, but I do want to point out some balance issues that I found to reduce the flow of the game for me. In the beginning of the rounds, base building has a great balance between resource gathering and construction. It's very easy to develop a flow and balance everything you need to advance. However, there's a point where you have to build a "Market" that is designed to somehow generate a new resource (by that point), a gold coin. This coin is a requirement to upgrade buildings and certain units. I unfortunately couldn't get this to work, even when trading for resources that I didn't need. The ability to trade for resources only becomes valuable when you get a map that doesn't spawn a specific resource within your starting area... I assume. This rarely happens however, so this building becomes extremely pointless for me and forced my strategy to successfully function without it. Maybe it's a glitch or something I was doing wrong, but after ten trades in one round, I was unable to generate one single coin. So I found that you can just create an old "Zerg" defense setup to overcome the lack of upgrades allowed by this building. I have beat the couple rounds that the game currently has, but I am a little frustrated that I haven't been able to see or try ANY of the buildings or units that require these coins. With all that being said, I still think it's a great game! With it still being in development, I'm sure we'll see some adjustments/fixes that will make things like this much better.This game has some great potential and is a great addition to the genre! With the fun humor, well balanced difficulty, and attention to quality, this game goes high on my recommendation list. Can't wait to see what else this title has to bring!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a review of the game as it was on initial early access release.It contains an endless mode and two campaign missions - further campaign missions are promised.Graphics:The game is gorgeous and runs well on my machine, you can scroll to a very low level of detail and it's enjoyable to watch your little peons run around doing their thing.Gameplay: This game has 3 game modes and the experience is drastically different between them. The 'easy' game mode is the only one where as a player you can actually enjoy building up your settlement and taking time to watch battles/workers. Medium and hard scale up with limited starting resources, more regular and larger waves of enemies. If you want a challenge you will get it in spades. It can be brutal. Having to manually collect magic crystals forces you out of your turtle which is a good bonus for cowardly players like me.HOWEVER - if you enjoy building up a settlement you risk bouncing off this game on anything other than easy as the frantic racing around the screen desperately micro-managing units in your army for peak efficiency, building specific builds in exactly the right order will leave little time for 'enjoying' the colony builder aspect. So you would be right to approach this as a medieval They Are Billions.Content? I'm a little disappointed - the endless mode and two campaign missions feels slightly lightweight. However the game mechanics and breadth of unit types/buildings and enemies I have seen are very impressive and show an extremely sturdy start.Don't leave bodies lying around. They get back up and start eating your peons.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game! Reminds me of an updated version of Firefly Studio's Stronghold which I absolutely loved back in the day. I also get strong Banished vibes, only this is better because it has a combat mechanic where the former did not. Positives: + Cool graphical style. Works well for this type of game.+ Fun and addicting gameplay. I've already sunk 9 hours into this and I always look forward to playing more. + Good variety of buildings and units. + Interesting tech tree with lots of options. It's difficult to choose which research to go with, but that's how it should be.Negatives:- Difficulty is a little unbalanced. You can make it easier by choosing the easiest difficulty, but where's the fun in that? Also, your choices in the game affect how difficult it is. Want to side with the people and fight the monach? Yeah, it's going to be harder than siding with the king and fight peasants. - Not a ton of content at the moment, but it is in early access, so that's to be expected. Thankfully, you get a lot of mileage out of the content that is there.Looking forward to upcoming updates. Well worth the $25 entry fee. I've paid way more for way less game. If you're an RTS fan, this is a no brainer. Just be ready to play the same levels over and over again until you figure out the winning strategy.

name: Dordogne
detailed_description: Immerse yourself in a unique narrative experience, embarking on a vibrant journey that will awaken your senses and evoke warm memories. Play as Mimi, exploring the precious recollections of your childhood and the times shared with your late grandmother. As past meets present, confront your adult choices with fond childhood memories to uncover lost family secrets. Explore Dordogne landscapes of a thousand summer colors, within sumptuous hand-painted watercolor environments. During your adventure, recall the moments, the panoramas, the scents, the sounds, and the sensations. Recount these vivid memories in your journal as a recollection of Mimi’s family past that’s unique to your experience and a nostalgic, touching reflection of your journey. • Explore the stunning landscapes of Dordogne in hand-painted watercolors • Embark on a unique and heartwarming narrative experience • Awaken your senses as you explore childhood memories • Collect photos, sounds and scents to create your journal, unique to your adventure

_childDocuments_.review: Dordogne is a heartwarming linear narrative adventure game with strikingly vibrant watercolour art. It is a story about remembering forgotten childhood memories and recognising their importance going into adulthood. It is a moving short story told through impressive visual displays, but one that will only last a few hours.You play as Mimi in both the past and present. Present Mimi is an adult and is having difficulties with her father. He does not acknowledge her desire to remember more about her grandmother, Nora. The topic is always contentious when it is brought up in conversation, but no one in her family will answer why she has large portions of memory missing. Now that Nora has recently passed away, she is more determined than ever to finally have her questions answered.Beginning her adventure, Mimi ventures out to Nora’s old house and her memories start flooding back. She recalls being there, and all of the fun she had with her grandmother. Why were these precious recollections hidden from her? What happened, and where did it all go wrong?The story is generally very uplifting, but the darker undertones are still present, they just do not take centre stage. Collect letters to find out more, carefully reading between the lines in dialogue with Nora. Now that Mimi is analysing her memories through an adult perspective, it is easier to spot the strain in Nora’s voice when certain topics are brought up, or the way specific topics are quickly brushed off or changed. I enjoyed this angle, as it kept the game purposefully light-hearted, but the full context is there for players who wish to delve deeper into the narrative, especially with the character Renaud and his indirectly explained past. The focus is on Nora and her relationship with Mimi, and how this shaped her as an adult. There is an abundance of self-reflection that Mimi does, on her emotions and how she felt during specific moments or days. Whilst there is no villain or looming threat in the story, the game fantastically submerses players into its vibrant watercolour wonderland, and into the life of Mimi. Switching between young and adult Mimi, the entirety of the game is set in and around Nora’s house, and of course the Dordogne river. Adult Mimi is searching for clues to spark her memories in order to find a box that her grandmother left behind for her. After finding an object of significance, the game will switch to childhood Mimi and play a scene to show how that specific object fits into the timeline. Dordogne is extremely linear and with small explorable areas in each chapter, it is near impossible to become lost or unsure of what to do next. Young Mimi is an explorer, and loves to record sounds, take photos, and collect stickers. There are also tapes scattered around that help give further insight into the past. Alongside the stickers and tapes, there is another collectable to find which are words. These words portray Mimi’s emotions in a literal sense and can be used to create a notebook page at the end of the chapter. This is where players creativity can shine through. Decorate the page with stickers found from that chapter, photos and recorded sounds, as well as making a short three sentences based on the words discovered. I found these binder pages to signify Mimi’s self-reflection as it seems to be a popular theme in the game, with her grandmother often asking how she feels, how did she find today and so forth. All encouraging young Mimi to be free to think for herself and recognise her emotions. Despite Dordogne being such a short game, I was disappointed to see that the menu is void of a chapter select option. Given that the chapters end abruptly and without warning, it can be difficult to know what exact action you do will lead to the ending of the chapter, and thus the ending of your opportunity to explore and collect more items. I loved exploring and collecting the adorable stickers, and wished to go back to specific locations, but without a chapter select, this becomes more time consuming.There are no puzzles, but basic tasks are made enjoyable with their interactivity. Direct Mimi’s left and right hands with left and right mouse buttons to catch objects, unscrew lids by holding down left click and shaking the mouse, or direct the key into the keyhole by moving the mouse to the right spot. Each of these simple tasks would typically be automated in games, but in Dordogne, it matches the calm, relaxing pace and overall cozy atmosphere of the game. Helping to bring something new to the gameplay loop which was always a welcome addition.  Dordogne’s striking watercolour visuals breathe life into each and every scene. Each summer landscape oozes authenticity and individuality, giving off a childish, yet beautiful view of the world, as seen through Mimi’s eyes. The impressive illustrations are the most alluring and distinctive feature of the game and do not disappoint.Characters are voiced during cutscenes, but not in their narration when exploring the world. With the ability to record sounds, its easy to zone in on background sounds such as dogs barking, crickets chirping or the sound of the river flowing down a stream. Everything about the sounds resembled peacefulness and sentimentality. Despite the game being obviously called Dordogne, a river in France, there seemed to be an immense lack of French culture or direct references to the setting present in the game, at least from a foreigner’s perspective. The default language is English, and I felt the need to search online for more information about this area, as opposed to being able to learn about it in the game. This was disappointing, given the especially beautiful and culturally rich setting which the game alludes to, even with its own title. Playing with French voice overs and English subtitles is possible, but unfortunately the game does not make this a clear option. I would recommend a prompt at the start of the game for players to choose their preferred option. 3.5 hours. Player choice.  None, it is a linear narrative adventure. Only for achievement hunting.Dordogne is a visually distinctive and heart-warming narrative adventure. It misses an opportunity to better explore its culturally rich setting, but its short and peaceful story are sure to provide a relaxing few hours of nostalgia. Its simple gameplay and sticker-collecting exploration help refocus players attention on the story, all whilst being absorbed in the beautiful summer landscapes and watercolour art.

_childDocuments_.review: Dordogne is a lovely gentle heart warming game about childhood memories which hits all the nostalgic buttons accompanied by good voice acting and watercolour graphics.You play as the adult Mimi who visits her late grandmother's home against the wishes of her parents.  You already know there is breakdown in the relationship between your father and his mother.  You have no memory of visiting your grandmother's house and once there, certain objects trigger off memories.  These memories take you back as the child Mimi when you were staying with your grandmother.You were 12 years old when you visited your grandmother whilst your parents were preparing to move the family to USA.  The game highlights well the innocent and simple days of childhood free from adult responsibilities and worries.  The natural beauty of the French countryside is around the river Dordogne and you meet some of the local residents.  As a city girl, you have to adapt to country life and food plus getting to know your grandmother.  Mimi often looks and acts much younger than a 12 year old and that may be due to being an only child.The natural beauty of the countryside is beautifully portrayed in vivid watercolour art style and I particularly loved the river scenes whilst kayaking.  The art style is accompanied by gentle sounds and music and excellent voice overs.At the time of writing this, the developer has added a chapter select where you are able to go back and find missing collectables.  There are 8 chapters and you collect stickers, sounds, photos, words, letters and make up a journal as well.  There are quite a few of these and a lot of achievements are linked to getting them all.  So there is a bit of a grind to achieve 100% which I didn't manage to get.I did find the gameplay a bit clunky at time when trying to open a jar or pour the milk.  I managed to make a great mess with that!  There are a few activities like cooking which you have to do as well as trying to lure a cat!  Yes, there is a resident cat in the game.I'm sure many of us will resonate with this game, especially if you spent holidays with other relatives as a child.  Dordogne has a mystery at the heart of its story and it unfolded very well and kept your interest.  I did shed a tear at the end when Mimi realised how much her grandmother loved her. That is not a spoiler!It is a fairly short game, but well worth playing.  Don't take any notice of my time as I was trying to hunt down the collectables!  There is a warning at the beginning about epilepsy triggers.  When the scene changes to the past, there is like a whirlpool action which can make you dizzy too.  Be aware also that there are adult themes in the letters you have to read.Highly recommend for those who enjoy gentle, charming games with an interesting story.  8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: This game tries to be many things, with controls that feel clunky more often than not, with short mini-games, collectibles and even quick time events. And while it doesn't really manage to actually be all those things, it does manage to capture a glimpse of long forgotten summer days. _childDocuments_.review: Dordogne is a game about the childhood memories of one city girl, living for one summer with her grandmother in a peaceful and quiet region of the French countryside. This game was made by someone who knows about this duality between life in the city and "Going outside" and reconnecting with your other world.Sometimes it can feel (living in the city) as if you are no longer there. You are outside of yourself in a way. Falling apart as if trying to escape.And then you go outside the city and you cannot find yourself either, you are trapped between two states. You are not free.Dordogne may help us free ourselves by taking us on a trip with the protagonist, finding her memories and finding herself, giving us this small experience, a really nice one to be had, in which we breath organically through its watercolors visuals. If you experienced life outside the city before, and you want to remember how it was, to be blissfully quiet one summer afternoon... or maybe you want to know how it could be, then I recommend playing through Dordogne.

_childDocuments_.review: Dordogne (i can't pronounce that) is a beautiful story driven game which takes you back, accompanied by beautiful art and story it delivers a wonderful experience.You play as Mimi – a woman who goes back to a town in France from USA after her grandma died. While she's there she starts remembering her childhood she spent with grandma there. That's when gameplay shifts to when Mimi was a child. Piece by piece you uncover the past which is mysterious and you finally make peace in your mind.The game is done amazingly well. Great atmosphere which makes you feel nostalgic, the way you uncover the story and write the story yourself is very simple yet it delivers an emotional impact.The gameplay is extremely simple – you just walk around while looking for collectibles and doing the main tasks to advance the story. It has some simple mini-games but mostly it's story driven and everything is in the text and images presented by the game.It's a very short game but it's diverse and not for a second you think it's boring. You just want to proceed with the story and relive the memories.This game has only one downside and it's not having a chapter select. It's filled with collectibles and some challenges. If you miss one you must replay the game. That's just bad design. Either add chapter select or stop with collectible related achievements. It's too annoying.Graphically the game is wonderful. Artistic style is beautiful and each scene is true art. Usually those artistic graphics in other games look very similar to each other due to using same tools and technique but not here. Every scene is painted beautifully.Sound design is very good. While the game is only partially voiced, the voice acting is good and music accompanies the story well and takes you down the memory lane.It's a wonderful game which could definitely be called a piece of art. It's a short one so people may think twice before paying full price. But at least wishlist it or if you can afford to pay, buy it.

_childDocuments_.review: 4/10 Beautiful artwork but terrible otherwise.I loved the graphics style, but that is this game's one and only redeeming feature, and, in the face of everything else, just not enough to merit a positive review.The world is tiny, the game itself short enough to finish in 3 hours, with next to no replay-ability due to its completely linear nature. The story, though very occasionally cute, is painfully unoriginal, filled with plot holes and entirely forgettable.Worse still, the gameplay itself is just one frustration after another. Something as straightforward as opening a door or pouring cereal into a bowl is needlessly difficult due to abysmally poor mouse control responses. Even with the game literally showing you on screen which direction to move the mouse, the controls often just don't work.Honestly, the devs should have given up trying to make a game and simply used their awesome graphical talent to make an animated movie. Unfortunately, as a gaming experience, this one fails miserably.

_childDocuments_.review: Fixed Multicam as an approach was invented by French developers, so I was really looking forward to the prospect of a 'Boku no Vacance'... a Gallic take on the 'summer vacation' sub-genre of fixed multicam games, pioneered by Japan's Millennium Kitchen with 2000's 'Boku no Natsuyasumi'.DORDOGNE (as the developers insist on shouting the title) takes place on twin timelines, as Mimi older attempts to recover her recollections of Mimi younger's visits to her grandmother's house in (all together, now:) DORDOGNE. The game makes a strong first impression through the extraordinary visuals from developers Un Je Ne Sais Quoi and Umanimation. 3D models blend perfectly with their gorgeous, parallaxing handpainted backgrounds, achieving an incredibly strong (and distinctively 'bandes dessinées') 'interactive cartoon' aesthetic. The visual techniques on display are - to my knowledge - unique in gaming and sometimes the sense of depth is unreal...!DORDOGNE tells a tale of family, innocence and loss through strong writing and characterisation, with some distinctive and flavourful language - grandmother Nora's description of a diary/binder as a 'never-ending book' - and some fantastic animation - young Mimi sulks adorably...!The game offers a little virtual tourism, with enticing renderings of village markets, idyllic riverside tracks and one pantry in particular that never failed to conjure heady scents of preserved meats and jams and mmm... good stuff. Nora's house especially screams FRANCE, THIS IS A LOVELY OLD FRENCH HOUSE BELONGING TO A FRENCH LADY IN (together now) DORDOGNE.Micro activities (possibly inspired by fellow countrymen Quantic Dream's Fahrenheit and Heavy Rain) provide a change of pace - you'll glue toys together, you'll cook food with Nora, you'll find stickers and sound effects and take photographs and solve incredibly simple puzzles... and none of it will disguise that this game is painfully linear.Broken into eight chapters spread over the four-week holiday, DORDOGNE (!) will set you a series of fairly linear tasks per chapter. Contrast this with the Boku games, where you're allocated 30 days, to do with as you wish! Explore! Participate in bug battles! Catch fish! Investigate mysteries! Or don't, it's your vacation! DORDOGNE, on the other hand, has a singular story to tell, and sticks rigidly to this schedule.The gameplay is casual, and faithfully serves the tale, and, in principle, there's nothing wrong with that - I'm just a little sad I didn't get to explore this incredible environment a little more...! But if you knowingly go into the game looking for a nice, slightly predictable but gorgeously executed melancholy tale of childhood adventure and family tension... DORDOGNE (SCREAM ITS NAME) will 100% deliver.Bonnes vacances!

_childDocuments_.review: It's a beautiful game, but the actual interactivity feels like it's for a little kid. Every item you interact with tells you exactly what to do, and it feels like the interaction is just for the sake of saying it's there. It doesn't require thought like a puzzle or have consequences for choices. There's also a word collecting aspect that feels like a children's vocabulary game, but the framing story is way too mature for this game to be meant for kids. It's a bit odd, and I'm not sure who the intended audience is. It almost feels like two different games mashed together.My other complaint is that walkable paths aren't clearly marked, and perspective is not controllable or consistent. Sometimes you'll be walking down to go south, and the perspective shifts on you, so then down becomes west and suddenly you're going in the wrong direction. And sometimes the art looks like an area is somewhere you can walk, but it's not, or the actual walkable path is narrower than the painted path, so you get stuck if you don't have your character lined up with something you can't see. It's really annoying.

_childDocuments_.review: Dordogne is a very wholesome adventure with amazing water colors and a deep story to dive right in.I bought the game because the art style looked unique and interesting, and wow! It really is good in both its colors and in the way the story is told. Since I don't want to spoil anything, I will keep it short and hope many more people can enjoy this remarkable story.You jump between the long-forgotten past and present to discover lost memories that are yours to reclaim.The colors are more dim with a sad touch when you play in the present, but as you jump into the past, it fully unleashes the most vibrant colors you can imagine.It reminds me of how I used to see the world as a child, full of colors and surprises around every corner.Not that the world has lost colors over time, but there is a difference in how the world is viewed when you are grown, and I think the game portrays this very well.There are also valuable lessons you might or might not learn/be reminded of through the game, so keep an open mind for these messages.A game that makes you shed tears, usually counts for a well told story, at least it does for me.

_childDocuments_.review: The reason I'm giving this a negative review is because, while playing this game, I kept being reminded of Season: A Letter to the Future and how it's a VASTLY superior game compared to this one. Both games have a scrapbooking mechanic; you're encouraged to make memories last by taking pictures, recording sounds, and finding words and stickers to fill in your journal. However, the difference between how the two games implement this mechanic is like night and day. For starters, the camera works way better in Season than it does in Dordogne. In Season, the camera allows you to be very creative; you can zoom in and out, add filters, resize, etc. You are also free to take pictures absolutely anywhere. Dordogne, by contrast, gives you a less advanced camera, and you can only take pictures in designated areas. One achievement requires you to take 50 pictures, and you're stuck taking the same pictures over and over again because you can only take pictures in the exact same places every chapter and have no ability to edit or enhance them.  Secondly, the scrapbooking mechanic in Dordogne is just vastly inferior to Season. In Dordogne, you HAVE to add a picture, a sticker, a sound effect, and a poem every time you make a new page, and depending on the chapter there's very little variety of what you can add. Season, by contrast, gives the player complete freedom to craft pages however they choose. In other words, scrapbooking in Dordogne felt more like a chore, whereas Season felt more like making actual memories. Season left you free to explore the world at your own pace, taking in the beauty of the environments and forming genuine bonds with different people, whereas Dordogne forces you into a linear story that leaves little room for exploration; I didn't really feel like I was enjoying my summer in the French countryside so much as going from point A to point B and gathering pointless collectables. Overall, Season genuinely felt like a chill game, whereas Dordogne was just boring; the small world and overly simplistic gameplay don't do it for me anymore. If you don't care about any of that and just want to explore a beautiful watercolour world, then go ahead and check this game out, but if you REALLY want to see how good chill games can be, just skip this one and play Season. I will likely be exploring the world of Season again, but I have no desire to go back to Dordogne any time soon.

_childDocuments_.review: 2023 was an amazing year for games in general, particularly for indie titles. However, among all these games, it's quite easy to overlook titles that haven't garnered a lot of attention but are otherwise great experiences: Dordogne is one such game.Set in a beautiful French village, it showcases the carefree childhood days, paired with a deep and meaningful story, all tailored with an eye-catching graphical direction.However, as much as I want to, I simply cannot overlook the game's shortcomings: the abundance of animations in multiple places, the graphical glitches, and the minigames, which make the experience more tedious than relaxing after a certain point.+ Absolutely fabulous graphical direction, paired with soothing audio pieces+ Deep and emotional narrative which isn’t afraid to delve into more serious topics+ A relaxing, laid-back narrative...- … which gets repetitive after a certain point- A number of graphical glitches and weird issuesWe get thrown into the narrative in medias res: in the opening moments, we meet a woman in her 30s named Mimi, our protagonist, who, despite her father’s wishes (and strong urges), decides to travel all the way to a small village in France, set near the Dordogne river, to find answers about her late grandmother’s, Nora's, life.She knows as a fact that she’s spent an entire summer with her grandmother many years ago - but seemingly Mimi doesn’t remember it at all!How could this happen? What exactly happened before her 13th birthday? Why does her father want to stop her? Throughout the game, you will gradually get all the answers you need while you rediscover the house and relive your past memories. The narrative unfolds in a well-structured manner within several chapters. It is an emotional roller-coaster filled with many amazing scenes: the thing that makes Dordogne stand out from other ‘cozy-games’ is the fact that it manages to encapsulate a wide variety of different emotions, all presented in a really believable and realistic way.The story itself isn’t anything grand or new: the main emphasis is on getting the player to feel something - feelings of nostalgia, sorrow, and joy all culminate in the short, three hours playtime. Mimi’s journey spoke to me and made me remember long forgotten memories about my own grandparents - only a handful of games managed to do something similar by far.Throughout the game, you will play as Mimi in various life stages; however, the gameplay will stay essentially the same. The main emphasis is on exploration: both Nora’s house and the area surrounding the Dordogne hold a great number of secrets and mysteries to uncover. While the game itself is completely linear, all these areas have a wide variety of objects you can interact with, including a great deal of collectible items!The game also features numerous different mechanics that make the game more enjoyable but get a bit repetitive after a certain point. This includes taking a key and manually opening a door with it, planting flowers, or creating a character out of sticks and a cone. For sure, these little things do feel refreshing; however, due to their limited nature, they start to feel like a drag after a certain while.Another interesting addition to Dordogne is a binder that you will acquire early into the game, which gives you the opportunity to design your own page consisting of multiple elements like an image, a poem, or a sound that you recorded. This is an awesome mechanic that I enjoyed quite a lot. Each page represents a chapter in the game, and this way you can easily keep track of your progress. One of the game’s main selling points is its graphical direction, which can be best described as absolutely breathtaking. Each scene feels like a watercolor painting, with vivid and blissful colors, mesmerizing scenery - and clunky animations!One of the game’s biggest shortcomings, in my eyes, is the stiffness of most animations. In some instances, I felt like it heavily broke the immersion - also, I played the game on ultrawide resolution, and while it is completely supported, on many occasions the characters simply glitched out of the scene after their animation finished.  is a heavily enjoyable game that’s perfect for everyone who wants to feel something. The story - while not grandiose - unfolds at a pleasant pace and features a lovable cast of characters. The graphical direction is incredible, and if paired with the soothing soundtrack, one can easily get lost in the breathtaking scenery. Some issues exist that affected my experience, but not the types that would heavily impact my enjoyment. : GreatYou can find my review chart

_childDocuments_.review: AVOID | LACKING | MAYBE | WORTHWHILE |  | UNMISSABLEDordogne is a narrative-based point & click game focusing on a young woman, Mimi, as she revisits the house of her late grandma where she spent summers as a kid. The game is broken into 8 chapters where you switch back and forth between present-day Mimi and past Mimi to rediscover memories and solve a family secret. The game is beautiful in its presentation, as it has hand-painted watercolor artwork. It is very relaxing, with a soundtrack to match. The storyline is engaging and interesting throughout and the characters are charming. The only critique I have about this game is that I found the controls to be rather frustrating. I think it would be solved almost completely by being able to see your cursor in game, but to have a point & click game where you can't actually see what you're clicking is irritating at absolute best. Luckily, precision isn't needed to progress and I got used to it somewhat over the course of the game, but it would be a significant quality of life improvement if a change was made to fix this. The game took me 4.5 hours to complete.If you're looking for a relaxing game that relies on beautiful artwork and a compelling story to carry it through, this is a solid game to pick!

_childDocuments_.review: I love relaxing and cozy adventure games, and Dordogne scratches this itch for me. The art style is very much like a watercolor painting and the voice acting is great. The plot is interesting and so is the "time shift/memory" gameplay mechanic. Overall this is a great game for players looking to enjoy a (relatively) calm, peaceful game where you can take your time and soak in the experience.Now if you are a gamer and are planning to unlock every achievement in the game, I do have a warning for you. The developers were kind enough to include a system by which you can replay every chapter in the game in order to unlock every achievement, which is great. As the game relies on a single save point if you use this method you will lose any progress in the chapter you were on before the skip, so it is only best to do so either at the start of a new chapter or after you complete the game. The drawback being that you need to play each chapter from the very beginning each time it's loaded using the chapter skip, so if the unlock is further into the chapter you will find yourself playing through that chapter a second time to reach it.What the developers did not account for is the fact that ONE achievement, which needs you to perform a very specific action once in EVERY chapter, is reset by the chapter skip option. I never realized this fact and by chapter skipping before I completed the game I accidentally reset this achievement's "counter". Meaning that even though I had performed the action in previous chapters the game "forgot" I did it. Bottom line, in order to complete this ONE achievement I would need to replay the entire game a second time as you cannot just reach the unlock and chapter skip to the next chapter... or it will reset the achievement's counter again back to zero negating your progress to unlock it.That one issue aside, if you are the type of gamer who investigates everything odds are good you will perform this hidden action (yes, it's a hidden achievement in Steam) as their is a small "event" connected to it that has nothing to do with the main plot so it stands out. If so, just play the entire game and avoid using the chapter skip until after you have already completed the game. As odds are, you will unlock this achievement naturally and without spoiler help. I chapter skipped before finishing my game, which is how I ran into this issue. If reading this still makes you anxious about missing it, the secret task you need to do in every chapter is... My only other advice for players looking to unlock EVERY achievement without first using a walkthrough guide (which ruins the plot)... .I truly hope everyone who plays Dordogne has as wonderful an experience as I did and has no regrets over not unlocking every achievement. This game is a real gem and worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: Dordogne captured my attention from the start with its beautiful concept and outstanding art style. The visuals feel like a watercolor painting come to life, and the early chapters evoke a cozy sense of nostalgia that took me back to my childhood visits to my grandmother’s house in the Italian countryside.However, as I progressed through the game, the gameplay mechanics started to detract from that initial magic. While the controls and interactions are simple and intuitive at first, they quickly became more of a hindrance than a joy. Some mechanics felt needlessly drawn out, almost as if they were slowing down the whole experience. There were several moments where I found myself thinking, "Please, speed this up!"—the pacing could have benefited from a tighter focus, allowing players to stay immersed in the narrative without getting bogged down by clunky or repetitive tasks.The promise of exploration, something that felt very exciting at the start, ultimately falls short. You are often tied to what the game wants you to see, with little room for genuine discovery or free-roaming. A more open-world approach would have given the game so much more depth, allowing for a true sense of adventure and the joy of uncovering secrets at your own pace. This is a missed opportunity, as the world is so beautifully crafted that being able to wander more freely through it would have been incredibly rewarding!Also I feel like the game didn’t quite live up to its initial promise. Infact, the story hints at a big secret early on, but by the end, I was left feeling a little bit underwhelmed. That said, I believe this is intentional to some degree. Rather than leading to a grand revelation or a satisfying resolution, the game’s ending reflects the realities of life—there is no hidden treasure waiting at the end of the path, just adulthood, acceptance, and the weight of human experiences. In this sense, the developers chose to tell a story that feels raw, human, and real. It’s less about uncovering a mystery and more about coming to terms with the complex emotions of growing up, grief, and letting go. This direction, while admirable in its authenticity, may not satisfy all players who were hoping for a more traditionally rewarding conclusion.Overall, I’d recommend this game if you’re looking for a short, emotionally driven narrative that explores themes of grief, loss, and acceptance. The game is more about personal reflection and nostalgia than about intricate gameplay or world exploration. Be prepared for a linear experience that feels more like reading a beautifully illustrated children book than venturing through a videogame. While the game's pacing and mechanics may occasionally frustrate, the heartfelt story and breathtaking visuals make it worth experiencing—especially if you’re someone who appreciates art and narrative over gameplay complexity.

_childDocuments_.review: Dordogne is a beautifully whimsical game that you can relax, explore and unwind with. The visuals comprise these vibrantly excellent watercolour-like animations, that are sometimes interactive - quite delightful and impressionistic.The game mechanic of mending things, sorting and unpacking things, etc are also fun and interesting without being too difficult. Often you get these hint arrows or discreet footstep symbols indicating what to next head for; this really gave my brain a rest, and I really appreciated the experience.I also liked the camera+tape recorder+journal feature: Inserting self-created pages into the journal was fun and satisfying, although I wished to create more pages. Technically the game allowed me to create more pages, only I had not collected enough different objects to store in any additional pages - so the page creation would not *validate*. There are in-game achievements for creating 10 or 20 journal pages, so something must be more possible than what I actually got.The mobile phone was also fun, either when checking my objectives or choosing what to text in response to other peoples messages. I always chose to be polite in my texts. I might like to play the game again and be more rude in response!The background music is fitting and appropriate, if not a touch too melancholic at times, for my liking. There were several occasions when the game suddenly sounded like Mimi was having a crisis, when in actual fact, she was only being lazy and explorative ! I wasn't hurt by it, it was just kind of ironic, really.The story was nice although it didn't really develop into much for me. There seemed to be two or three chapters of introductory game mechanic, without much plot cohesion, then just as things were warming up, after 4.2 hours of game play, the game suddenly ended. So was left with this feeling that there was a lot of beautiful visuals and game mechanic that was still waiting to be exploited and transformed into something via the story, and it didn't quite deliver the impact I was expecting.All in all, I would definitely recommend Dordogne to a prospective gamer as a wholesome, fun, casual and chill game. Enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: My stationary computer broke down with some classic BSOD, so while I put it on some much needed bedrest with some people who actually know hardware, I decided to pick up some games off my never-ending list.The one I really wanted to finish for a long time now is Dordogne, and I’m happy I finally did. The aesthetics of this game are really quite stunning, I really appreciate when we’re getting to the stage of game art where we can truly see unique art styles come alive so clearly in 3D. I feel like for a long time either production companies were aiming for such a broad audience that they could never gamble on going on a unique artstyle, or didn’t have the technology to support artistic flexibility. And now I’m happy to see more and more games being able to become an extension of an artist’s vision. I really do love that Dordogne gives the feeling of constantly walking in someone’s painting, and it just fits the narrative of living through a story of their childhood so well. In terms of art, I think the combination of using billboards and just a lot of 3D-models with alphas and just allowing the brush-strokes create imperfections in the shapes to make it look more organic. I think what works so well is that the different ways of creating 3D has been interwoven so well, usually I feel like there’s a risk of these techniques clashing, especially with VFX or casting shadows in 3D, but Dordogne pulls it off really well.I didn’t necessarily find the puzzles too intriguing, mostly because I’ve never really enjoyed gamified “regular actions” like brushing teeth or shaking a pan, and I feel like it would’ve done better with creating just easy puzzles instead.I think what I adore most of all is that Dordogne is really becoming a pillarstone in terms of what aesthetics in games can be, and it really galvanizes me to one day create my own game where I get to infuse my style and my story into an experience as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Dordogne

_childDocuments_.review: Dordogne is a gorgeous little game about a woman reminiscing about her past summer vacation staying at her grandma's house and learning more about her familiy's broken relationships.While the game is visually stunning with it's watercolour paintings and it has lots of cute moments I enjoyed, it mostly plays like a walking sim with some very  light interactive elements.The most involved activity you get is your scrapbook, which you can add a page to after each chapter.Here you can add pictures you have taken that day, sounds you have recorded, stickers you found and poems you wrote.These were my favorite part, but sadly there isn't very many spots the game let's you take photos or record sounds in, so the pages can feel a bit samey.I also wish there was more free exploration around the countryside, but each chapter mostly takes you to a defined, small extra section of the game.I would still recommend the game for it's beautiful art alone, but be aware it is *very* light on gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Dordogne

_childDocuments_.review: This game exceeded my expectations. It doesn't only look beautiful but it also sounds right in every way. The game is well written and I was interested in the story. The cut-scenes were also well directed. There is gameplay but it might not be enough for some. I'm happy enough that I could explore the areas by moving the character, there were lots of collectibles, you can take pictures and sounds (in specific spots) and there are some mini games where you are supposed to do something. You can think of cooking, planting a seed etc. However, the game still has 2 clear flaws imo. There is no chapter select or a way to return to collect what you missed. When you finish the game and load your save, the credits are repeated again. This is unacceptable for a game that puts great emphasis on collectibles. Creating pages in your book is a neat idea but I don't like the fact that you have to create a page from scratch if you want to modify anything minor. Maybe it is possible and I don't know how but I haven't been able to. And last but not least, the game has 2 minor bugs that are not game breaking but it would be nice to get rid of them to make the game 100% polished. One has monologues getting repeated if you enter and exit one recording spot. The second one happened in chapter 6 when I left the house and was told I found a tape when I didn't and the tape wasn't in my inventory.I almost wanted to give a negative rating for not being able to select chapters and collect what you missed but the game does too many things right. The developers perfectly captured a child's mind during Summer. It was a great Summer to experience. The ones who don't like those kind of games won't be persuaded by this, but the ones who do, rest assured that this is worth playing. It took me around 5.5 hours to complete this game while taking my sweet time. The game was on pause for 30 minutes.Edit:One of the bugs (with repeated dialogue) is supposedly fixed with the newest patch. I didn’t test this to confirm.Also one more thing. Some people thought the story was too slow and therefore boring. I didn’t ever feel that way. I was feeling immersed and thought the way things happened made sense for a child. The story and characters were introduced slowly while you were living your life. While the focus is Summer vibe, it made sense how things got introduced. It offered a bigger pay off imo. But, it might be something to think about if you’re expecting big plots and twists all the time.

_childDocuments_.review: The watercolor style immediately caught my eye, and I went in confident that the game would look stunning.   I'm happy to say that in addition to beautiful environments, the game has a cute little story with characters that feel like believable people.   And the game just has an extremely pleasant vibe to it.   I played this game with my mom, who loves drawing and painting as well.  This game is an excellent one to share with relatives who may not be gamer hobbyists but can appreciate beautiful art.   You'll be spending most of your game time traveling through the environments on very basic quests to find items or to go do very simple tasks.   When you find items there are often basic object puzzles.   Nothing super difficult or deep, they mostly are there to take you through the story and the paintings.   Without any spoilers the story rotates between flashbacks to the character Mimi's childhood and the present, with each flashback and the story around it in the present serving as a chapter.   There are eight chapters in total, and we completed the game with around four hours of playtime split into a couple two hour sessions.   A player who's trying to find all the collectibles will probably add a couple/few hours of playtime for a single run.I think this game is absolutely worth its full price.   There is a ton of artistic talent on display, and it feels like a personal story that comes from a place of love.   It is a short and sweet experience so it's a premium spend compared to some games, but if you can spare the money, I wholeheartedly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: The ideas behind this game are great. The art design is gorgeous, and the story is touching and heartfelt. The primary focus is effectively a nostalgic collectathon in the form of a story. You go through chapters of a young girl's life as she tries to remember a misremembered Summer of the past. It has childish purity, adult contemplation, and nostalgic moments of growing up.However, it's not without faults, and it comes down to the mechanics of the game. The game is desperately married to those mechanics. You're mostly walking around, inspecting the world for telegraphed pick-ups. The game is meant to be immersive, but because there were so many objectives, I kept getting pulled out of the mood. The same goes for the text messages. They're so distracting! Every time I was appreciating the space, I'd get another dang text from someone I didn't want to talk to. I could have ignored them, but I would rather the protag just chuck her phone in the river!The story also feels a bit padded. Why were there so many kayaking scenes? Why were there so many sequences of just walking around with little consequence? Why were some scripted sequences so long for the sake of walking? When the game is letting the characters talk, or featuring a gorgeously animated cutscene, or letting you decorate your binder, it's an absolute treat. But when it's obsessively making you do rote tasks over and over, it can be very frustrating, as if the game were an hour and a half too long because they wanted it to be A GAME rather than A STORY.But, at the end of the day, the story is the main appeal here, and it's a nice story. In classic French fashion, it's a little bittersweet, and a little nihilistic, but ultimately beautiful. The game mechanics bog this down a bit, but it's still a nice time. This is great if you're into cozy games but want a story to go with it. Also, the voice acting is best in French, so change the language! Bonus points to the studio for fully voice-acting and translating everything into Occitan.

_childDocuments_.review: “Places, objects, should have many lives” I’ve been following the publisher Focus Entertainment throughout 2023, since I learned that they published my favourite game of 2023, A Plague Tale Requiem. They have an interesting catalogue of AA, Indie and cozy games across a range of genres. When I saw their announcement of Dordogne I was immediately attracted to the gorgeous water colour art style, and in this respect, the game does not disappoint. What is the Dordogne? It is a river and a region in south-west France. The river winds through the ancient and beautiful countryside, and so the game brings this to bucolic setting to life through the broad brushstrokes of it’s eye-catching art style. The protagonist of the game is Mimi, and throughout the game we explore two time periods of her life, the present-day, and a childhood holiday she spent in the Dordogne with her grandmother, Nora. The story sets an immediate undercurrent of familial discord, but Mimi has no memory of her childhood holiday, or the reasons for that discord. The game’s 8 chapters gradually explore the reasons for both of these mysteries. This is done through simple but effective storytelling, a series of small interactive moments where the player must carefully control Mimi’s actions, and a series of emotions and words that appear in the world around her. I found the interactions to be charming, and the floating words to be an interesting way of expressing Mimi’s inner monologue, but also the decisions she has to take to express those thoughts and emotions to her Grandmother. At the end of each chapter, Mimi collects her thoughts, photographs and unique memories into pages of her binder, and I found this to be a charming way to contextualise the game’s collectibles, but also to express those in a way that felt genuine through the eyes of the 12-year old protagonist. I played this game on Steam Deck, and as you might imagine from the graphical style, it played excellently on that device. The entire game could easily be completed on a single charge of the battery. Visual highlights were kayaking down the river Dordogne, seeing the blend of 3D objects, applied with their watercolour style textures, but with 2D water coloured surfaces for the distant items provided an eye-catching scenes Despite the game’s indie background, no aspect of the story, gameplay or visuals felt unfinished, or cheap. The animation quality is superb throughout – most likely the result of the work by Umanimation and their experience animating with the Unity engine, on which this game is built. I did have one point that I felt detracted from the game’s overall feeling – the music choice. I felt the game’s bright, vibrant colour palette and style, and bucolic setting, did not mesh with the electronic, almost sci-fi soundtrack. Something a little lighter, and more acoustic, might have gelled better with the overall vibe of this game. In conclusion, while Dordogne doesn’t break any new ground, it tells it’s story effectively, and I would recommend it to anyone looking for a more casual game, a shorter, simpler game, or someone who wants to soak up the gorgeous art style.

_childDocuments_.review: Dordogne is a real gem. If this game caught your attention, it will most likely be for the same reason it caught mine - the gorgeous watercolor painted art style. Yet, the screenshots don't quite do it justice the way playing it would. The way angles transition with some scenes looks spectacular. And, because you play as both the modern day, adult Mimi and the childhood Mimi of her memories, you get to see the same rooms/areas, but with different color palettes across the time periods. It's wonderful to be able to experience the same spaces under two different, equally beautiful visual effects. While the artwork is the clear draw of the game, the story itself is well executed. Much of it feels casual and lighthearted. And even when the narrative's more serious conflicts are explored, they never seem to veer into anything too extreme or ugly. For the most part, it evolves as a warm, touching story of a grandmother and granddaughter forming a bond.The soundtrack is wonderful and relaxing. I don't remember ever growing tired of it (in fact, there was one song I remember thinking I would miss when I had to move on to the next scene haha).The controls/interface is simple and gives you clear direction (though I did get a wee bit stuck pouring cereal ^_^'). So don't expect any serious brain teasers or puzzles.The game itself is relatively short, which can be (and in this case is) a good thing. I'm sure I could have finished Dordogne in 2 or 3 hours if I rushed. But the beauty is that I never felt inclined to rush. I WANTED to take my time, to enjoy the artwork, enjoy the music, read Mimi's dialogue on everything around with each passing scene.I left this game feeling good. Easy recommend for me <3

_childDocuments_.review: I appreciate the dedication put into crafting the intricate atmosphere and visually stunning art style of this game. However, despite its aesthetic allure, I find myself unable to wholeheartedly recommend it due to several significant shortcomings that hinder its overall enjoyability and immersion.One of the primary issues I encountered while playing was the game's excessively linear and overly guided nature. While I understand the desire to create a cohesive narrative experience, the lack of player agency and freedom to explore detracts from the sense of immersion and engagement. Instead of feeling like an active participant in the unfolding story, I often felt like a passive observer being led from one predetermined point to another. This lack of interactivity ultimately diminished my investment in the game's world and characters.Speaking of characters, I found the portrayal of certain individuals within the game to be particularly troubling. The constant belittlement and demeaning treatment of the protagonist by her family and peers felt not only unnecessary but also detrimental to the intended wholesome atmosphere. Rather than fostering empathy or understanding, these interactions left me feeling uncomfortable and disheartened. It reminded me of a similar issue I encountered in another indie game, "Epiphany City," where attempts at creating a lighthearted tone were overshadowed by underlying negativity and toxicity.As someone who values honesty and authenticity, I must admit that this game hit uncomfortably close to home for me. The depiction of emotional abuse and toxic relationships resonated with my own personal experiences, and as such, I found it difficult to fully immerse myself in the game without being reminded of past traumas. This is a deeply personal aspect of my critique, but one that I believe is important to acknowledge given the impact it had on my overall enjoyment of the game.Furthermore, the portrayal of familial dynamics within the game struck a particularly sensitive chord with me. Having personally experienced similar dynamics within my own family, I found it challenging to engage with the narrative without being reminded of the pain and trauma associated with those experiences. In particular, the interactions between the protagonist and her grandmother evoked memories of my own grandmother, further heightening my emotional response to the game.Despite these criticisms, I recognize that the game does have its merits. There are moments of brilliance scattered throughout, reminiscent of other beloved titles in the genre such as "Another Code" and "Hotel Dusk." The attention to detail and the occasional glimpses of genuine emotional depth serve as reminders of the potential this game had to offer.In conclusion, while I admire the ambition and creativity behind this game, I ultimately cannot wholeheartedly recommend it due to its significant flaws. It is my hope that future iterations or projects from the developers will address these issues and deliver a more cohesive and fulfilling experience for players.

A heartwarming journey into the summer memories of childhood."It's a "Boku no Natsuyasumi-like" set in the 1982 French Dordogne, although with more emphasis on narrative and collection mechanics similar to "Season: A Letter to the Future", being able to make a personal archive with stickers, photos, poems and audio recordings per chapter. Impregnated with a nostalgic tone (with tinges of melancholy), two timelines are proposed in which we discover the evolution of the relationship between Mimi, her grandmother and her parents. There are also some letters and cassettes that reveal the story of her grandparents.Of course, I have to mention its exquisite artistic section, based on three-dimensional environments with watercolor textures and fixed camera in most cases. All created by @Cedric_Babouche (and even his little daughters) in situ in real places.I've loved the insane detail of the organic interaction with objects and people, something that intensifies the costumbrism that emanates from preparing breakfast, running errands or brushing your teeth.And then, there are these kayak fragments, which despite not being so extensive, do provide a variety very well received by the player.A linear narrative title that, through a packaging that reminds us of those books that were sent to us as homework during school vacations, conveys a vital message that is really necessary.

_childDocuments_.review: A heartwarming story of formative childhood memories presented through stunning hand-drawn watercolor art. Gameplay is minimal and the click-and-drag interaction mechanic can misbehave; but if you can look past the minor annoyance, you'll find an experience that's sure to leave a lasting impression. Completionists beware, though: one achievement is bugged (not impossible to get, just more frustrating), and no further updates/patches are expected in the future.  is a narrative-focused game about a woman named Mimi, who travels to her late grandmother's home in rural France to rediscover childhood memories from a summer spent there along the Dordogne river. Along the way, she'll learn more about herself and her family than she ever expected, and dive into a decades-long mystery that's kept her away all these years. Something to note before you pick it up: it's very light on gameplay, focusing more on telling its story than acting like a traditional video game. I don't think that's a bad thing, just something you should know in advance. Gameplay mainly consists of simple exploration with some very light puzzle elements; and I use that qualifier because it often spells out rather plainly what you're expected to do any time you reach an obstacle. The central mechanic is that you need to interact with most objects through click-and-drag gestures based on the action you're trying to perform, like twisting open doorknobs or brushing items to the side to reveal what's underneath.  as all the different gestures feel designed specifically with a mouse in mind. Each chapter has you exploring through mostly linear spaces, with the occasional ability to step off the main path and find one of the game's several types of collectibles. All the collectibles are used for this little end-of-day scrapbooking minigame, where you get to add a page to a binder using collected stickers, photographs, audio snippets you record around town (don't ask me how adding sound to paper is physically possible), and finally craft a poem using keywords you pick up either by exploring or through important story beats. Due to the minimal gameplay, it's up to the story and artistic elements to do the heavy lifting, and neither one disappoints. , and it uses this blend of 2D and 3D assets that makes it feel like you're playing through one of those pop-up picture books. Every landscape is full of vibrant colors, every set piece packed with little details, and even the more muted or somber locations look so good that they make you want to run off the path to see what's hiding just out of frame. Sadly, you're rarely if ever allowed to stray from the required path; and  if for no other reason than to give me more artwork to look at. Each chapter has you jumping between past 12-year-old Mimi and present day adult Mimi, reliving the memories of an uncertain but hopeful summer trip through the introspective eyes of an adult as she comes to realize just how important those memories are to her. It maintains a largely lighthearted tone, but viewing these scenes from an adult's perspective allows you to see hints that there's more going on under the surface, something that's given further context through collectibles acquired in the present day sections. I feel like I might've said too much already, so I'll stop here and just say that I think it did a solid job.The only other complaint I have is that . The most common problem was that the swipe mouse movement could be rather finicky, especially with larger motions that involve sweeping across most of the display (e.g. putting a key in a keyhole). Aside from that, there were minor bugs that only popped up once or twice like animation glitches, an instance where my controls got locked and I had to restart, and one time where I went to the main menu during the scrapbooking minigame and returned to find that the keywords I picked up in the chapter's last conversation had disappeared. The completion issue stems from the achievement "Like a Swiss clock", which, unlike the others, cannot be earned by revisiting chapters through the chapter select and demands a new save file (and the loss of previously-earned collectibles) to earn if you miss a step. The developer stated in a discussion surrounding the achievement issue that , so be warned that any bugs you may run into, such as the ones I mentioned, will not be resolved., but I elected not to try for 100% completion due to the bugged achievement. Technical problems aside, I still really enjoyed my time with the game. It brought me a lot of nostalgia, not really for a specific place or event, but rather a type of experience I was lucky to have a few times growing up: getting to visit a place far from home with the kind of curiosity and wonder only a child can have, making fast new friends with the knowledge that you may never see them again, and having little to worry about other than what kind of fun you're going to get yourself into tomorrow. Taking a step back after playing it brought back memories that I'd long since forgotten about; and  does its best to not just convey how important those kinds of memories can be, but how important it is to share those memories and the things we keep that remind us of them so that they can be used to help create lasting memories for others. This is devolving into a weird tangent, but the point is:

_childDocuments_.review: Dordogne is a loving, wistful experience of one summer spent in the French countryside. The game jumps between the perspectives of Mimi, a woman in her thirties sorting through her estranged passed grandmother's estate, and Mimi as a young girl reluctantly spending a summer with her grandmother and the mystery of how their family unraveled. Gameplay is simplistic, there are few "true" puzzles, and interactions are mostly kept to looking at the wonderfully detailed world.And what a world that is! Dordogne features hand painted watercolor textures directed by French cartoonist Cedric Babouche and it looks great. Every screen is littered with detail and I spent a long time on each screen trying to break down how they modeled and textured with paints all the intricacies of the world. The art and music stands head over heels but I can't ignore a wonderful localization and writing that, in indie game tradition, presents a layer of whimsy over a core of melancholy. Dordogne is a game about the events that lead people to drifting apart and the ending, while satisfying, left a bittersweet taste in my mouth. I'm writing this review as someone who beat the game before they patched in chapter select, and while I was satisfied with the 4-or-so hours it's a testament to its charm that I'm preparing to dive back in to collect all the achievements.
_childDocuments_.name: Dordogne

_childDocuments_.review: PROS:*wonderful art and music (both of these are the games highlights imo, phenomenal)*chill vibes for a lot of the game, until the latter chapters, the happy parts of the game were amazing*the UX is novel and immersive, but see also cons*the voice acting is really goodCONS:*this game is VERY short, its like a story that could go somewhere better than this but it doesnt, and im torn on being ok with that and *maybe* should have had an hour or more. there's things alluded to that are never deeply explored, characters that aren't developed as much as they should be and it seems to build a wonderful world that you only see a fragment of. For the genre of the game and the story sake, maybe there isn't much more you can do, but its such a downer to realize "well thats it" when you finish.This is the games core problem, if you can handle 3 or so hours (really only if you're 100% otherwise it's faster) for a story that doesn't have the most satisfying resolution, go for it. Just realize what you're getting.*the UX is largely good but on keyboard and mouse some of it is a bit clunky, probably better with gamepadOverall, this is a 7/10 but ill give it an 8 just because the art is so good. It's a hard sell for anyone who isn't into adventure/walking sim/narrative games

_childDocuments_.review: You can read my other reviews Video review: Childhood memories, in most cases, are wholesome moments that make our hearts full, happy moments that reflect the longing for events that we cannot return to in person, but that will always live in a well-hidden corner of our memory.Dordogne is an adventure that explores the memories of Mimi, who after being confronted with the reality of the loss of her grandmother, returns to a place that had been very happy but inexplicably does not remember most of the things that happened at that time. The house of Nora, her grandmother, is for sale and the adventurous Mimi decides to visit the place. Through exploration, the player will collect objects that trigger important flashbacks and that help her to re-establish the moments spent together with her grandmother, in a hot summer in this French village. Who knows, maybe even find the key moment that led to the loss of memories of this very picturesque place.Although all the action moments are events from Mimi’s past, through mini-games, it is interesting to absorb how there is a parallelism between the different moments of the same character. The exploration made by the adult Mimi is essentially based on the search for the next object that will provide the critical moment of her memory and that can be interrupted by the vibration of her cell phone, with the super upset messages from her father’s, or with her friend’s concerned lines of text. It’s interesting to have a window to understand a little better the characters and their personality strokes that inhabit Mimi’s life, even if it’s just the messages on her cell phone that add more color to this whole adventure.Speaking of brushstrokes and color, the entire hand-painted watercolor environment of Dordogne is super vibrant, inspiring the player to take breaths of air along with the character’s movement, attributing a sense of life and energy.All chapters of the story follow a common thread in Mimi’s past adventures. Mimi could thus see a notebook, a quite special one, being given to her, where she had been putting moments captured with a camera and with that making its pages quite colorful and full of juicy memories. Even though it’s a linear story, there are places to explore and elements to collect. Although these collectible elements are secondary, they can be translated into special moments in constructing the notebook of memories. A special moment is also the kayak trip to the local market, to buy ingredients to cook with her grandmother and the introduction of a new character who becomes quite important. Yes, because without friends everything becomes quite boring, right?As these characters’ stories intertwine, each chapter tasks the player with a small task. These small activities add a little “je ne sais quoi” to the adventure, which often translates into important moments. For example, Kayake’s adventure to the center of the village was triggered by the simple search for a trowel to help Nora with the gardening activities that the player will have to carry out.Dordogne’s message is to appreciate every moment in life, because as good as that moment is, it will never last forever. It’s not a demanding title in any way, the puzzles are simple, the message although important doesn’t leave the player overwhelmed. An adventure to be enjoyed over 3 hours, with landscapes and very colorful moments that will undoubtedly remain in your memory.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this game, it's gorgeous, atmospheric, and the story is hitting every department of the emotional register. I cried my eyes out over the ending. It's made with so much love, and I highly recommend to play it and dwell in the childhood nostalgia that is a summer vacation on the countryside. I LOVE this game. Still, I felt like I should write down a few accessibility notes for those who need it.- there are  at the start and in chapter 7 of the game (you will notice it when it's raining). There's no way to turn off flashes, so be careful if you are photosensitive.- the story contains  without explicit content warnings. It is not explicitly shown, but mentioned/implied. I'll put the emotional content warning into a spoiler: I used mouse and keyboard, so these notes are specifically for those peripherals:- With mouse and keyboard, you will need the  to get through the game. Sometimes you have to press the mouse button down and perform some movement with the mouse (dragging).- You will have to  to get through some of the puzzles. There's unfortunately . I'm gonna say you never hold the mouse button for more than 5 seconds at a time, but it can still be challenging. Not sure if controller offers an alternative.- Cutscenes are , so you can't "click" to continue the dialogue and take more time to read. The dialogue speed is not extremely fast, but it definitely requires to follow. Cutscenes have both subtitles and voice acting. Visuals:- Due to the watercolor style, . I have good vision and even I took a couple of seconds sometimes to identify the object. Within puzzles, the object you have to use has a soft white glow on the surface, that might blend into the environment.Summary:The game and its puzzles are solved visually and there's unfortunately no second channel to assist with that. There is no text to speech ingame. Apart from spoken dialogue, there's no audio descriptions.Subtitles are consistent and there's visualization of text and elements, so players don't have to rely on audio to get through.You have to hold down the left mouse button/click+drag to complete the puzzles (controllers however might differ). It might work with custom hardware or click lock via Windows OS, but there's no in game options provided to switch between holding and letting go. Hope this helps ♥

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoy puzzle-solving and exploration games, Dordogne is perfect. It's a unique blend of adventure, storytelling, and art that creates an engaging experience. The game's beautifully crafted world, set in the French countryside, is impressive. The colors and lighting create a peaceful and serene atmosphere that makes exploring the world a joy. The story follows a young woman named Mimi, who visits her grandmother in Dordogne and discovers her grandmother's past and a hidden family secret. It's well-written and keeps you engaged throughout the game. The puzzles are challenging and rewarding, using a unique mechanic that involves creating paintings to progress through the game. The small mechanics scattered throughout the game, like pouring tea or using a key to unlock a door, add an extra layer of immersion and engagement. Dordogne is an excellent adventure game that offers a unique and enjoyable experience. _childDocuments_.review: Dordogne is an absolutely beautiful game that tells a quaint and simple story. The art style is truly one-of-a-kind and it perfectly captures the culture of France in the late 70's.It is full of wholesome vibes that will take you back to a simpler time, when you were a kid playing in your grandparent's home and exploring the wilderness like you were crossing a mythical land.My only major complaint is the English voice acting sounds too - for lack of a better word - American-y. Native French speakers who could speak fluent English would have been a better choice. As is, for every English player, I must recommend you set the voice acting to French to fully appreciate the game's culture.Other than that, I don't have much to say. I only wish there was more of this game. I do feel there are several key plot elements left unexplored. But what's there is still a sweet story that wouldn't have felt out-of-place in a Ghibli movie.

_childDocuments_.review:
Dordogne is a narrative adventure game in which you play as Mimi, a 32-year-old woman visiting the house of her recently deceased grandmother.

As a souvenir of the childhood summers Mimi spent with her in Dordogne, her grandmother left her letters and puzzles to solve, to remind her to make the most out of life.

In this colourful region, full of wonderful scents and feelings, Mimi will immerse herself back into her childhood memories, and see once again through the eyes of the little girl who marveled at everything.

name: DeathSprint 66
detailed_description: Run for Fame. Die for Glory. In the year 2066, the Bachman Media Network is yet again, set to dominate the world of brutal entertainment with the latest series of their headline show. DEATHSPRINT 66 sees challengers take on the role of a Clone Jockey with an endless supply of clones at their disposal to compete in the visceral velocity of DEATHSPRINT. RACE Take part in thrilling 8 player PvP on-foot races across extreme obstacle courses that push the boundaries of entertainment. Run, jump, drift and slide your way through a series of deadly tracks, chaining together traversals to enter a flow state and earn HYPE. Collect Tributes to gain access to exiting and deadly abilities including Enraged Charge, Seeker Drone, Mag Shield and everyone’s favourite the GIGA SAW. A well-deployed ability can be the difference between winning and losing, making those split-second strategic decisions is vital to your race. ENTERTAIN Winning is not enough. Entertaining the audience on track leads to bigger rewards off it. Your FAME rank is a measure of how attractive you are to sponsors, the higher the rank, the more interested they’ll be, unlocking a greater variety of cosmetics for your runner. Tracks are filled with deadly booby traps, thrilling traversals and opportunities to take out your rivals meaning that each race is an unpredictable, unique and gripping experience. SURVIVE In the ruins of long-abandoned cities of the old world, the Bachman Media Network has built a series of deadly racetracks designed for one purpose – to keep their blood-thirsty viewers entertained. Deadly traps and difficult traversals litter each track, but with an endless supply of human clones to race with, contestants must fight a bloody battle to the finish and claim victory.
