_childDocuments_.review: It's not clean, but this is one of the better games in the genre.  The visuals are clearly high production value, though they lack the more specific inspiration of top competitors like Blasphemous--I can't really fault the devs for wanting to recreate a Bloodborne aesthetic, though.  The combat is tight, and the game implements a fairly traditional set of soulslike RPG features (the stat system, weapon upgrades, strength/dex/magic/guns-based build variety, etc.).  Very little here is novel, but I don't imagine anyone is here looking for anything other than a standard 2D soulslike Metroidvania, which is exactly what you'll get with The Last Faith.My nitpicks are not insubstantial, but I'm including them here mainly as feedback for the devs and secondarily as a light heads-up for interested players.  I don't intend any of this to be a warning away from the game (unless one of these things is a particular pet peeve of yours).The roughest patch by far is the writing.  The devs seem to be Italian, so I don't want to put translation issues (or possibly just ESL) on blast, but I do want to be clear that this part wasn't done right.  From Software's writing style is tricky to imitate.  Most soulslike games kind of just blandly regurgitate a stripped down version of it (see Salt & Sanctuary or, more recently, Thymesia).  Some (e.g. Death's Gambit) instead opt for a more traditional, character-focused story where everyone is pretty normal--just in a dark and isolating situation.  The Last Faith seems to try to take the first option without understanding that in stories like this, the way that characters speak is varied and based on their intent, their culture, and, of course, their level of derangement.  In Elden Ring, for instance Melina, Ranni, and, say, the Finger crones all speak with ornate diction.  The Finger crones are highly deranged and use archaic words to describe vague and abstruse things.  Ranni, meanwhile, isn't vaguebooking--she's just withholding information from you, so gaps in what she says are flavored by her plans for you.  And Melina is just telling you things, but she talks weird.  And then, of course, there are characters like Thops and Rogier who will just tell you everything they know in plain English, etc., etc.  All of these characters have different voices, and their dialogue serves to convey different sorts of information, both about who they are and literally about the things they're telling you.  In The Last Faith, you can sort of intuit some measure of the NPCs' derangement from whether or not they can stay on topic, but not one of them seems capable of discussing anything with you in any format other than insufferably dense, vague word salad.  This, by itself, made it very difficult both to follow what was going on in the story and to care about any of it (since when, e.g., Mark refuses to get to the point in 250 overwrought words, one of the results is that I get annoyed and form a negative association with Mark).  And the fact that many English words are used incorrectly (one of many examples: the devs should consider the definition and connotations of "relinquish") pushes the writing from "confusing" to "an active hindrance in the game's storytelling".  All of this is then made slightly worse by the voice acting being...poorly directed.  I don't want to look a gift horse in the mouth here--voice acting is a nice bow on the package of a game like this--but I struggle to understand why many of the voice takes used for dialogue in the game were considered acceptable.  Insufficient energy, slightly-incorrect pronunciations/accents, and highly awkward delivery cadences abound.Beyond the writing, The Last Faith struggles a bit with polish in areas past the core combat and platforming bones, in particular usability and quality of life.  The map--both a solved problem for the genre and the heart and soul of modern Metroidvania--needs a few more QA passes.  There are rooms where the map shows space that simply isn't there, random bleed-off lines from doorways, "open door" icons floating in empty space where the game will never take you--all of this is pretty annoying in a game where repeatedly backtracking and evaluating how your new navigational skills can solve old puzzles is part of the fun.  The fast travel system could use some QoL improvements as well: It presents a list of locations in an order that isn't *not* useful, but it's a poor organization of options if you know what vague area of the game you want to go to (or really if you're doing anything other than trying to suss out what "the next area" is).  The fact that it seems to default randomly when accessing the menu and that it doesn't have wraparound collectively also wasted a lot of button presses throughout my playthrough.In a similar vein, I mostly didn't have complaints about enemy variety or difficulty (I thought I might, but then it turned out that the first boss was just one of the game's most annoying enemy types, which, in moderation, is okay).  If I had any gripe there, it would be that enemies seem to be designed in a way that wears you down rather than threatens to kill you.  The vast majority of enemies in the game have attacks that are finicky to avoid but not especially dangerous to get hit by.  This may be a stylistic quibble, but I enjoy when soulslikes tilt those scales in the opposite direction, where the danger isn't the swarm--it's my own overconfidence that's more likely to get me killed.Also a stylistic quibble: I thought the game handled its secrets (in particular its secret *walls*) in a kind of obtuse way.  It neither seemeed to have a particular language that it used to communicate the presence of a secret wall nor did it seem to give you any tools for finding them (there was an item in the game that promised to show me specters leading me to treasure, but I never encountered anything like this that led me to the secret walls--I ended up having to look them up online).  Ender Lilies' solution to this was to color code its map to indicate whether there was anything in a room that you haven't collected, and I wish more games would adopt that convention.  Alas, The Last Faith did not.All told, I enjoyed my time with this game quite a bit, all of the words above notwithstanding (I wouldn't write them if I didn't care), and I would recommend it at full price to anyone looking for a 2D soulslike.

_childDocuments_.review: I really tried to make it through this game before making a review, but after 50% I don't want to play anymore. Its been a long time since I've had so little fun playing a game. They tried to follow the souls and hollow knight formulas, but instead of grabbing the fun aspects of those games they took all the worst. Instant death traps, unblockable/no-iframe grab attacks, multiple double boss fights, animations are slow and recovery for any action feels like dial-up, some internal cool down (not stamina) for dodging/dashing without an indicator of when its ready, very few weapons to choose from (and most are so late game they are basically NG+ weapons, for a game that has no point for NG+), the weapons you do get are so poorly balanced, that not going strength feels bad, areas where enemies are all ranged for the very limited range options you have, and flying enemies require you to bunny hop constantly to even hit them (seriously they made magic wind up so slow they couldn't allow you to cast in the air as there would be no point, by the time you cast you would be back on the ground anyways) just to name a few. Even things like the finisher mechanic was frustrating, since it took 30+ sec to finish an enemy that was already 1 hit from dead anyways. They at least got the mysterious air and red string map quest connections that gave it a Bloodborne feel. It was also missing the rewarding feeling, in most Soulsborne games when you beat a difficult boss or area it usually meant a new weapon or spell or something cool. The amount of times I got through something frustrating only to get money or consumables was so disappointing. I'm all for challenging/punishing and rewarding, but this was just frustrating/annoying and pointless.

_childDocuments_.review: I give it a negative review for one main reason. These devs don't respect my time.For no valid reason, you can lock yourself out of major content if you go beyond a certain point (including the poster child boss: The hydra). Pass a certain point key NPCs disappear and the only thing you can do is to start a new playthrough. Most metroidvania will either bring you back to a spot where you can wrap up everything after beating the last boss or at the very least give you a warning. No such things here and it's unacceptable.The rest of the game is fairly good but not to the point of justifying a 2nd playthrough. It's very much a souls game but the closest game to it in design is clearly Blasphemous who isn't a souls game:+ They nailed the atmosphere with a spot-on art direction and a pretty nice soundtrack+ Good level design+ The game's short (<20 hours) but it's the right length for the gameplays depth it offers.+ Combat is simple but feels nice and dynamic+ Exploration is rewarded- Very basic build system. The stats can't be more basic: One for life and 4 for 4 kind of damage scalling/damage reduction- Some controls like grabbing ledges are clunky.- Enemies are stupid easy. They have very little tracking. You can get behind their back a very long time before their attack and stay there safe. Some bosses suffers from the same issue.- Simple boss design. They are very easy to figure out and beat on a 1st try.- The game's is on the easy side of metroivanias. In part for the reason above but also due to how generous the game is with healing. You can carry an absurd amount of healing even at the start.- Healing is done though consumables you can buy or farm. It's very bad design choice even if you'll always have a large stock of it. They should have gone for the vastly better x number of healing per rest.- Spikes or pits are insta-death. Really unnecessary. Blasphemous was criticized for it and they changed that in Blasphemous 2.- Game locks you out of content without any warning6/10

_childDocuments_.review: After finishing 100% of the game and experiencing two out of three possible endings, I feel prepared to offer a fair review. In short, this game had incredible potential, but it missed the mark in a lot of ways. I’d give it a 5/10—worth playing if you get a good deal, but not much beyond that.The game's lore and visuals stand out as its strongest points. Set in a dark, Victorian fantasy world, it tells a twisted tale of four noble houses with complex histories, interesting characters, and a somewhat predictable but fitting plot twist at the end. The game explores themes of greed, sacrifice, and consequence, adding layers to its world. However, the story could have been better conveyed. Characters speak in a highly stylized, overly complex manner that detracts from the experience, making it tempting to skip dialogue. Several subplots and character arcs are left hanging, and the overall story feels incomplete. A sequel or DLC could potentially resolve these loose ends.The visuals are another highlight. The game’s art style, combining gothic, grotesque, and steampunk elements, is unique and memorable. The settings create a haunting world filled with bloodthirsty beasts, and the boss designs are both terrifying and visually compelling. Each boss has a unique look and story, with Dr. Hermann, the mutated scientist, being a particular favorite. For a non-horror game, it delivers some genuine chills on first encounters.Despite these positives, the game falls short in many critical areas. The lack of updates since early 2024 suggests the developers may have moved on, leaving promised features like New Game+ undelivered. The game’s endings also feel underwhelming, and with many unresolved plot points, it seems incomplete.Gameplay-wise, the game struggles with design and technical issues. Bugs, some of which are game-breaking, remain unaddressed. Additionally, some design choices are questionable—like numerous flying enemies without an option to aim up. And unlike most Souls-like games, healing items don’t automatically refill at safe points, forcing you to either farm or use currency to restock, which disrupts the flow.The game also suffers from limited enemy variety, with models reused across areas, which feels lazy and repetitive. Similarly, while the weapons are beautifully designed, only a few are viable, forcing players to use the same weapon for hours on end. The leveling system also limits variety, making it costly to switch builds, which can lead to an unbalanced experience for certain playstyles.In conclusion, The Last Faith has promising lore and visuals but is held back by gameplay flaws and a sense of abandonment from the developers. If you're looking for something similar to Blasphemous, you might enjoy it, but I’d still recommend Blasphemous over this one. Thanks for reading, and enjoy your gaming!

_childDocuments_.review: Let's get the biggest negatives out of the way first:The control scheme is absolutely horrible. I don't remember the last time a game made me put the control scheme as the #1 negative point, but The Last Faith does. The control scheme is so increndibly unintuitive and backwards, the game would go from a 7/10 to an 8/10 just by allowing you to remap the controls.The stat system is also, in my opinion, affecting The Last Faith negatively overall. As much as I like the idea of splitting your ressources between buying items, levelling up weapons or yourself, coupling a small number of weapons with a stat system that makes a number of 'em inefficient to use means that you feel locked into one or two weapons per run.Third, when I bought it, it was about 25 bucks. A bundle of Blasphemous 1 + 2 was just over 30. So, definitely not best the bang for your buck.Now, why would I still recommend it?It pulls off the Metroidvania formuala well enough so far, the Soulslike elements (mostly) feel like they fit the design and formula well, the enemy variety feels fun and progressing through the game is rewarding enough to keep me engaged and entertained.Lastly, I gotta highlight the aesthetic and atmosphere. It's highly derivative, obviously: It's essentially Castlevania x Bloodborne. But it also nails the late 90s high-end spritework artstyle in a way that few games capture really well. Basically, it looks a lot like Symphony of the Night and I love that.  I wish more Metroidvanias looked like the game that put the vania in Metroidvania. So, big plus for me, maybe irrelevant for you.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a pretty great metroidvania that has some issues, but is overall a good time. As always my list of gripes is very long, but there is more than enough excellence here to make this a solid recommend.What I liked:1. The artwork is phenomenal. This is some of the best pixel art I've seen all year and it really does speak for itself. Monster and environment designs are somewhat by the numbers, but the detailing and animation really elevates the material. I'd go so far as to say this is the main reason for my recommend. 2. The weapons and spells you find are very cool and clearly had a lot of thought put into them. Every weapon in the game has an interesting gimmick that complements it's basic attack in a clever way. 3. Exploration is generally interesting and rewarding. The game world is absolutely brimming with hidden passages and collectibles to find.4. The game is mechanically sound. That might not sound like high praise, but I don't take it for granted when everything works as advertised anymore. While I do have some complaints, the combat and leveling systems are all fit to purpose and behave as expected.I have a fair amount of criticism for this one as well, and a lot of it stems from the derivative nature of the game. It's clear this project was inspired by both Blasphemous and Bloodborne, and there are a few nonsensical design decisions here that can only be explained by that influence. In a strictly single player game, why does accessing the map or menu not pause the game? Well, because that's how it was in Bloodborne. Why do you have the ability to execute some enemies, an action that has no gameplay advantage, disrupts the flow of combat with animations that go on way too long, and forces you to circle back and finish off enemies who will randomly survive a fatal blow with a single hit point? Well, because that's how it was in Blasphemous. There's a fine line between having influences and uncritically copying the features of other games, even where it doesn't make sense. Aside from that, some other issues:1. Controls feel a bit sluggish. While things are responsive enough overall, there is just a hint of lag to everything you do, just enough where your dodges, jumps, and heals will occasionally fail to trigger in the heat of the moment. 2. The map feature is subpar. From a quality of life perspective, it is generally expected that a map will at least clearly communicate the location of insta-kill hazards like spikes or bottomless pits. A large number of rooms will auto-map in such a way that tricks you into thinking there is a hidden area below you, when in fact it's yet another death pit. It's also extremely annoying that when you die, the resources you drop do not show up on your map.3. The story is "Zanzibart forgive me" level nonsense. If you've every watched Aqua Teen Hunger Force, the plot here is practically ripped straight from one of the Cybernetic Ghost of Christmas Past rants. "Thousands of years ago, the Merovingians of Baskerville gave rise to the bloodquickening of the Dragonoids, but they were deceived by the ethereal goblins of retrograde Neptune!" It's all overwrought nonsense, and why? Because, once again, that's how it was in Dark Souls.Overall this is a pretty great game. It has it's issues, but they don't detract too much from the things it does very well. Solid recommend, give it a shot if you're a genre fan and looking to scratch the itch.

While 2 bosses do have some annoying patterns, most of the fights are fair and explosively funI'm looking forward to future updates!

_childDocuments_.review: 6/10It's better than a lot of the "we wish we made Dark Souls" side scrollers. But the bar is low. Dying by hazard in this game usually feels pretty fair. However, every one of your combat deaths is going to feel like the controls just stopped working. Then there's the little things that'll start to irk you. Enemies are immune to traps. Shocking pads on the floor, falling spikes, etc. That's true of a lot of games, especially old platformers, but after you've played games where enemies can hurt each other and hazards affect the NPCs this sort of game design becomes painful. It doesn't really feel like you and the enemies are playing in the same world.Game's art and voice acting are beautiful, but quality is suspect in many other areas. Example, there's no cooldown on the "you just entered a new area" noise. So, you go to the manor, noise happens. Go outside of level up lady, noise happens. Realize you want to buy items instead of talk to level up lady? Go back inside, noise. The game is full of small things like this.Might still beat it at some point. It's not bad, but the polish you see in the art and the acting is not available for the actual gameplay in my opinion.Edit: Gave it another few hours. Not worth your time. You begin to really feel how the game either fails to buffer inputs, or simply drops them. One too many "Pretty sure I hit jump" and "I swear I hit the attack button" and you begin to wish you could get a refund.

_childDocuments_.review: I was waiting on this game since first I saw it, attracted by the style and atmosphere and being a fan of Metroidvanias. I was a bit worried about the soulslike imprint because I am not a fan of those games. After playing the demo, and trying hard on the first boss ( that it is not the giant you encounter first, in the full version) my fears grew that I would not be able to progress and enjoy the game. Even the normal monsters felt like a chore. Now after playing it and beating the first boss I think that I can enjoy it. As all metroidvanias, there is a learning curve that, with patience, let you overcome the challenges before you. I hope that this is the case for the rest of the game as well :D. I really don't get people who think the game is average or clunky. I feel the controls are good. It is a little different from other metroidvanias and requires maybe a little adjustment, but I think it is solid. As for the average part, well I think people want originality at all costs, even if it is not good. I prefer something that recalls to other things but does it good. And, for me, that is the case here. Sure it can look a bit like Blasphemous, but I think it has its own stile. And let's not forget that Simphony of the Night came first, so...Only complaints for me, at this point:  the lack of infos in game for what each player stat do,  making it a little frustrating and confusing leveling up. And then, the lack of a feature to refund points and reassign them, even more felt because of the lack of infos. And seeing as different weapons have different stats prefences, and new weapons are found as you progress, I think that the option to rearrange the progress of your characther shoud be a given. One other thing: I understand no pause during game is a souls feature, but It Is a stupid one. People have things to do, responsiblities, emergencies, other people demanding attention, they have to eat, drink and go to the bathroom. There should be an option to abilitate the pause for those that want It.In any case, for all who enjoy metroidvanias, I reccomend this game. It can be a little more challenging maybe but it can be done.

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost, my experience with souls-like games is so little that I don’t even know whether I’m qualified to write a proper review for this game, but I’ll do my best within my limited knowledge. The Last Faith is a metroidvania/souls-like title that initially got my attention with its beautiful pixel art and enemy executions. Those two things were enough to convince me that it was my cup of tea and I started waiting for its arrival with anticipation, without even watching a single gameplay video or playing its demo. Due to this carelessness, I realized very late that it was actually a souls-like game. Adding my former prejudice about the souls-like genre into the mix, I ended up quite frustrated due to my lack of attention. My former prejudice about the genre itself was mostly because of the toxic members of its community which made me avoid the proper souls-like games despite knowing that the games themselves are actually good. I agree that this was very stupid of me hence, I’m grateful for the existence of The Last Faith that encouraged me to try out other games from the genre which I will be doing very soon. Now that I got my personal feelings out of the way, let’s get to reviewing this fine game, shall we? As I have mentioned above, The Last Faith is a metroidvania/souls-like title that was inspired by Castlevania and Bloodborne. The main aspect that will catch your attention is probably its beautiful pixel art and haunting atmosphere. Just a single glance is enough to see that the world you’re diving into is by no means safe, but a hostile environment in every way, and boy, doesn’t it show. You start by escaping a prison and you immediately notice upon the second cutscene that there’s something wrong with the protagonist Eryk, and that is being explained by other characters not long after. You find out that there’s a curse placed on Eryk, and it slowly takes over his body. And thus, your hopeless journey to your uncertain salvation begins. The whole story is explained in a very cryptic way and on top of that, every single character, including Eryk, speaks Shakespearean. Apparently, this is the way of storytelling that Miyazaki came up with in his games and I can understand that several developers were influenced by the gameplay mechanics that got invented by him, but why try to reproduce the storytelling as well? The dialogue in The Last Faith tries to be pathos and tragic, but it actually sounds like a parody most of the time. I had a very, very hard time taking it seriously on my first playthrough. The second playthrough? It was not that bad, but still sounded weird at times. Maybe this is just me, I don’t know, but I didn’t like it. The atmosphere of the environment on the other hand is well done since you get the feeling of the environment you’re in thanks to echoes and other creative sound effects. Very few games made use of this feature in the past and it makes me sad that it’s still not a common practice at this point. The soundtrack also fits well with the gothic ambiance, but it’s not something extraordinary or noteworthy. Furthermore, it’s quite forgettable. The gameplay is solid, it feels like the offspring of Symphony of the Night and Aria of Sorrow with souls-like mechanics. You have four different play styles that you can choose before starting the game, but ultimately, they don’t have many differences. The progression feels smooth, there are a considerate number of secret areas that will reward you with weapons or upgrades, new powers as you progress through the game, and satisfying magic powers. The whole game feels extremely balanced thus leaving no room for the frustration caused by difficulty. However, many things need addressing immediately such as:-  (Need confirmation after 1.5 patch)-  - - - No NG+. This feature has been funded in the Kickstarter campaign, so I’ll be replaying the game once it is implemented. Apart from that, the game is quite good. Its length is just right as well. It took me about 20 hours on my first playthrough to see everything the game has to offer, and after that, I did another playthrough with a different playstyle to completely grasp the story and other stuff. The Last Faith is definitely a notable metroidvania/souls-like entry. I personally haven’t played them yet, but apparently, it’s quite close to Blasphemous gameplay-wise, and Bloodborne story-wise, so if you’re into those games, the chances that you’ll like The Last Faith is quite high.A solid metroidvania/souls-like entry with extremely cryptic storytelling. Despite cryptic storytelling being one of the signature features of the souls-like genre, I find it quite funny that many indie developers are trying to reproduce it since the characters in The Last Faith sound weird at times. Some issues need to be resolved such as having no option to rebind buttons and the inability to turn off controller rumble as well as the lack of NG+ mode. Nonetheless, it’s nearly perfect gameplay-wise since it's quite balanced.

_childDocuments_.review: Ehh, I don't know, kinda feels like this game is missing some secret sauce.There are baffling design choices right out of the gate - why does the right trigger activate the left-side skill? Why does the left trigger activate the right-side skill? Why does the game rip off absolutely every mechanic of Dark Souls EXCEPT the Estus Flask? There are weird quirks like this apparent within the first 5 minutes of play. The Last Faith is also clearly trying to be Blasphemous - the visual design of the first boss is ripped straight from Cvstodia. Seriously, I could show my girlfriend both games, and she wouldn't be able to tell the difference.The most egregious thing so far, though, is that not a single facet of the game really comes off as interesting to me. The RPG mechanics are the same tired Soulslike stuff we've all seen a million times: gain exp, use it to level up stats at "bonfires", drop it on death, yadda yadda. The combat feels fine, not great - it's weirdly floaty. And, beyond gameplay, the "Ooo, something spooky happened recently!" worldbuilding of the narrative feels forced.I know I haven't played for too long, but I really don't feel the need to fire this game up again. The Last Faith feels like a B-side mish-mash of Blasphemous and Death's Gambit without the things that made either of those games good. If you've played both those games and want more, maybe check this out. If not, play those first. As it is currently, this is a strong candidate for a refund for me.

_childDocuments_.review: I’ve played so many Souls-likes and metroidvanias over the years, and somehow this game manages to miss the mark on both ends. It’s marred with so many baffling design choices that create an overall frustrating experience. Platforming especially is horrendous. Until you are able to double jump, expect to have problems with navigation. Ledges can be grabbed and clambered up but its jank, the platform edge needs to be hit within such a narrow window or else you’ll end up falling into a pit. By itself it's annoying, but when you combine enemies that are constantly throwing projectiles at you, it becomes infuriating. Remember Blasphemous's insta-death spikes? People loved them so much that they were removed altogether from the 2nd game. Guess what this game has? I still tried to give the game a chance though, playing it all the way to the end, but the frustrating moments only continued to pile on, and my mood was soured by the time I finished it. The pixel art is gorgeous and the environmental detail is great, but everything else feels extremely jank. The story manages to be even more obfuscated than any of the Souls games combined, I think the narrative upset me the most. -Descriptions and dialogue are so vague and abstract that little information is provided at all about the world. This game reminds me the most of Blasphemous, and even when the writing was drenched with church jargon, Blasphemous at least attempted to describe the setting and characters in a coherent matter. But in this title, every item description goes on about “the darkness found in the pit of humanity’s souls” and “the path of ascension”, without actually developing these ideas or explaining anything interesting about the world or narrative. By the time you finish the game, you have hundreds of key items in your inventory and no clue or understanding about what they aim to accomplish or why you even need them. -Side quests consist of a character asking you for an item, you collect it from somewhere in the map, bring it back, an achievement pops up and...nothing. Nothing changes, nothing happens, they disappear and it’s over. No new world elements, no new story beats, they say their thanks and then vaporize into the ether. And suddenly the world feels even emptier than before. -Interesting locations, but that feel detached from the narrative. You enter a palace of broken mirrors. You find a perpetually frozen lake. Only the latter is mentioned as being extremely important in item descriptions and even then, it just becomes a set piece for a single room that’s a boss arena. There’s no developed atmosphere at all.-Uninteresting enemy designs. Eventually you realize just how many of them are another spin of “large bat”. I think there were only two that I found memorable.Despite the grievances that I have, I would like to see what these devs create next. There are similar games out there (e.g. Blasphemous) that had lukewarm reception on release, but were polished post-release until they became some of the most beloved titles out there. Something similar could occur here, but in its current state, I think too much exists to frustrate the player.

_childDocuments_.review: Very good game, it was fun to explore the world and fight the enemies in it. The execution moves were brutal and very reminiscent of Blasphemous, as a lot of other people have mentioned.I will say though, that there wasn't much need for variety in fighting things. Sure, there were guns, but since I was speccing into dexterity, between the limited (albeit extremely common) ammo and lower damage compared to my weapons, I never really bothered with those. I also never really bothered with spells or even really the stigma moves, because slashing things with my scythe was all I needed to win most fights. I'd have to go out of my way to actually use other things. Because of that, I didn't even get the achievement to parry 50 enemies until right at the end of the game, when I was wrapping up all the achievements. I also never really had a reason to use items apart from healing or nycrux gathering, so I had a huge stock of debuff reducing items (except the nightmare ones, I used those a lot) and items that applied status effects to my weapon.The weapon selection is decent, although I went through about half of the game with my starting dagger because nothing I could find for dexterity was nearly as good until I got the blood sword, and that eventually got replaced by the scythe. All in all, I used about three different primary weapons the entire game.Bosses were really thematic and I enjoyed them (Except for the starlight beast of illygarth, I hated that thing) though they got especially tanky the further you got into the game. It wasn't really an issue for me personally, but they do take a lot of hits to go down even with high level equipment, so keep that in mind.One big gripe I have is the mapping system, though. I like to fully map out areas, but the map in this game reveals rooms as you cover them instead of revealing the entire room upon entering it. This is fine, but it makes for a lot of oddly-shaped rooms on the map because they were wide open and you couldn't reach the top half. Another thing I had a major issue with, and I honestly don't know why this was done, is the fact you can only have a limited number of specific map markers on screen at once. If I saw a treasure I couldn't reach yet, I'd mark it with the treasure icon and move on, but those add up, and eventually it gets to a point where you have to remove old ones to put down new ones, and there are a lot of items you will not be able to reach until later, so there's a lot of things to mark. I had to start marking things with the other marker types instead because I was out of treasure markers. I would like it if that restriction wasn't a thing.All in all, very good game, with cool bosses, fun combat, and an interesting world to explore, but again, I would have liked it if there was a bit more of an incentive to use any of the other things in my arsenal other than my primary weapon.
_childDocuments_.name: The Last Faith

_childDocuments_.review: Review after 100% Achievements (~25 Hours, difficulty 6/10)To start with  -  the good news is that the latest patch/version (played January 2024) works great out the box, and maintained a steady 60fps with no bugs/crashes/glitches throughout my entire playthrough."The Last Faith" is IMO a slightly 'above average' entry in its field of Metroid/Souls/Vania, but provides a solid enough 6-7/10 experience if you've already exhausted the superior counterparts in this genre portfolio. The atmosphere and graphical style are great, but the gameplay and shallow depth of mechanics/builds do let this game down somewhat.I'd describe it as Blasphemous-lite, and the things that TLF does get right are things I've seen before in other games (and done much better).On the positive - some of the boss fights are very good, although many will feel very very easy compared to similar games. Nothing rivals the brilliance/frustration/challenge of Eviterno in Blasphemous 2, or Nameless Puppet in the recent Lies of P.But ultimately this is still a recommend for fans of the genre. If you've already played Metroid Dread, Hollow Knight, Lies of P, Blasphemous 1 and 2  -  then Last Faith will fill the void.

_childDocuments_.review: The Last Faith was a fun game to play period. It brings a lot of good ideas from Bloodborne to the Metroidvania genre, namely the weapon variety, a large map with multiple pathways available at any point, and some incredible moments like the hydra boss fight.What detracts from this experience is copying even the bad design choices from Bloodborne and the technical implementation of bosses. Even Blasphemous 2 learned to make spikes non-lethal and no one likes to grind currency to purchase healing items in the middle of trying to kill a difficulty boss. It truly astonishes me how the team discussed these and agreed to implement them. And the programming for the bosses' AI definitely needs more love as picking random attacks is a recipe for player frustration.All in all, I still recommend people to play The Last Faith. It will be a good time exploring the different areas, testing new weapons, and backtracking with new abilities to find even more cool stuff. It pains me to say this but boss fights should be memorable in these games and they were a painful experience in The Last Faith. If you're a PC player who wants to play Bloodborne and likes MetroidVanias, then give The Last Faith a try. I think you'll dig it but if you get stuck on a boss go somewhere else to level up and upgrade your weapon, and then come back to buffer your frustration.
_childDocuments_.name: The Last Faith

_childDocuments_.review: Last Faith doesn't try to introduce some never-before-seen mechanics to the genre and its Blasphemous meets Bloodborne crossover inspirations are obvious, but instead it grabs its roots with a confident hand and delivers precisely what most people hoped for.The combat depth, character building and world progression is spot on. Obviously excellent visuals and animation need no highlight - they sell the game on their own merit. It's also quite hard, at least in some of the multiple waves secret rooms I've seen so far.Somehow it also manages to capture the "weirdness" of Souls design - characters speak as if they have LSD-laced Macbeth up their butt and the otherworldly bizarro atmosphere and precise sound tie it all together into a faithful "you died" simulator that is addicting enough to try and die just one more time.Not much to think about here if you're a fan of the genres - the devs delivered, lovely game all around. Looking forward to the speedruns!

_childDocuments_.review: I played the Brawler, beat the first boss, and just refunded the game. It's not enjoyable in it's basic mechanics and it's  not worth paying thirty bucks.Pretty weak movement in the game, everything feels sluggish and slow. Rolling doesn't have appropriate I-frames, if any, so when you try to dodge out of the way of incoming attacks you just get hit anyway. This might be an issue with wonky hit boxes getting in front of the attack visual, the attack having precedent over the roll when they happen on the same frame, or they might just not have I-frames at all. The point is, you don't move fast enough, far enough on screen with your roll to make rolling better than just walking out of range of an attack unless you provide the I-frames and make them actually work.I found this to be true for the basic mobs, as well as for the first boss. I hit a basic mob twice to trigger their attack, and then rolled into the mob and got clipped by the mob's attack anyway. I reacted to the boss' attacks by rolling and got clipped by the attacks anyway.In the case of the mob, the best way to deal with them is just walk forward to trigger the attack, walk back so they fall face first, and then walk forward again to hit them four times before they can get up. This is a  feeling for the intro mobs and it doesn't bode well for the rest of the game. In the case of the boss, you just stand in front of them to swing, walk behind them, and continue swinging while they do their attacks. Rolling around is not reliable enough damage mitigation, so you just have to DPS check your way through it by spamming attacks and heals.There's no hit stun on enemies or any way to block so it's going to be walk into range to trigger the attack animation, walk out of range, then walk back to hit them. I charged the attack and timed it so when a mob walked into range, I'd let it go thinking the charge would either stun them or do enough damage to kill them. It did not, I got hit anyway. Why even put that feature in the game if spamming light attacks kills them faster than a charged attack? It doesn't serve a purpose. In either case, you still need to bait the attack from the mob before you start attacking.There also aren't quality of life features like coyote time to let you jump a few frames after you leave a ledge, so get ready for those obnoxious min / maxed jump tests where you have to jump on the last pixel of a ledge to make it. Jumping at the ledge is so poorly handled, that if you roll off the ledge you immediately end the roll animation and drop like a rock. It's the most standard implementation of air mechanics you can get. IF IN AIR, FALL. IMMEDIATELY FALL. ALWAYS FALL. NEVER NOT FALLING IF IN AIR.You don't have any input forgiveness, so if you try to jump in the air, hold your charged melee attack, and let it go it disregards the input completely. You're not going to be able to buffer inputs.That these pretty basic, expected quality of life mechanics aren't in the game is not a good sign. There are expected ease of use mechanics that indie devs making side scrollers should know to include in their titles. I'm not talking about some crunchy rollback netcode, I mean these are day 1 tutorials you can find for every game engine on YouTube. It would only be worst if this was intended, because all it does is make the game less consistent to play.There's no menu option for graphics settings, which is disconcerting. I don't like the idea that I can't adjust my resolution, set it to windowed mode, choose the monitor it boots on, adjust the framerate, and there doesn't seem to be a way of using the mouse cursor. That these options are not in the game makes me question the game's programming pretty harshly. How much of the game just  if the resolution changes? Is the game  to the render engine's frame rate, because the dev didn't know how to leverage the physics engine independently from the frame rate? I also can't just exit the game from the menu, I have to go to the main menu first. Not great quality of life on the menus.The keyboard button navigation is also leaving a lot to be desired. Tab and left shift to move right and left between character inventory screens, but then X AND Z to move left and right WITHIN the screens? Ew. That's disgusting. I really don't know why it was coded that way. I expected the same WASD character navigation to be default to move around between inventory screens, and then going down into those screens to navigate around the grid.I don't think I could equip items from my inventory screen, I had to go to the equip slot menu, select the equip slot, and then select the item and doing so  the item from my inventory screen. That means I'd have to bounce between screens to see what I have equipped and what I have unequipped, rather than just having all my equip items together and a UI indicator telling me what's equipped with my equip slots in the same screen.Animations leave a lot to be desired, it's about as bare bones as it can get. There's a backstep animation that plays when you change directions and a ledge grab animation that plays when you have to mantle up onto a ledge. The dodge forward is a roll and the dodge backwards has a vanish look to it, but that's about it for interesting animations. The jumping animation is pretty stiff and landing after a jump attack looks like a cardboard cut out of a character landing on the ground. I would have liked to see animation cancelling when you land on the ground so you could air attack, land with a cushioning animation, and then immediately go back to attacking.The whole aesthetic and "punishing" gameplay seems lifted straight from Bloodeborne / Dark Souls. Everything's got that same drab, dreary grey, black, and dark blue look to it like you're wandering around the set to an emo band's music video. The audio in this game is also pretty lackluster, just another bog standard piano track over another bog standard pixelated metroidvania.If the game was 9.99, then I would consider it a stronger purchase, but I can't justify the lack of features, boring boss fighting, bare bones animations, missing settings, and weak, core gameplay loop for thirty bucks.

_childDocuments_.review: I was on the fence about this game after playing the demo and finding it rather dull, saw it was on sale and decided ♥♥♥♥ it, I'll give it a shot, I regret nothing. What I got was a really incredible world that was fun to navigate having tons of different branching paths that really make it feel more believable, other games like blasphemous just feel like a series of rooms and the good old '' fight x number of bosses for thing to open'' in this game it just really feels like you can move around and I love the fact that there are hidden optional bosses. I also like the variety of build which can sometimes be lacking in metroidvenia games where you only unlock more abilities and upgrades, in this one you have multiple stats and weapons that can be used for different builds, all the weapons bring something different to the table and I enjoy them a lot.A lot of people complain about the healing being an item drop rather than refilling at a resting point but I have not once ran out of healing in the entire game, the fact this game is easier than other metroidvanias also makes it less punishing for having that mechanic.I found the bosses to be really entertaining and all feeling fresh and different, I experienced one bug in the entirety of the game which made my buffs last infinitely but a quick restart of the game fixed itOverall this game was a really great surprise and I am looking forward to seeing what they do nextps : please add ng+ I beg

_childDocuments_.review: The bones of a really good game are here. I give it a lukewarm "yes" recommendation.The Last Faith has a lot of the pieces of a great Metroidvania, but falls short in a few different ways. The biggest one is its input handling and blocked input windows. The simplest examples here are attempting to attack immediately after jumping and attempting to heal immediately after rolling, both of which typically don't get recognized as inputs unless you mash the button or get the timing just right. This could largely be fixed with a little bit of input buffering. Interestingly, the dodge-roll typically cancels out of whatever else you were doing, so the developer took the time to ensure that at least one input felt responsive, it's unfortunate that a similar level of attention wasn't given to every other input.Another way that The Last Faith could be improved is with its seemingly arbitrary difficulty spikes in certain areas. There's no visible way to know that you've just entered a more difficult area, and in some cases you'll be fighting the exact same enemy in one zone that you can easily kill in another, and it will inexplicably have a ton more health and deal a ton more damage than the one you've been fighting. I don't mind having higher-level areas, but there needs to be a way to communicate that to the player without them needing to get killed to find it out.Much has been said about the healing system being based off consumables, so I won't belabor that point any more than to say it's a thing. If you're willing to do a little bit of farming and can make it far enough into the game to get one of the earlier vendors in your hub area, it becomes a non-issue, but it's annoying nonetheless.And finally, the death pits and spikes have also been talked about a lot but are important enough to warrant a mention. I can, to a degree, understand visible spikes being an instant-kill if that's how you want to design your game (though I wish it just took some health and put you back where you jumped from), but the bigger sin here is death pits in the intended path that you can't see from your jumping-off point, and dying to a large fall where an elevator would be if you sat and waited for it to arrive after activating it. There's no fall damage, and we know there's an elevator at that location on the next screen down, but for *only some* of the elevators, you will die if you attempt to jump down the elevator shaft without waiting for it to arrive.All of that being said, I love the style of the game, the exploration, and the combat itself feels good (outside of the input buffering issues), I just wish different design decisions had been made in the above areas. If those things don't sound like dealbreakers for you, The Last Faith is a solid entry into the genre that you will probably enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a huge fan of Souls-Like, but not as much for Metroidvania. Hence i was skeptical about this game when i first knew about it.I decided to give it a try because some friends of mine suggested me to do so, saying that "bruh you're just gonna love it".Hell they were right! This indie game is a complete masterpiece!The ambience is heavilly inspired by Bloodborne (as many features are aswell), and it's mixed with different gameplay elements inspired by Blasphemous and Castlevania. The result is so gorgeous to watch that this game has been nominated by Steam for the best ambience!The game map is big, filled with secrets and very well integrated with backtracking elements, all of them carefully placed in order to make up for a lore scheme well crafted.If you like exploration, then this game is definitely for you. 90% of the game is exploring the world and find all secrets and secret weapons!Combat is very simple to learn, and yet hard to master. There are a lot of different playstyles based off your own character progression, as different scaling weapons behave differently and offer repliability for up to 4 playthroughs (one for each main attribute, but you could also go wider by making quality builds and mixed builds).Commands wise, you can play the game with both KBM and Controller.The devs suggest to play using the controller, but i assure you KBM does a good job aswell. You can also customize KBM keys, while you can't do that on controllers.In conclusion, The Last Faith is a very well crafted indie game which provides a very good art direction and a bloodborne-like feeling with its own ambience, mixed with souls-like gameplay and elements from Blasphemous and Castlevania. Therefore, if you like one of those, this is a full go and you won't ever regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Last Faith

_childDocuments_.review: The last faith was nothing short of phenomenal... It's probably the only game you can find in the sidescroller genre that can rival blasphemous which is saying a lot! I'd argue that in some regards like visuals & music but especially bossfights, it's even better! Blasphemous still wins out ever so slighly due to better worldbuilding, voice acting & story but it's a close one! If that isn't enough to convince you to play this masterpiece then let me further indulge you in why the last faith is as good as it is! The only flaw I should mention though is that there is a point of no return. So if you want to 100% your save i'll give you a hintAlso if you're worried about difficulty, don't be. The game is very generous with the healing so no boss should have you stumped for too long. For those looking for a challenge like me, doing bosses flaskless is very satisfying and provides a proper challenge!In fact why don't we start of this review with said bosses, easily the highlight of this game! Every single boss, and i mean literally EVERY SINGLE ONE, is an absolute blast to fight. From their amazing designs & arena's to the amazing soundtracks and ofcourse their mechanics. Each boss posseses a diverse set of well-telegraphed attacks that seem intimidating at first but you can get down after a few attempts. Each attack has clear ways to identify & dodge them, that you can discover. So defeating the boss then becomes a test of skill to see if you can properly dodge them well enough for a few minutes. The amount of different attacks never becomes overwhelming or boring all the while remaining challenging but fair. They truly nailed the difficulty on these, if anything they're on the easy side but as mentioned doing it flaskless or even hitless makes the game (in my opinion) even more fun! I even once force quit the game to fight a boss again because i was having such a good time!What also helps with this is the fact that the respawn point is always right next to the boss or at most 2 rooms away from it. This makes jumping back in fast & addictive. You can even skip the boss cutscenes after your first encounter so no time's wasted here. In fact this game respects your time in every facet (well other than locking you out of some stuff if you do a certain thing first, but you've been warned). There's your standard corpse running if you die but the pleasant suprise here is that dying to a boss gives you back your nycrux at the spawn point. I hate it when games lock my hard earned currency in the boss room forcing me to stay at it or forfeit it forever. None of that BS here, just straight up challenging but fair mechanics. You can lose your nycrux on regular enemies but i found out that if you die again before collecting your corpse without having gathered any new nycrux, your old corpse still remains there for the taking.And gather nycrux you should because it's used in many ways. Not only do you level with this currency but it's also used for the most usefull upgrades in the game, those being weapon upgrades. These make an enormous difference and the game scales along very well. They really nailed the balance as well, with each weapon, gun and spell being usefull. Although i did stick with the greatsword for pretty much the whole game because it's VERY satisfying! However when i eventually finally revisit this game, i shall play as a different class and use (a) different weapon(s). In fact the game is so damn fun that i'm already looking forward to it. Alas i've too many games to play for now but one day! I digress, let's get back to the point shall we? The final usage of the nycrux is buying weapons, materials and consumables. Now normally i HATE consumables but in this game the traders' stock is infinite and the consumables are cheap so really it's not even an issue like some people make it out to be.At first i was stingey with my pots, not wanting to waste them unless i really needed to. But the game has so many laying around the map and from drops that i never once ran out. After about 5 hours i started to freely use them during exploration when fighting regular enemies. These enemies pose a fair challenge but the healing is so generous that this shouldn't really be too difficult. The handfull of gauntlet sections do up the challenge a fair bit, locking you into a room with a multitude of enemies. These were also tons of fun thanks to the great enemy variety and difficulty. Just like bosses these have perfectly telegraphed & diverse attacks, and even though some are reused i never felt there was a lack for enemies. Even though i find blasphemous' regular enemies to be a bit more fun, the last faith came as close as one could to such perfection and thus it's also a masterpiece. Also there's the awesome & brutal exections like blasphemous! Stomping demonic children never felt so satisfying! That came out wrong, but once one of those lil ♥♥♥♥♥ jumps you you'll get what i mean.These diverse enemies inhabit an equally diverse range of environments. From ruined cities to haunted tombs, from foggy forests to spiraling cathedrals and from damp prisons to even damper swamps, this game has it all. Each environment is beautifully realized with some of the best pixel art i've ever seen, maybe even my favorite! Each area is thus visually distinct as well as wonderfully made in terms of level design. The game easily deserves the metroidvania tag and while you can complete most of an area on your first pass through some collectibles will stay out of reach till later. The whole map is very well interconnected in my opinion so combined with the responsive controls a real joy to explore. I heard some people say they felt the game was clunky but i found that everything had just the right amount of weight to it. And if you wonder if the game is heavy on platforming the answer is no. There's no tough platforming sections to speak off but i don't hink the mechanics of this game would've allowed for that anyways. A shame as I did really enjoy it when grime did that near the end but oh well...Just like grime and blasphemous though this game has some quirky and creepy npc's for you to meet. They speak in cryptic language but the writing is pretty solid. Sometimes it tries a little too hard but it does fit in very well with the setting. I'm not sure i picked up everything the story had going for it, as some parts at the end felt out of left field but i was never too good at piecing together stories from item descriptions anyways. In any case what i did get though was very intrueging, and the storytelling both environmental and spoken was done very well. In fact the voice acting was pretty amazing for an indie title so i enjoyed this part of the audio very much. What i loved even more though was the games soundtrack, from the soothing melancholy and ominous ambient soundtracks to the epic, grandiose boss themes. Each track was wonderful in it's own right. The only gripe i have is that the save room music cuts out and starts again when you warp between save points which gets annoying a bit but it's no biggie!Speaking of warping this game allows you to warp between save points at any time from the start of the game. This is such a great quality of life feature that i wish more games would adopt but alas not all of them are as benevolent as the last faith. The game treated me very well throughout it's runtime with its astounding visuals, amazing combat and fun exploration. There were also no technical hiccups. No crashes, no bugs and no lag either although it did stutter for the first minute after startup but that's it. The game is fun and works, so really there's no reason not to play it. An easy recommendation for any MV, soulslike or sidescroller fan! At the very least it's one of my absolute favorites and maybe soon yours too?

_childDocuments_.review: I like The Last Faith over all; the visuals are great, combat is solid, the levels are well designed and the music is suitable.It does suffer from being a pastiche of better and more well known games, (chiefly Blasphemous and Bloodborne) which draws obvious comparisons. On the one hand there are a few ways which it improves on the Blasphemous formula but only insofar as it 'fixed' a lot of the common complaints regarding Blasphemous.Over-all, the similarities to other games, without any truly unique aspects, drag it down a little.The bosses are all pretty solid but towards the midpoint they become very spongey (unless i was just under-levelled).There's very little replay value, as yet, but with a dynamic NG+ like Blasphemous there could be, especially given how many weapons and spells are in the back half of the game.Also,  and the credits should be skip-able. Over all worth a play on discount.

_childDocuments_.review: To the point========================The epitome of "we have bloodborne at home" is an annoying experience. Worth it on sale if you're curious but I wouldn't pay full priceGood Stuff=======================- The pixel art is really beautiful and it is at least on par with it's main competitor Blasphemous- The visual themes of the different sections of the game are similarly lovely to look at and the designers have done a wonderful job of making it feel like a living, breathing world.-You certainly get a lot of bang for your buck, I couldn't stomach more then 11 hours but I'm betting it would be 15-20 for 100% I just stopped caring.Bad Stuff===================- Ok so the biggest sin: Your character controls like complete trash. You are slow, your dodges almost seem like rolling the dice, you turn like a 16 wheeler, and none of that becomes evident until the mid game bosses where staying mobile is the best way to approach large encounters. The worst part is that you get a transformation later on that makes movement and combat more dynamic and fun but it only lasts for a few seconds in combat.- The enemies are perhaps, the most frustrating I've encountered in a game recently. They have large health pools that just continue to grow through the game, making it so that you'll never really feel like you've made progress leveling or improving your weapon. They will almost all have homing projectiles or ways to hit you without risking themselves or they have tracking to be able to completely 180 mid swing and the worst part? So many of them deal damage on death by exploding, lighting themselves on fire, shooting icicles etc. combat becomes: Engage group of enemies, kill one, back away to let it explode, repeat. Makes the flow of combat in the mid to late game awful.- Ledges are really more of a dice roll, sometimes you'll grab them, sometimes you won't. Especially fun over instant death pits.- While the sprite work is fantastic, it is criminally overused, you will be fighting the same enemies the entire game with larger and larger health and damage pools. Sometimes you'll get palette swap characters and new areas do have 1 or 2 new enemies but it gets old quickly.- The fast travel system has a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ UI, please just let me move my cursor around the map freely to pick the point I want to go to as opposed to locking me in place.- The sidequests are just bad. Usually you'll have to find an item for an NPC, they'll thank you and vanish. No aftermath and sometimes not even an item, it's weird and makes the whole process forgettable.- The late game areas put little traps everywhere. Icicles that explode when you hit them, powder kegs that explode too, stalactites that fall from the ceiling. Couple this with the exploding enemy deaths I mentioned before and it just feels awful- Even at very high level your character is incredibly fragile because there is no hit stun. Basically there's no period of immunity so things like this happen:Engage bomb throwing enemy and melee enemy. Kill bomb thrower with 2 swings, he drops 3 bomb on the spot where he dies and one bomb in front and behind himMelee enemy hits me during this, I fall backwards into a dropped bomb that explodesI am thrown forward by the explosion and into the spot where the bomber died3 bomb explosions do most of my healthMelee enemy kills me with a follow upLike a 1 second immunity would be so helpful here to make the process more manageable.- Really the game isn't bad/hard but the above choices make it so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ tedious, I was ready to be done by the end of it.

_childDocuments_.review: The Last Faith brings a great experience to the 2D Souls-like genre, blending gothic aesthetics with punishing gameplay.The game's visuals are nothing short of stunning, with beautifully detailed environments in a dark, atmospheric style. The music also underlines the game's atmosphere with a fitting soundtrack in most areas, adding layers of melancholy to further enhance the overall experience. The story is good and fits perfectly into the dark-themed world of The Last Faith.However, the game's map system leaves much to be desired. It could really use some quality-of-life improvements, like better controls and making it clearer overall. Over time, you do get used to it, but it could be more user-friendly from the start. Most of the enemies look amazing and have interesting movesets. Unfortunately, there are some areas that are just bombarded with enemies, which disrupts the pacing and makes exploration feel more overwhelming than rewarding. Aside from the sometimes unclear progression where you're supposed to go next, there is an abundance of hidden walls and secret paths, which can make you feel like you're missing out on something important. While this adds to the game's mystique, it can also create frustration for players who aren't keen on hitting every wall as they explore.Despite these drawbacks, The Last Faith offers a visually impressive, challenging, and fun experience that will appeal to fans of the genre. It's definitely worth checking out if you're interested in a beautifully crafted 2D adventure!

_childDocuments_.review: A really fun gothic themed metroidvania that's inspired by souls like games. It doesn't overwhelm you with a lot of weapon or spell choices like SOTN or Order of Ecclesia but the weapon arts and make the weapons distinct. (There are 10 main hand weapons, 16 spells and 6 off hand firearms)  It's has that 8 bit Castlevania type of difficulty and it doesn't hold your hand and the early hours are quite tough especially if you don't scale into strength.  I did a full play through with Dex/Mind and I probably made the game more difficult for myself but I enjoyed the battle mage type of build. The problem with most metroidvania is that you are so overpowered once you get past a certain point that you blow up the bosses so easily. This game brought back the old NES type of difficulty where you have to learn the bosses' patterns and execute which I really enjoyed. You will die if you try to button mash and face tank a boss. The quests are surprisingly not very obtuse and I managed to get all trophies in one play through of 30 hours and saw all 3 endings.  There's a lot of secret bosses which is nice to see. Stages do lack a lot of variety though since it mostly consisted of dungeons and castles in a gothic world with muted colours. If you're looking for pretty and colourful backdrops like Bloodstained you won't find it here. What's also missing is good music tracks. A lot of is not memorable and completely missing. I can see they're going for that dark and moody feel so I understand why some tracks are like that. The writing is very much a souls game, where you have to piece together the story from item description and cryptic dialogue from NPCs.  The stories seem a bit rushed towards the end with no resolution from some NPCs that you meet and the endings are all kind of lame. Maybe they're hoping to make a sequel and expand?  Some design choices are questionable, like having to farm HP and MP pots instead of getting a refillable flask.  This is probably the worst thing it copied from Bloodborne.  The parry system is hit and miss doesn't reward you enough for it to try and regen your MP and HP.  The dodge roll is nebulous too since it doesn't tell you what you can roll through.  Sometimes it gives you iframes, other times you will get hit out of it.  You also have to find an item for an NPC to respec your stats and she actually disappears from the game towards the end if you go up the elevator in the last dungeon.  A lot of it is probably due to this being the dev's first game and I'm hoping they will revisit these things in future patches or a sequel.Despite all the issues, I'm surprised at how much I liked this game though. It has just enough souls borne type of game play mixed with metroidvania.  I would probably rate it in my top 5 metroidvanias.  SOTN, Order of Ecclesia, Dawn of Sorrow, Bloodstained, and this, The Last Faith. If you like Bloodborne or Metroidvania, I would recommend you give this game a try. I got this for less than $30 bucks so if you see it on sale I think it's worth picking it up.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is NOT blasphemous, so if you are looking for that blasphemous itch, don't buy this. It doesn't even come close to blasphemous. If there was a third option of "I wouldn't recommend it, but I also wouldn't say don't try it" that's what I would pick.It's not a bad game per se, but there's so much developer oversight missing that makes it frustrating for me:1- You can't pause if you are using your inventory or map. Why? Half the game requires you to switch out weapons and consumables2- You can't hit upwards or do a landing attack, and when you are jumping you can't shoot your gun. Because of this flying enemies are difficult to hit.3- There's a subtle cooldown to when you can attack again that makes it super frustrating 4- No blocking mechanic, not so bad because you can dodge, but personally I would like it, but it's just personal preference.5- Enemies have too much health6- Using the map on controller is frustrating as you can use the left joystick to navigate.There's plenty more if I kept playing I'm sure, the game is a good game, but I personally did not like it and it frustrated me two hours in.Good game, terrible execution.

_childDocuments_.review: A really good Souls-like with heavy Metroidvania elements, but with some questionable design decisions. These include, but are not limited to:1. The lack of being able to quick travel back to your last checkpoint if you're in the middle of an area. Not even a rare item. This can result in a lot of unnecessary backtracking, especially when you need to go through previously explored areas to progress.2. Movement is pretty limited for a majority of the game. This would be fine if there was some advance movement options (Backdash cancelling, divekicks, etc.). but none of that is here. As a result moving around can be pretty boring. You do get movement upgrades that makes it feel better, but they're pretty late into the game. 3. Spending currency to refresh supplies (ammo, healing, buffs, etc.). It's not like souls games where you have an infinite amount for a checkpoint. You'll have to balance between leveling and getting consumables. Especially if you're dying a lot.If you're okay with some of this, I'd definitely recommend. The combat and boss fights are really fun.

_childDocuments_.review: The Last Faith is a game that I cannot recommend at its full price to anyone. This game is only good to get at a big discount, as it has a lot of flaws that make the experience towards the end of the game super tedious and frustrating.The good:- Excellent visuals, style, animations.- Combat is fun and there's a lot of variety with weapons and spells.- Some boss fights and arenas are very fun to play.- Music fits the game really well.- Metroidvania tropes are done well, albeit a bit weird with the traversal items (I don't like the order they are given in).The bad:- Controls are clunky and unresponsive at times. For example, you cannot jump -> attack -> jump in the air again (with the double jump). This has caused me a lot of unnecessary deaths and it's not like the game doesn't allow for that type of inputs (you can jump, dodge in the air and jump again for example).- Sound design is pretty bad in some areas, there are a lot of over saturated sounds for weapons which makes playing the game at a loud volume a bit uncomfortable.- Over use of traps and annoying enemies that slow down the pace of map traversal. A literal third of the game is an Ice map filled to the brim with traps that freeze you, enemies that alzo freeze you, and enemies that cause damage after dying and freeze you. There are also ice floors that make you skate, in places filled with ice traps and enemies, which is not challenging, but it's insanely frustrating because you cannot go fast.- Traversal feels weird, they give you the double-jump basically at the final third of the game, which makes some places very annoying to go to.The ugly:- This is NOT and RPG. I made a build following the stats and the descriptions of items. But ended up at level 100 with a weapon that did VERY POOR damage even when levelling the stats correctly. Ended up having to grind 30 levels in the endgame to respec my character into another weapon I had which had an ENORMOUS damage difference for no other reason that it having more damage. This is TERRIBLE, the game should be balanced so that every class or build or even weapon can be viable to finish the game, this is NOT true for this game, so it's better to just read a guide on which weapon has the most damage and use that. This made me turn from a positive to a negative review, this is COMPLETELY UNACCEPTABLE.- The story is an absolutely convoluted mess and the way dialogue and information on items are written if frustratingly complicated for no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ reason other than to make it "sound cool". I completely lost interest in the story after a couple of hours of trying to decipher whatever the ♥♥♥♥ the developers meant to say in their texts and dialogues.- There is no mana regeneration and both health items and mana items are a consumable that you have to farm for or buy at vendors. I haven't found a vendor that sold mana items so those are 100% farm items, which makes it unnecessarily annoying, especially into the endgame where bosses are harder and you need to use your powers more often.

_childDocuments_.review: You could be forgiven if, half an hour into The Last Faith, you were to dismiss the game as a cheap ripoff of the Blasphemous series.   It’s a Pixel Art hack-and -slash Metroidvania with a lot of the same visual cues as that excellent series.  But it would be a mistake to stop there without elaborating on all of the good qualities that it brings to the table — many of which only become evident after at least a few hours of gameplay.  It benefits tremendously from its terrific level design and challenging boss battles, as well as a pretty decent character and weapon customization system that allows for different builds and play styles (enough to at least give you a different experience your second time through).  Combat, for the most part, is an asset to the game.  There are a ton of different enemies  that attack you with a wide variety of ranged, melee, physical, and magical attacks.  Many of them, if you aren’t careful, can drain you of your health in mere seconds. The combat keeps you on your toes while providing ample incentive to gain levels and purchase upgrades.  It’s a fairly open-ended game too, which means that you can access areas fairly early on that you are woefully underpowered for.  One brutally difficult boss, for example, can be accessed about eight hours before you can reasonably be expected to defeat it.  Secrets and collectibles are a huge part of a good Metroidvania game.  You’ll be happy to hear then that The Last Faith truly excels in this area.  The desire to constantly see what is around the next corner or behind the next fake wall is a driving force that lends this game the addictive quality that constantly keeps you coming back for more.  That is not to say that the game is perfect.  Some of the items that yiu get (namely, the grenades) are fairly useless).  There are a few questionable control decisions too — chief among them being the piss poor implementation of blocking/parrying.  Blocking is a risk/reward proposition where the former vastly outweighs the latter — so much that you may find yourself abandoning the mechanic outright and resorting instead to dodging through enemy attacks.  For a game that is as melee- heavy as The Last Faith — this is a pretty big deal.  The interface is a bit clumsy in spots too, and the lack of a pause feature is likely to be occasionally frustrating for you.Overall though, I can recommend The Last Faith quite wholeheartedly.  It’s definitely not perfect, but it’s a 4/5 caliber game that should scratch that Metroidvania itch for you, if that’s what you’re in the mood for.

_childDocuments_.review: Another case where I would rather have "neutral" review.I've mostly enjoyed my playthrough of The Last Faith. Combat... works, exploration is interesting and engaging, visuals are really good. But there are just so many issues:First of all, developers clearly used approach "hey, let's add <feature> to our game, it was good in another game, it would look cool in ours", without considering what would this feature bring to the game, and what makes this feature good in other games. Good example of this is finishers. I've stopped using them after 1 hour of game - there is simply no point. Yes, it is cool animation, but it is extremely long, and the only benefit is minuscule bonus to nycrom ("souls" in the TLF world). This also goes to a lot of other mechanics (basically everything that uses Focus gauge), a lot of equipment, offensive consumables, and even shortcuts (what is the point of shortcut if its placement does not save you any time?).Some other issues I have with the gameBasically, play only if you are starving for this kind of games, and maybe wait for discount first.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has serious issues that have been stated in other reviews regarding pausing, or healing, but my personal issues on top of those are as follows:1. I can't tell when I do and do not have i-frames for some attacks from both bosses and regular enemies. 2. Enemy animation quality varies from Metal Slug levels of detail to GBC Castlevania games. I find this jarring when both types of animations are playing on screen3. Jumping is a pain. Sometimes I'm able to grapple onto the side of a platform, and other times the game just didn't think I was close enough by a handful of pixels and I move past the grab point. This hasn't been an issue in platforming.4. The writing is abysmal. Every character talks so slow and at such a length that I found myself skipping dialogue because it was like being stuck in a stage performance with someone who had just discovered a thesaurus and etymology. I cannot bring myself to care about half of the characters I run into.5. Whoever mixed the audio levels needs to be taught what the hell equalization is. Some music is blaring in my ears, and then I move to the next room and it is dead quiet in comparison.6. The travel mechanic does not tell me where I last traveled from after I've obtained a certain number of locations have been unlocked.7. I've found switching items in the menu sometimes requires me to select the item multiple times for it to actually stick. I assume this is because the devs are checking "on down" events and not "on up" events for an input, but it is a PITA when I'm not even in combat. 8. There are no weapon combos and once I've stunlocked enemies there's just no challenge9. I cannot tell when I can and cannot touch an enemy. Some of them hurt you slightly if you are on top of them. Others don't matter. More still have "the world's worst hit box" and you end up attacking while they attack and neither of your attacks land. It isn't even infuriating from a gameplay perspective, it's just a nuisance and a waste of my time. Overall, this game is visually stunning but the combat needs some rework.
